snuffbox vs styloid vs thumb base · occult scaphoid fracture · carpal tunnel and its mimics · when not to imageWhere exactly is the tenderness or numbness, and would a negative test change anything?

Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise: a normal film does not clear it, so a thumb spica now and repeat films in about 2 weeks, or MRI now Night numbness of the thumb to the radial ring finger, eased by shaking, thenar skin spared: carpal tunnel syndrome; a night splint, and release for thenar atrophy Radial styloid pain with a positive Finkelstein test: de Quervain tenosynovitis (de Quervain tendinopathy), clinical; no imaging; a thumb spica splint and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) first

What it is Wrist or hand pain, or hand numbness, in an adult Sort by Where the tenderness sits (snuffbox, radial styloid, thumb base) and which skin is numb (median, ulnar, radial, a root) Hands off Thumb base osteoarthritis: Osteoarthritis; a hot, swollen wrist: Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult Osteoarthritis Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult

Missed proximal pole fractureSnuffbox tenderness, normal first film If a scaphoid fracture is possible, choose immobilize now; never send home unsplinted. Why cast on suspicionRetrograde blood supplyThe scaphoid is fed from its distal end, so a fracture cuts off the proximal pole: a missed one may die (avascular necrosis) or fail to heal (nonunion), and the proximal pole fares worst. Pancoast tumorHand muscle atrophy with shoulder pain and Horner syndrome: a lung apex tumor on the lower trunk (C8 to T1) Acute carpal tunnel syndromeMedian numbness right after a wrist injury: a lunate dislocation

Wrist and thumb pain, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Scaphoid fracture Fall on the outstretched hand; tender anatomic snuffbox First films normal in up to about 30%: treat on suspicion; proximal pole worst Colles fracture Older adult with osteoporosis, a fall; distal radius tender, not the snuffbox Dinner fork deformity: distal radius fracture De Quervain tenosynovitis (de Quervain tendinopathy) Repetitive wrist use, as in a new mother; radial styloid pain Finkelstein test positive TendonsDe QuervainStenosing tenosynovitis of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first extensor compartment. First carpometacarpal osteoarthritis Older adult, thumb base pain Radiograph: joint space narrowing and osteophytes Osteoarthritis Intersection syndrome Rower; dorsal forearm pain Swelling and crepitus 3 to 8 cm above the wrist Disseminated gonococcal infection Young, sexually active; migratory joint pain, pustules, fever Ceftriaxone and doxycycline Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult Ganglion cyst Dorsal wrist swelling Non-tender and cystic

Hand numbness: which nerve or root Lesion Distribution Decides it Carpal tunnel syndrome Palmar thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger Nocturnal, eased by shaking; Tinel and Phalen signs; thenar skin spared ManeuversPhalen and TinelPhalen: full wrist flexion reproduces the tingling. Tinel: tapping over the nerve does. Median nerve above the wrist The same fingers plus the thenar eminence Thenar numbness: the palmar branch leaves before the tunnel C6 radiculopathy Thumb Biceps reflex lost Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel Ring and little fingers, elbow pain Elbow flexion or leaning; chronic: claw hand Ulnar nerve at the Guyon canal Ring and little fingers Cyclist; hook of hamate fracture Radial nerve Dorsal hand Wrist drop (Saturday night palsy)
Thenar atrophy means the median nerve; hypothenar atrophy, the ulnar.

Hand arthritis by joint Arthritis Joints Decides it Osteoarthritis Distal and proximal interphalangeal (DIP, PIP), first carpometacarpal Heberden and Bouchard nodes Rheumatoid arthritis Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and PIP, symmetric Spares the DIP Psoriatic arthritis DIP Nail pitting; pencil-in-cup on radiograph

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Snuffbox tenderness after a fall → Wrist radiographs with scaphoid views Nondisplaced fracture Thumb spica cast, 6 to 8 weeks Displaced or proximal pole fracture Surgical fixation Normal Still presumed fracture Targeted tests TestResultMeans Classic night numbness, no weakness → Neutral wrist splint at night; thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) if hypothyroid features TSH high Hypothyroidism: treat it Severe symptoms or an unclear diagnosis → Nerve conduction studies Median slowing at the wrist Carpal tunnel syndrome confirmed and graded Next step TestResultMeans Normal films, fracture still suspected → Thumb spica and repeat films in about 2 weeks, or MRI now Fracture line Treat as a fracture No fracture, pain gone Remove the splint SkipImaging and labs for de Quervain tenosynovitis, and nerve studies before a splint trial when the history is classic.

Suspected scaphoid fracture Day 0First films miss up to about 30%: splint, or MRI About 2 weeksReexamine and repeat films In practiceRepeat windowIn practice: the Merck Manual re-examines at 1 week and repeats imaging if the wrist is still tender. 6 to 8 weeksCast a nondisplaced fracture

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Third-trimester numb hands Carpal tunnel syndrome of pregnancy Night splint CausesCarpal tunnel causesPressing Down HARD: pregnancy, dialysis-related amyloidosis (beta-2 microglobulin), hypothyroidism, acromegaly, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes. Treating the cause can relieve the symptoms. Rings no longer fit, coarse features Acromegaly Insulin-like growth factor 1 Years of hemodialysis Beta-2 microglobulin amyloidosis Treat as carpal tunnel Thenar atrophy, weak opposition Severe carpal tunnel syndrome Surgical release De Quervain still painful after splinting Failed splint and NSAID Corticosteroid injection, then first dorsal compartment release A finger that catches and pops on forced extension Trigger finger Conservative care; a corticosteroid injection if it fails Ring and little fingers drawn into flexion; diabetes or alcohol Dupuytren contracture Surgery when the hand cannot lie flat on a table

Pause point Tender snuffbox, negative film Read as clearing the snuffbox A negative test cannot rule out a likely fracture → A likely fracture is not ruled out Classic de Quervain or classic carpal tunnel Offered: imaging, labs or a nerve study A clinical diagnosis → De Quervain: no imaging or labs; carpal tunnel: no nerve study before a splint trial

A negative test cannot rule out disease when pretest probability is high, as with a D-dimer in high-probability pulmonary embolism; and when the diagnosis is clinical with a positive provocative test and no red flags, restraint is the answer.

briefs.title: Low Back Pain in an Adult
briefs.sub: red flags and when to image · acute pain with no red flags · inflammatory back pain and spondyloarthritisIs there a red flag or a neurologic deficit, and does the pain improve when the patient moves?
blocks: Low Back Pain in an Adult
red flags and when to image · acute pain with no red flags · inflammatory back pain and spondyloarthritisIs there a red flag or a neurologic deficit, and does the pain improve when the patient moves?

Acute low back pain, no red flag, normal neurologic exam: no imaging; an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or acetaminophen, and stay active Why no imagingWhy no imagingDisc herniations and bulges are common in people without symptoms, so an early scan mostly finds lesions unrelated to the pain; up to 85% of patients recover without surgery within 6 weeks whatever the cause. A history of cancer, fever or injection drug use, or a bladder or saddle change, means imaging even when the neurologic exam is normal Night pain that eases on getting up is inflammatory; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves, with a cancer history or weight loss, points to malignancy

What it is Usually mechanical; a few cases are infection, inflammation, cancer or fracture Sort by Red flags and the neurologic exam, then how the pain answers rest and movement Hands off A fragility fracture: Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment; anterior uveitis: The Red Eye; buttock pain from the hip or piriformis: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment The Red Eye Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

Cauda equina syndromeUrinary retention or incontinence, saddle anesthesia, sciatica on one side or both, lost anal tone and ankle reflexes If the bladder or the saddle is involved, choose emergent MRI and surgical decompression. Spinal cord compressionUpper motor neuron signs: hyperreflexia (reflexes may be low at first when the onset is acute), an extensor plantar response, a sensory level If cancer is known or suspected, choose dexamethasone first, then emergent MRI of the whole spine. Spinal epidural abscessFever, focal spinal tenderness and neurologic signs after injection drug use or bacteremia If fever comes with a neurologic sign, choose MRI and blood cultures. Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysmOlder smoker; sudden back pain with syncope or hypotension; a pulsatile mass If the patient is unstable, choose straight to surgery.

Low back pain, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Lumbosacral strain After lifting; paraspinal tenderness; a symmetric, belt-like ache Acute, settles within weeks; normal neurologic exam, negative straight-leg raise Lumbar radiculopathy from a disc Pain shooting below the knee; positive straight-leg raise Sudden onset; most settle within 6 weeks; imaging (MRI) for a deficit or pain past 6 weeks (the ladder, rung 2) Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication) Older; buttock and leg pain on walking or standing Chronic; eased by sitting or leaning forward (shopping cart, uphill, cycling); pulses normal, unlike vascular claudication Ankylosing spondylitis SpondyloarthritisThe familySeronegative spondyloarthritis (PAIR: psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, reactive arthritis, formerly Reiter syndrome) shares human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27), enthesitis and anterior uveitis. Ankylosing spondylitis also brings aortic regurgitation (aortitis), stiffens the chest wall (restrictive lung disease), may scar the upper lobes, and thins bone. Its mimic, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, affects an older man with flowing ossification over 4 or more vertebrae and normal sacroiliac joints; it is not spondyloarthritis. Man, most often aged 20 to 40; morning stiffness that eases with use; night pain Insidious, over 3 months; sacroiliitis on imaging Vertebral metastasis Batson plexusRouteProstate cancer reaches the lumbar spine through the vertebral (Batson) venous plexus, often as osteoblastic lesions. Prior cancer (prostate, breast, kidney, thyroid, lung); weight loss Weeks, worsening; night pain that no position or analgesic relieves; MRI with contrast Vertebral osteomyelitis Injection drug use, hemodialysis or bacteremia; focal tenderness Continuous pain; fever often absent; ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) high; MRI Vertebral compression fracture Older, osteoporosis or chronic glucocorticoids; a minor fall or lift Sudden; point tenderness over one vertebra; radiograph first Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment

Course of low back pain Under 4 to 6 weeksNo imaging without a red flag; most recover Past 6 weeksRadicular pain or a deficit: MRI (the ladder, rung 2) Over 3 months, onset by 40Inflammatory back pain

Inflammatory versus mechanical back pain Feature Inflammatory Mechanical Onset By age 40, gradual, over 3 months Any age, often sudden after an event Night Wakes the patient; eases on getting up Usually absent Morning stiffness Marked, eases with use Brief Rest and activity Worse with rest, better with exercise Better with rest

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any low back pain → Red-flag history and a neurologic exam No red flag, exam normal, under 4 to 6 weeks No imaging: treat Bladder, saddle or upper motor neuron signs Emergent MRI Any other red flag Image by cause, below Targeted tests TestResultMeans Prior cancer, night pain, weight loss → MRI of the spine with contrast MRI not possible CT, or a radiograph with ESR or CRP Lesion Metastasis Fever, injection drug use, bacteremia → MRI; blood cultures, ESR and CRP Infected vertebra Vertebral osteomyelitis Epidural collection Spinal epidural abscess Older, osteoporosis, minor trauma → Radiograph Collapsed vertebra Compression fracture Inflammatory pattern → Sacroiliac joint radiographs Sacroiliitis Ankylosing spondylitis Radiographs normal, suspicion still high MRI of the sacroiliac joints SkipImaging for acute pain with no red flag; rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (spondyloarthritis is seronegative) unless peripheral arthritis suggests another diagnosis; HLA-B27 as proof. HLA-B27HLA-B27Human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) is present in about 90% of White patients with ankylosing spondylitis but also in up to 10% of the general population, so it supports the diagnosis and rarely makes it.

Acute low back pain: start on the lowest rung not yet tried Rung Do Move on when 1 An NSAID or acetaminophen; stay active; a nonbenzodiazepine muscle relaxant second line Still painful at 4 to 6 weeks, or a new red flag 2 Physical therapy and exercise Radicular pain past 6 weeks: MRI 3 Epidural glucocorticoid injection, severe or persistent radicular pain Conservative care fails 4 Surgical referral Cauda equina, or an unequivocal disc herniation with a progressive deficit or intractable pain after 6 weeks

Treatment by cause Cause Treatment Ankylosing spondylitis An NSAID and daily exercise, then a TNF (tumor necrosis factor) or IL-17 (interleukin-17) inhibitor Beyond the NSAIDSecond lineMethotrexate and sulfasalazine help only peripheral arthritis. Blocking TNF impairs granulomas and can reactivate latent tuberculosis. Malignant spinal cord compression Dexamethasone, then decompression, or radiation for a radiosensitive tumor

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Foot drop or trouble heel-walking L4 to L5 disc on the L5 root A motor deficit: MRI promptly Young man, back pain, cough and lung nodules Testicular cancer Scrotal ultrasound and tumor markers Fused (bamboo) spine, new pain after a minor fall Fracture of the rigid spine Image for a fracture Diarrhea or urethritis, then knee and ankle arthritis and red eyes Reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome) Diagnose it clinically from the history and exam; the joint fluid is sterile Ankylosing spondylitis with a painful red eye and photophobia Anterior uveitis, its most common complication outside the joints Follow the red-eye workup The Red Eye

Pause point Back pain Offered: imaging every back pain Read the history first → Image by cause Back pain with a normal neurologic exam Cancer pain called mechanical because the exam is normal Read the history first → Then image by cause

Diagnosis19 of 19 68-year-old man with diabetes has back stiffness radiograph: flowing ossification along the front of 4 or more vertebrae sacroiliac joints normal No morning stiffness over 30 minutes Afebrile · HLA-B27 negative · Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis · Ankylosing spondylitis · Spinal osteoarthritis 68-year-old man with diabetes has back stiffness radiograph: flowing ossification along the front of 4 or more vertebrae sacroiliac joints normal No morning stiffness over 30 minutes Afebrile · HLA-B27 negative Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosisflowing anterior ossification with spared sacroiliac joints in an older man with diabetes is diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, not spondyloarthritis

Bed rest: harmful, delays recovery. CT of the lumbosacral spine: not indicated at 1 week, and MRI is the modality for disc and nerve root. Epidural injection: only after 4 to 6 weeks of failed conservative care. Oral prednisone: does not improve acute sciatica.

When most patients do not need a test, ask whether this patient is the exception. A dense list of pertinent negatives supports doing less. When a symptom fits two categories, its behavior separates them: here, what happens when the patient gets up.

briefs.title: Hip Injury in an Adult
briefs.sub: fracture vs posterior dislocation by leg position · the 6-hour and 72-hour clocks · the shoulder mirror · reduction within about 6 hoursIs the leg externally rotated and abducted, or internally rotated, adducted and flexed?
blocks: fracture vs posterior dislocation by leg position · the 6-hour and 72-hour clocks · the shoulder mirror · reduction within about 6 hoursIs the leg externally rotated and abducted, or internally rotated, adducted and flexed?

Older adult after a fall, groin pain, often cannot walk, leg may be shortened, abducted and externally rotated hip fracture: radiograph, then surgery once medically stable, within 72 hours After a dashboard injury, leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated posterior dislocation: closed reduction as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours A normal radiograph with a fracture still suspected is not the end: MRI

What it is An injured hip in an adult: a fracture of the femoral neck or between the trochanters, or a dislocation of the femoral head Sort by The leg position: shortened and turned out is a fracture; shortened, flexed and turned in is a posterior dislocation; flexed, abducted and turned out is the rare anterior one Hands off A fragility fracture: Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment; hip pain without injury: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness; a child: The Limping Child Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness The Limping Child

Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (avascular necrosis)After a displaced femoral neck fracture or a dislocation If the hip is dislocated, choose closed reduction as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours; open reduction if there is a fracture. Blood supply to the femoral headBlood supplyThe femoral head depends on the medial circumflex femoral artery: a displaced neck fracture often disrupts it, and a dislocation left unreduced threatens the same tenuous supply. Sciatic nerve injuryAfter a posterior dislocation If a posterior dislocation, choose check sciatic nerve function, because the dislocation can injure it. Venous thromboembolismImmobility after hip fracture surgery If a hip fracture is repaired, choose prophylactic anticoagulation after surgery.

Time limits Within 6 hoursReduce a dislocation as soon as possible; a later reduction raises the osteonecrosis risk Up to 72 hoursFracture surgery once medically stable; earlier surgery lowers mortality After surgeryProphylactic anticoagulation and early walking

Hip injury in an adult, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Femoral neck fracture Older and osteopenic, a ground-level fall; leg shortened, abducted, externally rotated Radiograph; displaced in an older patient: arthroplasty Which operationFemoral neck fractureA displaced femoral neck fracture in an older patient usually takes arthroplasty, so weight-bearing starts early; one who walks little usually gets a hemiarthroplasty. A nondisplaced or impacted fracture typically takes open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), and a younger patient may have early ORIF, within 6 hours. Intertrochanteric fractures usually take ORIF with an intramedullary nail or a dynamic hip screw. Intertrochanteric fracture Older, ground-level fall; leg shortened, abducted, externally rotated Fracture between the trochanters on radiograph; ORIF Posterior hip dislocation The most common dislocation; dashboard injury; leg shortened, flexed, adducted, internally rotated Reduce as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours; CT after reduction for acetabular and femoral head fractures and loose bodies (an acetabular fracture in about 70% of these dislocations) Anterior hip dislocation Rare; leg flexed, abducted, externally rotated Reduce as soon as possible, preferably within 6 hours; the femoral head may be impacted or the cartilage injured Impacted femoral neck fracture Walks with mild pain and no deformity Radiograph may be normal: MRI Pubic ramus fracture Groin pain after a fall Radiograph Osteonecrosis without injury (avascular necrosis) Long-term glucocorticoids or sickle cell disease; pain with weight bearing, no warmth or fever Weeks of progressive groin pain; radiograph often normal: MRI

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Hip injury, pain, cannot bear weight → Anteroposterior pelvis and cross-table lateral radiographs Fracture of the neck or between the trochanters Radiograph the whole femur; surgery Femoral head out of the socket Dislocation: reduce now Radiograph normal Fracture not excluded Targeted tests TestResultMeans A dislocation, reduced → CT of the hip Acetabular or femoral head fracture, loose bodies Open reduction Older patient after an unexplained fall → Electrocardiogram (ECG) and a search for the cause of the fall Syncope or another cause Treat it while medically stabilizing, up to 72 hours Next step TestResultMeans Normal radiograph, fracture still suspected → MRI Fracture line Occult hip fracture: surgery SkipCT for a suspected occult fracture: it misses up to 30% of acute fractures; MRI is preferred.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Knee pain after a fall in an older adult Hip fracture with referred pain Hip radiographs Displaced femoral neck fracture, 78 years old Fixation risks osteonecrosis Arthroplasty Dislocation reduced at 10 hours Higher osteonecrosis risk Watch the femoral head Fracture from a fall from standing Osteoporosis Treat the bone too Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment Shoulder after a seizure or electrocution, arm held turned in Posterior shoulder dislocation, the mirror of the hip Axillary and lateral radiographs Shoulder Pain
The shoulder mirrors the hip: the common anterior shoulder dislocation is held turned out (axillary nerve at risk), the rare posterior one turned in.
Pause point Shortened leg after a dashboard injury Offered as a fracture Turned in and adducted → A dislocation; the 6-hour window is closing

Posterior dislocation needs reduction within ~6 hours to avoid femoral head AVN (avascular necrosis). In an older patient, a displaced femoral neck fracture carries osteonecrosis risk from retinacular vessel disruption; treat it with arthroplasty.

briefs.title: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness
briefs.sub: groin vs lateral vs buttock · tendon vs nerve · which nerves have motor fibers · when to imageWhere is the pain, and is there tenderness, weakness or only numbness?
blocks: Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness
groin vs lateral vs buttock · tendon vs nerve · which nerves have motor fibers · when to imageWhere is the pain, and is there tenderness, weakness or only numbness?

Sort by place: the groin is the joint; the lateral hip is the gluteal tendons or a sensory nerve; the buttock is the spine, the sacroiliac joint or the piriformis Point tenderness over the greater trochanter, worse lying on that side, with a normal neurologic exam is greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS), however burning the pain sounds A numb upper lateral thigh with full strength is meralgia paresthetica: the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve carries no motor fibers, so the diagnosis is clinical Sensory-only nervesSensory-only nervesLateral femoral cutaneous: anterior and lateral thigh. Saphenous (from the femoral nerve): medial leg. Sural: posterior lateral leg. A digital nerve between the third and fourth metatarsal heads: Morton neuroma, pain and a click when the heads are squeezed.

What it is Pain or numbness around the hip and thigh in an adult: the joint, a tendon, or a nerve Sort by Where it hurts, then tenderness, weakness, or numbness alone Hands off A fall with a shortened, turned-out leg: Hip Injury in an Adult; back pain with sciatica: Low Back Pain in an Adult; treating hip osteoarthritis: Osteoarthritis Hip Injury in an Adult Low Back Pain in an Adult Osteoarthritis

Femoral neck stress fractureRunner or recruit with groin pain on hopping; the radiograph is normal early If groin pain follows overuse and the film is normal, choose MRI now; if missed, it can become a complete fracture. Osteonecrosis of the femoral headGlucocorticoids, alcohol or sickle cell disease; groin pain on weight bearing; motion limited If a risk factor comes with a normal film, choose MRI. Hip Injury in an Adult

Hip and thigh pain, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (trochanteric bursitis) Most often a woman aged 40 to 60; lateral hip pain lying on it, walking, or after long sitting Typically no inciting injury; point tenderness over the trochanter; no groin pain Gluteus medius tendon tear Lateral hip pain, weak abduction, Trendelenburg gait GTPS still failing after an injection, or weak abduction: MRI or ultrasound Hip osteoarthritis Older; groin pain into the thigh or knee Typically gradual onset; internal rotation painful and reduced; crepitus; stiffness under 30 minutes; radiograph Osteoarthritis Femoral neck stress fracture Runner, possibly with energy imbalance (female athlete triad) Overuse in training; groin pain on hopping; MRI Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (avascular necrosis) Glucocorticoids, alcohol, sickle cell disease Progressive groin pain, motion limited; no fever; MRI Labral tear Active; clicking, catching or locking FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation) painful; MRI Piriformis syndrome Buttock pain down the back of the thigh, worse sitting Deep buttock tenderness; normal neurologic exam Osteoid osteoma Male under 25; femoral pain at night Relieved by an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug); a small lucent nidus Iliotibial band syndrome Runner or cyclist; lateral knee pain Tender at the lateral femoral epicondyle: a knee diagnosis

Numbness or weakness: which nerve Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Meralgia paresthetica Burning patch on the upper lateral thigh; tight belt, obesity, pregnancy, diabetes Sensory only; strength and reflexes normal; no testing; loosen tight clothing L2 to L3 radiculopathy Back pain into the anterior thigh; weak hip flexion Patellar reflex reduced, with back pain Low Back Pain in an Adult Femoral neuropathy Anterior thigh and medial leg numbness after a pelvic fracture or a retroperitoneal hematoma Weak knee extension and hip flexion; patellar reflex reduced Diabetic amyotrophy Diabetes; severe thigh pain and weight loss Asymmetric proximal weakness and wasting

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any hip or thigh complaint → Where it hurts; a motor and reflex exam Groin The joint: radiograph Lateral, trochanter tender GTPS: clinical Buttock or posterior Spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis Numb patch, strength normal Meralgia paresthetica: no testing Targeted tests TestResultMeans Groin pain → Standing pelvis and hip radiographs Joint space narrowing, osteophytes Osteoarthritis Normal, with overuse or a necrosis risk MRI: stress fracture, osteonecrosis or labral tear Lateral pain despite an injection, or weak abduction at any point → MRI or ultrasound Torn gluteus medius tendon Orthopedic referral for a large tear Weak quadriceps, low patellar reflex → Ask about back pain Yes L2 to L3 radiculopathy No Femoral neuropathy SkipImaging for typical GTPS or meralgia paresthetica: both are clinical. A normal radiograph does not exclude a stress fracture or early osteonecrosis.

GTPS: start on the lowest rung not yet tried Rung Do Move on when 1 Activity change, an NSAID, physical therapy Symptoms persist 2 Glucocorticoid injection at the trochanter Still failing, or weak abduction at any rung: MRI for a tear

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Years of metformin, numb feet Vitamin B12 deficiency: a distal symmetric neuropathy Check vitamin B12; a one-sided thigh patch is not this Foot drop after habitual leg crossing or weight loss Peroneal palsy at the fibular neck Test hip abduction: weakness favors L5 radiculopathy Lateral hip pain with a leg-length difference GTPS, often from an overworked gluteus medius Activity change, an NSAID and physical therapy, as for GTPS
Pause point Lateral hip pain described as “burning” Bait: trusting the word “burning” Lateral tenderness with a normal neurologic exam → A tendon Numbness with full strength is a sensory nerve.

Next step2 of 16 58-year-old woman was diagnosed with greater trochanteric pain syndrome 2 months ago still tender over the trochanter 8 weeks of an NSAID and abductor-strengthening therapy No weakness or limp Afebrile · hip range of motion full · MRI of the hip · Continue NSAIDs and physical therapy · Corticosteroid injection 58-year-old woman was diagnosed with greater trochanteric pain syndrome 2 months ago still tender over the trochanter 8 weeks of an NSAID and abductor-strengthening therapy No weakness or limp Afebrile · hip range of motion full Corticosteroid injectionrefractory to an NSAID and physical therapy: corticosteroid injection; MRI is for suspected tendon tear

Diagnosis4 of 16 67-year-old man has 2 years of groin pain pain radiates to the knee, worse after walking internal rotation reduced, with crepitus Morning stiffness under 30 minutes Afebrile · body mass index 29 · no trochanteric tenderness · Femoral neck stress fracture · Greater trochanteric pain syndrome · Hip OA 67-year-old man has 2 years of groin pain pain radiates to the knee, worse after walking internal rotation reduced, with crepitus Morning stiffness under 30 minutes Afebrile · body mass index 29 · no trochanteric tenderness Hip OAgroin pain with reduced internal rotation and crepitus is the joint itself, hip osteoarthritis: radiograph

Diagnosis5 of 16 26-year-old woman training for a marathon has groin pain pain when she hops on that leg log-roll of the leg reproduces the groin pain Hip radiograph normal; irregular periods Afebrile · body mass index 18 · Hip osteoarthritis · Osteonecrosis of the femoral head · Femoral neck stress fracture 26-year-old woman training for a marathon has groin pain pain when she hops on that leg log-roll of the leg reproduces the groin pain Hip radiograph normal; irregular periods Afebrile · body mass index 18 Femoral neck stress fracturegroin pain on hopping in a runner with a normal film is a femoral neck stress fracture: MRI; irregular periods and low weight suggest the female athlete triad

Diagnosis6 of 16 30-year-old man, a cyclist, has lateral knee pain tender over the lateral femoral condyle Noble test reproduces it Hip examination normal; rides 200 km a week Afebrile · BP 118/70 mm Hg · no knee effusion · Pes anserine bursitis · Greater trochanteric pain syndrome · IT band syndrome 30-year-old man, a cyclist, has lateral knee pain tender over the lateral femoral condyle Noble test reproduces it Hip examination normal; rides 200 km a week Afebrile · BP 118/70 mm Hg · no knee effusion IT band syndromelateral knee pain at the femoral condyle with a positive Noble test is iliotibial (IT) band syndrome, a knee diagnosis, not a hip one

Diagnosis7 of 16 40-year-old man has numbness over the upper lateral thigh a patch that burns when he wears a tight belt no tenderness over the trochanter; no back pain Strength normal; reflexes normal Afebrile · body mass index 36 · Lumbar radiculopathy · Meralgia paresthetica · Ilioinguinal neuralgia 40-year-old man has numbness over the upper lateral thigh a patch that burns when he wears a tight belt no tenderness over the trochanter; no back pain Strength normal; reflexes normal Afebrile · body mass index 36 Meralgia parestheticaa sensory-only patch on the upper lateral thigh with normal strength is meralgia paresthetica; a radiculopathy usually brings back pain, a dermatomal pattern or weakness

Diagnosis8 of 16 16-year-old boy has 3 months of thigh pain pain wakes him at night ibuprofen relieves it dramatically No trauma; no weight loss Afebrile · radiograph: small lucency with sclerosis in the proximal femur · Femoral neck stress fracture · Osteosarcoma · Osteoid osteoma 16-year-old boy has 3 months of thigh pain pain wakes him at night ibuprofen relieves it dramatically No trauma; no weight loss Afebrile · radiograph: small lucency with sclerosis in the proximal femur Osteoid osteomanight pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs in a young patient is an osteoid osteoma; CT (computed tomography) shows the nidus

Diagnosis9 of 16 45-year-old man on prednisone for 2 years has progressive groin pain drinks heavily range of motion reduced in all planes Hip radiograph normal; no trauma Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal · Hip osteoarthritis · AVN · Femoral neck stress fracture 45-year-old man on prednisone for 2 years has progressive groin pain drinks heavily range of motion reduced in all planes Hip radiograph normal; no trauma Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal AVNsteroids or alcohol with groin pain and a normal film is avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)

Diagnosis10 of 16 38-year-old woman has 2 months of right buttock pain pain runs down the back of the thigh worse sitting, tender deep in the buttock No back pain; straight-leg raise negative Afebrile · strength, reflexes and sensation normal · Greater trochanteric pain syndrome · Piriformis syndrome · Lumbar radiculopathy 38-year-old woman has 2 months of right buttock pain pain runs down the back of the thigh worse sitting, tender deep in the buttock No back pain; straight-leg raise negative Afebrile · strength, reflexes and sensation normal Piriformis syndromebuttock pain sorts to the spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis; worse sitting with piriformis tenderness and a normal neurologic exam fits piriformis syndrome

Diagnosis11 of 16 44-year-old man, obese, has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh wears a tight work belt every day no back pain Strength 5/5 throughout Afebrile · BP 136/86 mm Hg · reflexes normal · body mass index 37 · Femoral neuropathy · L2–L3 radiculopathy · Meralgia paresthetica 44-year-old man, obese, has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh wears a tight work belt every day no back pain Strength 5/5 throughout Afebrile · BP 136/86 mm Hg · reflexes normal · body mass index 37 Meralgia parestheticathe lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory, so full strength confirms meralgia paresthetica: weight loss and loosening restrictive belts

Diagnosis12 of 16 44-year-old man has numbness over the anterior thigh and medial leg weak knee extension reduced patellar reflex Began after a long procedure in the lithotomy position; no back pain Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg · Femoral neuropathy · Meralgia paresthetica · Trochanteric bursitis 44-year-old man has numbness over the anterior thigh and medial leg weak knee extension reduced patellar reflex Began after a long procedure in the lithotomy position; no back pain Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg Femoral neuropathyanterior thigh and medial leg numbness with quadriceps weakness and a reduced patellar reflex is a femoral neuropathy

Diagnosis13 of 16 44-year-old man has 2 months of lateral thigh numbness back pain radiating to the knee reduced patellar reflex, weak hip flexion Femoral stretch test positive; no bladder symptoms Afebrile · BP 132/84 mm Hg · L2–L3 radiculopathy · Diabetic polyneuropathy · Meralgia paresthetica 44-year-old man has 2 months of lateral thigh numbness back pain radiating to the knee reduced patellar reflex, weak hip flexion Femoral stretch test positive; no bladder symptoms Afebrile · BP 132/84 mm Hg L2–L3 radiculopathyback pain with weakness, a reduced reflex and a positive femoral stretch test is an L2 to L3 radiculopathy; meralgia has no motor or reflex loss

Diagnosis14 of 16 56-year-old woman has 2 months of lateral hip pain point tenderness over the bony lateral hip no numbness Worse lying on that side and climbing stairs Afebrile · strength normal · knee examination normal · Trochanteric bursitis · Iliotibial band syndrome · Femoral neuropathy 56-year-old woman has 2 months of lateral hip pain point tenderness over the bony lateral hip no numbness Worse lying on that side and climbing stairs Afebrile · strength normal · knee examination normal Trochanteric bursitistrochanteric tenderness without numbness is trochanteric bursitis, the older, misnamed label for greater trochanteric pain syndrome; the exam may still use it

Diagnosis15 of 16 60-year-old man with diabetes has severe right thigh pain proximal leg weakness and thigh wasting lost 7 kg in 2 months Asymmetric; the left leg is spared Afebrile · hemoglobin A1c 9.1% · Diabetic amyotrophy · Diabetic polyneuropathy · Femoral neuropathy 60-year-old man with diabetes has severe right thigh pain proximal leg weakness and thigh wasting lost 7 kg in 2 months Asymmetric; the left leg is spared Afebrile · hemoglobin A1c 9.1% Diabetic amyotrophysevere asymmetric thigh pain, proximal weakness and weight loss in diabetes is diabetic amyotrophy; polyneuropathy is symmetric and starts in the feet

Workup16 of 16 44-year-old man has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh since he started wearing a tool belt strength and reflexes normal No back pain Afebrile · sensory loss in a patch on the upper lateral thigh · Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies · MRI of the lumbar spine · No testing; it is a clinical diagnosis 44-year-old man has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh since he started wearing a tool belt strength and reflexes normal No back pain Afebrile · sensory loss in a patch on the upper lateral thigh No testing; it is a clinical diagnosismeralgia paresthetica is a clinical diagnosis; no imaging or electrodiagnostic testing is needed

When the pain quality and the findings disagree, rely on the findings. A nerve's motor content sets what its lesion can look like: if it has no motor fibers, a normal motor exam confirms rather than refutes.

briefs.title: Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult
briefs.sub: septic arthritis, crystal arthritis and septic bursitis · synovial fluid thresholds · prosthetic joint and gonococcal branches · post-injection flareIs joint motion preserved, and has the fluid been sampled before any treatment?
blocks: Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult

septic arthritis, crystal arthritis and septic bursitis · synovial fluid thresholds · prosthetic joint and gonococcal branches · post-injection flareIs joint motion preserved, and has the fluid been sampled before any treatment?

Aspirate before you treat: no exam finding excludes infection, and a septic joint can destroy cartilage within days Passive motion picks the space: kept, with swelling over the bursa, is bursitis; pain with any passive motion and a diffuse effusion is the joint Nothing goes in before the sample (no antibiotic, colchicine, glucocorticoid or repeat injection), unless the patient is septic: then antibiotics do not wait for the tap

What it is A hot, swollen joint or bursa in an adult: infection, crystals, or a reaction to an injection Sort by Passive range of motion, then the fluid Hands off Shoulder pain without a hot joint: Shoulder Pain; noninflammatory fluid: Osteoarthritis; arthritis after diarrhea or urethritis: Low Back Pain in an Adult (reactive arthritis, also called Reiter syndrome) Shoulder Pain Osteoarthritis Low Back Pain in an Adult

Septic arthritisA hot, swollen joint that hurts with any passive motion; fever If passive motion of the joint hurts, choose arthrocentesis, then IV antibiotics at once, without waiting for culture results (the ladder, rung 2).

Hot joint or bursa, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Septic arthritis Diabetes, inflammatory arthritis, a prosthesis, injection drug use Hours to days; fluid over 50,000 white cells, over 75% neutrophils; usually Staphylococcus aureus Gout Man; the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra); alcohol, diuretics An untreated early flare typically settles in 7 to 10 days; negatively birefringent urate needles Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease) Chondrocalcinosis on the radiograph Weakly positively birefringent, rhomboid crystals Septic bursitis Red, warm swelling over the olecranon or kneecap (housemaid's knee); leaning, kneeling or an abrasion Joint motion kept; fever often absent; bursal Gram stain or culture, usually Staphylococcus aureus Noninfectious bursitis Swelling over the bursa, as in septic bursitis Bursal Gram stain and culture negative Prosthetic joint infection A knee or hip replacement; pain Lower cut-offs: over 3,000 white cells, over 80% neutrophils Disseminated gonococcal infection Sexually active; migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustules Fluid count lower and Gram stain often negative; NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) of the cervix, urethra, pharynx, rectum Post-injection flare Pain within 24 hours of a glucocorticoid injection Settles within 48 hours; infection worsens over days instead
After a joint or bursa injection Within 24 hoursA post-injection flare begins By 48 hoursThe flare has settled Days laterWorsening infection: aspirate

Synovial fluid Fluid White cells/mm³ Normal Under 200 Noninflammatory (osteoarthritis) Under 2,000 Inflammatory (crystals, rheumatoid arthritis) 2,000 to 100,000 Septic Over 50,000; over 75% neutrophils Prosthetic joint infection Over 3,000; over 80% neutrophils

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any hot joint or bursa → Passive range of motion Kept, swelling over the bursa Bursa: aspirate the bursa Pain with any passive motion, effusion Joint: arthrocentesis Targeted tests TestResultMeans Joint fluid → Cell count and differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals Over 50,000 white cells Septic arthritis Crystals, but over 50,000 Treat as septic until culture Crystals, lower count Gout or pseudogout Bursal fluid → Gram stain, culture, crystals Gram stain or culture positive Septic bursitis Negative An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and activity change Prosthetic joint → Aspirate the joint Over 3,000, over 80% neutrophils Prosthetic joint infection Migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustules → NAAT and cultures of cervix, urethra, pharynx and rectum Positive Disseminated gonococcal infection Deep bursa worse days after an injection → Ultrasound- or radiograph-guided aspiration Infected fluid Iatrogenic septic bursitis SkipSerum uric acid: normal in at least 30% of patients during a flare, so it settles neither gout nor infection.

The hot joint: start on the lowest rung not yet tried Rung Do Move on when 1 Arthrocentesis through clean skin or with ultrasound, never through cellulitis Always, first 2 IV antibiotics once culture samples are taken: vancomycin; add a gram-negative drug (ceftriaxone, or an antipseudomonal agent with immunosuppression or injection drug use) when gram-negative infection is suspected or vancomycin is not working; in sickle cell disease add Salmonella coverage (asplenic patients also need coverage for encapsulated organisms) Purulent fluid or over 50,000; do not wait for culture 3 Drain the joint: repeated aspiration, or arthroscopic or open washout Septic arthritis confirmed

Treatment by cause Cause Treatment Septic bursitis Aspirate, then antibiotics against Staphylococcus aureus; drainage, and incision and drainage when antibiotics fail Gout flare, infection excluded An NSAID first, or colchicine as the next choice; a glucocorticoid third, but first in kidney failure; colchicine or a glucocorticoid in heart failure or cirrhosis Urate loweringBetween flaresBetween flares, allopurinol or febuxostat comes first; probenecid suits only patients who underexcrete uric acid. Started without NSAID or colchicine cover, urate lowering can set off a flare. Pseudogout An NSAID, a glucocorticoid or colchicine Disseminated gonococcal infection IV ceftriaxone with oral doxycycline Any suspected infection No glucocorticoid injection into a joint or a bursa
Pause point Bursitis with a crystal on the slide, or a history of gout Read as the end of the search: gout Crystals do not exclude infection → A high count is treated as septic until culture

Next step1 of 15 54-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen, red right knee severe pain on passive range of motion obesity, hypertension and diabetes Radiograph: joint space narrowing T 38.5 °C · HR 102/min · no rash · Arthrocentesis · Naproxen · Serum uric acid 54-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen, red right knee severe pain on passive range of motion obesity, hypertension and diabetes Radiograph: joint space narrowing T 38.5 °C · HR 102/min · no rash Arthrocentesisnothing on exam excludes infection, and diabetes and joint space narrowing are risk factors for it: aspirate before any treatment

Diagnosis2 of 15 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate: 68,000 white cells/mm³, 85% neutrophils No crystals seen under polarized light T 38.6 °C · Gram stain pending · Septic arthritis · Gout · Calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate: 68,000 white cells/mm³, 85% neutrophils No crystals seen under polarized light T 38.6 °C · Gram stain pending Septic arthritisover 50,000 white cells with over 75% neutrophils and no crystals is septic arthritis: vancomycin after cultures, then drainage

Diagnosis3 of 15 55-year-old man woke with severe pain at the base of the big toe red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint began after a steak dinner Aspirate: 12,000 white cells/mm³ T 37.6 °C · negatively birefringent needles · Gout · Pseudogout · Septic arthritis 55-year-old man woke with severe pain at the base of the big toe red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint began after a steak dinner Aspirate: 12,000 white cells/mm³ T 37.6 °C · negatively birefringent needles Goutan inflammatory count with negatively birefringent needles is gout: an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or colchicine

Next step4 of 15 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen right knee aspirate shows negatively birefringent needle crystals and 60,000 white cells/mm³ Gram stain shows no organisms T 38.2 °C · culture pending · Treat as septic · Treat as a gout flare · Treat as pseudogout 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen right knee aspirate shows negatively birefringent needle crystals and 60,000 white cells/mm³ Gram stain shows no organisms T 38.2 °C · culture pending Treat as septiccrystals do not exclude coexisting infection: over 50,000 white cells is treated as septic until culture says otherwise

Diagnosis5 of 15 72-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen right knee radiograph shows chondrocalcinosis aspirate: positively birefringent rhomboid crystals Gram stain shows no organisms T 37.8 °C · aspirate 18,000 white cells/mm³ · Septic arthritis · Gout · Pseudogout 72-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen right knee radiograph shows chondrocalcinosis aspirate: positively birefringent rhomboid crystals Gram stain shows no organisms T 37.8 °C · aspirate 18,000 white cells/mm³ Pseudogoutpositively birefringent rhomboids with chondrocalcinosis are calcium pyrophosphate crystals: pseudogout

Diagnosis6 of 15 68-year-old man has 3 weeks of right knee pain had a knee replacement 2 years ago aspirate: 3,200 white cells/mm³, 82% neutrophils No crystals seen T 37.4 °C · radiograph: no loosening seen · Gout · Prosthetic joint infection · Aseptic loosening of the prosthesis 68-year-old man has 3 weeks of right knee pain had a knee replacement 2 years ago aspirate: 3,200 white cells/mm³, 82% neutrophils No crystals seen T 37.4 °C · radiograph: no loosening seen Prosthetic joint infectionaround a prosthesis the 50,000 threshold does not apply: over 3,000 white cells with over 80% neutrophils is prosthetic joint infection

Diagnosis7 of 15 24-year-old woman has 4 days of joint pain moving from knee to wrist tenosynovitis over the wrist extensors a few pustules on the hands Sexually active, inconsistent condom use T 38.1 °C · no back pain or conjunctivitis · Reactive arthritis · Disseminated gonococcal infection · Staphylococcal septic arthritis 24-year-old woman has 4 days of joint pain moving from knee to wrist tenosynovitis over the wrist extensors a few pustules on the hands Sexually active, inconsistent condom use T 38.1 °C · no back pain or conjunctivitis Disseminated gonococcal infectionmigratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustules are disseminated gonococcal infection: NAAT and cultures of cervix, urethra, pharynx and rectum

Avoid8 of 15 47-year-old woman has a hot, swollen left knee and fever red, warm cellulitis over the front of the knee the joint must be sampled Diabetes, on metformin T 38.4 °C · pain with passive motion · knee effusion · Aspiration through an uninvolved approach · Image-guided aspiration of the joint · Arthrocentesis straight through the cellulitis 47-year-old woman has a hot, swollen left knee and fever red, warm cellulitis over the front of the knee the joint must be sampled Diabetes, on metformin T 38.4 °C · pain with passive motion · knee effusion Arthrocentesis straight through the cellulitisa needle through cellulitis seeds the joint: aspirate through clean skin or under image guidance

Next step9 of 15 60-year-old man with sickle cell disease has a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate cloudy, cultures drawn Empiric antibiotics are being chosen T 38.7 °C · aspirate 90,000 white cells/mm³ · Add Pseudomonas aeruginosa coverage · Add Salmonella to coverage · Vancomycin alone 60-year-old man with sickle cell disease has a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate cloudy, cultures drawn Empiric antibiotics are being chosen T 38.7 °C · aspirate 90,000 white cells/mm³ Add Salmonella to coveragesickle cell disease adds Salmonella to the organisms to cover

Diagnosis10 of 15 70-year-old man has 2 days of a diffusely swollen right knee severe pain with any passive motion fever and chills No swelling localized over the kneecap T 38.8 °C · large knee effusion · Septic arthritis · Noninfectious overuse bursitis · Septic prepatellar bursitis 70-year-old man has 2 days of a diffusely swollen right knee severe pain with any passive motion fever and chills No swelling localized over the kneecap T 38.8 °C · large knee effusion Septic arthritispain with any passive motion and a diffuse effusion is the joint, not the bursa: aspirate the joint

Diagnosis11 of 15 52-year-old man has a red, hot, tender swelling over the kneecap fever since yesterday full, painless passive knee motion Kneels on concrete at work T 38.6 °C · no knee effusion · Prepatellar hematoma · Septic prepatellar bursitis · Septic arthritis of the knee 52-year-old man has a red, hot, tender swelling over the kneecap fever since yesterday full, painless passive knee motion Kneels on concrete at work T 38.6 °C · no knee effusion Septic prepatellar bursitispreserved joint motion with swelling over the bursa is extraarticular: septic prepatellar bursitis, aspirate the bursa

Next step12 of 15 45-year-old man, a floor installer, has 3 days of knee swelling boggy swelling over the kneecap, red and warm knee range of motion intact Serum uric acid not yet drawn T 37.4 °C · no knee effusion · Compression wrap, ice and rest from kneeling · Empiric colchicine · Aspirate the bursal fluid 45-year-old man, a floor installer, has 3 days of knee swelling boggy swelling over the kneecap, red and warm knee range of motion intact Serum uric acid not yet drawn T 37.4 °C · no knee effusion Aspirate the bursal fluidredness and warmth make infection plausible: aspirate the bursal fluid before presuming crystals or overuse

Next step13 of 15 49-year-old man was diagnosed with septic prepatellar bursitis no improvement after 3 days of antibiotics swelling and redness unchanged Culture grew Staphylococcus aureus T 38.0 °C · knee motion still full · MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the knee · Incision and drainage of the bursa · Stop antibiotics and start colchicine 49-year-old man was diagnosed with septic prepatellar bursitis no improvement after 3 days of antibiotics swelling and redness unchanged Culture grew Staphylococcus aureus T 38.0 °C · knee motion still full Incision and drainage of the bursafailure to improve on antibiotics is the drainage gate: incision and drainage of the bursa

Next step14 of 15 58-year-old woman has worsening right shoulder pain began 4 days after a subacromial corticosteroid injection fever and myalgias Pain was mild the day after the injection T 38.4 °C · white cells 14,000/mm³ · Shoulder x-ray · Repeat corticosteroid injection · Image-guided aspiration of the bursa 58-year-old woman has worsening right shoulder pain began 4 days after a subacromial corticosteroid injection fever and myalgias Pain was mild the day after the injection T 38.4 °C · white cells 14,000/mm³ Image-guided aspiration of the bursapain worsening days after an injection is iatrogenic inoculation of skin flora: image-guided aspiration of the deep bursa

Diagnosis15 of 15 60-year-old man has severe right shoulder pain began 6 hours after a corticosteroid injection already easing by the next morning No chills or redness at the injection site Afebrile · white cells normal · no swelling · Post-injection steroid flare · Iatrogenic septic bursitis · Rotator cuff tear 60-year-old man has severe right shoulder pain began 6 hours after a corticosteroid injection already easing by the next morning No chills or redness at the injection site Afebrile · white cells normal · no swelling Post-injection steroid flarepain within hours that settles within 48 hours is a post-injection steroid flare; infection worsens over days
Naproxen: skips a rung; treats a diagnosis not yet made and delays drainage. Serum uric acid: wrong parameter; neither rules gout in nor infection out.

Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Childin adults every acute hot joint is aspirated at rung 1; only in children does rung 1 depend on toxicity and inflammatory signs, not on the presence of fluid Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: in adults every acute hot joint is aspirated at rung 1; only in children does rung 1 depend on toxicity and inflammatory signs, not on the presence of fluid.

When a test is both diagnostic and therapeutic and the disease it excludes is time-destructive, the test comes before every treatment outside sepsis, even one right for the more likely diagnosis. Aspirate the space that may be infected, because infection cannot be excluded.

Sick first: fever or refusal to bear weight is septic arthritis until the Kocher criteria and the tap say otherwise Night pain, bruising or weight loss: CBC with smear for leukemia before calling a limp benign Then match the age and the duration: a limp past about 2 weeks makes transient synovitis (toxic synovitis) unlikely; weeks to months points to Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), juvenile idiopathic arthritis or a tumor

What it is A child who walks unevenly, with or without pain Sort by Sick or well, then age, then duration Knee pain With a normal knee exam: examine the hip Hands off Infection, the slipped epiphysis, arthritis, leukemia and bone lesions each have their own brief Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis Acute Leukemia in a Child Bone Lesions in a Child Leg Pain in a Child

Septic arthritisFever, a toxic child, refuses to bear weight; pain on any hip motion Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child If there is fever or no weight bearing, choose Kocher criteria and hip US; aspirate before antibiotics. LeukemiaNight pain that wakes the child, bruising, pallor, weight loss Acute Leukemia in a Child If any of these comes with the limp, choose CBC with smear before anything is called benign. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)Age 10 to 15; groin, thigh or knee pain; lost internal rotation Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis If the radiograph shows a slip, choose no weight bearing; urgent pinning in situ. AbuseA corner fracture, or an injury the story does not explain Suspected Child Abuse

The limping child, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis) Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child Days after a cold; looks well, walks with a limp; exam, labs and radiograph normal Days; gone within about 2 weeks; afebrile, markers normal Septic arthritis Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child Fever, toxic, will not bear weight; pain on any motion Hours to days; fever with a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count Osteomyelitis Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a ChildFoot Puncture Wounds and Osteomyelitis Fever and malaise; point bone tenderness Hours to days; marrow signal on MRI Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease Avascular necrosisAvascular necrosis (osteonecrosis)Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease and SCFE both cause avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head; in Perthes disease the blood supply is cut off for no known reason (idiopathic), and the head flattens and fragments before it heals. Boy of 5 to 10, peak 5 to 7, about 4 to 5 times more often than girls; painless limp, then hip, thigh or knee pain Weeks to months; abduction and internal rotation lost; flat, fragmented femoral head Early filmPerthes disease on radiographsThe first radiograph in Perthes disease is often normal or shows only slight flattening; fragmentation comes later in the course. A normal film with a persistent limp is followed by MRI. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis Age 10 to 15, the growth spurt; often obese; groin, thigh or knee pain Weeks to months; internal rotation lost; the hip rotates outward on flexion Toddler's fracture Most often 9 months to 3 years; will not bear weight after a trip or fall Days; tibial shaft tenderness; spiral fracture of the tibia Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) Infant: positive Barlow or Ortolani maneuver; breech, girl, firstborn, family history (the 4 Fs); asymmetric skin folds Since walking began; painless limp, short leg, limited abduction Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis Swollen joint, morning stiffness that eases with activity 6 weeks or more Leukemia Acute Leukemia in a Child Night pain, bruising, pallor, weight loss Weeks to months; cytopenias or blasts on the smear Growing pains Leg Pain in a Child Both legs, late in the day or at night; exam normal No limp: growing pains do not cause one Bone tumor Bone Lesions in a Child Bone pain worse at night Weeks to months; osteoid osteoma eases with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs Acute rheumatic fever Acute Rheumatic Fever Migratory large-joint arthritis 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis; timed to the throat, not the joint Osgood-Schlatter disease Adolescent athlete after the growth spurt; pain below the knee Tender, prominent tibial tubercle; hip normal Psoas abscess or appendicitis Pain when the hip is extended (psoas sign) The hip joint itself is normal

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Every limping child → Temperature and weight bearing Fever or no weight bearing Septic arthritis: Kocher criteria, hip US, tap → CBC with smear, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) Cytopenias or blasts Leukemia → Hip rotation and abduction Internal rotation lost Hip disease: Perthes disease or SCFE Abduction limited DDH Targeted tests TestResultMeans Under 5, well, no fever, nothing localized → Radiographs of both tibias and fibulas Spiral fracture of the tibia Toddler's fracture Corner fracture Suspect abuse Walker with a painless limp, short leg, limited abduction → Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis; hip US under 4 months Shallow acetabulum, head displaced Missed DDH Limp past about 2 weeks, or internal rotation lost → Anteroposterior and frog-leg radiographs of both hips Flat, fragmented femoral head Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease Slipped epiphysis SCFE Next step TestResultMeans Fever with point bone tenderness, or a normal film and a persistent limp → MRI Marrow signal Osteomyelitis, or early Perthes disease SkipKnee films for knee pain with a normal knee exam: the hip refers pain to the knee. Hip US in an infant past 4 months: the femoral head has ossified.

Treatment by cause Cause Treatment DDH Under 6 months: Pavlik harness, hips flexed and abducted; if it fails, or past 6 months: usually closed or open reduction with a spica cast; untreated, a short leg and a painful hip Perthes disease Under 6: limited weight bearing and physical therapy; casting and bracing if refractory; 6 or older: femoral osteotomy; usually self-limited over 2 to 3 years, with later osteoarthritis Toddler's fracture Immobilization and pain control; no further workup when the story fits Osgood-Schlatter disease Analgesics and rest

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Knee pain with a normal knee exam Hip disease: Perthes disease or SCFE Examine and image the hip Morning stiffness easing through the day, 6 weeks or more Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis Slit-lamp exam for uveitis; highest risk when antinuclear antibody is positive Migratory joint pain 2 to 4 weeks after a sore throat Acute rheumatic fever Acute Rheumatic Fever Antistreptolysin O titer and the Jones criteria A nail through a shoe weeks ago, little fever Puncture-wound osteomyelitis Foot Puncture Wounds and Osteomyelitis MRI of the foot Adolescent athlete, pain below the knee, tender tibial tubercle Osgood-Schlatter disease Analgesics and rest Breech girl, or a family history of DDH High risk for DDH Hip US at 6 weeks of age

Diagnosis4 of 9 6-year-old boy with a limp for 2 months, worse after play intermittent groin and knee pain hip abduction and internal rotation limited No fever, trauma or night pain Afebrile · CBC and ESR normal · radiograph: flattened, fragmented femoral head · Legg-Calvé-PerthesBoy of 6, limp for months; flat, fragmented head · Transient synovitisGone within about 2 weeks; this limp is 2 months old · Slipped capital femoral epiphysisAges 10 to 15; the epiphysis slips, it does not fragment 6-year-old boy with a limp for 2 months, worse after play intermittent groin and knee pain hip abduction and internal rotation limited No fever, trauma or night pain Afebrile · CBC and ESR normal · radiograph: flattened, fragmented femoral head Legg-Calvé-Perthesan insidious limp over weeks with normal labs at about 5 to 10 years; early films can be normal, so MRI when they are

Workup8 of 9 5-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a limp leg pain that wakes him at night tired; bruises easily pale; lost weight this month T 37.8 °C · hip and knee motion full · Hip ultrasound for an effusionHip and knee motion are full; no effusion to find · CBC with smearNight pain, bruising, pallor, weight loss: leukemia · Tibial radiographsFor a well toddler after a fall; he looks ill 5-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a limp leg pain that wakes him at night tired; bruises easily pale; lost weight this month T 37.8 °C · hip and knee motion full CBC with smeara limp with night pain, bruising, fatigue or weight loss: CBC with smear for leukemia before calling anything benign

Diagnosis9 of 9 14-year-old boy with 3 months of anterior knee pain worse with running and jumping in basketball tender, prominent tibial tubercle hip motion full and painless Afebrile · no night pain or weight loss · Patellofemoral pain syndromePain around the patella, not at the tubercle · Osteosarcoma of the proximal tibiaNight pain or weight loss; he has neither · Osgood-Schlatter diseaseTeen athlete; tender, prominent tibial tubercle 14-year-old boy with 3 months of anterior knee pain worse with running and jumping in basketball tender, prominent tibial tubercle hip motion full and painless Afebrile · no night pain or weight loss Osgood-Schlatter diseasethe hip is cleared and the tibial tubercle is tender in an active adolescent: activity modification and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

Healthy 16-month-old girl with a painless right-sided limp since she began walking 4 months ago term; cesarean delivery for breech presentation no family history of musculoskeletal disorders left leg shorter than the right left hip abduction limited to 30 degrees; right hip normal Sensation, circulation and strength normal Most likely underlying mechanism? Competing answers Acute epiphyseal fracture: a toddler's limp; but it needs trauma, with pain, bruising and guarding; this limp is painless and 4 months old. Acute suppurative arthritis: limited hip motion; but it brings fever and pain; she is healthy and painless. Avulsion of muscle origin: a limp; but it follows an injury and hurts, often with a defect or mass. Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis: limited hip motion and a limp; but that is the adolescent slip, which limits internal rotation. Failure of osteoid to mineralize: a toddler's leg problem; but rickets bows both legs; it does not shorten one or limit one hip. Down to two: poorly developed acetabulum or displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis. Poorly developed acetabulum: a breech girl with a painless limp from her first steps, a short leg and limited abduction has DDH missed in infancy. Every option was a disease written as its mechanism. (As in the source stem, the limp is on the right and the signs on the left.)

Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Childfever, a toxic child or refusal to bear weight Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysisage 10 to 15 with lost internal rotation Leg Pain in a Childleg pain with a normal gait Suspected Child Abusea fracture the history does not explain, such as a corner fracture, or a femur fracture before walking Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infanta breech infant also needs a hip exam Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: fever, a toxic child or refusal to bear weight. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: age 10 to 15 with lost internal rotation. Leg Pain in a Child: leg pain with a normal gait. Suspected Child Abuse: a fracture the history does not explain, such as a corner fracture, or a femur fracture before walking. Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: a breech infant also needs a hip exam.
Ask sick or well, then how old, then how long; a limp with night pain is a blood count first.

pull or fall · reduce or radiograph · after reduction · supracondylar nerves and artery · suspecting abuse · treatment by cause

A pull on the arm, a child under 5 holding the forearm pronated, and no swelling, deformity or bony tenderness: radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow); reduce without a radiograph A fall on an outstretched hand with a swollen elbow: radiographs first; a posterior fat pad is an occult fracture A story that does not fit, or a long-bone fracture before walking: suspect abuse; report to child protective services and order a skeletal survey under 2 years

What it is A young child who will not move or use one arm Sort by The mechanism (a pull or a fall), then the elbow exam, then age; the reduction maneuver both diagnoses and treats Hands off Suspected abuse has its own brief Suspected Child Abuse The Limping Child

Brachial artery injuryPale, cool or pulseless hand: a supracondylar fracture may injure the brachial artery If the hand is pale or pulseless, choose urgent orthopedics; splint the elbow as it lies, no reduction in the emergency department. Compartment syndromeTense, painful forearm after an elbow fracture; untreated, Volkmann ischemic contracture, a clawlike hand If the forearm is tense and painful, choose fasciotomy without delay. AbuseA long-bone fracture before walking, a delay in care, or a story that does not fit the injury How oftenHumerus fractures and abuseAbuse causes up to 54% of humerus fractures under age 3; a displaced physeal fracture of the humerus is 13 times as likely as a displaced supracondylar fracture to be abuse Suspected Child Abuse If abuse is suspected, choose report to child protective services; skeletal survey under 2 years.

Arm injury in a young child, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow) Why under 5MechanismAt 2 to 3 years the head of the radius is only as wide as its neck, so a pull slides the annular ligament over it and into the radiocapitellar joint Under 5, most often 2 to 3; lifted or pulled by the hand or wrist Minutes: uses the arm within about 30 minutes of reduction; elbow slightly flexed, forearm pronated, no swelling or bony tenderness Which nerveRadial head subluxation and the radial nerveThe deep (motor) branch of the radial nerve is pinched, so the forearm extensors are weak; the wrist still extends and the back of the hand keeps its feeling Supracondylar humerus fracture Ages 3 to 11; usually a fall onto an outstretched hand that hyperextends the elbow Swollen, painful elbow with limited motion; posterior fat pad on the lateral film Fat padsElbow radiographA posterior fat pad on a true lateral film is always abnormal: specific for an effusion, though not sensitive. A posterior fat pad, or a large anterior one (sail sign), is treated as an occult fracture Abuse (non-accidental trauma) Suspected Child Abuse Not yet walking; a delay in care, or a history that does not fit Spiral long-bone or rib fractures, or fractures of different ages Osteogenesis imperfecta Repeated fractures with minimal trauma; mimics abuse with bruising Blue sclerae, short stature Midshaft humerus fracture Humeral shaft injury with radial nerve injury at the spiral groove Wrist drop; radial head subluxation spares wrist extension and the back of the hand

Age at onsetnot to scale Suspected abuseUnder 2 years: skeletal survey with any fracture Birth1 yr23511 yr→ Report and survey Oldera survey when suspicion is high Radial head subluxationUnder 5; most often 2 to 3 Birth1 yr23511 yr→ Reduce Supracondylar humerus fracture3 to 11 years Birth1 yr23511 yr→ Radiograph first Rankthe most common elbow fracture in children Report and surveyReduceRadiograph first

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Every young child who will not use an arm → History: a pull or a fall, and whether it fits Lifted or pulled by the hand Radial head subluxation Fall on an outstretched hand Supracondylar fracture No mechanism, or one that does not fit Suspect abuse → Elbow exam: swelling, deformity, bony tenderness; pulses and hand nerves Forearm pronated; no swelling, deformity or bony tenderness Reduce: hyperpronation first Swelling, deformity or point tenderness Radiographs before any maneuver Pale or pulseless hand Urgent orthopedics Targeted tests TestResultMeans After reduction → Watch the child use the arm for about 30 minutes Reaches and uses the arm Done: no radiograph or sling Still unused at about 30 minutes Second reduction attempt Unused after a second attempt, or a fall with a swollen elbow → Anteroposterior and lateral elbow radiographs Posterior fat pad, or a large anterior one (sail sign) Occult fracture: splint, orthopedic follow-up Displaced supracondylar fracture Splint as it lies; orthopedics Normal film, arm still unused Splint and close follow-up Next step TestResultMeans A fracture before walking, or a story that does not fit → Report to child protective services Home not safe Admit for immediate safety → Skeletal survey under 2 years Occult fractures of different ages Abuse workup continues in its own brief SkipA radiograph before reducing a classic pull with a normal exam, and films after a reduction the child confirms by using the arm. Reducing a swollen elbow after a fall, or a displaced supracondylar fracture in the emergency department.

After reductionnot to scale Uses the armUsually 10 to 20 minutes; nearly all by about 30 Reduction10 minutes20 minutes30 minutes24 hours→ Expected Unused at about 30 minutesSecond attempt; still unused after it: elbow radiographs Reduction10 minutes20 minutes30 minutes24 hours→ Reassess Pain or disuse past 24 hoursIncomplete reduction or an occult fracture Reduction10 minutes20 minutes30 minutes24 hours→ Suspect a fracture ExpectedReassessSuspect a fracture

Treatment by cause Cause Treatment Radial head subluxation Hyperpronation (more first-attempt success) or supination with flexion; no immobilization; teach lifting under the arms, not by the hand; recurs in 27 to 46% Supracondylar fracture Nondisplaced or occult: splint, orthopedic follow-up. Displaced: splint as it lies, early orthopedics, often open reduction and internal fixation; most are admitted for neurovascular checks Compartment syndrome Fasciotomy without delay Suspected abuse Suspected Child Abuse Report to child protective services; keep the child safe, admitting if needed

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Wrist drop, numb back of the hand Radial nerve at the spiral groove: midshaft humerus fracture Radiograph the injured area Cannot oppose the thumb; index and middle fingers stay straight in a fist Median nerve: anteromedial supracondylar fracture (anterolateral displacement typically injures the radial nerve) Check the radial pulse; orthopedics After a pull, an older child usually points to the back of the upper forearm, not the lateral elbow Still radial head subluxation; do not mistake it for a buckle fracture of the proximal radius Reduce when there is no swelling or bony tenderness; the maneuver diagnoses and treats A second pulled elbow with the same fitting story; well child, no fracture Recurrence (27 to 46%) Reduce again; teach lifting under the arms; a skeletal survey is for a fracture or a story that does not fit Spiral humerus fracture in an infant not yet crawling Abuse Suspected Child Abuse Report; skeletal survey Repeated fractures with minimal trauma and blue sclerae Osteogenesis imperfecta White sclerae and a story that does not fit favor abuse over osteogenesis imperfecta

Pause point Classic pull Offered: a radiograph before reducing, or a skeletal survey for a recurrence with a fitting story A pull with a normal exam → The reduction Elbow problem in a child Offered: a maneuver A fall or swelling → The radiograph first

Let the mechanism and the elbow exam decide: reduce a pull with a normal exam, and image when the mechanism or the elbow says fracture, or when the arm stays unused after two attempts.
