Both legs, pain in the evening or night with pain-free days, and a normal exam: growing pains; reassure, with no labs or radiographs Tender calves a few days into influenza, reflexes kept: benign acute childhood myositis; CK (creatine kinase) is high, and dark urine points to rhabdomyolysis Ascending weakness with absent reflexes: Guillain-Barré syndrome. Bone tenderness with pallor or bruising: CBC with smear. One side or a focal spot: radiograph

What it is Pain in the legs of a child, sorted by the exam Sort by The exam first: gait, joints, bones, calves, reflexes and skin, then the side, the timing and any systemic signs Night painShared by benign and serious causesGrowing pains, osteoid osteoma and leukemia can all hurt at night, and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) often eases both growing pains and osteoid osteoma; the side, the exam and systemic signs decide Hands off Bone tumors, leukemia, the hot limb and dark urine have their own briefs Bone Lesions in a Child Acute Leukemia in a Child The Limping Child Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood

Respiratory failureAscending weakness with absent reflexes: Guillain-Barré syndrome can paralyze the breathing muscles If the weakness rises and the reflexes are gone, choose admit; serial spirometry, intubating when the forced vital capacity falls to 20 mL/kg or less (the threshold taught for the exam). In practiceVital capacitya standard clinical reference sets a lower threshold: intubation when the vital capacity falls below 15 mL/kg, checked every 6 to 8 hours RhabdomyolysisTea-colored urine, a dipstick positive for blood with few red cells, and a CK above 1,000 Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood If the dipstick shows blood with few red cells, choose IV fluids; follow creatinine and potassium. LeukemiaBone pain with pallor, bruising or fever; the pain can be worse at night and in both legs Acute Leukemia in a Child If the bones are tender with pallor or bruising, choose CBC with peripheral smear. Hot limbFever with one-sided point tenderness, warmth or refusal to bear weight: osteomyelitis or septic arthritis The Limping Child Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child If one leg is tender and the child is febrile, choose ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and urgent imaging.

Leg pain in a child, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Growing pains (benign nocturnal limb pains of childhood) How commonGrowing painsBetween 80% and 90% describe both legs; episodes last minutes to hours Onset usually 3 to 6 years; calves, thighs, shins or behind the knee, often after active days; late in the day or at night, not during play Months, with pain-free days: both legs, evening or night, gone by morning; normal exam and gait; no systemic signs Benign acute childhood myositis (influenza-induced myositis) School-age, more often boys; about 3 days after a flu-like illness, most often influenza B; sudden calf pain, difficulty or refusal to walk Days: calves tender to touch; reflexes preserved; CK high, CRP usually normal WeaknessMyositis and Guillain-Barré syndromeInfluenza myositis can weaken a child, from mild weakness to quadriparesis, so strength does not separate it from Guillain-Barré syndrome; preserved reflexes do Guillain-Barré syndrome After an infection, influenza among them; symmetric weakness that usually starts in the legs and rises Days to weeks: deep tendon reflexes lost; no calf tenderness; CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) protein may be high with a normal cell count Acute lymphoblastic leukemia Acute Leukemia in a Child Dull bone pain, worse at night; refuses to walk; fever, pallor, bruising Tender long bones with pallor or bruising; cytopenias and blasts on the CBC and smear Bone tumor (osteoid osteoma, osteosarcoma) Bone Lesions in a Child One side; persistent or progressive pain; osteoid osteoma hurts at night and NSAIDs relieve it Radiograph: a small lucent nidus (osteoid osteoma), or a destructive lesion with periosteal reaction and a soft-tissue mass (osteosarcoma) Juvenile dermatomyositis Proximal weakness: trouble climbing stairs or rising from a seat Weeks to months: heliotrope rash on the eyelids, Gottron papules on the knuckles; CK high Arthritis (juvenile idiopathic arthritis, parvovirus B19, rheumatic fever) Juvenile Idiopathic ArthritisFever and Rash in a ChildAcute Rheumatic Fever Pain in the joint, worse in the morning Joint swelling or reduced range of motion; morning stiffness Overuse injury (Osgood-Schlatter disease) The Limping Child Active child after the growth spurt; pain with activity Tender tibial tubercle; pain on resisted knee extension

Time coursenot to scale Benign acute childhood myositisAbout 3 days after the illness begins; self-limited Illness1 week1 month3 monthsYears→ Days Guillain-Barré syndromeDays to weeks; weakness peaks by 3 to 4 weeks in 90% Illness1 week1 month3 monthsYears→ Do not miss Juvenile dermatomyositisWeakness may build over weeks to months Illness1 week1 month3 monthsYears→ Weeks or longer Growing painsEpisodes for months to years, with pain-free days; gone by adolescence Illness1 week1 month3 monthsYears→ Weeks or longer Bone tumorOne side; persistent or progressive Illness1 week1 month3 monthsYears→ Do not miss DaysWeeks or longerDo not miss

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Every child with leg pain → History: side, timing, activity, a recent illness, systemic symptoms Both legs, evening or night, pain-free days Growing pains pattern A few days after a flu-like illness Myositis or Guillain-Barré syndrome Fever, fatigue, weight loss, pallor or bruising Systemic cause: not growing pains → Exam: gait, joints, palpation of bones and calves, strength and reflexes, skin Normal exam and gait Growing pains: no tests Tender calves, reflexes kept Myositis: CK and urinalysis Weakness rising from the legs, reflexes absent Guillain-Barré syndrome: admit; CSF analysis, nerve conduction studies; serial spirometry Bone tenderness, a focal spot, a mass or joint swelling Radiograph or laboratory tests Targeted tests TestResultMeans Tender calves after influenza → Serum CK CK elevated Muscle disease, not a joint or nerve → Urinalysis with microscopy Dipstick positive for blood, few red cells, CK above 1,000 Myoglobin: rhabdomyolysis; IV fluids Urinalysis normal Home: rest, analgesics and fluids Bone tenderness with pallor, bruising or fever → CBC with peripheral smear Cytopenias, blasts Leukemia Acute Leukemia in a Child One side, a focal tender spot, progressive pain or a mass → Plain radiograph Small lucent nidus Osteoid osteoma Bone Lesions in a Child Destructive lesion, periosteal reaction, soft-tissue mass Osteosarcoma Bone Lesions in a Child Normal film, focal signs persist MRI or bone scan Next step TestResultMeans Ascending weakness, absent reflexes → Admit; CSF analysis, nerve conduction studies; serial spirometry CSF protein may be high, cell count normal Supports Guillain-Barré syndrome; it may take up to a week to appear Weeks of proximal weakness with a rash → CK; muscle biopsy is the definitive test Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, CK high Juvenile dermatomyositis SkipBlood tests and radiographs for a classic history with a normal exam, and new tests when growing pains recur with a normal exam: episodes with pain-free weeks are expected until adolescence.

Treatment by cause Cause Treatment Growing pains Explain the benign, self-limited course; massage, sometimes with heat; ibuprofen or acetaminophen; stretching may help; keep usual activity, no braces ⚠︎ Benign acute childhood myositis Rest, analgesics and fluids; avoid aspirin in children with influenza (Reye syndrome); use a non-aspirin analgesic such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen instead Encephalopathy and Cerebral Edema in a Child Rhabdomyolysis IV fluids to prevent acute kidney injury; follow creatinine and potassium; admit ⚠︎ Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood Guillain-Barré syndrome IVIG (intravenous immune globulin) or plasma exchange, with respiratory support; no glucocorticoids Juvenile dermatomyositis Glucocorticoids, then long-term methotrexate

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Night pain in one leg that ibuprofen relieves Osteoid osteoma: relief by NSAIDs does not make it growing pains Bone Lesions in a Child Radiograph Pain that limits sports or comes during activity Not growing pains: an overuse injury or trauma Examine the tibial tubercle and the joints Calf pain with weakness Myositis or Guillain-Barré syndrome: weakness does not separate them Test the reflexes: kept in myositis, lost in Guillain-Barré syndrome Morning pain and stiffness, joint swelling Inflammatory arthritis Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis ESR, CRP and a CBC

Pause point Classic growing pains Offered: blood tests or films Both legs with a normal exam → Reassurance Night pain that NSAIDs relieve Offered: reassurance because NSAIDs work One side or a focal finding → The radiograph Rising weakness with calf pain Offered as myositis because the calves hurt The reflexes → The reflexes separate myositis from Guillain-Barré syndrome

12-year-old boy with 2 days of severe pain in both calves a week ago: dry cough, sore throat, headache and fever all resolved on ibuprofen after 5 days; no medications now Marked tenderness of both calves T 37 °C Most likely diagnosis? Competing answers Dermatomyositis: a myositis; but it brings proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; the stem describes no rash and no weakness. Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease): the fever may have just reached its 5-day threshold; but it has resolved, with no conjunctivitis, rash, node, hand, foot or lip change. NBME used the formal name. Parvovirus B19-induced arthritis: a post-viral ache; but it is symmetric arthritis of the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet; this tenderness is in muscle. Rheumatic fever: a sore throat came first; but it follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and is diagnosed by the Jones criteria (carditis, arthritis, nodules, erythema marginatum, chorea); calf tenderness is none of them. Down to two: influenza-induced myositis or dermatomyositis. Influenza-induced myositis: tender calves a few days after a flu-like illness, with no rash or proximal weakness. The stem never names influenza, and the key names the cause rather than the syndrome.

The Limping Childthe gait is abnormal Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysisone-sided hip, thigh or knee pain in an adolescent Acute Leukemia in a Childthe systemic picture Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Bloodheme on the dipstick, no red cells The Limping Child: the gait is abnormal. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: one-sided hip, thigh or knee pain in an adolescent. Acute Leukemia in a Child: the systemic picture. Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood: heme on the dipstick, no red cells.
A symptom shared by benign and serious causes does not separate them; find the feature that does. In leg pain, it is the exam and the side, not the hour.

briefs.title: Bone Lesions in a Child
briefs.sub: bone lesions by site, age and periosteum · the aggressive film and MRI before biopsy · Ewing sarcoma or osteomyelitis · natural history · treatment by cause
blocks: bone lesions by site, age and periosteum · the aggressive film and MRI before biopsy · Ewing sarcoma or osteomyelitis · natural history · treatment by cause

Sunburst periosteum or a Codman triangle at the metaphysis near the knee in a teenager: osteosarcoma. Onion skin in the shaft or pelvis, sometimes with fever: Ewing sarcoma An aggressive film gets MRI of the bone, then the biopsy; chest CT stages the lungs. Fever does not exclude a tumor Benign lesions are named by site and age and observed: a painless spur is an osteochondroma; night pain relieved by a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) is an osteoid osteoma; a central metaphyseal lucency is a unicameral bone cyst (simple bone cyst)

What it is A bone lesion on a child's plain film, named by where it sits, the child's age and the periosteum Sort by The site (epiphysis, metaphysis or shaft), then the age (physes open or closed), then the periosteum (quiet, or aggressive: sunburst, Codman triangle, onion skin) FeverEwing sarcoma or osteosarcomaFever, leukocytosis and high inflammatory markers occur in Ewing sarcoma and often mean it has spread; osteosarcoma rarely brings them Hands off Leukemia, the febrile limp, one-sided leg pain and the mass after an injury have their own briefs Acute Leukemia in a Child The Limping Child Leg Pain in a Child Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans

OsteosarcomaA painful, enlarging mass near the knee in a teenager, or a pathologic fracture If the film shows sunburst periosteum or a Codman triangle, choose MRI of the bone, then biopsy; chest CT for lung metastases. Ewing sarcomaWeeks of pain and swelling in the shaft or pelvis; fever and high markers can mimic infection If the film shows a permeative lytic lesion with onion-skin layers, choose MRI, then biopsy; fever does not exclude it. OsteomyelitisDays of fever with point tenderness at a long-bone metaphysis; the film is normal early The Limping Child If the child is febrile and the bone is tender, choose CBC, ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and blood culture. LeukemiaBone pain with fever, pallor or bruising, and no lytic lesion on the film Acute Leukemia in a Child If the film shows no lesion and the child is pale or bruised, choose CBC with peripheral smear.

Aggressive film or a painful bone, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Ewing sarcoma Peak 10 to 15, more often boys; pain and swelling in the shaft, pelvis or axial skeleton; fever, leukocytosis and high markers in some Weeks: permeative, moth-eaten lytic lesion with onion-skin (lamellated) periosteum; biopsy: sheets of small round blue cells; t(11;22) Osteosarcoma Teens; painful enlarging mass at the distal femur or proximal tibia; rarely febrile; prior radiation or hereditary retinoblastoma Chronic, progressive pain: metaphyseal lesion, lytic and sclerotic, with sunburst periosteum and a Codman triangle; high alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and lactate dehydrogenase; biopsy: osteoid-producing cells Osteomyelitis The Limping Child Fever, focal pain and swelling; long-bone metaphysis; trauma or immunodeficiency support it Days: point tenderness; the film turns abnormal after 2 to 4 weeks; biopsy: inflammatory cells and necrotic bone Acute lymphoblastic leukemia Acute Leukemia in a Child Bone pain with fever, pallor or bruising No lytic lesion: the pain comes from the marrow; cytopenias on the CBC with smear Langerhans cell histiocytosis Children; bone and skin Lytic lesion with a pathologic fracture and no skin disease (eosinophilic granuloma); lytic skull lesions with a scalp rash, diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency) and exophthalmos; biopsy: S-100 stain Chondrosarcoma Adults, over 40 to 50; pelvis, proximal femur or humerus Growth of an osteochondroma after the physes close suggests it; ring-and-arc calcifications

Quiet lesion on a film, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Osteoid osteoma Teens, more often boys; proximal femur most often, or the spine Night pain unrelated to activity, relieved by NSAIDs; nidus under 2 cm in a sclerotic rim; CT shows the nidus best Unicameral bone cyst (simple bone cyst) Physes open; humerus or femur; painless and incidental, or a pathologic fracture Central metaphyseal lucency, narrow transition zone, no periosteal reaction Osteochondroma Teens; the most common benign bone tumor; a painless hard bump near the knee; multiple if hereditary Spur from the metaphysis pointing away from the joint, continuous with the cortex and medulla Nonossifying fibroma Common in children; femur or tibia; found by chance on a film Well-circumscribed lytic lesion, no symptoms Chondroblastoma Age 10 to 21, more often boys, physes open; distal femur, proximal tibia or proximal humerus; constant joint pain Epiphyseal lucency with a thin sclerotic rim; may cross the physis Giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma) Age 20 to 40, skeletally mature; distal femur or proximal tibia; joint pain and swelling Eccentric, expansile lytic lesion in the epiphysis with a soap-bubble look Aneurysmal bone cyst Adolescents; rapid growth Expansile lytic lesion with a thin sclerotic rim; MRI shows fluid-fluid levels

Site and age Site Lesion Epiphysis Chondroblastoma (physes open); giant cell tumor (mature) Metaphysis Osteochondroma, unicameral bone cyst, osteosarcoma, nonossifying fibroma Shaft (diaphysis) Ewing sarcoma; osteoid osteoma Pelvis Ewing sarcoma in a child; chondrosarcoma in an adult

Natural historynot to scale OsteochondromaGrows with the skeleton, then stops at physeal closure ChildTeenPhyses closeAdult→ Benign: stops or resolves Warninggrowth after the physes close suggests chondrosarcoma Unicameral bone cystResolves, typically by physeal closure; may fracture first ChildTeenPhyses closeAdult→ Benign: stops or resolves Osteoid osteomaResolves on its own ChildTeenPhyses closeAdult→ Benign: stops or resolves Ewing sarcomaPeak 10 to 15; progressive; early metastases to lung and bone ChildTeenPhyses closeAdult→ Malignant: progresses OsteosarcomaTeens; progressive; metastases usually to lung ChildTeenPhyses closeAdult→ Malignant: progresses Benign: stops or resolvesMalignant: progresses

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Every child with a bone lesion or focal bone pain → History and exam: age, night pain, response to NSAIDs, fever, weight loss Night pain relieved by NSAIDs Osteoid osteoma pattern Fever or weight loss, and pain that wakes the child at night Malignancy or infection, not a benign lesion → Plain radiograph of the bone Spur continuous with the cortex and medulla Osteochondroma: observe; no biopsy Central metaphyseal lucency, narrow transition, quiet periosteum Unicameral bone cyst: watch it on serial films Epiphyseal lucency, thin sclerotic rim Physes open: chondroblastoma; mature skeleton: giant cell tumor; both need curettage A small lucent nidus ringed by sclerosis Osteoid osteoma; CT shows the nidus best Sunburst, Codman triangle or onion skin Aggressive: MRI of the whole involved extremity, then biopsy Targeted tests TestResultMeans Fever and focal bone pain → CBC, ESR, CRP, blood culture Fever for days, a tender long-bone metaphysis, the film still normal Osteomyelitis The Limping Child Weeks, shaft, pelvis or spine, lytic lesion MRI, then biopsy: Ewing sarcoma also raises the inflammatory markers Bone pain with pallor, bruising or fever → CBC with peripheral smear Cytopenias, no lytic lesion Leukemia: the marrow, not the bone Acute Leukemia in a Child Next step TestResultMeans Aggressive film → MRI of the whole involved extremity Extent in bone, soft tissue and vessels mapped Plans the biopsy and the resection Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Aggressive lesion after MRI → Biopsy Osteoid-producing pleomorphic cells Osteosarcoma Sheets of small round blue cells Ewing sarcoma Inflammatory cells and necrotic bone Osteomyelitis Malignant on biopsy → Chest CT Nodules Lung metastases SkipBiopsy of a spur continuous with the bone, a typical unicameral bone cyst or a typical osteoid osteoma: the history and the film make the diagnosis. Repeat films for a sunburst or onion skin: MRI and biopsy come first.

Treatment by cause Cause Treatment Osteochondroma Observe; excision if it grows, hurts or disturbs growth In practiceOsteochondromaboard sources teach about 1%; a standard clinical reference puts malignant change at well under 1% of single osteochondromas Osteoid osteoma NSAIDs and serial films until it resolves In practiceOsteoid osteomaradiofrequency ablation of the nidus gives lasting relief in most cases Unicameral bone cyst (simple bone cyst) Observe with serial films until it resolves; the risk is fracture In practiceUnicameral bone cystsmaller cysts sometimes heal on their own; larger cysts in children may need an intervention Nonossifying fibroma Observe Chondroblastoma Curettage and bone grafting Giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma) Curettage or excision; high local recurrence; denosumab if unresectable Aneurysmal bone cyst Resection Osteosarcoma Chemotherapy plus en bloc resection Ewing sarcoma Chemotherapy plus resection, with or without radiation

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Fever with a lytic lesion over weeks Ewing sarcoma, not only osteomyelitis MRI, then biopsy Night pain that an NSAID relieves Osteoid osteoma: the nidus makes prostaglandins Radiograph; CT for the nidus Fracture through a lucent lesion after a minor fall Unicameral bone cyst; eosinophilic granuloma if lytic with no skin disease Serial radiographs for a classic cyst An osteochondroma that grows after the physes close Chondrosarcoma Excision or biopsy Bone pain with cytopenias and a normal film Leukemia Acute Leukemia in a Child CBC with smear

Pause point Febrile child with a lytic lesion in the shaft Offered as osteomyelitis Onion-skin periosteum; fever does not exclude a tumor → Ewing sarcoma: MRI, then biopsy A lesion the film already names Offered: biopsy A benign name → Observed Sunburst or onion skin on the film Offered: repeating the film An aggressive film → MRI, then biopsy

briefs.title: Shoulder Pain
briefs.sub: tendon vs joint by range of motion · cuff, impingement and biceps · red flags and referred pain · no sling for tendon painIs passive motion preserved, and what has the patient already tried?
blocks: tendon vs joint by range of motion · cuff, impingement and biceps · red flags and referred pain · no sling for tendon painIs passive motion preserved, and what has the patient already tried?

Sort by range of motion: active lost with passive kept is a tendon; both lost is the joint; a normal shoulder exam means referred pain Cuff tendinopathy is clinical (painful arc, Neer, Hawkins): rest and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug), then cuff strengthening, then occasionally an injection for short-term relief; MRI for weakness or failed therapy Rest never means a sling for tendon pain: prolonged immobilization is a risk factor for adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

What it is Shoulder pain in an adult, from a tendon, the joint, or somewhere else Sort by Active against passive range of motion, then the maneuvers Hands off A hot, swollen shoulder: Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult; glenohumeral osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease): Osteoarthritis Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult Hip Injury in an Adult Osteoarthritis

Septic arthritisFever, a red swollen shoulder that refuses all motion If the joint is hot and swollen, choose arthrocentesis before antibiotics. Referred cardiac painExertional pain with a normal shoulder exam If the shoulder exam is normal and the pain is exertional, choose an electrocardiogram (ECG). Pancoast tumorA stiff, painful shoulder with cough or dyspnea

Shoulder pain, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Rotator cuff tendinopathy or impingement Overhead use; pain worst between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction Passive motion kept; Neer, Hawkins or empty can positive ManeuversCuff maneuversEmpty can (Jobe): resisted downward pressure on the arms forward-flexed with thumbs down tests the supraspinatus. Neer: a positive test is impingement of the cuff tendons under the coracoacromial arch. Weak resisted external rotation suggests significant cuff dysfunction, such as a full-thickness tear. Full-thickness rotator cuff tear Weakness more than pain, in abduction and external rotation Acute, after a fall or injury: MRI confirms Biceps tendinopathy (biceps tendinitis) Anterior shoulder pain Tender long head of the biceps; Speed or Yergason test positive Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) Woman aged 40 to 60; diabetes, thyroid disease or dyslipidemia; or after immobilization Chronic, over months; active and passive motion lost in two or more planes, external rotation and abduction most Calcific tendinopathy Severe pain on abduction Passive motion kept; calcium in the tendon on the radiograph Glenohumeral osteoarthritis Older; prior shoulder trauma or surgery Motion lost like adhesive capsulitis; radiograph Acromioclavicular joint injury Trauma to the top of the shoulder Pain on cross-arm adduction; glenohumeral motion kept C5 to C6 radiculopathy Neck pain on movement, hand weakness or numbness Normal shoulder exam; neck signs

Adhesive capsulitis course Painful, about 2 to 9 monthsSevere pain that disturbs sleep, then stiffness sets in Stiff, about 4 to 12 monthsPain eases while the stiffness worsens Recovery, months to yearsMotion returns; 1 to 3 years in all, often with some stiffness left In practiceCourseIn practice: a 2019 family medicine review traditionally expects most untreated patients to recover within 1 to 2 years; board teaching allows up to 3.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any painful shoulder → Range of motion, the patient moving it, then you Only active motion down Tendon: cuff or biceps Both lost Joint: adhesive capsulitis or osteoarthritis Normal shoulder exam Referred: neck, heart or gallbladder Targeted tests TestResultMeans Tendon pattern → Painful arc, Neer, Hawkins, empty can, external rotation strength Pain, strength kept Tendinopathy: clinical Weakness Full-thickness tear: MRI Both motions lost → Glucose testing and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) Diabetes or hypothyroidism Adhesive capsulitis with its cause Fever, effusion, refuses motion → Arthrocentesis Purulent fluid Septic arthritis Next step TestResultMeans Weakness, a suspected tear, or tendon pain after every lower rung → MRI Full-thickness tear Surgical repair SkipMRI before a trial of treatment for tendinopathy, and imaging to diagnose adhesive capsulitis (its radiographs are typically normal).

Tendon pain: start on the lowest rung not yet tried Rung Do Move on when 1 Stop the offending activity; an NSAID; no sling No better after a brief trial 2 Physical therapy to strengthen the cuff Pain persists 3 Subacromial glucocorticoid injection InjectionsSteroid injectionA subacromial glucocorticoid injection gives short-term relief; repeated injections risk tendon degeneration, so limit them. Still failing, or a tear suspected 4 MRI, then surgery Top rung

Adhesive capsulitis takes a different plan: Its treatmentAdhesive capsulitis treatmentAn NSAID and gentle physical therapy (aggressive stretching makes it worse); an intra-articular glucocorticoid injection early, alongside therapy; oral glucocorticoids help only briefly; surgical release when refractory.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Weeks in a sling after a minor injury, now stiff in every direction Adhesive capsulitis from immobilization Physical therapy, not more rest Young patient, traumatic full-thickness tear A repairable tear Prompt orthopedic referral for repair Bulge in the arm after a sudden load on the flexed elbow Biceps tendon rupture, proximal (long head) or distal Proximal: reassurance and follow-up; distal: surgical repair, especially if young or active Scapular winging after axillary node dissection, or supraspinatus and infraspinatus atrophy Long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior) or suprascapular nerve (C5 to C6) Recognize the nerve lesion Fall on the shoulder, midshaft tenderness Clavicle fracture Usually conservative; a sling is right here Force on an arm held out and turned out; it stays that way, deltoid flattened Anterior dislocation, by far the most common; labrum (Bankart) and humeral head (Hill-Sachs) injuries Radiographs, prompt closed reduction; test lateral shoulder sensation (axillary nerve) Seizure or electrocution; arm held in and turned in, cannot turn out Posterior dislocation, easy to miss on films Axillary view Dislocation with a humeral neck fracture Fracture-dislocation: no closed reduction Emergency orthopedic consultation for surgical reduction A dislocation, reduced Recurrence if under 25 in contact sports; a cuff tear if over 40 Sling for 1 to 3 weeks, then physical therapy
Pause point Shoulder tendon pain Offered: a sling, “just rest”, or MRI first Start on the lowest rung not yet tried → Keep the shoulder moving

Next step13 of 13 45-year-old man has sudden antecubital pain after lifting a heavy cabinet weak supination of the forearm gap palpable above the elbow crease Bruising spreads into the forearm the next day Afebrile · biceps hook test abnormal · Sling and observation · Physical therapy alone · Urgent orthopedic referral for surgical repair 45-year-old man has sudden antecubital pain after lifting a heavy cabinet weak supination of the forearm gap palpable above the elbow crease Bruising spreads into the forearm the next day Afebrile · biceps hook test abnormal Urgent orthopedic referral for surgical repaira distal biceps rupture is repaired surgically, unlike a proximal one: urgent orthopedic referral
Range of motion sorts tendon from joint before any test. The next step is usually the next rung not yet tried, and every instruction to rest says what to do instead.

briefs.title: Heart Murmurs in a Child
briefs.sub: innocent vs pathologic murmurs · one pathologic feature buys the echo · louder on standing · the continuous murmur by locationIs any single feature pathologic, and does the murmur get louder or softer on standing?
blocks: innocent vs pathologic murmurs · one pathologic feature buys the echo · louder on standing · the continuous murmur by locationIs any single feature pathologic, and does the murmur get louder or softer on standing?

An innocent murmur is grade 1 to 2, early or midsystolic, musical or vibratory and softer on standing or Valsalva, in a well child with normal vitals, first and second heart sounds (S1, S2), pulses and growth: reassure. Any single pathologic feature (grade 3 or higher, holosystolic or diastolic, harsh, abnormal S2, weak femoral pulses, symptoms) calls for an electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiography. A systolic murmur louder on standing or Valsalva is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded: hold sports.
Innocent murmurs are mildly turbulent flow through a normal heart; a diastolic murmur is never innocent. The one benign continuous murmur, the venous hum, disappears supine or with head flexion.

Act now Finding Action Murmur louder on standing in an athlete, or syncope on exertion Hold sports; obtain ECG and echocardiography: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a common cause of sudden death in young athletes. Weak femoral pulses with arm hypertension Coarctation: measure four-extremity pressures and obtain echocardiography. Infant with poor weight gain, feeding difficulty or breathing fast Heart failure from a shunt: obtain echocardiography. Central cyanosis with a murmur Cyanotic heart disease: obtain echocardiography.

Innocent murmurs Murmur Decides it Next best step Still murmur Often ages 2 to 6: vibratory or musical, left lower sternal border; louder supine, softer standing. Reassure. Pulmonic flow murmur Any age: soft ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border; normal, moving S2. Reassure. Venous hum Often ages 3 to 8: continuous, above the right clavicle; gone supine or with head flexion. Reassure. Peripheral pulmonary stenosis Under 1 year: grade 1 or 2 ejection murmur spreading to the axillae and back. Reassure if well; it should be gone by age 1. In practiceThe American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) advises echocardiography or considering cardiology referral for any newborn murmur, even when well, because structural lesions are more prevalent at that age.

Pathologic murmurs Lesion Decides it Next best step Ventricular septal defect Holosystolic, left lower sternal border; small is loud and harsh, large tends to be softer. Obtain echocardiography. Atrial septal defect Ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border with a wide, fixed split S2. Obtain echocardiography. Patent ductus arteriosus Continuous, machine-like, loudest just below the medial end of the left clavicle; congenital rubella. Obtain echocardiography. Coarctation of the aorta Arm hypertension, weak femoral pulses; a systolic or continuous murmur between the shoulder blades on the back. Measure four-extremity pressures; obtain echocardiography. Pulmonary valve stenosis Ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border spreading to the back; ejection click; S2 widely split but moving. Obtain echocardiography. Aortic stenosis Ejection murmur at the upper right sternal border spreading to the carotids. Obtain echocardiography. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border, louder standing or with Valsalva, softer squatting or with handgrip; fourth heart sound (S4); family history of sudden death. Hold sports; obtain ECG and echocardiography. Infant of a diabetic motherA transient hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from myocardial fat and glycogen deposition resolves by age 1; beta-blockers if symptomatic.

Innocent or pathologic: the screening exam Axis Innocent Pathologic History Asymptomatic, normal growth Infant: poor weight gain, feeding difficulty, fast breathing; older: chest pain, syncope, exertional intolerance Murmur Early or midsystolic, musical or vibratory, grade 1 to 2, softer upright Holosystolic or diastolic, harsh, grade 3 or higher, louder or persistent upright (a venous hum aside) Other findings Normal vitals, normal S1 and S2, symmetric pulses Central cyanosis; loud, fixed or single S2; weak femoral pulses; hepatomegaly

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any murmur in a child → Auscultation supine, sitting and standing Grade 1 to 2, vibratory, softer on standing, normal examination Innocent murmur: reassure; no testing Systolic, louder on standing or Valsalva Treat as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: no sports until ECG and echocardiography Harsh, holosystolic or diastolic, grade 3 or higher, or an abnormal S2 ECG and echocardiography Targeted tests TestResultMeans Weak femoral pulses → Four-extremity blood pressures Arm pressure above leg Coarctation Any pathologic feature → ECG Hypertrophy or a conduction abnormality Supports a structural lesion; pair it with echocardiography Diagnostic test TestResultMeans A pathologic feature, or an innocent murmur outliving its age → Echocardiography Structural lesion Names the lesion (Congenital Heart Disease covers each) SkipEchocardiography, ECG or chest radiography for a child with every benign feature: they rarely add to the examination.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step A new soft murmur on day 3 after a normal birth examination A shunt as pulmonary resistance falls, or peripheral pulmonary stenosis Check where it spreads. Loudest in the axilla, spreading to the lung fields Peripheral pulmonary stenosis Reassure if well; confirm it is gone by age 1. Saturation 99% with normal pulses Against cyanotic disease and coarctation Check the murmur grade and where it spreads. S2 split that moves with breathing Excludes an atrial septal defect, whose split is fixed Keep atrial septal defect off the list.
Pause point Murmur with mostly benign features Offered: reassurance Reassurance needs every benign feature; one pathologic feature is enough → ECG and echocardiography

Diagnosis1 of 18 5 yo M, grade 2 vibratory murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder supine, vanishes on standing · Ventricular septal defectA ventricular septal defect is holosystolic and does not vanish on standing. · Still murmurA soft vibratory murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder supine and gone on standing, is a Still murmur. · Hypertrophic cardiomyopathyHypertrophic cardiomyopathy gets louder on standing, not softer. 5 yo M, grade 2 vibratory murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder supine, vanishes on standing Still murmurreassurance

Diagnosis2 of 18 14 yo athlete, systolic murmur that grows louder with standing and Valsalva · Still murmurA Still murmur softens on standing. · Hypertrophic cardiomyopathyA systolic murmur louder with standing and Valsalva is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded. · Aortic stenosisAortic stenosis sits at the upper right sternal border, radiates to the carotids and softens with Valsalva. 14 yo athlete, systolic murmur that grows louder with standing and Valsalva Hypertrophic cardiomyopathyechocardiography before sports

Diagnosis3 of 18 6 yo F, continuous right supraclavicular hum that disappears with head flexion · Venous humA continuous hum above the right clavicle that disappears with head flexion is a venous hum. · Patent ductus arteriosusA patent ductus does not change with head position. · Aortic coarctationCoarctation brings arm hypertension and weak femoral pulses. 6 yo F, continuous right supraclavicular hum that disappears with head flexion Venous humreassurance

Next step4 of 18 3 yo M, harsh grade 3 holosystolic murmur, otherwise well · ECG and echocardiographyGrade 3, harsh and holosystolic are each pathologic: ECG and echocardiography. · Chest x-ray aloneA chest radiograph rarely helps and cannot name the lesion. · Reassurance with follow-upReassurance needs every benign feature. 3 yo M, harsh grade 3 holosystolic murmur, otherwise well ECG and echocardiographyone pathologic feature is enough

Diagnosis5 of 18 Infant with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension, continuous murmur over the back · Patent ductus arteriosusA patent ductus is heard below the left clavicle, with bounding pulses. · Essential hypertensionEssential hypertension does not weaken the femoral pulses. · Aortic coarctationWeak femoral pulses with arm hypertension and a murmur over the back is coarctation with collateral flow. Infant with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension, continuous murmur over the back Aortic coarctationcollateral flow murmur

Diagnosis6 of 18 Well 4 yo, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla, normal S2 · Pulmonic valve stenosisPulmonic valve stenosis adds an ejection click. · Atrial septal defectAn atrial septal defect has a wide fixed split S2. · Pulmonic flow murmurA soft midsystolic murmur at the upper left sternal border with a normal S2 in a well child is a pulmonic flow murmur. Well 4 yo, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla, normal S2 Pulmonic flow murmurinnocent; a wide fixed split or ejection click would change the answer

Mechanism7 of 18 4 yo with a soft continuous murmur above the right clavicle that fades with head flexion and when supine · Increased flow across the pulmonary valveExtra pulmonary valve flow makes a systolic ejection murmur, not a continuous one. · Turbulent flow through the curved jugular and subclavian veinsThe hum is turbulent venous flow into the superior vena cava, which head flexion and lying down change. · Shunting from aorta to pulmonary artery through a patent ductusDuctal shunting is unchanged by head position. 4 yo with a soft continuous murmur above the right clavicle that fades with head flexion and when supine Turbulent flow through the curved jugular and subclavian veinsvenous hum, and why it is usually right-sided

Diagnosis8 of 18 3 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur under the left clavicle that does not change with head position or posture · Patent ductus arteriosusA fixed, continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle is a patent ductus arteriosus. · Coarctation of the aorta with intercostal collateralsCoarctation collaterals are heard over the back, with weak femoral pulses. · Venous humA venous hum changes with head position and posture. 3 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur under the left clavicle that does not change with head position or posture Patent ductus arteriosusechocardiography

Diagnosis9 of 18 9 yo with a continuous murmur heard best over the back, upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses · Coarctation with intercostal collateral flowA continuous murmur over the back with arm hypertension and weak femoral pulses is coarctation collateral flow. · Venous humA venous hum is heard at the clavicle and changes with position. · Patent ductus arteriosusA patent ductus is heard below the left clavicle, without weak femoral pulses. 9 yo with a continuous murmur heard best over the back, upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses Coarctation with intercostal collateral flowechocardiography and four-extremity pressures

Mechanism10 of 18 6-week-old with a large ventricular septal defect and tachypnea with feeds, the chamber that receives the increased preload · Right atriumThe right atrium receives systemic venous return, which the shunt does not increase. · Left atriumThe left-to-right shunt returns extra blood from the lungs to the left atrium. · Right ventricleThe right ventricle passes shunted blood straight to the lungs; the extra filling load falls on the left heart. 6-week-old with a large ventricular septal defect and tachypnea with feeds, the chamber that receives the increased preload Left atriumleft-to-right shunt increases pulmonary venous return

Diagnosis11 of 18 2 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle that runs through S2, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure · Ventricular septal defectA ventricular septal defect is holosystolic. · Aortic regurgitationAortic regurgitation is diastolic, not continuous. · Patent ductus arteriosusA continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle with bounding pulses is a patent ductus. 2 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle that runs through S2, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure Patent ductus arteriosusthe machine-like continuous murmur, with a wide pulse pressure

Diagnosis12 of 18 6 d old M, well and thriving, a soft 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, normal apical impulse, 2+ equal femoral pulses, saturation 98% · A large ventricular septal defectA soft holosystolic murmur in a well 6-day-old points to a large defect: equal pressures leave little turbulence. · A small ventricular septal defectA small defect is loud and harsh because of its high gradient. · An innocent Still murmurA Still murmur is vibratory and occurs in older children, not a holosystolic newborn murmur. 6 d old M, well and thriving, a soft 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, normal apical impulse, 2+ equal femoral pulses, saturation 98% A large ventricular septal defectsoft because a wide defect creates little turbulence

Diagnosis13 of 18 3 wk old, well and feeding normally, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, normal S2 with symmetric pulses · Pulmonic flow murmurA pulmonic flow murmur is soft and does not spread to both axillae and the back. · Atrial septal defectAn atrial septal defect has a wide fixed split S2. · Peripheral pulmonary stenosisA soft murmur spreading to both axillae and the back in a well infant is peripheral pulmonary stenosis. 3 wk old, well and feeding normally, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, normal S2 with symmetric pulses Peripheral pulmonary stenosisan innocent murmur of the first year

Diagnosis14 of 18 5 yo F with a continuous grade 2 hum above the right clavicle that is louder when she sits up and disappears when she lies down · Still murmurA Still murmur is systolic and louder supine. · Venous humA hum louder sitting up that disappears lying down is a venous hum. · Patent ductus arteriosusA patent ductus does not change with posture. 5 yo F with a continuous grade 2 hum above the right clavicle that is louder when she sits up and disappears when she lies down Venous humthe one benign murmur that increases upright

Mechanism15 of 18 Why a venous hum is typically louder on the right than the left · Left-sided flow is damped by the aortic archThe aortic arch does not dampen venous flow. · The right atrium is closer to the chest wallThe position of the right atrium does not generate the hum. · The right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more verticalThe right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical, so flow into the superior vena cava is faster. Why a venous hum is typically louder on the right than the left The right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more verticalmore turbulent flow into the superior vena cava

Next step16 of 18 18 mo old whose neonatal murmur radiating to the axillae and back is unchanged, with normal growth and no symptoms · Continued observationAn innocent murmur that outlives its age is a pathologic feature. · EchocardiographyPeripheral pulmonary stenosis is a first-year murmur; still present at 18 months, it needs echocardiography. · Reassurance with no follow-upReassurance without follow-up misses a persisting lesion. 18 mo old whose neonatal murmur radiating to the axillae and back is unchanged, with normal growth and no symptoms Echocardiographyperipheral pulmonary stenosis is a first-year murmur

Next step17 of 18 7 yo F, well and growing normally, with a grade 2 vibratory midsystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that softens on standing; normal S2 and pulses · ReassuranceEvery feature of the benign profile is present: reassure. · ECG and echocardiographyTesting is for a pathologic feature, and none is present. · Chest X-rayA chest radiograph rarely helps with a murmur. 7 yo F, well and growing normally, with a grade 2 vibratory midsystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that softens on standing; normal S2 and pulses Reassurancethe full benign profile is present

Next step18 of 18 15 yo soccer player, asymptomatic, with a grade 2 systolic murmur that grows louder when he stands from a squat · Hold sports pending ECG and echoA murmur louder on standing is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded: hold sports pending ECG and echocardiography. · Exercise stress test aloneA stress test alone cannot exclude hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. · Reassurance and clearance for sportsClearing him now risks sudden death. 15 yo soccer player, asymptomatic, with a grade 2 systolic murmur that grows louder when he stands from a squat Hold sports pending ECG and echolouder on standing is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded

Still murmur: vibratory, lower left sternal border, louder supine Pulmonic flow murmur: systolic ejection, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla Venous hum: continuous, above the clavicle, usually right-sided because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical, so flow velocity into the superior vena cava is higher; disappears with head flexion and when supine.

A continuous murmur in a child has three causes, separated by location: Right supraclavicular and positional: venous hum, benign, fades with head flexion and when supine Left infraclavicular and fixed: patent ductus arteriosus, machine-like, unchanged by head position or posture; runs through S2, with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure Over the back with weak femoral pulses: coarctation collateral flow, with upper-extremity hypertension. Separately, a fixed split S2 is the atrial septal defect sign, so an S2 split that moves with respiration excludes atrial septal defect.

Congenital Heart Diseasecovers the cyanosis and single S2 of the pathologic column Heart Murmurs in an Adultcovers the pathologic counterpart of the innocent pulmonic flow murmur. Ask: "what does standing do to it?" Congenital Heart Disease covers the cyanosis and single S2 of the pathologic column. Heart Murmurs in an Adult covers the pathologic counterpart of the innocent pulmonic flow murmur. Ask: "what does standing do to it?"

Still murmur: younger children, left lower sternal border, midsystolic, vibratory or musical, louder supine and softer standing; resolves by adolescence Pulmonic flow murmur: childhood through adolescence, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla; appears or intensifies in high-output states such as fever, anemia and anxiety Venous hum: continuous, above the clavicle, right louder than left because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical; the one benign murmur that increases sitting up, and it disappears supine or with head flexion Peripheral pulmonary stenosis: the neonatal benign murmur, upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, from physiologically narrow proximal pulmonary arteries while fetal resistance is still falling; typical under 1 year Persistence past the expected age: a benign murmur that outlives its window is itself a pathologic feature Intensity and defect size: a small ventricular septal defect is loud and a large one is soft or silent, because turbulence falls as the orifice widens

A murmur new on day 3 after a normal birth examination pulls toward a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus; its soft grade and spread to the axilla mark peripheral pulmonary stenosis. The options were the five common acyanotic lesions, so the key was the umbrella term, pulmonary stenosis.
In screening, reassurance requires the entire benign profile. One pathologic feature on exam, in the vitals or in the history is sufficient to start the workup.

Unchecked attributePatent ductus arteriosus: it is the right category for a continuous murmur near a clavicle. Check the side and the positional change; a ductus murmur does not change with head position. Unchecked attributeAtrial septal defect: the split S2 here moves with respiration, the opposite of the fixed split it requires. Mirror twinHypertrophic cardiomyopathy: it is the dangerous mimic of the innocent murmur; the direction the murmur moves on standing separates them. Uniform-answer doubtReassurance: accept it only after naming the full benign profile.

briefs.title: Heart Murmurs in an Adult
briefs.sub: shape first, then breathing · the click and the second heart sound (S2) decide · prior congenital repair can explain adult complications
blocks: shape first, then breathing · the click and the second heart sound (S2) decide · prior congenital repair can explain adult complications

Identify systolic, diastolic or continuous timing, then use site, radiation, breathing, the click and second heart sound (S2) to choose the lesion. Inspiration usually accentuates right-sided murmurs. Standing or Valsalva accentuates hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and shifts a prolapse click earlier. In a patient with repaired tetralogy of Fallot, think pulmonic regurgitation; palpitations with syncope require evaluation for ventricular arrhythmia.
Right inspiration, left expiration (RILE): breathing helps localize the murmur. A repaired congenital lesion can explain the adult presentation.

High-risk presentations Finding Action Syncope, angina or exertional dyspnea with an aortic ejection murmur Arrange prompt echocardiography and valve assessment. Palpitations or syncope after tetralogy repair Obtain an electrocardiogram (ECG), ambulatory rhythm monitoring and specialist assessment. Exertional syncope with a dynamic systolic murmur and a sudden-death family history Evaluate urgently for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; ventricular arrhythmia can cause sudden death in young athletes.

Murmur patterns Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Pulmonic (pulmonary) stenosis Ejection click and crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border; wide S2 split varies with breathing. Confirm the valve obstruction and gradient with Doppler echo. Atrial septal defect Wide, fixed S2 split; increased pulmonic flow without a stenotic-valve click. Obtain echocardiography to define the shunt. Tricuspid regurgitation Holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder on inspiration; moderate to severe disease may cause prominent venous waves, and severe disease may cause a pulsatile liver. Use echo to assess the regurgitation and right ventricular (RV) size; identify the cause. Mitral regurgitation Holosystolic apical murmur with axillary radiation. Obtain echo to assess the valve and ventricle. Aortic stenosis Crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids; softer with Valsalva. A bicuspid valve can present prematurely. Confirm with transthoracic echo. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Systolic ejection murmur becomes louder with standing or Valsalva, softer with squatting or handgrip. Obtain echo to assess dynamic outflow obstruction. Aortic regurgitation Early diastolic decrescendo murmur with a wide pulse pressure. Obtain echo to quantify regurgitation. Pulmonic (pulmonary) regurgitation Early diastolic murmur after repaired tetralogy; with pulmonary hypertension, a loud pulmonic component of S2 (P2) suggests a Graham Steell murmur. Order echocardiography to assess regurgitation and RV dilation. Mitral or tricuspid stenosis Diastolic rumble; an apical opening snap favors mitral stenosis, inspiration favors the tricuspid valve. Use echo to define the obstructed valve. Mitral valve prolapse A mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur; standing moves the click earlier. Order echocardiography if structural disease or associated regurgitation is suspected. Functional flow murmur Soft systolic murmur, no click, normal S2 and a high-output cause such as anemia or fever. Treat the underlying cause; reassess the murmur. Left atrial myxoma A diastolic plop or position-dependent rumble with constitutional symptoms; myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults. Obtain echo to look for a mass. Patent ductus arteriosus A continuous, machine-like murmur spans S2. Obtain echo to define the shunt.

Heart sounds: first (S1) and second (S2) S2 finding Interpretation Wide split that varies with respiration Delayed pulmonic closure, as in pulmonic stenosis. Wide, fixed split Atrial septal defect. Paradoxical splitting Delayed aortic closure, as in severe aortic stenosis or left bundle branch block. Loud P2 Pulmonary hypertension; with a pulmonary diastolic murmur, consider Graham Steell. Single S2 Several congenital or severe valve conditions can merge or remove a component; use the complete examination.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Adult murmur → Characterize timing, location and radiation Systolic, diastolic or continuous Narrow to the corresponding murmur patterns. → Listen with inspiration, standing or Valsalva as appropriate Right-sided accentuation or a dynamic response Use the response to separate valve flow from dynamic outflow obstruction. Targeted tests TestResultMeans High-output flow pattern or suspected anemia → CBC Anemia Treat the cause and reassess the flow murmur. Tricuspid regurgitation with pulmonic stenosis → Urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) Elevated result in the appropriate context Evaluate carcinoid syndrome as an acquired cause. Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Suspected structural valve lesion, shunt or cardiac mass → Transthoracic echocardiography Valve gradient, regurgitant jet or chamber dilation Define lesion severity and the treatment branch.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Prior tetralogy repair and a new diastolic murmur Pulmonic regurgitation Order echo to assess RV size and regurgitation; obtain rhythm monitoring for palpitations or syncope. A wide fixed split rather than a variable split Atrial septal defect rather than isolated pulmonic stenosis Confirm the shunt with echo.

Pause point Early diastolic or holosystolic murmur Named by its shape alone Match both the phase and the side → Aortic and pulmonic regurgitation share an early diastolic shape; tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic

Treatment by cause Cause Action Severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis Refer for balloon valvuloplasty when the valve anatomy is suitable. Pulmonic regurgitation after repair Follow RV size and function; symptoms with progressive dilation or impaired function can require pulmonary valve replacement. Tricuspid regurgitation or Graham Steell murmur Identify and treat the cause of tricuspid regurgitation, including intrinsic valve disease. A Graham Steell murmur requires treatment of the pulmonary hypertension.

After congenital heart repairThe repair can determine the adult complication Pulmonic regurgitation, RV dilation and ventricular arrhythmia risk.Palpitations or syncope need rhythm evaluation. Aortic regurgitation. Recurrent narrowing or persistent hypertension. Protein-losing enteropathy and arrhythmia. Baffle obstruction or systemic RV failure.

Diagnosis1 of 16 30-year-old man has exertional dyspnea tetralogy of Fallot repaired at age 3 decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, louder with inspiration single S2; parasternal heave Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 84/min · Aortic regurgitationEarly diastolic decrescendo murmur with a wide pulse pressure. · Pulmonic regurgitationA repaired tetralogy plus a right-sided diastolic murmur favors pulmonic regurgitation. · Tricuspid regurgitationHolosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder on inspiration; moderate to severe disease may cause prominent venous waves, and severe disease may cause a pulsatile liver. 30-year-old man has exertional dyspnea tetralogy of Fallot repaired at age 3 decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, louder with inspiration single S2; parasternal heave Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 84/min Pulmonic regurgitationThe repaired tetralogy and right-sided diastolic murmur favor pulmonic regurgitation. Echocardiography assesses regurgitation and RV size; progressive symptomatic RV dilation warrants valve replacement assessment.

Diagnosis2 of 16 18-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur ejection click, then a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace widely split S2 that varies with respiration Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 72/min · Atrial septal defectWide, fixed S2 split; increased pulmonic flow without a stenotic-valve click. · Innocent pulmonic flow murmurSoft systolic murmur, no click, normal S2 and a high-output cause such as anemia or fever. · Pulmonic valve stenosisAn ejection click and variable wide S2 split favor pulmonic stenosis. 18-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur ejection click, then a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace widely split S2 that varies with respiration Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 72/min Pulmonic valve stenosisan ejection click and a widened split that varies with breathing are pulmonic stenosis; an atrial septal defect splits S2 wide but fixed, with no click, and the innocent pulmonic flow murmur has no click and a normal S2; confirm with echocardiography

Diagnosis3 of 16 38-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap loud S1 ECG shows atrial fibrillation Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 112/min, irregularly irregular · Left atrial myxomaA diastolic plop or position-dependent rumble with constitutional symptoms; myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults. · Tricuspid stenosisDiastolic rumble; an apical opening snap favors mitral stenosis, inspiration favors the tricuspid valve. · Mitral stenosisAn apical rumble with an opening snap favors mitral stenosis. 38-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap loud S1 ECG shows atrial fibrillation Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 112/min, irregularly irregular Mitral stenosisAn apical diastolic rumble with an opening snap favors mitral stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis is accentuated by inspiration; a positional plop or rumble suggests a myxoma.

Diagnosis4 of 16 17-year-old boy is evaluated for a murmur harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left mid-sternal border louder with Valsalva and on standing Family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 120/74 mm Hg · HR 70/min · Pulmonic stenosisEjection click and crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border; wide S2 split varies with breathing. · Hypertrophic cardiomyopathyA murmur accentuated by standing and Valsalva suggests dynamic outflow obstruction. · Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valveCrescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids; softer with Valsalva. A bicuspid valve can present prematurely. 17-year-old boy is evaluated for a murmur harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left mid-sternal border louder with Valsalva and on standing Family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 120/74 mm Hg · HR 70/min Hypertrophic cardiomyopathyStanding and Valsalva reduce filling and accentuate the dynamic outflow murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valve usually radiates toward the carotids; pulmonic stenosis is left upper sternal and accentuated by inspiration. Confirm the obstruction with echocardiography.

Diagnosis5 of 16 64-year-old man has leg edema and ascites distended jugular veins with large v waves pulsatile, tender, enlarged liver holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min · Mitral regurgitationHolosystolic apical murmur with axillary radiation. · Tricuspid regurgitationA right-sided holosystolic murmur with venous v waves and hepatic pulsation favors tricuspid regurgitation. · Ventricular septal defectA septal defect is harsh at the lower sternal border; the venous pattern favors tricuspid regurgitation. 64-year-old man has leg edema and ascites distended jugular veins with large v waves pulsatile, tender, enlarged liver holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min Tricuspid regurgitationA holosystolic murmur accentuated by inspiration, with venous v waves and hepatic pulsation, favors tricuspid regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation usually radiates toward the axilla; a ventricular septal defect is usually a harsh lower sternal murmur.

Diagnosis6 of 16 45-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur that decreases with inspiration bounding pulses No history of heart surgery or lung disease Afebrile · BP 158/52 mm Hg, a wide pulse pressure · HR 76/min · Aortic regurgitationAn early diastolic murmur with wide pulse pressure favors aortic regurgitation. · Mitral stenosisDiastolic rumble; an apical opening snap favors mitral stenosis, inspiration favors the tricuspid valve. · Pulmonic regurgitationEarly diastolic murmur after repaired tetralogy; with pulmonary hypertension, a loud pulmonic component of S2 (P2) suggests a Graham Steell murmur. 45-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur that decreases with inspiration bounding pulses No history of heart surgery or lung disease Afebrile · BP 158/52 mm Hg, a wide pulse pressure · HR 76/min Aortic regurgitationAn early diastolic murmur with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure favors aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic regurgitation is right-sided; mitral stenosis causes an apical rumble.

Diagnosis7 of 16 20-year-old woman has 6 months of heavy menstrual periods soft midsystolic murmur normal S2; no click No syncope or chest pain on exertion Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 8 g/dL · Pulmonic valve stenosisEjection click and crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border; wide S2 split varies with breathing. · Functional flow murmurSevere anemia explains a soft flow murmur with normal S2 and no click. · Atrial septal defectWide, fixed S2 split; increased pulmonic flow without a stenotic-valve click. 20-year-old woman has 6 months of heavy menstrual periods soft midsystolic murmur normal S2; no click No syncope or chest pain on exertion Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 8 g/dL Functional flow murmurAnemia can cause a soft systolic flow murmur. A normal S2 and absent click support that pattern here; Pulmonic valve stenosis usually has an ejection click and a variable split; an atrial septal defect has a fixed split. Treat the anemia and reassess the murmur.

Diagnosis8 of 16 55-year-old woman has dyspnea that changes with body position a plop and a rumble that vary with body position fever and weight loss T 38.1 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 92/min · Infective endocarditisConstitutional symptoms alone fit infection, but the positional plop favors a mass. · Mitral stenosisDiastolic rumble; an apical opening snap favors mitral stenosis, inspiration favors the tricuspid valve. · Left atrial myxomaA positional plop or rumble with constitutional symptoms favors myxoma. 55-year-old woman has dyspnea that changes with body position a plop and a rumble that vary with body position fever and weight loss T 38.1 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 92/min Left atrial myxomaa plop and a rumble that shift with position, with fever and weight loss, are a left atrial myxoma; mitral stenosis gives an apical rumble with an opening snap, and fever with weight loss also fit endocarditis, but a plop and rumble that shift with position point to a mass

Diagnosis9 of 16 20-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border S2 split widely, and fixed with breathing; no click Lungs clear; no edema Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min · Tricuspid regurgitationHolosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder on inspiration; moderate to severe disease may cause prominent venous waves, and severe disease may cause a pulsatile liver. · Atrial septal defectA wide fixed S2 split reflects an atrial septal defect. · Pulmonic valve stenosisEjection click and crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border; wide S2 split varies with breathing. 20-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border S2 split widely, and fixed with breathing; no click Lungs clear; no edema Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min Atrial septal defecta wide, fixed split with no click is an atrial septal defect, more right-sided flow across a normal pulmonic valve; pulmonic stenosis splits S2 widely but the split varies, after an ejection click, and tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic at the lower border

Diagnosis10 of 16 78-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of syncope crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids softer with Valsalva delayed carotid upstroke No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 128/84 mm Hg · HR 70/min · Hypertrophic cardiomyopathySystolic ejection murmur becomes louder with standing or Valsalva, softer with squatting or handgrip. · Aortic stenosisCarotid radiation, delayed upstroke and softening with Valsalva favor aortic stenosis. · Mitral regurgitationHolosystolic apical murmur with axillary radiation. 78-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of syncope crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids softer with Valsalva delayed carotid upstroke No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 128/84 mm Hg · HR 70/min Aortic stenosisCarotid radiation, a delayed upstroke and reduced intensity with Valsalva favor aortic stenosis. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy becomes louder as preload falls; mitral regurgitation is holosystolic.

Diagnosis11 of 16 28-year-old man has 2 weeks of palpitations and one episode of syncope repaired tetralogy of Fallot No chest pain, fever or seizure activity Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 92/min · Pulmonic regurgitationEarly diastolic murmur after repaired tetralogy; with pulmonary hypertension, a loud pulmonic component of S2 (P2) suggests a Graham Steell murmur. · Residual ventricular septal defectA residual septal defect does not explain the episodic rhythm symptoms. · Ventricular arrhythmiaPalpitations with syncope after tetralogy repair raise concern for ventricular arrhythmia. 28-year-old man has 2 weeks of palpitations and one episode of syncope repaired tetralogy of Fallot No chest pain, fever or seizure activity Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 92/min Ventricular arrhythmiaPalpitations with syncope after tetralogy repair require ECG, ambulatory monitoring and specialist assessment for ventricular arrhythmia. Pulmonic regurgitation with RV dilation can be the substrate.

Diagnosis12 of 16 30-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border loud P2 echocardiogram shows pulmonary hypertension No prior heart surgery Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 80/min · Graham Steell murmurPulmonic regurgitation with a loud P2 and pulmonary hypertension is a Graham Steell murmur. · Aortic regurgitationEarly diastolic decrescendo murmur with a wide pulse pressure. · Post-surgical pulmonic regurgitationEarly diastolic murmur after repaired tetralogy; with pulmonary hypertension, a loud pulmonic component of S2 (P2) suggests a Graham Steell murmur. 30-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border loud P2 echocardiogram shows pulmonary hypertension No prior heart surgery Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 80/min Graham Steell murmurGraham Steell is pulmonic regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension: a loud P2 in pulmonary hypertension, contrasted with the prior congenital-repair setting, and there was no surgery; aortic regurgitation brings a wide pulse pressure, and this one is normal; treat the pulmonary hypertension

Diagnosis13 of 16 28-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur the click moves earlier on standing No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg · HR 72/min · Mitral valve prolapseA click moving earlier with reduced filling is mitral valve prolapse. · Hypertrophic cardiomyopathySystolic ejection murmur becomes louder with standing or Valsalva, softer with squatting or handgrip. · Aortic stenosisCrescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids; softer with Valsalva. A bicuspid valve can present prematurely. 28-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur the click moves earlier on standing No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg · HR 72/min Mitral valve prolapsea click that moves earlier with standing (reduced preload) is mitral valve prolapse; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also grows louder with reduced preload but is a harsh diamond-shaped murmur, and aortic stenosis has no mid-systolic click and gets softer with reduced preload

Next step14 of 16 22-year-old woman has exertional dyspnea ejection click and a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace echocardiogram shows a doming pulmonic valve with a severe gradient Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 84/min · Observation with serial echocardiographySevere symptomatic obstruction has passed the surveillance-only branch. · Surgical valve replacementAn appropriate native valve is usually treated with a balloon before surgical replacement. · Percutaneous balloon valvulotomySevere symptomatic valvular pulmonic stenosis is treated with balloon valvuloplasty when suitable. 22-year-old woman has exertional dyspnea ejection click and a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace echocardiogram shows a doming pulmonic valve with a severe gradient Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 84/min Percutaneous balloon valvulotomycongenital pulmonic stenosis, often silent until adult exertional dyspnea, now severe and symptomatic: percutaneous balloon valvulotomy is preferred over surgical replacement, and a severe, symptomatic valve is past observation

Diagnosis15 of 16 52-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur systolic murmur at the right 2nd interspace S2 splits paradoxically ECG shows no bundle branch block Afebrile · BP 134/82 mm Hg · HR 70/min · Pulmonic valve stenosisEjection click and crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border; wide S2 split varies with breathing. · Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valvePremature aortic calcification with a right upper sternal murmur suggests a bicuspid valve. · Functional flow murmurSoft systolic murmur, no click, normal S2 and a high-output cause such as anemia or fever. 52-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur systolic murmur at the right 2nd interspace S2 splits paradoxically ECG shows no bundle branch block Afebrile · BP 134/82 mm Hg · HR 70/min Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valveAn aortic ejection murmur with paradoxical S2 splitting supports aortic stenosis. Premature adult presentation suggests a bicuspid valve; echocardiography establishes the lesion.

Next step16 of 16 30-year-old man has worsening exertional dyspnea repaired tetralogy of Fallot echocardiogram shows a severely regurgitant pulmonic valve right ventricle more dilated than a year ago Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 86/min · Pulmonic valve replacementSymptoms with severe regurgitation and progressive RV dilation warrant valve replacement assessment. · Continue serial echocardiographySurveillance alone does not address progressive symptomatic RV volume overload. · Start diuretics and reassess in one yearDiuretics alone leave the worsening valve lesion uncorrected. 30-year-old man has worsening exertional dyspnea repaired tetralogy of Fallot echocardiogram shows a severely regurgitant pulmonic valve right ventricle more dilated than a year ago Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 86/min Pulmonic valve replacementsevere pulmonic regurgitation after repair with progressive right ventricular dilation and symptoms needs pulmonic valve replacement; serial echocardiography is surveillance, and diuretics with a recheck in a year leave the dilating ventricle untreated

Tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic and grows with inspiration; a pulmonic ejection click and variable split instead favor stenosis. Aortic regurgitation is an early diastolic left-sided murmur, often with a wide pulse pressure. Atrial septal defect has a wide fixed split. A soft systolic murmur with anemia, no click and a normal S2 supports a flow murmur; reassess after treating the cause rather than using S2 alone to exclude valve disease.

Heart Murmurs in a Childthe innocent pulmonic flow murmur, the benign counterpart of pulmonic stenosis; ask: is there a click, and what is S2 doing? Congenital Heart Diseasewhen a murmur appears and why; this brief covers what the murmur is Heart Murmurs in a Child: the innocent pulmonic flow murmur, the benign counterpart of pulmonic stenosis; ask: is there a click, and what is S2 doing?
