Fix phase and side before you name a valve, and check inspiration in every murmur. Then separate look-alikes by the accompanying findings, not the sound.

briefs.title: Cyanosis in the Newborn
briefs.sub: lung, heart or airway before a lesion · work of breathing, oxygen response, two limbs · normal exam: the trigger decidesIs he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?
blocks: lung, heart or airway before a lesion · work of breathing, oxygen response, two limbs · normal exam: the trigger decidesIs he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?

A cyanotic newborn who is working to breathe (grunting, flaring, retractions) and pinks up on oxygen has lung disease; comfortable tachypnea with no rise on 100% oxygen is a fixed right-to-left shunt. A preductal saturation above postductal means right-to-left flow across the ductus: persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), or coarctation, which can give lower-extremity cyanosis from birth. With a normal examination, the trigger decides: worse with feeding, better with crying is bilateral choanal atresia; worse with crying is a tetralogy of Fallot (tet) spell.

Central cyanosis shows in the lips and mucous membranes. Blue hands and feet with pink mucous membranes is acrocyanosis, common in the first hours of life and normal. Other causes of tachypneaPersistent pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, transient tachypnea, respiratory distress syndrome, heart anomalies and pneumothorax.

Act now Finding Action No rise on 100% oxygen with weak pulses or falling blood pressure Start prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) and obtain echocardiography; instability raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion. No rise on 100% oxygen Start PGE1 when cyanosis is severe or a ductal-dependent lesion such as transposition is likely; obtain echocardiography. Preductal saturation above postductal with distress after meconium Treat PPHN: oxygen, ventilation as needed and inhaled nitric oxide; echocardiography confirms. Cyanosis with every feed that clears with crying Place an oral airway and feed by orogastric tube while the nasal passages are checked.

Sorting by physiology Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Respiratory distress syndrome Minutes to hours after a preterm birth: grunting, retractions, oxygen-responsive; ground-glass with air bronchograms. Start CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure); surfactant if it fails. Transient tachypnea of the newborn Soon after a term cesarean: mild distress; perihilar streaking, fluid often in the fissures; usually clears in 2 to 3 days. Give oxygen and supportive care. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Term, after meconium or perinatal stress: preductal above postductal, poor response to oxygen, a film often clear; maternal selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) use. Obtain echocardiography; give inhaled nitric oxide. Transposition of the great arteries Within hours of birth: comfortable tachypnea, no murmur, single loud S2; no rise on oxygen. Start PGE1 to keep the ductus open; echocardiography confirms. Coarctation of the aorta Often from birth, with shock as the ductus closes by day 10: postductal below preductal, weak femoral pulses. Start PGE1; obtain echocardiography. Group B streptococcal pneumonia or sepsis After preterm prelabor rupture of membranes, even with intrapartum penicillin; looks like respiratory distress syndrome. Obtain cultures and start antibiotics while awaiting them.

Normal examination: sorting by trigger Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Bilateral choanal atresia From birth: blue at rest or with feeding, pink with crying. Pass a catheter through each naris; CT confirms. Tetralogy of Fallot Cyanosis worse with crying and agitation, plus a harsh murmur. Place in knee-chest position and give oxygen; obtain echocardiography. Transposition of the great arteries Constant cyanosis, unchanged by feeding or crying or oxygen. Start PGE1 to keep the ductus open; echocardiography confirms. Esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula Coughing, choking and cyanosis with feeds. Pass an orogastric tube and obtain a radiograph. Laryngomalacia Inspiratory stridor worse supine and with exertion; cyanosis uncommon. Evaluate it as noisy breathing; it does not explain cyanosis at rest. Methemoglobinemia Cyanosis unchanged by crying or oxygen; chocolate-colored blood, normal arterial oxygen pressure (PaO2); benzocaine or nitrites in well water. Check a methemoglobin level; treat with methylene blue. Neonatal sepsis Temperature instability, lethargy, poor feeding. Obtain cultures and start antibiotics. Intraventricular hemorrhage Preterm; lethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures. Obtain a head ultrasound.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Central cyanosis → Pulse oximetry, right hand and a foot Preductal above postductal Right-to-left flow across the ductus: PPHN, or coarctation (lower-extremity cyanosis) Hand and foot equal No ductal shunt → Trial of 100% oxygen Saturation rises substantially Lung disease Saturation barely rises Fixed right-to-left shunt, such as transposition Targeted tests TestResultMeans Distress with an oxygen response → Chest radiograph Ground-glass, air bronchograms, low volumes Respiratory distress syndrome in a preterm Perihilar streaking, fluid in the fissures Transient tachypnea of the newborn Clear or dark lung fields PPHN or cyanotic heart disease Worse with feeding, better with crying → Catheter through each naris Blocked Bilateral choanal atresia Coughing and choking with feeds → Orogastric tube and radiograph Stops short Esophageal atresia Unchanged by crying or oxygen, normal PaO2 → Methemoglobin level Elevated Methemoglobinemia: methylene blue Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Hypoxemia that oxygen does not correct → Echocardiography Structural lesion or high pulmonary pressures Names the lesion or confirms PPHN; PGE1 for a ductal-dependent lesion Posterior nasal obstruction → CT or nasal endoscopy Posterior nasal obstruction Choanal atresia; check for the other features of CHARGE syndrome CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia of the choanae, retarded growth, genital and ear anomalies). SkipAny test for acrocyanosis with pink mucous membranes; and echocardiography, a methemoglobin level, cultures or head ultrasound for cyanosis only with feeds before the nose is checked.

Pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours or later: positive with any reading under 90%, or, on repeat checks 1 hour apart, both hand and foot under 95% or a hand-foot gap over 3%. A positive screen calls for a full evaluation for congenital heart disease and for other causes of hypoxemia.

Approach to neonatal cyanosis Cyanosis at birth Distal extremities and lips, normal saturation Mucosal or diffuse, low saturation Peripheral cyanosis Central cyanosis Give supplemental oxygen saturation unchanged saturation rises Anatomic right-to-left shunt: the blood never reaches the lung Ventilation-perfusion mismatch: lung disease, or failed transition Start prostaglandin E1 if a ductal lesion is likely; echocardiography confirms. Respiratory support and treat the lung disease; consider pulmonary hypertension Reassurance Instability raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion; it also licenses the drug before the picture. Oxygen improves a mismatch because normally aerated lung is still available; it cannot improve a fixed shunt. Redrawn rather than reproduced. Prostaglandin E1 starts when cyanosis is severe or a ductal-dependent lesion such as transposition is likely; echocardiography then names the lesion.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Grunting, flaring, retractions Lung disease; cyanotic heart disease gives comfortable tachypnea Obtain a chest radiograph. Saturation 65% rising to 92% on oxygen Recruitable alveoli; this excludes transposition Treat the lung disease. Right hand and foot both 65% No ductal gradient: against PPHN and coarctation Obtain a chest radiograph. Thirty minutes old Too early for a ductal-dependent lesion: ductal closure typically begins within 10 to 15 hours Repeat pulse oximetry at 24 hours or later. One dose of antenatal glucocorticoids Lowers the risk of respiratory distress syndrome; never excludes it Keep respiratory distress syndrome on the list.

Pause point Cyanotic newborn who is grunting and retracting Offered: prostaglandin E1 Saturation rises on oxygen → Lung disease, not a ductal-dependent lesion: obtain a chest radiograph and treat the lung disease Cyanotic newborn with comfortable tachypnea Offered: exogenous surfactant No rise on 100% oxygen → A fixed right-to-left shunt; echocardiography confirms

Treatment by cause Cause Action Respiratory distress syndrome CPAP; intubation and surfactant for severe or failing cases. Ductal-dependent heart lesion PGE1 infusion to hold the ductus open. Persistent pulmonary hypertension Oxygen and inhaled nitric oxide. Bilateral choanal atresia Oral airway with orogastric feeding; definitive surgical repair. Methemoglobinemia Methylene blue.

Diagnosis1 of 18 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms · Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newbornPPHN gives a preductal-postductal gap and responds poorly to oxygen. · Respiratory distress syndromeGrunting and retractions in a 32-week infant who rises to 92% on oxygen, with ground-glass and air bronchograms, is respiratory distress syndrome. · D-Transposition of the great arteriesTransposition gives comfortable tachypnea and no rise on oxygen. 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms Respiratory distress syndromeSurfactant deficiency

Next step2 of 18 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously · Observe on room airRoom air leaves the hypoxemia and collapsing alveoli untreated. · Start CPAPA spontaneously breathing preterm with respiratory distress syndrome starts on CPAP. · Intubate and give surfactant immediatelyIntubation and surfactant are kept for severe disease or CPAP failure. 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously Start CPAPSurfactant and intubation are reserved for severe disease

Next step3 of 18 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours · Start inhaled nitric oxideInhaled nitric oxide treats pulmonary hypertension, not surfactant deficiency. · Increase CPAP pressure and continueMore pressure delays the specific treatment once CPAP has failed. · Intubate and give exogenous surfactantA rising oxygen need with worsening retractions on CPAP is failure: intubate and give surfactant. 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours Intubate and give exogenous surfactantCPAP has failed

Next step4 of 18 Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen · Obtain echocardiographyEchocardiography confirms the anatomic shunt that comfortable tachypnea with no rise on oxygen points to. · Arterial blood gas on room airA blood gas confirms the hypoxemia, not its cause. · Chest radiographA chest radiograph may suggest the lesion but cannot confirm the anatomy. Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen Obtain echocardiographyan anatomic right-to-left shunt; PGE1 keeps the ductus open while echocardiography confirms the lesion

Next step5 of 18 Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity · Inhaled nitric oxideA preductal-postductal gap with a clear film after meconium is PPHN: inhaled nitric oxide. · Prostaglandin E1 infusionPGE1 treats a ductal-dependent heart lesion, not high pulmonary resistance. · Exogenous surfactantSurfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome, which shows ground-glass lungs. Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity Inhaled nitric oxidePersistent pulmonary hypertension

Mechanism6 of 18 Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts · To lower airway resistance during inspirationLowering airway resistance is what nasal flaring does. · To recruit accessory muscles and raise tidal volumeAccessory muscles show as retractions; grunting is expiratory. · To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli openGrunting is expiration against a partly closed glottis, holding pressure that keeps alveoli open. Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli openFlaring lowers airway resistance

Diagnosis7 of 18 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures · Tetralogy of FallotTetralogy worsens with crying and has a harsh murmur. · Bilateral choanal atresiaBlue at the breast and pink with crying, with a normal heart and lungs, is bilateral choanal atresia. · Transposition of the great arteriesTransposition is constant cyanosis, unchanged by feeding or crying. 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures Bilateral choanal atresiaObligate nasal breathing

Workup8 of 18 Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying · EchocardiographyEchocardiography is for cyanosis that oxygen does not correct, not this pattern. · Arterial blood gas on 100 percent oxygenA blood gas on oxygen sorts lung from heart; the nose is the suspect here. · Pass a catheter through each narisCyanosis worse with feeding and better with crying points to the nose: pass a catheter first. Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying Pass a catheter through each narisCT or nasal endoscopy confirms it

Next step9 of 18 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying · Place an oral airwayAn oral airway treats choanal atresia, which crying relieves. · Withhold oxygen and observeOxygen is part of first-line spell care; withholding it is wrong. · Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygenA tet spell is treated with knee-chest positioning and oxygen. 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygenA tet spell, triggered by crying

Mechanism10 of 18 Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia · Crying bypasses the obstructed noseNewborns breathe through the nose; crying opens the mouth and bypasses the blocked choanae. · Crying raises pulmonary blood flow across the ductusThe ductus is not involved; the obstruction is in the nose. · Crying recruits collapsed alveoliThe lungs are normal; nothing needs recruiting. Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia Crying bypasses the obstructed noseby opening the oral airway; Neonates are obligate nasal breathers

Next step11 of 18 Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure · Obtain echocardiography aloneEchocardiography alone delays the drug while the ductus closes. · Initiate continuous positive airway pressureCPAP treats lung disease, not a ductal-dependent lesion. · Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiographyNo rise on oxygen with weak pulses and falling pressure suggests a closing ductus: start PGE1 and obtain echocardiography. Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiographyinstability licenses the drug before the picture

Mechanism12 of 18 Why supplemental oxygen fails to raise the saturation in transposition of the great arteries · Alveolar collapse prevents oxygen reaching the capillaryAlveolar collapse is respiratory distress syndrome, which oxygen improves. · Pulmonary vasoconstriction reduces pulmonary blood flowPulmonary vasoconstriction is PPHN, with a preductal-postductal gap. · Parallel circulations bypass the lungsIn transposition, systemic venous blood returns to the aorta without passing the lungs, so added oxygen cannot reach it. Antenatal glucocorticoids are genuinely protective, but they only lower the risk of RDS (respiratory distress syndrome); they do not treat it away. A grade 1/6 murmur is soft and non-specific. In a 30-minute-old it is almost certainly a physiologically open duct rather than a lesion. PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) raises concern for group B streptococcal pneumonia even after intrapartum penicillin; that pneumonia is clinically very hard to tell from RDS, so antibiotics are started empirically pending cultures. In the normal-examination case, six normal findings each exclude one diagnosis, and the only positive finding is the timing. A primigravida with an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and an infant who voided and passed meconium, are inert findings. They only establish that the baby is well, which is the precondition for the sort.

Grunting with retractions that improves on oxygen is lung disease; in a preterm infant with ground-glass and air bronchograms that is surfactant deficiency. Work of breathing is the first sort: grunting, flaring and retractions mean lung; comfortable tachypnea with cyanosis means heart. Oxygen is diagnostic and therapeutic: it separates alveolar disease from a fixed shunt and treats RDS (respiratory distress syndrome). It is occasionally harmful: in hypoplastic left heart syndrome it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and shifts right ventricular output to the lungs. A lesion that depends on the duct presents as the duct closes, which typically begins within 10 to 15 hours. Cyanosis in the delivery room is lung disease, failed transition or transposition. Antenatal glucocorticoids stimulate fetal surfactant synthesis and lower the risk of RDS; a dosed 32-week infant can still have it. Hypoxia in RDS is self-amplifying. Collapse causes hypoxia, hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vasculature, and the resulting right-to-left shunt deepens the cyanosis. Shunt physiology can therefore be present without a shunt lesion. Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. Nasal obstruction therefore gives cyanosis that worsens when the mouth is occluded by feeding and improves when it opens with crying. The inverse pattern is the tet spell: cyanosis worsens with crying and agitation and is relieved by knee-to-chest positioning. Pass a catheter through each naris first. It is a free bedside test, and imaging only confirms what the catheter suggested. Choanal atresia may be part of CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth, genital and ear abnormalities). Unilateral disease often goes unrecognized until childhood, when it presents as chronic unilateral nasal discharge. Tachypnea without distress points to the heart: fast breathing with no flaring, grunting or retractions, and clear lungs. Work of breathing points to the lung. A loud single S2 with no murmur is characteristic of transposition. The absent murmur is a positive finding rather than a missing one, because flow through the mixing shunts is too low-velocity to generate sound.

Ask: is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, do the limbs differ, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing? When a finding has both a lung and a heart cause, sort by physiology before naming a disease. The bedside triad of work of breathing, oxygen response and a pre-to-postductal difference decides which group of diagnoses to consider. When the sort finds nothing abnormal, the pattern in time is the key finding. A trigger that runs the opposite way excludes the lesion it resembles.

briefs.title: Heart Failure in a Child
briefs.sub: the viral prodrome that is not bronchiolitis · gallop, apical murmur and weak pulses · cardiogenic shock: cautious fluidIs there a gallop or a new murmur, and are the pulses weak with a low pressure?
blocks: the viral prodrome that is not bronchiolitis · gallop, apical murmur and weak pulses · cardiogenic shock: cautious fluidIs there a gallop or a new murmur, and are the pulses weak with a low pressure?

A gallop, a new apical holosystolic murmur and weak pulses with low blood pressure days after a viral illness point to heart failure from viral myocarditis, whatever the lungs sound like. Order an electrocardiogram (ECG), troponin, chest radiograph and echocardiography; diffuse hypokinesis with a reduced ejection fraction confirms the failing ventricle. The shock is cardiogenic: no rapid fluid bolus; diurese, reduce afterload and give inotropes.

The respiratory findings come from the heart: basal rales are pulmonary edema, and the apical murmur is mitral regurgitation from a dilated ventricle. Coxsackievirus B and adenovirus are the viruses most often linked to viral myocarditis. Other virusesParvovirus B19, human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and COVID-19 can also cause myocarditis.

Act now Finding Action Hypotension with weak pulses and low urine output Cardiogenic shock: inotropes such as dobutamine; fluid only in small, cautious aliquots; no beta-blocker. Palpitations, syncope or an irregular pulse Continuous cardiac monitoring; arrhythmia is how myocarditis causes sudden death.

Respiratory distress after a viral illness Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Viral myocarditis Days after a viral illness: gallop, new apical holosystolic murmur, poor perfusion; tachycardia out of proportion to fever. Echocardiography with troponin and ECG. Bronchiolitis Under 2 years, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), coryza then wheeze or crackles; heart sounds normal. Give supportive care. Acute rheumatic fever About 2 to 3 weeks after strep pharyngitis; migratory arthritis or chorea. Send strep titers and count the Jones criteria. Kawasaki disease Fever 5 days or more plus 4 criteria; a node at least 1.5 cm. Count the criteria against the days of fever. Glomerulonephritis Hematuria, hypertension and edema after an infection. Order a urinalysis. Large ventricular septal defect Infant of 4 to 6 weeks: failure as pulmonary resistance falls, holosystolic murmur, poor feeding. Obtain echocardiography.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Heart failure signs after a viral prodrome → ECG Sinus tachycardia, nonspecific ST changes Supports myocarditis; watch for arrhythmia → Troponin Elevated Myocyte injury Targeted tests TestResultMeans Rales or hypoxemia → Chest radiograph Cardiomegaly with pulmonary edema The rales are edema, not bronchiolitis or pneumonia Diagnosis still uncertain → Cardiac MRI or endomyocardial biopsy Myocardial inflammation; lymphocytic infiltrate with necrosis Tissue-level confirmation Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Suspected myocarditis → Echocardiography Diffuse hypokinesis, reduced ejection fraction Myocarditis with heart failure; no structural lesion SkipAn antistreptolysin O titer with no pharyngitis weeks earlier and no Jones criteria: a concurrent cold is the wrong illness at the wrong time.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Gallop rhythm An S3 from a failing, overloaded ventricle Obtain echocardiography. Basal rales with hypoxemia, no wheeze Pulmonary edema with the cardiac findings; no wheeze argues against bronchiolitis Give a diuretic, cautiously. Fever 4 days, no rash or conjunctivitis, subcentimeter nodes The Kawasaki criteria are not met Order echocardiography for myocarditis. No pulsus paradoxus Typical of myocarditis; tamponade would show it Obtain echocardiography, which also excludes an effusion.
Pause point Low pressure in cardiogenic shock Offered: a rapid large bolus It worsens pulmonary edema → Inotropes such as dobutamine; fluid only in small, cautious aliquots, or not at all

Treatment by cause Cause Action Viral myocarditis Support the heart with diuretics, afterload reduction and inotropes; intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is often given, but its benefit in children is not established. Giant cell or other immune myocarditis Immunosuppression, starting with glucocorticoids. Arrhythmia Continuous monitoring and arrhythmia treatment.

Next step8 of 8 5 yo recovering from biopsy-proven myocarditis who has a syncopal episode and an irregular pulse · Discharge with outpatient Holter in 2 weeksDischarge with an outpatient monitor leaves a dangerous arrhythmia unwatched. · Continuous cardiac monitoringSyncope with an irregular pulse after myocarditis signals arrhythmia, the cause of sudden death: monitor continuously. · Begin high-dose corticosteroidsSteroids treat specific immune forms such as giant cell myocarditis, not this arrhythmia. 5 yo recovering from biopsy-proven myocarditis who has a syncopal episode and an irregular pulse Continuous cardiac monitoringarrhythmia is the mechanism of sudden death

S3 or new murmur in any child in respiratory distress: heart failure until an echocardiogram says otherwise, however viral the story sounds A new holosystolic murmur at the apex in a failing ventricle is functional mitral regurgitation: a consequence, not a second disease Hypotension in myocarditis is cardiogenic: fluid loading fills the lungs and is the commonest management error Rheumatic fever is defined by its interval, about 2 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis; a murmur appearing during a viral illness is myocarditis Kawasaki's fever requirement is five days, and it is mandatory

Shock in Childrencovers the perfusion categories and the cardiogenic-versus-distributive fork Acute Rheumatic Fevercovers Jones and the post-streptococcal interval Kawasaki Diseasecovers the five-day fever requirement. Ask: is there a gallop or a new murmur, and how long has the fever run? Shock in Children covers the perfusion categories and the cardiogenic-versus-distributive fork. Acute Rheumatic Fever covers Jones and the post-streptococcal interval. Kawasaki Disease covers the five-day fever requirement. Ask: is there a gallop or a new murmur, and how long has the fever run?

When respiratory findings are prominent and cardiac findings are subtle, read the cardiac findings first. A gallop, a new murmur or weak pulses point to the heart as the failing organ. The lung signs are then a consequence rather than a cause.

Unchecked attributeAcute rheumatic fever: fever with a new murmur after an infection is its exact shape, but the antecedent is coryza not pharyngitis, the illness is concurrent, not about 2 to 3 weeks earlier, and no Jones criteria are met. Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: genuinely causes myocarditis, but fever is 4 days and no criteria are met; the nodes are subcentimeter, below the 1.5 cm node criterion. True-fact-wrong-slotGlomerulonephritis: oliguria after a URI (upper respiratory infection) fits, but it presents with hematuria and hypertension, and this child is hypotensive with unexplained cardiac findings. Salient decoyBronchiolitis: the whole respiratory picture and the age fit, but it explains nothing cardiac and the classic wheeze is absent and the rales come with cardiac findings.

briefs.sub: five mechanisms · A-a gradient · response to oxygen · shunt vs ventilation-perfusion mismatch · saturation gapIs the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia correct when inspired oxygen rises?
blocks: five mechanisms · A-a gradient · response to oxygen · shunt vs ventilation-perfusion mismatch · saturation gapIs the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia correct when inspired oxygen rises?

Low saturation an arterial blood gas first: a normal PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) means the hemoglobin is the problem (methemoglobin, carbon monoxide) Low PaO2 the A-a (alveolar-arterial) gradient: normal means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; widened means V/Q (ventilation-perfusion) mismatch, shunt or a diffusion defect Widened and corrects on oxygen V/Q mismatch; stays low shunt: recruit the alveoli (CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure; PEEP; surfactant) rather than turning the oxygen up

What it is Low arterial oxygen; the mechanism is named before the disease Sort by PaO2 low or only the reading the A-a gradientNormal valueAlveolar minus arterial oxygen pressure; normal is approximately (age/4) + 4 the response to oxygen Hands off Surfactant deficiency: Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant; cyanosis at rest in a newborn: Cyanosis in the Newborn; oxygen in carbon dioxide retainers: COPD; embolism: Venous Thromboembolism

ShuntSaturation stays below 90% on supplemental oxygen More oxygen will not fix it If alveoli are collapsed or flooded, choose recruit them: CPAP or PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), surfactant in the preterm newborn. Carbon monoxideHeadache and nausea in people sharing a heated home (furnace, gas heater); a normal pulse oximeter reading If exposure is possible, choose co-oximetry, and 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask without waiting. HypoventilationSlow breathing, pinpoint pupils, PaCO2 ↑ If opioid overdose is suspected, choose naloxone, a diagnostic and therapeutic step. Carbon dioxide retentionCOPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) on supplemental oxygen Oxygen can raise dead space and the PaCO2 COPD If a carbon dioxide retainer needs oxygen, choose titrate to a saturation of 88 to 92%, not higher.

Normal A-a means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; widened and oxygen-responsive means V/Q mismatch; widened and oxygen-refractory means shunt. Shunt is the hypoxemia that oxygen will not fix. When the FiO2 goes up and the saturation does not follow, stop titrating and start recruiting. Recruit with PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), surfactant, drainage, or a diuretic for the edema behind it. Hypoventilation is the one hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient and a high PaCO2; low inspired PO2 is the one with a normal gradient and a low PaCO2 from the compensatory hyperventilation. A normal PaO2 in a cyanotic patient means the hemoglobin cannot carry oxygen: think of methemoglobin. Boundary: refractory hypoxemia with clear lungs and no cardiac history can still be an embolus. If it raises right-sided pressures enough to open a PFO (patent foramen ovale), a dead-space disease presents as a right-to-left shunt. Look for the cause of the raised pressure, not just the shunt.

Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infantcovers the parenchymal differential by chest film (ground glass and air bronchograms versus retained fluid, meconium, or air leak) Congenital Heart Diseasecovers the lesions themselves Cyanosis in the Newborncovers sorting at-rest physiology in the delivery room. This brief covers the mechanism categories above all three. Ask: is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia respond to oxygen? Treat hypoxemia as a physiology question. Compute the A-a gradient, then check what happens on supplemental oxygen. Those two answers name the mechanism before the illness is named.

blocks: stridor vs wheeze · toxic vs well · the phase of the noise localizes · airway before imagingWhich phase is the noise in, and is the child toxic or well?

Stridor is the upper airway, wheeze the lower; the phase localizes: inspiratory above the chest, expiratory intrathoracic trachea, biphasic fixed, usually subglottic Toxic, drooling, tripoding, unvaccinated epiglottitis: secure the airway in the operating room before any throat exam or x-ray Sudden choking, afebrile foreign body, rigid bronchoscopy; barky and nontoxic croup, dexamethasone, with racemic epinephrine for stridor at rest

What it is Stridor or wheeze in a child Sort by the phase of the noise Why the phaseMechanismInspiration lowers the pressure inside the airway and pulls collapsible tissue above the chest inward; expiration raises the pressure in the chest and compresses a soft trachea; a fixed ring cannot change caliber, so it sounds in both phases, and a tight vascular ring is often biphasic too. toxic or well sudden or gradual, febrile or not vaccination status Hands off Retropharyngeal and peritonsillar abscess and Ludwig angina: Deep Neck Infections; paradoxical vocal fold motion: Asthma

EpiglottitisToxic, drooling without a barking cough, tripoding, muffled voice No tongue depressor and no lateral neck film first: agitation can complete the obstruction 4 Ds EpiglottitisDrooling, dysphagia, dysphonia (muffled voice), distress (tripod position) If epiglottitis is suspected, choose intubation in the operating room, then ceftriaxone with or without vancomycin. CroupStridor at rest or respiratory distress If stridor is present at rest, choose racemic epinephrine with dexamethasone; no response points to bacterial tracheitis. Foreign bodySudden choking or stridor in a well, afebrile child If aspiration is suspected, choose rigid bronchoscopy, which diagnoses and removes it.

Causes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) Barky cough, hoarse, inspiratory stridor, worse at night, nontoxic; parainfluenza 6 months to 3 years; steeple sign; improves with racemic epinephrine Epiglottitis Abrupt high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod, muffled voice; unvaccinated Abrupt onset; thumbprint sign, but the airway comes first Bacterial tracheitis Worsening "croup": abrupt toxicity and pus in the trachea after a viral illness No response to racemic epinephrine; S. aureus Foreign body aspiration Sudden choking in a well, afebrile toddler; unilateral wheeze Unilateral hyperinflation on the expiratory film; usually the right mainstem Bronchiolitis Under 2 years, winter, after a cold; wheeze and crackles, retractions Clinical; respiratory syncytial virus; supportive care Pertussis (whooping cough) Paroxysms ending in a whoop, vomiting after coughing; apnea in infants Marked lymphocytosis Laryngomalacia Inspiratory stridor since early infancy; louder supine, with crying or feeds Better prone; supraglottic collapse on inspiration Tracheomalacia Expiratory noise with a brassy cough; after tracheoesophageal fistula repair No change with position or albuterol Vascular ring Biphasic stridor with dysphagia Better with neck extension, not prone; posterior esophageal indentation Subglottic stenosis Constant biphasic stridor after weeks of intubation; worse with colds Fixed narrowing: no change with position Paradoxical vocal fold motion (vocal cord dysfunction) Episodic stridor taken for wheeze; normal between episodes No response to asthma therapy; cords close on inspiration Retropharyngeal abscess Fever, drooling, neck pain, refuses to extend the neck Widened prevertebral space; CT Peritonsillar abscess Adolescent; trismus, hot-potato voice Uvula deviated away

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Croup that worsens: abrupt toxicity, pus in the trachea, no response to racemic epinephrine Bacterial tracheitis Secure the airway; IV antibiotics covering S. aureus and streptococci Unimmunized child Epiglottitis: absent Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) immunization is the strongest risk factor Airway first Paroxysms with a whoop, vomiting, lymphocytosis Pertussis Azithromycin; household contacts within 21 days of the cough Former preterm intubated for weeks; constant biphasic stridor Subglottic stenosis Fixed narrowing after prolonged intubation Laryngomalacia with failure to thrive, cyanosis or distress Severe laryngomalacia Refer for airway surgery; otherwise reassure, it resolves by 18 months Bad teeth, soft submandibular space Not Ludwig angina That needs firm bilateral submandibular swelling Deep Neck Infections

1. Stridor (upper) or wheeze (lower)? Then which phase: inspiratory is extrathoracic, expiratory is the intrathoracic trachea, biphasic is fixed and usually subglottic. 2. Sudden + afebrile → foreign body; the absence of fever is a key clue. 3. Toxic + drooling + tripod → epiglottitis, airway first in the OR (operating room). Getting a throat exam or X-ray first is an error. 4. Barky + nontoxic → croup. 5. Croup that is not behaving like croup → bacterial tracheitis. 6. Vaccination status always matters.
Risk factors, and the ones th…

Absent Hib immunization is the strongest risk factor for epiglottitis in a child Diabetes mellitus ⚠︎ is linked to epiglottitis in adults, not in children Secondhand smoke raises the risk of otitis media, asthma and respiratory infections in children, not the answer for epiglottitis Poor dental hygiene points instead at Ludwig angina, which needs tender bilateral submandibular induration and an elevated floor of mouth; a soft submandibular space excludes it

Croup improves with racemic epi, tracheitis doesn't laryngomalacia better prone, croup worse at night bronchiolitis gets nothing expiratory film for foreign body because the trapped lung stays inflated.
Part II Deep Neck Infections covers Ludwig angina and the retropharyngeal space. These are the two deep-neck mimics of a toxic child with a sore throat. Ask: is the submandibular space soft?

Sequencing trapThroat exam or lateral neck film in a toxic, drooling child: the airway is secured in the operating room first Unchecked attributeExpiratory stridor: the sound of the floppy intrathoracic trachea (tracheomalacia); laryngomalacia is above the thoracic inlet, so it collapses on inspiration Unchecked attributeBiphasic stridor: needs a fixed lesion such as subglottic stenosis; the arytenoid tissue in laryngomalacia is mobile and position-dependent

briefs.title: Respiratory Infection in a Child
briefs.sub: green mucus is not a bacterial sign · one side is a foreign body · typical vs atypical pneumoniaWhich side, how long and how sick, and does the illness span the upper and lower airway?
blocks: green mucus is not a bacterial sign · one side is a foreign body · typical vs atypical pneumoniaWhich side, how long and how sick, and does the illness span the upper and lower airway?

Read the side and the days before the color: pus alone is not bacterial; one foul side in a well toddler nasal foreign body; bilateral sinusitis must pass one of the three doorsBacterial sinusitisSymptoms for 10 days or more without improvement; fever of 39 °C or more with severe symptoms for 3 to 4 days; or worsening after a cold had begun to improve ("double sickening") Sore throat in a child: test before treating; penicillin prevents rheumatic fever, not poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis Pneumonia: abrupt, febrile, productive and lobar pneumococcus, amoxicillin; gradual dry cough at school age with a film worse than the child Mycoplasma, a macrolide

What it is Nasal discharge, sore throat, ear pain or cough with fever in a child Sort by one side or both how many days how sick upper airway or chest Hands off Allergic rhinitis: Rhinitis; orbital and other complications: Sinusitis and Its Complications; rheumatic fever: Acute Rheumatic Fever; cold agglutinin hemolysis: Hemolytic Anemia; subacute cough with a known contact: Tuberculosis

MucormycosisBlack or white turbinates or palate in ketoacidosis, neutropenia or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection with a CD4 (helper T-cell) count under 50 If the nasal tissue is necrotic, choose surgical debridement with amphotericin B. Button batteryA button battery or paired magnets in the nose If one is seen, choose emergency removal before the septum perforates.

Causes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Acute bacterial sinusitis Bilateral pus, often with fever and cough, after a cold Passes a door; amoxicillin-clavulanate, no imaging Nasal foreign body One side, foul, purulent, at times bloody; well, afebrile, 1 to 6 years; the insertion usually unseen Other side normal; remove it: blow with the other side shut, then instruments Parent's kissNasal foreign bodyWith the open nostril held closed, a parent covers the child’s mouth with theirs and blows once; left in place, it brings sinusitis, periorbital cellulitis or aspiration. Viral upper respiratory infection (URI) Afebrile, well, a few days of runny nose and cough Clear eardrums, no exudate, clear lungs; supportive care Adenoid hypertrophy Mouth breathing, snoring, nasal voice Chronic bilateral obstruction Strep pharyngitis Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough Positive rapid test or culture; penicillin or amoxicillin Acute otitis media Bulging, red eardrum Reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; high-dose amoxicillin Typical pneumonia (S. pneumoniae) Abrupt high fever, productive cough, chest pain; looks ill One lobe consolidated; amoxicillin Organism by agePneumonia1 to 3 months: Chlamydia trachomatis, afebrile, with a staccato cough and eosinophilia. Under 5: mostly viruses, led by respiratory syncytial virus, then adenovirus, parainfluenza and human metapneumovirus. From 5: S. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila. Atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma pneumoniae) Gradual over 1 to 2 weeks, dry cough, low fever, still active; school age Bilateral diffuse film, worse than the child; macrolide In practiceAtypical pneumoniaDoxycycline is an alternative; short courses are now accepted under 8 years. Mycoplasma extrasComplicationsNo cell wall, so Gram stain misses it and penicillin does not work. Cold agglutinin (IgM) hemolysis; erythema multiforme, its second infectious cause after herpes simplex virus; Guillain-Barré syndrome. Adult atypicalsOlder patientsWater systems, hotels or cruise ships, diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia: Legionella, urine antigen. Birds: Chlamydophila psittaci. Farm animals: Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), later hepatitis or culture-negative endocarditis. Hoarseness in a young adult: Chlamydophila pneumoniae. Viral pneumonia Under 5; bilateral crackles, with or without wheeze Most often a virus at this age: RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) and others Allergic rhinitis Sneezing and itch; clear discharge on both sides; smoke and pets raise the risk Pale, boggy turbinates; intranasal corticosteroid

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Nasal discharge → Name the side; count the days One side, foul, well toddler Nasal foreign body Both sides, through a door Bacterial sinusitis Both sides, a few days, well Viral URI Targeted tests TestResultMeans Sore throat, exudate, no cough → Rapid antigen test, culture if negative Positive Strep pharyngitis: treat Ear pain, fever → Pneumatic otoscopy Bulging, immobile drum Acute otitis media Next step TestResultMeans Cough, fever, crackles → Chest X-ray One lobe consolidated Typical pneumonia Bilateral diffuse interstitial Atypical pneumonia; under 5, often viral Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Atypical picture, if a test is needed → Mycoplasma polymerase chain reaction (PCR), throat or nasopharyngeal swab Positive Mycoplasma; often treated empirically, as the diagnosis is usually clinical SkipSinus imaging without signs of a complication, and a film for a nasal foreign body: most objects do not show.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Anemia or dark urine during a Mycoplasma pneumonia Cold agglutinin (IgM) hemolysis Supports Mycoplasma Otitis no better after 2 to 3 days of amoxicillin, or back within 30 days Resistant otitis Amoxicillin-clavulanate Febrile child with no heart disease and a perihilar infiltrate Pneumonia, not heart failure Heart failure in children follows congenital heart disease or malnutrition Smoking parent, pet dog Allergic rhinitis risk Allergy is bilateral and clear, never one foul side HIV infection with a CD4 count well over 50, red swollen turbinates Not mucormycosis That needs white or black tissue

Pause point Green discharge or a single high fever Read as bacterial sinusitis Count the days and check the side → The days and the side decide Child who looks better than the film Offered as pneumococcus Looks better than the film → Mycoplasma

Diagnosis1 of 22 3-year-old boy has had 2 days of green nasal discharge playful and eating well tympanic membranes clear and mobile on pneumatic otoscopy no pharyngeal exudate; lungs clear Discharge from both nostrils Afebrile · HR 110/min · oxygen saturation 99% · Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis · Viral upper respiratory infection · Acute otitis media 3-year-old boy has had 2 days of green nasal discharge playful and eating well tympanic membranes clear and mobile on pneumatic otoscopy no pharyngeal exudate; lungs clear Discharge from both nostrils Afebrile · HR 110/min · oxygen saturation 99% Viral upper respiratory infectionthe green comes from neutrophil myeloperoxidase in any inflammation, so 2 days of colored discharge in a well, afebrile child is viral: supportive care. Sinusitis must pass a door (10 days, 3 to 4 consecutive days or more of high fever with purulence, or double worsening); otitis media needs a bulging, immobile membrane

Mechanism2 of 22 6-year-old boy has a sudden onset of high fever with shaking chills cough productive of rust-colored sputum chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation Ill appearing; right-sided chest pain T 39.8°C · HR 140/min · Mycoplasma pneumoniae · Streptococcus pneumoniae · Legionella pneumophila 6-year-old boy has a sudden onset of high fever with shaking chills cough productive of rust-colored sputum chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation Ill appearing; right-sided chest pain T 39.8°C · HR 140/min Streptococcus pneumoniaeabrupt onset, rigors, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation and an ill appearance separate pneumococcus from Mycoplasma, which is gradual and diffuse; Legionella brings diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia in an older smoker

Next step3 of 22 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of foul-smelling, purulent discharge from the left naris only white bead visible just inside the left naris right naris normal Active, eating well, calm and cooperative; no cough Afebrile · Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses · Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days · Positive-pressure expulsion 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of foul-smelling, purulent discharge from the left naris only white bead visible just inside the left naris right naris normal Active, eating well, calm and cooperative; no cough Afebrile Positive-pressure expulsiona visible bead in a calm child comes out first with positive pressure (the parent's kiss, or blowing with the other naris closed); instruments if it fails, ENT endoscopy if not visible. No imaging, since most objects are radiolucent, and antibiotics leave the object in place

Diagnosis4 of 22 9-year-old girl is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia now jaundiced and pale hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positive for C3 Fingers turn white in the cold T 37.9°C · HR 118/min · Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia · Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia · Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency 9-year-old girl is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia now jaundiced and pale hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positive for C3 Fingers turn white in the cold T 37.9°C · HR 118/min Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemiaMycoplasma triggers IgM against the I antigen: a Coombs-positive cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia, sometimes with Raynaud. Fingers that blanch in the cold and a C3-positive direct antiglobulin test pick the cold type over warm autoimmune hemolysis or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

Mechanism5 of 22 4-year-old girl has had 2 days of runny nose with green discharge her mother asks whether the green color means she needs an antibiotic Playful; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · lungs clear · No; neutrophils color it in any inflammation · Only if the color lasts beyond 3 days · Yes, green discharge means a bacterial infection 4-year-old girl has had 2 days of runny nose with green discharge her mother asks whether the green color means she needs an antibiotic Playful; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · lungs clear No; neutrophils color it in any inflammationthe green is myeloperoxidase in neutrophils recruited by any inflammation, viral included, so color never proves bacteria; duration, fever and double worsening decide

Mechanism6 of 22 35-year-old woman who breeds parrots at home has 1 week of dry cough and fever severe headache spleen tip palpable chest x-ray: patchy infiltrate, no hilar adenopathy No farm animal contact; no travel T 39.0°C · HR 96/min · Chlamydophila psittaci · Histoplasma capsulatum · Coxiella burnetii 35-year-old woman who breeds parrots at home has 1 week of dry cough and fever severe headache spleen tip palpable chest x-ray: patchy infiltrate, no hilar adenopathy No farm animal contact; no travel T 39.0°C · HR 96/min Chlamydophila psittacia pet parrot with severe headache and splenomegaly is psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci). Histoplasma comes from soil rich in bird or bat droppings and typically enlarges the hilar or mediastinal nodes, which this film lacks; Coxiella needs farm animals, sheep or parturient cats

Diagnosis7 of 22 3-year-old boy has had 12 days of nasal discharge without improvement thick purulent discharge from both nostrils daytime cough No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.1°C · HR 112/min · tympanic membranes mobile · Viral upper respiratory infection · Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis · Allergic rhinitis 3-year-old boy has had 12 days of nasal discharge without improvement thick purulent discharge from both nostrils daytime cough No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.1°C · HR 112/min · tympanic membranes mobile Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis10 days or more without improvement is the first door to acute bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate, with no imaging. The persistence, not the color, is what separates it from a viral cold; allergy gives clear discharge with sneezing and itch

Mechanism8 of 22 10-year-old boy has had 2 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough no improvement after 4 days of amoxicillin bilateral crackles; diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray Walking around and attending school T 37.9°C · white blood cell count 7,800/mm³ · Beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae · Penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae · Mycoplasma has no cell wall 10-year-old boy has had 2 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough no improvement after 4 days of amoxicillin bilateral crackles; diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray Walking around and attending school T 37.9°C · white blood cell count 7,800/mm³ Mycoplasma has no cell walla gradual, diffuse picture in a school-aged child is Mycoplasma, which has no cell wall, so beta-lactams cannot work: switch to a macrolide. Resistant H. influenzae or pneumococcus would still be a typical, focal pneumonia

Diagnosis9 of 22 3-year-old boy has clear rhinorrhea and frequent sneezing itchy, watery eyes seasonal recurrence each spring for 2 years pale, boggy nasal turbinates Father smokes; a cat at home Afebrile · HR 100/min · Vasomotor rhinitis · Allergic rhinitis · Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis 3-year-old boy has clear rhinorrhea and frequent sneezing itchy, watery eyes seasonal recurrence each spring for 2 years pale, boggy nasal turbinates Father smokes; a cat at home Afebrile · HR 100/min Allergic rhinitisbilateral clear discharge, itch and pale, boggy turbinates are allergic rhinitis, and smoke and pets raise its risk: an intranasal corticosteroid. Sinusitis is purulent and must pass a door; the itch and the seasonal pattern point to allergy over a vasomotor cause

Next step10 of 22 2-year-old girl pushed something from the television remote into her nose 2 hours ago her brother saw it now right-sided nosebleed and dark discharge smooth, gray, coin-shaped object deep in the right naris Afebrile · breathing comfortably · oxygen saturation 99% · Outpatient ENT referral for nasal endoscopy · Immediate removal in the emergency department · Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and recheck in 48 hours 2-year-old girl pushed something from the television remote into her nose 2 hours ago her brother saw it now right-sided nosebleed and dark discharge smooth, gray, coin-shaped object deep in the right naris Afebrile · breathing comfortably · oxygen saturation 99% Immediate removal in the emergency departmenta coin-shaped object from a remote is a button battery: pressure and current necrose the mucosa and can perforate the septum, and a nosebleed or dark discharge is the tell, so remove it now. An outpatient endoscopy or an antibiotic recheck lets the injury progress

Diagnosis11 of 22 2-year-old boy has 3 days of cough, runny nose and wheeze diffuse wheezes and crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial pattern, no consolidation Attends daycare T 38.3°C · respiratory rate 44/min · oxygen saturation 95% · Lobar bacterial pneumonia · Viral pneumonia · Mycoplasma pneumoniae 2-year-old boy has 3 days of cough, runny nose and wheeze diffuse wheezes and crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial pattern, no consolidation Attends daycare T 38.3°C · respiratory rate 44/min · oxygen saturation 95% Viral pneumoniaunder 5, viruses lead: RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus. Mycoplasma is typical at age 5 and older, and lobar bacterial pneumonia gives a focal consolidation

Next step12 of 22 5-year-old girl had an upper respiratory illness that improved over 5 days on day 8, new fever worsening purulent nasal discharge Tympanic membranes mobile; lungs clear; eating less T 39.5°C · HR 124/min · Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate · Supportive care alone · Computed tomography of the sinuses 5-year-old girl had an upper respiratory illness that improved over 5 days on day 8, new fever worsening purulent nasal discharge Tympanic membranes mobile; lungs clear; eating less T 39.5°C · HR 124/min Oral amoxicillin-clavulanatean illness that improves and then worsens with new fever is double worsening: acute bacterial sinusitis, treated with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Supportive care alone ignores a door already crossed; the diagnosis is clinical, so no sinus computed tomography (CT)

Mechanism13 of 22 28-year-old woman who works on a sheep farm has 10 days of fever and dry cough helped with lambing and a cat's delivery last month No rash, joint pain or bird contact T 39.2°C · alanine aminotransferase 140 U/L · Coxiella burnetii · Chlamydophila psittaci · Brucella melitensis 28-year-old woman who works on a sheep farm has 10 days of fever and dry cough helped with lambing and a cat's delivery last month No rash, joint pain or bird contact T 39.2°C · alanine aminotransferase 140 U/L Coxiella burnetiifarm animals, sheep and parturient cats with hepatitis and no rash are Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), which can cause culture-negative endocarditis later. Brucella also spreads to people in contact with livestock, but it brings cyclical fever with migratory arthralgia or sacroiliitis, often from unpasteurized dairy; psittacosis needs bird exposure, which she denies

Diagnosis14 of 22 3-year-old boy: 2 weeks of nasal discharge, first clear, now thick, foul right naris: pus, red swollen mucosa and turbinates; left normal Human immunodeficiency virus since birth, treated; CD4 520/mm³ Father smokes; pet dog Afebrile · playful · no cough · Nasal foreign body · Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis · Allergic rhinitis 3-year-old boy: 2 weeks of nasal discharge, first clear, now thick, foul right naris: pus, red swollen mucosa and turbinates; left normal Human immunodeficiency virus since birth, treated; CD4 520/mm³ Father smokes; pet dog Afebrile · playful · no cough Nasal foreign bodyone-sided foul pus in a well, afebrile toddler is a nasal foreign body: remove it with positive pressure or instruments. Sinusitis is bilateral and usually brings fever and cough; the smoking father and the pet dog raise allergy risk, but allergy is bilateral and clear; human immunodeficiency virus invites mucormycosis, but a CD4 count of 520 and red, not white or black, turbinates leave mucormycosis out. Afebrile, playful and without cough, he has no systemic signs

Diagnosis15 of 22 11-year-old girl had a dry cough and low-grade fever 3 weeks ago weakness rising from feet to thighs over 4 days absent ankle and knee reflexes sensation normal, no sensory level Pupils and bladder function normal HR 98/min · Transverse myelitis · Guillain-Barré syndrome · Botulism 11-year-old girl had a dry cough and low-grade fever 3 weeks ago weakness rising from feet to thighs over 4 days absent ankle and knee reflexes sensation normal, no sensory level Pupils and bladder function normal HR 98/min Guillain-Barré syndromeascending weakness weeks after a respiratory illness is a postinfectious complication: Guillain-Barré syndrome. Mycoplasma can also cause encephalitis and transverse myelitis, but normal sensation with no sensory level and normal bladder function argue against a cord lesion, and normal pupils argue against botulism

Next step16 of 22 7-year-old boy has had 3 days of runny nose and cough mild maxillary pain profuse yellow-green nasal discharge tender upper cheeks Well appearing; no fever for the past 48 hours T 37.2°C · HR 96/min · Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days · Saline irrigation and analgesics · Oral antihistamine 7-year-old boy has had 3 days of runny nose and cough mild maxillary pain profuse yellow-green nasal discharge tender upper cheeks Well appearing; no fever for the past 48 hours T 37.2°C · HR 96/min Saline irrigation and analgesics3 days of symptoms, afebrile for 48 hours, meets no door, so this is viral rhinosinusitis despite the colored discharge: supportive care with saline irrigation and analgesics. Amoxicillin-clavulanate waits for a door; an antihistamine treats allergy, which gives clear discharge with itch

Diagnosis17 of 22 8-year-old boy is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia target lesions on the hands and feet painful oral mucositis with crusted lips raised three-ring targets; no skin sloughing Cough improving over the past week T 38.2°C · HR 110/min · Kawasaki disease · Erythema multiforme / MIRM · Stevens-Johnson syndrome 8-year-old boy is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia target lesions on the hands and feet painful oral mucositis with crusted lips raised three-ring targets; no skin sloughing Cough improving over the past week T 38.2°C · HR 110/min Erythema multiforme / MIRMtarget lesions with mucositis during Mycoplasma infection are erythema multiforme or MIRM (Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis); Mycoplasma is the leading infectious cause of erythema multiforme after herpes simplex virus. Raised, typical targets with three rings and no epidermal detachment pick erythema multiforme over Stevens-Johnson syndrome, whose target-like lesions are atypical, with two zones. The Mycoplasma link to targets and mucositis is what this stem shows; nothing in it builds a Kawasaki picture

Avoid18 of 22 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of a viral upper respiratory illness green nasal discharge from both nostrils improving each day Eating and sleeping normally; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · HR 104/min · Prescribe intranasal saline · Prescribe antibiotics · Continue supportive care 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of a viral upper respiratory illness green nasal discharge from both nostrils improving each day Eating and sleeping normally; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · HR 104/min Prescribe antibioticsan improving viral illness meets no door; antibiotics do not shorten it and carry adverse effects. Supportive care and intranasal saline are both appropriate

Next step19 of 22 12-year-old girl has had 2 weeks of dry cough and headache scattered crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial infiltrates Well appearing; eating normally T 38.0°C · oxygen saturation 97% on room air · Oral amoxicillin · Oral azithromycin · Intravenous ceftriaxone 12-year-old girl has had 2 weeks of dry cough and headache scattered crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial infiltrates Well appearing; eating normally T 38.0°C · oxygen saturation 97% on room air Oral azithromycinpresumed Mycoplasma pneumonia in a well child is treated as an outpatient with a macrolide, or doxycycline (short courses are accepted under 8 years); it lacks a cell wall, so amoxicillin and intravenous ceftriaxone fail

Diagnosis20 of 22 3-year-old boy has had fever and a runny nose for 3 days and is irritable right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous no movement on pneumatic otoscopy External canal normal T 38.9°C · HR 128/min · Acute otitis media · Otitis externa · Otitis media with effusion 3-year-old boy has had fever and a runny nose for 3 days and is irritable right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous no movement on pneumatic otoscopy External canal normal T 38.9°C · HR 128/min Acute otitis mediaa bulging, immobile, erythematous membrane is acute otitis media; mobility on pneumatic otoscopy is the discriminator. With fever and a bulging red membrane this is acute infection rather than effusion alone, and the normal canal leaves otitis externa out

Mechanism21 of 22 64-year-old man who smokes has 2 days of high fever and confusion watery diarrhea crackles at the right base Returned from a cruise last week T 40.1°C · sodium 128 mEq/L · Mycoplasma pneumoniae · Legionella pneumophila · Streptococcus pneumoniae 64-year-old man who smokes has 2 days of high fever and confusion watery diarrhea crackles at the right base Returned from a cruise last week T 40.1°C · sodium 128 mEq/L Legionella pneumophilahigh fever, diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia in an older smoker after a cruise is Legionella: the urine antigen confirms. Mycoplasma is indolent in the young, and pneumococcus is the rigors and rusty sputum picture

Diagnosis22 of 22 3-year-old boy had a cold that was improving by day 5 on day 7, new fever nasal discharge worsening again, from both nostrils No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.8°C · HR 120/min · tympanic membranes mobile · Allergic rhinitis · Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis · Viral upper respiratory infection 3-year-old boy had a cold that was improving by day 5 on day 7, new fever nasal discharge worsening again, from both nostrils No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.8°C · HR 120/min · tympanic membranes mobile Acute bacterial rhinosinusitisimprovement, then new fever and worse discharge, is double worsening, the third door to acute bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate. The turn, not the day count or the color, crosses the door; allergy gives clear discharge with sneezing and itch

Previously healthy 10-year-old boy with 10 days of worsening cough a low-grade fever mild dyspnea on exertion diffuse crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: diffuse perihilar infiltrate Most likely diagnosis? Competing answers Pneumonia due to respiratory syncytial virus: viral, with diffuse bilateral findings; but it causes wheezy lower respiratory disease in infants and children under 2, not at 10. Congestive heart failure: a diffuse perihilar infiltrate with bilateral crackles also describes pulmonary edema; but in children it usually follows congenital heart disease, an arteriovenous fistula or severe malnutrition, and this child was previously healthy and febrile. Tuberculosis: the cough is subacute; but there is no exposure, weight loss or night sweats, and the film shows no hilar adenopathy or cavitation. Down to two: Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Streptococcus pneumoniae. Mycoplasma over pneumococcus: pneumococcus brings a productive cough, pleuritic chest pain and a single-lobe consolidation, not a gradual 10-day course with a diffuse film. A film that looks worse than the child is the Mycoplasma pattern. The stem never says atypical; age, onset and film carry the answer, and a macrolide treats it.

Acute bacterial sinusitis for one-sided pus: purulence fits, but sinusitis is bilateral and usually febrile with cough; one-sided discharge in a playful, afebrile toddler is a foreign body. Allergic rhinitis because of a smoking father and a pet dog: risk factors, but allergy gives bilateral clear discharge with pale turbinates, not unilateral foul pus. Mucormycosis because of his human immunodeficiency virus infection: a CD4 count of 520/mm³ and red, swollen turbinates, not white or black, rule it out.

Part I Hemolytic Anemia: the cold-agglutinin hemolysis Mycoplasma causes and the direct antiglobulin pattern that identifies it. Part I Tuberculosis: the child with a subacute cough and a known contact; is there weight loss, night sweats or hilar adenopathy?

For each striking detail, ask what it adds to the diagnosis; a detail that only raises alarm is a distractor. When symptoms involve two compartments at once (upper and lower airway, as pharyngitis with an interstitial pneumonia in adults), ask which organisms span both: typical bacterial pneumonia does not cause pharyngitis.

briefs.title: Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant
briefs.sub: neonatal respiratory distress causes · bronchopulmonary dysplasiaHow preterm, did labor occur, when did it start, and what does the film show?
blocks: Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant
neonatal respiratory distress causes · bronchopulmonary dysplasiaHow preterm, did labor occur, when did it start, and what does the film show?

Time it first: gestational age, labor or not, onset and the film decide; then the oxygen response splits lung from shunt Term after cesarean without labor, wet fissures, gone in 2 to 3 days transient tachypnea; preterm with ground glass, air bronchograms and small lungs respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), surfactant Each preterm complication keeps its own window: apnea from day 2 or 3, well between spells caffeine; oxygen still needed at 28 days bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), arrested alveolar growth

What it is Breathing trouble at birth, or in the weeks after a preterm birth Sort by gestational age labor or cesarean onset the film response to oxygen Hands off Little change on oxygen with a heart cause: Cyanosis in the Newborn; necrotizing enterocolitis: The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn; sepsis: Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn; the physiology: Hypoxemia

Diaphragmatic herniaScaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the chest, heart sounds shifted Why no bag-mask Diaphragmatic herniaBag-mask air fills the bowel inside the chest and crushes the lung further; the small lung also carries pulmonary hypertension after repair. If a hernia is suspected, choose intubation at once, never bag-mask, with nasogastric suction. Pulmonary hypertensionCyanosis that oxygen barely changes; foot saturation below the right hand If the postductal saturation is 5% or more below the preductal, choose echocardiogram, then inhaled nitric oxide for severe disease. Tension pneumothoraxDistended, hyperresonant side in an infant who is getting worse If it is suspected, choose needle decompression, which also confirms it. Group B streptococcal pneumoniaTemperature instability, neutropenia; a film like RDS If sepsis is possible, choose blood culture, then ampicillin and gentamicin.

Distress at birth, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Transient tachypnea of the newborn Term or near term; cesarean before labor, a large baby, a mother with diabetes or asthma Wet lungs, fluid in the fissures, volumes normal or high; gone in 2 to 3 days Respiratory distress syndrome Preterm surfactant deficiency; distress from birth Low volumes, diffuse ground glass, air bronchograms; surfactant Group B streptococcal pneumonia Maternal fever, membranes ruptured 18 hours or more, no intrapartum prophylaxis Film can look exactly like RDS, but onset can be later (days) and it is commoner at term; temperature instability, neutropenia Meconium aspiration Term or post-term, meconium-stained fluid Hyperinflation with patchy, streaky opacities Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Failed transition after asphyxia or meconium Postductal saturation lower than preductal; oxygen barely helps Congenital diaphragmatic hernia Sunken (scaphoid) abdomen, displaced heart sounds Film: bowel in the chest, heart pushed aside Polycythemia Plethora with low glucose; clear film Venous hematocrit above 65% at term

The preterm clock Complication Window Tell Pulmonary interstitial emphysema First days, on a ventilator for RDS Air dissects the interstitium; worsening can be sudden Apnea of prematurity From day 2 or 3; gone by about 40 weeks postmenstrual age Pause over 20 seconds, or shorter with bradycardia; well between spells Bronchopulmonary dysplasia Oxygen toxicityMnemonicRetinopathy of prematurity, Intraventricular hemorrhage, Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (RIB) Oxygen still needed at 28 days, or at 36 weeks postmenstrual age Arrested alveolar development, not scarring CareBronchopulmonary dysplasiaSupportive: nutrition, fluid restriction, diuretics; alveoli go on forming for months. Antenatal glucocorticoids, gentle ventilation, surfactant and caffeine lower the risk. Pulmonary hypertension Months later, after BPD Poor growth; loud P2; echocardiogram Necrotizing enterocolitis On enteral feeds Bloody stools, pneumatosis intestinalis

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Distress at birth → Pulse oximetry on room air, then oxygen Corrects on modest oxygen Lung disease Little change Shunt or heart Targeted tests TestResultMeans Little change on oxygen → Pre- and postductal saturations Foot 5% or more below the right hand Right-to-left ductal shunt: pulmonary hypertension Gap present → Echocardiogram High pressure, normal structure Pulmonary hypertension, not cyanotic heart disease Next step TestResultMeans Lung disease → Chest film Fluid in the fissures Transient tachypnea Ground glass, low volumes RDS, or group B streptococcal pneumonia Patchy, hyperinflated Meconium aspiration Bowel in the chest Diaphragmatic hernia Temperature instability or neutropenia → Blood culture and complete blood count Positive or ill Group B streptococcal pneumonia: ampicillin and gentamicin Diagnostic test TestResultMeans A wet, term film → Time Settled by day 3 Transient tachypnea; persistence means another diagnosis SkipRestarting antibiotics for apnea in a preterm infant who is well between spells: look for anemia, infection and hemorrhage, then give caffeine.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Maternal diabetes Transient tachypnea; RDS can appear at an age that would otherwise be safe Fetal insulin delays surfactant maturation Apnea with lethargy, a tense fontanelle or seizures Intraventricular hemorrhage Cranial ultrasound BPD with an RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) season ahead High-risk infant Nirsevimab, preferred over palivizumab Well infant, heart on the right, no distress Dextrocardia No emergency
Pause point Newborn with a scaphoid abdomen Offered: bag-mask ventilation The hernia → Intubate Preterm infant with apnea Offered: a sepsis restart Well between spells → Caffeine

Diagnosis1 of 24 1-hour-old boy born at 40 weeks by cesarean without labor is tachypneic chest x-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures Afebrile · birth weight 4200 g · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 88% on room air, 98% on oxygen · Transient tachypnea of the newborn · Respiratory distress syndrome · Group B streptococcal pneumonia 1-hour-old boy born at 40 weeks by cesarean without labor is tachypneic chest x-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures Afebrile · birth weight 4200 g · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 88% on room air, 98% on oxygen Transient tachypnea of the newbornretained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs: fluid in the fissures appears in no competing diagnosis, and saturation correcting from 88% to 98% on oxygen is alveolar fluid, not a shunt. Cesarean without labor misses the catecholamine surge that switches the epithelium to absorbing fluid; macrosomia adds risk. Respiratory distress syndrome is the right category but a preterm member, and group B streptococcal pneumonia needs risk factors the stem never supplies. Supportive care: onset within 2 hours, and it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so an infant breathing normally by 48 hours fits

Mechanism2 of 24 6-week-old boy born at 26 weeks still needs supplemental oxygen on nasal cannula oxygen every day since birth enteral feeds introduced today Weight gain appropriate on total parenteral nutrition Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on 0.5 L/min · Interstitial air leak · Fibrotic ventilator-induced injury · Arrested alveolar development 6-week-old boy born at 26 weeks still needs supplemental oxygen on nasal cannula oxygen every day since birth enteral feeds introduced today Weight gain appropriate on total parenteral nutrition Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on 0.5 L/min Arrested alveolar developmenta preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days or more has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and since surfactant and gentler ventilation it is arrested alveolar development: fewer alveoli, less septation, disrupted vasculogenesis. Fibrotic ventilator injury is the old form, and air leak occurs in the first days on high pressures, weeks before this. Feeds introduced today suggest refeeding syndrome, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition

Next step3 of 24 6-hour-old girl born at term has tachypnea and grunting membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery maternal fever 38.5 °C in labor; no intrapartum prophylaxis Temperature unstable since birth T 35.9 °C · HR 176/min · respiratory rate 74/min · Observe for 48 hours without antibiotics · Blood culture and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin · Surfactant administration 6-hour-old girl born at term has tachypnea and grunting membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery maternal fever 38.5 °C in labor; no intrapartum prophylaxis Temperature unstable since birth T 35.9 °C · HR 176/min · respiratory rate 74/min Blood culture and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicinrupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever and no intrapartum prophylaxis, with temperature instability, is early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis. Its film mimics respiratory distress syndrome exactly, so surfactant misses it, and observing without antibiotics leaves the infection untreated: culture and start ampicillin and gentamicin

Next step4 of 24 Term newborn boy has severe respiratory distress at delivery scaphoid abdomen heart sounds displaced to the right chest x-ray shows bowel gas in the left hemithorax T 36.6 °C · HR 92/min · oxygen saturation 64% · Bag-mask ventilation while preparing for transfer · Needle decompression of the left chest · Intubate with limited peak pressures and decompress the stomach Term newborn boy has severe respiratory distress at delivery scaphoid abdomen heart sounds displaced to the right chest x-ray shows bowel gas in the left hemithorax T 36.6 °C · HR 92/min · oxygen saturation 64% Intubate with limited peak pressures and decompress the stomacha scaphoid abdomen with displaced heart sounds and bowel in the chest is a diaphragmatic hernia. Bag-mask ventilation inflates bowel inside the chest, so intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma) and decompress with a nasogastric tube. Needle decompression is for a tension pneumothorax: a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant

Next step5 of 24 4-day-old boy born at 29 weeks in neonatal intensive care several 20-second breathing pauses today, bradycardia and desaturation ends with stimulation; pink, active, feeding well between Cultures negative; antibiotics stopped T 36.9 °C, stable · glucose, electrolytes, hemoglobin, ultrasound normal · Begin caffeine · Begin dexamethasone · Restart empiric antibiotics 4-day-old boy born at 29 weeks in neonatal intensive care several 20-second breathing pauses today, bradycardia and desaturation ends with stimulation; pink, active, feeding well between Cultures negative; antibiotics stopped T 36.9 °C, stable · glucose, electrolytes, hemoglobin, ultrasound normal Begin caffeinea central pause from an immature brainstem, starting on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between spells, with the mimics checked (infection, anemia, intraventricular hemorrhage, glucose, electrolytes), is apnea of prematurity. Caffeine is a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue. Antibiotics answer the infant who is ill between spells; dexamethasone and albuterol are used for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, not for apnea

Diagnosis6 of 24 2-hour-old boy born at 29 weeks is grunting and retracting chest x-ray shows low lung volumes diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms Membranes ruptured at delivery T 36.8 °C · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 86% on room air · Respiratory distress syndrome · Transient tachypnea of the newborn · Group B streptococcal pneumonia 2-hour-old boy born at 29 weeks is grunting and retracting chest x-ray shows low lung volumes diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms Membranes ruptured at delivery T 36.8 °C · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 86% on room air Respiratory distress syndromesurfactant deficiency in a preterm infant (under 34 weeks) gives distress at birth, worsening over 48 to 72 hours, with low volumes, ground glass and air bronchograms: give surfactant and CPAP. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures in a term infant; group B streptococcal pneumonia mimics this film exactly but needs risk factors (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) this stem does not supply

Next step7 of 24 2-day-old boy born at term is plethoric, lethargic and feeding poorly venous hematocrit 72% no better after 12 hours of intravenous fluids Born after delayed cord clamping Afebrile · glucose 48 mg/dL · HR 156/min · Intravenous furosemide · Double-volume exchange transfusion · Partial exchange transfusion 2-day-old boy born at term is plethoric, lethargic and feeding poorly venous hematocrit 72% no better after 12 hours of intravenous fluids Born after delayed cord clamping Afebrile · glucose 48 mg/dL · HR 156/min Partial exchange transfusionmost polycythemic infants are ruddy and asymptomatic; hyperviscosity brings lethargy, irritability and jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, respiratory distress, poor feeding and cyanosis. Hydration by feeds or glucose-containing intravenous fluids comes first; symptomatic hyperviscosity despite it needs a partial exchange transfusion, which swaps blood for saline to lower viscosity. A double-volume exchange replaces the infant's blood with donor red cells and is used for severe hyperbilirubinemia, and furosemide adds fluid loss, which can make the blood even thicker; true dehydration is rare in the first 2 days, while the neonate still carries excess extracellular fluid

Next step8 of 24 8-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks is cyanotic preductal saturation 88%, postductal 76% minimal improvement on 100% oxygen chest x-ray nearly clear Delivered through meconium-stained fluid Afebrile · HR 168/min · BP 62/38 mm Hg · Give surfactant · Obtain an echocardiogram · Reassure the parents and observe 8-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks is cyanotic preductal saturation 88%, postductal 76% minimal improvement on 100% oxygen chest x-ray nearly clear Delivered through meconium-stained fluid Afebrile · HR 168/min · BP 62/38 mm Hg Obtain an echocardiograma pre- to postductal gap that barely responds to oxygen is right-to-left ductal shunting: persistent pulmonary hypertension, a failed transition often after asphyxia or aspiration.
