Echocardiography shows high pulmonary pressure in a structurally normal heart and excludes cyanotic heart disease. Surfactant treats alveolar disease, which corrects on oxygen, and reassurance misses a can't-miss diagnosis

Diagnosis9 of 24 12-day-old girl born at 26 weeks has abdominal distension bloody stools on day 10 of enteral feeds abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis T 35.9 °C · HR 182/min · capillary refill 4 seconds · Malrotation with volvulus · Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis · Necrotizing enterocolitis 12-day-old girl born at 26 weeks has abdominal distension bloody stools on day 10 of enteral feeds abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis T 35.9 °C · HR 182/min · capillary refill 4 seconds Necrotizing enterocolitisa preterm infant on enteral feeds with distension, bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis has bacterial invasion of the bowel wall: keep nil by mouth, give intravenous antibiotics and consult surgery. Allergic proctocolitis is the well infant with bloody stool; pneumatosis intestinalis is the tell that names this can't-miss diagnosis over it and over malrotation with volvulus

Next step10 of 24 1-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks by cesarean without labor is breathing fast chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures with perihilar streaking Mother asks to breastfeed now Afebrile · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 93% on oxygen · Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen · Intubate and give surfactant · Begin oral feeding now 1-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks by cesarean without labor is breathing fast chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures with perihilar streaking Mother asks to breastfeed now Afebrile · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 93% on oxygen Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygenneonatal tachypnea is a respiratory rate above 60 per minute, and feeding at a rate of 80 risks aspiration: keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and oxygen. Intubation and surfactant are for the preterm surfactant-deficient lung, not retained fluid in a term infant

Next step11 of 24 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, is in preterm labor at 29 weeks cervix dilated 5 cm delivery expected within 48 hours T 37.0 °C · BP 118/72 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 140/min · Antenatal betamethasone · Tocolysis with nifedipine · Postnatal surfactant 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, is in preterm labor at 29 weeks cervix dilated 5 cm delivery expected within 48 hours T 37.0 °C · BP 118/72 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 140/min Antenatal betamethasoneantenatal betamethasone gives the fetal lung the cortisol signal that drives surfactant maturation (the signal fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes); corticosteroid exposure before delivery lowers rates of respiratory distress syndrome, intracranial hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis and death, while surfactant can only be given after birth; tocolysis buys time for the steroid course and has not been shown to improve neonatal outcomes on its own

Mechanism12 of 24 1-hour-old boy born at 37 weeks has grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled diabetes chest x-ray shows diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms Afebrile · birth weight 4300 g · oxygen saturation 85% on room air · Placental insufficiency causes chronic fetal hypoxia · Maternal hyperglycemia directly injures the type II pneumocytes of the fetal lung · Fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol, delaying surfactant maturation 1-hour-old boy born at 37 weeks has grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled diabetes chest x-ray shows diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms Afebrile · birth weight 4300 g · oxygen saturation 85% on room air Fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol, delaying surfactant maturationfetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol and suppresses phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol production, delaying surfactant maturation; the pneumocytes are not directly injured, and placental vessel disease from diabetic vascular complications can give a small-for-gestational-age infant, not a 4300 g one

Next step13 of 24 5-day-old girl born at 30 weeks has new apnea and bradycardia since this morning lethargic and mottled between episodes abdominal distension and feeding intolerance No antibiotics so far T 35.8 °C, unstable · HR 188/min · capillary refill 4 seconds · Begin caffeine · Red blood cell transfusion · Blood culture and empiric antibiotics 5-day-old girl born at 30 weeks has new apnea and bradycardia since this morning lethargic and mottled between episodes abdominal distension and feeding intolerance No antibiotics so far T 35.8 °C, unstable · HR 188/min · capillary refill 4 seconds Blood culture and empiric antibioticsan infant who is ill between spells (temperature instability, feeding intolerance or poor perfusion) has suspected sepsis, not simple apnea of prematurity: culture and treat. Caffeine is for the infant well between spells; anemia of prematurity comes weeks later, pale with a low hemoglobin; this tachycardia is sepsis

Next step14 of 24 2-day-old girl was diagnosed with a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia at birth intubated; saturations now falling echocardiogram shows suprasystemic pulmonary pressures right hand saturation 92% · foot saturation 78% · HR 170/min · Inhaled nitric oxide · Prostaglandin E1 infusion · Chest tube placement 2-day-old girl was diagnosed with a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia at birth intubated; saturations now falling echocardiogram shows suprasystemic pulmonary pressures right hand saturation 92% · foot saturation 78% · HR 170/min Inhaled nitric oxidea hand-foot gap is right-to-left ductal shunting from pulmonary hypertension of the hypoplastic lung. Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) is the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but this cyanosis is not a closing duct; a chest tube treats a pneumothorax, not shunting. The lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists; the gap itself shows the duct is already open, so the target is pulmonary vasodilation

Diagnosis15 of 24 3-day-old boy born at 27 weeks has abrupt hypoxia on high-pressure mechanical ventilation since birth chest x-ray shows unilateral perivascular cystic lucencies No distended, hyperresonant hemithorax Afebrile · HR 172/min · oxygen saturation 78% · Worsening respiratory distress syndrome · Tension pneumothorax · Pulmonary interstitial emphysema 3-day-old boy born at 27 weeks has abrupt hypoxia on high-pressure mechanical ventilation since birth chest x-ray shows unilateral perivascular cystic lucencies No distended, hyperresonant hemithorax Afebrile · HR 172/min · oxygen saturation 78% Pulmonary interstitial emphysemaair dissects into the interstitium on high ventilator pressures in the first days: cystic lucencies and abrupt decompensation; reduce ventilator pressures. Tension pneumothorax gives a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax needing needle decompression, and respiratory distress syndrome, though it worsens over 48 to 72 hours, shows ground glass with air bronchograms

Next step16 of 24 10-hour-old girl born at 29 weeks has needed CPAP since birth rising oxygen requirement, now 60% worsening retractions chest x-ray shows ground glass with air bronchograms T 36.8 °C · oxygen saturation 86% on CPAP · Continue CPAP and observe closely · Start antibiotics alone · Intubate and give surfactant 10-hour-old girl born at 29 weeks has needed CPAP since birth rising oxygen requirement, now 60% worsening retractions chest x-ray shows ground glass with air bronchograms T 36.8 °C · oxygen saturation 86% on CPAP Intubate and give surfactantworsening surfactant deficiency despite CPAP means CPAP has failed: intubate and give surfactant. Closer observation leaves the failure untreated, and antibiotics alone do not replace surfactant

Diagnosis17 of 24 6-hour-old boy born at term is ruddy and jittery breathing fast with no retractions chest x-ray is clear; no hepatomegaly; normal heart sounds Mother had preeclampsia Afebrile · glucose 32 mg/dL · respiratory rate 70/min · HR 150/min · Glycogen storage disease · Transient tachypnea of the newborn · Polycythemia 6-hour-old boy born at term is ruddy and jittery breathing fast with no retractions chest x-ray is clear; no hepatomegaly; normal heart sounds Mother had preeclampsia Afebrile · glucose 32 mg/dL · respiratory rate 70/min · HR 150/min Polycythemiaplethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film is polycythemia. Intrauterine hypoxia drives erythropoietin (preeclampsia, maternal diabetes or hypertension, smoking, growth restriction), or placental transfusion adds blood (delayed cord clamping, twin-twin transfusion); hyperviscosity brings jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea; check a venous hematocrit (above 65%). Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, glycogen storage disease type I brings hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis, and cyanotic heart disease is excluded by a normal heart and exam

Screening18 of 24 14-month-old boy born at 30 weeks is seen at a well visit has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, on diuretics until 3 months ago his second RSV season starts next month Afebrile · respiratory rate 36/min · oxygen saturation 96% on room air · Infant RSV vaccination · Nirsevimab prophylaxis · Palivizumab monthly 14-month-old boy born at 30 weeks is seen at a well visit has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, on diuretics until 3 months ago his second RSV season starts next month Afebrile · respiratory rate 36/min · oxygen saturation 96% on room air Nirsevimab prophylaxischronic lung disease of prematurity that needed medical support (supplemental oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids) in the 6 months before the second season qualifies for a second-season dose, and nirsevimab is the product recommended and is preferred over palivizumab; the prophylaxis is an antibody, not an infant vaccine

Next step19 of 24 Term newborn girl has severe cyanosis at 12 hours no improvement on 100% oxygen no retractions; comfortable tachypnea chest radiograph structurally normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 68% on 100% oxygen · HR 160/min · Inhaled nitric oxide · Prostaglandin E1 infusion · Surfactant through an endotracheal tube Term newborn girl has severe cyanosis at 12 hours no improvement on 100% oxygen no retractions; comfortable tachypnea chest radiograph structurally normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 68% on 100% oxygen · HR 160/min Prostaglandin E1 infusioncyanosis that does not correct on oxygen in a comfortable infant with a normal film is a shunt (the hyperoxia test, still keyed on exams though largely abandoned clinically): suspect cyanotic congenital heart disease and start prostaglandin E1 pending echocardiography. Surfactant treats alveolar disease that corrects on oxygen; inhaled nitric oxide treats pulmonary hypertension, whose tell is a ductal saturation gap

Mechanism20 of 24 3-week-old boy born at 28 weeks is given caffeine for central apneic spells well between spells His parents ask when the spells should stop Afebrile · HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% on room air · By 28 days of life · By about 1 year of chronological age · By about his expected due date 3-week-old boy born at 28 weeks is given caffeine for central apneic spells well between spells His parents ask when the spells should stop Afebrile · HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% on room air By about his expected due datethe brainstem breathing center matures by term corrected age, so spells resolve by about the expected due date; 28 days is the bronchopulmonary dysplasia clock, not the apnea clock

Diagnosis21 of 24 1-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks has tachypnea and retractions delivered through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress chest x-ray shows coarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation Afebrile · respiratory rate 84/min · oxygen saturation 87% · Meconium aspiration syndrome · Transient tachypnea of the newborn · Congenital pneumonia 1-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks has tachypnea and retractions delivered through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress chest x-ray shows coarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation Afebrile · respiratory rate 84/min · oxygen saturation 87% Meconium aspiration syndrometerm or post-term delivery through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress, with coarse patchy asymmetric infiltrates and hyperinflation; watch for pneumothorax and pulmonary hypertension. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, and for congenital pneumonia nothing in this stem points to infection (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis)

Next step22 of 24 2-hour-old girl born at 36 weeks has central cyanosis, grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes chest x-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacities Afebrile · saturation 64% rising to 82% on oxygen · pre- and postductal readings equal · Prostaglandin E1 infusion · Surfactant · Corticosteroids 2-hour-old girl born at 36 weeks has central cyanosis, grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes chest x-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacities Afebrile · saturation 64% rising to 82% on oxygen · pre- and postductal readings equal Surfactantmaternal diabetes delays surfactant maturation, so an infant of a diabetic mother can develop respiratory distress syndrome at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe. Ground glass with equal pre- and postductal readings and a partial oxygen response is lung disease, not a ductal shunt, so prostaglandin E1 is not the answer; steroids for the lung are the antenatal betamethasone given before delivery

Diagnosis23 of 24 4-month-old boy born at 28 weeks has poor weight gain needed supplemental oxygen until 3 months of age loud P2 liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · respiratory rate 56/min · oxygen saturation 93% on room air · Pulmonary artery hypertension · Chronic aspiration · Systemic arterial hypertension 4-month-old boy born at 28 weeks has poor weight gain needed supplemental oxygen until 3 months of age loud P2 liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · respiratory rate 56/min · oxygen saturation 93% on room air Pulmonary artery hypertensionpulmonary hypertension is a complication of bronchopulmonary dysplasia that arrives months later, with a loud P2 and poor growth: obtain an echocardiogram. Systemic hypertension and recurrent respiratory infections are also complications, but a loud P2 is the pulmonic sound, and aspiration is a trigger to screen for in this pulmonary hypertension, not the diagnosis; the enlarged liver can reflect right heart failure

Next step24 of 24 4-day-old girl born at term was diagnosed with transient tachypnea on day 1 still breathing fast at 96 hours of life Feeding by nasogastric tube Afebrile · respiratory rate 74/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air · Continue observation · Re-evaluate for another diagnosis · Discharge with outpatient follow-up 4-day-old girl born at term was diagnosed with transient tachypnea on day 1 still breathing fast at 96 hours of life Feeding by nasogastric tube Afebrile · respiratory rate 74/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air Re-evaluate for another diagnosistransient is a diagnostic criterion, not a description: it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so tachypnea beyond 72 hours means the diagnosis was wrong; look again. Continued observation and discharge both keep the wrong label

Refeeding syndrome: feeds introduced today suggest it, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition. Pulmonary interstitial emphysema at 28 days: real ventilator pathology, but it occurs in the first days. RDS in a term infant: the right category, a preterm member. Group B streptococcal pneumonia: needs risk factors the stem must supply. Prostaglandin in a diaphragmatic hernia: the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but the cyanosis comes from hypoplastic lungs and pulmonary hypertension, not a closing duct. Diaphragmatic hernia at an hour with fissural fluid: it presents at delivery with a scaphoid abdomen.

Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant: the well infant with bloody stool; here, the ill preterm infant. Ask: is the infant preterm, distended and unwell? Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant: intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia of prematurity, the mimics to exclude before calling a spell apnea of prematurity. Ask: is the infant well between episodes? Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the same distress in the first hours. Ask: is this fluid in normal lungs, or lungs that never developed? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the step before, where work of breathing, the oxygen response and the limb gradient sort lung from heart. Part I Hypoxemia: the physiology under the oxygen response.

Match the clock before the findings. Birth: RDS or transient tachypnea, sorted by gestational age, labor, onset and the film. Ventilator days: air leak. Day 2 to 3 spells in a well infant: apnea of prematurity. Oxygen at 28 days: BPD. Months: pulmonary hypertension. When the history states a diagnostic criterion exactly, make that diagnosis directly.

briefs.title: Abnormal Liver Tests
briefs.sub: hepatocellular vs cholestatic · liver or bone source · ducts on ultrasound · biliary vs sclerosing cholangitisWhich pattern is it, and are the ducts dilated on ultrasound?
blocks: hepatocellular vs cholestatic · liver or bone source · ducts on ultrasound · biliary vs sclerosing cholangitisWhich pattern is it, and are the ducts dilated on ultrasound?

Sort the pattern before chasing causes: AST and ALT high is hepatocellular; alkaline phosphatase (ALP) high with direct bilirubin is cholestatic; bilirubin alone is an isolated hyperbilirubinemia. An ALP rise with normal aminotransferases needs a gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT): a high GGT puts the source in the liver; a normal GGT means bone, growth or placenta. A cholestatic pattern goes to right upper quadrant ultrasound first: dilated ducts mean extrahepatic obstruction, imaged next by magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or CT; nondilated ducts mean intrahepatic disease, tested next with the antimitochondrial antibody.

Injured hepatocytes leak aminotransferases; blocked bile flow raises ALP and backs conjugated bilirubin into the blood. Excess unconjugated bilirubin comes from overproduction (hemolysis) or weak conjugation (Gilbert syndrome).

Act now Finding Action Fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice (Charcot triad); hypotension and confusion may add the Reynolds pentad Acute (ascending) cholangitis: blood cultures and antibiotics, then endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) to remove the stone as soon as possible. Painless jaundice with weight loss and a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) Pancreatic head cancer until excluded: abdominal CT.

Cholestatic causes Cause Decides it Confirm with Choledocholithiasis Biliary pain with a dilated common bile duct; ALP, GGT and direct bilirubin often up. Ultrasound; MRCP if unclear. Acute cholangitis (ascending cholangitis) Charcot triad on top of a duct stone. Blood cultures and antibiotics, then ERCP to remove the stone. Pancreatic head cancer Painless jaundice, weight loss, Courvoisier sign; a dilated duct ending at a head mass. Abdominal CT. Drug-induced cholestasis ALP and bilirubin up after amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids, chlorpromazine or oral contraceptives. Timing after the drug; tests usually improve once it is withdrawn. Sarcoidosis (infiltrative liver disease) Cholestasis with bilateral hilar lymph nodes and hypercalcemia; portal granulomas. Liver biopsy shows the granulomas. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy Pregnancy with intense itching, worst at night, and raised aminotransferases. Fasting bile acids; ursodeoxycholic acid and timed delivery.
Two chronic bile duct diseases to tell apart: primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), formerly primary biliary cirrhosis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

PBC or PSC Axis PBC PSC Patient Middle-aged women with itching and fatigue Men, young to middle-aged, with inflammatory bowel disease In practiceThe Merck Sharp and Dohme (MSD) Manual gives a peak age at diagnosis of 25 to 45 years, about two-thirds men, and inflammatory bowel disease in 60 to 90%. Antibody Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), positive in 90 to 95% p-ANCA (perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody); AMA negative Association Sjögren syndrome, Hashimoto thyroiditis, rheumatoid arthritis, celiac disease Ulcerative colitis in about 90%; screening colonoscopy at diagnosis Ducts and histology Small intrahepatic ducts, so MRCP looks normal; destructive cholangitis, with granulomas in some Beading of intra- and extrahepatic ducts on MRCP; onion-skin periductal fibrosis Course Jaundice and xanthelasma often come late Raised risk of cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer and, with colitis, colon cancer

Hepatocellular pattern: AST and ALT lead Cause Clue or first test Viral hepatitis Serologies first Alcohol-related liver disease AST:ALT above 2 Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly nonalcoholic fatty liver disease ALT above AST Autoimmune hepatitis Anti-smooth muscle antibody (type 1) or anti-liver-kidney microsomal type 1 antibody (type 2) Wilson disease Low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper Hereditary hemochromatosis Iron studies first Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level, with genotype or phenotype testing Drug-induced liver injury Timing after the drug; stop it Cause still unclear Liver biopsy

Isolated bilirubin or isolated ALP Cause Decides it Next best step Gilbert syndrome Indirect bilirubin up alone, rising with fasting, stress or illness; mildly low conjugating enzyme. Fractionate; normal CBC, smear and reticulocytes settle it. Hemolysis Indirect bilirubin up with a high reticulocyte count. CBC, smear, reticulocyte count. Crigler-Najjar syndrome Indirect bilirubin from absent (type I) or reduced (type II) conjugating enzyme. Give a phenobarbital trial: type II, the less severe form, responds. Dubin-Johnson or Rotor syndrome Direct bilirubin up with normal liver enzymes and CBC; Dubin-Johnson has a black liver. No further testing: the pattern is benign. Bone or placental ALP ALP up with a normal GGT: Paget disease (the commonest isolated rise after 40), a growing child, pregnancy, bone metastases, vitamin D deficiency, a healing fracture. Order calcium, phosphate, vitamin D and bone imaging.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any abnormal liver test → Hepatic panel with fractionated bilirubin AST and ALT lead Hepatocellular: serologies and the first hepatocellular tests ALP and direct bilirubin lead Cholestatic: ultrasound next Bilirubin alone Indirect: CBC, smear, reticulocytes; direct with normal enzymes: Dubin-Johnson or Rotor ALP up, aminotransferases normal → GGT GGT high Hepatic: work up as cholestatic GGT normal Bone or placenta: calcium, phosphate, vitamin D and bone imaging Cholestatic pattern → Right upper quadrant ultrasound Ducts dilated Extrahepatic: MRCP or CT Ducts not dilated Intrahepatic: antimitochondrial antibody Targeted tests TestResultMeans Nondilated ducts in a middle-aged woman with itching → Antimitochondrial antibody Positive PBC: biopsy usually not needed Negative MRCP, then biopsy if still unexplained Dilated duct with biliary pain → MRCP if ultrasound is unclear Filling defect in the common bile duct Choledocholithiasis Dilated duct, painless jaundice, weight loss → Abdominal CT Mass where the dilated duct ends Pancreatic cancer Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Inflammatory bowel disease with a cholestatic pattern → MRCP Beading of intra- and extrahepatic ducts PSC; colonoscopy if colitis is not yet known Cause still unclear after antibodies and imaging → Liver biopsy Granulomas, duct destruction or drug injury Sarcoidosis, AMA-negative PBC or drug-induced injury SkipERCP to diagnose: MRCP shows the ducts without procedural risk; ERCP is kept for removing a stone, opening a stricture or taking tissue.

Treatment by cause Cause Treat Choledocholithiasis ERCP with sphincterotomy to remove the stone; cholecystectomy afterward. Acute cholangitis Blood cultures and antibiotics, then ERCP to remove the stone. PBC Ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol) first line; it slows damage and delays transplant. A second agent if the response is poor. In practiceThe MSD Manual says a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) agonist, including some fibrates, may be used second line; the board cards name obeticholic acid. PSC No drug clearly improves survival (ursodiol evidence is mixed); ERCP dilation and stenting for a dominant stricture; liver transplant for end-stage disease. Drug-induced cholestasis Withdraw the drug early; most recover. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy Ursodiol first line; delivery timing in Liver Disease in Pregnancy. Gilbert, Dubin-Johnson or Rotor syndrome Reassure; no treatment.

Pause point Itching with a cholestatic pattern Offered: ERCP or a liver biopsy first Duct size decides the next test → Right upper quadrant ultrasound first Middle-aged woman with itching and a cholestatic pattern Offered as primary sclerosing cholangitis Nondilated ducts; antimitochondrial antibody positive → Primary biliary cholangitis

Next step1 of 9 Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct and a pancreatic head mass · Repeat ultrasound in 3 monthsRepeating the ultrasound later delays the diagnosis of a likely cancer. · ERCP firstERCP is kept for removing a stone, opening a stricture or taking tissue, not the first look at a mass. · CT abdomenA head mass behind a dilated duct is imaged and staged with abdominal CT first. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct and a pancreatic head mass CT abdomenpancreatic adenocarcinoma

Diagnosis2 of 9 Normal ducts + AMA positive in a woman with pruritus · Primary biliary cholangitisNondilated ducts with a positive antimitochondrial antibody in a woman with itching is primary biliary cholangitis. · Primary sclerosing cholangitisPrimary sclerosing cholangitis is a man with inflammatory bowel disease and beading on MRCP; AMA is negative. · Autoimmune hepatitisAutoimmune hepatitis is hepatocellular, with anti-smooth muscle antibody. Normal ducts + AMA positive in a woman with pruritus Primary biliary cholangitisursodiol

Workup3 of 9 Young man with ulcerative colitis and a cholestatic pattern · MRCPMRCP shows the beading of primary sclerosing cholangitis without procedural risk. · Liver biopsyBiopsy is for disease that MRCP cannot show. · ERCPERCP is kept for a stricture that needs dilation, a stent or tissue. Young man with ulcerative colitis and a cholestatic pattern MRCPbeads on a string → PSC

Diagnosis4 of 9 Alk phos elevated with a normal GGT · Bile duct obstructionDuct obstruction raises GGT and direct bilirubin. · Bone source or pregnancyA normal GGT places the ALP outside the liver: bone, growth or placenta. · Cholestatic liver injuryCholestatic liver injury raises GGT along with ALP. Alk phos elevated with a normal GGT Bone source or pregnancynot liver disease at all

Diagnosis5 of 9 Charcot triad (fever + right upper quadrant pain + jaundice) · Ascending cholangitisFever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice together are the Charcot triad of acute cholangitis. · Choledocholithiasis without cholangitisA duct stone without fever is choledocholithiasis; fever on top makes it cholangitis. · Acute cholecystitisAcute cholecystitis is a blocked cystic duct; the common duct stays open, so jaundice is not part of it. Charcot triad (fever + right upper quadrant pain + jaundice) Ascending cholangitisurgent ERCP

Diagnosis6 of 9 Painless jaundice + weight loss + palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) · Pancreatic head malignancyPainless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) point to a pancreatic head tumor. · Primary biliary cholangitisPrimary biliary cholangitis leaves the ducts nondilated. · CholedocholithiasisA duct stone causes biliary pain. Painless jaundice + weight loss + palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) Pancreatic head malignancynot stones

Diagnosis7 of 9 Isolated indirect hyperbilirubinemia appearing with fasting or illness, all else normal · Gilbert syndromeMild indirect bilirubin that rises with fasting or illness, with everything else normal, is Gilbert syndrome. · Crigler-Najjar type IICrigler-Najjar type II is a reduced conjugating enzyme, not a mild fasting rise. · HemolysisHemolysis brings a high reticulocyte count. Isolated indirect hyperbilirubinemia appearing with fasting or illness, all else normal Gilbert syndromereassurance

Next step8 of 9 Cholestatic pattern after amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids, oral contraceptives, or chlorpromazine · Stop the drug, then monitorDrug-induced cholestasis usually recovers when the drug is withdrawn early. · Liver biopsyBiopsy is for a cause still unclear after antibodies and imaging. · Start ursodiolUrsodiol treats primary biliary cholangitis, not a reversible drug reaction. Cholestatic pattern after amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids, oral contraceptives, or chlorpromazine Stop the drug, then monitor

Diagnosis9 of 9 Cholestasis + hilar lymphadenopathy + hypercalcemia · Primary biliary cholangitisPrimary biliary cholangitis brings no hilar nodes or hypercalcemia. · LymphomaLiver granulomas with bilateral hilar nodes fit sarcoidosis, not lymphoma. · SarcoidosisCholestasis with bilateral hilar lymph nodes and hypercalcemia is sarcoidosis with portal granulomas. Cholestasis + hilar lymphadenopathy + hypercalcemia Sarcoidosis

Anti-smooth muscle antibody and iron studies look for hepatocellular disease, the wrong pattern for a cholestatic picture. ERCP waits until imaging shows a lesion to treat. Repeating the liver tests later fits only once a reversible cause has been found and removed.

Use the liver test pattern as a triage instrument to choose tests. Tests are pattern-specific: an autoimmune hepatitis antibody looks for hepatocellular disease and does not belong in the workup of a cholestatic pattern.

briefs.title: Stool Changes in a Well Infant
briefs.sub: dyschezia, allergic proctocolitis, secondary lactase deficiency · ill-appearing mimics · reassure, eliminate, or work upIs the infant well and thriving, and what do the stool and its timing after the trigger show?
blocks: Stool Changes in a Well Infant

dyschezia, allergic proctocolitis, secondary lactase deficiency · ill-appearing mimics · reassure, eliminate, or work upIs the infant well and thriving, and what do the stool and its timing after the trigger show?

In a well, thriving infant, read the stool and its timing after the trigger. Straining and crying for minutes, then a soft stool, under 9 months: infant dyschezia, reassurance only; a hard stool makes it constipation. An ill-appearing infant is treated as an emergency first. Painless blood streaks in a well infant aged 1 week to 6 months: food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP). A breastfeeding mother drops cow's milk and soy; a formula-fed infant goes to extensively hydrolyzed formula, not soy. Watery diarrhea and bloating once dairy returns after gastroenteritis: secondary lactase deficiency, a lactose-free spell with no workup.

Dyschezia is poor coordination: the infant pushes before learning to relax the anal sphincter, so a soft stool still takes effort. FPIAP is a reaction to milk or soy protein, not mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE), in the distal colon; breast milk carries what the mother eats. Gastroenteritis can strip brush-border lactase, so unabsorbed lactose pulls water into the bowel and colonic bacteria ferment it to gas and acid.

Act now: the ill-appearing mimics Finding Points to Action Profuse, repeated vomiting, pallor and lethargy hours after a trigger food (typically over 2 hours); no hives or wheeze Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES), also not IgE-mediated Intravenous fluids for the hypovolemia; epinephrine does not treat it. Hives, wheeze, angioedema or hypotension within minutes of a food (anaphylaxis typically within 15 minutes) IgE-mediated food allergy, which may progress to anaphylaxis Intramuscular epinephrine in the outer thigh; then strict avoidance and an allergist. A preterm infant on enteral feeds with a distended abdomen and bloody stool Necrotizing enterocolitis Abdominal x-ray for pneumatosis intestinalis; bowel rest, nasogastric suction, IV fluids and IV antibiotics; surgery for perforation. Never a well-infant diagnosis.

The well, thriving infant with a stool complaint Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Infant dyschezia Under 9 months; strains, cries and reddens for minutes, then passes a soft stool; growing well. Reassure; it resolves on its own. Functional constipation Hard or pellet stools passed infrequently, often when the diet changes (formula, rice cereal or cow's milk). Diet change and a laxative. Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP; milk protein proctocolitis) Well infant, 1 week to 6 months, with painless blood streaks or mucus in a soft stool; breastfed or formula-fed. Remove cow's milk and soy protein; no scope. Anal fissure Blood streaks on a hard stool that hurts to pass (as in older children and adults). Examine the anus; past infancy, see GI Bleeding in a Child. Secondary lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance after gastroenteritis) Watery diarrhea, bloating and gas when dairy returns after gastroenteritis; no fever, no vomiting. Start a lactose-free trial, with no stool tests, when dairy is the clear trigger; stool tests only when the cause is unclear.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Straining, crying or a changed stool in an infant → Growth chart, general appearance and a look at the stool Thriving, soft stool after the effort Infant dyschezia: no further tests Hard or pellet stool Functional constipation Vomiting, lethargy, hives or wheeze Ill-appearing mimic: treat it urgently Blood streaks in a thriving infant → Anal exam Tear seen at the anal verge, hard stool Anal fissure No tear, soft stool FPIAP: elimination trial next Targeted tests TestResultMeans Painless streaks, no fissure, under 6 months → Cow's milk and soy elimination trial Bleeding settles FPIAP: resolves spontaneously, tolerating the protein by 12 months Watery diarrhea and bloating once dairy returns after gastroenteritis → Lactose-free trial Diarrhea stops Secondary lactase deficiency: reintroduce dairy as the bowel heals Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Diarrhea that stops with fasting but the cause is unclear → Stool pH and stool osmotic gap; hydrogen breath test Acidic stool (pH under 6), osmotic gap above 100, breath hydrogen up Osmotic diarrhea from carbohydrate malabsorption, as in secondary lactase deficiency: lactose-free diet, then dairy back as the bowel heals SkipStool culture, stool ova and parasite testing, colonoscopy or skin-prick tests in a thriving infant, and a glycerin suppository or formula switch for straining that ends in a soft stool. Each tests or treats a disease the stool and appearance have excluded; skin and IgE tests are most useful for IgE-mediated reactions, and FPIAP is not one.

Treatment by cause Cause Treat Infant dyschezia Reassurance and parent education; no laxative, suppository or formula change. FPIAP, breastfed Keep breastfeeding; remove cow's milk and soy from the maternal diet. FPIAP, formula-fed Extensively hydrolyzed formula; soy formula is the other trigger. Secondary lactase deficiency Lactose-free for a while, then dairy back once the brush border recovers. FPIES, IgE allergy, necrotizing enterocolitis IV fluids for FPIES; epinephrine for IgE allergy; bowel rest and IV antibiotics for necrotizing enterocolitis.

Pause point Infant straining at stool Offered: a formula switch or a suppository A thriving infant with a soft stool → Reassurance Appearance first, then the stool: blood streaks get milk and soy out, and only an ill-appearing infant gets fluids or epinephrine.

Next step1 of 10 3-month-old girl, breastfed and growing along her curve; turns red, grunts and cries for several minutes before most bowel movements, then passes a soft yellow stool; abdomen soft, anal exam normal · Reassurance and parental educationA thriving infant who strains, then passes a soft stool, has infant dyschezia: reassure and teach the parents. · Glycerin suppository before feedsA suppository treats hard stool; dyschezia ends in a soft one. · Switch to an extensively hydrolyzed formulaHydrolyzed formula treats milk protein proctocolitis, which brings blood streaks, not straining. 3-month-old girl, breastfed and growing along her curve; turns red, grunts and cries for several minutes before most bowel movements, then passes a soft yellow stool; abdomen soft, anal exam normal Reassurance and parental educationinfant dyschezia resolves by about 9 months

Diagnosis2 of 10 5 mo F, passed meconium on day 1, now hard pellet stools every 3 days with straining since starting solids, thriving · Infant dyscheziaInfant dyschezia ends in a soft stool; hard pellets mean constipation. · Functional constipationHard pellet stools after starting solids, with meconium on day 1, is functional constipation. · Hirschsprung diseaseHirschsprung disease delays meconium past 24 to 48 hours; this infant passed it on day 1. 5 mo F, passed meconium on day 1, now hard pellet stools every 3 days with straining since starting solids, thriving Functional constipationdietary change, then an osmotic laxative

Next step3 of 10 6 wk F, exclusively breastfed, thriving, blood-streaked soft stools for a week, comfortable and well · Switch to a soy-based formulaSoy protein triggers the same reaction, and breastfeeding need not stop. · Stool culture and observationInfectious colitis brings fever and diarrhea; a thriving infant with streaks needs no culture. · Eliminate cow's milk and soy from the maternal dietA thriving breastfed infant with painless streaks has FPIAP: keep breastfeeding, the mother drops dairy and soy. 6 wk F, exclusively breastfed, thriving, blood-streaked soft stools for a week, comfortable and well Eliminate cow's milk and soy from the maternal dietfood protein-induced allergic proctocolitis

Next step4 of 10 3 mo M on cow's milk formula, well-appearing, gaining weight, blood streaks and mucus in soft stools · Extensively hydrolyzed formulaA formula-fed infant with FPIAP switches to extensively hydrolyzed formula. · Soy-based formulaSoy is the other trigger protein, so it is not the substitute. · Colonoscopy with biopsyA thriving infant with blood streaks needs an elimination trial, not a scope. 3 mo M on cow's milk formula, well-appearing, gaining weight, blood streaks and mucus in soft stools Extensively hydrolyzed formulasoy cross-reacts, so it is not the substitute

Avoid5 of 10 2 mo F, breastfed, with food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis; the recommendation to avoid · Extensively hydrolyzed formula if maternal elimination failsHydrolyzed formula is the formula-fed answer, an acceptable fallback, not the move to avoid. · Stop breastfeeding and start a soy-based formulaStopping breastfeeding for soy formula is the move to avoid: soy triggers the same reaction. · Continue breastfeeding with maternal dairy and soy eliminationThis is the board answer for a breastfed infant, so it is not the move to avoid. 2 mo F, breastfed, with food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis; the recommendation to avoid Stop breastfeeding and start a soy-based formulasoy protein triggers the same reaction and breastfeeding need not stop

Next step6 of 10 7 mo M, 2 hours after his first cow's-milk formula, repetitive profuse vomiting, pale, limp and lethargic, no urticaria or wheeze · Skin-prick testing to cow's milkSkin-prick tests detect IgE; FPIES is not IgE-mediated, and a limp infant needs fluids now. · Intravenous fluid resuscitationRepeated vomiting and lethargy hours after a new food, with no hives, is FPIES: restore volume with intravenous fluids. · Intramuscular epinephrineEpinephrine is for IgE reactions within minutes, with hives or wheeze; FPIES is not IgE-mediated. 7 mo M, 2 hours after his first cow's-milk formula, repetitive profuse vomiting, pale, limp and lethargic, no urticaria or wheeze Intravenous fluid resuscitationfood protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome is non-IgE, so epinephrine does nothing

Next step7 of 10 9 mo F, hives and wheezing within 15 minutes of her first scrambled egg · Intramuscular epinephrineHives with wheeze within minutes of a food is anaphylaxis: intramuscular epinephrine. · Intravenous fluid bolusFluids alone are the FPIES answer, vomiting hours later with no hives. · Oral antihistamine and observationAntihistamines ease hives but do not treat wheeze or shock. 9 mo F, hives and wheezing within 15 minutes of her first scrambled egg Intramuscular epinephrineIgE-mediated food allergy, strict avoidance and allergist referral

Next step8 of 10 6 yo M, viral gastroenteritis 10 days ago that was improving, now watery diarrhea and bloating since milk was reintroduced, afebrile, no vomiting · Empiric metronidazoleMetronidazole treats giardiasis; there is no infection to treat here. · Stool ova and parasite testingOva and parasite testing is a workup; diarrhea that tracks dairy after a resolving illness needs only a lactose-free trial. · Temporary lactose avoidance, then reintroduceDiarrhea and bloating when milk returns after gastroenteritis is secondary lactase deficiency: a lactose-free spell, then reintroduce. 6 yo M, viral gastroenteritis 10 days ago that was improving, now watery diarrhea and bloating since milk was reintroduced, afebrile, no vomiting Temporary lactose avoidance, then reintroducesecondary lactase deficiency needs no workup

Mechanism9 of 10 5 yo F, diarrhea after a resolving gastroenteritis that stops when she fasts, acidic stool pH, raised stool osmotic gap · Transient loss of brush-border lactaseGastroenteritis can strip brush-border lactase; unabsorbed lactose gives osmotic, acidic diarrhea that stops with fasting. · Clostridioides difficile colitisClostridioides difficile colitis follows antibiotic exposure, and inflammatory diarrhea does not stop with fasting. · Giardia lamblia infectionGiardiasis is an active infection; this diarrhea tracks dairy and stops with fasting, the osmotic pattern. 5 yo F, diarrhea after a resolving gastroenteritis that stops when she fasts, acidic stool pH, raised stool osmotic gap Transient loss of brush-border lactasecolonic bacteria ferment the unabsorbed lactose

Next step10 of 10 5-day-old born at 32 weeks, bilious and coffee-grounds emesis, distended tender abdomen, pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal x-ray · Blood cultures and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics with bowel restA preterm infant with pneumatosis intestinalis has necrotizing enterocolitis: bowel rest, blood cultures and broad IV antibiotics. · Immediate exploratory laparotomySurgery waits for perforation or failure of medical therapy. · Continue breast milk feeds and observeFeeds stop: bowel rest is the first measure. 5-day-old born at 32 weeks, bilious and coffee-grounds emesis, distended tender abdomen, pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal x-ray Blood cultures and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics with bowel restnecrotizing enterocolitis

Reassurance or an elimination trial fits only an infant who is well-appearing and thriving. Lethargy, dehydration or profuse vomiting hours after a food is FPIES; hives or wheeze within minutes is IgE-mediated allergy; a preterm infant with distension and bloody stool has necrotizing enterocolitis. Fever or vomiting after gastroenteritis does not fit secondary lactase deficiency and needs a workup. A laxative or suppository is wrong for dyschezia; it fits only a hard stool.

Dyschezia is a coordination problem: the infant pushes before learning to relax the anal sphincter, and the muscles that help a bowel movement develop gradually FPIAP and FPIES are both reactions not mediated by IgE: FPIAP leaves the infant well and settles by 12 months, FPIES makes the infant ill hours after the food Only IgE-mediated reactions get epinephrine Secondary lactase deficiency is osmotic: it stops with fasting, the stool is acidic, and celiac disease can strip the brush border too

Constipation in a Childcovers hard stools and the withholding cycle once the stool itself is hard The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infantcovers necrotizing enterocolitis beside malrotation with volvulus and intussusception GI Bleeding in a Childcovers bleeding past infancy, the anal fissure among it Feeding an Infant or Toddlercovers when cow's milk starts, at 12 months, and why it waits Constipation in a Child covers hard stools and the withholding cycle once the stool itself is hard. The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers necrotizing enterocolitis beside malrotation with volvulus and intussusception. GI Bleeding in a Child covers bleeding past infancy, the anal fissure among it. Feeding an Infant or Toddler covers when cow's milk starts, at 12 months, and why it waits.
In a thriving child with worried parents, base management on the stool, the timing after the trigger, and the child's appearance. Reassure or eliminate the trigger before testing.

Uniform-answer doubtReassurance feels like doing nothing, but for dyschezia every active option is a named wrong answer. Class-vs-memberSoy formula removes cow's milk, but soy protein cross-reacts. True-fact-wrong-slotEpinephrine treats IgE-mediated food allergy; FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome) vomiting hours later is non-IgE and needs fluids. Sequencing trapIn a well child whose diarrhea followed dairy, the lactose-free trial comes before any stool workup.

briefs.title: Feeding an Infant or Toddler
briefs.sub: the feeding ladder by age · the toddler who refuses food · eosinophilic esophagitisIs the child well and due for the next age-gated step, or refusing a texture, a food group, or eating altogether?
blocks: the feeding ladder by age · the toddler who refuses food · eosinophilic esophagitisIs the child well and due for the next age-gated step, or refusing a texture, a food group, or eating altogether?

A well infant: read the age, since each step has a gate. Breast milk or formula alone to about 6 months, solids at about 6 months, whole cow's milk at 12 months. A child who refuses food: plot weight and height first, then name the pattern: texture (the esophagus), food group (gluten: celiac disease) or appetite (systemic disease). An atopic toddler on purees only with a normal swallow study needs endoscopy with esophageal biopsy; a count of 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, with other causes excluded, makes it eosinophilic esophagitis.
Iron leads the first solids because fetal stores run low at 4 to 6 months; cow's milk is poor in iron, blocks its absorption and can bleed occultly, so it waits for the first birthday.

The feeding ladder Age Feed Advance when 0 to 6 months Breast milk or formula only. Breastfed or partly breastfed: vitamin D 400 IU (international units) daily from the first days through the first year, against rickets. Breastfed: from 4 months, iron 1 mg/kg a day. About 6 months, once ready: sits with support, holds the head steady, has lost the tongue-thrust (extrusion) reflex, wants food About 6 months Iron-rich foods first (fortified cereal, pureed meat), then pureed vegetables and fruit, adding one new food every 3 to 5 days. Supplemental iron stops once iron-rich foods are in. Sits alone; the grasp moves from raking toward pincer 8 to 9 months Soft foods to pick up, lumpier textures, a cup, feeding themselves First birthday 12 months Whole cow's milk, about 16 oz a day and always under 24 oz a day; family foods; bottle traded for a cup Why wholeMilk fat supports myelination through the second year. Age 2: reduced-fat milk
Hold until 12 months Food Why Whole cow's milk Low in iron, blocks absorption, occult gut bleeding: iron deficiency Honey Botulinum spores: infant botulism

Fruit juice also waits until 12 months. Allergenic foods are not delayed: offer them as solids begin, at about 4 to 6 months when risk is low. With severe eczema or egg allergy (high risk), test for allergy first, then start peanut at 4 to 6 months.

Act now Finding Action Food stuck, drooling, cannot swallow saliva Food impaction: urgent endoscopy. Coughing and choking with most feeds, or repeated pneumonias Aspiration risk: video swallow study. Infant with constipation, then ptosis and a floppy head, after honey or soil exposure Infant botulism: human botulism immune globulin. Weight percentile falling while height holds A caloric deficit: work it up now rather than calling it picky eating.

Why the child stops advancing Cause Decides it Next best step Eosinophilic esophagitis Atopic child, often young; toddler refuses solids, school age has pain and vomiting, adolescent has dysphagia or impaction. Endoscopy with esophageal biopsy. Gastroesophageal reflux disease Reflux symptoms; suspect eosinophilic esophagitis when acid suppression fails. Biopsy if symptoms persist on acid suppression. Oropharyngeal dysphagia Coughing and choking with feeds; aspiration pneumonias. Obtain a video swallow study. Anatomic obstruction (stricture, ring, vascular ring) Sudden onset, or past caustic ingestion or reflux. Obtain an esophagram or endoscopy. Celiac disease Refuses gluten foods only (bread, pasta); diarrhea or constipation, pain, distension. Send tissue transglutaminase IgA (immunoglobulin A) with total IgA. Behavioral feeding disorder, such as avoidant restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) Avoids foods for texture or other sensory features; developmental delay or autism spectrum; weight loss; normal endoscopy. Feeding therapy once the esophagus is cleared. Iron deficiency, often from excess cow's milk Toddler drinking over 24 oz of milk a day and eating little else; pale. Cut milk to under 24 oz a day and start oral iron. Systemic or metabolic disease Appetite changed: big appetite with tachycardia and goiter (hyperthyroidism); poor appetite with a palpable mass. Look for the systemic cause and test for it.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any child refusing food → Weight and height on the growth chart Percentiles hold, no sign of disease Reassure and guide the family Weight falls, height holds Caloric deficit: name the pattern, then test Targeted tests TestResultMeans Coughing and choking with feeds, or textures refused → Video swallow study Abnormal Oropharyngeal dysphagia Normal The lesion is below the pharynx: endoscopy next, no repeat study Gluten foods refused, with diarrhea or distension → Tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA Positive Celiac disease; confirming it is not covered by this page Sudden onset, or past caustic ingestion or reflux → Esophagram Stricture or ring Anatomic obstruction Appetite lost, or increased with poor gain → Examination and tests for a systemic cause Big appetite, tachycardia, goiter Hyperthyroidism Anorexia, palpable mass Abdominal US first, then CT or MRI, as for Wilms tumor Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Atopic child refusing textures, normal swallow study → Endoscopy with esophageal biopsy Eosinophils at 15 or more per high-power field, other causes excluded Eosinophilic esophagitis; rings and furrows may show Normal biopsies Behavioral feeding disorder: feeding therapy SkipAllergy skin testing to make the diagnosis: it shows IgE (immunoglobulin E) sensitization only. A proton pump inhibitor trial in place of biopsy: no longer a diagnostic step.

Treatment by cause Cause Treat Eosinophilic esophagitis First line, any of three: a proton pump inhibitor, a swallowed topical glucocorticoid (fluticasone, budesonide) or an elimination diet; about half do not respond to acid suppression. Careful dilation may be needed for a significant stricture. After biopsy, skin testing may help pick foods to remove, though its accuracy is limited. In practiceThe Merck Sharp and Dohme (MSD) Manual notes that in children a proton pump inhibitor is often preferred when diet fails, and that dupilumab, from age 1 and at least 15 kg, is kept for disease that fails other drugs. Food impaction Urgent endoscopy. Behavioral cause, endoscopy normal Feeding therapy. Iron deficiency, often from cow's milk Milk under 24 oz a day plus oral iron.
Pause point Atopic toddler refuses every texture after a normal swallow study Offered: allergy skin testing or celiac serology Neither decides it → The biopsy decides it

briefs.title: Right Lower Quadrant Pain
briefs.sub: appendix, ileocecum, or neither · Campylobacter and Yersinia · appendix-sparing imaging · when to treat CampylobacterIs there profuse mucoid diarrhea, and is there a sick contact?
blocks: appendix, ileocecum, or neither · Campylobacter and Yersinia · appendix-sparing imaging · when to treat CampylobacterIs there profuse mucoid diarrhea, and is there a sick contact?

Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness and a neutrophil leukocytosis fit appendicitis and infectious ileocecitis alike and decide nothing. Profuse mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact points to infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) from Campylobacter or Yersinia: supportive care, no surgery. Appendicitis is periumbilical pain that settles at the McBurney point, with anorexia, vomiting and little or no diarrhea: surgical consultation, with imaging before the operation (US first in a child, CT otherwise). In practiceClinical references treat the classic picture as a clinical diagnosis, because delaying surgery for imaging only raises the risk of perforation; the board cards image first. In an adolescent girl, a pregnancy test comes first: ectopic pregnancy is often mistaken for appendicitis.

Campylobacter and Yersinia favor the ileocecum, and Yersinia also inflames the mesenteric nodes (mesenteric adenitis); imaging shows ileocecal inflammation with a normal appendix. Campylobacter can begin in the jejunum and then reach the ileum and cecum, so its pain can migrate like appendicitis. In children, appendicitis follows obstruction of the lumen, usually by lymphoid hyperplasia. Diarrhea in appendicitisBowel movements usually slow or stop in appendicitis; when diarrhea is present, suspect a retrocecal appendix.

Act now Finding Points to Action Rebound tenderness, guarding or rigidity Peritonitis from a ruptured appendix Surgical consultation now; IV fluids and a third-generation cephalosporin before appendectomy. Adolescent girl with a positive pregnancy test Ectopic pregnancy Work up ectopic pregnancy before anything else. Sudden, severe pain in a girl, usually with vomiting Adnexal (ovarian) torsion Pelvic US with Doppler and immediate surgery to save the ovary. Bloody diarrhea with little fever in a child E. coli O157:H7 No antibiotics; isotonic IV fluids, which may limit kidney injury; watch for hemolytic uremic syndrome.

Right lower quadrant pain in a young patient Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis): Campylobacter, Yersinia Profuse mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact, with fever, right lower quadrant pain and leukocytosis; Campylobacter after undercooked poultry or a puppy, Yersinia after pork or unpasteurized milk, often in toddlers; puppies carry both. Supportive care; a stool culture or nucleic acid amplification test names the organism. Acute appendicitis Periumbilical pain moving to the McBurney point, anorexia, vomiting; little or no diarrhea, no sick contact; rebound once it ruptures. Surgical consultation and imaging (US first in a child); appendectomy. E. coli O157:H7 Undercooked beef or an outbreak; bloody stool within 1 to 3 days; fever above 38.5 °C is rare. No antibiotics; watch for hemolytic uremic syndrome. Norovirus Outbreak with prominent vomiting; watery stools that rarely contain mucus or blood; normal white blood cell count. Supportive care. Ectopic pregnancy Adolescent girl with a positive pregnancy test; often mistaken for appendicitis. Order the ectopic workup before anything else. Adnexal torsion Girl with sudden, severe pain, usually with vomiting; an enlarged ovary; decreased or absent Doppler flow supports the diagnosis. Immediate surgery to untwist the ovary. Crohn ileitis Chronic, relapsing pain, weight loss, perianal disease; the terminal ileum is its usual site. Colonoscopy with ileal intubation and biopsy. Cecal diverticulitis Right-sided diverticular inflammation in an adult; exceedingly rare at 17; mild or no diarrhea. Exclude it by age; order the workup for the other rows.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any adolescent girl with right lower quadrant pain → Pregnancy test (human chorionic gonadotropin, hCG) Positive Ectopic pregnancy until excluded Negative Go on to the examination and the stool history Fever with right lower quadrant tenderness → CBC Neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis Fits appendicitis and ileocecitis alike; decides nothing Targeted tests TestResultMeans Suspected appendicitis, or a diagnosis still unclear after examination → US in a child; CT otherwise Inflamed appendix Appendicitis: surgery (treatment by cause below) Ileocecal inflammation, enlarged mesenteric nodes, normal appendix Infectious ileocecitis: no surgery A girl with sudden, severe pain, usually with vomiting → Pelvic US with Doppler Enlarged ovary; decreased or absent flow supports it Adnexal torsion (treatment by cause below) Diarrhea with right lower quadrant pain, or a day-care outbreak → Stool culture or nucleic acid amplification test Campylobacter or Yersinia Names the organism; a susceptibility report by itself does not justify treatment Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Months of pain, weight loss or perianal disease → Colonoscopy with ileal intubation Chronic ileal inflammation on biopsy Crohn ileitis SkipDiagnostic laparoscopy when imaging can decide; empiric antibiotics for a mild diarrheal illness; colonoscopy for a few days of acute illness with a sick contact.

Treatment by cause Cause First line When it changes Campylobacter Supportive care with rehydration; usually self-limited within 7 days. Beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fever, pregnancy, immunocompromise or old age: azithromycin; with resistance, an agent the susceptibility panel shows is active (amoxicillin in the practice question below); avoid doxycycline under age 8 when another agent covers the organism. Yersinia Supportive care; self-limited. Septic complications: a third-generation cephalosporin, a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, by susceptibility. Appendicitis IV third-generation cephalosporin, then appendectomy. Perforated: continue the antibiotic after surgery, for 4 days. Pain for 5 days or more with a contained abscess: bowel rest, IV fluids and antibiotics, then interval appendectomy at 6 to 8 weeks. Adnexal torsion Immediate laparoscopy to untwist the ovary and try to restore its blood flow. Surgery is not delayed: suspicion alone is enough to operate.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step A dozen mucus-laden stools in a day with fever, and a sibling or day-care contact with the same illness Infectious ileocecitis, which appendicitis cannot explain Supportive care. Pork, unpasteurized milk or a puppy in a toddler (a puppy fits Campylobacter too) Yersinia Supportive care. Migratory pain with profuse diarrhea Campylobacter spreading from the jejunum to the ileocecum Supportive care; the migration alone is no reason to operate. A susceptibility panel in a mild, improving child The susceptibility panel is not an indication Symptomatic care only. Diarrhea with otherwise classic appendicitis signs A retrocecal appendix Image before setting appendicitis aside.

Pause point Migratory right lower quadrant pain Pulled by the migratory pain Profuse diarrhea or a sick contact → Infectious ileocecitis, which needs no surgery Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness and leukocytosis are shared.

That 6 year old with suspected Shiga toxin producing E coli; which intervention should be withheld Empiric antibioticsRisk of precipitating hemolytic uremic syndrome

Two weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis Reactive arthritisThe second named sequela

Next step12 of 13 6 yo with Campylobacter coli enteritis now on day 9 with bloody stools; ciprofloxacin resistant, erythromycin intermediate, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive · LevofloxacinLevofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone, and this isolate is ciprofloxacin resistant. · DoxycyclineDoxycycline stains teeth under 8 when another agent covers the organism. · AmoxicillinBloody stools on day 9 meet the criteria; ampicillin-sensitive, so amoxicillin, which is safe under 8. 6 yo with Campylobacter coli enteritis now on day 9 with bloody stools; ciprofloxacin resistant, erythromycin intermediate, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive Amoxicillinsensitive, and safe under 8

Next step13 of 13 4 yo in day care with high fever, bloody diarrhea and a brief generalized seizure; stool grows Shigella · AzithromycinHigh fever, bloody diarrhea and a seizure are severe Shigella: azithromycin shortens illness and shedding. · Symptomatic care onlySevere Shigella in a child is treated, not left to resolve. · LoperamideLoperamide slows the stool but does not clear Shigella. 4 yo in day care with high fever, bloody diarrhea and a brief generalized seizure; stool grows Shigella Azithromycintreating shortens illness and spread

A contact's bloody stools can pull toward Shiga toxin E. coli in a patient whose own stool has no blood: a contact's findings describe the exposure, not this patient's illness. Migratory pain is also explained by Campylobacter spread, so it does not confirm appendicitis.

Campylobacter and Yersinia: treated by cause Shiga toxin-producing E. coli: bloody diarrhea with little fever; no antibiotics, which can raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome Shigella: high fever with mucoid, bloody diarrhea, sometimes a seizure; antibiotics such as azithromycin shorten illness and shedding Clostridioides difficile: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin first line

Appendicitis explains neither a dozen mucoid stools nor a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia explains both. Profuse diarrhea or a sick contact should halt a planned appendectomy for a second look. In pseudoappendicitis, imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix. Campylobacter can begin in the jejunum, so its pain may migrate like appendicitis. The two tested Campylobacter sequelae are Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis.

Acute Kidney Injury in a Childcovers hemolytic uremic syndrome from the renal side, where the E. coli O157:H7 branch ends Anemia with Thrombocytopeniacovers hemolytic uremic syndrome as hemolysis with low platelets Infectious Diarrheacovers the organism by exposure. Ask: whose stool was bloody, and how many days into the illness? Acute Kidney Injury in a Child covers hemolytic uremic syndrome from the renal side, where the E. coli O157:H7 branch ends. Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers hemolytic uremic syndrome as hemolysis with low platelets. Infectious Diarrhea covers the organism by exposure. Ask: whose stool was bloody, and how many days into the illness?
When a presentation fits a textbook script, look for the finding the script cannot explain, such as a symptom the disease does not produce or an exposure it cannot have.

Salient decoyAcute appendicitis is not associated with profuse watery then mucoid diarrhea and cannot explain a sibling with the same illness. There are no peritoneal signs. True-fact-wrong-slotE. coli O157:H7 causes hematochezia in the patient within 1 to 3 days, and fever above 38.5 °C rarely occurs. Bloody stools in a contact are not this patient's. Class-vs-memberNorovirus gives watery stools that rarely contain mucus, a normal white blood cell count, and prominent vomiting. Unchecked attributeCecal diverticulitis is exceedingly rare at this age and does not produce profuse mucoid diarrhea. Test-overrides-findingsA susceptibility panel invites treatment, but a mild, improving, afebrile child is treated by the clinical picture, not the culture report.

briefs.title: Constipation in a Child
briefs.sub: withholding cycle · alarm signs · impacted or not · oral laxative before any rectal treatment · maintenance for monthsIs growth normal and the examination benign, and is there stool in the rectum?
blocks: withholding cycle · alarm signs · impacted or not · oral laxative before any rectal treatment · maintenance for monthsIs growth normal and the examination benign, and is there stool in the rectum?

Functional constipation, the most common cause in children (about 95%), is hard, painful stools starting at a transition (solid food and cow's milk, toilet training, school entry) in a child with normal growth and examination: no tests unless treatment fails. First step: an oral osmotic laxative (polyethylene glycol) with more water and fiber, cow's milk kept under 24 oz daily and time on the toilet after meals; not an enema or a radiograph. An alarm sign (meconium delayed beyond 48 hours, poor growth, vomiting or fever, a displaced anus or sacral tuft, abnormal gait or reflexes) points to an organic cause: the test follows the sign.

A painful stool makes the child tighten the external sphincter and hold; the rectum stretches around the retained stool, the urge fades and the stool hardens, so the next one hurts more. A fissure from hard stool feeds the same cycle.

Act now Finding Points to Action Vomiting, severe distension and pain Severe impaction that mimics obstruction Abdominal radiograph. Newborn with no meconium by 48 hours, a distended abdomen and bilious vomiting Hirschsprung disease Contrast enema, then suction rectal biopsy (The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers it). Infant with constipation, poor suck, ptosis and a floppy head Infant botulism A clinical diagnosis: a botulinum toxin assay or electromyography supports it; ask about honey before age 12 months. Abnormal gait or leg reflexes, or new urinary incontinence Spinal cord involvement, such as a tethered cord Spinal MRI.

Constipation in a child Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Functional constipation Onset at a transition; withholding, painful hard stools, an anal fissure; normal growth and examination. Start an oral osmotic laxative and diet changes. Impaction with overflow incontinence (encopresis) Soiling that looks like diarrhea: soft stool leaks around a hard mass, often palpable; encopresis is not diagnosed before age 4. Clear the impaction, then give a daily maintenance laxative. Excess cow's milk intake Over 24 oz a day with little else eaten; often pallor from iron deficiency. Cut milk to under 24 oz a day; check for iron deficiency. Hirschsprung disease Usually declares as a newborn: meconium delayed beyond 48 hours; distension, ribbon stools, poor growth; a tight anal canal with explosive stool (squirt sign) and an empty rectum. Contrast enema or anorectal manometry, then suction rectal biopsy. Congenital hypothyroidism Poor linear growth, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, a large fontanelle. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroxine. Occult spinal dysraphism or tethered cord Sacral hair tuft or pit, a displaced anus, urinary incontinence, leg or gait findings; a shallow dimple with no tuft is normal. Spinal MRI. Celiac disease Falling weight percentile, distension, onset after wheat enters the diet. Tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibody.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Constipation in a child → History, growth chart, and abdominal, anal and perineal examination No alarm sign Functional constipation: treat (ladder below); no tests An alarm sign Organic cause: order the test that sign points to Targeted tests TestResultMeans Meconium delayed beyond 48 hours, explosive stool on rectal examination, or constipation persisting despite standard therapy → Anorectal manometry or contrast enema Absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex, or a transition zone Hirschsprung disease likely: suction rectal biopsy next Normal Functional: keep up maintenance and work on withholding Poor growth → Thyroid-stimulating hormone and tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibody Abnormal Hypothyroidism or celiac disease Sacral tuft or pit, a displaced anus, urinary or gait findings → Spinal MRI Abnormal result Spinal dysraphism Severe pain and vomiting → Abdominal radiograph Large stool load without obstruction Severe impaction: disimpact Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Abnormal result → Suction rectal biopsy Absent ganglion cells Hirschsprung disease: resect the aganglionic segment SkipAbdominal radiograph, enema or manometry for an untreated child with no alarm sign: no test is needed.

1 First lineNo impaction Oral osmotic laxative (polyethylene glycol) plus more water and fiber, cow's milk kept under 24 oz daily, and time on the toilet after meals. Juice and toiletingDiluted prune or apple juice works as an osmotic laxative through its sorbitol, in infants as well; a child midway through toilet training can take a break from it until the constipation resolves. 2 ImpactedStool mass or overflow soiling Disimpact first: high-dose oral polyethylene glycol, or an enema; with an anal fissure go oral, because an enema adds rectal trauma. InfantsInfants usually need no more than a glycerin suppository when intervention is needed. 3 MaintenanceAfter clearing, always A daily osmotic laxative long term, so the stretched rectum can return to size and the child unlearns withholding; restart it on relapse. 4 RefractoryPersisting despite adequate therapy Anorectal manometry or contrast enema (workup above); pediatric gastroenterology if abnormal. In practiceNot the board answer: the Merck Manual also orders an abdominal radiograph when a child does not respond to treatment.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Anal fissure A complication that fits functional constipation Keep to the oral route; disimpact by mouth if needed. Soiling mistaken for diarrhea Overflow around an impaction Clear the impaction, then give maintenance; the soiling is not deliberate. Recurrent urinary tract infections or bedwetting A full rectum pressing on the bladder Treat the constipation. Exactly 24 oz of milk a day At the limit: trim it, do not stop it Trim milk to under 24 oz, add fiber and water; do not stop milk. Shallow sacral dimple with no hair tuft A normal finding Reassure; skip spinal imaging. A normal first stool after birth A structural cause is unlikely Treat as functional when growth and examination are normal.
Pause point Constipated child with a fissure or a benign abdomen Offered: a rectal enema or a radiograph No alarm sign → An oral osmotic laxative An alarm sign picks the one test it points to.

Next step1 of 11 3 yo M with hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, a nontender abdomen and an anal fissure · Initiate an oral osmotic laxativeNo alarm sign and no treatment yet: an oral osmotic laxative makes the next stool painless. · Obtain an abdominal radiographA radiograph does not change treatment for an untreated child with a benign abdomen. · Administer a rectal enemaThere is no impaction, and the anal fissure makes the rectal route harmful. 3 yo M with hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, a nontender abdomen and an anal fissure Initiate an oral osmotic laxativeFunctional constipation

Next step2 of 11 6 yo M with involuntary soiling of his underwear and a palpable suprapubic stool mass, without an anal fissure · Maintenance laxative aloneMaintenance alone leaves the impaction in place, so the leakage goes on. · Anorectal manometryManometry is for constipation persisting despite standard therapy, not yet tried here. · Disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapySoiling with a palpable stool mass is overflow around an impaction: clear it, then maintain. 6 yo M with involuntary soiling of his underwear and a palpable suprapubic stool mass, without an anal fissure Disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapyImpaction with overflow incontinence

Next step3 of 11 4 yo F with fecal impaction requiring disimpaction who has a painful anal fissure on examination · Rectal enemaAn enema adds rectal trauma to the fissure. · Glycerin suppositoryA glycerin suppository is still rectal, and it is the measure for infants. · High-dose oral polyethylene glycolWith an anal fissure, disimpact by mouth: high-dose oral polyethylene glycol. 4 yo F with fecal impaction requiring disimpaction who has a painful anal fissure on examination High-dose oral polyethylene glycolEnemas cause further rectal trauma
