Next step5 of 11 3 yo F with constipation, daytime urinary incontinence and a tuft of hair over the sacrum · Obtain an abdominal radiographAn abdominal radiograph does not show the spinal cord. · Initiate an oral osmotic laxativeA laxative treats functional constipation; this alarm sign needs imaging first. · Magnetic resonance imaging of the spineA sacral hair tuft with urinary incontinence points to occult dysraphism: spinal MRI. 3 yo F with constipation, daytime urinary incontinence and a tuft of hair over the sacrum Magnetic resonance imaging of the spineOccult spinal dysraphism

Next step6 of 11 5 yo M whose constipation persists after 3 months of adequate laxative and dietary therapy, with normal growth and examination · Rectal enemaAn enema treats an impaction, and none is described. · Increase the laxative dose and continueRaising the dose of a treatment that has already failed delays the workup. · Anorectal manometryConstipation persisting despite adequate laxative and diet earns anorectal manometry to look for Hirschsprung disease. 5 yo M whose constipation persists after 3 months of adequate laxative and dietary therapy, with normal growth and examination Anorectal manometryRefractory to standard therapy

Diagnosis7 of 11 Newborn who first passed meconium at 60 hours, now with ribbon-like stools, abdominal distension and poor weight gain · Functional constipationFunctional constipation starts at a transition in a thriving child, after a normal first stool. · Hirschsprung diseaseMeconium after 48 hours, ribbon stools, distension and poor weight gain are Hirschsprung disease. · Congenital hypothyroidismCongenital hypothyroidism brings prolonged jaundice, hypotonia and a large fontanelle. Newborn who first passed meconium at 60 hours, now with ribbon-like stools, abdominal distension and poor weight gain Hirschsprung diseaseContrast enema or manometry, then rectal suction biopsy

Diagnosis8 of 11 8-month-old with constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia and a large anterior fontanelle · Congenital hypothyroidismProlonged jaundice, hypotonia and a large fontanelle with constipation are congenital hypothyroidism. · Hirschsprung diseaseHirschsprung disease declares with delayed meconium and distension, not jaundice and hypotonia. · Functional constipationFunctional constipation comes with normal growth and examination. 8-month-old with constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia and a large anterior fontanelle Congenital hypothyroidismCheck the TSH

Mechanism9 of 11 Why one painful bowel movement can produce weeks of worsening constipation in a toddler · Aganglionosis of the distal rectumAganglionosis is Hirschsprung disease, which usually declares at birth with delayed meconium. · Reduced colonic smooth muscle contractility from cow's-milk proteinCow's milk slows transit by crowding out fiber; withholding drives the cycle. · Withholding desiccates stool in the rectumHolding lets the rectum stretch and the stool harden, so the next stool hurts more. Why one painful bowel movement can produce weeks of worsening constipation in a toddler Withholding desiccates stool in the rectumthe next bowel movement hurts more and withholding continues; the cycle is the disease

Avoid10 of 11 3 yo M with functional constipation who drinks 24 oz of cow's milk daily; which management is inappropriate · Discontinuing cow's milk entirely24 oz is at the limit: trim milk to under 24 oz a day rather than stop it. · Initiating an oral osmotic laxativeAn oral osmotic laxative is first line, so it is appropriate. · Increasing dietary fiber and waterMore fiber and water is first-line care, so it is appropriate. 3 yo M with functional constipation who drinks 24 oz of cow's milk daily; which management is inappropriate Discontinuing cow's milk entirelyMilk is trimmed to under 24 oz a day, not stopped

Next step11 of 11 15-month-old with constipation since infancy refractory to dietary changes, thin caliber stools, distended abdomen, explosive stool and gas on rectal exam · Begin polyethylene glycolA laxative treats functional constipation; this alarm picture needs testing first. · Contrast enemaThin stools since infancy with explosive stool on rectal examination point to Hirschsprung disease: a contrast enema shows the transition zone. · Replace dairy with soy productsExplosive stool on rectal examination is the Hirschsprung sign, not a milk protein problem. 15-month-old with constipation since infancy refractory to dietary changes, thin caliber stools, distended abdomen, explosive stool and gas on rectal exam Contrast enemaHirschsprung disease

Refusing fruit and a high milk volume suggest a dietary cause, but milk at 24 oz is at the limit, not above it: trim it to under 24 oz and add fiber and water; do not stop it. A firm, mildly distended abdomen is not an alarm sign; severe distension with pain and vomiting is the picture that gets a radiograph, and it is usually a severe impaction rather than another disease. The anal fissure is an expected complication of functional constipation, not evidence of another diagnosis; its only effect on management is to rule out the rectal route.

A growing child with painful hard stools and a normal examination gets an oral osmotic laxative, not a rectal procedure or imaging. Childhood constipation is a behavioral cycle with a mechanical consequence: the laxative makes stools painless so the child stops withholding, and maintenance continues long after the first soft stool. The three common triggers are solid food and cow's milk, toilet training, and school entry; onset at one of them supports the diagnosis. An anal fissure is a complication of constipation, not a competing diagnosis, and is the reason to disimpact by mouth rather than by rectum. Hirschsprung disease presents with meconium delayed beyond 48 hours and explosive stool on rectal examination; a child whose first stool came normally is unlikely to have a structural cause. Poor growth is a clue to an organic cause; a child tracking a percentile with a normal examination likely has functional disease. Enuresis (bedwetting) and urinary tract infections are complications of constipation, so in a child with both, treat the bowel first.

Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adultcovers the adult side: fecal impaction in an older adult and when new constipation needs a colonoscopy Stool Changes in a Well Infantcovers straining with a soft stool in an infant, which needs no laxative Spinal Dysraphismcovers the hair tuft, lipoma or dimple above the gluteal cleft and the spinal imaging that follows The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infantcovers Hirschsprung disease declared in the newborn, with no meconium by 48 hours Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult covers the adult side: fecal impaction in an older adult and when new constipation needs a colonoscopy. Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers straining with a soft stool in an infant, which needs no laxative. Spinal Dysraphism covers the hair tuft, lipoma or dimple above the gluteal cleft and the spinal imaging that follows. The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers Hirschsprung disease declared in the newborn, with no meconium by 48 hours.

With no alarm signs and a normal examination, treat; investigate only when an alarm sign is present. A complication of the diagnosis supports it but can still change management, as an anal fissure rules out the rectal route.

Unchecked attributeDiscontinue milk: 24 oz is at the limit (keep it under 24 oz a day), so trim it rather than stop it Sequencing trapObtain abdominal radiograph: The film is for severe impaction that mimics obstruction, with pain and vomiting; a nontender, benign abdomen does not need it Salient decoyAdminister rectal enema: With no impaction there is nothing to disimpact, and an anal fissure makes the rectal route actively harmful Sequencing trapObtain anorectal manometry: Reserved for constipation that persists despite standard therapy or an alarm sign; not before therapy has been tried when no alarm sign is present

briefs.title: Recurrent Vomiting in a Child
briefs.sub: stereotyped episodes, well in between · the migraine link · dental erosion is not purging · findings that argue against itAre the episodes identical and self-limited, and is the child well and growing between them?
blocks: stereotyped episodes, well in between · the migraine link · dental erosion is not purging · findings that argue against itAre the episodes identical and self-limited, and is the child well and growing between them?

Cyclic vomiting syndrome is stereotyped, self-limited bouts of vomiting, often at about the same time each month, with the child entirely well and growing normally between them. Migraine in the child or the family often goes with it, and stress or infection often sets off a bout. It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion: the tests only rule out mimics. Bilious vomiting or an abnormal neurologic exam means act first; weight loss, fever or faltering growth points to another disease.

Worn enamel or erosive caries in a child who vomits often is acid damage from real, repeated vomiting. It does not mean purging unless there is bingeing, restriction or preoccupation with shape. Natural historyOnset averages age 5, and it tends to remit by adulthood. In practiceThe Merck Sharp and Dohme (MSD) Manual describes attacks at varying intervals; the board teaching times them at about the same time each month.

Act now Finding Points to Action Bilious (green) vomiting, which may come with a distended abdomen Malrotation with midgut volvulus, or another obstruction past the ampulla A surgical emergency: abdominal X-ray, then an upper GI series, as in a newborn (The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers it). Abnormal neurologic exam, a change in mental status or a focal deficit A brain mass or hydrocephalus Brain MRI before calling it cyclic vomiting.

Recurrent vomiting: what happens between the episodes Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Cyclic vomiting syndrome Entirely well and growing normally between stereotyped, self-limited bouts; often migraine in the child or family. No confirming test: exclude mimics, then treat by cause. Bulimia nervosa Binges, then compensates; overvalues body shape and weight; parotid swelling and enamel erosion at normal or slightly high weight. Refer for psychiatric assessment. Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome Bouts like cyclic vomiting with chronic cannabis use; relieved by hot showers or baths (the MSD Manual describes it in adults). Ask about cannabis; urine drug screen. Factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen syndrome by proxy) Inconsistent history, symptoms no one else witnesses; illness caused or fabricated by the caregiver. Notify child protective services. Gastroesophageal reflux disease Low-grade symptoms that persist between bouts; regurgitation and burning substernal pain rather than discrete bursts. Start a trial of acid suppression. Chronic pancreatitis Poor growth and diarrhea; epigastric tenderness on exam. Order pancreatic imaging and enzyme studies. Inflammatory bowel disease Weight loss and fever; diarrhea and a tender abdomen that persist between bouts. Order blood markers and a colonoscopy.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Mid-bout, vomiting repeatedly → Electrolytes, glucose and BUN Dehydration changes only Rehydrate; drawn during the bout, when urgent causes would show Targeted tests TestResultMeans An atypical pattern (bilious vomiting is a surgical emergency) → Upper GI contrast series Normal rotation Malrotation excluded Pain or tenderness that could be pancreatic, hepatobiliary or urinary → Lipase, liver enzymes and urinalysis Normal Pancreatitis, hepatobiliary and urinary causes excluded Abnormal neurologic exam → Brain MRI Mass or hydrocephalus An intracranial cause, not cyclic vomiting Chronic cannabis use, or relief in a hot shower → Urine drug screen Positive result Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome Weight loss, diarrhea or bleeding → Colonoscopy Mucosal inflammation Inflammatory bowel disease Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Stereotyped bouts, well between them, normal growth and neurologic exam → None: clinical diagnosis Mimics excluded Cyclic vomiting syndrome SkipUpper endoscopy with normal growth and no alarm features, which adds nothing; testing between bouts, when the results are normal anyway.

Treatment by cause Cause Treat Cyclic vomiting syndrome During a bout: IV fluids and an antiemetic; anti-migraine agents such as sumatriptan may help abort it. Between boutsAvoid its triggers, which are often stress or infection. Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome Stop cannabis, which ends it; antiemetics and supportive care for the bout. Factitious disorder imposed on another It is child abuse: notify child protective services.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Erosive caries Real, repeated vomiting, not purging Take a history for bingeing, restriction and shape concerns; with none, treat as cyclic vomiting. Worse at the start of the school year A stress trigger Treat as cyclic vomiting syndrome. Weight on the same percentile at each visit Normal growth: inflammatory bowel disease and chronic pancreatitis unlikely Do not order upper endoscopy. Relief in a hot shower Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome Ask about cannabis; urine drug screen.

Pause point Stereotyped vomiting bouts Erosive caries read as purging, or a well, growing child sent for endoscopy Self-limited bouts with complete wellness and normal growth between them → Cyclic vomiting syndrome The tests only rule out mimics.

Diagnosis1 of 6 10-year-old boy; a year of vomiting bouts lasting about 2 days each, roughly monthly; plays and eats normally between them; weight steady on his curve; mother has migraine; normal neurologic exam; worn enamel on the upper molars · Bulimia nervosaBulimia nervosa binges, then compensates, and overvalues body shape and weight. · Factitious disorder imposed on anotherFactitious disorder imposed on another has an inconsistent history and symptoms no one else witnesses. · Cyclic vomiting syndromeStereotyped, self-limited bouts with the child well and growing between them are cyclic vomiting syndrome. 10-year-old boy; a year of vomiting bouts lasting about 2 days each, roughly monthly; plays and eats normally between them; weight steady on his curve; mother has migraine; normal neurologic exam; worn enamel on the upper molars Cyclic vomiting syndromeA diagnosis of exclusion with predictable intervals

Mechanism2 of 6 The historical association that supports cyclic vomiting syndrome · A family history of peptic ulcer diseasePeptic ulcer disease in the family is not the history linked to cyclic vomiting; migraine is. · Recent travel or food exposureTravel or a food exposure suggests gastroenteritis: vomiting with diarrhea, not stereotyped bouts. · Personal or family history of migraineMigraine in the child or the family supports cyclic vomiting syndrome. The historical association that supports cyclic vomiting syndrome Personal or family history of migraineTriggers are often infection or stress

Next step3 of 6 Child with established cyclic vomiting syndrome presenting mid-episode, dehydrated · Psychiatric admissionPsychiatric care is for bulimia nervosa, with bingeing and preoccupation with shape and weight. · Intravenous rehydration with an antiemeticA bout of known cyclic vomiting with dehydration needs IV fluids and an antiemetic; sumatriptan may help abort it. · Upper endoscopy during the episodeUpper endoscopy adds nothing with normal growth and no alarm features. Child with established cyclic vomiting syndrome presenting mid-episode, dehydrated Intravenous rehydration with an antiemeticAbortive triptans may shorten the episode

Diagnosis4 of 6 Adolescent with self-induced vomiting after binge eating, preoccupied with body shape, normal weight · Gastroesophageal reflux diseaseGastroesophageal reflux disease brings regurgitation and substernal pain, not self-induced vomiting. · Bulimia nervosaSelf-induced vomiting after binges with preoccupation with body shape is bulimia nervosa. · Cyclic vomiting syndromeCyclic vomiting syndrome is stereotyped bouts with the child entirely well between them and no bingeing. Adolescent with self-induced vomiting after binge eating, preoccupied with body shape, normal weight Bulimia nervosaBingeing and compensatory behavior, not stereotyped episodes

Diagnosis5 of 6 Child with recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, poor growth and epigastric tenderness · Inflammatory bowel diseaseInflammatory bowel disease brings weight loss, fever and diarrhea with abdominal tenderness, not epigastric tenderness. · Chronic pancreatitisPoor growth and diarrhea with epigastric tenderness point to chronic pancreatitis. · Cyclic vomiting syndromeCyclic vomiting syndrome leaves the child entirely well and growing normally between bouts. Child with recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, poor growth and epigastric tenderness Chronic pancreatitisGrowth failure and tenderness, unlike the well-between-episodes pattern

Mechanism6 of 6 What the erosive dental caries in a child with recurrent vomiting indicates · An independent nutritional deficiencyThe erosion is acid damage from vomiting, not a sign of a nutritional deficiency. · Evidence that the vomiting is real and recurrentErosive caries show real, repeated acid exposure from vomiting, whatever its cause. · Proof of self-induced vomitingPurging needs bingeing, restriction or preoccupation with shape; erosion alone does not prove it. What the erosive dental caries in a child with recurrent vomiting indicates Evidence that the vomiting is real and recurrentIt supports the history rather than implying purging

Bilious vomiting or an abnormal neurologic exam: act first, not cyclic vomiting Weight loss, fever or faltering growth points to another disease, such as inflammatory bowel disease or chronic pancreatitis Laboratory tests are usually drawn during a bout, not between bouts

Symptom-free intervals: the bouts are stereotyped, often at about the same time each month, and the child is well between them Dental erosion shows repeated acid exposure, not its cause Migraine in the child or the family often goes with it As a diagnosis of exclusion, the workup looks for dangerous mimics

Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatmentcovers migraine and its treatment ladder Eating Disorderscovers bulimia nervosa, the purging that enamel erosion can suggest Substance Intoxication and Withdrawalcovers cannabis, whose hyperemesis is eased by hot showers The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infantcovers malrotation behind bilious vomiting Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment covers migraine and its treatment ladder. Eating Disorders covers bulimia nervosa, the purging that enamel erosion can suggest. Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal covers cannabis, whose hyperemesis is eased by hot showers. The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers malrotation behind bilious vomiting.
For episodic illness, ask how the patient is between episodes. Most of the diagnostic information comes from the interval between episodes.

Salient decoyDental erosion suggests purging, but this child has no bingeing, restriction or preoccupation with shape. Unchecked attributeNormal growth argues against inflammatory bowel disease and chronic pancreatitis.

briefs.title: GI Bleeding in a Child
briefs.sub: both scopes first · pertechnetate scan in a child · capsule endoscopy in an adult · visible Meckel bleedingHave both scopes come back negative, and is the patient a child or an adult?
blocks: both scopes first · pertechnetate scan in a child · capsule endoscopy in an adult · visible Meckel bleedingHave both scopes come back negative, and is the patient a child or an adult?

Occult GI bleeding is iron deficiency anemia with a positive stool occult blood test and no visible blood; at any age the first step is upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Both scopes clean: a child gets a technetium 99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan; an adult gets capsule endoscopy. A toddler with painless dark red or maroon stool and a soft, nontender abdomen goes straight to the pertechnetate scan; pain suggests a complication or another disease, and ultrasound comes first when intussusception is the concern.

A Meckel diverticulum is the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct left partly open, the most common congenital GI anomaly, and most never cause symptoms. Acid from its ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates the neighboring ileum, which bleeds. The scan images that mucosa rather than the blood, so it works between bleeds. Scan yieldThe scan may find the diverticulum in 85 to 97% of bleeding children; a diverticulum with no gastric mucosa does not show.

Act now Finding Points to Action Visible bleeding with unstable vital signs A brisk active bleed Resuscitate first (intravenous access, fluids, blood); then upper endoscopy for hematemesis or melena, and CT angiography for brisk hematochezia (as for adults); not a Meckel scan. Infant with bilious vomiting, a distended abdomen and bloody stool Midgut volvulus A surgical emergency: upper GI series if stable (The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers it).

Bleeding in a well child Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Meckel diverticulum Toddler, classically under 2 though any age is possible; painless dark red or maroon stool, or occult blood with iron deficiency; soft, nontender abdomen. Rule of 2sOften presents by age 2, shorter than 2 inches, 2 feet or less from the ileocecal valve; twice as common in boys. Pertechnetate scan; resect it once it has bled. Milk protein proctocolitis Infant, well, taking cow's milk protein, with painless blood-streaked stool; resolves by age 1. Remove cow's milk protein from the diet or formula. Juvenile polyp Child with rectal bleeding from a single rectal polyp, which may prolapse. Colonoscopy, which can remove it. Natural historyJuvenile polyps typically outgrow their blood supply and fall off during or after puberty; removal is needed only for bleeding that will not stop or for intussusception. Celiac disease Iron deficiency with negative occult blood and suspected malabsorption, not bleeding. Send tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A.

Bleeding with pain, diarrhea or fever Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Intussusception Most often under 2; bouts of severe colicky pain, often with vomiting, with the child well between them; currant jelly stool; a sausage-shaped mass is sometimes present; a Meckel diverticulum can be the lead point. Order abdominal US, then an air enema. Bacterial colitis Bloody diarrhea with crampy pain and fever. Send a stool culture. Inflammatory bowel disease Pain, diarrhea and weight loss. Send fecal calprotectin. Anal fissure Painful passage of a hard stool streaked with bright red blood. Examine the anus.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Pallor or tiredness in a child → CBC Microcytic anemia Iron deficiency: test the stool for blood Iron deficiency with no visible blood → Stool occult blood test Positive Occult GI bleeding: upper endoscopy and colonoscopy next Negative Bleeding unlikely: ask about excess cow's milk; tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A if malabsorption is suspected Targeted tests TestResultMeans Occult blood positive, any age → Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy Unremarkable, biopsies clean The source is in the small bowel, beyond both scopes Bouts of severe colicky pain, with or without bloody stool → Abdominal US Target sign Intussusception: an air enema confirms and reduces it; surgery if it fails or the bowel has perforated Bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and fever → Stool culture A pathogen grows Bacterial colitis A hard, painful stool streaked with bright red blood → Anal exam A fissure is seen Anal fissure Rectal bleeding in a well child with a polyp prolapsing at the anus → Colonoscopy A single juvenile polyp Can be removed during the same colonoscopy Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Both scopes clean in a child, or painless dark red stool in a toddler → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan Uptake by ectopic gastric mucosa Meckel diverticulum: surgical resection Both scopes clean in an adult → Capsule endoscopy Angiodysplasia, neoplasia or ulcer The adult small-bowel source; then CT or magnetic resonance enterography SkipCT angiography for occult bleeding, which is too slow to show; abdominal CT, which cannot tell the diverticulum from other bowel loops; upper endoscopy for dark red stool without hematemesis or black, sticky melena; fecal deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) testing, a screen for average-risk adults.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Dark red or maroon stool, with no hematemesis or black, sticky melena A lower source, in a toddler usually the small bowel Pertechnetate scan, not upper endoscopy. Goats or cattle at home Bacterial colitis only with bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and fever Skip the culture when the stool is formed and there is no fever. Past the first birthday Beyond milk protein proctocolitis Do not order a milk elimination trial. Iron deficiency with negative occult blood Often diet (excess cow's milk) or malabsorption, not bleeding Take a milk history; send tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A if malabsorption is suspected. Pain, vomiting or a mass with the bleed Intussusception first, or another painful complication of a Meckel diverticulum Order abdominal US first.

Pause point Toddler with painless maroon stool Offered as intussusception No colicky pain; soft, nontender abdomen → Meckel diverticulum: technetium 99m pertechnetate scan Pain changes the first test.

Workup1 of 11 10 year old with 2 months of exertional fatigue, pallor, hemoglobin 9.4 with mean corpuscular volume 74, stool positive for occult blood; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies are unremarkable · Tissue transglutaminase antibodiesCeliac disease causes iron deficiency by malabsorption; positive occult blood points to bleeding. · CT angiographyCT angiography needs brisk active bleeding; occult bleeding is too slow to show. · Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanBoth scopes clean in a child: the pertechnetate scan finds the ectopic gastric mucosa of a Meckel diverticulum. 10 year old with 2 months of exertional fatigue, pallor, hemoglobin 9.4 with mean corpuscular volume 74, stool positive for occult blood; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies are unremarkable Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanMeckel scan – it images ectopic gastric mucosa

Mechanism2 of 11 How a Meckel diverticulum causes occult bleeding · Ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acidAcid from ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates the adjacent ileum, which bleeds. · Venous congestion from a twisted mesenteryA twisted mesentery is midgut volvulus: bilious vomiting and an acute abdomen, not slow painless loss. · Autoimmune villous atrophyVillous atrophy is celiac disease, which causes iron deficiency without occult blood. How a Meckel diverticulum causes occult bleeding Ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acidUlcerating adjacent small bowel

Next step3 of 11 Child with iron deficiency anemia and a positive fecal occult blood test; the first step · Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanThe pertechnetate scan comes only after both scopes are clean. · Upper endoscopy and colonoscopyOccult bleeding at any age starts with upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. · Capsule endoscopyCapsule endoscopy is the adult small-bowel study, after both scopes are clean. Child with iron deficiency anemia and a positive fecal occult blood test; the first step Upper endoscopy and colonoscopyLocalize before reaching for small-bowel studies

Workup4 of 11 Adult with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy · Fecal DNA testingFecal DNA testing screens average-risk adults for colorectal neoplasia; it does not find a bleeding source. · Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanThe pertechnetate scan is the child branch, for a Meckel diverticulum. · Capsule endoscopyBoth scopes clean in an adult: capsule endoscopy looks for angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers. Adult with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy Capsule endoscopyAngiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers – the adult small-bowel causes

Diagnosis5 of 11 Child with painless hematochezia and no abdominal pain, age under 2 · Meckel diverticulumPainless hematochezia in a child under 2 is a Meckel diverticulum until proven otherwise. · Milk protein proctocolitisMilk protein proctocolitis is blood-streaked stool in an infant and is gone by age 1. · IntussusceptionIntussusception brings bouts of severe colicky pain, with or without bloody stool. Child with painless hematochezia and no abdominal pain, age under 2 Meckel diverticulumFailed closure of the vitelline duct

Avoid6 of 11 Child with slow occult blood loss and stable vital signs; which study is least likely to help · Capsule endoscopyCapsule endoscopy looks at the small-bowel lining directly and does not need active bleeding. · Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanThe pertechnetate scan images gastric mucosa, so it works between bleeds. · CT angiographyCT angiography needs brisk active bleeding; slow occult loss shows nothing. Child with slow occult blood loss and stable vital signs; which study is least likely to help CT angiographyIt needs brisk active bleeding to see anything

Diagnosis7 of 11 Child with microcytic anemia, chronic diarrhea and a negative fecal occult blood test · Celiac diseaseIron deficiency with diarrhea and negative occult blood is malabsorption: celiac disease. · Meckel diverticulumA Meckel diverticulum bleeds, so the occult blood would be positive. · Inflammatory bowel diseaseInflammatory bowel disease brings pain and weight loss and inflamed mucosa that bleeds. Child with microcytic anemia, chronic diarrhea and a negative fecal occult blood test Celiac diseaseMalabsorption, not blood loss – the occult blood is negative

Workup8 of 11 22-month-old boy with a large, dark red, formed stool; playful and feeding well; the family keeps goats; afebrile and pale; abdomen soft and nontender, no mass; anal exam normal; stool positive for occult blood · Cow's milk elimination dietMilk protein proctocolitis is an infant disease and is gone by age 1. · Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanPainless dark red stool in a toddler with a soft abdomen goes straight to the pertechnetate scan. · Upper endoscopyUpper endoscopy is for hematemesis or black, sticky melena; dark red stool without either is a lower source. 22-month-old boy with a large, dark red, formed stool; playful and feeding well; the family keeps goats; afebrile and pale; abdomen soft and nontender, no mass; anal exam normal; stool positive for occult blood Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanMeckel diverticulum: ectopic gastric mucosa takes up the tracer; painless small-bowel bleeding in a toddler, and dark red stool without hematemesis or melena is not an upper GI bleed

Next step9 of 11 10-week-old boy fed cow's milk-based formula with several days of mucus and streaks of blood in otherwise soft stools; feeding well, gaining weight, afebrile and playful; mild eczema on the cheeks; abdomen soft and nontender; no anal fissure on exam · Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanThe pertechnetate scan is for painless small-bowel bleeding in a toddler, not streaks in a thriving infant. · Bacterial stool cultureBacterial colitis brings bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and fever. · Switch to an extensively hydrolyzed formulaA thriving infant with mucus and blood streaks on cow's milk formula has milk protein proctocolitis: remove the protein. 10-week-old boy fed cow's milk-based formula with several days of mucus and streaks of blood in otherwise soft stools; feeding well, gaining weight, afebrile and playful; mild eczema on the cheeks; abdomen soft and nontender; no anal fissure on exam Switch to an extensively hydrolyzed formulamilk protein proctocolitis: a reaction not mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE) in infants; bleeding clears once cow's milk protein is removed, and it resolves by age 1

Workup10 of 11 2-year-old boy with 12 hours of sudden episodes of severe crying with his legs drawn up, quiet and sleepy between episodes; vomited twice; one stool of dark red blood and mucus (currant jelly); afebrile; a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant · Abdominal ultrasoundBouts of severe pain with currant jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass are intussusception: ultrasound shows the target sign. · Abdominal CTUltrasound is the preferred first study for intussusception, and the air enema follows it. · Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanThe Meckel bleed is painless; pain changes the first test. 2-year-old boy with 12 hours of sudden episodes of severe crying with his legs drawn up, quiet and sleepy between episodes; vomited twice; one stool of dark red blood and mucus (currant jelly); afebrile; a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant Abdominal ultrasoundintussusception: pain is the tell; target sign on ultrasound, then air enema to confirm and reduce; a Meckel diverticulum can be the lead point

Next step11 of 11 3-year-old girl with two episodes of painless maroon stool over the past month; pale, hematocrit 28%, vital signs normal; abdomen soft and nontender; technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower quadrant · Surgical resectionA Meckel diverticulum that has bled is resected to stop the bleeding and prevent complications. · Oral iron and observationIron treats the anemia, not the source; the ectopic mucosa keeps ulcerating. · Proton pump inhibitor therapyAcid suppression does not remove the ectopic gastric mucosa. 3-year-old girl with two episodes of painless maroon stool over the past month; pale, hematocrit 28%, vital signs normal; abdomen soft and nontender; technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower quadrant Surgical resectiona symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is removed to stop the bleeding and prevent intussusception, diverticulitis and obstruction; iron treats the anemia, not the source

Stool color follows transit time, not only where the blood started. Dark red or maroon stool in a toddler is a lower source, usually the small bowel, because the blood passes quickly. The upper GI (gastrointestinal) picture is hematemesis with black, sticky melena, and it is more common in adults. A toddler with dark red stool and neither of these does not start with upper endoscopy.

Visible bleeding with instability: resuscitate first; hematemesis or melena goes to upper endoscopy and brisk hematochezia to CT angiography (as for adults), not a Meckel scan Scope first for occult bleeding: small-bowel studies are for after a clean upper endoscopy and colonoscopy; a toddler with visible, painless dark red stool goes straight to the pertechnetate scan Meckel is classically under 2, but any age is possible, so age does not exclude it Balloon-assisted enteroscopy is the fallback when the source stays hidden

The Meckel scan detects gastric mucosa, not blood, so it works when the lesion is not actively bleeding Occult bleeding is too slow for angiography Celiac gives iron deficiency without occult blood; the FOBT (fecal occult blood test) separates them Here, small bowel means the segment the two scopes cannot reach Painless hematochezia in a toddler is Meckel until proven otherwise Rule of 2s: often presents by age 2, usually under 2 inches long, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve The bleed is painless; pain comes from complications: intussusception with the diverticulum as lead point, diverticulitis that mimics appendicitis, obstruction or perforation A symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is surgically resected to stop the bleeding and prevent those complications

The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infantcovers the obstructed and acutely bleeding infant gut Microcytic Anemiacovers the iron-versus-thalassemia fork that precedes this workup. Ask: is the bleeding visible, and have both ends been scoped? The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers the obstructed and acutely bleeding infant gut. Microcytic Anemia covers the iron-versus-thalassemia fork that precedes this workup. Ask: is the bleeding visible, and have both ends been scoped?
When an algorithm branches on age, the same negative workup can send a child and an adult to different tests.

Class-vs-memberCapsule endoscopy is the adult small-bowel study; a child gets the pertechnetate scan. Sequencing trapOrdering a small-bowel study before upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are done. Salient decoyMicrocytic anemia in a child pulls toward celiac serology, which the positive FOBT (fecal occult blood test) excludes. Unchecked attributeMilk elimination fits painless blood in an infant, but milk protein proctocolitis resolves by age 1; a 2-year-old is past it. Salient decoyFarm animals at home pull toward bacterial colitis, which needs bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and fever. True-fact-wrong-slotEndoscopy is right for hematemesis and black melena; dark red stool without either points below.

briefs.title: Umbilical Findings in a Newborn
briefs.sub: hernia vs omphalocele vs gastroschisis · skin-covered and reducible: observe · 1.5 cm and age 5 cutoffs · incarcerationIs there skin over it, and how big and how old is it?
blocks: hernia vs omphalocele vs gastroschisis · skin-covered and reducible: observe · 1.5 cm and age 5 cutoffs · incarcerationIs there skin over it, and how big and how old is it?

Pt 4-hour-old boy, 38 wk, 3.6 kg, mother 18 with no prenatal care, normal vitals; soft, nontender, skin-covered 1.4 cm bulge just below the umbilical stump that enlarges with crying and reduces with gentle pressure Q the most appropriate next step for the mass; options spanned observation, abdominal ultrasound, karyotype, immediate surgery and topical silver nitrate

Ask first whether skin covers it. A soft bulge under skin that reduces and enlarges with crying is a congenital umbilical hernia: observe; the diagnosis is clinical. Repair a hernia still present at about age 5, and an incarcerated one urgently at any age; one over 1.5 cm is less likely to close. A moist nub after the cord falls off is a granuloma (silver nitrate); urine or stool from the umbilicus is a remnant tract (US, then excision). Bowel with no skin over it goes to surgery after birth: a membrane sac with the cord on it is an omphalocele, which adds a karyotype and echocardiogram; bare bowel beside a normal cord is gastroschisis.

The umbilical ring normally closes after the intestines return from their physiologic herniation into the cord; a hernia is a ring that has not closed yet, so skin covers it. Incarceration is very rare, and small hernias usually close on their own. In practiceElective repair of a very large defect may be offered after age 2; the board answer stays repair at about age 5 for a persistent hernia.

Act now Finding Points to Action Bowel outside the abdomen at delivery, with or without a membrane Gastroschisis or omphalocele Cover it with a sterile, moist dressing, place a nasogastric tube, start IV fluids and antibiotics and keep the infant warm; then surgery. Too big to closeWhen the bowel will not fit, a silo covers it and is tightened over several days: a staged silo repair. A known hernia now firm, tender, discolored or irreducible, with vomiting Incarcerated umbilical hernia Urgent surgical repair at any age.

A bulge at the umbilicus Finding Decides it Next best step Umbilical hernia Skin-covered, soft, reducible, grows with crying; common in normal newborns, more with Down syndrome, hypothyroidism, Beckwith-Wiedemann and Ehlers-Danlos; most common in African-American infants. Observe; repair at about age 5 if it persists. Omphalocele Midline, at the umbilical ring; bowel, often liver, in a membrane sac with the cord inserting on it; other major malformations, trisomy 13 or 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann. Repair after birth; order a karyotype and echocardiogram first. Gastroschisis Full-thickness defect, usually right of a normal cord; bare, swollen bowel with no sac; not linked to chromosomal abnormalities. Immediate surgery. Associated defectsOther anomalies are uncommon, but malrotation or intestinal atresia comes with it in about a quarter of infants.

A moist or draining umbilicus Finding Decides it Next best step Umbilical granuloma A soft, moist, pink or red, pedunculated nub that appears after the cord falls off; no urine or stool. Treat with topical silver nitrate. Patent urachus (urachal fistula) Clear, urine-like fluid from the umbilicus, more with crying, straining or lying prone; a tract to the bladder. Order abdominal US, then surgical excision. Patent omphalomesenteric duct (vitelline fistula, persistent vitelline duct) Meconium, stool or mucus from the umbilicus; a tract to the ileum. Order abdominal US, then surgical excision.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any umbilical finding in a newborn → Look and feel: is there skin over it, does it reduce, does anything drain? Skin-covered, soft, reducible Umbilical hernia: observe; no imaging or genetic test Bowel in a membrane sac, or bare bowel beside the cord Omphalocele or gastroschisis: cover it with a sterile, moist dressing, place a nasogastric tube, start IV fluids and antibiotics and keep the infant warm; then surgery Moist red nub after the cord falls off Umbilical granuloma: topical silver nitrate Targeted tests TestResultMeans Hernia with prolonged jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone or constipation, or a missed newborn screen → Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (T4) High TSH, low free T4 Congenital hypothyroidism : levothyroxine (Congenital Hypothyroidism covers it) Hernia with macroglossia plus macrosomia, hypoglycemia or one side larger → Abdominal US and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), repeated at intervals A renal or liver mass Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome : Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) or hepatoblastoma (Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers the screening schedule) Omphalocele → Karyotype and echocardiogram Trisomy 13 or 18, or a heart defect Associated anomaly found before the repair Hernia with Down syndrome features → Karyotype Down syndrome confirmed The hernia is still observed Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Urine-like fluid, meconium or stool from the umbilicus → Abdominal US Tract to the bladder Patent urachus: surgical excision Tract to the ileum Patent omphalomesenteric duct: surgical excision SkipAbdominal US, karyotype or immediate surgery for a skin-covered, reducible hernia in a well newborn: the diagnosis is clinical, US is for an acquired hernia in an older child or adult, and a karyotype needs Down features.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Defect over 1.5 cm in a well infant A hernia less likely to close Keep observing; repair if still present at about age 5. Wet, red midline mucosa below the umbilicus, with urine dripping Bladder exstrophy; an omphalocele sits at the umbilicus and is not wet Examine for separated pubic bones and epispadias. Cord still attached after 30 days Leukocyte adhesion deficiency Order a CBC: marked neutrophilia, with infections that form no pus. Single umbilical artery (two-vessel cord) Congenital and chromosomal anomalies, often renal Order a renal US.

Term newborn with loops of bare, edematous bowel protruding through a defect to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, with no covering membrane; vital signs stable Cover the bowel and arrange immediate surgeryGastroschisis

Workup7 of 8 Term newborn with a 5 cm midline membrane-covered sac containing bowel and liver at the base of the umbilical cord, with the cord inserting on the sac · Karyotype and echocardiogramA membrane sac with the cord on it is an omphalocele, linked to trisomy 13 or 18 and heart defects: karyotype and echocardiogram. · Serum TSH and free T4TSH and free T4 are for a skin-covered hernia with prolonged jaundice, a large tongue or poor tone. · No further evaluation is neededAn omphalocele is linked to other major malformations, so skipping the search misses them. Term newborn with a 5 cm midline membrane-covered sac containing bowel and liver at the base of the umbilical cord, with the cord inserting on the sac Karyotype and echocardiogramOmphalocele

Workup8 of 8 7-week-old girl born at home without newborn screening, with a reducible skin-covered umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone, constipation and a wide posterior fontanelle · Serum TSH and free T4A hernia with prolonged jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone and constipation, with no newborn screen, is congenital hypothyroidism: TSH and free T4. · Abdominal ultrasoundThe hernia is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging does not test the thyroid. · KaryotypeA karyotype needs Down features or an omphalocele. 7-week-old girl born at home without newborn screening, with a reducible skin-covered umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone, constipation and a wide posterior fontanelle Serum TSH and free T4Congenital hypothyroidism

Exposed bowel dries and loses heat and water, so the cover, decompression, fluids and antibiotics come before surgery. An omphalocele also needs a karyotype and echocardiogram, because it is linked to trisomy 13 and 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann and heart defects. Gastroschisis is usually free of chromosomal and other anomalies outside the gut.

An umbilical hernia with prolonged jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone, constipation or a large fontanelle is a reason to check TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), because congenital hypothyroidism is the treatable association Karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, never for an isolated hernia in a normal infant Silver nitrate is the treatment for a granuloma; an umbilical lesion that keeps draining urine or stool is a remnant tract and needs US and excision

Congenital Hypothyroidismcovers the screen and treatment when a hernia comes with prolonged jaundice or a large tongue Inherited Tumor Syndromescovers Beckwith-Wiedemann tumor surveillance Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Functioncovers delayed cord separation Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresiacovers the anomaly screen after a structural defect: VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb) anomalies Congenital Hypothyroidism covers the screen and treatment when a hernia comes with prolonged jaundice or a large tongue. Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers Beckwith-Wiedemann tumor surveillance. Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers delayed cord separation. Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers the anomaly screen after a structural defect: VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb) anomalies.
A sleepy 2-month-old at his first visit, with an umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice and cool extremities, needed thyroid function tests, not karyotype, sweat chloride or head or liver CT.

For a newborn umbilical finding, ask first whether skin covers it. Observe a skin-covered, reducible bulge, and repair it if still present at about age 5 or incarcerated at any age. Bowel without skin goes to surgery at birth.

Redundant workupAbdominal ultrasound adds nothing to a clinical diagnosis; it is for an acquired hernia in an older child or adult. True-fact-wrong-slotImmediate surgery is for gastroschisis and omphalocele, where no skin covers the bowel. Salient decoyA young mother without prenatal care invites a genetic workup, but karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, and this infant has neither. Mirror twinSilver nitrate treats an umbilical granuloma, the moist red nub that appears after the cord falls off, not a skin-covered bulge at 4 hours.

briefs.sub: painful scrotum and painless mass: separate workups · torsion vs epididymitis · the two hard pairs · tumor markersWas the onset sudden or gradual, and does the mass transilluminate or change with Valsalva?

Sudden pain, a high-riding transverse testis and no cremasteric reflex is torsion: straight to surgery; imaging only when the exam is equivocal Pain building over days with fever, dysuria and tenderness behind the testis is epididymitis, diagnosed clinically: treat without imaging A painless mass is sorted by transillumination, position and Valsalva; a firm mass on the testis is a tumor: ultrasound and markers, then inguinal orchiectomy

What it is Scrotal pain or a scrotal mass in a boy or young man Sort by Painful: onset, location, cremasteric reflex painless: transillumination, position, Valsalva Hands off A right or fixed varicocele in a young child: Abdominal Mass in a Young Child; purpura with scrotal pain: Bruising and Purpura in a Child Abdominal Mass in a Young Child Bruising and Purpura in a Child

TorsionSudden severe pain, nausea and vomiting, a high-riding transverse testis, no cremasteric reflex If the exam fits, choose emergent detorsion with bilateral orchiopexy; no waiting for imaging; salvage window about 6 hours. Undescended testisAn acute abdomen in a boy with an empty scrotum: intra-abdominal torsion Fournier gangreneToxic, crepitus, necrosis; diabetic If there is crepitus or necrosis, choose emergent debridement.

The acute scrotum, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Testicular torsion Age 12 to 18, bell-clapper deformity; nausea and vomiting, no fever; no relief of pain on lifting the testis (negative Prehn sign) Minutes to hours; high-riding transverse testis; cremasteric reflex absent Epididymitis Posterior tenderness, dysuria, fever, pyuria; pain eases on lifting the testis (Prehn sign) Over 35Epididymitis by ageOver 35 or at low risk of a sexually transmitted infection, the organism is usually Escherichia coli: levofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Days; reflex intact; under 35, chlamydia or gonorrhea Torsion of the appendix testis Prepubertal boy; blue dot at the upper pole Gradual; reflex intact; supportive care Orchitis Mumps in an unvaccinated boy; sterility risk in teenagers Days, after parotitis; reflex intact; supportive IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) Bruising and Purpura in a Child Palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, joint and belly pain, after a cold Days; the rash, with scrotal pain

The painless scrotal mass, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Hydrocele Painless, uniform; in an infant, larger by midday if communicating Transilluminates; the testis is felt within Varicocele Why leftVaricoceleThe left gonadal vein meets the left renal vein at a right angle, and the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery can pinch the renal vein; the right one joins the inferior vena cava at a slant. A raised scrotal temperature impairs spermatogenesis, and a varicocele may also shrink the testis on its side. A new left varicocele can follow a left renal vein thrombosis. Older men not seeking fertility: scrotal support and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Bag of worms, about 90% left-sided Larger standing or with Valsalva, smaller supine; does not transilluminate Indirect inguinal hernia Enlarges with Valsalva; soft tissue or bowel Reducible, and you cannot get above it Spermatocele Above and separate from the testis, as a varicocele also is Transilluminates; no change with position or Valsalva Testicular tumor MarkersTumor markersA raised alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) means a yolk sac, embryonal or teratoma component, never a pure seminoma. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) can rise in either kind; only AFP excludes. Both normal with a solid mass: a pure seminoma or a stromal tumor (Leydig, Sertoli), separated by a hormonal syndrome. Lactate dehydrogenase tracks tumor burden, not histology. A teratoma, heterogeneous with calcified and cystic areas on ultrasound, is malignant in adults whatever its maturity and benign in prepubertal boys; it resists chemotherapy, so residual masses are resected. A Leydig cell tumor, a mostly benign stromal tumor with Reinke crystals, shows itself by its hormones; a Sertoli cell tumor, also stromal and usually benign, is typically hormonally silent. Firm, fixed, painless, on the testis; seminoma is the commonest, a yolk sac tumor under age 3; cryptorchidism or Klinefelter syndrome raises the risk Does not transilluminate; solid on ultrasound

A transscrotal biopsy of a testicular mass.

briefs.title: Polyuria
briefs.sub: urine osmolality first · solute vs water diuresis · when water deprivation is indicated · desmopressin responseIs the urine dilute, and has the serum sodium already answered what the deprivation test would?

Urine osmolality first: under 300 is a water diuresis; 600 or more before any deprivation means the kidney concentrates, so look for solute Then the sodium: high has already proven an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder, low means primary polydipsia; only a normal sodium needs water deprivation Desmopressin after deprivation: urine concentrates in AVP deficiency, stays dilute in AVP resistance

Workup9 of 10 Child with polyuria whose urine remains dilute when fluids are withheld · Serum arginine vasopressin level · MRI of the brain · Desmopressin after water deprivation Child with polyuria whose urine remains dilute when fluids are withheld Desmopressin after water deprivationthe hormone itself is too unstable in a sample to measure routinely; serial urine osmolality is what is read

Mechanism10 of 10 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 · Hypercalcemia blunts the response to vasopressin · Excess pituitary vasopressin release · Filtered calcium driving an osmotic diuresis 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 Hypercalcemia blunts the response to vasopressinan acquired, reversible AVP resistance at the collecting duct

A sodium above 145 makes the test redundant. A sodium below normal already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test. Serum vasopressin is rarely measured: its half-life is short and it is unstable in the sample, so the desmopressin response is the assay AVP deficiency – the current name for central diabetes insipidus AVP resistance – the current name for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Damage to the hypothalamic nuclei often makes the deficiency permanent; damage to the posterior pituitary is usually transient, because the hypothalamic neurons survive Pregnancy can produce a transient deficiency through placental vasopressinase, secreted in its latter half Lithium causes resistance by inhibiting aquaporin-2, and amiloride is the agent that blocks lithium's entry into the cell

Part I Enuresis already links a very low specific gravity to diabetes insipidus and to this test. This brief covers what happens after the test is ordered. Brain Tumors in a Child covers the causes of AVP (arginine vasopressin) deficiency and the post-operative case where the diagnosis is not in doubt. Hypercalcemia covers a common, reversible acquired resistance. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?

When the kidney is making dilute urine, the serum sodium shows whether a water deprivation test is still needed. A high sodium already confirms an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder; a low sodium already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test.

Sequencing trapMRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain: the right study once a deficiency is proven, and nothing has been proven yet. Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography: it images the kidney, which is implicated only if desmopressin fails. Salient decoyA BUN (blood urea nitrogen) of 30 pulls toward renal disease, but the creatinine is 1.0 and the defect is concentration, not filtration. True-fact-wrong-slotFractional excretion of sodium: it measures perfusion, and perfusion is not in question here. Salient decoyChest radiography: it looks for SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), which produces concentrated urine and hyponatremia, both opposite to the findings here.

briefs.title: Urinary Incontinence
briefs.sub: stress, urge, overflow, fistula · the postvoid residual splits the differential · cough stress test · drug pairingsWhat is the postvoid residual, and which diagnosis does that number make impossible?
blocks: stress, urge, overflow, fistula · the postvoid residual splits the differential · cough stress test · drug pairingsWhat is the postvoid residual, and which diagnosis does that number make impossible?

Pt woman with urinary leakage; no pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy or radiation Labs postvoid residual 800 mL Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned overflow, stress and urge incontinence and vesicovaginal fistula

The postvoid residual (PVR) splits the differential before any symptom is weighed: under 50 mL is normal, a high residual means overflow A bladder holding 800 mL cannot be draining through a fistula Oxybutynin treats urge incontinence and worsens overflow

What it is Involuntary loss of urine; stress, urge, overflow, functional, fistula, or a mix Sort by The residual (low or high) what sets off the leak: cough, urgency, constant dribbling, or the trip to the toilet Hands off Overflow from the prostate: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention

InfectionUrgency and frequency with dysuria, pyuria and nitrites If the urinalysis is positive, choose treat the infection; it is not chronic incontinence. RetentionA high residual with dribbling and recurrent infection If the bladder does not empty, choose catheterize and stop anticholinergics.

Incontinence types, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Stress incontinence Leaks with cough, sneeze or lifting; pregnancy, childbirth, menopause, obesity Low residual; leak starts and stops with the cough Urge incontinence (overactive bladder) Sudden urge, then leakage; frequency, nocturia Low residual; detrusor overactivity Overflow incontinence Hesitancy, weak stream, dribbling, recurrent infection High residual: an underactive detrusor or an obstructed outlet Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention Functional incontinence Dementia or immobility; cannot reach the toilet Normal residual and a normal tract Vesicovaginal fistula Continuous leakage; urine pooling in the vagina After surgery, delivery or radiation; dye in the vagina Normal pressure hydrocephalus Incontinence with a magnetic gait and dementia The triad: wet, wobbly and wacky; enlarged ventricles; sometimes reversible Mixed incontinence Stress and urge features together Both histories, low residual

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any new incontinence → Urinalysis Pyuria and nitrites Infection: treat it first Urinalysis clean → PVR by bladder ultrasound Under 50 mL Stress, urge or functional High Overflow: detrusor underactivity or outlet obstruction Targeted tests TestResultMeans Leaks with effort, low residual → Cough stress test Leak with the cough Stress incontinence Retention with urgency; multiple sclerosis → Urodynamics Mixed retention and urgency Neurogenic bladder Continuous leak after pelvic surgery, delivery or radiation → Dye test, cystoscopy Dye in the vagina Vesicovaginal fistula High residual in diabetes → Autonomic neuropathy screen Orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, resting tachycardia Diabetic autonomic neuropathy underactivating the detrusor SkipA cough stress test once the residual is high: overdistension alone can make it positive. Why it failsCough stress testA chronically overdistended bladder leaks with any rise in abdominal pressure, so a positive cough test loses its specificity once the residual is high. So a positive result can mislead here, just as a negative one can miss.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Leaks with cough, low residual Stress incontinence Pelvic floor exercises, then a pessary, then a midurethral sling Urgency, low residual Urge incontinence Bladder training, then an antimuscarinic or mirabegron, then botulinum toxin High residual, enlarged prostate Overflow from outlet obstruction Alpha-blocker Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention High residual, no obstruction Detrusor underactivity Intermittent catheterization; bethanechol In practiceIn practiceIn practice: a clinical reference calls bethanechol usually ineffective; catheterization carries the treatment. Spinal cord lesion Above the sacral cord: spastic bladder; at the sacral cord: atonic bladder A spastic bladder leaks with urgency; an atonic bladder overflows Rising residual on oxybutynin Anticholinergic retention Stop the drug; check for fecal impaction

Pause point Woman with a positive cough test and a residual of 800 mL Offered as stress incontinence or a fistula The residual names overflow → Overflow No fistula, surgery, delivery injury or radiation is present.

Screening9 of 9 32 yo F, T1DM, PVR 800 · Screen for nephropathy with UACR · Screen for autonomic neuropathy · Screen for neuropathy with monofilament 32 yo F, T1DM, PVR 800 Screen for autonomic neuropathygastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and resting tachycardia

A high PVR (postvoid residual) suggests that overflow is present, not that it is the only mechanism; mixed incontinence is common. A positive cough test may reflect a real coexisting stress component. A PVR is only interpretable when measured after a normal void. PVR thresholds in adults: under 50 mL is normal and argues against overflow; over 100 mL may suggest detrusor underactivity or outlet obstruction.

When a quantitative measure of organ function is given, check whether each candidate diagnosis is compatible with that number before weighing symptoms. Exclude a diagnosis the physiology forbids without arguing from symptoms.

briefs.title: Abdominal Mass in a Young Child
briefs.sub: organ of origin · age · Wilms tumor vs neuroblastoma · cystic newborn masses · ultrasound, then computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)Where does the mass arise, and how old is the child?
blocks: Abdominal Mass in a Young Child

organ of origin · age · Wilms tumor vs neuroblastoma · cystic newborn masses · ultrasound, then computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)Where does the mass arise, and how old is the child?

Pt 3 yo F at a well-child visit, normal development and immunizations; BP 156/96; mild right upper and lower quadrant tenderness with a palpable right-sided abdominal mass Imaging ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solitary mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, polycystic kidney disease and renal cell carcinoma

Ask two questions of any solid mass: which organ it arises from, and how old the child is Within the kidney at 2 to 5, smooth and not crossing the midline: Wilms tumor; adrenal or sympathetic chain, irregular, crossing the midline, usually under 2: neuroblastoma Ultrasound first; a solid kidney mass usually goes to excision rather than a needle biopsy

What it is A palpable abdominal mass in an infant or young child, most often painless Sort by Organ of origin: kidney, adrenal or sympathetic chain, liver age: cystic masses in the newborn, solid tumors in the toddler Hands off Syndromes that need tumor screening: Inherited Tumor Syndromes; hydronephrosis by level: Posterior Urethral Valves Inherited Tumor Syndromes Posterior Urethral Valves

NeuroblastomaLeg weakness or other new neurologic deficit: tumor in the spinal canal If a child with a mass has new weakness, choose MRI of the spine, as for any cord compression. Wilms tumorA needle biopsy can spill tumor into the peritoneum and raise the stage If the solid mass arises within the kidney, choose image, then excise; no percutaneous biopsy.

Abdominal mass look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) Well child; smooth, unilateral flank mass; high blood pressure, hematuria; WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann Denys-DrashDenys-Drash syndromeWilms tumor with early-onset nephrotic syndrome from diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and gonadal dysgenesis in a genetic boy (a WT1 mutation). Blood pressureWhy the pressure is highWilms tumor raises it through renin or by compressing the renal vessels. Neuroblastoma can raise it through catecholamines, though rarely severely, because it seldom secretes epinephrine. Age 2 to 5; arises within the kidney; does not cross the midline Neuroblastoma Often an ill child: bone pain, fever, weight loss; periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes), opsoclonus-myoclonus; calcifications Usually under 2 (median 18 months); adrenal or sympathetic chain, displaces the kidney, may cross the midline; urine vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA) raised Pheochromocytoma Episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with high blood pressure; often syndromic Inherited Tumor Syndromes Older child or adult; adrenal, sits on the kidney; metanephrines raised Hepatoblastoma Right upper quadrant mass; Beckwith-Wiedemann Infant or toddler; arises in the liver; alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) raised Hydronephrosis or multicystic dysplastic kidney The commonest newborn abdominal masses; fluid-filled on ultrasound Posterior Urethral Valves Newborn or infant; a dilated collecting system; or cysts that do not connect, with no working kidney tissue (usually one side, not inherited) Polycystic kidney disease Both kidneys enlarged and cystic Recessive form in newborns: large echogenic kidneys, hepatic fibrosis, portal hypertension; dominant form in adults Renal vein thrombosis A stressed newborn: diabetic mother, birth asphyxia, dehydration or polycythemia Newborn; enlarged kidney with hematuria and thrombocytopenia Renal cell carcinoma Flank pain, hematuria and a mass; von Hippel-Lindau presents earlier Adult

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any abdominal mass in a child → Abdominal US with Doppler Fluid-filled, in a newborn Hydronephrosis or multicystic dysplastic kidney Solid, within the kidney Wilms tumor: CT or MRI next Solid, above the kidney, calcified Neuroblastoma: urine VMA and HVA Solid, within the liver Hepatoblastoma: serum AFP Targeted tests TestResultMeans Opsoclonus-myoclonus (dancing eyes), raccoon eyes or bone pain → Urine VMA and HVA Raised Neuroblastoma: CT or MRI, then biopsy Episodes of headache, sweating, palpitations → Metanephrines Raised Pheochromocytoma Prepubertal boy, right varicocele that stays when supine Scrotal Pain and Masses → Abdominal US Kidney mass Wilms tumor compressing the vein Next step TestResultMeans Solid kidney mass → CT or MRI of the abdomenChest CT Extent, nodes, other kidney, liver Staging and surgical planning Lung nodules Wilms tumor has spread; the lung is its commonest distant site Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Wilms tumor → Excision with pathology Nephroblastoma Staged for chemotherapy, with or without radiation Neuroblastoma → Biopsy of the mass Small round blue cells, Homer-Wright rosettes Neuroblastoma confirmed SkipA needle biopsy of a solid kidney mass: it can spill tumor and raise the stage. AFP for a kidney mass: it is raised only in hepatoblastoma.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele, low glucose Beckwith-Wiedemann: Wilms tumor more often than hepatoblastoma US every 3 months to age 8; AFP every 3 months to age 4 Inherited Tumor Syndromes Aniridia, genitourinary anomalies WAGR (WT1 deletion); Wilms tumor more often on both sides US every 3 months in early childhood Inherited Tumor Syndromes High blood pressure with the mass Wilms tumor or neuroblastoma The organ of origin on ultrasound decides
Pause point Abdominal mass Offered first: CT or a needle biopsy; AFP for a kidney mass Ultrasound shows the organ of origin → Ultrasound; the organ picks the next test

Diagnosis1 of 11 3 yo F at a well-child visit, BP 156/96, palpable right abdominal mass; ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solid mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney · Neuroblastoma · Wilms tumor · Pheochromocytoma 3 yo F at a well-child visit, BP 156/96, palpable right abdominal mass; ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solid mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney Wilms tumorexcision with chemotherapy, with or without radiation

Diagnosis2 of 11 14 mo M, irritable for weeks, with rapid chaotic eye movements, jerking of the limbs, and a firm irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline; ultrasound shows calcifications · Neuroblastoma · Hepatoblastoma · Wilms tumor 14 mo M, irritable for weeks, with rapid chaotic eye movements, jerking of the limbs, and a firm irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline; ultrasound shows calcifications Neuroblastomaurine VMA and HVA

Workup3 of 11 18 mo M with weight loss, bruising around both eyes and a firm left upper quadrant mass lying above the kidney on ultrasound · Plasma renin activity · Urine VMA and HVA · Serum alpha-fetoprotein 18 mo M with weight loss, bruising around both eyes and a firm left upper quadrant mass lying above the kidney on ultrasound Urine VMA and HVAneuroblastoma

Workup4 of 11 2 yo F, well, whose mother felt a firm painless mass in her left flank while bathing her; BP 118/76, mass smooth and does not cross the midline · Percutaneous needle biopsy of the mass · Abdominal ultrasound · CT of the abdomen and pelvis 2 yo F, well, whose mother felt a firm painless mass in her left flank while bathing her; BP 118/76, mass smooth and does not cross the midline Abdominal ultrasoundsuspected Wilms tumor

Diagnosis5 of 11 3-day-old boy with a smooth left flank mass; ultrasound shows multiple noncommunicating cysts of varying size replacing the left kidney with no normal parenchyma, right kidney normal · Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease · Multicystic dysplastic kidney · Wilms tumor 3-day-old boy with a smooth left flank mass; ultrasound shows multiple noncommunicating cysts of varying size replacing the left kidney with no normal parenchyma, right kidney normal Multicystic dysplastic kidneynonfunctioning kidney; the other kidney must be checked

Diagnosis6 of 11 15 yo F with episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, BP 172/104 during an episode, and a 4-cm mass above the left kidney · Neuroblastoma · Pheochromocytoma · Wilms tumor 15 yo F with episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, BP 172/104 during an episode, and a 4-cm mass above the left kidney Pheochromocytomaplasma free metanephrines

Diagnosis7 of 11 6 mo F with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, 1 week of intermittent vomiting and fussiness, macroglossia, right-sided hemihypertrophy and a firm right upper quadrant mass; serum alpha-fetoprotein 15,678 ng/mL, urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid normal · Hepatoblastoma · Neuroblastoma · Wilms tumor 6 mo F with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, 1 week of intermittent vomiting and fussiness, macroglossia, right-sided hemihypertrophy and a firm right upper quadrant mass; serum alpha-fetoprotein 15,678 ng/mL, urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid normal Hepatoblastomaliver mass with a very high alpha-fetoprotein

Diagnosis8 of 11 3 yo M with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; a screening ultrasound shows a 7-cm solid mass arising within the left kidney; serum alpha-fetoprotein and urine catecholamine metabolites are normal · Wilms tumor · Hepatoblastoma · Neuroblastoma 3 yo M with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; a screening ultrasound shows a 7-cm solid mass arising within the left kidney; serum alpha-fetoprotein and urine catecholamine metabolites are normal Wilms tumorkidney origin with a normal alpha-fetoprotein

Workup9 of 11 9 mo F, fussy, with a firm right upper quadrant mass that ultrasound places within the right lobe of the liver; the kidneys and adrenals are normal · Serum alpha-fetoprotein · Plasma free metanephrines · Urine VMA and HVA 9 mo F, fussy, with a firm right upper quadrant mass that ultrasound places within the right lobe of the liver; the kidneys and adrenals are normal Serum alpha-fetoproteinhepatoblastoma

Diagnosis10 of 11 Male newborn at 38 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, Apgar scores 8 and 9, normal examination except bilateral flank masses; hematocrit 50%, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urine with moderate blood and trace protein; ultrasound shows both kidneys enlarged with mixed echogenicity · Renal vein thrombosis · Polycystic kidney disease · Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) Male newborn at 38 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, Apgar scores 8 and 9, normal examination except bilateral flank masses; hematocrit 50%, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urine with moderate blood and trace protein; ultrasound shows both kidneys enlarged with mixed echogenicity Polycystic kidney diseasethe recessive form; look for hepatic fibrosis

Diagnosis11 of 11 2-day-old boy whose mother has poorly controlled diabetes, with a new right flank mass, gross hematuria and a platelet count of 70,000/mm3; ultrasound shows one enlarged kidney and a normal left kidney · Renal vein thrombosis · Multicystic dysplastic kidney · Polycystic kidney disease 2-day-old boy whose mother has poorly controlled diabetes, with a new right flank mass, gross hematuria and a platelet count of 70,000/mm3; ultrasound shows one enlarged kidney and a normal left kidney Renal vein thrombosisconfirm with Doppler ultrasound of the renal vein

Wilms tumor is treated with excision plus chemotherapy, with or without radiation; with favorable histology about 90% are cured. Tissue at excision or biopsy makes the diagnosis. Ultrasound, not CT (computed tomography), is the first study.

Establish the origin before weighing age: a mass within the kidney is Wilms tumor; an adrenal or paraspinal mass is neuroblastoma or pheochromocytoma Hypertension does not separate the two tumors: Wilms raises renin, neuroblastoma releases catecholamines A well child with a smooth flank mass favors Wilms; an irritable child with weight loss, bone pain or raccoon eyes favors neuroblastoma Rapid chaotic eye movements with myoclonic jerks in a toddler is opsoclonus-myoclonus, a paraneoplastic sign of neuroblastoma Two enlarged kidneys in a well newborn suggest ARPKD (autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease); ultrasound shows large echogenic kidneys ARPKD comes from PKHD1 mutations and brings congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli syndrome Severe ARPKD in utero causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) is the adult form, with kidney and liver cysts and cerebral aneurysms A creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL on day 1 mirrors the mother's creatinine and does not prove neonatal kidney failure Neonatal renal vein thrombosis also gives a flank mass and hematuria, usually with thrombocytopenia, in a stressed infant Avoid repeated deep palpation of a suspected Wilms tumor, because rupture of the capsule spreads tumor Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome raises the risk of both Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma, so the syndrome alone cannot pick between them A firm right upper quadrant mass with a very high AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) in an infant is hepatoblastoma NBME framing: the stem names the syndrome and hides the answer in a lab panel, a very high AFP with normal urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) A syndrome that carries Wilms risk earns surveillance ultrasounds, covered in Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes

For the newborn with two flank masses, the key reads only polycystic kidney disease, and the ultrasound says mixed echogenicity rather than cysts The options are a mass family sorted by age, three tumors plus one vascular mimic, and the labs plant hematuria and a raised creatinine to fit the decoys

Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann and the surveillance that follows. Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the neonatal flank mass, where hydronephrosis and multicystic dysplastic kidney come first. Part II Acute Leukemia in a Child shares marrow infiltration and periorbital ecchymoses with neuroblastoma. Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the day-1 creatinine that reflects the mother's kidneys: is the value the mother's or the baby's? Ask: does the mass arise within the kidney, and is the child older than 2?
For a solid mass in a child, name the organ it arises from before naming the tumor, then use age to decide among the rest. A finding two tumors share, such as hypertension, cannot distinguish them.

Unchecked attributeNeuroblastoma is the famous childhood abdominal tumor, but it arises from the adrenal or sympathetic chain and usually before age 2. Salient decoyPheochromocytoma matches the hypertension and the upper-pole location, but it is adrenal and episodic. Unchecked attributePolycystic kidney disease gives bilateral cystic kidneys, not one solid mass. Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma arises within the kidney too, but in adults. Salient decoyWilms tumor (nephroblastoma): the best-known Beckwith-Wiedemann tumor, but it is a flank mass within the kidney and does not raise AFP (alpha-fetoprotein). Test-overrides-findingsNeuroblastoma: age 6 months fits it better than Wilms tumor, but urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) are normal. Unchecked attributeGerm cell tumor: a yolk sac tumor also raises AFP, but in a young child it presents as a pelvic mass, not a firm upper abdominal one. True-fact-wrong-slotSpina bifida occulta: a raised AFP goes with open neural tube defects in pregnancy, not the closed form, and it makes no abdominal mass. Unchecked attributeNephroblastoma (Wilms tumor): it shares the flank mass and hematuria; it is usually unilateral and peaks at ages 2 to 5, and this newborn has two masses. Salient decoyNeuroblastoma: it is the most common solid tumor of infancy; it arises in the adrenal, displaces the kidney rather than enlarging it, and is rarely bilateral. Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma: it shares a mass within the kidney and hematuria; it is a tumor of adults and adolescents, not newborns. Unchecked attributeRenal vein thrombosis: it shares a newborn flank mass, hematuria and an enlarged kidney; this baby has no risk factor, with an uncomplicated delivery, good Apgar scores and a normal hematocrit.

briefs.title: Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child
briefs.sub: potassium, acid-base, then blood pressure · anion gap · urine pH during acidosis · distal vs proximal vs type 4Is the gap normal, and is the urine pH above 5.5 during the acidosis?
blocks: Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child
potassium, acid-base, then blood pressure · anion gap · urine pH during acidosis · distal vs proximal vs type 4Is the gap normal, and is the urine pH above 5.5 during the acidosis?

Pt 18 mo M with poor linear growth; no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 90/60 Labs Na 138, Cl 112, K 3.1, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L; urine pH 7.6; arterial pH 7.28 and Pco2 26 mm Hg, with normal oxygenation on room air Q the most likely cause of the hypokalemia; options spanned Addison disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperparathyroidism, juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia, pheochromocytoma, primary hyperaldosteronism, pseudohypoaldosteronism, renal artery stenosis and renal tubular acidosis

Sort by potassium and the acid-base state first, then by blood pressure Low potassium with a normal-gap acidosis is diarrhea or RTA (renal tubular acidosis); with no diarrhea, a urine pH above 5.5 during the acidosis means the distal tubule cannot secrete acid: distal (type 1) RTA Low potassium with an alkalosis: urine chloride and blood pressure decide
