What it is Low potassium, or a metabolic acidosis or alkalosis, in a child with poor growth, weakness or a history of vomiting Sort by Potassium and pH anion gap, urine pH, urine chloride, blood pressure Hands off By the clue: high calcium, high blood pressure, slow growth Hypercalcemia High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent Abnormal Growth in a Child

High potassiumLow sodium and low blood pressure: adrenal crisis, or salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency in an infant If the child is in shock, choose immediate glucocorticoid and fluid resuscitation. Low potassiumWeakness, hyporeflexia or paralysis; U waves, flat T waves and arrhythmia on the ECG (electrocardiogram) Vomiting infantHypochloremic, hypokalemic alkalosis, as in pyloric stenosis If the urine chloride is low, choose IV normal saline.

Low and high potassium, sorted by pattern, most tempting first Pattern Causes Decides it Normal-gap acidosis with low potassium; normal blood pressure Anion gapNormal gapSodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate; normal is about 8 to 12. When chloride replaces the lost bicarbonate, the gap stays normal (hyperchloremic acidosis). In the source vignette, 138 minus (112 plus 16) gives 10: a normal gap. Distal (type 1) RTA; proximal (type 2) RTA; diarrhea Urine pH above 5.5 during the acidosis is distal; proximal fails to reclaim bicarbonate and acidifies only once bicarbonate is low; it often wastes glucose and phosphate; for diarrhea, the history decides Urine anion gapGut or kidneyUrine sodium plus potassium minus chloride. Negative in diarrhea, where the kidney excretes acid normally; a negative gap also occurs in proximal RTA. Alkalosis with low potassium; normal blood pressure Vomiting; diuretics; Bartter syndrome (juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia); Gitelman syndrome; cystic fibrosis Urine chloride low after vomiting, high in Bartter, Gitelman and diuretic abuse; Bartter acts like a loop diuretic and raises urine calcium, Gitelman like a thiazide, milder, with low calcium and magnesium; renin and aldosterone high in both Alkalosis with low potassium; high blood pressure High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent Primary hyperaldosteronism; renal artery stenosis; 11-beta- or 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency; Liddle syndrome Renin is low in primary aldosteronism and high in renal artery stenosis; Liddle syndrome mimics aldosterone excess with both renin and aldosterone low Normal-gap acidosis with high potassium; blood pressure low or normal Addison disease; salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency; type 1 pseudohypoaldosteronism; type 4 RTA Aldosterone is high in pseudohypoaldosteronism, low in Addison disease and 21-hydroxylase deficiency, often with low sodium; urine pH usually below 5.5 Low potassium, normal pH Shift into cells: beta-2 agonists such as albuterol, insulin The drug history; the potassium has moved, not been lost Episodic high blood pressure Inherited Tumor Syndromes Pheochromocytoma Paroxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations; raised metanephrines High calcium, sometimes a mild normal-gap acidosis Hypercalcemia Hyperparathyroidism High calcium with a high parathyroid hormone level

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Low potassium or a low or high bicarbonate → Electrolytes with the anion gapBlood gas Acidosis, gap 8 to 12 Normal gap: diarrhea or RTA Alkalosis Urine chloride and blood pressure High potassium with acidosis Low aldosterone effect Next step TestResultMeans Normal-gap acidosis, no diarrhea → Urine pH during the acidosis Above 5.5 Distal (type 1) RTA, usually with low potassium Below 5.5, glucose and phosphate in the urine Proximal (type 2) RTA, as in Fanconi syndrome Alkalosis, normal blood pressure → Urine chloride Under 20 mEq/L Chloride-responsive, as after vomiting: IV normal saline Over 20 mEq/L Bartter, Gitelman or diuretic use: urine calcium Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Alkalosis, high blood pressure → Plasma renin and aldosterone Renin low, aldosterone high Primary hyperaldosteronism Both high Renal artery stenosis Both low Liddle syndrome or apparent mineralocorticoid excess SkipThe potassium to type the RTA: distal and proximal are both low; the urine pH during the acidosis decides.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Poor growth, nephrocalcinosis or calcium phosphate stones Distal RTA Oral alkali, citrate or bicarbonate; untreated, growth slows Amphotericin B, lithium, autoimmune disease (Sjögren syndrome) Acquired distal RTA Urine pH during the acidosis Rickets, glucose and phosphate in the urine; acetazolamide Proximal RTA Alkali; phosphate and vitamin D for the bones High blood pressure, renin and aldosterone both low Liddle syndrome Amiloride or triamterene Potassium-sparing diuretic, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor Type 4 RTA Potassium restriction and a potassium-wasting diuretic; a few need mineralocorticoid

Pause point Low potassium with high blood pressure Read as aldosterone excess from the potassium and blood pressure alone Renin and aldosterone sort the hypertensive child → Renin and aldosterone levels Acidotic child with an RTA Typed by its potassium The urine pH sorts the acidotic one → Urine pH

Diagnosis1 of 6 18 mo M with poor linear growth and no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 90/60; Na 138, Cl 112, K 3.1, HCO3 16 mEq/L; urine pH 7.6; arterial pH 7.28, Pco2 26 mm Hg · Pseudohypoaldosteronism · Renal tubular acidosis · Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia 18 mo M with poor linear growth and no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 90/60; Na 138, Cl 112, K 3.1, HCO3 16 mEq/L; urine pH 7.6; arterial pH 7.28, Pco2 26 mm Hg Renal tubular acidosisnormal-gap acidosis with urine pH above 5.5 is distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis

Diagnosis2 of 6 2 yo F with poor weight gain and polyuria; no vomiting and no diuretic use; BP 88/54; Na 135, Cl 92, K 2.8, HCO3 32 mEq/L; high urine calcium · Distal renal tubular acidosis · Bartter syndrome · Gitelman syndrome 2 yo F with poor weight gain and polyuria; no vomiting and no diuretic use; BP 88/54; Na 135, Cl 92, K 2.8, HCO3 32 mEq/L; high urine calcium Bartter syndromelow potassium with alkalosis, normal blood pressure and high urine calcium

Diagnosis3 of 6 3 yo M with poor growth and bowed legs; no diarrhea; BP 92/58; Na 138, Cl 113, K 3.2, HCO3 15 mEq/L; normal serum glucose with glucose and phosphate in the urine; urine pH 5.0 · Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis · Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets · Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis 3 yo M with poor growth and bowed legs; no diarrhea; BP 92/58; Na 138, Cl 113, K 3.2, HCO3 15 mEq/L; normal serum glucose with glucose and phosphate in the urine; urine pH 5.0 Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosisFanconi syndrome: the urine acidifies once bicarbonate is low, and glucose and phosphate are wasted

Workup4 of 6 20 mo F with length below the 3rd percentile; no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 88/56; Na 139, Cl 113, K 3.0, HCO3 15 mEq/L · Urine pH during the acidosis · Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone · Plasma renin activity and aldosterone 20 mo F with length below the 3rd percentile; no vomiting or diarrhea; BP 88/56; Na 139, Cl 113, K 3.0, HCO3 15 mEq/L Urine pH during the acidosisabove 5.5 with a normal-gap acidosis indicates distal renal tubular acidosis

Next step5 of 6 2 yo M with distal renal tubular acidosis; urine pH 7.0 with HCO3 15 mEq/L and K 3.0 mEq/L; weight and length below the 3rd percentile; nephrocalcinosis on renal ultrasound · Oral potassium chloride supplements alone · Oral alkali therapy with citrate or bicarbonate · Oral hydrochlorothiazide with a low-salt diet 2 yo M with distal renal tubular acidosis; urine pH 7.0 with HCO3 15 mEq/L and K 3.0 mEq/L; weight and length below the 3rd percentile; nephrocalcinosis on renal ultrasound Oral alkali therapy with citrate or bicarbonatecorrecting the acidosis lets growth recover and lowers urine calcium

Mechanism6 of 6 4 yo F with poor growth and nephrocalcinosis on ultrasound; no diarrhea; normal-gap metabolic acidosis with K 3.0 mEq/L; urine pH 6.8 · Impaired hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephron · Reduced aldosterone effect on the collecting duct · Impaired bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule 4 yo F with poor growth and nephrocalcinosis on ultrasound; no diarrhea; normal-gap metabolic acidosis with K 3.0 mEq/L; urine pH 6.8 Impaired hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephrondistal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis
Treat distal renal tubular acidosis with oral alkali, citrate or bicarbonate, and add potassium when it stays low. Untreated acidosis slows growth in children.

Distal renal tubular acidosis raises urine calcium and lowers urine citrate, so nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones can follow; serum calcium stays normal The urine anion gap (urine sodium plus potassium minus chloride) is positive in distal renal tubular acidosis and negative in diarrhea Winter's formula predicts a Pco2 of 1.5 times 16 plus 8, or 32, plus or minus 2 The measured 26 is below that range, which suggests an added respiratory alkalosis Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia is the kidney lesion of Bartter syndrome, which gives low potassium with alkalosis and a normal blood pressure

The lead-in asked for the cause of the hypokalemia, a secondary finding, although the acid-base values decided the answer. The nine options formed a grid of potassium, acid-base status and blood pressure, and only one option fit this child.

Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers the first step, electrolytes with a venous blood gas when length is also low; this brief covers reading that panel. Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers low potassium with alkalosis and hypertension, where renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renal artery stenosis. Part I Polyuria covers the dilute urine that severe hypokalemia can cause. Part I Hypercalcemia covers hyperparathyroidism; distal renal tubular acidosis raises urine calcium, not serum calcium. Ask: is the child acidotic or alkalotic, and is the blood pressure high?
Sort low potassium by acid-base status first, then by blood pressure. Low potassium with a normal-gap acidosis and no diarrhea is renal tubular acidosis, and a urine pH above 5.5 makes it distal.

Unchecked attributeAddison disease: it causes acidosis with a low-normal blood pressure; potassium would be high and sodium low. Salient decoyCongenital adrenal hyperplasia: an adrenal disorder that affects growth; the salt-wasting form raises potassium, and the hypertensive forms cause alkalosis with high blood pressure. True-fact-wrong-slotHyperparathyroidism: excess parathyroid hormone can cause a mild normal-gap acidosis; its hallmark is high calcium, and it does not explain low potassium. Unchecked attributeJuxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia: this is Bartter syndrome, the closest mimic, with low potassium, normal blood pressure and poor growth in a young child; Bartter syndrome causes alkalosis, and this child is acidotic. Class-vs-memberPheochromocytoma: an adrenal tumor on a list of hormonal causes; it causes episodic hypertension with headache and sweating, and this child is normotensive. Unchecked attributePrimary hyperaldosteronism: the textbook cause of low potassium; it brings hypertension and alkalosis, and both are absent. Unchecked attributePseudohypoaldosteronism: it causes a normal-gap acidosis and poor growth in infants; potassium is high in every form. True-fact-wrong-slotRenal artery stenosis: renin excess does cause low potassium; it brings hypertension and alkalosis, and both are absent.

briefs.title: Child with Puffy Eyes
briefs.sub: local to the eye, or the first sign of edema everywhere · red flags · the dipstick splits the branches · minimal change diseaseIs the swelling confined to the eye or spread over the whole child, and what does the urine dipstick show?
blocks: local to the eye, or the first sign of edema everywhere · red flags · the dipstick splits the branches · minimal change diseaseIs the swelling confined to the eye or spread over the whole child, and what does the urine dipstick show?

First decide whether the swelling is the eye's or the whole child's; check the airway and the orbit before anything else Local swelling is allergy or infection; generalized edema means protein is lost or not made, or salt and water are retained In the generalized branch the dipstick sorts it: 3+ to 4+ protein with no blood is nephrotic syndrome; blood or red cell casts, glomerulonephritis

What it is Swollen lids, on one side or both Sort by Eye or whole child the urine: protein, blood, or clean Hands off Nephrotic syndrome, nephritis, anaphylaxis, the infected lid Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome Anaphylaxis Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child

AirwayStridor, wheeze or low blood pressure; swollen lips or tongue, or a hoarse voice If there are hives or a likely allergen, choose intramuscular epinephrine first. OrbitProptosis, pain with eye movement, blurred vision If any orbital sign is present, choose CT of the orbits and sinuses, and IV antibiotics. BellyEdema with fever, belly pain and rebound: spontaneous peritonitis If a nephrotic child has peritoneal signs, choose cultures, then antibiotics. PressureNephritis with a high pressure and headache, vomiting or confusion: hypertensive encephalopathy If volume overload drives it, choose furosemide; nifedipine if it stays high. ClotA nephrotic child with flank pain and hematuria, or one swollen leg: a clot

Puffy eyes in a child, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Nephrotic syndrome Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child CourseMinimal change diseaseThe filter loses its negative charge, so albumin leaks; it often follows a cold, an immunization or an insect bite. Prednisone daily for 4 to 6 weeks, then tapered; restrict salt. Give albumin with furosemide only when edema is severe: a diuretic alone can lower a plasma volume that is already low. Home urine dipstick: relapse is common and is treated with prednisone again. Pneumococcal and yearly influenza vaccines in remission; no live vaccines on high-dose steroids. During a relapse, watch for infection (spontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal) from low immunoglobulin G, and for venous clots, the renal vein included, as antithrombin III is lost in the urine. Both eyes, worst on waking; then the legs, belly and scrotum Blood pressure normal; 4+ protein without blood; albumin low WhyBlood pressureLow oncotic pressure moves fluid into the tissues and leaves the plasma volume low, so the pressure stays normal; nephritis retains salt and water, so it rises. Allergic conjunctivitis The Red Eye Both eyes itchy and watery, ropey mucus; sneezing, clear runny nose; seasonal Itch, and a clean urine Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (postinfectious glomerulonephritis) Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome CoursePoststreptococcal glomerulonephritisTreatment is supportive: salt and fluid restriction, and furosemide for volume overload; nifedipine when the pressure stays high. C3 is normal again by 8 weeks. Puffy eyes with cola-colored urine; edema over days Blood pressure high; about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 after impetigo; C3 low Periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child One red, warm, tender lid after a bite, scratch or sinusitis The eye moves freely; normal vision, no proptosis Orbital cellulitis Sinusitis and Its Complications Fever, proptosis, pain with eye movement Ophthalmoplegia or a change in vision; sinusitis is the usual source Acute allergic reaction Anaphylaxis Abrupt swelling of the lids, lips or tongue Hives within minutes of a food, a drug or a sting Hereditary angioedema Anaphylaxis BradykininHereditary angioedemaHereditary angioedema is autosomal dominant C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency; bradykinin, not histamine, causes the swelling, so angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are contraindicated, and an attack does not answer to epinephrine: it is treated with C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant. Death is usually from airway swelling. Recurrent swelling without hives; after dental work or stress Low C4; no response to epinephrine Infectious conjunctivitis NewbornConjunctivitis in the newbornGonococcal conjunctivitis at 2 to 5 days, with marked lid swelling and pus; chlamydial at 5 to 14 days, with mild swelling. Red eye, pus crusting the lids, mild lid swelling Begins in one eye; under 6, usually bacterial Heart failure Heart Failure in a Child Tires or breathes fast with activity; edema is uncommon Big liver, gallop, no protein in the urine Liver failure or protein-losing enteropathy Ascites with jaundice, or edema with chronic diarrhea Low albumin with a clean urine Malnutrition (kwashiorkor) Edema with thin hair, poor growth Diet history

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Generalized edema, or no local cause → Urinalysis, dipstick and microscopy 3+ to 4+ protein, no blood Nephrotic syndrome: then albumin, lipids and creatinine Blood or red cell casts with some protein Glomerulonephritis: creatinine and C3 Normal Not the kidney: allergy, infection, or albumin lost by another route Next step TestResultMeans Nephrotic dipstick → Serum albumin, cholesterol, creatinine Albumin under 2.5 g/dL, high cholesterol, normal creatinine Nephrotic syndrome Low albumin, clean urine → Liver tests, bilirubin, international normalized ratio (INR)Stool alpha-1 antitrypsin Bilirubin and INR high Liver failure Stool alpha-1 antitrypsin high Protein-losing enteropathy Gallop, big liver → Chest radiograph and echocardiogram Big heart, poor function Heart failure Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Nephrotic syndrome → Spot urine protein/creatinine ratio Above 2 mg/mg with low albumin Nephrotic range A typical child → Daily prednisone Protein gone within weeks Presumed minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis); no biopsy No response by 8 weeks, hematuria, hypertension, high creatinine, or age over 10 to 12 → Renal biopsy Effaced foot processes, nothing else Minimal change disease; if steroid resistant, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) SkipSerum immunoglobulin E or allergy testing: often high in atopic children, and it cannot exclude a kidney cause. CT of the orbits without orbital signs.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Puffiness worst on waking, better by afternoon Allergy and edema alike: lying flat moves fluid to the lids Test the urine Tight shoes and waistband, pitting over the shins, scrotal or labial swelling, a fluid wave Generalized edema and ascites Urinalysis first Dark circles under the eyes, a second crease below the lower lid, a bumpy conjunctiva Allergy Avoid the allergen; antihistamine eye drops One red, tender lid; eye movements full and painless; vision normal Preseptal cellulitis Oral antibiotics; recheck in 1 to 2 days Dark urine about 1 to 3 weeks after a sore throat, or up to about 6 after skin sores Glomerulonephritis Creatinine, C3; antistreptolysin O or anti-deoxyribonuclease B
Pause point Puffiness on both sides each morning Offered: allergy testing or orbit imaging Waking puffiness separates neither allergy nor edema → The dipstick

Diagnosis1 of 17 5 yo boy with a week of puffy eyelids on both sides, worst when he wakes and better by afternoon, now with swollen ankles, a bigger belly, tiredness and a poor appetite; no itching, redness or discharge; blood pressure normal; urine dipstick 4+ protein and negative for blood · Minimal change disease · Allergic conjunctivitis · Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 5 yo boy with a week of puffy eyelids on both sides, worst when he wakes and better by afternoon, now with swollen ankles, a bigger belly, tiredness and a poor appetite; no itching, redness or discharge; blood pressure normal; urine dipstick 4+ protein and negative for blood Minimal change diseaseNephrotic syndrome: protein without blood at a normal blood pressure

Workup2 of 17 5 yo girl with 4 days of puffiness around both eyes, worst on waking; no itching, redness, discharge or fever; her shoes have felt tight since yesterday · CT of the orbits · Serum IgE level · Urinalysis 5 yo girl with 4 days of puffiness around both eyes, worst on waking; no itching, redness, discharge or fever; her shoes have felt tight since yesterday UrinalysisThe dipstick shows whether the kidney is leaking protein

Mechanism3 of 17 6 yo with hay fever and 5 days of puffy eyelids on both sides each morning, now with ankle swelling; a serum IgE level is high; no urine has been tested · It confirms allergic eyelid swelling · It does not exclude a kidney cause · It makes nephrotic syndrome unlikely 6 yo with hay fever and 5 days of puffy eyelids on both sides each morning, now with ankle swelling; a serum IgE level is high; no urine has been tested It does not exclude a kidney causeAtopy is common; the urine dipstick is still the next test

Diagnosis4 of 17 7 yo with puffy, itchy eyes on both sides every spring, clear watery discharge, sneezing and a runny nose; dark circles and an extra crease below both lower lids; afebrile; urine dipstick negative · Nephrotic syndrome · Allergic conjunctivitis · Periorbital cellulitis 7 yo with puffy, itchy eyes on both sides every spring, clear watery discharge, sneezing and a runny nose; dark circles and an extra crease below both lower lids; afebrile; urine dipstick negative Allergic conjunctivitisItch and a clean urine separate it from edema; antihistamine eye drops

Diagnosis5 of 17 3 yo whose eyelids and lips swell within 20 minutes of eating a cashew for the first time, with raised, itchy wheals on the chest; no hoarseness, wheeze or vomiting; blood pressure and oxygen saturation normal · Contact dermatitis · Hereditary angioedema · IgE-mediated food allergy 3 yo whose eyelids and lips swell within 20 minutes of eating a cashew for the first time, with raised, itchy wheals on the chest; no hoarseness, wheeze or vomiting; blood pressure and oxygen saturation normal IgE-mediated food allergyAbrupt swelling with hives; hereditary angioedema brings no hives

Diagnosis6 of 17 4 yo with 2 days of swelling and redness of the right upper eyelid, which is warm and tender, around a scratch from the family cat; T 38.3 C; full, painless eye movements, normal vision, no proptosis · Bacterial conjunctivitis · Periorbital cellulitis · Allergic conjunctivitis 4 yo with 2 days of swelling and redness of the right upper eyelid, which is warm and tender, around a scratch from the family cat; T 38.3 C; full, painless eye movements, normal vision, no proptosis Periorbital cellulitisOne eye, warm and tender, orbit spared: oral antibiotics

Diagnosis7 of 17 4 yo with 2 days of a red left eye, thick yellow discharge and lids stuck together each morning, with mild lid puffiness; the eyelid skin is not red, warm or tender; afebrile; vision normal · Allergic conjunctivitis · Bacterial conjunctivitis · Periorbital cellulitis 4 yo with 2 days of a red left eye, thick yellow discharge and lids stuck together each morning, with mild lid puffiness; the eyelid skin is not red, warm or tender; afebrile; vision normal Bacterial conjunctivitisPus and crusting; under 6, bacterial is more likely than viral

Workup8 of 17 5 yo with puffy eyes and swelling of the ankles and scrotum; BP 96/58; urine dipstick 4+ protein, no blood; serum albumin 1.8 g/dL · Serum C3 and C4 levels · Spot urine protein/creatinine ratio · Renal biopsy with electron microscopy 5 yo with puffy eyes and swelling of the ankles and scrotum; BP 96/58; urine dipstick 4+ protein, no blood; serum albumin 1.8 g/dL Spot urine protein/creatinine ratioAbove 2 mg/mg with low albumin is nephrotic syndrome

Diagnosis9 of 17 3 yo with 2 weeks of puffy eyelids who tires after a few minutes of play and sweats and breathes fast with meals; RR 44, HR 150; liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin; gallop rhythm; urine dipstick negative for protein · Nephrotic syndrome · Liver failure · Heart failure 3 yo with 2 weeks of puffy eyelids who tires after a few minutes of play and sweats and breathes fast with meals; RR 44, HR 150; liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin; gallop rhythm; urine dipstick negative for protein Heart failureBig liver and a gallop with a clean urine: echocardiogram next

Diagnosis10 of 17 2 yo with 3 weeks of swollen eyelids and legs and 2 months of loose stools; weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile; albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine dipstick negative for protein; bilirubin and INR normal · Minimal change disease · Chronic liver failure · Protein-losing enteropathy 2 yo with 3 weeks of swollen eyelids and legs and 2 months of loose stools; weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile; albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine dipstick negative for protein; bilirubin and INR normal Protein-losing enteropathyAlbumin lost in the gut; stool alpha-1 antitrypsin is high

Next step11 of 17 4 yo with periorbital and leg edema; BP 132/88; urinalysis 4+ protein with 30 red cells per high-power field; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; C3 normal · Renal biopsy · Oral prednisone without biopsy · Antistreptolysin O titer 4 yo with periorbital and leg edema; BP 132/88; urinalysis 4+ protein with 30 red cells per high-power field; creatinine 1.1 mg/dL; C3 normal Renal biopsyHematuria, hypertension and a high creatinine are atypical for minimal change disease

Next step12 of 17 6 yo with minimal change disease that went into remission on prednisone, off steroids for 5 months; his home urine dipstick has shown 3+ to 4+ protein for 3 days and his eyes are puffy again; blood pressure normal, no blood in the urine · Renal biopsy before treatment · Start a calcineurin inhibitor · Restart daily prednisone 6 yo with minimal change disease that went into remission on prednisone, off steroids for 5 months; his home urine dipstick has shown 3+ to 4+ protein for 3 days and his eyes are puffy again; blood pressure normal, no blood in the urine Restart daily prednisoneA relapse in a steroid-responsive child; relapses are common and do not harm the kidney

Mechanism13 of 17 5 yo in a relapse of nephrotic syndrome, before steroids have been restarted, who develops pneumococcal peritonitis · Consumption of complement by immune complexes · Urinary loss of immunoglobulin and factor B · Bacterial translocation from portal hypertension 5 yo in a relapse of nephrotic syndrome, before steroids have been restarted, who develops pneumococcal peritonitis Urinary loss of immunoglobulin and factor BOpsonins for encapsulated organisms leak into the urine

Next step14 of 17 5 yo with nephrotic syndrome in relapse and ascites, now with T 39.2 C, severe abdominal pain, guarding and rebound tenderness; HR 140, BP 90/54 · Increase the prednisone dose · IV albumin and furosemide · Cultures and IV antibiotics 5 yo with nephrotic syndrome in relapse and ascites, now with T 39.2 C, severe abdominal pain, guarding and rebound tenderness; HR 140, BP 90/54 Cultures and IV antibioticsSpontaneous peritonitis, usually pneumococcal; blood and peritoneal fluid cultures, then broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative cover

Diagnosis15 of 17 6 yo with severe nephrotic syndrome, albumin 1.4 g/dL, who develops sudden left flank pain, gross hematuria and an enlarged, palpable left kidney; creatinine has risen from 0.4 to 0.9 mg/dL; afebrile · Obstructing kidney stone · Acute pyelonephritis · Renal vein thrombosis 6 yo with severe nephrotic syndrome, albumin 1.4 g/dL, who develops sudden left flank pain, gross hematuria and an enlarged, palpable left kidney; creatinine has risen from 0.4 to 0.9 mg/dL; afebrile Renal vein thrombosisUrinary loss of antithrombin III and hemoconcentration; Doppler ultrasound

Avoid16 of 17 5 yo in week 3 of daily prednisone, 2 mg/kg, for a first episode of nephrotic syndrome; his kindergarten vaccines are due · Inactivated polio vaccine · DTaP vaccine · Varicella vaccine 5 yo in week 3 of daily prednisone, 2 mg/kg, for a first episode of nephrotic syndrome; his kindergarten vaccines are due Varicella vaccineLive vaccines wait until the child is off high-dose steroids

Screening17 of 17 5 yo discharged in remission from a first episode of minimal change disease; the parents ask how a relapse will be caught early · Monthly serum albumin · Renal ultrasound every 6 months · Home urine dipstick testing 5 yo discharged in remission from a first episode of minimal change disease; the parents ask how a relapse will be caught early Home urine dipstick testingProtein on the morning dipstick comes before the swelling

Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child covers the lesion: minimal change disease versus membranous and FSGS (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis). It also covers starting steroids without a biopsy. Part II Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome covers PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) and its C3 clock. Part II Anaphylaxis covers the acute allergic reaction and angioedema without hives. Part I Sinusitis and Its Complications covers preseptal versus orbital cellulitis and the orbital CT (computed tomography). Part I The Red Eye covers the conjunctivitis types.

For puffy eyes in a child, decide first whether the swelling is confined to the eye or spread over the whole child. If it is generalized, the urinalysis sorts it: protein alone means nephrotic syndrome, and blood with high blood pressure means nephritis.

Salient decoyPuffiness worst in the morning in an allergic child, treated as allergy without a urine dipstick. Mirror twinPSGN also starts with puffy eyes; blood in the urine and a high blood pressure separate it. Unchecked attributeA swollen lid called cellulitis without checking whether one eye or both, or whether the legs are swollen too. Treat-the-numberFurosemide alone for nephrotic edema, when the plasma volume is already low.

briefs.title: Lymphadenopathy
briefs.sub: tempo and laterality sort every neck node · acute and unilateral is bacterial · covering staph, strep, anaerobesHow fast did the node appear, on one side or both, and which organisms must the drug cover?
blocks: tempo and laterality sort every neck node · acute and unilateral is bacterial · covering staph, strep, anaerobesHow fast did the node appear, on one side or both, and which organisms must the drug cover?

Sort an enlarged node by site, tempo and side: one acute, unilateral, tender, warm, red neck node in a young child is bacterial lymphadenitis (Staphylococcus aureus, then Streptococcus pyogenes), treated with clindamycin. Bilateral, small, mobile nodes with a current URI (upper respiratory infection) are reactive: observe. A node that grows over weeks is cat-scratch disease when tender and draining a scratch, or nontuberculous mycobacteria when painless and violaceous. Malignancy flags: supraclavicular, firm or immobile, larger than 2 cm without infection, generalized, or with systemic symptoms; these get a CBC and chest radiograph, not observation, and a firm, immobile or enlarging node, or one that persists longer than six weeks, goes on to biopsy.

Nodes swell where they drain: a neck node reports on the throat, mouth and scalp, and an arm node on a scratch farther down the limb. An acute hot node is the node itself infected; reactive nodes are many and small; malignant nodes in children are usually painless. In practiceIn practice: a small node with no flags is rechecked after 10 to 14 days on the board answer; another reference allows up to 4 weeks of observation when there are no other findings.

Act now Finding Points to Action Fever, neck pain, drooling or a muffled voice with a tender node Retropharyngeal abscess CT of the neck, then drainage with antibiotics (Deep Neck Infections covers it). Nontender nodes with bruising, pallor, bone pain or hepatosplenomegaly Acute lymphoblastic leukemia CBC with a smear now (Acute Leukemia in a Child covers the marrow test). Fever for 5 days or more with a unilateral cervical node, red eyes, rash, strawberry tongue or swollen hands Kawasaki disease Count the criteria: fever plus 4 of the 5 (Kawasaki Disease covers the workup and treatment).

Acute neck swelling, over days Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Bacterial lymphadenitis (acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis) Under age 5; one acute, unilateral, tender, warm, red node, often 3 to 6 cm, with or without fever; S. aureus, then S. pyogenes; oral anaerobes after age 5 with poor dental hygiene. Empiric clindamycin, which covers S. aureus including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), S. pyogenes and oral anaerobes; fluctuance adds incision and drainage. In practiceIn practice: guideline authors, on expert opinion, also accept a 10-day oral course of cephalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate; the board answer is clindamycin. Reactive viral adenopathy Bilateral, small, mobile, mildly tender nodes during a current URI; shotty nodes. Supportive care and observation. Infectious mononucleosis (EBV, Epstein-Barr virus) Fatigue, fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical nodes and hepatosplenomegaly. Heterophile (monospot) test. Infected thyroglossal duct cyst Fever with midline neck pain that worsens with swallowing or tongue protrusion; the cyst rises with the tongue. Ultrasound first; Sistrunk excision, but not during the acute infection. Infected branchial cleft cyst Cystic lateral mass anterior to the sternocleidomastoid, sometimes with a draining pit; does not move with swallowing; flares after a URI. Refer for excision once the infection is treated. Tularemia (Francisella tularensis) Rabbit, tick or deerfly contact; an ulcer with a black base and a regional node. Examine the entry site for a black-based ulcer and take an animal and tick history.

A node over weeks, or a red flag Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) A papule at a cat scratch, then a tender regional node proximal to it, on its drainage path, within 2 weeks, axillary most often, then cervical; may suppurate; fever in some; fails drugs aimed at S. aureus and S. pyogenes. Ask about cats; often clinical, and Bartonella serology confirms; generally self-limited, and azithromycin speeds recovery. In practiceIn practice: adult references often skip antibiotics for localized disease in a healthy host and give azithromycin to shorten it. Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis Age 1 to 5; a chronic, painless, violaceous submandibular node in a well child. Excisional biopsy, which usually also treats it. Tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula) A chronic, single, usually cervical, nontender node with TB (tuberculosis) risk. Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, then node biopsy with acid-fast culture. Toxoplasmosis Bilateral, symmetric, nontender nodes after cat exposure. Send Toxoplasma serology. HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) Generalized painless nodes. HIV antigen/antibody test. Lymphoma Classically Hodgkin lymphoma: firm, nontender cervical or supraclavicular nodes, or a mediastinal mass, may be the first sign; fever and night sweats. CBC and chest radiograph, then excisional biopsy. Disseminated histoplasmosis Lung disease with mediastinal nodes, or hepatosplenomegaly with generalized nodes, mostly in the immunosuppressed; Mississippi and Ohio River valleys. Order Histoplasma testing for that picture only, never for a single hot node.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any enlarged node → Exam: site, tempo, one side or both, size, tenderness and fixation; other node regions, liver and spleen Acute, unilateral, tender, warm and red Bacterial lymphadenitis: clindamycin is typically the empiric drug; no test needed Bilateral or shotty with a URI; or one node under 2 cm, soft, mobile, not red and not exquisitely tender in an afebrile child Reactive or low risk: observe 10 to 14 days; work up if it persists, grows or symptoms appear Supraclavicular, firm or immobile, larger than 2 cm without infection, generalized, or systemic symptoms Red flag: CBC and chest radiograph; biopsy if the node is firm, immobile or enlarging, or persists longer than six weeks Targeted tests TestResultMeans Fluctuance, or no response to oral antibiotics → Neck ultrasound Abscess Incision and drainage with continued antibiotics, intravenous if oral therapy failed Pus from a drained node → Gram stain and culture Gram-positive cocci in clusters S. aureus; susceptibilities show MRSA and narrow the drug Tender regional node draining a skin lesion or scratch, not better on antistaphylococcal drugs → Bartonella henselae serology Positive Cat-scratch disease: azithromycin speeds recovery Chronic, single, nontender cervical node with TB risk → Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay Positive Tuberculous lymphadenitis: node biopsy or aspirate with acid-fast culture Bilateral, symmetric, nontender nodes with cat exposure → Toxoplasma serology Positive Toxoplasmosis Generalized painless nodes → HIV antigen/antibody test Positive HIV infection Posterior cervical nodes, pharyngitis, fatigue and splenomegaly → Heterophile (monospot) test Positive EBV infectious mononucleosis Recurrent abscesses and tender nodes with S. aureus, Serratia or Aspergillus → Dihydrorhodamine test Abnormal Chronic granulomatous disease Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Chronic, painless, violaceous node at age 1 to 5 → Excisional biopsy Granulomas, acid-fast bacilli Nontuberculous mycobacteria: the excision is the treatment Red-flag node that is firm, immobile or enlarging, persists longer than six weeks, or grows on antibiotics → Excisional biopsy Malignant cells Lymphoma or metastatic cancer SkipHistoplasma testing for a single hot node; broad routine labs, rarely indicated when the node pattern already names the cause.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Cat scratches, but midline neck pain worse on swallowing or tongue protrusion Infected thyroglossal duct cyst, not cat-scratch disease Ultrasound, then Sistrunk excision after the infection settles. Eastern Arkansas or a river valley, one hot neck node Bacterial lymphadenitis; the geography is a decoy Give clindamycin and skip Histoplasma testing. Caries or poor dental hygiene in a child over 5 Oral anaerobes beside S. aureus and S. pyogenes Give clindamycin, which still covers all three. A resolved URI a week before the node The portal of entry, not reactive adenopathy Treat the single hot node as bacterial. Recurrent skin abscesses, osteomyelitis or pneumonia Chronic granulomatous disease Dihydrorhodamine test (Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers it).

Pause point Child with fever and anterior neck pain, scratches from the family cat Offered as cat-scratch disease or infectious mononucleosis Is the pain midline and worse with swallowing or tongue protrusion? → Infected thyroglossal duct cyst; the cat is a distractor Teen on clindamycin for a red lump at the elbow, now tender axillary nodes and fever Offered as interferon-gamma release assay or HIV test Is the node tender, regional and draining a skin lesion, and did antistaphylococcal therapy fail? → Cat-scratch disease: Bartonella serology Toddler from eastern Arkansas with one hot, 5 cm neck node and fever Offered as itraconazole or supportive care One acute hot node, or lung disease with organomegaly? → Bacterial lymphadenitis: clindamycin

Next step1 of 19 3 yo M with a 5 cm tender, warm, erythematous, poorly mobile right anterior cervical node appearing over 2 days, T 38.6, with a resolved upper respiratory illness a week earlier · ClindamycinAn acute, unilateral, hot node with fever needs coverage of S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes and oral anaerobes: clindamycin. · CefdinirCefdinir misses MRSA and oral anaerobes. · Supportive care onlySupportive care alone fits only an afebrile child with a small, minimally tender node; this one is 5 cm and febrile. 3 yo M with a 5 cm tender, warm, erythematous, poorly mobile right anterior cervical node appearing over 2 days, T 38.6, with a resolved upper respiratory illness a week earlier Clindamycincovers MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes

Next step2 of 19 4 yo with a 1.5 cm mildly tender unilateral cervical node, afebrile, well-appearing, no overlying erythema · Incision and drainageIncision and drainage needs fluctuance. · ClindamycinClindamycin is for fever, marked tenderness, erythema or a large node. · Supportive care with reassessmentAfebrile, well, 1.5 cm, mildly tender and not red: observe and recheck in 10 to 14 days. 4 yo with a 1.5 cm mildly tender unilateral cervical node, afebrile, well-appearing, no overlying erythema Supportive care with reassessmentsmall, afebrile and not red: observe and recheck in 10 to 14 days

Next step3 of 19 3 yo who has taken clindamycin for 48 hours whose node is now fluctuant with spreading erythema · Incision and drainage with continued antibioticsFluctuance means an abscess: drain it and keep the antibiotic going. · Switch to amoxicillin-clavulanateAmoxicillin-clavulanate drops MRSA coverage and leaves the pus in place. · Continue the current antibiotic aloneAntibiotics alone do not clear an abscess; fluctuance adds drainage. 3 yo who has taken clindamycin for 48 hours whose node is now fluctuant with spreading erythema Incision and drainage with continued antibioticssuppuration has developed

Diagnosis4 of 19 8 yo with a 3-week history of a slowly enlarging tender axillary node and a papule where his kitten clawed him · Cat-scratch diseaseWeeks of a tender node draining a kitten scratch with a papule is cat-scratch disease. · Acute bacterial lymphadenitisAcute bacterial lymphadenitis appears over days and has no inoculation papule. · Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisNontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis is a painless, violaceous neck node at age 1 to 5. 8 yo with a 3-week history of a slowly enlarging tender axillary node and a papule where his kitten clawed him Cat-scratch diseaseazithromycin

Diagnosis5 of 19 3 yo with a 6-week painless violaceous submandibular node, afebrile and otherwise well · Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisAge 1 to 5 with a chronic, painless, violaceous submandibular node: nontuberculous mycobacteria, treated by excision. · Hodgkin lymphomaHodgkin lymphoma brings firm, nontender cervical or supraclavicular nodes or a mediastinal mass, not violaceous skin. · Acute bacterial lymphadenitisAcute bacterial lymphadenitis is acute, tender, warm and red. 3 yo with a 6-week painless violaceous submandibular node, afebrile and otherwise well Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitissurgical excision

Avoid6 of 19 7 yo with poor dental hygiene and acute unilateral bacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a community where MRSA is uncommon · Amoxicillin-clavulanateAmoxicillin-clavulanate covers methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, S. pyogenes and oral anaerobes: an accepted oral choice where MRSA is uncommon. · CefdinirPoor dental hygiene after age 5 adds oral anaerobes, which cefdinir misses, so it is the agent to avoid. · ClindamycinClindamycin covers S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes and oral anaerobes. 7 yo with poor dental hygiene and acute unilateral bacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a community where MRSA is uncommon Cefdinirno coverage of oral anaerobes, which poor dental hygiene brings

Diagnosis7 of 19 5 yo from the Mississippi River Valley with cough, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse adenopathy · Disseminated histoplasmosisLung disease with mediastinal nodes, hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse nodes in a river-valley child is disseminated histoplasmosis. · Acute bacterial lymphadenitisAcute bacterial lymphadenitis is one hot neck node, not diffuse nodes with organomegaly. · Cat-scratch diseaseCat-scratch disease is a tender regional node draining a scratch. 5 yo from the Mississippi River Valley with cough, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse adenopathy Disseminated histoplasmosisamphotericin B, as for any disseminated histoplasmosis

Diagnosis8 of 19 2 yo with fever, cough and rhinorrhea with bilateral small mobile mildly tender cervical nodes · Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisNontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis is chronic, unilateral and painless. · Reactive viral adenopathyBilateral, small, mobile, mildly tender nodes during a current URI are reactive: supportive care. · Acute bacterial lymphadenitisAcute bacterial lymphadenitis is one unilateral, warm, red node. 2 yo with fever, cough and rhinorrhea with bilateral small mobile mildly tender cervical nodes Reactive viral adenopathysupportive care

Mechanism9 of 19 4 year old with 1 day of fever and a red, tender, fluctuant 2 cm anterior cervical node; normal dentition, no animal contact, no rash · Bartonella henselaeBartonella henselae needs a cat scratch and builds over weeks. · Prevotella speciesPrevotella and other oral anaerobes need poor dental hygiene, usually after age 5. · Staphylococcus aureusAn acute, unilateral, suppurative node with good teeth and no exposure: S. aureus first, then S. pyogenes. 4 year old with 1 day of fever and a red, tender, fluctuant 2 cm anterior cervical node; normal dentition, no animal contact, no rash Staphylococcus aureusWith Streptococcus pyogenes – acute, unilateral, suppurative

Mechanism10 of 19 Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis and extensive dental caries · Francisella tularensisFrancisella tularensis needs rabbit, tick or deerfly exposure. · Anaerobic oral floraCaries adds oral anaerobes to S. aureus and S. pyogenes. · Staphylococcus aureusS. aureus leads without dental disease; caries points to the anaerobes. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis and extensive dental caries Anaerobic oral floraPrevotella and relatives follow periodontal disease

Mechanism11 of 19 Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis after skinning a rabbit · Bartonella henselaeBartonella henselae comes from a cat scratch or bite. · Francisella tularensisSkinning a rabbit names Francisella tularensis. · Mycobacterium aviumMycobacterium avium causes a chronic, painless node in a young child, not an acute one after an exposure. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis after skinning a rabbit Francisella tularensisThe exposure names the organism

Diagnosis12 of 19 Child with bilateral tender cervical nodes, coryza and pharyngitis for 3 days · Infectious mononucleosisInfectious mononucleosis brings fatigue, posterior cervical nodes and hepatosplenomegaly. · Bacterial cervical lymphadenitisBacterial cervical lymphadenitis is one unilateral hot node. · Acute viral adenitisBilateral tender nodes with coryza and pharyngitis for 3 days are viral. Child with bilateral tender cervical nodes, coryza and pharyngitis for 3 days Acute viral adenitisBilateral and acute points at adenovirus and its relatives

Diagnosis13 of 19 3 yo with cough and rhinorrhea last week, now resolved, and a single neck node noticed yesterday that is 4 cm, tender, warm and red today; T 38.5 · Acute bacterial lymphadenitisA single acute, tender, warm, red node after a resolved URI is bacterial lymphadenitis. · Reactive viral adenopathyReactive viral adenopathy is bilateral and small, with a current URI. · Cat-scratch diseaseCat-scratch disease builds over weeks after a scratch. 3 yo with cough and rhinorrhea last week, now resolved, and a single neck node noticed yesterday that is 4 cm, tender, warm and red today; T 38.5 Acute bacterial lymphadenitisempiric clindamycin

Diagnosis14 of 19 12 yo M with a painful left neck lump a week after a febrile URI, now cystic, with a small pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoid draining mucopurulent fluid · Branchial cleft cystA lateral cyst anterior to the sternocleidomastoid with a draining pit is an infected branchial cleft cyst. · Actinomyces lymphadenitisActinomyces drains yellow sulfur granules. · Thyroglossal duct cystA thyroglossal duct cyst is midline and rises with the tongue. 12 yo M with a painful left neck lump a week after a febrile URI, now cystic, with a small pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoid draining mucopurulent fluid Branchial cleft cystsecond-arch remnant infected after a URI; resect cyst and tract

Diagnosis15 of 19 8 yo with a tender midline neck cyst after a cold that rises when she sticks out her tongue · Branchial cleft cystA branchial cleft cyst is lateral, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid. · Dermoid cystA dermoid cyst is midline but moves with the overlying skin, not the tongue. · Thyroglossal duct cystA midline cyst that rises with tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst. 8 yo with a tender midline neck cyst after a cold that rises when she sticks out her tongue Thyroglossal duct cystfollows the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum

Diagnosis16 of 19 Adult trumpet player with a soft lateral neck swelling that enlarges when he bears down · Branchial cleft cystA branchial cleft cyst sits anterior to the sternocleidomastoid and does not change with straining. · Cystic hygromaA cystic hygroma is a lymphatic malformation of the posterior neck, linked to Turner syndrome. · LaryngoceleA lateral swelling that inflates with bearing down in a wind player is a laryngocele. Adult trumpet player with a soft lateral neck swelling that enlarges when he bears down Laryngocelelaryngeal mucosa pouching through the thyrohyoid membrane, inflated by pressure

Workup17 of 19 16 yo F with a tender red lump at the left elbow 5 days ago, diagnosed as lymphadenitis and treated with clindamycin taken as prescribed; now fever and increasing swelling in the left armpit; T 38.3; a 1 cm tender mobile epitrochlear node and several 2 to 3 cm tender left axillary nodes; no other enlarged nodes · Interferon-gamma release assayAn interferon-gamma release assay is for a chronic, single, nontender node with TB risk. · HIV antigen/antibody testHIV testing is for generalized painless nodes. · Bartonella henselae serologyA tender node draining a skin lesion that fails clindamycin is cat-scratch disease: Bartonella serology. 16 yo F with a tender red lump at the left elbow 5 days ago, diagnosed as lymphadenitis and treated with clindamycin taken as prescribed; now fever and increasing swelling in the left armpit; T 38.3; a 1 cm tender mobile epitrochlear node and several 2 to 3 cm tender left axillary nodes; no other enlarged nodes Bartonella henselae serologycat-scratch disease; ask about cats; azithromycin speeds recovery

Diagnosis18 of 19 24 yo F who adopted a stray cat 2 months ago, with 3 weeks of fatigue and low-grade fever; 1 to 2 cm nontender, mobile posterior cervical nodes on both sides, symmetric; no pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, no skin lesions; heterophile antibody test negative · Cat-scratch diseaseCat-scratch disease is a tender regional node draining a scratch. · Infectious mononucleosisInfectious mononucleosis brings pharyngitis and splenomegaly with a positive heterophile test. · ToxoplasmosisBilateral, symmetric, nontender nodes after a new cat, with a negative heterophile test, is toxoplasmosis. 24 yo F who adopted a stray cat 2 months ago, with 3 weeks of fatigue and low-grade fever; 1 to 2 cm nontender, mobile posterior cervical nodes on both sides, symmetric; no pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, no skin lesions; heterophile antibody test negative ToxoplasmosisToxoplasma serology; self-limited in an immunocompetent adult

Diagnosis19 of 19 26 yo M who moved from the Philippines 2 years ago, with a single firm, nontender, 3 cm right cervical node that has enlarged slowly over 2 months; no pain, no overlying warmth, no animal exposure; other node regions normal · Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisNontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis is a disease of children aged 1 to 5. · Cat-scratch diseaseCat-scratch disease is tender and follows a scratch. · Tuberculous lymphadenitisA chronic, single, firm, nontender cervical node in an adult from a high-burden country is tuberculous lymphadenitis. 26 yo M who moved from the Philippines 2 years ago, with a single firm, nontender, 3 cm right cervical node that has enlarged slowly over 2 months; no pain, no overlying warmth, no animal exposure; other node regions normal Tuberculous lymphadenitisinterferon-gamma release assay, then node biopsy with acid-fast culture

The location, eastern Arkansas, is genuinely endemic for histoplasmosis. Mentioned in a stem beside relatives with colds, it reads as an exposure history. It is not one: sick contacts explain a recent URI. The location explains nothing, because histoplasmosis does not present as a single hot node.

Midline, moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion thyroglossal duct cyst, often found after a URI Midline, does not move with the tongue dermoid cyst, along an embryologic fusion plane Lateral, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid, below the mandible branchial cleft cyst, usually second arch, between the internal and external carotids; cured by resecting the cyst and its tract Lateral, necrotic node with violaceous skin and a fistula nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis Posterior triangle, from birth or on prenatal ultrasound cystic hygroma Lateral, enlarges with Valsalva laryngocele, through the thyrohyoid membrane; often in wind-instrument players Submandibular sinus draining sulfur granules actinomyces, after dental infection or trauma

Tempo and laterality sort neck nodes before anything else acute and unilateral is bacterial, chronic and unilateral is Bartonella or mycobacterial, acute and bilateral is viral Clindamycin is chosen for its spectrum, not its class a cephalosporin that misses MRSA and oral anaerobes can fail Violaceous and nontender is mycobacterial, and its preferred treatment is surgical excision rather than antibiotics Fluctuance adds drainage the drug stays the same A resolved URI a week earlier is a portal of entry, not a competing diagnosis; a concurrent URI would point at reactive adenopathy instead

Respiratory Infection in a Childcovers pharyngitis and reactive nodes with a URI Deep Neck Infectionscovers retropharyngeal and peritonsillar abscess Kawasaki Diseasecovers prolonged fever with a unilateral cervical node Acute Leukemia in a Childcovers nontender nodes with cytopenias Tuberculosiscovers tuberculous lymphadenitis Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Functioncovers chronic granulomatous disease Respiratory Infection in a Child covers pharyngitis and reactive nodes with a URI. Deep Neck Infections covers retropharyngeal and peritonsillar abscess. Kawasaki Disease covers prolonged fever with a unilateral cervical node. Acute Leukemia in a Child covers nontender nodes with cytopenias. Tuberculosis covers tuberculous lymphadenitis. Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers chronic granulomatous disease.
Scratches from a pet cat were placed beside a cat-scratch disease option, but acute midline pain that worsens with swallowing or tongue protrusion names an infected thyroglossal duct cyst.

When every option is a drug, name the organisms you must cover, then find the single agent that covers all of them. A geographic detail matters only when the syndrome matches the endemic disease, not merely the location.

Unchecked attributeSupportive care only: observation suits an afebrile child with a small, minimally tender node; a child with a temperature of 38.6 C and a 5 cm inflamed node is at risk of abscess. Unchecked attributeAzithromycin: correct for cat-scratch and part of mycobacterial therapy, but both are chronic and indolent, unlike a node that appeared yesterday. Class-vs-memberCefdinir: covers S. pyogenes but not MRSA or oral anaerobes, and the organisms cannot be told apart at the bedside. Salient decoyItraconazole: eastern Arkansas is histoplasmosis country, but histoplasmosis presents with pulmonary or disseminated disease, not an isolated hot node. True-fact-wrong-slotOseltamivir: influenza adenopathy is bilateral and accompanies active respiratory symptoms, not a URI that has already resolved.

briefs.title: Oral Lesions in a Child
briefs.sub: vesicles vs exudate · front of the mouth or back · herpangina vs herpetic gingivostomatitis · the palm and sole rashAre the lesions vesicles or exudate, and do they sit at the front of the mouth or the back?
blocks: vesicles vs exudate · front of the mouth or back · herpangina vs herpetic gingivostomatitis · the palm and sole rashAre the lesions vesicles or exudate, and do they sit at the front of the mouth or the back?

Sort mouth lesions by type, then site, then the skin: vesicles and ulcers are viral, while tonsillar exudate points to strep, Epstein-Barr virus or adenovirus pharyngitis. Back of the mouth (soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars) and no rash: herpangina (coxsackievirus A), supportive care. Front of the mouth with red, swollen gums: herpetic gingivostomatitis (herpes simplex virus type 1), oral acyclovir. Mouth ulcers plus vesicles on the palms and soles: hand-foot-and-mouth disease, supportive care. In all three, watch for dehydration in a child who will not drink.

Coxsackievirus A spreads by the fecal-oral route and peaks in summer and early fall; it causes both herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and the skin tells them apart. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) usually causes gingivostomatitis as its first infection, typically in children, then lies dormant in the trigeminal ganglion and can return as cold sores.

Act now Finding Points to Action Refuses all fluids; dry mouth, decreased urine output Dehydration, the main complication Check hydration now (mouth, urine output, heart rate); oral rehydration in small, frequent amounts, IV fluids if severe. Fever 5 days or more with red lips or a strawberry tongue, plus conjunctivitis, rash or swollen hands Kawasaki disease Count the criteria (fever plus 4 of 5); Kawasaki Disease covers the rest. Thrush with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea and recurrent infections Severe combined immunodeficiency Not simple thrush: look for a T-cell or autoimmune defect.

Mouth lesions in a child Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Herpangina (coxsackievirus A) Age 3 to 10, summer or early fall; abrupt fever and sore throat; small gray vesicles that become shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars; no rash. SiteMost often the tonsillar pillars and soft palate; the tonsils, uvula or tongue can be involved too. Give fluids and pain control and offer a soft diet without acidic foods; it heals within a week. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackievirus A) Young child; painful ulcers on the tongue, cheeks and palate plus a maculopapular, partly vesicular rash on the palms and soles, sometimes the buttocks. OverlapIts throat lesions can look just like herpangina; the skin decides. Clinical diagnosis; supportive care and hand hygiene after diaper changes. Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1) From 6 months to 5 years, in any season; drools and will not drink; clusters of vesicles at the front (gums, tongue, lips) with red, swollen gums. Give oral acyclovir. In practiceIn practice: oral antivirals are an option for a first infection, with topical anesthetics for mouth pain. Recurrent aphthous ulcers (canker sores) Painful shallow ulcers with a gray base and red rim; they come back, often with stress; rarely in the pharynx; usually no fever. Treat with a topical anesthetic or coating; recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms suggest Crohn or celiac disease. Cyclic neutropenia Mouth ulcers with fever every 3 weeks, each bout 3 to 5 days. CBC during a bout; repeat the count a few times each week for 6 weeks or more to confirm. Oral thrush (oral candidiasis) White plaques that scrape off and may bleed; after antibiotics or corticosteroids, inhaled ones included, or with a weak immune system. Give nystatin suspension; chronic thrush suggests a T-cell or autoimmune defect.

Exudate, not vesicles Diagnosis Decides it Excluded by Streptococcal pharyngitis Sore throat and fever without cough; exudate on the tonsils, tender nodes at the front of the neck, petechiae on the palate. Blisters and ulcers in place of exudate. Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) Adolescent with prolonged fatigue; exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly. SpleenNo contact sports for a month: the enlarged spleen can rupture. No exudate, nodes or big spleen. Adenoviral tonsillitis Sore throat with fever and cough, at times red eyes (conjunctivitis); exudate but no blisters. Vesicles are not its picture.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Fever with mouth sores in a child → Look in the mouth: lesion type, then site Vesicles and ulcers at the back, skin clear Herpangina: supportive care, no testing Vesicles at the front, red swollen gums Herpetic gingivostomatitis: oral acyclovir Tonsillar exudate, no vesicles Exudative pharyngitis Mouth ulcers with fever → Check the palms and soles Vesicles or papules found Hand-foot-and-mouth disease: supportive care, hand hygiene Skin clear Herpangina or gingivostomatitis: sort by site Drooling, not drinking → Hydration check: mouth, urine output, heart rate Mild or moderate dehydration Oral rehydration in small, frequent amounts, even if unwilling to drink Severe: circulatory compromise IV fluids Targeted tests TestResultMeans White plaques on the tongue or cheeks → Scrape a plaque Wipes off; may leave a raw, bleeding base Thrush: nystatin suspension Mouth ulcers with fever every 3 weeks → CBC during a bout Neutropenia during a bout Cyclic neutropenia: serial counts confirm Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Severe or atypical lesions, or a weak immune system → Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of a swab from an ulcer base Herpes simplex virus Herpetic infection: acyclovir Enterovirus Herpangina or hand-foot-and-mouth disease: still supportive SkipStrep testing for vesicles without exudate; viral testing for typical herpangina or hand-foot-and-mouth disease, both clinical diagnoses; acyclovir for herpangina, an enterovirus infection.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Tongue, lips and gums described as normal Not herpes simplex virus: the front of the mouth is spared No acyclovir; supportive care. Late summer, about to start school The coxsackievirus season, not an exposure Use it only with the site; season alone does not decide. Runny nose and cough with vesicles at the back of the throat Still herpangina Reassure and observe; no workup. Blue-white spots on red cheek mucosa with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis Measles (Koplik spots) Watch for a rash spreading from the face down; Fever and Rash in a Child covers it.

Pause point 5-year-old with gray ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; gums normal Offered as herpetic gingivostomatitis or oral acyclovir Where are the lesions, and are the gums red and swollen? → Back of the mouth, gums spared: herpangina, supportive care Young child with mouth ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles Offered as herpangina Is the skin involved? → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease: supportive care Toddler with mouth ulcers and fever every 3 weeks, well between Offered as aphthous ulcers or a viral illness Do the bouts come back on a fixed cycle, with fever? → Cyclic neutropenia: CBC during a bout Site first, then the skin, then the season or the 3-week cycle.

Mechanism1 of 9 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the tonsillar pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash · Streptococcus pyogenesStreptococcus pyogenes makes tonsillar exudate, not vesicles or ulcers. · Herpes simplex virus type 1Herpes simplex virus type 1 causes gingivostomatitis: vesicles at the front with red, swollen gums. · Coxsackievirus ABack-of-mouth gray vesicles and ulcers, front spared, no rash: herpangina, from coxsackievirus A. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the tonsillar pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash Coxsackievirus Aherpangina

Diagnosis2 of 9 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the tongue, lips and gums, which are red and swollen · HerpanginaHerpangina sits at the back of the mouth and spares the gums. · Herpetic gingivostomatitisClusters of vesicles at the front with red, swollen gums in a toddler: herpetic gingivostomatitis. · Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseHand-foot-and-mouth disease adds vesicles on the palms and soles. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the tongue, lips and gums, which are red and swollen Herpetic gingivostomatitisoral acyclovir

Diagnosis3 of 9 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles · Herpetic gingivostomatitisHerpetic gingivostomatitis brings red, swollen gums and no hand or foot lesions. · HerpanginaHerpangina has no rash. · Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseMouth ulcers plus vesicles on the palms and soles: hand-foot-and-mouth disease. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles Hand-foot-and-mouth diseasesupportive care

Next step4 of 9 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs · Oral amoxicillinAmoxicillin treats strep pharyngitis, which makes exudate, not vesicles. · Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesiaHerpangina is self-limited: fluids that avoid acid, plus pain control, keep the child drinking. · Oral acyclovirAcyclovir targets herpes simplex virus; herpangina is an enterovirus infection. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesiaherpangina resolves within a week

Diagnosis5 of 9 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles · Group A streptococcal pharyngitisFever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior nodes without cough: streptococcal pharyngitis. · Adenoviral tonsillitisAdenovirus brings cough, sometimes conjunctivitis, with its exudate. · HerpanginaHerpangina makes back-of-mouth vesicles and ulcers, not exudate. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles Group A streptococcal pharyngitisrapid antigen testing before treating

Diagnosis6 of 9 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly · Group A streptococcal pharyngitisStrep pharyngitis brings tender anterior nodes, not posterior nodes with a big spleen. · Epstein-Barr virus infectionAdolescent, prolonged fatigue, exudate, posterior cervical nodes and splenomegaly: infectious mononucleosis. · HerpanginaHerpangina makes vesicles, not exudate, and no splenomegaly. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly Epstein-Barr virus infectionavoid contact sports

Avoid7 of 9 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated · Acetaminophen for fever and painFever and pain control is part of the supportive care. · Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesiaFluids that avoid acid are part of the supportive care. · Oral acyclovirAcyclovir is the one to avoid: herpangina is an enterovirus infection, and acyclovir targets herpes simplex virus. 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated Oral acyclovirherpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one

Next step8 of 9 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours; HR 160, cool hands, capillary refill 4 seconds · Reassurance and oral fluids at homeOral fluids suit mild or moderate dehydration, not circulatory compromise. · Intravenous rehydrationDry mouth, no urine, a fast heart rate and slow capillary refill mark severe dehydration: IV fluids. · Oral acyclovirAcyclovir treats neither an enterovirus infection nor dehydration. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours; HR 160, cool hands, capillary refill 4 seconds Intravenous rehydrationdehydration is the principal complication

Diagnosis9 of 9 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash · Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseHand-foot-and-mouth disease adds a palm and sole rash. · Herpetic gingivostomatitisHerpetic gingivostomatitis involves the gums, lips and tongue. · HerpanginaLate summer, back-of-mouth gray vesicles and ulcers, normal gums and no rash: herpangina. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash Herpanginacoxsackievirus A; supportive care

Between herpangina and gingivostomatitis, the front of the mouth (gums, tongue, lips) is herpes; the back (soft palate, uvula, tonsillar pillars) is coxsackie – both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, Epstein-Barr virus and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does – same virus family, separated by the skin Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure Hand hygiene, above all around diaper changes, is the public-health answer

Respiratory Infection in a Childcovers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Fever and Rash in a Childcovers the other rashes with fever and points here for hand-foot-and-mouth disease Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule ; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Fever and Rash in a Child covers the other rashes with fever and points here for hand-foot-and-mouth disease.

When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where the lesions are before asking what they are. Treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.

Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus: oral vesicles in a child bring HSV to mind, but HSV sits at the front of the mouth; when the gums, tongue and lips are spared and the gums are not swollen, it does not fit. Class-vs-memberAdenovirus: a common cause of pediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers. Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes: exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it. True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus: needs exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age, none of which herpangina brings.
