blocks: Fever and Rash in a Child
itchy crops of blisters, a rash that begins on the face, or hives partway through an antibioticWhich lesion is it, where did it begin, how did it time with the fever, and what came before it?

Classify the lesion first: among whole-body exanthems, varicella alone makes vesicles, itchy crops at several stages at once; hand-foot-and-mouth blisters are centered on the palms, soles and mouth. Next, find where it began and how it timed with the fever: face first and spreading down is measles (ill, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) or rubella (well, posterior nodes); trunk first as the fever breaks is roseola. When the joints hurt too, date the rash against the exposure: 5 to 14 days into a drug is a serum sickness-like reaction; 2 to 4 weeks after untreated strep throat is acute rheumatic fever. An unvaccinated teenager with face-first spots and aching joints is rubella.

Most childhood exanthems are diagnosed at the bedside from the lesion, where it started, how it spread and the prodrome; serology or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is kept for severe or atypical cases. Scarlet fever, from group A Streptococcus, is the one bacterial rash among the classic six.

Act now Finding Points to Action Within minutes of an exposure: wheezing, hypotension or angioedema; joints and nodes spared Anaphylaxis Epinephrine; an antihistamine alone treats only itch and hives. Painful dusky skin that blisters, with hemorrhagic oral erosions, days to weeks into a drug Stevens-Johnson syndrome Stop the drug. Fever for 5 days or more with 4 of 5 criteria and negative strep testing, usually under age 5 Kawasaki disease Kawasaki Disease covers treatment and the echocardiogram. Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a face-first rash in an unvaccinated child Measles (rubeola) Airborne precautions: a respirator (N95) and an isolation room. Isolation Precautions

The classic exanthems Diagnosis Rash Tell Varicella (chickenpox; varicella-zoster virus) Crops of itchy spots that pass from macule to papule to vesicle to crust; starts on the trunk or face, then the limbs Lesions of every stage side by side in a well child. At age 3 a child has usually had one of the two doses, so a milder breakthrough case (lower fever, fewer lesions) still counts. Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackievirus) Spots and small blisters on the palms and soles, sometimes the buttocks and limbs Fever with painful mouth ulcers; drinks poorly Oral Lesions in a Child Measles (rubeola) Spreads from the face to the trunk over several days and turns confluent; palms and soles spared Ill, unvaccinated child with fever of 40 °C or more, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis; Koplik spots (gray-white dots on a red buccal base); joints spared Rubella (German measles) Fine, separate pink spots that reach the feet from the face within a day; palms and soles clear Well, unvaccinated, low fever; tender nodes behind the ears and at the occiput; in teenage girls and women, finger and wrist pain that may last up to a month Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease; parvovirus B19) Slapped cheeks that spare the nasolabial folds, followed by a lacy rash over the trunk and limbs Well, after a passing cold-like illness; the rash fades and returns with sun, heat or stress; teenagers and adults get symmetric polyarthritis Roseola (exanthem subitum, sixth disease; human herpesvirus 6) Maculopapular, starting on the trunk and spreading to the face and limbs; never vesicular Well infant or toddler; high fever for 3 to 4 days, then the rash as it breaks; febrile seizures Scarlet fever (scarlatina; group A Streptococcus) Rough, sandpaper-like papules, densest in the axillae and groin, with dark lines in skin folds and circumoral pallor; peels as it fades School-age child with sore throat, tonsillar exudate and palatal petechiae; tender anterior neck nodes; strawberry tongue
Joints hurt too: date the rash against the exposure.

Minutesanaphylaxis: wheezing, hypotension, angioedema; joints and nodes spared 5 to 14 days into a drugserum sickness-like reaction: itchy hives, low fever; complement near normal 5 to 14 days after a foreign proteinserum sickness: high fever; low complement 2 to 4 weeks after strep throat that went untreatedacute rheumatic fever Weeks to months after a painless chancresecondary syphilis Months after erythema migransLyme arthritis

Rash with joint pain Diagnosis Rash Joints and tell Serum sickness-like reaction Itchy hives that last more than a day; mouth and eyes spared Joints tender and painful to move but not swollen; low fever; nodes; mild proteinuria possible; starts 5 to 14 days into a drug such as a penicillin, cefaclor or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Commoner in children than serum sickness, and milder. Serum sickness Hives High fever and low complement 5 to 14 days after a foreign protein: antivenom, antitoxin or a monoclonal antibody Acute rheumatic fever Erythema marginatum: pale pink rings with clear centers that do not itch, usually on the trunk and proximal limbs, not the face Hot, swollen joints, each settling as the next flares; carditis; begins 2 to 4 weeks after a sore throat that went untreated; extremely rare once strep is treated promptly Disseminated gonococcal infection A few painless pustules or vesiculopustules on the distal limbs, rarely the face Sexually active; tenosynovitis with migrating joint pain, or a single hot, swollen knee Lyme arthritis Erythema migrans months earlier Typically recurring swelling of a few large joints, the knee most of all Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis Evanescent rash Arthritis for 6 weeks or more with a daily (quotidian) fever for 2 weeks or more Immunoglobulin A (IgA) vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) Palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs, not hives Platelets normal; belly pain; blood in the urine

Other mimics Diagnosis Rash Tell Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) Maculopapular rash, mainly after a beta-lactam, classically amoxicillin Teenager with exudative pharyngitis, fatigue, a big spleen and posterior cervical nodes Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Tender red skin, then flaccid bullae and large sheets of peeling; mucosa spared Irritable, febrile infant or child under 5 (rare after that); throat normal Eczema herpeticum (herpes simplex virus) Uniform, painful vesicles and punched-out erosions grouped on atopic skin Fever; looks ill Scabies Itchy papules with burrows; in infants, vesicles on the palms and soles Afebrile; others at home itch; finger webs, wrists, around the navel Secondary syphilis Maculopapular, with a rash on the palms and soles Nodes everywhere, condylomata lata; weeks to months after a painless chancre

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any child with fever and rash → Dated history of drugs, foreign proteins, vaccines, sore throat and sexual contact; look at the lesion and where it began Classic exanthem in a well child Clinical diagnosis; no test A drug 5 to 14 days ago, hives, tender unswollen joints Serum sickness-like reaction: clinical; stop the drug if still taking it Unvaccinated, sore throat weeks ago, or sexually active Test only the matching branch below Targeted tests TestResultMeans Sandpaper rash with a sore throat → Rapid strep antigen test or throat culture Positive Scarlet fever Swollen, migratory joints weeks after a sore throat → Antistreptolysin O (ASO) and anti-DNase B (anti-deoxyribonuclease B) titers Raised Recent strep: Acute Rheumatic Fever covers the Jones criteria Unvaccinated teenager, face-first fine rash, posterior nodes → Rubella immunoglobulin M (IgM) serology Positive Rubella Hives, high fever and joint pain after antivenom or a monoclonal antibody → Serum complement Low Serum sickness Pustules or tenosynovitis in a sexually active teenager → Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for gonorrhea Positive Disseminated gonococcal infection Sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis with sudden pallor → CBC and reticulocyte count Falling hemoglobin, low reticulocytes Transient aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19, which a child with sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis can develop SkipSerology or PCR for a classic exanthem in a well child; a parvovirus test before a return to school; complement or strep titers when a drug 5 to 14 days earlier explains hives with unswollen joints.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Two blisters on a palm with crops on the scalp and trunk; mouth normal Varicella, not hand-foot-and-mouth disease Give supportive care. A toddler with fever, then a rash Roseola only if the rash came as the fever broke and is not vesicular No test; reassure. Mild itch with a face-first maculopapular rash and no vesicles Rubella or measles, not varicella, which needs vesicles in crops Isolate with airborne precautions if measles is possible; order rubella IgM serology. Peeling skin after fever Scarlet fever peels as it fades; scalded skin syndrome starts with flaccid bullae under age 5 Rapid strep antigen test or throat culture. Rash after amoxicillin in a teenager with exudative pharyngitis Infectious mononucleosis, not a drug allergy alone Examine for splenomegaly and posterior cervical nodes. A rash on the palms and soles in a sexually active teenager Secondary syphilis Examine for condylomata lata; ask about a painless chancre weeks earlier. Intense itch, no fever, finger webs and wrists Scabies Examine the finger webs and wrists for burrows.

Treatment by cause Cause Action Serum sickness-like reaction Stop the drug if still taking it; an antihistamine for itch; it resolves on its own. Epinephrine only for anaphylaxis. Scarlet fever Penicillin or amoxicillin; the rash needs nothing extra. Varicella, healthy child Supportive care with antihistamines; no acyclovir for otherwise healthy children with typical varicella; home until every lesion has crusted. Who gets acyclovirAcyclovir is for high-risk patients or complicated disease (secondary bacterial skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis): oral for people at risk of moderate to severe disease, intravenous for the immunocompromised and others at risk of severe disease. Varicella exposure Immune (past chickenpox or 2 doses): observe. Healthy, nonimmune, age 1 or older, not pregnant: varicella vaccine within 5 days. Nonimmune and either immunocompromised or pregnant, or a newborn whose mother's varicella began 5 days before to 2 days after delivery: varicella-zoster immune globulin (VariZIG) within 10 days; the live vaccine cannot be given to the immunocompromised or pregnant. In practiceIn practice: the MSD (Merck Sharp and Dohme) Manual and the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) give the vaccine within 3 days and possibly up to 5; VariZIG also covers hospitalized preterm infants born at 28 weeks or later to a nonimmune mother, and any born before 28 weeks or at 1,000 g or less. Measles Airborne precautions for 4 days after the rash appears (contagious from 4 days before); vitamin A for severe measles or deficiency. In practiceIn practice: the MSD Manual recommends vitamin A for every child with measles. Rubella Supportive care; the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine prevents it; keep away from pregnant contacts, mainly in early pregnancy (miscarriage, stillbirth, congenital rubella syndrome). Erythema infectiosum No longer contagious once the rash appears, because the rash is immune mediated: back to school; the rash may recur with sun, heat or stress. Disseminated gonococcal infection Ceftriaxone.

Pause point Hives and sore wrists on day 9 of penicillin for strep throat Offered as acute rheumatic fever or scarlet fever Are the joints swollen, and did the rash start 5 to 14 days into a drug? → Serum sickness-like reaction: stop the drug Itchy crops of blisters in a once-vaccinated 3-year-old Offered as hand-foot-and-mouth disease or roseola Vesicles at several stages, beyond the palms, soles and mouth? → Breakthrough varicella after one dose Unvaccinated teenager with a face-first rash and finger pain Offered as disseminated gonococcal infection or measles Well, with posterior nodes and no pustules or cough? → Rubella

Diagnosis19 of 19 5-year-old boy who finished amoxicillin for otitis media 6 days ago raised, nonblanching purple spots on buttocks and legs painful, swollen ankles Colicky abdominal pain T 37.9 °C · platelet count normal · IgA vasculitisPalpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with normal platelets, joint and abdominal pain: IgA vasculitis. · Serum sickness-like reactionA serum sickness-like reaction gives hives, not purpura. · Immune thrombocytopeniaImmune thrombocytopenia has a low platelet count; this child's is normal. 5-year-old boy who finished amoxicillin for otitis media 6 days ago raised, nonblanching purple spots on buttocks and legs painful, swollen ankles Colicky abdominal pain T 37.9 °C · platelet count normal IgA vasculitispalpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with normal platelets, joint pain and colicky abdominal pain is IgA vasculitis, not a drug reaction: check a urinalysis

10-year-old girl, new to the United States from Central America with her family Vaccine history not given Five days of fatigue, mild itching all over, a low-grade fever and a slightly runny nose Rash for 1 day: began on the face, now covers the whole body No diarrhea or abdominal discomfort T 37.8 °C discrete maculopapules on face, trunk, back and limbs no lesions in the eyes or mouth Which vaccine is most likely to have prevented her illness? Competing answers Varicella: itching and a whole-body rash suggest chickenpox; but her lesions are discrete maculopapules with no vesicles, and varicella needs vesicles in crops. Typhoid: fever and a rash in a child from Central America suggest typhoid rose spots; but she has no abdominal pain or diarrhea, and her rash began on the face and covers the whole body. Influenza virus: fever, fatigue and a runny nose fit influenza; but influenza does not typically cause a rash. Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis: a routine childhood vaccine a recent immigrant may have missed; but diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis do not cause a spreading maculopapular rash. Haemophilus influenzae type b: another routine vaccine she may have missed; but this organism causes epiglottitis, meningitis and pneumonia, not a face-first rash. Hepatitis B: a routine infant vaccine she may have missed; but acute hepatitis B brings right upper quadrant pain and nausea, and she has no abdominal symptoms. Inactivated poliovirus: a routine vaccine she may have missed abroad; but polio causes flaccid paralysis, not a rash. Pneumococcal: a routine childhood vaccine she may have missed; but pneumococcus causes otitis media, pneumonia and meningitis, not a viral exanthem. Down to two: measles-mumps-rubella or varicella. Measles-mumps-rubella: a face-first maculopapular rash that spreads down is measles or rubella, and the MMR vaccine prevents both, so the lead-in skips the diagnosis. The low fever, discrete spots and clear eyes and mouth fit rubella better than measles; the NBME explanation teaches measles, but the stem sets the facts. The options were the routine childhood vaccines plus one travel vaccine, typhoid.

Classify the lesion first (vesicles in crops, maculopapular, lacy, sandpaper, hives), then where it began and whether it came with or after the fever; when joints hurt too, put it on a clock against the exposure. For a varicella exposure, check immunity, then risk group, then the days since exposure (up to 5 for vaccine, 10 for VariZIG).

briefs.title: Fever in an Infant
briefs.sub: urine, blood, meninges, lungs, or a virus · red flags · workup by age, appearance and vaccines · the culture confirmsDoes the infant look ill, and if well, how old and how vaccinated is the infant?
blocks: urine, blood, meninges, lungs, or a virus · red flags · workup by age, appearance and vaccines · the culture confirmsDoes the infant look ill, and if well, how old and how vaccinated is the infant?

A febrile neonate (28 days or younger) has sepsis until proven otherwise, however well: CBC, blood culture, catheter urine culture and lumbar puncture, then admission on ampicillin plus gentamicin. In practiceIn practice: the 2021 guideline for well-appearing febrile infants 8 to 60 days old, which the Aquifer case teaches, narrows the 28-day rule above: it taps every infant 21 days or younger, and from 22 to 60 days a well infant may skip the lumbar puncture when inflammatory markers (including procalcitonin, C-reactive protein and absolute neutrophil count) are normal. An ill-appearing infant at any age gets blood and urine cultures and admission, plus a lumbar puncture under 3 months; after the first month the usual drug is IV ceftriaxone. A well child of 3 to 36 months with no source: fully immunized gets only a catheter urine if at risk for a urinary tract infection (UTI); underimmunized adds a CBC and blood culture.

When a full history and examination find no focus, a virus is the usual cause; among bacterial sources the urine comes first; the blood, the meninges and the lungs follow. Neonates often do not contain infection locally, and meningeal signs are usually absent under 12 months, so age sets the floor of testing and appearance raises it.

Act before the full history Finding Points to Action Delayed capillary refill, hypotension, altered mental status Septic shock Support circulation, airway and breathing first; cultures, then IV antibiotics. Fast heart or breathing rate in an ill-appearing infant Early sepsis Cultures and antibiotics now. Hypothermia or temperature instability in a young infant, poor feeding, lethargy Sepsis, with fever absent Treat as a febrile infant: full workup and admission. Bulging fontanelle, lethargy, seizure, cries when picked up Bacterial meningitis Perform a lumbar puncture. Ill-appearing neonate, or one with skin or mouth vesicles, seizures, or maternal genital herpes Neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection Add acyclovir to the antibiotics.

Fever in an infant, most tempting first Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Febrile UTI (pyelonephritis) Fever with no focus, fussy and eating less; girl under 2 or uncircumcised boy under 1; fever puts the infection in the kidney. Catheter urinalysis and culture. Occult bacteremia Positive blood culture in a well-appearing child; the risk is higher if underimmunized. Recall and reexamine when the culture grows. Bacterial meningitis Lethargy or irritability, a bulging fontanelle, poor feeding, crying when picked up; neck signs usually absent. Perform a lumbar puncture. Sepsis Ill-appearing, fast heart and breathing rates, poor perfusion; hypothermia in young infants. Cultures, then IV antibiotics and admission. Roseola (exanthem subitum, sixth disease) 3 to 5 days of high fever in a well child under 2, then a rash as the fever breaks; human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6). Reassure; no tests or treatment. Viral meningitis Milder; loose stools, rash or cold symptoms; enterovirus. Lumbar puncture: lymphocytes, normal glucose. Pneumonia Cough, fast breathing, crackles, low saturation; rarely silent; a lower-lobe pneumonia can cause belly pain. Chest x-ray. Acute otitis media Bulging, poorly mobile, red eardrum; redness alone has no predictive value. A source: treat the ear. HSV gingivostomatitis Usually 6 months to 5 years; fever and fussiness, then mouth vesicles and ulcers. Treat the source; Oral Lesions in a Child covers it. Viral upper respiratory infection Congestion, cough, runny nose. Treat it as a viral source, not fever without one. Kawasaki disease Fever 5 days or more with red eyes, red lips and rash; infants often have incomplete forms. Check the criteria in Kawasaki Disease.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans No source; girl under 2, uncircumcised boy under 1, circumcised boy under 6 months, prior UTI or urinary tract anomaly, fever over 48 hours, or underimmunized → Catheter urinalysis Leukocyte esterase and nitrite positive UTI strongly suggested: culture and start antibiotics Leukocyte esterase alone Pyuria has other causes; the culture decides Nitrite negative Does not exclude UTI; infants void often Normal UTI unlikely; look elsewhere or follow closely Well, fully immunized, 3 to 36 months, none of those risks → No test: clinical follow-up Still febrile after 48 hours Reexamine and test the urine Targeted tests TestResultMeans Neonate, 28 days or younger, well or ill → CBC, blood culture, catheter urine culture, lumbar puncture All sent before antibiotics Admit on empiric antibiotics until a dangerous infection is ruled out 1 to 3 months, ill-appearing or high risk (premature, unvaccinated) → CBC, blood and urine cultures, lumbar puncture All sent before antibiotics Admit on IV ceftriaxone until serious bacterial infection is ruled out 1 to 3 months, well-appearing 61 to 90 days Many experts wait for the urinalysis before blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies in a well infant of 61 to 90 days. → Catheter urine, blood culture, inflammatory markers All normal Home with a recheck in 24 to 36 hours; admit if follow-up is doubtful Any abnormal Lumbar puncture, then admission on parenteral antibiotics 3 to 36 months, well, missing a second dose of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) or Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine In practice In practice: an underimmunized child with fever over 39 C, no source and a white count of 15,000 or more also gets parenteral ceftriaxone pending blood and urine cultures. → CBC with differential and blood culture, with the urine High white count, bands More likely bacterial Positive days later in a well child Occult bacteremia: recall and reexamine 3 to 36 months, ill-appearing → CBC, blood and urine cultures All sent before antibiotics Admit on IV ceftriaxone pending cultures Bulging fontanelle, lethargy, irritability, cries when picked up → Lumbar puncture Neutrophils, low glucose, high protein Bacterial meningitis Lymphocytes, normal glucose Viral meningitis Cough, fast breathing, crackles; or fever over 39 C with a white count of 20,000 or more and no other source → Chest x-ray Infiltrate Pneumonia Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Positive urinalysis → Catheter urine culture A single uropathogen UTI; E. coli in 85 to 90%, the rest Klebsiella, Proteus or enterococcus Blood drawn for an ill or underimmunized infant → Blood culture Positive in a well child Occult bacteremia Positive in an ill child Sepsis Lumbar puncture done → CSF culture Positive, even when the Gram stain is negative Bacterial meningitis 3 to 5 days of high fever in a well child → None: clinical Rash as the fever breaks Roseola SkipA CBC in a well, fully immunized child (a high count is almost always a false positive); a bag urine for culture (contaminated, screening only); group A strep testing under age 3; a lumbar puncture in a well child over 3 months with no meningeal signs.

Treatment by cause Cause Setting Treatment Febrile neonate, any source, before cultures return Admit IV ampicillin plus gentamicin; ampicillin plus cefotaxime if meningitis is suspected; add acyclovir for herpes signs or an ill appearance. No ceftriaxone under 1 month: it displaces bilirubin. These target the common neonatal pathogens: group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria. Bacterial Meningitis covers the meningitis regimen. Ill-appearing infant over 1 month Admit IV ceftriaxone until serious bacterial infection is ruled out; vancomycin joins it when meningitis is suspected (Bacterial Meningitis). Febrile UTI in an older infant or child, well, keeping oral medicine down, reliable family Home An oral cephalosporin (cefixime or cephalexin); not nitrofurantoin, which reaches an acceptable level only in the urine. DosingWeight times milligrams per kilogram per day, split by the number of daily doses; choose the fewest doses a day and a volume in whole milliliters. Febrile UTI, toxic, vomiting doses, or doubtful adherence Admit IV ceftriaxone; switch to ampicillin if enterococcus grows, since ceftriaxone misses it. After a first febrile UTI under age 2 Follow-up Renal and bladder ultrasound; Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers the voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG). Occult bacteremia, now well Recall Reexamine when the blood culture grows. Roseola Home Reassurance; no treatment.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Fussy and eating less, nothing else Separates nothing: UTI, meningitis and viruses all do it Use age, appearance and vaccines to set the tests. Missing a second dose of PCV or Hib Underimmunized: bacteremia risk higher Add CBC and blood culture. Diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis or pneumococcal vaccine in the last few days Immunization fever Watch: it comes within a few days; a live vaccine (measles, mumps and rubella, or varicella) brings fever at 6-14 days. Circumcised boy 6 months or older, immunized, well Low UTI risk Clinical follow-up, no urine. No Kernig or Brudzinski sign under 12 months Excludes nothing: usually absent in infant meningitis Examine the fontanelle, feeding and alertness. Eardrum red but mobile and not bulging Not acute otitis media Keep working it up as fever without a source. High white count in a well, immunized child Almost always a false positive Avoid further blood tests.

Pause point 6-month-old girl, well, fully immunized, febrile, no source Offered as CBC and blood culture or lumbar puncture Ill-appearing or underimmunized? At risk for UTI? → Catheter urinalysis and culture only: a girl under 2 is at risk Febrile neonate, feeding well and alert Offered as home with a recheck or urine only 28 days or younger? → Full workup with lumbar puncture, admission, ampicillin plus gentamicin Febrile UTI, still febrile on ceftriaxone; enterococcus grows Offered as add gentamicin or continue ceftriaxone Does the drug cover the organism? → Switch to ampicillin

In an infant with fever and no source, appearance, age and vaccine status decide how much testing is needed. Test the urine of any child at risk, and collect it by catheter. The culture, not the dipstick, confirms the infection.

Salient decoyFussiness and poor feeding come with UTI, meningitis and viral illness alike and cannot separate them. Unchecked attributeA supple neck and no Kernig or Brudzinski sign under 12 months do not exclude meningitis. Test-overrides-findingsA high white count in a well, fully immunized infant is almost always a false positive. Class-vs-memberNitrofurantoin treats bladder infection but never reaches the kidney, so it cannot treat a febrile UTI.

First rule out a drug or a medical illness, including delirium; a trauma disorder alone does not typically explain psychosis Then: does the psychosis persist, and is it only inside mood episodes? Lifelong odd traits that may include odd perceptions, with no persistent psychosis a personality disorder

What it is Psychosis: a distorted perception of reality, with delusions, hallucinations or disorganized thought or speech Sort by Cause (drug, illness, trauma) course (persistent, inside mood episodes, lifelong traits) Hands off Timing and treatment of each psychotic disorder: Psychosis; a manic episode: Bipolar Disorder; a drug or disease: Medication- and Illness-Induced Psychiatric Disorders

DeliriumFluctuating attention and disorientation; any psychosis is secondary Delirium If attention fails over hours to days, choose find and treat the drug or illness causing it. Drug or illnessA new medication, drug use or a disease known to cause psychosis Medication- and Illness-Induced Psychiatric Disorders If the timing ties it to a drug or disease, choose treat the cause before naming a primary disorder.

(healthy; most common at 3 to 6, can last into school age; aids creativity and rehearses social skills, with no harm to real friendships); autism spectrum disorder No withdrawal or fall in function; autism has no hallucinations

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans New voices or odd beliefs → Medication and substance history, with timing → Chemistry panel → Blood count → Liver and thyroid tests → Vitamin B12 → Urine drug screen → Urinalysis → HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) serology A drug, a disease or delirium Treat the cause first No cause found Sort by the course Next step TestResultMeans No cause found → Course of the symptoms Persistent delusions or voices Primary psychotic disorder: time it Only inside a mood episode Mood disorder with psychotic features Hours, under stress Borderline personality disorder Lifelong traits, no frank psychosis A personality disorder SkipNo test sorts the primary look-alikes; the course does.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step A young child who sees and hears a companion, with organized speech and behavior A normal imaginary friend Reassure; no referral or therapy A teen whose voice comes with withdrawal and falling grades; or disorganization, isolation or lost milestones; or hallucinations in an older child A hallucination, not an imaginary friend Psychiatric evaluation; time the psychosis Psychosis High-functioning with one fixed belief Delusional disorder Low function points to schizophrenia Elated or irritable mood, less sleep, pressured speech Mania with psychotic features Bipolar Disorder

briefs.title: Cognitive Decline and Dementia in an Adult
briefs.sub: tempo · first domain lost · companion signsOver years, stepwise, or weeks to months, and what came with it?
blocks: Cognitive Decline and Dementia in an Adult
tempo · first domain lost · companion signsOver years, stepwise, or weeks to months, and what came with it?

Dementia: decline in memory or thinking with intact consciousness that costs independence in daily activities. First exclude delirium and depression Every new decline: CBC, metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and vitamin B12, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) and syphilis testing by risk; brain MRI may be added to exclude a structural cause Tempo and companions name the cause: memory loss over years (Alzheimer), stepwise (vascular), fluctuation, visual hallucinations, dream enactment (dementia with Lewy bodies, or Lewy body dementia), weeks to months with startle myoclonus (Creutzfeldt-Jakob)

What it is Acquired decline in memory or thinking, with intact consciousness, enough to need help with daily activities Who Older adults; Alzheimer disease is the most common cause, vascular dementia the second Sort by Tempo: years, stepwise, or weeks to months first domain lost: memory, executive or visuospatial function, or personality companions: parkinsonism, gait and incontinence, myoclonus, alcohol use Treatment in Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism Delirium Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal Major Depressive Disorder

Acute changeSudden confusion in a patient with known dementia Delirium If attention and alertness wax and wane, choose look for infection, pain, a metabolic derangement or a medication effect. Alcohol or malnutritionAlcohol use or malnutrition with confusion, ataxia or eye-movement abnormalities Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal If Wernicke encephalopathy is possible, choose thiamine; glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. HallucinationsVisual hallucinations in suspected dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia) Antipsychotic Adverse Effects If the hallucinations need treatment, choose avoid typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol; a cholinesterase inhibitor is first-line; if psychosis is severe or distressing, low-dose quetiapine may be used with extreme caution. Rapid declineDementia progressing over weeks to months If startle myoclonus or cerebellar signs appear, choose MRI, electroencephalogram (EEG), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 14-3-3 protein and real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) for prion disease.

Causes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Timeline Decides it Alzheimer disease Short-term memory lost first, then language and spatial disorientation; personality changes later Insidious, over years Memory lost first; no focal deficits early; medial temporal (hippocampal) atrophy is the earliest imaging finding Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia); see Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism Fluctuating attention, early well-formed visual hallucinations, dream enactment, parkinsonism; executive and visuospatial loss before memory Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism; dream enactment may come years earlier Dementia plus 2 of 4 core features: fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM (rapid eye movement) sleep behavior disorder Delirium; see Delirium Waxing and waning attention and alertness Acute Consciousness altered; dementia leaves it intact Depression-related cognitive impairment (pseudodementia); see Major Depressive Disorder Depressed mood; distressed by memory loss; often answers "I don't know" Acute onset with the depressive episode Aware and distressed, unlike dementia; does not explain parkinsonism, fluctuation or dream enactment Vascular dementia Typically early executive dysfunction, focal neurologic signs, vascular risk factors Stepwise decline Infarcts or white matter changes on imaging Frontotemporal dementia Early disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behavior such as hyperorality Onset typically in the 40s or 50s Memory and visuospatial function relatively spared early; frontal and anterior temporal atrophy Normal pressure hydrocephalus Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, slowed attention and apathy; a reversible cause Wet, wobbly, wackyMnemonicWet is urinary incontinence, wobbly is gait apraxia, wacky is dementia Gait problem early Dilated ventricles; gait improves after lumbar puncture Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Mood or sleep disturbance, startle myoclonus, cerebellar and upper motor neuron signs WhoSporadic or acquiredUsually sporadic, after age 50; rarely iatrogenic (neurosurgical instruments, corneal or dura grafts, growth hormone) or variant, from contaminated beef Weeks to months; fatal within about a year Positive CSF RT-QuIC; cortical ribboning on MRI; periodic sharp waves on EEG Korsakoff syndrome; see Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal Alcohol use disorder; confabulation without concern; recent memory lost, remote memory kept; anterograde amnesia more prominent than retrograde Chronic; may follow a Wernicke episode or develop without one Alert, with no ataxia or eye findings, unlike Wernicke encephalopathy; rarely recovers Parkinson disease dementia; see Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism Established parkinsonian motor disease Dementia more than 1 year after motor onset Timing of dementia against motor onset Encephalitis (herpes simplex, autoimmune or paraneoplastic) Usually fever, headache, seizures and focal deficits (herpes); a tumor such as small cell lung cancer (paraneoplastic) Under 1 week (herpes) MRI, CSF and EEG separate it from prion disease
Tempo of declinenot to scale Creutzfeldt-Jakob diseaseWeeks to months; death usually within a year WeeksYears Alzheimer diseaseInsidious, over years WeeksYears

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any suspected dementia → Ask which daily activities the patient needs help with Help needed with daily activities Dementia: find the cause Waxing and waning attention Delirium: treat the trigger → Cognitive testing, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment Low score with intact alertness Cognitive impairment confirmed Every new cognitive decline → CBC → Metabolic panel → TSH Abnormal TSH A reversible contributor: treat it → Vitamin B12 Low B12 A reversible contributor: treat it → HIV and syphilis testing, by risk Positive syphilis test Neurosyphilis: a reversible cause Positive HIV test HIV-associated dementia: not reversible Treated HIV Almost only untreated, advanced HIVHIV-associated dementia occurs almost exclusively in untreated, advanced disease (CD4 <200/mm3). With antiretroviral therapy, common dementias such as Alzheimer disease are a much more likely cause. Structural cause possible → Brain MRI Tumor, subdural hematoma or enlarged ventricles A structural cause Infarcts or white matter changes Vascular dementia Targeted tests TestResultMeans Weeks to months of decline with startle myoclonus → MRI (diffusion-weighted imaging or fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) Cortical ribboning; high signal in the caudate and putamen Suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease → EEG Periodic sharp wave complexes Suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease → CSF analysis with 14-3-3 protein No white cells; 14-3-3 elevated Noninflammatory; 14-3-3 is not specific Gait problem early, urinary incontinence → Lumbar puncture to remove CSF Gait improves Normal pressure hydrocephalus: shunt Low mood, distressed about memory → Screen for depression Depressive episode Treat with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Suspected prion disease → CSF RT-QuIC Positive Confirms Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease SkipA normal head CT as reassurance in suspected prion disease: CT is often normal early

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Dream enactment, good and bad days, rigidity Dementia with Lewy bodies Cholinesterase inhibitor; avoid haloperidol Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism Alcohol use disorder, confabulation, remote memory intact, unconcerned Korsakoff syndrome Thiamine, as for any undernourished patient; memory rarely recovers Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal Startle myoclonus after months of decline Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease CSF RT-QuIC; supportive care, counseling and social services HIV with missed doses and CD4 count <200/mm3; personality change; decline in memory, attention and calculation; diffuse white matter change, large ventricles, no focal deficit HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HIV-associated dementia) Diffuse and symmetric; progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) brings focal deficits with well-delineated, asymmetric white matter lesions Slow memory loss over years, no focal deficits Alzheimer disease Cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil; memantine is an option CourseExpectationsCholinesterase inhibitors improve cognitive function but do not alter the course Stepwise decline with focal signs, typically with stroke risk factors Vascular dementia MRI for infarcts Early disinhibition or apathy with memory relatively spared Frontotemporal dementia MRI for frontal and anterior temporal atrophy Gait problem, incontinence, enlarged ventricles Normal pressure hydrocephalus Lumbar puncture; shunt if gait improves Depressed, aware of and distressed by memory loss Depression-related cognitive impairment Treat the depression with an SSRI Major Depressive Disorder

Pause point Suspected prion disease Answered by a head CT or a nonspecific 14-3-3 Head CT is often normal early in prion disease → Name the tempo and the companion signs first Hallucinations in Lewy body dementia Offered: haloperidol Neuroleptic sensitivity worsens rigidity and confusion → A cholinesterase inhibitor first; low-dose quetiapine, with extreme caution, if psychosis is severe or distressing

Diagnosis1 of 8 74-year-old man; his wife reports he punches and shouts while asleep Some mornings he seems himself; by afternoon he is confused. He recently got lost driving home Exam: rigidity and slow gait, new this year; recall near normal · Parkinson disease dementiaDementia comes more than 1 year after motor onset · Alzheimer diseaseShort-term memory is lost first · Dementia with Lewy bodiesFluctuation, dream enactment and parkinsonism with early visuospatial loss 74-year-old man; his wife reports he punches and shouts while asleep Some mornings he seems himself; by afternoon he is confused. He recently got lost driving home Exam: rigidity and slow gait, new this year; recall near normal Dementia with Lewy bodiesDream enactment, fluctuation and parkinsonism with early visuospatial loss and relatively spared memory fit Lewy body dementia; Alzheimer disease starts with memory loss, and Parkinson disease dementia follows motor disease by over a year

Diagnosis2 of 8 61-year-old man who drinks heavily is found entering a neighbor's house He gives a fluent, false reason and is unbothered by gaps in his story He recalls his school years in detail; gait and eye movements are normal · Korsakoff syndromeConfabulation, recent memory loss and preserved remote memory in alcohol use · Wernicke encephalopathyBrings confusion, ataxia or eye-movement findings; none are present here · Alzheimer diseaseGradual memory loss without confabulation in alcohol use 61-year-old man who drinks heavily is found entering a neighbor's house He gives a fluent, false reason and is unbothered by gaps in his story He recalls his school years in detail; gait and eye movements are normal Korsakoff syndromeConfabulation with lost recent memory, preserved remote memory and no concern, in alcohol use disorder, is Korsakoff syndrome; Wernicke encephalopathy brings confusion, ataxia or eye findings

Next step3 of 8 58-year-old woman has declined over 3 months and can no longer dress herself A slammed door makes her arms jerk; she now sleeps most of the day Head CT is normal; routine CSF shows no white cells · Repeat head CTCT is often normal early in prion disease · Empiric IV acyclovirHerpes encephalitis typically evolves in under a week, usually with fever and seizures · CSF RT-QuICThe most sensitive and specific test for prion disease 58-year-old woman has declined over 3 months and can no longer dress herself A slammed door makes her arms jerk; she now sleeps most of the day Head CT is normal; routine CSF shows no white cells CSF RT-QuICRapid decline with startle myoclonus and sleep disturbance suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease; a positive RT-QuIC confirms it, while CT is often normal and herpes encephalitis evolves within a week with fever

Diagnosis4 of 8 55-year-old man now sleeps 14 hours a day and drifts into the right lane when driving Over 2 months he developed a wide-based gait and dysmetria CSF RT-QuIC is positive; reflexes and sensation are normal · Flaccid paralysisUpper motor neuron involvement brings increased tone instead · Cogwheel rigidityA parkinsonian sign; startle myoclonus is the finding that usually develops in prion disease · MyoclonusUsually develops in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, provoked by startle 55-year-old man now sleeps 14 hours a day and drifts into the right lane when driving Over 2 months he developed a wide-based gait and dysmetria CSF RT-QuIC is positive; reflexes and sensation are normal MyoclonusA positive RT-QuIC confirms Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, in which startle myoclonus usually develops; prion disease affects upper motor neurons, so flaccid paralysis is not expected

Diagnosis5 of 8 70-year-old woman has 6 weeks of poor sleep, low appetite and slowed thinking She insists her memory is failing and often answers "I don't know" She is tearful and worried; no parkinsonism or focal deficits · Frontotemporal dementiaEarly disinhibition or apathy with memory relatively spared · Depression-related cognitive impairmentAcute onset, depressed mood and distress about memory · Alzheimer diseaseGradual memory loss with relative unconcern 70-year-old woman has 6 weeks of poor sleep, low appetite and slowed thinking She insists her memory is failing and often answers "I don't know" She is tearful and worried; no parkinsonism or focal deficits Depression-related cognitive impairmentAcute onset with depressive symptoms and distress about memory point to depression-related cognitive impairment; patients with Alzheimer disease are typically relatively unconcerned

Next step6 of 8 76-year-old man first developed an unsteady gait, then urinary accidents Over several months he became slow to answer and apathetic Brain MRI shows dilated ventricles; no infarcts or mass lesion · Ventriculoperitoneal shunt nowDefinitive treatment once lumbar puncture improves gait · DonepezilTreats Alzheimer-type dementia, not a reversible hydrocephalus · Lumbar puncture to remove CSFImproved gait afterward supports the diagnosis 76-year-old man first developed an unsteady gait, then urinary accidents Over several months he became slow to answer and apathetic Brain MRI shows dilated ventricles; no infarcts or mass lesion Lumbar puncture to remove CSFGait disturbance, incontinence and cognitive slowing with dilated ventricles suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus; gait improvement after lumbar puncture supports it, and a shunt is the definitive treatment

Next step7 of 8 68-year-old man has forgotten appointments and repeated questions for a year He now needs help paying bills; his wife says he is alert and calm Exam shows no focal deficits; no recent medication changes · Start donepezil todayTreatment follows the evaluation for reversible causes · CSF 14-3-3 proteinFor rapid decline; it is not specific for prion disease · CBC, metabolic panel, TSH and B12Excludes reversible contributors to cognitive decline 68-year-old man has forgotten appointments and repeated questions for a year He now needs help paying bills; his wife says he is alert and calm Exam shows no focal deficits; no recent medication changes CBC, metabolic panel, TSH and B12A slow decline with intact alertness and lost independence is dementia; laboratory testing first excludes reversible contributors before a cause is named

Avoid8 of 8 80-year-old man with Lewy body dementia sees strangers in his room at night The visions frighten him; attention fluctuates and his limbs are rigid His family asks for medication to stop the hallucinations · RivastigmineFirst-line; can improve visual hallucinations · Low-dose quetiapineMay be used with extreme caution if psychosis is severe · HaloperidolNeuroleptic sensitivity worsens rigidity and confusion 80-year-old man with Lewy body dementia sees strangers in his room at night The visions frighten him; attention fluctuates and his limbs are rigid His family asks for medication to stop the hallucinations HaloperidolTypical antipsychotics such as haloperidol can markedly worsen rigidity, confusion and falls in Lewy body dementia; a cholinesterase inhibitor is first-line, and low-dose quetiapine is a cautious option for severe psychosis

Deliriuman acute change on top of dementia Parkinson Disease and ParkinsonismLewy body and Parkinson disease dementia Substance Intoxication and WithdrawalWernicke encephalopathy Major Depressive Disorderdepression-related cognitive impairment Delirium: an acute change on top of dementia. Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism: Lewy body and Parkinson disease dementia. Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal: Wernicke encephalopathy. Major Depressive Disorder: depression-related cognitive impairment.
Exclude delirium and depression before naming a dementia; then the tempo and the companion signs choose the cause.

briefs.title: Suspected Overdose or Toxidrome
briefs.sub: anticholinergic · stimulant · serotonin syndrome · neuroleptic malignant syndrome · lithium · opioid and sedative · cholinergic · salicylate and acetaminophenWhich toxidrome, and what must be checked in every overdose?
blocks: anticholinergic · stimulant · serotonin syndrome · neuroleptic malignant syndrome · lithium · opioid and sedative · cholinergic · salicylate and acetaminophenWhich toxidrome, and what must be checked in every overdose?

Stabilize first: airway and breathing, a fingerstick glucose and an ECG (electrocardiogram); naloxone for slow breathing with pinpoint pupils In every intentional overdose, check acetaminophen and salicylate levels, and suspect more than one substance Then name the toxidrome from the pupils, the skin, the bowel sounds and the muscle tone

What it is A toxidrome: a cluster of signs that points to a class of poison Who Intentional overdose is common in adolescents and adults, often with more than one substance Sort by Pupils sweating or dry skin bowel sounds tone and reflexes Timing: minutes to hours, or days, after a drug is started or raised Treatment in Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity SSRI Adverse Effects Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Lithium Therapy Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal

BreathingSlow, shallow breathing with pinpoint pupils respirations are 6/min and shallow Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal If breathing is slow or the airway is at risk, choose assisted ventilation and IV naloxone. GlucoseAltered consciousness or a depressed nervous system If a bedside glucose has not ruled out hypoglycemia, choose IV dextrose, with thiamine given with or before it in alcohol use or undernutrition. HeartA wide QRS, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity If the QRS is over 100 ms after a tricyclic, choose sodium bicarbonate. Another causeInfection, head injury, hypoglycemia, stroke or Wernicke encephalopathy can also alter consciousness Delirium If the toxidrome does not fit the picture, choose look for another cause of altered consciousness. Suicide attemptAny intentional ingestion Suicide Risk Assessment If the patient is medically stable and thinking clearly, choose assess suicide risk.

Which toxidrome, most tempting first Toxidrome Fingerprint Decides it Anticholinergic (tricyclic, antihistamine, clozapine) Big pupils; hot, dry, flushed skin; ileus; urinary retention; delirium MnemonicAnticholinergic toxidromeHot as a hare (fever), dry as a bone (no sweating), red as a beet (flushing), blind as a bat (big pupils), mad as a hatter (delirium) Dry skin with normal tone; a tricyclic may add a wide QRS Stimulant (cocaine, amphetamine) Big pupils, fast pulse, hypertension, agitation, fever, seizures Sweating, with the same big pupils and fever Serotonin syndrome Clonus, hyperreflexia, sweating, increased bowel sounds Minutes to hours after a serotonergic drug is added or raised; clonus Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, unstable vital signs Builds over 1 to 3 days after a dopamine blocker is started or raised; rigid, with slow reflexes Lithium toxicity Acute: vomiting and diarrhea first. Chronic: tremor, ataxia, seizures Usually within 10 days of adding a thiazide; an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor also raises the level Opioid Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, sedation Pupils under 1 mm with slow breathing Sedative (benzodiazepine) Sedation with normal-sized pupils Breathing only mildly slowed; abnormal vital signs suggest alcohol taken as well Barbiturate Somnolence to coma, slow pulse, low blood pressure, slow breathing; sluggish pupils Versus a benzodiazepineBarbiturate overdoseBenzodiazepines carry less risk of respiratory depression and coma, and flumazenil does not reverse barbiturates. Breathing slows too; beta blockers and calcium channel blockers can slow the pulse and lower the pressure but would not slow or stop breathing Cholinergic (organophosphate) Pinpoint pupils, sweating, salivation, tearing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia Secretions everywhere, with increased bowel sounds Salicylate (aspirin) Fever, tinnitus, fast breathing Respiratory alkalosis early, metabolic acidosis late; a salicylate level confirms Acetaminophen Often no symptoms early Liver failure may follow 1 to a few days later

Onset after the exposure Minutes1 day3 days10 days Serotonin syndromeMinutes to hours Neuroleptic malignant syndromeBuilds over 1 to 3 days Acetaminophen liver injuryMay follow 1 to a few days later Lithium after a thiazideUsually within 10 days

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any suspected overdose → Fingerstick glucose Low glucose IV dextrose; thiamine with or before it in alcohol use or undernutrition → ECG and cardiac monitoring QRS over 100 ms Tricyclic cardiotoxicity: bicarbonate An intentional or mixed ingestion → Acetaminophen level Acetaminophen detected N-acetylcysteine, best given before liver injury → Salicylate level → Urine drug screen A positive urine screen Does not prove that drug caused the picture Targeted tests TestResultMeans Takes lithium → Lithium level Fever, tinnitus and fast breathing → Salicylate level Rigid and febrile on a dopamine blocker → CK (creatine kinase) CK very high Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Next step TestResultMeans Still no named poison → Examine pupils, skin, bowel sounds and tone Big pupils, dry skin Anticholinergic Big pupils, sweating Stimulant Clonus, hyperreflexia Serotonin syndrome Lead-pipe rigidity Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Pinpoint pupils, secretions everywhere Cholinergic (organophosphate) Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing Opioid SkipBlood levels of most drugs: they do not guide treatment; acetaminophen, salicylate and lithium are among the exceptions.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) overdose with confusion or an abnormal exam A coingestant: an SSRI alone is usually well tolerated Levels of common coingestants, such as salicylate and ethanol Agitated, hallucinating and febrile on clozapine or a tricyclic Anticholinergic toxicity; haloperidol would worsen it A benzodiazepine Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity Normal muscle tone in an agitated, febrile patient on clozapine or a tricyclic Not neuroleptic malignant syndrome No bromocriptine; ECG Farmer with pinpoint pupils, tearing, vomiting and increased bowel sounds Organophosphate poisoning Atropine first, then pralidoxime Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, sedation Opioid toxicity IV naloxone; intubation if no quick response On a mood stabilizer: vomiting and diarrhea, then tremor and ataxia Lithium toxicity Lithium level Lithium Therapy Acetaminophen taken, no symptoms yet Delayed liver injury N-acetylcysteine; activated charcoal within 4 hours

Pause point Agitated, febrile patient on psychiatric drugs Offered: haloperidol The exam names the toxidrome → Name the toxidrome from the exam Negative urine screen Read as no poisoning Screens miss many drugs → Check the acetaminophen level anyway

In a suspected overdose, stabilize breathing, glucose and the heart, check acetaminophen and salicylate levels, then let the pupils, skin, bowel sounds and tone name the toxidrome.

briefs.title: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
briefs.sub: aching with normal strength · sedimentation rate and creatine kinase · giant cell arteritis overlap · prednisone responseIs this pain and stiffness with normal strength after 50, and does low-dose prednisone clear it within days?
blocks: aching with normal strength · sedimentation rate and creatine kinase · giant cell arteritis overlap · prednisone responseIs this pain and stiffness with normal strength after 50, and does low-dose prednisone clear it within days?

Over 50, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching with morning stiffness, normal strength, a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and a normal creatine kinase (CK) polymyalgia rheumatica Low-dose prednisone, 15 to 20 mg; a dramatic response within days supports the diagnosis, and no response means another diagnosis should be suspected Headache, jaw claudication or vision change is giant cell arteritis: high-dose glucocorticoids now, the biopsy after

What it is An inflammatory syndrome of proximal aching and stiffness in adults over 50, without true weakness, closely tied to giant cell arteritis Driver Likely low-grade synovitis and bursitis around the girdles, not muscle injury, so the CK stays normal Triggers Age over 50 (non-modifiable) Female sex, about 2 to 1 (non-modifiable) Chain Inflammation: girdle bursitis and synovitis ESR and C-reactive protein (CRP) rise Clinical: shoulder and hip girdle aching morning stiffness over an hour pain limits movement while strength stays normal Insights Pain, not weakness, keeps the patient in bed: true weakness with a high CK points to myositis The steroid response is part of the diagnosis: relief comes in hours to days on low-dose prednisone, and no response by a week points elsewhere

Who age over 50 Pain bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness over 60 minutes, normal strength Labs ESR raised, usually over 50; CRP raised; CK normal Response dramatic improvement on low-dose prednisone within days

Giant cell arteritisNew headache, jaw claudication, vision loss or amaurosis fugax; untreated, a high risk of blindness, higher with jaw claudication or diplopia; about half of patients with arteritis also have polymyalgia rheumatica If it is suspected, choose high-dose glucocorticoids at once, without waiting for the biopsy; consider IV pulse first if vision is impaired; the temporal artery biopsy follows. BiopsyTemporal artery biopsyThe arteritis is segmental, so the biopsy takes a long segment, and a negative biopsy does not exclude it. Treatment is not delayed for it: the biopsy can be done up to 2 weeks after glucocorticoids start. Jaw claudication and diplopia carry a higher risk of blindness.

Proximal pain or weakness after 50, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Polymyalgia rheumatica Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching and stiffness; strength normal Sudden onset; stiffness over an hour each morning; ESR and CRP high, CK normal Polymyositis or dermatomyositis Proximal weakness more than pain; dermatomyositis adds a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules and can signal a cancer CK high; anti-Jo-1; muscle biopsy confirms Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) Headache, jaw claudication, vision loss Over 50; ESR often over 50; temporal artery biopsy shows giant cells Elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis Small-joint synovitis of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, erosions Rheumatoid factor or anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) positive Statin myopathy Lipid Screening and Statin Therapy Aching on a statin After a statin is started; CK high Hypothyroid myopathy Thyroid Disease in an Adult Fatigue, weight gain, bradycardia Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) high, CK high Glucocorticoid-induced myopathy Painless proximal weakness on long-term glucocorticoids, as for arteritis ESR and CK both normal; no pain Fibromyalgia Widespread pain with tender points, often a young to middle-aged woman Chronic; ESR, CRP and CK normal

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Proximal aching and stiffness after 50 → ESR and CRP, CK, TSH ESR high, usually over 50; CK and TSH normal Fits polymyalgia rheumatica CK high Myositis, hypothyroid or statin myopathy: not polymyalgia ESR and CRP normal Fibromyalgia or another cause Targeted tests TestResultMeans Headache, jaw claudication or vision change → High-dose glucocorticoids, then temporal artery biopsy Granulomatous arteritis Giant cell arteritis Swollen MCPs or PIPs → Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP Positive Elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis Myalgias, weakness, high CK → TSH and free T4 TSH high Hypothyroid myopathy Next step TestResultMeans Weakness with a high CK → Anti-Jo-1 and electromyography, then muscle biopsy Inflammatory infiltrate Polymyositis or dermatomyositis: glucocorticoids, then methotrexate Diagnostic test TestResultMeans The picture fits; no arteritis symptoms → Prednisone 15 to 20 mg daily Dramatic relief in hours to days Polymyalgia rheumatica, a clinical diagnosis No response after a week Reconsider the diagnosis SkipElectromyography and muscle biopsy when strength is normal: both are normal in polymyalgia rheumatica.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Painless proximal weakness on long-term glucocorticoids; ESR and CK normal Glucocorticoid-induced myopathy, not a flare Not more prednisone: the ESR is normal and there is no pain Aching on a statin with a raised CK Statin myopathy Stop the statin Widespread tender points, normal ESR, CRP and CK Fibromyalgia Exercise; duloxetine or another antidepressant, or an anticonvulsant Small-joint synovitis, erosions Elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP; methotrexate

Pause point Patient who “cannot get out of bed” Read as weakness: sent for electromyography and biopsy Strength is normal; pain and stiffness limit movement → Polymyalgia rheumatica: check the ESR and CRP Polymyalgia Offered: the high arteritis dose No arteritis symptoms → The polymyalgia dose, not the arteritis dose

What raises the stakes Finding Means Do Headache, jaw claudication, vision change Giant cell arteritis, with a blindness risk High-dose glucocorticoids now; consider IV pulse if vision is impaired Long-term prednisone Osteoporosis, diabetes, hypertension Protect bone and monitor glucose and blood pressure Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment Relapse whenever the dose is lowered Glucocorticoid dependence The lowest dose that controls symptoms In practiceSteroid-sparingIn practice: methotrexate is an option when the glucocorticoid cannot be tapered without a relapse, though the data are limited; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs alone are rarely enough.

1 Startpolymyalgia without arteritis symptoms Low-dose prednisone, 15 to 20 mg daily 2 Tapersymptoms subside Taper to the lowest effective dose, guided by symptoms and CRP rather than the ESR 3 Reconsiderno response after a week Not a higher dose: reconsider the diagnosis 4 Switchheadache, jaw claudication or vision change High-dose glucocorticoids, about 40 to 60 mg of prednisone; consider IV pulse if vision is impaired; biopsy after

Course on treatment Hours to daysRelief on low-dose prednisone Weeks to monthsTaper as symptoms subside About 2 yearsSome patients stop; others need small doses for years Any timeArteritis can appear, even after apparent cure

Follow-up decisions When Do Every visit, during and after treatment Ask about headache, pain on chewing and vision change: report them at once While tapering Check symptoms and CRP at each visit, not the ESR On long-term prednisone A bisphosphonate; watch for diabetes and hypertension

PMR (polymyalgia rheumatica) = pain with normal CK (creatine kinase); polymyositis = weakness with high CK PMR responds to low-dose steroids, GCA (giant cell arteritis) needs high dose every PMR diagnosis gets a GCA symptom screen, and about half of GCA patients have PMR NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) fail in PMR; they are a close but inadequate therapy.

briefs.title: Osteoarthritis
briefs.sub: pharmacotherapy ladder · class right, member wrong · ketorolac's 5-day maximum · excluding inflammatory arthritisIs the offered drug the right member of the right class for a chronic condition in this patient?
blocks: pharmacotherapy ladder · class right, member wrong · ketorolac's 5-day maximum · excluding inflammatory arthritisIs the offered drug the right member of the right class for a chronic condition in this patient?

Older adult, pain in a weight-bearing joint after use that rest relieves, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus, no fever osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease) Exercise and weight loss first; a topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) for the knee or hand, an oral NSAID next; acetaminophen only when NSAIDs cannot be taken Right class, wrong member: ketorolac stops at 5 days, so it never treats a chronic joint; there is generally no role for oral glucocorticoids, and none for hydroxychloroquine or methotrexate

What it is The most common arthritis: progressive loss of joint cartilage with bony overgrowth, a mechanical rather than inflammatory joint disease Driver Activated chondrocytes release matrix metalloproteinases and cytokines that break down the cartilage matrix Triggers Age over 60 (non-modifiable) Obesity Joint trauma Female sex (non-modifiable) An earlier deformity of the joint, such as Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease or avascular necrosis of the scaphoid (non-modifiable) Chain Molecular: chondrocyte enzymes and cytokines cartilage matrix breaks down Structural: joint space narrows osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts bone polishes on bone (eburnation) Clinical: pain after use, worse by evening brief stiffness crepitus and lost range of motion Insights The pattern is mechanical, so oral steroids and disease-modifying drugs miss: no fever, no long stiffness, no synovitis, and joint fluid usually under 2,000 white cells Topical comes first because the knee and hand are superficial: the drug may reach the joint with limited systemic exposure, which matters most in older patients

Who older adult, risk highest over 60 Pain weight-bearing joint, worse with use, eased by rest Stiffness under 30 minutes, easing with movement Exam bony enlargement, crepitus, less range of motion Radiograph LOSS: the joint space narrows, osteophytes form, and the bone under the cartilage turns sclerotic and cystic

Hot, swollen jointA single red, swollen, painful joint, usually the knee, developing over hours or days If a joint is warm with an effusion, choose arthrocentesis first: septic arthritis must be excluded. Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult NSAID harm in an older patientGastrointestinal bleeding, kidney injury and cardiovascular events If there is kidney injury or insufficiency, or a prior gastrointestinal bleed, choose a topical NSAID or acetaminophen rather than a systemic NSAID, which may be contraindicated. KetorolacWhy not ketorolacThe label limits ketorolac to 5 days in all, for moderately severe acute pain. It is contraindicated after a gastrointestinal bleed or peptic ulcer and in advanced kidney disease, it inhibits platelets, and older patients carry more gastrointestinal risk.

Chronic joint pain in an adult, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease) Knees, where wear begins medially, hips and lower spine; distal and proximal interphalangeal (DIP, PIP) and first carpometacarpal (CMC) joints; asymmetric Gradual onset, chronic and progressive; stiffness under 30 minutes; Heberden and Bouchard nodes; spares the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints Rheumatoid arthritis Symmetric MCP and PIP synovitis with fatigue or fever Morning stiffness over an hour; anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibody; erosions and periarticular osteopenia Septic arthritis Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult One red, hot, swollen joint, usually the knee Hours to days; joint fluid over 50,000 white cells Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition disease) Flares in a degenerated joint, most often the knee Acute flares; rhomboid, weakly positive birefringent crystals; chondrocalcinosis on the radiograph Hemochromatosis arthropathy Second and third MCP joints Hook-like osteophytes; high ferritin and transferrin saturation Medial meniscal tear Knee pain with a small effusion Locking or catching Patellofemoral pain syndrome Pain around or behind the patella Pain on quadriceps contraction against the patella (grind test)
Morning stiffness, by diagnosis 030 minutes1 hourLonger Osteoarthritisunder 30 minutes Rheumatoid arthritisover 1 hour
Spine osteoarthritis is the usual cause of spinal stenosis; hip osteoarthritis can mimic trochanteric pain.
Low Back Pain in an Adult Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Joint pain worse with use in an older adult → History, exam and a weight-bearing radiograph Joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts Osteoarthritis Erosions and periarticular osteopenia Rheumatoid arthritis Chondrocalcinosis Pseudogout Targeted tests TestResultMeans Warm joint with an effusion → Arthrocentesis: cell count, crystals, Gram stain and culture Under 2,000 white cells Osteoarthritis Over 50,000 white cells Septic arthritis Rhomboid, weakly positive crystals Pseudogout Symmetric MCP synovitis, stiffness over an hour → Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP Positive Rheumatoid arthritis Second and third MCP hook-like osteophytes → Ferritin and transferrin saturation Both high Hemochromatosis SkipBlood tests when the picture is mechanical: they are normal in osteoarthritis. Treat the patient, not the film, since pain and radiographic severity often disagree.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Months of knee pain in a 72-year-old; the only NSAID offered is ketorolac Right class, wrong member: a 5-day drug Acetaminophen, when no other NSAID is among the options Kidney injury or insufficiency, or a prior gastrointestinal bleed Avoid a systemic NSAID A topical NSAID or acetaminophen Body mass index 35 Weight loss is the highest-value step Weight loss with exercise Morning stiffness over an hour with symmetric MCP synovitis Rheumatoid arthritis, not osteoarthritis Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP; disease-modifying drugs

Pause point Months of knee pain, NSAID chosen Offered: ketorolac Ketorolac stops at 5 days → Acetaminophen when ketorolac is the only NSAID offered; otherwise a topical NSAID for the knee or hand, or an oral NSAID A joint with no inflammation Offered: an oral steroid or hydroxychloroquine Brief stiffness; no fever or synovitis → Exercise and weight loss, then a topical or oral NSAID

What raises the stakes Finding Means Do Older age or heart disease Higher NSAID risk Topical first; lowest oral dose for the shortest time, with gastric protection considered Kidney injury or insufficiency, or a prior bleed A systemic NSAID may be contraindicated A topical NSAID or acetaminophen Pain despite exercise, weight loss and NSAIDs Severe disease Intra-articular glucocorticoid InjectionsIntra-articular glucocorticoidIntra-articular glucocorticoids give short-term relief; frequent injections may speed cartilage loss. End-stage joint, all conservative measures failed Refractory disease Total joint replacement

1 Alwaysevery patient Exercise, with quadriceps strengthening for the knee; weight loss when overweight; a self-management program 2 First drugknee or hand Topical NSAID, such as diclofenac Hip Hip osteoarthritisA hip joint lies deep, so a topical NSAID is unlikely to help, and hip or many-joint disease starts with an oral NSAID. Hip pain is felt in the groin (likely the most specific site), sometimes at the greater trochanter or referred to the thigh and knee. 3 Raisepain persists, or the hip or many joints Oral NSAID at the lowest dose for the shortest time; a proton pump inhibitor if gastrointestinal risk 4 If NSAIDs cannot be takenintolerance or contraindication Acetaminophen, short-term; duloxetine, a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; topical capsaicin for the knee In practice AcetaminophenIn practice: the 2019 American College of Rheumatology guideline keeps topical NSAIDs for the knee and oral NSAIDs strongly recommended and lists acetaminophen only conditionally, for short-term use when NSAIDs cannot be taken, because its trial effects are very small. Older board items still key acetaminophen. 5 Injectsevere pain despite the above Intra-articular glucocorticoid 6 Replacerefractory, end-stage joint Total joint replacement

Not on the ladder Drug Why not Ketorolac A 5-day limit, for acute pain only Oral glucocorticoids No role; the steroid route in osteoarthritis is intra-articular Hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate Strongly recommended against: no inflammation to treat Glucosamine, bisphosphonates Strongly recommended against Opioids Few benefits and high risk; the American College of Rheumatology guideline allows tramadol only as a conditional recommendation

Follow-up decisions When Do On an oral NSAID Watch for gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and kidney effects On a long-term NSAID Gastric protection On repeated injections Space them: frequent injections may speed cartilage loss Pain despite every nonsurgical step Refer for joint replacement

When choosing initial pharmacotherapy, read which specific agent represents each class. A class can be right while the offered member is wrong: ketorolac for chronic OA (osteoarthritis), gentamicin for simple cystitis, chloramphenicol for otitis. Check the offered drug rather than rejecting the guideline.

briefs.title: Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child
briefs.sub: Kocher criteria count · ultrasound for an effusion · aspirate at 3 or 4, or at 2 with an effusion and raised blood tests · transient synovitis vs Perthes by the courseHow many Kocher criteria are present: aspirate now, or treat with NSAIDs and recheck?
blocks: Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child

Kocher criteria count · ultrasound for an effusion · aspirate at 3 or 4, or at 2 with an effusion and raised blood tests · transient synovitis vs Perthes by the courseHow many Kocher criteria are present: aspirate now, or treat with NSAIDs and recheck?

A febrile child who refuses to bear weight on a painful hip may have septic arthritis: count the Kocher criteria; 3 or 4, or an effusion with raised blood tests, means aspirate before antibiotics Count the Kocher criteria: fever, non-weight-bearing, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) over 40 mm/h, white blood cell count (WBC) over 12,000/mm³. 3 or 4: aspirate; 0 or 1 in a well child after a cold: transient synovitis (toxic synovitis), rest and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) Joint fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant, is septic: surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics

What it is Septic arthritis: a bacterial infection of one joint, in a child usually blood-borne and usually the knee, hip or ankle Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis): a sterile, self-limited effusion after a viral illness, the commonest nontraumatic cause of a limp Bug Staphylococcus aureus overall Kingella kingae in children 3 years and under Gonococcus in sexually active adolescents Sickle cell disease: Haemophilus influenzae in the joint; Salmonella is its bone (osteomyelitis) organism Spread Blood-borne seeding of the joint in children Age under 4, the commonest age (non-modifiable) Sickle cell disease (non-modifiable) An immunosuppressant such as methotrexate Chain Joint: bacteria seed the synovium pus fills the capsule the hip is held flexed, abducted and externally rotated Damage: cartilage destroyed within hours or days femoral head blood supply lost osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) and growth arrest Insights The position shows an effusion, not infection. Transient synovitis can hold the hip the same way, so the count and the fluid decide Why the hip sits flexedPositionFlexion, abduction and external rotation lower the pressure inside the capsule, which eases the pain; an effusion of any cause does it. Antibiotics before the tap hide the organism. Cultures are limited after prior antibiotics, so the blood culture and the aspirate come first

Fever present Non-weight-bearing will not stand on the leg ESR above 40 mm/h WBC above 12,000/mm³ C-reactive protein (CRP) over 2 mg/dL adds to the likelihood Count one point each; 3 or 4 aspirate; 2 aspirate if the child looks toxic or an effusion comes with raised blood tests; 0 or 1 observe Confirm joint fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³ or a positive culture Kocher 1999 derivationBy countBy criteria count in the 1999 derivation: 0 under 0.2%, 1 about 3%, 2 about 40%, 3 about 93%, 4 about 99.6%; fever was scored as over 38.5 °C. The rule has not been checked in other groups of children and may mislead when the risk is low.

Septic hipFever, refuses to bear weight, pain on any motion of the hip If 3 or 4 Kocher criteria, or a toxic child with an effusion, choose blood culture, then ultrasound-guided aspiration today, before antibiotics. InfantMay be afebrile; ESR and CRP may be barely raised even with pus in the joint If an infant who will not move the leg has an effusion, choose aspirate; normal blood tests do not exclude infection. ImmunosuppressedOne hot joint out of step with the rest, on methotrexate Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis If fever or septic fluid, choose treat as infection until the fluid says otherwise; no steroid into the joint.

briefs.sub: six weeks of arthritis, then joints and fever set the subtype · mimics · macrophage activation syndrome and leukemia · uveitis screening · the treatment ladder

Arthritis for 6 weeks or more, starting before age 16, with no other cause is juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), a clinical diagnosis; the first 6 months set the subtype: systemic (any joints plus daily fever spikes for 2 weeks or more), polyarticular (5 or more joints), oligoarticular (4 or fewer) Treat with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) first; methotrexate when arthritis persists; systemic JIA moves to an interleukin-1 (IL-1) or IL-6 blocker; systemic steroids are usually avoided, except for refractory or severe disease or macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), which usually takes high-dose steroids Screen for silent uveitis with a slit lamp every 3 months in a young, antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive child with oligoarticular or rheumatoid factor (RF) negative polyarticular JIA; with two or more cell lines low in a child labeled systemic JIA, aspirate the bone marrow first

What it is Chronic arthritis of childhood with no other cause, grouped into subtypes by the joint count and systemic features of the first 6 months Systemic JIA (Still disease): arthritis with daily fever, rash, hepatosplenomegaly, nodes or serositis Driver Cause unknown: a genetic predisposition with autoimmune and autoinflammatory inflammation Systemic JIA responds well to blocking IL-1 (anakinra) or IL-6 (tocilizumab) Triggers Oligoarticular: typically young girls, ages 2 to 4, the commonest subtype (non-modifiable) Polyarticular: girls, peaks at 2 to 5 and 10 to 14 (non-modifiable) Systemic: boys and girls equally, peak 2 to 4 (non-modifiable) Enthesitis-related: older boys; HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen B27) more common (non-modifiable) Chain Joint: synovium inflamed swelling and stiffness on waking that eases through the day a limp or a joint not used Systemic: daily fever spikes with a salmon rash anemia, high white count and platelets macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) in about 1 in 10 Eye: usually silent anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) synechiae, cataract, glaucoma Insights Systemic JIA comes and goes; MAS does not. The fever spikes daily and the rash fades; in MAS the fever is unremitting, the rash constant, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) falls Why the ESR falls in MASESRThe ESR depends on fibrinogen; MAS consumes fibrinogen, so the ESR drops even as inflammation peaks. The uveitis usually gives no symptoms. A slit lamp on a schedule finds it, not a complaint

Age onset before 16 Arthritis 6 weeks or more, no other cause Systemic daily fever 2 weeks or more plus rash, nodes, hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, or serositis; boys and girls equally Polyarticular 5 or more joints in the first 6 months; girls more Oligoarticular 4 or fewer joints in the first 6 months; typically young girls Enthesitis-related older boys; HLA-B27

LeukemiaLabeled systemic JIA, now pale, petechiae, nodes, hepatosplenomegaly Acute Leukemia in a Child If two or more cell lines low, choose bone marrow aspiration before treating as JIA or MAS. MASKnown systemic JIA, now unremitting fever, bleeding, a falling ESR If ferritin up with platelets, fibrinogen and ESR falling, choose high-dose steroids; high mortality from multiorgan failure. MAS classification criteriaCriteriaIn a febrile child with systemic JIA: ferritin above 684 ng/mL plus any 2 of platelets 181,000/mm³ or less, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) above 48 units/L, triglycerides above 156 mg/dL, fibrinogen 360 mg/dL or less. Built for research; clinicians use them to support the diagnosis. Septic jointOne hot joint in a child on methotrexate Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child If fever or one joint out of step with the rest, choose aspirate: septic until the fluid says otherwise.
