Pause point Positive ANA Read as lupus, or as proof against systemic JIA ANA does not decide; the counts do → Lupus tends to lower the white cells and platelets; systemic JIA often raises them

What sets the outcome Finding Means Do Unremitting fever, bleeding, falling ESR in systemic JIA MAS: high mortality from multiorgan failure High-dose steroids RF-positive polyarticular JIA A less favorable prognosis Methotrexate; a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor if it fails Uveitis found Synechiae, cataract, glaucoma Steroid and dilating drops; methotrexate or anti-TNF if refractory Long systemic steroid courses Growth retardation, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) Inject the joint instead where possible

Follow-up decisions When Do Oligo- or RF-negative polyarticular, ANA positive, under 7 at onset, within 4 years Slit-lamp exam every 3 months Uveitis screening by riskAmerican College of Rheumatology 2019High risk, every 3 months: oligoarticular, RF-negative polyarticular, psoriatic or undifferentiated JIA that is also ANA positive, under 7 at onset and within 4 years of onset. Everyone else (ANA negative, 7 or older at onset, past 4 years, systemic JIA, RF-positive polyarticular JIA, enthesitis-related arthritis): every 6 to 12 months. A simpler rule for recently diagnosed oligoarticular or polyarticular JIA: every 3 months if ANA positive, every 6 if negative; where the two differ, this brief teaches the risk rule above. Other subtypes, ANA negative, 7 or older at onset, or past 4 years Slit-lamp exam every 6 to 12 months Systemic JIA Slit-lamp exam every 6 to 12 months On methotrexate CBC, AST, ALT and albumin; one hot joint is septic until the fluid says otherwise Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child

briefs.title: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
briefs.sub: lost internal rotation · films of both hips · stable vs unstable · atypical: look for an endocrine or renal cause · keep off it and pin in situDoes a child of 10 to 16 with a limp and hip-to-knee pain have films of both hips, and can the child walk even with crutches?
blocks: lost internal rotation · films of both hips · stable vs unstable · atypical: look for an endocrine or renal cause · keep off it and pin in situDoes a child of 10 to 16 with a limp and hip-to-knee pain have films of both hips, and can the child walk even with crutches?

Age 10 to 16 limp hip, groin, thigh or knee pain films of both hips; cross-table lateral if the slip is unstable (cannot walk even with crutches); lost internal rotation supports it Suspected slip off the leg now (crutches or a wheelchair) urgent in situ screw fixation; never force it back Under 8, underweight or short consider an endocrine or renal cause

What it is Femoral epiphysis slips back and down off the neck, through the growth plate (physis) Most common hip disorder of adolescence, usually at 10 to 16 years; average age 12 in girls, 13.5 in boysIn practice:In practice: the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) gives 8 to 15 years, and films for any child of that age with a new limp and hip, groin, thigh or knee pain. Driver Probably a weakened physis shear force, greater with obesity the slip Triggers Obesity: 63% weigh at or above the 90th percentile, but it is not required Growth spurt: tall, thin adolescents slip too non-modifiable Male sex non-modifiable Genetic factors non-modifiable Endocrine abnormalities (hypothyroidism, growth hormone treatment, hypogonadism, panhypopituitarism); renal disease Chain Physis, proposed: weak plate shear epiphysis slips through the hypertrophic zone Exam: limp; lost internal rotation; hip turns outward on passive flexion Vessels: kinked, or pressed by a hematoma osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) often early osteoarthritis Insights Knee pain can come from the hip: the obturator nerve usually carries it Walking sets the risk: a child who cannot walk even with crutches has an unstable slip, with more complications

Course, stage by stagedetail behind the chain May begin as stiffness that eases with rest, then a limp, then pain down the front and inner thigh to the knee Poorly localized: hip, groin, thigh, buttock, low back or knee; worse with squatting, long sitting, cyclingThe hip may be missed until the slip worsens Painful hip motion with limited flexion, abduction and internal rotation; limp or Trendelenburg gait; leg turned outAn early exam may not show it About 90% are stable; by duration, acute under 3 weeks, chronic 3 weeks or more, acute-on-chronic a flare of a chronic slipAbout 88% of unstable slips had earlier symptoms Usually progresses; osteonecrosis and collapse of the epiphysis can follow if the blood supply fails

Views AP (anteroposterior) and frog-leg lateral of both hips Unstable AP of both hips and a cross-table lateral of the slipped side Klein line drawn along the top of the femoral neck, it normally crosses the epiphysis; in a slip the epiphysis sits below it Physis wider than the other side: a slip even before the head moves Films normal MRI or ultrasound helps when a slip is still suspected
Both hipsWhy order itSlipped capital femoral epiphysis is bilateral in about one-fifth of patients; 18 to 50% across series.

SlipA suspected slip, at any stage Usually progresses If a slip is suspected, choose no weight bearing until it is ruled out or fixed, plus urgent orthopedic referral. UnstableCannot walk, even with crutches If the slip is unstable, choose urgent fixation, never a forceful reduction. FeverFebrile and toxic, hip held flexed and turned out Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child If fever or toxicity comes with the hip pain, choose a Kocher criteria count, then urgent ultrasound-guided aspiration if septic arthritis is suspected. AbuseThe story is vague or does not fit the age or the injury Suspected Child Abuse If the history does not fit, choose an evaluation for inflicted injury, with child and caregivers interviewed apart.

Look-alikes in school age and adolescence, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Slipped capital femoral epiphysis Limp, vague hip to knee pain, lost internal rotation 10 to 16; symptoms over weeks; turns outward on passive flexion; epiphysis below the Klein line Adductor strain (groin pull) Groin pain Follows an injury or activity; lost internal rotation points to the hip instead Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease Limp and vague hip pain over weeks to months; lost internal rotation About 4 to 10; femoral head flattened or fragmented rather than displaced; early films may be normal Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis) Limp, sometimes after a viral illness Under 10; a course of weeks argues against it Septic arthritis Febrile, toxic, hip held flexed and turned out Any age; Kocher criteria: fever, non-weight-bearing, ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) >40 mm/h, white cell count >12,000/µL Femoral neck stress fracture Runner whose training just went up; groin pain Adolescent athlete; hurts to hop; films normal, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) shows it Avulsion fracture of an anterior iliac spine Hip pain, age 12 to 25 Sudden, after a forceful movement; seen on the film Osgood-Schlatter disease Knee pain in an adolescent Adolescent; the tibial tubercle is tender Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) Limp, groin pain, limited abduction Film shows a chronically dislocated hip, not a slipped epiphysis Bone tumor Limp with pain Night pain

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Age 10 to 16 with a limp, or hip, groin, thigh or knee pain → Hip exam Internal rotation lost Disease inside the hip joint: suspect a slip Turns outward on passive flexion Obligate external rotation (Drehmann sign) Targeted tests TestResultMeans After films confirm a slip, only if atypical: under 8, underweight or short → Thyroid, growth hormone and kidney tests (find a cause) Abnormal Hypothyroidism, a growth hormone disorder or renal osteodystrophy Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Exam or story fits a slip → Films of both hips to confirm Epiphysis below the Klein line, or a widened physis A slip: no weight bearing, urgent orthopedic referral
Why the hip exam firstWhy it goes firstLost internal rotation is the most telling sign, yet an early exam can miss it: film the hips whenever the story fits.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Knee pain; knee exam and knee films normal Hip disease felt in the knee Examine the hip; films of both hips Weeks of groin pain, then a minor fall and now unable to walk Acute-on-chronic unstable slip Off the leg; urgent fixation A cold last week, but 13 years old with 3 weeks of pain Not transient synovitis Films of both hips Short, underweight, or under 8 Possibly an endocrine or renal cause Thyroid, growth hormone and kidney tests as well as fixation

Pause point Groin pain in an adolescent Offered as a muscle strain, sent to physical therapy Lost internal rotation with a widened, irregular physis; strain is rare at this age → A slip, before the head visibly moves Stiff hip Offered: bracing or a spica cast Bracing and casting treat infant dysplasia → Only fixation stops the slip

Stability, by weight bearing Type Recognize it It means Stable Walks, with or without crutches; about 90% of slips Osteonecrosis under 10% Unstable Cannot walk, even with crutches Osteonecrosis in as many as 20 to 50%
Slip gradeAlso gradedOn the frog-leg film the head is displaced under one-third of the neck width (mild), one-third to one-half (moderate) or over one-half (severe).

1 Nowslip suspected or seen No weight bearing (crutches or a wheelchair) and urgent orthopedic referral The aim is to stop the slip and prevent osteonecrosis, chondrolysis and impingement. 2 Surgeryas soon as it is diagnosed In situ fixation with a single screw across the physis Never force the head back: forceful reduction can cause osteonecrosis. 3 Complicationnew pain or stiffness after fixation Image the hip for osteonecrosis or chondrolysis Chondrolysis is sudden cartilage loss, most often from a pin that entered the joint unseen, so the joint space narrows; osteonecrosis shows first as sclerosis and lucency, then collapse of the head.

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Stable slip Single screw in situ Bracing, casting, traction and physical therapy do not stop a slip Unstable slip Urgent fixation, usually in situ Timing of surgery and the value and manner of reduction are debated; never a forceful reduction Atypical patient Fixation plus an endocrine and renal workup Hypothyroidism, growth hormone treatment, hypogonadism Other hip painless Films now; consider pinning only if risk is highWho gets itYounger patients, obesity, an endocrine disorder, or follow-up unlikely. Prophylactic pinning of the healthy hip is not recommended for most patients

Follow-up decisions When Do After fixation Graded return over about 6 months; after a stable slip, running and contact sport may resume once the growth plate closes The next 18 months Watch the other hip: when it slips, it is often within 18 months Years later Early osteoarthritis can follow osteonecrosis, or impingement after a severe slip heals out of position

Next step3 of 7 12-year-old boy was diagnosed with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis today pinning is scheduled right hip: no pain, full internal rotation Body mass index above the 95th percentile Afebrile · radiographs were taken of the left hip only · Image only if it becomes symptomatic · Radiographs of the right hip now · Reassure; bilateral slips are rare 12-year-old boy was diagnosed with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis today pinning is scheduled right hip: no pain, full internal rotation Body mass index above the 95th percentile Afebrile · radiographs were taken of the left hip only Radiographs of the right hip nowboth hips are imaged at diagnosis: about one-fifth of patients have bilateral slips (18 to 50% across series)

Next step4 of 7 13-year-old boy with 3 weeks of aching right knee pain and a limp knee: no effusion, no tenderness, full painless motion ligament tests normal Plays football; no specific injury Afebrile · knee radiographs normal · Knee arthroscopy · Examine the hip · MRI of the knee 13-year-old boy with 3 weeks of aching right knee pain and a limp knee: no effusion, no tenderness, full painless motion ligament tests normal Plays football; no specific injury Afebrile · knee radiographs normal Examine the hipa normal knee exam sends you to the hip: a slip refers pain to the knee through the obturator nerve

Mechanism5 of 7 14-year-old girl 5 months after screw fixation of a slipped left capital femoral epiphysis new left groin pain and stiffness hip motion now limited in all directions Afebrile · radiograph: narrowed joint space; femoral head round, without sclerosis; screw position unchanged · Chondrolysis · Osteonecrosis of the femoral head · Hardware failure 14-year-old girl 5 months after screw fixation of a slipped left capital femoral epiphysis new left groin pain and stiffness hip motion now limited in all directions Afebrile · radiograph: narrowed joint space; femoral head round, without sclerosis; screw position unchanged Chondrolysisa narrowed joint space means lost cartilage, and a stiff, painful hip with that film after fixation is chondrolysis, most often from a pin that entered the joint unseen; osteonecrosis shows first as sclerosis and lucency, then collapse of the head; an unchanged screw argues against hardware failure

Diagnosis6 of 7 16-year-old girl, a cross-country runner, with 3 weeks of right groin pain worse with each run; now hurts to hop on the right leg recently doubled her weekly mileage Afebrile · radiographs of both hips normal · Osteoid osteoma · Femoral neck stress fracture · Slipped capital femoral epiphysis 16-year-old girl, a cross-country runner, with 3 weeks of right groin pain worse with each run; now hurts to hop on the right leg recently doubled her weekly mileage Afebrile · radiographs of both hips normal Femoral neck stress fracturegroin pain on hopping with normal films after a training increase: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) for a femoral neck stress fracture

Avoid7 of 7 12-year-old girl with 3 weeks of right thigh pain since a minor fall today she cannot bear weight on the right leg right leg held externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: right femoral epiphysis displaced off the neck · Radiographs of the opposite hip · Forceful closed reduction of the slip · Urgent in situ fixation with a single screw 12-year-old girl with 3 weeks of right thigh pain since a minor fall today she cannot bear weight on the right leg right leg held externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: right femoral epiphysis displaced off the neck Forceful closed reduction of the slipforcing the epiphysis back raises the risk of osteonecrosis: keep her off the leg and pin it where it lies

Previously healthy 13-year-old boy with 4 weeks of intermittent left groin pain and a limp no fever; not in acute distress height 50th percentile, weight 97th, body mass index above the 97th left hip: internal rotation and abduction limited; internal and external rotation to 75 degrees hurt; externally rotates on passive flexion Right hip and both knees normal T 37 °C · pulse 90/min · RR 20/min · BP 116/75 mm Hg AP and cross-table lateral films: irregular widening of the left femoral physis; mild osteopenia of the left femoral head and neck Analgesia and weight-loss counseling given; next step? Competing answers Physical therapy: weeks of pain and stiffness; but it treats a strain after an injury, and there was none. Abduction bracing: limited abduction; but it treats DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip) in infants. Traction: a painful hip and a limp; but it pulls a fractured bone to length; there was no trauma. Spica cast immobilization: holding the hip still; but it holds an infant hip reduced for DDH. Down to two: internal fixation or spica cast immobilization. Internal fixation: groin pain, lost internal rotation and a widened, irregular physis are a slip even before the epiphysis visibly moves; every other option treats another hip problem.

briefs.title: Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans
briefs.sub: post-traumatic muscle mass · peripheral ossification · motion and function
blocks: post-traumatic muscle mass · peripheral ossification · motion and function

After a muscle contusion, a painful intramuscular mass with lost motion suggests myositis ossificans (post-traumatic heterotopic ossification). Symptoms can persist or worsen about 2 to 4 weeks after injury; a pain-free interval may occur. A film showing peripheral ossification within muscle, separate from bone supports it. Start with gentle range of motion and symptom relief; refer an atypical or enlarging mass before biopsy. Rapidly worsening pain, spreading redness or systemic illness means possible necrotizing infection: urgent surgical assessment and antibiotics.

What it is Benign bone formation in soft tissue, often in the quadriceps or brachialis Driver Muscle injury inflammation bone-forming cells; the proposed mechanism is fibroblast-to-osteoblast differentiation Triggers A direct sporting injury; may also follow surgery Brain or spinal cord injury; less often stroke: a neurogenic form (non-modifiable) Chain Injured muscle an ossifying mass stiffness and restricted adjacent-joint motion Insights Movement helps localize it. Knee flexion can reproduce pain at a quadriceps mass. The tissue matters. A muscular lesion separate from cortex favors this process over an osteosarcoma.

What the disease does, by systemSupporting detail A firm, painful intramuscular massOssification limits movement nearby Early in the course, alkaline phosphatase is often raised; inflammatory markers can be elevatedResults are nonspecific; assess infection from the clinical findings An autosomal dominant progressive form is associated with an activin-receptor mutationKeep that inherited disorder distinct from an isolated mass after a contusion

Findings that support the diagnosis Finding Meaning Pain and motion may worsen after about 2 to 4 weeks Compatible with the developing ossified lesion Radiographs can show the lesion at 3 to 4 weeks A normal earlier film is not definitive Peripheral zonal ossification in muscle A nonmalignant ossification pattern; assess the entire lesion

InfectionSevere pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema or a toxic patient If necrotizing infection is suspected, choose urgent surgery plus broad antibiotic treatment; do not delay for imaging.

TumorA growing or fixed mass, or an uncertain diagnosis Bone Lesions in a Child If malignancy is a concern, choose MRI with contrast and orthopedic oncology referral; the treating team plans the biopsy.

Pain and a mass after a thigh injury Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Myositis ossificans (post-traumatic heterotopic ossification) A localized, firm mass after a muscle injury; motion hurts Weeks after injury; peripheral calcification in muscle, separated from the cortex Osteosarcoma Bone Lesions in a Child An adolescent with persistent bone pain or swelling near a metaphysis A bone-centered lesion; investigate a growing or suspicious mass Necrotizing soft-tissue infection Pain out of proportion, spreading red swollen tissue; systemic illness Rapid progression; immediate surgical assessment and antibiotics Quadriceps tendon rupture Cannot actively extend the knee; a gap above the patella A low patella with an extensor-mechanism deficit; surgical repair Venous thrombosis Venous Thromboembolism Swelling involves the thigh and calf rather than a discrete muscle mass Venous duplex identifies the clot Osteoid osteoma Night pain improves with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID); no muscular mass A bone lesion rather than peripheral muscle ossification Neurogenic heterotopic ossification Painful restricted joint after brain or spinal cord injury; less often stroke The neurologic history and joint findings support the neurogenic form
Time course 2 to 4 weeks Pain and restriction may worsen after the injury 3 to 4 weeks The lesion may become apparent on radiographs

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans A painful thigh mass after a contusion → Examine motion, strength, sensation and the extent of swelling Pain at the mass with passive knee flexion Localizes to the quadriceps rather than a complete tendon tear → Plain radiograph of the affected region Peripheral calcification within soft tissue Supports myositis ossificans No calcification on an early film Does not exclude evolving ossification; reassess the mass and its course Targeted tests TestResultMeans Rapid progression or systemic illness → Immediate surgical exploration and antibiotics Necrotic fascia or muscle Necrotizing infection; debride An enlarging or otherwise suspicious mass → MRI with contrast and orthopedic oncology referral A concerning bone or soft-tissue lesion The treating specialist plans biopsy Diffuse thigh and calf swelling → Venous duplex A venous thrombus Venous thrombosis Next step TestResultMeans A typical stable post-traumatic mass with an early nondiagnostic film → Re-examine and repeat radiographs at follow-up Developing peripheral ossification Supports the muscular diagnosis; continued growth or uncertainty needs referral Diagnostic test TestResultMeans A mineralized intramuscular mass → Assess the imaging pattern and relation to adjacent bone Bone formed in muscle with a separate cortex Myositis ossificans rather than a primary bone tumor SkipAn unplanned biopsy of an uncertain mass. Obtain appropriate imaging and let the treating oncology team choose the biopsy route.

Clues that change the next step Clue Points to Next best step A stable mass with an early normal film Evolving intramuscular ossification remains possible Reassess and repeat imaging at follow-up A growing or uncertain mass Possible tumor MRI and specialist-planned biopsy assessment Cannot actively extend the knee; a gap above the patella Quadriceps tendon rupture Arrange surgical repair
Pause point Growing or uncertain mass after a prior injury Read as reassurance No fever or weight loss does not by itself exclude a sarcoma → Imaging and specialist review

What changes management Finding Do Pain or loss of joint motion Gentle rehabilitation and symptom relief Persistent disabling symptoms Orthopedic assessment for further treatment Systemic illness or rapid progression Immediate surgical assessment and antibiotics

1 Conservativean established, typical post-traumatic lesion Gentle range-of-motion exercise; an NSAID for symptoms In practice Acute contusionFor a fresh contusion, ice and activity restriction come first. Gentle, static stretching starts no earlier than 48 hours after injury; acetaminophen is initially favored because an NSAID can increase bleeding. This differs from treating an established ossified lesion weeks later. 2 Reassesspain or restricted movement persists Re-examine, review imaging and refer if function remains limited 3 Excisiona mature lesion remains symptomatic despite conservative care Surgical excision may be considered if the lesion persists beyond 6 to 12 months

Follow-up decisions When Do At reassessment Check pain, knee motion and the mass; repeat imaging when the initial film was early The mass enlarges or remains uncertain Refer for MRI and a specialist diagnosis During rehabilitation Avoid forceful stretching or deep massage; use gentle motion

briefs.title: Adolescent Kyphosis
briefs.sub: flexible and structural roundback · vertebral wedging · growth and progression
blocks: flexible and structural roundback · vertebral wedging · growth and progression

Adolescent roundback: a curve that corrects with extension or a change of position is postural; a rigid curve needs spinal radiographs for Scheuermann disease (Scheuermann kyphosis). Anterior wedging of at least 5 degrees in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae supports Scheuermann disease. Use the curve, progression, symptoms and growth remaining to plan treatment. Mild, stable curve: conservative care. Progressing curve with growth remaining: consider a brace. Refractory pain, neurologic impairment or severe deformity: orthopedic assessment for intervention.

What it is Structural kyphosis from abnormal vertebral growth during adolescence Driver The cause is uncertain; vertebral endplate growth is disturbed Triggers Adolescent growth; boys somewhat more often affected (non-modifiable) Some cases run in families (non-modifiable) Chain Endplate disturbance anterior vertebral wedging a rigid forward curve Insights Test flexibility before interpreting the film. Postural roundback corrects; a structural deformity does not. Growth changes the treatment. Bracing is used for a growing child whose curve increases; persistent severe symptoms require a different discussion.

Diagnostic findings Finding Meaning Rigid kyphosis that does not correct in extension A structural deformity Anterior wedging of at least 5 degrees in 3 or more consecutive vertebral bodies Radiographic pattern of Scheuermann disease Schmorl nodes: disc material passes through an endplate into the adjacent vertebral body Supporting change, not required by the wedging criterion

Red flagsNight pain, weight loss, neurologic changes or systemic illness If the presentation is atypical for uncomplicated kyphosis, choose evaluate promptly for tumor, infection or neural compression; obtain MRI as indicated.

Roundback in an adolescent Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Postural kyphosis Flexible rounded posture Corrects with position or extension; vertebral shape is normal Scheuermann disease (Scheuermann kyphosis) Rigid roundback; often a mild persistent ache During adolescent growth; consecutive anterior wedge-shaped vertebrae Compression fracture Trauma with acute focal pain, or an osteoporosis risk context Focal vertebral height loss in a trauma or osteoporosis setting Ankylosing spondylitis Morning stiffness and sacroiliac or buttock pain in a young adult Sacroiliac disease rather than isolated thoracic vertebral wedging Vertebral tumor Night pain, weight loss or neurologic findings MRI evaluates the concerning lesion
Time course Growth spurt A structural curve may become more prominent Skeletal maturity Pain often improves; residual deformity may remain

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans A teenager with thoracic roundback → Examine the curve during extension and positional correction The curve straightens Postural kyphosis The curve remains rigid Assess for structural kyphosis with radiographs Targeted tests TestResultMeans A rigid curve → Standing anteroposterior and lateral spinal radiographs At least 5 degrees of anterior wedging in 3 or more adjacent vertebrae Scheuermann disease The Cobb angle and skeletal maturity Help choose conservative care, bracing or surgical assessment Night pain, weight loss or neurologic findings → MRI of the spine A focal or compressive lesion Evaluate tumor or another serious cause Morning stiffness with sacroiliac pain → Radiographs for suspected inflammatory spondyloarthropathy Sacroiliitis Ankylosing spondylitis rather than isolated Scheuermann disease Next step TestResultMeans Radiographs show structural kyphosis → Assess curve progression, symptoms and growth remaining Progression or refractory symptoms Conservative care; a brace if the curve progresses with growth remaining Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Typical structural roundback → Confirm the consecutive wedging on lateral radiographs Endplate irregularity or associated scoliosis Can support the structural pattern SkipMRI as the first study for an otherwise typical rigid curve with a normal neurologic examination; radiographs establish the structural pattern.

Clues that change the next step Clue Points to Next best step Curve corrects with extension Postural kyphosis Offer observation and posture-strengthening exercises Rigid curve during growth Possible structural kyphosis Obtain standing spinal radiographs Night pain, weight loss or neurologic changes Possible serious spinal disease Prompt evaluation with MRI as indicated
Pause point Rounded posture Offered as Scheuermann disease A rounded posture is not enough: test correction → Then look for the characteristic vertebral wedging

What sets the treatment Pattern Do Mild and nonprogressive Reduce painful loading and strenuous activity; follow the curve Progressing while the skeleton is immature Orthopedic assessment for bracing Persistent pain despite conservative care, neural impairment or severe deformity Orthopedic assessment for intervention

1 Conservativea mild stable curve Activity modification, physical therapy and symptom relief 2 Bracea growing child with an increasing curve Brace during remaining growth under orthopedic care 3 Surgerysevere deformity or persistent symptoms despite nonoperative care Discuss corrective stabilization or spinal fusion with the specialist

Whether the curve corrects with extension separates structural from postural kyphosis; radiographs confirm the vertebral pattern.

briefs.title: Foot Puncture Wounds and Osteomyelitis
briefs.sub: shoe and water exposures · persistent focal pain · MRI and bone cultures
blocks: shoe and water exposures · persistent focal pain · MRI and bone cultures

Nail through a shoe with persistent or returning deep foot pain weeks later: think Pseudomonas osteomyelitis, even in an otherwise well, afebrile child. Plain radiograph first for bone and retained material. Normal early films do not exclude bone infection; persistent focal pain calls for MRI. Confirmed deep puncture-wound infection: orthopedic treatment with debridement, bone cultures and antibiotics covering Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus. Fresh water favors Aeromonas; salt water favors Vibrio.

What it is Infection of bone after a penetrating foot wound; nearby cartilage may also be involved Bug Pseudomonas aeruginosa after a shoe-sole puncture; Staphylococcus aureus remains the usual organism overall Spread A penetrating wound introduces organisms directly; contamination and retained material matter Chain Puncture inoculation persistent deep pain and inflammation bone infection Insights Exposure changes the organism. The same puncture has different likely pathogens through footwear, in fresh water or in seawater. An early film can miss the infection. Radiographic changes lag, while MRI detects early disease more sensitively.

Imaging and microbiology Finding Means Persistent localized bone pain after a puncture A compatible clinical setting; normal temperature is not an exclusion MRI changes of bone infection Defines the extent of suspected osteomyelitis Bone or operative cultures Identify the organism for directed treatment

Deep infectionIncreasing focal bone pain, swelling or reduced weight bearing after a puncture If osteomyelitis is suspected despite a normal early film, choose obtain MRI and arrange orthopedic assessment; do not wait for fever.
UnstableShock in a patient with suspected bone infection If the patient is unstable, choose start antibiotics while arranging source control and cultures; do not delay treatment for biopsy.

Exposure and depth of infection Diagnosis or organism Fingerprint Decides it Pseudomonas osteomyelitis Persistent deep pain after a nail traverses a shoe Weeks after injury; minimal fever does not remove the concern Staphylococcal or streptococcal cellulitis Spreading skin redness around a puncture Early skin infection; S. aureus remains the commonest bone pathogen without the special exposure Aeromonas hydrophila A contaminated freshwater wound Fresh water or soil at injury, rather than the shoe-associated bone-infection pattern Vibrio vulnificus Saltwater or brackish-water wound contamination Marine exposure; consider severe soft-tissue infection Retained foreign body Persistent local pain or an infected puncture site Radiographs detect radiopaque material; ultrasound can find wood or vegetation Salmonella osteomyelitis Sickle Cell Disease and Trait Bone infection in a child with sickle cell disease This host favors Salmonella; empiric treatment also covers S. aureus

Time course Early after injury Skin redness can represent cellulitis Persistent or returning pain Reassess for retained material or deep infection Weeks after a shoe puncture Deep focal pain can signal Pseudomonas bone infection

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans A painful or infected foot puncture → Inspect the wound and examine focal bone tenderness and weight bearing Persistent focal pain or deep tenderness Evaluate for bone involvement rather than assuming a superficial wound → Plain radiographs of the foot Radiopaque material Retained foreign body No early bone change Does not exclude osteomyelitis Targeted tests TestResultMeans Deep pain persists but the radiograph is normal → MRI of the foot MRI abnormalities supporting bone infection Osteomyelitis; proceed to microbiologic diagnosis and treatment Wood or another radiolucent foreign body is suspected → Ultrasound of the puncture site Retained radiolucent material Plan targeted removal Osteomyelitis is suspected → CBC, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) Elevated inflammatory markers Support infection; interpret with the examination and imaging Normal markers Do not use them alone to dismiss an indolent infection Next step TestResultMeans Imaging supports deep bone infection → Arrange orthopedic cultures and treatment Culture and susceptibility results Tailor antibiotics when susceptibilities return Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Deep puncture-wound bone infection → Bone or operative tissue cultures during orthopedic treatment Organism and antibiotic susceptibility identified Narrow antimicrobial treatment to the result SkipWaiting for a follow-up radiograph when focal bone pain persists and osteomyelitis is suspected; obtain MRI rather than treating the normal film as reassurance.

Clues that change the next step Clue Points to Next best step Persistent focal pain after a shoe puncture Possible deep infection MRI if early radiographs do not explain the pain A freshwater-contaminated wound Aeromonas infection is possible Choose antibiotics for the freshwater exposure A possible wooden fragment Retained radiolucent foreign body Use ultrasound to locate it

Pause point Delayed focal pain after a puncture through a shoe Offered as staphylococci, which cause most osteomyelitis overall The shoe puncture and delayed focal pain → Pseudomonas moves ahead in this case

Depth and stability Finding Do Superficial skin infection Treat the skin pathogens; reassess if pain persists or deepens Bone infection after a shoe puncture Orthopedic debridement, deep cultures and antibiotics Shock Urgent antibiotics and source-control assessment

1 Wound carean acute puncture Clean the wound, assess for retained material and review tetanus immunization In practice Wound careSimple low-risk wounds do not automatically need antibiotic prophylaxis. Risk, contamination and the exposure guide the decision; a footwear puncture can introduce Pseudomonas. 2 Infectionclinical infection after footwear penetration Ensure Pseudomonas coverage as well as the appropriate skin-pathogen coverage 3 Bone infectionconfirmed deep post-puncture osteomyelitis Debride, obtain operative cultures and give empiric antibiotics; tailor treatment when susceptibilities return

Follow-up and prevention When Do Pain persists, returns or becomes more focal Look for retained material, deep infection or osteomyelitis Cultures return Use susceptibility-directed antibiotics Tetanus-prone puncture, at least 3 prior vaccine doses Booster if the last dose was at least 5 years ago; a recent booster does not identify the wound organism

A child aged 7 has ongoing foot tenderness, redness and warmth at a follow-up visit, 3 weeks after stepping on a nail through footwear. The wound had been cleaned. Temperature is 37.2 degrees C, and the child otherwise appears well. Tetanus immunization was last given at age 5. Which organism best fits this exposure and course? Competing answers Aeromonas hydrophila: consider contamination by fresh water or soil; neither is the distinguishing exposure here. Group A streptococcus: fits superficial spreading cellulitis better than the persistent deep shoe-puncture pattern. Klebsiella pneumoniae: lacks the characteristic footwear association. Staphylococcus aureus: leads overall in bone infection; the route of injury shifts this case toward another organism. Down to two Pseudomonas aeruginosa versus Staphylococcus aureus. Footwear penetration followed by persistent focal pain favors Pseudomonas bone infection, despite the near-normal temperature. Recent tetanus immunization changes wound prophylaxis, not the organism.

briefs.title: Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant
briefs.sub: neck rotation and head shape · ear position and sutures · hips and feet
blocks: Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant
neck rotation and head shape · ear position and sutures · hips and feet

Head tilts toward a tight sternocleidomastoid (SCM), chin turns away: congenital muscular torticollis. A firm muscle mass differs from a soft, transilluminating lymphatic malformation. Flat occiput, same-side ear forward: positional plagiocephaly. Ear displaced backward with a suture ridge: suspect lambdoid craniosynostosis and refer for craniofacial evaluation. Stretching and physical therapy, repositioning and awake tummy time; keep supine sleep. Examine hips and feet; a new tilt with neurologic signs needs brain MRI.

What it is A shortened or fibrotic SCM producing a tilted head usually noticed within the first 3 months Driver Intrauterine constraint or neck-muscle injury may contribute Triggers Breech positioning or other intrauterine constraint (non-modifiable) A persistent head-position preference; prematurity increases positional flattening risk Chain Restricted neck rotation one-sided positioning pressure-related skull flattening Insights The tilt identifies the tight side. The chin points toward the opposite shoulder. Skull position separates two processes. Forward ear displacement favors pressure-related molding; posterior displacement with a ridge suggests suture fusion.

Clinical findings Finding Interpretation Fixed tilt with restricted rotation and a firm SCM Muscular torticollis Anterior ear displacement and same-side forehead prominence Positional deformity is favored Posterior ear displacement and a suture ridge Suture fusion is suspected

NeurologicNew head tilt in an older child with neurologic findings or chronic-progressive headache Brain Tumors in a Child If a central cause is possible, choose obtain brain MRI to evaluate a posterior fossa lesion.
Suture fusionA posteriorly displaced ear on the flat side with a ridge If craniosynostosis is suspected, choose refer to a craniofacial or neurosurgical team; confirm the suture abnormality.

Head tilt, a flat occiput or a neck mass Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Congenital muscular torticollis Early infant; tight SCM, tilt toward it and chin away Early infancy; firm muscle mass that does not transilluminate, with limited neck rotation Positional plagiocephaly Flat occiput; same-side ear and forehead project forward A parallelogram shape, without a fused-suture ridge Lambdoid craniosynostosis Flat occiput with the same-side ear farther back A ridge and trapezoid shape suggest fusion rather than positional molding Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) Soft, compressible posterior-neck mass Transilluminates; not a firm contracted SCM Cervical lymphadenitis Tender enlarging node, fever or overlying warmth and redness Inflammation outside the SCM rather than its painless shortening Posterior fossa tumor Brain Tumors in a Child Acquired head tilt with neurologic findings in an older child Acquired tilt in an older child; brain MRI, rather than treating it as an infant muscle contracture
Time course Early infancy Congenital muscle restriction becomes apparent During growth A one-sided preference can perpetuate skull flattening

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans An infant with a head tilt or asymmetric occiput → Examine the neck and its rotation A tight, firm SCM; tilt toward it, chin away Congenital muscular torticollis A soft, transilluminating mass Cystic hygroma rather than a muscle mass → Look down at skull shape, ear position and sutures Ear forward, forehead prominent Positional plagiocephaly Ear backward with a ridge Suspected craniosynostosis; craniofacial referral → Examine both hips and the feet Breech, hip instability or torticollis Hip ultrasound for dysplasia Targeted tests TestResultMeans An atypical or uncertain neck mass → Ultrasound of the neck mass A cystic rather than muscular lesion Evaluate a developmental neck mass instead of assuming torticollis Posterior ear displacement and a suture ridge → Craniofacial evaluation; head CT when confirming suspected fusion Fused lambdoid suture Craniosynostosis; specialist treatment New acquired tilt with neurologic findings → MRI of the brain A posterior fossa lesion Treat the central cause Next step TestResultMeans Persistent flattening despite repositioning and therapy → Reassess the diagnosis and refer if the skull shape is uncertain Patent sutures with persistent deformity A helmet may be considered after physical therapy SkipRoutine head imaging for an otherwise typical positional head shape. Keep the infant sleeping supine; prone positioning is for supervised awake play.

Imaging pathwayThe 2003 head-deformity pathway recommends skull radiographs after 4 to 8 weeks without improvement, followed by CT if sutures are unclear or appear closed. An uncertain head shape warrants craniofacial or neurosurgical referral.

Clues that change the next step Clue Points to Next best step Firm SCM; chin turns away from the tilted side Muscular torticollis Begin gentle stretching and physical therapy The flat-side ear lies farther back, with a ridge Possible suture fusion Refer for craniofacial evaluation Acquired tilt with neurologic abnormalities A possible central cause Obtain brain MRI

Pause point Infant with a head tilt and a neck mass Offered as a lymphatic malformation A firm mass in a tight sternocleidomastoid that does not transilluminate → Congenital muscular torticollis Flat occiput in an infant Offered as craniosynostosis Ear and forehead on the flat side pushed forward; no suture ridge → Positional plagiocephaly

Findings that change the plan Finding Do Persistent neck restriction despite physical therapy Resistance to first-line care; pediatric orthopedic reassessment Persistent severe skull flattening Confirm the diagnosis and consider orthotic treatment A dislocatable hip that reduces with Ortolani Developmental dysplasia of the hip: refer and use age-appropriate treatment, usually a Pavlik harness in infancyThe Limping Child

Persistent neck restriction needs pediatric orthopedic reassessment

Follow-up decisions When Do During therapy Track active neck rotation, tilt and head-shape symmetry Persistent neck restriction despite therapy Compare rotation and tilt with prior visits; pediatric orthopedic reassessment if restriction persists Atypical progression or new neurologic signs Investigate another cause rather than continuing stretching alone

The underlying cause explains every finding: crowding gives the tilt and the hip, and the tilt gives the flat head; reject a diagnosis that leaves one out.

briefs.title: Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth
briefs.sub: birth trauma · upper and lower plexus · Moro, biceps and grasp
blocks: birth trauma · upper and lower plexus · Moro, biceps and grasp

Absent grasp with preserved Moro and biceps reflexes, a clawed hand and same-side ptosis or miosis point to Klumpke palsy (C8-T1). Moro and biceps decreased, grasp preserved: Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5-C6) (Erb palsy, waiter's tip palsy). Crepitus with biceps and grasp preserved favors a fracture. Start protective positioning and gentle physical therapy. No improvement over 1 to 2 months needs specialist evaluation; consider repair for persistent deficits rather than simply reassuring.

What it is Delivery-associated injury to the nerves supplying the arm and hand Driver Traction or compression may stretch, tear or avulse the involved nerves Triggers Shoulder dystocia, difficult extraction or a large infant (non-modifiable) Maternal diabetes may contribute through a large infant Chain Lateral neck traction upper-trunk injury shoulder and elbow weakness Upward arm traction lower-trunk injury intrinsic-hand weakness Insights Use the reflex pattern. Grasp tests the lower distribution; biceps and the upper-arm component of Moro distinguish the classic upper palsy. Horner changes prognosis. Lower-root sympathetic involvement can cause ptosis and miosis and predicts a poorer outcome.

What the injury does, by levelMotor localization Deltoid and supraspinatus weakness leaves the arm adductedInfraspinatus weakness leaves it internally rotated Biceps weakness impairs flexion and supinationThe forearm rests extended and pronated Biceps, infraspinatus, wrist extensors, deltoid and supraspinatus Lumbricals, interossei and thenar/hypothenar muscles can be weakLoss of intrinsic muscle balance allows clawing

Clinical localization Finding Interpretation Waiter's-tip posture with biceps and Moro decreased, grasp intact Classic C5-C6 upper-trunk injury Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints extended, interphalangeal (IP) joints flexed; grasp absent Claw hand from lower C8-T1 injury Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis Horner syndrome from sympathetic involvement; poorer prognosis

BreathingArm weakness with respiratory distress or reduced breath sounds on one side If a phrenic injury may accompany the plexus injury, choose assess breathing urgently and support ventilation as needed.
Extensive injuryA flail arm, absent reflexes or a sensory deficit If the entire plexus or cord may be involved, choose obtain urgent specialist assessment; cord signs require MRI.

A weak arm at birth: reflexes by lesion Diagnosis Moro / biceps / grasp, or central pattern Decides it Erb-Duchenne palsy (Erb palsy, waiter's tip palsy) Decreased / decreased / preserved At birth; adducted, internally rotated arm; extended elbow, pronated forearm, flexed wrist; C5-C6 In practiceRoot extentUpper-plexus injury may include C7 as well as C5 and C6. The classic Erb pattern used here localizes to C5-C6; an extensive injury can involve more roots. Klumpke palsy Preserved / preserved / absent At birth; a clawed hand, sometimes Horner syndrome; C8-T1 Clavicle fracture Pain-limited / preserved / preserved Clavicular crepitus or irregularity; pain inhibits the Moro response Humerus fracture Pain-limited / preserved / preserved Crepitus or swelling in the upper arm Total plexus palsy Absent / absent / absent Flaccid arm; sensory loss and Horner suggest more extensive injury Perinatal ischemic stroke Upper motor neuron signs may emerge Upper motor neuron signs rather than an isolated peripheral-nerve pattern Perinatal asphyxia Poor tone with altered alertness Altered alertness, poor tone, feeding or breathing problems, seizures
Time course Birth Weakness follows delivery Early recovery Movement often improves rapidly 1 to 2 months An unchanged deficit raises concern for long-term weakness and impaired growth

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans A newborn moves one arm less after delivery → Compare shoulder, elbow and hand movement Upper-arm weakness with grasp preserved Upper-trunk pattern Weak clawed hand Lower-trunk pattern → Compare Moro, biceps and grasp reflexes; palpate for crepitus Moro and biceps reduced, grasp preserved Erb-Duchenne palsy Grasp absent, Moro and biceps preserved Klumpke palsy Crepitus with biceps and grasp intact A fracture can limit movement through pain Targeted tests TestResultMeans Bony tenderness, crepitus or painful movement → Radiograph the suspected clavicle or humerus injury A fracture at the painful site Pain-related pseudoparalysis rather than a pure plexus deficit Pyramidal signs suggesting associated spinal cord trauma → MRI and specialist assessment Cord trauma A more extensive injury than an isolated upper or lower palsy Next step TestResultMeans Weakness persists at follow-up → Reassess motor recovery; refer if no improvement over 1 to 2 months Persistent deficit Assess the likelihood of recovery and need for repair Diagnostic test TestResultMeans A classic isolated upper or lower palsy → Clinical localization by posture, movement and reflexes The pattern matches C5-C6 or C8-T1 Classify the injury and follow motor recovery SkipRoutine reassurance for an unchanged deficit. Normal fracture films do not establish nerve recovery.

Clues that change the next step Clue Points to Next best step Moro and biceps reduced; grasp preserved Upper-trunk palsy Assess movement and follow recovery Crepitus with biceps and grasp preserved A painful fracture Obtain a radiograph at the tender site Pyramidal signs after birth trauma Possible associated cord injury MRI with urgent specialist assessment
Pause point Newborn with a reduced Moro reflex Read as proof of a nerve injury A fracture can make the response painful → Grasp and biceps, plus the bony examination, separate the two

Recovery and extent Finding Means Early return of movement Improvement is expected in many stretch injuries; continue observation and therapy Horner syndrome or persistent sensory loss Greater concern for severe root injury and a poor recovery Flail arm and absent reflexes Possible total plexus injury; more extensive than isolated Erb or Klumpke palsy

1 Protectimmediately after birth injury Protect the shoulder and position the arm; avoid excessive motion 2 Therapyduring early recovery Usually supportive: gentle passive range of motion with physical therapy; begin daily joint motion from about 1 week 3 Specialistno improvement over 1 to 2 months, or a severe deficit Refer for neurologic and orthopedic assessment of recovery and possible repair 4 Repairdeficits persist despite therapy Consider nerve surgery when there is no improvement by 3 to 9 months

Follow-up decisions When Do During the first weeks Record return of shoulder movement, elbow flexion and grasp; prevent joint contractures Motor recovery remains incomplete Track shoulder, elbow and hand movement; refer if no improvement over 1 to 2 months Persistent motor deficit Monitor limb growth and discuss reconstructive options with the team

Grasp is absent; Moro and biceps reflexes are symmetric. The wrist is extended and fingers clawed. Right ptosis and miosis; no crepitus Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injuryKlumpke palsy

Mechanism6 of 6 3-day-old girl with weakness of the right arm after a difficult vaginal delivery · Ipsilateral ptosis and miosisHorner syndrome signals sympathetic involvement near T1 and poorer recovery · Crepitus over the clavicleCrepitus suggests a fracture, not severe root injury · Absent biceps reflex with an intact graspAn upper-trunk pattern localizes the lesion but is less prognostically adverse 3-day-old girl with weakness of the right arm after a difficult vaginal delivery Ipsilateral ptosis and miosisHorner syndrome from a T1 injury

Gentle range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy to prevent contractures; most infants recover within months. Refer if no improvement over 1 to 2 months; persistent deficits may need surgical nerve repair. Horner syndrome marks a T1 injury and predicts a poorer outcome. A birth clavicle fracture generally heals with gentle handling and pain control.

Risk factors: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and maternal diabetes · Traction on the head and neck during shoulder dystocia stretches the upper roots (Erb); traction on a raised arm, as in delivering the posterior arm, stretches C8-T1 (Klumpke) · An intact, symmetric Moro does not exclude a plexus injury, because Klumpke spares the shoulder; check the grasp

Arm Injury in a Young Childsorts pediatric arm and elbow injuries Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infantevaluates infant neck position and head shape Stroke in a Child or Adolescentevaluates central focal weakness and seizures Arm Injury in a Young Child: sorts pediatric arm and elbow injuries. Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: evaluates infant neck position and head shape. Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: evaluates central focal weakness and seizures.

When a newborn will not move one arm, read three reflexes before the posture. A lower Moro alone with crepitus is a fracture. Lost Moro and biceps with a kept grasp is C5-C6. A lost grasp with Moro and biceps kept is C8-T1. With a lower-plexus injury, ptosis and miosis suggest T1 sympathetic involvement and a poorer outcome.

Upper and lower plexusThe classic C5-C6 pattern reduces Moro and biceps while preserving grasp. Lower-trunk injury instead weakens the hand and removes grasp. Fracture comparisonClavicular crepitus with a pain-limited Moro and preserved grasp favors a fracture. An absent grasp instead supports the lower-trunk pattern. Central weaknessUpper motor neuron signs favor a central lesion. A clawed hand with absent grasp and preserved upper reflexes supports lower-plexus localization. Generalized weaknessAltered alertness and poor tone favor a generalized neonatal insult. Isolated hand weakness with absent grasp and preserved Moro and biceps favors the lower plexus.

Birth weight is regained by 10–14 days, doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 1 year and quadruples by 2 years. When the numbers match a milestone rule and the exam is normal, management is reassurance; any other intervention is unnecessary.

Not you!" 12 mo The Little Person – cruises, pinches a Cheerio, first word ONE year = ONE word, ONE-finger pinch

Persistence beyond these windows indicates a UMN (upper motor neuron) lesion or cerebral palsy. Note: the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) 2022 revision moved milestones from the 50th to the 75th percentile. As a result, "sits without support" is now listed at 9 months, where older sources say 6.

NBME framing: the stem gives one skill present and one missing in each domain, and the options grid normal or delayed across three domains.

briefs.title: Maternal Effects in the Newborn
briefs.sub: maternal creatinine, antibodies and hormones · carryover or the baby's own disease · what is physiologic and what is notIs the infant well and inside the window, and does the mother's chart explain the finding?
blocks: maternal creatinine, antibodies and hormones · carryover or the baby's own disease · what is physiologic and what is notIs the infant well and inside the window, and does the mother's chart explain the finding?

In the first days a newborn's value or finding can be the mother's. Read her chart first. Creatinine: crosses the placenta; the day-1 value is the mother's. IgG (immunoglobulin G) antibodies: cross and cause disease, mostly transient (heart block is permanent); IgM (immunoglobulin M) and TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) do not cross. Estrogen: withdrawal bleeding, leukorrhea, labial swelling, breast hypertrophy with or without galactorrhea. When a value disagrees with urine output, growth and exam, those decide. Reassure only on positive criteria, and only after checking for each disqualifying finding.

Output at least one void per day of life; none by 24 hours is abnormal Weight loss under 10% in the first days; beyond that, look for feeding failure with hypernatremia and prerenal azotemia Red flags oliguria, edema, hypertension, or a risk factor: ultrasound and trended creatinine; risk factors: a nephrotoxic drug (gentamicin) or perinatal hypoxia

Diagnostic workup 1Mother first, then the baby Every abnormal day-1 value Maternal history Renal failure on dialysisThe creatinine is hers Anti-Ro/SSA (Sjögren syndrome antigen A), Graves, immune thrombocytopeniaTransplacental IgG disease Voids, weight, blood pressure, examination One void per day of life, loss under 10%, normalKidneys work: repeat the value Oliguria, edema or hypertensionThe baby's own kidney Red flag or risk factor Renal ultrasound, trended creatinine, medication list No void by 24 hours with respiratory distressObstruction or agenesis: image now Then A maternal creatinine falls over 2 weeks; a value that fails to fall is the baby's.

Bilateral renal agenesis no or minimal urine, respiratory distress, Potter facies, limb deformities Hypoxic-ischemic injury low Apgars, abnormal neurologic exam; creatinine rises over days Dehydration loss of 10% or more with fewer voids; breastfeeding jaundice reaches creatinine only this way

Anti-Ro/SSA with maternal SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) or no overt autoimmune disease, with fetal or neonatal bradycardia: congenital heart block Graves TSI (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin), neonatal thyrotoxicosis ITP (immune thrombocytopenia) antiplatelet IgG, neonatal thrombocytopenia; thyrotoxicosis and thrombocytopenia usually resolve as maternal IgG clears; complete heart block is permanent

Bilirubin: why the panel was drawn; it does not explain the creatinine. Arrest of labor, cesarean: suggest an insult; normal Apgars counter it. A newborn finding can be the mother's. Read her chart with the panel, let output, growth and exam decide, and reassure only on positive criteria, and only after checking for each disqualifying finding: fever, pain, odor, purulence, systemic illness, or a finding outside its window.

blocks: trisomies, cri-du-chat and Turner · the newborn with multiple anomalies · the floppy newborn · the trisomy 18 murmurWhich finding is unique to one syndrome: the hands, the tone, the nose or the eye?

Name the syndrome by its rarest finding, never its commonest: a heart defect, cleft palate and cryptorchidism appear on several lists. Trisomy 18 (Edwards): overlapping fingers, hypertonia, micrognathia. Trisomy 21 (Down): hypotonia, transverse palmar crease. Cri-du-chat (5p deletion): the cat-like cry. Turner (45,X): the webbed neck. CHARGE (coloboma, heart defect, atresia choanae, retarded growth and development, genitourinary and ear anomalies): among these, the only one with choanal atresia; coloboma is CHARGE or trisomy 13. Trisomy 13 (Patau): midline defects; a small head separates it from CHARGE. VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb): no eye or nasal component. Maternal age acts through meiotic nondisjunction: sporadic, not inherited.

The feature map: one signature finding each Syndrome Signature Also Trisomy 18 Clenched fists, overlapping fingers; hypertonia Growth restriction, microcephaly with prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set pointed ears, absent palmar creases, limited hip abduction, rocker-bottom feet; ventricular septal defect (VSD); Meckel diverticulum, malrotation and omphalocele in over three quarters; about 95% die in the first year Trisomy 13 Cutis aplasia, microphthalmia Microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, omphalocele, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, coloboma, cryptorchidism; highly lethal Trisomy 21 Transverse palmar crease; hypotonia Up-slanting fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots, protruding tongue; under 2.5 kg; heart defects, intestinal atresia; young mothers too Cri-du-chat Cat-like cry Microcephaly with protruding metopic suture, hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, hypotonia Turner Webbed neck Low hairline, widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, short stature; coarctation CHARGE Choanal atresia; coloboma Cleft lip or palate, hypotonia, anosmia: common, not identifying 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) Hypocalcemic seizure, absent thymic shadow Conotruncal defect such as truncus arteriosus, cleft palate VACTERL Imperforate anus or radial ray defect Hemivertebrae, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal anomaly Fanconi anemia Abnormal thumbs with abnormal pigmentation Café-au-lait macules, short stature, renal and ear anomalies; marrow failure later

C: coloboma a gap in an eye structure H: heart defect tetralogy of Fallot or VSD, commonly A: atresia choanae a 5-French catheter will not pass either naris R: retarded growth and development postnatal, not visible at an hour of life G: genitourinary cryptorchidism E: ear short, wide, lobeless; hearing loss

Wrong trisomy: right family, another trisomy's signature finding. Tone ignored: hypertonia rules out trisomy 21. Ready slot: VACTERL fits anomalies in several systems, but needs its own components. Head not read: trisomy 13 shares coloboma, cleft palate, cryptorchidism and a heart defect with CHARGE; microcephaly and choanal atresia separate them. Loud murmur: the most striking finding and the least useful; every option carries a heart defect. Blue hands, pink mouth: acrocyanosis, not a cyanotic lesion. Truncus arteriosus: real, but a 22q11 lesion with a single S2. Atrial septal defect: also seen in trisomy 18, but heard at the left upper border.

Mosaic trisomy arises after fertilization, so the parents carry no recurrence risk. Isolated choanal atresia still sends you looking for the other CHARGE features. VACTERL and CHARGE overlap only in cardiac and renal anomalies. The gene CHD7 and the syndrome share their first two letters.

briefs.title: School Difficulty in a Child
briefs.sub: behavior confined to school · the child's private interview · learning vs behavioral disorders · hearing and visionDoes the behavior stay at school, and what does the child say when interviewed alone?

Pt 9 yo M, irritable and fighting at school since third grade began, with school refusal; privately reports classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly; behavior normal at home Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned specific learning disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, social anxiety disorder and oppositional defiant disorder

The mother's chief complaint is irritability, a fight and school refusal. In a private interview, the child says his classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly. This private disclosure identifies the diagnosis. Each behavioral disorder in the differential explains the behavior, but only specific learning disorder also explains the failing grades. Onset coincides with an academic transition: third grade, where learning to read becomes reading to learn. The symptoms are confined to school, with normal behavior at home.

Specific learning disorder achievement below intellectual potential in reading, writing or math for at least 6 months despite support attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms in at least 2 settings with onset before age 12, so school-only behavior excludes it Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder severe outbursts at least 3 times weekly for at least 12 months with persistently irritable mood between them Oppositional defiant disorder a pattern of defiance, argumentativeness and vindictiveness toward authority for at least 6 months Social anxiety disorder fear of scrutiny across situations, and not diagnosed when better explained by another disorder

briefs.title: Suspected Child Abuse
briefs.sub: fractures that mean abuse · red flags · the bone-disease mimics · a risk factor is not a findingDoes the fracture need a pull, twist or squeeze, and does the film or exam give a bone disease its own sign?
blocks: fractures that mean abuse · red flags · the bone-disease mimics · a risk factor is not a findingDoes the fracture need a pull, twist or squeeze, and does the film or exam give a bone disease its own sign?

Pt 13-month-old boy brought by an aunt for left leg pain; irritable, refuses to stand, cries when the leg is touched; born at home without prenatal care, exclusively breastfed without vitamin D, no routine care; his mother broke her forearm and wrist as a child Exam weight 5th percentile, height 50th; swelling and point tenderness of the distal left thigh; no bruises; beefy red diaper plaques with satellite papules Imaging medial metaphyseal corner fracture of the distal femur Q the most likely cause of the x-ray findings; options spanned abuse, two metabolic or genetic bone diseases, an infection and a histiocytic disorder

In a young child, three fractures are abuse until proven otherwise. A metaphyseal corner (bucket-handle) fracture needs a forcible pull or twist of the limb. A posterior rib fracture comes from squeezing the chest. The third is a femur fracture in a child who does not yet walk. The bone-disease mimics each need their own finding on the film or exam. Rickets needs osteopenia with cupped, frayed metaphyses. Osteogenesis imperfecta needs blue sclerae and many low-energy fractures. Langerhans cell histiocytosis needs a punched-out lytic lesion. A risk factor in the history (breastfeeding without vitamin D, no prenatal care, a parent's single childhood fracture) is not that finding. A film with normal bone density and a classic abuse fracture outweighs that risk factor; the fracture stays abuse until proven otherwise.

History injury inconsistent with the child's developmental stage, delay in seeking care, a story that changes or conflicts between caregivers Bruises patterned (belt, buckle, hand), any bruise in an infant who is not yet mobile, or bruises over the ears, neck or trunk rather than shins and forehead Burns linear or sharply demarcated, such as immersion burns with a clean line Fractures metaphyseal corner, posterior rib, femur before walking, multiple in different stages of healing, skull Head subdural and retinal hemorrhages

Fracture in an infant or toddler: the differential Diagnosis Illness script The NBME tell Why less likely here Child abuse History that does not fit the injury or the child's development; delay in care Metaphyseal corner, posterior rib, or femur fracture before walking, on a film with normal bone density The key: a pull-or-twist fracture with no sign of bone disease Osteogenesis imperfecta Type I collagen defect, usually autosomal dominant; fractures with minimal trauma Blue sclerae, easy bruising, short stature, hearing loss, a family history of many fractures; osteopenia on film No blue sclerae, normal height; a parent's single childhood fracture is not that history Rickets Vitamin D deficiency in an exclusively breastfed infant without supplements; X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets looks similar on film Film: osteopenia, cupped and frayed metaphyses, widened physes; exam: bowed legs, widened wrists, rachitic rosary Risk factor present, film findings absent; the metaphysis is fractured, not frayed Congenital syphilis Untreated maternal infection; early (under 2 years): snuffles, palm and sole rash, hepatosplenomegaly, periostitis; late: saber shin, frontal bossing, saddle nose Rash, snuffles, big liver; later saber shin None of its findings; it does not cause corner fractures Langerhans cell histiocytosis A rash that looks seborrheic or candidal but is petechial or crusted and persists; sometimes diabetes insipidus Punched-out lytic skull or long-bone lesion The film shows a fracture, not a lytic lesion Toddler's fracture (accidental) A child who has started walking; new limp after a minor, often unwitnessed twist Nondisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibia Wrong bone and wrong pattern

Next step7 of 7 6-month-old boy seen for cough; chest radiograph shows a healing posterior rib fracture; the mother says he has never been injured; a small bruise is on the left ear; the physician is not certain the injury was inflicted · Report to child protective services · Discuss concerns with the parents and recheck in 1 week · Report only if the skeletal survey finds more fractures 6-month-old boy seen for cough; chest radiograph shows a healing posterior rib fracture; the mother says he has never been injured; a small bruise is on the left ear; the physician is not certain the injury was inflicted Report to child protective servicesphysicians are mandated reporters on reasonable suspicion, not proof; admit and obtain the skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy alongside the report

Safety first admit the child to the hospital rather than discharge to the suspected caregivers while the workup runs Report to child protective services on reasonable suspicion; physicians are mandated reporters and do not need proof, and the report is not delayed for the skeletal survey or other results Evaluate skeletal survey, head CT and funduscopy, plus the by-branch labs above

Abuse also presents as a posterior rib fracture or a femur fracture before walking, or with an added bruise on the ear or trunk A walking toddler with a spiral distal tibial fracture after a minor twist has an accidental injury. The same child with a corner fracture does not Caregivers who were themselves abused or neglected, an unstable home and a child with chronic medical problems raise the risk. The diagnosis rests on the fracture pattern

Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child covers bruising. Ask: is the bruise somewhere a child of this age could bump, and are the platelets normal? Part I The Limping Child master table covers the toddler's fracture. Ask: does the child walk, and is it a spiral tibial fracture or a corner fracture? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin D deficiency rickets and the 400 international units supplement for breastfed infants. Part I Bone Lesions in a Child covers the lytic lesion. Ask: is the bone destroyed, or broken?

Some fractures in a young child need a force the child could not generate. Treat these as abuse until the film or exam shows a sign specific to a bone disease. A risk factor in the history is not that sign.

Unchecked attributeRickets: exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D is a real risk factor, but the film never showed osteopenia, cupping, fraying or widened physes. Salient decoyLangerhans cell histiocytosis: the beefy diaper rash with satellite papules is ordinary candida; Langerhans cell histiocytosis causes punched-out lytic lesions, not corner fractures. Salient decoyOsteogenesis imperfecta: the mother's one childhood forearm fracture is common; without blue sclerae, short stature, bruising or many fractures, this is not osteogenesis imperfecta. True-fact-wrong-slotCongenital syphilis: no prenatal care is a real risk, but saber shin, frontal bossing and saddle nose are late findings, and none of its signs is a corner fracture.

briefs.title: Shock in Children
briefs.sub: four categories by mechanism, not appearance · cold shock in children · perfusion before pressure · septic shock ladderIs perfusion abnormal, and what is wrong with the circulation rather than with the skin?
blocks: four categories by mechanism, not appearance · cold shock in children · perfusion before pressure · septic shock ladderIs perfusion abnormal, and what is wrong with the circulation rather than with the skin?

Pt 4 yo F, fever to 40 C, petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds, no response to three fluid boluses; no blood pressure reported Q the category of shock; options spanned distributive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic and obstructive

Fever, a petechial rash and shock in a preschooler indicate septic shock. Septic shock is by definition distributive. Inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation and capillary leak, so blood is maldistributed rather than absent, inadequate or obstructed. She does not look vasodilated. Capillary refill of 4 seconds is cold shock, which is how children usually present. Children compensate by vasoconstricting and raising the heart rate, so the bedside picture mimics hypovolemia. The vignette gives no blood pressure, because in children hypotension is a late, pre-arrest finding.

Distributive shock vasodilation and capillary leak with maldistributed flow despite normal or high cardiac output Shock in a child a perfusion diagnosis: mental status, capillary refill above 2 seconds, weak pulses, urine output under 1 mL/kg/h Hypotension not required, and marks decompensation when present Fluid-refractory shock persistent after 40 to 60 mL/kg, the trigger to start a vasoactive infusion

The four categories of shock – what to look for Category Mechanism The NBME tell Distributive Vasodilation and capillary leak Fever with a source, urticaria, or a spinal injury; wide pulse pressure when warm Hypovolemic Volume loss – gastrointestinal, hemorrhage, burns, ketoacidosis A stated route of loss, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes Cardiogenic Pump failure – myocarditis, arrhythmia, congenital lesion Gallop, hepatomegaly, crackles; worsens with fluid Obstructive Mechanical block – tamponade, tension pneumothorax, ductal-dependent lesion Distended neck veins with clear or asymmetric lungs, muffled sounds Anaphylactic distributive subtype Immunoglobulin E-mediated vasodilation Urticaria, angioedema, wheeze within minutes of exposure Neurogenic distributive subtype Loss of sympathetic tone above T6 Hypotension with bradycardia, warm dry skin

Management ladder – pediatric septic shock Tier Intervention Escalate when 1 Recognise, obtain access, balanced crystalloid 10 to 20 mL/kg per bolus up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in the first hour, reassessing after each Shock persists after 40 to 60 mL/kg, or rales or hepatomegaly appear, which stops the fluid 2 Start a vasoactive infusion – epinephrine or norepinephrine Catecholamine-resistant shock 3 Hydrocortisone for catecholamine-resistant shock or suspected adrenal insufficiency No response; consider extracorporeal support Parallel Antimicrobials within 1 hour for septic shock, cultures first only if they cause no substantial delay –

Diagnosis9 of 9 17 yo M after a cervical spine injury, hypotensive with bradycardia and warm dry skin · Cardiogenic shock · Hypovolemic shock from occult hemorrhage · Neurogenic shock 17 yo M after a cervical spine injury, hypotensive with bradycardia and warm dry skin Neurogenic shockalso a distributive subtype

Where intensive care is not available and the child has sepsis without hypotension, bolus fluid is recommended against. This is a strong, high-certainty recommendation. Also, adolescence is never itself a reason to admit; the same hospitalization thresholds apply as for adults.

Hypotension is a late sign in children; they defend pressure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then decompensate abruptly Children get cold shock and adults get warm shock; a vasoconstricted child's shock is still distributive Anaphylactic and neurogenic shock are distributive subtypes, so classify the shock as distributive, not as the subtype, unless the subtype's trigger is present Neurogenic shock is the one form of shock with hypotension and bradycardia; all other shock is tachycardic Fever plus petechiae plus toxicity is meningococcemia until excluded; petechiae in a well child point instead at immune thrombocytopenia

Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid and meningococcal disease; this brief covers only recognition and resuscitation. Ask: is perfusion abnormal? If yes, resuscitate before you investigate.
Shock is classified by mechanism rather than appearance, so ask what is wrong with the circulation instead of what the skin looks like.

True-fact-wrong-slotFluid refractoriness in sepsis reflects leak and vasodilation, not pump failure. Class-vs-memberAnaphylaxis: it is in the right class but is the wrong member, with no exposure and no urticaria.

briefs.sub: corrected age · milestones at corrected age · growth faltering thresholds · vaccines at chronological ageWhat is the corrected age, and do growth and milestones fit it?
blocks: corrected age · milestones at corrected age · growth faltering thresholds · vaccines at chronological ageWhat is the corrected age, and do growth and milestones fit it?

Pt 18 mo F, former 26-week preterm infant, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles; height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile Q the most likely assessment; options spanned normal growth and development for corrected age, global developmental delay and failure to thrive

Calculate the corrected age first. Born at 26 weeks, she was 14 weeks early. At 18 months chronological age, her corrected age is about 14 and a half months. Judge every milestone against that age. She has just started walking, which is on time. Her vocabulary of 10 words is ahead of the three to five words expected at 15 months. Following a call, imitating and scribbling are age-appropriate. All three parameters sit together at the 15th percentile. They are proportionate, symmetric and well within normal. Faltering growth requires a parameter below about the 2nd percentile or a downward crossing of two major lines, and she has neither.

Corrected age chronological age minus the weeks born before 40 weeks How long to correct through 24 months for growth and development; newer data support 36 months in extremely and very preterm children What is never corrected immunizations, given at chronological age regardless of gestational age or birth weight; the one weight rule is the birth hepatitis B dose at 2 kg or more, and it is a weight threshold rather than an age correction Normal percentile range the 15th percentile is normal; faltering growth needs under about the 2nd percentile or a crossing of two major lines

Assessing the former preterm infant – the differential Assessment Illness script The NBME tell Normal for corrected age Preterm child meeting milestones and tracking a normal percentile once corrected Corrected-age milestones met, parameters proportionate above the 2nd percentile Global developmental delay Significant delay in two or more domains at corrected age Not walking or no words at 18 months corrected, often with a falling head circumference Isolated growth faltering Weight crosses percentiles downward with intact development Weight disproportionately low with length and head preserved Failure to thrive Inadequate calories, malabsorption or increased demand Parameter below the 2nd percentile or crossing two major lines Constitutional smallness Small but healthy child on a low-normal curve Normal growth velocity along their own percentile
