Former 26-week premature sets the age correction; it is not the problem. Mild bronchopulmonary dysplasia with normal head ultrasounds looks like a list of morbidities but is reassuring. Normal cranial imaging excludes the intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia that drive adverse neurodevelopmental outcome at this gestational age.

Mechanism fragile germinal matrix vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion (hypotension, hypoxia, hypo- or hyperventilation), and the blood can extend into the lateral ventricles Who under 32 weeks gestation or under 1500 g When the first few days of life, and often asymptomatic Symptomatic signs lethargy, hypotonia, seizures, apnea, bradycardia, a bulging fontanelle, a rapidly rising head circumference, acute anemia Diagnosis cranial ultrasound, repeated to follow progression; routine screening under 32 weeks Versus hypoglycemia or hypocalcemia lethargy, hypotonia and seizures, but never a growing head Versus hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy needs perinatal asphyxia and acidosis, not a day-3 onset after Apgar scores of 8 and 9 Versus meningitis needs fever or risk factors such as maternal fever or prolonged rupture of membranes

Mechanism oxygenation at birth (breathing, ductus closure) switches off erythropoietin; a preterm infant has also missed the third-trimester shift of erythropoietin production from liver to kidney Why worse than term lower hematocrit at birth, shorter red cell life span, frequent NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) blood draws, iron depletion Timing term physiologic anemia bottoms out at 9 to 11 g/dL at 2 to 3 months; the preterm nadir is deeper (about 7 g/dL) and earlier (1 to 2 months) Presentation often asymptomatic; tachycardia, a flow murmur, apnea, poor weight gain Labs normocytic, normochromic, normal platelets and white count; the absolute reticulocyte count may be normal for age, but there is no reticulocytosis for the degree of anemia Management iron supplementation and fewer blood draws; red cell transfusion if severe or symptomatic Versus thalassemia microcytic and hypochromic with target cells Versus hemolysis erythropoietin rises and the reticulocytes climb Versus iron deficiency microcytic, and unlikely on fortified formula with ferrous sulfate Versus anemia of chronic disease iron trapped in macrophages by chronic inflammation, infection or malignancy, in older children and adults

Head circumference is the parameter that predicts neurodevelopment, so preserved head growth in a former preemie is the most reassuring single measurement A percentile by itself is not a pathology; the concerning patterns are crossing lines downward and disproportion between parameters Retinopathy of prematurity and hearing screening are required by gestational age, however well the infant looks A preterm infant is more vulnerable to vaccine-preventable disease, so the vaccine schedule is never delayed

Part II Abnormal Growth in a Child covers the contrasting case. Ask: are the three parameters together or apart? Parameters that are together and steady are normal. Parameters that are apart, with weight lowest, indicate inadequate calories. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the imaging diagnosis when the delay does not resolve with corrected age. Part I Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers apnea of prematurity, the diagnosis for the spells once intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia are excluded. Ask: did the spells start on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between episodes?
When a gestational age is given, do the arithmetic before interpreting anything. An option claiming that assessment is impossible is almost always wrong.

Uniform-answer doubtDeclining to assess is not caution; correction exists to make the assessment possible. Treat-the-numberThe 15th percentile sounds low only against an unexamined assumption that normal means the 50th. Class-vs-memberGlobal delay is a valid framework, but here it is judged against chronological rather than corrected age.

briefs.title: Hypotonia in an Infant
briefs.sub: brain, anterior horn cell, neuromuscular junction or muscle · strength and reflexes · genetic confirmation · Down syndrome careIs the infant floppy but strong, or weak with absent reflexes, and which test confirms the level?
blocks: brain, anterior horn cell, neuromuscular junction or muscle · strength and reflexes · genetic confirmation · Down syndrome careIs the infant floppy but strong, or weak with absent reflexes, and which test confirms the level?

Pt infant with low tone, Aquifer Pediatrics 29; the case works from the hypotonia differential to Down syndrome, its confirmation and its health supervision Q decide whether the low tone comes from the brain or from the motor unit, confirm the chromosomal cause, then plan the child’s care for the first years

Hypotonia is a finding, not a diagnosis. Localize where it starts. Causes in the brain include Down syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, congenital hypothyroidism and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Other levels are the anterior horn cell (spinal muscular atrophy), the neuromuscular junction (infant botulism) and the muscle (congenital myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies). A central cause produces an infant who is floppy but strong for the tone, often dysmorphic or sleepy, with normal or brisk reflexes. A peripheral cause produces a weak, alert infant with low or absent reflexes. Check breathing and feeding first. Send the confirmatory test, usually genetic, once the level is known.

Red flags: act before the full history Finding What it points to Weak cry, pooled secretions, belly breathing, falling saturation Respiratory or bulbar failure: circulation, airway, breathing first Seizures or a sleepy infant after a hard delivery Brain injury: glucose, then imaging Ptosis, weak suck and constipation in a previously well infant Infant botulism: admit and watch the airway Tongue fasciculations with absent reflexes Spinal muscular atrophy: breathing fails next

What it is the commonest chromosomal cause of intellectual disability, about 1 in 700 US births Who any couple; risk climbs from the mid-30s, but most affected infants have mothers under 35 because younger women have more pregnancies Mechanism extra chromosome 21 material: free trisomy (most likely at any maternal age), an unbalanced translocation (relatively likelier with a younger mother), or mosaicism, with features from classic to almost none Features hypotonia, upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds, flat midface, small ears, loose nuchal skin; Brushfield spots, single palmar crease, clinodactyly, sandal gap; intellectual disability usually mild (intelligence quotient (IQ) 50 to 70) or moderate (35 to 50) Diagnosis prenatal serum analytes, nuchal ultrasound and cell-free DNA estimate risk; CVS (chorionic villus sampling) or amniocentesis diagnose; after birth a lymphocyte karyotype Treatment early intervention at diagnosis; an IEP (individualized education program) at school entry, with parents as advocates Complications heart disease in about half, some silent; duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease; hypothyroidism at any age; hearing and vision loss; transient myeloproliferative disorder and leukemia; atlantoaxial instability Follow-up the grid below Return for neck pain, head tilt, a change in walking, new weakness or wetting; pallor, bruising or fever; poor feeding or weight gain

Down syndrome: health supervision Check When Why CBC First 3 days, then yearly Polycythemia, leukemoid reaction, transient myeloproliferative disorder; later iron deficiency Echocardiogram First month, read by pediatric cardiology Heart disease in about half, some not heard on auscultation Hearing Newborn, then repeated Hearing loss is more common Eyes Cataract check from birth; ophthalmology at least yearly Cataracts and other vision problems TSH Newborn screen, then yearly Hypothyroidism can appear after a normal screen Early intervention At diagnosis Therapies before delay shows Neck History and examination every visit; positioning precautions discussed at least every 2 years Atlantoaxial instability; imaging for symptoms, not routinely Gut and growth Pediatric gastroenterology for feeding or weight problems; celiac serology for symptoms Structural anomalies, celiac disease Sleep Sleep study for all at ages 3 to 4 Obstructive sleep apnea Immunology If infections recur Immunodeficiency Head MRI Not indicated No consistent finding

For a floppy infant, first decide whether the problem is in the brain or the motor unit. An infant who is strong for the tone with normal reflexes has a central cause, often chromosomal. A weak infant with absent reflexes has a peripheral cause. Then send the genetic test for that level.

briefs.title: Heart Failure
briefs.sub: congestion and perfusion · echocardiographic phenotype · foundational therapy · diuresis and monitoring
blocks: congestion and perfusion · echocardiographic phenotype · foundational therapy · diuresis and monitoring

Congestion or poor perfusion suggests heart failure (HF); confirm cardiac dysfunction with echocardiography. A preserved ejection fraction does not exclude HF. Symptomatic chronic HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): use the four foundational drug classes; add a loop diuretic for congestion. HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and hypertension: control the pressure. Match the intervention to the outcome: blood pressure control for uncontrolled hypertension; statins for atherosclerotic risk, rather than as HF treatment.

What it is Inadequate cardiac performance with congestion, reduced tissue perfusion, or both. Driver Systolic failure: impaired contractility; diastolic failure: impaired filling of a stiff ventricle. Triggers Ischemia or a dilated ventricle; chronic uncontrolled hypertension is the leading cause of preserved-fraction HF. Chain Reduced kidney perfusion activates the renin-angiotensin system; retained fluid worsens congestion. Insights Orthopnea and waking breathless at night suggest left-sided congestion. Raised jugular venous pressure and dependent edema suggest systemic venous congestion.

Afterload and ventricular remodelingA mechanism behind pressure-driven decompensation Uncontrolled pressure raises afterload and ventricular wall stress.Remodeling can contribute to pump dysfunction and admission.

Ejection fraction Category Definition Reduced-fraction HF Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 40% or less. Mildly reduced-fraction HF LVEF 41% to 49% with increased filling pressures. Preserved-fraction HF In a patient with clinical HF: LVEF 50% or more and evidence of increased left ventricular filling pressures.

Decompensation Finding Action Dyspnea with hypotension, hypoxia or altered mentation Arrange urgent hospital assessment for acute HF or cardiogenic shock. Acute pulmonary congestion Give a loop diuretic; treat precipitating ischemia or an arrhythmia. Inotropes may be needed for cardiogenic shock.

Patterns of heart failure Pattern Decides it Next best step Systolic HF Poor contraction; reduced LVEF. Start the foundational regimen for symptomatic chronic HFrEF when stable. Diastolic HF Stiff ventricle; LVEF preserved, often after longstanding hypertension. Treat hypertension and relieve congestion. Obstructive Lung Disease Breathlessness can resemble HF; wheeze does not exclude pulmonary edema. Use chest imaging, natriuretic peptides and echo to distinguish cardiac from pulmonary disease.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans New dyspnea or suspected congestion → Chest radiograph Pulmonary congestion on imaging Supports HF; evaluate cardiac function. → Electrocardiogram (ECG) Evidence of infarction, hypertrophy or arrhythmia Assess a cause or precipitant. → Electrolytes and renal function Renal dysfunction or electrolyte abnormality Guide safe drug and diuretic use. Targeted tests TestResultMeans Cardiac versus pulmonary cause remains uncertain → B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) Elevated BNP Supports HF in the clinical context. Diagnostic test TestResultMeans HF suspected clinically → Transthoracic echocardiography Reduced LVEF Classify systolic dysfunction. Preserved LVEF with abnormal filling Evaluate diastolic dysfunction; preserved LVEF alone does not exclude HF.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step High blood pressure in established HF Afterload driving decompensation Treat the pressure using Hypertension in an Adult Atherosclerotic disease or increased lipid risk A separate indication for a statin Assess eligibility with Lipid Screening and Statin Therapy Potassium elevated while taking potassium-raising therapy Hyperkalemia requiring evaluation Obtain an ECG and review dietary and medication contributors; repeat potassium if the result does not fit the clinical presentation.

Pause point Heart failure decompensation with uncontrolled blood pressure and an abnormal lipid value Offered: cholesterol lowering A statin treats atherosclerotic risk, not the decompensation → Blood pressure control
Clinical assessment Assess Meaning Congestion Guides diuresis. Perfusion and mental status Hypotension or confusion can indicate shock and require urgent care.

1 FoundationalStable reduced-fraction HF Use an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI); an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) is an alternative when appropriate. Use an evidence-based beta-blocker: carvedilol, metoprolol succinate or bisoprolol. Add a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) when appropriate. For symptomatic chronic HFrEF, add a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. 2 CongestionFluid retention Add a loop diuretic and monitor kidney function and electrolytes. Titrate to relief of congestion. 3 Persistent symptomsHFrEF despite the foundational regimen Digoxin may improve symptoms and reduce HF admissions, without a proven survival advantage. 4 Preserved fractionHypertension or volume overload Treat hypertension and congestion; SGLT2 inhibitors may reduce HF admissions. 5 AvoidDecompensation or hyperkalemia Start a beta-blocker after stabilization, rather than during active congestion. Avoid use of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), which can worsen fluid retention. Avoid excess potassium when potassium is elevated; do not intensify potassium-raising drugs before evaluation.

Monitoring When Do During drug titration Recheck renal function and electrolytes after dose increases; reassess congestion and blood pressure. At home Check morning weight; seek care for continued weight gain or worsening symptoms. Avoid excessive dietary sodium; individualize the restriction.

briefs.title: Lipid Screening and Statin Therapy
briefs.sub: who gets lipids measured · no-calculation statin groups · the 10-year risk calculator · secondary causes · risk enhancers and the calcium score · high-density lipoprotein (HDL) as a marker
blocks: who gets lipids measured · no-calculation statin groups · the 10-year risk calculator · secondary causes · risk enhancers and the calcium score · high-density lipoprotein (HDL) as a marker

Clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) 190 mg/dL or more, or diabetes at 40 to 75 identifies a statin-benefit group before calculation. For remaining adults in the board-style Pooled Cohort Equations pathway, use the 10-year risk, risk enhancers and shared discussion. Low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) is a risk marker, not a drug target. Keep the calculator and its thresholds together. In practiceCurrent risk assessmentThe 2026 guideline recommends Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events (PREVENT) equations for primary prevention in adults ages 30 to 79 without known ASCVD or subclinical atherosclerosis and with LDL 70 to 189 mg/dL. Its risk bands differ: under 3%, 3% to under 5%, 5% to under 10%, and 10% or more. Do not apply the Pooled Cohort cutoffs to a PREVENT result.
Ages in the board-style lipid pathway not to scale Lipid assessment From age 20 20 years 40 years 75 years → Diabetes statin-benefit age range 40 to 75 years 20 years 40 years 75 years →

Statin-benefit groups Finding Action Clinical ASCVD: prior myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke or peripheral artery disease Use a high-intensity statin if tolerated; after age 75, a moderate-intensity statin is an option. LDL ≥ 190 mg/dL Use a high-intensity statin without a risk calculation. Severe LDL elevation is often familial; evaluate for familial hypercholesterolemia and assess relatives. Diabetes, age 40 to 75 Use at least moderate intensity; the board deck favors high intensity when Pooled Cohort risk is 7.5% or more.

Lipid assessment and calculator ages. Periodic risk assessment at ages 40 to 75 includes lipid measurement. The Pooled Cohort Equations are not validated under 40. Other ages and legacy screeningScreening agesThe US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) standalone adult lipid-screening recommendation is archived; its statin recommendation is risk-based. The board deck also teaches lipid screening from age 20, repeated every 4 to 6 years when normal. Pediatric universal screening is usually during ages 9 to 11, with a second screen during ages 17 to 21. Older USPSTF wording used men 35 or older, women 45 or older at increased risk, and younger adults with risk factors; the conventional interval was about every 5 years. These are legacy screening statements, not the current statin-benefit algorithm.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Lipid assessment or cardiovascular risk review → Lipid panel, fasting or nonfasting as appropriate Clinical ASCVD, severe LDL elevation or diabetes in the statin-benefit age range Use the statin-benefit group rather than making treatment depend on a calculator. No automatic-benefit group in the board-style pathway Estimate 10-year risk with the Pooled Cohort Equations when age-appropriate. Targeted tests TestResultMeans Nonfasting triglycerides above 400 mg/dL → Repeat a fasting lipid panel High triglycerides impair calculated LDL estimation Use the fasting results to clarify the lipid abnormality. A new or unexpectedly worsening lipid abnormality → Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), glucose or hemoglobin A1c, liver tests, creatinine and urine protein Hypothyroidism, diabetes, nephrotic syndrome or cholestasis. In hypothyroidism, reduced LDL receptor expression can raise cholesterol. Treat the secondary cause and reassess the lipid profile. A borderline or intermediate Pooled Cohort result leaves the statin decision uncertain → Coronary artery calcium (CAC) score CAC is zero A statin may be deferred unless diabetes, smoking or a strong premature family history is present. CAC is at least 100 Favors starting a statin after a risk discussion.

Pause point A low HDL value alone Offered: niacin or a cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitor A low HDL value alone is not an indication → Treat LDL-related and overall atherosclerotic risk, not the HDL number

Pooled Cohort risk bands 10-year risk Category Action Under 5% Low Emphasize lifestyle. 5% to under 7.5% Borderline Discuss a statin when risk enhancers favor treatment. 7.5% to under 20% Intermediate Discuss moderate-intensity statin therapy; use CAC selectively if uncertain. 20% or more High Use high-intensity statin therapy when tolerated.

Risk enhancers. Risk enhancers include premature family history, chronic kidney disease, metabolic syndrome, preeclampsia or premature menopause before age 40, chronic inflammatory disease, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and South Asian ancestry. Persistently elevated LDL (160 mg/dL or more) or triglycerides (175 mg/dL or more), apolipoprotein B, lipoprotein(a) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein may also refine risk.

USPSTF primary prevention. For primary prevention without prior cardiovascular disease, the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends a statin at ages 40 to 75 with a cardiovascular risk factor and estimated 10-year risk of at least 10%; offer one selectively at 7.5% to under 10%. In practiceDifferent recommendation frameworksThe USPSTF recommendation and the older Pooled Cohort-based American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) risk discussion are different frameworks. The 2026 PREVENT framework has different risk categories again. Read the calculator and recommendation named in the question.

Reassessment Situation Do After lifestyle or lipid-lowering treatment changes Reassess the lipid response, adherence and treatment tolerance. Myositis or hepatitis while taking a statin Stop the statin and evaluate the adverse effect.

briefs.title: Stable Ischemic Heart Disease
briefs.sub: three angina criteria, not location · anginal equivalents · retired terminology · stress test choice · high-risk findings
blocks: three angina criteria, not location · anginal equivalents · retired terminology · stress test choice · high-risk findings

Exertional discomfort relieved by rest suggests myocardial ischemia, even when described as epigastric burning. For a stable patient, choose testing from pretest probability, exercise ability and the resting electrocardiogram (ECG). New, worsening or rest pain needs urgent evaluation for an acute coronary syndrome. The board-style three-feature definition remains useful; current clinical terminology is cardiac, possibly cardiac or noncardiac.

What it is Transient myocardial ischemia without infarction, producing discomfort or pressure. Driver Coronary narrowing limits blood supply when myocardial oxygen demand rises. Triggers Exertion or emotional stress; symptoms usually improve with rest or nitroglycerin. Chain Faster heart rate and greater systolic wall tension increase oxygen demand beyond coronary supply. Insights An upper-abdominal or burning description does not exclude ischemia. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) increases the risk of premature coronary disease. Antiphospholipid syndrome can occur with SLE and is associated with thrombosis. Pain at rest with transient ST elevation in a young smoker suggests coronary spasm.

Angina classification Use Definition Board description of typical angina Substernal location, exertional precipitation and relief with rest or nitroglycerin. Legacy feature count All 3 features: typical; 2: atypical; fewer than 2: nonanginal. Clinical documentation Describe the pain as cardiac, possibly cardiac or noncardiac; avoid the label atypical.

Change in pattern Finding Action New, worsening or rest pain Evaluate promptly for an acute coronary syndrome with ECG and cardiac troponin testing. Unstable angina suspected Do not send the patient for routine early exercise stress testing.
Anginal symptom duration not to scale Stable angina Often under 20 minutes Onset 20 minutes Prolonged → Myocardial infarction Classically over 20 minutes Onset 20 minutes Prolonged →

Chest pain patterns Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Stable angina Often under 20 minutes: exertion-related pressure relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Select a test for ischemia according to probability and exercise/ECG suitability. Unstable angina Pain at rest or an accelerating pattern; no troponin-defined myocardial infarction. Obtain ECG and serial cardiac troponins in an acute evaluation. Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) Episodic rest pain, often nocturnal, with transient ST elevation. Use nitrates or a calcium channel blocker; stop smoking. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) Heartburn can mimic cardiac discomfort; the exertional pattern favors ischemia. Obtain ECG and assess ischemic risk when the clinical pattern is concerning. Costochondritis (costosternal syndrome; anterior chest wall syndrome) Localized pain reproduced by palpation and movement. Use the clinical examination; obtain ECG if ischemia remains plausible.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Stable symptoms concerning for ischemia → Resting 12-lead ECG Interpretable resting tracing and able to exercise Exercise ECG is a board-standard choice at intermediate probability. Baseline ECG is uninterpretable (for example, left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) with strain, digoxin effect, resting ST depression or Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern), or exercise is limited. Choose stress imaging, with pharmacologic stress when needed. Targeted tests TestResultMeans Able to exercise with an interpretable ECG → Exercise ECG Inducible ST-segment depression Supports myocardial ischemia; interpret with symptoms and overall risk. Left bundle branch block (LBBB) or paced rhythm → Vasodilator perfusion imaging Exercise-related septal artifact Do not rely on exercise perfusion imaging for this branch. Severe asthma when pharmacologic stress is needed → Dobutamine stress echocardiography Vasodilator agents are unsuitable because of bronchospasm risk Use dobutamine when appropriate. Diagnostic test TestResultMeans High pretest probability or high-risk abnormal stress findings. Deeper ST depression, especially 2 mm or more, indicates worse prognosis. → Coronary angiography Obstructive coronary lesions Define anatomy and consider revascularization. SkipExercise ECG when baseline ST changes cannot be interpreted; routine stress testing during suspected unstable angina.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Epigastric burning with exertion, relieved by rest An anginal equivalent Obtain ECG and select ischemia testing from the overall clinical risk. New troponin elevation in an acute presentation Myocardial injury rather than unstable angina alone Arrange urgent cardiac evaluation with ECG and serial troponins.
Pause point Chest pain described by its location Weighed by location Location is less useful → The exertional trigger, relief pattern and change from baseline

1 PreventEstablished stable ischemic disease Use a statin and aspirin for cardiovascular event prevention; address smoking and other risk factors. 2 SymptomsStable angina A beta-blocker reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Nitrates relieve acute symptoms. 3 EscalateSymptoms persist despite medical therapy or high-risk anatomy Consider coronary revascularization; the anatomy and clinical risk guide the procedure. 4 CautionRest pain or a changing symptom pattern Reassess urgently for an acute coronary syndrome instead of treating a new pattern as stable angina.

Reassessment When Do New rest symptoms or an accelerating pattern Arrange urgent reassessment. Stable follow-up Review symptoms and medication response; persistent activity limitation may warrant revascularization assessment.

The stress test follows whether the patient can exercise and whether the resting ECG can be read.

Systemic lupus erythematosus increases atherosclerotic and premature coronary risk. Antiphospholipid syndrome can occur with SLE and is associated with thrombosis. Assess exertional symptoms through the workup above.

For chest or epigastric discomfort, use the trigger, reliever and associated findings. Exertional symptoms relieved by rest favor ischemia even when the patient points to the epigastrium. Meal-related burning or antacid response can suggest a gastrointestinal cause but does not exclude ischemia. Pleuritic, positional or reproducible pain needs its own differential; new or concerning symptoms still require acute assessment.
True-fact-wrong-slotGastroesophageal reflux: epigastric burning is a real GI symptom, but burning brought on by exertion, eased by rest and not by antacids is an anginal equivalent.

briefs.title: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis
briefs.sub: cardiac eligibility · procedure eligibility · adult dental antibiotic selection
blocks: cardiac eligibility · procedure eligibility · adult dental antibiotic selection

Give endocarditis prophylaxis only when both a high-risk cardiac condition and a qualifying procedure are present. For qualifying dental work in an adult without penicillin allergy: amoxicillin 2 g orally one hour before. Mitral valve prolapse, bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic valve disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy alone do not qualify.

High-risk cardiac conditions Condition Qualifies when Prosthetic valve or valve repair An implanted valve, including a transcatheter valve, or prosthetic repair material. Previous infective endocarditis Prior infection qualifies, even without a prosthetic valve. Congenital heart disease Unrepaired cyanotic disease; a prosthetic repair within 6 months; or a residual defect at or beside prosthetic repair material. Heart transplant Associated valvulopathy.

Procedure selection Procedure Action Dental extraction, gingival manipulation or oral mucosal perforation Give prophylaxis when the cardiac condition qualifies. Respiratory mucosa incision or an intervention on infected skin or musculoskeletal tissue Consider the high-risk cardiac condition and procedure; match antibiotics to the infected site. Routine gastrointestinal or genitourinary procedure without infection Do not give antibiotics solely to prevent endocarditis. An established infection is a separate indication for organism-directed treatment.

Dental antibiotic selection Situation Choose Able to take oral medication; no penicillin allergy Amoxicillin 2 g orally one hour before. Penicillin allergy Azithromycin or doxycycline. Cephalexin is an option only without prior penicillin-associated anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria. Unable to take oral medication An appropriate parenteral regimen can use cefazolin or ceftriaxone when the allergy history permits. Avoid cephalosporins after penicillin-associated anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria.

Pause point A murmur before a procedure Offered: an antibiotic for the murmur alone A murmur alone is insufficient → Check the cardiac indication and the planned procedure separately, before selecting an antibiotic

Next step1 of 6 45 yo F with mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, due for a dental cleaning · Amoxicillin 2 gThe cardiac gate is closed; an antibiotic dose does not make it appropriate. · Clindamycin 600 mgThe cardiac gate is closed; no prophylactic antibiotic is indicated. · No prophylaxisMitral valve prolapse alone is not a qualifying high-risk cardiac condition. 45 yo F with mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, due for a dental cleaning No prophylaxis

briefs.title: Venous Thromboembolism
briefs.sub: pretest probability governs the test · D-dimer only rules out · imaging by stability · swollen-leg mimics
blocks: pretest probability governs the test · D-dimer only rules out · imaging by stability · swollen-leg mimics

Pretest probability selects the test: D-dimer rules out in a low-probability patient; high probability goes directly to imaging. A positive D-dimer does not confirm a clot. Unstable suspected pulmonary embolism (PE): bedside echocardiography and urgent treatment; hemodynamic compromise can require thrombolysis when no contraindication is present. Treat most confirmed proximal deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or PE with anticoagulation for at least 3 months; persistent or unprovoked risk may justify longer treatment.

What it is Venous thromboembolism (VTE): a venous clot, usually in the leg or pelvis, that may embolize to a pulmonary artery. Driver Virchow triad: venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. Triggers Immobility, surgery or trauma; cancer, pregnancy, estrogen exposure or inherited thrombophilia. Chain A venous thrombus obstructs flow; embolization can cause pulmonary vascular obstruction and hypotension. Insights D-dimer can rise with inflammation, pregnancy, surgery or cancer; it is not a rule-in test. A palpable superficial cord or a bruised calf after sudden pain can point to a DVT mimic.
Confirmation Site Evidence DVT A noncompressible vein on ultrasound. PE A pulmonary arterial filling defect on CT angiography; use an alternative diagnostic pathway when contrast is unsuitable.

Hemodynamic instability Finding Action Suspected PE with hypotension or shock Arrange urgent bedside assessment of the right ventricle with echocardiography; stabilize and treat without delaying for an unsafe CT transfer. PE causing hemodynamic compromise Give thrombolysis if appropriate and no contraindication exists; consider catheter or surgical treatment when thrombolysis is unsuitable. Massive painful leg swelling with cyanosis or ischemia: phlegmasia Arrange urgent vascular assessment and treatment to prevent venous gangrene.

The swollen leg Diagnosis Decides it Next best step DVT Diffuse unilateral swelling with thrombotic risk and calf tenderness. Estimate probability; obtain compression ultrasound when indicated. Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Fever with spreading skin erythema and a portal of entry. Treat the skin infection after assessing whether DVT also needs exclusion. Ruptured Baker cyst Sudden calf pain with knee disease; bruising can track below the malleolus. Use ultrasound if the distinction from DVT remains uncertain. Superficial thrombophlebitis A tender, palpable cord along a superficial vein. Order duplex ultrasound if associated DVT is clinically suspected. Chronic venous insufficiency Chronic: dependent swelling, worse with standing, and hemosiderin staining. Order duplex ultrasound if an acute clot remains clinically plausible. Lymphedema Painless, often non-pitting swelling involving the dorsal foot; a positive Stemmer sign. Exclude DVT with ultrasound if suspected, then evaluate a lymphatic cause.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Symptoms of DVT or PE → Assess clinical probability and hemodynamic stability Low probability and suitable for rule-out testing Use D-dimer; a negative result can exclude VTE in the appropriate setting. High probability Proceed directly to the appropriate imaging test. Targeted tests TestResultMeans Stable, low clinical risk for PE → Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC) All eight low-risk criteria met No PE testing is needed. Leg swelling with moderate or high DVT probability, or a positive D-dimer → Compression ultrasound with Doppler A noncompressible deep vein Confirms DVT; begin appropriate treatment. Stable suspected PE with high probability or a positive D-dimer → CT pulmonary angiography Pulmonary arterial filling defect Confirms PE; anticoagulate when appropriate. Iodinated contrast is unsuitable, including significant renal insufficiency → Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan High-probability or normal scan A normal scan excludes PE; a high-probability scan supports PE when the clinical probability agrees. A nondiagnostic scan needs leg duplex or further imaging; a negative leg study does not exclude PE. SkipDo not use a positive D-dimer as confirmation, or delay high-probability imaging while waiting for D-dimer.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Low probability and negative D-dimer VTE can be excluded in the appropriate setting Stop the clot-testing branch. High probability D-dimer is not the next test Order imaging. Pregnancy and suspected PE Imaging selection depends on the clinical context Consider V/Q imaging when suitable, especially with a normal chest radiograph.

Pause point Suspected VTE with a positive D-dimer Read as established VTE A positive D-dimer does not establish VTE → Separate clot probability from stability Unstable patient with suspected VTE Offered: waiting for CT Unstable → May be unable to wait for CT

Treatment branch Status Action Hemodynamically stable Anticoagulate appropriate confirmed events; if PE is strongly suspected and bleeding risk is low, begin while confirmation is pending. Hemodynamic compromise Assess urgently for reperfusion treatment.

1 AnticoagulationStable proximal DVT or PE Rivaroxaban or apixaban can be started without heparin bridging in suitable patients. Heparin followed by warfarin is an alternative. 2 Choose by contextPregnancy or important renal impairment Use low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) in pregnancy; warfarin is teratogenic. Unfractionated heparin may be preferred initially with renal insufficiency; assess the full clinical setting. 3 DurationAfter the initial treatment phase The initial course for most proximal events is 3 to 6 months. A major transient provoking factor commonly permits stopping after 3 months; consider extended treatment for unprovoked, recurrent or persistent-risk events after weighing bleeding risk. 4 CautionAnticoagulation contraindicated Consider a temporary inferior vena cava (IVC) filter. Recurrent PE despite adequate anticoagulation is a selected additional indication, rather than a routine alternative to anticoagulation.

Anticoagulation phases not to scale Initial treatment At least 3 months for most proximal events Start 3 months Later → Extended treatment Selected unprovoked, recurrent or persistent-risk events Start 3 months Later →

Reassessment When Do Before stopping or extending anticoagulation Reassess provoking factors, recurrence risk, bleeding risk and patient preferences. Persistent leg symptoms after DVT Assess for post-thrombotic syndrome and chronic venous complications.

ECG (electrocardiogram) may show sinus tachycardia. S1Q3T3 means an S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III and T-wave inversion in lead III; it is an insensitive and only moderately specific pattern, so use the probability-based diagnostic workup. Treatment depends on stability, provoking factors and bleeding risk. Contraceptive eligibility: see Contraception.
Test-overrides-findingsD-dimer: it rises with infection, malignancy, pregnancy and surgery, so a positive result confirms nothing; with high pretest probability, go straight to imaging.

briefs.title: Congenital Heart Disease
briefs.sub: cyanotic lesions · left-to-right shunts · ductal-dependent lesions · pulse oximetry screen · tet spells · timing: days for the ductus, weeks for shuntsWhen did it declare, and which structure makes the murmur?
blocks: cyanotic lesions · left-to-right shunts · ductal-dependent lesions · pulse oximetry screen · tet spells · timing: days for the ductus, weeks for shuntsWhen did it declare, and which structure makes the murmur?

Cyanosis within hours of birth that 100% oxygen does not fix is a right-to-left shunt (the 5 Ts); a holosystolic murmur by 2 to 3 weeks (moderate defect) and heart failure by 4 to 6 weeks (larger defect) is a left-to-right shunt. A newborn in shock as the ductus closes gets prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) before echocardiography; a preterm ductus flooding the lungs with respiratory compromise can sometimes be closed with indomethacin or ibuprofen. Tetralogy of Fallot (tet) spell: cyanosis deepens and the murmur fades with crying; knee-chest position and oxygen first, then morphine, fluids, phenylephrine or propranolol may help.

What it is Structural heart lesions sorted by shunt direction: right to left (cyanotic: the 5 Ts, which are truncus arteriosus, transposition, tricuspid atresia, tetralogy of Fallot and total anomalous pulmonary venous return; Ebstein anomaly; hypoplastic left heart), left to right (septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus) or obstruction (coarctation). Driver A murmur needs a pressure gradient, and blood takes the lower resistance: the balance of pulmonary and systemic resistance sets each shunt and when it declares. Triggers Down syndrome : atrioventricular septal defect non-modifiable ; 22q11.2 deletion : truncus arteriosus, tetralogy non-modifiable ; Turner syndrome: coarctation non-modifiable ; maternal diabetes: transposition ; maternal lithium: Ebstein anomaly ; fetal alcohol: tetralogy ; congenital rubella, prematurity and respiratory distress syndrome: patent ductus arteriosus Chain At birth pulmonary resistance is high, so little crosses a septal defect resistance falls over weeks; the left-to-right shunt and its murmur grow overcirculation brings heart failure by 4 to 6 weeks left unrepaired, pulmonary resistance often rises and the shunt reverses: Eisenmenger syndrome Insights The murmur tracks the gradient: a small ventricular defect is loud and a large one quiet; in tetralogy the large septal defect is usually silent and the murmur is the narrowed outflow tract, so it fades as a spell tightens it. Ductal-dependent lesions stay hidden until the ductus constricts at about 24 to 72 hours, and the pulse oximetry screen is done at 24 hours or later.

Hourstransposition: severe cyanosis; obstructed venous return: pulmonary edema 24 to 72 hoursductus constricts; hypoplastic left heart declares; pulse oximetry screen By day 10critical coarctation in shock Weeks 2 to 6ventricular septal defect murmur, then heart failure Months 2 to 4peak of tet spells YearsEisenmenger syndrome; an atrial septal defect may first be found

Positive pulse oximetry screen (24 hours or later) Measurement Positive if Any single reading Under 90% Right hand and foot Both under 95% on repeat checks 1 hour apart Hand-foot difference Over 3% on repeat paired checks 1 hour apart

Tetralogy of Fallot: four components (PROVe) Component Consequence Pulmonary infundibular stenosis Sets the shunt and makes the murmur Right ventricular hypertrophy Follows the outflow obstruction Overriding aorta Sits directly over the defect Ventricular septal defect Large, so it makes no murmur

Act now Finding Action Newborn with weak pulses, pallor or shock in the first days Ductal-dependent lesion: start PGE1 now; echocardiography follows. Hypoplastic left heart on PGE1 Give as little oxygen as possible: oxygen lowers pulmonary resistance and steals systemic flow. Tet spell: deeper cyanosis with crying, a fading murmur Knee-chest position and oxygen; morphine, fluids, phenylephrine or propranolol may help. Cyanosis with pulmonary edema shortly after birth Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return: emergent surgical repair. Transposition still hypoxemic on PGE1 Balloon atrial septostomy.
Sort lung from heart and airway first in Cyanosis in the Newborn; for a murmur in a well child, see Heart Murmurs in a Child.

Cyanotic lesions Lesion Decides it Next best step Transposition of the great arteries Within hours of birth: severe cyanosis, no murmur, single loud second heart sound (S2); egg on a string. Start PGE1; arterial switch, typically in the first week. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return At birth: pulmonary veins drain to the right heart, so survival needs an atrial defect; no significant murmur; obstructed drainage brings pulmonary edema. Echocardiography; emergent repair if obstructed. Hypoplastic left heart syndrome First 24 to 48 hours: shock as the ductus closes; no murmur. Start PGE1 with minimal oxygen; plan staged operations. Tricuspid atresia At birth: no tricuspid valve and a small right ventricle; cyanosis, a septal defect murmur, left axis deviation. Start PGE1 if severe; plan staged operations. Truncus arteriosus First weeks: usually mild cyanosis with heart failure; one arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect; 22q11.2 deletion in about 35%. Treat the failure; early surgical repair; check calcium and T cells. Tetralogy of Fallot Spells peak at 2 to 4 months: the most common cyanotic lesion; harsh systolic ejection murmur, left upper sternal border; boot-shaped heart. Echocardiography; repair at 2 to 6 months, earlier if symptoms are severe. Ebstein anomaly At birth if severe: tricuspid leaflets displaced into the right ventricle; regurgitation, widely split first heart sound (S1), a massive heart; maternal lithium. Obtain echocardiography; start PGE1 when severely cyanotic.

Left-to-right shunts and obstruction Lesion Decides it Next best step Ventricular septal defect Moderate defect: murmur by 2 to 3 weeks; larger defect: failure by 4 to 6: this is the most common lesion in infancy; holosystolic, left lower sternal border; louder means smaller. Diuretics and feeding; surgical closure if failure persists. Complete atrioventricular septal defect (atrioventricular canal) Down syndrome; heart failure by 4 to 6 weeks; single loud S2. Echocardiography; repair by 2 to 4 months. Atrial septal defect Often silent into childhood: fixed split S2, soft ejection murmur; no cyanosis. Obtain echocardiography; small central defects often close. Patent ductus arteriosus Common in preterm infants: continuous machine-like murmur; bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure with a significant shunt. Preterm with compromise: give indomethacin or ibuprofen. Coarctation of the aorta Days 1 to 10: weak femoral pulses, arm pressure above leg; Turner syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve. PGE1 when symptomatic; then repair. Isolated pulmonary stenosis Systolic ejection murmur radiating to the back; no septal defect, so no cyanotic spells. Obtain echocardiography. Eisenmenger syndrome Years after an unrepaired shunt: late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia; a reversed ductus turns only the legs blue. Prevent by timely repair; once established, transplantation.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Every newborn at 24 hours or later → Pulse oximetry, right hand and a foot Any reading under 90%; or, on repeat checks 1 hour apart, both under 95% or a hand-foot gap over 3% Positive: evaluate for critical heart disease and other causes of hypoxemia Normal Passed, but sensitivity is only about 75%; coarctation is the lesion most often missed Targeted tests TestResultMeans Weak femoral pulses → Four-extremity blood pressures Arm above leg Coarctation: PGE1 if the ductus is closing Cyanosis → 100% oxygen trial Saturation unchanged Fixed right-to-left shunt, not lung disease; PGE1 first if unstable Cyanotic heart disease suspected → Chest radiograph Boot-shaped heart, dark lung fields Tetralogy of Fallot Egg on a string, narrow mediastinum Transposition Massive, wall-to-wall heart Severe Ebstein anomaly Cyanosis with a septal defect murmur → ECG (electrocardiogram) Left axis deviation Tricuspid atresia Right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy Tetralogy of Fallot Truncus arteriosus or tetralogy → 22q11.2 deletion testing, calcium and T cells Positive result 22q11.2 deletion syndrome Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Any suspected lesion → Echocardiography Anatomy, defect size, shunt direction Names the lesion; right-to-left flow across a septal defect beyond the newborn period means pulmonary resistance has risen SkipHolding PGE1 until echocardiography is done in an unstable newborn: the ductus keeps closing, so PGE1 goes first.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Fever, vomiting and diarrhea in a 3-month-old with a harsh murmur Dehydration and crying can trigger a spell Monitor the saturation and re-examine the murmur. Saturation falls to 60% and the murmur fades while crying Tet spell: less outflow, less murmur Place him knee to chest and give oxygen. Harsh systolic ejection murmur in a cyanotic infant The narrowed outflow tract, not the septal defect Obtain echocardiography. Fixed split S2, no cyanosis Atrial septal defect Obtain echocardiography.
Pause point Tetralogy spell A softer murmur read as improvement A softer tetralogy murmur during a spell means less pulmonary flow → A worsening spell: knee-chest position and oxygen first

What the ductus supplies Group Lesions Meaning Ductal-dependent pulmonary flow Severe tetralogy, tricuspid atresia, severe Ebstein anomaly PGE1 keeps the ductus open; cyanosis deepens as it closes Ductal-dependent systemic flow Hypoplastic left heart, critical coarctation PGE1 before echocardiography; shock as it closes Parallel circulations Transposition Survival depends on mixing; PGE1, then septostomy if needed Not ductal-dependent Septal defects; a preterm patent ductus Overcirculation; a symptomatic preterm ductus is closed

1 Ductal-dependentCyanosis or shock as the ductus closes PGE1 (alprostadil) infusion; minimal oxygen in hypoplastic left heart. 2 Tet spellDeep cyanosis with crying Knee-chest position and oxygen; morphine, fluids, phenylephrine or propranolol may help; ketamine, intubation or surgery if refractory. Why knee-chestIt raises systemic vascular resistance, so less blood crosses right to left. 3 After a spellUnrepaired tetralogy Oral propranolol until repair; one significant spell calls for prompt surgery. 4 Shunt failureHeart failure at 4 to 6 weeks Diuretics, digoxin or an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor to control the failure, with fortified feeds; surgical closure if failure or poor growth persists. 5 Preterm ductusSignificant shunt with respiratory compromise Indomethacin or ibuprofen; typically no treatment without compromise. 6 DefinitiveOnce stable Arterial switch, typically in the first week, for transposition; tetralogy repair at 2 to 6 months, earlier if symptoms are severe; staged operations for hypoplastic left heart and tricuspid atresia.

After diagnosis or repair When Do Small ventricular septal defect, under 5 mm Observe; small defects often close in the first few years. Unrepaired large shunt with a softening murmur Urgent cardiology review: pulmonary resistance may be rising, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome. After repair Endocarditis prophylaxis for 6 months, longer with a residual defect beside a patch; see Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis. After tetralogy repair Watch for pulmonic regurgitation. Ebstein anomaly ECG for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, present in 20%.

The ductus was already closed by the normal 2-week visit, and its closure removes a continuous murmur rather than creating a holosystolic one; rising pulmonary pressure would soften the murmur

Next step6 of 20 1-day-old girl has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows a severely underdeveloped left ventricle Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 82% on room air · HR 166/min · Prostaglandin E1 infusionA hypoplastic left ventricle lives on the ductus, so PGE1 keeps it open. · Supplemental oxygen aloneOxygen alone lets the ductus close and lowers pulmonary resistance, stealing systemic flow. · IndomethacinIndomethacin closes the ductus and cuts off systemic flow. 1-day-old girl has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows a severely underdeveloped left ventricle Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 82% on room air · HR 166/min Prostaglandin E1 infusionthe ductus and the atrial defect are the only route to the systemic circulation, so the shunts must stay open: prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open; indomethacin closes it, and oxygen alone leaves it to close over days

Diagnosis7 of 20 3-week-old girl is seen for a weight check fixed splitting of S2 soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Thriving and gaining weight Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air · Patent ductus arteriosusA patent ductus is continuous and machine-like. · Atrial septal defectA fixed split S2 with a soft ejection murmur in a thriving, pink infant is an atrial septal defect. · Ventricular septal defectA ventricular septal defect is holosystolic at the lower sternal border. 3-week-old girl is seen for a weight check fixed splitting of S2 soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Thriving and gaining weight Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air Atrial septal defecta fixed split S2 with a soft pulmonic flow murmur and no cyanosis is an atrial septal defect; the atrial gradient stays low, so it is often silent into childhood. A ventricular septal defect is holosystolic at the lower sternal border, and a patent ductus is continuous and machine-like

Mechanism8 of 20 2-month-old boy was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth deeply cyanotic while crying improves when his mother holds his knees to his chest Afebrile · oxygen saturation 62% while crying, 84% after · Increased systemic vascular resistance reduces right-to-left shuntingKnee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, so less blood crosses right to left. · Decreased systemic venous returnThe lever is systemic resistance, not venous return. · Coronary vasodilationSpells come from the outflow tract and the shunt, not the coronary circulation. 2-month-old boy was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth deeply cyanotic while crying improves when his mother holds his knees to his chest Afebrile · oxygen saturation 62% while crying, 84% after Increased systemic vascular resistance reduces right-to-left shuntingknee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, which reverses the right-to-left shunt; the lever is systemic vascular resistance, not venous return or the coronary circulation

Diagnosis9 of 20 2-month-old girl is evaluated for a murmur holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur at the left lower sternal border widely split S1 early systolic sail sound Feeding and growing well Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on room air · Tricuspid atresiaTricuspid atresia has no tricuspid flow to regurgitate and shows left axis deviation. · Ebstein anomalyTricuspid regurgitation, a widely split S1 and a sail sound is Ebstein anomaly. · Pulmonic valve stenosisPulmonic stenosis makes an ejection murmur, not tricuspid regurgitation. 2-month-old girl is evaluated for a murmur holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur at the left lower sternal border widely split S1 early systolic sail sound Feeding and growing well Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on room air Ebstein anomalyapical displacement of the tricuspid valve atrializes the right ventricle and makes the regurgitation murmur, the widely split S1 and the sail sound; tricuspid atresia has no right atrium to right ventricle path, and pulmonic stenosis makes an outflow murmur

Next step10 of 20 4-month-old girl was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 1 month never repaired murmur has softened now desaturates with crying Parents say the quieter murmur means it is closing Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% at rest · Urgent cardiology referralA softening murmur with new desaturation in an unrepaired large defect can mean the shunt is reversing: refer urgently. · Start an afterload-reducing agent and recheck in 3 monthsAfterload reduction treats overcirculation; delay here risks Eisenmenger syndrome. · Reassurance that the defect is closingThe murmur softens because the gradient falls, not because the defect is closing. 4-month-old girl was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 1 month never repaired murmur has softened now desaturates with crying Parents say the quieter murmur means it is closing Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% at rest Urgent cardiology referrala softening murmur in an unrepaired large shunt is a warning, not an improvement: it can mean pulmonary vascular resistance is rising and the shunt is starting to reverse, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome; refer urgently while repair is still possible. Reassurance reads it as closure; an afterload reducer with a 3-month recheck treats overcirculation that is already reversing and delays repair

Diagnosis11 of 20 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border ECG shows left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces No spells with crying Afebrile · oxygen saturation 78% on room air · Ebstein anomalyEbstein anomaly adds a widely split S1, a sail sound and a massive heart. · Tricuspid atresiaCyanosis at birth, a septal defect murmur and left axis deviation is tricuspid atresia. · Tetralogy of FallotTetralogy shows right axis deviation and an ejection murmur. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border ECG shows left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces No spells with crying Afebrile · oxygen saturation 78% on room air Tricuspid atresiawith no right atrium to right ventricle path, flow depends on the atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductus, whose murmur is heard; left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces is its ECG. Tetralogy has right ventricular hypertrophy and an outflow murmur. Ebstein, cyanotic at birth when severe, also gives a regurgitation murmur, but adds a widely split S1, a sail sound and a massive box-shaped heart; left axis with small right ventricular forces is the tricuspid atresia ECG

Next step12 of 20 2-day-old boy is pale and mottled weak femoral pulses right arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg above the leg In shock on arrival Afebrile · BP 86/50 mm Hg in the right arm · HR 190/min · Start diuretics and observeDiuretics leave the closing ductus untouched. · Start prostaglandin E1Shock with weak femoral pulses and an arm-leg gap on day 2 is coarctation as the ductus closes: start PGE1. · Give a fluid bolus and reassessFluid does not reopen the ductus. 2-day-old boy is pale and mottled weak femoral pulses right arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg above the leg In shock on arrival Afebrile · BP 86/50 mm Hg in the right arm · HR 190/min Start prostaglandin E1coarctation declares in days, as the ductus closes: prostaglandin E1 reopens it. Diuretics and a fluid bolus leave the closing ductus untouched

Diagnosis13 of 20 2-month-old boy has cyanosis that began in recent weeks holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a single arterial trunk over a large defect in the ventricular septum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 86% · Total anomalous pulmonary venous returnTotal anomalous pulmonary venous return has no significant murmur. · Tetralogy of FallotTetralogy has a narrowed outflow tract and spells, not a single trunk. · Truncus arteriosusA single arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect is truncus arteriosus. 2-month-old boy has cyanosis that began in recent weeks holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a single arterial trunk over a large defect in the ventricular septum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 86% Truncus arteriosusa single shared arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect gives cyanosis characteristically in infancy, not at birth, with a holosystolic murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur and spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur

Mechanism14 of 20 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with a ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks loud grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a small defect Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile · A small defect produces high-velocity turbulent flowA small defect keeps a high gradient and makes high-velocity, loud flow. · Loud murmurs indicate higher right ventricular pressureHigher right ventricular pressure shrinks the gradient and softens the murmur. · Murmur intensity is unrelated to defect sizeIntensity does relate to size: louder means smaller. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with a ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks loud grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a small defect Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile A small defect produces high-velocity turbulent flowa small defect makes high-velocity turbulent flow; large defects are quieter and shunt more, so murmur intensity runs opposite to severity. A loud murmur reflects a high gradient, not a high right ventricular pressure, which would soften it

Workup15 of 20 3-month-old girl has episodes of deeper cyanosis with crying episodes resolve when she is calm harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · baseline oxygen saturation 86% · ElectrocardiographyRight axis deviation on ECG supports but does not confirm. · Chest radiographyA boot-shaped heart on chest radiograph supports but does not confirm. · EchocardiographyEchocardiography shows the septal defect, overriding aorta and narrowed outflow tract. 3-month-old girl has episodes of deeper cyanosis with crying episodes resolve when she is calm harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · baseline oxygen saturation 86% Echocardiographyechocardiography confirms the ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and narrowed outflow tract; a chest radiograph (boot-shaped heart) and an ECG only support

Next step16 of 20 3-day-old preterm boy born at 28 weeks continuous murmur below the left clavicle bounding pulses widened pulse pressure Murmur first heard today on rounds Afebrile · BP 58/24 mm Hg · respiratory rate 64/min · Prostaglandin E1PGE1 keeps a ductus open. · Observation aloneWith compromise present, observation leaves the shunt in place. · Indomethacin or ibuprofenA significant preterm ductus with bounding pulses and tachypnea is closed with indomethacin or ibuprofen. 3-day-old preterm boy born at 28 weeks continuous murmur below the left clavicle bounding pulses widened pulse pressure Murmur first heard today on rounds Afebrile · BP 58/24 mm Hg · respiratory rate 64/min Indomethacin or ibuprofena hemodynamically significant preterm ductus (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, tachypnea) shunting into the lungs is the problem, so close it with indomethacin or ibuprofen; prostaglandin E1 keeps a ductus open, and observation alone leaves the shunt in place

Diagnosis17 of 20 2-day-old girl with Down syndrome has a murmur grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border single loud S2 Feeding well; echocardiography is ordered before discharge Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% on room air · Coarctation of the aortaCoarctation is linked to Turner syndrome. · Tetralogy of FallotTetralogy is linked to 22q11.2 deletion and fetal alcohol, not Down syndrome. · Complete atrioventricular canal defectComplete atrioventricular septal defect is the most common heart lesion in Down syndrome. 2-day-old girl with Down syndrome has a murmur grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border single loud S2 Feeding well; echocardiography is ordered before discharge Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% on room air Complete atrioventricular canal defectmost children with the complete form of atrioventricular septal defect have Down syndrome; the single loud S2 reflects pulmonary hypertension, and heart failure follows by 4 to 6 weeks. Tetralogy of Fallot is linked to 22q11.2 deletion and fetal alcohol syndrome, and coarctation to Turner syndrome

Next step18 of 20 3-day-old girl has cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen single S2 now weak pulses with poor perfusion Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding poorly today Afebrile · oxygen saturation 70% on 100% oxygen · HR 190/min · Increase supplemental oxygenMore oxygen cannot fix a fixed shunt. · Obtain echocardiography before starting any infusionWaiting for echocardiography lets the ductus close. · Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiographyUnchanged saturation on 100% oxygen with failing pulses is a closing ductus: start PGE1, then image. 3-day-old girl has cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen single S2 now weak pulses with poor perfusion Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding poorly today Afebrile · oxygen saturation 70% on 100% oxygen · HR 190/min Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiographyunchanged saturation on 100% oxygen is a fixed shunt, not lung disease; weak pulses mean the ductus is closing, so instability licenses prostaglandin E1 before the picture; waiting for echocardiography or adding oxygen lets it close

Mechanism19 of 20 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border echocardiogram shows a large ventricular septal defect and an overriding aorta Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% · Regurgitation through the overriding aortaThe overriding aorta adds no murmur. · Flow across the ventricular septal defectThe ventricular septal defect is large, with no gradient, so it is silent. · Flow through the narrowed RV outflow tractThe narrowed outflow tract makes the murmur. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border echocardiogram shows a large ventricular septal defect and an overriding aorta Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% Flow through the narrowed RV outflow tractthe ventricular septal defect is real anatomy but too large to generate a murmur; the murmur comes from the narrowed right ventricular (RV) outflow tract, and the overriding aorta adds none

Diagnosis20 of 20 6-week-old boy has fed poorly for 1 week tachypneic and acyanotic holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination; born at term Afebrile · respiratory rate 68/min · oxygen saturation 98% · Ventricular septal defectAn acyanotic infant with a holosystolic lower-sternal-border murmur and failure at 6 weeks has a ventricular septal defect. · Patent ductus arteriosusA patent ductus makes a continuous murmur. · Atrial septal defectAn atrial septal defect gives a fixed split S2 and is often silent into childhood. 6-week-old boy has fed poorly for 1 week tachypneic and acyanotic holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination; born at term Afebrile · respiratory rate 68/min · oxygen saturation 98% Ventricular septal defecta holosystolic lower-sternal-border murmur in an acyanotic infant is a ventricular septal defect, appearing as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; an atrial septal defect gives a fixed split S2 and is often silent into childhood, and a patent ductus is continuous

3-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 3 days of pallor, low-grade fever, vomiting, occasional diarrhea and poor feeding Mildly dehydrated and cyanotic; perfusion and muscle tone normal T 37.8 °C · pulse 165/min · respirations 35/min · BP 80/48 mm Hg · oxygen saturation 85% on room air harsh grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur over the whole precordium cries and becomes agitated as an intravenous catheter is attempted saturation then drops to 60% and the murmur is barely audible Supplemental oxygen is given Most likely diagnosis? Competing answers Atrial septal defect: a common defect with a systolic murmur; but it shunts left to right with a fixed split S2 and causes no cyanosis. Coarctation of the aorta: a can't-miss lesion in an ill infant; but it gives arm hypertension, weak leg pulses and lower leg pressures, not cyanotic spells. Ventricular septal defect: a harsh murmur in an infant; but an isolated defect is holosystolic and acyanotic; a murmur that fades as cyanosis develops over months can mean rising resistance reversing the shunt, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome, not an acute spell with crying. Down to two: tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary stenosis. Tetralogy of Fallot: isolated pulmonary stenosis makes a similar outflow murmur, but with no ventricular septal defect it causes no cyanotic spells with crying. Crying tightens the outflow obstruction (the trigger is not fully understood), pulmonary flow drops, and less flow makes a softer murmur. The stem reads like a febrile stomach illness; the witnessed spell names the lesion, and the oxygen given treats the number, not the shunt.

Oxygen alone in a spell: it is given, but the shunt is anatomic; knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, the lever. Flow across the ventricular septal defect: real anatomy, wrong source of the tetralogy murmur. Ductal closure: removes a continuous murmur, cannot create a holosystolic one. Rising pulmonary pressure: the opposite direction; it would soften the murmur.

Heart Murmurs in a Childcentral cyanosis and a single or fixed S2 are pathologic; ask, cyanosis at birth, and is there a murmur? Cyanosis in the Newbornthe sort to finish first Heart Murmurs in an Adultmurmur shape and location Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infantlung versus heart Heart Murmurs in a Child: central cyanosis and a single or fixed S2 are pathologic; ask, cyanosis at birth, and is there a murmur? Cyanosis in the Newborn: the sort to finish first. Heart Murmurs in an Adult: murmur shape and location. Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant: lung versus heart.
Time it, then hear it: when did cyanosis or the murmur arrive, and which structure makes the sound? A murmur that appears or fades means the gradient changed, not the heart.

briefs.title: Hypertension in an Adult
briefs.sub: baseline panel · end-organ injury starts the drug · comorbidity picks it · secondary causes and how renin separates them
blocks: baseline panel · end-organ injury starts the drug · comorbidity picks it · secondary causes and how renin separates them

Confirm persistent blood pressure (BP) elevation, then assess organ injury, cardiovascular risk and comorbidities. Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) on the ECG is established organ injury: do not delay indicated pressure treatment for an echo or stress test. Resistant or young-onset hypertension, hypokalemia or a suggestive examination warrants a secondary-cause evaluation; renin separates primary aldosteronism from renovascular disease.

What it is Sustained elevation of resting systolic or diastolic pressure, often without symptoms. Driver Primary hypertension has no single established cause; secondary hypertension has an identifiable disorder. Triggers Inherited susceptibility interacts with modifiable contributors: sodium intake, obesity or a sedentary lifestyle, and alcohol intake. Chain Increased vascular pressure and wall stress lead to cardiac hypertrophy and vascular or renal injury. Insights The comorbidity can select the drug: gout favors losartan; calcium stones or osteoporosis may favor a thiazide. Hypokalemic alkalosis with hypertension suggests mineralocorticoid excess even if sodium is normal.

Hypertension is sustained systolic pressure 130 mm Hg or more, diastolic pressure 80 mm Hg or more, or both. Confirm routine outpatient hypertension with ambulatory monitoring (preferred) or home readings before treatment.

Acute injury versus chronic damage Finding Action Severe BP elevation with acute organ injury Evaluate and treat as a hypertensive emergency. Chronic LVH alone is not the acute injury that defines an emergency. Established LVH without an acute syndrome Begin indicated outpatient pressure treatment; further cardiac testing does not replace BP control.

Secondary hypertension Cause Decides it First test Medication or substance effect Cocaine or methamphetamine exposure; a corticosteroid, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or an oral contraceptive can also raise pressure. Review prescribed drugs, over-the-counter agents and substance exposure before attributing the pressure to a primary disorder. Primary aldosteronism (primary hyperaldosteronism; Conn syndrome) Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis; aldosterone elevated with renin suppressed. Measure an aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Renal artery stenosis or fibromuscular dysplasia Renovascular disease raises renin; unilateral renal artery stenosis can cause atrophy of the affected kidney. A young woman with an abdominal bruit suggests fibromuscular dysplasia. Order renal artery duplex or CT angiography as appropriate. Pheochromocytoma Spells of hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating. Measure plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines. Obstructive sleep apnea Snoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity, often with resistant hypertension. Obtain a sleep study; polysomnography can confirm the diagnosis. Coarctation of the aorta Delayed or weak femoral pulses and higher arm than leg pressure; rib notching can support the diagnosis. Measure arm-leg pressures and obtain echocardiography or angiographic imaging. Cushing syndrome Central obesity, wide striae, proximal weakness and glucose or potassium abnormalities; mood and sleep symptoms may coexist. Screen cortisol production with an appropriate suppression, urine or salivary test.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Hypertension confirmed with ambulatory or home blood pressure measurements → Electrolytes and creatinine Low potassium or impaired renal function Assess a secondary cause and drug safety. → Urinalysis and urine albumin Albuminuria Identify kidney injury that favors an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB). → Glucose or hemoglobin A1c, lipids and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) Diabetes, dyslipidemia or thyroid disease Treat the comorbidity and account for it in cardiovascular risk. → Electrocardiogram (ECG) LVH Recognize chronic organ injury and start indicated treatment. Targeted tests TestResultMeans Suspected primary aldosteronism → Aldosterone and renin, then suppression testing when appropriate Autonomous aldosterone fails to suppress Confirm the diagnosis; use adrenal imaging and usually adrenal venous sampling before selecting unilateral surgery. Pheochromocytoma phenotype → Plasma or urine metanephrines Biochemical evidence of catecholamine excess Localize with CT or MRI after biochemical testing. Cushing phenotype → Low-dose dexamethasone suppression, 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol Abnormal screening tests confirm cortisol excess Measure adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) to direct localization.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Renin suppressed Primary aldosteronism Continue the aldosterone workup. Renin elevated with a renal artery lesion Renovascular hypertension Order renal artery duplex or CT angiography; angiotensin II mediates vasoconstriction. Normal sodium despite mineralocorticoid excess Aldosterone escape can limit sodium retention Do not exclude primary aldosteronism because sodium is normal. New mood or sleep symptoms with proximal weakness, central obesity and metabolic abnormalities Cortisol excess rather than a primary mood disorder alone Measure 24-hour urinary free cortisol, one accepted initial screen, before assigning a primary psychiatric cause.
Pause point Excess aldosterone and an adrenal nodule Read as proof of the producing gland A nodule shows anatomy → It does not by itself prove which gland is producing aldosterone

Initial drug count once treatment is indicated BP category Action Below 140/90 mm Hg A single first-line agent can be used; choose it by comorbidity. 140/90 mm Hg or more Usually begin a pair of different first-line agents; a fixed combination tablet can simplify the regimen.

1 InitialNo selecting comorbidity Choose an ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide or dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB). In Black adults without a compelling renal or cardiac indication, a thiazide or dihydropyridine CCB is favored. 2 ComorbidityHypertension with a comorbidity Choose an agent that also treats the relevant comorbidity. 3 CautionBilateral renal artery stenosis or additive rate-slowing drugs ACE inhibition can cause acute kidney injury (AKI) when severe bilateral renal artery stenosis threatens filtration. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB. Do not routinely combine a beta-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem because of bradycardia, heart block and depressed contractility.

Antihypertensive choice Condition Preferred approach Gout Favor losartan when possible; avoid hydrochlorothiazide when a suitable alternative exists. Albuminuric chronic kidney disease Use an ACE inhibitor or ARB; monitor potassium and renal function. Osteoporosis or calcium kidney stones A thiazide reduces urinary calcium; it may help bone loss and recurrent calcium stones. Migraine A beta-blocker can treat both hypertension and migraine prophylaxis. Atrial fibrillation or flutter Use a beta-blocker or a nondihydropyridine CCB for rate control as appropriate; avoid the latter in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Coronary disease Stable Ischemic Heart Disease Reduced-fraction heart failure Heart Failure

Monitoring Situation Do About 1 month after starting or adjusting therapy Reassess BP, adherence, adverse effects and the relevant renal or electrolyte results. Persistent hypertension despite treatment Reassess the regimen and evaluate a secondary cause when indicated by the clinical pattern.

Mineralocorticoid physiologyExplains the potassium and renin pattern Aldosterone increases epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) activity; sodium uptake promotes potassium and hydrogen secretion.Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis can result. Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and pressure natriuresis limit retained sodium.Clinically significant edema or hypernatremia is usually absent in primary aldosteronism. Reduced renal perfusion activates renin and angiotensin II.Angiotensin II both constricts vessels and supports glomerular filtration rate (GFR) when perfusion is compromised.

The drug-selection cases below assume persistent hypertension has been confirmed with out-of-office readings. If confirmation is the question, obtain ambulatory or home measurements before routine outpatient treatment.

Next step1 of 15 48-year-old man has hypertension confirmed on 3 separate visits gout, no flares in a year on allopurinol ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy No chest pain or dyspnea BP 136/86 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · uric acid 8.4 mg/dL · HydrochlorothiazideA thiazide can raise urate and precipitate gout. · Discontinue the allopurinolStopping allopurinol does not treat hypertension and can destabilize gout. · LosartanGout favors losartan rather than hydrochlorothiazide. 48-year-old man has hypertension confirmed on 3 separate visits gout, no flares in a year on allopurinol ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy No chest pain or dyspnea BP 136/86 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · uric acid 8.4 mg/dL Losartangout picks losartan, which is mildly uricosuric; a thiazide raises urate, and stopping allopurinol treats neither the pressure nor the hypertrophy

Next step2 of 15 62-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated office readings osteoporosis, with a hip T-score of -2.7 BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or migraine BP 134/84 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL · Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockerA dihydropyridine CCB does not provide the thiazide bone benefit. · LosartanLosartan treats BP but lacks this calcium-conserving benefit. · Thiazide diureticThiazides conserve calcium and may attenuate bone loss. 62-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated office readings osteoporosis, with a hip T-score of -2.7 BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or migraine BP 134/84 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL Thiazide diuretica thiazide lowers blood pressure and may attenuate bone loss by reducing urinary calcium loss; losartan and a dihydropyridine CCB lack this calcium-conserving benefit

Next step3 of 15 60-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings chronic kidney disease, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 420 mg/g No diabetes, gout or heart failure; takes no medications BP 138/86 mm Hg · potassium 4.6 mEq/L · ACE inhibitorAlbuminuric kidney disease favors an ACE inhibitor or ARB. · Thiazide diureticA thiazide lacks the same preferred albuminuric kidney indication. · Nondihydropyridine CCBA nondihydropyridine CCB is not the preferred initial renal-protective choice here. 60-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings chronic kidney disease, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 420 mg/g No diabetes, gout or heart failure; takes no medications BP 138/86 mm Hg · potassium 4.6 mEq/L ACE inhibitoralbuminuric chronic kidney disease takes an ACE inhibitor or ARB; a thiazide or a nondihydropyridine CCB treats only the pressure
