Next step4 of 15 45-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated readings migraine headaches 6 times a month BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or osteoporosis BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 78/min · Thiazide diureticA thiazide does not provide migraine prophylaxis. · HydralazineHydralazine is not a standard first-line drug for this comorbidity choice. · Beta-blockerA beta-blocker can lower BP and prevent migraine. 45-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated readings migraine headaches 6 times a month BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or osteoporosis BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 78/min Beta-blockera beta-blocker treats both the pressure and the migraine, one drug for both diagnoses; a thiazide treats only the pressure, and hydralazine is not a first-line class

Next step5 of 15 58-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings 3 calcium kidney stones in 4 years urine calcium high on a 24-hour collection No gout or kidney disease BP 134/86 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL · Thiazide diureticThiazides lower urinary calcium and help prevent calcium stones. · Loop diuretic (furosemide)Loop diuretics increase urinary calcium. · LosartanLosartan does not provide the thiazide urinary-calcium effect. 58-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings 3 calcium kidney stones in 4 years urine calcium high on a 24-hour collection No gout or kidney disease BP 134/86 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL Thiazide diuretica thiazide reduces urinary calcium and treats both; a loop diuretic increases urinary calcium, and losartan treats only the pressure

Next step6 of 15 55-year-old man has hypertension newly confirmed on home readings ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy no chest pain, exertional dyspnea or syncope Baseline electrolytes, creatinine and urinalysis normal BP 138/88 mm Hg · HR 72/min · Exercise stress testingNo ischemic symptoms are given to justify delaying BP treatment for a stress test. · Start an antihypertensive nowConfirmed hypertension with LVH warrants indicated treatment without waiting for another cardiac test. · Echocardiography before any medicationEcho can characterize LVH but should not delay indicated pressure treatment. 55-year-old man has hypertension newly confirmed on home readings ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy no chest pain, exertional dyspnea or syncope Baseline electrolytes, creatinine and urinalysis normal BP 138/88 mm Hg · HR 72/min Start an antihypertensive nowleft ventricular hypertrophy is end-organ injury, the treatment gate; echo or stress testing only characterizes it and never delays the first drug

Workup7 of 15 29-year-old man has hypertension found at a work physical potassium 2.8 mEq/L bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis No headaches, sweating or abdominal bruit BP 168/102 mm Hg · sodium 142 mEq/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · Plasma free metanephrinesMetanephrines fit catecholamine spells, which are absent here. · Renal artery duplex ultrasoundA bruit or a high-renin pattern would favor renovascular disease. · Aldosterone-to-renin ratioHypokalemic alkalosis with hypertension suggests autonomous aldosterone excess. 29-year-old man has hypertension found at a work physical potassium 2.8 mEq/L bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis No headaches, sweating or abdominal bruit BP 168/102 mm Hg · sodium 142 mEq/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Aldosterone-to-renin ratiohypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with normal renal function are mineralocorticoid excess; a suppressed renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renovascular disease, and a normal sodium (aldosterone escape) does not argue against it. Duplex fits a bruit, metanephrines fit spells

Diagnosis8 of 15 32-year-old woman has new hypertension found at a routine visit abdominal bruit lateral to the umbilicus plasma renin activity elevated Femoral pulses normal and equal to radial pulses BP 166/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.0 mEq/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL · Primary hyperaldosteronismHypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis; aldosterone elevated with renin suppressed. · Fibromuscular dysplasiaA young woman with a bruit and elevated renin suggests fibromuscular dysplasia. · Coarctation of the aortaDelayed or weak femoral pulses and higher arm than leg pressure; rib notching can support the diagnosis. 32-year-old woman has new hypertension found at a routine visit abdominal bruit lateral to the umbilicus plasma renin activity elevated Femoral pulses normal and equal to radial pulses BP 166/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.0 mEq/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL Fibromuscular dysplasiaa young woman with an abdominal bruit and high renin has fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, a disease of the media): CT angiography. Primary hyperaldosteronism suppresses renin; coarctation weakens the femoral pulses

Diagnosis9 of 15 38-year-old man has spells of pounding headache palpitations and drenching sweats during spells hypertension during spells, normal pressure between Thyroid-stimulating hormone normal BP 188/110 mm Hg during a spell · HR 124/min · HyperthyroidismNormal TSH argues against thyroid-driven symptoms. · Panic disorderExclude the endocrine explanation before assigning panic disorder. · PheochromocytomaEpisodic headache, palpitations, sweating and hypertension suggest pheochromocytoma. 38-year-old man has spells of pounding headache palpitations and drenching sweats during spells hypertension during spells, normal pressure between Thyroid-stimulating hormone normal BP 188/110 mm Hg during a spell · HR 124/min Pheochromocytomaepisodic hypertension with headache, palpitations and sweating is pheochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines, several-fold high, then adrenal CT or MRI. A normal thyroid-stimulating hormone argues against hyperthyroidism, and panic disorder is not diagnosed when another condition better explains the spells

Diagnosis10 of 15 16-year-old boy has headaches and hypertension at a sports physical weak, delayed femoral pulses chest radiograph shows rib notching No palpitations, sweating or snoring right arm BP 162/94 mm Hg · leg BP 118/70 mm Hg · Coarctation of the aortaAn arm-leg gradient and delayed femoral pulses favor coarctation. · Renal artery stenosisRenovascular disease raises renin; unilateral renal artery stenosis can cause atrophy of the affected kidney. A young woman with an abdominal bruit suggests fibromuscular dysplasia. · PheochromocytomaSpells of hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating. 16-year-old boy has headaches and hypertension at a sports physical weak, delayed femoral pulses chest radiograph shows rib notching No palpitations, sweating or snoring right arm BP 162/94 mm Hg · leg BP 118/70 mm Hg Coarctation of the aortaweak femoral pulses, rib notching and an arm-leg pressure gradient are coarctation of the aorta; CT or magnetic resonance angiography defines the narrowing. Renal artery stenosis does not explain weak femoral pulses, rib notching or an arm-leg gradient, and pheochromocytoma commonly brings episodic headaches, sweating and a racing heart, and he has neither sweating nor palpitations

Diagnosis11 of 15 48-year-old man has hypertension resistant to 3 medications loud snoring and daytime sleepiness body mass index 38 kg/m², obese No striae; neck circumference 46 cm BP 158/98 mm Hg · potassium 4.3 mEq/L · Cushing syndromeCentral obesity, wide striae, proximal weakness and glucose or potassium abnormalities; mood and sleep symptoms may coexist. · Obstructive sleep apneaSnoring, obesity and daytime sleepiness favor obstructive sleep apnea. · Primary hyperaldosteronismHypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis; aldosterone elevated with renin suppressed. 48-year-old man has hypertension resistant to 3 medications loud snoring and daytime sleepiness body mass index 38 kg/m², obese No striae; neck circumference 46 cm BP 158/98 mm Hg · potassium 4.3 mEq/L Obstructive sleep apneasnoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity with resistant hypertension are obstructive sleep apnea: polysomnography, itself the confirmatory test. Snoring, sleepiness and a thick neck point to the airway first, and there are no striae to suggest Cushing syndrome

Diagnosis12 of 15 42-year-old woman has new hypertension and 6 months of weight gain wide purple abdominal striae round, full face Snoring absent; no episodic headache, palpitations or sweating BP 158/96 mm Hg · fasting glucose 168 mg/dL · PheochromocytomaSpells of hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating. · Obstructive sleep apneaSnoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity, often with resistant hypertension. · Cushing syndromeStriae, facial fullness, weight gain and hyperglycemia suggest cortisol excess. 42-year-old woman has new hypertension and 6 months of weight gain wide purple abdominal striae round, full face Snoring absent; no episodic headache, palpitations or sweating BP 158/96 mm Hg · fasting glucose 168 mg/dL Cushing syndromestriae, moon facies and hyperglycemia are Cushing syndrome: an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, then a second, different screening test, then ACTH to localize

Next step13 of 15 44-year-old woman has hypertension and potassium 3.0 mEq/L was diagnosed with primary hyperaldosteronism after salt loading CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule She is willing to undergo surgery BP 162/98 mm Hg · renin suppressed · Left adrenalectomyA nodule alone does not establish unilateral aldosterone production. · Adrenal venous samplingAdrenal venous sampling identifies the functional source before unilateral surgery in most candidates. · Repeat adrenal computed tomographyRepeating structural imaging does not determine which gland secretes aldosterone. 44-year-old woman has hypertension and potassium 3.0 mEq/L was diagnosed with primary hyperaldosteronism after salt loading CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule She is willing to undergo surgery BP 162/98 mm Hg · renin suppressed Adrenal venous samplingAn adrenal nodule identifies anatomy but not autonomous hormone production. Adrenal venous sampling lateralizes aldosterone secretion before unilateral surgery in most candidates.

Avoid14 of 15 74-year-old man has severe hypertension peripheral vascular disease with claudication was diagnosed with bilateral renal artery stenosis on CT angiography A new antihypertensive is being chosen BP 186/104 mm Hg · creatinine 1.4 mg/dL · An ACE inhibitorACE inhibition can impair filtration with severe bilateral renal artery stenosis. · A thiazide diureticA thiazide does not directly block the angiotensin support of filtration. · A calcium channel blockerA CCB lowers BP without blocking angiotensin-dependent efferent tone. 74-year-old man has severe hypertension peripheral vascular disease with claudication was diagnosed with bilateral renal artery stenosis on CT angiography A new antihypertensive is being chosen BP 186/104 mm Hg · creatinine 1.4 mg/dL An ACE inhibitorthe efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR, so with bilateral lesions an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated: it can cause AKI; a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide are effective at controlling pressure in renal artery stenosis

Mechanism15 of 15 66-year-old man has hypertension that has worsened over a year abdominal bruit and high plasma renin CT angiography: 80% narrowing of the left renal artery BP 174/100 mm Hg · potassium 3.3 mEq/L · creatinine 1.2 mg/dL · Angiotensin IIAngiotensin II is the direct vasoconstrictor in the renin cascade. · AldosteroneAldosterone chiefly increases sodium retention and potassium excretion. · ReninRenin starts the enzymatic cascade rather than directly constricting vessels. 66-year-old man has hypertension that has worsened over a year abdominal bruit and high plasma renin CT angiography: 80% narrowing of the left renal artery BP 174/100 mm Hg · potassium 3.3 mEq/L · creatinine 1.2 mg/dL Angiotensin IIrenin initiates the cascade and aldosterone causes the hypokalemia, but angiotensin II directly mediates the vasoconstriction
Discontinue the allopurinol: stopping it treats neither the pressure nor the LVH. Echo or stress testing first: characterizing injury does not replace indicated blood-pressure treatment.

Inherited Tumor Syndromesthe hypertension is one organ in a heritable pattern Stroke in a Child or Adolescentfibromuscular dysplasia versus Takayasu arteritis, the inflammatory cause of renal artery stenosis in a young patient Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Childlow potassium without hypertension, sorted by acid-base status Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the hypertension is one organ in a heritable pattern. Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: fibromuscular dysplasia versus Takayasu arteritis, the inflammatory cause of renal artery stenosis in a young patient. Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child: low potassium without hypertension, sorted by acid-base status.

Match the drug to the comorbidity. Biochemical testing establishes primary aldosteronism; imaging defines adrenal anatomy. For most surgical candidates, adrenal venous sampling is needed to identify unilateral secretion; an adrenal nodule alone does not establish a functional adenoma.

briefs.title: Kawasaki Disease
briefs.sub: CRASH and Burn criteria · incomplete disease · intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin within 10 days · echocardiogram · mimics · coronary complicationsHas fever lasted 5 days with 4 criteria, and is the child still inside the 10-day window?
blocks: CRASH and Burn criteria · incomplete disease · intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin within 10 days · echocardiogram · mimics · coronary complicationsHas fever lasted 5 days with 4 criteria, and is the child still inside the 10-day window?

Fever 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 CRASH criteria is Kawasaki disease; with only 2 or 3, check C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) for incomplete disease. Give IVIG plus high-dose aspirin, ideally within 10 days of fever onset; obtain an echocardiogram at diagnosis without delaying treatment. Sterile pyuria is part of the disease; aspirin is given despite the usual rule against aspirin in children.

What it is Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome): a medium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries. Driver Immune-mediated arteritis; the cause is unknown. Triggers None proven. Age under 5, peak 6 to 24 months non-modifiable ; Asian, especially Japanese, ancestry non-modifiable Chain Inflamed medium-sized arteries, mainly the coronaries the coronary wall dilates into an aneurysm the aneurysm expands, ruptures or thromboses ischemia, infarction or heart failure Insights Untreated, about 25% have some coronary artery involvement; treatment cuts coronary aneurysms from 20% to under 5%. Aneurysms form after the first week, so heart failure can arrive weeks after an untreated, self-limited illness.

Days 1 to 2nonexudative conjunctivitis By day 5rash and red lips; 5 days of fever opens the criteria Day 10target for IVIG; peeling at the nails begins Weeks 2 to 3thrombocytosis; periungual desquamation Weeks to monthscoronary aneurysm, infarction, heart failure

CRASH and Burn Criterion Feature Conjunctivitis Bilateral, nonexudative, limbal sparing Rash Polymorphous, perineal accentuation Adenopathy Cervical, at least 1.5 cm, usually a single node; the least common criterion Strawberry tongue Or cracked red lips; no ulcers, no exudate Hands and feet Erythema and edema; periungual peeling in weeks 2 to 3 Burn Fever 5 days or more

Rules Diagnosis Requires Kawasaki disease Fever 5 days or more plus at least 4 criteria Incomplete disease Fever 5 days or more with 2 or 3 criteria Infant: evaluate for incomplete disease Infant 6 months or younger with fever 7 days or more and no other explanation

Act now Finding Action Fast breathing, fast pulse, low blood pressure and a big heart weeks after a Kawasaki illness Heart failure from coronary disease: obtain an electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiography now. Infant with fever and fewer than 4 criteria Evaluate for incomplete disease now; infants under 1 year still develop aneurysms. Shock with vomiting or diarrhea weeks after COVID-19 Consider MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children) rather than Kawasaki disease.

Kawasaki mimics Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Scarlet fever Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines and no conjunctivitis; both can show a strawberry tongue. Rapid strep test; throat culture if negative. Adenovirus Exudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis; Kawasaki conjunctivitis is nonexudative. Send viral testing on a throat or eye swab. Measles Unvaccinated, cough and coryza, Koplik spots, rash spreading from the face down. Measles antibody serology or viral testing. MIS-C (multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children) Weeks after COVID-19, older child, prominent GI symptoms and shock. COVID-19 test or antibodies with the clinical criteria. Toxic shock syndrome Hypotension with multiorgan failure; desquamation later. Support the circulation and apply the clinical criteria; cultures are often negative. Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis Drug exposure, target lesions, mucosal erosions and ulcers. Stop the drug; skin biopsy when unclear. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Perioral crusting; Nikolsky sign positive. Diagnose clinically.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Fever 5 days or more with CRASH findings → CRP and ESR Elevated Supports Kawasaki disease → Echocardiogram and ECG Coronary dilation or aneurysm Baseline coronary study; in suspected incomplete disease, these changes alone justify IVIG Arrhythmia, low voltage or left ventricular hypertrophy Cardiac involvement such as myocarditis Targeted tests TestResultMeans Only 2 or 3 criteria, with a raised CRP or ESR → CBC, albumin, ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and urinalysis Anemia, albumin down, ALT up, urine white cells without bacteria; high platelets after day 7 Supports incomplete disease Sandpaper rash, no conjunctivitis → Rapid strep test Positive Scarlet fever: penicillin Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Clinical diagnosis → Five or more days of fever and at least 4 of the 5 criteria Criteria met Kawasaki disease; tests support and stage it, and IVIG within 10 days is not delayed for them SkipUrine culture for the pyuria: the white cells come from urethral inflammation caused by the disease, so IVIG proceeds.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step High fever, red eyes, red swollen hands, nodes and cracked lips that cleared on their own An earlier, untreated Kawasaki illness Look for coronary disease: ECG and echocardiography. Temperature 38 C two months later Low grade, not a new episode Obtain ECG and echocardiography for the complication. No murmur Argues against mitral stenosis; Kawasaki disease causes mitral regurgitation Treat as heart failure from coronary disease; obtain echocardiography. No raised jugular venous pressure or pulsus paradoxus Argues against tamponade Obtain echocardiography, which also shows any effusion. Cardiomegaly and ST depression in leads II and III Ischemic heart failure Echocardiography now. Urinalysis: many white cells, no bacteria Sterile pyuria from the disease itself Continue IVIG and aspirin.
Pause point Fewer than four criteria, coronary dilation or aneurysm on echocardiography Offered: waiting for a fourth criterion A fourth criterion is not required → Start IVIG

Coronary result and response Finding Meaning No coronary change on follow-up echocardiography Aspirin may be stopped once ESR and platelets normalize Coronary aneurysm Aspirin continues indefinitely Giant aneurysm, over 8 mm Greatest risk; added anticoagulant therapy may be needed Fever persisting 36 h after IVIG IVIG resistance: a second dose; higher aneurysm risk

1 Diagnosis madeWithin 10 days of fever onset IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin. 2 After day 10Seen after day 10 Give IVIG when fever without another cause or coronary changes continue, with a raised CRP or ESR. 3 AfebrileFever gone Step down to low-dose aspirin until follow-up echocardiography, at least 8 weeks after onset. Why aspirinAspirin is given for its antithrombotic effect; the usual rule against aspirin in children does not apply here. 4 IVIG resistanceFever persisting 36 h after IVIG Second IVIG dose; steroids or infliximab are alternatives.

After treatment Situation Do Uncomplicated disease Echocardiography at diagnosis, repeated 1 to 2 weeks after treatment and again at 4 to 6 weeks Counted from onsetAnKing counts from onset: at 1 to 2 weeks and at 6 to 8 weeks after onset. Fast breathing or irritability weeks later ECG and echocardiogram Live vaccines after IVIG Generally defer MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella 11 months On long-term aspirin Annual influenza vaccine

Next step1 of 13 4-year-old boy brought in on day 12 of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands since the first week; CRP 12 mg/dL · Aspirin aloneAspirin alone does not prevent coronary aneurysms; IVIG does most of that work. · No IVIG; supportive care onlyDay 10 is a target, not a cutoff; ongoing fever with a raised CRP still needs IVIG. · IVIG nowPast day 10, IVIG is still given when fever or inflammation persists. 4-year-old boy brought in on day 12 of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands since the first week; CRP 12 mg/dL IVIG nowgive IVIG even beyond day 10 when unexplained fever or coronary changes persist with a raised CRP or ESR

Mechanism2 of 13 18-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasingly fast breathing and irritability; 2 months earlier he had a high fever, red eyes, cracked red lips, enlarged lymph nodes and red swollen hands, all of which cleared without treatment within 14 days; in obvious discomfort; T 38 C (100.4 F); HR 150/min; RR 60/min; BP 60/40 mm Hg; the rest of the examination is normal; chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly; ECG: ST-segment depression in leads II and III, left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation · Congestive heart failureWeeks after untreated Kawasaki disease, coronary ischemia causes heart failure: fast breathing, hypotension, a big heart. · Pericardial effusionTamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus, absent here. · Mitral valve obstructionMitral stenosis would give a murmur; Kawasaki disease causes mitral regurgitation. 18-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 2 days of increasingly fast breathing and irritability; 2 months earlier he had a high fever, red eyes, cracked red lips, enlarged lymph nodes and red swollen hands, all of which cleared without treatment within 14 days; in obvious discomfort; T 38 C (100.4 F); HR 150/min; RR 60/min; BP 60/40 mm Hg; the rest of the examination is normal; chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly; ECG: ST-segment depression in leads II and III, left ventricular hypertrophy, right-axis deviation Congestive heart failurelate cardiac complication of untreated Kawasaki disease: cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression, and no murmur or signs of tamponade

Diagnosis3 of 13 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.5 C; bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge; strawberry tongue; a polymorphous rash; edema of both hands; one cervical lymph node 1.8 cm · AdenovirusAdenovirus causes exudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis. · Kawasaki diseaseSix days of fever with conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, hand edema and a 1.8 cm node meets the criteria. · Scarlet feverScarlet fever brings a sandpaper rash and no conjunctivitis. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.5 C; bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge; strawberry tongue; a polymorphous rash; edema of both hands; one cervical lymph node 1.8 cm Kawasaki diseasefever 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 criteria; IVIG plus aspirin

Next step4 of 13 4-year-old boy with 5 days of fever; T 39.0 C; only 3 of the 5 criteria are present: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips and a polymorphous rash; echocardiogram shows coronary artery dilation · Treat only once a fourth criterion appearsA fourth criterion is not needed once the echocardiogram shows coronary dilation. · Observe and repeat the echocardiogram in 48 hoursWaiting delays IVIG while the coronary disease progresses. · IVIG and aspirin nowIn incomplete disease, coronary changes on the echocardiogram justify treatment now. 4-year-old boy with 5 days of fever; T 39.0 C; only 3 of the 5 criteria are present: bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips and a polymorphous rash; echocardiogram shows coronary artery dilation IVIG and aspirin nowincomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on the coronary finding

Diagnosis5 of 13 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and sore throat; T 39.4 C; exudative pharyngitis; strawberry tongue; a fine sandpaper-like rash, densest in the skin creases; no conjunctivitis · Kawasaki diseaseKawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever and brings nonexudative conjunctivitis. · MeaslesMeasles brings cough, coryza, Koplik spots and a rash spreading downward. · Scarlet feverExudative pharyngitis and a sandpaper rash without conjunctivitis is scarlet fever. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and sore throat; T 39.4 C; exudative pharyngitis; strawberry tongue; a fine sandpaper-like rash, densest in the skin creases; no conjunctivitis Scarlet fevera positive rapid strep test confirms it; penicillin

Diagnosis6 of 13 4-year-old boy who is unvaccinated; 4 days of fever, cough and runny nose; T 39.8 C; bilateral conjunctivitis; Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa; a red rash that began on the face and is spreading downward · AdenovirusAdenovirus does not cause Koplik spots or a descending rash. · MeaslesKoplik spots and a rash spreading down from the face in an unvaccinated child is measles. · Kawasaki diseaseFour days of fever with cough and coryza does not meet the Kawasaki criteria. 4-year-old boy who is unvaccinated; 4 days of fever, cough and runny nose; T 39.8 C; bilateral conjunctivitis; Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa; a red rash that began on the face and is spreading downward MeaslesKoplik spots and a descending rash decide it; measles antibody serology confirms

Next step7 of 13 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands; IVIG and aspirin are ordered; urinalysis shows many white blood cells and no bacteria · Continue IVIG and aspirin as plannedWhite cells without bacteria are sterile pyuria, part of Kawasaki disease. · Renal ultrasoundKidney imaging adds nothing for sterile pyuria. · Urine culture and empiric antibioticsThis is not a urinary infection; do not hold IVIG for it. 4-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.1 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands; IVIG and aspirin are ordered; urinalysis shows many white blood cells and no bacteria Continue IVIG and aspirin as plannedsterile pyuria is Kawasaki urethritis, a feature of the disease, not a second diagnosis

Diagnosis8 of 13 9-year-old boy with 3 days of fever, abdominal pain and vomiting, 4 weeks after COVID-19; T 39.5 C; HR 168/min; BP 70/40 mm Hg; a diffuse red rash; cool hands and feet; creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; troponin raised · Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in childrenShock with GI symptoms weeks after COVID-19 in an older child is MIS-C. · Toxic shock syndromeToxic shock syndrome has no tie to a recent COVID-19 illness. · Kawasaki diseaseKawasaki disease favors children under 5 and causes fewer GI symptoms. 9-year-old boy with 3 days of fever, abdominal pain and vomiting, 4 weeks after COVID-19; T 39.5 C; HR 168/min; BP 70/40 mm Hg; a diffuse red rash; cool hands and feet; creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; troponin raised Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in childrenweeks after COVID-19, with prominent GI symptoms and shock

Workup9 of 13 3-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.4 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands · Rapid strep testConjunctivitis and swollen hands point away from strep. · EchocardiogramThe echocardiogram gives the coronary baseline at diagnosis; IVIG is not delayed for it. · Urine culturePyuria in Kawasaki disease is sterile; culture is not the next test. 3-year-old boy with 6 days of fever; T 39.4 C; bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen red hands Echocardiogrambaseline coronary assessment at diagnosis; IVIG is not delayed for it

Mechanism10 of 13 2-year-old girl, 3 weeks after 7 days of fever with conjunctivitis, cracked lips, rash and hand swelling that were never treated; afebrile now; peeling skin around the fingernails; platelet count 780,000/mm³ · Coronary artery aneurysmUntreated disease in the subacute phase, with peeling and high platelets, risks coronary aneurysm. · Mitral valve stenosisKawasaki disease affects the mitral valve as regurgitation, not stenosis. · Interstitial lung diseaseKawasaki disease rarely involves the lungs. 2-year-old girl, 3 weeks after 7 days of fever with conjunctivitis, cracked lips, rash and hand swelling that were never treated; afebrile now; peeling skin around the fingernails; platelet count 780,000/mm³ Coronary artery aneurysmechocardiogram now; untreated aneurysms can progress to infarction or heart failure

Next step11 of 13 5-year-old girl who received IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin for Kawasaki disease; the infusion ended 40 hours ago; T 39.3 C; conjunctivitis and rash persist · Switch to low-dose aspirin and dischargeLow-dose aspirin follows defervescence; this child is still febrile. · Continue aspirin and observe for 3 more daysObserving persistent fever after IVIG leaves the coronary risk untreated. · Second dose of IVIGFever persisting 36 h after IVIG is resistance: give a second dose. 5-year-old girl who received IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin for Kawasaki disease; the infusion ended 40 hours ago; T 39.3 C; conjunctivitis and rash persist Second dose of IVIGfever persisting 36 h after IVIG defines resistance

Avoid12 of 13 3-year-old boy at a well visit 2 months after he was given IVIG 2 g/kg for Kawasaki disease; afebrile; aspirin stopped after a normal echocardiogram; due for routine vaccines · Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines todayIVIG blunts live vaccines, so MMR and varicella wait 11 months. · Hepatitis A vaccine todayHepatitis A vaccine is inactivated and can be given today. · Inactivated influenza vaccine todayInactivated influenza vaccine needs no delay after IVIG. 3-year-old boy at a well visit 2 months after he was given IVIG 2 g/kg for Kawasaki disease; afebrile; aspirin stopped after a normal echocardiogram; due for routine vaccines Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines todaylive vaccines are deferred 11 months after IVIG; inactivated vaccines are not

Next step13 of 13 6-year-old boy treated with IVIG and aspirin for Kawasaki disease; afebrile since the day after the infusion; echocardiogram at diagnosis normal · Repeat echocardiogram at 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weeksCoronary changes can appear after a normal first study, so it is repeated on schedule. · Repeat echocardiogram only if fever returnsAneurysms are silent until they cause ischemia, so the schedule does not wait for fever. · No repeat echocardiogram; the first was normalA normal first echocardiogram does not exclude later aneurysms. 6-year-old boy treated with IVIG and aspirin for Kawasaki disease; afebrile since the day after the infusion; echocardiogram at diagnosis normal Repeat echocardiogram at 1 to 2 weeks and 4 to 6 weekscoronary changes can appear after a normal first study

The untreated Kawasaki illness is in the past history as an episode that resolved on its own, and the mechanism lead-in is keyed to heart failure. The criteria appear in lay words ("pink eye," swollen hands) and are never named.

True-fact-wrong-slotPericardial effusion: a real Kawasaki complication, but tamponade adds raised jugular venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus; cardiomegaly with ischemic ST depression fits heart failure. Unchecked attributeMitral valve obstruction: Kawasaki affects the mitral valve as regurgitation, not stenosis, and no stenotic murmur is heard. Salient decoyChronic inflammatory interstitial lung disease: Kawasaki rarely involves the lungs, and the film shows cardiomegaly rather than interstitial fibrosis. Class-vs-memberThickened internal layer of pulmonary arterioles: Kawasaki is a medium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries and rarely involves the pulmonary vessels.

Heart Failure in a Childis the failing heart from an untreated Kawasaki illness in the history or from an acute viral myocarditis? Heart Failure in a Child: is the failing heart from an untreated Kawasaki illness in the history or from an acute viral myocarditis?

A candidate diagnosis that explains only a subset of the findings is wrong. With sterile pyuria, a UTI (urinary tract infection) explains only the fever and the urine white cells; Kawasaki disease explains all the findings. Check which findings a diagnosis leaves unexplained.

briefs.title: Acute Rheumatic Fever
briefs.sub: Jones criteria · strep evidence · echocardiography for carditis · aspirin or prednisone · years of penicillin prophylaxisDid a sore throat come weeks before, and do the findings meet the Jones criteria?
blocks: Jones criteria · strep evidence · echocardiography for carditis · aspirin or prednisone · years of penicillin prophylaxisDid a sore throat come weeks before, and do the findings meet the Jones criteria?

Migratory large-joint arthritis or a new apical holosystolic murmur about 2 to 3 weeks after strep pharyngitis: apply the Jones criteria, which also need evidence of recent group A strep. Order antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers, because the throat swab is often negative by now, and echocardiography for every suspected case. Give penicillin to clear the strep and aspirin for arthritis or mild carditis; then penicillin G benzathine every 3 to 4 weeks for years.

What it is A nonsuppurative inflammatory complication of group A strep pharyngitis: arthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum and chorea. Bug Group A strep (Streptococcus pyogenes) pharyngitis, not strep skin infection (impetigo). Spread Untreated group A strep pharyngitis (early treatment can prevent rheumatic fever); incidence remains high in resource-poor regions (the family in one NBME stem had lived in a refugee camp). A prior attack: with untreated strep pharyngitis, recurrence approaches 50%. Chain Strep pharyngitis antibodies to the M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and basal ganglia antigens ( type II hypersensitivityPathologyAntibodies to strep M protein also bind look-alike self antigens; Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells are the pathology findings. ) valvulitis: mitral regurgitation now in some, valve stenosis, chiefly mitral, years to decades later Insights Valvulitis is the most constant part of carditis: the acute lesion is mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis is the late scar. Chorea can arrive alone, often months after the sore throat, and still meets the criteria once other movement disorders are excluded.

Day 0strep pharyngitis About 2 to 3 weeksarthritis, carditis, fever 3 to 6 weeksantistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B typically peak MonthsSydenham chorea, often after the rest has settled Years to decadeschronic rheumatic valve disease

Jones criteria, first episode Group Criteria Major (JONES) Joints: migratory polyarthritis; O: carditis, clinical or found only on echo; Nodules on extensor surfaces; Erythema marginatum, a fleeting pink rash with sharp edges; Sydenham chorea Minor Fever 38.5 C or higher; polyarthralgia; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) >60 mm/hour or C-reactive protein (CRP) >30 mg/L; prolonged PR interval Required Evidence of recent group A strep: raised or rising antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase B titer, or a positive culture or rapid test Rule 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor; chorea alone suffices once other movement disorders are excluded
Polyarthralgia does not count when polyarthritis is the major criterion; a long PR does not count when carditis is.

Urgent findings Finding Action Moderate to severe carditis: cardiomegaly or heart failure Give prednisone instead of aspirin. Severe carditis is the main cause of death in the acute phase. New strep pharyngitis after a prior attack Treat it promptly and continue prophylaxis; untreated, recurrence approaches 50%.

Arthritis or a murmur after an infection Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Acute rheumatic fever About 2 to 3 weeks after strep pharyngitis: migratory large-joint arthritis and a new mitral regurgitation murmur; chorea often months later. Strep titers and echocardiography; count the Jones criteria. Poststreptococcal reactive arthritis After strep, but typically only 1 or 2 joints, less migratory, and slower to respond to aspirin. Order echocardiography to look for carditis. Lyme disease Tick exposure and erythema migrans; later arthritis and atrioventricular block, not a new valve murmur. Check for erythema migrans and atrioventricular block; a new valve murmur points away from Lyme. Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) Fever 5 days or more with nonexudative conjunctivitis, rash, node and hand and foot changes. Count the Kawasaki criteria; the fever comes first, not a sore throat. Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome) Arthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis, often after diarrhea. Check for recent diarrhea or urethritis; it is linked to human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27). Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Arthritis over 6 weeks with no other cause; no strep latency or new murmur. Follow the arthritis beyond 6 weeks and exclude other causes.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Arthritis or carditis weeks after a sore throat, or chorea months after → Antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers Elevated or rising titer Recent group A strep, which the Jones criteria require → Throat culture or rapid strep test Often negative by now A negative swab does not exclude it; rely on the titers Targeted tests TestResultMeans Every suspected case, murmur or not → Echocardiography Mitral regurgitation Counts as carditis (major), with or without an audible murmur Inflammation to count as a minor criterion → ESR and CRP ESR >60 mm/hour or CRP >30 mg/L Minor criterion Conduction to count as a minor criterion → Electrocardiogram (ECG) Prolonged PR interval for age Minor criterion; not counted when carditis is already a major criterion Diagnostic test TestResultMeans No single test confirms it → Jones criteria Two major, or one major plus two minor, and strep evidence Acute rheumatic fever SkipLyme serology after a camping trip with no erythema migrans or tick bite: Lyme gives late arthritis and heart block, not a new valve murmur.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step A camping or travel detail, no tick bite, no rash A setting, not a mechanism Count the Jones criteria and send strep titers. Abnormal movements months after the sore throat Sydenham chorea, enough on its own once other movement disorders are excluded Exclude other movement disorders; order echocardiography.
Pause point Suspected rheumatic fever, negative throat swab Read as excluding rheumatic fever A negative throat swab does not exclude rheumatic fever → Strep titers supply the evidence

Carditis sets the treatment Finding Meaning Arthritis, no carditis or mild carditis Aspirin Moderate to severe carditis: cardiomegaly or heart failure Prednisone instead of aspirin Residual valve damage after carditis The longest prophylaxis

1 Clear the strepEvery case 10 days of oral penicillin or amoxicillin, or one injection of penicillin G benzathine. 2 Treat inflammationArthritis or mild carditis Aspirin; acetaminophen does not treat it. 3 Moderate to severe carditisCardiomegaly or heart failure Prednisone instead of aspirin; treat the heart failure. 4 Prevent recurrenceAfter the first attack Penicillin G benzathine IM every 3 to 4 weeks, continued for years.

Prophylaxis duration After the attack Continue for No carditis 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer Carditis, no residual heart damage 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer Carditis with residual heart damage Over 10 years; many experts continue until age 40 or for life

Later When Do Mitral stenosis years later, symptoms or not Start or continue penicillin prophylaxis. Dental work with rheumatic valve disease No endocarditis prophylaxis unless a prosthetic valve is present; see Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis. Chronic rheumatic valve disease Be alert for infective endocarditis, a complication of chronic rheumatic heart disease.

Diagnosis1 of 7 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis · Acute rheumatic feverMigratory arthritis and a new mitral murmur weeks after pharyngitis are two major Jones criteria. · Juvenile idiopathic arthritisJuvenile idiopathic arthritis lasts over 6 weeks and does not follow a sore throat with a new murmur. · Reactive arthritisReactive arthritis follows diarrhea or urethritis, with conjunctivitis, not carditis. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis Acute rheumatic feverpenicillin plus anti-inflammatories

Workup2 of 7 9 yo M with suspected acute rheumatic fever · HLA-B27HLA-B27 points to a spondyloarthritis such as reactive arthritis. · Anti-streptolysin O titerThe criteria need evidence of recent strep, and titers stay high after the swab turns negative. · Rheumatoid factorRheumatoid factor does not show a recent strep infection. 9 yo M with suspected acute rheumatic fever Anti-streptolysin O titer

Mechanism3 of 7 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever; which valve is most often involved · MitralThe mitral valve is affected most often; the acute lesion is regurgitation. · TricuspidThe tricuspid valve is seldom affected, and almost never alone. · AorticThe aortic valve is affected second most often, after the mitral. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever; which valve is most often involved Mitral

Diagnosis4 of 7 9 yo M with arthritis 10 days after a diarrheal illness, with conjunctivitis and urethritis · Acute rheumatic feverRheumatic fever follows strep pharyngitis, not a diarrheal illness. · Reactive arthritisArthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis after diarrhea is reactive arthritis. · Juvenile idiopathic arthritisJuvenile idiopathic arthritis needs over 6 weeks of arthritis with no infectious trigger. 9 yo M with arthritis 10 days after a diarrheal illness, with conjunctivitis and urethritis Reactive arthritis

Diagnosis5 of 7 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever and new choreiform movements · Tic disorderTics are brief, repeated, stereotyped movements, not irregular flowing jerks. · Sydenham chorea; a major criterionChorea in rheumatic fever is Sydenham chorea, a major criterion. · Cerebellar ataxiaCerebellar ataxia causes incoordination, not involuntary jerking. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever and new choreiform movements Sydenham chorea; a major criterion

Screening6 of 7 9 yo M recovering from acute rheumatic fever · A single treatment course of penicillinOne course treats this infection and prevents nothing later. · Long-term penicillin prophylaxisUntreated strep brings recurrence in up to half, so penicillin prophylaxis continues for years. · Annual echocardiography aloneEchocardiography follows the valves but prevents no recurrence. 9 yo M recovering from acute rheumatic fever Long-term penicillin prophylaxis

Diagnosis7 of 7 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis; history mentions a recent camping trip · Acute rheumatic feverTwo major criteria weeks after pharyngitis; the camping trip is only a setting. · Lyme carditisLyme carditis causes heart block, not a new mitral murmur, after a tick bite or erythema migrans. · Rocky Mountain spotted feverRocky Mountain spotted fever brings fever, headache and a petechial rash after a tick exposure. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis; history mentions a recent camping trip Acute rheumatic feverthe trip is a setting, not a mechanism; no tick bite, no rash, and the latency fits the pharyngitis

Lyme usually brings erythema migrans. Its arthritis is late (months) and usually involves one or a few large joints, and its cardiac finding is AV block (atrioventricular block), not a valvular murmur. RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) usually brings headache and a rash that spreads to the palms and soles; it is a vasculitis, not an arthritis. JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) needs arthritis beyond 6 weeks by definition.

No sore throat was mentioned, only a recent refugee camp, which also invited the travel-fever decoys; Kawasaki disease appeared as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, and the mitral murmur was described, not named.
Salient decoyLyme carditis: the camping trip is a setting, not a mechanism; there is no tick bite or erythema migrans, and Lyme gives atrioventricular block, not a new valve murmur.

briefs.title: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
briefs.sub: the syndrome is given; find the missing piece · calcium, T cells and microarray · which syndrome has which findingWhich component did the vignette leave out, and which bedside sign in the exam shows it?
blocks: the syndrome is given; find the missing piece · calcium, T cells and microarray · which syndrome has which findingWhich component did the vignette leave out, and which bedside sign in the exam shows it?

A conotruncal heart defect with an absent thymic shadow, cleft palate or an abnormal face suggests 22q11.2 deletion; recite CATCH (cardiac outflow anomaly, abnormal face, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia; 22 for the chromosome) to find the missing piece, often hypocalcemia. Check ionized calcium and obtain echocardiography; confirm with chromosomal microarray or FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization), not a standard karyotype. Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia with IV calcium; until T-cell immunity is confirmed, give no live vaccines and only irradiated blood products.

What it is 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome): a microdeletion causing thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia with conotruncal heart defects. Driver Loss of the genes for third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development and neural crest migration. Triggers Usually a sporadic deletion; autosomal dominant when inherited non-modifiable Chain 22q11.2 microdeletion third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail the thymus, parathyroid glands, palate, face and outflow tract all develop abnormally T-cell deficiency, hypocalcemia, cyanotic heart disease Insights The stem often names the syndrome; the question asks for the missing CATCH component, usually hypocalcemia shown as a tremulous infant. DiGeorge needs thymic involvement; facies and cleft palate do not have to be present.

CATCH-22 Component Finding Cardiac Outflow tract anomaly: truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch Abnormal face Low-set ears, micrognathia, prominent nasal bridge Thymus Hypoplasia or aplasia: low T cells Cleft palate Palate fails to close Hypocalcemia From parathyroid hypoplasia; tetany 22 The chromosome deleted
Phenotypes Name Requires DiGeorge syndrome Thymic involvement, CD3 count under 500/mm3 Velocardiofacial syndrome Facial abnormalities

Act now Finding Action Tremor, tetany or seizure in the first days Give IV calcium; tetany from low calcium can appear in the first 24 to 48 hours of life. Cyanosis unchanged on 100% oxygen A fixed shunt: obtain echocardiography; see Congenital Heart Disease. Low T-cell count Withhold live vaccines; transfuse only irradiated blood.

Dysmorphic newborn with a heart defect Diagnosis Decides it Next best step 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) Absent thymus with a conotruncal defect and cleft palate, often with low calcium. Order calcium, T-cell subsets and microarray or FISH. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) Atrioventricular septal (endocardial cushion) defect, duodenal atresia with a double bubble, single palmar crease. Order a karyotype for trisomy 21. Turner syndrome (45,X) Girl with preductal coarctation, webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples, horseshoe kidney. Order a karyotype for 45,X. CHARGE syndromeLettersCHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia of the choanae, retarded growth, genital and ear anomalies) Coloboma and choanal atresia with heart defects, growth delay, genital and ear anomalies. Examine the eyes and nasal passages. Infant of a diabetic mother Macrosomia, transposition or septal hypertrophy, hypoglycemia in the first hours. Check glucose.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Cyanosis or a murmur in a dysmorphic newborn → Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygen No rise on oxygen; hand and leg match A fixed right-to-left shunt inside the heart → Echocardiography Truncus, tetralogy or interrupted aortic arch Raises suspicion for 22q11.2 deletion Targeted tests TestResultMeans Conotruncal defect, tremor or seizure → Ionized calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) Low calcium with a low or low-normal PTH Hypoparathyroidism; IV calcium if tremulous or seizing Possible thymic loss → Chest radiograph Absent thymic shadow Thymic hypoplasia or aplasia Infections or a planned vaccine or transfusion → T-cell subsets and immunoglobulins CD3 count under 500/mm3 T-cell deficient: transfuse irradiated products and hold live vaccines Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Suspected 22q11.2 deletion → Chromosomal microarray or FISH for 22q11.2 Microdeletion at 22q11.2 22q11.2 deletion syndrome SkipA standard karyotype: the microdeletion is too small to see on it.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Tremulous newborn Hypocalcemia before tetany Check ionized calcium; the pregnancy history separates it from low glucose. Same saturation in the right hand and the leg No differential cyanosis, which points to a shunt inside the heart Image the heart for an intracardiac shunt. Apgars 8 and 8, uncomplicated pregnancy No asphyxia, no maternal diabetes Check calcium rather than glucose. Recurrent viral and fungal infections T-cell deficiency Order T-cell subsets and immunoglobulins.
Pause point Stem describing the syndrome Answered with the syndrome Read the last sentence first → It may ask for a missing condition

T-cell function Form Meaning Partial: some T-cell function Calcium plus calcitriol (active vitamin D) for the hypoparathyroidism; survival not affected by the immune defect Complete: no T-cell function Fatal without thymus or stem cell transplantation

1 AcuteTetany or seizure IV calcium gluconate. 2 OngoingHypoparathyroidism Calcium plus calcitriol (active vitamin D). 3 Low T-cell countBefore transfusion or vaccines Irradiated blood products only; no live vaccines. 4 Complete DiGeorgeNo T-cell function Thymus transplantation or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Over time When Do Recurrent infections or poor vaccine responses Recheck T-cell subsets and immunoglobulins; T-cell function may improve on its own. Heart defect Cardiology follow-up; prognosis often depends on the heart. Relatives No screening needed for most, because most cases are sporadic.

Diagnosis1 of 8 3 h old F, cyanosis refractory to 100% oxygen, saturation 72% in right hand and leg, low-set ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, absent thymus on chest film, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, tremulous on examination · Neutropenia22q11.2 deletion lowers T cells, not neutrophils. · HypocalcemiaFour CATCH letters are printed; tremulousness shows the fifth, hypocalcemia. · Horseshoe kidneyA horseshoe kidney points to Turner syndrome. 3 h old F, cyanosis refractory to 100% oxygen, saturation 72% in right hand and leg, low-set ears, micrognathia, cleft palate, absent thymus on chest film, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, tremulous on examination Hypocalcemiaparathyroid hypoplasia in 22q11.2 deletion

Workup2 of 8 Term neonate with truncus arteriosus, cleft palate and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph · Standard karyotypeA standard karyotype cannot resolve a deletion this small. · T-cell receptor excision circle assayA T-cell receptor excision circle test screens for low T cells but does not name the deletion. · Chromosomal microarray for the 22q11.2 deletionMicroarray (or FISH) detects the 22q11.2 microdeletion. Term neonate with truncus arteriosus, cleft palate and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph Chromosomal microarray for the 22q11.2 deletiona standard karyotype does not resolve a microdeletion

Next step3 of 8 Neonate with known 22q11.2 deletion who develops a generalized seizure; ionized calcium is low · Intravenous calcium gluconateA seizure from low calcium is treated with IV calcium. · Intravenous lorazepamA benzodiazepine does not correct the low calcium driving the seizure. · Intravenous dextroseDextrose treats hypoglycemia; here the calcium is low. Neonate with known 22q11.2 deletion who develops a generalized seizure; ionized calcium is low Intravenous calcium gluconatehypocalcemic seizure from parathyroid hypoplasia

Avoid4 of 8 4 mo old with 22q11.2 deletion and a CD3+ T-cell count of 210/mm3, presenting for routine immunizations · DTaP vaccineDTaP is inactivated and safe with low T cells. · Pneumococcal conjugate vaccinePneumococcal conjugate vaccine is not live. · The live attenuated rotavirus vaccineWith a CD3 count of 210/mm3, live vaccines such as rotavirus are withheld. 4 mo old with 22q11.2 deletion and a CD3+ T-cell count of 210/mm3, presenting for routine immunizations The live attenuated rotavirus vaccinelive vaccines are withheld until T-cell immunity is confirmed

Diagnosis5 of 8 Newborn with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph, a single transverse palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect · 22q11.2 deletion syndrome22q11.2 deletion brings conotruncal defects and an absent thymus, not duodenal atresia. · Down syndromeA double bubble, a single palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect point to Down syndrome. · Turner syndromeTurner syndrome brings coarctation, a webbed neck and a horseshoe kidney. Newborn with a double-bubble sign on abdominal radiograph, a single transverse palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect Down syndromeduodenal atresia

Diagnosis6 of 8 Newborn girl with coarctation of the aorta, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney · Noonan syndromeNoonan syndrome is not tied to a horseshoe kidney; with coarctation, that points to Turner syndrome. · 22q11.2 deletion syndrome22q11.2 deletion brings conotruncal defects and thymic loss. · Turner syndromeCoarctation, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney in a girl is Turner syndrome. Newborn girl with coarctation of the aorta, a webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples and a horseshoe kidney Turner syndrome45,X

Mechanism7 of 8 Why the thymus, parathyroids, palate and cardiac outflow tract fail together in this syndrome · Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development with abnormal neural crest migrationFailed third and fourth pouch development with abnormal neural crest migration takes the thymus, parathyroids, palate and outflow tract together. · Failure of endocardial cushion fusionEndocardial cushion failure gives an atrioventricular septal defect, as in Down syndrome. · Nondisjunction of chromosome 21Nondisjunction causes trisomies; 22q11.2 is a microdeletion. Why the thymus, parathyroids, palate and cardiac outflow tract fail together in this syndrome Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development with abnormal neural crest migrationone embryologic field, four organs

Next step8 of 8 6 yo with 22q11.2 deletion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and poor responses to polysaccharide vaccines · T-cell subsets with quantitative immunoglobulinsRecurrent infections with poor vaccine responses call for immune testing: lymphocyte subsets with immunoglobulin levels. · Sweat chloride testingSweat chloride tests for cystic fibrosis, which this picture does not suggest. · Bone marrow biopsyA marrow biopsy does not assess T-cell function. 6 yo with 22q11.2 deletion, recurrent sinopulmonary infections and poor responses to polysaccharide vaccines T-cell subsets with quantitative immunoglobulinsimmunoglobulins, vaccine titers and lymphocyte subsets assess immune function

Tremulous is the bedside sign of both neonatal hypoglycemia and neonatal hypocalcemia. An uncomplicated pregnancy in a primigravida with Apgars of 8 closes off the hypoglycemia route. The equal right-hand and leg saturations read as an incidental vital sign, but they exclude differential cyanosis and point to a shunt inside the heart.

Syndrome with a missing component: when a vignette describes most of a syndrome, recite the mnemonic and cross off what is printed. Answer with the remainder; CATCH is tested this way, as are other syndrome mnemonics Hypocalcemia and hypoglycemia share a neonatal presentation of jitteriness, tremor and seizure, and the pregnancy history separates them Differential cyanosis means ductal or arch pathology; equal pre- and postductal saturations mean a fixed intracardiac shunt, which is what truncus produces DiGeorge takes lymphocytes, so an option of neutropenia or anemia tests which lineage the thymus governs Until normal T-cell immunity is confirmed, these infants need irradiated blood and no live vaccines The same deletion has two names: thymic involvement makes it DiGeorge, and facial abnormality makes it velocardiofacial

Congenital Heart Diseasecovers truncus arteriosus within the cyanosis differential, and the oxygen-refractory shunt logic that leads to it Antibody Deficienciescovers the downstream question of which immunodeficiency the absent thymus produces. Ask: is the thymic shadow present, and does the face carry a syndrome? Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birthplaces this syndrome beside CHARGE, VACTERL, trisomy 13 and Fanconi anemia. There, the deciding finding is the one on the fewest lists Congenital Heart Disease covers truncus arteriosus within the cyanosis differential, and the oxygen-refractory shunt logic that leads to it. Antibody Deficiencies covers the downstream question of which immunodeficiency the absent thymus produces. Ask: is the thymic shadow present, and does the face carry a syndrome? Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth places this syndrome beside CHARGE, VACTERL, trisomy 13 and Fanconi anemia. There, the deciding finding is the one on the fewest lists.

Read the last sentence before the vignette. When a vignette assembles a recognizable syndrome, the diagnosis is given, and the question asks for the component it left out. That component usually has a one-word bedside sign in the physical examination.

True-fact-wrong-slotHorseshoe kidney: a real and memorable syndrome pairing, but it is a Turner finding, and nothing else here points to Turner. True-fact-wrong-slotDuodenal atresia: congenital heart disease with low-set ears reads as Down syndrome, but that is where duodenal atresia belongs and Down has no thymic aplasia. Unchecked attributeNeutropenia: DiGeorge genuinely causes a cytopenia, but the lineage is lymphocytes; red cell and neutrophil counts are unaffected. Mirror twinHypoglycemia: a tremulous neonate is the classic hypoglycemia cue and also the hypocalcemia cue, but this pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal Apgars.

briefs.title: High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent
briefs.sub: device vs auscultation · adult cutoffs from age 13 · staging · recheck interval by stage · ambulatory monitoringHas auscultation confirmed the device reading, and what stage does the averaged value set?
blocks: High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent

device vs auscultation · adult cutoffs from age 13 · staging · recheck interval by stage · ambulatory monitoringHas auscultation confirmed the device reading, and what stage does the averaged value set?

Pt 17 yo M at a pre-participation examination for football; feels well; no illnesses, medications or family history; body mass index (BMI) 29; automated oscillometric reading 138/88 mm Hg, stated as the 95th percentile for age and height, then 140/89 mm Hg on the same device; rest of the examination normal Q the most appropriate next step in diagnosis; options spanned auscultatory measurement, echocardiography, 24-hour ambulatory monitoring and repeat device readings daily for 3 days or in 2 weeks

A high oscillometric reading is confirmed by auscultation at the same visit: at least two readings, averaged; the device reading is not staged. From age 13, adult cutoffs apply: elevated 120 to 129 systolic with diastolic below 80; hypertension 130/80 or higher. The averaged auscultatory stage sets the recheck interval; ambulatory monitoring confirms hypertension; lifestyle change comes first.

Who is screened Group How often Every child from age 3 Yearly; an oscillometric device is acceptable for the screen Obesity, kidney disease, coarctation or other aortic arch obstruction, diabetes, a drug that raises pressure At every visit

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Screening reading of 120/80 mm Hg or higher (from age 13) → Two or more auscultatory readings during this visit Average of those readings Sets the category for the visit Next step TestResultMeans Elevated for 1 year, or stage 1 at 3 visits → 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring Hypertension confirmed Baseline tests; a secondary cause is sought only when the history or examination suggests one SkipEchocardiography, ambulatory monitoring or drugs before auscultation confirms the device reading; home cuffs and wrist monitors lack good validation in children and are not used.

Categories, age 13 and older Category Averaged auscultatory value Elevated blood pressure Systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg with diastolic below 80 Stage 1 hypertension 130/80 to 139/89 mm Hg Stage 2 hypertension 140/90 mm Hg or higher
Under age 13, the cutoffs are percentiles for age, height and sex: elevated at the 90th percentile, hypertension at the 95th.

What the category sets Category Next Elevated Advise lifestyle change; repeat auscultation at 6 months Stage 1 Advise lifestyle change; repeat in 1 to 2 weeks Stage 2 Advise lifestyle change and refer to a specialist within 1 week Elevated for 1 year, or stage 1 at 3 visits Ambulatory monitoring to confirm hypertension

Once hypertension is confirmed When Do Persistently high readings Pressure in both arms seated and in a leg prone; the leg normally reads 10 to 20 mm Hg higher, so a leg lower than the arm suggests coarctation of the aorta Every confirmed case Urinalysis, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine and lipids; with obesity, screen for diabetes and fatty liver First treatment DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet and physical activity of moderate to vigorous intensity, 30 to 60 minutes on at least 3 to 5 days each week Drug therapy considered Echocardiography for left ventricular hypertrophy Symptoms, stage 2 without a modifiable cause, left ventricular hypertrophy, kidney disease or diabetes, or lifestyle failure Start a drug: ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, angiotensin receptor blocker, calcium channel blocker or thiazide; beta blockers are not first line Goal from age 13 Below 130/80 mm Hg Goal under age 13 Below the 90th percentile for age, height and sex

Pause point Obese adolescent with hypertension and a normal examination Offered: an extensive search for a secondary cause Most childhood hypertension is now primary → Baseline tests and lifestyle change; an extensive search for a secondary cause only when the history or examination suggests one

Next step1 of 6 17 yo M at a football pre-participation examination, well, BMI 29, automated oscillometric blood pressure 138/88 mm Hg and 140/89 mm Hg on repeat with the same device, otherwise normal examination · Blood pressure measurement by auscultationOscillometric devices read high, so auscultation at this visit confirms the reading before staging. · Repeat oscillometric measurement in the office in 2 weeksRepeating the same device repeats its overestimate. · 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoringAmbulatory monitoring comes after auscultation confirms the high pressure. 17 yo M at a football pre-participation examination, well, BMI 29, automated oscillometric blood pressure 138/88 mm Hg and 140/89 mm Hg on repeat with the same device, otherwise normal examination Blood pressure measurement by auscultationthe averaged auscultatory readings set the stage

Diagnosis2 of 6 15 yo F at a well visit with an automated reading of 136/82 mm Hg; two auscultatory readings at the same visit average 132/78 mm Hg · Elevated blood pressureElevated pressure needs a systolic of 120 to 129 with a diastolic below 80. · Stage 2 hypertensionStage 2 starts at 140/90. · Stage 1 hypertensionAn averaged 132/78 has a systolic of 130 to 139, which is stage 1 whatever the diastolic. 15 yo F at a well visit with an automated reading of 136/82 mm Hg; two auscultatory readings at the same visit average 132/78 mm Hg Stage 1 hypertensiona systolic of 130 to 139 mm Hg sets stage 1 even with a diastolic below 80

Next step3 of 6 14 yo M at a well visit whose auscultatory readings average 124/76 mm Hg, with a normal examination · Recheck blood pressure in 1 to 2 weeksA recheck in 1 to 2 weeks is for stage 1 readings. · Reassurance and recheck at the next annual visitElevated pressure needs lifestyle advice and a scheduled recheck, not reassurance. · Lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 monthsAn average of 124/76 is elevated: lifestyle advice and a recheck in 6 months. 14 yo M at a well visit whose auscultatory readings average 124/76 mm Hg, with a normal examination Lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 monthselevated blood pressure

Next step4 of 6 16 yo F with obesity whose auscultatory averages are 134/84, 132/82 and 136/86 mm Hg at three visits over 3 months · EchocardiographyEchocardiography is ordered when drug therapy is considered. · 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoringStage 1 readings at three visits are confirmed with ambulatory monitoring before workup and treatment. · Start an antihypertensive medicationLifestyle change comes first; drugs follow confirmation and a clear indication. 16 yo F with obesity whose auscultatory averages are 134/84, 132/82 and 136/86 mm Hg at three visits over 3 months 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoringconfirms hypertension before workup and treatment

Next step5 of 6 17 yo M, asymptomatic with a normal examination, whose auscultatory readings at one visit average 146/94 mm Hg · Lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 monthsA recheck in 6 months is for elevated pressure. · Lifestyle advice and referral within 1 weekAn average of 146/94 is stage 2: lifestyle advice and referral within 1 week. · Lifestyle advice and recheck in 3 monthsStage 2 pressure cannot wait 3 months. 17 yo M, asymptomatic with a normal examination, whose auscultatory readings at one visit average 146/94 mm Hg Lifestyle advice and referral within 1 weekstage 2 hypertension

Workup6 of 6 16 yo M with obesity and hypertension confirmed by ambulatory monitoring whose blood pressure stays high after a trial of diet and exercise, so drug therapy is planned · Chest radiographA chest radiograph does not measure ventricular mass. · EchocardiographyEchocardiography measures left ventricular mass before drug therapy. · ElectrocardiographyEchocardiography, which measures ventricular mass, is the test the guideline names for cardiac damage. 16 yo M with obesity and hypertension confirmed by ambulatory monitoring whose blood pressure stays high after a trial of diet and exercise, so drug therapy is planned Echocardiographymeasures left ventricular mass before drug therapy

The 2017 AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) guideline set fixed adult cutoffs from age 13 and kept percentiles only for children under 13. Under 13, hypertension starts at the 95th percentile for age, height and sex. From age 13, stage 1 starts at 130/80 mm Hg regardless of percentile.

Symptoms such as headache or cognitive change call for drug therapy Persistently high readings call for both arms seated and a leg prone; the leg normally reads higher, so a leg lower than the arm suggests coarctation of the aorta Confirmed hypertension: baseline tests; a wider search for a secondary cause only when the history or examination points to one

Echocardiography is the test for cardiac damage once drug therapy is considered Lifestyle change aimed at obesity is the first treatment for most adolescent hypertension NBME framing: with the device reading already repeated, the key is a measurement method, not a diagnosis, heart test or later recheck

Hypertension in an Adultcovers confirmation, baseline tests, the secondary causes to test for, and drug choice in adults Hypertension in an Adult covers confirmation, baseline tests, the secondary causes to test for, and drug choice in adults.
A high blood pressure from an automated device is confirmed by averaged auscultatory readings before it is staged, monitored, imaged or treated.

Sequencing trapEchocardiography looks for left ventricular hypertrophy once drug therapy is considered, and this reading is not yet confirmed. Sequencing trapAmbulatory monitoring is accurate, but it follows auscultatory office readings that stay elevated for 1 year or in stage 1 across 3 visits. Unchecked attributeDaily device readings for 3 days repeat the same overestimate; the method must change, not the number of readings. True-fact-wrong-slotA 1 to 2 week recheck follows stage 1 confirmed by auscultation, but a repeat device reading in 2 weeks confirms nothing.

briefs.title: Obstructive Lung Disease
briefs.sub: asthma vs COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) by spirometry · alpha-1 antitrypsin · what lowers COPD mortality · long-term oxygenIs the obstruction reversible, and does the intervention change survival or only symptoms?
blocks: asthma vs COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) by spirometry · alpha-1 antitrypsin · what lowers COPD mortality · long-term oxygenIs the obstruction reversible, and does the intervention change survival or only symptoms?

After a bronchodilator, FEV1/FVC (forced expiratory volume in 1 second over forced vital capacity) <0.70, no asthma history COPD; FEV1 ↑ >12% and >200 mL, ratio normal asthma; ratio <0.70 asthma history smoke exposure overlap, whatever the gain Survival: quit smoking long-term oxygen for resting PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) ≤55 mm HgOxygen cutoffsLong-term oxygen: PaO2 ≤55 mm Hg or SaO2 (arterial oxygen saturation) ≤88% at rest on room air; or PaO2 56 to 59 mm Hg or SaO2 89% with cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension or hematocrit >55%. (or SaO2, arterial oxygen saturation, ≤88%) yearly influenza vaccine; bronchodilators treat symptoms Emphysema under 45, in a nonsmoker or at the bases alpha-1 antitrypsin level

What it is Airways (bronchitis), alveoli (emphysema), or both persistent, often progressive obstruction Chronic bronchitis: productive cough most days, at least 3 months a year, 2 years running Driver Inhaled smoke inflamed airways and alveoli in susceptible people Protease (neutrophil elastase) outruns antiprotease (alpha-1 antitrypsin) Triggers Cigarettes, rising with pack-years; only about 15% of smokers get clinical COPD Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency non-modifiable Cooking smoke, workplace dust, air pollution childhood asthma, low body weight Chain Enzymes Proteases elastin, alveolar septa broken down mucus hypersecretion Structure Lost recoil and airway tethering collapse on expiration air trapping, hyperinflation Circulation Chronic alveolar hypoxia pulmonary vasoconstriction pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale Exam Barrel chest, long expiration, wheeze later edema, neck vein distention Insights Oxygen prolongs life in severe resting hypoxemia; bronchodilators do not. Oxygen eases pulmonary hemodynamics and lowers hematocrit Basal panlobular emphysema in a young adult points to alpha-1: elastase goes unchecked; smoking favors the upper lobes

What the disease does, by systemdetail behind the chain Alpha-1: misfolded protein in hepatocytes; neonatal cholestatic jaundice; cirrhosis in some adults Flat diaphragm, bullae; bronchitis: normal or more basal markings
Symptoms dyspnea, chronic cough or sputum, with exposure Ratio stays <0.70 after a bronchodilator; any gain does not exclude it

Spirometry confirms it Bronchodilator gain threshold Exam and practiceExam threshold: more than 12% and more than 200 mL (AAFP, American Academy of Family Physicians). In practice: the Merck Manual (MSD) asthma page uses over 10% of predicted.

ExacerbationMore dyspnea, more sputum, purulent sputum Every patient: albuterol with ipratropium; systemic steroids unless mild Intensive care: acidosis, uncorrected hypoxemia, new arrhythmia, or worse despite treatment If 2 or more of dyspnea, sputum volume and purulence increase, or ventilation is neededIn practice:In practice: MSD gives antibiotics when purulent sputum is one of the two, or all three increase., choose an antibiotic: amoxicillin-clavulanate, doxycycline or azithromycin. FailureAcute respiratory failure with acidemia (pH <7.35): PaCO2 >50 mm Hg or PaO2 <50 Worse gases, mental status or fatigue, or failing noninvasive support: intubate If pH <7.35 with ↑ PaCO2, choose noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation; benefit is clearest <7.30. OxygenHypoxemia with CO2 (carbon dioxide) retention Aim for PaO2 about 60 mm Hg; more adds little and raises CO2 Hypoxemia If CO2 retention is likely, choose controlled oxygen by nasal prongs or Venturi mask, never withheld. SuddenAbrupt worsening, any COPD If breathing suddenly worsens, choose a chest film for pneumothorax.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it COPD Smoker; productive cough, then exertional dyspnea 40s onward, over years; ratio <0.70 after a bronchodilator; any gain does not exclude it Asthma Wheeze, cough, tight chest that vary; often atopic; often normal between attacks Usually before 40; FEV1 ↑ >12% and >200 mL, ratio returns to normal Asthma-COPD overlap Asthma features (eosinophilia, reversibility) plus smoke exposure Years of asthma, then smoking; ratio stays <0.70, whatever the gain Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Emphysema in a nonsmoker or young smoker; lower lobes; liver disease Under 45; ↓ serum level, then genetic testing (phenotype) Cough-variant asthma Cough alone, often worse at night Spirometry normal; methacholine drops FEV1 by ≥20% Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener) Bronchiectasis with chronic sinus or ear disease Since childhood; situs inversus if Kartagener Bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis Chronic purulent sputum; clubbing as cystic fibrosis progresses Thick-walled, dilated bronchi on CT; sweat chloride confirms cystic fibrosis Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Refractory asthma; brown mucus plugs Aspergillus skin test, then total IgE (immunoglobulin E) Heart failure Dyspnea that mimics COPD Big heart, effusion, sometimes edema on the film

Grade airflow and assign a treatment group. Why spirometry firstWhy order itExam signs are insensitive and nonspecific. Methacholine: watch forWatch forFEV1 can also fall in COPD, so a positive test is only relatively specific for asthma.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Edema, neck vein distention, loud pulmonic second sound Cor pulmonale Oxygen at PaO2 ≤59 mm Hg or SaO2 ≤89% ↑ hematocrit, normal white cells and platelets Secondary erythrocytosis from hypoxemia (secondary polycythemia) Oxygen; phlebotomy only for symptoms All three cell lines usually ↑, erythropoietin usually ↓ Polycythemia vera JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) testing

Airflow grade (GOLD, Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease), once the ratio is below 0.70: predicts survival, not drug choice Grade FEV1, % predicted GOLD 1, mild 80 or more GOLD 2, moderate 50 to 79 GOLD 3, severe 30 to 49 GOLD 4, very severe Below 30

Treatment group (GOLD A, B, E): the past year Group Defined by Start A 0 or 1 moderate exacerbation, none admitted; mMRC (modified Medical Research Council dyspnea scale) 0 to 1 or CAT (COPD Assessment Test) under 10 A LAMA (long-acting muscarinic antagonist) over a LABA (long-acting beta-agonist) B Same exacerbations; mMRC 2 or more, or CAT 10 or more LAMA plus LABA E 2 or more moderate, or 1 or more admitted LAMA plus LABA; consider an ICS (inhaled corticosteroid) if eosinophils ≥300/μL

1 Every patientfrom diagnosis Stop smoking; vaccines; a rescue short-acting bronchodilator; rehabilitation if symptoms are heavy or an admission was recent Quitting slows FEV1 loss and lengthens survival. Influenza (lowers mortality), pneumococcal, COVID-19, RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) from age 50. Preventive Care: Ranking Interventions 2 Startgroup A: few exacerbations, mild symptoms A LAMA; a LABA if not tolerated 3 Start or step upgroup B or E, or group A with symptoms that persist on one drug LAMA plus LABA Before any step up: check inhaler technique and look for other causes of dyspnea. 4 Addexacerbations on two drugs; eosinophils ≥300/μL (consider from 150) An ICS: triple therapy Fewer exacerbations, more pneumonia; low-certainty evidence it may lower mortality. Never an ICS alone. 5 Add-onexacerbations recur despite inhaled therapy Roflumilast (FEV1 <50%, chronic bronchitis) or azithromycin (better in former smokers) 6 Refersevere emphysema despite all of this Lung volume reduction surgery: upper-lobe emphysema, low exercise capacity Surgery improves survival in these patients; transplant improves quality of life, not survival.

Long-term oxygen: who qualifies Resting level When Then PaO2 ≤55 mm Hg or SaO2 ≤88% Room air at rest; on optimal therapy 30 days or more Oxygen 15 hours a day or more: lowers mortalityOxygen targetAAFP: saturation 88 to 92%. MSD: PaO2 above 60 mm Hg (saturation above 90%). PaO2 56 to 59 mm Hg or SaO2 89% Cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension or hematocrit >55% Oxygen, same schedule Above these, or ↓ only on exertion or at night No tissue hypoxia No survival gain Symptom relief: sources differSources differMSD: may ease exertional symptoms. AAFP: no gain in outcomes or quality of life.
