Diagnosis16 of 16 15-year-old boy has had a wet cough since infancy recurrent sinusitis and two pneumonias digital clubbing; weight below the 5th percentile Never smoked; eats well but stays thin Afebrile · SaO2 94% · chest x-ray: hyperinflation · Cystic fibrosis · Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency · Severe persistent asthma 15-year-old boy has had a wet cough since infancy recurrent sinusitis and two pneumonias digital clubbing; weight below the 5th percentile Never smoked; eats well but stays thin Afebrile · SaO2 94% · chest x-ray: hyperinflation Cystic fibrosisclubbing with a lifelong wet cough and poor growth points to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride test confirms it; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency instead causes emphysema in young adults, not a wet cough and poor growth from infancy

16-year-old girl in the emergency department with 3 days of cough with thick yellowish sputum and 1 day of shortness of breath No fever. Asthma on albuterol and inhaled corticosteroids, hospitalized 10 times between ages 8 and 10 Smokes 1.5 packs a day for 4 years T 37 °C · pulse 102/min · respirations 42/min · BP 108/80 mm Hg mild clubbing; increased anteroposterior chest diameter; occasional end-expiratory wheezes chest x-ray: severe bilateral hyperinflation, nothing else Most likely diagnosis? Competing answers Congenital lobar emphysema: emphysema and hyperinflation; but it overinflates one lobe, not both lungs diffusely, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is more common. Kartagener syndrome: thick sputum and clubbing; but there is no situs inversus, chronic sinusitis or lifelong wet cough. Pulmonary sequestration: a congenital lung lesion; but it gives recurrent pneumonia in one region, and this film shows only hyperinflation. Sarcoidosis: chronic lung disease in the young; but there is no hilar adenopathy or infiltrate. Down to two: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or Kartagener syndrome. Emphysema this young, with barrel chest and diffuse hyperinflation, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: unopposed neutrophil elastase, panlobular and basal; misfolded protein in the liver causes cirrhosis. The common answer (severe asthma in a smoker) is not offered, the childhood asthma admissions pull toward it, and the clubbing is a planted pull toward Kartagener syndrome. Confirm with a serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level.

Asthmacovers severity and step therapy once asthma is confirmed Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Diseasecovers cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Ask: which test measures the defining variable? Asthma covers severity and step therapy once asthma is confirmed. Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease covers cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Ask: which test measures the defining variable?

When two choices test the same variable, pick the one that yields a number: post-bronchodilator spirometry over relief after albuterol. An association is not a discriminator, and an intervention is ranked by the outcome the question names.

briefs.title: Occupational Lung Disease
briefs.sub: matching occupational exposure to lung disease · upper vs lower lobes · pleural plaques · cancer and tuberculosis riskWhat did the patient breathe at work, which lobes are involved, and is the pleura involved?
blocks: matching occupational exposure to lung disease · upper vs lower lobes · pleural plaques · cancer and tuberculosis riskWhat did the patient breathe at work, which lobes are involved, and is the pleura involved?

The job names the dust the lobes and the pleura confirm it: asbestos at the bases with pleural plaques; silica, coal and beryllium at the apices Asbestos bronchogenic carcinoma far more than mesothelioma; smoking multiplies only the carcinoma Silicosis tuberculosis risk, a yearly tuberculin test; berylliosis granulomas like sarcoidosis

What it is Lung fibrosis from a mineral dust inhaled at work; hypersensitivity pneumonitis is the organic-antigen look-alike Driver Years of exposure dust-laden macrophages inflammation and fibrosis Triggers Asbestos: shipyards, construction, plumbing, insulation, brake linings Silica: sandblasting, mining, foundries, stone countertops; coal: coal mining Beryllium: aerospace and electronics manufacturing Chain Nodules coalesce progressive massive fibrosis restrictive lungs with a low diffusing capacity Fibrosis cor pulmonale, most with berylliosis and silicosis Insights Latency runs 20 to 30 years, so a job left decades ago still counts Pleural plaques alone mark exposure; they are benign and need no treatment

Which dust, by job, most tested first Disease Job and lobes Decides it Asbestosis Shipyard, construction, plumbing; lower lobes Pleural plaques; ferruginous bodies Silicosis Sandblasting, mining, foundry; upper lobes Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (black lung) Coal mining; upper lobes Nodules coalescing to progressive massive fibrosis; with rheumatoid arthritis, Caplan syndrome Berylliosis Aerospace, electronics; upper lobes Noncaseating granulomas: a sarcoidosis mimic Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Birds, moldy hay Hours after each exposure: fever, cough, dyspnea; clears away from it Byssinosis Cotton and textile mills Worst on the first workday of the week; obstructive, not restrictive Drug-induced fibrosis Nitrofurantoin, no dust history The drug list, not the job
The lobes in one word: USB-CLobe mnemonicUpper lobes: Silica, Beryllium, Coal. Asbestos is the one at the bases.

Next step9 of 11 66 yo M, retired shipyard worker, asymptomatic, with calcified pleural plaques and normal lung parenchyma on imaging · Oral corticosteroids · No treatment · CT-guided pleural biopsy 66 yo M, retired shipyard worker, asymptomatic, with calcified pleural plaques and normal lung parenchyma on imaging No treatmentplaques alone mark exposure and are benign

Next step11 of 11 50 yo M aerospace machinist with progressive dyspnea and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, now removed from exposure · Antituberculous therapy · Observation alone · Oral corticosteroids 50 yo M aerospace machinist with progressive dyspnea and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, now removed from exposure Oral corticosteroidsberylliosis is granulomatous, so it is occasionally steroid-responsive

Asbestos comes from the roof but affects the base; silica and coal come from the ground but affect the top. Latency is typically 20–30 years, so exposure that ended decades ago still counts. Pleural plaques alone are a marker of exposure, benign, and need no treatment.

Answering a long stem in under 40 seconds means one cue was pattern-matched and the verification pass was skipped. This costs the most in occupational stems. The lobe distribution usually decides the diagnosis, and it comes at the end of the stem.

briefs.title: Rhinitis
briefs.sub: the step-up ladder · nasal steroid after antihistamines fail · start 2 weeks before pollen · immunotherapy is the baitWhich step has the patient already failed, and how far off is the pollen season?
blocks: the step-up ladder · nasal steroid after antihistamines fail · start 2 weeks before pollen · immunotherapy is the baitWhich step has the patient already failed, and how far off is the pollen season?

Moderate to severe seasonal rhinitis that has failed antihistamines an intranasal corticosteroid, the most effective drug class Seen in late winter start it about 2 weeks before pollen season; it needs lead time Immunotherapy only after drug therapy fails; a decongestant spray past 3 days rebound congestion

What it is Allergic rhinitis: a type I hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa, for example to pollen Driver Allergen IgE (immunoglobulin E)-mediated reaction eosinophil-rich mucosal inflammation Triggers Pollen, dust, animal dander Atopy: asthma and eczema travel with it Chain Exposure sneezing, itch, clear rhinorrhea, congestion pale, boggy turbinates Repeated bouts nasal polyps Insights Itchy, watery eyes point to allergic rhinitis; vasomotor rhinitis spares the eyes A first-generation antihistamine in the stem is usually there to be replaced, not continued

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Allergic rhinitis Sneezing, itch, clear rhinorrhea; pale, boggy mucosa With exposure, eg pollen season; eye symptoms Vasomotor rhinitis (nonallergic rhinitis) Clear rhinorrhea set off by temperature change; no itch or sneezing No eye symptoms; no response to oral antihistamines Rhinitis medicamentosa Worse congestion on a decongestant spray Spray used past 3 days; rebound vasodilation Viral rhinitis (common cold) Sneezing, congestion, runny nose A cold; rhinovirus the usual cause Nasal foreign body A young child with nasal discharge One side, foul-smelling, purulent or bloody

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Sneezing, congestion, clear rhinorrhea → Nasal exam and the eyes Pale, boggy mucosa; itchy, watery eyes Allergic rhinitis No itch, no eye symptoms; temperature triggers Vasomotor rhinitis Targeted tests TestResultMeans Congestion worse despite a decongestant spray → Ask how long the spray has been used More than 3 days Rhinitis medicamentosa Child, discharge from one nostril, foul smell → Look in that nostril Object seen Nasal foreign body

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Seen in late winter, before pollen season Prophylaxis Start the nasal steroid about 2 weeks before the season Rhinitis with asthma, wants one oral drug Montelukast Counsel on neuropsychiatric effects
Pause point Never tried a nasal steroid Offered: immunotherapy, the only option that changes the disease Desensitization waits until drug therapy fails → A nasal steroid first

1 Avoidwhen practical Allergen avoidance Practical for dust mites or pets; not for pollen, where limiting time outdoors fails. 2 1st linemoderate to severe, or antihistamines failing An intranasal corticosteroid It suppresses the mucosal inflammation and needs lead time: start about 2 weeks before pollen season. 3 Addsymptoms persist A second-generation antihistamine, oral or intranasal First-generation agents sedate and are anticholinergic: replace them. 4 Lastdrug therapy fails Allergen immunotherapy (desensitization) Rising allergen doses shift the response from IgE to IgG (immunoglobulin G); the only disease-modifying option.

cystic fibrosis · primary ciliary dyskinesia · antibody deficiency · foreign body · allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis when antibiotics failWhich exam finding could no immune defect produce, and when an adequate antibiotic course fails, are the eosinophils and immunoglobulin E (IgE) up?

Recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia that need antibiotics cross the gate; up to 12 self-limited colds a year is normal Heart on the right situs inversus with recurrent infection, a ciliary defect: primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD); poor growth or greasy stools cystic fibrosis, sweat chloride A week of adequate antibiotics fails in asthma or cystic fibrosis eosinophils and IgE (immunoglobulin E) allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)

What it is Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infection from secretions the airway cannot clear, or from a missing defense Driver Retained secretions: dysmotile cilia, thick cystic fibrosis mucus, a trapped object missing antibody or immune cells Triggers Autosomal recessive defects: dynein arms (PCD), CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) non-modifiable A choking episode in a toddler Asthma or cystic fibrosis for ABPA Chain Retained secretions repeated infection bronchiectasis, the permanent endpoint Damaged airway traps inhaled Aspergillus colonization an IgE-driven reaction, ABPA Insights A heart on the right is the one finding no immune defect can produce; only a ciliary defect randomizes laterality Bronchiectasis is never the cause; name what kept the secretions in

Mechanisms behind the chaindetail behind the chain Airway cilia dysmotile; nodal cilia in the embryo cannot set left-right asymmetry, so laterality is random Everyone inhales the spores and clearance removes them; asthma or cystic fibrosis traps them, and chronic colonization turns into a Th2 (type 2 helper T cell) hypersensitivity

Foreign bodyA toddler, abrupt choking, then focal wheeze If the onset was abrupt after choking, choose rigid bronchoscopy to find and remove it. SteroidsEosinophilia after tropical or subtropical exposure Systemic steroids can turn strongyloidiasis into hyperinfection or dissemination If steroids are planned, choose screen for and treat strongyloidiasis first.

Recurrent infection: the finding that picks the cause Diagnosis The stem shows Sets it apart Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome with situs inversus) Wet cough, ear and sinus infections since infancy; breathing trouble as a term newborn From infancy; heart on the right in about half ⚠︎ Cystic fibrosis Thick secretions, repeated infection, bronchiectasis Poor growth, fatty stools, meconium ileus, nasal polyps, clubbing; heart on the left Retained foreign body Toddler, abrupt choking episode Abrupt; focal wheeze, one-sided hyperinflation on an expiratory or decubitus film Antibody deficiency: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA), common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) Encapsulated sinopulmonary infection, normal airway anatomy XLA after 6 months, CVID after puberty; XLA: absent tonsils and B cells; CVID: B cells present HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection Otitis, pneumonia and recurrent thrush; a mother with thrush, diarrhea and weight loss The mother's illness; thrush with bacterial infections Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) Infant with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, thrush Absent tonsils and thymus; no T cells Neutrophil killing defect (chronic granulomatous disease) Abscesses, osteomyelitis, pneumonia Dihydrorhodamine test Heterotaxy (situs ambiguus) Heart defects and a liver in the midline No spleen, or several small spleens (asplenia, polysplenia)

When antibiotics fail in a structural lung Diagnosis The stem shows Sets it apart ABPA Asthma or cystic fibrosis, worse despite antibiotics Eosinophilia and a high IgE Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Organic antigen; fever, malaise, infiltrates Improves in hospital; no eosinophilia, normal IgE Strongyloidiasis Lived in the rural tropics or subtropics; eosinophilia, high IgE Migrating hives, gut symptoms Granulomatosis with polyangiitis Necrotizing bronchiectasis that looks like refractory pneumonia Older adults; destroyed sinuses, hemoptysis, glomerulonephritis; eosinophils normal Nontuberculous mycobacteria Mycobacterium avium complex, often in the bronchiectasis of cystic fibrosis Over months to years; nodules, then cavities; eosinophils and IgE not raised

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Recurrent infection needing antibiotics → Chest x-ray; examine where the heart lies Heart and stomach bubble both on the right Situs inversus: the PCD axis Heart on the left Go by the branch below Targeted tests TestResultMeans Poor growth, greasy stools, polyps → Sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L Cystic fibrosis Abrupt onset after choking → Rigid bronchoscopy Object seen and removed Retained foreign body Normal anatomy, absent tonsils or onset after puberty → Immunoglobulin levels and B-cell counts by flow cytometry Every class low, no B cells XLA Low, B cells present CVID PCD suspected, heart on the left → Nasal nitric oxide Low Supports PCD; confirm with ciliary electron microscopy, then genetic testing Next step TestResultMeans A week of adequate antibiotics fails → Blood count with differential, then total IgE Eosinophilia; IgE >417 IU/mL (1,000 ng/mL) Allergic sensitization: ABPA likely Resistant organism; eosinophils and IgE normal Bacterial: adjust to sensitivities Diagnostic test TestResultMeans ABPA suspected → Aspergillus-specific IgE or skin test Positive Sensitization confirmed Chronic cough, recurrent pneumonia, hemoptysis → High-resolution CT of the chest Dilated bronchi; mucoid impaction, finger-in-glove opacities Bronchiectasis; with the allergic markers, ABPA SkipAn immune workup when colds pass on their own and growth is normal: reassure. Aspergillus IgG (immunoglobulin G) only supports ABPA; it does not diagnose it.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Cystic fibrosis, pneumonia, under 20 years Staphylococcus aureus Over 20: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Adult with bronchiectasis and sinus or ear disease since childhood PCD, missed in childhood Nasal nitric oxide, then ciliary testing Eosinophilia with travel, urticaria or gut symptoms Strongyloidiasis Strongyloides serology before any steroid
Pause point Child whose heart is on the right Offered: another antibiotic course or an immune workup No antibody defect moves the heart → The exam finding picks the test

First treatment by diagnosis Diagnosis Choose Watch for PCD Daily airway clearance Bronchiectasis progresses without it ABPA A systemic glucocorticoid with itraconazole An antifungal alone treats the antigen, not the response In practiceIn practiceIn practice: clinical references start the steroid alone and add itraconazole when ABPA persists despite it. XLA or CVID Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), long term Heterotaxy with asplenia Prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms Eosinophilia with tropical exposure Treat strongyloidiasis before systemic steroids Hyperinfection, dissemination
Follow-up decisions When Do Cystic fibrosis Total IgE every year to screen for ABPA ABPA on treatment Chest film, eosinophils and IgE every 3 months for response

Diagnosis1 of 23 11-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has a week of fever and productive cough no improvement after a week of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia IgE 3,225 IU/mL No travel, rash or gastrointestinal symptoms T 38.4°C · bilateral crackles · Hypersensitivity pneumonitis · Granulomatosis with polyangiitis · Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis 11-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has a week of fever and productive cough no improvement after a week of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia IgE 3,225 IU/mL No travel, rash or gastrointestinal symptoms T 38.4°C · bilateral crackles Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosisantibiotic failure plus eosinophilia and an IgE more than triple the usual threshold make it allergic, not bacterial. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis improves in hospital and gives no eosinophilia and a normal IgE; granulomatosis with polyangiitis affects older adults, without eosinophilia

Diagnosis2 of 23 3-year-old girl has had a chronic wet cough since infancy recurrent otitis media since infancy chest film: cardiac silhouette on the right stomach bubble on the right Growth normal for age Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% · Cystic fibrosis · Heterotaxy syndrome with congenital heart disease · Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) 3-year-old girl has had a chronic wet cough since infancy recurrent otitis media since infancy chest film: cardiac silhouette on the right stomach bubble on the right Growth normal for age Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)a heart on the right with chronic wet cough and otitis points to a ciliary defect: the dynein-arm defect leaves nodal cilia unable to set left-right asymmetry. Without normal ciliary function during embryogenesis, abnormal orientation can result; cystic fibrosis does not involve this defect; heterotaxy is situs ambiguus with asplenia or polysplenia and heart disease. Confirm with nasal nitric oxide, then ciliary electron microscopy

Next step3 of 23 15-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has an exacerbation that fails initial therapy sputum grows Pseudomonas resistant to the current antibiotic eosinophil count normal IgE normal T 38.3°C · oxygen saturation 93% · Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent · Adjust antibiotics according to culture sensitivities · Repeat total serum IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE testing 15-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has an exacerbation that fails initial therapy sputum grows Pseudomonas resistant to the current antibiotic eosinophil count normal IgE normal T 38.3°C · oxygen saturation 93% Adjust antibiotics according to culture sensitivitiesa resistant organism with normal eosinophils and IgE is still a bacterial exacerbation: adjust to culture sensitivities. Without the allergic markers, neither glucocorticoids nor repeat Aspergillus serology fits

Next step4 of 23 2-year-old boy has his third pneumonia this year chronic loose, greasy stools weight below the 3rd percentile point of maximal impulse in the left chest No choking episode; tonsils present T 38.6°C · oxygen saturation 95% · Nasal nitric oxide measurement · Sweat chloride testing · Quantitative serum immunoglobulins 2-year-old boy has his third pneumonia this year chronic loose, greasy stools weight below the 3rd percentile point of maximal impulse in the left chest No choking episode; tonsils present T 38.6°C · oxygen saturation 95% Sweat chloride testingwith the heart on the left, poor growth and greasy stools open the cystic fibrosis axis: sweat chloride, 60 mmol/L or more. Immunoglobulins fit normal anatomy without tonsils; nasal nitric oxide fits a ciliary picture with normal growth

Next step5 of 23 16-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis this week Aspergillus-specific IgE positive CT: mucoid impaction, finger-in-glove opacities Productive cough despite a week of antibiotics T 37.9°C · total IgE 2,600 IU/mL · Broadened intravenous antibacterial coverage for Pseudomonas · Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent · Voriconazole alone 16-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis this week Aspergillus-specific IgE positive CT: mucoid impaction, finger-in-glove opacities Productive cough despite a week of antibiotics T 37.9°C · total IgE 2,600 IU/mL Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agentthe pathology is allergic inflammation: a systemic glucocorticoid first-line, with an antifungal added to reduce spore burden. Voriconazole alone treats the antigen, not the response; more antibacterial coverage treats an infection that is not there

Next step6 of 23 14-month-old boy choked while eating nuts 3 weeks ago now a focal right-sided wheeze second right lower lobe pneumonia film: right-sided hyperinflation Well before the choking episode T 38.2°C · oxygen saturation 95% · High-resolution chest CT · Rigid bronchoscopy · Another course of oral antibiotics with a repeat film in 4 weeks 14-month-old boy choked while eating nuts 3 weeks ago now a focal right-sided wheeze second right lower lobe pneumonia film: right-sided hyperinflation Well before the choking episode T 38.2°C · oxygen saturation 95% Rigid bronchoscopyabrupt onset after choking, focal wheeze and unilateral hyperinflation are a retained foreign body: rigid bronchoscopy finds and removes it. Another antibiotic course or a CT leaves the obstruction in place

Screening7 of 23 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis comes for her routine annual review feels well baseline cough unchanged No wheeze or new sputum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · lung function at her baseline · High-resolution chest CT · Aspergillus skin testing · Total serum IgE 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis comes for her routine annual review feels well baseline cough unchanged No wheeze or new sputum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · lung function at her baseline Total serum IgEcystic fibrosis earns an annual total serum IgE, one of the few purely serologic screening intervals; CT and skin testing are not the yearly screen

Next step8 of 23 5-year-old boy has had recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia since 9 months of age no palpable tonsils no cervical lymphadenopathy Heart sounds loudest in the left chest; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · Sweat chloride testing · Quantitative serum immunoglobulins with B-cell flow cytometry · Bronchoscopic ciliary biopsy 5-year-old boy has had recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia since 9 months of age no palpable tonsils no cervical lymphadenopathy Heart sounds loudest in the left chest; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% Quantitative serum immunoglobulins with B-cell flow cytometrynormal anatomy with absent lymphoid tissue is the antibody axis; all immunoglobulins low with B cells absent is X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Sweat chloride needs poor growth or greasy stools, and ciliary biopsy needs a ciliary picture

Diagnosis9 of 23 45-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has several months of cough and weight loss CT: nodular and cavitary opacities No hemoptysis; no recent travel eosinophils 2% · IgE 90 IU/mL · oxygen saturation 94% · Reactivation of latent pulmonary tuberculosis · Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis · Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease 45-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has several months of cough and weight loss CT: nodular and cavitary opacities No hemoptysis; no recent travel eosinophils 2% · IgE 90 IU/mL · oxygen saturation 94% Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung diseasecystic fibrosis bronchiectasis is colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria such as Mycobacterium avium complex, rather than Mycobacterium tuberculosis: chronic over months to years, nodular then cavitary. No eosinophilia or IgE rise removes the allergic cause

Next step10 of 23 8-year-old boy has a year-round wet cough unexplained respiratory distress as a term newborn chronic otitis media point of maximal impulse in the left chest Growth and stools normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · Nasal nitric oxide measurement · Repeat chest radiograph in 6 weeks · Monthly IVIG replacement 8-year-old boy has a year-round wet cough unexplained respiratory distress as a term newborn chronic otitis media point of maximal impulse in the left chest Growth and stools normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% Nasal nitric oxide measurementsitus inversus appears in only 40% to 50% of PCD, so a heart on the left does not exclude it; low nasal nitric oxide supports PCD with normal situs. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and a repeat film adds nothing

Next step11 of 23 34-year-old woman has asthma that is difficult to control recurrent brown mucus plugs central bronchiectasis on CT IgE 2,400 IU/mL Aspergillus skin test positive T 37.2°C · peripheral eosinophilia · oxygen saturation 95% · Prolonged oral antibacterial therapy for the bronchiectasis · Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent · Inhaled corticosteroid dose escalation 34-year-old woman has asthma that is difficult to control recurrent brown mucus plugs central bronchiectasis on CT IgE 2,400 IU/mL Aspergillus skin test positive T 37.2°C · peripheral eosinophilia · oxygen saturation 95% Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agentsame disease, different structural host: asthma, like cystic fibrosis, traps the spores. A systemic glucocorticoid with an antifungal; more inhaled steroid or antibacterial therapy leaves the allergic response untreated

Diagnosis12 of 23 3-year-old girl in daycare has had 9 upper respiratory illnesses this year each self-limited without antibiotics normal examination between illnesses Older brother is well growth at the 50th percentile · Afebrile · Primary ciliary dyskinesia without situs inversus · Normal frequency of childhood viral infection · Selective IgA deficiency 3-year-old girl in daycare has had 9 upper respiratory illnesses this year each self-limited without antibiotics normal examination between illnesses Older brother is well growth at the 50th percentile · Afebrile Normal frequency of childhood viral infectionup to 12 viral illnesses a year is normal in daycare or with older siblings: reassure, no immune workup. Ciliary disease and antibody defects give antibiotic-requiring bacterial infection, not colds that clear alone

Next step13 of 23 52-year-old man who farms has fever, malaise and airspace infiltrates no response to a week of antibiotics symptoms improve over 3 days in hospital No travel or rash IgE 40 IU/mL · eosinophils 1% · Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent · Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy · Identify and eliminate the inciting antigen exposure 52-year-old man who farms has fever, malaise and airspace infiltrates no response to a week of antibiotics symptoms improve over 3 days in hospital No travel or rash IgE 40 IU/mL · eosinophils 1% Identify and eliminate the inciting antigen exposureimprovement in hospital, away from the exposure, with a normal IgE and no eosinophilia is hypersensitivity pneumonitis: identify and eliminate the antigen, since removal from the exposure is what brings improvement. The allergic fungal disease needs eosinophilia and a high IgE, and the improvement already explains the picture without a biopsy

Diagnosis14 of 23 18-month-old boy has had 8 antibiotic courses for sinusitis and pneumonia older brother has the same illness mildly enlarged tonsils point of maximal impulse in the right chest Delivered vaginally without complications oxygen saturation 99% · bilateral rales and rhonchi · Common variable immunodeficiency · Primary ciliary dyskinesia · X-linked agammaglobulinemia 18-month-old boy has had 8 antibiotic courses for sinusitis and pneumonia older brother has the same illness mildly enlarged tonsils point of maximal impulse in the right chest Delivered vaginally without complications oxygen saturation 99% · bilateral rales and rhonchi Primary ciliary dyskinesiathe heart on the right decides: visceral rotation needs normal ciliary movement, which an antibody defect leaves intact. Tonsils exclude X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and 18 months excludes CVID; bilateral rales with a normal saturation argue against a foreign body; the affected brother alone separates none of them

Next step15 of 23 40-year-old man from the rural tropics has refractory pulmonary infiltrates migratory urticaria abdominal pain IgE 4,100 IU/mL Infiltrates persist after 10 days of antibiotics T 37.8°C · eosinophils 18% · oxygen saturation 94% · Empiric antituberculous therapy · Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent · Treat for strongyloidiasis before giving systemic glucocorticoids 40-year-old man from the rural tropics has refractory pulmonary infiltrates migratory urticaria abdominal pain IgE 4,100 IU/mL Infiltrates persist after 10 days of antibiotics T 37.8°C · eosinophils 18% · oxygen saturation 94% Treat for strongyloidiasis before giving systemic glucocorticoidseosinophilia and a high IgE with roaming urticaria, gut symptoms and tropical exposure are strongyloidiasis: treat it before any systemic glucocorticoid, which risks hyperinfection or dissemination. Antituberculous therapy explains neither the eosinophilia nor the urticaria

Diagnosis16 of 23 4-year-old boy adopted at 6 months has 6 months of nasal obstruction recurrent nosebleeds repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia bilateral nasal polyps; digital clubbing Diffuse coarse crackles weight 3rd, height 5th percentile · oxygen saturation 93% · Cystic fibrosis · Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis · Severe allergic rhinitis 4-year-old boy adopted at 6 months has 6 months of nasal obstruction recurrent nosebleeds repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia bilateral nasal polyps; digital clubbing Diffuse coarse crackles weight 3rd, height 5th percentile · oxygen saturation 93% Cystic fibrosisnasal polyps, clubbing and poor growth with recurrent infection point to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride testing; newborn screening misses rarer CFTR mutations. Allergic rhinitis causes neither poor growth nor clubbing, and a vasculitis explains neither in a 4-year-old with recurrent sinopulmonary infection

Workup17 of 23 15-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 2 weeks of productive cough no improvement after 10 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia total IgE 1,850 IU/mL No travel or rash Afebrile · oxygen saturation 95% · Aspergillus-specific IgE or Aspergillus skin testing · Serum galactomannan assay · Sputum fungal culture 15-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 2 weeks of productive cough no improvement after 10 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia total IgE 1,850 IU/mL No travel or rash Afebrile · oxygen saturation 95% Aspergillus-specific IgE or Aspergillus skin testingtotal IgE suggests; Aspergillus-specific IgE or a skin test confirms sensitization. A sputum culture or galactomannan looks for the fungus, but everyone inhales it: the disease is the immune response

Workup18 of 23 17-year-old boy has had sinusitis all his life chronic productive cough infertility evaluation with his partner semen analysis: normal sperm count, absent motility No greasy stools; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% · Sweat chloride testing · Electron microscopy of respiratory cilia for dynein-arm defects · Peripheral blood karyotype to evaluate for Klinefelter syndrome 17-year-old boy has had sinusitis all his life chronic productive cough infertility evaluation with his partner semen analysis: normal sperm count, absent motility No greasy stools; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% Electron microscopy of respiratory cilia for dynein-arm defectsa normal count with absent motility is the ciliary pattern, and electron microscopy shows the dynein-arm defect. Cystic fibrosis often gives obstructive azoospermia or severe oligospermia from congenital absence of the vas deferens, which a normal count excludes. Klinefelter syndrome typically gives small testes with reduced testosterone, not a normal count with immotile sperm, and no sinusitis

Mechanism19 of 23 13-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis sputum has grown Aspergillus repeatedly IgE 2,900 IU/mL Neutrophil count normal; no cavity on CT Afebrile · eosinophils 12% · oxygen saturation 96% · Mucus trapping defeats mucociliary clearance, allowing colonization and Th2 sensitization · Cavitary lung disease providing a space for a fungus ball · Neutropenia permitting tissue invasion 13-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis sputum has grown Aspergillus repeatedly IgE 2,900 IU/mL Neutrophil count normal; no cavity on CT Afebrile · eosinophils 12% · oxygen saturation 96% Mucus trapping defeats mucociliary clearance, allowing colonization and Th2 sensitizationeveryone inhales the spores, and the mucociliary escalator clears them; trapped mucus allows colonization, then Th2 sensitization. A normal neutrophil count and no cavity remove the other two

Next step20 of 23 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with primary ciliary dyskinesia at age 4 daily purulent sputum high-resolution CT: lower-lobe bronchiectasis crackles at both lung bases Takes no maintenance therapy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% · Begin daily airway clearance therapy · Antibiotics only during acute exacerbations, no maintenance · Surgical resection of the bronchiectatic lobe 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with primary ciliary dyskinesia at age 4 daily purulent sputum high-resolution CT: lower-lobe bronchiectasis crackles at both lung bases Takes no maintenance therapy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% Begin daily airway clearance therapythe bronchiectasis comes from failed mucociliary clearance, so start daily airway clearance; antibiotics only during exacerbations leave the secretions in place, and resection removes one lobe of a disease of the whole airway

Next step21 of 23 10-year-old girl has had two pneumococcal bacteremias midline liver complex congenital heart disease no spleen on abdominal imaging Growth normal; no chronic wet cough Afebrile · HR 96/min · oxygen saturation 96% · Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination plus daily antibiotic prophylaxis · Monthly IVIG replacement · Daily airway clearance therapy 10-year-old girl has had two pneumococcal bacteremias midline liver complex congenital heart disease no spleen on abdominal imaging Growth normal; no chronic wet cough Afebrile · HR 96/min · oxygen saturation 96% Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination plus daily antibiotic prophylaxissitus ambiguus with no spleen is the asplenia of heterotaxy: protect against encapsulated organisms with vaccination and daily prophylaxis. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and airway clearance a ciliary one

Mechanism22 of 23 4-year-old boy has a chronic wet cough recurrent otitis media recurrent sinusitis since infancy chest film: situs inversus totalis Growth normal; tonsils present; stools normal Afebrile · HR 104/min · oxygen saturation 97% · Dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme · CFTR chloride channel of the airway epithelium · Bruton tyrosine kinase 4-year-old boy has a chronic wet cough recurrent otitis media recurrent sinusitis since infancy chest film: situs inversus totalis Growth normal; tonsils present; stools normal Afebrile · HR 104/min · oxygen saturation 97% Dynein arms of the ciliary axonemedynein arms power ciliary beating; their defect impairs mucociliary clearance and randomizes laterality. CFTR and Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause infection without the ciliary dysfunction that misplaces the heart

Mechanism23 of 23 6-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has recurrent nosebleeds greasy, foul-smelling stools weight below the 3rd percentile repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia Bruises easily on the shins platelets 280,000/mm³ · prothrombin time prolonged · Platelet dysfunction from chronic infection · Pancreatic insufficiency with vitamin K malabsorption · Chronic sinus inflammation eroding mucosal vessels 6-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has recurrent nosebleeds greasy, foul-smelling stools weight below the 3rd percentile repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia Bruises easily on the shins platelets 280,000/mm³ · prothrombin time prolonged Pancreatic insufficiency with vitamin K malabsorptionpancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamins, and vitamin K deficiency causes the bleeding; neither sinus inflammation nor platelet dysfunction prolongs the prothrombin time

XLA with tonsils present: it has no tonsillar or adenoidal tissue. CVID at 18 months: it presents in adolescence or adulthood. Normal childhood infection: those are viral and need no antibiotics; eight antibiotic courses are a disease pattern. Fever as proof of infection: fever, malaise and blood-streaked sputum are common in ABPA. Broader antibiotics: antibiotic failure is a finding, not a dosing problem; change the category (allergic, mycobacterial, vasculitic) before the spectrum. Tuberculosis: cystic fibrosis airways are colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria.

Part I Antibody Deficiencies: the airway is structurally normal, so immunoglobulin levels and the B-cell count decide. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies: what pancreatic insufficiency does to vitamins A, D, E and K; is the prothrombin time long? Part I Obstructive Lung Disease: the adult with brown mucus plugs.

A physical finding that no immune defect could produce decides the cause of recurrent infection. When a treatment that should work fails, the failure is the finding: change the category of disease, most often infection to hypersensitivity, rather than intensifying treatment.

briefs.title: Sickle Cell Disease and Trait
briefs.sub: trait or disease: read the electrophoresis first · what each causes · chronic dyspnea: the timing pattern picks the testIs any adult hemoglobin (HbA) present, and are the symptoms nocturnal and intermittent, or exertional and progressive?
blocks: trait or disease: read the electrophoresis first · what each causes · chronic dyspnea: the timing pattern picks the testIs any adult hemoglobin (HbA) present, and are the symptoms nocturnal and intermittent, or exertional and progressive?

Read the electrophoresis: adult hemoglobin (HbA) about 60%, sickle hemoglobin (HbS) about 40%, normal complete blood count (CBC) trait; no HbA sickle cell anemia, hemoglobin SC (HbSC) or sickle-beta-zero; HbA present but below HbS with a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV) sickle-beta-plus Fever in sickle cell disease cultures and ceftriaxone now; new infiltrate with chest pain or hypoxemia acute chest syndrome: antibiotics, oxygen, transfusion Weeks of dyspnea: nocturnal and intermittent spirometry for asthma; exertional and progressive echocardiogram or chest CT

What it is Autosomal recessive beta-globin disease: two sickle genes, or one with HbC or a beta-thalassemia gene disease; one sickle gene trait, no anemia Driver Valine for glutamic acid at beta-6 deoxygenated HbS polymerizes rigid sickled red cells Triggers Hypoxemia, dehydration, acidosis (infection) Falling fetal hemoglobin (HbF): newborns are spared; pain crises can start by 6 months non-modifiable Chain Molecular deoxygenated HbS polymerizes cells sickle Vessel rigid cells plug small vessels infarcts from bone to brain Blood fragile cells hemolyze chronic anemia; reticulocytes often 10% or more Clinical pain crises, acute chest syndrome, stroke; the spleen infarcts itself encapsulated infections Insights Trait sickles only in the renal medulla under 50% HbS stays fluid except where blood is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic painless hematuria, dilute urine Asthma and acute chest syndrome feed each other asthma raises the risk of the next episode, so treating it is prevention

What the disease does, by systemdetail behind the chain Large in young children, then autosplenectomy; Howell-Jolly bodies on the smearnot seen in trait Pneumococcus; Salmonella osteomyelitis Dactylitis in infants and toddlers; avascular necrosis: progressive hip pain without fever Concentrating defect, papillary necrosis, chronic kidney disease SAND MnemonicRenal papillary necrosis: Sickle cell disease or trait, Acute pyelonephritis, Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), Diabetes mellitus Acute chest syndrome; pulmonary hypertension and fibrosis later Retinopathy; ankle ulcers; gallstones Ischemic priapism: painful erection over 4 hours Hematuria, usually left-sided and self-limited; rare medullary carcinoma; rhabdomyolysis with exhausting exercise; more kidney disease and pulmonary embolism
Trait HbA more than HbS Sickle cell anemia no HbA; HbS with a variable HbF
Infiltrate new on the chest film With fever, chest pain or dyspnea
No test confirms a vaso-occlusive crisis; it is diagnosed clinically

FeverFever in a child with sickle cell disease Pneumococcus leads despite vaccination; infection is the leading killer in childhood If the child looks ill with a temperature above 38 °C, choose cultures, chest film, admission and ceftriaxone now. Acute chest syndromeFever, chest pain, new infiltrate; hypoxemia can come fast Pneumonia looks the same and can trigger it If a new infiltrate appears, choose ceftriaxone plus azithromycin, oxygen and transfusion. Splenic sequestrationYoung child, pale or in shock, with a fast-growing spleen Why it happensSplenic sequestrationYoung children still have a working spleen; once repeated infarcts scar it, sequestration stops and infection becomes the main risk. Hemoglobin down 2 g/dL or more; reticulocytes up, platelets down If anemia is symptomatic, choose transfusion, given slowly. Aplastic crisisWorsening anemia after a viral illness; spleen not enlarged Reticulocytes under 1%; platelets normal; parvovirus B19 If hemoglobin falls below baseline, choose simple transfusion. StrokeNew focal weakness or hemiparesis Sickle cell disease is the commonest cause of stroke in children Stroke in a Child or Adolescent If a deficit appears, choose exchange transfusion.

Electrophoresis after infancy, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Sickle cell trait HbA about 60%, HbS about 40%; CBC normal HbA exceeds HbS Why A beats SReading itIn trait, alpha chains bind normal beta chains with higher affinity, so HbA always exceeds HbS; learn the inequality, not the numbers. Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia HbA present but low; low MCV HbS exceeds HbA: the sharpest mimic of trait Sickle cell anemia (HbSS) HbA 0%, HbS about 90%, HbF 5 to 25%; reticulocytes often 10% or more No HbA, cells normocytic HbF by ageReading itFetal hemoglobin falls after birth, to under 10% by 6 months, which is when sickle pain can begin. Sickle-beta-zero thalassemia HbA 0%; HbS high; HbA2 (minor adult hemoglobin) raised No HbA, cells small: looks like HbSS Hemoglobin SC disease HbA 0%; HbS about equal to hemoglobin C (HbC) Anemia milder, yet retinopathy and avascular necrosis exceed what it predicts Normal HbA about 97%; HbA2 about 2.5%; HbF under 2% No HbS

Sudden anemia in sickle cell disease, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Splenic sequestration Young child; big, tender spleen; shock Reticulocytes up, platelets down Aplastic crisis After a viral illness: parvovirus B19 halts red cell production Reticulocytes under 1%; platelets normal; no big spleen Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction Hemolysis after an initial rise Days to weeks after a transfusion Folate deficiency Chronic hemolysis uses up folate MCV up, reticulocytes down

Weeks of dyspnea in sickle cell disease, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Asthma Wheeze, tightness or cough; worse at night, with exercise or a cold; film normal Nocturnal and intermittent; obstruction that reverses Pulmonary hypertension Raised neck veins, edema, enlarged pulmonary arteries Exertional and progressive; echocardiogram Pulmonary fibrosis Reticular markings, restrictive function Exertional and progressive; honeycombing on chest CT Acute chest syndrome Fever, chest pain, hypoxemia, new infiltrate Sudden onset Pulmonary embolism Tachycardia, hypoxia, pleuritic pain Acute and persistent; hypoxemia with a clear film Sarcoidosis Bilateral hilar adenopathy Not linked to sickle cell disease

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Newborn screen → Hemoglobin electrophoresis pattern FAS (fetal, adult, sickle) Trait; F leads because HbF predominates at birth FS (fetal, sickle) Disease; repeat at 3 to 6 months may be needed to confirm Targeted tests TestResultMeans Painless hematuria, otherwise well → Urinalysis, then renal imaging Blood, imaging clear Medullary sickling: consider trait Renal mass Renal medullary carcinoma Next step TestResultMeans Family history or anemia → CBC with MCV and reticulocytes Completely normal Trait Anemia, high reticulocytes Disease Low MCV A beta-thalassemia combination Diagnostic test TestResultMeans After infancy → Hemoglobin electrophoresis HbA exceeds HbS Sickle cell trait No HbA HbSS, HbSC or sickle-beta-zero SkipA sickle solubility (metabisulfite) test: positive in trait and disease alike, and unreliable in the first months; only electrophoresis separates them.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Known disease: pain, fever or pallor → CBC, reticulocyte count, metabolic panelCultures and chest film if febrile Reticulocytes under 1% Aplastic crisis Hemoglobin down 2 g/dL or more, big spleen Splenic sequestration Pain, labs at baseline Vaso-occlusive crisis: a clinical diagnosis Targeted tests TestResultMeans Chest pain or hard breathing → Chest film and pulse oximetry New infiltrate Acute chest syndrome or pneumonia Hypoxemia, clear film Pulmonary embolism: CT pulmonary angiography Weeks of cough or tightness → Chest x-ray Normal Expected in asthma; acute chest syndrome, fibrosis and sarcoid unlikely Next step TestResultMeans Exertional and progressive → EchocardiographyChest CT Tricuspid regurgitation, raised estimated pressure Pulmonary hypertension; catheterization confirms Honeycombing Fibrosis; restrictive function Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Nocturnal and intermittent → Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator Obstruction that reverses Asthma SkipSerum angiotensin-converting enzyme: neither sensitive nor specific, even with sarcoid suspected; sarcoid has no link to sickle cell disease, and the chest film leads.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Polyuria and nocturia with dilute urine in a well patient Hyposthenuria of sickle cell trait Hemoglobin electrophoresis if trait is not known Trait with a stressor: air travel, dehydration, sepsis Splenic infarction Hemoglobin electrophoresis Infant with swollen, tender hands and feet Dactylitis Analgesics and fluids Fever and bone pain Osteomyelitis: Salmonella most often, then S. aureus Cover both: vancomycin or clindamycin plus ceftriaxone

Pause point Trait or disease? Offered: a solubility test Electrophoresis reads the genotype → Electrophoresis Uncomplicated pain crisis Offered: a transfusion Uncomplicated → Analgesics and fluids Weeks of night cough Offered: a CT angiogram The night cough → Spirometry

1 Alongsideevery child with sickle cell disease Daily oral penicillin until at least 5 years; pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae, meningococcal and influenza vaccines; folic acid 2 1st lineall children, to prevent crises Hydroxyurea How it worksHydroxyureaRaises fetal hemoglobin, which dilutes HbS and slows sickling: fewer pain crises, less acute chest syndrome, fewer transfusions. Watch the counts: neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; not in pregnancy. 3 Pain crisisuncomplicated vaso-occlusive pain Opioids; a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), with care in kidney disease; normal intravascular volume; oxygen only for hypoxia Transfusion does not help an uncomplicated pain crisis. 4 Transfuseacute chest syndrome, stroke, sepsis, symptomatic sequestration or aplastic crisis Simple transfusion to correct anemia; exchange for severe acute chest syndrome or stroke 5 Curerepeated severe complications Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only cure

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Fever, looks ill Cultures, admission, ceftriaxone Fever alone may not need admission Acute chest syndrome Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; oxygen; transfusion Severe: exchange transfusion Splenic sequestration Transfuse slowly Hyperviscosity as trapped cells return Aplastic crisis Simple transfusion Recovers as the infection clears Stroke Exchange transfusion Then chronic transfusion, HbS under 30% Asthma Inhaled bronchodilator and corticosteroid, as for anyone Treating it also prevents acute chest syndrome

Follow-up decisions When Do Sickle cell disease, ages 2 to 16 Transcranial Doppler yearly; high risk chronic exchange transfusion, HbS under 30% Frequent transfusions Screen for iron overload; chelation On hydroxyurea Blood counts; dose adjusted to counts and side effects Two parents with trait Autosomal recessive: genetic counseling; prenatal DNA testing Sickle cell trait No anemia or crises; explain the hematuria and hard-exertion risks
Life span now over 50 years; acute chest syndrome and infection lead the causes of death.

Workup1 of 27 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night Prior acute chest syndrome; family sarcoid history Normal vital signs · lungs clear · no edema · normal chest x-ray · Echocardiography · Computed tomography pulmonary angiography · Spirometry with bronchodilator testing 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night Prior acute chest syndrome; family sarcoid history Normal vital signs · lungs clear · no edema · normal chest x-ray Spirometry with bronchodilator testingnocturnal and intermittent means airway, so the first test is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, looking for obstruction that reverses; clear lungs do not argue against it, since wheezing is often absent when symptoms are mild or intermittent. The angiogram answers an embolism, acute and persistent with tachycardia and hypoxia; the echocardiogram answers exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs. The prior acute chest syndrome makes asthma more likely, and a family history of sarcoidosis does not explain this picture

Diagnosis2 of 27 1-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 60%, HbS 40% complete blood count normal Asymptomatic; her older sister has sickle cell anemia Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile · Sickle cell trait · Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia · Sickle cell anemia 1-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 60%, HbS 40% complete blood count normal Asymptomatic; her older sister has sickle cell anemia Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile Sickle cell traitHbA exceeding HbS with a completely normal blood count is trait, not disease. Sickle cell anemia has no HbA at all; sickle-beta-plus thalassemia has HbA but S exceeds A, with a low MCV. The affected sister makes the disease complications look plausible; the most common complication of trait is painless hematuria

Next step3 of 27 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of pleuritic chest pain chest x-ray shows a new left lower lobe infiltrate T 38.9 °C · oxygen saturation 88% on room air · HR 118/min · Spirometry with bronchodilator testing · Echocardiography · Transfusion with antibiotic therapy 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of pleuritic chest pain chest x-ray shows a new left lower lobe infiltrate T 38.9 °C · oxygen saturation 88% on room air · HR 118/min Transfusion with antibiotic therapyfever, hypoxia, chest pain and a new infiltrate are acute chest syndrome, pulmonary vasoocclusion often with infection: transfuse and give antibiotics. Spirometry is for chronic, nocturnal airway symptoms, and echocardiography for exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs

Diagnosis4 of 27 20-year-old man with sickle cell trait nocturia and polyuria Otherwise healthy; takes no medications or diuretics urinalysis shows no glucose and no protein Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · Central diabetes insipidus · Chronic kidney disease · Hyposthenuria 20-year-old man with sickle cell trait nocturia and polyuria Otherwise healthy; takes no medications or diuretics urinalysis shows no glucose and no protein Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Hyposthenuriathe renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic, the one site that sickles a carrier's cells, so trait impairs urinary concentrating ability: hyposthenuria. Central diabetes insipidus is a pituitary defect; trait alone explains a medullary concentrating defect, and a normal creatinine with no protein argues against chronic kidney disease

Workup5 of 27 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease exertional dyspnea jugular venous distension and pedal edema loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound No nocturnal cough or chest tightness Afebrile · HR 98/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air · Spirometry with bronchodilator testing · CT scan of the chest · Echocardiography 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease exertional dyspnea jugular venous distension and pedal edema loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound No nocturnal cough or chest tightness Afebrile · HR 98/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air Echocardiographyexertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs is pulmonary hypertension from chronic hemolysis and vasculopathy: echocardiography shows tricuspid regurgitation with a raised estimated pulmonary pressure, and catheterization confirms. Spirometry answers nocturnal, intermittent airway symptoms, and chest computed tomography answers progressive fibrosis

Diagnosis6 of 27 1-year-old girl has laboratory results reviewed at a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 90% hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL reticulocytes 14% Parents ask what her results mean Afebrile · growth at the 25th percentile · Hemoglobin SC disease · Sickle cell trait · Sickle cell anemia 1-year-old girl has laboratory results reviewed at a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 90% hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL reticulocytes 14% Parents ask what her results mean Afebrile · growth at the 25th percentile Sickle cell anemiano HbA with about 90% HbS, anemia and reticulocytes of 10 to 20% is sickle cell anemia: ensure penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination. Trait keeps HbA above HbS with a normal blood count, and hemoglobin SC has HbS about equal to HbC with no HbA and a milder anemia

Diagnosis7 of 27 9-month-old boy has painful swelling of the hands and feet Previously well; no recent trauma; family history unknown fingers and toes diffusely swollen and tender Afebrile · hemoglobin 7 g/dL · reticulocytes 12% · Juvenile idiopathic arthritis · Sickle cell trait · Dactylitis 9-month-old boy has painful swelling of the hands and feet Previously well; no recent trauma; family history unknown fingers and toes diffusely swollen and tender Afebrile · hemoglobin 7 g/dL · reticulocytes 12% Dactylitispainful swelling of the hands and feet is dactylitis, often the first presentation of sickle cell disease; trait carries no anemia and none of the disease complications, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis does not explain a hemoglobin of 7 with a high reticulocyte count

Workup8 of 27 24-year-old woman with sickle cell disease 1 year of progressive dyspnea on exertion chest x-ray shows increased reticular markings No edema; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 93% on room air · CT pulmonary angiogram · Spirometry with bronchodilator testing · CT scan of the chest 24-year-old woman with sickle cell disease 1 year of progressive dyspnea on exertion chest x-ray shows increased reticular markings No edema; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 93% on room air CT scan of the chestprogressive exertional dyspnea with reticular markings is fibrosis from repeated vasoocclusive lung injury; chest computed tomography shows honeycombing, and pulmonary function testing is restrictive. Spirometry with bronchodilator testing answers nocturnal, intermittent airway symptoms, and the pulmonary angiogram answers an acute, persistent embolism with tachycardia and hypoxia

Diagnosis9 of 27 2-year-old boy is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 15%, HbS 70% mean corpuscular volume 68 fL Parents ask whether he has sickle cell trait Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL · Sickle cell trait · Sickle-beta-zero thalassemia · Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia 2-year-old boy is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 15%, HbS 70% mean corpuscular volume 68 fL Parents ask whether he has sickle cell trait Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL Sickle-beta-plus thalassemiaHbA present but S exceeding A, with a low MCV, is sickle-beta-plus thalassemia, the sharpest mimic of trait. In trait HbA exceeds HbS with a normal blood count, and sickle-beta-zero has no HbA at all

Diagnosis10 of 27 22-year-old man with sickle cell trait collapses during military basic training diffuse muscle pain and weakness dark urine Lungs clear on examination T 37.4 °C · HR 116/min · creatine kinase 48,000 U/L · Heat stroke alone · Exertional rhabdomyolysis · Acute chest syndrome 22-year-old man with sickle cell trait collapses during military basic training diffuse muscle pain and weakness dark urine Lungs clear on examination T 37.4 °C · HR 116/min · creatine kinase 48,000 U/L Exertional rhabdomyolysistrait carries a real risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis and sudden death under extreme exertion, which is why it matters in recruits. Acute chest syndrome is a complication of disease, not of a carrier, and the lungs are clear; heat stroke alone does not fit a normal temperature

Next step11 of 27 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night spirometry shows airway obstruction that improves after albuterol Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air · Oral glucocorticoid taper alone · Chronic transfusion therapy · Inhaled corticosteroid with a short-acting bronchodilator 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night spirometry shows airway obstruction that improves after albuterol Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air Inhaled corticosteroid with a short-acting bronchodilatorasthma in sickle cell disease is treated as asthma is in anyone else, with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids, and control also lowers the risk of the next acute chest syndrome. Chronic transfusion does not treat reversible airway obstruction, and an oral glucocorticoid taper alone leaves out the inhaled treatment

Diagnosis12 of 27 3-year-old boy with sickle cell anemia has a high fever hypotension and tachycardia leukocytosis with bandemia Vaccinations up to date; no bone pain T 39.5 °C · BP 70/40 mm Hg · HR 168/min · leukocytes 24,000/mm3 · Salmonella species · Staphylococcus aureus · Streptococcus pneumoniae 3-year-old boy with sickle cell anemia has a high fever hypotension and tachycardia leukocytosis with bandemia Vaccinations up to date; no bone pain T 39.5 °C · BP 70/40 mm Hg · HR 168/min · leukocytes 24,000/mm3 Streptococcus pneumoniaepneumococcus remains the leading cause of sepsis in sickle cell disease despite vaccination (non-vaccine serotypes): start empiric ceftriaxone. Salmonella is the leading cause of osteomyelitis, and there is no bone pain; Staphylococcus aureus is not the leading septic organism

Diagnosis13 of 27 16-year-old boy has 3 months of right hip pain radiograph shows avascular necrosis of the femoral head retinopathy on dilated eye examination hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 50%, HbC 48% Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL · Hemoglobin SC disease · Sickle cell anemia · Sickle-beta-zero thalassemia 16-year-old boy has 3 months of right hip pain radiograph shows avascular necrosis of the femoral head retinopathy on dilated eye examination hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 50%, HbC 48% Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL Hemoglobin SC diseaseno HbA with HbS about equal to HbC and a milder anemia is hemoglobin SC disease, whose retinopathy and avascular necrosis run out of proportion to the anemia. Sickle cell anemia and sickle-beta-zero thalassemia both have high HbS with no HbC; the 48% HbC decides

Workup14 of 27 20-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has sudden pleuritic chest pain tachycardic and short of breath at rest Chest x-ray clear; no new infiltrate Afebrile · HR 124/min · oxygen saturation 89% on room air · CT pulmonary angiogram · Serum ACE activity · Spirometry with bronchodilator testing 20-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has sudden pleuritic chest pain tachycardic and short of breath at rest Chest x-ray clear; no new infiltrate Afebrile · HR 124/min · oxygen saturation 89% on room air CT pulmonary angiogramacute, persistent pleuritic pain with tachycardia and hypoxia and a clear film is embolism, and sickle cell disease raises thrombotic risk: computed tomography angiography shows the filling defect. Spirometry answers chronic nocturnal airway symptoms, and serum ACE answers sarcoidosis, which is not associated with sickle cell disease

Diagnosis15 of 27 19-year-old woman with sickle cell trait left upper quadrant pain began after a high-altitude flight yesterday Lungs clear; no chest pain Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL · oxygen saturation 98% · Splenic infarction · Splenic sequestration · Acute chest syndrome 19-year-old woman with sickle cell trait left upper quadrant pain began after a high-altitude flight yesterday Lungs clear; no chest pain Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL · oxygen saturation 98% Splenic infarctionsplenic infarction is real in trait, at altitude, though uncommon. Acute chest syndrome is a complication of disease, not of a carrier, and the lungs are clear; a normal hemoglobin argues against sequestration

Mechanism16 of 27 13-year-old boy with sickle cell disease was diagnosed with asthma last year His mother asks why his asthma and his acute chest syndrome episodes each seem to raise the risk of the other Afebrile · Hydroxyurea causes bronchial irritation · Chronic transfusion raises pulmonary vascular iron deposition · Parenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculature 13-year-old boy with sickle cell disease was diagnosed with asthma last year His mother asks why his asthma and his acute chest syndrome episodes each seem to raise the risk of the other Afebrile Parenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculatureparenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculature, and acute chest syndrome in turn worsens airway hyperreactivity, so treating the asthma is also acute chest syndrome prevention. Hydroxyurea bronchial irritation and transfusional iron in the pulmonary vessels are not the link

Diagnosis17 of 27 2-week-old boy is seen for a weight check newborn screen reported as FAS Parents ask what the result means and whether he needs treatment Born at term; feeding well Afebrile · examination normal · Hemoglobin SC disease · Sickle cell anemia · Sickle cell trait 2-week-old boy is seen for a weight check newborn screen reported as FAS Parents ask what the result means and whether he needs treatment Born at term; feeding well Afebrile · examination normal Sickle cell traitFAS is trait and FS is disease; F leads because fetal hemoglobin predominates at birth, and the A shows HbA is present, which excludes sickle cell anemia; hemoglobin SC has no HbA. Counsel the parents; no treatment

Diagnosis18 of 27 22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has a cough chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy anterior uveitis and hypercalcemia No exertional dyspnea; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · Asthma · Pulmonary fibrosis from sickle cell disease · Sarcoidosis 22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has a cough chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy anterior uveitis and hypercalcemia No exertional dyspnea; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% Sarcoidosisbilateral hilar adenopathy with uveitis and hypercalcemia points to sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas); the chest film makes the diagnosis, and it is not associated with sickle cell disease, so the film decides, not the sickle history. Fibrosis shows reticular markings and honeycombing rather than hilar nodes, and asthma leaves the film normal

Diagnosis19 of 27 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has sudden pallor reticulocyte count 0.2% spleen not palpable Tired for 3 days; no jaundice or dark urine Afebrile · HR 124/min · hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL · Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis · Hyperhemolytic crisis · Splenic sequestration 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has sudden pallor reticulocyte count 0.2% spleen not palpable Tired for 3 days; no jaundice or dark urine Afebrile · HR 124/min · hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisisa reticulocyte count near zero means the marrow has stopped: parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis. Splenic sequestration would bring an enlarging spleen, and hyperhemolysis would bring jaundice and dark urine with a responding marrow

Diagnosis20 of 27 28-year-old man with sickle cell trait has 2 weeks of painless hematuria imaging shows a mass in the right kidney No flank pain or fever Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg · Papillary necrosis · Clear cell renal carcinoma · Renal medullary carcinoma 28-year-old man with sickle cell trait has 2 weeks of painless hematuria imaging shows a mass in the right kidney No flank pain or fever Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg Renal medullary carcinomarenal medullary carcinoma is rare but nearly pathognomonic for trait; painless hematuria in a carrier is usually medullary sickling, and imaging is what excludes the carcinoma. Clear cell carcinoma is not the trait-linked tumor, and papillary necrosis makes no mass

Workup21 of 27 15-year-old boy with sickle cell disease intermittent chest tightness and cough worse at night and with exercise no wheezing on examination Pulmonary function testing is ordered Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% · chest x-ray normal · Airway obstruction that reverses after bronchodilator administration · Reduced diffusing capacity with normal spirometry · A restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity 15-year-old boy with sickle cell disease intermittent chest tightness and cough worse at night and with exercise no wheezing on examination Pulmonary function testing is ordered Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% · chest x-ray normal Airway obstruction that reverses after bronchodilator administrationasthma is confirmed by pulmonary function testing showing airway obstruction that reverses with a bronchodilator; absent wheeze does not exclude it. A restrictive pattern points to fibrosis, and a low diffusing capacity with normal spirometry shows no obstruction to reverse

Diagnosis22 of 27 3-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 88%, HbA2 elevated mean corpuscular volume 64 fL Painful swelling of the hands at 10 months Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · reticulocytes 11% · Sickle cell anemia · Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia · Sickle-beta-zero thalassemia 3-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 88%, HbA2 elevated mean corpuscular volume 64 fL Painful swelling of the hands at 10 months Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · reticulocytes 11% Sickle-beta-zero thalassemiano HbA, high HbS and a raised HbA2 with a low MCV is sickle-beta-zero thalassemia: it looks like HbSS but is microcytic. Sickle cell anemia shares the absent HbA but is not microcytic, and sickle-beta-plus keeps some HbA; the raised HbA2 decides

Diagnosis23 of 27 14-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has chest pain chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate Cough began yesterday; no leg swelling T 38.6 °C · oxygen saturation 87% on room air · HR 120/min · Acute chest syndrome · Pulmonary embolism · Pneumonia alone 14-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has chest pain chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate Cough began yesterday; no leg swelling T 38.6 °C · oxygen saturation 87% on room air · HR 120/min Acute chest syndromechest pain, hypoxia and a new infiltrate in sickle cell disease is acute chest syndrome, pulmonary vasoocclusion often with infection, treated with transfusion and antibiotics. Calling it pneumonia alone leaves out the transfusion, and embolism gives a clear film with a filling defect on angiography

Mechanism24 of 27 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait asks about future children her partner also carries sickle cell trait Neither has anemia; both have normal blood counts They plan their first pregnancy next year · 50% Disease per pregnancy · All children will carry trait · 25% Disease, 50% trait, 25% unaffected 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait asks about future children her partner also carries sickle cell trait Neither has anemia; both have normal blood counts They plan their first pregnancy next year 25% Disease, 50% trait, 25% unaffectedtwo carriers each pass a sickle gene half the time, so each pregnancy carries 25% disease, 50% trait and 25% unaffected; 50% disease overstates the risk, and not every child carries trait

Avoid25 of 27 14-year-old girl with sickle cell disease intermittent dry nocturnal cough for several weeks Family history of sarcoidosis; no exertional dyspnea Her parents ask which tests she needs Afebrile · lungs clear · no film yet · Spirometry with bronchodilator testing · Serum ACE activity · Chest x-ray 14-year-old girl with sickle cell disease intermittent dry nocturnal cough for several weeks Family history of sarcoidosis; no exertional dyspnea Her parents ask which tests she needs Afebrile · lungs clear · no film yet Serum ACE activityserum ACE has poor sensitivity and specificity, sarcoidosis is not associated with sickle cell disease, and nothing suggests hilar adenopathy, so it should not be ordered first. The chest x-ray comes first and is expected to be normal in asthma; spirometry with bronchodilator testing then confirms

Diagnosis26 of 27 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops sudden hemiparesis right arm and leg weaker than left no headache before onset Noncontrast computed tomography of the head shows no bleeding Afebrile · BP 104/62 mm Hg · glucose 92 mg/dL · Complicated migraine · Hemorrhagic stroke · Ischemic stroke 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops sudden hemiparesis right arm and leg weaker than left no headache before onset Noncontrast computed tomography of the head shows no bleeding Afebrile · BP 104/62 mm Hg · glucose 92 mg/dL Ischemic strokesudden hemiparesis in sickle cell disease is an ischemic stroke, a disease complication no carrier gets: treat with exchange transfusion. A scan without blood argues against hemorrhage, and no headache argues against a complicated migraine

Diagnosis27 of 27 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait is 24 weeks pregnant 2 days of dysuria No flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase and nitrites Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 88/min · Urinary tract infection · Painless hematuria · Pyelonephritis from papillary necrosis 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait is 24 weeks pregnant 2 days of dysuria No flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase and nitrites Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 88/min Urinary tract infectiondysuria in a pregnant carrier is a urinary tract infection. Hematuria is the commonest trait complication but is painless, and pyelonephritis would bring fever and flank pain

Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome: painless hematuria, the commonest trait complication. Part II Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: the sickle cell stroke among the other pediatric causes. Part I Asthma: what follows once spirometry confirms. Part I Obstructive Lung Disease: the adult version of the which-test question.

Read a supplied lab panel first; it usually excludes most of the differential in one line. A dramatic chronic disease sets the prior for its own complications but does not suspend the base rate of common disease. Ask what the timing of the complaint means before asking what the known diagnosis predisposes to.
