Day symptoms, night wakings and FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) set the severity the NAEPP (National Asthma Education and Prevention Program) step: intermittent, a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) alone; persistent, add an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS), then a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator: FEV1 up >12% asthma; normal spirometry, still suspected methacholine challenge Severe attack: SABA ipratropium systemic steroids oxygen; wheeze fading while hypoxemia persists intubate

What it is Hyperresponsive airways that narrow reversibly Driver Airway inflammation parasympathetic tone bronchoconstriction Triggers Allergens (atopic asthma), smoke, irritant fumes, cold air, viral infections, exercise Aspirin in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease; nonselective beta-blockers Reflux at night Chain Inflamed, twitchy airways reversible narrowing wheeze, cough, tight chest; worse at night as it gets more severe Severe attack air trapping too little airflow to wheeze hypoxemia, then respiratory failure Insights A rescue inhaler used 4 days a week is not intermittent asthma: count the days, then step up to a daily controller A quiet chest in a tiring patient is air trapping, not recovery
Symptoms episodic wheeze, cough, tight chest Reversibility FEV1 up >12% and >200 mL after a bronchodilator

Severe attackAcute, severe exacerbation Every patient: albuterol (SABA) with ipratropium, systemic steroids, oxygen Steroid route Watch forOral prednisone preferred; intravenous is acceptable. At discharge, prednisone 40 to 60 mg daily for 5 to 7 days lowers relapse and admission. If there is no improvement after an hour, choose one dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate. FailingAltered consciousness, cyanosis, saturation <90%, PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) <60 mm Hg, PaCO2 (arterial carbon dioxide) >45 mm Hg Wheeze fades while hypoxemia persists: silent chest from air trapping Hypoxemia If respiratory failure persists despite escalating treatment, choose intubation. HistoryPast respiratory failure needing ventilation The single greatest risk factor for a life-threatening attack

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Asthma Episodic wheeze, cough, tight chest; worse at night; lungs usually normal between attacks Usually before 40; FEV1 up >12% after a bronchodilator COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) Smoker; productive cough first 40s and 50s; partial or no reversal after the bronchodilator Paradoxical vocal fold motion (vocal cord dysfunction) "Asthma" that fails usual therapy; inspiratory stridor, not expiratory wheeze Flat inspiratory loop; FVC (forced vital capacity) and ratio normal Cough-variant asthma Chronic dry cough is the main symptom; often at night Normal spirometry; methacholine challenge Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Asthma or cystic fibrosis with eosinophilia An IgE-mediated (immunoglobulin E) reaction; worked up in the structural lung brief Heart failure (cardiac asthma) Wheeze with progressive dyspnea and orthopnea Bilateral crackles and leg edema

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Episodic wheeze, cough or chest tightness → Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator FEV1 up >12% (and >200 mL) Asthma Little or no reversal COPD more likely Targeted tests TestResultMeans Symptoms at work, better at home → Serial peak flow at home and at work 20% or more lower at work Occupational asthma Fails asthma therapy; inspiratory stridor → Flow-volume loop Flat inspiratory loop, normal ratio Paradoxical vocal fold motion Next step TestResultMeans Normal spirometry, asthma still suspected → Methacholine challenge FEV1 falls ≥20% (>12% in a child) Supports asthma Negative Rules asthma out (sensitive, not specific) SkipA chest film to diagnose asthma: often normal between attacks.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Sickle cell disease with wheeze Asthma: common, and it raises acute chest syndrome risk Spirometry first, as for anyone Sickle Cell Disease and Trait Night cough while already on a proton pump inhibitor Reflux unlikely; asthma Pulmonary function tests for bronchodilator response Asthma, nasal polyps, wheeze after aspirin Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease Avoid aspirin and other cyclooxygenase-1 inhibitors

Pause point Wheezes “only now and then” but reaches for the rescue inhaler 4 days a week Read as “only now and then” Severity comes from the counts, not the impression → Persistent asthma: a daily controller

NAEPP severity, age 5 and older Class Day symptoms Night wakings FEV1 Start Intermittent ≤2 days a week ≤2 a month >80% SABA as needed Mild persistent >2 days a week, not daily 3 to 4 a month >80% Add low-dose ICS Moderate persistent Daily >1 a week, not nightly 60 to 80% Low-dose ICS with a LABA, or medium-dose ICS Severe persistent Throughout the day Often nightly <60% High-dose ICS with a LABA

In practice In practiceIn practice: UWorld now follows GINA (Global Initiative for Asthma), which does not support a short-acting beta-agonist alone at any step; even intermittent asthma gets an inhaled corticosteroid, as needed with formoterol or with the reliever. Intermittent symptoms still mean ongoing airway inflammation. NBME still keys NAEPP: a ladder of "nothing extra, montelukast, low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, add a long-acting beta-agonist" marks a NAEPP question.

1 Every patientfrom diagnosis A SABA for quick relief at every step; avoid triggers; a written action plan Before exercise, the SABA prevents exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. 2 Mildmild persistent Add a daily low-dose ICS Montelukast (a leukotriene antagonist) can be added at any step. 3 Moderatemoderate persistent, or not controlled Low-dose ICS plus a LABA, or a medium-dose ICS Before any step up: adherence, inhaler technique, triggers, other conditions. 4 Severesevere persistent High-dose ICS plus a LABA 5 Addstill not controlled Add oral steroids

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Symptoms only with exercise A SABA before exercise; not exercise avoidance Daily symptoms, or the SABA fails: start a controller A LABA is considered Always with an ICS Never a LABA alone Theophylline among the options Never the answer on the exam An old oral adenosine antagonist, kept for its low cost Pregnancy Expect worsening if asthma was severe or poorly controlled Often in the second trimester Needs a beta-blocker Avoid nonselective agents They worsen asthma

Follow-up decisions When Do Well controlled for 3 months or more Consider stepping down Thrush on an ICS A spacer and rinsing the mouth after each dose Every patient Spirometry at least every 1 to 2 years

Diagnosis1 of 6 9 yo M, symptoms 1 day per week, night waking once a month, normal FEV₁ · Intermittent · Mild persistent · Moderate persistent 9 yo M, symptoms 1 day per week, night waking once a month, normal FEV₁ IntermittentSABA as needed

Diagnosis2 of 6 9 yo M, symptoms 4 days per week, 3 nights a month, FEV₁ 85% · Intermittent · Moderate persistent · Mild persistent 9 yo M, symptoms 4 days per week, 3 nights a month, FEV₁ 85% Mild persistentlow-dose inhaled corticosteroid

Diagnosis3 of 6 9 yo M with daily symptoms, weekly night waking, FEV₁ 70% · Moderate persistent · Mild persistent · Severe persistent 9 yo M with daily symptoms, weekly night waking, FEV₁ 70% Moderate persistentlow-dose ICS plus LABA

Diagnosis4 of 6 9 yo M with symptoms throughout the day, nightly waking, FEV₁ 55% · Moderate persistent · Severe persistent · Mild persistent 9 yo M with symptoms throughout the day, nightly waking, FEV₁ 55% Severe persistent

Next step5 of 6 9 yo M using his rescue inhaler four times a week · Add a LABA without an ICS · Step up to a daily controller – this is not intermittent asthma · Continue SABA alone 9 yo M using his rescue inhaler four times a week Step up to a daily controller – this is not intermittent asthma

Next step6 of 6 9 yo M with symptoms only on exertion, otherwise well · Daily montelukast · Daily inhaled corticosteroid · SABA before exercise 9 yo M with symptoms only on exertion, otherwise well SABA before exercise

briefs.title: Liver Disease in Pregnancy
briefs.sub: normal pregnancy liver tests · the gestational age clock · placental alkaline phosphatase · bile acids · acute fatty liver vs hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets (HELLP)Which liver disease fits this week of pregnancy, and is the pregnancy causing it at all?
blocks: normal pregnancy liver tests · the gestational age clock · placental alkaline phosphatase · bile acids · acute fatty liver vs hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets (HELLP)Which liver disease fits this week of pregnancy, and is the pregnancy causing it at all?

Gestational age sorts it: severe vomiting with weight loss from about 5 to 18 weeks is hyperemesis gravidarum; itching in the 2nd or 3rd trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis; after 20 weeks with hemolysis and low platelets is HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets); near term, liver failure is acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP). An isolated alkaline phosphatase rise, up to 2 to 3 times normal at term with normal AST, ALT and bilirubin, is placental: reassure. HELLP and AFLP are treated by delivery; intrahepatic cholestasis gets ursodeoxycholic acid and delivery at 37 weeks.

What it is Liver test changes in pregnancy: physiologic (placental alkaline phosphatase), pregnancy-specific (hyperemesis, intrahepatic cholestasis, HELLP, AFLP) or unrelated to pregnancy (viral hepatitis, the most common cause of jaundice). Driver A different driver for each: hormones apparently exaggerating bile stasis, a possible inherited defect in fatty acid oxidation, platelet activation possibly from endothelial dysfunction, or vomiting. Triggers Maternal LCHAD (long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) variant: AFLP risk 20 times higher non-modifiable ; cholestasis in an earlier pregnancy non-modifiable ; ancestry from Bolivia or Chile (cholestasis) non-modifiable ; twins or a molar pregnancy behind hyperemesis non-modifiable ; oral contraceptives tend to bring the itch back Chain Intrahepatic cholestasis: pregnancy estrogen and progesterone normal bile stasis is exaggerated and bile excretion falls serum bile acids rise intense itching; preterm birth and stillbirth risk Insights Only alkaline phosphatase rises in a normal pregnancy, because the placenta makes it; a raised AST, ALT or bilirubin is disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid eases the itch and the labs but does not lower fetal complications, so the timing of delivery protects the fetus.

What each disease doesby disease; supports, never diagnoses Itching first, then sometimes dark urine and jaundice; no painHormones apparently exaggerate the normal bile stasis of pregnancy Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, anemia, bruisingEndothelial dysfunction possibly activates platelets; a swollen liver may stretch its capsule Nausea, vomiting, jaundice, then in severe cases liver failureSmall fat droplets fill hepatocytes; tied to LCHAD variants Vomiting with weight loss and ketosis; jaundice, if present, usually mildLosing gastric acid causes a metabolic alkalosis Alkaline phosphatase up to 2 to 3 times normal at termThe placenta makes the enzyme; the liver is normal

5 to 18 weekshyperemesis gravidarum; vomiting usually peaks near 9 weeks After 20 weekspreeclampsia and HELLP possible; most after 34 weeks 2nd or 3rd trimesterintrahepatic cholestasis; itching comes first Third trimesteralkaline phosphatase climbs from the placenta Near termacute fatty liver of pregnancy Up to 6 weeks postpartumpreeclampsia can still begin, most often within 4 days

HELLP syndrome Criterion Cutoff Hemolysis Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 600 units/L or more; schistocytes on smear Elevated Liver enzymes Aminotransferases over 2 times normal Low Platelets Under 100,000
Intrahepatic cholestasis Test Cutoff Fasting total bile acids Above 10 micromol/L; may be the only abnormal test

Act now Finding Action Near term with vomiting, jaundice, low glucose and prolonged clotting Acute fatty liver of pregnancy: deliver promptly. After 20 weeks with hypertension, right upper quadrant pain and platelets under 100,000 HELLP syndrome: magnesium sulfate and blood pressure control, then delivery. HELLP syndrome with sudden severe hypotension Suspect rupture of a subcapsular liver hematoma. Prolonged vomiting with confusion, ataxia or abnormal eye movements Wernicke encephalopathy: thiamine before any dextrose.

Liver disease in pregnancy Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2nd or 3rd trimester; intense itching, worst at night, classically of the palms and soles ⚠︎; no rash, no pain. Order fasting serum bile acids. HELLP syndrome After 20 weeks; right upper quadrant pain, hemolysis with schistocytes, platelets under 100,000; up to 15% may lack hypertension. CBC with smear and LDH; delivery. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) Near term; nausea, vomiting, jaundice and liver failure, in which low glucose may occur and prolonged clotting is common; aminotransferases may stay under 500. Glucose and clotting tests; prompt delivery. Placental alkaline phosphatase Third trimester; alkaline phosphatase up to 2 to 3 times normal; AST, ALT and bilirubin normal; no symptoms. Reassure; no further tests. Hyperemesis gravidarum 5 to 18 weeks; vomiting with weight loss over 5%, ketosis, metabolic alkalosis; jaundice, if present, usually mild. Check urine ketones, electrolytes, BUN and creatinine; give IV fluids. Acute viral hepatitis Any trimester; the most common cause of jaundice in pregnancy; hepatitis E may run more severe. Order A to E serologies. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) Before 20 weeks; obesity, diabetes, raised ALT, echogenic liver; not pregnancy-specific. Order a liver US and hepatitis serologies.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Pregnant patient with abnormal liver tests or itching → AST, ALT, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase Alkaline phosphatase alone, up to 2 to 3 times normal Placental: reassure AST or ALT raised Disease: match the gestational age to the targeted tests Targeted tests TestResultMeans Itching in the 2nd or 3rd trimester, no rash → Fasting serum bile acids Above 10 micromol/L Intrahepatic cholestasis: ursodeoxycholic acid 100 micromol/L or more Deliver at 36 weeks After 20 weeks with hypertension or right upper quadrant pain → CBC with smear and LDH; blood pressure and urine protein Schistocytes, platelets under 100,000, LDH 600 or more, aminotransferases over twice normal HELLP syndrome: delivery Near term with vomiting, jaundice or confusion → Glucose, prothrombin time with international normalized ratio (INR), creatinine and ammonia Low glucose, prolonged clotting, rising creatinine AFLP, a liver failure: delivery Vomiting from 5 to 18 weeks with weight loss → Urine ketones, electrolytes, BUN and creatinine Ketonuria, metabolic alkalosis Hyperemesis gravidarum Ketonuria and metabolic alkalosis: next test → Obstetric US Molar pregnancy or twins A cause of the vomiting Raised ALT before 20 weeks, or jaundice at any stage → Hepatitis A to E serologies Positive Viral hepatitis Negative result, liver tests still raised → Liver US Echogenic liver with obesity or diabetes MASLD, unrelated to pregnancy Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Suspected AFLP → Clinical criteria, liver tests and hepatitis serologies; biopsy when done Small fat droplets in hepatocytes, usually with little necrosis Acute fatty liver of pregnancy SkipRight upper quadrant US or bile acids for an isolated alkaline phosphatase rise late in pregnancy: the placenta makes it, and AST, ALT and bilirubin stay normal.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Itching with no rash, pain or systemic symptoms Intrahepatic cholestasis Order fasting bile acids. Low glucose and prolonged clotting near term AFLP, which is liver failure Plan prompt delivery. Normal blood pressure with hemolysis and low platelets after 20 weeks HELLP still: up to 15% may lack hypertension CBC with smear and LDH. The same itch in a past pregnancy or on oral contraceptives Recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis Order fasting bile acids. Vomiting that began near 5 weeks Hyperemesis gravidarum Check urine ketones, electrolytes, BUN and creatinine. Alkaline phosphatase 3 times normal in the third trimester, all else normal Placental enzyme Reassure.
Pause point Raised alkaline phosphatase late in pregnancy Read as cholestatic No itching, normal bile acids and normal AST, ALT and bilirubin → Placental

Risk and timing Finding Meaning Bile acids above 40 micromol/L Fetal demise more likely Bile acids 100 micromol/L or more Deliver at 36 weeks HELLP at 34 weeks or more Deliver now, after stabilizing HELLP under 34 weeks, mother and fetus stable Corticosteroids for the fetal lungs, then delivery AFLP with rapidly progressive liver failure High maternal and fetal mortality: deliver promptly

1 First lineIntrahepatic cholestasis Ursodeoxycholic acid for the itch and the labs; deliver at 37 weeks, or at 36 weeks when bile acids are 100 micromol/L or more. In practiceIn practice: the Merck Sharp and Dohme (MSD) Manual times delivery at 36 to 39 weeks when bile acids are under 100 micromol/L. 2 DefinitiveHELLP syndrome Magnesium sulfate against seizures and antihypertensives, then delivery; under 34 weeks and stable, corticosteroids first. 3 DefinitiveAcute fatty liver of pregnancy Prompt delivery is usually advised; depending on gestational age, this may mean ending the pregnancy. 4 First lineHyperemesis gravidarum IV fluids, electrolytes and antiemetics such as the antihistamine dimenhydrinate; thiamine before any dextrose.

After delivery Situation Do After intrahepatic cholestasis Itching usually settles within about 48 h of delivery; it tends to recur in later pregnancies and on oral contraceptives. After AFLP Test mother and infant for LCHAD variants; survivors recover fully without recurrence. After HELLP or preeclampsia Watch for postpartum onset, most often within 4 days and up to 6 weeks.

Diagnosis1 of 9 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intense palmar pruritus, raised bile acids and no rash · Acute fatty liver of pregnancyAFLP brings vomiting, jaundice and liver failure, not itching alone. · HELLP syndromeHELLP brings hemolysis, low platelets and usually hypertension. · Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancyItching with raised bile acids and no rash in the third trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intense palmar pruritus, raised bile acids and no rash Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancyursodeoxycholic acid

Diagnosis2 of 9 26 yo F at 36 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy and raised transaminases · Viral hepatitisViral hepatitis fits any trimester; near-term low glucose and clotting failure point to AFLP. · Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancyIntrahepatic cholestasis itches but does not cause liver failure. · Acute fatty liver of pregnancyLow glucose and prolonged clotting near term mean liver failure: acute fatty liver of pregnancy. 26 yo F at 36 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy and raised transaminases Acute fatty liver of pregnancyurgent delivery

Diagnosis3 of 9 26 yo F at 34 weeks with hypertension, hemolysis, high LFTs and platelets 68,000 · Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancyIntrahepatic cholestasis causes itching and raised bile acids, not hemolysis or low platelets. · HELLP syndromeHypertension, hemolysis, raised liver enzymes and platelets under 100,000 after 20 weeks is HELLP. · Acute fatty liver of pregnancyAFLP is liver failure with low glucose and prolonged clotting. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with hypertension, hemolysis, high LFTs and platelets 68,000 HELLP syndromedelivery

Diagnosis4 of 9 26 yo F at 9 weeks with intractable vomiting, ketonuria and mildly raised transaminases · Hyperemesis gravidarumIntractable vomiting at 9 weeks with ketonuria is hyperemesis gravidarum. · Acute fatty liver of pregnancyAFLP comes near term, not at 9 weeks. · Viral hepatitisViral hepatitis fits any trimester, but ketonuria from intractable vomiting points to hyperemesis. 26 yo F at 9 weeks with intractable vomiting, ketonuria and mildly raised transaminases Hyperemesis gravidarum

Diagnosis5 of 9 26 yo F at 14 weeks, obese with diabetes and raised transaminases · Viral hepatitisViral hepatitis fits any trimester, but obesity and diabetes point to MASLD; serologies sort it. · HELLP syndromeHELLP comes after 20 weeks, with hemolysis and low platelets. · Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease – the third-trimester diseases do not fit at 14 weeksAt 14 weeks, obesity and diabetes with raised transaminases fit MASLD, not a pregnancy-specific disease. 26 yo F at 14 weeks, obese with diabetes and raised transaminases Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease – the third-trimester diseases do not fit at 14 weeks

Diagnosis6 of 9 26 yo F at 30 weeks with an isolated alkaline phosphatase twice normal, all else normal · Cholestasis of pregnancyIntrahepatic cholestasis needs itching and raised bile acids. · Placental alkaline phosphatase – physiologicAn isolated alkaline phosphatase twice normal at 30 weeks is placental. · Biliary obstructionBiliary obstruction raises bilirubin and bile acids; here everything but alkaline phosphatase is normal. 26 yo F at 30 weeks with an isolated alkaline phosphatase twice normal, all else normal Placental alkaline phosphatase – physiologicreassurance

Next step7 of 9 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intractable palmar pruritus and raised bile acids, taking ursodeoxycholic acid · Immediate deliveryImmediate delivery at 34 weeks is for HELLP or AFLP, not stable cholestasis. · Delivery at 36 to 37 weeksIntrahepatic cholestasis is delivered at 37 weeks, or 36 if bile acids are 100 or more, for the stillbirth risk. · Delivery at 40 weeksWaiting to 40 weeks leaves the stillbirth risk; ursodeoxycholic acid does not lower fetal complications. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intractable palmar pruritus and raised bile acids, taking ursodeoxycholic acid Delivery at 36 to 37 weeksintrahepatic cholestasis carries stillbirth risk

Next step8 of 9 29 yo F at 35 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia and rising creatinine · Emergent deliveryAcute fatty liver of pregnancy is treated by prompt delivery. · Magnesium sulfate and expectant managementMagnesium sulfate is for preeclampsia with severe features; expectant care delays delivery, the treatment for AFLP. · Ursodeoxycholic acidUrsodeoxycholic acid treats intrahepatic cholestasis, not liver failure. 29 yo F at 35 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia and rising creatinine Emergent deliveryacute fatty liver of pregnancy is treated by delivering

Next step9 of 9 28 yo F at 32 weeks with alkaline phosphatase three times normal on routine labs; AST, ALT and bilirubin normal; no symptoms · Right upper quadrant ultrasoundRight upper quadrant US adds nothing when only alkaline phosphatase is raised. · ReassuranceAlkaline phosphatase 3 times normal at 32 weeks with normal AST, ALT and bilirubin is placental: reassure. · Serum bile acidsBile acids are for itching; this patient has no symptoms. 28 yo F at 32 weeks with alkaline phosphatase three times normal on routine labs; AST, ALT and bilirubin normal; no symptoms Reassurancethe placenta makes alkaline phosphatase

Alkaline phosphatase normally rises in pregnancy because the placenta makes its own isoenzyme; levels may reach 2 to 3 times normal at term. AST (aspartate aminotransferase), ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and bilirubin do not rise physiologically; any elevation is pathologic.

Liver labs in normal pregnancy Rises physiologically Falls physiologically Should stay normal Alkaline phosphatase (placental), white blood cell count (to ~15,000), erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen and factors VII/VIII/X, total thyroxine and thyroxine-binding globulin, cholesterol, glomerular filtration rate Hemoglobin (dilutional), platelets (mild gestational), creatinine and BUN, arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO₂), thyroid-stimulating hormone in the first trimester AST, ALT, bilirubin

Liver disease in pregnancy: by timing Condition Timing The tell Management Hyperemesis gravidarum About 5 to 18 weeks Vomiting, ketonuria, >5% weight loss Supportive Intrahepatic cholestasis 2nd or 3rd trimester Pruritus of palms and soles, worse at night; ↑bile acids, bilirubin sometimes raised; stillbirth risk Ursodeoxycholic acid; deliver at 37 weeks (36 if bile acids are 100 micromol/L or more) Preeclampsia / HELLP Emergency >20 wk Hypertension + proteinuria; Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets, right upper quadrant pain, schistocytes Delivery Acute fatty liver Emergency Near term Hypoglycemia, ↑ammonia, coagulopathy, ↑creatinine, encephalopathy; long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency link Emergent delivery

Hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, high ammonia and renal failure indicate AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy). Hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and more hypertension indicate HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome. Both are treated by delivering.
Before diagnosing a pregnancy-specific liver disease, check that the gestational age fits it.

briefs.title: Fatty Liver Disease
briefs.sub: aspartate aminotransferase (AST):alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio · causes to exclude · fibrosis staging · weight loss first · formerly nonalcoholic fatty liver diseaseIs the picture metabolic with ALT above AST, and have the other liver diseases been excluded?
blocks: aspartate aminotransferase (AST):alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio · causes to exclude · fibrosis staging · weight loss first · formerly nonalcoholic fatty liver diseaseIs the picture metabolic with ALT above AST, and have the other liver diseases been excluded?

Metabolic risk factors with ALT above AST (ratio usually under 1) and a bright liver on ultrasound is MASLD once alcohol, viral hepatitis, iron overload and drugs are excluded. Stage fibrosis noninvasively: the Fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4), then elastography; biopsy when the diagnosis or stage is unclear or portal hypertension is unexplained. Weight loss of 7 to 10% treats the liver; statins are safe and are used for dyslipidemia, since cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death.

What it is Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) or fatty liver: a fatty liver with at least one cardiometabolic risk factor and little or no alcohol. Driver Insulin resistance: free fatty acids flood the liver and hepatocytes make new fat. Triggers Obesity, the strongest; type 2 diabetes mellitus; dyslipidemia and hypertension ; older age non-modifiable ; male sex, Hispanic or Native American ancestry non-modifiable Chain Fat accumulates in hepatocytes (steatosis) ballooned hepatocytes and inflammation: metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), formerly nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) stellate cells lay down fibrosis cirrhosis with portal hypertension hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) Insights Fibrosis stage, not fat or enzyme level, predicts liver death; AST rising above ALT suggests advanced fibrosis. Cardiovascular disease, not liver failure, is the most common cause of death, so statins are used for dyslipidemia, not avoided.

MASLD requires Criterion Requires Steatosis On imaging, blood markers or biopsy Cardiometabolic factor At least 1 of the 5 below Limited alcohol No more than 2 drinks a day (women) or 3 (men) No other cause Viral hepatitis, iron overload, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, drugs

Cardiometabolic factors Factor Cutoff Weight Body mass index (BMI) over 25, over 23 in Asian patients, or a large waist Glucose Fasting over 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c over 5.7%, or diabetes Blood pressure Over 130/85 mm Hg or treated Triglycerides Over 150 mg/dL or treated High-density lipoprotein (HDL) Under 40 mg/dL (men) or 50 (women)

Board stems still call it a diagnosis of exclusion. In practiceIn practice: the newer criteria are positive ones, steatosis plus a cardiometabolic factor; in them hepatitis serology is helpful but not required, while the first workup still takes an alcohol and drug history and tests for hepatitis B and C.

Act now Finding Action Splenomegaly or low platelets in a patient with fatty liver Advanced fibrosis may be present: splenomegaly is usually the first sign of portal hypertension. Stage now: FIB-4, then elastography; biopsy if the cause is unclear. Normal examination in long-standing MASLD Does not exclude cirrhosis: MASH cirrhosis can be silent, so stage every patient.

Other causes of a fatty liver Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Alcohol-associated liver disease AST:ALT 2 or more; more than 2 drinks a day (women) or 3 (men) Obtain a corroborated drinking history; abstinence can reverse the steatosis. Drug-induced steatosis Amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, glucocorticoids or valproate on the list Review the drug list and stop the drug where possible. Chronic hepatitis B or C Positive hepatitis B surface antigen or hepatitis C virus antibody Viral hepatitis workup; the serology is part of the first panel. Hereditary hemochromatosis High ferritin; ferritin alone also rises in MASH Check transferrin saturation; if high, order genetic testing. Wilson disease Low ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings Measure urinary copper; Wilson Disease covers the workup.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Metabolic risk factors with raised liver enzymes, or a fatty liver seen by chance → AST and ALT ALT above AST, ratio usually under 1 Fits MASLD; a ratio of 2 or more points to alcohol → Liver ultrasound Hyperechoic (bright) liver Steatosis; ultrasound shows fat but not inflammation or fibrosis Targeted tests TestResultMeans Steatosis on ultrasound: exclude the other causes → Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody Negative Viral hepatitis excluded → Ferritin and transferrin saturation Ferritin up Common in MASH; with high transferrin saturation as well, it may suggest hemochromatosis Tremor, cognitive change or Kayser-Fleischer rings → Ceruloplasmin Low Wilson disease, not MASLD Every suspected MASLD → Lipids and fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c Abnormal Supplies the cardiometabolic risk factor Next step TestResultMeans MASLD established: stage fibrosis → FIB-4 score (age, platelets, AST, ALT) Low Advanced fibrosis unlikely; recheck periodically Not low (indeterminate or high) FIB-4 not low → Transient elastography Stiff liver Advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis: hepatology referral Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Clinical diagnosis → Steatosis, a cardiometabolic risk factor, limited alcohol and no other cause All present MASLD; MASH itself needs a biopsy, which many patients never need SkipLiver biopsy in every patient: invasive, so noninvasive staging comes first; keep it for an unclear diagnosis, discordant staging or unexplained portal hypertension.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step AST at least twice the ALT Alcohol-associated liver disease Obtain a corroborated drinking history; abstinence can reverse the steatosis. Mildly raised ferritin Common in MASH Check transferrin saturation for hemochromatosis. Low ceruloplasmin with Kayser-Fleischer rings Wilson disease Measure urinary copper. High low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol in MASLD Cardiovascular risk, the leading cause of death Start a statin.
Pause point Normal liver enzymes Read as excluding MASLD Enzyme levels are often normal in it → MASLD is not excluded

Stage and meaning Finding Meaning Simple steatosis Usually silent; progresses to MASH in 12 to 40% MASH Risk of fibrosis, cirrhosis and HCC; it can regress to steatosis Moderate to severe fibrosis (stage F2 to F3) Resmetirom candidate AST rising above ALT Suggests advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis, or another cause Cirrhosis Highest liver risk: HCC and varices

1 EveryoneEvery patient with MASLD Diet and exercise for 7 to 10% weight loss; avoid alcohol; treat diabetes and dyslipidemia. Why 7 to 10%A 3 to 5% loss improves the fat; 7 to 10% is needed to reduce the inflammation and fibrosis. 2 DyslipidemiaDyslipidemia Statin: no added risk of serious liver injury in MASLD. 3 ObesityBMI 35 or more, or 30 or more with type 2 diabetes Bariatric surgery. EffectIn one study, MASH resolved in 85% within a year of surgery. 4 FibrosisMASH with stage F2 to F3 fibrosis Add resmetirom, a thyroid hormone beta receptor agonist. In practiceIn practice: preliminary evidence suggests pioglitazone and vitamin E can improve histology in MASH but may not reduce fibrosis, and high-dose vitamin E is avoided in diabetes; glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) drugs are under study; metformin and ursodeoxycholic acid are not proven for the liver.

After diagnosis Situation Do Lifestyle change started Repeat liver enzymes and ultrasound in 6 to 12 months Low fibrosis risk, abnormalities persist CBC, liver enzymes, lipids, glucose and a fibrosis score every 12 to 24 months Advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis Consider hepatology referral; in cirrhosis, ultrasound for HCC; screen for varices

Diagnosis1 of 6 48 yo M, BMI 34, type 2 diabetes, ALT 70, AST 45, hyperechoic liver · MASLDObesity, type 2 diabetes, ALT above AST and a bright liver on ultrasound is MASLD. · Chronic hepatitis CChronic hepatitis C is decided by a positive hepatitis C virus antibody, not by a bright liver. · Alcohol-associated liver diseaseAlcohol-associated liver disease gives AST:ALT of 2 or more, not ALT above AST. 48 yo M, BMI 34, type 2 diabetes, ALT 70, AST 45, hyperechoic liver MASLD

Diagnosis2 of 6 48 yo M with AST 180 and ALT 70 and a history of heavy drinking · MASLDMASLD gives ALT above AST, a ratio under 1. · Autoimmune hepatitisAutoimmune hepatitis does not explain heavy drinking with AST:ALT of 2 or more. · Alcohol-associated liver diseaseAST at least twice the ALT with heavy drinking is alcohol-associated liver disease. 48 yo M with AST 180 and ALT 70 and a history of heavy drinking Alcohol-associated liver diseaseAST:ALT of 2 or more

Next step3 of 6 48 yo M with MASLD asking what most improves liver histology · 7 to 10% weight lossLosing 7 to 10% of body weight reduces the inflammation and fibrosis. · Ursodeoxycholic acidUrsodeoxycholic acid is not proven to help MASLD. · A statinA statin treats cardiovascular risk, not the liver histology. 48 yo M with MASLD asking what most improves liver histology 7 to 10% weight loss

Next step4 of 6 48 yo M with MASLD and a high FIB-4 score · Assess fibrosis with elastographyA high FIB-4 score means possible advanced fibrosis: elastography next. · Reassure and recheck in a yearReassurance misses fibrosis, the stage that predicts liver death. · Liver biopsy in every patientBiopsy is kept for an unclear diagnosis or discordant staging. 48 yo M with MASLD and a high FIB-4 score Assess fibrosis with elastography

Mechanism5 of 6 48 yo M with MASLD and low-density lipoprotein 160 · Withhold until the ALT normalizesWaiting for ALT to normalize delays needed cardiovascular protection. · Statins are safe and indicatedStatins carry no added risk of serious liver injury in MASLD and treat its leading cause of death. · Statins are contraindicated in fatty liverFatty liver is not a contraindication; statins are indicated. 48 yo M with MASLD and low-density lipoprotein 160 Statins are safe and indicated

Diagnosis6 of 6 32 yo M with fatty liver, low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings · Wilson diseaseLow ceruloplasmin with Kayser-Fleischer rings is Wilson disease, a genetic cause of fatty liver. · Hereditary hemochromatosisHemochromatosis is found by high ferritin with high transferrin saturation, not low ceruloplasmin. · MASLDMASLD is a diagnosis of exclusion; low ceruloplasmin points to another cause. 32 yo M with fatty liver, low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings Wilson disease

Significant alcohol: more than 2 drinks a day (women) or 3 (men) gallstones in pregnancy are common (progesterone → gallbladder stasis) and usually incidental without wall thickening, fever, or pain young patient with steatosis + tremor + Kayser-Fleischer rings → Wilson disease.

Wilson Diseasecovers the copper exclusion: is the patient under about 40, with a tremor, psychiatric change or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low? Wilson Disease covers the copper exclusion: is the patient under about 40, with a tremor, psychiatric change or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

briefs.title: Zenker Diverticulum
briefs.sub: undigested regurgitation in an older man · the barium esophagram before any scope or tube · achalasia and cancer · myotomyIs the regurgitated food undigested, and is the finding in the neck or in the chest?
blocks: undigested regurgitation in an older man · the barium esophagram before any scope or tube · achalasia and cancer · myotomyIs the regurgitated food undigested, and is the finding in the neck or in the chest?

An older man with undigested food regurgitation, halitosis and a gurgle in the neck has a Zenker diverticulum (pharyngeal diverticulum). Image with a barium esophagram first; passing a scope or nasogastric tube blind can perforate the pouch ⚠︎. Treat with cricopharyngeal myotomy plus a pouch procedure against recurrence; the main complication is aspiration pneumonia.

What it is Zenker diverticulum (pharyngeal diverticulum): a false, pulsion pouch of mucosa and submucosa pushed out through the posterior wall above the upper esophageal sphincter. Driver Cricopharyngeal motor dysfunction: the sphincter muscle fails to relax as the pharynx pushes the bolus down, probably a timing mismatch. Triggers Older age non-modifiable ; male sex non-modifiable Chain Cricopharyngeus does not relax pressure in the pharynx rises with each swallow mucosa herniates through Killian triangle, a weak gap just above the cricopharyngeus the pouch fills with food regurgitation, halitosis, aspiration Insights The pouch sits above the sphincter, so the food it returns is undigested and the finding is in the neck, not the chest. A blind pouch catches instruments: a scope or tube passed before imaging can enter it and tear through it ⚠︎.

At presentationoropharyngeal dysphagia, undigested regurgitation As it fillshalitosis, neck gurgle, regurgitation that may come on bending or lying down At nightregurgitated contents may be aspirated Rarely, a large pouchsometimes a palpable neck mass, obstruction

Where the pouch sits Pouch Site Tied to Zenker Posterior, above the upper sphincter (Killian triangle) Pulsion: cricopharyngeal dysfunction Traction (Rokitansky) Midesophagus Pull from mediastinal inflammation, historically tuberculosis Epiphrenic Just above the diaphragm Usually a motility disorder such as achalasia

Act now Finding Action Suspected pouch and a scope or feeding tube is planned Image first with a barium esophagram; a blind scope or nasogastric tube can perforate the pouch ⚠︎. Fever, productive cough and a lower lobe infiltrate in a patient with a pouch Aspiration pneumonia from pouch contents, the main complication. Weight loss with progressive dysphagia in a smoker or drinker Esophageal cancer cannot be missed: endoscopy with biopsy.

Adult dysphagia mimics Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Achalasia Solids and liquids from the start; also regurgitates undigested food; bird beak on esophagram. Confirm with esophageal manometry. Esophageal cancer, must not miss Progressive solid then liquid dysphagia with weight loss; smoking or alcohol (squamous) or long-standing reflux (adenocarcinoma). Upper endoscopy with biopsy. Oropharyngeal (neurologic) dysphagia Stroke, Parkinson disease or myasthenia; cough or choke as the swallow begins, food or fluid out the nose. Videofluoroscopic swallow study, then speech therapy. Diffuse esophageal spasm Chest pain radiating to the back and neck with intermittent dysphagia; non-peristaltic contractions. Order manometry. Schatzki ring or peptic stricture Intermittent impaction with meat or bread, no weight loss; distal ring from chronic reflux. Treat with dilation.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Undigested regurgitation, halitosis, a neck gurgle → Barium esophagram Posterior pouch above the cricopharyngeus This study is the diagnostic test Dilated esophagus tapering to a bird beak Esophageal manometry, then upper endoscopy Targeted tests TestResultMeans Trouble starting the swallow, coughing at its onset, nasal regurgitation → Videofluoroscopic swallow study Delayed swallow initiation, aspiration Oropharyngeal neurologic dysphagia: speech therapy Weight loss, smoking or alcohol, progressive solid then liquid dysphagia → Upper endoscopy with biopsy Malignant tissue Esophageal cancer; with these alarm features and no neck sign, the scope comes first Next step TestResultMeans Bird beak on the esophagram → Esophageal manometry Absent peristalsis; the lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax Achalasia → Upper endoscopy Tumor at the gastroesophageal junction Pseudoachalasia, the reason endoscopy follows Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Pouch suspected from the history → Barium esophagram, the first-step study Posterior pouch above the cricopharyngeus Zenker diverticulum confirmed; no scope is needed to make the diagnosis In practice In practice: diverticula are often confirmed on upper endoscopy; the board answer images first and never passes a blind scope. SkipIn a suspected pouch, upper endoscopy or a blind nasogastric tube before imaging: either can enter the pouch and perforate it ⚠︎.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Regurgitates undigested food hours after meals Food held above the stomach in a pouch or a non-emptying esophagus Order a barium esophagram. Gurgling in the neck on swallowing, halitosis Zenker diverticulum Order a barium esophagram before any scope. Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start Achalasia Order an esophagram, then manometry. Weight loss with progressive solid-food dysphagia Esophageal cancer Endoscopy with biopsy. Coughing at the start of the swallow after a stroke Oropharyngeal neurologic dysphagia Order a videofluoroscopic swallow study. Food that may come back on bending or lying down, night cough Pouch spilling into the airway Order a barium esophagram; treat any pneumonia.
Pause point Older patient with dysphagia Pulled toward endoscopy for cancer Undigested food with a neck gurgle and stable weight → A pouch: the esophagram goes first

Pouch and symptoms Finding Action Pouch with dysphagia, regurgitation or aspiration Symptomatic: cricopharyngeal myotomy plus a pouch procedure Large pouch, sometimes a palpable neck mass Same repair; the size of the defect sets which pouch procedure Small pouch, no symptoms Usually no specific treatment WhyFor esophageal diverticula in general, treatment is usually not required; resection is occasionally needed for large or symptomatic ones. A symptomatic Zenker pouch needs cricopharyngeal myotomy plus a pouch procedure.

1 SymptomaticPouch on the esophagram with symptoms Cricopharyngeal myotomy plus diverticulectomy, diverticulopexy or diverticulotomy to lower recurrence; the size of the defect sets the choice. Why myotomyCutting the non-relaxing cricopharyngeus removes the high pressure that pushed the pouch out; the pouch procedure is added against recurrence. In practiceIn practice: an endoscopic diverticulectomy is an alternative to open diverticulectomy. 2 AvoidBefore or instead of repair Image before any tube or scope.

After diagnosis or repair Situation Do Fever, productive cough, lower lobe infiltrate Treat the aspiration pneumonia; it can recur until the pouch is repaired Symptoms return after repair Image the pouch again with a barium esophagram, as at diagnosis; recurrence is lower when a pouch procedure was done

Diagnosis1 of 7 74 yo M, months of dysphagia, regurgitates undigested food hours after meals, halitosis, gurgling in the neck when he swallows, weight stable · AchalasiaAchalasia: solids and liquids from the start, with a bird beak on esophagram. · Zenker diverticulumUndigested regurgitation, halitosis and a neck gurgle in an older man is a Zenker pouch. · Esophageal squamous cell carcinomaEsophageal cancer brings progressive dysphagia with weight loss; his weight is stable. 74 yo M, months of dysphagia, regurgitates undigested food hours after meals, halitosis, gurgling in the neck when he swallows, weight stable Zenker diverticulumbarium esophagram

Workup2 of 7 79 yo M with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis and a gurgling neck · Upper endoscopyA blind scope can enter the pouch and perforate it; image first. · Barium esophagramThe esophagram shows the pouch safely before any instrument passes. · Esophageal manometryManometry tests esophageal motility, as in achalasia, not a pharyngeal pouch. 79 yo M with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis and a gurgling neck Barium esophagrama blind scope or tube risks perforating the pouch

Avoid3 of 7 81 yo M with suspected Zenker diverticulum and poor oral intake; the intervention to avoid · Barium esophagramThe esophagram is the safe first study, not the step to avoid. · Cricopharyngeal myotomyMyotomy treats a symptomatic pouch; it is not the hazard here. · Blind nasogastric tube placementA blind tube can enter the pouch and perforate it. 81 yo M with suspected Zenker diverticulum and poor oral intake; the intervention to avoid Blind nasogastric tube placementthe tube enters the pouch and perforates it

Next step4 of 7 72 yo M whose esophagram shows a posterior pharyngoesophageal outpouching above the cricopharyngeus · EsophagectomyEsophagectomy is a cancer operation; this pouch is benign and above the esophagus. · Proton pump inhibitor and dietary modificationAcid suppression does not treat a motor pouch above the upper sphincter. · Cricopharyngeal myotomy with a pouch procedureMyotomy cuts the non-relaxing cricopharyngeus that drives the pouch; a pouch procedure lowers recurrence. 72 yo M whose esophagram shows a posterior pharyngoesophageal outpouching above the cricopharyngeus Cricopharyngeal myotomy with a pouch procedurethe pouch is the symptom, the non-relaxing muscle is the cause

Mechanism5 of 7 76 yo M with known Zenker diverticulum, 3 days of fever, productive cough and a right lower lobe infiltrate · Squamous cell carcinoma of the pouchCancer in a pouch would not explain 3 days of fever and a new infiltrate. · Esophageal perforationPerforation follows a scope or tube and presents as mediastinitis, not a lobar infiltrate. · Aspiration pneumoniaPouch contents regurgitated at night are aspirated into the lung. 76 yo M with known Zenker diverticulum, 3 days of fever, productive cough and a right lower lobe infiltrate Aspiration pneumoniapooled contents aspirate at night

Diagnosis6 of 7 46 yo F, dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset, regurgitation of undigested food, 5 kg weight loss, esophagram with a dilated esophagus tapering to a bird's beak · Zenker diverticulumZenker diverticulum: undigested regurgitation with halitosis and a neck gurgle, no bird beak. · AchalasiaAchalasia: solids and liquids from the start, with a bird beak on esophagram. · Diffuse esophageal spasmDiffuse esophageal spasm: chest pain with intermittent dysphagia, no bird beak. 46 yo F, dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset, regurgitation of undigested food, 5 kg weight loss, esophagram with a dilated esophagus tapering to a bird's beak Achalasiamanometry, then pneumatic dilation or myotomy

Diagnosis7 of 7 63 yo M, 40 pack-years and daily alcohol, 3 months of progressive solid-food dysphagia now with liquids, 8 kg weight loss · Schatzki ringSchatzki ring: intermittent impaction with meat or bread, no weight loss. · Esophageal squamous cell carcinomaSmoking, alcohol, progressive solid then liquid dysphagia and weight loss point to squamous cell cancer. · Zenker diverticulumZenker diverticulum brings undigested regurgitation and a neck gurgle, not progressive weight loss. 63 yo M, 40 pack-years and daily alcohol, 3 months of progressive solid-food dysphagia now with liquids, 8 kg weight loss Esophageal squamous cell carcinomaendoscopy with biopsy

Regurgitated undigested food never reached the stomach; a pouch or a non-emptying esophagus held it. With a neck finding it is a Zenker pouch; with dysphagia to liquids from day one it is achalasia. In both, the first study is the esophagram. Endoscopy comes first only with an alarm feature for cancer (weight loss, smoking, progressive solid dysphagia) and no neck finding.

Zenker is a false (pulsion) diverticulum: mucosa and submucosa herniate through the posterior wall at Killian triangle, between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor the mechanism is cricopharyngeal motor dysfunction (diminished relaxation), not structural weakness alone halitosis comes from food decaying in the pouch the main complication is aspiration pneumonia treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy plus a pouch procedure (diverticulectomy, diverticulopexy or diverticulotomy), chosen by the size of the defect
Ask: is the regurgitated food undigested, and is the finding in the neck or in the chest?

When the diagnosis implies a blind pouch or cavity the instrument cannot see, image it before instrumenting it: esophagram before endoscopy in Zenker, as with ultrasound before aspirating a hip effusion.

Sequencing trapUpper endoscopy is ordered too early; a blind scope can perforate the pouch that the esophagram would have shown. Salient decoyWeight loss and age suggest cancer, but undigested regurgitation with a neck gurgle indicates a pouch, and the esophagram evaluates both. Class-vs-memberManometry evaluates motility disorders such as achalasia, not a pharyngeal pouch.

briefs.title: Hereditary Polyposis Syndromes
briefs.sub: adenomas or hamartomas: count the polyps, find the pigment · when a known carrier is scoped and operated on · lip macules that redirect an anemia workupHow many polyps, is there an adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) mutation, and where exactly is the pigment?
blocks: adenomas or hamartomas: count the polyps, find the pigment · when a known carrier is scoped and operated on · lip macules that redirect an anemia workupHow many polyps, is there an adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) mutation, and where exactly is the pigment?

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): an autosomal dominant loss of APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) that carpets the colon and rectum with 100 or more adenomas; untreated, nearly all have cancer by 40. A child of an affected parent gets APC testing; a carrier has yearly endoscopy from age 10 to 12, and proctocolectomy follows in the teens to early 20s, or at once for bleeding ⚠︎, a polyp larger than 1 cm ⚠︎, innumerable polyps or high-grade dysplasia; upper endoscopy goes on after colectomy. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: an STK11 (serine/threonine kinase 11) variant, hamartomatous polyps and macules on lips, mouth, hands and feet; microcytic anemia or intussusception sends the patient to upper and lower endoscopy.

What it is FAP: an inherited adenoma syndrome of the whole colon; Gardner syndrome is FAP with extracolonic tumors; Turcot syndrome is polyposis with a brain tumor, medulloblastoma with FAP or glioma with Lynch syndrome. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: an inherited hamartoma syndrome of stomach, small bowel and colon, with pigmented macules. Driver FAP: APC, a tumor suppressor that holds the beta-catenin and Wnt signaling pathway in check. Peutz-Jeghers: STK11, also a tumor suppressor. Triggers An affected parent: both syndromes are autosomal dominant, so every child of a carrier is at risk non-modifiable ; age: adenomas arrive after puberty non-modifiable Chain FAP: one inherited APC copy a second hit in colonic epithelium thousands of adenomas after puberty colorectal cancer in nearly all untreated patients by 40 Peutz-Jeghers: STK11 variant hamartomas through the gut occult bleeding with iron deficiency, or obstruction and intussusception Insights Colectomy leaves the duodenum and ampulla behind, so their adenomas still need upper endoscopy. A hamartoma itself rarely turns malignant, yet Peutz-Jeghers raises cancer risk in the gut and beyond it, and its colorectal and gastric cancers can grow from accompanying adenomas.

Age 10 to 12a carrier starts yearly sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy By 15polyps in half of carriers Teens to early 20splanned proctocolectomy By 35polyps in 95% of carriers By 40cancer in nearly all who are untreated

Rules Diagnosis Requires FAP 100 or more adenomas, with endoscopy and genetic testing Attenuated FAP 10 to 99 adenomas Gardner syndrome FAP plus osteomas, desmoids or other extracolonic growths Turcot syndrome Polyposis plus a malignant brain tumor: medulloblastoma with FAP, glioma with Lynch Peutz-Jeghers syndrome Pigment, 2 or more hamartomatous polyps or a family history prompt STK11 testing; an STK11 variant confirms Juvenile polyposis syndrome Many juvenile hamartomas, no pigment

Act now Finding Action FAP with rectal bleeding, visible or occult An any-age trigger ⚠︎: proctocolectomy now. Colicky pain in a child or adolescent with lip macules Suspect obstruction or intussusception from a hamartoma, which can be the lead point. Microcytic anemia with lip or buccal macules Occult polyp bleeding until proven otherwise: upper and lower endoscopy.

Hereditary polyposis syndromes Syndrome Decides it Next best step Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) 100 or more adenomas covering colon and rectum from adolescence; a parent with FAP Test for the APC mutation, then screen yearly by scope Gardner syndrome Polyposis plus osteomas of skull or mandible and desmoid tumors Follow the FAP pathway; it is FAP with extracolonic growths Turcot syndrome Polyposis plus a malignant brain tumor, such as medulloblastoma Medulloblastoma: follow the FAP pathway for the colon; glioma: Lynch syndrome, not covered here Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC) Few polyps, early right-sided cancer, endometrial cancer in the pedigree; mismatch-repair defect Follow its own screening schedule, outside this page Peutz-Jeghers syndrome Hamartomas that bleed or intussuscept, with lip and buccal macules Upper and lower endoscopy; STK11 testing Juvenile polyposis syndrome Hamartomas of stomach, colon and small bowel without pigment; can bleed massively Remove the colon for massive bleeding; colorectal cancer risk is raised Attenuated FAP 10 to 99 adenomas, sitting more proximally Use colonoscopy rather than sigmoidoscopy

Look-alikes of pigment with anemia Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Peutz-Jeghers syndrome Discrete brown macules of the lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles; slow polyp bleeding drains iron Upper and lower endoscopy, then genetic testing Menstrual iron deficiency Abnormal Uterine Bleeding No pigment; microcytic, from heavy or long menses Give iron, and add hormonal control if bleeding is heavy Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) Diffuse pigment, darkest on pressure points and sun-exposed skin; anemia, if any, usually normocytic Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test Lead poisoning A blue line along the gums where they meet the teeth; small red cells with basophilic stippling Blood lead level Aplastic anemia or leukemia No pigment; usually normocytic, with other cytopenias Examine a bone marrow sample

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Child of a parent with FAP → APC testing for the family mutation The family mutation is present Carrier: yearly endoscopy starting at 10 to 12 The family mutation is absent Not a carrier: screen as average risk Lip or buccal macules with fatigue or pallor → CBC with mean corpuscular volume (MCV) Microcytic; other cell lines normal Blood loss is draining iron; the marrow itself is working Targeted tests TestResultMeans Carrier from age 10 to 12, or an at-risk child when testing is unavailable → Yearly sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy Adenomas by the hundreds Polyposis: schedule proctocolectomy for the teens to early 20s Any surgical trigger: bleeding ⚠︎, a polyp larger than 1 cm ⚠︎, innumerable polyps, high-grade dysplasia Operate now, whatever the age Pigment with microcytic anemia → Upper and lower endoscopy, biopsying the polyps Hamartomas, 2 or more With the macules this is Peutz-Jeghers, and the polyps explain the anemia Next step TestResultMeans FAP, before or after colectomy → Upper endoscopy Duodenal or ampullary adenomas Upper-tract surveillance continues after colectomy Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Hundreds of colonic adenomas → Colonoscopy with genetic testing 100 or more adenomas FAP; 10 to 99 is attenuated FAP Pigment, 2 or more hamartomas, or a family history → STK11 genetic testing STK11 variant Peutz-Jeghers confirmed; autosomal dominant, so test first-degree relatives SkipFor an APC carrier, colonoscopy at 40 or yearly fecal immunochemical testing: that is the sporadic family-history pathway. For lip macules, the ACTH stimulation test or a lead level: Addison pigment is diffuse and lead gives a gingival line.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step APC-positive 12-year-old with no symptoms A carrier with no trigger yet Start yearly sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy now Parent with FAP and no genetic test available Treat the child as affected Start yearly sigmoidoscopy at age 10 to 12 Mandibular osteoma or an abdominal-wall desmoid Gardner syndrome Follow the FAP pathway and its colectomy rules Intussusception in an older child with lip macules A hamartoma lead point Evaluate for Peutz-Jeghers: upper and lower endoscopy Parent whose macules have faded Family history still counts Offer the child STK11 testing Lip or buccal macules with microcytic anemia and normal platelets and leukocytes Blood loss, not marrow failure Order upper and lower endoscopy for the source
Pause point Child with a positive APC test Pulled toward colectomy now No trigger → Yearly endoscopy; the operation is planned for the teens to early 20s

Colectomy triggers in FAP Finding Action Gastrointestinal bleeding ⚠︎ Operate now, at any age A polyp over 1 cm ⚠︎ Operate now, at any age Innumerable polyps Operate now, at any age High-grade dysplasia Operate now, at any age A few adenomas under 1 cm ⚠︎, no dysplasia, no bleeding No trigger: yearly endoscopy toward the planned operation

1 CarrierFrom age 10 to 12 Yearly sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy; colonoscopy is usually done, since it can find a more proximal cancer. 2 PolyposisTeens to early 20s Planned prophylactic proctocolectomy. In practiceIn practice: total proctocolectomy is usually done soon after diagnosis, because nearly all untreated patients have colon cancer by 40; for a carrier with no trigger, it is planned for the teens to early 20s. 3 Trigger metAny age, with a surgical trigger Proctocolectomy now. 4 The operationColectomy planned or triggered Total proctocolectomy removes colon and rectum, and with them the colorectal cancer risk. Colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis keeps a rectum that needs frequent endoscopy. 5 Peutz-JeghersA colonic polyp over 1 cm Such polyps are usually removed; surveillance is lifelong.

After the diagnosis Situation Do FAP after colectomy Periodic upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas WhenIn practice: the American College of Gastroenterology starts upper endoscopy with duodenoscopy at age 25 to 30. Rectum kept after ileorectal anastomosis Frequent endoscopy of the rectal remnant FAP, other organs Yearly thyroid ultrasound; the duodenum (FAP after colectomy row), pancreas, brain and liver also carry raised cancer risk ChildrenIn practice: hepatoblastoma screening may be offered to the children of an affected parent from birth to age 5. Peutz-Jeghers, newly diagnosed Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, then lifelong surveillance that includes the small bowel AgesIn practice: colonoscopy, upper endoscopy and capsule endoscopy begin at age 8, breast MRI or mammography at 25, pancreatic imaging at 30. Peutz-Jeghers, cancers beyond the gut Breast and genital tract screening; testicular Sertoli cell tumors in boys Peutz-Jeghers family STK11 testing of first-degree relatives; faded macules in a parent do not exclude the syndrome

Screening1 of 15 12-year-old boy is seen for a well visit His father has familial adenomatous polyposis genetic testing shows the family APC mutation Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL · abdomen soft and nontender · Colonoscopy at age 40Colonoscopy at 40 is the sporadic family-history schedule, not a carrier pathway. · Annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy starting nowA known APC carrier at puberty starts yearly sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy now. · Prophylactic colectomy nowColectomy is planned for the teens to early 20s; no trigger is present. 12-year-old boy is seen for a well visit His father has familial adenomatous polyposis genetic testing shows the family APC mutation Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL · abdomen soft and nontender Annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy starting nowthe screening gate opens at puberty, age 10 to 12, so a known APC carrier starts annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy now. Colonoscopy at 40 is the sporadic family-history schedule and does not apply to a carrier; prophylactic colectomy is planned for the teens to early 20s, or sooner only for bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps or high-grade dysplasia, and none is present

Next step2 of 15 13-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue Regular menses lasting 6 days; no medications pale conjunctivae; brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 70 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal · Blood lead levelLead gives a blue gingival line at the tooth margin, not lip macules. · Iron therapy and oral contraception onlyIron and an oral contraceptive treat the anemia but leave the syndrome undiagnosed. · Upper and lower endoscopyLip and buccal macules with microcytic anemia mean bleeding hamartomas: upper and lower endoscopy. 13-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue Regular menses lasting 6 days; no medications pale conjunctivae; brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 70 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal Upper and lower endoscopysix-day menses with a microcytic anemia suggest menstrual iron deficiency, but brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa mark Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, so the anemia is occult bleeding from hamartomatous polyps: scope above and below. Iron with an oral contraceptive treats the anemia but leaves the syndrome undiagnosed; lead gives a blue gingival line, not mucosal macules

Diagnosis3 of 15 28-year-old man has a firm mass in the abdominal wall biopsy shows a desmoid tumor radiograph shows a mandibular osteoma colonoscopy shows hundreds of colonic adenomas No headaches or neurologic deficits Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL · Gardner syndromePolyposis plus osteomas and desmoid tumors is Gardner syndrome. · Turcot syndromeTurcot syndrome is polyposis plus a brain tumor, and there are no neurologic findings. · Peutz-Jeghers syndromePeutz-Jeghers gives hamartomas with lip and buccal macules. 28-year-old man has a firm mass in the abdominal wall biopsy shows a desmoid tumor radiograph shows a mandibular osteoma colonoscopy shows hundreds of colonic adenomas No headaches or neurologic deficits Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL Gardner syndromepolyposis plus osteomas and desmoid tumors is Gardner syndrome, an FAP variant managed on the same pathway with the same colectomy rules. Turcot syndrome adds central nervous system tumors, and there are no neurologic findings; Peutz-Jeghers polyps are hamartomas that come with lip and buccal pigmentation

Next step4 of 15 19-year-old man is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis Annual colonoscopy since age 11 2 weeks of rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL · low ferritin consistent with iron deficiency · Colonoscopy with polypectomy and iron supplementationPolypectomy with iron treats the symptom and leaves the polyposis colon. · Colectomy nowBleeding is an any-age colectomy trigger, so operate now. · Repeat colonoscopy in 1 yearWaiting a year delays a trigger that is already met. 19-year-old man is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis Annual colonoscopy since age 11 2 weeks of rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL · low ferritin consistent with iron deficiency Colectomy nowbleeding is an any-age indication, so the operation planned for the teens to early 20s happens now. Polypectomy with iron treats the symptom and leaves a colon that adenomas carpet, and repeating colonoscopy in a year delays a trigger that is already met

Diagnosis5 of 15 15-year-old boy has 3 months of fatigue, anorexia and weight loss diffuse hyperpigmentation, darkest over the elbows, knees and sun-exposed skin No lip macules; gums normal BP 106/64 mm Hg · hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 88 fL · Peutz-Jeghers syndromePeutz-Jeghers gives discrete brown macules on lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles. · Lead poisoningLead gives a blue gingival line with a microcytic anemia. · Addison diseaseDiffuse pigment, darkest on pressure points and sun-exposed skin, with a normocytic anemia is Addison disease. 15-year-old boy has 3 months of fatigue, anorexia and weight loss diffuse hyperpigmentation, darkest over the elbows, knees and sun-exposed skin No lip macules; gums normal BP 106/64 mm Hg · hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 88 fL Addison diseasediffuse pigmentation, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areas, is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), with an anemia that is usually normocytic if present; the adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test answers it. Peutz-Jeghers gives discrete brown macules on the lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles, and lead a blue gingival line with a microcytic anemia

Screening6 of 15 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit Her mother has familial adenomatous polyposis the girl has never had genetic testing Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile · hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL · Reassure and begin average-risk screening as an adultAverage-risk screening presumes she is not a carrier before she is tested. · Annual fecal immunochemical testingYearly fecal immunochemical testing is the wrong pathway for a possible carrier. · APC genetic testingEach child of an affected parent has a one-in-two risk, so test for the family APC mutation. 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit Her mother has familial adenomatous polyposis the girl has never had genetic testing Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile · hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL APC genetic testingAPC is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a one-in-two risk and is tested rather than presumed: a positive result starts annual endoscopic screening, and a negative result for the known family mutation means average-risk screening. Average-risk screening presumes she is not a carrier, and annual fecal immunochemical testing is the wrong pathway for a carrier

Mechanism7 of 15 16-year-old girl has 4 months of fatigue dark brown macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms Regular menses lasting 5 days; intermittent cramping abdominal pain Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 68 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal · Occult polyp bleedingThe macules mark Peutz-Jeghers, whose hamartomas bleed slowly into iron deficiency. · Prolonged menstrual blood lossMicrocytic anemia in an adolescent girl is not automatically menstrual once the macules are seen. · Bone marrow failureMarrow failure is usually normocytic, with other cytopenias; her other counts are normal. 16-year-old girl has 4 months of fatigue dark brown macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms Regular menses lasting 5 days; intermittent cramping abdominal pain Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 68 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal Occult polyp bleedingthe macules mark Peutz-Jeghers, whose hamartomatous polyps bleed slowly and cause iron deficiency. The low MCV separates the bleeding causes from the marrow causes, and normal platelet and leukocyte counts argue against marrow failure, which is usually normocytic; microcytic anemia in an adolescent girl is not automatically menstrual once the macules are seen

Next step8 of 15 14-year-old boy is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis annual colonoscopy shows a few small adenomas, all under 1 cm biopsies show no dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL · Continue annual colonoscopy and plan colectomy for the late teens to early 20sA few small adenomas with no dysplasia or bleeding meet no trigger: keep yearly endoscopy. · Proctocolectomy nowOperating now is for a met trigger, and none is present. · Repeat colonoscopy in 5 yearsA 5-year interval is not the yearly schedule a carrier needs. 14-year-old boy is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis annual colonoscopy shows a few small adenomas, all under 1 cm biopsies show no dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL Continue annual colonoscopy and plan colectomy for the late teens to early 20sno immediate trigger is present: no bleeding, no polyp over 1 cm, the polyps are few rather than innumerable, and there is no high-grade dysplasia, so annual surveillance continues toward a planned prophylactic proctocolectomy. Operating now is for a met trigger, and a 5-year interval is not the annual schedule a carrier needs

Diagnosis9 of 15 15-year-old boy has recurrent cramping abdominal pain ultrasound shows a small-bowel intussusception pigmented macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms No vomiting; stools without visible blood Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL · Familial adenomatous polyposisFAP brings 100 or more colonic adenomas, not pigment. · Peutz-Jeghers syndromeMucocutaneous macules with an intussuscepting hamartoma is Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. · Addison diseaseAddison pigment is diffuse, darkest on pressure points and sun-exposed skin. 15-year-old boy has recurrent cramping abdominal pain ultrasound shows a small-bowel intussusception pigmented macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms No vomiting; stools without visible blood Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL Peutz-Jeghers syndromemucocutaneous macules with hamartomatous polyps that intussuscept is Peutz-Jeghers, autosomal dominant; intussusception in an older child has a lead point until proven otherwise, and a hamartoma can be one. The tell of FAP is hundreds of colonic adenomas, and Addison pigmentation is diffuse, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areas, not discrete macules

Screening10 of 15 23-year-old woman is seen for follow-up Total proctocolectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis 2 years ago Asymptomatic; eating well; no abdominal mass Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 72/min · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL · Upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomasColectomy leaves the duodenum and ampulla behind, so upper endoscopy continues. · No further surveillance is neededSurveillance does not stop after colectomy; the upper tract stays at risk. · Annual abdominal CT for desmoid tumorsDesmoid tumors mark the Gardner variant; the surveillance after colectomy is upper endoscopy. 23-year-old woman is seen for follow-up Total proctocolectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis 2 years ago Asymptomatic; eating well; no abdominal mass Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 72/min · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL Upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomascolectomy does not address duodenal and ampullary adenomas, so upper endoscopy surveillance continues; the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk, so stopping surveillance is wrong. A desmoid tumor marks Gardner syndrome, a feature of the variant rather than the surveillance that continues after colectomy, which is upper endoscopy

Diagnosis11 of 15 14-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue a blue line along the gingival margin at the teeth No lip or buccal macules; regular 4-day menses Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 66 fL · basophilic stippling on the smear · Iron deficiency from menorrhagiaMenstrual iron deficiency needs heavy or long menses; hers last 4 days. · Peutz-Jeghers syndromePeutz-Jeghers pigment is discrete macules on the lips and buccal mucosa. · Lead poisoningA blue gingival line with microcytic anemia and basophilic stippling is lead poisoning. 14-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue a blue line along the gingival margin at the teeth No lip or buccal macules; regular 4-day menses Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 66 fL · basophilic stippling on the smear Lead poisoninga blue gingival line at the tooth margin with a microcytic anemia and basophilic stippling is lead poisoning: check a blood lead level. Peutz-Jeghers pigment is discrete macules on the lips and buccal mucosa, and menstrual iron deficiency brings no pigment and needs heavy or prolonged menses

Next step12 of 15 17-year-old girl is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis colonoscopy shows innumerable polyps, several over 1 cm biopsy of one polyp shows high-grade dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL · Endoscopic polypectomy of the largest polypsRemoving the largest polyps leaves a colon that keeps forming adenomas. · Total proctocolectomyInnumerable polyps, polyps over 1 cm and high-grade dysplasia are each an any-age trigger. · Segmental colectomy of the involved regionFAP covers the whole colon and the rectum, so a segment is not enough. 17-year-old girl is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis colonoscopy shows innumerable polyps, several over 1 cm biopsy of one polyp shows high-grade dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL Total proctocolectomyinnumerable polyps, polyps over 1 cm and high-grade dysplasia are each an any-age colectomy trigger. Polypectomy of the largest lesions is not enough once innumerable polyps or dysplasia indicate colectomy, and a segmental resection leaves the rest of a colon that adenomas carpet

Avoid13 of 15 15-year-old girl has fatigue Regular menses every 28 days, lasting 6 days brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa No medications; no visible blood in stool Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 72 fL · platelets normal · Iron and an oral contraceptiveIron and an oral contraceptive treat the anemia but leave the syndrome undiagnosed. · STK11 testing and upper and lower endoscopySTK11 testing with endoscopy finds the source and confirms the syndrome. · Upper and lower endoscopyUpper and lower endoscopy finds the bleeding hamartomas, so it names the cause. 15-year-old girl has fatigue Regular menses every 28 days, lasting 6 days brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa No medications; no visible blood in stool Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 72 fL · platelets normal Iron and an oral contraceptiveiron and an oral contraceptive treat the anemia but leave the syndrome undiagnosed. Upper and lower endoscopy finds the bleeding hamartomas, the source of the anemia, and adding STK11 testing confirms the syndrome, after which first-degree relatives are tested because inheritance is autosomal dominant

Diagnosis14 of 15 36-year-old woman has a right-sided colon cancer on colonoscopy 12 polyps elsewhere in the colon Her mother had endometrial cancer at 45; her brother had colon cancer at 42 Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL · no mucocutaneous pigmentation · Lynch syndromeFew polyps, early right-sided cancer and endometrial cancer in the pedigree is Lynch syndrome. · Familial adenomatous polyposisFAP brings 100 or more adenomas, not 12; even attenuated FAP at 10 to 99 does not explain the endometrial cancer in the pedigree. · Peutz-Jeghers syndromePeutz-Jeghers brings hamartomas with lip and buccal macules; she has none. 36-year-old woman has a right-sided colon cancer on colonoscopy 12 polyps elsewhere in the colon Her mother had endometrial cancer at 45; her brother had colon cancer at 42 Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL · no mucocutaneous pigmentation Lynch syndromeearly right-sided colon cancer with few polyps and an endometrial cancer in the pedigree is Lynch syndrome, a mismatch-repair mutation: test the tumor for mismatch repair. FAP brings hundreds to thousands of adenomas, and Peutz-Jeghers brings hamartomas with lip and buccal pigmentation

Screening15 of 15 20-year-old woman is seen for follow-up of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome STK11 mutation confirmed at age 14 Asymptomatic; her lip macules have faded Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL · Periodic upper and lower endoscopy with small-bowel examinationPeutz-Jeghers surveillance is lifelong endoscopy of the gut, plus breast and genital tract screening. · Colonoscopy only, from age 40 or 10 years before a relative's cancerThe age-40 schedule is for sporadic family history and misses the upper gut. · Prophylactic proctocolectomy in the early 20sProphylactic proctocolectomy is the FAP pathway. 20-year-old woman is seen for follow-up of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome STK11 mutation confirmed at age 14 Asymptomatic; her lip macules have faded Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL Periodic upper and lower endoscopy with small-bowel examinationsurveillance is lifelong, upper and lower endoscopy and small-bowel examination from age 8, with later intervals set by the findings, plus breast and genital tract cancer screening, because the risk includes gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast and genital tract (ovary, cervix) cancers, plus testicular Sertoli cell tumors; faded macules do not end the polyp risk. Prophylactic proctocolectomy is the FAP pathway, and the age-40 schedule is for sporadic family history

Colonoscopy at 40: the sporadic family-history schedule; an APC carrier is scoped annually from puberty. Polypectomy of the largest lesions: not enough once innumerable polyps or dysplasia indicate colectomy. Stopping surveillance after colectomy: the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk. Iron with an oral contraceptive: an adolescent girl with menses and microcytic anemia looks like menstrual iron deficiency until the oral macules are noted. ACTH stimulation or a lead level: Addison disease and lead also cause pigmentation, but in a different distribution.

Abnormal Uterine Bleedinglists Lynch syndrome among the endometrial cancer risk factors; Lynch syndrome and its colorectal screening intervals are not covered on this page Abnormal Uterine Bleeding lists Lynch syndrome among the endometrial cancer risk factors; Lynch syndrome and its colorectal screening intervals are not covered on this page.

Identify the hereditary syndrome first: start age, interval and operation all depend on it, and sporadic family-history numbers do not apply to a known carrier. When one finding does not fit an otherwise ordinary explanation, that finding usually determines the diagnosis.

briefs.title: Jaundice in a Newborn
briefs.sub: timing, direct fraction and Coombs · the sick neonate with a positive screenIs the infant well, and is any of it direct?
blocks: timing, direct fraction and Coombs · the sick neonate with a positive screenIs the infant well, and is any of it direct?
