Physiologic jaundice is a conjugation lag: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while hepatic uridine diphosphate (UDP) glucuronosyltransferase is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. A raised direct fraction makes newborn jaundice urgent. Physiologic jaundice: begins after 24 hours, peaks around day 3 to 5, predominantly indirect, resolving by 1 to 2 weeks. Pathologic jaundice: within the first 24 hours, any raised direct fraction, or persistence beyond 2 weeks. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: direct bilirubin above 1.0 mg/dL; never physiologic and never breast-milk jaundice. Classic galactosemia: galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency; galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in the liver. Conjugated jaundice, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar in the urine after milk feeds; it predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: indirect jaundice with anemia and Coombs-negative hemolysis, often after an oxidant.

Diagnostic workup 1Bilirubin fractions first, then branch First Total and direct bilirubin Indirect, after 24 hours, well infantPhysiologic or intake-related; plot on an hour-specific chart for phototherapy Direct fraction raisedNever physiologic: cholestasis, galactosemia, sepsis or biliary atresia; check it in any infant still jaundiced past 2 weeks By branch: indirect Blood type and direct Coombs test Coombs positive, mother group O or Rh-negativeIsoimmune hemolysis: phototherapy, exchange above threshold Complete blood count, smear, reticulocytes, G6PD Anemia with Coombs-negative hemolysisG6PD deficiency or spherocytosis By branch: direct Urine reducing substances with dipstick glucose Reducing substance positive, glucose negativeGalactose or fructose: stop lactose now; falsely negative once feeds stop Blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures Escherichia coliFebrile neonate: intravenous (IV) antibiotics in parallel, not after Liver panel with gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) High GGT and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), transaminases normal or mildly highBile duct injury: biliary atresia Normal GGTProgressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) Next Abdominal ultrasound, then hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan Small or absent gallbladder, triangular cord sign; no excretion into the bowelSupports biliary atresia Confirms Red cell galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT) activity Absent or near absentClassic galactosemia; invalid after transfusion Intraoperative cholangiogram (or liver biopsy) No contrast reaches the bowel; duct proliferation and fibrosisBiliary atresia: Kasai before about 60 days; most eventually need a liver transplant
Causes: timing and the direct fraction

Well or sick, indirect or direct Cause When The tell Physiologic After 24 hours, peak day 3 to 5 Well infant, feeding and voiding normally; indirect; nothing but time Suboptimal-intake (breast-feeding) jaundice Day 3 to 5 Weight loss, few wet diapers; feed more often, lactation support Breast-milk jaundice Day 7 onward, peak about 2 weeks, can persist weeks Thriving, indirect, normal GGT and stools; continue breast-feeding Blood group or Rh hemolytic disease Often within 24 hours Coombs positive; mother group O or Rh-negative; high reticulocytes G6PD deficiency Can't miss Variable, can be abrupt Coombs negative, anemia, high reticulocytes, often an oxidant; X-linked, mostly boys; Mediterranean, African or Asian ancestry; remove the trigger, phototherapy Biliary atresia Can't miss Well at birth; jaundice and hepatomegaly at 2 to 8 weeks Direct, high GGT and ALP, normal reticulocytes; acholic stools, dark urine; reducing substances negative PFIC Infancy Direct with a normal GGT; gallbladder present; specialist evaluation Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Infancy, acute Febrile and ill; direct and GGT high, cytopenias, low reticulocytes, normal gallbladder; urgent hematology Crigler-Najjar or Gilbert Persistent indirect The same enzyme absent or reduced, not immature; depends on type Classic galactosemia Within days of milk feeds Sick; conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly, urine reducing substances

Visible above about 5 mg/dL Physiologic ceiling peak around 14 to 15 mg/dL, indirect over 90% Exchange range generally above 20 mg/dL; kernicterus risk rises at 25 to 30 mg/dL Under 24 hours never physiologic: bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs Any direct fraction not physiologic: consider obstruction or infection Beyond 2 weeks check the direct fraction and the stool color before reassuring Phototherapy versus exchange phototherapy first; exchange for the severe range or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold Feeding almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding; more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut
The sick neonate with a positive screen

Stop all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing Feed soy-based formula in place of breast milk and standard formula In parallel blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures and empiric neonatal antibiotics for Escherichia coli Confirm afterwards red cell GALT activity Urine test needs recent intake, so a negative test after feeds stop does not exclude galactosemia

Screen-positive and sick: the liver and the urine name it Diagnosis The tell Galactokinase deficiency Cataracts in a well infant; no liver disease, no sepsis Congenital rubella syndrome Cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, blueberry muffin rash; present at birth, not triggered by milk Hereditary fructose intolerance Aldolase B; same liver picture plus hypoglycemia, at weaning with fruit, juice or sucrose Maple syrup urine disease Encephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis; sweet-smelling urine, ketosis

Mechanism1 of 28 4-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery is jaundiced breast-feeding without difficulty; eight wet diapers daily alert; Apgar scores 10 and 10 Afebrile · total bilirubin 11 mg/dL · Decreased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin · Increased hepatocyte ligandin concentration · Immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity 4-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery is jaundiced breast-feeding without difficulty; eight wet diapers daily alert; Apgar scores 10 and 10 Afebrile · total bilirubin 11 mg/dL Immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activitya well infant, feeding and voiding normally, jaundiced on day 4 at 11 mg/dL has physiologic jaundice: fetal hemoglobin breaks down quickly while the conjugating enzyme is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates. Enterohepatic circulation is increased in the newborn, not decreased, and ligandin is low at birth, not high: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction. Cholestasis would make the bilirubin direct, and albumin displacement needs a displacing drug

Next step2 of 28 3-day-old girl born at term is seen at a follow-up visit newborn screen reported positive for galactosemia by telephone asymptomatic and breastfeeding well Afebrile · weight 3% below birth weight · no jaundice · Admit for intravenous antibiotics · Continue breastfeeding until confirmatory testing returns · Stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula pending confirmation 3-day-old girl born at term is seen at a follow-up visit newborn screen reported positive for galactosemia by telephone asymptomatic and breastfeeding well Afebrile · weight 3% below birth weight · no jaundice Stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula pending confirmationpresumptive galactosemia: stop all lactose and galactose immediately, without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing; replace breast milk with soy-based formula and confirm afterwards with red cell GALT activity. Continuing feeds continues the injury, and intravenous antibiotics answer a febrile or septic neonate, not this well one

Workup3 of 28 6-week-old girl: ultrasound shows no gallbladder stools pale gray since week 3; urine dark jaundice deepening over 4 weeks; exclusively breastfed liver 2 cm below the costal margin Well-appearing, afebrile · HR 148/min · total bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL · Direct bilirubin high, GGT high, reticulocyte count normal · Direct bilirubin normal, GGT normal, reticulocyte count high · Direct bilirubin high, GGT normal, reticulocyte count normal 6-week-old girl: ultrasound shows no gallbladder stools pale gray since week 3; urine dark jaundice deepening over 4 weeks; exclusively breastfed liver 2 cm below the costal margin Well-appearing, afebrile · HR 148/min · total bilirubin 10.2 mg/dL Direct bilirubin high, GGT high, reticulocyte count normalpale stools and an absent gallbladder mean bile duct destruction, which raises the direct fraction and the GGT while the reticulocytes stay normal: biliary atresia. A direct rise with a normal GGT is progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, and an indirect rise with high reticulocytes is hemolysis. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis also raises both, but in a febrile, ill infant with low reticulocytes. Exclusive breastfeeding suggests breast-milk jaundice, but that is indirect and leaves the stools yellow and the gallbladder normal. Intraoperative cholangiography confirms, then Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy

Diagnosis4 of 28 9-month-old girl has vomiting and jaundice began after juice and fruit were introduced liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · glucose 38 mg/dL · Classic galactosemia · Glycogen storage disease type I · Hereditary fructose intolerance 9-month-old girl has vomiting and jaundice began after juice and fruit were introduced liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · glucose 38 mg/dL Hereditary fructose intolerancealdolase B deficiency gives the same hepatic picture as galactosemia plus hypoglycemia, but it starts with fruit, juice or sucrose at weaning, months old rather than days; remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol. Glycogen storage disease type I brings hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with no dietary trigger; essential fructosuria is the benign cousin, a urinary sugar with no illness

Next step5 of 28 2-day-old girl born at term has jaundice to the chest infant blood group B, mother group O direct Coombs test positive Alert and breast-feeding well Afebrile · total bilirubin 19 mg/dL · direct 0.6 mg/dL · Exchange transfusion · Restriction of breast-feeding · Phototherapy 2-day-old girl born at term has jaundice to the chest infant blood group B, mother group O direct Coombs test positive Alert and breast-feeding well Afebrile · total bilirubin 19 mg/dL · direct 0.6 mg/dL Phototherapya positive Coombs test with a group O mother is isoimmune hemolysis, still below the exchange range. Phototherapy comes first; exchange transfusion is for the severe range (generally above 20 mg/dL) or signs of encephalopathy, not a level near threshold. Jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: more milk increases bilirubin excretion through the gut

Avoid6 of 28 2-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia last week parents ask what she can be fed jaundice resolving on her current feeds Mother hopes to resume breastfeeding Afebrile · weight gain 25 g/day · Elemental lactose-free formula · Soy-based formula · Breast milk 2-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia last week parents ask what she can be fed jaundice resolving on her current feeds Mother hopes to resume breastfeeding Afebrile · weight gain 25 g/day Breast milkbreast milk and standard formula carry lactose, so they are replaced with soy-based formula; the diet reverses the acute illness. An elemental lactose-free formula carries no lactose either

Diagnosis7 of 28 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed weight 11% below birth weight three wet diapers in the past day Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL, direct 0.4 mg/dL · Extrahepatic biliary atresia · Breast-milk jaundice · Suboptimal-intake jaundice 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed weight 11% below birth weight three wet diapers in the past day Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL, direct 0.4 mg/dL Suboptimal-intake jaundiceweight loss and few wet diapers in the first week are a hungry infant: too little milk, not the milk itself, raising bilirubin through increased enterohepatic reabsorption (also called breast-feeding jaundice). Feed more often, with lactation support. Breast-milk jaundice is a thriving infant still jaundiced in the second week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction

Workup8 of 28 10-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Newborn screen flagged a disorder of galactose metabolism Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL · Liver biopsy · Red cell GALT enzyme activity · Serum galactose level 10-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances Newborn screen flagged a disorder of galactose metabolism Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL Red cell GALT enzyme activityred cell GALT activity names the enzyme defect: absent or near absent in classic galactosemia, and invalid after transfusion. Reduced red cell GALT activity establishes the diagnosis, so red cell enzyme analysis confirms it without hepatic tissue, and a serum galactose level only supports it

Diagnosis9 of 28 6-week-old girl born at term has jaundice acholic stools and dark urine liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin exclusively breast-fed; gaining weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 8 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL · Biliary atresia · Physiologic jaundice · Breast-milk jaundice 6-week-old girl born at term has jaundice acholic stools and dark urine liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin exclusively breast-fed; gaining weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 8 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL Biliary atresiaa direct fraction is never physiologic, and acholic stools with dark urine at 2 to 8 weeks in an infant well at birth is duct obstruction. An exclusively breastfed infant can still have it: breast-milk jaundice is indirect, peaks around 2 weeks and leaves the stools yellow. Physiologic jaundice is predominantly indirect and resolves by 1 to 2 weeks

Next step10 of 28 5-day-old boy born at term has poor feeding and lethargy seizures today urine smells like maple syrup Newborn screen reported positive T 36.9 °C · glucose 72 mg/dL · no hepatomegaly or jaundice · Leucine-free formula with dextrose · Switch to soy-based formula · Empiric antibiotics and observation 5-day-old boy born at term has poor feeding and lethargy seizures today urine smells like maple syrup Newborn screen reported positive T 36.9 °C · glucose 72 mg/dL · no hepatomegaly or jaundice Leucine-free formula with dextrosebranched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency (signs from day 2 to 3) is encephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis, with sweet-smelling urine and ketosis: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error to confuse with galactosemia, but it carries ketoacids, not a reducing sugar. Soy formula, the galactosemia substitute, still contains protein, including the branched-chain amino acids, so it keeps feeding the block; protein is given as amino acids free of the branched chains, with isoleucine and valine added back, so the formula is leucine-free, and high calories come as dextrose and lipid. Antibiotics with observation do not lower plasma leucine

Mechanism11 of 28 5-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the abdomen breast-feeding poorly with few wet diapers dry mucous membranes; weight 10% below birth weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 16 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL · Reduced hepatic conjugation capacity · Increased enterohepatic reabsorption · Displacement of bilirubin from albumin 5-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the abdomen breast-feeding poorly with few wet diapers dry mucous membranes; weight 10% below birth weight Afebrile · total bilirubin 16 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL Increased enterohepatic reabsorptionthe newborn gut reabsorbs bilirubin, so anything that slows transit raises the indirect fraction: too little milk slows it and lets intestinal bilirubin return to the circulation. Conjugation is immature in every newborn, and albumin displacement requires a displacing drug

Diagnosis12 of 28 10-day-old girl born at term vomits after starting formula jaundiced, with the liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL · Glycogen storage disease type I · Hereditary fructose intolerance · Classic galactosemia 10-day-old girl born at term vomits after starting formula jaundiced, with the liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts urine positive for reducing substances Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3 mg/dL Classic galactosemiaconjugated jaundice with hepatomegaly, cataracts and urine reducing substances within days of milk feeds: liver, kidney, brain and lens are affected; eliminate galactose and lactose. Glycogen storage disease type I has no galactose trigger and no cataracts; hereditary fructose intolerance appears at weaning

Workup13 of 28 14-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice of the face and chest breast-feeding well Uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · HR 140/min · transcutaneous bilirubin 9 mg/dL · Total and direct bilirubin with a Coombs test · Serum albumin concentration · Ultrasonography of the liver and biliary tree 14-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice of the face and chest breast-feeding well Uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · HR 140/min · transcutaneous bilirubin 9 mg/dL Total and direct bilirubin with a Coombs testonset inside 24 hours is never physiologic, so it is pathologic until proven otherwise: send bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs test. Hepatic ultrasound and serum albumin cannot show hemolysis or immature conjugation

Mechanism14 of 28 3-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia at 1 week bilateral cataracts seen on red reflex examination on soy formula; jaundice resolving Liver edge now 1 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · weight gain 30 g/day · Sorbitol accumulation · Galactose-1-phosphate deposition in the lens · Galactitol accumulation via aldose reductase 3-week-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia at 1 week bilateral cataracts seen on red reflex examination on soy formula; jaundice resolving Liver edge now 1 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · weight gain 30 g/day Galactitol accumulation via aldose reductasecataracts in both galactose disorders come from galactitol, made by aldose reductase, the same enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens: an osmotic lens injury. Galactokinase deficiency makes cataracts without ever forming galactose-1-phosphate, so the lens injury is galactitol, not galactose-1-phosphate; sorbitol is the diabetic product

Workup15 of 28 4-day-old term boy of Greek descent is jaundiced to the abdomen feeding well Mother and infant both group A, Rh-positive direct Coombs negative; no spherocytes on smear hematocrit 36% · reticulocytes high · bilirubin 17 mg/dL, direct 0.6 mg/dL · Liver panel with GGT · G6PD enzyme activity level · Osmotic fragility testing 4-day-old term boy of Greek descent is jaundiced to the abdomen feeding well Mother and infant both group A, Rh-positive direct Coombs negative; no spherocytes on smear hematocrit 36% · reticulocytes high · bilirubin 17 mg/dL, direct 0.6 mg/dL G6PD enzyme activity levelCoombs-negative hemolysis (anemia with high reticulocytes) in a boy of Mediterranean ancestry is G6PD deficiency: X-linked, so mostly boys, and often an oxidant trigger. Osmotic fragility testing looks for spherocytosis, which the smear argues against, and a liver panel answers a raised direct fraction

Next step16 of 28 8-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced vomits after breastfeeds liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances, dipstick glucose negative Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL · Stop breast milk and start soy-based formula · Phototherapy and continue breastfeeding · Liver transplant evaluation 8-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced vomits after breastfeeds liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin urine positive for reducing substances, dipstick glucose negative Afebrile · direct bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL Stop breast milk and start soy-based formulaa conjugated fraction, a large liver and a non-glucose reducing sugar after days of milk feeds indicate classic galactosemia: stop breast milk now and start soy formula. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise, and continuing feeds continues the injury; the diet reverses the liver disease, so transplant evaluation is not the step

Mechanism17 of 28 3-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the chest a sulfonamide is proposed for a suspected urinary tract infection Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 15 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL · Inhibition of glucuronosyltransferase · Displacement of bilirubin from albumin · Increased heme oxygenase activity 3-day-old boy born at term is jaundiced to the chest a sulfonamide is proposed for a suspected urinary tract infection Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity is normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 15 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL Displacement of bilirubin from albuminfree bilirubin crosses into the basal ganglia. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, so they are avoided in jaundiced newborns; when G6PD is deficient a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis, a second way it harms, excluded here by the normal enzyme. Glucuronosyltransferase activity sets how much bilirubin is conjugated and heme breakdown how much is made; the sulfonamide instead competes with bilirubin for albumin, raising the unbound fraction.

Diagnosis18 of 28 6-week-old boy born at term is well and growing bilateral cataracts on red reflex examination no hepatomegaly; no jaundice urine positive for reducing substances Passed newborn hearing screen; no murmur Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile · Congenital rubella syndrome · Classic galactosemia · Galactokinase deficiency 6-week-old boy born at term is well and growing bilateral cataracts on red reflex examination no hepatomegaly; no jaundice urine positive for reducing substances Passed newborn hearing screen; no murmur Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile Galactokinase deficiencya block one step earlier diverts galactose to galactitol: cataracts in a well infant, with no liver disease and no sepsis; lactose-free diet. Classic galactosemia traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate and makes the whole sick-neonate picture; congenital rubella brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth and not triggered by milk

Next step19 of 28 4-week-old boy born at term is well and feeding well jaundiced, with acholic stools urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · weight at the 40th percentile · total bilirubin 7 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL · Phototherapy · Abdominal ultrasound and HIDA scan · Kasai portoenterostomy now 4-week-old boy born at term is well and feeding well jaundiced, with acholic stools urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · weight at the 40th percentile · total bilirubin 7 mg/dL · direct bilirubin 5 mg/dL Abdominal ultrasound and HIDA scana direct fraction in a well infant with acholic stools and negative reducing substances is biliary atresia: image first, then intraoperative cholangiogram confirms, and Kasai follows confirmation, before about 60 days. Phototherapy treats an indirect rise

Diagnosis20 of 28 3-day-old boy, formula-fed, has increasing lethargy and vomiting breathing rapidly; no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, clear lenses Urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · arterial pH 7.50, low carbon dioxide · ammonia markedly elevated · glucose 80 mg/dL · Maple syrup urine disease · Classic galactosemia · Urea cycle disorder 3-day-old boy, formula-fed, has increasing lethargy and vomiting breathing rapidly; no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, clear lenses Urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · arterial pH 7.50, low carbon dioxide · ammonia markedly elevated · glucose 80 mg/dL Urea cycle disordervery high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis in the first days of feeding, with no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts: hyperammonemia; stop protein and lower the ammonia. Classic galactosemia brings conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly and urine reducing sugar; maple syrup urine disease brings sweet-smelling urine and ketosis

Avoid21 of 28 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed; weight 9% below birth weight only three wet diapers today; alert and well Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL · direct 0.4 mg/dL · Stopping breast-feeding · Lactation support with more frequent feeds · Phototherapy if the level crosses threshold 4-day-old girl born at term is jaundiced exclusively breast-fed; weight 9% below birth weight only three wet diapers today; alert and well Afebrile · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL · direct 0.4 mg/dL Stopping breast-feedingthis is suboptimal intake, and jaundice is almost never a reason to stop breast-feeding: feed more often, not less, because milk intake drives bilirubin out through the gut. Lactation support with more frequent feeds, and phototherapy if the level crosses threshold, are both appropriate

Diagnosis22 of 28 3-month-old boy has a protuberant abdomen and doll-like facies massive hepatomegaly hypoglycemia after a 4-hour fast No cataracts; urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · lactate 6 mmol/L · triglycerides 450 mg/dL · glucose 35 mg/dL · Classic galactosemia · Hereditary fructose intolerance · Glycogen storage disease type I 3-month-old boy has a protuberant abdomen and doll-like facies massive hepatomegaly hypoglycemia after a 4-hour fast No cataracts; urine negative for reducing substances Afebrile · lactate 6 mmol/L · triglycerides 450 mg/dL · glucose 35 mg/dL Glycogen storage disease type Ihepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis and hypertriglyceridemia, with hypoglycemia within hours of fasting, no galactose trigger and no cataracts; treat with frequent cornstarch feeds. Galactosemia needs milk feeds and urine reducing sugar; hereditary fructose intolerance starts with fruit or sucrose at weaning

Next step23 of 28 6-week-old boy born at term, jaundiced since 3 weeks of age clay-colored stools, dark urine ultrasound: small gallbladder, triangular cord sign intraoperative cholangiogram: no contrast reaches the duodenum Afebrile · direct bilirubin 6 mg/dL · GGT high · Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy · Ursodeoxycholic acid and fat-soluble vitamins · Primary liver transplantation 6-week-old boy born at term, jaundiced since 3 weeks of age clay-colored stools, dark urine ultrasound: small gallbladder, triangular cord sign intraoperative cholangiogram: no contrast reaches the duodenum Afebrile · direct bilirubin 6 mg/dL · GGT high Kasai hepatoportoenterostomyno contrast reaching the bowel confirms biliary atresia: Kasai before about 60 days, best done early, and most eventually need a liver transplant, so transplant is the later step, not the first. Ursodeoxycholic acid is given after the Kasai, not in place of it

Next step24 of 28 12-day-old girl was diagnosed with galactosemia on day 6 on soy formula since diagnosis now lethargic and feeding poorly Jaundice improving; liver smaller T 38.8 °C · HR 186/min · capillary refill 3 seconds · Blood and urine cultures, then intravenous ceftriaxone · Blood and urine cultures, then observe off antibiotics · Blood, urine and CSF cultures, then IV ampicillin and gentamicin 12-day-old girl was diagnosed with galactosemia on day 6 on soy formula since diagnosis now lethargic and feeding poorly Jaundice improving; liver smaller T 38.8 °C · HR 186/min · capillary refill 3 seconds Blood, urine and CSF cultures, then IV ampicillin and gentamicingalactosemia predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis, and a neonate with suspected sepsis gets a lumbar puncture once able to tolerate it: culture blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, then start empiric neonatal antibiotics. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin, so it is avoided in a jaundiced newborn, and observing off antibiotics leaves the infection untreated

Workup25 of 28 3-week-old girl born at term is still jaundiced to the chest exclusively breastfed and gaining weight well yellow stools and pale urine Seen at a routine visit; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · Transcutaneous bilirubin measurement · Serum total and direct bilirubin · Blood type and direct Coombs test 3-week-old girl born at term is still jaundiced to the chest exclusively breastfed and gaining weight well yellow stools and pale urine Seen at a routine visit; examination otherwise normal Afebrile Serum total and direct bilirubinjaundice past 2 weeks needs a direct fraction, and the stool color, before reassurance; an indirect result in a thriving infant is breast-milk jaundice. A transcutaneous reading gives no direct fraction, and a Coombs test answers jaundice inside 24 hours, not prolonged jaundice

Mechanism26 of 28 9-day-old breastfed girl has 3 days of vomiting and poor feeding jaundiced; liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts Normal hearing screen, no murmur; mother 39, declined vaccines T 38.4 °C · blood culture: Escherichia coli · Maternal nonadherence to recommended vaccinations · Advanced maternal age at conception · Inability to metabolize galactose in breast milk 9-day-old breastfed girl has 3 days of vomiting and poor feeding jaundiced; liver 4 cm below the costal margin bilateral cataracts Normal hearing screen, no murmur; mother 39, declined vaccines T 38.4 °C · blood culture: Escherichia coli Inability to metabolize galactose in breast milka milk-fed neonate with conjugated jaundice, a large liver, cataracts and Escherichia coli sepsis has classic galactosemia: stop breast milk and start soy formula without waiting for confirmation, and treat the sepsis in parallel. Congenital rubella, the vaccine decoy, brings cataracts with deafness and a patent ductus arteriosus, present at birth; a normal hearing screen and no murmur argue against it. Classic galactosemia is autosomal recessive, so the mother's age is a decoy

Mechanism27 of 28 2-year-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia on newborn screening fed soy formula since day 5 parents ask about her long-term outlook Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile · Speech and learning problems and ovarian insufficiency can occur despite the diet · Normal development and normal fertility are expected as long as the diet is strict · Progressive cirrhosis is expected even if the diet is strict 2-year-old girl was diagnosed with classic galactosemia on newborn screening fed soy formula since day 5 parents ask about her long-term outlook Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile Speech and learning problems and ovarian insufficiency can occur despite the dieteven with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems (verbal dyspraxia), and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency. The diet reverses the acute liver, sepsis and cataract illness but does not prevent these, so normal fertility is not expected, and neither is progressive cirrhosis

Diagnosis28 of 28 3-week-old boy born at term is still jaundiced at a weight check exclusively breast-fed and gaining weight well yellow stools; thriving Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 13 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL · Biliary atresia · Suboptimal-intake jaundice · Breast-milk jaundice 3-week-old boy born at term is still jaundiced at a weight check exclusively breast-fed and gaining weight well yellow stools; thriving Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · total bilirubin 13 mg/dL · direct 0.5 mg/dL Breast-milk jaundicemilk beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin and increases enterohepatic circulation: from day 7, peaking around 2 weeks and able to persist for weeks, in a thriving infant with normal stools; continue breast-feeding. Suboptimal intake is a hungry infant losing weight in the first week, and biliary atresia raises the direct fraction and turns the stools pale

5-day-old boy of Mediterranean descent with 2 days of progressive jaundice Five yellow, seedy stools a day; 2 ounces of cow's milk formula every 2 hours Born at term to a 32-year-old primigravida, who took an old sulfamethoxazole prescription for cystitis in the third trimester Mother and infant both group O, Rh-positive examination normal except jaundice from the head to the upper thighs hematocrit 33% · total bilirubin 20 mg/dL, direct 0.9 mg/dL direct and indirect Coombs tests negative Most likely explanation for the jaundice? Competing answers Dehydration: raises indirect bilirubin through enterohepatic reabsorption; but feeds every 2 hours and five stools a day argue against it, and it does not cause anemia. Sepsis: can raise indirect bilirubin; but he is well on examination, and Coombs-negative anemia after an oxidant exposure points to hemolysis. Milk protein allergy: the cow's milk formula is the decoy; allergy causes reflux, enterocolitis, enteropathy or urticaria, not hemolysis. Down to two: enzyme deficiency or physiologic jaundice. Enzyme deficiency: a total of 20 mg/dL exceeds the physiologic peak of about 15, and a hematocrit of 33% points to hemolysis. A negative Coombs removes isoimmune hemolysis; Mediterranean ancestry and a maternal sulfonamide point to G6PD deficiency. G6PD makes NADPH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate), which keeps glutathione reduced; without it, sulfonamides and other oxidants cause hemolysis. The key named only the class.

Direct high, GGT high, reticulocytes normal duct obstruction: biliary atresia in a well infant with pale stools Direct high, GGT normal progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis Direct and GGT high, reticulocytes low, cytopenias hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in a febrile, ill infant Indirect, reticulocytes high hemolysis Indirect, everything else normal breast-milk jaundice in a thriving infant; an exclusively breastfed infant can still have biliary atresia, so pale stools and a direct fraction decide it

Reducing substances positive with dipstick glucose negative means galactose or fructose, because glucose is itself a reducing sugar, so read both tests. Galactokinase makes galactose-1-phosphate, and GALT converts it to uridine diphosphate galactose and glucose-1-phosphate. A galactokinase block leaves only galactitol, so cataracts alone; a GALT block traps toxic galactose-1-phosphate, so the whole sick-neonate picture, affecting liver, kidney, brain and lens. Cataracts in both come from galactitol via aldose reductase, the enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens. Even with an early, strict diet, children can have cognitive deficits and speech problems, and girls develop primary ovarian insufficiency.

Ligandin or enterohepatic circulation: real mechanisms stated in the wrong direction (ligandin is low and enterohepatic circulation increased in the newborn). Exchange transfusion at a level still in the phototherapy range. Maple syrup urine disease for a sick jaundiced neonate: the right class of screen-flagged inborn error, but no hepatomegaly, and ketoacids rather than a reducing sugar. Cystic fibrosis because the screen is positive: screened by immunoreactive trypsinogen, it presents with meconium ileus or quiet cholestasis, not fever with urinary sugar. Sickle cell or neonatal hyperthyroidism: screen-positive with no hepatic picture; sickle cell jaundice is unconjugated and silent at 10 days because fetal hemoglobin protects. Urea cycle disorder: very high ammonia with lethargy and respiratory alkalosis, but no jaundice, hepatomegaly or cataracts. Glycogen storage disease type I: hypoglycemia within hours of fasting with lactic acidosis, but no galactose trigger and no cataracts. Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, and a sulfonamide also causes hemolysis when G6PD is deficient.

Board questions use 60 days as the Kasai cutoff, and the Kasai is ideally done before 60 days. The evidence shows no sharp cutoff: native-liver survival falls continuously with age at operation, and a 2023 meta-analysis found operating at 30 days or earlier still better than at 31 to 60 days. Use 60 days as the exam threshold, not as a deadline with room to spare.

Part I Abnormal Liver Tests: the conjugated-versus-unconjugated workup in adults. Hereditary fructose intolerance has no brief of its own: did symptoms start with fruit or sucrose? Biliary atresia: is the infant sick or well, and are reducing substances present? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism: another positive newborn screen, where the thyroid-stimulating hormone level and the neck locate the defect; in galactosemia, the enzyme deficiency and the organism locate it.

When every option names a real mechanism, check which direction each one moves in this patient before choosing. A positive newborn screen never names the disease when every disorder under consideration is on the panel: the bilirubin fraction, the liver and the urine identify it, and a febrile neonate is cultured and treated for sepsis in parallel with the metabolic diagnosis, not after it.

Pt 7-day-old term F with truncus arteriosus in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) awaiting repair, poor feeding and abdominal distension; T 35 C, BP 60/30, pulse 180, respirations 65, saturation 82% Exam lethargic and cyanotic, moderate distension, absent bowel sounds, bright red blood in stool; nasogastric tube returns bilious fluid Imaging abdominal x-ray Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), malrotation with volvulus, intussusception, milk protein proctocolitis and C difficile colitis

The combination of temperature instability, abdominal distension with bloody stools, and pneumatosis intestinalis on the film indicates NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis). NEC is mainly a disease of prematurity, but this infant is term. In a term infant, cyanotic congenital heart disease and hypotension reduce mesenteric oxygen delivery and cause the same ischemic bowel injury. The bilious return also fits volvulus, so rule it out. Volvulus gives abrupt vomiting in a previously well infant, with proximal gas and a gasless distal abdomen. NEC gives air in the bowel wall with gas still visible in the large bowel. Read the gas pattern first; if malrotation is still possible, only an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes it.

Pneumatosis intestinalis air within the bowel wall; highly specific for NEC, often with portal venous gas (branching lucencies over the liver) Pneumoperitoneum free air under the diaphragm; means perforation and an operation NEC risk factors prematurity (the most important), very low birth weight under 1.5 kg, enteral feeding (especially formula), prolonged antibiotics, and in term infants a hypoxic-ischemic insult such as cyanotic heart disease, hypotension or perinatal asphyxia Volvulus film proximal gaseous distension with a gasless distal abdomen Intussusception age 6 months to 3 years

The distended abdomen in a newborn or infant: the differentialtiming, the stool, and the gas pattern Diagnosis The picture Key discriminator What to do Necrotizing enterocolitis Emergency Preterm infant on enteral feeds; lethargy, apnea, hypothermia rather than fever, distension, feeding intolerance, bilious emesis, bloody stools (may be absent early); leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis Pneumatosis intestinalis with or without portal venous gas; gas still present distally Nothing by mouth (NPO), nasogastric (NG) decompression, parenteral nutrition, broad-spectrum antibiotics now; surgery for perforation or worsening despite medical care Malrotation with midgut volvulus Emergency Previously well, then abrupt bilious vomiting and pain; any age, most often the first month; older children can have intermittent pain and vomiting instead Proximal gas, gasless distal abdomen; upper GI series shows the ligament of Treitz on the right and a corkscrew or bird's-beak duodenum Upper GI series if stable; emergency laparotomy if not; the operation is the Ladd procedure Duodenal atresia Bilious vomiting in the first 1 to 2 days, polyhydramnios, trisomy 21; abdomen not distended Double bubble with no distal gas, present from birth rather than abrupt Stop feeds, NG decompression, echocardiogram, then surgical repair Hirschsprung disease No meconium by 48 hours, poor feeding, distension, bilious vomiting; failed neural crest migration leaves an aganglionic segment, usually rectosigmoid, that cannot relax and stays contracted; usually isolated, but associated with Down syndrome Normal meconium once it passes; tight rectum with an explosive squirt of stool and gas on rectal exam; enema shows a rectosigmoid transition zone with dilated proximal colon; a newborn under 48 hours is not yet late Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy (absent ganglion cells confirms); surgical resection of the aganglionic segment Meconium ileus No meconium, distension, ± bilious vomiting; thick, sticky meconium obstructs the terminal ileum; cystic fibrosis in about 90% Dilated small bowel with little colonic gas; contrast enema shows a microcolon; empty rectum, no squirt; not a Down syndrome association Hyperosmolar contrast enema, which can also relieve it; surgery if it fails or for free air; sweat chloride test Intussusception Colicky pain, currant-jelly stool, right upper quadrant mass Age 6 months to 3 years; target sign on ultrasound Air-contrast enema Milk protein-induced proctocolitis Blood-streaked stools at 2 to 8 weeks The infant is well – thriving, undistended, normal vitals Maternal dairy elimination or hydrolyzed formula Clostridioides difficile colitis Distension with watery, sometimes bloody stool Neonates are colonized but lack the toxin receptors Not a neonatal diagnosis

Diagnostic workup Test Order Result What it points to Abdominal radiograph First Pneumatosis intestinalis with or without portal venous gas, distal gas present NEC: NPO, decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics Proximal gas, gasless distal abdomen Volvulus: upper GI series if stable, laparotomy if not Double bubble, no distal gas Duodenal atresia: NG decompression and surgical repair Diffusely dilated loops, distended abdomen, no air in the rectum, no free air Distal obstruction: Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus Free air under the diaphragm Perforation: laparotomy Echocardiogram By branch Duodenal atresia with trisomy 21 features About half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease (ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, atrioventricular canal); obtain before surgery, murmur or not Karyotype Confirms Trisomy 21 Confirms Down syndrome but is not urgent and does not change the operation Upper GI series after a diagnostic double bubble Skip Film already diagnostic Upper GI is for malrotation, which has distal gas Contrast enema, then rectal suction biopsy By branch Transition zone; absent ganglion cells Hirschsprung disease: no meconium by 48 hours with distension Contrast enema, then sweat chloride test By branch Microcolon with inspissated meconium in the terminal ileum Meconium ileus: a hyperosmolar enema can relieve it; about 90% have cystic fibrosis Complete blood count, blood gas and blood culture By branch Leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis NEC: the platelet fall tracks severity; a rising count is often the first sign of improvement Upper GI contrast series Confirms Ligament of Treitz on the right; corkscrew or bird's-beak duodenum Malrotation with midgut volvulus: Ladd procedure; skip it and operate if the infant is unstable Abdominal ultrasound By branch Target sign Intussusception at 6 months to 3 years: air-contrast enema C difficile toxin testing Skip Neonates lack the toxin receptors Not a neonatal diagnosis
