Workup21 of 24 3-week-old boy in the NICU born at 28 weeks weighing 900 g, extubated to nasal cannula last week, on continuous nasogastric formula feeds and gaining weight, with small yellow seedy stools until none in the past 24 hours, now has 6 hours of nonbloody bilious vomiting; temperature 35.6 C, BP 75/45, pulse 165, respirations 70; lethargic, with a tense distended abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds; leukocytosis and metabolic acidosis · Abdominal x-ray with air in the bowel wall and portal veins · Abdominal x-ray with air in the stomach and duodenum but no distal air · Contrast enema with a narrow rectosigmoid and a dilated proximal colon 3-week-old boy in the NICU born at 28 weeks weighing 900 g, extubated to nasal cannula last week, on continuous nasogastric formula feeds and gaining weight, with small yellow seedy stools until none in the past 24 hours, now has 6 hours of nonbloody bilious vomiting; temperature 35.6 C, BP 75/45, pulse 165, respirations 70; lethargic, with a tense distended abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds; leukocytosis and metabolic acidosis Abdominal x-ray with air in the bowel wall and portal veinsNecrotizing enterocolitis; stop feeds, NG decompression and broad-spectrum antibiotics

Screening22 of 24 Girl born at 27 weeks weighing 950 g, now 4 days old, stable on room air in the NICU and about to start enteral feeds; her mother is expressing milk · Prophylactic broad-spectrum IV antibiotics · Exclusive feeding with breast milk · Calorie-dense preterm infant formula Girl born at 27 weeks weighing 950 g, now 4 days old, stable on room air in the NICU and about to start enteral feeds; her mother is expressing milk Exclusive feeding with breast milkThe most effective measure against necrotizing enterocolitis

Diagnosis23 of 24 7-month-old boy with 6 hours of persistent bilious vomiting, no fever, diarrhea or recent illness, last bowel movement 24 hours ago and no prior surgery; temperature 37 C, BP 70/50, pulse 180, respirations 65; moans with light palpation of a distended, hypertympanic abdomen with absent bowel sounds · Necrotizing enterocolitis · Intestinal malrotation with midgut volvulus · Pyloric stenosis 7-month-old boy with 6 hours of persistent bilious vomiting, no fever, diarrhea or recent illness, last bowel movement 24 hours ago and no prior surgery; temperature 37 C, BP 70/50, pulse 180, respirations 65; moans with light palpation of a distended, hypertympanic abdomen with absent bowel sounds Intestinal malrotation with midgut volvulusEmergency laparotomy, Ladd procedure

Next step24 of 24 5-week-old term girl with 4 hours of bilious vomiting and inconsolable crying; after a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, pulse is 190, BP 55/30 and capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen distended and diffusely tender; film shows a dilated stomach and duodenum with little distal gas · Emergency laparotomy · Nasogastric decompression and serial abdominal exams · Upper gastrointestinal contrast series 5-week-old term girl with 4 hours of bilious vomiting and inconsolable crying; after a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, pulse is 190, BP 55/30 and capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen distended and diffusely tender; film shows a dilated stomach and duodenum with little distal gas Emergency laparotomyUnstable malrotation with midgut volvulus; Ladd procedure without waiting for contrast

Free air – stop investigating and operate Unstable with bilious vomiting – laparotomy without waiting for contrast In a term infant with NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis), look for the perfusion insult: cyanotic heart disease, hypotension, sepsis NEC worsening despite bowel rest and antibiotics: surgery Late NEC sequelae – strictures and short-bowel syndrome Bilious emesis in any infant, at any age, is malrotation until an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes it

Maternal fentanyl epidural maternal opioids can slow the newborn bowel and delay meconium, but they do not raise rectal tone or cause an explosive release of stool on rectal exam Mother aged 38 advanced maternal age raises the risk of Down syndrome, which goes with Hirschsprung disease; most Hirschsprung disease is isolated, so a nondysmorphic infant still fits Shallow sacral dimple with intact skin and no hair a normal finding; spina bifida occulta severe enough to cause a neurogenic bowel brings a hair tuft or neurologic deficits, and this exam has normal strength and reflexes Tight rectum, then a release of normal stool the squirt sign; meconium ileus gives normal tone, no release, and inspissated meconium in the ileum

The order stop feeds, NG (nasogastric) decompression and IV (intravenous) fluids, echocardiogram, then surgical repair Echocardiogram about half of infants with Down syndrome have heart disease. A loud holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border is a VSD (ventricular septal defect) No distension the block is proximal, so the rest of the abdomen stays flat; distension points to a distal obstruction Meconium timing about 99% of healthy term newborns pass meconium within 24 hours, so a distended infant with none by then needs evaluation; none by 48 hours is delayed and raises Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus; a well, undistended newborn a few hours old is not yet late Pyloric stenosis nonbilious projectile vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks, not bilious emesis on day 1

Pneumatosis – gas made by bacteria that have invaded the wall, which is why it is specific Bilious vomiting means the obstruction is distal to the ampulla; it is urgent until an upper GI (gastrointestinal) series excludes malrotation NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis) and volvulus both give a distended, bilious, unwell neonate; the gas pattern separates them A well infant with blood in the stool is almost never surgical; distension and instability suggest a surgical cause Prematurity is the commonest NEC risk factor, not a required one Meconium ileus means cystic fibrosis – nearly all patients with cystic fibrosis develop sinopulmonary disease, including chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (sinus opacification by age 1); hypothyroidism and early-onset Alzheimer disease point to Down syndrome, which goes with Hirschsprung disease

Mild: lethargy, temperature instability, apnea, feeding intolerance, bilious residuals, heme-positive stool; labs and film normal or mild dilation Moderate: adds absent bowel sounds, tenderness, abdominal wall erythema, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis and pneumatosis Severe: adds hypotension, peritonitis, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) and pneumoperitoneum Platelets: the fall tracks severity, and a rising count is often the first sign of improvement Prevention: exclusive breast milk is the most effective measure; antenatal corticosteroids for a mother likely to deliver preterm within 7 days also lower the risk, along with respiratory distress syndrome and intraventricular hemorrhage

Age: most present in the first month, but volvulus can happen at any age. In a 7-month-old with bilious vomiting, tachycardia and a silent distended abdomen, malrotation is still the first diagnosis Older children: intermittent abdominal pain and vomiting, sometimes failure to thrive Late signs: hematochezia, peritonitis and shock mean the bowel is already ischemic Not NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis): a disease of preterm infants in the first weeks on feeds Not pyloric stenosis: that vomiting is nonbilious and projectile at 3 to 6 weeks, in a well infant with an olive-shaped mass

Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers the well infant with blood in the stool; this brief covers the sick one. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers obstruction above the pylorus. Ask: is the infant well, and what is the gas pattern?
In a distended neonate, the stool and vital signs show severity and the gas pattern identifies the disease: air in the wall, air where bowel should be, or no air at all.

Unchecked attributeIf NEC (necrotizing enterocolitis) is filed under prematurity, a term infant is ruled out without checking perfusion. Salient decoyBilious nasogastric return pulls toward volvulus before the film is read. Class-vs-memberRight category of neonatal bowel emergency, wrong member of it. Sequencing trapKaryotype confirms trisomy 21, but it is not urgent and does not change the need for repair. Redundant workupAn upper GI (gastrointestinal) series adds nothing once the film shows a double bubble with no distal gas; it is for malrotation. Unchecked attributeNo meconium sounds like Hirschsprung disease, but a 10-hour-old is not yet late and the abdomen is not distended. True-fact-wrong-slotEarly-onset Alzheimer disease and hypothyroidism are real Down syndrome associations, but Down syndrome goes with Hirschsprung disease; thick meconium in the ileum with a microcolon is meconium ileus, which means cystic fibrosis and later sinus disease. Class-vs-memberInspissated meconium is the other cause of no meconium with distension, but it obstructs the ileum with a microcolon, normal rectal tone and no squirt; it is cystic fibrosis, not Hirschsprung disease. Salient decoyA shallow sacral dimple without a hair tuft is normal; spinal cord dysfunction would bring neurologic deficits, and strength and reflexes are normal. Salient decoyA maternal fentanyl epidural can cause neonatal ileus, but not increased rectal tone with an explosive release of stool. Salient decoyBilious vomiting pulls toward a proximal block, but air in the stomach and duodenum with no distal gas is duodenal atresia, which presents with the first feeds; an infant who has been passing yellow seedy stools on full feeds is not obstructed there. Salient decoyNo stool for a day suggests Hirschsprung disease, but that shows no meconium by 48 hours or chronic constipation, not sudden hypothermia, acidosis and a tense abdomen in a 3-week-old preterm infant. Unchecked attributeNEC is the right category of sick distended bowel, but it affects preterm infants in their first weeks on feeds; a term 7-month-old with bilious vomiting has volvulus. Unchecked attributePyloric stenosis causes vomiting in infancy, but it is nonbilious and projectile at 3 to 6 weeks; bilious vomiting in any infant is malrotation until proven otherwise.

briefs.title: Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult
briefs.sub: firm stool in the vault · overflow diarrhea · anticholinergic cause · enema, then manual disimpaction · treat the causeWhat does the rectal exam find, and which drug is slowing the colon?
blocks: Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult
firm stool in the vault · overflow diarrhea · anticholinergic cause · enema, then manual disimpaction · treat the causeWhat does the rectal exam find, and which drug is slowing the colon?

Pt 77 yo F taking oxybutynin; last bowel movement 5 days ago, and it was loose stool; colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities; no hematochezia Exam afebrile, warm dry skin, soft abdomen without distension, diffuse tenderness, firm stool in the rectal vault Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned fecal impaction, adhesions, colon cancer, diverticulitis, ischemic bowel and volvulus

Firm stool in the rectal vault on rectal exam is fecal impaction; loose stool after days without a bowel movement is overflow around it, not diarrhea. Clear it with an enema first; manual disimpaction follows only when the enema fails. Then remove the cause when possible, such as an anticholinergic like oxybutynin, and start daily polyethylene glycol (PEG) to prevent recurrence.

What it is Fecal impaction: a hard stool mass blocking the rectum, which may cause or follow constipation. Driver Slowed colonic transit, commonly from a drug (anticholinergics, opioids) Triggers Constipating drugs: anticholinergics, opioids, calcium channel blockers, iron, calcium, aluminum, ondansetron ; older age non-modifiable ; bed rest or low activity ; hypothyroidism, hypercalcemia, diabetes ; neurologic disease such as Parkinson disease non-modifiable Chain Drug slows colonic transit hard stool collects in the rectum liquid stool leaks around the mass overflow diarrhea or fecal incontinence Insights Only a small volume of liquid stool can leak around a hard rectal mass, so the diarrhea is scant and can come with incontinence. Older adults have a more compliant rectum and blunted rectal sensation, so a larger mass builds before the urge comes.

Clinical diagnosis Diagnosis Requires Fecal impaction A hard stool mass on digital rectal exam; no imaging when the abdomen is soft Overflow diarrhea Watery stool or mucus passing around a hard stool mass Drug-induced constipation Onset with a constipating drug and no red flags; may be treated without further study

Act now Finding Action Tympanitic abdomen with vomiting, or an empty rectal vault with a distended abdomen Treat as suspected mechanical obstruction: flat and upright abdominal films or CT, and nasogastric suction. Severe or persistent abdominal pain of unknown cause Hold laxatives until obstruction and other acute causes are excluded. Blood in stool or weight loss, or severe constipation of recent onset or worsening in an older adult with no known cause Colonoscopy to exclude colon cancer.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Typical picture Decides it Adhesive small bowel obstruction Prior abdominal surgery; colicky pain, early vomiting, high-pitched bowel sounds Empty rectum with a distended abdomen Sigmoid volvulus Chronically constipated older adult; abrupt pain, distended tympanitic abdomen Coffee-bean loop on the abdominal film Colon cancer (colorectal carcinoma) New or progressive constipation, narrower stools; blood in stool or weight loss Colonoscopy; a recent normal one argues against it Diverticulitis Fever with focal left lower quadrant (LLQ) pain and tenderness CT of the abdomen and pelvis, the preferred test Ischemic colitis Atrial fibrillation or atherosclerotic risk; crampy pain Hematochezia Dyssynergic defecation (pelvic floor dysfunction) Typically straining, incomplete evacuation, digital disimpaction Fails fiber and laxatives; anorectal manometry with balloon expulsion

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Older patient on a constipating drug, days without a bowel movement, then loose stool → Digital rectal exam Firm stool in the vault Impaction pattern; clear it Empty vault with a distended abdomen Obstruction above the rectum: abdominal films or CT Targeted tests TestResultMeans Distended, tympanitic abdomen or vomiting → Flat and upright abdominal radiographs, or CT Multiple air-fluid levels Small bowel obstruction: nasogastric suction Coffee-bean loop Sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic decompression, which can reduce the twist noninvasively Severe new or worsening constipation with no clear cause, or blood in stool or weight loss → Colonoscopy Mass or stricture Colon cancer → Alongside the colonoscopy: CBC, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), glucose, electrolytes and calcium Raised TSH or calcium Hypothyroidism or hypercalcemia as the cause Typically straining and incomplete evacuation despite fiber and laxatives → Anorectal manometry with balloon expulsion Abnormal Pelvic floor dysfunction such as dyssynergic defecation Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Firm stool on the first-step rectal exam → No further test: a clinical diagnosis Soft abdomen and a clear drug cause Fecal impaction SkipRepeat colonoscopy here: a normal one 3 years ago and a clear drug cause make cancer unlikely, so treatment comes first.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Loose stool after 5 days without a bowel movement Overflow around an impaction Perform a digital rectal exam Warm, dry skin on oxybutynin Anticholinergic effect: the drug is the cause Stop or reduce it once the rectum is clear Soft abdomen without distension Argues against obstruction and volvulus Treat the impaction; no film needed Normal colonoscopy 3 years ago Argues against colon cancer Treat the impaction first No fever; diffuse rather than focal tenderness Argues against diverticulitis Treat the impaction No hematochezia Argues against ischemic colitis Treat the impaction
Pause point Constipated patient with loose stool Offered as a diarrheal illness Firm stool in the vault: overflow → Impaction

1 First lineFirm stool in the vault Enema: tap water, then a small hypertonic enema. 2 Mass remainsMass still in the rectum Manual fragmentation and disimpaction may be needed, with a topical local anesthetic. 3 After clearingAlways, once the rectum is clear Stop or reduce the constipating drug when possible; daily PEG to prevent recurrence, with fluids and activity. Why PEG worksAn osmotic laxative stays in the colon and holds water there; the larger, softer stool distends the bowel and drives peristalsis. 4 Opioid continuesOpioid-induced constipation, the opioid still needed A scheduled osmotic or stimulant laxative (senna, bisacodyl) first; a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (methylnaltrexone, naloxegol) only when laxatives fail. Not with obstructionThese antagonists are contraindicated when bowel obstruction is known or suspected.

After clearing Situation Do Constipation began with a new drug Stop the drug when possible; with no red flags, the constipation may be treated without further testing Daily habits A set toilet time after breakfast, when eating stimulates the colon; fluids and activity Still constipated on fiber and laxatives Anorectal manometry

Diagnosis1 of 7 77 yo F, 5 days without a bowel movement (BM), empty rectal vault, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, prior laparotomy · Fecal impactionFecal impaction leaves firm stool in the vault; this vault is empty. · Sigmoid volvulusSigmoid volvulus shows a coffee-bean loop on the abdominal film. · Adhesive small bowel obstructionAn empty rectum, distension and high-pitched bowel sounds after a laparotomy are adhesive small bowel obstruction. 77 yo F, 5 days without a bowel movement (BM), empty rectal vault, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, prior laparotomy Adhesive small bowel obstructionnasogastric decompression + imaging

Diagnosis2 of 7 77 yo F, sudden severe pain, distended tympanitic abdomen, coffee-bean sign · Adhesive small bowel obstructionAdhesive small bowel obstruction gives air-fluid levels in small bowel loops, not a coffee-bean loop. · Sigmoid volvulusA coffee-bean loop with a distended, tympanitic abdomen is sigmoid volvulus. · Cecal volvulusCecal volvulus is the rarer twist; its gas bubble sits in the mid-abdomen or left upper quadrant. 77 yo F, sudden severe pain, distended tympanitic abdomen, coffee-bean sign Sigmoid volvulusendoscopic decompression

Diagnosis3 of 7 68 yo M, LLQ pain with fever 38.5 and focal tenderness · Ischemic colitisIschemic colitis brings hematochezia in a patient with atrial fibrillation or atherosclerosis. · DiverticulitisFever with focal left lower quadrant pain and tenderness is diverticulitis; CT confirms it. · Colon cancerColon cancer changes bowel habits over weeks; it does not bring acute fever with focal pain. 68 yo M, LLQ pain with fever 38.5 and focal tenderness DiverticulitisCT

Diagnosis4 of 7 72 yo F with atrial fibrillation, crampy pain and hematochezia · DiverticulitisDiverticulitis brings fever with focal left lower quadrant tenderness. · Infectious colitisInfectious colitis brings fever and diarrhea after an exposure, neither given here. · Ischemic colitisCrampy pain with hematochezia in a patient with atrial fibrillation is ischemic colitis. 72 yo F with atrial fibrillation, crampy pain and hematochezia Ischemic colitis

Diagnosis5 of 7 60 yo M, progressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss, no recent colonoscopy · Diverticular strictureA diverticular stricture follows diverticulitis and does not explain the anemia. · Chronic functional constipationFunctional constipation is long-standing, without anemia or weight loss. · Colon cancerProgressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss in an older adult needs colonoscopy for colon cancer. 60 yo M, progressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss, no recent colonoscopy Colon cancercolonoscopy

Next step6 of 7 77 yo F, impaction cleared by enema, still constipated · Add senna, continue oxybutyninAdding a laxative while the oxybutynin continues leaves the cause in place. · Stop the oxybutynin, start PEGAfter clearing, remove the anticholinergic cause and prevent recurrence with daily PEG. · Start lubiprostoneLubiprostone is a later option for chronic constipation; the drug cause comes off first. 77 yo F, impaction cleared by enema, still constipated Stop the oxybutynin, start PEG

Next step7 of 7 80 yo M on chronic opioids, 6 days without a BM, hard stool in the vault · Start PEG alonePEG alone does not clear a hard mass already sitting in the vault. · Disimpaction, then a scheduled stimulant or osmotic laxativeClear the impaction first; then a scheduled stimulant or osmotic laxative, with a peripherally acting opioid antagonist only if laxatives fail. · Increase the opioid and add sennaA higher opioid dose worsens the constipation. 80 yo M on chronic opioids, 6 days without a BM, hard stool in the vault Disimpaction, then a scheduled stimulant or osmotic laxative

Impaction can sit distal to a second lesion, such as a slow-growing tumor or partial obstruction. Here, a normal colonoscopy 3 years ago, no blood in the stool and a clear drug cause mean no further workup is needed. If any one of these is missing, relieve the impaction and also investigate.

Constipation in a Childcovers the pediatric case, where an oral laxative comes before any rectal treatment and an anal fissure is a reason to avoid the rectal route that is first-line here Constipation in a Child covers the pediatric case, where an oral laxative comes before any rectal treatment and an anal fissure is a reason to avoid the rectal route that is first-line here.
When two answers both seem plausible, choose the one the stem's findings do not exclude. Here, firm stool in the rectal vault with a soft, undistended abdomen excludes small bowel obstruction.
Salient decoyLoose stool suggests a diarrheal illness, but with firm stool in the vault it is overflow around an impaction.

briefs.title: Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia
briefs.sub: choking on the first feed · pass a tube before you order a picture · fistula type by abdominal gas · age at presentationDid it start with the first feed, and will a nasogastric tube pass?
blocks: choking on the first feed · pass a tube before you order a picture · fistula type by abdominal gas · age at presentationDid it start with the first feed, and will a nasogastric tube pass?

Pt term newborn boy delivered at home, 3 hours old, who coughs and brings back his first breastfeed while milk and saliva pool in his mouth Exam coarse breath sounds, retractions, a soft systolic murmur, upper left sternal border Q best next step

Drooling, choking and vomiting with the first feed plus a nasogastric tube that will not pass is esophageal atresia; a film showing the tube coiled in the upper chest confirms it. Gas in the abdomen means a distal fistula, the common type at about 85%; a gasless abdomen means pure atresia. Before repair: nothing by mouth and continuous pouch suction; screen for VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb) anomalies with an echocardiogram and renal US.

What it is Esophageal atresia (EA): the upper esophagus ends in a blind pouch; most types also carry a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), a channel between trachea and esophagus. Driver The foregut fails to partition from the airway in the embryonic period, weeks 4 to 7. Triggers A congenital mesodermal defect; other malformations in up to 50%, about 20% meeting VACTERL criteria non-modifiable Chain The upper esophagus ends blind saliva and milk fill the pouch and spill into the larynx drooling, coughing and choking with the first feed a distal fistula lets crying force air into the stomach and acid reflux into the lungs abdominal distension and aspiration pneumonia Insights The fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid, so polyhydramnios may be the prenatal clue; it is not specific, since many disorders cause it. Cyanosis with feeds can be reflex laryngospasm guarding the airway, so together with drooling and choking it points to the esophagus, not the heart.
In uteropolyhydramnios First feeddrooling, choking and vomiting Late infancy or childhoodH-type fistula, usually found after aspiration pneumonia

Type by tube and gas Finding Type Tube coils; gas in the abdomen Atresia with a distal fistula (the common type, type C), about 85% Tube coils; gasless abdomen Pure atresia, no fistula Tube passes; cough with feeds and recurrent pneumonia, usually found later H-type fistula, no atresia

Act now Finding Action Choking, drooling or cyanosis with the first feed Hold oral feeds; the tube test comes before any further feed. Coarse breath sounds or crackles before repair Keep feeds held, with continuous upper pouch suction and acid suppression; aspiration pneumonia makes repair more hazardous and can defer it. Abdominal distension with a distal fistula Gastrostomy to decompress the stomach if repair is deferred; air is forced through the fistula into the stomach.

Neonatal choking, vomiting and distress, most tempting first Diagnosis Decides it Esophageal atresia (EA) with distal tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) Frothy secretions and choking from the first feed, maternal polyhydramnios; tube will not pass Pure esophageal atresia Same feeding picture; gasless abdomen on the film H-type fistula The tube reaches the stomach; cough with feeds for months, repeated pneumonia Congenital heart disease Cyanosis and sweating with feeds; no excess secretions Congenital diaphragmatic hernia Scaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest, bowel sounds over the left lung; severe distress from delivery Respiratory distress syndrome Preterm surfactant deficiency; low lung volumes, ground-glass with air bronchograms Duodenal atresia Bilious vomiting, Down syndrome, double bubble Neonatal abstinence syndrome Maternal opioid use; typically starts at 24 hours or later, with hypertonia and irritability Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis Age 3 to 6 weeks, nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after, olive mass Epiglottitis Drooling and stridor with fever in a school-aged child; not a newborn disease

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Drooling, choking or vomiting with the first feed → Nasogastric tube passage at the bedside Meets resistance and will not advance Esophageal atresia likely; film it with the tube in place Passes into the stomach Atresia is excluded; persistent cough with feeds raises an H-type fistula (targeted tests) Targeted tests TestResultMeans Atresia confirmed, before repair → Echocardiogram and renal US Cardiac or renal anomaly VACTERL association; examine the spine, anus and limbs too Tube reaches the stomach, yet feeds bring cough and repeated pneumonia → Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagram Fistula without atresia H-type fistula Anatomy unclear on the plain film → Water-soluble contrast may be needed: a small volume, aspirated back at once Pouch outlined Defines the anatomy; done by a radiologist at the surgical center Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Tube will not pass → Chest and abdominal x-ray with the tube in place Tube coiled in the upper chest Esophageal atresia confirmed; the gas pattern sorts the type SkipBarium esophagram or endoscopy as the first test: contrast can spill from the blind pouch into the lungs, and the coiled tube on film already confirms atresia.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Formula mixed with saliva in the mouth Milk filled a blind pouch and spilled back Check whether a nasogastric tube passes. Soft murmur at the upper left sternal border A possible VACTERL heart lesion, not the cause of the choking Echocardiogram after the tube and film, before repair. Maternal polyhydramnios The fetus could not swallow amniotic fluid; not specific At birth, check whether a nasogastric tube passes when atresia is suspected. Imperforate anus in a newborn VACTERL association Pass a nasogastric tube; echocardiogram and US of the other systems.
Pause point Suspected fistula with a murmur Offered first: an echocardiogram or a barium study The heart is screened after the diagnosis, before repair → The bedside tube decides

Timing of repair Finding Meaning Stable infant Repair now Extreme prematurity, aspiration pneumonia or other major malformations Defer repair; a gastrostomy decompresses the stomach so acid does not reflux into the lungs Extremely long gap between the two ends The ends cannot be joined directly; a replacement operation

1 Before repairAtresia confirmed Nothing by mouth, parenteral nutrition, continuous suction of the upper pouch, head elevated, acid suppression. In practiceIn the neonatal intensive care unit the infant lies prone, head up 30 to 40 degrees, right side down. 2 StableCondition stable Surgery: ligate the fistula and join the esophageal ends; primary anastomosis is possible in about 80%. 3 Long gapExtremely long gap Gastric transposition or colon interposition may be performed. 4 DeferredRepair deferred Gastrostomy tube to decompress the stomach until repair. 5 After repairAll infants Acid suppression for reflux; fundoplication may be needed if medical treatment fails.

After repair Problem Detail Leak or stricture at the anastomosis The most common acute complications Feeding difficulty and dysphagia Poor motility of the distal segment, in 80 to 90% Reflux More than 40%; acid suppression

Next step1 of 10 5 h old term girl, born after a pregnancy with polyhydramnios, drools frothy saliva, coughs and turns blue during her first bottle; crackles at both bases and a soft systolic murmur · Nasogastric tube placementFrothy drool with choking and cyanosis at the first feed is atresia until a tube fails to pass. · EchocardiogramThe murmur is screened with an echocardiogram after the diagnosis, before repair. · Lateral neck radiographA neck film looks for epiglottitis: drooling and stridor with fever in a school-aged child, not a newborn. 5 h old term girl, born after a pregnancy with polyhydramnios, drools frothy saliva, coughs and turns blue during her first bottle; crackles at both bases and a soft systolic murmur Nasogastric tube placementEsophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula

Next step2 of 10 2 h old term girl drooling frothy secretions who choked on her first feed; a nasogastric tube meets firm resistance and will not advance · Barium esophagramContrast can spill from the blind pouch into the lungs; the film already confirms. · Chest x-ray with the tube in placeThe film shows the tube coiled in the pouch and whether gas reached the abdomen. · Flexible upper endoscopyEndoscopy adds risk and shows nothing the coiled tube on film does not. 2 h old term girl drooling frothy secretions who choked on her first feed; a nasogastric tube meets firm resistance and will not advance Chest x-ray with the tube in placeA coiled tube confirms atresia; gas below the diaphragm means a distal fistula

Diagnosis3 of 10 Term newborn girl, maternal polyhydramnios, drooling; the feeding tube coils in the upper chest on x-ray and the abdomen is completely gasless · Esophageal atresia with a distal fistulaA distal fistula lets air into the stomach, so the abdomen would hold gas. · Esophageal atresia without a fistulaA coiled tube with a gasless abdomen means no fistula carried air to the stomach. · Duodenal atresiaDuodenal atresia brings bilious vomiting and a double bubble. Term newborn girl, maternal polyhydramnios, drooling; the feeding tube coils in the upper chest on x-ray and the abdomen is completely gasless Esophageal atresia without a fistulaNo tracheal connection, so no air reaches the stomach

Diagnosis4 of 10 8 mo old boy with three right upper lobe pneumonias and coughing and choking with liquid feeds since birth; a feeding tube passes easily into the stomach · H-type tracheoesophageal fistulaA tube that passes, with months of cough on feeds and recurrent pneumonia, is a fistula without atresia. · LaryngomalaciaLaryngomalacia causes inspiratory stridor, not repeated pneumonia with feeds. · Gastroesophageal reflux diseaseReflux spits up after feeds; choking with each swallow points to an airway connection. 8 mo old boy with three right upper lobe pneumonias and coughing and choking with liquid feeds since birth; a feeding tube passes easily into the stomach H-type tracheoesophageal fistulaBronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagram

Screening5 of 10 Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, before surgical repair · Echocardiogram and renal ultrasoundAtresia flags VACTERL, so the heart and kidneys are screened before repair. · Head ultrasoundThe VACTERL screen does not include the brain. · TORCH titersCongenital infection is not part of the atresia picture. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, before surgical repair Echocardiogram and renal ultrasoundVACTERL association

Next step6 of 10 4 wk old boy with a week of nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after each episode, ultrasound showing a thickened elongated pylorus, low chloride and high bicarbonate · Thickened feeds and reflux precautionsPyloric stenosis is a fixed obstruction; feeding changes do not relieve it. · Immediate pyloromyotomyPyloromyotomy comes after the alkalosis is corrected. · IV fluids and electrolyte repletionFluids correct the hypochloremic alkalosis first; surgery waits for normal electrolytes. 4 wk old boy with a week of nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after each episode, ultrasound showing a thickened elongated pylorus, low chloride and high bicarbonate IV fluids and electrolyte repletionHypertrophic pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy once the alkalosis corrects

Next step7 of 10 Newborn girl with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, maternal polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting on day 1, abdominal x-ray with a double bubble and no distal gas · Nasogastric decompression and IV fluidsBilious vomiting with a double bubble in Down syndrome is duodenal atresia; decompress and hydrate first. · Upper GI contrast seriesThe double bubble with no distal gas already makes the diagnosis. · Emergency laparotomyRepair follows stabilization and the cardiac check. Newborn girl with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, maternal polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting on day 1, abdominal x-ray with a double bubble and no distal gas Nasogastric decompression and IV fluidsDuodenal atresia; repair after stabilization and an echocardiogram

Diagnosis8 of 10 30 wk preterm boy grunting and retracting at 1 h of life, x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes · Transient tachypnea of the newbornTransient tachypnea follows term birth and shows fluid in the fissures. · Respiratory distress syndromeA preterm infant with ground-glass, air bronchograms and low lung volumes lacks surfactant. · Meconium aspiration syndromeMeconium aspiration affects term or post-term infants with patchy infiltrates. 30 wk preterm boy grunting and retracting at 1 h of life, x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes Respiratory distress syndromecontinuous positive airway pressure, then surfactant if the oxygen requirement rises

Next step9 of 10 36 h old girl, irritable and tremulous with a high-pitched cry, sneezing and feeding poorly; mother maintained on methadone · Swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-inWithdrawal is treated first with swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-in. · Oral morphineMorphine is for withdrawal that nonpharmacologic care does not control. · NaloxoneNaloxone can precipitate withdrawal in an opioid-exposed newborn. 36 h old girl, irritable and tremulous with a high-pitched cry, sneezing and feeding poorly; mother maintained on methadone Swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-inNeonatal abstinence syndrome; morphine only if nonpharmacologic care fails

Next step10 of 10 Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, saturating 96% in room air, awaiting surgical repair · NPO, head elevated, continuous pouch suctionBefore repair, suction keeps saliva out of the lungs and head-up positioning limits acid reflux through the fistula. · Intubation and positive-pressure ventilationShe saturates 96% in room air and needs no airway support. · Small, frequent oral feeds held uprightAny oral feed fills the blind pouch and is aspirated. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, saturating 96% in room air, awaiting surgical repair NPO, head elevated, continuous pouch suctionKeeps pooled saliva out of the lungs and gastric acid out of the fistula

Age at presentation narrows the differential. First feed: TEF (tracheoesophageal fistula) with EA (esophageal atresia). From delivery: diaphragmatic hernia; in a preterm infant, respiratory distress syndrome. 24 hours or later: neonatal abstinence. 3 to 6 weeks: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Late infancy or childhood: H-type fistula; inspiratory stridor in infancy is laryngomalacia.

Polyhydramnios in utero is the prenatal clue, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid The tube that will not pass makes the diagnosis; the film with the tube in place confirms it The abdominal gas pattern shows the anatomic type without endoscopy VACTERL screening after diagnosis: echocardiogram and renal US

Posterior Urethral Valvescovers the opposite amniotic fluid clue: too little fluid, because no fetal urine leaves the bladder, leading to Potter sequence Cyanosis in the Newborncovers bilateral choanal atresia, the other newborn who turns blue with feeds; a catheter will not pass the nose, and crying turns the infant pink Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birthcovers VACTERL beside CHARGE, trisomy 13 and DiGeorge syndrome, each told apart by the finding only it has Posterior Urethral Valves covers the opposite amniotic fluid clue: too little fluid, because no fetal urine leaves the bladder, leading to Potter sequence. Cyanosis in the Newborn covers bilateral choanal atresia, the other newborn who turns blue with feeds; a catheter will not pass the nose, and crying turns the infant pink. Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers VACTERL beside CHARGE, trisomy 13 and DiGeorge syndrome, each told apart by the finding only it has.
When a newborn chokes or vomits with the first feed, first check whether a nasogastric tube reaches the stomach, before any imaging or drug. Imaging only confirms what the tube found.

True-fact-wrong-slotEpiglottitis is a febrile school-age disease; a 3-hour-old cannot have it. Sequencing trapEchocardiography is indicated for VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after the diagnosis, not before it. True-fact-wrong-slotPyloric stenosis needs 3 to 6 weeks for the muscle to hypertrophy, and it gives projectile vomiting, not coughing with saliva-mixed formula at 3 hours. True-fact-wrong-slotSurfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome in the preterm lung; this is a term newborn whose retractions come from aspirated secretions, which surfactant does not fix. Salient decoyThe maternal drug history points at neonatal abstinence syndrome, but withdrawal typically begins at 24 hours or later, never pools saliva or causes coughing with feeds, and is treated first without drugs.

briefs.title: Wilson Disease
briefs.sub: copper and ATP7B · liver plus brain, eye or red cells · ceruloplasmin, slit lamp, urine copper · chelation or transplantDoes unexplained liver disease come with brain, eye or red-cell findings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?
blocks: copper and ATP7B · liver plus brain, eye or red cells · ceruloplasmin, slit lamp, urine copper · chelation or transplantDoes unexplained liver disease come with brain, eye or red-cell findings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

Pt teen whose hepatitis may be advancing toward cirrhosis, now with tremor, slurred speech and a change in behavior Exam golden-brown rings at the rim of the cornea Labs raised transaminases Q which mechanism underlies the disease

Screen for Wilson disease in unexplained liver disease under 40, above all with tremor, dysarthria or psychiatric change, Kayser-Fleischer rings or Coombs-negative hemolysis. Screen with serum ceruloplasmin (low) plus a slit-lamp exam; confirm with a high 24-hour urine copper, and let liver biopsy copper settle tests that disagree. Treat for life: a chelator (penicillamine or trientine), then zinc or a lower dose for maintenance; fulminant liver failure needs a liver transplant.

What it is Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration): autosomal recessive copper overload of the liver, then the brain, cornea, red cells and kidneys. Driver Loss of ATP7B (chromosome 13), the hepatocyte copper pump; its relative, copper-transporting ATPase 7A (ATP7A), causes Menkes disease. Triggers Copper builds from birth, so none is needed. A sibling, parent or cousin with the disease non-modifiable ; age under 40, with symptoms usually from 5 to 35 non-modifiable Chain ATP7B fails in the hepatocyte copper is neither excreted into bile nor loaded onto ceruloplasmin, so ceruloplasmin falls copper accumulates in the liver: hepatitis, then fibrosis and cirrhosis free copper spills into the blood it deposits in the basal ganglia, the Descemet membrane of the cornea, red cells and the renal tubule movement and psychiatric signs, Kayser-Fleischer rings, hemolysis, Fanconi syndrome Insights Ceruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant, so active hepatitis can lift it to normal; carriers and other liver diseases can also run low, so one borderline value does not decide it. Total serum copper usually runs low because most of it rides on ceruloplasmin, while free copper runs high and does the damage in the brain, cornea and red cells.

Birthcopper starts to build in the liver Childhood and adolescencehepatitis is the first sign in almost half: acute, chronic or fulminant Young adultsneurologic or psychiatric onset in about 40% Untreatedfatal, usually by age 30

Rules Result Means Low ceruloplasmin plus a Kayser-Fleischer ring Diagnostic Low ceruloplasmin plus high 24-hour urine copper Diagnosis clear Rings plus typical motor signs Nearly pathognomonic Ceruloplasmin under 5 mg/dL Highly suggestive, whatever the clinical picture Indeterminate tests and no rings Liver biopsy for hepatic copper

Act now Finding Action Jaundice and confusion with a high international normalized ratio (INR) and Coombs-negative hemolysis in a teen or young adult Fulminant Wilson disease: liver transplant may be lifesaving, so refer now. New psychosis or a movement disorder with ataxia, dysarthria or abnormal liver tests Add serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper to the workup. A treated patient plans to stop medication Do not stop: stopping can bring on acute liver failure.

Unexplained liver disease, young patient Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Autoimmune hepatitis Young woman, often with another autoimmune disease; no neurologic signs or corneal rings. Antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibody (in children, anti-liver kidney microsomal type 1 antibody) and immunoglobulin G; check ceruloplasmin too, since Wilson disease can mimic it. Viral hepatitis The most common cause: exposure risk for hepatitis B or C, or an acute hepatitis A illness; no neurologic signs, rings or hemolysis. Order A, B and C serologies. Hereditary hemochromatosis Autosomal recessive iron overload that presents after 40: diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy; iron does not cause tremor or corneal rings. Check transferrin saturation and ferritin. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Hepatocytes retain a misfolded protein: cholestasis in newborns, cirrhosis in adults, early basal emphysema; the lung, not the brain or eye, is its second organ. Measure its serum level. MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) Fatty Liver Disease Obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia, a mild ALT-predominant rise and a bright liver on ultrasound; nothing outside the liver. Diagnose it by exclusion after testing for the other causes. Antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Tremor, rigidity or dystonia that follows a dopamine blocker; liver tests normal, so it does not explain liver disease. Match the onset to the drug start.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Unexplained hepatitis or persistently raised transaminases in a patient under 40 → Liver tests: AST, ALT, bilirubin, INR Hepatocellular rise, mild up to acute liver failure Liver injury whose cause still needs testing → Hepatitis serologies, iron studies, ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, alpha-1 antitrypsin level All normal The common mimics are excluded; screen for Wilson disease Targeted tests TestResultMeans Mimics excluded, or liver disease with neuropsychiatric signs → Serum ceruloplasmin Low, below about 20 mg/dL Supports Wilson disease, where it is usually low; under 5 mg/dL is highly suggestive Normal Does not exclude it in active hepatitis, since ceruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant → Slit-lamp exam Kayser-Fleischer rings Corneal copper; with a low ceruloplasmin, diagnostic No rings Does not exclude liver-only disease: rings in over 9 of 10 with neurologic signs, 5 or 6 of 10 with liver signs alone Anemia with the liver disease → CBC, reticulocytes, direct Coombs test Anemia, high reticulocytes, Coombs negative Copper hemolysis; with acute liver failure, fulminant Wilson disease Movement or psychiatric signs → Brain MRI Signal change in the basal ganglia Shows brain involvement; the diagnosis does not require it Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Low ceruloplasmin or Kayser-Fleischer rings → 24-hour urine copper High, usually over 100 mcg per day (normal up to 30) With a low ceruloplasmin, the diagnosis is clear; the same test monitors chelation Ceruloplasmin, urine copper and slit lamp disagree → Liver biopsy with copper measurement High hepatic copper Wilson disease SkipTotal serum copper: usually low with the ceruloplasmin, but it can be high in acute liver failure, so it does not decide the diagnosis.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Golden-brown ring at the corneal margin Kayser-Fleischer ring: copper in the Descemet membrane Order serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper Tremor, slurred speech or falling grades in a teen with hepatitis Neurologic Wilson disease Order a slit-lamp exam; rings are almost always present Normal ceruloplasmin during active hepatitis A false normal from the acute phase rise Send a 24-hour urine copper
Pause point Active hepatitis with a normal ceruloplasmin Read as the end of the search A normal ceruloplasmin in active hepatitis does not end it → The urine copper or the liver biopsy decides

Presentation and what it means Finding Meaning Raised transaminases without symptoms Early disease Cirrhosis Treated with a chelator; transplant for severe liver failure despite drugs; adds hepatocellular carcinoma risk Neurologic or psychiatric signs Copper has left the liver; Kayser-Fleischer rings almost always present Acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis Fulminant disease: liver transplant

1 SymptomaticHepatic or neurologic disease First line: a chelator, penicillamine (most used) or trientine (the alternative; penicillamine is more likely to cause side effects), plus a low-copper diet. Penicillamine harmsFever, rash, low neutrophils and platelets, proteinuria and membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulonephritis); pyridoxine is given with it, and neurologic signs can worsen when chelation starts. 2 MaintenanceCopper removed and symptoms improved Lower-dose chelator or oral zinc, which reduces gut copper absorption; zinc is not given at the same time as a chelator. 3 PresymptomaticRelative found by screening, no symptoms Zinc for a presymptomatic relative. 4 Chelator failsChelator not tolerated, or neurologic signs not responding Zinc acetate as the alternative. 5 Liver failureAcute (fulminant) liver failure, or severe liver failure despite drugs Liver transplant, which cures the disease in most cases.

After diagnosis Situation Do Every patient Lifelong therapy, with or without symptoms; stopping can bring on acute liver failure. On treatment Follow 24-hour urine copper; penicillamine is dosed to urine copper and free serum copper. Sibling, parent or cousin Screen: slit-lamp exam, liver tests, ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urine copper and, if available, ATP7B testing. Infant relative Test after age 1 year; ceruloplasmin is low in the first months of life. Pregnancy Continue treatment throughout.

Mechanism1 of 7 16 yo M with several months of fatigue and mild jaundice, a new hand tremor, slurred speech and irritability with falling grades; elevated AST and ALT; golden-brown rings at the corneal margins on slit-lamp exam · Defective copper transport in hepatocytesATP7B failure blocks biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin loading, so copper reaches the brain and cornea. · Hepatocyte retention of a misfolded protease inhibitorAlpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: the lung, not the brain or eye, is its second organ. · Increased intestinal iron absorptionHemochromatosis presents after 40; iron does not cause tremor or corneal rings. 16 yo M with several months of fatigue and mild jaundice, a new hand tremor, slurred speech and irritability with falling grades; elevated AST and ALT; golden-brown rings at the corneal margins on slit-lamp exam Defective copper transport in hepatocytesWilson disease: ATP7B failure blocks biliary copper excretion and copper loading onto ceruloplasmin, so copper deposits in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea

Workup2 of 7 19 yo F with 3 months of fatigue and a fine hand tremor; ALT 240, AST 190, bilirubin normal; hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody negative; normal body mass index and no alcohol use · Liver biopsy with copper measurementLiver biopsy copper is for when ceruloplasmin, urine copper and the slit lamp disagree. · Serum ceruloplasminCommon mimics are excluded in a young patient with hepatitis and tremor: screen with ceruloplasmin. · MRI of the brainBrain MRI shows neurologic involvement but is not needed for the diagnosis. 19 yo F with 3 months of fatigue and a fine hand tremor; ALT 240, AST 190, bilirubin normal; hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody negative; normal body mass index and no alcohol use Serum ceruloplasminscreen for Wilson disease in a young patient with unexplained hepatitis and a tremor; slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper follow

Diagnosis3 of 7 17 yo F with Hashimoto thyroiditis and 6 weeks of fatigue, joint aches and jaundice; ALT 850, AST 700; serum IgG high; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positive; ceruloplasmin normal; no Kayser-Fleischer rings; normal neurologic exam · Acute hepatitis AHepatitis A is an acute illness found by serology; autoantibodies and high immunoglobulin G point elsewhere. · Autoimmune hepatitisYoung woman with another autoimmune disease, antinuclear and anti-smooth muscle antibodies and high immunoglobulin G. · Wilson diseaseNo neurologic signs or corneal rings, and the autoantibodies explain the hepatitis. 17 yo F with Hashimoto thyroiditis and 6 weeks of fatigue, joint aches and jaundice; ALT 850, AST 700; serum IgG high; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positive; ceruloplasmin normal; no Kayser-Fleischer rings; normal neurologic exam Autoimmune hepatitiscorticosteroids, with azathioprine to spare steroids

Next step4 of 7 21 yo M with 1 year of hand tremor and dysarthria; compensated cirrhosis on imaging, INR 1.3, no ascites or encephalopathy; ceruloplasmin low, 24-hour urine copper high, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam · Oral zinc acetateZinc is for maintenance after chelation, presymptomatic relatives or chelator failure. · Liver transplantationTransplant is for fulminant failure or failure refractory to drugs; this liver is compensated. · Oral penicillamineSymptomatic disease with compensated cirrhosis: start a chelator, penicillamine or trientine. 21 yo M with 1 year of hand tremor and dysarthria; compensated cirrhosis on imaging, INR 1.3, no ascites or encephalopathy; ceruloplasmin low, 24-hour urine copper high, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam Oral penicillaminesymptomatic Wilson disease: lifelong chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc later for maintenance

Next step5 of 7 18 yo F with 1 week of jaundice, now confused; INR 3.2; hemoglobin 7.8 with high reticulocytes and a negative direct Coombs test; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam; no acetaminophen ingestion · Intravenous acetylcysteineAcetylcysteine treats acetaminophen toxicity, and there was no ingestion. · Oral penicillamineA chelator treats compensated disease; fulminant failure needs a transplant. · Urgent liver transplantationAcute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis is fulminant Wilson disease: transplant is lifesaving. 18 yo F with 1 week of jaundice, now confused; INR 3.2; hemoglobin 7.8 with high reticulocytes and a negative direct Coombs test; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam; no acetaminophen ingestion Urgent liver transplantationfulminant Wilson disease: acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis does not recover with chelation alone

Screening6 of 7 14 yo M, asymptomatic, whose 17-year-old sister was just diagnosed with Wilson disease; normal growth and development; normal physical and neurologic exam · Serum ferritin and transferrin saturationIron studies screen for hemochromatosis, not Wilson disease. · Serum ceruloplasmin and liver testsRelatives are screened before symptoms: ceruloplasmin, liver tests, slit lamp and urine copper. · No testing unless symptoms developEarly treatment works best, so screening does not wait for symptoms. 14 yo M, asymptomatic, whose 17-year-old sister was just diagnosed with Wilson disease; normal growth and development; normal physical and neurologic exam Serum ceruloplasmin and liver testssiblings carry a 1 in 4 risk; add a slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper, and treat presymptomatic disease with zinc

Avoid7 of 7 24 yo M with Wilson disease treated with penicillamine for 3 years; tremor resolved, liver tests now normal, urine copper at target; asks about coming off medication · Stopping copper-lowering therapyTreatment is lifelong; stopping can bring on acute liver failure. · Switching to zinc maintenanceZinc after chelation is an accepted maintenance choice. · Continuing yearly urine copper checksUrine copper checks are how treatment is monitored, so they continue. 24 yo M with Wilson disease treated with penicillamine for 3 years; tremor resolved, liver tests now normal, urine copper at target; asks about coming off medication Stopping copper-lowering therapytreatment is lifelong; stopping can precipitate acute liver failure

Symptomatic disease: copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine, lifelong, with a low-copper diet (avoid shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate and mushrooms) Maintenance or presymptomatic disease: zinc, which reduces intestinal copper absorption Fulminant liver failure: urgent liver transplantation, which corrects the liver defect Family: screen first-degree relatives, siblings above all (a 1 in 4 chance of disease, since it is autosomal recessive), with ceruloplasmin, liver tests, a slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper Never stop: stopping therapy can precipitate acute liver failure

Psychiatric change or falling school performance can precede the liver findings. A young patient with new psychiatric illness and abnormal liver tests needs a ceruloplasmin Acute liver failure with a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia in a teen or young adult is fulminant Wilson disease. It needs a transplant center, not chelation alone A presumed autoimmune hepatitis in a young patient should have ceruloplasmin checked before steroids Serum total copper is usually low; urine copper is high

Fatty Liver Diseaselists Wilson disease among the exclusions: is there tremor or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low? Abnormal Liver Testsplaces Wilson in the hepatocellular pattern: are the transaminases, not the alkaline phosphatase, leading? Hemolytic Anemiacovers the other Coombs-negative hemolysis of the young: are there spherocytes and an affected parent, or liver disease with corneal rings? Tick-Borne Illnessholds the acute mimic: did confusion with transaminitis arrive over hours with fever and a rash, or over months with a tremor? Fatty Liver Disease lists Wilson disease among the exclusions: is there tremor or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low? Abnormal Liver Tests places Wilson in the hepatocellular pattern: are the transaminases, not the alkaline phosphatase, leading? Hemolytic Anemia covers the other Coombs-negative hemolysis of the young: are there spherocytes and an affected parent, or liver disease with corneal rings? Tick-Borne Illness holds the acute mimic: did confusion with transaminitis arrive over hours with fever and a rash, or over months with a tremor?

When unexplained liver disease comes with a finding outside the liver, identify the organ. Brain, cornea or red cells point to copper, and the lung points to alpha-1 antitrypsin. The pancreas, skin, joints and heart in an older patient point to iron.

Class-vs-memberIncreased intestinal iron absorption: the right class, an inherited metal overload of the liver, but the wrong metal; HFE hemochromatosis presents in middle age with diabetes, skin and joint findings, never tremor or corneal rings. Unchecked attributeHepatocyte retention of a misfolded protease inhibitor: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited liver disease of the young, but its second organ is the lung; it does not explain neuropsychiatric signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings.

briefs.title: Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism
briefs.sub: motor diagnosis · mimics · motor and nonmotor complicationsTypical Parkinson disease, a mimic, or a treatment complication?
blocks: motor diagnosis · mimics · motor and nonmotor complicationsTypical Parkinson disease, a mimic, or a treatment complication?

Bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity establishes parkinsonism. Asymmetric onset and a clear levodopa response support Parkinson disease (PD); diagnosis is clinical Early falls, vertical gaze palsy or early severe autonomic failure suggest another parkinsonian disorder. Dementia before or within 1 year of motor onset favors dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia) Treat functional motor impairment with carbidopa-levodopa; distinguish wearing off from dyskinesia. Recognize nonmotor symptoms, including depression, even when movement improves

What it is Progressive neurodegeneration; the commonest cause of parkinsonism Driver Loss of dopamine-producing substantia nigra neurons; alpha-synuclein aggregates form Lewy bodies Triggers Older age and inherited susceptibility (non-modifiable); male sex (non-modifiable) Pesticides or solvents may raise risk; repeated severe head trauma is associated Chain Nigrostriatal dopamine falls thalamic inhibition increases motor-cortex activation falls Insights What can precede motor findings? A motor disorder can begin with nonmotor symptoms WhyNonmotor diseaseAlpha-synuclein pathology extends to olfactory, autonomic and brainstem structures; constipation, reduced smell and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder can precede motor findings Why combine carbidopa with levodopa? Carbidopa limits peripheral conversion; levodopa reaches the brain MechanismDrug pairingLevodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and becomes dopamine. Carbidopa blocks peripheral dopa decarboxylase, reducing nausea and orthostasis while increasing brain delivery; central adverse effects such as agitation and visual hallucinations may still occur ProgressionTreatment courseLoss of dopamine storage narrows the response window as disease progresses. Delaying levodopa has not been shown to prevent motor complications

What the disease does, by systemSupporting features, not diagnostic alone Small handwriting, a quiet voice, reduced facial movement, reduced arm swing and short shuffling steps Constipation, orthostasis, urinary or sexual dysfunction Insomnia and dream enactment; REM sleep behavior disorder reflects loss of normal REM paralysis Executive and visuospatial impairment may precede memory loss Depression and anxiety may overlap motor slowing and masked facial expression Loss of nigral pigment; Lewy bodies also involve cortex and autonomic structures Multiple system atrophy involves glial alpha-synuclein; progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration are tauopathiesIn progressive supranuclear palsy, midbrain degeneration can give a hummingbird appearance on MRI
Motor Bradykinesia plus rigidity or resting tremor PD additionally requires no exclusion feature, supportive findings and few or no red flags

Tremor at rest Rigidity cogwheel resistance Akinesia/bradykinesia slow voluntary movement Postural instability usually late, not required for diagnosis Shuffling gait short steps Small handwriting micrographia

SwallowingDysphagia can lead to aspiration pneumonia If swallowing symptoms develop, choose assess swallowing and aspiration risk. New confusionAcute mental change requires assessment for infection and medication triggers If confusion or hallucinations newly appear, choose look for a reversible trigger. Delirium

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Parkinson disease Asymmetric slowing with rest tremor or rigidity Progressive; clear dopaminergic response; falls usually occur later Toxic parkinsonism Carbon monoxide exposure or MPTP (an illicit-drug contaminant) Toxin exposure precedes motor disease Essential tremor Bilateral action tremor; head or voice may be involved Action, rather than rest, brings out the tremor Drug-induced parkinsonism Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Dopamine-blocking antipsychotic or antiemetic exposure After a drug start or increase; often symmetric; improves after withdrawal Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia) Fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations and dream enactment Dementia before or within 1 year of motor onset; marked antipsychotic sensitivity Progressive supranuclear palsy Vertical gaze limitation, gait freezing, early falls Early falls with vertical gaze palsy; usually poor levodopa response Multiple system atrophy Severe orthostasis or incontinence with ataxia or pyramidal signs Early autonomic failure; poor dopaminergic response Corticobasal degeneration Asymmetric motor signs with apraxia, cortical sensory loss or an alien limb Cortical dysfunction accompanying parkinsonism; usually little levodopa benefit Normal pressure hydrocephalus Gait impairment, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline Asymmetric rest tremor and rigidity are less typical Wilson Disease Younger patient; liver disease with movement or psychiatric changes Copper-related disease, rather than typical aging-associated PD

Nonmotor and cognitive timingnot to scale Prodromal nonmotor featuresConstipation, loss of smell or dream enactment may precede motor signs by years Before motorMotor onsetLater Parkinson disease dementiaDementia begins more than 1 year after established parkinsonism Before motorMotor onsetLater Dementia with Lewy bodiesDementia before, or within 1 year of, motor onset Before motorMotor onsetLater

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Slowing, tremor or rigidity → Motor and neurologic examination Bradykinesia with rest tremor or rigidity Parkinsonism is present Vertical gaze palsy, early falls or marked ataxia Consider an atypical syndrome → Drug history and nonmotor chronology Dopamine-blocking drug exposure Assess a drug-induced cause Dementia starts before or near motor onset Consider dementia with Lewy bodies Targeted tests TestResultMeans Atypical neurologic findings or a structural mimic suspected → Brain MRI Stroke or hydrocephalus A structural alternative to idiopathic PD Uncertain essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism → Dopamine transporter imaging, if uncertainty remains Reduced striatal uptake Supports degeneration; does not separate PD from degenerative Parkinson-plus syndromes Normal uptake Favors essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Typical examination without exclusion features → Clinical assessment and response to dopaminergic therapy Marked improvement Supports PD; poor response warrants reconsidering the diagnosis SkipRoutine brain imaging is usually unnecessary for a classic presentation with a clear treatment response

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Early falls or vertical gaze palsy Atypical parkinsonism Reassess for progressive supranuclear palsy Psychosis during dopaminergic therapy Drug effect or advanced disease; also check triggers Check infection and other drugs; reduce an implicated dopamine agonist first if feasible Controlled motor symptoms with new anhedonia Depression may need separate treatment Assess and treat the mood syndrome Medication- and Illness-Induced Psychiatric Disorders
Pause point Tremor Offered as PD A tremor alone does not establish PD → Demonstrate bradykinesia, review dopamine-blocking drugs, and look for early atypical features

Function and complications guide treatment Pattern Action Mild disease with little functional interference Individualize a lower-potency option or levodopa Motor symptoms impair daily activities Carbidopa-levodopa provides the greatest motor benefit Fluctuations or dyskinesia despite medication Adjust therapy; consider advanced treatment when refractory

1 Firstmotor symptoms need treatment Carbidopa-levodopa is preferred for most patients Supportive care In practicePhysical or occupational therapy with exercise may improve conditioning Alternatives Drug selectionFor selected younger patients with mild disease, pramipexole or ropinirole can be alternatives. Selegiline or rasagiline, monoamine oxidase B (MAO-B) inhibitors, offer less potent symptom relief 2 Raiseend-of-dose slowing or recurrent off periods Adjust levodopa dose timing; consider a dopamine agonist, MAO-B inhibitor or entacapone adjunct 3 Complicationtroublesome dyskinesia Reduce or adjust levodopa for excess involuntary movement; amantadine can help Adverse effects AmantadineAmantadine can cause mottled skin (livedo reticularis), ataxia, peripheral edema and orthostatic symptoms 4 Rescuesudden off episode Apomorphine provides rapid, short-acting dopaminergic rescue 5 Referrefractory tremor or persistent motor complications despite drug adjustment Evaluate deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus or internal globus pallidus

Medication complications Finding Action or caution Gambling, compulsive shopping or hypersexuality on a dopamine agonist Reduce or discontinue the agonist; these drugs carry more psychosis risk than carbidopa-levodopa and may cause hallucinations or confusion Older adult or cognitive impairment Avoid dopamine agonists when possible; anticholinergics can worsen cognition, retention and constipation Tremor predominates in a younger patient Benztropine or trihexyphenidyl may help tremor and rigidity, not bradykinesia; use cautiously because of anticholinergic effects Levodopa adverse effects Dizziness, headache, agitation or visual hallucinations can occur early Later effectsTiming and riskDyskinesia typically develops after 5 to 10 years of treatment; psychiatric adverse-effect risk rises with age, prior psychiatric illness, treatment duration and higher dose Levodopa adjunct selected Entacapone inhibits peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT); selegiline and rasagiline may amplify levodopa adverse effects MechanismsAdjunct actionsTolcapone inhibits COMT both centrally and peripherally; the nonergot agonists ropinirole and pramipexole are preferred over ergot agents such as bromocriptine; ropinirole favors D2 receptors and pramipexole D3 receptors. Amantadine reduces N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor activity and alters dopamine release/reuptake

Nonmotor management Problem Do Hallucinations or delusions Treat triggers; reduce the implicated dopaminergic drug if feasible. Persistent symptoms may require quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin; strong dopamine blockade worsens movement Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Depression or anxiety Recognize the mood syndrome even with effective motor therapy; for assessment and treatment, see Medication- and Illness-Induced Psychiatric Disorders Dream enactment Melatonin or clonazepam may reduce episodes Orthostatic symptoms Review medications; consider salt intake or an abdominal binder when appropriate; persistent symptoms may need fludrocortisone or droxidopa Parkinson disease dementia Consider a cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine Lewy body dementiaCognitive symptomsFor dementia with Lewy bodies, a cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil is a treatment option

Follow-up decisions When Do Every functional review Review dose timing, falls, swallowing, cognition, mood, sleep and orthostasis Response becomes shorter or unpredictable Separate off periods from excess involuntary movement before adjusting medication Poor response or new atypical findings Reconsider the diagnosis

Action tremor favors essential tremor; early falls and vertical gaze palsy suggest progressive supranuclear palsy

Fever, flank or costovertebral angle tenderness and urinary symptoms make it a clinical diagnosis; a benign abdomen needs no imaging Stable, not pregnant, keeping tablets down home on an oral fluoroquinolone; otherwise admit for IV (intravenous) ceftriaxone No better after 48 to 72 hours of the right antibiotic CT for an abscess or obstruction; in pregnancy, ultrasound

What it is Bacterial infection of the kidney parenchyma, ascending from the bladder Bug Escherichia coli in about 80%; then Klebsiella, Proteus catheter or hospital: Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Serratia Triggers Obstruction: stones, an enlarged prostate A catheter or instrumentation Pregnancy Why pregnancyPregnancyProgesterone widens the ureters, so urine stalls and bacteria ascend. Vesicoureteral reflux (non-modifiable) Chain Bladder bacteria ascend infected parenchyma fever, flank pain, nausea and vomiting Obstruction or a gas-forming infection abscess, sepsis Papillary necrosisComplicationAcute pyelonephritis is the A of SAND (sickle cell disease, acute pyelonephritis, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, diabetes): the swollen interstitium compresses the medullary vessels. Insights Nitrofurantoin cures cystitis but does not treat the kidney Failure on the right antibiotic is a drainage problem: image for pus or a blockage, do not broaden
Clinical fever and chills, flank or costovertebral angle tenderness, urinary symptoms Urine pyuria; the culture names the organism

In practice In practiceIn practice: the IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) 2025 guideline calls every pyelonephritis a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI), treated for typically 7 days by mouth or IV, changing to oral once the patient improves (older teaching 5 to 14 days, by drug). Cystitis in a man may be uncomplicated, whereas older teaching labeled all male infections complicated.

SepsisHypotension judged against the usual pressure: 104/68 is low after years of hypertension If the patient is unstable, choose admission for IV antibiotics. EmphysematousDiabetic, worsening on antibiotics; gas in the parenchyma on CT If there is gas in the kidney, choose IV antibiotics and urgent urology. ObstructedFever behind a stone or other blockage If the infected kidney is obstructed, choose relieve the obstruction.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Pyelonephritis Fever, chills, flank or costovertebral angle tenderness, vomiting Systemic signs; clinical diagnosis Cystitis Dysuria and frequency; no fever, no flank tenderness Afebrile; nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) or fosfomycin Acute prostatitis A man with dysuria and fever Tender, boggy prostate on rectal exam Perinephric abscess Still febrile after 48 to 72 hours of the right antibiotic CT; drainage Chlamydial or gonococcal urethritis Sexually active; pyuria with a sterile culture NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test)

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Fever, flank pain, dysuria → Urinalysis and urine culture Nitrite positive Gram-negative, usually E. coli Nitrite negative Does not exclude infection: the test is specific, not sensitive; Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus are nitrite negative Targeted tests TestResultMeans Sexually active, pyuria, sterile culture → NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea Positive Urethritis Urine pH over 7, staghorn calculus → Urine culture Urease organism Usually Proteus mirabilis: struvite Gram-positive cocci, coagulase negative → Novobiocin Resistant Staphylococcus saprophyticus Next step TestResultMeans No better at 48 to 72 hours → CT; ultrasound in pregnancy Abscess or obstruction Drain it or relieve it Diabetic, worsening → CT Gas in the parenchyma Emphysematous pyelonephritis: urgent urology SkipImaging in a patient who is improving with a benign abdomen: the diagnosis is clinical.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Pregnant, with fever and flank pain Admission, even with oral intake intact IV third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin; no fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX Vomiting her tablets, or only clear fluids for days Cannot take oral therapy Admit for IV antibiotics Catheter, instrumentation, prior antibiotics or hospital Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Serratia Treat by the culture, not by the E. coli default Febrile urinary tract infection in a well child Oral therapy Oral third-generation cephalosporin such as cefixime; no fluoroquinolone under 18

Pause point Febrile patient with flank tenderness Offered: nitrofurantoin Fever and flank tenderness → Nitrofurantoin does not treat the kidney Fever persists at 72 hours on the right drug Offered: broader antibiotics Failure on the right drug → Imaging for an abscess or obstruction

Home or admit Finding Where Cannot keep oral therapy down: vomiting, or days of clear fluids only Admit, IV Unstable: sepsis or hypotension against the baseline Admit, IV Pregnancy, obstruction, stones or a catheter Admit, IV Immunocompromise or extremes of age (a well child is the exception) Admit, IV Outpatient therapy failed, or the organism resists every oral agent Admit, IV None of these: healthy, stable, tolerating oral intake Home, oral

1 Outpatientstable, not pregnant, oral intake An oral fluoroquinolone; TMP-SMX only if the organism is sensitive Local resistance drives the empiric choice. 2 Admitany admission finding IV ceftriaxone; switch to oral as soon as the patient improves Pregnancy: an IV third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin. 3 Imageno better at 48 to 72 hours CT for an abscess or obstruction; in pregnancy, ultrasound 4 Source controlabscess, obstruction or gas Drain the abscess or relieve the obstruction; urgent urology for emphysematous pyelonephritis

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Cystitis: no fever, no flank tenderness Nitrofurantoin 5 days, TMP-SMX 3 days, or fosfomycin once Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated with creatinine clearance under 60 mL/min; it can cause pulmonary fibrosis, and hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency Asymptomatic bacteriuria or cystitis in pregnancy Treat it: cephalexin or another cephalosporin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, fosfomycin or nitrofurantoin Repeat the culture after treatment; avoid TMP-SMX and fluoroquinolones, and nitrofurantoin in the third trimester Pyelonephritis in pregnancy, refractory Ultrasound for an abscess; 14 days of antibiotics Not CT A child An oral third-generation cephalosporin if well; IV ceftriaxone if toxic or vomiting No fluoroquinolone under 18: cartilage damage

Follow-up decisions When Do Improving on IV therapy Switch to oral and finish the course at home Still febrile at 48 to 72 hours CT for an abscess or obstruction; in pregnancy, ultrasound Pregnancy, first prenatal visit Urine culture to screen for asymptomatic bacteriuria Recurrent cystitis after intercourse Postcoital TMP-SMX or nitrofurantoin Recurrent infections growing Proteus, alkaline urine Look for a struvite staghorn stone
