blocks: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention
three-stage history · retention, infection and kidney injury as complications · 1+ blood is not a stone · catheter firstWhich process came first, and does it explain every other finding?

Months of hesitancy, weak stream and nocturia come first; retention, infection and a rising creatinine are its complications, not the cause Acute retention: catheter first an alpha-1 blocker such as tamsulosin add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for a large gland A hard, nodular or asymmetric prostate, or a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) over 10, needs a biopsy

What it is Nonmalignant overgrowth of the periurethral (transition zone) prostate with age; it does not raise cancer risk Driver DHT (dihydrotestosterone) drives the hyperplasia Triggers Age (non-modifiable) For acute retention: anticholinergics (tricyclics, first-generation antihistamines), sympathomimetics, opioids, alcohol, anesthesia An infection that swells the prostate Chain Narrowed urethra incomplete emptying stasis: infection and stones Prolonged obstruction bilateral hydronephrosis postrenal kidney injury Insights Find the process that came first: the prostate explains the retention, the infection and the creatinine 1+ blood on a dipstick does not make it a stone Why 1+ bloodHematuriaTrace to 1+ hematuria is expected with infection, a distended bladder and the vascular prostate itself; a stone needs colicky flank pain to the groin, and does not explain months of hesitancy.
Symptoms weak stream, hesitancy, nocturia, incomplete emptying Exam smooth, rubbery, symmetric enlargement Exclude infection, hematuria and cancer (urinalysis, PSA)

RetentionNo urine, suprapubic pain, a distended bladder If the bladder is full, choose a urethral catheter now; coudé tip if it will not pass, suprapubic if neither does. Kidney injuryCreatinine rising behind the obstruction If the creatinine is up, choose decompress, then renal ultrasound for hydronephrosis.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Benign prostatic hyperplasia Months of hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, dribbling in an older man Smooth, firm, symmetric, nontender gland Prostate cancer Hard nodule, asymmetric enlargement PSA over 10 is worrisome; biopsy confirms Drug-induced retention Retention after a new anticholinergic, opioid or decongestant Stop the drug Acute prostatitis Fever, dysuria Tender, boggy prostate Urethral stricture A younger man, weak stream after urethral trauma, infection or radiation; high postvoid residual Urethrography or cystoscopy shows the narrowing Kidney stone Hematuria Colicky flank pain to the groin

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Hesitancy, frequency, nocturia → Urinalysis, rectal exam, PSA Smooth, symmetric, enlarged BPH Hard, nodular, asymmetric Prostate cancer: biopsy Infection or hematuria Treat it; evaluate the blood Targeted tests TestResultMeans No urine, suprapubic fullness → Bladder catheter Drains a large volume Acute urinary retention Creatinine rising → Renal ultrasound Bilateral hydronephrosis Postrenal kidney injury from the prostate Next step TestResultMeans Moderate or severe symptoms → Postvoid residual by bladder ultrasound Over 50 mL Outlet obstruction In practice In practiceIn practice: a clinical reference reads a postvoid residual over 100 mL as retention; the board card reads over 50 mL as outlet obstruction. SkipDiagnosing cancer from the PSA alone: the biopsy confirms it.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step PSA mildly raised, smooth gland BPH can raise the PSA Read it with the rectal exam 1+ blood on the dipstick after months of hesitancy Expected with infection, distension and BPH Not a stone without the colic BPH with hypertension One drug for both Terazosin BPH with erectile dysfunction One drug for both Daily tadalafil

Pause point Retention, infection, a high creatinine and 1+ blood after six months of hesitancy Offered as the cause: the retention, the infection or the creatinine; 1+ blood read as a stone The six months of hesitancy came first → The prostate explains every later finding

1 Every patientfrom diagnosis Stop anticholinergics, sympathomimetics and opioids; treat any infection 2 Retentiona full bladder Catheter first; suprapubic only if a urethral catheter fails 3 1st linebothersome symptoms An alpha-1 blocker: tamsulosin, or terazosin if also hypertensive Watch for orthostatic hypotension. 4 Addlarge gland A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride); together they beat either alone Shrinks the gland over 6 to 12 months; gynecomastia can follow. 5 Surgeryno response, or a complication TURP (transurethral resection of the prostate) For recurrent infection, stones, bladder damage or hydronephrosis; retrograde ejaculation is common after it.

Follow-up decisions When Do Retention relieved by the catheter Start an alpha-1 blocker Retention after a new anticholinergic Stop it before adding drugs Recurrent infections, stones or hydronephrosis Refer for surgery

Acute retention → bladder catheterization first (suprapubic if the urethra is impassable). Then treat the UTI (urinary tract infection) and watch for post-obstructive diuresis. Expect the creatinine to fall; the fall proves the AKI (acute kidney injury) was post-renal. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis if confirmation is needed. Long-term, give tamsulosin ± finasteride, with TURP (transurethral resection of the prostate) if refractory.
A single lab value should change the diagnosis only if it is incompatible with it, not merely compatible with another diagnosis.

briefs.sub: the annual care bundle and the outcome noun · kidney screening by detection threshold · foot ulcers read by exam, not risk profileIs the outcome morbidity, mortality, hospitalization or benefit, which test catches the reversible stage, and does the exam overrule the risk profile?
blocks: the annual care bundle and the outcome noun · kidney screening by detection threshold · foot ulcers read by exam, not risk profileIs the outcome morbidity, mortality, hospitalization or benefit, which test catches the reversible stage, and does the exam overrule the risk profile?

Read the outcome noun first: morbidity screen for a complication; mortality smoking cessation Kidney screen: spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), the most sensitive test, at diagnosis in type 2, 5 years after it in type 1, then yearly A painless, warm, plantar ulcer is neuropathic, but pulses and the ankle-brachial index (ABI) are still checked

What it is Diabetes damages retina, kidney and nerve; retinopathy is the most common preventable complication; each can be silent until late Driver Glycation of small vessels and the glomerular basement membrane Triggers Diabetes duration (non-modifiable) and degree of hyperglycemia Hypertension, smoking Chain Hyperfiltration albuminuria 30 to 300 mg/g overt proteinuria falling GFR Neuropathy unfelt trauma at pressure points ulcer contiguous osteomyelitis NeuropathyFiber typesSmall fibers: pain, burning, autonomic dysfunction (dry skin). Large fibers: sensory loss, which lets injury go unnoticed. It can be present when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed, and diabetes is the most common cause of neuropathic ulcers. Mononeuropathies include cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies. Insights A normal creatinine does not exclude early kidney disease: hyperfiltration may keep it normal The exam overrules the risk profile: a neuropathic ulcer still needs its perfusion checked Why still checkPerfusionNeuropathy hides ischemic pain, and calcified vessels raise the ABI, so a normal index makes arterial disease less likely without excluding it.
Ratio UACR 30 mg/g or more Persistence 2 of 3 samples over 3 to 6 months Exclude exercise, fever, infection, heart failure, hyperglycemia

Leg and foot ulcers, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Neuropathic (diabetic) ulcer Painless, plantar over a metatarsal head or heel, callus Warm, dry foot; normal pulses; monofilament not felt Arterial ulcer Painful toe tips or lateral malleolus, worse elevated Cool, hairless skin; absent pulses; ABI 0.9 or less Venous stasis ulcer Shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus Hemosiderin, edema, normal pulses; duplex ultrasound Charcot arthropathy (neuropathic joint) Weeks of a warm, swollen foot, no ulcer, no fever Neuropathy, normal labs; radiographs or MRI; casting Pressure ulcer Sacrum, heel or trochanter in an immobile patient Staged by depth Pyoderma gangrenosum Days of rapid, very painful growth; violaceous undermined border Inflammatory bowel disease; biopsy and steroids, never debride Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a scar) Over 3 months unhealed in a scar; rolled edges Biopsy

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Diabetes, yearly kidney screen → Spot UACRCreatinine with eGFR (estimated GFR) 30 to 300 mg/g The reversible stage: moderately increased albuminuria Normal creatinine Does not exclude early disease Next step TestResultMeans One abnormal ratio → Two more ratios within 3 to 6 months Two of the three high Persistent albuminuria: treat Targeted tests TestResultMeans Albuminuria found → Dilated eye exam Retinopathy Supports a diabetic cause None A biopsy trigger No retinopathy, active sediment or a rapid GFR fall → Microscopy of the urine sediment Red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells Points away from diabetic nephropathy Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Atypical features, including heavy proteinuria too early or diabetes too short → Renal biopsy Nodular glomerulosclerosis Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesion of diabetes SkipA urine dipstick: it turns positive only at about 300 mg/day, past the reversible stage.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Diabetic foot ulcer → Pulses and ABI Normal pulses, ABI normal Foot criteria CriteriaInternational Working Group on the Diabetic Foot: pulses present, ABI 0.9 to 1.3, toe-brachial index at least 0.70, and pedal waveforms biphasic or triphasic. Arterial disease less likely, not excluded ABI 0.9 or less Arterial disease Same visit → 10-g monofilament Not felt Lost protective sensation No known diabetes → Hemoglobin A1c 6.5% or higher Diabetes, the cause of the neuropathic ulcer Targeted tests TestResultMeans ABI over 1.4 → Toe-brachial index 0.7 or less Arterial disease hidden by calcified vessels Deep or long-standing ulcer → Probe-to-bone test, ESR (sedimentation rate), plain films Bone felt with the probe; ESR above 70 Likely osteomyelitis; early films can look normal Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Osteomyelitis likely → MRI, then a bone biopsy Edema in the marrow; organism grown from bone Osteomyelitis, with its organism named SkipA superficial wound swab: it grows colonizers. Culture deep tissue or bone from an infected ulcer.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step "Prevent morbidity" Complications, disability Screen for one: the dilated eye exam "Reduce mortality" Death Smoking cessation "Reduce hospitalization" Admissions Treat the driver of decompensation "Most beneficial" Largest effect, any outcome Usually smoking cessation Total protein needed, or myeloma suspected UACR and dipstick miss light chains MyelomaLight chainsThe dipstick stays negative while the sulfosalicylic acid test is positive; urine electrophoresis shows an M-spike. Protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine Most accurate GFR needed; amputee, cachexia Creatinine unreliable Inulin or iothalamate clearance; cystatin C
Pause point Screening for nephropathy Offered: a urine dipstick, or reassured by a normal creatinine Hyperfiltration may keep the creatinine normal early → The UACR catches the reversible stage

ABI bands Stage ABI Means Noncompressible Over 1.4 Calcified vessels: use the toe-brachial index Normal About 0.91 to 1.3 No arterial disease In practiceIn practiceIn practice: the American Heart Association reads 1.0 to 1.4 as normal and 0.91 to 0.99 as borderline. Arterial disease 0.9 or less Claudication range down to 0.4 Critical limb ischemia Under 0.4 Rest pain, ulcers, gangrene

1 Every patientfrom diagnosis Glycemic control (A1c goal under 7%) and blood pressure control; a statin from age 40 to 75 2 1st linepersistent albuminuria ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker), especially with BP over 130/80 In practiceIn practiceIn practice: some guidance ties the ACE inhibitor or ARB to hypertension; a clinical reference starts it at the first albuminuria whatever the pressure. Never both together; neither in pregnancy. 3 Addtype 2 diabetes, albuminuria persisting SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitor if the eGFR is 20 or more It also cuts hyperfiltration. 4 Foot ulcerneuropathic ulcer Off-load the foot until it heals; inspection at each visit and podiatry 5 Neuropathic painpainful neuropathy First line: a tricyclic or a gabapentinoid (gabapentin, pregabalin); a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) such as duloxetine is an alternative Avoid tricyclics over 65 or with heart disease. 6 Referretinopathy moderate or worse Ophthalmology: macular edema, any proliferative retinopathy, or nonproliferative that is moderate or worse Proliferative retinopathy: photocoagulation or anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) therapy.

Annual care When Do Type 2: at diagnosis, then yearly Dilated eye exam, UACR with creatinine, monofilament foot exam In practiceIn practiceIn practice: after normal exams with well-controlled glycemia, every 1 to 2 years may be considered. Type 1: within 5 years of onset, then yearly First dilated eye exam Type 1: from 5 years after diagnosis, then yearly Kidney screen Every visit Blood pressure; inspect the feet once sensation is lost A1c not at goal or after a therapy change A1c every 3 months A1c stable at goal A1c every 6 months Age 19 to 49 with diabetes; every adult 50 or older Pneumococcal vaccine Hypertension, kidney disease, lupus, sickle cell disease, nephrotoxic drugs or human immunodeficiency virus infection Kidney screen at diagnosis, then yearly or by risk Routine visits Depression screen; weight and tobacco counseling Healthy adult without risk factors No kidney screen (USPSTF: insufficient evidence)

Screening1 of 21 28-year-old woman had type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 month ago Asymptomatic; walks daily and has cut out sugary drinks takes metformin; no other medical history BP 122/78 mm Hg · A1c 6.1% · Annual dilated eye exam · Pneumococcal vaccination · Monthly A1c measurement 28-year-old woman had type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 month ago Asymptomatic; walks daily and has cut out sugary drinks takes metformin; no other medical history BP 122/78 mm Hg · A1c 6.1% Annual dilated eye exammorbidity means the complications of diabetes, so the answer screens for one: the dilated eye exam finds retinopathy while it is still asymptomatic. Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated too, but it addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes; monthly A1c measures overlapping windows

Screening2 of 21 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years Due for his annual kidney screening; feels well takes metformin; no edema BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · A1c 7.4% · 24-Hour urine protein · Urine dipstick protein · Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years Due for his annual kidney screening; feels well takes metformin; no edema BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · A1c 7.4% Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratiothe most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold: the ratio detects 30 to 300 mg/g, the reversible stage. The dipstick stays negative until about 300 mg/day; a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection quantifies total protein when a non-albumin protein is suspected

Diagnosis3 of 21 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a foot ulcer for 3 weeks painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head surrounding callus; foot warm and dry T 36.9 °C · pedal pulses normal · A1c 9.1% · Neuropathic ulcer · Venous stasis ulcer · Arterial ischemic ulcer 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a foot ulcer for 3 weeks painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head surrounding callus; foot warm and dry T 36.9 °C · pedal pulses normal · A1c 9.1% Neuropathic ulcerpainless, plantar over a bony prominence and warm point away from arterial disease; normal pulses support a perfused foot, but neuropathy hides ischemic pain, so the ABI is still checked, and even a normal ABI and toe-brachial index only make arterial disease less likely; dry skin is autonomic denervation. Off-loading with a total contact cast is the single most important treatment, with debridement and glycemic control

Screening4 of 21 56-year-old man has type 2 diabetes diagnosed today Thirst and frequent urination for 2 months no medical care in the past 10 years BP 134/84 mm Hg · A1c 8.2% · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL · At diagnosis · At age 60 · Five years after diagnosis 56-year-old man has type 2 diabetes diagnosed today Thirst and frequent urination for 2 months no medical care in the past 10 years BP 134/84 mm Hg · A1c 8.2% · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL At diagnosisin type 2 diabetes kidney screening starts at diagnosis and repeats yearly, because silent hyperglycemia predates the diagnosis by years; in type 1 it starts 5 years after diagnosis

Next step5 of 21 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 2 years asks about A1c frequency A1c at goal on her last three checks No change in her metformin dose for a year BP 118/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.4% · Check the A1c every 6 months · Check the A1c every 3 months · Check the A1c monthly 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 2 years asks about A1c frequency A1c at goal on her last three checks No change in her metformin dose for a year BP 118/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.4% Check the A1c every 6 monthsstable at goal means every 6 months; every 3 months is for an A1c not at goal or after a therapy change. Monthly values measure overlapping windows of the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan

Diagnosis6 of 21 68-year-old man has had a painful ulcer at the toe tips for 1 month pain worse with the leg raised, better dangling cool pale foot; shiny, hairless skin T 36.8 °C · BP 148/86 mm Hg · absent pulses · Venous stasis ulcer · Arterial ischemic ulcer · Neuropathic diabetic ulcer 68-year-old man has had a painful ulcer at the toe tips for 1 month pain worse with the leg raised, better dangling cool pale foot; shiny, hairless skin T 36.8 °C · BP 148/86 mm Hg · absent pulses Arterial ischemic ulcera painful ulcer at the toe tips on a cool, pale, pulseless foot is arterial: confirm with the ankle-brachial index. A neuropathic ulcer is painless and plantar on a warm foot; a venous ulcer is wet and sits at the medial malleolus

Next step7 of 21 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a single abnormal albumin-to-creatinine ratio ratio 64 mg/g on his annual screen Ran a 10K race the day before the sample BP 126/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · Repeat the albumin-to-creatinine ratio · Start an ACE inhibitor immediately · Refer to nephrology now 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a single abnormal albumin-to-creatinine ratio ratio 64 mg/g on his annual screen Ran a 10K race the day before the sample BP 126/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Repeat the albumin-to-creatinine ratioconfirmation requires 2 of 3 abnormal samples over 3 to 6 months, which excludes transient albuminuria from exercise, fever, infection, heart failure or hyperglycemia; drug treatment starts once it persists

Screening8 of 21 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is due for vaccines Receives this season's influenza vaccine today no asplenia; no chronic lung or heart disease Does not smoke BP 120/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.8% · Pneumococcal vaccination · Zoster vaccination · No additional vaccines at this time 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is due for vaccines Receives this season's influenza vaccine today no asplenia; no chronic lung or heart disease Does not smoke BP 120/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.8% Pneumococcal vaccinationdiabetes is a risk-based indication for pneumococcal vaccination in adults 19 to 49, and every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age; asplenia is not required

Diagnosis9 of 21 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years is seen for his annual foot exam ABI 1.5 in both legs radiograph shows calcified tibial arteries BP 138/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL · Severe peripheral arterial disease · Normal arterial perfusion · Noncompressible vessels 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years is seen for his annual foot exam ABI 1.5 in both legs radiograph shows calcified tibial arteries BP 138/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL Noncompressible vesselsan index over 1.4 means calcified, noncompressible vessels, as in diabetes and end-stage renal disease; the next test is the toe-brachial index, abnormal at 0.7 or less, which can unmask arterial disease the ABI hides

Screening10 of 21 24-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 Establishing care at a new clinic after a move uses an insulin pump; no kidney screening on record BP 112/70 mm Hg · A1c 7.3% · At the time of diagnosis · 5 years after diagnosis · At age 30 24-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 Establishing care at a new clinic after a move uses an insulin pump; no kidney screening on record BP 112/70 mm Hg · A1c 7.3% 5 years after diagnosisin type 1 diabetes kidney screening starts 5 years after diagnosis, then yearly; it starts at diagnosis only in type 2, where hyperglycemia has been silent for years

Next step11 of 21 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes asks what most reduces his risk of death smokes one pack of cigarettes daily Overdue for his eye and foot exams BP 136/84 mm Hg · A1c 7.0% · Annual foot exam · Smoking cessation · Annual dilated eye exam 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes asks what most reduces his risk of death smokes one pack of cigarettes daily Overdue for his eye and foot exams BP 136/84 mm Hg · A1c 7.0% Smoking cessationmortality means death, so choose the intervention with survival data: smoking cessation, then blood pressure control and a statin. The eye and foot exams prevent morbidity, not death

Diagnosis12 of 21 62-year-old woman has had a leg ulcer for 2 months shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus brown hemosiderin staining and ankle edema Mild ache, better with the leg raised T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal · Arterial ischemic ulcer · Neuropathic ulcer · Venous stasis ulcer 62-year-old woman has had a leg ulcer for 2 months shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus brown hemosiderin staining and ankle edema Mild ache, better with the leg raised T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal Venous stasis ulcera shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus with hemosiderin and edema is venous stasis: duplex ultrasound, then compression

Next step13 of 21 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 9 years albumin-to-creatinine ratio 85 mg/g second elevated value in 4 months; the first was 72 mg/g BP 134/82 mm Hg (similar at her last visit) · A1c 7.1% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor · Add a sulfonylurea · Increase the metformin dose 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 9 years albumin-to-creatinine ratio 85 mg/g second elevated value in 4 months; the first was 72 mg/g BP 134/82 mm Hg (similar at her last visit) · A1c 7.1% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitorpersistent albuminuria (2 of 3 samples elevated over 3 to 6 months) with a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg calls for an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more an SGLT2 inhibitor as well; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts her eGFR well above 20. Together they are most likely to slow progression

Diagnosis14 of 21 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a foot ulcer that has not healed in 2 months plantar foot ulcer over a bony prominence; probe-to-bone test positive Foot radiograph normal T 37.2 °C · ESR 88 mm/h · Charcot arthropathy · Osteomyelitis · Cellulitis alone 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a foot ulcer that has not healed in 2 months plantar foot ulcer over a bony prominence; probe-to-bone test positive Foot radiograph normal T 37.2 °C · ESR 88 mm/h Osteomyelitisa probe that touches bone makes osteomyelitis likely, and an ESR over 70 supports it; plain films are insensitive early, so MRI comes next, then bone biopsy, which names the organism

Next step15 of 21 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes asks when to recheck her A1c A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent Takes metformin and sitagliptin; no low blood sugars BP 124/78 mm Hg · weight 82 kg · Check the A1c annually · Check the A1c every 6 months · Check the A1c every 3 months 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes asks when to recheck her A1c A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent Takes metformin and sitagliptin; no low blood sugars BP 124/78 mm Hg · weight 82 kg Check the A1c every 3 monthsan A1c not at goal and a therapy change each mean every 3 months; every 6 months is for an A1c stable at goal

Workup16 of 21 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is enrolling in a drug study below-knee amputation of the right leg last year The study protocol needs an exact filtration rate before dosing BP 130/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL · Serum creatinine · Creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rate · Inulin or iothalamate clearance 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is enrolling in a drug study below-knee amputation of the right leg last year The study protocol needs an exact filtration rate before dosing BP 130/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL Inulin or iothalamate clearancemeasured clearance is the most accurate; creatinine is unreliable in amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders and cirrhosis, where cystatin C helps

Diagnosis17 of 21 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a warm, swollen, erythematous right foot swelling for 3 weeks no ulcer or break in the skin; no fever Cannot feel the monofilament on either foot T 36.9 °C · white cells 7,400/mm³ · Cellulitis of the foot · Charcot arthropathy · Osteomyelitis 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a warm, swollen, erythematous right foot swelling for 3 weeks no ulcer or break in the skin; no fever Cannot feel the monofilament on either foot T 36.9 °C · white cells 7,400/mm³ Charcot arthropathya warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests Charcot arthropathy (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity

Screening18 of 21 32-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 26 Establishing care after a move; old records lost reports she has never had a dilated eye examination BP 116/72 mm Hg · A1c 7.6% · 10 years after diagnosis · Within 5 years after diagnosis · Only once visual symptoms appear 32-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 26 Establishing care after a move; old records lost reports she has never had a dilated eye examination BP 116/72 mm Hg · A1c 7.6% Within 5 years after diagnosisin an adult with type 1 diabetes the first dilated eye exam comes within 5 years after onset, then yearly; in type 2 diabetes it comes at diagnosis. Retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced, so waiting for symptoms misses it

Diagnosis19 of 21 34-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging painful ulcer on her lower leg violaceous, undermined border grew from a small sore over 10 days Has inflammatory bowel disease with a recent flare T 37.3 °C · white cells 9,800/mm³ · Pyoderma gangrenosum · Necrotizing fasciitis · Vasculitic ulcer 34-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging painful ulcer on her lower leg violaceous, undermined border grew from a small sore over 10 days Has inflammatory bowel disease with a recent flare T 37.3 °C · white cells 9,800/mm³ Pyoderma gangrenosuma rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border in inflammatory bowel disease or rheumatoid arthritis is pyoderma gangrenosum: biopsy and steroids, and never debride (pathergy)

Next step20 of 21 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has confirmed albuminuria ratio 140 mg/g, then 156 mg/g 3 months later Asks what most slows progression BP 138/86 mm Hg (similar at his last visit) · A1c 7.8% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor · Dietary protein restriction · Tight glycemic control alone 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has confirmed albuminuria ratio 140 mg/g, then 156 mg/g 3 months later Asks what most slows progression BP 138/86 mm Hg (similar at his last visit) · A1c 7.8% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitorwith albuminuria and a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg, an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus, in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more, an SGLT2 inhibitor slows progression; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts his eGFR well above 20. Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB

Next step21 of 21 66-year-old man has a chronic non-healing ulcer on his shin arose in an old burn scar 8 months ago rolled, everted edges No better despite compression and two courses of antibiotics T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal · Repeat wound culture · Continue compression therapy · Biopsy for Marjolin ulcer 66-year-old man has a chronic non-healing ulcer on his shin arose in an old burn scar 8 months ago rolled, everted edges No better despite compression and two courses of antibiotics T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal Biopsy for Marjolin ulceran ulcer in a chronic wound or scar with rolled, everted edges that has not healed in over 3 months needs a biopsy for Marjolin ulcer

Neuropathic ulcer off-loading (total contact cast) is the single most important intervention; debride callus and necrotic tissue; glycemic control Infection culture only if clinically infected, deep tissue rather than a swab Perfusion check the ABI anyway: mixed neuroischemic ulcers are common Charcot arthropathy warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests it (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity

A1c reflects glycation across the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan, so monthly values measure heavily overlapping windows; they add no information and prevent no complication. At goal, monthly testing is six times the 6-month schedule.

The source question for the first practice item (eye exam, pneumococcal vaccine or monthly A1c to prevent morbidity) came with two errors. 1. The pneumococcal rationale is wrong. It limited vaccination to patients over 65 or with asplenia, but every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age, and diabetes is itself a risk-based indication in adults 19 to 49, so she is a candidate. The eye exam wins because it targets a diabetes-specific complication; vaccination addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes. 2. The attribution is off. The annual bundle and A1c intervals come from the American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care, not the USPSTF.

“Microalbuminuria” → “UACR 85 mg/g” “hyperfiltration” → “creatinine 0.7” in a diabetic “Kimmelstiel-Wilson” → “nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy” “transient albuminuria” → “he ran a 10K yesterday.”

Read the outcome noun before the options: morbidity, mortality, hospitalization and benefit are four different targets, and a distractor can be the right intervention for the wrong target. The most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold; the most specific or confirmatory test is the least likely to give a false positive. Risk factors set the prior probability and physical findings the posterior: when the exam contradicts the risk profile on three separate axes, rely on the exam.

briefs.title: Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome
briefs.sub: glomerular or not, then symptomatic or not · nephritis weeks after strep: complement and volumeIs it glomerular, how long since the infection, is complement low, and is the child overloaded?
blocks: glomerular or not, then symptomatic or not · nephritis weeks after strep: complement and volumeIs it glomerular, how long since the infection, is complement low, and is the child overloaded?

With dysuria, leukocyte esterase and pyuria, the blood is part of the cystitis, not a separate workup. Otherwise ask in order: is it glomerular, and if not, does a symptom name the cause? Glomerular hematuria: any of brown, tea or cola urine, red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, protein, edema or hypertension; check creatinine, complement levels and a complete blood count (CBC). Non-glomerular hematuria: bright red urine or clots, normal red cell shape, no protein. With no symptom to name the cause: renal and bladder ultrasound, the first image for painless gross hematuria, since a young child's kidney stone is often painless; urine culture; and a spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio for hypercalciuria, a common cause of asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross, in a well child. Nephritic syndrome: hematuria with red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, hypertension, edema, oliguria and a rising creatinine; protein present but usually below the nephrotic range. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) (postinfectious glomerulonephritis): weeks, not days. About 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo; often summarized as 2 to 4 weeks. Hematuria during or within days of an upper respiratory infection is immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy (Berger disease). Complement clock: C3 (complement component 3) low at onset, back to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks; still low after 8 weeks suggests a different lesion.

Glomerular vs non-glomerular hematuria Glomerular Non-glomerular Color Brown, tea or cola Bright red, clots Sediment Red cell casts, dysmorphic red cells Normal red cell shape Protein Present Absent Other signs Edema, hypertension None, or a local symptom: dysuria, flank pain, trauma, meatal irritation Causes IgA nephropathy, PSGN, Alport (hereditary nephritis), thin basement membrane, lupus Urinary tract infection, stones, trauma, tumor, hypercalciuria, sickle trait, exercise

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Every case → Urinalysis with microscopy Dipstick blood, 3 or more red cells per high-power field (hpf) True hematuria Dipstick blood, no red cells Suggests myoglobin or hemoglobin Targeted tests TestResultMeans Dysuria, leukocyte esterase and pyuria → Urine culture Growth Cystitis: treat, repeat the urinalysis after antibiotics; image only if blood persists No growth, in a sexually active adolescent Chlamydia and gonorrhea nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) Protein, edema or hypertension → Urine sediment: casts and red cell shape Red cell casts, dysmorphic red cells, protein Glomerular: creatinine, complement levels, CBC, blood pressure; antistreptolysin O (ASO) after strep Abdominal or flank trauma → Contrast CT abdomen Renal injury Stable: managed without surgery, at any grade Flank pain with crystals → Renal ultrasound Stone Ultrasound is the first image in a child with flank pain, no radiation Meatal irritation → Exam of the urethral meatus and perineum Visible, painful irritation Reassurance, no imaging Well child, no symptom → Renal and bladder ultrasoundUrine cultureUrine calcium/creatinine ratio Ultrasound: stone, hydronephrosis or renal mass First image for painless gross hematuria: no radiation; excludes Wilms tumor Culture: growth Urinary tract infection Calcium/creatinine ratio high Hypercalciuria: a common cause of asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross, in a well child; a major stone risk Next step TestResultMeans Stone still suspected after a nondiagnostic ultrasound → Noncontrast CT of the abdomen Small stone the ultrasound missed CT is more sensitive, but uses radiation Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Painless gross hematuria in an older adult or smoker → CT urography and cystoscopy Mass or stone Not a first test in a child Glomerular, and history and complement do not settle it → Renal biopsy Names the glomerular lesion IgA nephropathy, Alport or lupus Skip24-hour urine protein or biopsy for bright red urine without protein, casts, edema or hypertension: nonglomerular.

Acute nephritis in a child: the differential Diagnosis Illness script and tell Against it 2 weeks after a sore throat PSGN (postinfectious glomerulonephritis) Immune complexes after group A strep pharyngitis or impetigo; edema, hypertension, cola urine; weeks later, low C3, normal by 6 to 8 weeks; positive ASO or anti-DNase B; children recover over weeks The answer IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) Mesangial IgA; recurrent gross hematuria in an older child or young adult, during or within days of an infection; normal C3 Two-week gap; edema and hypertension, not isolated episodes IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) nephritis Small-vessel IgA vasculitis; kidney disease can follow the rash by weeks; palpable purpura on legs and buttocks, arthritis, abdominal pain; normal C3 No rash, joint or abdominal pain Lupus nephritis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) Immune-complex nephritis that does not resolve; lupus mostly in adolescent girls; persistently low complement; lupus lowers C3 and C4 (complement component 4), with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) Decided at 8 weeks: an unrecovered C3 calls for further investigation, including a biopsy Alport syndrome (hereditary nephritis) Type IV collagen defect, usually X-linked; persistent hematuria with sensorineural hearing loss and family kidney failure; slow progression Acute onset after an infection; no deafness or family history Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhea; microangiopathy; hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, low platelets plus acute kidney injury (AKI) Normal blood count; sore throat, not diarrhea

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Cola urine, edema or hypertension → Urinalysis with microscopyCreatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), electrolytesCBC with smear Urine: blood and protein, red cell casts, dysmorphic red cells Glomerular (nephritic) bleeding Creatinine raised; potassium may be high AKI; a high potassium steers away from an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor Smear: schistocytes, low platelets HUS: Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhea Next step TestResultMeans Nephritic urine → C3 and C4 Low C3, C4 normal or mildly low PSGN Normal C3 IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis Low C3 and C4 Suggests lupus Low C3, weeks after strep throat or impetigo → ASO and anti-DNase B (streptozyme) Elevated titers Recent group A strep; anti-DNase B is the better marker after impetigo Diagnostic test TestResultMeans C3 still low after 8 weeks, or a worsening course → Renal biopsy Names the glomerular lesion MPGN or lupus nephritis SkipRenal biopsy in typical PSGN, with a C3 back to normal by 8 weeks.

Workup1 of 16 6-year-old boy has bright red urine since yesterday No dysuria, trauma or recent infection no edema or flank tenderness BP 100/65 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts; leukocyte esterase and nitrite negative · Cystoscopy · Noncontrast CT of the abdomen · Renal and bladder ultrasonography 6-year-old boy has bright red urine since yesterday No dysuria, trauma or recent infection no edema or flank tenderness BP 100/65 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts; leukocyte esterase and nitrite negative Renal and bladder ultrasonographybright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension is nonglomerular, and no symptom names a cause. In a young child a kidney stone is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone; the ultrasound finds many stones and any obstruction with no radiation and also excludes a renal mass such as Wilms tumor. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Noncontrast CT is more sensitive for small stones but carries radiation, so in a child it follows a nondiagnostic ultrasound

Diagnosis2 of 16 8-year-old boy has 2 days of tea-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago, resolved without treatment puffy eyelids; mild pretibial edema urine: red cell casts, 2+ protein BP 140/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL · IgA nephropathy · Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis · Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 8-year-old boy has 2 days of tea-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago, resolved without treatment puffy eyelids; mild pretibial edema urine: red cell casts, 2+ protein BP 140/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisa latent period of weeks, not days, with red cell casts, protein and hypertension: expect a low C3 that normalizes by 6 to 8 weeks and a positive ASO or anti-DNase B. IgA nephropathy bleeds during or within days of an upper respiratory infection with a normal C3. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is the nephritis that does not resolve, with a persistently low complement; it is raised when the C3 is still low at 8 weeks

Avoid3 of 16 8-year-old girl was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis yesterday periorbital and pedal edema Her physician considers drugs for her blood pressure BP 150/96 mm Hg · creatinine 1.7 mg/dL · potassium 6.0 mEq/L · Nifedipine · Furosemide · Lisinopril 8-year-old girl was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis yesterday periorbital and pedal edema Her physician considers drugs for her blood pressure BP 150/96 mm Hg · creatinine 1.7 mg/dL · potassium 6.0 mEq/L LisinoprilACE inhibitors raise potassium and can lower the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in AKI, and this potassium is already high. Furosemide treats the overload that drives the edema and pressure, and nifedipine follows if pressure stays high after diuresis

Diagnosis4 of 16 14-year-old boy receiving cyclophosphamide has 2 days of bright red urine with clots suprapubic discomfort; no flank pain Urine culture shows no growth Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · urine: protein negative, no casts · Bladder carcinoma · Hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein · Bacterial hemorrhagic cystitis 14-year-old boy receiving cyclophosphamide has 2 days of bright red urine with clots suprapubic discomfort; no flank pain Urine culture shows no growth Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · urine: protein negative, no casts Hemorrhagic cystitis from acroleinbright red urine with clots on cyclophosphamide is a hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein, which mesna and hydration given with the drug help prevent. After a transplant, think of BK (a polyomavirus) or adenovirus. A bacterial cystitis needs significant bacteriuria on culture, and bladder cancer is very rare in children

Workup5 of 16 7-year-old girl has microscopic hematuria on two routine urinalyses Well, with no dysuria, flank pain or edema urine: no protein, no casts, normal red cell shape BP 98/60 mm Hg · urine culture negative · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL · Cystoscopy · Renal biopsy · Urine calcium/creatinine ratio 7-year-old girl has microscopic hematuria on two routine urinalyses Well, with no dysuria, flank pain or edema urine: no protein, no casts, normal red cell shape BP 98/60 mm Hg · urine culture negative · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL Urine calcium/creatinine ratiohypercalciuria is a common cause of asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross, in a well child and a major risk factor for a stone; a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio finds it. A biopsy is a glomerular test, and this urine has no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, very rare in children

Diagnosis6 of 16 16-year-old boy has a third episode of cola-colored urine each began 1 to 2 days into a sore throat Between episodes he feels well urine: red cells, 1+ protein BP 118/74 mm Hg · C3 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · Thin basement membrane disease · IgA nephropathy · Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 16-year-old boy has a third episode of cola-colored urine each began 1 to 2 days into a sore throat Between episodes he feels well urine: red cells, 1+ protein BP 118/74 mm Hg · C3 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL IgA nephropathysynpharyngitic hematuria, within 1 to 2 days of the sore throat, recurrent, with a normal C3: mesangial IgA, typical in an older child or young adult. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis comes weeks, not days, after the infection: about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo, often summarized as 2 to 4 weeks; its C3 is low. Thin basement membrane disease usually presents as isolated microscopic hematuria; gross bleeds occur in only a minority, often after infection

Next step7 of 16 9-year-old boy has headache, lethargy and 2 days of low urine output Sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital, scrotal and pedal edema; no rash BP 170/102 mm Hg, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, normal blood count · urine: moderate blood, 2+ protein · Furosemide · Normal saline bolus · Plasmapheresis 9-year-old boy has headache, lethargy and 2 days of low urine output Sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital, scrotal and pedal edema; no rash BP 170/102 mm Hg, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, normal blood count · urine: moderate blood, 2+ protein Furosemidehematuria with protein, hypertension, edema and a rising creatinine two weeks after a sore throat is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water, and the edema and hypertension both come from that volume: the first drug is a loop diuretic, with sodium and fluid restriction. Saline answers the low urine output and raised creatinine, but this child is overloaded, not dry. Plasmapheresis treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease; this disease is immune-complex and self-limited. Headache and lethargy at this pressure are signs of hypertensive encephalopathy, so a calcium channel blocker is added alongside the diuretic now rather than after diuresis; it is not among these options

Workup8 of 16 68-year-old man has two episodes of painless bright red urine Smokes one pack daily for 45 years no dysuria or flank pain Afebrile · BP 136/84 mm Hg · urine: over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein, casts or leukocyte esterase · Repeat urinalysis in 6 weeks · Renal ultrasound alone · Cystoscopy + CT urography 68-year-old man has two episodes of painless bright red urine Smokes one pack daily for 45 years no dysuria or flank pain Afebrile · BP 136/84 mm Hg · urine: over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein, casts or leukocyte esterase Cystoscopy + CT urographypainless gross hematuria in an older adult or smoker earns CT urography and cystoscopy, which find a mass or stone; bladder cancer is the concern at this age. A repeat urinalysis in weeks delays that, and a renal ultrasound alone skips the cystoscopy and detects far fewer upper tract urothelial tumors than CT urography

Next step9 of 16 10-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 3 months ago Seen at a scheduled follow-up visit edema has resolved microscopic hematuria persists on urinalysis BP 108/68 mm Hg · C3 still low · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL · Repeat antistreptolysin O titer · Repeat serum C3 in 3 months · Renal biopsy 10-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 3 months ago Seen at a scheduled follow-up visit edema has resolved microscopic hematuria persists on urinalysis BP 108/68 mm Hg · C3 still low · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL Renal biopsya C3 that has not recovered by 8 weeks calls for further investigation, including a biopsy, to look for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis. Microscopic hematuria may persist for up to 5 years, but C3 returns to normal within 6 to 8 weeks in about 80%; waiting 3 more months delays the biopsy, and a repeat ASO shows only recent strep infection, not why the C3 stays low

Workup10 of 16 8-year-old boy has had 3 days of tea-colored urine He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital edema urine: red cell casts, 1+ protein Afebrile · BP 138/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL · Serum C3 level · Renal biopsy · Renal ultrasound 8-year-old boy has had 3 days of tea-colored urine He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital edema urine: red cell casts, 1+ protein Afebrile · BP 138/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL Serum C3 levelnephritis weeks after pharyngitis: a low C3 with a normal or mildly low C4 supports poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis; a normal C3 means IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis, and a low C3 and C4 suggest lupus. A biopsy is generally only for an atypical course (C3 still low after 8 weeks or worsening), and an ultrasound shows size and structure, not immune complexes

Diagnosis11 of 16 10-year-old boy has microscopic hematuria on every urinalysis since age 4 sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry His maternal uncle had kidney failure at 30 BP 112/70 mm Hg · urine: 1+ protein · C3 normal · Thin basement membrane disease · IgA nephropathy · Alport syndrome 10-year-old boy has microscopic hematuria on every urinalysis since age 4 sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry His maternal uncle had kidney failure at 30 BP 112/70 mm Hg · urine: 1+ protein · C3 normal Alport syndromepersistent hematuria with sensorineural hearing loss and a family history of kidney failure is a type IV collagen defect, usually X-linked, progressing slowly to kidney failure. Thin basement membrane disease does not bring deafness. IgA nephropathy bleeds in recurrent gross episodes during or within days of an upper respiratory infection

Workup12 of 16 11-year-old boy fell onto bicycle handlebars 3 hours ago left flank pain, bruising; bright red urine alert; abdomen soft, left flank tender HR 96/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · large blood, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts · Contrast CT of the abdomen · Renal and bladder ultrasonography · Repeat urinalysis in 1 week 11-year-old boy fell onto bicycle handlebars 3 hours ago left flank pain, bruising; bright red urine alert; abdomen soft, left flank tender HR 96/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · large blood, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts Contrast CT of the abdomenhematuria after abdominal or flank trauma: CT shows and stages the renal injury. Ultrasound may be used in children, but CT is preferred, and waiting a week to repeat the urinalysis leaves the injury unstaged

Next step13 of 16 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 2 days ago headache After 24 hours of furosemide with sodium and fluid restriction alert, no respiratory distress BP 165/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.8 mEq/L · Continue the current regimen and recheck in 24 hours · Add nifedipine · Begin hemodialysis 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 2 days ago headache After 24 hours of furosemide with sodium and fluid restriction alert, no respiratory distress BP 165/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.8 mEq/L Add nifedipinepressure that stays high after 24 hours of diuresis is the indication for a calcium channel blocker, so waiting another day is not the step. Watch for hypertensive encephalopathy: headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures. Dialysis is for refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia, none of which is present

Workup14 of 16 17-year-old girl has 5 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner; no fever or flank pain urine: leukocyte esterase positive, 20 white cells/hpf, a few red cells urine culture: no growth Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · Renal ultrasound · Chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT · Urine culture for bacterial cystitis 17-year-old girl has 5 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner; no fever or flank pain urine: leukocyte esterase positive, 20 white cells/hpf, a few red cells urine culture: no growth Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg Chlamydia and gonorrhea NAATsterile pyuria with dysuria in a sexually active adolescent: test for chlamydia and gonorrhea with a nucleic acid amplification test. Other causes of sterile pyuria are renal tuberculosis, interstitial nephritis, a partially treated urinary tract infection and appendicitis. A culture for bacterial cystitis already grew nothing, which is what makes this pyuria sterile, and a renal ultrasound answers flank pain with crystals or painless gross hematuria

Diagnosis15 of 16 6-year-old girl has cola-colored urine and puffy eyelids Crusted sores on her legs 4 weeks ago red cell casts; no rash or joint pain BP 138/90 mm Hg · C3 low · C4 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · IgA nephropathy · Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis · IgA vasculitis nephritis 6-year-old girl has cola-colored urine and puffy eyelids Crusted sores on her legs 4 weeks ago red cell casts; no rash or joint pain BP 138/90 mm Hg · C3 low · C4 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisnephritis up to about 6 weeks after impetigo, with a low C3 and normal C4, a C3 expected to normalize within 8 weeks; anti-DNase B is the better strep marker after impetigo. IgA nephropathy bleeds within days of an infection with a normal C3, and IgA vasculitis brings palpable purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain with a normal C3

Workup16 of 16 9-year-old girl has 2 days of brown urine puffy eyelids each morning mild pretibial edema BP 132/86 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, protein 2+, red cell casts · no leukocyte esterase or nitrite · Serum creatinine, complement levels and CBC · Urine calcium/creatinine ratio and urine culture · Renal and bladder ultrasonography and urine culture 9-year-old girl has 2 days of brown urine puffy eyelids each morning mild pretibial edema BP 132/86 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, protein 2+, red cell casts · no leukocyte esterase or nitrite Serum creatinine, complement levels and CBCbrown urine with protein, casts, edema and hypertension is glomerular hematuria: check creatinine, complement levels and a CBC. A low C3 after a recent strep infection points to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The ultrasound and calcium/creatinine ratio are for the nonglomerular branch

8-year-old girl with 6 days of intermittent headache, tiredness and little appetite, then 2 days of brown urine Vomited yesterday morning; no abdominal pain, diarrhea or dysuria Sore throat and fever 2 weeks ago that cleared without treatment; previously healthy, no medications; normal growth and development mildly pale, not distressed; height 50th percentile, weight 75th T 36.7 °C · HR 108/min · respiratory rate 16/min · BP 138/88 mm Hg large, mildly red tonsils without exudate; lungs clear grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, no rub or gallop; abdomen normal; warm extremities with 1+ edema serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL · urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL · sodium 132 mEq/L · potassium 5.2 mEq/L · chloride 100 mEq/L · bicarbonate 15 mEq/L urine: blood 2+ · protein 1+ · red cell casts too numerous to count · pH 5 · specific gravity 1.020 · Gram stain: no organisms Most appropriate next step in diagnosis? Competing answers Antinuclear antibody assay: pulls toward lupus nephritis; but it is neither sensitive nor specific for PSGN, and lupus would lower both C3 and C4. Urine culture: the urine is abnormal; but a culture answers a urinary tract infection; there is no dysuria and the Gram stain shows no organisms. Renal ultrasonography: the creatinine is rising; but immune-complex deposits are microscopic, not visible on ultrasound. Down to two: serum C3 or echocardiography. Serum C3: brown urine with casts, protein, hypertension and edema 2 weeks after a sore throat; deposited immune complexes consume C3, so the serum level falls. The soft ejection murmur after the sore throat baits rheumatic carditis, but the lungs are clear, so heart failure is unlikely.

Volume overload inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water; edema and hypertension both come from that volume; headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures mean hypertensive encephalopathy Every child supportive care with sodium and fluid restriction Loop diuretic furosemide first, for edema or hypertension from volume overload; saline for the oliguria would worsen it Calcium channel blocker nifedipine when pressure stays high after diuresis or encephalopathy appears; ACE inhibitors only with caution in AKI because of hyperkalemia Dialysis refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia No role plasmapheresis, since the disease is self-limited Antibiotics treat a still-active strep infection but do not change the renal course

It needs a nitrate-reducing organism (Enterococcus, S. saprophyticus and Pseudomonas are not) and adequate bladder dwell time. A negative nitrite never excludes a urinary tract infection when leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms agree.

A kidney stone in a young child is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone, and crystals are not always seen. Hypercalciuria is a major risk factor: look for earlier microscopic hematuria and a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio. The renal and bladder ultrasound comes first; noncontrast CT only if it is nondiagnostic. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Meatal irritation is painful and visible on exam: reassure.

Nephritis days after an upper respiratory infection is IgA nephropathy; weeks after pharyngitis or impetigo, PSGN. Treating strep pharyngitis promptly prevents rheumatic fever but does not reliably prevent PSGN. Children usually recover fully within weeks, although microscopic hematuria may persist for up to 5 years; adults are more likely to develop chronic kidney disease.

A negative nitrite overruling leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms. Cystoscopy in a child: right for an older adult, but bladder cancer is very rare in a 6-year-old, so the ultrasound comes first. Noncontrast CT before the ultrasound: more sensitive for small stones, but radiation. A 24-hour urine protein or kidney biopsy for bright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Normal saline for a low urine output in an overloaded child. Plasmapheresis: treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; PSGN is immune-complex and self-limited. Lisinopril first: risks hyperkalemia in AKI; diuresis first, then a calcium channel blocker. Protein restriction: for chronic kidney disease, not a self-limited acute nephritis.

Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child: protein without red cells, from the well child’s routine dipstick to the young child with periorbital edema who gets steroids without a biopsy. Ask: does the urine show red cells and casts, or protein alone? Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes starts one step earlier: is the swelling local to the eye? Part I Acute Kidney Injury in a Child: the AKI that does need fluids. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child sends the renal involvement of IgA vasculitis here. Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia: HUS.

With a full lab panel, base the diagnosis on the pattern of the panel, not the most alarming single value; a discordant component reflects a test's limited sensitivity and does not overrule the pattern. In a child with AKI, decide whether the kidney needs volume given or removed before choosing a drug: edema with hypertension means overload, so the loop diuretic comes first and saline is harmful.

briefs.title: Hypercalcemia
briefs.sub: parathyroid hormone first in every case · calcium and phosphorus patterns · normal labs that rule out alternativesIs the parathyroid hormone high or suppressed, and which way is the phosphorus going?
blocks: parathyroid hormone first in every case · calcium and phosphorus patterns · normal labs that rule out alternativesIs the parathyroid hormone high or suppressed, and which way is the phosphorus going?

Confirmed high calcium: PTH (parathyroid hormone) first. High or inappropriately normal primary hyperparathyroidism or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH); suppressed malignancy, vitamin D or granulomas High PTH with high urine calcium primary hyperparathyroidism, surgery; calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio under 1% FHH, no surgery Severe or confused: isotonic saline first calcitonin and a bisphosphonate

What it is Total calcium over 10.4 mg/dL; stones, bones, groans, thrones and psychiatric overtones Driver PTH (primary hyperparathyroidism, the commonest, usually an adenoma), PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein) from a tumor, calcitriol from granulomas or lymphoma, bone resorption from metastases, myeloma or immobilization Triggers Thiazides; lithium; calcium carbonate antacids (milk-alkali); vitamin D excess; immobilization Chain PTH or PTHrP bone resorption and renal phosphate loss high calcium, low phosphate High calcium urine cannot concentrate polyuria and volume depletion calcium rises further Insights Phosphate splits the drivers: low with PTH or PTHrP, high with vitamin D or immobilization A calcium over 13 points away from the parathyroid
Calcium total over 10.4 mg/dL PTH-driven PTH high or inappropriately normal FHH calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio under 1%

SevereCalcium 14 or more, confusion, dehydration Short QT interval on the ECG (electrocardiogram); arrhythmias If calcium is severe or the patient is confused, choose isotonic saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate.

Causes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Primary hyperparathyroidism Mild, often incidental; phosphate low PTH high or normal; urine calcium high Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy Calcium over 13, weight loss; squamous cell lung cancer PTH suppressed, PTHrP high Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia Lifelong, mild, no symptoms, relatives affected Calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio under 1%; no surgery Bone metastases or myeloma Breast cancer; anemia, renal failure, lytic lesions (CRAB) PTH and PTHrP low; lytic lesions Granulomatous disease or lymphoma Hilar adenopathy (sarcoidosis), lymphoma 1,25-OH vitamin D high Vitamin D excess Supplement excess 25-OH vitamin D high Milk-alkali syndrome Calcium carbonate antacids; metabolic alkalosis PTH suppressed Thiazide On a thiazide; mild Usually under 12 Immobilization New quadriplegia or bed rest Phosphate high too

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Calcium high on a screen → PTH, with phosphorus and albumin PTH high or inappropriately normal PTH-dependent: FHH or primary hyperparathyroidism PTH suppressed PTH-independent Targeted tests TestResultMeans PTH high or normal → 24-hour urine calcium Clearance ratio under 1% FHH: no surgery High Primary hyperparathyroidism Next step TestResultMeans PTH suppressed → PTHrP; 25-OH and 1,25-OH vitamin D PTHrP high Malignancy: imaging next 1,25-OH high Granulomatous disease or lymphoma 25-OH high Vitamin D excess SkipA sestamibi scan to make the diagnosis: the diagnosis is biochemical; the scan only localizes the gland before surgery.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Polyuria with a dilute urine Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from the calcium Treat the calcium Polyuria Antacids for dyspepsia, metabolic alkalosis Milk-alkali syndrome Check PTH (suppressed); isotonic saline Sarcoidosis with a high 1,25-OH vitamin D Calcitriol-driven Glucocorticoids help
Pause point Hypercalcemia Offered first: a PTHrP, a vitamin D level or a scan PTH splits the whole differential → PTH first, in every case

Severity by calcium Severity Calcium (mg/dL) Means Mild 10.5 to 11.9 Often no symptoms; find the cause Moderate 12.0 to 13.9 Confusion can start above 12 Severe 14 or more Saline, calcitonin, bisphosphonate

1 Severesevere or symptomatic Isotonic saline first: nearly all are volume depleted In practice In practiceIn practice: a clinical reference gives isotonic saline plus a loop diuretic; the board answer keeps the loop diuretic for fluid overload, because it deepens volume depletion. 2 Addcalcium still high Calcitonin for fast, short control and a bisphosphonate for lasting control Bisphosphonates are usually the drugs of choice in malignancy. 3 Calcitriolgranulomas, lymphoma, vitamin D toxicity Add a glucocorticoid 4 Dialysissevere symptoms, or renal failure Hemodialysis with a low-calcium bath

Treatment by cause Cause Choose Watch for Primary hyperparathyroidism, symptomatic Parathyroidectomy Sestamibi localizes the gland first Primary hyperparathyroidism, no symptoms Surgery if a criterion is met Surgery without symptomsPrimary hyperparathyroidismAge under 50; osteoporosis or a fragility fracture; kidney stones; GFR (glomerular filtration rate) under 60; calcium 1 mg/dL or more above normal; urine calcium over 400 mg a day. Otherwise surveillance FHH No surgery Autosomal dominant: relatives Thiazide Usually mild A calcium over 13 suggests another cause

Follow-up decisions When Do Calcium, phosphate and magnesium fall a week or more after parathyroidectomy Hungry bone syndrome: replace them Repeated IV bisphosphonate Watch for osteonecrosis of the jaw

Diagnosis5 of 6 58 yo F with hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH, high 1,25-OH vitamin D and hilar adenopathy · Granulomatous disease · Primary hyperparathyroidism · Malignancy 58 yo F with hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH, high 1,25-OH vitamin D and hilar adenopathy Granulomatous disease

Next step6 of 6 58 yo F with calcium 14.5, confusion and dehydration · Bisphosphonate alone · Loop diuretic first · Isotonic saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate 58 yo F with calcium 14.5, confusion and dehydration Isotonic saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate
Normal labs that rule out alt…

A normal albumin means the calcium is truly elevated, with no correction needed a specific gravity of 1.005 argues against diabetes mellitus, because glucosuria raises the specific gravity low phosphorus argues against vitamin D excess, which raises both calcium and phosphorus enalapril rather than a thiazide removes the drug confounder.

Part I Polyuria covers the polyuria hypercalcemia causes. It results from an acquired, reversible resistance to vasopressin at the collecting duct, which corrects when the calcium does. Ask: does the kidney concentrate after desmopressin?

blocks: Urinary Tract Infection in a Child
assign the tract, then name the risk factor · reflux grade sets treatment and outcomeIs this infection febrile or afebrile, does the bladder empty, and what grade did the cystourethrogram show?

Afebrile recurrent cystitis in a constipated child is stasis a long-term laxative; febrile recurrences point to reflux First febrile urinary tract infection (UTI) under 2 years renal and bladder US after treatment; recurrent febrile UTI voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) at any age Reflux grade I to II: prophylaxis under 5 years, observation over 5; grade III to V: prophylaxis at any age, surgery for breakthrough

What it is Bacterial infection of the bladder (cystitis) or kidney (pyelonephritis); a recurrence sends the search to the tract Bug Escherichia coli, then Klebsiella, Proteus Triggers Vesicoureteral reflux, a short intravesical ureter (non-modifiable) Bladder and bowel dysfunction: constipation, holding urine Female, or an uncircumcised boy under 12 months (non-modifiable) Outlet obstruction or a duplex collecting system (non-modifiable) Chain Reflux carries bladder bacteria up febrile pyelonephritis; stasis leaves residual urine afebrile cystitis Recurrent parenchymal infection focal scars at the upper and lower poles hypertension, proteinuria, chronic kidney disease (reflux nephropathy) Insights Assign the tract before the cause: anatomy gives febrile upper-tract recurrences, emptying problems give afebrile cystitis US shows dilation and scars but cannot show reflux; the VCUG grades it
I ureter only II reaches the pelvis, no dilation III ureter and pelvis dilated, little or no blunting IV fornices obliterated V gross dilation, tortuous ureter
A UTI itself needs pyuria and a culture at the clean-catch or catheter cutoff.

Young infantFebrile UTI under 2 months, or vomiting, unstable, or failing oral therapy If any of these, choose IV (intravenous) antibiotics, the drug chosen by age. Not improvingStill febrile at 48 to 72 hours on an antibiotic the organism is sensitive to If the organism is susceptible, choose renal and bladder US now, for an abscess or obstruction. Boy, weak streamMale infant with a weak stream, a palpable bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis Posterior Urethral Valves If the bladder does not empty, choose US, then VCUG for posterior urethral valves. Genital injuryGenital injury or bleeding, behavior change, disclosure Suspected Child Abuse If the genitalia are injured, choose evaluate for sexual abuse.

Reflux grade sets the plan Grade Course Plan Mild, I to II Usually resolves Why it resolvesMild refluxMild reflux usually resolves, probably because the intravesical ureter lengthens as the child grows. 1 Emptyingafebrile cystitis with constipation or holding Long-term laxative; behavioral therapy for holding Bladder and bowel dysfunction is preferably treated first, at every grade. 2 Prophylaxisreflux, by the grade rule Daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) or nitrofurantoin Grade I to II over 5 years: observation alone. In practice In practiceIn practice: the American Urological Association (AUA) guideline and current references differ from the board rule. There is no consensus on prophylaxis for mild to moderate reflux; most pediatric urologists give it for severe reflux at all ages, for grades III to V under 2 years, and with recurrent febrile infections or bladder and bowel dysfunction. A trial, Randomized Intervention for Children with Vesicoureteral Reflux (RIVUR), in children aged 2 to 72 months with reflux of grade I to IV after one or two symptomatic UTIs, found that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis halved recurrent infections, with no significant difference in renal scarring. 3 Surgeryfebrile breakthrough on prophylaxis Ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic bulking injection 4 Scarringestablished renal scars Chronic kidney disease care when BP, protein or function worsens

Reflux produces recurrent upper-tract, febrile disease, and a child with reflux would likely have had at least one febrile episode by now. Three days is an adequate course for a lower-tract infection, and a 6-week symptom-free gap means reinfection, not relapse

Empiric after the urinalysis, chosen by local sensitivity patterns and adjusted to the culture: oral options include cefixime, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole Route oral is preferred, pyelonephritis included; intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone for age under 2 months, vomiting, an unstable or ill child, or failure of oral therapy Blood tests complete blood count, blood culture and procalcitonin only if ill-appearing, unvaccinated or under 2 months No better by 48 to 72 hours resistant: switch to a susceptible drug; susceptible: ultrasound for abscess or obstruction, repeat culture, intravenous antibiotics and admission After a good response no routine repeat culture Prevention treat constipation, prophylaxis for reflux per the AUA rules, voiding habits, front-to-back wiping

Constipation is the commonest modifiable risk factor for recurrent cystitis in a young child, and the mechanism is purely mechanical. Functional constipation that dates to day-care entry is the stressor-driven withholding trigger. Hard stool with normal rectal tone argues against both a neurologic cause and anal trauma. Midline anal fissures are a complication of chronic constipation; alongside normal genitalia, they argue against injury, while a fissure off the midline may have another cause, such as Crohn disease. Treating the infection without the constipation treats the episode, not the disease; the maintenance laxative runs for at least 2 months, and the dilated rectum narrows on treatment.

Reflux scarring is tubulointerstitial: bacteria in the parenchyma cause inflammation and ischemia, which lead to wedge-shaped fibrosis, and the glomeruli are lost secondarily. Only the grade predicts the long-term outcome, and the course if untreated follows the severity in this patient: never carry a severity adjective from one study to another. Stasis from reflux favors stones, and urease-producing organisms make struvite stones.

Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the obstructive counterpart, with the same cystourethrogram and hydronephrosis but reflux secondary to outlet obstruction; is there a weak stream or a palpable bladder, and is the reflux the disease or its consequence? Aquifer Fever in an Infant: the first febrile UTI in an infant, with the catheter specimen, oral or intravenous treatment, the drug and the dose.

A disease name strongly associated with a complaint comes to mind before the finding that discriminates it, and recently learned associations come fastest. Convert each into a question: here, which tract is infected, and what grade did the cystourethrogram show?

What it is Repeated bedwetting, twice a week or more for at least 3 months, or with distress, in a child of 5 or older Driver Maturational in most primary cases: the child does not wake to a full bladder, and wetting comes in deep N3 sleep Triggers Family history (non-modifiable), the strongest risk factor; male sex (non-modifiable) Constipation: a full rectum shrinks bladder capacity and makes the bladder muscle (detrusor) unstable Obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy A stressor (a new sibling, illness, a hospital stay) Chain Full bladder in deep sleep no waking wetting; usually outgrown A new cause raises urine volume (diabetes, diabetes insipidus) or irritates the bladder (infection) wetting after 6 months dry Insights Tests only exclude a cause: enuresis itself is a clinical diagnosis, made once the urine and examination are normal The alarm retrains waking, so its cure lasts; desmopressin, an antidiuretic hormone analog, only raises water reabsorption overnight, so wetting returns when it stops

Enuresis bedwetting on 2 or more nights a week for at least 3 months, or causing distress or impairment, from age 5 (or the same developmental level) Primary never dry for 6 months Secondary wetting again after 6 months or more dry Nonmonosymptomatic bedwetting plus urinary symptoms by day

Glucose in urineGlucose with or without ketones; thirst, weight loss If the urine has glucose, choose serum glucose and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) for type 1 diabetes. On desmopressinHeadache, vomiting or a seizure If a child on desmopressin is unwell, choose hyponatremia: stop the drug; hypertonic saline for any neurologic symptom. Spinal signsSacral dimple or tuft, abnormal gait or reflexes, new daytime accidents Spinal Dysraphism If the spine or legs are abnormal, choose spinal MRI for a tethered cord. StressorNew wetting after a separation or another stressor; behavior change Suspected Child Abuse If a stressor is found, choose address it and screen for abuse, after the urinalysis.

With a normal examination and urinalysis and no daytime symptoms, no further tests.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Under 5 years Below the diagnostic age; most resolve Reassure Camp or a sleepover soon A fast effect is needed Desmopressin No better after 6 weeks of the alarm The alarm is failing Add or switch to desmopressin Desmopressin with evening drinks Water retention, hyponatremia Nothing to drink from an hour before the dose until 8 hours after it
Pause point New wetting after a divorce or a new sibling Blamed on the stressor Test the urine first → A urinalysis; then address the stressor

The type sets the plan Type Course Plan Under 5 Normal at this age Reassure; no treatment Primary monosymptomatic Resolves about 14% a year CourseUsually resolvesAbout 20% of children wet the bed at age 5 and 10% at age 10; about 14% a year resolve with no treatment, and the history and severity often follow the course of the affected family member. Behavioral therapy, then the ladder Nonmonosymptomatic Comorbid causes, such as constipation, may contribute Treat constipation and daytime symptoms first; no alarm while bladder capacity is small Secondary A cause is likelier Treat the cause; with none found, the ladder

1 Behavioralmonosymptomatic, no cause found Psychoeducation and behavioral training: reassurance, motivational therapy that rewards effort and routine, not dry nights Void every 3 hours by day and before bed; stop drinks in the 1 to 2 hours before bed and drink well in the morning; treat constipation. Move on after 3 to 6 months without improvement, if the family is bothered. 2 Alarmbehavioral therapy fails; a motivated family Bed-wetting alarm: the best long-term cure Usually over age 6; may take up to 4 months; after 14 dry nights in a row it can stop, and it restarts on relapse. Why it lasts AlarmThe child learns to link a full bladder with the alarm and wakes to void before wetting; the conditioning survives stopping the alarm, while desmopressin only lowers night urine output, so its effect does not. 3 Desmopressinpharmacotherapy, usually from age 7: nondrug therapy fails (the alarm after 6 weeks), or rapid improvement is desired Oral desmopressin, the first-line drug; alone or with the alarm Nothing to drink from an hour before the dose until 8 hours after it; not intranasal (hyponatremia); relapses more often after stopping. 4 Refractoryalarm and desmopressin both fail Imipramine, rarely; urology referral Oxybutynin only with desmopressin or imipramine, never alone. Imipramine ImipramineImipramine is second line for its worse side effects, rarely sudden death; an electrocardiogram (ECG) first, since a prolonged QT interval rules it out.

By situation Situation Choose Secondary enuresis with a cause Treat the cause Desmopressin toxicity with neurologic symptoms Stop the drug; hypertonic saline Desmopressin toxicity, no symptoms Stop the drug; strict water restriction

Follow-up decisions When Do Behavioral therapy, 3 to 6 months No better and the family is bothered: alarm or desmopressin Alarm, after 6 weeks No better: add or switch to desmopressin Alarm, 14 consecutive dry nights Consider stopping; restart on relapse Both fail Imipramine rarely, or urology referral
