briefs.title: Acute Kidney Injury in a Child
briefs.sub: the labs assign the compartment · prerenal pattern · ibuprofen with volume loss · sediment · fluids, stop the drugIs the kidney still concentrating, and what does the sediment show?
blocks: Acute Kidney Injury in a Child
the labs assign the compartment · prerenal pattern · ibuprofen with volume loss · sediment · fluids, stop the drugIs the kidney still concentrating, and what does the sediment show?

Assign the compartment from the labs before blaming the drug: BUN:creatinine over 20:1, specific gravity over 1.020 and a bland sediment are prerenal Vomiting or diarrhea on ibuprofen with a prerenal pattern isotonic fluids and stop the NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug); a falling creatinine confirms it Bloody diarrhea days before, then schistocytes and low platelets hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS): supportive care, no antibiotics

What it is Acute kidney injury (AKI): a rise in creatinine, a fall in urine output, or both, from a prerenal, intrarenal or postrenal cause Driver Prerenal: low renal blood flow, tubules intact; intrarenal: tubular necrosis, interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis or HUS; postrenal: obstruction of both outflows Triggers Volume loss from vomiting and diarrhea, or diabetic ketoacidosis An NSAID during volume loss, worse with an ACE inhibitor Shiga toxin Escherichia coli O157:H7 from undercooked beef, under age 5 Nephrotoxins: aminoglycosides, contrast, heme pigment from rhabdomyolysis Drug hypersensitivity: NSAIDs after weeks, beta-lactams, proton pump inhibitors Chain Volume loss glomerular filtration rate (GFR) leans on prostaglandins an NSAID constricts the afferent arteriole GFR falls Prolonged hypoperfusion tubular necrosis: oliguric maintenance with high potassium polyuric recovery with low potassium Insights Intact tubules still concentrate: a high specific gravity and urine sodium under 20 mean prerenal, not tubular, injury Ibuprofen in volume loss acts on blood flow, not by allergy: interstitial nephritis needs days to weeks of the drug and white cells in the urine MechanismIbuprofenProstaglandins normally dilate the afferent arteriole; NSAIDs block them, so the afferent arteriole constricts and GFR (glomerular filtration rate) falls. An ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor added on top loosens the efferent side as well.

Prerenal BUN:creatinine over 20:1, specific gravity over 1.020, bland sediment, fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) under 1%, urine sodium under 20 Acute tubular necrosis muddy brown casts, specific gravity about 1.010, BUN:creatinine under 15, FENa over 2%, urine sodium over 40 Postrenal obstruction of both outflows; early, FENa under 1% and BUN:creatinine over 15, like prerenal; long-standing, FENa over 2%, BUN:creatinine under 15, urine sodium over 40

High potassiumHyperkalemia with ECG (electrocardiogram) changes If the ECG has changed, choose IV calcium to stabilize the heart, then insulin with glucose. HUSBloody diarrhea 5 to 10 days ago; now pallor, petechiae, oliguria Anemia with Thrombocytopenia If the smear shows schistocytes, choose supportive care, dialysis if needed; no antibiotics. Refractory failureAcidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, volume overload or uremia beyond medical control If medical treatment fails, choose dialysis (AEIOU).

Acute kidney injury: the compartment, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Prerenal (NSAID and volume loss) (prerenal azotemia) Vomiting or diarrhea; an NSAID BUN:creatinine over 20:1, specific gravity over 1.020, bland sediment; fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) under 1% Acute interstitial nephritis DRAINSWhich drugsDrugs behind acute interstitial nephritis: DRAINS, for diuretics, rifampin, antibiotics and allopurinol, inhibitors of the proton pump, NSAIDs and sulfa drugs. Drug hypersensitivity: fever, rash, flank pain White cell casts, sterile pyuria with eosinophils Acute tubular necrosis Ischemia after shock, or a toxin (aminoglycoside, contrast); the commonest intrarenal cause Muddy brown casts; specific gravity about 1.010; FENa over 2% Hemolytic uremic syndrome Anemia with ThrombocytopeniaInfectious Diarrhea Under 5; bloody diarrhea 5 to 10 days before; Escherichia coli O157:H7 Schistocytes, low platelets, hematuria or proteinuria Immune-complex glomerulonephritis Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome Poststreptococcal (postinfectious glomerulonephritis): weeks, not days, after strep, about 1 to 3 weeks after the throat and up to about 6 after impetigo; IgA nephropathy (Berger disease): gross hematuria during an upper respiratory infection Hematuria and proteinuria, red cell casts; low C3 in poststreptococcal Postrenal obstruction Posterior Urethral Valves Obstruction of both kidneys' outflow, or of a solitary kidney Renal US or a postvoid residual Rhabdomyolysis Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood Muscle injury or a seizure; heme pigment injures the tubules Dipstick blood with few red cells on microscopy

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Rising creatinine or low urine output → BUN and creatinine; urinalysis with specific gravity BUN:creatinine over 20:1, specific gravity over 1.020, bland sediment Prerenal: the tubules still concentrate Muddy brown granular casts; specific gravity near 1.010 Acute tubular necrosis Hematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts Glomerulonephritis: check C3 Targeted tests TestResultMeans Bloody diarrhea days before; pallor, petechiae → CBC and peripheral smear Schistocytes with low platelets HUS: supportive care, no antibiotics Fever or rash, on a drug for days to weeks → Urine sediment, CBC with differential White cell casts, eosinophilia Acute interstitial nephritis: stop the drug Obstruction suspected → Renal and bladder US, postvoid residual Both outflows obstructed Postrenal acute kidney injury Next step TestResultMeans Pattern unclear → Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) Under 1% Prerenal Over 2%, urine sodium over 40 Acute tubular necrosis Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Prerenal pattern → Isotonic fluids and stopping the NSAID Creatinine falls after the fluids Prerenal injury: the response confirms it SkipRenal US in a prerenal pattern: usually normal, and it adds nothing once the labs assign the compartment.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Specific gravity about 1.010 after shock Tubules can no longer concentrate Supportive care; watch potassium Polyuria days into tubular necrosis Recovery phase Watch for low potassium An NSAID added to an ACE inhibitor The afferent arteriole constricts and the efferent dilates Stop the NSAID and give fluids
Pause point Prerenal pattern Offered: furosemide or a renal US Intact tubules need volume → Isotonic fluids and stopping the ibuprofen

Dialysis when medical treatment fails (AEIOU) Trigger Dialysis when Acidosis Refractory metabolic acidosis Electrolytes Hyperkalemia that does not respond Intoxication A dialyzable substance Overload Pulmonary edema or volume overload Uremia Uremic symptoms

1 Prerenalvolume loss with a prerenal pattern IV (intravenous) isotonic fluid bolus; stop the NSAID 2 Intrarenalthe cause is in the kidney Interstitial nephritis: stop the drug; tubular necrosis and HUS: supportive care HUS from Escherichia coli usually remits with supportive care; no antibiotics. 3 Postrenalobstruction of both outflows on US Relieve the obstruction; as in adults, recovery is likelier the shorter it lasted Posterior Urethral Valves 4 Potassiumhyperkalemia with ECG changes IV calcium, then insulin with glucose 5 Dialysisan AEIOU trigger despite treatment Hemodialysis or hemofiltration, as in adults Over half of patients with HUS need it.

Follow-up decisions When Do After isotonic fluids A falling creatinine confirms prerenal injury Tubular necrosis, maintenance phase Oliguria: watch for high potassium and uremia Tubular necrosis, recovery phase Polyuria: watch for low potassium and electrolyte wasting

Diagnosis4 of 7 60 yo M after septic hypotension, SG 1.010, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr 14:1 · Acute interstitial nephritis · Prerenal azotemia · Ischemic acute tubular necrosis 60 yo M after septic hypotension, SG 1.010, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr 14:1 Ischemic acute tubular necrosis

Next step5 of 7 74 yo M on lisinopril and furosemide who starts ibuprofen, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 2.0 · Start intravenous antibiotics · Discontinue the ibuprofen and give fluids · Renal biopsy 74 yo M on lisinopril and furosemide who starts ibuprofen, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 2.0 Discontinue the ibuprofen and give fluidsthe "triple whammy" of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID

Diagnosis6 of 7 16 yo M, gross hematuria 2 days into a URI, normal C3 · Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis · IgA nephropathy · Alport syndrome 16 yo M, gross hematuria 2 days into a URI, normal C3 IgA nephropathytiming with the URI and normal complement decide

Diagnosis7 of 7 7 yo M, cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after pharyngitis, low C3 · Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis · Minimal change disease · IgA nephropathy 7 yo M, cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after pharyngitis, low C3 Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritissupportive care

Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor drop GFR (glomerular filtration rate) from opposite ends. An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin II receptor blocker) plus a diuretic is the "triple whammy" FENa (fractional excretion of sodium) <1% supports prerenal but is unreliable after diuretics the AIN (acute interstitial nephritis) triad is present in a minority; WBC (white blood cell) casts carry the diagnosis PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) vs IgA nephropathy is timing plus complement. PSGN comes weeks, not days, after the infection (about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 after impetigo) with low C3; IgA nephropathy comes during the URI (upper respiratory infection) with normal C3.
Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers sorting by smear and coagulation studies when renal failure comes with a falling platelet count.
Read the ratio, then the specific gravity, then the sediment, and only then the drug. When a full chemistry panel is given, read it before answering.

Salient decoyDrug-induced interstitial nephritis: the named drug draws attention to it, but the timeline and the sediment are wrong. True-fact-wrong-slotHUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): gastroenteritis cues it, but it needs bloody diarrhea, schistocytes and an active sediment.

briefs.title: Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child
briefs.sub: protein on a routine dipstick in a well child · nephrotic or nephritic · the lesion, and the age-directed search for its causeIs the protein still there in a first-morning urine, are there red cells and casts, and how old is the patient?
blocks: Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child

protein on a routine dipstick in a well child · nephrotic or nephritic · the lesion, and the age-directed search for its causeIs the protein still there in a first-morning urine, are there red cells and casts, and how old is the patient?

Well child, protein on a dipstick first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio urinalysis; 0.2 or less, normal urinalysis and blood pressure reassure Child age 1 to under 12: edema 4+ protein, no blood, normal blood pressure and creatinine presumed minimal change (lipoid nephrosis) prednisone, no biopsy Biopsy for steroid failure or atypical features; membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulonephritis) in a child find the cause, hepatitis B first

What it is Nephrotic syndrome (classic definition): protein-to-creatinine ratio >2 albumin <2.5 g/dL edema ↑ lipids Protein alone on a screen: usually transient, or benign orthostatic Driver In minimal change disease, T-cell cytokines may injure podocytes albumin leaks more than larger proteins, probably through a lost negative charge barrier The T-cell permeability factor is proposed; the exact mechanism is unknown Triggers Age: minimal change most likely at 2 to 7 (median 3); boys more often under 8 non-modifiable Recent viral infection or allergy may precede minimal change disease Secondary: hepatitis B, syphilis, lupus (membranous); obesity, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), sickle cell (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, FSGS) Chain Filter podocyte injury albumin, immunoglobulins, antithrombin III lost in urine Blood ↓ albumin ↓ oncotic pressure capillary leak Exam puffy eyes, scrotum and shins, then ascites; blood pressure usually normal Insights Urine loses more than albumin lost antithrombin III, clots; lost immunoglobulins and opsonins, possibly infection Steroid response stands in for the biopsy: remission presumes minimal change; no remission may mean underlying focal sclerosis

Losses and complications, by systemdetail behind the chain Frothy; oval fat bodies and fatty casts. Cellulitis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitispossibly lost opsonins and immunoglobulins Protein undernutrition: brittle hair and nails, stunted growth Minimal change: more than 80% remit with treatment; most responders relapse
Protein ratio >2, or more than 1,000 mg/m² a day Albumin <2.5 g/dL Edema present Lipids ↑
Supine first-morning ratio 0.2 or less after a night lying down Upright ratio >0.2 after 4 to 6 hours upright
Minimal change is presumed clinically from age 1 to under 12: abrupt nephrotic-range protein, normal kidney function, no nephritic sediment
Tests to skip Test Why not 24-hour urine in a child May be impractical; a first-morning spot ratio is preferred Ultrasound or pyelography for a dipstick Cannot show whether the protein persists

InfectionNephrotic child with fever and belly pain Risk is highest in children, in relapse and on long steroid courses Which antibiotic Which antibioticA third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime, pending cultures, as for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis. In nephrotic syndrome: usually Streptococcus pneumoniae. If fever comes with belly pain or peritoneal signs in a child with ascites, choose diagnostic paracentesis, blood and fluid cultures, then intravenous antibiotics. ClotFlank pain, gross hematuria, falling urine output Most often membranous, but also minimal change If a nephrotic child has these, choose vascular imaging (usually magnetic resonance venography or CT angiography), then long-term anticoagulation unless an invasive intervention is planned. NephriticProtein with blood, casts, hypertension or ↓ complement Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome If the urine or blood pressure is nephritic, choose pediatric nephrology referral; biopsy considered.

Protein on a well child’s dipstick, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Orthostatic proteinuria Protein when upright, none after a night lying down Protein returns on an upright sample; first-morning 0.2 or less; especially adolescent boys Transient proteinuria Fever, exercise, stress, dehydration or cold Gone once the trigger passes Persistent proteinuria Abnormal urinalysis, or ratio >0.2 Still there on waking; needs a renal workup

Protein or blood in a child’s urine, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis) Abrupt edema; protein mainly albumin; no nephritic sediment; 70 to 90% of childhood cases Over 1 year, usually under 6; usually remits on steroids FSGS (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis) Insidious; hematuria, hypertension; obesity, HIV, sickle cell Older child or adolescent; often steroid resistant; segmental sclerosis Membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulonephritis) Insidious; granular immunoglobulin G (IgG), subepithelial deposits Rare in children: usually chronic hepatitis B, lupus or autoimmune thyroid disease; also syphilis Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (postinfectious glomerulonephritis) Nephritic: hematuria, hypertension, ↓ complement Weeks, not days: about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) Mixed nephritic and nephrotic; ↓ complement C3 still ↓ after 8 weeks; double contours on biopsy Lupus nephritis Hematuria, heavy protein, signs of lupus ↓ complement, ↑ anti-double-stranded DNA Immunoglobulin A (IgA) vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) Purpuric rash, joint and belly pain Hematuria with the rash IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) Hematuria with a respiratory infection During or within days of the infection Alport syndrome Hematuria, hypertension; sensorineural hearing loss Family history, usually X-linked; type IV collagen Congenital nephrotic syndrome Finnish type (nephrin gene); Denys-Drash syndrome First year of life Amyloidosis Restrictive cardiomyopathy; apple-green birefringence Adult; rare in children
Puffy eyes with a normal urinalysis: Child with Puffy Eyes

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Protein on a dipstick, or edema → Urinalysis with microscopy Red cells or casts, or hypertension Nephritic: pediatric nephrology referral 4+ protein, no blood or casts Nephrotic, not nephritic Targeted tests TestResultMeans Well child, protein on a dipstick → First-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio, with a bedtime sample, once any fever or hard exercise has passed Ratio 0.2 or less (0.5 or less at 6 to 24 months), urinalysis and blood pressure normal Transient or orthostatic: reassure; consider a repeat first-morning dipstick in 1 year Ratio >0.2, or white cells Persistent: CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine; albumin or complement as the history directs; renal US may help if anatomic or chronic kidney disease is suspected Edema with heavy protein → Spot protein-to-creatinine ratioAlbumin, lipids, creatinine, complement Ratio >2 Nephrotic range Albumin <2.5 g/dL, lipids ↑, creatinine and complement normal Nephrotic syndrome, typical of minimal change Next step TestResultMeans Typical child, age 1 to under 12 → Prednisone trial, no biopsy Remission Minimal change disease presumed No remission Genetic testing and renal biopsy Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Age under 1; age over 12, case by case; steroid failure; gross hematuria; sustained hypertension; ↓ complement; ↓ glomerular filtration rate not from low volume → Renal biopsy Normal light microscopy; foot processes effaced; no immune deposits Minimal change Segmental sclerosis FSGS Subepithelial deposits with spikes between them, granular IgG Membranous: hepatitis B and C and syphilis serologies, antinuclear antibody; consider thyroid disease
Why firstWhy order itA first-morning sample removes the upright leak. Trace onlyIf traceA trace reading is simply repeated on a first-morning urine. Membranous in a child: treat the cause.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Protein in the afternoon, none on waking Orthostatic proteinuria Reassure Obese adolescent, hematuria, hypertension, no steroid response FSGS Renal biopsy Hematuria, kidney failure in maternal uncles Alport syndrome Hearing test

Pause point Well child with one positive dipstick Offered: steroids, imaging or a biopsy Protein alone on a screen is usually transient or orthostatic → Repeat the urinalysis, with a first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio Child with a membranous biopsy Offered: an antistreptolysin O titer Strep causes nephritic disease, not membranous → The cause, hepatitis B first

First-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio (mg/mg) Band Ratio Do Normal 0.2 or less (0.5 or less at 6 to 24 months) Reassure if urinalysis and blood pressure are normal Persistent >0.2 up to 2 (>0.5 at 6 to 24 months) Basic renal blood tests Nephrotic range >2 Albumin and lipids; prednisone if typical

Steroid response Type Defined by Do Responsive Remission on steroids Minimal change presumed Infrequent relapse Occasional recurrence Glucocorticoids again Frequent relapse or dependent Frequent recurrence, or cannot stop steroids Add a steroid-sparing agent Resistant No improvement on steroids Genetic testing and biopsy; may be underlying focal sclerosis
Most responders relapse; resistance is under 5% of children with minimal change

1 Alongsideevery nephrotic child Salt restriction for edema; pneumococcal vaccine Loop diuretic only if salt restriction fails or fluid overloads: it can worsen low volume and clotting. 2 1st linetypical child, 1 to under 12, no biopsy Prednisone, daily then every other day CourseHow longOne course: 4 weeks daily, then 4 weeks every other day. 3 Relapsefirst or infrequent relapse Glucocorticoids again 4 Steroid-sparingfrequent relapse or steroid dependence Cyclophosphamide, a calcineurin inhibitor, mycophenolate, possibly rituximab 5 Referno remission after the steroid course Pediatric nephrology, genetic testing and renal biopsy With reduced kidney function, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) may cut protein and slow decline.

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Severe edema Intravenous albumin first; loop diuretic as in card 1 above Low volume, clots Membranous in a child Treat the cause, hepatitis B first; also lupus, autoimmune thyroid disease Renal vein thrombosis Renal vein thrombosis Long-term anticoagulation Pulmonary embolism Live vaccine due on high-dose steroids Defer until at least 1 month after stopping Usual cutoff: prednisone 2 mg/kg a day, or 20 mg a day if over 10 kg, for 14 days or more
Clot prevention is considered when risk is high, mainly in membranous.

Follow-up decisions When Do Transient or orthostatic Reassure; consider a repeat first-morning dipstick in 1 year Persistent proteinuria Blood pressure, urinalysis, creatinine and BUN every 6 to 12 months at first, then yearly once stable; no limits on diet or sport Nephrotic syndrome Pneumococcal vaccine; live vaccines deferred on high-dose steroids Relapse Expected in most responders: glucocorticoids again; frequent relapse adds a steroid-sparing agent

Workup1 of 17 17-year-old boy has 1 month of facial puffiness and fatigue periorbital and pretibial edema urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells, no casts renal biopsy: subepithelial deposits, granular IgG and C3 BP 110/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.2 g/dL · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · Hepatitis B serologies · Antistreptolysin O titer · No additional workup 17-year-old boy has 1 month of facial puffiness and fatigue periorbital and pretibial edema urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells, no casts renal biopsy: subepithelial deposits, granular IgG and C3 BP 110/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.2 g/dL · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Hepatitis B serologiesmembranous nephropathy in a child is usually secondary, so the biopsy names the lesion but obliges a search for its cause, and hepatitis B is the highest-yield cause to test. Antistreptolysin O chases poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is nephritic, with hematuria and often hypertension, and strep is not associated with membranous; stopping leaves the cause unfound, and in a child finding it is the management

Diagnosis2 of 17 15-year-old boy at a sports physical afternoon dipstick: 2+ protein; a second afternoon sample a week later shows the same first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.1 mg/mg microscopy normal BP 116/70 mm Hg · examination normal · Orthostatic proteinuria · Transient proteinuria · Persistent proteinuria 15-year-old boy at a sports physical afternoon dipstick: 2+ protein; a second afternoon sample a week later shows the same first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.1 mg/mg microscopy normal BP 116/70 mm Hg · examination normal Orthostatic proteinuriaprotein in urine made upright with a normal first-morning ratio (0.2 mg/mg or less) is orthostatic proteinuria: reassure and consider a repeat first-morning dipstick in 1 year. Transient protein follows fever, exercise or dehydration and is gone on any repeat; persistent proteinuria needs a first-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg or an abnormal urinalysis

Next step3 of 17 11-year-old boy with 2+ protein and 2+ blood on a routine dipstick microscopy shows red cell casts no edema Well; no recent fever or hard exercise BP 138/90 mm Hg · Repeat urinalysis on a first-morning sample · Trial of oral prednisone · Referral to pediatric nephrology 11-year-old boy with 2+ protein and 2+ blood on a routine dipstick microscopy shows red cell casts no edema Well; no recent fever or hard exercise BP 138/90 mm Hg Referral to pediatric nephrologyprotein with blood, casts and hypertension is glomerular disease from the start, not a benign pattern, so it goes straight to the renal workup and pediatric nephrology. A first-morning repeat is for protein alone in a well child, and a prednisone trial treats nephrotic syndrome, while this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet

Diagnosis4 of 17 4-year-old boy has periorbital swelling that began abruptly urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood renal biopsy: light microscopy normal, immunofluorescence negative electron microscopy: diffuse foot process effacement Afebrile · BP 94/56 mm Hg · Minimal change disease · Membranous nephropathy · Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis 4-year-old boy has periorbital swelling that began abruptly urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood renal biopsy: light microscopy normal, immunofluorescence negative electron microscopy: diffuse foot process effacement Afebrile · BP 94/56 mm Hg Minimal change diseaseabrupt onset with normal light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence and foot process effacement on electron microscopy is minimal change disease; a typical young child is treated with empiric corticosteroids without a biopsy, which is kept for atypical features. Membranous shows subepithelial deposits with granular IgG and C3 and a subacute onset; focal segmental glomerulosclerosis shows segmental sclerosis on light microscopy

Next step5 of 17 58-year-old man has 6 weeks of leg swelling biopsy: subepithelial deposits with granular IgG and C3 hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis serologies negative antinuclear antibody and thyroid studies normal Takes no medications BP 128/80 mm Hg · albumin 2.4 g/dL · No further evaluation · Malignancy screening for his age · Repeat renal biopsy in 6 months 58-year-old man has 6 weeks of leg swelling biopsy: subepithelial deposits with granular IgG and C3 hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis serologies negative antinuclear antibody and thyroid studies normal Takes no medications BP 128/80 mm Hg · albumin 2.4 g/dL Malignancy screening for his agewith infection, autoimmune disease (lupus, thyroiditis) and drugs excluded, the leading remaining secondary association in an adult is malignancy, mostly solid tumors, so screen as appropriate for his age. A repeat biopsy names the same lesion again but not its cause, and stopping is almost never right while a secondary-cause list remains

Diagnosis6 of 17 9-year-old girl with acute otitis media has 1+ protein on a dipstick T 39.2 °C 2 weeks later she is afebrile afternoon and first-morning urines both negative for protein Otherwise healthy · Orthostatic proteinuria · Transient proteinuria · Persistent proteinuria 9-year-old girl with acute otitis media has 1+ protein on a dipstick T 39.2 °C 2 weeks later she is afebrile afternoon and first-morning urines both negative for protein Otherwise healthy Transient proteinuriaprotein during a fever that is gone on a repeat once the trigger passes is transient proteinuria and needs no further testing. Orthostatic proteinuria keeps protein in the upright afternoon sample, and persistent proteinuria keeps it on the first-morning sample

Next step7 of 17 4-year-old girl has 5 days of periorbital and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood creatinine and complement levels normal Previously healthy; growth normal Afebrile · BP 94/58 mm Hg · albumin 1.9 g/dL · Renal biopsy before starting treatment · Furosemide alone and repeat urinalysis in 2 weeks · Oral prednisone without a renal biopsy 4-year-old girl has 5 days of periorbital and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood creatinine and complement levels normal Previously healthy; growth normal Afebrile · BP 94/58 mm Hg · albumin 1.9 g/dL Oral prednisone without a renal biopsya typical young child with edema, pure 4+ proteinuria and a normal blood pressure, creatinine and complement has presumed minimal change disease: corticosteroids without a biopsy, and most children remit. Biopsy is for an older child or atypical features, and furosemide alone with a repeat urinalysis delays the corticosteroids that bring the remission

Diagnosis8 of 17 8-year-old boy has cola-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago No prior episodes of dark urine urinalysis: blood and red cell casts BP 140/90 mm Hg · creatinine 1.6 mg/dL · C3 low · Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis · Membranous nephropathy · IgA nephropathy 8-year-old boy has cola-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago No prior episodes of dark urine urinalysis: blood and red cell casts BP 140/90 mm Hg · creatinine 1.6 mg/dL · C3 low Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisa nephritic picture weeks, not days, after strep (about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo), with hematuria, hypertension, a raised creatinine and a low C3, is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: supportive care and blood pressure control. Membranous is nephrotic, with protein and usually no red cells or casts; IgA nephropathy brings hematuria during or within days of a respiratory infection, not 2 weeks later

Mechanism9 of 17 16-year-old boy with chronic hepatitis B has 1 month of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells biopsy: granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops electron microscopy: subepithelial deposits BP 112/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.0 g/dL · Complement activation by the alternative pathway alone · Deposited hepatitis B e antigen immune complexes · Direct viral cytopathic injury to podocytes 16-year-old boy with chronic hepatitis B has 1 month of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells biopsy: granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops electron microscopy: subepithelial deposits BP 112/70 mm Hg · albumin 2.0 g/dL Deposited hepatitis B e antigen immune complexesimmune complexes of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and anti-HBeAg form in the subepithelial space and give the granular IgG and C3 along the loops. That granular IgG is antibody in the deposits, so neither direct viral injury to the podocytes nor complement activation alone accounts for the picture

Workup10 of 17 16-year-old boy with 1+ protein on a dipstick at a sports physical no blood in the urine No fever, illness or hard exercise this week Examination normal BP 114/70 mm Hg · First-morning urine protein-to-creatinine ratio · Late-afternoon urine protein-to-creatinine ratio · 24-hour urine protein collection 16-year-old boy with 1+ protein on a dipstick at a sports physical no blood in the urine No fever, illness or hard exercise this week Examination normal BP 114/70 mm Hg First-morning urine protein-to-creatinine ratioa first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.2 mg/mg or less on waking fits orthostatic or transient proteinuria. An afternoon sample is made upright, so it shows the orthostatic leak rather than excluding it, and the spot ratio stands in for the 24-hour collection, which may be impractical in children

Mechanism11 of 17 5-year-old girl: serum albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine protein 4+ with no blood and no casts 2 weeks of swollen eyelids, pitting leg edema, mild ascites Body mass index 97th percentile before this illness BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 96/min · Immune complex-mediated glomerular injury · Cytokine-induced glomerular injury · Glomerular sclerosis 5-year-old girl: serum albumin 1.7 g/dL; urine protein 4+ with no blood and no casts 2 weeks of swollen eyelids, pitting leg edema, mild ascites Body mass index 97th percentile before this illness BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 96/min Cytokine-induced glomerular injurypure proteinuria with no blood, a normal blood pressure and dependent edema at age 5 is minimal change disease: T-cell cytokines such as interleukin 13 are thought to injure the podocytes. Obesity is a real focal segmental glomerulosclerosis association, but that lesion is far less common at age 5 and usually brings hematuria and hypertension; immune complex deposition (poststreptococcal, membranoproliferative) brings hematuria, and membranous, the immune complex exception without hematuria, is rare at age 5

Next step12 of 17 13-year-old boy with 2+ protein on a dipstick at a well visit first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.6 mg/mg on two separate days microscopy: no blood or casts BP 108/66 mm Hg · no edema · Renal biopsy · Complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine · Reassurance and a repeat first-morning dipstick at next year's well visit 13-year-old boy with 2+ protein on a dipstick at a well visit first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.6 mg/mg on two separate days microscopy: no blood or casts BP 108/66 mm Hg · no edema Complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatininea first-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg is persistent proteinuria, which needs a basic renal workup; albumin or complement is added as the history and examination direct, and a renal ultrasound for suspected anatomic disease or chronic kidney disease. Reassurance is only for a normal first-morning sample, and biopsy is considered after hematuria, hypertension, low complement, falling kidney function or signs of vasculitis appear

Workup13 of 17 12-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria on repeated urinalyses Two maternal uncles have kidney failure No sore throat or recent illness; growth normal No edema; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · BP 108/66 mm Hg · creatinine 0.6 mg/dL · Hepatitis B serologies · Audiology evaluation · Antistreptolysin O titer 12-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria on repeated urinalyses Two maternal uncles have kidney failure No sore throat or recent illness; growth normal No edema; examination otherwise normal Afebrile · BP 108/66 mm Hg · creatinine 0.6 mg/dL Audiology evaluationpersistent hematuria with kidney failure in maternal uncles points to Alport syndrome, an X-linked type IV collagen defect whose partner finding is sensorineural hearing loss, so test hearing. Hepatitis B serologies search for the cause of membranous nephropathy, which is nephrotic; antistreptolysin O chases poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows strep by weeks, not days (about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo) with hypertension and a raised creatinine

Avoid14 of 17 17-year-old girl has 5 weeks of facial and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells or casts biopsy: granular IgG and C3, subepithelial deposits No serologies sent yet BP 108/68 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL · Sending hepatitis B and C serologies · Checking an antinuclear antibody · Stopping the workup at the biopsy 17-year-old girl has 5 weeks of facial and ankle swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells or casts biopsy: granular IgG and C3, subepithelial deposits No serologies sent yet BP 108/68 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL Stopping the workup at the biopsymembranous nephropathy in a child is usually secondary, so stopping at the biopsy leaves the cause unfound, and in a child finding the cause is the management. Hepatitis B and C serologies and an antinuclear antibody (for systemic lupus erythematosus) are the secondary-cause search and should go ahead

Diagnosis15 of 17 66-year-old man has 3 months of leg swelling and exertional dyspnea urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells echocardiography: restrictive cardiomyopathy renal biopsy: apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain BP 118/72 mm Hg · albumin 2.1 g/dL · Minimal change disease · Amyloidosis · Membranous nephropathy 66-year-old man has 3 months of leg swelling and exertional dyspnea urinalysis: 4+ protein, no red cells echocardiography: restrictive cardiomyopathy renal biopsy: apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain BP 118/72 mm Hg · albumin 2.1 g/dL Amyloidosisnephrotic-range protein in an older adult with apple-green birefringence and a restrictive cardiomyopathy is amyloidosis, and echocardiography shows the cardiac involvement. The biopsy shows amyloid, not the immune deposits with granular IgG and C3 of membranous nephropathy or the normal light microscopy of minimal change disease

Avoid16 of 17 14-year-old boy with 3+ protein on a dipstick at a routine visit no edema no blood in the urine No repeat sample collected yet; feels well BP 110/68 mm Hg · Urine microscopy for red cells and casts · Repeat urinalysis on a first-morning sample · Trial of oral prednisone 14-year-old boy with 3+ protein on a dipstick at a routine visit no edema no blood in the urine No repeat sample collected yet; feels well BP 110/68 mm Hg Trial of oral prednisonesteroids treat nephrotic syndrome, not an unconfirmed dipstick finding; this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet. A first-morning repeat and urine microscopy for red cells and casts are the right first steps

Diagnosis17 of 17 15-year-old boy with severe obesity has 2 months of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein and microscopic hematuria no remission after a full course of prednisone Afebrile · BP 138/90 mm Hg · Minimal change disease · Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis · Membranous nephropathy 15-year-old boy with severe obesity has 2 months of leg swelling urinalysis: 4+ protein and microscopic hematuria no remission after a full course of prednisone Afebrile · BP 138/90 mm Hg Focal segmental glomerulosclerosisobesity with hematuria, hypertension and steroid resistance points to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (segmental sclerosis on light microscopy), and these atypical features earn a renal biopsy. Minimal change disease brings no hematuria, a normal blood pressure and a steroid response; membranous is subacute, usually secondary in a child, and its blood pressure is typically normal

12-year-old boy at a well-child visit No illnesses since his visit a year ago HR 102/min · respiratory rate 21/min · BP 102/60 mm Hg examination normal urinalysis: 3+ protein Most appropriate next step in diagnosis? Competing answers Intravenous pyelography: images the collecting system for anatomic lesions and strictures; but it cannot show whether the protein persists. Trial of corticosteroids: treats nephrotic syndrome; but this boy has no edema and no diagnosis yet, and transient or orthostatic proteinuria is benign. Renal biopsy: diagnoses persistent glomerular disease; but it is invasive and comes only after persistence or red-flag features are shown. Down to two: repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking, or renal ultrasonography. Repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking: a well boy with protein on one dipstick most likely has transient or orthostatic proteinuria, and orthostatic proteinuria, common in adolescent boys, shows protein at bedtime and a normal first-morning sample. Ultrasonography looks for obstruction, abscess, cysts or masses and cannot show whether the protein persists; it is at most a later, selective test. The key named the timed procedure, not orthostatic proteinuria.

Hepatitis B evaluating every patient with membranous nephropathy for it is recommended; in a child it is close to mandatory Secondary causes infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis), malignancy (solid tumors in adults), autoimmune disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroiditis), drugs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, penicillamine) Tempo gradual podocyte damage gives a subacute onset over weeks to a month; deposits accumulate slowly, while foot processes efface suddenly in minimal change disease Course kidney function usually normal at onset; blood pressure normal or raised

Mechanism T-cell dysregulation releases cytokines such as interleukin 13 that are thought to injure podocytes; the capillary wall loses its charge selectivity, anionic albumin leaks, and low oncotic pressure gives dependent edema (periorbital, scrotal, pretibial) Diagnosis clinical; biopsy only for atypical features Treatment corticosteroids without a biopsy; most children remit, relapse is common, and the risk of chronic kidney disease is low when steroid responsive Obesity a real FSGS association, but FSGS is far less common at age 5 and usually brings hematuria and hypertension; no hematuria, a normal blood pressure and a pure 4+ protein urinalysis point to minimal change disease

Nephrotic versus nephritic is settled on the urinalysis, not the protein: 4+ protein with hypoalbuminemia and edema, without red cells or casts and with a normal blood pressure and creatinine, is nephrotic; red cells, hypertension and a rising creatinine are nephritic. Deposits: subepithelial is membranous (also the humps of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis), subendothelial is lupus nephritis, mesangial is IgA nephropathy. Up to 10% of school-age children show protein on a single screen; with repeated testing, about 0.1% do. Orthostatic proteinuria is the most common cause of proteinuria in children, especially adolescent boys, and long-term follow-up shows no progressive kidney disease. A first-morning spot ratio stands in for the 24-hour collection, which may be impractical in children. A dipstick can read falsely positive in very concentrated urine (specific gravity above 1.030) or alkaline urine (pH above 8).

After a membranous biopsy in a teenager, no additional workup: the biopsy names the lesion but not the cause, and stopping is almost never right when a secondary-cause list exists. Antistreptolysin O: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is nephritic, with hematuria, hypertension and a raised creatinine. Audiology or echocardiography after that biopsy: they chase Alport syndrome and amyloidosis, and neither shows subepithelial immune deposits. Renal biopsy for a well child's dipstick: invasive, and only after persistence or red-flag features. Corticosteroid trial: treats nephrotic syndrome, and the well child has no edema and no diagnosis. Renal ultrasonography and intravenous pyelography: they look for obstruction, abscess, cysts, masses, anatomic lesions or strictures, and cannot show whether the protein persists.

Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome: the nephritic side of this fork, the Alport link, the parallel well child with isolated microscopic hematuria, and red cells, hypertension, a rising creatinine and a low C3 weeks after strep. Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes: from the chief complaint to this diagnosis, with relapse, peritonitis, thrombosis and vaccines in the nephrotic child.

In a well child with protein on a routine dipstick, repeat the urine on a first-morning sample before any imaging, steroids or biopsy; only protein that persists on waking, or protein with blood, hypertension or edema, needs a renal workup. When a biopsy diagnosis is given, decide what it obliges you to do next: ask what the disease is associated with, and let the patient's age decide whether that list is the priority or an afterthought.

Pt term newborn boy, respiratory distress, flat facies, clubfeet, distended abdomen with a suprapubic midline mass Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned posterior urethral valves, bilateral renal agenesis and congenital diaphragmatic hernia

A newborn boy with Potter sequence and a palpable suprapubic bladder posterior urethral valves: one lesion upstream of every finding Renal and bladder US first, then, if the US is abnormal, a voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG); drain the bladder with a temporary catheter and correct the electrolytes The VCUG shows the dilated, elongated posterior urethra; cystoscopy confirms the valves and ablates them

What it is An obstructing membrane in the posterior urethra, males only: a mesonephric duct remnant and the commonest bladder outlet obstruction in male infants Driver Outlet obstruction: high bladder pressure can drive reflux and bilateral hydronephrosis Triggers Male sex: valves occur only in boys (non-modifiable) Congenital: may be diagnosed on prenatal US Chain Fetus: no urine leaves the bladder oligohydramnios Potter sequence pulmonary hypoplasia Urinary tract: high pressure thick, trabeculated bladder reflux and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis rising creatinine Insights Potter features establish the sequence, not its cause; a palpable bladder in a boy names the cause Why the lungs failLungsAfter about 16 weeks fetal urine is the major source of amniotic fluid; without it the alveoli are not distended by aspirated fluid, so the lungs stay hypoplastic. US shows the obstruction but cannot confirm valves; the VCUG while voiding shows the dilated posterior urethra

Oligohydramnios amniotic fluid index 5 cm or less, or the deepest single pocket under 2 cm Potter sequence the POTTER features: pulmonary hypoplasia, oligohydramnios, twisted facies and skin, extremity deformities such as hand and foot clubbing, and renal agenesis Sequence, not syndrome one initiating defect producing a cascade, not one cause producing independent anomalies

BreathingRespiratory distress at birth, low lung volumes Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant If the lungs are small, choose chest radiograph: pulmonary hypoplasia, the usual cause of death. KidneysDistended abdomen, poor urine output, rising creatinine If the bladder cannot empty, choose renal and bladder US to find the outlet obstruction; drain the bladder with a catheter and correct the electrolytes.

The newborn with Potter sequence: the cause, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Posterior urethral valves A boy; obstructing membrane in the posterior urethra Potter sequence with a palpable suprapubic bladder; weak stream Bilateral renal agenesis No kidneys, no urine, no amniotic fluid Potter sequence, no bladder to palpate, anuria Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease Large echogenic kidneys with liver fibrosis Bilateral flank masses with hepatomegaly Preterm premature rupture of membranes Normal kidneys; the fluid is lost through the membranes The mother reports leaking fluid; renal US is normal Placental insufficiency The placenta cannot exchange fluid Normal kidneys and bladder Prune belly syndrome Deficient abdominal wall muscle Wrinkled lax abdomen, both testes undescended Congenital diaphragmatic hernia Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant Bowel herniates into the chest and compresses the lung Scaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest; explains the breathing only Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) Abdominal Mass in a Young Child A renal mass in an older child Explains the mass only Duodenal atresia The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant Blocks fetal swallowing Polyhydramnios, the opposite direction; double bubble

Prenatal hydronephrosis: the level, most tempting first Diagnosis Dilated parts and bladder wall Decides it Posterior urethral valves Both ureters and pelves dilated; the bladder wall thick and trabeculated A boy with a weak, dribbling stream Ureterocele A ureterocele rarely prolapses past the bladder neck and obstructs the outlet A girl, sometimes with an interlabial mass; US, then VCUG Neurogenic bladder Spinal Dysraphism Both sides dilated, as with valves; a thick, trabeculated bladder Spinal dysraphism or an abnormal lower-limb neurologic exam Vesicoureteral reflux Urinary Tract Infection in a Child Pelvis and ureter, one or both sides; normal bladder wall Normal stream; the VCUG shows reflux into the ureters Duplicated renal collecting system Usually one side, one of two moieties; normal bladder Two ureters draining one kidney Ureteropelvic junction obstruction Renal pelvis only, usually one side; normal bladder No hydroureter; the commonest obstructive cause of prenatal hydronephrosis

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Newborn boy: distended abdomen, poor urine output, respiratory distress → Renal and bladder US; BUN, creatinine and electrolytes Thick-walled distended bladder, both sides dilated Outlet obstruction: a bladder catheter to drain it; correct the electrolytes during drainage Targeted tests TestResultMeans Hydronephrosis on prenatal US → Renal and bladder US Thick-walled distended bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, keyhole sign Outlet obstruction; US cannot confirm the valves Keyhole sign KeyholeThe bladder wall thickens because the detrusor hypertrophies against the outlet; above the valves the posterior urethra dilates, giving the keyhole shape on US. Respiratory distress → Chest radiograph Low lung volumes Pulmonary hypoplasia Next step TestResultMeans US abnormal → VCUG Dilated, elongated posterior urethra; trabeculated bladder Valves, the gold-standard image, often with secondary reflux Diagnostic test TestResultMeans VCUG shows valves → Cystoscopy Leaflets seen at cystoscopy Diagnosis and treatment at once: ablate them SkipUS alone as proof: postnatal US is not sensitive and does not confirm valves.

Image first, drain the bladder alongside, and confirm before surgery. Obtain a renal and bladder ultrasound, then a voiding cystourethrogram, and drain the bladder with a urethral catheter alongside. The cystourethrogram is the gold-standard imaging study; it shows a dilated posterior urethra and a thick-walled trabeculated bladder. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis but cannot confirm the diagnosis. Then perform cystoscopic valve ablation.

Fetal urine is needed for lung growth, so pulmonary hypoplasia rather than renal failure is the cause of death in Potter sequence Posterior urethral valves is a male-only diagnosis; a newborn girl with the same picture may have a ureterocele prolapsing past the bladder neck, which is rare A sequence is one defect cascading; a syndrome is independent anomalies from a shared cause The neonatal renal mass differential is hydronephrosis first, then multicystic dysplastic kidney; the neonatal renal tumor is congenital mesoblastic nephroma, not Wilms Neuroblastoma crosses the midline and Wilms does not

The stem split the level of obstruction across three findings (prenatal image, voiding exam, postnatal image), and normal urine output drew attention away from obstruction. Every option was a congenital urinary tract cause of hydronephrosis, separated only by the level of the lesion.

Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia is the mechanistic counterpart. A fetus that cannot make urine develops oligohydramnios, and one that cannot swallow develops polyhydramnios. Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant also pairs with this brief; there the fork is whether the lungs are structurally normal. Part I Urinary Tract Infection in a Child is the other end of the same imaging pathway. There the voiding cystourethrogram grades reflux; here it finds the obstructing valve. Part II Abdominal Mass in a Young Child covers the solid flank mass after infancy. Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the neurogenic bladder that mimics valves: is the spine or lower-limb neurologic exam abnormal?

Order renal and bladder ultrasound first, then a voiding cystourethrogram if the ultrasound is abnormal, then cystoscopy to confirm and ablate; bladder drainage and electrolyte correction run alongside Weight gain in the first 48 hours is abnormal newborns lose weight, so a gaining newborn is retaining, and in a boy with a distended abdomen what he is retaining is urine
When findings span three unrelated organ systems, look for the one lesion upstream of all of them. For each candidate, name the findings it leaves unexplained, and reject it if any remain.

Class-vs-memberDiaphragmatic hernia and Wilms: each explains the most prominent finding and leaves the rest unexplained. Trump-card inversionDuodenal atresia: it causes polyhydramnios, the opposite of the oligohydramnios the clubfeet prove. True-fact-wrong-slotTransient tachypnea: it is mild and self-limited, and cannot explain a mass or clubfeet. Unchecked attributeDuplicated renal collecting system: it can cause prenatal hydronephrosis with a dilated ureter; it usually involves one kidney and does not thicken the bladder wall or weaken the stream. Mirror twinNeurogenic bladder: it shares the thick-walled bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and dribbling; a normal spine and normal neurologic exam leave the urethral outlet as the lesion. Salient decoyUreteropelvic junction obstruction: it is the most common obstructive cause of prenatal hydronephrosis; it dilates the renal pelvis only, so dilated ureters and a thick bladder wall exclude it. True-fact-wrong-slotVesicoureteral reflux: it also causes bilateral hydroureteronephrosis; primary reflux leaves the bladder wall and stream normal, and reflux in a boy with valves is secondary to them.

briefs.title: Thyroid Disease in an Adult
briefs.sub: thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) first, then uptake splits making from leaking · levothyroxine recheck timing and its exceptions · the 30% rule and pregnancy-specific normsIs the gland making or leaking, has the TSH had 6 to 8 weeks to settle, and is she pregnant right now?
blocks: thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) first, then uptake splits making from leaking · levothyroxine recheck timing and its exceptions · the 30% rule and pregnancy-specific normsIs the gland making or leaking, has the TSH had 6 to 8 weeks to settle, and is she pregnant right now?

Check TSH first, then T4 (thyroxine): Thyrotoxicosis: low TSH with high T4. Radioactive iodine uptake is the next step, but not in a woman who is pregnant (except a molar pregnancy) or breastfeeding. Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH with low T4. Central hypothyroidism: both low, or a normal TSH with a low T4; check cortisol first. High uptake: the gland is making hormone. Low uptake: the hormone is leaking from the gland or is exogenous; antithyroid drugs are useless there. Levothyroxine: TSH lags a dose change by 6 to 8 weeks; pregnancy is the exception, where the dose goes up before the TSH moves.

Thyroid disease: the differential Diagnosis The picture Labs and uptake Treatment Graves disease Young woman; the most common hyperthyroidism; diffuse goiter, with or without a bruit; exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema: Graves only TSH-receptor antibodies positive; diffuse high uptake Methimazole, or propylthiouracil (PTU) in the first trimester; radioactive iodine; or surgery Toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer) Elderly, longstanding lumpy goiter; apathetic hyperthyroidism: new atrial fibrillation, weight loss, depression Patchy multifocal hot nodules Radioactive iodine or surgery; autonomous nodules, not a thyroiditis Toxic adenoma Single autonomous nodule One hot nodule, rest cold Radioactive iodine or lobectomy; hot nodules are almost never cancer Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis Post-viral: painful, tender gland after a viral upper respiratory infection; pain to the jaw or ear High erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), low uptake; hyper, then hypo, then recovery Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), with or without steroids; the only painful thyrotoxicosis Painless or postpartum thyroiditis Painless small goiter; classically 2 to 6 months postpartum Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies positive, low uptake, normal ESR Beta-blocker only: nothing is being made Hashimoto thyroiditis The most common hypothyroidism; firm, rubbery goiter; may have a brief hashitoxicosis Anti-TPO; Hürthle cells, germinal centers Levothyroxine; a rapidly enlarging gland points to B-cell lymphoma Factitious thyrotoxicosis Supplements or healthcare access; no goiter Low uptake and low thyroglobulin Stop the hormone; thyroglobulin is high when a gland leaks Riedel thyroiditis, IgG4 (immunoglobulin G subclass 4)-related Rock-hard, fixed, painless; mimics anaplastic carcinoma Fibrosis, IgG4 plasma cells Steroids or tamoxifen; young and hard: Riedel; old: anaplastic Thyroid storm (emergency) Fever, tachyarrhythmia and delirium; precipitant: surgery, infection, iodine load Clinical diagnosis: do not wait for labs Beta-blocker, then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids (iodine first fuels synthesis) Central hypothyroidism Hypothyroid with other pituitary deficits; after Sheehan syndrome, a mass or apoplexy TSH low or normal with a low T4 Titrate to free T4, not TSH; screen cortisol first

Diagnostic workup 1Is TSH low or high, and is the gland making or leaking? First Serum TSH Low, with a high T4Thyrotoxicosis High, with a low T4Primary hypothyroidism Next Free T4 Low, with a low or normal TSHCentral hypothyroidism: check cortisol and the other pituitary axes By branch: thyrotoxicosis Radioactive iodine uptake; not if pregnant (except a molar pregnancy) or breastfeeding High: diffuse, patchy or one hot noduleGland making hormone: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter or toxic adenoma LowLeaking or exogenous hormone: thyroiditis or factitious; antithyroid drugs useless Serum thyroglobulin Low, with low uptakeFactitious thyrotoxicosis; high when an inflamed gland leaks Confirms TSH-receptor antibodies: thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) PositiveGraves disease; proptosis or pretibial myxedema already makes the diagnosis Skip Thyroid ultrasound or fine-needle aspiration to name the cause: they show structure, not function, so they cannot split making from leaking. Fine-needle aspiration is for a cold nodule.

Recheck interval TSH lags dose changes by 6 to 8 weeks; earlier values are untrustworthy. At 8 weeks it is reliable: a TSH of 9.5 then means the dose is genuinely inadequate, so increase it Rechecked too soon under 6 weeks after a change: recheck in 6 weeks, not a dose change (outside pregnancy; in pregnancy, TSH may be rechecked 4 to 6 weeks after a change) TSH stays high despite escalating doses adherence, then absorption: empty stomach; iron, calcium, proton pump inhibitors and cholestyramine bind it; consider celiac disease Elderly or coronary artery disease start low, go slow (25 to 50 µg) to avoid angina or arrhythmia Central hypothyroidism titrate to free T4; TSH is the broken variable Subclinical hypothyroidism high TSH, normal T4: treat if TSH is over 10, TPO-positive, pregnant, or symptomatic Pregnancy levothyroxine requirements frequently increase, usually by 25 to 50%; increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed

Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG). β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) shares an alpha subunit with TSH and stimulates the TSH receptor. As a result, a normal pregnancy makes more thyroxine on its own; a patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate.

Dose rule increase levothyroxine by 20 to 30% (for example, two extra daily doses a week) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even with a currently normal TSH; do not wait for the TSH to rise Monitoring TSH may be checked at confirmation, approximately every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy, at least once in the third trimester, and 4 to 6 weeks after any dose change, using pregnancy-specific norms; target a TSH between the lower limit of the reference range and 2.5 mU/L. Free T4 (analog assay) is an appropriate marker in the first half of pregnancy Mechanism estrogen raises TBG, so more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; as pregnancy progresses, transfer of maternal T4 to the fetus and T4 degradation by placental type 3 deiodinase add to the need. Separately, β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor, which lowers TSH in the first trimester Drug levothyroxine; T3 (triiodothyronine), given as liothyronine, is never the right drug in pregnancy Graves disease in pregnancy PTU is the recommended drug in the first trimester (American Thyroid Association, 2017); whether to switch to methimazole after it is a clinical choice; never radioactive iodine

Thyroid labs in normal first-trimester pregnancy Hormone Change Interpretation Total T4 Increased Physiologic: TBG excess binds more hormone Free T4 Unchanged or mildly increased The value to trust in the first half of pregnancy TSH Decreased β-hCG cross-reactivity: not hyperthyroidism

Toxic multinodular goiter is a lumpy gland in an older patient with patchy uptake; subacute thyroiditis is painful, with low uptake

Waiting until the TSH rises is the titration rule in the wrong slot; liothyronine is never the right drug in pregnancy

It runs hyper, then hypo, then recovery; treat with NSAIDs, with or without steroids. Hashimoto thyroiditis is a firm, rubbery goiter with anti-TPO antibodies; painless thyroiditis has a normal ESR

Diagnosis7 of 22 55-year-old woman with untreated hyperthyroidism is brought in for agitation Received iodinated contrast for imaging 3 days ago confused and diaphoretic no neck stiffness; lungs clear T 40.0 °C · atrial fibrillation, HR 156/min · BP 150/60 mm Hg · Graves disease without storm · Thyroid storm · Sepsis 55-year-old woman with untreated hyperthyroidism is brought in for agitation Received iodinated contrast for imaging 3 days ago confused and diaphoretic no neck stiffness; lungs clear T 40.0 °C · atrial fibrillation, HR 156/min · BP 150/60 mm Hg Thyroid stormfever, tachyarrhythmia and delirium in a thyrotoxic patient after an iodine load: a clinical diagnosis, so treatment does not wait for labs. Give a beta-blocker, then a thionamide (PTU), then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids. Graves disease without storm lacks the fever and delirium. Sepsis has no evident source (lungs clear, no neck stiffness), while untreated hyperthyroidism after an iodine load, a known storm precipitant, explains the whole picture

Free T4 is the value to trust, and it distinguishes physiology from Graves disease

Mechanism22 of 22 29-year-old woman with hypothyroidism is 10 weeks pregnant Her levothyroxine dose was raised when pregnancy was confirmed total T4 elevated; free T4 normal HR 78/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · TSH 2.0 mU/L · Accelerated hepatic T4 clearance · Estrogen-induced rise in thyroxine-binding globulin · Suppression of TSH by β-hCG 29-year-old woman with hypothyroidism is 10 weeks pregnant Her levothyroxine dose was raised when pregnancy was confirmed total T4 elevated; free T4 normal HR 78/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · TSH 2.0 mU/L Estrogen-induced rise in thyroxine-binding globulinestrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, so more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; as pregnancy progresses, transfer of maternal T4 to the fetus and T4 degradation by placental type 3 deiodinase add to the need; the added degradation is placental, not hepatic. At 10 weeks, thyroxine-binding globulin is still rising toward its peak near week 16. β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor, which is why TSH falls in the first trimester; it also stimulates thyroid hormone production, so it does not explain the rising requirement.

Lid lag and stare occur in any thyrotoxicosis (sympathetic); proptosis and pretibial myxedema occur in Graves only. A hot nodule is almost never cancer; a cold nodule needs fine-needle aspiration. Nodule workup starts with TSH: if low, get an uptake scan; if normal or high, get an ultrasound, then fine-needle aspiration.

Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks impaired fetal neurodevelopment, because the fetus depends on maternal T4 early. A low TSH with a high total T4 in the first trimester is physiology, not Graves; free T4 distinguishes the two.

Antithyroid workup for a TSH of 0.3 in early pregnancy: β-hCG cross-reactivity explains the low TSH. “Recheck in 6 to 8 weeks” at conception: correct as a titration rule, but pregnancy is the one setting where acting first is right.
Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism is the neonatal version, where the TSH direction and the neck locate the defect.

Apply an exception to the standard titration rule only when its trigger condition is actually present; otherwise, follow the standard rule. When physiology predictably outruns a fixed drug dose, adjust the dose pre-emptively; do not recheck and react, although that approach is correct in every other setting.

briefs.title: Hyperprolactinemia
briefs.sub: inferring the unnamed drug · antipsychotic ranking · causes by category · cheap tests before magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) · cabergoline firstIs the prolactin in the drug range or the prolactinoma range, and which drug is behind it?
blocks: inferring the unnamed drug · antipsychotic ranking · causes by category · cheap tests before magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) · cabergoline firstIs the prolactin in the drug range or the prolactinoma range, and which drug is behind it?

When a patient with a known illness remains on an unnamed medication, identify the drug by two-step inference. First identify the drug class the illness requires. Then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. In psychosis, the class is an antipsychotic, and the member is the one with the highest prolactin liability. The prolactin level separates drug-induced hyperprolactinemia from prolactinoma. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. In this patient, a level of 70 is in the drug-induced range and excludes prolactinoma without any imaging.

Dopamine is prolactin-inhibiting factor. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes that inhibition. Highest prolactin effect: risperidone and paliperidone, plus high-potency typicals such as haloperidol. Lowest: aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist that can lower prolactin), quetiapine and clozapine. Aripiprazole is therefore the antipsychotic least likely to cause hyperprolactinemia and the one to switch to.

Hyperprolactinemia – causes by category Category Examples Discriminator Physiologic Pregnancy, nipple stimulation, stress, exercise, sleep Pregnancy test first Drugs Antipsychotics, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), opioids, estrogens, H2 blockers Level 25–100 Prolactinoma Micro- or macroadenoma Level >200; macroadenoma adds headache and bitemporal hemianopsia Stalk effect Any sellar mass compressing the stalk Modest elevation (<100) with a large mass on MRI Hypothyroidism ↑thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates lactotrophs Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) elevated Chronic kidney disease (CKD), cirrhosis Reduced clearance –

For elevated prolactin, first get a pregnancy test, TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), medication review and renal function. Order an MRI pituitary only if all are negative. Do not image before excluding the cheap causes. Hook effect: a very large prolactinoma can saturate the assay and give a falsely low value; repeat with dilution. Prolactinoma is the pituitary tumor you treat medically. First-line treatment is dopamine agonists (cabergoline > bromocriptine), even for macroadenomas, because they shrink the tumor. Surgery is for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy.

briefs.title: Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment
briefs.sub: who is screened early · T-score vs Z-score · when to treat · drug cautionsHas every risk factor been counted, and does each one point the way you assume?
blocks: who is screened early · T-score vs Z-score · when to treat · drug cautionsHas every risk factor been counted, and does each one point the way you assume?

Screen every woman at 65 with DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry). Run the risk-factor list before applying that default: Exam shorthand (question banks): any one risk factor (prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, low body weight, chronic glucocorticoids) means DEXA now; the BHOF (Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation) 2022 guide likewise says to consider DEXA in younger postmenopausal women with a clinical risk factor. The task force rule differs (next line). USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) 2025: postmenopausal and under 65 with a risk factor such as low body weight, parental hip fracture, smoking or excess alcohol (the USPSTF also lists menopausal status), use a clinical risk tool such as FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool), then DEXA if the risk is raised; no fixed threshold. Men: evidence insufficient (not a recommendation against). Androgen deprivation therapy: BHOF says to consider DEXA. Obesity protects bone; low body weight (under 58 kg) is the risk factor. A hip or vertebral fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis without a scan.

briefs.title: Congenital Hypothyroidism
briefs.sub: newborn screen · thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) direction locates the defect · goiter or none · dysgenesis as the default · treat before imagingIs TSH high or low, and is there a goiter?
blocks: newborn screen · thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) direction locates the defect · goiter or none · dysgenesis as the default · treat before imagingIs TSH high or low, and is there a goiter?

Pt 1 mo old, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since the first week, large tongue; no goiter described, maternal diet balanced with prenatal vitamins Labs TSH 110, thyroxine (T4) 0.6 Q the most likely cause; options spanned thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, iodine deficiency, panhypopituitarism and neonatal Graves disease

TSH 110 with T4 0.6 (TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone; T4, thyroxine) puts the lesion below the pituitary. The feedback loop is intact, so panhypopituitarism is excluded outright. Neonatal Graves gives a suppressed TSH with high T4, so it is excluded in the opposite direction. Among the primary causes, the exam is silent on goiter and the maternal history is clean (balanced diet, prenatal vitamins). This removes the tell of the two goitrous causes, dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency. The default remains: dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland arrested along the thyroglossal tract). The home birth is not a cause. It explains only why a screen-detected, asymptomatic diagnosis instead presented at one month, as maternal T4 washed out.

Primary congenital hypothyroidism elevated TSH with low T4 (in-context: "increased TSH and decreased T4"); the diagnosis is made by newborn screening, not by symptoms Prolonged (pathologic) neonatal jaundice unconjugated jaundice persisting beyond age 2 weeks; it is the finding that converts a sleepy feeder into a thyroid workup

TSH 110 with T4 0.6 primary (glandular) failure; excludes panhypopituitarism and any central cause Macroglossia + hoarse cry mucopolysaccharide deposition in tongue and larynx; the specific soft-tissue signature of thyroid hormone deficiency, not of sepsis or a storage disease at this age Direct bilirubin 0.7 of 8 unconjugated; excludes biliary atresia and the cholestatic causes of the sick jaundiced neonate, and points at slowed gut motility plus reduced hepatic conjugating enzyme activity No goiter described argues against dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency, both of which enlarge the gland under TSH drive Mother ate well and took prenatal vitamins; infant is formula-fed iodine deficiency is excluded (formula is iodine-supplemented) Normal tone with decreased activity hypometabolism, not a neuromuscular disease; hypotonia may appear later and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis Symptomatic at 1 month, not at birth maternal T4 crossed the placenta and masked the deficit; this timing is characteristic of the disease

Congenital hypothyroidism: locating the defect Diagnosis Illness script + buzzwords The National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tell Excluded here by Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis/hypoplasia/ectopy) Failed formation or descent of the thyroid diverticulum from the pharyngeal floor along the thyroglossal duct; sporadic, no family history High TSH, low T4, NO goiter, unremarkable maternal history; ectopic lingual tissue on scintigraphy (the answer) Dyshormonogenesis (e.g., thyroid peroxidase defect) Autosomal recessive enzyme block in organification; gland present but cannot make hormone, so TSH drive enlarges it Goiter in a hypothyroid newborn; consanguinity or affected sibling; deafness if Pendred No goiter, no family history; a minority of cases Iodine deficiency Maternal dietary lack in an endemic region; substrate, not machinery, is missing; goitrous Maternal diet/geography stated; goiter in mother and infant Balanced diet + prenatal vitamins; all formula contains iodine Central (panhypopituitarism) Pituitary/hypothalamic failure; TSH is the deficient hormone LOW or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4; midline defects (cleft lip/palate), micropenis, hypoglycemia TSH 110: the axis is intact and driving Transplacental TSH-receptor stimulating antibody Maternal Graves immunoglobulin G (IgG) crosses to the fetus → neonatal Graves, usually transient as antibody clears, generally within 6 months Low TSH, high T4, tachycardia, irritability, hyperphagia with poor weight gain Direction is inverted: TSH 110, T4 0.6, poor feeding and lethargy

A maternal blocking antibody against the TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) receptor is the rare counterpart of the stimulating antibody. It causes transient primary hypothyroidism with high TSH; scintigraphy can show no uptake, so ultrasound is needed to show the gland is present.

Is TSH high or low? High → primary; the pituitary causes are excluded Is T4 low? Yes → hypothyroid, not a compensated or antibody-stimulated state Is there a goiter? No → not dyshormonogenesis, not iodine deficiency Is there a maternal story? Diet fine, no Graves → no acquired/transplacental cause What's left is the default dysgenesis, the most common cause; the home birth explains the delay in detection, not the disease

The home birth is not a cause. It explains the missed newborn screen and therefore the unusual symptomatic presentation. The balanced maternal diet with prenatal vitamins excludes iodine deficiency. Primigravida, age 24, unremarkable family history: none of these points to a cause, although the absent family history modestly argues against a recessive enzyme defect.

High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), low T4 (thyroxine) and no goiter mean dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. Symptom onset at weeks to months, not at birth, is characteristic of congenital hypothyroidism. Placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age calls for considering thyroid disease and galactosemia; conjugated jaundice at any age calls for considering a biliary cause. Macroglossia plus hoarse cry is mucopolysaccharide deposition in hypothyroid soft tissue. It is distinct from Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia). Treat on the screening result. Imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks. Most children treated early and adequately have normal neurodevelopmental outcomes. A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn points to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem; dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge. In central hypothyroidism, give cortisol before levothyroxine unless adrenal function is shown to be intact: thyroid hormone is thought to accelerate cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.

Jaundice in a Newbornshares the complaint of a jaundiced newborn with an abnormal screen. Ask: is the hyperbilirubinemia conjugated, and is the infant ill or merely slow? Thyroid Disease in an Adultcovers the adult version of the same TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) direction logic. It also covers the dosing loop that this brief only points at. In any hormone deficiency, the trophic hormone's direction locates the lesion. High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) puts it in the gland; low TSH puts it in the pituitary. Within the gland, the presence or absence of an organ (goiter or none) separates a machinery defect from a formation defect.
