Pt 16 yo M, bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, mother had an adrenal tumor resected, one light brown facial patch without freckling Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1 and Sturge-Weber syndrome

Bilateral retinal hemangioblastoma points to von Hippel-Lindau, because no other listed syndrome produces one. NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) gives optic gliomas and Lisch nodules. MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) gives conjunctival and corneal neuromas. Sturge-Weber gives a leptomeningeal and choroidal vascular malformation. Li-Fraumeni gives sarcomas with no characteristic eye finding. The mother's resected adrenal tumor reads as a pheochromocytoma transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion. Hemangioblastoma plus adrenal medullary tumor is the von Hippel-Lindau organ pattern, with clear cell renal carcinoma the third member. A single light brown facial macule is a normal café-au-lait spot. It is not the multiple macules of NF1 and not a red-purple port-wine stain. Consider a teenager found confused after an unwitnessed fall. A fibroma growing from under a toenail and calcified nodules lining the lateral ventricles on CT (computed tomography) indicate tuberous sclerosis complex. The fall was a seizure, and the nodules are subependymal hamartomas. The nail lesion is a periungual fibroma, which appears in adolescence. NF1 puts neurofibromas on the trunk and a glioma on the optic nerve. Ataxia-telangiectasia starts with ataxia in early childhood. The nail-bed sign of endocarditis is a splinter hemorrhage, not a fibroma.

The VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing gate any patient with a retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma undergoes VHL gene testing, family history or not The café-au-lait gate an isolated macule is normal; six or more with regular borders plus axillary freckling is NF1 (each macule over 5 mm before puberty or over 15 mm after puberty); macules with jagged, irregular borders that usually respect the midline and follow the lines of Blaschko suggest McCune-Albright. Count, border, distribution and freckling are four separate criteria, and the exam varies whichever one is not being checked Patch color as a criterion Sturge-Weber's lesion is a red-purple vascular port-wine stain; a light brown patch is pigmented and points to a different family

Bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas essentially syndrome-defining; retinal hemangioblastoma may be the first neoplasm of VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) and by itself triggers gene testing Mother's adrenal tumor removed pheochromocytoma in a first-degree relative; autosomal dominant transmission, and the second organ of the VHL pattern A single light brown 4-cm patch one café-au-lait macule, a normal finding, lacking the multiplicity of NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and the color of Sturge-Weber Age 16 with painless progressive blurring VHL can present at any age but usually presents in early adulthood. Vision falls from retinal edema and distortion Blood pressure 110/72 mm Hg and an otherwise normal examination no clinically active pheochromocytoma today, which does not exclude one and is why surveillance is needed

Inherited tumor syndromes: the differential Syndrome Illness script The NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) tell Excluded here by Von Hippel-Lindau Autosomal dominant loss of the VHL tumor suppressor on chromosome 3; tumors of retina, central nervous system, adrenal medulla and kidney Retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, clear cell renal carcinoma (the answer) Neurofibromatosis type 1 Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder of skin, nerve and eye Multiple café-au-lait macules with axillary freckling; cutaneous neurofibromas on the trunk; optic glioma and Lisch nodules; seizures in some One macule only, which is normal; the retinal lesion is a hemangioblastoma Sturge-Weber syndrome Leptomeningeal and ocular capillary-venous malformation Red-purple port-wine stain, seizures, glaucoma The patch is light brown and pigmented, not vascular Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2B RET proto-oncogene; medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma Conjunctival or corneal neuromas, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus Eye lesion is a hemangioblastoma; no thyroid disease Li-Fraumeni syndrome Autosomal dominant TP53 loss; many tumor types across a young family Soft tissue sarcoma, early breast cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma; no characteristic eye or skin lesion Hemangioblastoma is not part of it Tuberous sclerosis complex Autosomal dominant TSC1 or TSC2 mutation, inherited or new; benign hamartomas of brain, eye, skin, heart and kidney; epilepsy in most, intellectual disability and autism Ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas; calcified subependymal nodules on CT; cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma No skin hamartoma here, and its brain lesions are nodules and tubers, not hemangioblastomas Neurofibromatosis type 2 Autosomal dominant tumors of nerve sheath and meninges Bilateral vestibular schwannomas The eighth nerve, not the retina

Confirm with VHL gene testing (VHL: von Hippel-Lindau). Then begin lifelong surveillance: retinal examination, plasma or urine metanephrines, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen. Resect tumors as they appear. For the retinal lesions, laser therapy is the preferred treatment.

Skin hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas over the cheeks and nose, a shagreen patch (orange-peel plaque on the lower back), and periungual fibromas, which appear in adolescence or adulthood Brain subependymal nodules, calcified on CT along the ventricles; cortical tubers, best seen on MRI; a nodule can grow into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma that obstructs CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) flow and causes hydrocephalus, which needs resection Seizures epilepsy in most, often infantile spasms, but the first seizure can come at any age, adolescence included; intellectual disability, autism and behavior disorders Heart and kidney cardiac rhabdomyoma; renal angiomyolipoma Surveillance skin and eye exams, serial MRI of brain and kidneys, baseline echocardiogram and serial ECGs (electrocardiograms), baseline EEG (electroencephalogram), and neuropsychiatric screening Not tuberous sclerosis NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1): café-au-lait macules, trunk neurofibromas, optic glioma; VHL (von Hippel-Lindau): cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas; ataxia-telangiectasia: ataxia from early childhood, poorly coordinated eye movements, conjunctival telangiectasias; endocarditis: fever, murmur and splinter hemorrhages

Optic nerve glioma the most common brain tumor in neurofibromatosis type 1; usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma of one or both optic nerves or the chiasm Presentation insidious vision loss, proptosis and optic atrophy Eye surveillance children with neurofibromatosis type 1 need an eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18 Pheochromocytoma risk also raised No established link medulloblastoma, craniopharyngioma, and arteriovenous malformation, which points to Wyburn-Mason syndrome

Name the retinal lesion exactly. Hemangioblastoma → VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) If it is a different eye lesion: optic glioma or Lisch nodules point to NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1). Conjunctival neuromas point to MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B). Glaucoma with a choroidal malformation points to Sturge-Weber Read the skin patch's color. Light brown pigmented = café-au-lait; red-purple vascular = port-wine Count the skin lesions. One café-au-lait macule is normal; multiple plus axillary freckling is NF1 Read the family's tumor for its organ. Adrenal medulla with kidney and CNS (central nervous system) points to VHL. Adrenal medulla with thyroid points to MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2)

The skin patch drew nearly two in five readers: 20% chose NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and 18% chose Sturge-Weber. A solitary café-au-lait macule is normal, so this most conspicuous physical finding does not discriminate. The mother's adrenal tumor supplies both the inheritance pattern and the second organ. The normal blood pressure does not help the diagnosis, but it indicates that no pheochromocytoma is active yet.

Retinal hemangioblastoma is von Hippel-Lindau until gene testing says otherwise; the pheochromocytoma and clear cell renal carcinoma follow. A retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma by itself warrants referral to genetics. VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing follows the lesion, with or without a family history. Eye lesions by syndrome: hemangioblastoma → VHL optic glioma with Lisch nodules → NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) conjunctival and corneal neuromas → MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) choroidal malformation with glaucoma → Sturge-Weber. Read a patch's color, not merely its presence. Light brown pigmented is café-au-lait, red-purple vascular is port-wine, and they point to different syndromes. VHL surveillance covers its organs: retina, brain and spine, adrenal medulla and kidney. The follow-up is therefore an eye exam, metanephrines, and two MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans. Up to 35% of pheochromocytomas may be germline, so genetic testing should be considered for every patient; a younger age at presentation or bilateral tumors make a hereditary syndrome more likely. The syndromes include VHL, MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), NF1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene variants. Before resecting a pheochromocytoma, alpha blockade precedes beta blockade; reversing the order leaves alpha stimulation unopposed. NBME framing: a well 17-year-old at a sports physical has about 10 light brown macules and axillary freckling, and the syndrome is never named. After puberty only macules over 15 mm count, so the axillary freckling supplies the second criterion. The lead-in asks which lesion carries a raised risk compared with the general population.

Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers pheochromocytoma from the blood-pressure side, reaching the same tumor from a different complaint. Ask: is the pheochromocytoma isolated, or is it one organ of a syndrome? Related conditions without their own brief: the neurocutaneous syndromes as a set, namely NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1), NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2), tuberous sclerosis and Sturge-Weber. Part I Puberty covers the border and distribution attributes of café-au-lait macules. Part II Abdominal Mass in a Young Child covers the mass itself. Ask: is it within the kidney, and is the child older than 2? Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers ataxia-telangiectasia and its infections. Ask: is the skin lesion vascular, or a fibrous tumor? Part I Brain Tumors in a Child covers optic pathway glioma and craniopharyngioma as masses. Ask: does the visual field loss come from the optic nerve or from the sella?

When a visible lesion identifies a syndrome, the lesion's category is shared across syndromes, but its identity is not. Name the tissue and the color before matching. The most conspicuous physical finding may be the one that does not discriminate.

Unchecked attributeNeurofibromatosis type 1, for two café-au-lait macules: Two macules sit between the isolated-is-normal rule and the six of NF1. A count rule alone therefore lands on NF1. The border, the distribution that respects the midline and the absent freckling all argue against it. Salient decoyNeurofibromatosis type 1: One macule is normal; NF1 requires multiple with axillary freckling, and its eye lesions are optic glioma and Lisch nodules, never a hemangioblastoma Unchecked attributeSturge-Weber syndrome: The patch is the wrong kind; port-wine stains are red-purple vascular malformations, and this one is light brown and pigmented True-fact-wrong-slotLi-Fraumeni syndrome: TP53 disease is sarcomas, early breast and adrenocortical carcinoma, with no characteristic eye or skin lesion and no hemangioblastoma Class-vs-memberMultiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B: Its eye findings are conjunctival and corneal neuromas, and it brings medullary thyroid carcinoma, which nobody in this stem has Class-vs-memberNeurofibromatosis type 1, for the teenager with the toenail fibroma: Also autosomal dominant with seizures, but its skin tumors are neurofibromas on the trunk and its brain tumor is an optic glioma; calcified subependymal nodules point to tuberous sclerosis Unchecked attributeAtaxia-telangiectasia: Autosomal recessive, with ataxia from early childhood and vascular telangiectasias rather than a fibrous nail tumor, and no ventricular nodules Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: The nail finding pulls toward it, but endocarditis gives splinter hemorrhages with fever and a murmur, not a firm periungual fibroma Salient decoyMedulloblastoma, for the teenager with 10 café-au-lait macules: The most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, with raised intracranial pressure and ataxia, but neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk True-fact-wrong-slotCraniopharyngioma: A Rathke pouch remnant that causes bitemporal field loss; neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk True-fact-wrong-slotArteriovenous malformation: Retinal and midbrain arteriovenous malformations point to Wyburn-Mason syndrome, not neurofibromatosis type 1 True-fact-wrong-slotCerebral aneurysm: An adult cause of intracranial hemorrhage; the tumor this skin pattern predicts is an optic nerve glioma

briefs.title: Puberty
briefs.sub: normal staging: sexual maturity rating (SMR) · early puberty: central or peripheral · virilization in a girlIs the stage right for the age, and if not, which hormones are on board, from where?
blocks: normal staging: sexual maturity rating (SMR) · early puberty: central or peripheral · virilization in a girlIs the stage right for the age, and if not, which hormones are on board, from where?

Stage breast and hair separately; a stage wrong for the age needs a workup. Precocious puberty: secondary sexual characteristics before 8 in girls or 9 in boys. Delayed puberty: no breast development by 13, or no testicular enlargement by 14. Central, GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) dependent: the whole axis turns on; consonant, progressive, LH (luteinizing hormone) pubertal. Peripheral, GnRH-independent: sex hormone from gonad, adrenal or an exogenous source. Virilization: clitoral enlargement in a girl; normal adrenarche never causes it. Breast tissue means estrogen; an androgen-only source gives hair, acne and odor without breasts.

Sexual maturity rating: the phrase that decides each stage Stage Breast Pubic hair 1 Papilla elevation only None, or vellus only 2 Bud: small mound under a widening areola Sparse, straight, lightly pigmented 3 Beyond the areola, one contour Darker, coarser, curled; sparse over the pubis 4 Areola and papilla form a second mound Adult quality across the pubis, sparing the medial thighs 5 Areola recedes; papilla projects alone Adult quantity, spreads to the medial thighs

One number only when breast and hair agree Discordant stages a finding; hair well ahead of breast suggests an adrenal source First sign thelarche in girls; testes 4 mL or more in boys Peak height velocity SMR 2 to 3 in girls, SMR 4 in boys Menarche SMR 4, about 2 to 3 years after thelarche, about 6 months after peak velocity

Diagnostic workup 1Bone age, then: is the axis on? Every child with early signs Bone age radiograph AdvancedTrue progressive puberty: go on Matches ageSuggests premature thelarche or adrenarche; observe if isolated and no virilization Next: is the axis on? Basal LH Pubertal levelCentral, GnRH-dependent Not diagnosticGnRH stimulation: LH rises in central, stays flat in peripheral Central confirmed Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Girls under 6, boys under 9, or neurologic signsHypothalamic or pituitary lesion Virilized: by branch 17-hydroxyprogesterone HighCongenital adrenal hyperplasia DHEAS (dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate) with testosterone; pelvic ultrasound DHEAS markedly high, testosterone normalAdrenal tumor until proven otherwise: adrenal computed tomography Testosterone high with an adnexal massAndrogen-secreting ovarian tumor, such as Sertoli-Leydig Then Skip estradiol alone: it cannot tell which axis drives. McCune-Albright is clinical; check other glands, such as thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).

Triad peripheral precocious puberty, irregular café-au-lait macules, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (recurrent fractures) Mechanism a somatic mosaic activating GNAS (the G protein alpha-s gene) mutation keeps a G protein switched on; any tissue carrying it secretes autonomously, so thyrotoxicosis, acromegaly or Cushing syndrome can accompany or replace the precocity Family history silent; postzygotic, not inherited; no added recurrence risk

Read a pigmented patch: number, border, distribution, color Syndrome The skin McCune-Albright Often large and segmental; irregular; respecting the midline Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) Six or more, smooth, axillary freckling; precocity via optic glioma Tuberous sclerosis Hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch; seizures Sturge-Weber; Peutz-Jeghers Red-purple port-wine stain; 1 to 5 mm perioral macules; no precocity
Central GnRH agonist, because the axis drives it Peripheral treat the source; a GnRH agonist does nothing McCune-Albright in girls, aromatase inhibitor or estrogen-receptor blockade
Virilization in a girl: which source?

DHEAS almost only from the adrenal zona reticularis; urine 17-ketosteroids rise with it Testosterone mostly ovarian in a girl High DHEAS, normal testosterone, normal pelvic ultrasound adrenal; far above range in a child is a tumor until proven otherwise; many pediatric virilizing adrenal tumors are carcinomas High 17-hydroxyprogesterone nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the commoner adrenal cause

Diagnosis1 of 18 6-year-old girl is evaluated for breast budding and pubic hair two large hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders confined to the left chest and back, without freckling Long-bone fractures at ages 4 and 5 Afebrile · no headache, emesis or visual change · Neurofibromatosis type 1 · McCune-Albright syndrome · Adrenal tumor 6-year-old girl is evaluated for breast budding and pubic hair two large hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders confined to the left chest and back, without freckling Long-bone fractures at ages 4 and 5 Afebrile · no headache, emesis or visual change McCune-Albright syndromeperipheral precocity, irregular segmental macules and recurrent fractures (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia) are the triad; only two macules, irregular borders and no freckling argue against neurofibromatosis type 1 (six or more smooth macules, usually with freckling), and breast budding excludes an androgen-only adrenal tumor

Next step2 of 18 6-year-old girl has breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced to 9 years Skin entirely normal; no headache, emesis or visual change Afebrile · blood pressure (BP) 100/62 mm Hg · Measure basal LH with GnRH-stimulation testing if not diagnostic · Reassurance with a repeat bone age and height check in 6 months · Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any hormone testing 6-year-old girl has breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced to 9 years Skin entirely normal; no headache, emesis or visual change Afebrile · blood pressure (BP) 100/62 mm Hg Measure basal LH with GnRH-stimulation testing if not diagnosticconsonant, progressive puberty with an advanced bone age suggests the axis is on, and normal skin argues against McCune-Albright: a pubertal basal LH confirms it, and a GnRH stimulation test settles a nondiagnostic level; waiting misses progressive puberty, and brain imaging follows confirmation

Next step3 of 18 5-year-old girl was diagnosed with central precocious puberty this week LH rose after GnRH stimulation bone age advanced No headache, emesis or visual change; parents ask about next steps Afebrile · neurologic examination normal · Reassurance and a repeat bone age in 6 months · Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain · Begin a GnRH agonist without imaging 5-year-old girl was diagnosed with central precocious puberty this week LH rose after GnRH stimulation bone age advanced No headache, emesis or visual change; parents ask about next steps Afebrile · neurologic examination normal Magnetic resonance imaging of the brainyounger onset raises the risk of a central nervous system lesion: image the brain for confirmed central puberty in a girl under 6 or a boy under 9, before treating or reassuring

Next step4 of 18 2-year-old girl has breast budding noticed 3 months ago no pubic or axillary hair growth velocity normal Bone age matches her chronological age Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile · Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain · Measure basal LH · Reassurance and observation 2-year-old girl has breast budding noticed 3 months ago no pubic or axillary hair growth velocity normal Bone age matches her chronological age Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile Reassurance and observationisolated breast development with normal growth velocity and a bone age matching age is premature thelarche: observe, without hormone testing or imaging

Next step5 of 18 14-year-old boy is brought in because he is the shortest in his class no testicular enlargement height at the 3rd percentile His father entered puberty late Afebrile · examination otherwise normal · Obtain a bone age · Start testosterone therapy now · Reassure without further testing 14-year-old boy is brought in because he is the shortest in his class no testicular enlargement height at the 3rd percentile His father entered puberty late Afebrile · examination otherwise normal Obtain a bone ageno testicular enlargement by 14 is delayed puberty; the bone age comes before treatment or reassurance; delayed, with a late-blooming parent, it fits constitutional delay of growth and puberty

Next step6 of 18 7-year-old girl has 6 months of pubic and axillary hair and body odor no breast development growth velocity normal No clitoral enlargement; bone age matches age Afebrile · height at the 60th percentile · Reassurance with interval follow-up · Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain · Begin a GnRH agonist 7-year-old girl has 6 months of pubic and axillary hair and body odor no breast development growth velocity normal No clitoral enlargement; bone age matches age Afebrile · height at the 60th percentile Reassurance with interval follow-upisolated hair and odor with normal growth and bone age is premature adrenarche: reassure and follow; nothing points to the axis or the brain, and clitoral enlargement or fast growth would change that

Next step7 of 18 6-year-old girl has 5 months of pubic hair and severe acne clitoral enlargement linear growth rapidly accelerating No breast budding; no hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg · Measure 17-hydroxyprogesterone · Begin a GnRH agonist · Reassurance and observation 6-year-old girl has 5 months of pubic hair and severe acne clitoral enlargement linear growth rapidly accelerating No breast budding; no hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg Measure 17-hydroxyprogesteroneclitoral enlargement is virilization, which normal adrenarche never causes; it points to an adrenal source, not the axis, so neither a GnRH agonist nor reassurance fits; congenital adrenal hyperplasia shows a high 17-hydroxyprogesterone

Next step8 of 18 7-year-old boy has pubic hair and acne testes remain prepubertal in size growing faster than his classmates No headache or visual change; no hormone creams at home Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg · Evaluate for a peripheral androgen source · Begin a GnRH agonist to suppress the axis · Reassurance and observation 7-year-old boy has pubic hair and acne testes remain prepubertal in size growing faster than his classmates No headache or visual change; no hormone creams at home Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg Evaluate for a peripheral androgen sourceandrogen signs with small testes mean the testes are not being driven: a peripheral source, which a GnRH agonist cannot suppress; bilateral testicular enlargement would indicate a central cause

Diagnosis9 of 18 4-year-old girl is evaluated after a femoral fracture one large hyperpigmented macule with an irregular border free thyroxine high, thyroid-stimulating hormone suppressed No goiter or eye findings noted Afebrile · heart rate 128/min · Graves disease · Neurofibromatosis type 1 · McCune-Albright syndrome 4-year-old girl is evaluated after a femoral fracture one large hyperpigmented macule with an irregular border free thyroxine high, thyroid-stimulating hormone suppressed No goiter or eye findings noted Afebrile · heart rate 128/min McCune-Albright syndromethe mutation is organ-agnostic: any endocrine organ carrying it can secrete autonomously, here the thyroid; Graves disease would not explain the irregular macule and fracture, and neurofibromatosis macules are six or more and smooth, usually with freckling

Workup10 of 18 7-year-old girl has 6 months of breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced Skin normal; no headache or visual change Afebrile · BP 100/60 mm Hg · LH response to GnRH stimulation · Bone age radiograph of the hand · Random serum estradiol level 7-year-old girl has 6 months of breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced Skin normal; no headache or visual change Afebrile · BP 100/60 mm Hg LH response to GnRH stimulationa rise in LH after GnRH stimulation means the axis is driving it (central); a flat LH points to a peripheral source; estradiol alone cannot tell which axis, and bone age shows progression, not its source

Avoid11 of 18 7-year-old girl was diagnosed with McCune-Albright syndrome last year breast development progressing basal LH prepubertal; one large irregular macule over the right flank Parents ask about treatment for the early puberty Afebrile · bone age advanced · Estrogen-receptor blockade · GnRH agonist · Aromatase inhibitor 7-year-old girl was diagnosed with McCune-Albright syndrome last year breast development progressing basal LH prepubertal; one large irregular macule over the right flank Parents ask about treatment for the early puberty Afebrile · bone age advanced GnRH agonistthe axis is not the driver, so a GnRH agonist does nothing; treat the source, here with aromatase inhibitors or estrogen-receptor blockade

Next step12 of 18 6-year-old girl has 4 months of pubic hair, acne and clitoral enlargement no breast development 17-hydroxyprogesterone normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate markedly high, testosterone normal No hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 108/70 mm Hg · Computed tomography of the adrenal glands · Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain · Pelvic ultrasound to look for an ovarian mass 6-year-old girl has 4 months of pubic hair, acne and clitoral enlargement no breast development 17-hydroxyprogesterone normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate markedly high, testosterone normal No hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 108/70 mm Hg Computed tomography of the adrenal glandsa markedly high adrenal androgen with normal testosterone is an adrenal tumor until proven otherwise: image the adrenals, not the brain; normal testosterone points away from the ovary; histology, not labs, separates adenoma from carcinoma

Diagnosis13 of 18 12-year-old girl is seen for a well visit breast tissue extends beyond the areola without a separate contour pubic hair curled, spread partially across the pubis Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile · Stage 3 · Stage 2 · Stage 4 12-year-old girl is seen for a well visit breast tissue extends beyond the areola without a separate contour pubic hair curled, spread partially across the pubis Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile Stage 3one contour is 3, a second mound is 4; curled hair is past 2, partial spread is below 4; both agree, so one number is acceptable, and it is normal for age

Diagnosis14 of 18 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit areola and papilla form a secondary mound above the breast contour adult-type pubic hair that spares the medial thighs Afebrile · height at the 40th percentile · Stage 4 · Stage 3 · Stage 5 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit areola and papilla form a secondary mound above the breast contour adult-type pubic hair that spares the medial thighs Afebrile · height at the 40th percentile Stage 4a second mound is the stage 4 tell; stage 5 needs the areola to recede and hair on the thighs; menarche typically occurs at this stage

Diagnosis15 of 18 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit small mound of breast beneath a widened areola a few straight, lightly pigmented hairs along the labia Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile · Stage 3 · Stage 2 · Stage 1 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit small mound of breast beneath a widened areola a few straight, lightly pigmented hairs along the labia Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile Stage 2a bud and straight hair are stage 2: thelarche, the first sign in girls, at a normal age; curled hair would make it 3

Diagnosis16 of 18 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit her first menstrual period began last month breast development began about 2 years ago Her mother asks how much taller she will grow Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile · SMR 4 · SMR 5 · SMR 2 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit her first menstrual period began last month breast development began about 2 years ago Her mother asks how much taller she will grow Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile SMR 4menarche comes at SMR 4, about 6 months after peak height velocity (SMR 2 to 3 in girls), so little growth is left

Next step17 of 18 13-year-old girl is brought in because she has no breast development short stature webbed neck and widely spaced nipples No headaches or visual change Afebrile · height below the 3rd percentile · Obtain a karyotype · Obtain a bone age · Reassure and recheck at age 15 13-year-old girl is brought in because she has no breast development short stature webbed neck and widely spaced nipples No headaches or visual change Afebrile · height below the 3rd percentile Obtain a karyotypeno breast development by 13 is delayed puberty, and the dysmorphic features point to Turner syndrome: a karyotype, which a bone age or waiting would miss

Next step18 of 18 13-year-old boy has tender lumps beneath both nipples 2 cm of subareolar breast tissue on each side sexual maturity rating 3 pubic hair and genitals Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · growing fast this year · Reassurance and follow-up · Start an aromatase inhibitor · Breast ultrasound 13-year-old boy has tender lumps beneath both nipples 2 cm of subareolar breast tissue on each side sexual maturity rating 3 pubic hair and genitals Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · growing fast this year Reassurance and follow-uppubertal gynecomastia is normal at SMR 3 to 4 and coincides with peak height velocity; it resolves within 1 to 2 years, so reassure rather than image

10-year-old girl with 6 months of increased facial hair growth and facial acne At the 50th percentile for height and weight T 37 °C · pulse 64/min · respirations 12/min · BP 110/60 mm Hg mild clitoral enlargement; early male pubic hair pattern serum testosterone 0.2 nmol/L (normal 0.17 to 0.7) dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate 9 μg/mL (normal 0.5 to 5.4); urine 17-ketosteroids 20 mg/24 h (normal 6 to 15) pelvic ultrasonography: no abnormalities Most likely diagnosis? Competing answers Androgen insensitivity syndrome: an androgen disorder in a genital-examination stem; but it is a receptor defect in a genetically male child with no androgen effect, so it cannot virilize. Pituitary adenoma: the third adenoma, and a pituitary cause of early puberty; but there is no headache or visual field loss, and pituitary adenomas rarely virilize. Polycystic ovarian syndrome: hirsutism and acne; but testosterone and ovaries are normal, weight is at the 50th percentile, and it does not enlarge the clitoris. Down to two: adrenal adenoma or ovarian adenoma. Adrenal adenoma: DHEAS comes almost only from the adrenal, and testosterone in a girl mostly from the ovary; a high DHEAS and 17-ketosteroids with normal testosterone and a normal pelvic ultrasound localize the source to the adrenal. An ovarian tumor would raise testosterone. Three options are adenomas at different glands, so it is a location question; at 10, pubic hair alone would be ordinary, and the clitoral enlargement is what makes it virilization.

Precocity is a complaint, not a diagnosis: sort central from peripheral, then look outside the endocrine system. Fractures in a preschooler: not incidental, one of the triad. No headache, emesis or visual change: nothing intracranial. Stage 4: the adjacent stage the stem negates (no second mound). Enlarged areola: in stage 2, but stage 2 hair is straight.

Developmental Milestones and Normal Growthis bone age ahead of, matching, or behind the age? Inherited Tumor Syndromescafé-au-lait macules from the tumor side Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth: is bone age ahead of, matching, or behind the age? Inherited Tumor Syndromes: café-au-lait macules from the tumor side.
When staging, find the phrase that fits exactly one level. When every option is a syndrome sharing the complaint, find the finding only one produces.

briefs.title: Tall Stature and Marfanoid Habitus
briefs.sub: homocystinuria vs Marfan vs Ehlers-Danlos · lens down or up and out · homocysteine before Marfan is called · B6 firstWhat is this child doing that Marfan cannot: clots, learning problems, fair skin or a downward lens?
blocks: homocystinuria vs Marfan vs Ehlers-Danlos · lens down or up and out · homocysteine before Marfan is called · B6 firstWhat is this child doing that Marfan cannot: clots, learning problems, fair skin or a downward lens?

A Marfanoid child: look for what Marfan does not do. Intellectual disability, a thrombotic stroke or clot, fair skin and hair, lens dislocated down: homocystinuria. Plasma homocysteine and methionine are both high. Normal intellect, lens up and out, aortic root dilation: Marfan syndrome. Echocardiographic surveillance and a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker. Stretchy skin, easy bruising and lax joints with normal proportions: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not a Marfanoid disorder. Treat homocystinuria with pyridoxine (B6) first (about half respond), plus folate and vitamin B12 (cobalamin); nonresponders need methionine restriction and betaine. Never nitrous oxide.

Marfanoid child: which one? Feature Marfan syndrome Homocystinuria Inheritance Autosomal dominant; fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1) Autosomal recessive (cystathionine beta-synthase) Lens Up and out Down Intellect Normal Often impaired Vessels Aortic root dilation, dissection Clots: stroke, DVT (deep vein thrombosis), PE (pulmonary embolism) Skin, hair, joints Usual coloring; joints often lax Fair, fine hair; joints often stiff, not lax

Diagnostic workup 1Lens, then homocysteine, then B6 First Slit-lamp exam Lens downHomocystinuria Lens up and outMarfan Lens down, or any lens dislocation with learning problems or a clot Plasma total homocysteine and methionine Both highCystathionine beta-synthase deficiency Diagnosis made (both high) Pyridoxine trial Level fallsB6-responsive: pyridoxine, folate, B12 No fallMethionine restriction and betaine Then Echocardiography and FBN1 testing look for Marfan; when learning problems or clots come with a dislocated lens, check homocysteine first.

Ehlers-Danlos lax joints, hyperextensible skin, fragile tissue; vascular EDS (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) ruptures arteries rather than clotting them; no Marfanoid build or learning problems Phenylketonuria fair skin and intellectual disability, with a musty odor and eczema; no Marfanoid build or clots

Homocystinuria pyridoxine trial; folate and B12; methionine restriction and betaine if B6 fails Surgery avoid nitrous oxide: it inhibits methionine synthase, raises homocysteine and invites thrombosis Marfan echocardiographic surveillance of the aortic root; beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker

Workup5 of 6 16-year-old boy, tall and thin with long fingers both lenses subluxed struggles in school; repeated a grade No family history of sudden death BP 118/72 mm Hg · slit lamp: direction unclear · Genetic testing for FBN1 mutation · Echocardiogram · Serum homocysteine level 16-year-old boy, tall and thin with long fingers both lenses subluxed struggles in school; repeated a grade No family history of sudden death BP 118/72 mm Hg · slit lamp: direction unclear Serum homocysteine levela Marfanoid build with lens subluxation fits Marfan and homocystinuria; serum (plasma) homocysteine separates them, and it comes before echocardiography or FBN1 testing when learning problems or clots are present

Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the Marfanoid habitus of MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B).

briefs.title: Abnormal Growth in a Child
briefs.sub: short stature and growth velocity · faltering weight · normal variants, endocrine, nutritional and genetic causesIs velocity normal, which parameter fell first, and what is the bone age?
blocks: short stature and growth velocity · faltering weight · normal variants, endocrine, nutritional and genetic causesIs velocity normal, which parameter fell first, and what is the bone age?

Velocity matters more than the percentile. A low, steady channel is a normal variant; height crossing 2 or more major percentile lines downward is growth failure. Then ask which parameter fell first: Weight first, length and head preserved: inadequate intake (up to 80%, mostly psychosocial), malabsorption or increased demand. Height first, weight preserved or rising: endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, glucocorticoid excess). All three from birth: genetic, congenital infection or intrauterine insult. Bone age comes first among tests: delayed means growth potential remains; advanced means sex steroid exposure. Choose a rare organic cause over inadequate intake only when a symptom, sign or admission supports it.

Short stature height at or below the 2nd percentile for age and sex Faltering weight weight below the 2nd percentile, or crossing 2 or more major percentile lines downward Not pathologic catch-up growth in a preterm infant; shifts toward genetic potential in the first 2 years Midparental height average of the parents' heights, plus 6.5 cm for a boy or minus 6.5 cm for a girl

Pt 7 yo, bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric Q the expected laboratory value; options spanned a decreased platelet count, an increased serum haptoglobin and a positive direct Coombs test

Scleral icterus with fatigue is hemolytic anemia, and anuria for 24 hours with pedal edema is acute kidney injury. The third feature of hemolytic uremic syndrome is thrombocytopenia. Shiga toxin damages endothelium, platelets are consumed into microthrombi, and red cells are sheared as they pass. The platelet count falls because of the same process that produces the schistocytes and the bilirubin. The exposure is bloody diarrhea a week ago, in a cluster of people who ate together and recovered.

HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) triad microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (rising blood urea nitrogen [BUN] and creatinine) Microangiopathic hemolysis red cells sheared by platelet microthrombi, giving schistocytes, increased indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin The preceding illness Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae; bloody diarrhea first, with HUS appearing about a week later Coombs in HUS negative, because the red cells are destroyed mechanically rather than coated by antibody

Bloody diarrhea one week ago Shiga toxin colitis; the one-week latency between the diarrhea and the syndrome is characteristic Shared meal with relatives who recovered a point-source exposure that confirms the organism but does not explain the labs; most infected people never develop HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) Anuria for 24 hours with normal intake, plus 2+ pedal edema acute kidney injury with volume overload, the renal feature of the triad Scleral icterus indirect hyperbilirubinemia from hemolysis, the hemolytic feature of the triad Fatigue and refusing to get out of bed symptomatic anemia rather than ongoing volume loss; the diarrhea has resolved No bruising or petechiae described consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS is often not severe enough to bleed; its absence never argues against the diagnosis No fever or neurologic change the absent neurologic change argues against TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) is treated supportively with fluid and electrolyte management, transfusion, and dialysis when needed. Withhold antibiotics and antimotility agents in suspected Shiga toxin infection.

How many cell lines are down? Anemia plus a consumed platelet count → the microangiopathy family, not a single-lineage problem Is the hemolysis mechanical or immune? Schistocytes with a negative Coombs → mechanical shearing Are the coagulation studies normal? Yes → HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) or TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura), not DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) Which organ, and what came first? Kidney, after bloody diarrhea in a child → HUS Marker directions from the mechanism haptoglobin consumed and falling, reticulocytes rising, indirect bilirubin rising, Coombs negative

TTP pentad (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura): microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, neurologic signs, renal injury. Most patients do not have all five; anemia with schistocytes plus low platelets is enough to act.

The cookout and the recovered relatives are epidemiology: they confirm a point-source Shiga toxin exposure but settle no laboratory value. The stool blood "has since resolved"; it stopped days ago and was never chronic, so it does not support iron deficiency. The absence of bruising or petechiae does not argue against a low platelet count. Consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) frequently produces no bleeding at all.

Bloody diarrhea a week ago plus anuria and jaundice is HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): schistocytes, low platelets, rising creatinine and a negative Coombs test. Two cytopenias with schistocytes mean mechanical destruction. In mechanical destruction the Coombs test is by definition negative, because no cell is antibody-coated. Haptoglobin is consumed in hemolysis, while ferritin and other acute-phase reactants rise. A marker falls if the process uses it up and rises if the liver makes more of it. Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis and fall in marrow failure. A reticulocyte count that fails to rise in a known hemolytic patient is a hematologic emergency. Normal coagulation studies separate HUS and TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) from DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). Kidney injury after bloody diarrhea in a child points to HUS; brain involvement in an adult points to TTP. Withhold platelet transfusion in TTP unless there is overt bleeding or an invasive procedure, because it can worsen TTP. Withhold antibiotics in suspected Shiga toxin colitis, because they may increase the risk of HUS.

Part II Acute Kidney Injury in a Child covers the acute-kidney-injury compartments and carries the hemolytic uremic syndrome row from the renal side. Part II Hemolytic Anemia covers Coombs-negative hemolysis when the platelets and kidneys are normal. This brief covers the case where both cell lines fall together. Ask: is a second cell line down, and is the smear sheared or spherocytic? Part I Hemolytic Anemia covers hemolysis with a normal platelet count and an antibody rather than a clot. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child starts one step earlier, from the bruise, and sorts it by the platelet count.

For a laboratory abnormality "associated" with a stated mechanism, what matters is the direction each marker moves, not the marker's name. Derive the direction from the mechanism: consumed or produced, mechanical or immune. When the findings form a named syndrome, list its triad rather than re-deriving each component.

Unchecked attributeIncreased serum haptoglobin: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed, so it falls in hemolysis True-fact-wrong-slotPositive direct Coombs test: Coombs detects antibody-coated cells; HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome) destroys red cells mechanically, so the test is negative. Antibody hemolysis would not cause anuria and edema Salient decoyDecreased ferritin level: The bleeding was acute and has resolved; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and rises with inflammation Class-vs-memberIncreased PT: DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) also consumes clotting factors and needs a critically ill patient; in HUS the PT is normal Unchecked attributeDecreased reticulocyte count: Hemolysis is expected to produce reticulocytosis, a rise, as the marrow responds to the anemia

briefs.title: Hemolytic Anemia
briefs.sub: drug-induced immune hemolysis and hereditary spherocytosis · latency, the Coombs test and the smear name the mechanism, then map it to its assayWhich drug and how long ago, is the direct Coombs test positive, and are the platelets and liver enzymes normal?
blocks: drug-induced immune hemolysis and hereditary spherocytosis · latency, the Coombs test and the smear name the mechanism, then map it to its assayWhich drug and how long ago, is the direct Coombs test positive, and are the platelets and liver enzymes normal?

Confirm hemolysis, then name the mechanism. Anemia with an unconjugated bilirubin, dark urine and normal liver enzymes is hemolysis; the enzymes, not the pain, separate it from obstruction. Hapten drug hemolysis: a stable hapten such as high-dose penicillin or a cephalosporin such as cefotetan binds the red-cell surface, IgG (immunoglobulin G) attaches to the drug-cell complex, and splenic macrophages destroy the cell: extravascular, with spherocytes, typically after 7 to 10 days of high-dose penicillin. Immune-complex drug hemolysis: the drug, mainly ceftriaxone or piperacillin, forms complexes with drug-specific antibodies that fix complement for intravascular destruction; the Coombs test is usually positive for complement, not IgG; after earlier exposure it can follow a single dose within hours. Hereditary spherocytosis: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with jaundice and splenomegaly; mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) above 36%, because membrane loss dehydrates the cell, the one common anemia with a high MCHC; splenectomy needs pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccination first. Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia: IgG against red cells; a positive Coombs test is the only line separating it from hereditary spherocytosis. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: oxidant hemolysis 1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours) after the trigger, with bite cells, Heinz bodies and a negative Coombs test. Cold agglutinin hemolysis: IgM (immunoglobulin M) fixes complement, so the test shows C3 (complement component 3) only. Spherocytes mean a membrane defect (hereditary spherocytosis) or an IgG antibody (warm autoimmune or hapten drug hemolysis), plus ABO (blood group) incompatibility in a newborn. The Coombs test separates membrane (negative) from antibody (positive); the history (a drug, lupus, the first day of life) separates the antibodies. A normal platelet count excludes the consumptive causes.

Hemolysis in a child: the differential Diagnosis Illness script The tell Drug-induced immune hemolysis High-dose penicillin or a cephalosporin such as cefotetan: stable hapten, IgG, extravascular; ceftriaxone or piperacillin: immune complexes fix complement, intravascular; also a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as diclofenac Hapten: typically after 7 to 10 days of high-dose penicillin, Coombs IgG. Immune complex: can follow a single dose within hours after earlier exposure, Coombs C3. Drug hemolysis may take hours or several months. Platelets usually normal Hereditary spherocytosis Autosomal dominant ankyrin, spectrin or band 3 defect; extravascular splenic hemolysis, pigment stones Spherocytes, Coombs negative, MCHC above 36% Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia IgG against red cells with lupus, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, methyldopa or penicillins; subacute Spherocytes, Coombs positive G6PD deficiency X-linked, so mostly boys; normal between episodes; oxidant stress depletes glutathione: infection, sulfonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine or fava beans; African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern or Asian ancestry 1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours) after the trigger; sudden dark urine with back or abdominal pain; bite cells, Heinz bodies on crystal violet stain, Coombs negative, MCHC normal Mycoplasma cold agglutinin hemolysis Atypical pneumonia drives IgM against the I antigen, which fixes complement C3 only, cold agglutinins that can turn positive after 7 to 10 days of the infection Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) Acquired PIGA (phosphatidylinositol glycan anchor biosynthesis class A) clone; complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis; adults Cytopenias, thrombosis at odd sites, bland smear, Coombs negative Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), can't miss Consumptive coagulopathy from sepsis or shock Schistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, prolonged clotting times Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction ABO incompatibility; complement-mediated intravascular lysis Fever, back pain, dark urine minutes into a transfusion Biliary obstruction A stone or sludge blocks the duct Severe pain, raised alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, conjugated bilirubin Hemoglobinopathy Sickle cell disease or thalassemia; chronic inherited hemolysis with splenomegaly Target cells or sickled forms; low mean corpuscular volume (MCV) in thalassemia Production failure Iron, vitamin B12 (cobalamin) or folate deficiency, or marrow disease; pallor without jaundice Low reticulocytes; the MCV points the way

Diagnostic workup 1Is it hemolysis, and what is on the red cell? First Complete blood count (CBC) with platelets, reticulocytes and indices Anemia, high reticulocytes, normal plateletsHemolysis; the consumptive causes are excluded MCHC over 36%A membrane that has lost surface Liver enzymes and fractionated bilirubin Unconjugated bilirubin up, alkaline phosphatase and transaminases normalHemolysis, not obstruction: no abdominal imaging Peripheral smear SpherocytesMembrane defect or IgG antibody; ABO disease in a newborn Bite cellsOxidant injury in G6PD deficiency Schistocytes, low plateletsA clot: DIC, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) Supports Haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), bilirubin Haptoglobin low; LDH and indirect bilirubin upHemolysis; mainly extravascular when IgG or the membrane drives it Next Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test IgG aloneConfirms immune hemolysis: hapten drug or warm autoimmune C3 with IgGImmune-complex drug (ceftriaxone) or warm autoimmune C3 onlySuggests cold agglutinins or immune-complex drug hemolysis NegativeA membrane defect or oxidant injury, not antibody By branch Eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry Reduced fluorescenceHereditary spherocytosis; osmotic fragility is the older, less sensitive equivalent G6PD activity, measured after recovery LowOxidative hemolysis; during the episode young cells read falsely normal Flow cytometry for CD55 (cluster of differentiation 55) and CD59 (cluster of differentiation 59) Missing on the red cellsParoxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria: cytopenias, bland smear; skip it for spherocytes Skip Abdominal imaging for the pain of acute hemolysis with normal enzymes (biliary colic in chronic hemolysis still earns an ultrasound, the test of choice for gallstones); fibrinogen with normal platelets.

Workup1 of 23 5-year-old girl treated for pneumonia has dark urine and abdominal pain Received ceftriaxone for otitis media last year Began one hour after today's intravenous ceftriaxone dose mild upper abdominal tenderness hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL · platelets 285,000/mm³ · liver enzymes normal · Serum fibrinogen level · Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level · Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test 5-year-old girl treated for pneumonia has dark urine and abdominal pain Received ceftriaxone for otitis media last year Began one hour after today's intravenous ceftriaxone dose mild upper abdominal tenderness hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL · platelets 285,000/mm³ · liver enzymes normal Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) testhemolysis within an hour of a ceftriaxone dose, in a child sensitized by the earlier course, is immune: ceftriaxone mainly forms drug-antibody immune complexes that fix complement, so the direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3, with or without IgG. Oxidative hemolysis begins 24 to 72 hours after exposure, and ceftriaxone is not a typical oxidant. A normal platelet count excludes disseminated intravascular coagulation, so a fibrinogen level adds nothing

Workup2 of 23 7-year-old boy has had intermittent jaundice for months His father has the same anemia spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin spherocytes on the smear hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL · MCHC 38% · direct Coombs negative · Hemoglobin electrophoresis · Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 · Eosin-5-maleimide binding test 7-year-old boy has had intermittent jaundice for months His father has the same anemia spleen palpable 3 cm below the costal margin spherocytes on the smear hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL · MCHC 38% · direct Coombs negative Eosin-5-maleimide binding testspherocytes with a negative Coombs test mean a membrane defect; the MCHC above 36% and the affected father support it but do not decide it. Eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry shows reduced fluorescence; osmotic fragility is the older equivalent. CD55 and CD59 testing is for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, and hemoglobinopathies give target cells or sickled forms, never spherocytes

Next step3 of 23 7-year-old boy has dark urine on day 3 of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole bite cells on the smear Heinz bodies on a crystal violet stain Direct antiglobulin test negative HR 118/min · hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL · platelets 240,000/mm³ · Direct antiglobulin testing with anti-C3 · Serum haptoglobin and fibrinogen · Stop the drug and measure glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase after recovery 7-year-old boy has dark urine on day 3 of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole bite cells on the smear Heinz bodies on a crystal violet stain Direct antiglobulin test negative HR 118/min · hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL · platelets 240,000/mm³ Stop the drug and measure glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase after recoverybite cells and Heinz bodies with a negative direct antiglobulin test 1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours) after an oxidant are oxidative, not immune, hemolysis. Stop the drug; measured during the episode, the surviving young cells carry near-normal enzyme and read falsely normal, so the level waits until weeks after recovery

Next step4 of 23 24-year-old woman has 2 weeks of fatigue and jaundice Systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 3 years ago spherocytes on the smear direct Coombs test positive for IgG HR 104/min · hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL · platelets 220,000/mm³ · Eosin-5-maleimide binding test · Prednisone · Splenectomy 24-year-old woman has 2 weeks of fatigue and jaundice Systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed 3 years ago spherocytes on the smear direct Coombs test positive for IgG HR 104/min · hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL · platelets 220,000/mm³ Prednisonespherocytes with a positive direct Coombs test in lupus are warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia: IgG against red cells, subacute. The Coombs test is the only line separating it from hereditary spherocytosis, so eosin-5-maleimide binding, which confirms a membrane defect, is not needed; splenectomy is not the first step

Next step5 of 23 4-year-old girl hospitalized with sepsis has oozing from line sites and dark urine Receiving intravenous antibiotics schistocytes on the smear BP 82/48 mm Hg · hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL · platelets 18,000/mm³ · fibrinogen 80 mg/dL · Direct antiglobulin test and glucocorticoids · Discontinue the antibiotic and observe · Treat the underlying sepsis with coagulation support 4-year-old girl hospitalized with sepsis has oozing from line sites and dark urine Receiving intravenous antibiotics schistocytes on the smear BP 82/48 mm Hg · hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL · platelets 18,000/mm³ · fibrinogen 80 mg/dL Treat the underlying sepsis with coagulation supportschistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia and a low fibrinogen in sepsis are a consumptive coagulopathy: treat the cause. Drug-induced immune hemolysis does not usually explain schistocytes with a low fibrinogen, so stopping the antibiotic answers the wrong process, and the direct antiglobulin test looks for an antibody when schistocytes with a low platelet count mean a clot

Diagnosis6 of 23 7-year-old boy has intermittent jaundice and an enlarged spleen No family history of anemia, jaundice or gallstones spherocytes on the smear hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL · MCHC 37% · direct Coombs test negative · Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia · Hereditary spherocytosis · Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria 7-year-old boy has intermittent jaundice and an enlarged spleen No family history of anemia, jaundice or gallstones spherocytes on the smear hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL · MCHC 37% · direct Coombs test negative Hereditary spherocytosisspherocytes with a negative Coombs test and an MCHC above 36% are a membrane defect even without an affected parent: a meaningful fraction are de novo or recessive. Warm autoimmune hemolysis is Coombs positive, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria brings cytopenias and a bland smear in an adult

Next step7 of 23 5-year-old girl has dark urine and pallor on day 2 of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumonia Had a ceftriaxone course last year hemoglobinuria on urinalysis Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 and IgG HR 112/min · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · platelets 250,000/mm³ · Add intravenous immunoglobulin and continue the antibiotic · Begin plasma exchange · Discontinue the ceftriaxone 5-year-old girl has dark urine and pallor on day 2 of intravenous ceftriaxone for pneumonia Had a ceftriaxone course last year hemoglobinuria on urinalysis Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 and IgG HR 112/min · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · platelets 250,000/mm³ Discontinue the ceftriaxonehemoglobinuria suggests the immune-complex mechanism, and stopping the drug is the treatment and usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days. Glucocorticoids and intravenous immunoglobulin are reserved for severe cases and never justify continuing the drug; plasma exchange has been reported as a rescue in life-threatening cases, not a first step in a stable child. Ceftriaxone hemolysis is C3-positive, often with IgG, and is more common after an earlier course

Workup8 of 23 30-year-old man has dark urine on waking most mornings new hepatic vein thrombosis on ultrasound Direct Coombs test negative; smear bland Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL · white cells 2,900/mm³ · platelets 88,000/mm³ · Bone marrow biopsy alone · Eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry · Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 30-year-old man has dark urine on waking most mornings new hepatic vein thrombosis on ultrasound Direct Coombs test negative; smear bland Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL · white cells 2,900/mm³ · platelets 88,000/mm³ Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59Coombs-negative hemolysis with cytopenias, thrombosis at an odd site and a bland smear: an acquired clone whose red cells lack CD55 and CD59 and undergo complement-mediated intravascular lysis. Eosin-5-maleimide binding confirms a spherocytic membrane defect, and a marrow biopsy further characterizes the disease in the setting of another marrow abnormality; flow cytometry is the gold standard

Diagnosis9 of 23 15-year-old girl has jaundice and fatigue 10 days into an atypical pneumonia No new medications direct antiglobulin test positive for C3, negative for IgG cold agglutinins present Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · platelets 230,000/mm³ · Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency · Mycoplasma-associated cold agglutinin hemolysis · Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemia 15-year-old girl has jaundice and fatigue 10 days into an atypical pneumonia No new medications direct antiglobulin test positive for C3, negative for IgG cold agglutinins present Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · platelets 230,000/mm³ Mycoplasma-associated cold agglutinin hemolysisatypical pneumonia drives IgM against the I antigen, which fixes complement, so the direct antiglobulin test shows C3 only; the hemolysis follows the infection, whose cold agglutinins can turn positive after 7 to 10 days. Drug-induced immune hemolysis needs a drug, although its immune-complex type also shows complement without IgG, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency gives bite cells with a negative test

Next step10 of 23 10-year-old girl has a week of increasing pallor and fatigue Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 2 slapped-cheek rashes among classmates at school hemoglobin 5 g/dL, 12 g/dL a week ago · reticulocytes 0.1% · Transfusion · Urgent splenectomy · Folic acid and recheck in 1 week 10-year-old girl has a week of increasing pallor and fatigue Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 2 slapped-cheek rashes among classmates at school hemoglobin 5 g/dL, 12 g/dL a week ago · reticulocytes 0.1% Transfusiona falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count in a chronic hemolytic patient is parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis until proven otherwise, and transfusion treats an aplastic or hemolytic crisis. Folic acid is for chronic reticulocytosis, and splenectomy is indicated for symptomatic hemolysis or complications such as biliary colic or a persistent aplastic crisis

Avoid11 of 23 8-year-old boy needs an antibiotic for pneumonia Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency was diagnosed at age 3 after an episode of dark urine cough; right lower lobe crackles T 38.6 °C · HR 110/min · oxygen saturation 95% · Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole · Azithromycin · Ceftriaxone 8-year-old boy needs an antibiotic for pneumonia Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency was diagnosed at age 3 after an episode of dark urine cough; right lower lobe crackles T 38.6 °C · HR 110/min · oxygen saturation 95% Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazoleoxidant stress depletes glutathione and precipitates hemolysis: sulfonamides do it, as do dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine and fava beans. Neither ceftriaxone nor azithromycin is a typical oxidant

Workup12 of 23 14-year-old boy has colicky right upper quadrant pain after meals Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia since infancy; father affected mild scleral icterus; spleen tip palpable Afebrile · HR 88/min · hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · transaminases normal · Hepatitis serologies · Right upper quadrant ultrasound · Supine and upright abdominal radiographs 14-year-old boy has colicky right upper quadrant pain after meals Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia since infancy; father affected mild scleral icterus; spleen tip palpable Afebrile · HR 88/min · hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · transaminases normal Right upper quadrant ultrasoundextravascular splenic hemolysis raises the indirect bilirubin and forms pigment stones, so colic after meals earns an ultrasound, the imaging test of choice for gallbladder stones, with cholecystectomy if stones are present. Plain radiographs miss most gallstones, and hepatitis serologies answer a hepatitis that normal transaminases make unlikely

Next step13 of 23 9-year-old boy develops fever, back pain and dark urine 15 minutes into a packed red cell transfusion after surgery flushed and anxious; no wheeze or rash T 39.0 °C · HR 132/min · BP 92/54 mm Hg · Slow the transfusion and give an antipyretic · Give diphenhydramine and continue · Stop the transfusion immediately 9-year-old boy develops fever, back pain and dark urine 15 minutes into a packed red cell transfusion after surgery flushed and anxious; no wheeze or rash T 39.0 °C · HR 132/min · BP 92/54 mm Hg Stop the transfusion immediatelyfever, back pain and dark urine minutes into a transfusion are an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: ABO incompatibility drives complement-mediated intravascular lysis, so the transfusion stops at once. Slowing it with an antipyretic, or an antihistamine and continuing, keeps the incompatible blood running

Diagnosis14 of 23 10-year-old Black boy has back pain and dark urine since waking First episode; cough and fever 2 days ago, treated with ibuprofen scleral icterus; mild abdominal tenderness Afebrile · HR 104/min · hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL bite cells; crystal violet stain shows inclusions · G6PD deficiency · Acute intermittent porphyria · Sickle cell disease 10-year-old Black boy has back pain and dark urine since waking First episode; cough and fever 2 days ago, treated with ibuprofen scleral icterus; mild abdominal tenderness Afebrile · HR 104/min · hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL bite cells; crystal violet stain shows inclusions G6PD deficiencybite cells, with Heinz bodies as the inclusions on a crystal violet stain, after an infection: activated leukocytes release oxidants that denature hemoglobin, and the episode brings sudden dark urine with back or abdominal pain. Infection is the leading cause of acute hemolysis in this deficiency, so the ibuprofen is not needed to explain it. Sickle cell disease shows sickled forms on the smear, and acute intermittent porphyria darkens the urine without anemia or bite cells

Next step15 of 23 5-year-old girl with pneumonia has dark urine since this morning after intravenous ceftriaxone Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 lethargic and pale; dark urine continuing HR 168/min · hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL · platelets 260,000/mm³ · Discontinue the drug and observe alone · Transfuse and discontinue the offending drug · Begin high-dose glucocorticoids without transfusion 5-year-old girl with pneumonia has dark urine since this morning after intravenous ceftriaxone Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 lethargic and pale; dark urine continuing HR 168/min · hemoglobin 4.5 g/dL · platelets 260,000/mm³ Transfuse and discontinue the offending drugseverity gates transfusion: stop the drug and transfuse when the anemia is severe. Glucocorticoids are for severe cases but do not replace the transfusion, and observation alone leaves a hemoglobin of 4.5 with tachycardia and lethargy untreated

Next step16 of 23 8-year-old boy has fever and looks ill Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 2; splenectomy a year ago ill-appearing; no focal source found T 39.5 °C · HR 150/min · BP 90/56 mm Hg · Oral antibiotics and review in 24 hours · Blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone now · Observation with antipyretics 8-year-old boy has fever and looks ill Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 2; splenectomy a year ago ill-appearing; no focal source found T 39.5 °C · HR 150/min · BP 90/56 mm Hg Blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone nowtreat every fever after splenectomy as sepsis until proven otherwise: blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics now, not oral antibiotics or observation

Mechanism17 of 23 7-year-old boy has pallor and dark urine on day 9 of high-dose intravenous penicillin Direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG spherocytes on the smear; liver enzymes normal hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL · platelets 270,000/mm³ · The drug binds the erythrocyte surface as a hapten, IgG attaches, and splenic macrophages destroy the cell · Oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin into Heinz bodies · Complement-mediated intravascular lysis by preformed IgM 7-year-old boy has pallor and dark urine on day 9 of high-dose intravenous penicillin Direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG spherocytes on the smear; liver enzymes normal hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL · platelets 270,000/mm³ The drug binds the erythrocyte surface as a hapten, IgG attaches, and splenic macrophages destroy the cellhigh-dose penicillin is a stable hapten, and its hemolysis typically follows 7 to 10 days of the drug: it binds the red-cell membrane, IgG attaches to the drug-cell complex and splenic macrophages clear it, an extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes and a direct antiglobulin test positive for IgG. Heinz bodies come from oxidant injury with a negative test, and complement-fixing IgM gives a C3-only result

Next step18 of 23 18-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice Mother blood group O positive; infant A positive spherocytes on the smear direct antiglobulin test weakly positive Total serum bilirubin above the phototherapy threshold, below the exchange level HR 142/min · Phototherapy · Eosin-5-maleimide binding test · Exchange transfusion 18-hour-old boy born at term has visible jaundice Mother blood group O positive; infant A positive spherocytes on the smear direct antiglobulin test weakly positive Total serum bilirubin above the phototherapy threshold, below the exchange level HR 142/min Phototherapyjaundice on the first day with a group O mother, a group A infant, spherocytes and a weakly positive direct antiglobulin test is ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn, the antibody cause of spherocytes on the first day of life; phototherapy treats a bilirubin above the phototherapy threshold. Eosin-5-maleimide binding looks for hereditary spherocytosis, and the bilirubin is below the exchange level, so exchange transfusion is not indicated

Mechanism19 of 23 8-year-old boy has pallor, jaundice and dark urine on day 2 of a febrile pneumonia G6PD deficiency was diagnosed at age 1; no antibiotic given bite cells on the smear; direct antiglobulin test negative T 38.9 °C · hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL · Oxidants from activated leukocytes denature hemoglobin · Cold-reacting IgM against the organism fixes complement · Red cells lacking CD55 and CD59 undergo complement lysis 8-year-old boy has pallor, jaundice and dark urine on day 2 of a febrile pneumonia G6PD deficiency was diagnosed at age 1; no antibiotic given bite cells on the smear; direct antiglobulin test negative T 38.9 °C · hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL Oxidants from activated leukocytes denature hemoglobininfection alone is an oxidant stress: activated leukocytes release oxidants, and red cells short of NADPH (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) cannot regenerate glutathione. Cold-reacting IgM gives a C3-positive test, and red cells lacking CD55 and CD59 point to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, with cytopenias

Next step20 of 23 6-year-old boy is reviewed 2 days after his piperacillin was stopped Treated for hemolysis with a positive direct antiglobulin test mild residual jaundice; energy improving hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, up from 7.9 g/dL · HR 96/min · Begin an intravenous immunoglobulin infusion · Observation without glucocorticoids · Begin prednisone 6-year-old boy is reviewed 2 days after his piperacillin was stopped Treated for hemolysis with a positive direct antiglobulin test mild residual jaundice; energy improving hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, up from 7.9 g/dL · HR 96/min Observation without glucocorticoidsdrug withdrawal is the treatment and usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days; a stable, rising hemoglobin shows it working. Glucocorticoids and intravenous immunoglobulin are reserved for severe cases

Workup21 of 23 5-year-old boy from a Greek family has pallor, jaundice and dark urine since this morning Ate fava beans 2 days ago Direct antiglobulin test negative hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL · reticulocytes raised · HR 118/min · Spherocytes · Schistocytes · Bite cells 5-year-old boy from a Greek family has pallor, jaundice and dark urine since this morning Ate fava beans 2 days ago Direct antiglobulin test negative hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL · reticulocytes raised · HR 118/min Bite cellsoxidized hemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages bite them out; the Heinz bodies themselves need a supravital stain such as crystal violet. Spherocytes mean a membrane defect or a warm antibody, and schistocytes mean cells sheared in damaged small vessels

Screening22 of 23 16-year-old girl has fatigue that limits her sport Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 4; splenectomy is planned gallstones on ultrasound; cholecystectomy planned alongside hemoglobin 8 g/dL · reticulocytes 12% · HR 96/min · No additional vaccination is required · Annual influenza vaccine alone · Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination before surgery 16-year-old girl has fatigue that limits her sport Hereditary spherocytosis was diagnosed at age 4; splenectomy is planned gallstones on ultrasound; cholecystectomy planned alongside hemoglobin 8 g/dL · reticulocytes 12% · HR 96/min Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination before surgeryHib vaccination joins the pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines before splenectomy for moderate to severe disease, deferred, ideally, until after age 6, so neither an influenza vaccine alone nor no vaccination is enough

Avoid23 of 23 5-year-old boy has dark urine 3 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole bite cells on the smear; Heinz bodies on supravital stain He is still actively hemolyzing today HR 124/min · hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL · reticulocytes 9% · Measuring G6PD activity during the acute episode · Supportive hydration and monitoring · Stopping the offending drug 5-year-old boy has dark urine 3 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole bite cells on the smear; Heinz bodies on supravital stain He is still actively hemolyzing today HR 124/min · hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL · reticulocytes 9% Measuring G6PD activity during the acute episodeduring acute hemolysis the surviving young cells carry near-normal enzyme and read falsely normal, so the assay waits weeks. Stopping the drug and supportive care are right now

Drug-induced immune hemolysis stop the drug, which usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days (penicillin hapten hemolysis typically ceases a few days to 2 weeks after stopping); transfuse if the anemia is severe; glucocorticoids, of questionable benefit, and intravenous immunoglobulin only for severe cases, and never while continuing the drug Hereditary spherocytosis folic acid for chronic reticulocytosis; transfusion for an aplastic or hemolytic crisis Splenectomy for moderate to severe disease, deferred, ideally, until after age 6, preceded by pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination; cholecystectomy too if pigment stones are present After splenectomy the hemolysis stops but the defect does not: spherocytes persist and Howell-Jolly bodies appear; treat every fever as sepsis until proven otherwise
A falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count in any chronic hemolytic patient is parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis until proven otherwise.

Smear clues in hemolysis Smear finding What made it Points to Sickle cells Crescent cells from polymerized hemoglobin S Sickle cell disease; a crisis brings severe pain Target cells Too much membrane for the hemoglobin inside Thalassemia, microcytic and chronic rather than acute; also hemoglobin C and liver disease Spherocytes Membrane lost, leaving small round cells without central pallor Hereditary spherocytosis, warm autoimmune or hapten drug hemolysis; ABO disease in a newborn Bite cells and Heinz bodies Oxidized hemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages bite them out G6PD deficiency after an oxidant trigger Schistocytes Red cells sheared in damaged small vessels or on a mechanical valve Microangiopathic hemolysis: HUS, TTP, DIC

Immune-complex drug hemolysis can arrive within hours of a dose in a patient sensitized by earlier exposure; hapten hemolysis typically builds over 7 to 10 days of high-dose penicillin; oxidative hemolysis comes in 1 to 3 days (24 to 72 hours); cold agglutinin hemolysis follows the pneumonia that caused it, whose cold agglutinins can turn positive after 7 to 10 days. Symptoms one hour after a dose are too fast for oxidative injury. Hemolysis within hours of a ceftriaxone or piperacillin dose is immune-complex, and the direct antiglobulin test reveals it, positive for C3; IgG without C3 usually marks the hapten type.
Reading the labs and the pain

The MCHC is the only red-cell index that rises in a common anemia, and the red cell distribution width (RDW) rises with it. A normal MCV does not exclude hemolysis, because a 10% reticulocytosis inflates it. Hereditary spherocytosis hemolyzes extravascularly, with indirect bilirubin, splenomegaly and pigment stones; PNH and severe G6PD deficiency hemolyze intravascularly, with hemoglobinuria, low haptoglobin and high LDH. Dark urine is hemoglobinuria or urobilinogen; with normal liver tests it is red cells, not bile. Severe hemolysis causes abdominal or back pain from red-cell destruction in the vertebral bodies, liver and spleen, while biliary obstruction would hurt considerably more. A normal creatinine argues against a microangiopathy and against massive intravascular hemolysis.

A G6PD level during the episode, or for hemolysis one hour after a drug that is not a typical oxidant. Abdominal computed tomography or liver ultrasound: obstruction brings severe pain with raised alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, and imaging cannot explain a hemoglobin of 6.3. Serum fibrinogen: DIC needs severe thrombocytopenia with prolonged clotting times. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage: back pain with acute anemia, but it follows trauma or a coagulopathy; a normal prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count and no injury exclude it. Anaphylaxis to a beta-lactam: seconds to minutes, with rash and edema, and no anemia. CD55 and CD59 testing just because the hemolysis is Coombs negative: PNH means cytopenias, a bland smear and acquired disease, not spherocytes in a boy whose father is affected. G6PD deficiency for a boy with jaundice: it needs an oxidant trigger and is not passed father to son. Hemoglobinopathy: the right class of inherited red-cell disorder, but it gives targets or sickles, never spherocytes.

In the first item, upper abdominal tenderness and dark urine tempt a biliary reading when symptoms are read before the laboratory values. Mycoplasma cold agglutinins also give a C3-positive direct antiglobulin test, so the test is still the right one, and the one-hour latency after a ceftriaxone dose points to the drug.

Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia: hemolysis with thrombocytopenia, where the smear and the coagulation studies identify a different process; an isolated hemolytic anemia is one process, a hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia another. Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child carries the Mycoplasma cold agglutinin association. Related conditions without their own brief: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (ask: is the direct Coombs test positive?) shares jaundice, anemia and spherocytes with hereditary spherocytosis, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (ask: are the white cells and platelets normal?).

When two mechanisms or diagnoses share a syndrome or a smear finding, the case supplies the attribute that separates them, usually an exposure and an interval or one test; choose the test for the mechanism, not the finding they share, then map the disease to its confirmatory assay. Spherocytes with a normal platelet count mean an antibody or a membrane; schistocytes with a low platelet count mean a clot.
