blocks: Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood
heme-positive dipstick, no red cells · hemoglobin vs myoglobin · creatine kinase and hemolysis labs · valve hemolysisDoes microscopy show red cells, and is the pigment hemoglobin or myoglobin?

Pt 62 yo M with a mechanical mitral valve, dark urine Labs dipstick heme-positive with 1 RBC (red blood cell) per high-power field, LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) 380, haptoglobin undetectable Smear schistocytes Q the most likely cause; options spanned intravascular hemolysis from the prosthetic valve, warfarin-related hematuria and infective endocarditis

The urine dipstick detects the heme moiety; it cannot distinguish hemoglobin, myoglobin and intact red blood cells. When the dipstick is positive but microscopy shows 0–2 RBC/hpf (red blood cells per high-power field), the urine contains free hemoglobin or myoglobin, not blood. This patient has a mechanical valve, schistocytes, a high LDH and low haptoglobin, the classic picture of intravascular hemolysis. The free pigment is hemoglobin released from red cells sheared as they pass through the prosthetic valve. Do not read the dark urine as gross hematuria when the dipstick is positive and microscopy is not.

Dipstick-microscopy mismatch heme-positive dipstick with ≤2 RBC/hpf on microscopy means free pigment, not bleeding Hemoglobinuria clues low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, schistocytes, indirect hyperbilirubinemia Myoglobinuria clues CK (creatine kinase) >10,000, muscle pain, recent crush/exertion/seizure

Heme-positive urine – the differential Diagnosis Illness script The NBME tell Excluded by Mechanical valve hemolysis Prosthetic valve, chronic mild hemolysis, dark urine Dipstick+, no RBCs, schistocytes, low haptoglobin – Anticoagulant hematuria On warfarin; dark/red urine RBCs present on microscopy 0–2 RBC/hpf Rhabdomyolysis Crush injury, exertion, seizure; dark urine CK >10,000; also dipstick+/RBC− No muscle symptoms, no CK elevation Glomerulonephritis Proteinuria, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts RBCs and casts on microscopy No RBCs, no casts Endocarditis Prosthetic valve + fever, new murmur Fever, positive blood cultures, vegetations Afebrile, no systemic infection

Diagnostic workup Test Order Result What it points to Urine dipstick Screen Heme-positive Blood, hemoglobin or myoglobin; the strip cannot tell them apart Urine microscopy First 0 to 2 RBCs per high-power field Free pigment, not bleeding; many RBCs or casts mean true hematuria Serum creatine kinase Next Markedly high, often over 10,000 Myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis; normal CK points to hemoglobin LDH, haptoglobin and indirect bilirubin By branch LDH up, haptoglobin low Intravascular hemolysis releasing hemoglobin into the urine Peripheral smear Confirms Schistocytes Mechanical fragmentation, here from the prosthetic valve Echocardiogram, if hemolysis worsens By branch Paravalvular leak Valve repair or replacement Renal ultrasound or urine culture Skip No RBCs means no bleeding source to find Pigment in the urine is not a urinary tract problem

Diagnosis2 of 7 28 yo M found unconscious after a building collapse, dark brown urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 45,000 · Rhabdomyolysis · Hemoglobinuria from intravascular hemolysis · Acute glomerulonephritis 28 yo M found unconscious after a building collapse, dark brown urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 45,000 Rhabdomyolysisaggressive IV normal saline

Workup3 of 7 45 yo F with dark urine and a heme-positive dipstick showing 0 RBCs on microscopy · Serum aspartate aminotransferase · Serum creatine kinase · Serum lactate dehydrogenase 45 yo F with dark urine and a heme-positive dipstick showing 0 RBCs on microscopy Serum creatine kinaseCK is the most sensitive marker of muscle injury; LDH and aspartate aminotransferase also leak from injured muscle, but their rise is nonspecific

Mechanism5 of 7 Why the dipstick is positive for blood when no red blood cells are seen on microscopy · The dipstick is falsely positive due to alkaline pH · The dipstick detects the heme moiety in free hemoglobin or myoglobin, not intact red blood cells · Vitamin C in the urine caused a false-positive reaction Why the dipstick is positive for blood when no red blood cells are seen on microscopy The dipstick detects the heme moiety in free hemoglobin or myoglobin, not intact red blood cellsalkaline urine falsely raises the protein pad, and vitamin C causes false-negative, not false-positive, blood readings

Diagnosis6 of 7 35 yo F with systemic lupus erythematosus, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts · Intravascular hemolysis · Lupus nephritis · Rhabdomyolysis 35 yo F with systemic lupus erythematosus, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts Lupus nephritisrenal biopsy

Next step7 of 7 24 yo M after a marathon, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 32,000, creatinine 2.4 · Furosemide to increase urine output · Sodium bicarbonate drip · IV normal saline at 200 to 300 mL per hour 24 yo M after a marathon, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 32,000, creatinine 2.4 IV normal saline at 200 to 300 mL per hourrhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury

The dipstick detects heme, not cells; a positive dipstick with no RBCs (red blood cells) means free pigment Hemoglobin vs myoglobin: CK (creatine kinase) separates them: CK >10,000 with muscle symptoms means myoglobin, and normal CK with hemolysis markers means hemoglobin Mild chronic hemolysis from a well-functioning mechanical valve is expected; worsening anemia or rising LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) suggests paravalvular leak → echocardiography, then possible reoperation Schistocytes confirm mechanical fragmentation and tie the hemolysis to the valve rather than to an autoimmune or drug cause Haptoglobin: consumed by binding free hemoglobin; most sensitive marker of intravascular hemolysis but also an acute-phase reactant (can be falsely normal during infection)

Hemolytic Anemiaalso brings hemolysis labs and dark urine, but the cause is immune: spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not schistocytes. Ask: is there a mechanical source? Hemolytic Anemia also brings hemolysis labs and dark urine, but the cause is immune: spherocytes and a positive direct antiglobulin test, not schistocytes. Ask: is there a mechanical source?

When the dipstick is positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells, look for the source of free pigment, not a bleeding site. CK (creatine kinase) separates muscle from red cell, and the clinical context identifies the mechanism.

Unchecked attributeAnticoagulant hematuria: the patient is on warfarin, but urine microscopy shows almost no RBCs (red blood cells). Salient decoyEndocarditis: there is a prosthetic valve, but no fever or systemic infection. Mirror twinRhabdomyolysis: it also causes a positive dipstick with no RBCs, but there are no muscle symptoms and no CK (creatine kinase) elevation.

briefs.title: Microcytic Anemia
briefs.sub: iron studies before electrophoresis · iron deficiency masks thalassemia trait · lead and chronic disease · the complete blood count (CBC) aloneIs the patient iron replete yet, and do the red cell distribution width (RDW) and red cell count fit deficiency or trait?
blocks: iron studies before electrophoresis · iron deficiency masks thalassemia trait · lead and chronic disease · the complete blood count (CBC) aloneIs the patient iron replete yet, and do the red cell distribution width (RDW) and red cell count fit deficiency or trait?

Both iron deficiency anemia and beta-thalassemia trait produce a low MCV (mean corpuscular volume). Hemoglobin electrophoresis is not the first test, because iron deficiency lowers HbA2 (hemoglobin A2), the marker electrophoresis uses to diagnose beta-thalassemia trait. In an iron-deficient patient, a falsely normal HbA2 on electrophoresis will mask coexisting thalassemia. Order iron studies first, correct the iron, then electrophoresis.

Iron studies first ferritin, serum iron, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), transferrin saturation; iron deficiency must be corrected before electrophoresis is interpretable HbA2 masking iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 into the normal range Beta-thalassemia trait HbA2 elevated (>3.5%) only when iron stores are replete

Microcytic anemia – the differential Diagnosis Illness script The NBME tell First test Confirms, then Iron deficiency anemia Menstrual loss, vegan/poor diet, GI bleed; low MCV Low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin sat Iron studies Low ferritin; oral iron, then electrophoresis if the MCV stays low Beta-thalassemia minor Mediterranean/Asian, lifelong mild anemia, target cells Elevated HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis (only when iron-replete) Iron studies first HbA2 over 3.5% once iron-replete; genetic counseling Alpha-thalassemia minor Southeast Asian/African, mild microcytic anemia Normal electrophoresis; diagnosis by exclusion or gene testing Iron studies → electrophoresis → gene analysis Alpha-globin gene deletion analysis Lead poisoning Child in old housing, developmental delay, abdominal pain Basophilic stippling; elevated lead level Lead level Elevated venous lead level; chelation if high Anemia of chronic disease Chronic infection, autoimmunity, malignancy Low iron, low TIBC (iron sequestered, not absent); ferritin normal/high Iron studies Low iron and TIBC with normal or high ferritin; treat the underlying disease

Workup1 of 13 15 yo F vegan with heavy menses, MCV 68, hemoglobin 9.2 · Iron studies · Bone marrow biopsy · Hemoglobin electrophoresis 15 yo F vegan with heavy menses, MCV 68, hemoglobin 9.2 Iron studiesiron deficiency must be assessed before electrophoresis is interpretable

Workup8 of 13 2 yo M, well-child visit, five 8-oz cups of whole cow milk daily, pale with tachycardia and a flow murmur, Hb 8, MCV 70, erythrocytes 3.1 million/uL, platelets and leukocytes normal · Abnormal hemoglobin electrophoresis · Low serum total iron-binding capacity · Elevated red cell distribution width 2 yo M, well-child visit, five 8-oz cups of whole cow milk daily, pale with tachycardia and a flow murmur, Hb 8, MCV 70, erythrocytes 3.1 million/uL, platelets and leukocytes normal Elevated red cell distribution widthiron deficiency anemia

Diagnosis9 of 13 2 yo of Greek descent, MCV 65, Hb 10.2, erythrocytes 5.4 million/uL, RDW normal, ferritin and iron studies normal · Iron deficiency anemia · Beta-thalassemia trait · Anemia of chronic disease 2 yo of Greek descent, MCV 65, Hb 10.2, erythrocytes 5.4 million/uL, RDW normal, ferritin and iron studies normal Beta-thalassemia traita normal red cell count with a low MCV

Next step10 of 13 2 yo M with Hb 8 and MCV 70 whose diet is cheese, yogurt and roughly 40 oz of whole cow milk daily · Transfuse packed red blood cells · Limit cow milk below 24 oz per day and begin an empiric oral iron trial · Send hemoglobin electrophoresis now 2 yo M with Hb 8 and MCV 70 whose diet is cheese, yogurt and roughly 40 oz of whole cow milk daily Limit cow milk below 24 oz per day and begin an empiric oral iron trialiron deficiency from excessive milk intake

Mechanism11 of 13 Why the red cell distribution width rises in iron deficiency but stays normal in thalassemia trait · Iron deficiency shortens red cell survival · Thalassemic cells are cleared at varying rates by the spleen · Iron available for erythropoiesis fluctuates, so cells are made at varying sizes Why the red cell distribution width rises in iron deficiency but stays normal in thalassemia trait Iron available for erythropoiesis fluctuates, so cells are made at varying sizesthalassemia produces uniformly small cells

Diagnosis12 of 13 16 yo F with heavy menses, a low MCV, a low erythrocyte count, an elevated RDW and a low ferritin · Beta-thalassemia minor · Iron deficiency anemia · Anemia of chronic disease 16 yo F with heavy menses, a low MCV, a low erythrocyte count, an elevated RDW and a low ferritin Iron deficiency anemiaoral iron

Diagnosis13 of 13 58 yo M with rheumatoid arthritis and a microcytic anemia; serum iron low, TIBC low, ferritin normal · Anemia of chronic disease · Iron deficiency anemia · Beta-thalassemia minor 58 yo M with rheumatoid arthritis and a microcytic anemia; serum iron low, TIBC low, ferritin normal Anemia of chronic diseaseiron is sequestered, not absent

Iron studies → then electrophoresis: a required order, not a preference, because iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 (hemoglobin A2) into the normal range Ferritin is the most specific single test for iron deficiency; TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) and transferrin saturation add sensitivity when ferritin is borderline (ferritin is an acute-phase reactant) Alpha-thalassemia minor has a normal electrophoresis. It is diagnosed by exclusion or gene testing and is the one microcytic anemia that electrophoresis cannot diagnose The Mentzer index is MCV (mean corpuscular volume) divided by RBC (red blood cell count). It is a screening heuristic: under 13 suggests thalassemia and over 13 suggests IDA (iron deficiency anemia). It is not diagnostic and is never the most appropriate test If the anemia does not correct with iron, look for a second cause; that is when to order electrophoresis

Sickle Cell Disease and Traitalso uses hemoglobin electrophoresis. Ask: is the electrophoresis interpretable, or must iron be corrected first? Sickle Cell Disease and Trait also uses hemoglobin electrophoresis. Ask: is the electrophoresis interpretable, or must iron be corrected first?
Telling them apart on the CBC…

RDW elevated in iron deficiency because the iron available for erythropoiesis varies through the day, so cells are made at varying sizes; normal or low in thalassemia trait, where every cell is uniformly small Erythrocyte count low in iron deficiency because the marrow lacks substrate, but normal or elevated in thalassemia trait, which makes plenty of small cells Mentzer index MCV divided by RBC; over 13 favours iron deficiency and under 13 favours thalassemia trait TIBC direction elevated in iron deficiency as transferrin is upregulated, and low in anemia of chronic disease mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration low in both iron deficiency and thalassemia, and elevated in hereditary spherocytosis from loss of membrane surface area Cow milk threshold over 24 oz per day after age 1 is the named risk factor, because milk is iron-poor, its calcium and caseinophosphopeptide block absorption, and volume displaces iron-rich food

When two diseases share a lab value and one suppresses the marker used to diagnose the other, testing order is a dependency, not a preference. Correct the confounder first, then run the definitive test.

Sequencing trapHemoglobin electrophoresis: it checks for thalassemia, but iron deficiency makes it uninterpretable. Class-vs-memberBone marrow biopsy: it can look like the definitive hematology test, but it is invasive and unnecessary when a dietary cause is obvious.

briefs.title: Hemophilia
briefs.sub: refractory bleeding on replacement: alloantibodies · the mixing study proves it · bleeding to lab pattern · arthropathyIs the partial thromboplastin time still long on adequate factor, with normal platelets and prothrombin time?
blocks: refractory bleeding on replacement: alloantibodies · the mixing study proves it · bleeding to lab pattern · arthropathyIs the partial thromboplastin time still long on adequate factor, with normal platelets and prothrombin time?

A patient with known severe hemophilia A on factor VIII replacement has bleeding that does not respond to increased dosing. The aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) is 112 seconds, massively prolonged despite daily infusions that should be correcting it. The infused factor VIII is being neutralized by alloantibodies. This is inhibitor development, which occurs in ~25% of patients with severe hemophilia A. An aPTT of 112 on replacement therapy means the intrinsic pathway remains uncorrected even though the missing factor is being given. Platelets of 150K and a normal PT (prothrombin time) exclude every platelet and common-pathway cause.

Inhibitor development alloantibodies (IgG) against infused factor VIII; ~25% of severe hemophilia A patients Clinical clue bleeding refractory to adequate factor replacement therapy Lab clue prolonged aPTT that does not correct on a mixing study Bethesda assay quantifies inhibitor titer; guides treatment (low <5 Bethesda units (BU) vs high ≥5 BU)

Refractory bleeding in a hemophiliac – the differential Diagnosis Illness script The NBME tell Excluded by Inhibitor development Known hemophilia on replacement; increasing bleeds Refractory bleeding + prolonged aPTT on replacement + mixing study does not correct – Acquired von Willebrand disease Autoimmune, lymphoproliferative; mucocutaneous bleeding Mucosal bleeding; low vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor Hemarthrosis, not mucocutaneous Fibrinogen dysfunction Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), liver failure; diffuse bleeding Both PT and aPTT prolonged; low fibrinogen PT is normal Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Heparin exposure; thrombosis + falling platelets Thrombocytopenia + thrombosis; 4T score, platelet factor 4 antibody Platelets 150K (normal) Platelet dysfunction Uremia, aspirin; mucocutaneous bleeding Normal coagulation studies + prolonged PFA-100 aPTT 112; hemarthrosis, not petechiae

Factor (clotting) defect deep bleeding: hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, large ecchymoses, excess bleeding after surgery; the PT or aPTT is prolonged Platelet defect mucocutaneous bleeding: nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, petechiae, small bruises; the count is low or aggregation is abnormal PT factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen; factor VII is the only one the PT measures alone aPTT factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen Hemophilia by age easy bruising in infancy; hemarthroses and deep hematomas once the toddler walks Factor XI deficiency the hemophilia lab pattern, but bleeding mainly with surgery or major trauma

Hemophilia X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII (A) or factor IX (B); prolonged aPTT with normal PT and platelets; severity tracks factor activity Hemarthrosis spontaneous or trivial-trauma bleeding into a large joint, often a knee, with sudden severe swelling The link iron from the extravasated red cells is stored as hemosiderin in the synovium, which inflames it Then the synovium thickens and turns boggy, fibroses, and the cartilage and subchondral bone are destroyed Result chronic pain, swelling and loss of motion, including a joint that will not fully extend actively or passively Imaging radiographs show only late disease; MRI detects damage earlier Prevention early prophylaxis with factor concentrate lowers the risk Treatment factor replacement; desmopressin for mild hemophilia A Versus juvenile idiopathic arthritis or rheumatoid arthritis autoimmune cartilage destruction, no bleeding history Versus disseminated gonococcal infection acute onset, not 6 months Versus avascular necrosis sickle cell disease, or Legg-Calvé-Perthes at the hip between 4 and 12 Versus Lyme arthritis knee effusion, but no bleeding history

Mixing study mix patient plasma 1:1 with normal plasma. Correction of the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) means factor deficiency; no correction means an inhibitor. A factor VIII inhibitor is time- and temperature-dependent (incubate at 37°C for 1–2 hours before reading) Bethesda assay low-titer (<5 BU) may respond to high-dose factor VIII; high-titer (≥5 BU) requires bypassing agents: rFVIIa (recombinant activated factor VII) or activated PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate) Immune tolerance induction repeated high-dose factor VIII to desensitize the immune system; the long-term eradication strategy Acquired hemophilia A the adult analogue: autoantibodies in a patient with no prior bleeding history, often autoimmune, malignancy, or postpartum Hemarthrosis versus petechiae hemarthrosis indicates a factor problem and petechiae a platelet problem; this division sorts most bleeding disorders before any lab is read

Anemia with Thrombocytopeniaalso uses the coagulation workup. Ask: does the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) correct on mixing? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficienciescovers vitamin K deficiency. Ask: is the PT (prothrombin time) long first, and is factor V normal (vitamin K) or low (liver)? Anemia with Thrombocytopenia also uses the coagulation workup. Ask: does the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) correct on mixing? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin K deficiency. Ask: is the PT (prothrombin time) long first, and is factor V normal (vitamin K) or low (liver)?

Bleeding on factor replacement therapy that does not respond to dose escalation, with an aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) still prolonged despite adequate dosing, means the infused factor is being neutralized. The mixing study proves it.

Unchecked attributePlatelet dysfunction: platelets are normal, and the abnormal value is the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time), which is not a platelet test. True-fact-wrong-slotAcquired vWD (von Willebrand disease): it can lower factor VIII but presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, not hemarthrosis. The patient already has a known factor deficiency. Unchecked attributeFibrinogen dysfunction: the PT (prothrombin time) is normal, and a fibrinogen (common pathway) defect would prolong both the PT and the aPTT.

Pt 12 yo F with idiopathic aplastic anemia, new petechiae and bruising over a week; during a platelet transfusion a chest rash spreads over the body Labs absolute neutrophil count 420, platelets 7,000 Exam T 37.2 °C, blood pressure (BP) 110/82 mm Hg, heart rate (HR) 90/min, respiratory rate (RR) 18/min, saturation 98%; oropharynx normal, lungs clear; diffuse urticarial rash on trunk and limbs plus pinpoint nonblanching macules and bruises at the extremities Q the best next step in evaluation of the reaction; options spanned culture of the product, direct Coombs test, no additional evaluation, peripheral smear and coagulation studies

Blood pressure is normal, there is no wheeze, the lungs are clear and the oropharynx is normal. This is isolated urticaria in a hemodynamically stable patient. The rash improved after an antihistamine, with an hour of stable observation. It is an urticarial transfusion reaction, caused by preformed immunoglobulin E (IgE) reacting against a soluble allergen in the donated plasma, or the reverse. Management is what has already been done: stop the transfusion, give an antihistamine and observe. Improvement with the antihistamine confirms the diagnosis, and the transfusion may be resumed without additional evaluation.

Urticarial reaction hives and itching only, onset hours into the transfusion, from preformed IgE against a soluble plasma allergen; stop, antihistamine, resume if otherwise asymptomatic, no workup Anaphylactic reaction onset seconds to minutes, from antibodies to immunoglobulin A (IgA) in an IgA-deficient recipient reacting to donor IgA; respiratory distress or wheeze, angioedema, hypotension; epinephrine, and washed products thereafter Acute hemolytic reaction ABO incompatibility from clerical error; fever, flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, direct Coombs positive Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection fever, chills, hypotension, most common with platelets; culture both the recipient and the product

Transfusion reactions: timing, company and the movethe vitals sort them faster than the rash does Reaction Onset The company it keeps What to do Urticarial Hours Hives and itching, nothing else; vitals normal Stop, antihistamine, resume; no workup Anaphylactic Emergency Seconds to minutes Wheeze, angioedema, hypotension; IgA-deficient recipient Epinephrine; future transfusions washed Acute hemolytic Emergency Minutes to hours Fever, flank pain, hypotension, dark urine Stop; direct Coombs, smear, prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT); supportive Bacterial contamination Emergency Minutes to hours Fever, rigors, hypotension; platelets most often Culture recipient and product; empiric antibiotics Febrile nonhemolytic During or within 4 h Fever and chills without hemolysis Stop, antipyretic; leukoreduction reduces its incidence TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) / TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) TRALI within 6 h; TACO within 12 h Respiratory distress: volume overload vs noncardiogenic edema Stop; diuretic for TACO, supportive care for TRALI

BP 110/82 mm Hg, HR 90/min, saturation 98% hemodynamically stable, which excludes anaphylaxis, hemolysis and sepsis Lungs clear, oropharynx normal no bronchospasm, no angioedema; the two findings that would make this anaphylaxis Afebrile at 37.2 °C excludes both a febrile reaction and bacterial contamination Rash improved with diphenhydramine and stayed stable for an hour confirms the diagnosis Petechiae and bruises were present before the transfusion they reflect a platelet count of 7,000 from aplastic anemia, not a new consumptive process No flank pain, no dark urine the findings of a hemolytic reaction are absent It was a platelet transfusion platelets are the product most associated with bacterial contamination; without fever, culture is not indicated

What is the blood pressure and the saturation? Normal → the dangerous reactions are out Is there a fever? No → not hemolytic, not bacterial, not febrile Wheeze, angioedema or hypotension? None → urticaria is isolated, so not anaphylaxis How fast did it start? Late, not in the first minutes → urticarial Did it respond to the antihistamine? Yes → that is the confirmation So what is needed? Nothing further; the transfusion may be resumed

The petechiae and ecchymoses look like a new hemorrhagic complication, and they appear in the skin examination beside the urticaria as though they arrived together. They were present before the transfusion: she had bruising a week ago, and her platelet count is 7,000. A finding documented before the intervention cannot be a reaction to it.

Vital signs: normal blood pressure, no fever and no hypoxia eliminate anaphylaxis, hemolysis, bacterial contamination and TRALI Isolated urticaria is the only reaction in which the transfusion may continue: stop, give an antihistamine, observe, then resume the same unit Timing separates the two allergic reactions: seconds to minutes with wheeze and hypotension is anaphylaxis; hours with hives alone is urticarial Anaphylaxis to blood suggests IgA deficiency; the long-term fix is washed products Platelets carry the bacterial risk because they are stored at room temperature; fever and rigors during a platelet transfusion call for cultures

Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers selective IgA deficiency and already keys washed red cells; this brief covers the same topic from the transfusion side. Ask: what are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?

When a treatment has already been given and the response is reported, the response serves as the diagnostic test, and usually nothing further is needed. Check the reported response before ordering anything.

Redundant workupDirect Coombs test: answers "is this hemolysis?", already excluded by normal vitals, no fever, no flank pain and no dark urine. Salient decoyPT and PTT: indicated only for hemolysis complicated by disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); her bruising is thrombocytopenic and predates the transfusion. Redundant workupPeripheral smear: would show schistocytes if microangiopathy were present; there is no hemolysis to look for. Unchecked attributeCulture of the product: platelets do carry the bacterial risk, but culture requires fever, chills or hypotension; she is afebrile and stable.

Pt 5 yo M, 2 weeks of fatigue, 1 week of leg pain, 1 day of fever with petechiae; pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy Q the most useful test; options spanned complete blood count with differential and smear, C-reactive protein and partial thromboplastin time

Together, tri-lineage cytopenia, diaphyseal bone pain and diffuse nontender adenopathy with splenomegaly fit only one disease. They indicate marrow replacement, which is confirmed in the marrow. The complete blood count is the initial and most useful first test: cheap, fast, and enough to convert a vague illness into an oncologic emergency. It raises the suspicion of leukemia; the bone marrow aspirate is the diagnostic test that confirms it.

Pancytopenia reduction in all three lineages, the word that eliminates every single-lineage disease acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) diagnostic gate at least 20% lymphoblasts of marrow nucleated cells M1, M2, M3 marrow under 5%, 5 to 25%, over 25% blasts, a burden and response category rather than the diagnostic gate Leukemic bone pain diaphyseal or metaphyseal tenderness from marrow expansion, distinct from joint-line pain Petechiae a platelet problem, so prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) are normal

Corticosteroids partially treat ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia). They transiently improve the child while destroying the diagnostic specimen and degrading risk stratification. Separate systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) from ALL before treatment, not after. A normal white count does not exclude ALL; the cytopenias are the clue, not the blasts.

The story families often date leukemic bone pain to a fall; the pain is dull, in the long-bone shafts, worse at night, and the child limps or refuses to walk What makes it systemic fever, hepatomegaly, bilateral tibial tenderness and two or more cytopenias The bruises thrombocytopenia explains truncal bruising; trauma cannot depress three cell lines When to think abuse a vague history with bruising away from injury-prone areas, and normal counts The white count often low early, since normal production falls; later high as blasts spill into the blood Versus aplastic anemia pancytopenia from a hypocellular marrow, so no bone pain and rarely hepatomegaly Versus immune thrombocytopenia hemoglobin and white count normal, no bone pain or organomegaly Workup marrow biopsy with flow cytometry (20% or more blasts), then lumbar puncture for CNS (central nervous system) disease Prognosis 5-year survival above 85% in children with multidrug chemotherapy

Paternal uncle with hemophilia hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, so a boy inherits it through his mother; his father's brother cannot pass it to him Uneventful tonsillectomy last year a surgical challenge passed without bleeding argues against any inherited bleeding disorder New bleeding plus pallor, nodes and hepatosplenomegaly an acquired marrow problem: blasts crowd out megakaryocytes, so platelet production fails Hemophilia joint and muscle bleeds after trauma, prolonged PTT (partial thromboplastin time), normal counts and no organomegaly Von Willebrand disease lifelong mucosal bleeding with a normal platelet count and a normal exam

Leukemia lowers blood counts; systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) raises them, with ferritin, platelets and WBC (white blood cell count) all rising Neuroblastoma and ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia) are confirmed by the same test; periorbital ecchymoses and a midline-crossing mass separate them A mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL and can compress the airway or cause superior vena cava syndrome; a normal chest film does not exclude B-cell ALL About half of children with ALL present with bleeding (petechiae, bruising, gum oozing) from thrombocytopenia Extramedullary spread also shows as testicular enlargement and as leptomeningeal disease with cranial nerve deficits or meningismus, which is why a lumbar puncture is part of the workup Inflammatory markers monitor disease; they do not distinguish between diagnoses that all raise them Tumor lysis: potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down, with acute kidney injury

Part I Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis is the mirror twin, and Part I The Limping Child shares the presenting complaint. Ask: are the counts up or down? Part I Leg Pain in a Child covers the benign nocturnal limb pain whose normal examination excludes this diagnosis. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child places leukemia among the other causes of bruising in a child. Part I Hemophilia covers the bleeding-pattern-to-lab table: is the PT (prothrombin time) or the PTT (partial thromboplastin time) long, and are the platelets normal?

A systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis diagnosis made 2 months earlier, partly improved on ibuprofen, was the anchor; new pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly still meant bone marrow aspiration, not imaging or liver biopsy.

Choose laboratory tests by what a result could change, not by their sophistication. A test that is abnormal in every diagnosis on the differential discriminates nothing. A test of an uninvolved compartment does not address the clinical question.

Salient decoyEthnicity and travel are epidemiologic priors, not findings, and cannot outrank the blood count. True-fact-wrong-slotSplenomegaly and generalized adenopathy are not features of Kawasaki or of leukemia's mimics in the way offered. Class-vs-memberPTT is the right class of hematologic test on the wrong compartment. Salient decoyThe fall and the mother's boyfriend pull toward abuse, but trauma cannot explain fever, hepatomegaly or three low cell lines.

Pt 6 yo with new bruising, Aquifer Pediatrics 21; the case works through purpura and petechiae to IgA vasculitis Q build the differential for purpura in a school-age child, then narrow it by history, examination and a first set of tests

Bruising is a finding, not a diagnosis. Ask what failed: the vessel wall (IgA vasculitis), the platelets (immune thrombocytopenia, leukemia, von Willebrand disease), the clotting factors (hemophilia), or the story (accidental or nonaccidental trauma). Each leaves a different bruise, history and first test. First check whether the child needs intervention now. Then use the history, the examination and the platelet count to remove whole branches at a time. Order the confirmatory test last, once one branch is left.

Red flags: act before the full history Finding What it points to Altered mental status, labored breathing, slow capillary refill Unstable: circulation, airway, breathing first Fever with fast-spreading purpura, ill child Sepsis or meningococcemia: antibiotics before the workup Pallor, fatigue, bone pain, big spleen or nodes Marrow disease: complete blood count (CBC) and smear today Headache or confusion with low platelets Intracranial bleeding Sudden severe belly pain, vomiting, bloody stool Intussusception

Diagnostic workup Test Order Result What it points to CBC with platelet count First Normal platelets Vessel wall: IgA vasculitis Low platelets, nothing else abnormal ITP Low platelets with anemia or an abnormal white count Marrow or consumption: smear next Peripheral smear By branch Blasts or schistocytes Leukemia, or hemolytic uremic syndrome Urinalysis and blood pressure By branch Blood or protein, or high blood pressure Kidney involved: blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine Prothrombin time (PT) and aPTT By branch aPTT long, PT normal Hemophilia or von Willebrand disease Abdominal ultrasound By branch Intussusception A negative study does not exclude an intermittent one Bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry Confirms 20% or more blasts Leukemia Factor VIII, IX and von Willebrand studies Confirms Low level Names the bleeding disorder Skin biopsy, only if atypical Confirms IgA in the vessel walls IgA vasculitis; rarely needed Serum IgA Skip High in only about half Cannot confirm or exclude IgA vasculitis

Finalists On arrival CBC Next Confirms Treatment and follow-up IgA vasculitis Well; raised purpura on the legs, sore ankles, belly pain Platelets normal Urinalysis and blood pressure Clinical; biopsy only if atypical Supportive; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) unless GI bleeding or nephritis; urine and BP checks for a year Immune thrombocytopenia Well; flat petechiae, nose or gum bleeding Platelets low, nothing else Smear Low platelets alone, in a typical story Observe; intravenous immunoglobulin or steroids for serious bleeding; no NSAIDs, limit contact sports Leukemia Ill; fever, bone pain, big spleen or nodes Two or more cell lines abnormal Smear Marrow: 20% or more blasts; lumbar puncture for central nervous system spread Oncology

What it is the commonest vasculitis of childhood, about half of cases; an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis of the skin, gut, joints and kidneys that usually settles in about a month Who 4 to 6 years (range 2 to 17), boys about twice as often; about half follow an upper respiratory infection Mechanism an IgA-dominated immune response, often to an infection, inflames small vessels; biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits Features palpable purpura with a normal platelet count, symmetric and gravity-dependent, sometimes starting as macules or hives; arthritis of the knees and ankles; colicky belly pain, sometimes before the rash; hematuria; no big spleen Diagnosis clinical; the urinalysis is the one test it needs, with BUN and creatinine if the urine or blood pressure is abnormal Treatment acetaminophen or an NSAID unless there is GI bleeding or nephritis; steroids are debated, used for severe belly pain, and have not been shown to protect the kidney Complications kidney disease in about a third (about 5% chronic renal failure, under 1% end-stage); GI bleeding, with occult blood in about half; intussusception, usually ileoileal, so an enema cannot reduce it Follow-up urinalysis and blood pressure every 1 to 2 weeks for 1 to 2 months, then monthly to every other month for a year; about 30% recur, weeks to months later Return for severe belly pain, blood in the stool, vomiting that stops fluids, puffy face, hands or feet, severe headache, blurred vision or confusion

What sets it apart Versus What separates it ITP Platelets normal, and the purpura is raised Leukemia A well child with normal counts and no big spleen Hemolytic uremic syndrome No anemia or schistocytes; platelets normal Abuse Raised, symmetric, dependent lesions with joint, belly or kidney findings

Diagnosis1 of 19 6 yo boy, a week after a cold, with raised, nonblanching red-purple spots on the backs of both legs and the buttocks, swollen tender ankles and crampy periumbilical pain; platelets 280,000 · Immune thrombocytopenia · IgA vasculitis · Nonaccidental trauma 6 yo boy, a week after a cold, with raised, nonblanching red-purple spots on the backs of both legs and the buttocks, swollen tender ankles and crampy periumbilical pain; platelets 280,000 IgA vasculitisurinalysis next

Workup2 of 19 6 yo with 3 days of new bruises and pinpoint red spots on the legs and trunk; afebrile, alert, normal vital signs, no history of injury · CBC with smear · PT and aPTT · Skeletal survey 6 yo with 3 days of new bruises and pinpoint red spots on the legs and trunk; afebrile, alert, normal vital signs, no history of injury CBC with smearthe platelet count sorts every branch

Diagnosis3 of 19 4 yo, well-appearing, flat petechiae everywhere and a nosebleed two weeks after a viral illness; platelets 12,000, hemoglobin and white count normal, no organomegaly · Immune thrombocytopenia · Acute lymphoblastic leukemia · IgA vasculitis 4 yo, well-appearing, flat petechiae everywhere and a nosebleed two weeks after a viral illness; platelets 12,000, hemoglobin and white count normal, no organomegaly Immune thrombocytopenialow platelets and nothing else

Next step4 of 19 5 yo with petechiae and platelets of 20,000 who otherwise looks like ITP, except that the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin · Intravenous immunoglobulin · Bone marrow examination · Observe as ITP 5 yo with petechiae and platelets of 20,000 who otherwise looks like ITP, except that the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin Bone marrow examinationa spleen this size is not ITP

Diagnosis5 of 19 8 yo girl with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising and bleeding for a day after a tooth extraction; platelet count normal; her mother has heavy periods · Hemophilia · Immune thrombocytopenia · Von Willebrand disease 8 yo girl with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising and bleeding for a day after a tooth extraction; platelet count normal; her mother has heavy periods Von Willebrand diseaseplatelets that do not stick, at a normal count

Diagnosis6 of 19 7 yo boy, afebrile, with a warm, tense, swollen knee after a minor fall, a deep thigh hematoma last year, and an uncle who bled after surgery; platelet count normal · Septic arthritis · Hemophilia · Von Willebrand disease 7 yo boy, afebrile, with a warm, tense, swollen knee after a minor fall, a deep thigh hematoma last year, and an uncle who bled after surgery; platelet count normal Hemophiliadeep bleeding means a clotting factor

Workup7 of 19 7 yo boy with a swollen knee after a minor fall; platelet count and PT normal, aPTT prolonged · Mixing study · Von Willebrand factor antigen · Factor VIII and IX activity 7 yo boy with a swollen knee after a minor fall; platelet count and PT normal, aPTT prolonged Factor VIII and IX activitynames the missing factor

Next step8 of 19 9-month-old who cannot yet crawl, with a bruise on the ear and another on the upper back; the parent says he bruises easily; CBC and coagulation studies are normal · Skeletal survey · Hematology referral · Reassurance 9-month-old who cannot yet crawl, with a bruise on the ear and another on the upper back; the parent says he bruises easily; CBC and coagulation studies are normal Skeletal surveya child who cannot crawl cannot bruise his back by accident

Diagnosis9 of 19 5 yo with purpura on the legs, abdominal pain and hematuria a week after bloody diarrhea; hemoglobin 7, platelets 40,000, schistocytes on the smear · Immune thrombocytopenia · Hemolytic uremic syndrome · IgA vasculitis 5 yo with purpura on the legs, abdominal pain and hematuria a week after bloody diarrhea; hemoglobin 7, platelets 40,000, schistocytes on the smear Hemolytic uremic syndromelow platelets and hemolysis; IgA vasculitis keeps both normal

Workup10 of 19 6 yo diagnosed with IgA vasculitis on examination, platelet count normal · Serum IgA level · Skin biopsy · Urinalysis 6 yo diagnosed with IgA vasculitis on examination, platelet count normal Urinalysisthe only test the diagnosis itself requires

Mechanism11 of 19 6 yo with raised purpura on both legs, ankle pain and a normal platelet count, whose serum IgA level comes back normal · It does not exclude IgA vasculitis · It excludes IgA vasculitis · A skin biopsy is needed to decide 6 yo with raised purpura on both legs, ankle pain and a normal platelet count, whose serum IgA level comes back normal It does not exclude IgA vasculitisserum IgA is high in only about half

Workup12 of 19 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria · Renal ultrasound · BUN and creatinine · Serum IgA level 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria BUN and creatininemeasures the extent of renal disease

Workup13 of 19 5 yo with IgA vasculitis who develops sudden severe colicky abdominal pain with vomiting · Air contrast enema · Abdominal ultrasound · Abdominal radiograph 5 yo with IgA vasculitis who develops sudden severe colicky abdominal pain with vomiting Abdominal ultrasoundlooking for intussusception

Next step14 of 19 5 yo with IgA vasculitis and an ileoileal intussusception that is still present on repeat ultrasound hours later, with ongoing pain · Continued observation · Air contrast enema · Surgical reduction 5 yo with IgA vasculitis and an ileoileal intussusception that is still present on repeat ultrasound hours later, with ongoing pain Surgical reductionan enema cannot reach the small bowel

Next step15 of 19 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose purpura has faded; urinalysis and blood pressure were normal at diagnosis · Serial urine and BP checks · No further follow-up · Serial CBC and serum IgA 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose purpura has faded; urinalysis and blood pressure were normal at diagnosis Serial urine and BP checkskidney disease can come after the rash

Next step16 of 19 4 yo with ITP, platelets 15,000, skin petechiae only, no mucosal or other bleeding · Observation · Intravenous immunoglobulin · Platelet transfusion 4 yo with ITP, platelets 15,000, skin petechiae only, no mucosal or other bleeding Observationwith activity limits; the count alone does not call for treatment
Avoid17 of 19 4 yo with ITP and a painful sprained ankle · Ice and elevation · Ibuprofen · Acetaminophen 4 yo with ITP and a painful sprained ankle Ibuprofenimpairs platelet function

Mechanism18 of 19 Previously healthy 4 yo boy with 3 days of bruising that started on the arms and legs and has spread to the trunk; no injury recalled, and his parents call him very active; afebrile, normal vital signs; scattered petechiae and bruises of different ages, most on the limbs; hemoglobin 12 g/dL, white count 6,000, platelets 1,000, PT and aPTT normal · Decreased platelet production · Child abuse · Increased platelet destruction Previously healthy 4 yo boy with 3 days of bruising that started on the arms and legs and has spread to the trunk; no injury recalled, and his parents call him very active; afebrile, normal vital signs; scattered petechiae and bruises of different ages, most on the limbs; hemoglobin 12 g/dL, white count 6,000, platelets 1,000, PT and aPTT normal Increased platelet destructionimmune thrombocytopenia; antibody-coated platelets are cleared in the spleen

Mechanism19 of 19 5 yo with 2 weeks of bruising, pallor, fever and leg pain; liver and spleen enlarged; hemoglobin 7 g/dL, white count 2,000, platelets 15,000; PT and aPTT normal · Abnormal platelet function · Decreased platelet production · Increased platelet destruction 5 yo with 2 weeks of bruising, pallor, fever and leg pain; liver and spleen enlarged; hemoglobin 7 g/dL, white count 2,000, platelets 15,000; PT and aPTT normal Decreased platelet productionmarrow replacement, as in leukemia; peripheral smear next, and bone marrow examination confirms

Normal PT (prothrombin time) and aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) argue against a clotting factor deficiency and against DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). A low platelet count with a normal hemoglobin and white count in a well child means increased platelet destruction. In ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), antibodies coat platelets and splenic macrophages clear them; the antibodies also reduce platelet production. Decreased production from leukemia or aplastic anemia usually lowers two or more cell lines. Abnormal platelet function (von Willebrand disease, Glanzmann thrombasthenia) causes bleeding at a normal or near-normal count.

The key was a mechanism class, increased platelet destruction, not the name ITP (immune thrombocytopenia). Child abuse was the decoy, planted as an active boy with bruises in several stages of healing. Widespread petechiae, a platelet count of 1,000 and a normal PT (prothrombin time) and aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) explain the bruising.

Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers the child with two cell lines down. Part II Acute Leukemia in a Child covers the marrow branch and its confirmatory biopsy. Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome covers the glomerular workup that renal IgA vasculitis enters. Part II Suspected Child Abuse covers the fracture branch of nonaccidental trauma. Ask: does the fracture need a pull or a twist, and does the film show a bone disease?

For bruising in a child, decide whether the vessel, the platelets, the clotting factors or the story failed. The feel of the lesion, the platelet count and the spleen each remove a branch. Order the confirmatory test only after one branch is left.

Salient decoyThe recent cold is shared by ITP and IgA vasculitis and cannot separate them. Unchecked attributePurpura read as a platelet problem without checking whether it is raised. Mirror twinA child who looks like ITP but has a spleen more than 2 cm down is not ITP. Test-overrides-findingsA normal serum IgA offered as exclusion, when it is high in only about half. Salient decoyChild abuse: bruises of different colors on an active boy invite it, but bruise color cannot reliably date a bruise. Widespread petechiae, a platelet count of 1,000 and normal clotting times explain the bleeding; a platelet count and coagulation studies belong in most bruising workups for suspected abuse. Unchecked attributeAbnormal platelet function: von Willebrand disease and Glanzmann thrombasthenia cause bleeding at a normal or near-normal count; this count is 1,000. Unchecked attributeDecreased platelet production: leukemia and aplastic anemia usually lower more than one cell line; a hemoglobin of 12 and a white count of 6,000 are normal. True-fact-wrong-slotDisseminated intravascular coagulation: it occurs in an ill patient and prolongs the clotting times, with low fibrinogen and high D-dimer; this boy is well and his clotting times are normal.

briefs.title: Tuberculosis
briefs.sub: who to screen · skin test cutoffs by risk · latent versus active by symptoms and film · isolate first · four drugs and their toxicitiesAre there symptoms or an abnormal chest film, and must the patient be isolated before any drug?
blocks: who to screen · skin test cutoffs by risk · latent versus active by symptoms and film · isolate first · four drugs and their toxicitiesAre there symptoms or an abnormal chest film, and must the patient be isolated before any drug?

A positive purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) with no symptoms and a normal chest radiograph (CXR) is latent tuberculosis (TB) infection: not infectious, treated with a short rifamycin regimen. Cough over 2 to 3 weeks, night sweats, weight loss or an upper lobe cavity points to active TB: airborne isolation first, then 3 sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear, culture and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) to confirm it. Treat active TB with four drugs, RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), for 2 months, then rifampin and isoniazid for 4 months; never one drug alone.

What it is Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis: an asymptomatic latent stage often comes first, and in some it reactivates to active disease, most often in the lungs. Bug M. tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus: mycolic acids in its cell wall hold the stain. It lives inside macrophages and is walled off in granulomas. Spread Inhaled droplet nuclei from active pulmonary disease; a cavity holds a large number of bacteria and makes the patient especially contagious. Reactivation risk: human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, the strongest; organ transplant drugs; glucocorticoids and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) inhibitors; silicosis; diabetes; dialysis. Exposure risk: a high-prevalence area (birth there, or travel of more than 1 month), prison, a homeless shelter, substance use. Most new cases arise in Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific and Africa. Chain Inhaled bacilli macrophages take them up but cannot fuse the phagosome with the lysosome T cells build a caseating granuloma ( delayed-type, type IV, hypersensitivitySkin testThe same delayed-type response makes the PPD skin test turn hard 48 to 72 hours after injection. ) latent infection: test positive, CXR normal immunity falls: reactivation, most often in the apices, where oxygen tension is high upper lobe cavity: cough, night sweats, hemoptysis Insights No skin test or IGRA separates latent from active TB; the symptoms and the CXR do. TNF-α holds the granuloma together, so a TNF-α inhibitor can let latent TB reactivate; screen before the first dose.
Day 0droplet nuclei inhaled 2 to 12 weeksimmune containment; skin test and IGRA turn positive First 2 yearswhen most reactivation happens Lifetimeabout 5 to 15% reactivate if immunocompetent

Extrapulmonary TB Site Clue Lymph node: scrofula (tuberculous lymphadenitis) The most common extrapulmonary site Spine: Pott disease (tuberculous spondylitis) Vertebral body infection that often spreads to the next vertebra, narrowing the disc space; see Low Back Pain in an Adult. Meninges and brain Meningitis at the base of the brain, tuberculomas; see Bacterial Meningitis. Blood: miliary TB Countless 2 to 3 mm nodules through both lungs; seeds liver, spleen, adrenals, meninges Kidney Sterile pyuria: white cells with no growth on routine culture Adrenal, pericardium Addison disease; constrictive pericarditis, both chiefly in the developing world Pleura Lymphocytic effusion, very high protein, low glucose

Latent infection versus active disease State Criteria Latent TB infection Positive PPD or IGRA and no symptoms and a normal CXR; not infectious Active TB Symptoms or a CXR suggesting TB; confirmed by NAAT or culture (a positive smear supports but cannot confirm)

PPD cutoffs by risk group Induration Group 5 mm or more HIV; recent contact of an active case; fibrotic changes of old TB on CXR; organ transplant; TNF-α inhibitor; prednisone ≥15 mg/day for over 1 month 10 mm or more Injection drug use; immigrant within 5 years from a high-prevalence area; prison or homeless shelter; health care worker; diabetes; silicosis; chronic kidney diseaseIn practice: some references place end-stage kidney disease on dialysis at 5 mm.; child under 4 15 mm or more No risk factors

Urgent findings Finding Action Suspected active pulmonary TB: cough with an upper lobe cavity Airborne isolation in a negative-pressure room; staff wear a fitted N95 respirator, not a surgical mask. Precaution types by organism: Isolation Precautions. Miliary TB, TB meningitis or respiratory failure Admit and start four drugs promptly, before culture results; meningitis also gets glucocorticoids.

Weeks of cough, weight loss or a cavity Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Reactivation (secondary) pulmonary TB Cough over 2 to 3 weeks, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis; upper lobe infiltrate or cavity Airborne isolation, then 3 sputum samples for AFB smear, culture and NAAT. Primary or progressive primary TB Middle or lower lobe infiltrate with hilar nodes (Ghon complex) or effusion; no response to antibiotics Sputum AFB, culture and NAAT; a lymphocytic, high-protein pleural effusion supports TB. Pneumococcal pneumonia Acute fever, productive cough and pleuritic pain; one lobe Give antibiotics; failure to improve raises TB. Chronic histoplasmosis Upper lobe cavities and calcified nodules that mimic TB Check where the patient has lived; calcified hilar nodes may come from either. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (aspergilloma, fungus ball) An old TB cavity; hemoptysis and weight loss Image the cavity for a mass inside it. Nontuberculous mycobacteria AFB smear positive, NAAT negative Repeat AFB smear and NAAT; a second positive smear with a negative NAAT means nontuberculous mycobacteria.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Screening someone at risk with no symptoms: a contact, someone from a high-prevalence area, or before a TNF-α inhibitor, glucocorticoids or chemotherapy → PPD skin test, read at 48 to 72 hours Induration at the risk-group cutoff TB infection, latent or active; the test cannot tell which → IGRA, preferred after bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination Positive result Same meaning; BCG does not cause a false-positive IGRA Targeted tests TestResultMeans Any positive screen, or any TB symptom → Symptom review and CXR No symptoms, normal CXR Latent TB infection: treat it Symptoms or an abnormal CXR Airborne isolation, then sputum testing Once TB is diagnosed → HIV test Positive Changes the regimen and the antiretroviral timing; it also lowers the skin test cutoff Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Suspected active pulmonary TB → Sputum AFB smear: 3 samples, 1 early morning Positive Supports active TB; cannot tell TB from nontuberculous mycobacteria → Sputum NAAT Positive, with a rifampin resistance result Generally confirms pulmonary TB → Sputum mycobacterial culture Organism identified Confirms active TB and gives drug susceptibility SkipA PPD or IGRA to judge whether TB is active: neither separates latent from active, and suspected active TB goes straight to sputum testing and a CXR.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Health care worker: negative first PPD, positive on a repeat 1 to 3 weeks later A boosted old infection, not a recent conversion Treat it as latent infection once symptom review and CXR are clear. Positive PPD after a BCG vaccine given abroad (not used in the United States) Count it as true infection (Step 2 answer)In practice: the BCG effect on the skin test usually wanes after several years, and an IGRA avoids the question. Proceed as for any positive test: symptom review and CXR. HIV, especially with a CD4 (helper T cell) count under 200; fever; old age; heavy immunosuppression Anergy: a negative PPD does not exclude TB Prefer an IGRA; do not rely on a negative skin test.

Pause point A month of cough, night sweats and an upper lobe cavity on the CXR Offered as start RIPE now or send sputum and wait Isolation comes before any drug or sputum result → Airborne isolation in a negative-pressure room A positive IGRA, no symptoms, a normal CXR Offered as repeat the IGRA or four drugs No test separates latent from active; the film and symptoms do → Latent TB: a rifamycin regimen

What changes the regimen Finding Meaning Cavity on the first CXR and a positive culture at 2 months Isoniazid and rifampin for 7 more months: 9 months in all HIV diagnosed together with TB TB drugs first; antiretroviral therapy (ART) added once 2 weeks of TB drugs are done, to lower the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome; rifabutin in place of rifampin with protease inhibitors HIV with latent TB, on interacting ART Isoniazid with vitamin B6 for 9 months; rifamycins interact with ART

1 Latent TBPositive test, no symptoms, normal CXR Isoniazid plus rifapentine once weekly for 3 months, or rifampin daily for 4 months, both first line; isoniazid daily for 9 months only if neither can be taken. 2 Active TB, first 2 monthsSymptoms or an abnormal CXR; drug susceptible RIPE, started promptly once the patient is isolated, without waiting for cultures. 3 ContinuationAfter 2 months Stop pyrazinamide and ethambutol; rifampin and isoniazid for 4 more months, 6 months in all. 4 Hepatitis on treatmentSymptoms of hepatitis Stop isoniazid, rifampin and pyrazinamide; restart them one at a time.

RIPE toxicities by drug Drug Toxicity Do Rifampin Red-orange urine, sweat and tears; strong cytochrome P450 inducer: oral contraceptive and warfarin failure; hepatitis Counsel on the color change, which alone is no reason to stop it; switch the contraceptive; use rifabutin with HIV protease inhibitors Isoniazid Peripheral neuropathy from vitamin B6 loss; hepatitis; drug-induced lupus; sideroblastic anemia; seizures in severe cases Vitamin B6 for those at risk; stop isoniazid for symptomatic hepatitis (with rifampin and pyrazinamide if on them) Pyrazinamide Hyperuricemia, often; gout, rarely; hepatitis Usually mild; the drug stops after 2 months Ethambutol Optic neuritis: red-green color vision lossIn practice: a major reference describes trouble telling blue from green first; acuity may then fall., then acuity Baseline color vision and acuity, then monthly vision questions; substitute another drug if it occurs

After the diagnosis When Do Every active case Notify the health department, which traces close contacts. Close contacts of an active case PPD or IGRA now; repeat a negative test 8 to 10 weeks after the exposure; a close-contact child under 5 of a smear-positive case is treated even if negative. HIV, psychiatric illness, substance use, poor adherence Directly observed therapy: a public health worker watches each dose. Leaving airborne isolation Usually 3 negative sputum smears over 2 days, at least 1 early-morning sample. On isoniazid, rifampin or pyrazinamide Return for fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting or jaundice; liver tests then, not routinely unless liver risk factors. Mother with active, untreated TB Breastfeeding is contraindicated until it is treated.

Next step1 of 4 Booster / two-step: health care worker with a negative first PPD, positive on repeat 1–3 weeks later = old memory, not conversion · True recent conversion – treat as a contactTwo-step testing exists so that a boosted old response is not mistaken for a recent conversion. · Treat as latentA positive repeat 1 to 3 weeks after a negative first PPD is a boosted old infection, read as latent infection. · False positive from prior BCGStep 2 counts a positive PPD after BCG as true infection; boosting explains the late positive. Booster / two-step: health care worker with a negative first PPD, positive on repeat 1–3 weeks later = old memory, not conversion Treat as latent

Screening2 of 4 Window period: contact of an active case · A single PPD now onlyA single early test can be negative before the immune response forms. · PPD now and at 8–10 weeksThe immune response takes about 2 to 12 weeks to form, so a negative test soon after exposure is repeated. · IGRA now, treat only if positiveAn IGRA also turns positive only once the immune response forms; one early negative does not clear a contact. Window period: contact of an active case PPD now and at 8–10 weeksthe only time "repeat later" is correct

Screening3 of 4 Before biologics: starting a TNF-α inhibitor (rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease stem) · Chest radiograph onlyA normal CXR is expected in latent TB; only a PPD or IGRA finds it. · Screen for latent TB firstTNF-α holds granulomas together; blocking it can reactivate latent TB, so screen first. · Start the biologic and monitor symptomsWaiting for symptoms lets latent TB reactivate on the drug. Before biologics: starting a TNF-α inhibitor (rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease stem) Screen for latent TB first

Next step4 of 4 Sequencing trap: coughing + cavitary CXR · Send sputum AFB and await resultsIsolation and treatment do not wait for sputum results. · Start RIPE immediatelyFour drugs start promptly, but after the patient is isolated. · Airborne isolationSuspected active pulmonary TB is isolated first: a negative-pressure room and a respirator. Sequencing trap: coughing + cavitary CXR Airborne isolationbefore any medication is started

briefs.title: Bacterial Meningitis
briefs.sub: cell type by glucose · organism by host · when computed tomography (CT) precedes the tap · antibiotics before imaging · when to add ampicillin · dexamethasone · contact prophylaxisAre the cells neutrophils or lymphocytes, and is the glucose low?
blocks: cell type by glucose · organism by host · when computed tomography (CT) precedes the tap · antibiotics before imaging · when to add ampicillin · dexamethasone · contact prophylaxisAre the cells neutrophils or lymphocytes, and is the glucose low?

Fever with headache, a stiff neck or altered mental status in a child, or only lethargy, irritability, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle in an infant: suspect bacterial meningitis; a supple neck does not exclude it under 12 months. Blood cultures, then the lumbar puncture, then IV antibiotics; when a red flag for raised pressure or shock delays the tap, cultures and antibiotics come first and the CT after. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) decides: neutrophils with low glucose is bacterial, lymphocytes with normal glucose viral. Treat with ampicillin plus cefotaxime under 1 month, vancomycin plus ceftriaxone after, and dexamethasone with the first dose for Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) or pneumococcus.

What it is Bacterial infection of the leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid) and the subarachnoid space; lethal untreated, so even a small chance of it earns a lumbar puncture. Bug Under 1 month: group B Streptococcus (GBS), then Escherichia coli (K1 capsule strains), then Listeria monocytogenes; mnemonic newborn GEL (GBS, E. coli, Listeria). Children: Streptococcus pneumoniae. Adolescents: Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative diplococcus. Unvaccinated child: Hib, the only H. influenzae capsular type that causes meningitis. Adults: S. pneumoniae; in older adults, also Listeria and gram-negative rods; Listeria also in pregnancy or immunocompromise. Viral (aseptic) meningitis: enteroviruses, coxsackievirus and echovirus, are the most common cause of meningitis at every age. Spread Most often respiratory droplets and throat secretions; the organism most commonly reaches the meninges through the blood. Meningococcus: carriage peaks in adolescents and young adults; dormitories, military recruits; asplenia, terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9) or eculizumab. Pneumococcus and Hib: asplenia or sickle cell disease, a nearby sinus or ear infection or a CSF leak, and missed conjugate vaccines (given from 2 months). Listeria: contaminated food, the placenta or the birth canal. Ventricular shunt or neurosurgery: S. epidermidis and gram-negative rods. Chain Organism colonizes the nose and throat reaches the subarachnoid space through the blood bacterial lysis releases cytokines that open the blood-brain barrier neutrophils flood the CSF; cerebral edema raises intracranial pressure herniation; scarred arachnoid granulations that may cause hydrocephalus; hearing loss and seizures as later sequelae Insights Antibiotics sterilize the CSF, so the tap comes first when it can be done at once; when it cannot, blood cultures drawn before the first dose still name the organism. Dexamethasone protects the cochlea: it blunts the inflammation that injures cranial nerve VIII, so it goes in before or with the first antibiotic dose.

CSF patterns Diagnosis Cells Glucose Protein Bacterial Neutrophil-predominant; white cells often over 1,000/mm³ Low High NumbersMSD (Merck Sharp and Dohme) Manual: protein over 100 mg/dL; glucose under 40 mg/dL, often under 10, with a CSF to blood glucose ratio typically under 0.33. Viral Lymphocytes; neutrophils may be mixed in during the first 24 to 48 hours Normal Normal or raised Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis Lymphocytes with red cells Normal or mildly low Mildly raised Tuberculous Lymphocytes, often mixed with neutrophils Low High Fungal (cryptococcal) Lymphocytes Low High
Opening pressure is raised in bacterial, tuberculous and fungal meningitis and normal or raised in viral meningitis. Some neonates with meningitis have normal counts, so the culture decides.

Urgent findings Finding Action Papilledema, a focal deficit, a seizure or obtundation Blood cultures and antibiotics now; CT before any tap. Hypotension or shock (cardiorespiratory compromise, most often in young infants) Treat the shock, draw blood cultures and give antibiotics; the tap waits. Spreading nonblanching petechiae or purpura Meningococcemia: antibiotics without delay; check platelets and fibrinogen, typically low in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

Fever with meningeal signs or a lethargic infant Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Bacterial meningitis Neutrophils, low glucose, high protein, high opening pressure; the Gram stain may show the organism. Empiric antibiotics by age. Viral (aseptic) meningitis Late summer or fall in the United States; lymphocytes, normal glucose, normal or raised protein. CSF enterovirus polymerase chain reaction (PCR); supportive care. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis Altered mental status, seizures, aphasia or focal signs; lymphocytes with red cells; in a newborn, lethargy may be the only sign. Start IV acyclovir now; send a CSF HSV PCR to confirm. Meningococcemia Fever and myalgia, then nonblanching petechiae and purpura that spread rapidly, often on the legs; shock and DIC can follow. Blood cultures and antibiotics without waiting; droplet precautions. Tuberculous meningitis Lymphocytes or a mixed count, low glucose, high protein; basilar enhancement and hydrocephalus. CSF acid-fast stain, mycobacterial culture and PCR. Cryptococcal meningitis Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or other immunocompromise; lymphocytes with low glucose. Send a CSF antigen test. Simple febrile seizure A seizure with fever and no meningeal signs. No tap unless meningeal signs, or an unimmunized infant of 6-12 months; otherwise supportive care.

What makes it severe Finding Meaning Obtundation or coma; hypertension, bradycardia and slow breathing (Cushing triad); papilledema Raised intracranial pressure; herniation is the commonest cause of death in the acute stages Purpura with shock, low platelets and low fibrinogen Meningococcemia with DIC Shock that deepens after purpura Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: bilateral adrenal hemorrhage; the lost cortisol worsens the hypotension Low sodium Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) Neonate not improving on antibiotics Ventriculitis or brain abscess: repeat the tap and image the brain

1 NeonateUnder 1 month IV ampicillin plus cefotaxime, with or without gentamicin; cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone, because ceftriaxone raises bilirubin. WhyAmpicillin covers Listeria; cefotaxime enters the central nervous system better than gentamicin. Fever in an Infant Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn 2 Child or adultOver 1 month IV vancomycin plus ceftriaxone: ceftriaxone covers meningococcus and other gram-negatives; vancomycin is added for cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus. In practiceIn practice: once the organism and its susceptibilities are known, therapy narrows and vancomycin may stop. 3 Listeria riskOver 50, pregnancy or immunocompromise Add IV ampicillin for Listeria. 4 AdjunctSuspected Hib or pneumococcal meningitis after 6 weeks of age IV dexamethasone just before or with the first antibiotic dose, every 6 hours for 4 days, to cut hearing loss. LimitsIn adults it is best established for pneumococcal meningitis; high-dose steroids worsen meningococcal shock without meningitis. 5 HSV possibleEncephalitis signs or lymphocytes with red cells Add IV acyclovir until HSV is ruled out. 6 Shunt or neurosurgeryVentricular shunt or recent neurosurgery Vancomycin plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime.

Contacts, isolation and aftercare When Do Meningococcal disease Close contacts (household, child care in the prior 7 days, anyone exposed to oral secretions): rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone, whatever their vaccine status, ideally within 24 hours. Young childrenFor young children, rifampin by mouth or ceftriaxone by injection is the preferred choice; ciprofloxacin suits older contacts. Hib meningitis Rifampin for the household when it includes an incompletely immunized child under 4 or an infant under 12 months without the primary series. Pneumococcus or other bacteria No prophylaxis for contacts. Health care workers Prophylaxis only after managing the airway or direct exposure to respiratory secretions. Admission Droplet precautions for meningococcus and Hib until 24 hours of effective antibiotics. Isolation Precautions Every survivor Audiologic testing and developmental follow-up: hearing loss is the most common sequela in children; sensorineural loss is most common after pneumococcal meningitis. Hearing Loss and Chronic Ear Disease Recurrent or unusual Neisseria infection CH50 (total hemolytic complement) after recovery, for a terminal complement deficiency: the membrane attack complex is the main defense against Neisseria. Prevention Where given routinely, Hib and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, both from 2 months, make meningitis from these organisms rare; the schedule is in Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications

briefs.title: Vaccines in Special Populations
briefs.sub: live vaccines by CD4 count in HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) · extra vaccines by condition · HIV additions · hepatitis B serologyIs it live, and which defense has the condition removed?
blocks: live vaccines by CD4 count in HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) · extra vaccines by condition · HIV additions · hepatitis B serologyIs it live, and which defense has the condition removed?

Two checks decide most cases: whether the vaccine is live, and which defense the condition has removed. In HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), live MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella need a CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count of 200 or higher (MMR: both the count and a CD4 percentage of 15% or higher held for 6 months); LAIV (live attenuated influenza vaccine) is never given; vaccines that are not live, including recombinant zoster, go at any CD4 count. Asplenia: pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b); complement deficiency or eculizumab: meningococcal; cirrhosis: pneumococcal, hepatitis A and B; pregnancy: no MMR, varicella or LAIV.

Live vaccines can revert to a virulent form, so they are usually withheld in severe immunodeficiency (in HIV, a CD4 count under 200) and in pregnancy; inactivated vaccines follow the routine schedule, and each condition adds the vaccines its lost defense calls for.

Vaccines in HIV by CD4 count Vaccine CD4 under 200 CD4 200 or higher MMR Contraindicated Give once the count of 200 or higher and a CD4 percentage of 15% or higher have held for at least 6 months Varicella Contraindicated Give Not MMRVThe combined MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella and varicella) vaccine is not used in HIV at any severity; use the single-antigen varicella vaccine. Yellow fever Contraindicated Give with caution Live attenuated influenza (LAIV) Never Never: inactivated influenza instead BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) and oral polio Never Never Recombinant zoster Live zosterThe old live zoster vaccine was discontinued in 2020; only the recombinant vaccine is in use. Give Give

Extra vaccines by condition Condition Extra vaccines HIV Pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY (serogroups A, C, W and Y), hepatitis A and B, recombinant zoster, human papillomavirus (HPV), yearly inactivated influenza (next table) Cirrhosis or other chronic liver disease Pneumococcal; hepatitis A and B WhyThe liver makes complement, so cirrhosis loses opsonins; portosystemic shunting bypasses the Kupffer cells; hepatitis A on a cirrhotic liver can be fulminant. Asplenia, splenectomy or sickle cell disease (functional asplenia) Pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, Hib; before a planned splenectomy when possible WhyWithout splenic phagocytes, encapsulated organisms cause overwhelming bacteremia: pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b (SHiN: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis). Complement deficiency or eculizumab Meningococcal ACWY and B WhyEculizumab blocks C5; the terminal components, C5 through C9, form the membrane attack complex that kills Neisseria. Cerebrospinal fluid leak or cochlear implant Pneumococcal WhyBoth give pneumococcus direct access to the meninges. Pregnancy Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis) in every pregnancy, at 27 to 36 weeks, and inactivated influenza; no MMR, varicella or LAIV Vaccines in Pregnancy
