briefs.title: Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications
briefs.sub: sorting DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine) histories into contraindication, precaution or neither · the vaccines each visit allows and the age windows that open and closeIs the window open, and is there a named reason this child cannot have it?
blocks: sorting DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine) histories into contraindication, precaution or neither · the vaccines each visit allows and the age windows that open and closeIs the window open, and is there a named reason this child cannot have it?

Two checks at every visit: has the vaccine's age window opened for this child, and has it closed? If it is open, vaccinate unless you can name a contraindication or precaution; a history that only sounds disqualifying is neither. DTaP (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis) is contraindicated by anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component (no further doses of any component), or after encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose and with no other cause, which bars only the pertussis part: finish with DT (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids). Precautions defer or weigh the dose: a progressive or unstable neurologic disorder, such as uncontrolled seizures, or a moderate or severe acute illness; a cold with low fever is neither. Rotavirus vaccine is live and oral: never after intussusception or with SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency); the first dose by 14 weeks 6 days, no dose after 8 months 0 days. Up to date at 4 months: the child is due second doses of rotavirus, IPV (inactivated poliovirus vaccine), PCV (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine), Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) and DTaP; influenza waits for 6 months, MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) and varicella for 12 months.

A contraindication means the vaccine is not given; a precaution means defer in general, though the vaccine may still be given if its benefit is greater than its risk, for example during an outbreak; neither means vaccinate today. Live vaccines such as MMR and varicella add two bars, both in the child being vaccinated: pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency; rotavirus and nasal influenza add bars of their own (table below).

DTaP: contraindication, precaution or neither Category Histories Contraindication (any vaccine with pertussis) Anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component, so no further doses of any component Anaphylaxis · Encephalopathy within 7 days of a dose (coma, a lowered level of consciousness or prolonged seizures), with no other cause: give DT Precaution (defer or weigh) Moderate or severe acute illness, with or without feverModerate or severe illnessModerate or severe illness: an acute illness, with or without fever, that defers the dose; a fever over 39 °C or a severe illness without fever is a clear reason to delay, while a cold, even with low fever, is not. · Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a tetanus-toxoid dose · A progressive or unstable neurologic disorder (infantile spasms, uncontrolled epilepsy or progressive encephalopathy): the pertussis part waits until neurologic status is clarified and stable · Arthus-type reaction to a diphtheria- or tetanus-toxoid dose: wait at least 10 years from the last tetanus-toxoid dose Neither (vaccinate today) Reactions to an earlier dose: fever of 40.5 °C or higher within the first 48 hours; in the same 48 hours, a collapse or shock-like state (hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode) or 3 hours or more of inconsolable crying; an uncomplicated seizure in the first 3 days Older sources differThe MSD Manual and older sources list these four reactions as precautions, whereas current guidance from the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) names them among conditions incorrectly perceived as contraindications or precautions. · Family history of seizures or epilepsy; a neurologic condition that is stable or has resolved; the child's own febrile seizure · A mild illness, low fever included; a recent exposure to an infection

Other routine vaccines: when not to give Vaccine Do not give Defer Rotavirus (live, oral) Why the early cutoffThe vaccine enlarges the Peyer patches, which can act as a lead point; the risk rises with age, hence the early first dose and the cutoff at 8 months 0 days. SCID; any past intussusception; anaphylaxis to a dose or a component Moderate or severe illness, including moderate or severe vomiting or diarrhea; altered immunity other than SCID MMR and varicella (live, injected) Pregnancy or severe immunodeficiency in the child being vaccinated Vaccines in Special Populations Vaccines in Pregnancy Moderate or severe illness; blood products containing antibody within the past 11 months (the interval depends on the product) Nasal influenza (LAIV, live attenuated influenza vaccine) Under 2 years; aspirin or other salicylate therapy; immunocompromise; pregnancy; caring for a severely immunocompromised person in a protected environment Give the injected inactivated vaccine instead, from 6 months

Common histories at a vaccine visit History Ruling A cold or other mild illness, even with low fever Vaccinate today; moderate or severe illness is the precaution Egg allergy Any licensed influenza vaccine appropriate for age and health Breastfeeding Not a contraindication Pregnancy in the mother or another household contact Give MMR and varicella to the child: pregnancy bars live vaccines only in the person vaccinated Current antibiotics, or preterm birth Vaccinate; hepatitis B vaccine is an exception in some preterm infants Penicillin or another nonvaccine allergy, or relatives with allergies Vaccinate An immunosuppressed household contact Vaccinate; varicella is recommended for such contacts, and nasal influenza is avoided only beside a protected environment Fever and a mild rash 1 to 3 weeks after MMR Vaccine-strain reaction: reassure

Age windows that open or close Vaccine Window Doses Rotavirus Dose 1 between 2 months and 14 weeks 6 days, never on or after 15 weeks 0 days; nothing after 8 months 0 days Two doses of monovalent rotavirus vaccine (RV1), at 2 and 4 months, or three of pentavalent rotavirus vaccine (RV5), at 2, 4 and 6 months Influenza Each season, starting at 6 months Ages 6 months to 8 years in a first season (fewer than 2 earlier doses, or history unknown): 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart MMR and varicella First doses at 12 to 15 months and second doses at 4 to 6 years Live injected vaccines: the same day or at least 4 weeks apart

Vaccines due at each visit Visit Vaccines due Age limit that matters 2 months First doses of DTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus; the second hepatitis B dose (the first is given at birth) unless it was given at 1 month The first rotavirus dose cannot wait past 14 weeks 6 days 4 months Second doses of the same five: DTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus Influenza opens at 6 months; MMR and varicella at 12 months 6 months Third doses of DTaP and PCV; a third Hib dose unless the series used PedvaxHIB; a third rotavirus dose only with RV5; hepatitis B and IPV third doses, due between 6 and 18 months; influenza when in season No rotavirus after 8 months 0 days; a first influenza season takes 2 doses 12 to 15 months First MMR and varicella doses; hepatitis A, the first of 2 doses, given at 12 to 23 months; the fourth PCV dose and the Hib booster The live injected vaccines open at 12 months 15 to 18 months DTaP fourth dose If this dose slips to 4 years or older, at least 6 months after the third, no fifth dose is needed 4 to 6 years DTaP fifth dose; IPV, MMR and varicella last doses Before school entry; then Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis booster) from 11 years Adolescent Vaccines

Which childhood vaccines are live Class Vaccines Live attenuated Rotavirus, MMR, varicella; also nasal influenza, BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) and oral polio (no longer used in the United States) Inactivated (killed) IPV and injected influenza Toxoid Diphtheria and tetanus Subunit or conjugate Acellular pertussis, Hib and pneumococcal conjugate

Pause point Brief seizure the evening after the last DTaP dose, well since Offered as precaution or switch to DT Was it encephalopathy within 7 days, or an unstable disorder? → Neither: an uncomplicated seizure within 3 days of a dose does not bar DTaP; vaccinate today Past 15 weeks old, starting vaccines, no rotavirus yet Offered as rotavirus today or rotavirus at the next visit Has the window for the first rotavirus dose closed? → Yes, after 14 weeks 6 days: give the other 2-month vaccines without rotavirus Egg allergy with hives, due for influenza vaccine Offered as skip influenza vaccine or an egg-free vaccine only Does egg allergy bar any influenza vaccine? → No: any licensed influenza vaccine appropriate for age and health

Diagnosis1 of 13 2-month-old boy is at the well-child visit for his first vaccines His father has epilepsy, and an older sister had seizures with fever His mother asks to skip the pertussis vaccine development and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 140/min · PrecautionA precaution is the child's own unstable neurologic disorder or illness, not a relative's. · NeitherA family history of seizures or epilepsy is neither: vaccinate today. · ContraindicationContraindications are anaphylaxis, or encephalopathy within 7 days of a dose, in the child. 2-month-old boy is at the well-child visit for his first vaccines His father has epilepsy, and an older sister had seizures with fever His mother asks to skip the pertussis vaccine development and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 140/min Neithera family history of seizures or epilepsy is neither a contraindication nor a precaution: vaccinate today. The mother's request is a matter for counseling; it does not change the classification

A precaution is weighed; this is not

DTaP and the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine are 2-month vaccines he is due for

Moderate or severe acute illness is the precaution

Next step5 of 13 12-month-old boy is at his well-child visit with his mother She is 20 weeks pregnant and asks whether his vaccines could harm the fetus Healthy; up to date on infant vaccines examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 118/min · Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine today; varicella vaccine after deliveryVaricella, like MMR, is given to the child of a pregnant mother. · Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines todayPregnancy bars live vaccines only in the person vaccinated: give both today. · Defer measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines until after deliveryThe mother's pregnancy is not a reason to defer; deferring leaves the child unprotected. 12-month-old boy is at his well-child visit with his mother She is 20 weeks pregnant and asks whether his vaccines could harm the fetus Healthy; up to date on infant vaccines examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 118/min Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines todaythe CDC lists pregnancy of the recipient's mother or another close or household contact as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution for both vaccines. Pregnancy contraindicates them only in the person being vaccinated, so neither is deferred

Diagnosis6 of 13 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose Clusters of sudden flexion spasms began 3 weeks ago and continue daily despite treatment She has lost the ability to roll over T 36.8 °C · HR 122/min · NeitherOnly stable or resolved neurologic conditions are neither. · ContraindicationContraindications are anaphylaxis, or encephalopathy within 7 days of a dose. · PrecautionInfantile spasms are a progressive neurologic disorder: a precaution, so defer until stable. 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose Clusters of sudden flexion spasms began 3 weeks ago and continue daily despite treatment She has lost the ability to roll over T 36.8 °C · HR 122/min Precautioninfantile spasms are a progressive neurologic disorder: a precaution, so defer DTaP until neurologic status is clarified and stable. A brief seizure within 3 days of a dose, or a stable neurologic condition, would be neither

Next step7 of 13 7-month-old girl is at a well-child visit in November Up to date on her infant vaccines She has never received influenza vaccine growth and examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 130/min · Influenza vaccine at her 12-month visitInfluenza vaccine starts at 6 months; waiting for 12 months misses this season. · Influenza vaccine today and a second dose in 4 weeksA first influenza season from 6 months to 8 years needs 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart. · A single influenza vaccine dose todayOne dose is too few in a first season for a child aged 6 months to 8 years. 7-month-old girl is at a well-child visit in November Up to date on her infant vaccines She has never received influenza vaccine growth and examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 130/min Influenza vaccine today and a second dose in 4 weeksinfluenza vaccine starts at 6 months, every season; a child aged 6 months to 8 years with fewer than 2 earlier doses, or an unknown history, gets 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart. Waiting for the 12-month visit misses this season

Older sources called it a precaution

Next step9 of 13 12-month-old girl returns 2 weeks after her 12-month visit She received measles-mumps-rubella vaccine at that visit; varicella vaccine was out of stock Healthy; no immune problems examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 120/min · Varicella vaccine in 2 weeksLive injected vaccines not given the same day need at least 4 weeks between them. · Varicella vaccine at 4 to 6 yearsThe first varicella dose is due at 12 to 15 months, not 4 to 6 years. · Varicella vaccine todayTwo weeks after MMR is too soon; that varicella dose would not count. 12-month-old girl returns 2 weeks after her 12-month visit She received measles-mumps-rubella vaccine at that visit; varicella vaccine was out of stock Healthy; no immune problems examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 120/min Varicella vaccine in 2 weeksinjected live vaccines not given on the same day need at least 4 weeks between them; varicella vaccine given today, 2 weeks after measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, would not count and would have to be repeated at least 4 weeks later. Waiting until 4 to 6 years skips the first varicella dose, due at 12 to 15 months

Diagnosis10 of 13 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Within 10 minutes of her 2-month dose she developed hives, wheezing and low blood pressure She received epinephrine in the clinic T 37.0 °C · HR 132/min · NeitherHives, wheezing and hypotension within minutes are anaphylaxis, not a mild reaction. · ContraindicationAnaphylaxis after a previous dose is a contraindication to further doses. · PrecautionA precaution is weighed against benefit; anaphylaxis is not. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Within 10 minutes of her 2-month dose she developed hives, wheezing and low blood pressure She received epinephrine in the clinic T 37.0 °C · HR 132/min Contraindicationhives, wheezing and hypotension within minutes of a dose is anaphylaxis: a severe allergic reaction after a previous dose or to a vaccine component contraindicates that vaccine

Screening11 of 13 12-month-old boy is at a well-child visit Up to date on his vaccines, including the rotavirus series Healthy, with normal growth and development examination normal; no immune problems T 36.7 °C · HR 118/min · Measles-mumps-rubella onlyVaricella is due at 12 to 15 months with MMR. · RotavirusRotavirus is never given after 8 months 0 days. · Measles-mumps-rubella and varicellaMMR and varicella are the live vaccines first given at 12 to 15 months. 12-month-old boy is at a well-child visit Up to date on his vaccines, including the rotavirus series Healthy, with normal growth and development examination normal; no immune problems T 36.7 °C · HR 118/min Measles-mumps-rubella and varicellaMMR and varicella are the live injected vaccines first given at 12 to 15 months, with second doses at 4 to 6 years; the rotavirus series ended by 8 months 0 days

Diagnosis12 of 13 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Six hours after her 2-month dose she had a brief seizure that stopped on its own Since then she has been well, with normal development T 37.0 °C · HR 135/min · PrecautionUncontrolled seizures or a progressive disorder is the precaution; one brief seizure is not. · ContraindicationContraindications are anaphylaxis, or encephalopathy within 7 days of a dose. · NeitherAn uncomplicated seizure within 3 days of a dose is neither: vaccinate today. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Six hours after her 2-month dose she had a brief seizure that stopped on its own Since then she has been well, with normal development T 37.0 °C · HR 135/min Neithera seizure within 3 days of a previous dose is listed by the CDC as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution: vaccinate today. Older sources called it a precaution. Uncontrolled seizures or a progressive neurologic disorder would be the precaution

Diagnosis13 of 13 4-month-old boy is due for his 4-month vaccines Admitted yesterday with pneumonia; needs supplemental oxygen tachypneic with right-sided crackles T 39.2 °C · HR 170/min · oxygen saturation 91% on room air · NeitherOnly a mild illness is neither; pneumonia needing oxygen is moderate to severe. · PrecautionModerate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is a precaution: defer until recovered. · ContraindicationIllness is never a DTaP contraindication; those are anaphylaxis and encephalopathy. 4-month-old boy is due for his 4-month vaccines Admitted yesterday with pneumonia; needs supplemental oxygen tachypneic with right-sided crackles T 39.2 °C · HR 170/min · oxygen saturation 91% on room air Precautiona moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is a precaution: in general defer until he recovers. A mild illness, such as a cold with low fever, is neither

In January 2026 the CDC moved childhood rotavirus and influenza vaccines from routine to shared clinical decision-making. A federal court stayed that change in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts is the 2025 schedule, which lists both vaccines as routine; check the CDC site for the current schedule. The AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) publishes its own schedule and opposed the change, and the NBME item treats rotavirus as a routine 4-month vaccine.

4-month-old girl at a well-child visit in October Uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery; vaccines up to date Normal growth and development for age vital signs normal normal examination Immunization against which disease is most appropriate at this time? Competing answers Chickenpox: a routine live childhood vaccine; but the first varicella dose is not given until 12 months. Measles-mumps-rubella: routine and live, like rotavirus; but the first dose is at 12 months. Shingles: the same virus as chickenpox; but zoster vaccine is for adults from age 50; the NBME explanation, an older source, says 60. Down to two: rotavirus or influenza. Rotavirus: up to date at 4 months means the 2-month doses were given, so the second doses are due, rotavirus among them. The October date is a seasonal cue for influenza, but at 4 months she is below its 6-month age limit. The options form an age ladder, from rotavirus at 2 months through MMR and varicella at 12 months to zoster at 50.

Adolescent Vaccinescovers the 11 to 12 year visit and influenza timing by season Vaccines in Special Populationscovers live vaccines in HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), asplenia and immunodeficiency Vaccines in Pregnancycovers Tdap and influenza in pregnancy and the live vaccines it bars Anaphylaxiscovers treating a severe allergic reaction to a vaccine Adolescent Vaccines covers the 11 to 12 year visit and influenza timing by season. Vaccines in Special Populations covers live vaccines in HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), asplenia and immunodeficiency. Vaccines in Pregnancy covers Tdap and influenza in pregnancy and the live vaccines it bars. Anaphylaxis covers treating a severe allergic reaction to a vaccine.

Check the child's age against each vaccine's age window before the season or the disease; a vaccine whose window has not opened, or has closed, is not given at this visit. Then vaccinate unless you can name the criterion that makes the child ineligible.

briefs.title: Cervicitis and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
briefs.sub: chlamydia and gonorrhea at the cervix, then ascent to the upper tract · treat on the exam finding, before the test returns; the threshold is low by designIs there cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, is she pregnant, and does she meet an admission criterion?
blocks: chlamydia and gonorrhea at the cervix, then ascent to the upper tract · treat on the exam finding, before the test returns; the threshold is low by designIs there cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, is she pregnant, and does she meet an admission criterion?

A mucopurulent discharge and a friable cervix, with no pelvic tenderness, is cervicitis. Pelvic pain with any one of cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness and no other cause is pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Both are clinical diagnoses, usually treated at the same visit: order a pregnancy test and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for chlamydia and gonorrhea, but do not wait for the NAAT in PID, or in cervicitis at increased risk. Cervicitis at increased risk: ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. Outpatient PID: ceftriaxone once, then doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days. Admit for pregnancy, an abscess, severe illness or no response to oral therapy.

What it is Infection of the endocervical glands (cervicitis) that can ascend to the uterus, tubes and ovaries (PID, also called salpingo-oophoritis), usually from a sexually transmitted infection (STI). Bug Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D to K), the most common cause: an obligate intracellular bacterium that Gram stains poorly; subacute, so often missed. Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus: acute, with a creamy purulent discharge. The two often coinfect. PID is often polymicrobial: anaerobes and bacterial vaginosis flora join the two, which is why metronidazole is in the PID regimen. Spread Sexual contact. The strongest PID risk is multiple sexual partners; also age under 25 (non-modifiable), a new partner, or a partner with an STI or other partners. Rare before menarche, after menopause and in pregnancy. Chain Endocervical infection: mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix ascent through the uterus to the tubes: endometritis, salpingitis cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness; fever tubo-ovarian abscess, peritonitis, or perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome) tubal scarring may follow: infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain Insights Tenderness marks ascent, not infection: a cervix with no motion tenderness can still be infected, and a negative NAAT does not exclude PID, since only about half of cases test positive. The low threshold is deliberate: untreated mild PID still scars the tubes, and starting antibiotics does not hinder the workup of the alternatives.

PID: a presumptive diagnosis Criteria What counts Who A sexually active young woman, or another woman at risk for STIs, with pelvic or lower abdominal pain and no other cause Minimum: any one Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness or adnexal tenderness Additional: raise specificity Oral temperature above 38.3 °C; mucopurulent discharge or friability; abundant white cells on saline microscopy; raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP); documented gonorrhea or chlamydia

Cervicitis Criteria What counts Two major signs Mucopurulent endocervical discharge; friability, bleeding when touched with a swab Absent Cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness; fever. Any of these points to PID

Urgent findings Finding Action Positive pregnancy test with pelvic pain Consider ectopic pregnancy first: ultrasound; see Ectopic Pregnancy. Suspected ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess: worsening pain, peritoneal signs, shock Immediate laparoscopy or laparotomy. A surgical cause such as appendicitis cannot be excluded Surgical evaluation now; admit.

Pelvic pain or discharge in a young woman Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Cervicitis (chlamydia, gonorrhea) Most commonly silent; when not, mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix, postcoital or intermenstrual spotting; no pelvic tenderness, no fever NAAT; treat that day if she is at increased risk. PID (salpingo-oophoritis) Pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness; often fever and discharge Start antibiotics now; do not wait for the NAAT. Ectopic pregnancy, can't miss Missed period, then one-sided pain; positive human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), no intrauterine pregnancy Pregnancy test in every case; transvaginal ultrasound if positive. Tubo-ovarian abscess PID with an adnexal mass on exam or ultrasound Admit for intravenous antibiotics. Ovarian torsion (adnexal torsion) Sudden severe unilateral pain with an adnexal mass; vomiting; usually afebrile Doppler ultrasound; normal flow does not exclude it when suspicion is high. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis) Right upper quadrant pain that may come with PID; it can mimic cholecystitis Pelvic exam for salpingitis; ultrasound if needed. Appendicitis Pain that starts periumbilical and moves to the McBurney point; a normal cervix Surgical evaluation. Postpartum endometritis Most often 24 to 72 hours after delivery: typically lower abdominal pain and uterine tenderness, then fever Treat with intravenous clindamycin plus gentamicin, first line. Chlamydial urethritis Dysuria; leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative; cervical discharge NAAT; urine culture shows no growth. Pyelonephritis Fever with costovertebral angle tenderness and pyuria Urinalysis and urine culture; no cervical findings. Trichomoniasis Strawberry cervix: punctate cervical hemorrhages Test the vaginal fluid, and check for bacterial vaginosis as well. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) cervicitis Cervical ulcers or erosions, vulvar vesicles Treat with antivirals; they shorten symptoms but do not clear the infection.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Every woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain or discharge → Urine or serum hCG Positive Ultrasound for ectopic pregnancy; pregnancy changes the PID plan → Speculum exam Mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix Cervicitis: treat now if she is at increased risk → Bimanual exam Tender on moving the cervix, or a tender uterus or adnexa The infection has ascended: presumptive PID; start antibiotics now Targeted tests TestResultMeans Discharge whose source is unclear, or to support PID → Saline microscopy of vaginal fluid Abundant white blood cells Supports PID; no white cells, with normal discharge, makes it unlikely Dysuria → Urinalysis Leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative Points to urethritis from chlamydia, not a bladder infection Severe illness, an adnexal mass, or no response in 48 to 72 hours → Transvaginal ultrasound Complex adnexal mass Tubo-ovarian abscess: admit Any STI diagnosis → Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and syphilis tests Reactive A coexisting STI Diagnostic test TestResultMeans To name the organism, in both diagnoses: a cervical, vaginal or urine sample → NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea Positive for either Names the organism; PID treatment does not wait for it, nor does cervicitis treatment at increased risk Negative Does not exclude PID: about half of cases test negative Still unclear after imaging, and no response to antibiotics → Laparoscopy Purulent peritoneal material Confirms PID SkipUrine culture for dysuria with cervical discharge: it detects neither organism and often grows nothing. Ultrasound before antibiotics in uncomplicated PID: normal, and it delays treatment. Gram stain of a cervical swab: not recommended at that site.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Right upper quadrant pain, worse with breathing, that may follow PID Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome): violin-string adhesions on the liver capsule Examine the pelvis for salpingitis; it may mimic cholecystitis, but the exam usually tells them apart. Asymptomatic, sexually active, under 25 A routine screen, not a workup NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea. Cervicitis that persists after treatment Reinfection, or Mycoplasma genitalium Repeat the NAAT and test for M. genitalium.

Pause point Pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness; the NAAT is pending Offered as wait for the NAAT or pelvic ultrasound first The minimum criteria are met, and neither test could change today's plan → Start PID antibiotics now Chlamydia on a screen, gonorrhea negative, not pregnant Offered as ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or no treatment without symptoms Gonorrhea is excluded, and a silent infection still scars → Doxycycline alone for 7 days

Outpatient or admit Finding Meaning Mild to moderate PID, none of the findings below Outpatient treatment Pregnancy Admit Tubo-ovarian abscess Admit; drain if it fails antibiotics Severe illness, or oral temperature above 38.5 °C Admit Vomiting, or cannot follow an oral regimen Admit No response to oral therapy within 72 hours Admit, confirm the diagnosis, give intravenous therapy A surgical cause not excluded Admit

1 Cervicitis, presumptiveAt increased risk, or follow-up uncertain Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days; azithromycin if she cannot take doxycycline (Step 2 answer)In practice: the guideline gives doxycycline to all and adds ceftriaxone when she is at risk for gonorrhea or lives where it is common.. 2 Chlamydia aloneConfirmed, gonorrhea excluded, not pregnant Doxycycline for 7 days, first line; azithromycin 1 g once, second line. 3 PregnancyChlamydia or gonorrhea in pregnancy Azithromycin 1 g once for chlamydia, in place of doxycycline; ceftriaxone once for gonorrhea, as outside pregnancy. 4 PID, outpatientNo admission finding Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once, then doxycycline 100 mg and metronidazole 500 mgOlder question banksSome older question banks add metronidazole only for a tubo-ovarian abscess; current regimens give it to every patient, for the anaerobes., each orally twice daily for 14 days. 5 PID, inpatientAny admission finding Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 hours with doxycycline and metronidazole every 12 hours, continued until she has been afebrile for 24 hours, then oral therapy to complete 14 days. 6 Abscess not respondingIncomplete response, or larger than 7 cm Image-guided drainage; laparoscopy or laparotomy when needed.
Ceftriaxone 500 mg becomes 1 g at 150 kg or more when gonorrhea is treated.

After the diagnosis When Do Partners, after PID or a bacterial STI Test and treat everyone with sexual contact in the past 60 days, or the most recent partner; expedited partner therapy (a prescription she delivers) is an option. Until treatment is complete No sex until she and her partners are treated. Confirmed chlamydia or gonorrhea Retest 3 months after treatment; reinfection is common. Treated in pregnancy Test of cure 2 weeks after treatment (Step 2 answer)In practice: current guidelines advise a chlamydia test of cure about 4 weeks after treatment in pregnancy.. Confirmed gonorrhea, chlamydia or syphilis Report to the health department. Outpatient PID Reassess within 72 hours; no improvement means admission. PID with an intrauterine device Leave the device in; consider removal only if she does not improve within 48 to 72 hours. Sexually active and under 25, or older and at increased risk Screen every year with NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea, even with a normal exam: most infections are silent. Due for cervical cancer screening Pap or human papillomavirus testing on its own schedule; see Cervical Cancer Screening.

Next step1 of 15 17-year-old girl has had sudden pelvic pain since yesterday Sexually active; no other cause found cervical motion tenderness purulent cervical discharge no adnexal mass on bimanual exam T 39 °C · HR 104/min · urine pregnancy test negative · Start empiric antibiotics nowPelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness and no other cause meets the minimum criteria, so treatment starts now. · Obtain a pelvic ultrasound firstUltrasound is normal in uncomplicated PID and only delays treatment. · Await the cervical nucleic acid amplification test resultThe NAAT is positive in only about half of PID and cannot change today's decision. 17-year-old girl has had sudden pelvic pain since yesterday Sexually active; no other cause found cervical motion tenderness purulent cervical discharge no adnexal mass on bimanual exam T 39 °C · HR 104/min · urine pregnancy test negative Start empiric antibiotics nowpelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness and no other cause meets the minimum criteria, so presumptive treatment starts now. The purulent discharge and an oral temperature above 38.3 °C add specificity, and above 38.5 °C she meets an admission criterion. A pelvic ultrasound is normal in uncomplicated disease and delays treatment; the amplification test is positive in only about half, so neither result could change today's decision

Next step2 of 15 22-year-old woman has 1 week of vaginal discharge New male partner 2 months ago mucopurulent discharge at the cervical os cervix bleeds on contact with the swab no cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative · Await NAAT results before treatingUnder 25 with a new partner she is at increased risk, so treatment does not wait for the NAAT. · Ceftriaxone plus doxycyclineMucopurulent discharge and a friable cervix at increased risk: cover both organisms at the visit. · Azithromycin plus doxycyclineBoth drugs cover chlamydia, and gonorrhea is left untreated. 22-year-old woman has 1 week of vaginal discharge New male partner 2 months ago mucopurulent discharge at the cervical os cervix bleeds on contact with the swab no cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative Ceftriaxone plus doxycyclinemucopurulent discharge and a cervix that bleeds easily on swab contact are the two major signs. Under 25 with a new partner she is at increased risk, so presumptive treatment for both organisms is given at the visit while the nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) is pending: doxycycline for chlamydia, and ceftriaxone for gonorrhea, considered when she is at risk or lives in a high-prevalence community. Sexually active and under 25, she is in the group screened annually for gonorrhea. Azithromycin plus doxycycline covers chlamydia twice and leaves gonorrhea untreated

Diagnosis3 of 15 23-year-old woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain Mucopurulent vaginal discharge for 2 weeks No pregnancy or delivery in the past year uterine and adnexal tenderness cervical motion tenderness T 38.4 °C · HR 96/min · urine pregnancy test negative · Pelvic inflammatory diseasePelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness and no other cause is PID. · Postpartum endometritisPostpartum endometritis follows a recent delivery. · Acute cervicitisCervicitis has discharge and a friable cervix without pelvic tenderness. 23-year-old woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain Mucopurulent vaginal discharge for 2 weeks No pregnancy or delivery in the past year uterine and adnexal tenderness cervical motion tenderness T 38.4 °C · HR 96/min · urine pregnancy test negative Pelvic inflammatory diseasepelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness and no other cause meets the minimum criteria: the infection has ascended from the cervix. Cervicitis alone lacks that tenderness, and postpartum endometritis needs a recent delivery

Next step4 of 15 24-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a positive screening test for chlamydia First pregnancy; no symptoms Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg · Ceftriaxone aloneCeftriaxone treats gonorrhea, not chlamydia. · DoxycyclineDoxycycline is avoided in pregnancy; azithromycin replaces it. · AzithromycinAzithromycin 1 g once is the chlamydia regimen in pregnancy. 24-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has a positive screening test for chlamydia First pregnancy; no symptoms Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg Azithromycinazithromycin 1 g orally once is the recommended regimen in pregnancy; doxycycline is not the recommended regimen in pregnancy and is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of tooth discoloration, and ceftriaxone alone treats gonorrhea, not chlamydia. In pregnancy a test of cure follows: 2 weeks after treatment is the Step 2 answer, and current guidelines say about 4 weeks

Next step5 of 15 19-year-old woman has 4 days of pelvic pain and fever Sexually active; urine pregnancy test negative cervical motion and left adnexal tenderness 6-cm tubo-ovarian abscess on transvaginal ultrasound T 38.9 °C · HR 108/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg · Admit for intravenous antibioticsA tubo-ovarian abscess is an admission finding: intravenous antibiotics first. · Outpatient ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazoleOutpatient therapy is for PID with no admission finding. · Immediate laparotomySurgery is for a ruptured abscess or one that fails antibiotics. 19-year-old woman has 4 days of pelvic pain and fever Sexually active; urine pregnancy test negative cervical motion and left adnexal tenderness 6-cm tubo-ovarian abscess on transvaginal ultrasound T 38.9 °C · HR 108/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg Admit for intravenous antibioticsa tubo-ovarian abscess is a hospitalization criterion, and more than 24 hours of inpatient observation is recommended: intravenous antibiotics first, with drainage if the abscess fails medical therapy. Outpatient oral therapy is for women without an admission criterion, and laparotomy is not the first step

Diagnosis6 of 15 21-year-old woman has 4 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner no costovertebral angle tenderness mucopurulent cervical discharge on speculum exam Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive · nitrite negative · Acute simple cystitisCystitis brings no cervical discharge. · Chlamydial urethritis with cervicitisLeukocyte esterase without nitrite plus cervical discharge in a sexually active woman is chlamydial urethritis. · PyelonephritisPyelonephritis brings fever and costovertebral angle tenderness. 21-year-old woman has 4 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner no costovertebral angle tenderness mucopurulent cervical discharge on speculum exam Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive · nitrite negative Chlamydial urethritis with cervicitisleukocyte esterase without nitrite in a sexually active woman should prompt a pelvic exam for chlamydia: atypicals do not reduce nitrate, and the cervical discharge reframes the urinary tract infection. Send a NAAT; a urine culture often shows no growth. Cystitis lacks the discharge, and pyelonephritis brings costovertebral angle tenderness

Next step7 of 15 24-year-old woman has 2 days of lower abdominal pain Copper intrauterine device placed 2 years ago cervical motion and uterine tenderness no adnexal mass on ultrasound T 37.9 °C · HR 90/min · urine pregnancy test negative · Remove the device after completing 14 daysRemoval is considered only for no improvement, not after a full course. · Treat and leave the device in placeThe device can stay in during treatment; removal is considered only if she does not improve. · Remove the device before starting antibioticsRemoving the device first is not needed to treat PID. 24-year-old woman has 2 days of lower abdominal pain Copper intrauterine device placed 2 years ago cervical motion and uterine tenderness no adnexal mass on ultrasound T 37.9 °C · HR 90/min · urine pregnancy test negative Treat and leave the device in placethe intrauterine device does not need to be removed: treat with close clinical follow-up, and consider removal only if there is no improvement within 48 to 72 hours. All contraceptive methods can be continued during treatment

Next step8 of 15 25-year-old woman has fever and lower abdominal pain 3 days after vaginal delivery Membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery uterine tenderness foul-smelling lochia T 38.7 °C · HR 104/min · BP 116/70 mm Hg · Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazoleTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is not a regimen for endometritis or PID. · Ceftriaxone plus doxycyclineCeftriaxone plus doxycycline targets gonorrhea and chlamydia, not polymicrobial postpartum infection. · Clindamycin plus gentamicinFever and uterine tenderness days after delivery is postpartum endometritis: clindamycin plus gentamicin. 25-year-old woman has fever and lower abdominal pain 3 days after vaginal delivery Membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery uterine tenderness foul-smelling lochia T 38.7 °C · HR 104/min · BP 116/70 mm Hg Clindamycin plus gentamicinfever with uterine tenderness days after delivery, after prolonged rupture of membranes, is polymicrobial ascent from the lower genital or gastrointestinal tract; first-line treatment is intravenous clindamycin plus gentamicin, not an STI regimen. Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline treats gonorrhea and chlamydia, and TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) is not a regimen for gonorrhea, chlamydia or PID

Next step9 of 15 22-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has 2 days of pelvic pain Intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound mucopurulent cervical discharge cervical motion and adnexal tenderness T 38.1 °C · HR 98/min · Azithromycin alone as an outpatientAzithromycin alone leaves gonorrhea untreated, and pregnancy still needs admission. · Hospitalize for intravenous antibioticsPregnancy is an admission finding for PID. · Outpatient ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazoleOutpatient therapy is wrong in pregnancy, whatever the regimen. 22-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has 2 days of pelvic pain Intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound mucopurulent cervical discharge cervical motion and adnexal tenderness T 38.1 °C · HR 98/min Hospitalize for intravenous antibioticspregnancy is itself a hospitalization criterion: suspected ascending infection in pregnancy carries a high risk of maternal morbidity and preterm delivery, so she is admitted for intravenous antimicrobials in consultation with an infectious disease specialist. Outpatient therapy is wrong whatever the regimen because pregnancy mandates admission, and azithromycin alone also leaves gonorrhea untreated

Diagnosis10 of 15 17-year-old girl has 2 days of right upper quadrant pain that worsens with deep breaths Treated last week for lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness gallbladder normal on ultrasound T 38.2 °C · HR 96/min · chest radiograph normal · Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndromeRight upper quadrant pain after PID with a normal gallbladder is perihepatitis. · Acute cholecystitisCholecystitis would show on the gallbladder ultrasound. · Right lower lobe pneumonia with pleurisyA lower lobe pneumonia would show on the chest radiograph. 17-year-old girl has 2 days of right upper quadrant pain that worsens with deep breaths Treated last week for lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness gallbladder normal on ultrasound T 38.2 °C · HR 96/min · chest radiograph normal Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndromethe pelvic infection reached the liver capsule: perihepatitis with violin-string adhesions, which gives right upper quadrant pleuritic pain. Cholecystitis would show on the gallbladder ultrasound, and a lower lobe pneumonia on the chest radiograph

Next step11 of 15 18-year-old woman has worsening pelvic pain 72 hours after starting outpatient therapy Ceftriaxone injection, then oral doxycycline and metronidazole persistent cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 38.6 °C · HR 106/min · urine pregnancy test negative · Admit for intravenous therapy and reassess the diagnosisNo improvement within 72 hours of oral therapy means admission and a check of the diagnosis. · Add azithromycin and continue the oral regimen at homeAdding azithromycin keeps a failing outpatient plan. · Extend the oral course to 21 daysExtending a failing oral course keeps a failing plan. 18-year-old woman has worsening pelvic pain 72 hours after starting outpatient therapy Ceftriaxone injection, then oral doxycycline and metronidazole persistent cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 38.6 °C · HR 106/min · urine pregnancy test negative Admit for intravenous therapy and reassess the diagnosisno clinical improvement within 72 hours of outpatient intramuscular or oral therapy calls for hospitalization, assessment of the antimicrobial regimen and additional diagnostics, including consideration of diagnostic laparoscopy for an alternative diagnosis. Extending the oral course or adding azithromycin keeps a failing outpatient plan

Next step12 of 15 19-year-old woman has a positive screening test for chlamydia No symptoms; routine screening at her annual visit Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative · Ceftriaxone plus doxycyclineCeftriaxone is not needed once gonorrhea is excluded. · Doxycycline aloneConfirmed chlamydia with gonorrhea excluded, not pregnant: doxycycline for 7 days. · Observation without treatmentA silent positive screen is still treated, because silent infection still causes sequelae. 19-year-old woman has a positive screening test for chlamydia No symptoms; routine screening at her annual visit Same test negative for gonorrhea normal pelvic exam Afebrile · urine pregnancy test negative Doxycycline aloneconfirmed chlamydia alone in a nonpregnant patient is treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days; ceftriaxone is not needed once gonorrhea has been tested for and excluded. Treat partners from the previous 60 days, and retest her about 3 months after treatment; a test of cure is not advised

Next step13 of 15 20-year-old woman has 4 days of lower abdominal pain Starting outpatient treatment today; no other cause found Last sexual intercourse 3 weeks ago, with her only partner cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 37.9 °C · urine pregnancy test negative · Evaluate, test and treat the partner nowPartners from the past 60 days are tested and treated now, whatever her results. · Treat her partner only after her own NAAT returns positivePartner treatment does not wait for her test results. · No partner treatment is neededUntreated partners reinfect her; reinfection is common. 20-year-old woman has 4 days of lower abdominal pain Starting outpatient treatment today; no other cause found Last sexual intercourse 3 weeks ago, with her only partner cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness T 37.9 °C · urine pregnancy test negative Evaluate, test and treat the partner nowpelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness and no other cause is presumptive PID, so anyone who had sexual contact with her during the 60 days before symptom onset is evaluated, tested and presumptively treated for chlamydia and gonorrhea, regardless of the cause or pathogens found; if her last intercourse was more than 60 days ago, the most recent partner is treated

Diagnosis14 of 15 16-year-old girl has sudden severe right pelvic pain that began 3 hours ago Vomited twice tender right adnexal mass ultrasound: enlarged, edematous right ovary with reduced Doppler flow Afebrile · HR 112/min · urine pregnancy test negative · Ruptured ovarian cystReduced flow to an enlarged, edematous ovary points to torsion, not a ruptured cyst. · Ovarian torsionSudden severe one-sided pain, vomiting, an adnexal mass and reduced Doppler flow is torsion. · Pelvic inflammatory diseasePID brings cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness, often with fever. 16-year-old girl has sudden severe right pelvic pain that began 3 hours ago Vomited twice tender right adnexal mass ultrasound: enlarged, edematous right ovary with reduced Doppler flow Afebrile · HR 112/min · urine pregnancy test negative Ovarian torsionsudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting, an adnexal mass and no fever: Doppler ultrasound may show absent or reduced flow, though complete loss of flow is not necessary and preserved flow does not exclude it when suspicion is high; then laparoscopy. Pelvic inflammatory disease findings include cervical motion, uterine and bilateral adnexal tenderness, and ovarian edema, enlargement and abnormal flow are among the most sensitive ultrasound findings of torsion

Screening15 of 15 17-year-old girl is starting treatment today for pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness Cervical NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia sent No earlier testing for sexually transmitted infections T 38.0 °C · urine pregnancy test negative · HIV and syphilisEvery woman with an STI diagnosis such as PID is also tested for HIV and syphilis. · Hepatitis C aloneHepatitis C testing alone misses the recommended HIV and syphilis tests. · No additional testing is indicatedAn STI diagnosis always calls for HIV and syphilis testing. 17-year-old girl is starting treatment today for pelvic pain with cervical motion tenderness Cervical NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia sent No earlier testing for sexually transmitted infections T 38.0 °C · urine pregnancy test negative HIV and syphilisevery woman with this diagnosis is tested for gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV and syphilis, and a woman with chlamydial or gonococcal infection is retested 3 months after treatment. Hepatitis C testing alone misses the infections recommended here

16-year-old girl seen with her mother for a routine health maintenance visit Previously healthy; takes no medications; immunizations current Periods come every 28 to 35 days, irregularly; last one 3 weeks ago No tobacco, alcohol or illicit drugs One male partner for the past year; no condom use Family history: breast cancer in her mother at age 40 height 163 cm · weight 65 kg · body mass index 25 kg/m² · vital signs normal breasts: no masses, no nipple discharge external genitalia normal; no vaginal discharge sexual maturity rating 5 for breasts and pubic hair Most appropriate screening test now? Competing answers Mammography: her mother's breast cancer at 40 is the planted cue; but routine mammography starts at 40, not in adolescence. Fasting serum glucose: a body mass index of 25; but that alone does not meet the adolescent diabetes screening bar, which needs overweight plus risk factors such as insulin resistance. Hemoglobin concentration: irregular menses are the planted cue; but routine iron deficiency anemia screening is not a US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation. Down to two: a Pap smear or chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT. NAAT for both organisms: every sexually active woman under 25 is screened, even with no discharge and a normal exam, because most infections are silent and the two often coinfect. Cervical cytology starts at 21 whatever the sexual history.

Pt toddler with intensive care unit (ICU)-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic membrane perforation with otorrhea, weight below the 3rd percentile Labs immunoglobulin M (IgM) 450, immunoglobulin G (IgG) 250, immunoglobulin A (IgA) 24; neutropenia (15% of 9,000) Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned CD40 ligand deficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic perforation with otorrhea, and weight below the 3rd percentile establish a primary immunodeficiency rather than ordinary toddler illness. The infection history does not show which one. The panel shows IgM 450 against IgG 250 and IgA 24. XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) requires IgM to be low, and CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) requires it to be low or normal. Selective IgA deficiency and Job syndrome require a normal IgM. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) require a non-immunologic finding this child does not have: microthrombocytopenia and an inverted CD4/CD8, respectively. An isolated elevation of IgM with everything downstream absent is class-switch failure. CD40 ligand on the T cell cannot engage CD40 on the B cell, so the B cell stays locked on its native isotype. The neutropenia (15% of 9,000) is a confirmatory detail: it accompanies CD40 ligand deficiency and is not part of XLA or CVID.

Class switching (isotype switch recombination) the CD40L(T cell)–CD40(B cell) interaction that lets an IgM-committed B cell rearrange to IgG, IgA, or immunoglobulin E (IgE); when it fails, IgM is preserved or elevated and every other isotype falls The CD40L signature B cells normal, IgM ↑, IgG ↓, IgA ↓, IgE ↓. B and T cell counts are normal; they are dysfunctional, not absent The B-cell count is the first gate low or absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia; normal B cells → the block is downstream of B-cell development, and the isotype pattern names it

IgM 450 with IgG 250 and IgA 24 class-switch failure; simultaneously excludes XLA (all isotypes low) and CVID (IgM low or normal, never elevated) and selective IgA deficiency (requires normal IgG and IgM) Neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count, ANC ≈1,350) common in CD40L deficiency; not a feature of XLA or CVID Lymphocytes 75%, CD4/CD8 2.2 normal lymphocyte compartment; excludes HIV, where leukopenia and an inverted ratio are expected Platelets 260,000 excludes Wiskott-Aldrich, which requires small, low platelets Age 14 months with disease since early infancy argues against CVID, which surfaces in adolescents and young adults Vaccinations up to date, yet invasive pneumococcal disease vaccine failure from absent opsonizing IgG, not from missed doses Lymphadenopathy separates HIV from SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency): HIV causes generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly from chronic immune activation, while SCID has absent or tiny lymph nodes because there are no lymphocytes to populate them

Antibody deficiencies: reading the isotype panel Diagnosis Illness script + buzzwords The NBME tell Excluded here by Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency) X-linked recessive boy, infancy; recurrent AOM (acute otitis media)/sinusitis/pneumonia from encapsulated bacteria, plus opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis) because the T-cell–APC (antigen-presenting cell) limb is also broken IgM high, IgG/IgA/IgE low, B cells normal, plus neutropenia (the answer) X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia Boy, infections begin at 4 to 6 months as maternal IgG wanes; recurrent sinopulmonary and enteroviral disease B cells absent/low with ALL isotypes low; scant tonsils and lymph nodes IgM 450 (high) with a normal lymphocyte compartment Common variable immunodeficiency Normal early childhood, then onset at puberty or age 20 to 40; sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria → bronchiectasis; chronic lung disease including asthma and fibrosis; gastrointestinal (GI) infection (Giardia, Salmonella, Campylobacter) with low IgA, and chronic diarrhea; failure to thrive in children; atopic and autoimmune associations, granulomas, and lymphoma risk Low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, low vaccine titers, with a NORMAL B-cell count: B cells fail to become plasma cells IgM 450 (high); age 14 months Selective IgA deficiency Usually asymptomatic; otherwise recurrent respiratory/GI (giardiasis) or urogenital infection; anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products IgA alone low; IgG and IgM normal IgG 250: the deficiency is not isolated Syndromic defects with an Ig signature (Wiskott-Aldrich · Job/hyper-IgE) WAS: eczema + microthrombocytopenia + infection, X-linked. Job: cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, pneumatoceles The non-immunologic finding makes the diagnosis, not the panel: small platelets; IgE markedly high Platelets 260,000 and normal-sized; no eczema or abscess history Secondary immune defects (HIV; protein-losing states) Opportunistic infection, thrush, diarrhea, failure to thrive; in perinatal HIV, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and a mother with an acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-suggestive illness HIV: inverted CD4/CD8 with leukopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG and IgA high, IgM normal or high); protein loss: low IgG IgG 250 (low); CD4/CD8 2.2, WBC (white blood cell count) 9,000

Onset XLA: boys at 4 to 6 months as maternal IgG wanes; CVID: after a normal childhood, at puberty or age 20 to 40 B-cell count XLA: absent; CVID: normal, but they fail to mature into plasma cells Immunoglobulins XLA: all isotypes and vaccine titers absent; CVID: low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, low vaccine titers Family history XLA: affected maternal male relatives; CVID: usually none A few toddler ear infections that cleared promptly ordinary childhood illness, not the start of XLA

Infection pattern → immune compartmentwhich arm of immunity is broken Infection pattern Onset Labs Compartment and examples Recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated bacteria; enterovirus in XLA; Giardia and other GI infection in CVID After 4 to 6 months, as maternal IgG wanes, or later Low immunoglobulins and poor vaccine response B cell (antibody): XLA, CVID, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgM syndrome Viral, fungal (Candida, Pneumocystis) and bacterial infection with failure to thrive Before 4 to 6 months Low lymphocytes, ± low immunoglobulins T cell or combined: DiGeorge syndrome, SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia Skin and soft tissue infection and abscesses; fungi; catalase-positive organisms in CGD (chronic granulomatous disease) Early childhood Normal immunoglobulins; abnormal oxidative burst in CGD; high leukocyte count in leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) Phagocyte: chronic granulomatous disease, leukocyte adhesion deficiency Recurrent Neisseria infection; systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)-like autoimmunity Variable Low CH50 (total hemolytic complement); normal leukocytes and immunoglobulins Complement: C5–C9 (terminal) for Neisseria; C1q for SLE

Humoral defects – the isotype gridread B cells first, then which isotype is preserved or high B cells IgG IgA IgM IgE Defect Normal Normal Low Normal Normal Selective IgA deficiency Normal Normal Normal Normal High Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome Normal Low Low High Low Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency) Normal Low Low Low or normal Low Common variable immunodeficiency Absent or low Low Low Low Low X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia

Defect gene defects stop T-cell development; B cells fail without T-cell help, so antibody is low too; X-linked or autosomal recessive Presentation in the first months: severe viral, fungal (thrush) and opportunistic (Pneumocystis) infection, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive Labs and exam lymphopenia with low CD4 and CD8 counts, hypogammaglobulinemia, no palpable nodes or tonsils Newborn screen part of US newborn screening: absent T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on the dried blood spot; lymphocyte flow cytometry confirms Treatment hematopoietic stem cell transplant as early as possible; no live vaccines Not SCID Bruton agammaglobulinemia has absent B cells but normal T cells and bacterial rather than fungal or opportunistic infection; CVID starts later with normal T- and B-cell counts; CGD has normal lymphocytes and immunoglobulins

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome WATER: Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, Eczema, Recurrent infections; X-linked; bleeding at circumcision or from the umbilical stump in early infancy; T-cell dysfunction and low immunoglobulins worsen with age; stem cell transplant Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome FATED: coarse Facies (broad nose, prominent forehead), cold staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, high IgE with eosinophilia, Dermatologic eczema; autosomal dominant; impaired Th17 signaling; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis Ataxia-telangiectasia autosomal recessive defect in DNA break repair; early childhood progressive cerebellar ataxia and poorly coordinated eye and head movements, then telangiectasias of the conjunctivae and face; recurrent sinopulmonary infection; high malignancy risk; genetic testing confirms Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with polyendocrinopathy AIRE deficiency breaks thymic negative selection, giving a T-cell defect against Candida plus autoimmunity; chronic Candida of skin, mouth and nails with hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, seizure), adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis

Management is to replace what is missing and cover what the defect exposes. Give immunoglobulin replacement in XLA, CVID and CD40 ligand deficiency; in CD40 ligand deficiency, add TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) prophylaxis against Pneumocystis. In severe antibody deficiency, avoid live vaccines such as MMR (measles, mumps and rubella); in T-cell defects, avoid all live vaccines. In selective IgA deficiency, IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) does not help, and transfusions use washed or IgA-deficient products. Allogeneic HSCT (hematopoietic stem cell transplantation) is the curative therapy for CD40 ligand deficiency.

CVID and XLA lifelong IVIG: the B cells cannot make antibody, so it is supplied; infections fall, but the autoimmune and malignancy risk of CVID remains SCID hematopoietic stem cell transplant, as early as possible Complete DiGeorge syndrome (no thymus) cultured thymus tissue transplant CGD interferon gamma, the immunomodulator, plus TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis Cellular (T-cell) defects antiviral and antifungal prophylaxis CVID, an antibody defect with normal T cells needs antibody replacement, not a transplant or an immunomodulator, although each is right for some other defect

Is this beyond normal childhood illness? ICU pneumonia, perforated tympanic membranes, weight <3rd percentile → yes, work it up as primary immunodeficiency Are B cells / lymphocytes present? Normal → not XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) Is IgM high, normal, or low? High with everything else low → class-switch failure → CD40L deficiency Is any isotype normal or high? IgG normal with IgA alone low → selective IgA deficiency; IgE very high → Job Is every isotype high? IgG, IgA and IgM all high is polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The primary antibody deficiencies all lower IgG or IgA. With thrush, adenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, test for HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) Any finding off the panel? Small low platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich; inverted CD4/CD8 → HIV Now use the pattern: which organisms and which treatment does this specific block predict?

Diagnostic workup Test Order Result What it points to Complete blood count (CBC) with differential and smear First Platelets small and low, or neutropenia Small platelets: Wiskott-Aldrich; neutropenia fits CD40 ligand deficiency Serum IgG, IgA, IgM and IgE First IgM high, IgG and IgA low Class-switch failure; all low: XLA; IgG low with IgA and/or IgM low: CVID; IgA alone: selective IgA deficiency; all high: polyclonal rise, as in HIV Flow cytometry for CD19+ B cells Confirms B cells absent XLA; normal B cells with low IgG and low IgA and/or IgM is CVID Vaccine antibody titers (tetanus, diphtheria) Next Protective titers Antibody function intact: transient hypogammaglobulinemia, not CVID or XLA Flow cytometry for CD40 ligand on activated T cells Confirms CD40 ligand absent Hyper-IgM syndrome Newborn screen: T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) Screen TRECs absent on the dried blood spot SCID found before infection; confirm with lymphocyte flow cytometry, then transplant T-cell subsets and HIV testing By branch Absent CD3+ T cells, or inverted CD4/CD8 SCID; or HIV, confirmed in an infant by HIV DNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR) Dihydrorhodamine 123 assay Skip Normal in antibody defects Tests neutrophil oxidative burst, which is CGD
