Diagnosis28 of 28 14 mo boy with Pneumocystis pneumonia after two pneumococcal pneumonias; IgM high, IgG and IgA low; normal lymphocyte count and CD4/CD8 ratio · X-linked agammaglobulinemia · CD40 ligand deficiency · Perinatal HIV infection 14 mo boy with Pneumocystis pneumonia after two pneumococcal pneumonias; IgM high, IgG and IgA low; normal lymphocyte count and CD4/CD8 ratio CD40 ligand deficiencyClass-switch failure; low IgG and a normal CD4/CD8 ratio separate it from HIV

Lymphocytes at 75% look alarming but are expected. Lymphocytosis accompanies active infection. It also confirms that lymphocyte numbers are intact, which excludes XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). The three bronchiolitis episodes read as ordinary infant viral illness but support CD40 ligand deficiency, which impairs viral defense as well as opsonization. Up-to-date vaccination converts the pneumococcal ICU admission into vaccine failure, an immunodeficiency finding rather than a gap in care.

High IgM with low IgG/IgA is class-switch failure. Absent B cells is XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). Low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and B cells present is CVID (common variable immunodeficiency). Read the panel in a fixed order: B cells, then IgM, then IgG/IgA/IgE. The missing isotype predicts the organism. No opsonizing IgG → encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae). A broken CD40 ligand–CD40 axis also breaks T-cell licensing of macrophages → Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium. Neutropenia alongside hypogammaglobulinemia points at CD40L deficiency rather than XLA. Selective IgA deficiency is the defect whose management is what you withhold: no IVIG, and washed or IgA-deficient blood products for transfusion. A severe antibody deficiency contraindicates live vaccines such as MMR, and a defective T-cell limb contraindicates all of them; and replacement IgG likely interferes with later vaccine-titer testing. A mildly low IgG at 6–9 months in a thriving infant with normal IgM, normal B cells, and protective vaccine titers is transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy: recheck levels, and treatment is conservative. NBME framing: the lead-in asks for a mechanism but lists diseases, and the mother's thrush, chronic diarrhea and weight loss hold the deciding clue.

The nadir maternally derived IgG wanes after birth and troughs at 3 to 6 months, when the infant's own synthesis takes over Transient hypogammaglobulinemia that synthesis is delayed and the nadir is prolonged beyond 6 months, with recurrent respiratory infection and atopy Vaccine response is the most discriminating line on the panel a normal response excludes common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia at once, whatever the isotype levels say

Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease shares the complaint of recurrent otitis media and pneumonia in a child. Ask: does the immunoglobulin panel explain it, or does the anatomy? When the panel is normal, that brief covers the structural and mucociliary axis; when an isotype is out of step, this one does. Part I Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers the phagocyte defects: chronic granulomatous disease, leukocyte adhesion deficiency and Chédiak-Higashi. Ask: are the immunoglobulins normal, and is there pus? Part I 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome covers the thymic T-cell defect with hypocalcemia (CATCH-22); ask: is there a conotruncal heart lesion? Part II Infectious Diarrhea follows a patient with common variable immunodeficiency on immunoglobulin replacement who develops Salmonella gastroenteritis. Ask: does the organism point to the immune defect, or to the food it came from?

With recurrent sinopulmonary infection and an immunoglobulin panel, read the pattern rather than recall a disease. Count the B cells, then ask which isotype is preserved. The preserved isotype names the block, and the missing isotypes name the organisms you must cover.

Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: eczema plus recurrent infection fits its pattern, but it requires small, low platelets. A normal count excludes it, and atopy is itself a feature of transient hypogammaglobulinemia. Class-vs-memberBruton agammaglobulinemia: That member of the class requires absent B cells and low IgM; IgM is 450 and the lymphocyte compartment is intact True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: CVID leaves IgM low or normal but never high, and presents in adolescence or later, not at 14 months Salient decoyHIV infection: HIV would show leukopenia and a low CD4/CD8 ratio; here the ratio is 2.2 and WBC 9,000. HIV raises IgG in a polyclonal rise, while this panel has IgG 250. True-fact-wrong-slotIgA deficiency: Isolated IgA deficiency requires normal IgG and IgM; IgG 250 makes the deficiency global-with-a-block, not selective Class-vs-memberWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: The syndromic member is defined by microthrombocytopenia; platelets are 260,000 and normal-sized, and there is no eczema Class-vs-memberSevere combined immunodeficiency: It presents in early infancy with lymphopenia, low immunoglobulins and no palpable nodes. A 2-year-old with every isotype high and 2-cm axillary nodes does not fit. Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: Platelets of 95,000 are the lure. It classically has eczema and small platelets, and it is X-linked, while this patient with every isotype high is a girl. True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: It lowers IgG along with IgA and/or IgM, and it usually starts after puberty. Here every isotype is high at age 2. True-fact-wrong-slotChronic granulomatous disease: It causes catalase-positive abscesses and granulomas with an abnormal DHR (dihydrorhodamine) test. Immunoglobulins are normal or high in it, so this panel does not exclude it; the thrush, the adenopathy and the mother's illness point to HIV. Unchecked attributeChédiak-Higashi syndrome: It needs oculocutaneous albinism and neuropathy, and neither is described in the girl with every isotype high. True-fact-wrong-slotTerminal complement deficiency: It causes recurrent Neisseria infection, not pneumococcal disease with thrush and every isotype high. Salient decoyCystic fibrosis: Recurrent pneumonia and low weight fit. It causes lung and pancreatic disease, without thrush, adenopathy or a mother with an AIDS-suggestive illness.

briefs.title: Tick-Borne Illness
briefs.sub: treat suspected rickettsiosis before confirming it · a rash from the extremities inward · the platelet, sodium and liver triad · no rash: ehrlichiosis · an expanding ring: LymeWhere did the rash start, and what did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do?
blocks: treat suspected rickettsiosis before confirming it · a rash from the extremities inward · the platelet, sodium and liver triad · no rash: ehrlichiosis · an expanding ring: LymeWhere did the rash start, and what did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do?

Fever and headache for days, then a rash that starts on the wrists and ankles and moves to the trunk, palms and soles, with low platelets, low sodium and raised liver enzymes in spring or summer: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF). Start doxycycline on suspicion, in children of any age and in pregnancy; paired serology confirms it weeks later, and a negative early result changes nothing. The same tick season, usually with no rash and a low white count: ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis, also treated with doxycycline. A single expanding ring at a bite: Lyme disease, a diagnosis made on sight.

What it is Infections passed by tick bite. The Step 2 example is RMSF, a rickettsial small-vessel vasculitis that kills when treatment waits for proof. Bug RMSF: Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium that takes the Gram stain poorly and lives in vascular endothelium. Ehrlichiosis: Ehrlichia chaffeensis in monocytes. Anaplasmosis: Anaplasma phagocytophilum in granulocytes (MEGA: Monocytes with Ehrlichiosis, Granulocytes with Anaplasmosis). Lyme disease: the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Babesiosis: Babesia, a protozoan that lives inside red cells. Spread RMSF: Dermacentor ticks, spring and summer, most often the South Atlantic and southeastern states despite the name; only 55 to 60% recall a bite. Lyme, anaplasmosis and babesiosis: one vector, the Ixodes tick, with Lyme common in the Northeast and upper Midwest and anaplasmosis also in the mid-Atlantic and West Coast, so one bite can carry two infections. Ehrlichiosis: the lone star tick, in the southeastern and south-central states. Chain Tick bite R. rickettsii enters and multiplies in vascular endothelium small-vessel vasculitis with leaky capillaries rash, platelets used up in injured vessels, low sodium, liver injury untreated, it may progress to encephalitis, hypotension, circulatory failure and death Insights The rash can lag: most patients have one by the sixth day of fever, so the first visit may show fever and headache alone. Serology lags the illness: titers are often negative in the first week, so the test that confirms RMSF cannot decide when to treat it.

Day 0tick bite, often unnoticed 2 to 14 daysfever, severe headache, muscle aches In practice In practice: the MSD (Merck Sharp and Dohme) Manual gives an incubation of 3 to 12 days; the NBME explanation uses 2 to 14. By the sixth day of fevera rash in most, typically wrists and ankles first, then inward Days laterthe spots may turn petechial 2 to 10 weeksconvalescent titer: a fourfold rise confirms it

A clinical diagnosis: what makes RMSF the working diagnosis Element Finding Exposure Life, work or travel in or near wooded areas in spring or summer; a recalled bite is not required Tempo Days of fever and severe headache before any rash Rash Typically wrists and ankles first, then trunk, palms and soles; blanching, then may become petechial Labs Low platelets, low sodium, raised AST and ALT; prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times Rule No criteria set: the picture starts treatment; serology confirms it later
The rash can be missing: fever, headache and malaise in the right setting start doxycycline, rash or not.

Urgent findings Finding Action Confusion, seizures or coma with fever and rash Encephalitis: doxycycline now, then a lumbar puncture. Hypotension with a fast pulse Vascular collapse under way: doxycycline with fluid and organ support. Afebrile, rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis with normal sensation and no rash after a hike Tick paralysis: search the whole skin for the tick and remove it before breathing fails.

Fever and rash after outdoor exposure Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) Days of fever and headache, then a rash from the wrists and ankles inward to the palms and soles; low platelets, low sodium, high transaminases. Doxycycline now; send serology but do not wait for it. Ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis Same tick setting and prodrome; usually no rash; low white count; morulae, inclusions in monocytes or neutrophils. Send a blood smear and polymerase chain reaction (PCR); give doxycycline meanwhile. Lyme disease A single expanding ring at the bite, often clearing in the center; later facial palsy, heart block or arthritis of a large joint such as the knee. Diagnose erythema migrans on sight and give doxycycline. Babesiosis The same Ixodes tick; fever with hemolytic anemia, dark urine and jaundice; worst without a spleen. Order a blood smear for Maltese cross tetrads; treat with atovaquone plus azithromycin. Tick paralysis Afebrile, rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis with normal sensation; no rash Find and remove the tick. Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) Fever 5 days or more with nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, a node, red swollen hands and feet; platelets climb. Count the criteria; red eyes alone do not make it. Meningococcemia Hours, not days, from fever to petechiae and purpura, then shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Check the tempo: hours to purpura, against days of fever before an extremity rash. Dengue fever Tropical travel and Aedes mosquitoes; pain behind the eyes, severe bone and muscle pain; low white count and platelets. Obtain a travel history. Measles (rubeola) Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, then a rash from the head down that spares the palms and soles. None here: the rash direction and the missing prodrome exclude it. Roseola (exanthema subitum) Days of high fever in an infant, then a blanching rash on the neck and trunk as the fever breaks. Supportive care. Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) Slapped cheeks, then a lacy rash, in a school-age child who is otherwise well. Diagnose parvovirus B19; skip the tick-borne workup. Typhoid fever Salmonella Typhi in an endemic region; fever and chills with abdominal pain and diarrhea. Send blood cultures. Immune thrombocytopenia Low platelets alone in a well, afebrile child; normal liver tests. None here: fever, rash and raised transaminases exclude it. Wilson disease Kayser-Fleischer rings; liver and neuropsychiatric disease over months. None here: exclude it on tempo, a febrile rash over days, not disease over months. Amebiasis Bloody diarrhea with fever; a liver abscess on imaging. None: a normal CT and a rash exclude it; skip stool ova and parasites.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Fever, headache and an extremity rash after outdoor exposure in spring or summer → CBC Platelets low; white count normal or low Endothelial injury, which fits RMSF → Basic metabolic panel and liver enzymes Sodium low; AST and ALT raised The triad is complete: doxycycline now Targeted tests TestResultMeans Same exposure, no rash, a low white count → Peripheral smear and blood PCR Morulae in monocytes or neutrophils Ehrlichiosis (monocytes) or anaplasmosis (neutrophils); doxycycline treats both Confusion, seizures or meningeal signs → Lumbar puncture Central nervous system involvement RMSF encephalitis; the tap does not hold up doxycycline Facial palsy, heart block or knee arthritis, which can follow tick season by weeks to months → Lyme enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), then Western blot Both positive Disseminated or late Lyme disease Fever with hemolysis after an Ixodes bite → Blood smear Tetrads (Maltese cross) inside red cells Babesiosis Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Confirms RMSF after doxycycline has started → Rickettsia rickettsii immunoglobulin G (IgG) serology, acute and convalescent Usually a fourfold rise in titer between samples 2 to 10 weeks apart RMSF, confirmed in retrospect → PCR of blood or a skin biopsy Negative early Does not stop treatment SkipWaiting on any Rickettsia result before doxycycline; Lyme serology for a classic erythema migrans, which appears before antibodies.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step No tick bite recalled RMSF still fits: only 55 to 60% recall a bite Start doxycycline on the picture. Severe abdominal pain in a febrile child with the rash RMSF; its abdominal pain may mimic appendicitis and is frequent in children Doxycycline; skip the abdominal CT. Rash on the palms and soles A short list: RMSF, coxsackievirus A, toxic shock syndrome, secondary syphilis Start doxycycline when days of fever and headache came before the rash in tick season.

Pause point Febrile child, wrist and ankle petechiae, serology just sent Offered as wait for the titer or amoxicillin Can a test that turns positive weeks later decide when to treat? → Doxycycline now; the serology only confirms it later Under age 8, suspected RMSF, parents fear tooth staining Offered as amoxicillin or chloramphenicol Does a short course stain teeth, and does any other drug work as well? → Doxycycline: short courses spare the teeth, and other drugs raise the risk of death Summer tick bite, fever, a low white count, low platelets, no rash Offered as RMSF or babesiosis Is there a rash, and what sits inside the white cells? → Ehrlichiosis: morulae in monocytes; doxycycline as well

What makes it severe Finding Meaning Confusion, delirium, seizures or coma Encephalitis Hypotension Severe disease; circulatory failure may follow if untreated Bleeding with long clotting times Coagulopathy Doxycycline started late A worse outlook; early treatment improves it Babesiosis with asplenia, older age or advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection Severe, sometimes fatal hemolysis

1 Rickettsial diseaseRMSF, ehrlichiosis or anaplasmosis suspected Doxycycline at every age and in pregnancy; in RMSF, continue until at least 3 days after the fever ends and the patient is clearly improving. TeethShort courses (5 to 10 days) can be used without staining permanent teeth; the American Academy of Pediatrics calls the risk minimal under age 8 for courses up to 21 days. 2 Doxycycline not toleratedAllergy or intolerance Desensitize and still give doxycycline: other antibiotics raise the risk of death. Chloramphenicol is a rare second line for RMSF only; it fails in ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis. 3 Early Lyme diseaseErythema migrans Doxycycline, 10 days for a single lesion; in pregnancy, amoxicillin or cefuroxime; a child under 8 also takes doxycycline. In practiceIn practice: amoxicillin or cefuroxime remains an accepted choice for a young child who cannot take doxycycline. 4 Lyme heart or nervesMeningitis, carditis or heart block IV ceftriaxone; complete heart block may need a temporary pacemaker. 5 BabesiosisMild to moderate Oral atovaquone plus azithromycin; the azithromycin goes IV when the disease is severe.

After a tick bite and after the illness When Do Tick still attached Lift it out with fine forceps and steady traction on the head; never crush or squeeze it. A bite with no symptoms in an RMSF area No antibiotic; come back for fever, headache or a rash. Deer tick bite in a high-Lyme area No routine prophylaxis; one dose of doxycycline only in a narrow case. CriteriaGuideline criteria: the tick was attached 36 hours or more, it came off within the last 72 hours, and 20% or more of local ticks carry Lyme; the dose studied is oral doxycycline 200 mg once. Confirmed or probable RMSF Report it to public health: spotted fever rickettsioses are nationally notifiable.

Next step1 of 11 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal · DoxycyclineFever, an extremity rash, low platelets and raised transaminases after wooded exposure: doxycycline now for RMSF. · Stool for ova and parasitesAmebiasis brings bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess, and explains no rash. · AmoxicillinAmoxicillin treats early Lyme disease, a single expanding ring that spares the platelets and liver. 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal Doxycyclineempiric treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever

Avoid2 of 11 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent · Admitting for monitoring while treatingMonitoring while treating keeps doxycycline going; it is not the error. · Withholding antibiotics until serology returnsTiters are often negative in the first week; waiting lets the disease progress. · Starting doxycycline nowStarting doxycycline on suspicion is the right action, not the one to avoid. 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent Withholding antibiotics until serology returnsuntreated disease progresses to vascular collapse

Next step4 of 11 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining · Await serology before decidingSerology is often negative in the first week; waiting delays the only effective drug. · Give doxycyclineShort doxycycline courses can be given without staining permanent teeth, and any other drug raises the risk of death. · Substitute amoxicillinAntibiotics other than doxycycline raise the risk of severe illness and death. 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining Give doxycyclinea study found no staining of permanent teeth after short courses (5 to 10 days)

Diagnosis5 of 11 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash · Rocky Mountain spotted feverRMSF usually brings a rash that spreads in from the wrists and ankles. · BabesiosisBabesiosis is a fever with hemolytic anemia and tetrads in red cells. · EhrlichiosisTick exposure with a low white count, low platelets, raised transaminases and no rash: ehrlichiosis. 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash Ehrlichiosisdoxycycline treats it as well

The mechanism of thrombocytopenia in Rocky Mountain spotted fever Intravascular platelet destruction from infection of vascular endotheliumsmall-vessel vasculitis

Diagnosis7 of 11 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT · Acute appendicitisA normal abdominal CT argues against appendicitis, and appendicitis explains no rash. · Amebic liver abscessAn amebic abscess shows on imaging and brings no rash. · Rocky Mountain spotted feverFever with a wrist and ankle rash; abdominal pain that may mimic appendicitis is frequent in children with RMSF. 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT Rocky Mountain spotted feverabdominal pain in children mimics appendicitis

Child already started on doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever Rickettsia serologyconfirmation is retrospective and never delays therapy

Diagnosis9 of 11 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of high fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area, often bitten by mosquitoes; finished a steroid course for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill; T 39 C; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms · Kawasaki diseaseKawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria; this is day 4 with petechiae. · Rocky Mountain spotted feverSummer, rural life, days of fever and headache, then palm and distal arm petechiae: RMSF. · Dengue feverDengue needs tropical travel and brings pain behind the eyes and severe bone and muscle pain. 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of high fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area, often bitten by mosquitoes; finished a steroid course for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill; T 39 C; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms Rocky Mountain spotted feverdoxycycline now, without waiting for serology

Diagnosis10 of 11 10 yo F back 5 days from 2 weeks in the Dominican Republic; fever 39.5 °C, retro-orbital headache, severe bone and muscle pain; macular truncal rash; no outdoor exposure in the US; white blood cell count 2,800/µL, platelets 90,000/µL · Typhoid feverTyphoid brings fever and chills with abdominal pain and diarrhea. · Dengue feverTropical travel, pain behind the eyes, bone and muscle pain and a low white count: dengue. · Rocky Mountain spotted feverNo outdoor exposure in the US, and the rash is on the trunk, not spreading in from the wrists. 10 yo F back 5 days from 2 weeks in the Dominican Republic; fever 39.5 °C, retro-orbital headache, severe bone and muscle pain; macular truncal rash; no outdoor exposure in the US; white blood cell count 2,800/µL, platelets 90,000/µL Dengue feversupportive care with fluids; avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

Next step11 of 11 4 yo M on a Tennessee farm in July: 4 days of fever and headache; conjunctival injection; wrist and ankle macules, now petechial, spread to palms, soles and trunk; no cracked lips or hand swelling; platelets 85,000/µL, sodium 130 mEq/L · Start intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirinKawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria; there are no lip or hand changes. · Start doxycyclineWrist and ankle petechiae spreading inward with low platelets and sodium: doxycycline now, at any age. · Send Rickettsia serology and treat if positiveSerology is often negative early; treat on suspicion. 4 yo M on a Tennessee farm in July: 4 days of fever and headache; conjunctival injection; wrist and ankle macules, now petechial, spread to palms, soles and trunk; no cracked lips or hand swelling; platelets 85,000/µL, sodium 130 mEq/L Start doxycyclineRocky Mountain spotted fever; any age, treat on suspicion

Two details suggest abdominal and hepatic causes. Worsening abdominal pain with a normal CT fits RMSF: its abdominal pain may mimic appendicitis and is frequent in children. Once the scan is negative, stop pursuing an abdominal cause. Confusion with transaminitis suggests Wilson disease, but confusion in RMSF is early encephalitis arriving over hours, not over months.

No tick most RMSF stems never mention one; the clue is season (late spring to summer), rural or outdoor life, days of fever and severe headache, then a rash that starts on the wrists, ankles, palms or soles and spreads inward, turning petechial Mosquito bites point to dengue only with tropical travel, and dengue brings retro-orbital pain and severe bone and muscle pain Conjunctival injection occurs in RMSF too; Kawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria, and measles needs cough, coryza and a rash from the hairline down Steroids for poison ivy a month ago irrelevant; they explain none of the fever, headache or petechiae

Treat on suspicion, confirm retrospectively doxycycline treats the patient; serology only documents the diagnosis Doxycycline is given to children of any age for RMSF the staining concern applies to prolonged courses, and withholding it is the dangerous choice Low platelets plus transaminitis plus hyponatremia after outdoor exposure a rickettsial fingerprint the common viral exanthems rarely produce together The rash moves inward extremity onset spreading centrally with palms and soles is a short differential: RMSF, coxsackievirus A, toxic shock syndrome and secondary syphilis No recalled tick bite does not lower suspicion; the exposure history is habitat, not bite Abdominal pain in a febrile child with a rash is part of the illness a normal CT should redirect you to a systemic diagnosis, not a more invasive abdominal one

Fever and Rash in a Childcovers the febrile-rash differential, measles and roseola included Kawasaki Diseasecovers 5 days of fever with red eyes.Ask: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do? Fever and Rash in a Child covers the febrile-rash differential, measles and roseola included. Kawasaki Disease covers 5 days of fever with red eyes. Ask: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do?
Kawasaki disease appeared under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, as a decoy for a child with 4 days of fever, red eyes and a petechial rash on the palms.

When the confirmatory test is retrospective and the untreated disease is lethal, treat on the clinical picture. Let the serology arrive whenever it arrives. A pending test is not a reason to wait; treatment should already have started.

Salient decoyStool for ova and parasites: fever with abdominal pain and liver enzymes fits amebiasis, but that causes bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess and explains no rash. Treat-the-numberPrednisone: platelets of 46,000 invite ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), but ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not fever with rash, transaminitis and hypotension. True-fact-wrong-slotAmoxicillin: correct for Lyme, same season and habitat, but Lyme rash is a single expanding annular lesion and it spares the platelets and liver. Salient decoySerum ceruloplasmin: liver enzymes plus confusion reads as Wilson disease, a chronic disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not four days of fever with a rash. Sequencing trapLaparoscopy: the abdominal CT is already normal, which answers the surgical question. Salient decoyDengue fever: mosquito bites suggest it, but without tropical travel dengue is not on the table. It brings retro-orbital and bone pain rather than a rash spreading in from the wrists. Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: red eyes fit, but fever has run 4 days, not 5, and the rash is petechial on the palms, not polymorphous with swollen hands. Salient decoyMeasles: conjunctivitis tempts, but measles rash starts at the hairline, spares the palms and soles, and follows cough and coryza.

blocks: number vs function · catalase-positive organisms · granulomas and abscesses · oxidative burst test · low countsIs the neutrophil count low, or are there granulomas with infection outside the chest?

Pt 2 yo M, 3 days of fever, cough and irritability; perirectal abscess drained at 9 months; T 38.9, bilateral lower-lobe crackles Imaging bilateral pneumonia on chest film; after 3 days of antibiotics still febrile, computed tomography shows a small left effusion with paratracheal and hilar lymphadenopathy Labs lymph node and lung biopsy shows granuloma formation; culture grows Burkholderia (Pseudomonas) cepacia Q the mechanism responsible; options spanned decreased immunoglobulin production, decreased superoxide production, defective opsonization, impaired clearing of airway secretions and impaired neutrophil chemotaxis

Pt 2 yo M, 2 days of fever and mouth sores, fussy and refusing food, now improving; a year of similar episodes about every 3 weeks, each lasting 3 to 5 days; normal growth and development Exam T 38.4 C, HR 120; scattered aphthous ulcers; skin clear; no lymphadenopathy Labs Hb 11.5; white blood cell (WBC) count 4,000 with 4% segmented neutrophils, 84% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes; platelets 250,000 Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, dyskeratosis congenita, Fanconi syndrome, hypersplenism, leukemia, severe congenital neutropenia, viral illness and vitamin B12 deficiency

The pneumonia does not name the defect. Granulomas on biopsy and a Burkholderia cepacia culture together point at one disease: chronic granulomatous disease. It is a disorder of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms. The enzyme drives the neutrophil respiratory burst, so its loss means decreased superoxide production. Phagocytes migrate normally and ingest normally, but have impaired intracellular killing. Neutrophils can borrow hydrogen peroxide made by the pathogen itself. Susceptibility therefore particularly involves characteristic catalase-positive organisms that destroy their own peroxide; this is not an exclusive organism list. The granulomas are the same defect seen histologically: phagocytes arrive but clear pathogens poorly, contributing to granuloma formation.

Chronic granulomatous disease NADPH oxidase disorder, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms; impaired respiratory burst and reduced reactive oxygen species, so intracellular killing is impaired The organism pattern particular susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, because catalase degrades the pathogen's own hydrogen peroxide and denies the neutrophil a borrowed oxidant: S aureus, B cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus Sites lungs, skin, liver and lymph nodes; perirectal abscess is characteristic, with diffuse granulomas in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts Diagnosis measure neutrophil superoxide production: dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry preferred, nitroblue tetrazolium the older equivalent Treatment prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), itraconazole and interferon gamma; hematopoietic cell transplant is curative

Recurrent infection – reading the mechanismwhich defect, by organism and by histology Mechanism Disease The NBME tell Excluded here by ↓ superoxide production Chronic granulomatous disease Catalase-positive organisms + granulomas + abscesses (perirectal, liver) – (the answer) Impaired airway clearance Cystic fibrosis Nasal polyps, clubbing, steatorrhoea; also gets B cepacia No granulomas; infections confined to the sinopulmonary tract ↓ immunoglobulin production X-linked agammaglobulinemia Encapsulated organisms; all isotypes low, absent B cells No granulomas, no abscesses, wrong organism Defective opsonization Complement (C3) deficiency Encapsulated organisms, recurrent pyogenic infection Same – and B cepacia is not the pattern Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis Leukocyte adhesion deficiency Delayed umbilical cord separation (over 3 weeks), skin and mucosal infections without pus (cellulitis, periodontitis), poor wound healing, marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia; CD18 integrin defect Pus was present (abscess drained); no granulomas Impaired Th17 signaling (JAK-STAT) Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome Cold staphylococcal and Candida abscesses, severe eczema, eosinophilia with a normal white count No eczema or eosinophilia; granulomas and Burkholderia point to the oxidative burst

Granulomas on biopsy the most specific finding; excludes CF, X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA), complement deficiency and leukocyte adhesion deficiency, none of which form them Burkholderia cepacia catalase-positive, and shared with cystic fibrosis, which is exactly why it is not sufficient alone Perirectal abscess at 9 months extrapulmonary abscess; CF does not do this, and it is the finding that separates the two Persistent fever after 3 days of appropriate antibiotics killing is defective, not coverage Hilar and paratracheal lymphadenopathy node involvement, part of the chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) site pattern Male, age 2 consistent with the common X-linked form presenting in early childhood; autosomal recessive forms also occur Normal ear, nose and throat examination no chronic rhinosinusitis, arguing further against CF

Are there granulomas? Yes → CGD, essentially alone among the immunodeficiencies What grew? A catalase-positive organism → confirms Where are the infections? Lung and perirectal → extrapulmonary, so not CF Was there pus? Yes → chemotaxis and adhesion intact, so not leukocyte adhesion deficiency What is the mechanism of that defect? NADPH oxidase → decreased superoxide How is it confirmed? Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry

Diagnostic workup Test Order Result What it points to Complete blood count (CBC) with differential First Neutrophils present, count normal or high The defect is killing, not number; marked leukocytosis without pus suggests leukocyte adhesion deficiency; an absolute neutrophil count under 500 is a number problem instead Biopsy and culture of abscess or node Next Granulomas with a catalase-positive organism CGD pattern; B. cepacia alone also fits cystic fibrosis Dihydrorhodamine 123 flow cytometry Confirms Absent or reduced oxidative burst Chronic granulomatous disease Nitroblue tetrazolium test Confirms Neutrophils fail to turn the dye blue CGD; the older equivalent of the dihydrorhodamine test Neutrophil counts 2 to 3 times a week for 6 weeks, if the count is low By branch Nadirs about every 21 days, normal between; or persistently low Cyclic neutropenia if periodic; severe congenital neutropenia if persistent Sweat chloride, if no granulomas By branch 60 mmol/L or more Cystic fibrosis, which also grows B. cepacia Genetic testing of NADPH oxidase genes Cause X-linked or autosomal recessive variant Inheritance and family counseling Quantitative serum immunoglobulins Skip Normal or high in CGD Antibody production is intact

Number the neutrophil count is low; infections are bacterial, with fever, mouth ulcers, gingivitis and skin, lung or gut infection when the count is lowest Function the count is normal or high and the cells fail at a step: adhesion (leukocyte adhesion deficiency), killing (chronic granulomatous disease), granule traffic (Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which also lowers the count) Absolute neutrophil count WBC × (segmented neutrophils + bands); 4,000 × 4% is about 160; under 1,500 is neutropenia and under 500 is severe Name trap Fanconi syndrome is proximal renal tubule wasting of glucose, phosphate, bicarbonate and amino acids; Fanconi anemia is inherited marrow failure

Low neutrophil count in a child: the differential Diagnosis Illness script The tell Excluded in the periodic-fever child by Cyclic neutropenia Inherited, neutrophil elastase (ELANE) mutation; well between episodes Every 21 days, lasting 3 to 6 days: fever, oral ulcers, pharyngitis; periodontal disease and early tooth loss; absolute neutrophil count often under 200 at the nadir – (the answer) Severe congenital neutropenia Inherited, often ELANE; presents in the first months of life Persistent severe neutropenia with omphalitis, pneumonia, abscesses; high risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) Periodic episodes with health between; first symptoms after infancy Viral marrow suppression Parvovirus B19, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, other viruses Transient dip with the illness and its other symptoms A year of regular 3-week episodes; a virus does not keep a calendar Acute leukemia Malaise, weight loss, bone pain Anemia and thrombocytopenia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, blasts Normal platelets, no nodes or spleen, well between episodes Hypersplenism Splenic sequestration Splenomegaly with all three cell lines low No splenomegaly; hemoglobin and platelets preserved Fanconi anemia Inherited marrow failure Pancytopenia with short stature, thumb or radial anomalies, microcephaly, café au lait spots, developmental delay Normal growth, only one line low Dyskeratosis congenita Inherited marrow failure Reticular hyperpigmentation, dystrophic nails, oral leukoplakia; pancytopenia Skin and nails normal; only one line low Chédiak-Higashi syndrome Lysosomal trafficking defect (LYST) Oculocutaneous albinism, giant granules, neuropathy; frequent bacterial infections Normal pigment and neurologic examination Vitamin B12 deficiency Diet, malabsorption Macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils No macrocytic anemia; not periodic

Confirm one normal count between episodes proves nothing; check neutrophil counts 2 to 3 times a week for at least 6 weeks to catch the nadirs; genetic testing for the elastase mutation supports it During an episode treat any infection, keep up oral and dental hygiene Long term G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) keeps the count up and prevents episodes; the same drug treats severe congenital neutropenia

Mechanism1 of 18 2 yo M with a perirectal abscess drained at 9 months, now with bilateral pneumonia still febrile after 3 days of antibiotics; biopsy shows granulomas and culture grows Burkholderia cepacia · Decreased superoxide production · Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis · Impaired clearing of airway secretions 2 yo M with a perirectal abscess drained at 9 months, now with bilateral pneumonia still febrile after 3 days of antibiotics; biopsy shows granulomas and culture grows Burkholderia cepacia Decreased superoxide productionNADPH oxidase defect in chronic granulomatous disease

Workup2 of 18 3 yo M with recurrent Serratia marcescens skin abscesses and hepatic granulomas on imaging · Quantitative serum immunoglobulins · Sweat chloride testing · Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry 3 yo M with recurrent Serratia marcescens skin abscesses and hepatic granulomas on imaging Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometrymeasures the neutrophil respiratory burst

Mechanism3 of 18 Why are characteristic catalase-positive organisms associated with chronic granulomatous disease? · Catalase inactivates lysosomal proteases directly · Catalase-positive organisms have thicker capsules · Catalase degrades the organism's own hydrogen peroxide Why are characteristic catalase-positive organisms associated with chronic granulomatous disease? Catalase degrades the organism's own hydrogen peroxidethe neutrophil cannot borrow the pathogen's oxidant

Next step4 of 18 2 yo newly diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease, currently well between infections · Monthly immunoglobulin replacement · TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma prophylaxis · Observation with treatment of infections as they arise 2 yo newly diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease, currently well between infections TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma prophylaxisbacterial, fungal and immunomodulatory cover

Diagnosis6 of 18 Newborn with delayed umbilical cord separation and a soft tissue infection producing no pus, with a white blood cell count of 38,000 · Leukocyte adhesion deficiency · Chronic granulomatous disease · X-linked agammaglobulinemia Newborn with delayed umbilical cord separation and a soft tissue infection producing no pus, with a white blood cell count of 38,000 Leukocyte adhesion deficiencyimpaired chemotaxis and adhesion

Diagnosis7 of 18 4 yo with nasal polyps, digital clubbing, steatorrhea and Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia; biopsy shows no granulomas · Chronic granulomatous disease · Cystic fibrosis · Severe combined immunodeficiency 4 yo with nasal polyps, digital clubbing, steatorrhea and Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia; biopsy shows no granulomas Cystic fibrosissweat chloride testing

Diagnosis9 of 18 3 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess and a perirectal abscess drained in infancy · X-linked agammaglobulinemia · Chronic granulomatous disease · Leukocyte adhesion deficiency 3 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess and a perirectal abscess drained in infancy Chronic granulomatous diseaseconfirm with dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry

Diagnosis10 of 18 3 yo M with eczema since infancy and recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Candida abscesses, now a nontender fluctuant buttock abscess, afebrile; leukocytes 9,000 with 30% neutrophils and 40% eosinophils · Hyper-IgE syndrome · Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome · Myeloperoxidase deficiency 3 yo M with eczema since infancy and recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Candida abscesses, now a nontender fluctuant buttock abscess, afebrile; leukocytes 9,000 with 30% neutrophils and 40% eosinophils Hyper-IgE syndromeimpaired Th17 signaling blunts neutrophil recruitment

Next step13 of 18 2 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus perianal abscess drained at 2 months after failed oral antibiotics, left inguinal lymphadenitis at 7 months, and now a fluctuant right arm abscess that grows Serratia marcescens; leukocyte and platelet counts normal, B and T cells normal; dihydrorhodamine test abnormal · Itraconazole · Intravenous immunoglobulin · Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor 2 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus perianal abscess drained at 2 months after failed oral antibiotics, left inguinal lymphadenitis at 7 months, and now a fluctuant right arm abscess that grows Serratia marcescens; leukocyte and platelet counts normal, B and T cells normal; dihydrorhodamine test abnormal Itraconazoleantifungal prophylaxis in chronic granulomatous disease

Diagnosis18 of 18 2-month-old boy with omphalitis at 3 weeks and now a perianal abscess; the umbilical cord separated at 10 days and the wound drains pus; absolute neutrophil count under 200 on every CBC over 4 weeks, with normal hemoglobin and platelets · Cyclic neutropenia · Leukocyte adhesion deficiency · Severe congenital neutropenia 2-month-old boy with omphalitis at 3 weeks and now a perianal abscess; the umbilical cord separated at 10 days and the wound drains pus; absolute neutrophil count under 200 on every CBC over 4 weeks, with normal hemoglobin and platelets Severe congenital neutropeniaG-CSF; lifelong risk of myelodysplasia and AML

Burkholderia cepacia is seen in two diseases: cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease. It therefore identifies neither alone. Granulomas and extrapulmonary abscesses are what split them. In the vignette, a perirectal abscess in an infant is the single most specific clue to chronic granulomatous disease. It is in the past medical history, where it is easy to skim.

Eosinophilia, normal white count hyper-IgE syndrome Marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia leukocyte adhesion deficiency Neutropenia with oculocutaneous albinism Chédiak-Higashi syndrome: giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils on the smear, recurrent bacterial infection, progressive neurodegeneration with peripheral neuropathy; autosomal recessive lysosomal trafficking defect Small platelets with bruising Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome Lymphopenia DiGeorge syndrome, whose infections are invasive viral, fungal and bacterial rather than cold abscesses Unremarkable CBC with Candida infections myeloperoxidase deficiency Job syndrome, the rest autosomal dominant; eczema from the first weeks of life, recurrent sinopulmonary infection, broad nose and prominent forehead, retained primary teeth; genetic testing confirms; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis

Granulomas plus abscesses plus a catalase-positive organism is CGD, and no other immunodeficiency assembles that trio Catalase-positive is a mechanism, not a list – the neutrophil can use the organism's own peroxide, helping explain susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive organisms; other organisms are not excluded Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry has replaced nitroblue tetrazolium as the preferred test; both measure the same respiratory burst Prophylaxis – TMP-SMX for bacteria plus itraconazole for fungi such as Aspergillus, with interferon gamma added for severe disease; transplant is the only cure Not CGD prophylaxis – G-CSF, because the neutrophil count is normal; intravenous immunoglobulin, because immunoglobulins are normal (it treats antibody deficiency such as XLA); valacyclovir, which is for T-cell defects Vaccines – avoid BCG and other live bacterial vaccines; live viral and inactivated vaccines are safe Phagocytes in CGD migrate and ingest normally; the failure is intracellular killing, which is why pus forms and chemotaxis-defect diseases look different

Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers the antibody deficiencies, and this brief covers the phagocyte defects. Together the two cover the common primary immunodeficiencies. Ask: are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?

No organism or granuloma was named; the clue was a maternal uncle who died of fungal pneumonia, which points to X-linked disease. Four of the five options were steps in leukocyte function, and the key named the killing defect as impaired microbicidal activity.

When an organism is seen in two diseases, it cannot separate them; find the finding unique to one. Here the shared organism is B cepacia, and the findings unique to one disease are the granuloma and the perirectal abscess.

Unchecked attributeImpaired clearing of airway secretions: cystic fibrosis makes no granulomas, and its infections stay sinopulmonary; a perirectal abscess is outside its territory. Class-vs-memberDefective opsonization: complement deficiency gives encapsulated-organism infection without granulomas. Class-vs-memberImpaired neutrophil chemotaxis: leukocyte adhesion deficiency gives pus-free infections with delayed cord separation; pus was drained here. True-fact-wrong-slotDecreased immunoglobulin production: XLA gives encapsulated sinopulmonary infection; no granulomas, wrong organism. Unchecked attributeSevere congenital neutropenia: the right category and often the same gene, but it is persistent from the first months with severe infections; this child is well between regular 3-week episodes. Salient decoyViral illness: fever and mouth sores look viral, and viruses do lower the count, but once, not every 3 weeks for a year. True-fact-wrong-slotFanconi syndrome: a proximal tubule disorder, not a marrow one; the marrow disease is Fanconi anemia, which lowers all three lines and brings short stature and thumb anomalies.

briefs.title: Deep Neck Infections
briefs.sub: trismus with a deviated uvula needs no imaging · deep neck spaces by age · epiglottitis and Ludwig angina: airway firstHow old is the child, and is it trismus, pain on neck extension, or tripoding with stridor?
blocks: trismus with a deviated uvula needs no imaging · deep neck spaces by age · epiglottitis and Ludwig angina: airway firstHow old is the child, and is it trismus, pain on neck extension, or tripoding with stridor?

Pt boy of 14 whose throat pain on one side has grown worse over a week; he cannot open his jaw fully, his speech sounds muffled and the uvula leans to the left Q the likeliest diagnosis; choices covered peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess and infectious mononucleosis

Days of worsening one-sided throat pain, trismus, muffled speech and a uvula pushed away from a discrete tonsillar bulge in an adolescent is a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). It is a clinical diagnosis: no imaging unless the exam is limited, the diagnosis is in doubt or spread into the deep neck is suspected. Drain it, by needle aspiration or incision and drainage, and give antibiotics that cover aerobes and anaerobes; most patients go home. Usually under age 5, often after a cold, fever, drooling and a neck that will not extend: retropharyngeal abscess, imaged by CT neck with contrast. A tooth infection with a board-hard floor of the mouth: Ludwig angina. In both, and in a tripoding child, the airway comes first.

What it is Pus or spreading infection in the potential spaces of the neck. The Step 2 anchor is peritonsillar abscess, a collection between the tonsil and the superior pharyngeal constrictor and the most common deep neck infection. Bug Peritonsillar abscess: usually polymicrobial; streptococci (antibiotics should cover group A) and staphylococci, with oral anaerobes such as Fusobacterium and Bacteroides. Retropharyngeal abscess: group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus and Bacteroides. Ludwig angina: usually from a lower tooth; treat as mixed oral aerobes and anaerobes. Spread Peritonsillar: adolescents and young adults; virtually always one side, between the tonsil and the superior constrictor. Retropharyngeal: 6 months to 6 years, usually after an upper respiratory infection seeds the retropharyngeal nodes, which begin to regress after about age 5. Ludwig angina: usually an infected lower molar; poor dental hygiene, an extraction or jaw trauma may contribute. Chain Infection beside the tonsil pus collects between the tonsil and the superior constrictor a discrete one-sided bulge pushes the soft palate and uvula across jaw muscle spasm (trismus) and a muffled voice untreated, spread to the parapharyngeal space, the mediastinum or the carotid sheath, or rupture with aspiration Insights Pronounced trismus and a shifted uvula point to a discrete abscess; cellulitis swells the same area without the bulge; when the exam cannot tell them apart, ultrasound or the needle decides. Age sorts the spaces: the retropharyngeal nodes begin to regress after about age 5, so a retropharyngeal abscess is mostly a young child's disease, and a teenager with a one-sided bulge most likely has a peritonsillar one.

A clinical diagnosis: what makes it a peritonsillar abscess Element Finding Symptom Severe sore throat, one-sided and worsening over days, with fever and ear pain Signs Trismus, a muffled voice and a deviated uvula Abscess, not cellulitis A discrete bulge, palate and uvula pushed across, pronounced trismus; pus on the needle Imaging only when The exam is limited, the diagnosis is in doubt, or spread into the deep neck is suspected

Urgent findings Finding Action Stridor or drooling with any deep neck infection Airway first: secure it before imaging, antibiotics or drainage. Tripoding, drooling and stridor in an unvaccinated child whose throat often looks normal Epiglottitis: no tongue depressor; the airway is examined in the operating room. Board-hard floor of the mouth and a tongue pushed up after a tooth infection Ludwig angina: it can block the airway within hours; secure it first. Rigors, high fever and bacteremia, or bleeding from the throat, with a deep neck abscess May mean carotid sheath involvement from the posterior parapharyngeal space: contrast CT neck now.

The child or adolescent with a severe sore throat Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) Days of worsening one-sided throat pain in an adolescent; trismus, a muffled voice, the uvula pushed to the other side Needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics; no imaging in a classic case. Peritonsillar cellulitis The same throat, swelling above the tonsil with no discrete bulge; a needle that finds no pus may mean cellulitis Antibiotics and fluids; it usually settles within 48 hours. Infectious mononucleosis Exudative tonsils on both sides with posterior cervical nodes and splenomegaly Heterophile antibody test; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports. Streptococcal pharyngitis Swollen red tonsils, often with exudate, on both sides; nothing pushes the uvula aside Rapid antigen test or culture; penicillin if positive. Retropharyngeal abscess Usually under 5, often after an upper respiratory infection; will not extend the neck, drooling, a posterior pharyngeal wall that may bulge to one side Airway first, then CT neck with contrast; incision and drainage with IV antibiotics. Parapharyngeal abscess Mimics a peritonsillar abscess, but swelling below the angle of the jaw, medial bulging of the pharyngeal wall, torticollis Contrast CT neck, then IV antibiotics and drainage. Ludwig angina (submandibular space infection) Lower tooth infection; board-hard floor of the mouth on both sides, the tongue pushed up, drooling Airway first; the diagnosis is usually clinical, CT only when it is not. Epiglottitis Hours, not days, in an unvaccinated child; tripoding, drooling with no barking cough, stridor, often a normal-looking throat Secure the airway in the operating room, where laryngoscopy confirms it; no tongue depressor. Lemierre syndrome (septic jugular thrombophlebitis) May follow a throat infection: rigors, high fever, often bacteremia, then nodular lung infiltrates that cavitate Bug and spreadA usually anaerobic infection of the internal jugular vein and the tissue around it, most often Fusobacterium necrophorum, seeded mostly from the tonsils; spread goes mainly to the lungs, then the major joints. Contrast CT neck and prolonged antibiotics that cover anaerobes, the usual cause.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Severe one-sided sore throat with trismus, a muffled voice or drooling → Airway check, then oropharyngeal exam Discrete bulge above one tonsil, uvula pushed to the other side Peritonsillar abscess, a clinical diagnosis: go to the needle Stridor, drooling or tripoding Airway first; stop the examination Targeted tests TestResultMeans Abscess or cellulitis still unclear on the exam → Point-of-care (intraoral) ultrasound Fluid collection Abscess; it marks where to aspirate or cut Swelling below the angle of the jaw, torticollis, or a failed aspiration → CT neck with contrast Rim-enhancing collection beside the pharynx Parapharyngeal spread: IV antibiotics and drainage Under 5, fever and drooling, will not extend the neck, stridor → CT neck with contrast Collection behind the pharynx, with its extent Retropharyngeal abscess: drain it → Lateral neck radiograph, if taken first Prevertebral soft tissue wider than half a vertebral body Retropharyngeal abscess; CT shows the extent Exudates on both sides, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly → Heterophile antibody test Ages 2 to 5 The heterophile test is positive in only about half of children aged 2 to 5 years, against 85 to 90% of adolescents. Positive Mononucleosis: no amoxicillin, no contact sports Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Bulge and shifted uvula on the exam → Needle aspiration of the tonsillar mass, with culture Pus Abscess, drained in the same pass No pus May be cellulitis, or a missed pocket: image if aspiration fails SkipA lateral neck radiograph or CT for a classic peritonsillar abscess; a tongue depressor in a tripoding child.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step A rash after amoxicillin for a presumed strep throat Mononucleosis; the rash is not a true allergy Heterophile antibody test; the rash fades once the antibiotic stops. Retropharyngeal abscess in a teenager or adult Less common after age 5; in adults it may follow a swallowed foreign body or instrumentation CT neck to define the extent. Stridor that does not improve with racemic epinephrine Less likely croup: think epiglottitis or a deep neck abscess Airway first, in the operating room; CT only for a suspected abscess, once the airway is safe.

Pause point Teenager, one-sided sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula pushed across Offered as CT neck or lateral neck radiograph Can any image change a diagnosis the exam has already made? → Needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics; no imaging in a classic case A toddler, a week after a cold: fever, drooling, will not extend the neck, noisy breathing Offered as rapid strep test or oral antibiotics and home What comes before any test, and which study sees behind the pharynx? → Airway first, then CT neck with contrast; drainage and IV antibiotics Tooth infection, board-hard floor of the mouth, tongue pushed up, drooling Offered as CT first or oral intubation What kills first, and which route works when the floor of the mouth is swollen? → Airway first, by awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation or tracheotomy; then drainage and IV antibiotics

What makes it dangerous Finding Meaning Tonsils meeting in the midline Airway threat: a reason to admit Swelling below the angle of the jaw or torticollis Parapharyngeal spread A retropharyngeal infection tracking toward the chest Necrotizing mediastinitis Rigors, high fever, bacteremia, or bleeding from the throat The carotid sheath: septic jugular thrombophlebitis (Lemierre syndrome) or arterial erosion; contrast CT now

1 Drooling or stridorAny deep neck infection with drooling, stridor or a hard floor of the mouth Secure the airway before antibiotics, imaging or drainage. In Ludwig angina, awake fiberoptic nasotracheal intubation or a tracheotomy, because swelling makes oral intubation difficult. 2 EpiglottitisTripoding, drooling and stridor in an unvaccinated child Airway in the operating room; then antibiotics (Noisy Breathing in a Child). 3 Peritonsillar abscessClinical diagnosis Drain it, by needle aspiration or incision and drainage, and give antibiotics covering group A Streptococcus and oral anaerobes (for example ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin); most patients go home. In practiceIncision and drainage may carry a lower recurrence risk than aspiration alone (low-quality evidence), and corticosteroids may shorten symptoms. 4 Peritonsillar cellulitisNo pus on the needle, which may mean cellulitis Antibiotics and fluids; it usually settles within 48 hours. 5 Retropharyngeal abscessChild with a collection behind the pharynx Airway first, then incision and drainage with IV ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin. In practiceSmall abscesses in children are sometimes treated with IV antibiotics alone; surgery is kept for airway compromise, no response, a size over 3 cm, immune compromise or complications. 6 Parapharyngeal abscessCollection on contrast CT IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone, and surgical drainage. 7 Ludwig anginaOnce the airway is safe Incision and drainage and IV antibiotics covering oral aerobes and anaerobes. 8 Lemierre syndromeJugular thrombophlebitis on contrast CT Prolonged antibiotics covering anaerobes, 2 to 6 weeks. 9 Recurrent tonsillitisPeritonsillar abscess on a background of recurrent tonsillitis Elective tonsillectomy 4 to 6 weeks later. At presentation?Rarely: tonsillectomy at presentation is kept for a young or uncooperative child with other indications.

After the first aspiration or drainage When Do Dehydration, cannot drink, an airway concern, or failed outpatient care Admit for IV antibiotics, fluids and airway monitoring. Aspiration yields no pus but the picture persists Image to confirm an abscess and ask otolaryngology about incision and drainage. Group A Streptococcus grown Watch for poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (postinfectious glomerulonephritis) and rheumatic fever.

In Ludwig angina and epiglottitis, the airway is the emergency. Examination can precipitate obstruction, so do not depress the tongue or instrument the pharynx of a tripoding child outside the operating room. A peritonsillar abscess on a background of recurrent tonsillitis is an indication for elective tonsillectomy.

Peritonsillar abscess is diagnosed clinically; intraoral ultrasound helps when abscess versus cellulitis is uncertain and marks where to drain Retropharyngeal abscess makes neck extension painful, so the child holds the neck still Amoxicillin in undiagnosed mononucleosis brings a maculopapular rash that is not a true allergy Lemierre syndrome is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after a throat infection, most often Fusobacterium necrophorum, and it spreads most often to the lungs as nodular infiltrates

When a diagnosis is clinical and the complication is airway compromise, imaging is almost always the wrong next step. It cannot change what is already known, and it costs time the airway may not have.

Pt 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly Imaging periventricular calcifications Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned congenital cytomegalovirus, congenital toxoplasmosis and congenital rubella

Identify the organism, then its signature sequela. Calcifications along the ventricular margin (periventricular) indicate CMV (cytomegalovirus). Calcifications scattered through the parenchyma indicate toxoplasmosis. An indoor cat suggests toxoplasmosis but is compatible with congenital CMV.

Periventricular calcifications CMV Diffuse parenchymal calcifications toxoplasmosis, with chorioretinitis Subcortical calcifications with arthrogryposis Zika Diagnostic window urine or saliva PCR (polymerase chain reaction) within the first 3 weeks of life, after which congenital and perinatal acquisition cannot be separated; later, a positive PCR on the stored newborn dried blood spot may help, but a negative does not exclude it

Congenital infection – the differential Infection Illness script The NBME tell CMV Most common congenital infection; hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephaly Periventricular calcifications with microcephaly; sequela is sensorineural hearing loss Toxoplasmosis Cat litter, undercooked meat Diffuse parenchymal calcifications and chorioretinitis; sequela is obstructive hydrocephalus Rubella Unvaccinated mother Cataracts and a continuous machine-like PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) murmur Syphilis Untreated maternal infection Snuffles, palm-and-sole rash, periostitis; no CNS (central nervous system) calcifications HSV (herpes simplex virus) Can't miss Intrapartum acquisition Days 5 to 21, vesicles, seizures, temporal lobe; without vesicles, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with lymphocytes and red cells and normal glucose Zika Maternal travel Severe microcephaly with subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis Parvovirus B19 Maternal febrile illness with arthralgia; risk highest before 20 weeks Hydrops fetalis or fetal loss; congenital anomalies are rare in survivors; follow with serial ultrasonography and MCA (middle cerebral artery) Doppler Listeria monocytogenes Can't miss Nonspecific maternal febrile illness, often foodborne Severe neonatal sepsis with disseminated abscesses in liver, spleen, lung, kidney and brain

Rubella also causes sensorineural hearing loss. Hearing loss therefore does not separate rubella from CMV (cytomegalovirus); the calcification pattern does.

Sensorineural hearing loss a failed newborn hearing screen Cataracts an absent red reflex, or leukocoria Patent ductus arteriosus a continuous machine-like murmur at the left second interspace Plus growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly and a purpuric blueberry-muffin rash Maternal arthralgia after a febrile illness in pregnancy rubella causes organ malformation from first-trimester organogenesis; parvovirus B19 causes hydrops and no malformation

Exposure a child with slapped cheeks at home, school or day care; a child with the rash is no longer contagious, so exposure happened earlier; most maternal infections are asymptomatic, others flu-like with rash or symmetric arthralgia Maternal serology B19 IgM positive means acute infection; IgG positive with IgM negative means past infection and immunity; B19 DNA testing if immunocompromised Fetal risk the virus infects erythroid progenitors, so the danger is fetal anemia, then hydrops or fetal death, not malformation Acute infection serial ultrasonography with middle cerebral artery Doppler to detect fetal anemia and hydrops Severe fetal anemia intrauterine transfusion

Timing seizures, lethargy or apnea in the second or third week of life; vesicles are often absent Cerebrospinal fluid normal or mildly low glucose, mildly raised protein, a modest pleocytosis that is mostly lymphocytes, and many red cells Bacterial meningitis low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant leukocyte count, often over 1,000/mm3 Confirm herpes simplex virus PCR (polymerase chain reaction) of the cerebrospinal fluid Treat add intravenous acyclovir to empiric antibiotics without waiting for the PCR NBME framing: no vesicles are given and antibiotics are already begun, so the day of life and the lymphocytic, bloody cerebrospinal fluid identify the virus.

CMV (cytomegalovirus) is the most common congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss Only about 10% are symptomatic at birth, and that group carries up to 50% hearing-loss risk untreated Six months of valganciclovir is better than six weeks: 8% versus 13% hearing worsening at one year Hearing loss is progressive and can be late-onset, so passing the newborn screen does not discharge the child from audiology CMV – ventricles enlarge ex vacuo from volume loss Toxoplasmosis – ventricles enlarge from obstruction

Part I Hearing Loss and Chronic Ear Disease covers the childhood sensorineural causes. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the same imaging; the calcification pattern and the white-matter injury each point to a different cause. Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn: does the cerebrospinal fluid show low glucose with over 1,000 neutrophil-predominant leukocytes, or lymphocytes and red cells with normal glucose?

Identifying the complication of a syndrome takes two independent steps: name the syndrome, then its complication. When anatomic distribution and exposure history are both given, always rely on anatomic distribution.

Unchecked attributeCytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis both follow a mild maternal flu-like illness, but neither produces cataracts or a cardiac defect. The maternal history is shared; the fetal organ pattern separates them. Salient decoyToxoplasmosis: the indoor cat suggests it, but a cat is also compatible with cytomegalovirus. True-fact-wrong-slotRubella: it causes cataracts, but not periventricular calcifications. Salient decoyGroup B streptococcus: the antibiotics already begun point toward it, but neonatal bacterial meningitis gives low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant count, often over 1,000/mm3. Unchecked attributeEscherichia coli: a common cause of neonatal meningitis, but a count of 70 that is mostly lymphocytes, with normal glucose, does not fit a bacterial cause. True-fact-wrong-slotCytomegalovirus: symptomatic congenital infection shows at birth with periventricular calcifications and hearing loss, not as an acute encephalitis in the second week. True-fact-wrong-slotToxoplasma gondii: congenital infection shows chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications, not a new encephalitis on day 8.

blocks: Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn

neonatal sepsis, its mimics and the febrile infant to 60 days · a laboratory value decides when the temperature does not; every reliable negative closes a sourceIs a laboratory value the only sign, and which source remains?

Fever is unreliable in the first month: neonates with sepsis may be afebrile or hypothermic, so without fever the laboratory results decide. With fever, the age band sets the workup. Early-onset sepsis: onset within 72 hours; organisms from the maternal genital tract: group B Streptococcus (GBS), Escherichia coli and Listeria. Late-onset sepsis: onset 72 hours to 90 days; nosocomial organisms join: coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants. Leukopenia: the total white blood cell count (WBC) predicts early-onset sepsis poorly, but a low count in a neonate with these signs is sepsis until proven otherwise; it reflects marrow depletion by overwhelming infection and is more ominous than leukocytosis. Paradoxical irritability: quiet when undisturbed, crying on being picked up or moved, because handling stretches inflamed meninges: the meningeal sign of infancy. Neonatal empiric coverage: ampicillin plus gentamicin: ampicillin for GBS and Listeria (cephalosporins miss Listeria), gentamicin for gram-negative organisms (cefotaxime may be added or substituted if gram-negative meningitis is suspected); ampicillin plus cefotaxime when meningitis is strongly suspected or confirmed; ceftriaxone is avoided.

The irritable neonate: leukopenia separates sepsis from the behavioral mimics Diagnosis Illness script The tell Neonatal sepsis, can't miss Early onset within 72 hours, late onset after; maternal GBS or chorioamnionitis; subtle: poor feeding, temperature instability, apnea, tachycardia Leukopenia or leukocytosis with left shift; the neonate who “doesn’t look right” Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) Maternal opioid use; onset 24 to 72 hours High-pitched cry, tremor, sneezing, hyperactive Moro; normal WBC Neonatal hypoglycemia Infant of a diabetic mother, large or small for gestational age, preterm Jitteriness, lethargy, seizures; glucose below 40 to 45 mg/dL Neonatal thyrotoxicosis Maternal Graves disease, required Tachycardia, irritability, exophthalmos, goiter Inborn error of metabolism Poor feeding after protein or galactose, day 2 to 5 Metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, a specific dietary trigger

The toxic febrile infant: where is the source? Diagnosis Illness script The tell Bacterial meningitis Any age; infants show no neck signs Paradoxical irritability, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry Intussusception 6 to 36 months, ileocolic, often post-viral Paroxysmal crying with pain-free intervals, sausage mass, currant-jelly stool Urinary tract infection The commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infants Positive leukocyte esterase or nitrite with pyuria Bacterial gastroenteritis High fever with cramping Bloody or mucoid stools, many per day, sick contacts Viral respiratory infection Cough, congestion, coryza Rhinorrhea and cough Occult bacteremia or pneumonia Fever with leukocytosis, no localizing sign Tachypnea with hypoxia or focal crackles, not fever-driven tachypnea alone

Abnormal markers: temperature above 38.5 °C, procalcitonin above 0.5 ng/mL, C-reactive protein above 20 mg/L, absolute neutrophil count above 4,000/mm³ (5,200/mm³ without procalcitonin).

Ampicillin covers group B Streptococcus and Listeria, and gentamicin the gram-negative organisms. Intravenous dextrose answers a low glucose, and morphine answers neonatal abstinence, which brings tremor with a normal count. The total white cell count predicts early-onset sepsis poorly on its own, but here it is the one abnormal value

Workup2 of 17 7-month-old boy has fever and cries violently when picked up lies quietly when left undisturbed Three loose stools today; no cough or rhinorrhea T 39.5 °C · white blood cells 16,000/mm³ with 83% neutrophils · urine dipstick negative, specific gravity 1.030 · Lumbar puncture for Gram stain and culture · Abdominal ultrasound · Stool polymerase chain reaction panel for enteric pathogens 7-month-old boy has fever and cries violently when picked up lies quietly when left undisturbed Three loose stools today; no cough or rhinorrhea T 39.5 °C · white blood cells 16,000/mm³ with 83% neutrophils · urine dipstick negative, specific gravity 1.030 Lumbar puncture for Gram stain and culturecrying on being handled with calm when undisturbed is paradoxical irritability, the meningeal sign of infancy. No cough or rhinorrhea closes the respiratory branch; a negative dipstick in concentrated urine closes the urinary branch. Three loose stools are a nonspecific systemic response and do not explain the paradoxical irritability, and paroxysmal crying with a mass would earn the ultrasound

A normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia, and a normal count with a clear drug history argues against sepsis

Paroxysmal crying with calm intervals is the mirror of the constant paradoxical irritability that earns a lumbar puncture

Next step5 of 17 1-day-old girl is jittery and lethargic Mother had gestational diabetes large for gestational age Born at 39 weeks by cesarean delivery; Apgar scores 8 and 9 T 36.8 °C · HR 150/min · glucose 28 mg/dL · Ampicillin and gentamicin · Reassurance and observation with routine feeds · Intravenous dextrose infusion 1-day-old girl is jittery and lethargic Mother had gestational diabetes large for gestational age Born at 39 weeks by cesarean delivery; Apgar scores 8 and 9 T 36.8 °C · HR 150/min · glucose 28 mg/dL Intravenous dextrose infusionan infant of a diabetic mother with jitteriness, lethargy and a glucose below 40 to 45 mg/dL is symptomatic hypoglycemia, treated with intravenous dextrose. Antibiotics answer leukopenia, not a low glucose, and observation leaves a symptomatic infant untreated

Next step6 of 17 8-month-old girl has fever with no localizing findings No cough, rhinorrhea or diarrhea Immunizations are up to date; fever began 2 days ago catheterized urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase T 39.2 °C · HR 160/min · Observation with a repeat examination in 24 hours · Urine culture and empiric antibiotics · Lumbar puncture 8-month-old girl has fever with no localizing findings No cough, rhinorrhea or diarrhea Immunizations are up to date; fever began 2 days ago catheterized urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase T 39.2 °C · HR 160/min Urine culture and empiric antibioticsthe commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infants: a positive dipstick sends the urine for culture and starts antibiotics. A lumbar puncture tests the wrong fluid without a meningeal sign, and observation leaves a likely infection untreated

Diagnosis7 of 17 4-day-old girl has tachycardia and tremor Mother has Graves disease; no maternal drug use Born at 38 weeks poor weight gain since birth exophthalmos warm, moist skin T 37.4 °C · HR 196/min · white blood cells 9,000/mm³ · Neonatal abstinence syndrome · Neonatal thyrotoxicosis · Neonatal sepsis 4-day-old girl has tachycardia and tremor Mother has Graves disease; no maternal drug use Born at 38 weeks poor weight gain since birth exophthalmos warm, moist skin T 37.4 °C · HR 196/min · white blood cells 9,000/mm³ Neonatal thyrotoxicosismaternal Graves disease with tachycardia, tremor and exophthalmos; free thyroxine is high and thyroid-stimulating hormone low, and propranolol with methimazole treats it. Neonatal abstinence needs a maternal drug history

Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin leaves Listeria uncovered, and observation misses a bulging fontanelle

Diagnosis9 of 17 7-month-old boy has a rash on his trunk Fever to 39 °C for 3 days ended yesterday blanching rose-pink macules on the trunk playful and well appearing T 37.0 °C · HR 120/min · Bacterial meningitis · Roseola infantum · Measles 7-month-old boy has a rash on his trunk Fever to 39 °C for 3 days ended yesterday blanching rose-pink macules on the trunk playful and well appearing T 37.0 °C · HR 120/min Roseola infantumhigh fever that breaks before a blanching rose-pink truncal rash appears is human herpesvirus 6; no testing is needed. In measles, fever may spike when the rash appears, and a well, playful infant has no meningeal sign

Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is the right class at the wrong age, and observation delays treatment

Ampicillin and gentamicin are the neonatal regimen
