Escherichia coli now predominates among preterm and very low birth weight neonates, and Listeria is the organism ampicillin is kept for

Workup15 of 17 12-month-old girl has fever and vomiting papilledema on funduscopy; anterior fontanelle closed new weakness of the right arm and leg Empiric intravenous antibiotics have been given T 39.6 °C · HR 168/min · BP 96/58 mm Hg · Head CT before lumbar puncture · Await blood culture results before imaging · Immediate lumbar puncture 12-month-old girl has fever and vomiting papilledema on funduscopy; anterior fontanelle closed new weakness of the right arm and leg Empiric intravenous antibiotics have been given T 39.6 °C · HR 168/min · BP 96/58 mm Hg Head CT before lumbar puncturepapilledema or a focal deficit puts imaging before the tap, and antibiotics come first, then CT, then the lumbar puncture if imaging shows it is safe. An immediate tap is premature: signs of raised intracranial pressure and focal neurologic signs are reasons the tap may be delayed, and waiting for blood culture results holds up imaging that belongs during or right after the antibiotics

Next step16 of 17 21-day-old girl born at 39 weeks has a fever Well appearing and feeding normally Parents measured the fever an hour ago; no sick contacts no rash, cough or focal findings T 38.4 °C rectal · HR 168/min · Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, admission and empiric antibiotics · Urinalysis and urine culture only · Discharge with follow-up in 24 hours 21-day-old girl born at 39 weeks has a fever Well appearing and feeding normally Parents measured the fever an hour ago; no sick contacts no rash, cough or focal findings T 38.4 °C rectal · HR 168/min Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, admission and empiric antibioticsat 8 to 21 days the AAP guideline calls for a catheterized urinalysis, a blood culture and cerebrospinal fluid, parenteral antibiotics and hospital monitoring, even when the infant looks well. A urine-only workup or discharge without cerebrospinal fluid falls short in this band

Avoid17 of 17 8-month-old boy has fever, petechiae and lethargy Ill for 12 hours; capillary refill 5 seconds A lumbar puncture tray is being prepared T 39.8 °C · HR 190/min · BP 64/30 mm Hg · Obtaining blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose · Giving intravenous fluids · Delaying antibiotics to complete the lumbar puncture 8-month-old boy has fever, petechiae and lethargy Ill for 12 hours; capillary refill 5 seconds A lumbar puncture tray is being prepared T 39.8 °C · HR 190/min · BP 64/30 mm Hg Delaying antibiotics to complete the lumbar puncturetreat first, tap after: in shock with petechiae, a lumbar puncture never delays antibiotics. Blood cultures are right as long as they do not delay the first dose, and intravenous fluid boluses are suggested for the shock

Neonate (0 to 28 days) ampicillin plus gentamicin, covering GBS, E. coli and Listeria; cefotaxime may be added to or substituted for the gentamicin if gram-negative meningitis is suspected, and ampicillin plus cefotaxime is preferred when meningitis is strongly suspected or confirmed, for its superior cerebrospinal fluid penetration. The 2021 AAP table lists ampicillin with ceftazidime or gentamicin for 8 to 28 days. Where extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli circulates, gentamicin replaces ceftazidime for suspected bacteremia or sepsis, and meropenem replaces it when meningitis is suspected 29 to 60 days ceftriaxone, with vancomycin added when bacteremia or meningitis is a concern; the neonatal organisms recede and ceftriaxone’s biliary risk becomes acceptable Ceftriaxone in a neonate avoided: it displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and precipitates in the biliary tract as sludge; contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemic neonates or with calcium-containing intravenous solutions Herpes simplex virus (HSV) risk maternal genital HSV lesions or fever 48 hours before or after delivery; vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis with a negative Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or raised transaminases: acyclovir joins the parenteral antibiotics

With focal deficits or papilledema, give antibiotics first, obtain neuroimaging during or right after them, then tap if imaging shows it is safe. In an infant with an open fontanelle the requirement is generally suspended: the fontanelle decompresses rising pressure, so, without signs of raised intracranial pressure, tap without imaging first. If the tap will be delayed, give antibiotics first. Draw the blood culture, but never let it delay antibiotics.

8 to 21 days (AAP 2021) Decision Action and condition Urine Should: catheter or suprapubic aspiration specimen for urinalysis, and for culture if the urinalysis is positive Blood culture Should obtain Inflammatory markers May assess CSF Should obtain for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain and bacterial culture Antibiotics Should start parenteral therapy Where Should actively monitor in hospital, with staff experienced with neonates, while cultures are pending Stop Should stop parenteral antibiotics and discharge when cultures are negative for 24 to 36 hours (or grow only contaminants), the infant still appears well or is improving, and no other reason for hospitalization remains. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response HSV Should be considered with maternal genital HSV lesions or fever from 48 hours before to 48 hours after delivery, or vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase; then parenteral antibiotics including acyclovir

22 to 28 days (AAP 2021) Decision Action and condition Urine Should: catheter or suprapubic specimen for urinalysis and culture if positive, or a bag or voided specimen for urinalysis with a catheter or suprapubic culture if positive Blood culture Should obtain Inflammatory markers Should assess CSF Should obtain if any marker is abnormal. May obtain even if no marker is abnormal (urinalysis negative or positive), once blood and urine cultures are taken and the infant is hospitalized Antibiotics, hospital Should give parenteral therapy if CSF suggests bacterial meningitis or the urinalysis is positive. May give it if CSF and urinalysis are normal but a marker is abnormal, and may even if the urinalysis and all markers are normal and CSF is normal or enterovirus-positive Antibiotics, home Should give parenteral therapy before home management, even if the urinalysis, all markers and CSF are normal Home May manage at home if the urinalysis and all markers are normal, CSF is normal or enterovirus-positive, verbal and written instructions are given, a recheck in 24 hours is arranged, and plans for a change in condition (contact with providers, access to emergency care) are in place Hospital Should admit if CSF is not obtained or is uninterpretable Stop Should stop antibiotics and discharge hospitalized infants after 24 to 36 hours of negative cultures if the infant is well or improving, with no other reason for hospitalization and no other infection needing treatment (such as otitis media). At home, should stop when the infant is well or improving at reassessment, all cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours and no other infection needs treatment. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response HSV Should be considered (HSV can occur in this age group) with vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase

29 to 60 days (AAP 2021) Decision Action and condition Urine Should: bag or voided specimen for urinalysis with a catheter or suprapubic culture if positive, or a catheter or suprapubic specimen for both Blood culture Should obtain Inflammatory markers Should assess CSF Need not obtain if all markers are normal. May obtain if any marker is abnormal, testing for enterovirus when pleocytosis is found or in enterovirus season Antibiotics Should give parenteral therapy if CSF suggests bacterial meningitis. May give it if CSF (if obtained) is normal and any marker is abnormal. Should start oral therapy if the urinalysis is positive, no marker is abnormal and CSF (if obtained) is normal. Need not give any while cultures are pending if the urinalysis is negative, no marker is abnormal and CSF (if obtained) is normal or enterovirus-positive Hospital Should admit if CSF (if obtained) is abnormal. May admit if any marker is abnormal Home Should manage at home if CSF (if obtained) is normal, the urinalysis is negative and all markers are normal, with parental education, a recheck in 24 hours and plans for a change in condition. May manage at home without antibiotics or interpretable CSF if the urinalysis is negative, all markers are normal and parents can return promptly and agree to follow-up in 24 to 36 hours; reassess within 24 hours Stop Should stop antibiotics when all cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours, the infant is well or improving and no other infection needs treatment. With a positive urine culture, should discharge if blood and CSF (if obtained) cultures are negative, the infant is well or improving and no other reason for hospitalization remains; at home, should stop parenteral antibiotics (if started) and begin or continue oral therapy when other cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours and the infant is well or improving. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response HSV Should be considered, although uncommon, with maternal genital HSV lesions or vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase

Early-onset organisms come from the maternal genital tract: GBS, E. coli (often carrying the K1 (capsular antigen 1) capsule) and Listeria. Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis reduced early-onset GBS disease but did not change E. coli rates, and E. coli now predominates among preterm and VLBW neonates. No strategy yet prevents late-onset GBS disease, and its rate is unchanged. GBS remains a leading cause of meningitis and bloodstream infection under 3 months. For GBS disease the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) counts early onset as under 7 days and late onset as 7 to 89 days.

Fever without a source is documented fever with no localizing findings after history and examination. Nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable under roughly 12 to 18 months; look for paradoxical irritability, a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry. A dipstick is a screen, not a rule-out: leukocyte esterase is about 83% sensitive and nitrite about 53%, because infant bladder transit is too short for nitrate reduction; both negative in concentrated urine (specific gravity 1.030) is genuinely reassuring. Loose stools and mild tachypnea are nonspecific systemic responses in a septic infant, not localizing findings. When the sources are eliminated one by one and a meningeal sign remains, do a lumbar puncture. Dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis. In the first days, 5% weight loss at day 3 is physiologic (up to 7 to 10% in breastfed newborns).

Neonatal abstinence or hypoglycemia for an irritable, poorly feeding neonate: either fits the behavior, but leukopenia fits neither. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin under 29 days: the right class of empiric coverage at the wrong age. Propranolol: it treats neonatal thyrotoxicosis, which does not produce leukopenia. Abdominal ultrasound for paradoxical irritability: intussusception is the other inconsolable infant, but its crying is paroxysmal with calm intervals. Urine culture with a meningeal sign: the right class of test on the wrong fluid. Stool testing: three loose stools cannot produce a fever of 39.5 °C with 83% neutrophils.

Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF grid and the neonatal organism-by-host list, so this brief stops at the decision to tap. Ask: am I deciding whether to tap, or reading the fluid? Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child covers what a seizure adds to the decision to tap. Aquifer Fever in an Infant covers which tests the age, appearance and vaccines call for, and the febrile urinary tract infection that is most often found.

In a neonate the absence of fever does not exclude sepsis: without fever and with no maternal drug history, the WBC decides, not the behavioral pattern. In a febrile infant, name the disease first by elimination, then choose the test that follows from it; each reliable negative finding closes a source, and the diagnosis is the source that remains.

Pt 12 yo M, half an hour of burning, puffy eyes, a tight, scratchy throat and belly cramps, hours after starting amoxicillin for a sore throat; no known drug allergy Exam afebrile, blood pressure and pulse normal; swollen eyelids, mildly red conjunctivae, wheals on the trunk Q the mechanism; options included Epstein-Barr virus infection, immune complexes, impaired bradykinin breakdown, mast cell activation and vasculitis

Skin or mucosa plus one more system (airway, persistent gut symptoms or circulation) within minutes to hours of a likely allergen is anaphylaxis, and hypotension is not required; low blood pressure alone after a known allergen also qualifies. Give intramuscular (IM) epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh first; antihistamines, albuterol and glucocorticoids are adjuncts that never replace it. Swelling with no hives on an ACE inhibitor (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor), or with a low complement C4 level, is bradykinin angioedema; a rash days into a drug is a delayed reaction, not anaphylaxis.

What it is An acute, potentially fatal systemic allergic reaction: immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated, type I hypersensitivity in a sensitized person re-exposed to the antigen. Driver Mast cell and basophil degranulation. IgE type: the antigen cross-links IgE on sensitized cells. Non-IgE type (anaphylactoid): direct mast cell activation, no prior sensitization, clinically identical. Triggers Foods (nuts, eggs, seafood); drugs (beta-lactams, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); insect venom; latex; radiocontrast (non-IgE) Selective immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency: may react to blood products non-modifiable Chain Sensitized mast cells and basophils meet the antigen histamine, tryptase and leukotrienes are released vasodilation and plasma leakage; smooth muscle contraction hives, airway swelling, wheeze, vomiting; distributive shock with warm skin Insights Shock can be the only sign: cardiovascular collapse can occur without respiratory or other symptoms, which is why low blood pressure alone after a known allergen is a criterion. A first reaction is not a first exposure: an earlier, uneventful course sensitized the mast cells.
Minutesonset; shock can develop this fast Within 2 hoursbest window for a serum tryptase 4 to 6 hourstypical biphasic window, with no re-exposure

Anaphylaxis is likely with any 1 Criterion Requires First: skin or mucosa Hives, flushing or swelling of the lips, tongue or eyes, with breathing trouble or low blood pressure Second: likely allergen 2 or more of skin or mucosa, respiratory, low blood pressure, persistent gastrointestinal symptoms Third: known allergen Low blood pressure alone Low blood pressure in a child Age-specific low systolic pressure or a fall of more than 30%

Act now Finding Action Stridor or wheeze that does not answer epinephrine Oxygen and early intubation; waiting may let airway edema progress. Hypotension that persists after IM epinephrine Isotonic intravenous (IV) fluids, which usually work; IV epinephrine, preferably as an infusion, may be given next. Reaction in a patient taking a beta-blocker Give epinephrine anyway; if hypotension persists, add IV glucagon.

Anaphylaxis and its mimics Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Acute urticaria alone Hives and itch, but no second system: airway, gut and blood pressure are normal; mast cell activation, often IgE. Treat the hives with an oral antihistamine; epinephrine is not needed. Bradykinin angioedema (ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema) Over hours: swelling of the lips, tongue or bowel wall without hives or itch; on an ACE inhibitor it can begin after months or years of use. Why no hivesC1 inhibitor normally blocks kallikrein, which makes bradykinin; ACE breaks bradykinin down, so an ACE inhibitor lets it build. Hereditary angioedema is autosomal dominant C1 inhibitor deficiency that presents in childhood or adolescence, with colicky abdominal attacks from swelling of the bowel wall. Stop the ACE inhibitor; check C4 when no drug explains it. Vasovagal syncope Seconds after pain or fear, such as a needle; a vagal surge gives bradycardia, pallor and sweat, with no hives or wheeze. Check the pulse: slow, with clear skin and lungs, is vagal, not anaphylaxis. Serum sickness-like reaction Fever and Rash in a Child 5 to 14 days into a drug: urticarial rash with fever, joint pain and nodes; a delayed drug hypersensitivity (true serum sickness is immune complex). Stop the drug; it resolves on its own. Epstein-Barr virus rash with an aminopenicillin (infectious mononucleosis) Days into amoxicillin: a maculopapular rash, fever, exudative tonsils, posterior neck nodes and left upper quadrant pain. Treat as a virus-driven rash, not an IgE penicillin allergy. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) Days; immune complex vessel inflammation: palpable purpura, fever, joint pain, colicky abdominal pain. Examine the rash: palpable purpura is not urticaria. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (postinfectious glomerulonephritis) Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome Weeks, not days: about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo. Swelling that builds over days, with high blood pressure and cola-colored urine. Check the blood pressure and urine: immune complex nephritis, not anaphylaxis.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Skin or mucosa plus a second system minutes to hours after an exposure → Blood pressure and pulse Normal reading Does not exclude it; two systems already meet the criteria → Serum tryptase, ideally within 2 hours Elevated Supports mast cell activation afterward; epinephrine is never delayed for it Targeted tests TestResultMeans Recurrent swelling without hives, no drug cause, a family history → Serum C4 Low, even between episodes Points to hereditary angioedema; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function Anaphylaxis during a transfusion → Serum IgA level Undetectable IgA-depleted products from now on Transfusion Reactions Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Clinical diagnosis → Any 1 of the 3 criteria Met Anaphylaxis: give IM epinephrine now SkipTotal IgE or allergy testing during the reaction: the diagnosis is clinical and treatment is not delayed for testing.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step No known drug allergy; first reaction Sensitized by an earlier, uneventful exposure Treat as anaphylaxis. Hypotension alone after a known allergen Anaphylaxis by the third criterion Give IM epinephrine now. Swelling unchanged after epinephrine and an antihistamine Bradykinin, not mast cell Stop any ACE inhibitor; in hereditary angioedema give C1 inhibitor concentrate; secure the airway if it closes. More epinephrine is usually not effective. Flushing and hives after fish Scombroid fish poisoning can mimic it: flushing, hives, diarrhea and cramps minutes to hours after eating Give an antihistamine; albuterol or epinephrine may be added if needed.

Pause point Hives, throat tightness and cramps; blood pressure normal Offered as wait for hypotension or an oral antihistamine How many systems, and how soon after the exposure? → Anaphylaxis: three systems within minutes; give IM epinephrine Lip and tongue swelling, no hives, on lisinopril Offered as repeat epinephrine or mast cell activation Are there hives or itch? → Bradykinin angioedema: stop the ACE inhibitor Urticarial rash, fever and joint pain a week into penicillin Offered as anaphylaxis or acute rheumatic fever Minutes, or days? → Serum sickness-like reaction: stop the drug Epinephrine comes first; antihistamines and glucocorticoids never replace it.

Severity findings Finding Meaning Respiratory distress or hypotension Severe: admit for prolonged observation 2 or more IM doses, or any IV epinephrine, needed Admit for prolonged observation; higher biphasic risk Rash alone, or resolved with 1 dose May be discharged sooner Taking a beta-blocker Risk factor for a severe reaction

1 FirstCriteria met IM epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh: 0.01 mL/kg of the 1 mg/mL (1:1000) solution in children, 0.3 to 0.5 mL in adults. Why the thighAbsorption is greatest from the anterolateral thigh muscle. 2 PersistingSymptoms persist after 5 to 15 minutes Repeat IM epinephrine. 3 AirwayStridor or wheeze despite epinephrine Oxygen and early intubation. 4 ShockHypotension persists Isotonic IV fluids, which usually work; IV epinephrine, preferably as an infusion, may be given next; IV glucagon for a patient on a beta-blocker. 5 AdjunctsAfter epinephrine Antihistamines (diphenhydramine), inhaled albuterol for persistent bronchospasm; glucocorticoids are unproven, though they may help head off a late-phase reaction.

Hereditary angioedema: attacks and prevention Situation Do Laryngeal swelling with stridor or the airway closing Secure the airway first; airway swelling is usually the cause of death Laryngeal swelling with the airway still open Give C1 inhibitor concentrate now and be ready to secure the airway; intubation may be needed in severe cases Acute attack C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor blocker) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor); epinephrine, antihistamines and glucocorticoids are usually not effective Needs a blood pressure drug Avoid ACE inhibitors Triggers to plan around Dental work and other minor trauma; estrogen-containing medications First-degree relatives Screen with C1 inhibitor and C4 levels, with or without symptoms

After the reaction Situation Do Symptoms resolved Observe for several hours: a biphasic reaction typically returns within 4 to 6 hours Discharge Epinephrine autoinjector for every patient (0.15 mg child, 0.3 mg adult), alert identification, avoid the trigger Anaphylaxis to an insect sting Desensitization, since stings cannot reliably be avoided Anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications No further doses of that vaccine

Mechanism1 of 11 12 yo M, 30 minutes after starting amoxicillin for strep throat; a course at age 5 caused no reaction. Itchy wheals on the trunk, puffy eyelids, a tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; BP 116/68, HR 92 · Mast cell activationSkin, airway and gut signs within 30 minutes of amoxicillin: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation. · Impaired bradykinin degradationBradykinin angioedema brings swelling with no hives or itch; this boy has wheals. · Immune complex formationImmune complex reactions such as serum sickness arrive 5 to 14 days into a drug, not within minutes. 12 yo M, 30 minutes after starting amoxicillin for strep throat; a course at age 5 caused no reaction. Itchy wheals on the trunk, puffy eyelids, a tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; BP 116/68, HR 92 Mast cell activationanaphylaxis: skin, respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement within 30 minutes of amoxicillin, after sensitization by an earlier course; intramuscular (IM) epinephrine

Next step2 of 11 7 yo F at a birthday party, 10 minutes after eating a cookie made with peanut butter, develops hives on the face and trunk, wheezing and 2 episodes of vomiting; no previous reactions to food; T 37.0, BP 98/60, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 94% on room air; diffuse expiratory wheezes · Nebulized albuterolAlbuterol treats wheeze that persists after epinephrine; it does not replace it. · Intravenous diphenhydramineAntihistamines are adjuncts for itch and hives; they do not replace or delay epinephrine. · Intramuscular epinephrineHives, wheeze and vomiting minutes after peanut meet the criteria: IM epinephrine first. 7 yo F at a birthday party, 10 minutes after eating a cookie made with peanut butter, develops hives on the face and trunk, wheezing and 2 episodes of vomiting; no previous reactions to food; T 37.0, BP 98/60, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 94% on room air; diffuse expiratory wheezes Intramuscular epinephrineanaphylaxis by skin plus respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement; blood pressure need not fall

Next step3 of 11 9 yo M, itchy raised wheals on the trunk and arms 1 hour after eating strawberries for the first time this season; no lip or tongue swelling, throat symptoms, cough, vomiting or abdominal pain; BP 104/66, HR 90, SpO2 99%; lungs clear; blanching urticarial plaques · Intramuscular epinephrineEpinephrine is for anaphylaxis; one system does not meet the criteria. · Oral prednisone for 5 daysA steroid course is not the first treatment for hives alone; an antihistamine is. · Oral cetirizineHives with no second system is acute urticaria alone: an oral antihistamine treats it. 9 yo M, itchy raised wheals on the trunk and arms 1 hour after eating strawberries for the first time this season; no lip or tongue swelling, throat symptoms, cough, vomiting or abdominal pain; BP 104/66, HR 90, SpO2 99%; lungs clear; blanching urticarial plaques Oral cetirizineacute urticaria alone: one system, so criteria for anaphylaxis are not met

Next step4 of 11 15 yo M treated in the emergency department for hives, throat tightness and wheezing 20 minutes after eating cashews, his first reaction to food; one dose of intramuscular epinephrine was given, and after 6 hours of observation he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs and clear lungs · Epinephrine autoinjector prescriptionEvery patient leaves with self-injectable epinephrine, an action plan, avoidance and allergy referral. · Oral prednisone for 5 daysGlucocorticoids have no proven role and do not protect against the next exposure. · Daily oral cetirizineA daily antihistamine does not treat the next reaction to cashews. 15 yo M treated in the emergency department for hives, throat tightness and wheezing 20 minutes after eating cashews, his first reaction to food; one dose of intramuscular epinephrine was given, and after 6 hours of observation he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs and clear lungs Epinephrine autoinjector prescriptionanaphylaxis, observed for a biphasic reaction; discharge with self-injectable epinephrine, an action plan, avoidance and allergy referral

Mechanism5 of 11 58 yo M with hypertension and diabetes, 6 hours of progressive swelling of the lips and tongue; no itching, hives, wheezing or abdominal pain; takes lisinopril, which he started 2 years ago, and metformin; no new foods or medications; swelling did not improve after intramuscular epinephrine and diphenhydramine · Mast cell activationMast cell swelling comes with hives or itch and answers epinephrine. · Immune complex formationImmune complex disease brings fever, rash and joint pain, not isolated swelling. · Impaired bradykinin degradationSwelling with no hives on lisinopril, unchanged after epinephrine: the ACE inhibitor blocks bradykinin breakdown. 58 yo M with hypertension and diabetes, 6 hours of progressive swelling of the lips and tongue; no itching, hives, wheezing or abdominal pain; takes lisinopril, which he started 2 years ago, and metformin; no new foods or medications; swelling did not improve after intramuscular epinephrine and diphenhydramine Impaired bradykinin degradationACE inhibitor angioedema: no urticaria and little response to epinephrine; stop the ACE inhibitor permanently

Workup6 of 11 16 yo F with recurrent episodes over 3 years of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the hands, face and once the throat, each lasting 2 to 3 days, and separate episodes of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes no medications; her mother has similar episodes; antihistamines and epinephrine have not helped; examination between episodes is normal · Serum C4 levelRecurrent swelling without hives and a family history: C4, low even between episodes, screens for hereditary angioedema. · Total serum IgE levelTotal IgE does not test for C1 inhibitor deficiency. · Serum tryptase levelTryptase supports mast cell activation when drawn within 2 hours of a reaction, not between attacks. 16 yo F with recurrent episodes over 3 years of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the hands, face and once the throat, each lasting 2 to 3 days, and separate episodes of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes no medications; her mother has similar episodes; antihistamines and epinephrine have not helped; examination between episodes is normal Serum C4 levelhereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency; low C4, bradykinin-mediated, so epinephrine disappoints

Diagnosis7 of 11 17 yo F, 5 days of fever, sore throat and fatigue, treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep pharyngitis; 4 days later, a diffuse, mildly itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs; T 38.4, BP 112/70; tonsillar exudates, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, left upper quadrant tenderness; no wheals, no lip swelling, lungs clear · Infectious mononucleosisExudative pharyngitis, posterior nodes and left upper quadrant tenderness with a rash after amoxicillin: Epstein-Barr virus. · IgE-mediated penicillin allergyAn IgE allergy starts within minutes to hours with hives, not a maculopapular rash days later. · Serum sickness-like reactionA serum sickness-like reaction brings urticaria and joint pain 5 to 14 days into the drug. 17 yo F, 5 days of fever, sore throat and fatigue, treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep pharyngitis; 4 days later, a diffuse, mildly itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs; T 38.4, BP 112/70; tonsillar exudates, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, left upper quadrant tenderness; no wheals, no lip swelling, lungs clear Infectious mononucleosisan aminopenicillin rash during Epstein-Barr virus infection; not an IgE-mediated penicillin allergy

Diagnosis8 of 11 34 yo F with a known severe shellfish allergy becomes lightheaded 15 minutes after eating a dish she later learns contained shrimp; no rash, flushing, lip swelling, wheeze or vomiting; BP 76/44, HR 132, warm extremities; lungs clear · Vasovagal syncopeVasovagal syncope brings bradycardia and pallor; she is tachycardic with warm skin. · AnaphylaxisHypotension alone after a known allergen meets the third criterion: anaphylaxis. · Acute urticariaUrticaria alone has hives and a normal blood pressure; she has neither. 34 yo F with a known severe shellfish allergy becomes lightheaded 15 minutes after eating a dish she later learns contained shrimp; no rash, flushing, lip swelling, wheeze or vomiting; BP 76/44, HR 132, warm extremities; lungs clear Anaphylaxishypotension alone after a known allergen meets criteria; give IM epinephrine

Mechanism9 of 11 22 yo F with recurrent episodes since adolescence of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the lips and one hand lasting 2 to 3 days, the latest starting the day after a dental extraction; separate bouts of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes a combined oral contraceptive and no other medications; her father has similar episodes; epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the emergency department did not help; serum C4 low · Mast cell activationMast cell swelling comes with hives and answers epinephrine. · C1 inhibitor deficiencyRecurrent swelling without hives after dental work, on estrogen, with a low C4 and an affected father: C1 inhibitor deficiency. · Impaired bradykinin degradationImpaired bradykinin degradation is the ACE inhibitor mechanism; she takes none. 22 yo F with recurrent episodes since adolescence of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the lips and one hand lasting 2 to 3 days, the latest starting the day after a dental extraction; separate bouts of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes a combined oral contraceptive and no other medications; her father has similar episodes; epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the emergency department did not help; serum C4 low C1 inhibitor deficiencyhereditary angioedema: bradykinin-mediated swelling without urticaria; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function

Next step10 of 11 19 yo M with known hereditary angioedema, 4 hours of progressive swelling of the face and tongue with a hoarse voice after a facial injury in a basketball game; no stridor; SpO2 98% on room air; no hives; no improvement after intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous diphenhydramine · Repeat intramuscular epinephrineEpinephrine is usually not effective in bradykinin swelling, as the first dose showed. · Intravenous methylprednisoloneGlucocorticoids are usually not effective in bradykinin-mediated angioedema. · Intravenous C1 inhibitor concentrateA laryngeal hereditary angioedema attack needs specific therapy such as C1 inhibitor concentrate, with the airway secured if it closes. 19 yo M with known hereditary angioedema, 4 hours of progressive swelling of the face and tongue with a hoarse voice after a facial injury in a basketball game; no stridor; SpO2 98% on room air; no hives; no improvement after intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous diphenhydramine Intravenous C1 inhibitor concentrateacute hereditary angioedema attack with laryngeal involvement: give specific therapy and be ready to secure the airway

Avoid11 of 11 45 yo F with hereditary angioedema, low C4 and a family history, now with blood pressure 152/96 on three separate visits; no diabetes or kidney disease · ChlorthalidoneChlorthalidone does not act on bradykinin breakdown. · AmlodipineAmlodipine does not act on bradykinin breakdown. · LisinoprilACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown and are contraindicated in hereditary angioedema. 45 yo F with hereditary angioedema, low C4 and a family history, now with blood pressure 152/96 on three separate visits; no diabetes or kidney disease LisinoprilACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown and provoke attacks

Waiting for hypotension delays epinephrine: throat tightness or wheeze with hives already meets the criteria The diagnosis is clinical; a serum tryptase within 2 hours can support it afterward but never delays treatment Swelling with no hives is bradykinin, where epinephrine works poorly: stop the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, and check C4 when swelling recurs without a drug Common triggers are foods (nuts, eggs, seafood), drugs such as beta-lactams, and insect venom

Fever and Rash in a Childcovers the serum sickness-like reaction: did the hives start 5 to 14 days into the drug, with joint pain? Transfusion Reactionscovers anaphylaxis during transfusion: is the recipient IgA deficient? Shock in Childrencovers anaphylactic shock as a distributive subtype: is perfusion abnormal? Stool Changes in a Well Infantcovers FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome), the non-IgE mimic: is it hours of vomiting without hives? Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindicationscovers anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose as a contraindication: did it follow an earlier dose of the same vaccine? Child with Puffy Eyesplaces the acute allergic reaction among the other causes of swollen eyelids: is it one eye or both, and does the urine contain protein? Fever and Rash in a Child covers the serum sickness-like reaction: did the hives start 5 to 14 days into the drug, with joint pain? Transfusion Reactions covers anaphylaxis during transfusion: is the recipient IgA deficient? Shock in Children covers anaphylactic shock as a distributive subtype: is perfusion abnormal? Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome), the non-IgE mimic: is it hours of vomiting without hives? Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications covers anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose as a contraindication: did it follow an earlier dose of the same vaccine? Child with Puffy Eyes places the acute allergic reaction among the other causes of swollen eyelids: is it one eye or both, and does the urine contain protein?

Skin or mucosal involvement plus any second system within minutes to hours of an exposure is anaphylaxis. Treat it with IM (intramuscular) epinephrine first. Swelling with no hives points to bradykinin. A rash that arrives days later points to a delayed drug or immune complex reaction.

Unchecked attributeImpaired bradykinin degradation: the swollen eyes suggest angioedema, but bradykinin swelling has no wheals or itch; he has wheals on the trunk plus throat and gut symptoms, which is mast cell release. Unchecked attributeImmune complex formation: the sore throat invites poststreptococcal disease or serum sickness, but immune complexes take days to form; this began within hours of the drug, not days. True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus infection: mononucleosis really does cause a rash after amoxicillin, but that rash is maculopapular, comes days later and brings fever and nodes; he is afebrile with wheals. Salient decoySystemic vasculitis: crampy abdominal pain recalls IgA vasculitis, but vasculitis develops over days with fever and palpable purpura, not wheals within minutes.

briefs.title: Isolation Precautions
briefs.sub: precaution by route · when isolation ends · protective precautions in neutropeniaWhich way does it travel, and whom does the precaution shield?
blocks: precaution by route · when isolation ends · protective precautions in neutropeniaWhich way does it travel, and whom does the precaution shield?

Pt febrile, lethargic, hypotensive infant moving to intensive care on antibiotics Labs gram-negative diplococci on the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Gram stain Q which precaution to start; choices were airborne, contact, droplet, neutropenic and standard

Match the precaution to how the organism travels: droplets of 5 microns or more drop within 3 to 6 feet and need a surgical mask; airborne particles under 5 microns hang in room air and need an N95 respirator in a negative-pressure room; contact organisms ride on hands and surfaces and need a gown and gloves. Standard precautions already cover every patient, so they are never the added answer; neutropenic (protective) precautions reverse the direction and shield the patient from everyone else. Isolation ends by organism: 24 hours of effective antibiotics for meningococcus and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), 5 days of antibiotics for pertussis, every lesion crusted for varicella, and clinical improvement, usually with 3 negative sputum smears, for tuberculosis (TB).

Two questions sort every case: what size the particle is, and whose safety the precaution serves. A large droplet falls within 3 to 6 feet of the patient; a droplet nucleus can stay suspended in indoor air for several hours; a contact organism moves on hands, skin, stool and shared objects.

Precaution by route Precaution Organisms Gear and room Standard Every patient Hand hygiene for all; add gloves, gown, mask or eye protection when blood or body fluid exposure is expected WhyHand hygiene is the single most important step against hospital-acquired spread. Droplet Meningococcus (Neisseria meningitidis), Hib, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza, pertussis, adenovirus, mumps, rubella AdenovirusAdenovirus also spreads on fingers and shared objects, so adenovirus pneumonia adds contact precautions to droplet. Surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet; private room Airborne Tuberculosis, measles, SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome) SARSSARS adds droplet and contact precautions to airborne. Fitted N95 respirator; single negative-pressure room; staff without immunity kept out of a measles room Airborne plus contact Varicella; disseminated zoster N95 and a negative-pressure room, plus gown and gloves Contact RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), C. difficile, scabies, E. coli O157:H7 in a diapered or incontinent patient, MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers Staphylococcal food poisoningIt comes from a preformed toxin and does not pass from person to person, so it needs no contact precautions. Gown and gloves, ideally a private room; dedicated equipment; soap-and-water hand washing for C. difficile Why soapAlcohol-based hand rubs do not kill C. difficile spores. Protective (reverse) Severe neutropenia, ANC (absolute neutrophil count) under 500, as after chemotherapy or stem cell transplant Hand hygiene and a private, filtered-air room; bar fresh flowers, plants and animals; bar rectal thermometers, enemas and suppositories

When isolation ends Organism Ends when Meningococcus 24 hours of effective antibiotics Hib 24 hours of effective antibiotics Pertussis 5 days after antibiotics start UntreatedWithout antibiotics, isolation lasts 3 weeks. In practice: a patient treated at home is isolated for at least 4 weeks from onset and until symptoms subside. Mumps Gland swelling subsides Tuberculosis Clinical improvement, usually with 3 negative sputum AFB (acid-fast bacilli) smears in a row SmearsRelease usually requires 3 negative smears over 2 days, at least 1 from early morning. Measles 4 days after rash onset ImmunocompromisedAn immunocompromised patient may shed virus for longer, so isolation lasts the whole illness. After MMRIn a small fraction of patients, a self-limiting mild rash and fever 1 to 3 weeks after the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine come from the vaccine strain: no respiratory isolation, but keep the child away from immunocompromised people. Varicella and disseminated zoster Every lesion crusted Scabies 24 hours after effective therapy starts C. difficile and RSV Duration of illness Protective (reverse) Neutrophil count recovers

Isolate on suspicion: a child with suspected measles, or a patient under evaluation for TB, goes into airborne isolation before the results return. Close contacts of meningococcal disease also need chemoprophylaxis (see Bacterial Meningitis).

Pause point Infant in shock; CSF Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci Offered as airborne precautions or contact precautions What size of particle carries meningococcus? → Large droplets: droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics Fever and a faint rash 10 days after the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine Offered as airborne precautions, as for measles Wild virus, or the vaccine strain? → Vaccine-strain rash: no respiratory isolation; keep the child away from immunocompromised people Leukemia in induction chemotherapy, ANC 200, temperature check due Offered as a rectal thermometer or contact precautions Who is being protected from whom? → The patient: neutropenic precautions, so no rectal thermometer Every patient already gets standard precautions; the question asks what to add on top.

Next step1 of 7 3 yo F with 12 hours of fever, lethargy and a spreading petechial rash; BP 68/36; CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci; intravenous antibiotics are running, and she is moving to the pediatric ICU (intensive care unit) · Droplet precautionsGram-negative diplococci are meningococcus, carried in large droplets: droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective antibiotics. · Contact precautionsContact precautions are for spread by hands and surfaces; meningococcus travels in respiratory droplets. · Airborne precautionsAirborne precautions are for particles under 5 microns: TB, measles and varicella. 3 yo F with 12 hours of fever, lethargy and a spreading petechial rash; BP 68/36; CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci; intravenous antibiotics are running, and she is moving to the pediatric ICU (intensive care unit) Droplet precautionsNeisseria meningitidis: surgical mask within 3 to 6 feet until 24 hours of effective antibiotics

Next step2 of 7 2 yo M, unvaccinated, 4 days of fever to 40 C, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, then a maculopapular rash that began at the hairline and spread to the trunk; small gray-white spots on the buccal mucosa; admitted for dehydration · Contact precautionsGown and gloves do not stop an airborne virus. · Droplet precautionsDroplet precautions cover particles that fall within 3 to 6 feet; measles stays suspended in room air. · Airborne precautionsProdrome, Koplik spots and a rash spreading down from the hairline: measles, airborne precautions with an N95 and a negative-pressure room. 2 yo M, unvaccinated, 4 days of fever to 40 C, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, then a maculopapular rash that began at the hairline and spread to the trunk; small gray-white spots on the buccal mucosa; admitted for dehydration Airborne precautionsmeasles: N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room

Next step3 of 7 4 mo F admitted with 3 days of cough, rhinorrhea and increased work of breathing, SpO2 88% on room air; diffuse crackles and wheezes; nasal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus · Standard precautions onlyStandard precautions cover every patient; RSV needs contact precautions added. · Airborne precautionsAirborne precautions are for TB, measles and varicella, not RSV. · Contact precautionsRSV spreads mainly on hands and surfaces: contact precautions, gown and gloves. 4 mo F admitted with 3 days of cough, rhinorrhea and increased work of breathing, SpO2 88% on room air; diffuse crackles and wheezes; nasal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus Contact precautionsRSV spreads mainly by hands and contaminated surfaces: gown and gloves

Next step4 of 7 48 yo M with 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss, admitted with an upper lobe cavity on chest radiograph; sputum smear positive for acid-fast bacilli; four-drug therapy and airborne isolation were started 3 days ago · 24 hours of four-drug therapyThe 24-hour rule is for meningococcus and Hib, not TB. · Three negative sputum AFB smearsTB airborne isolation ends with clinical improvement on therapy and 3 consecutive negative sputum smears. · Clearing of the cavity on chest radiographRelease rests on sputum smears and clinical improvement, not on the radiograph. 48 yo M with 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss, admitted with an upper lobe cavity on chest radiograph; sputum smear positive for acid-fast bacilli; four-drug therapy and airborne isolation were started 3 days ago Three negative sputum AFB smearsactive pulmonary TB: airborne isolation ends when the patient is improving clinically on effective therapy and three consecutive sputum smears are negative

Next step5 of 7 3 yo F admitted with cellulitis of the thigh complicating chickenpox that began 3 days ago; several vesicles on the trunk and scalp have not yet crusted; T 38.9 · Airborne and contact precautionsVaricella needs airborne plus contact precautions until every lesion has crusted. · Contact precautionsContact alone misses the airborne spread of varicella. · Droplet and contact precautionsVaricella spreads through room air, beyond the 3 to 6 feet that droplets reach. 3 yo F admitted with cellulitis of the thigh complicating chickenpox that began 3 days ago; several vesicles on the trunk and scalp have not yet crusted; T 38.9 Airborne and contact precautionsvaricella: N95, negative-pressure room, gown and gloves until every lesion has crusted

Avoid6 of 7 6 yo F with acute lymphoblastic leukemia admitted during induction chemotherapy; afebrile; absolute neutrophil count 200/mm3; placed in a private room under neutropenic precautions · Oral temperature measurementAn oral temperature is not on the neutropenic list of things to avoid. · Axillary temperature measurementAn axillary temperature is not on the neutropenic list of things to avoid. · Rectal temperature measurementNeutropenic precautions bar rectal thermometers, enemas and suppositories. 6 yo F with acute lymphoblastic leukemia admitted during induction chemotherapy; afebrile; absolute neutrophil count 200/mm3; placed in a private room under neutropenic precautions Rectal temperature measurementneutropenic precautions protect the patient: no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositories, no fresh flowers or plants

Next step7 of 7 8 yo M on clindamycin for an abscess develops 6 watery stools a day and cramping; stool PCR (polymerase chain reaction) positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin; admitted for dehydration · Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washingC. difficile needs contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washing. · Contact precautions with alcohol-based hand rubAlcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores. · Droplet precautionsC. difficile spreads on hands and surfaces, not in droplets. 8 yo M on clindamycin for an abscess develops 6 watery stools a day and cramping; stool PCR (polymerase chain reaction) positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin; admitted for dehydration Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washingalcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores

Tuberculosiscovers latent versus active disease and its testing Scabiescovers the contact-spread rash whose treatment includes the household Infectious Diarrheacovers the workup and treatment of C. difficile and E. coli O157:H7 Tuberculosis covers latent versus active disease and its testing. Scabies covers the contact-spread rash whose treatment includes the household. Infectious Diarrhea covers the workup and treatment of C. difficile and E. coli O157:H7.

Size the particle, then name who is protected. Droplets that fall within 3 to 6 feet need a surgical mask; particles that hang in room air need an N95 and a negative-pressure room; organisms on skin, stool or surfaces need a gown and gloves; neutropenic precautions protect the patient.

Unchecked attributeAirborne precautions: the right idea, a respiratory route, with the wrong particle size; meningococcus travels in large droplets that fall within 3 to 6 feet, and airborne isolation is for TB, measles and varicella. Salient decoyContact precautions: a septic, possibly petechial infant in the ICU feels like a gown-and-gloves patient, but meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets, not by skin or surfaces. True-fact-wrong-slotStandard precautions: they apply to every patient, including this one, but they are the baseline, not the transmission-based precaution the organism requires. Unchecked attributeNeutropenic precautions: the direction is reversed; they protect an immunocompromised patient, and this infant is the source of infection.

briefs.title: Infectious Diarrhea
briefs.sub: timing gates · organism by food source · stool culture, blood culture or neither · who gets an antibioticWhat did the patient eat, how soon did it start, and does that organism need a blood culture or an antibiotic?
blocks: timing gates · organism by food source · stool culture, blood culture or neither · who gets an antibioticWhat did the patient eat, how soon did it start, and does that organism need a blood culture or an antibiotic?

Pt girl of 14 back from a summer camp that lasted a week, where she felt fine; for 2 days, cramps, nausea, vomiting and loose stools, and today fever with bloody stool; takes immunoglobulin replacement for common variable immunodeficiency (CVID); amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis one month ago Exam temperature 38.2 C, pulse 102; mild tenderness throughout the abdomen without peritoneal signs Labs ova and parasites negative; Salmonella grows on stool culture Q the likeliest underlying cause; choices covered food handling, seafood, contaminated infusions, antibiotic disruption of the gut flora and failed typhoid vaccination

Name the organism from the exposure and the hours to onset: vomiting within 1 to 6 hours with no fever is a toxin already in the food; fever and bloody diarrhea within about 3 days is an invasive bacterium. Bloody diarrhea with little or no fever after undercooked ground beef is Shiga toxin Escherichia coli: no antibiotics and no antimotility drugs, then a CBC and creatinine about a week later for hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Most infectious diarrhea needs only rehydration. The antibiotic follows the organism and its severity, for example typhoid, moderate to severe Shigella, Clostridioides difficile, and nontyphoidal Salmonella only in high-risk hosts.

What it is Acute diarrhea from an organism or its toxin, taken in with food, water, an animal or another person; each organism keeps its own source, timing and treatment. Bug Preformed toxin: Staphylococcus aureus and the emetic Bacillus cereus toxin; the staphylococcal toxin is heat stable, so cooking does not remove it. Invasive bacteria: nontyphoidal Salmonella (Enteritidis, Typhimurium), Campylobacter, and Shigella, which causes disease from as few as 10 to 100 organisms. Shiga toxin E. coli: enterohemorrhagic, serotype O157:H7. Typhoidal Salmonella: Typhi and Paratyphi. Watery-diarrhea organismsWatery diarrheaEnterotoxigenic E. coli, norovirus, rotavirus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus; the parasites Giardia and Cryptosporidium.. Bloody, from a parasite: Entamoeba histolytica. After antibiotics: C. difficile, which starts watery. Spread Food: poultry and eggs (Salmonella, Campylobacter); undercooked ground beef (Shiga toxin E. coli); meats, mayonnaise and custard (S. aureus); reheated rice (B. cereus); raw shellfish (Vibrio). Animals: pet turtles and other reptiles (Salmonella); puppies and unpasteurized milk (Campylobacter). Water and people: unpurified stream water on a camping trip (Giardia); pools and day care (Cryptosporidium); travel to areas of poor sanitation (typhoid, enterotoxigenic E. coli, amebiasis); person to person (Shigella, norovirus). Host: antibody deficiency such as common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) raises Salmonella, Campylobacter and Giardia; sickle cell disease raises Salmonella, including osteomyelitis; recent antibiotics raise C. difficile. Chain Invasive bacteria: swallowed with foodthey penetrate the colonic mucosafever, white cells in the stool, then blood Shiga toxin E. coli: most often swallowed in undercooked ground beefthe toxin binds glomerular endotheliumplatelet microthrombi form and shear red cellsHUS: hemolytic anemia, low platelets, kidney injury Insights The risk factor in the history is not always the exposure: recent antibiotics point to C. difficile, which starts watery, not to fever and bloody stools after camp food. Antibiotics may shorten Shigella and its spread but raise the HUS risk with Shiga toxin E. coli, so bloody diarrhea gets a culture before any antibiotic.

1 to 6 hoursS. aureus or emetic B. cereus: vomiting, no fever 8 to 18 hoursdiarrheal B. cereus: watery, nonbloody 15 to 24 hoursV. parahaemolyticus after shellfish Within 3 daysnontyphoidal Salmonella; Shigella at 1 to 4 days Watery 1 to 2 days, then bloodShiga toxin E. coli: usually watery, then bloody About a week laterHUS after Shiga toxin E. coli 8 to 14 daystyphoid: usually gradual fever, constipation, abdominal pain 5 to 10 days into antibioticsC. difficile; up to 2 months after

Inflammatory versus watery diarrhea Pattern Features Usual organisms Inflammatory Fever, blood or white cells in the stool Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Shiga toxin E. coli, E. histolytica Watery Rarely blood Viruses, preformed toxins, enterotoxigenic E. coli, Vibrio, Giardia, Cryptosporidium

HUS after Shiga toxin E. coli Criterion Finding Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia Fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the smear Thrombocytopenia Low platelet count (consumed in microthrombi) Acute kidney injury Rising creatinine; over half need dialysis Setting A child with bloody diarrhea about a week before

Urgent findings Finding Action A week after Shiga toxin E. coli diarrhea CBC and creatinine to find HUS early; supportive care, and over half need dialysis. Nontyphoidal Salmonella in an infant Typically blood culture and cerebrospinal fluid testing for bacteremia and meningitis; antibiotics. Typhoid in the third week: an acute abdomen and rising white count may suggest perforation Surgery for a distal ileal perforation. C. difficile with distension, fever or shock Toxic megacolon: abdominal imaging and a surgery consult.

Diarrhea by exposure Diagnosis Decides it Next best step Nontyphoidal Salmonella Within 3 days: undercooked poultry or eggs, food left warm, a pet reptile; fever, cramps, vomiting; bloody stools in children Stool culture; supportive care unless high risk Campylobacter jejuni Undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk, puppies; fever, bloody diarrhea, pain that can mimic appendicitis Stool culture; supportive care; azithromycin if severe or high risk Shigella 1 to 4 days: person to person from a tiny inoculum; a young child with sudden high fever, mucus and blood in the stool, sometimes seizures Stool culture; azithromycin if moderate to severe or high risk Shiga toxin E. coli (enterohemorrhagic, O157:H7) Watery stool for 1 to 2 days, then bloody: undercooked ground beef, a petting zoo; little or no fever Stool culture and Shiga toxin test; fluids, no antibiotics or antimotility drugs Typhoid fever (enteric fever, S. Typhi) Usually 8 to 14 days after exposure while traveling in an area of poor sanitation: days of fever first, constipation, relative bradycardia, rose spots; later splenomegaly Blood cultures, then ceftriaxone C. difficile infection (pseudomembranous colitis) Typically 5 to 10 days into antibiotics, up to 2 months after, classically clindamycin or ampicillin; watery diarrhea, cramps, fever, leukocytosis Stool toxin or nucleic acid test; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin S. aureus or B. cereus toxin 1 to 6 hours: meats, mayonnaise, custard or reheated rice; vomiting, no fever, several diners ill Clinical diagnosis; fluids, antibiotics do not help Vibrio parahaemolyticus 15 to 24 hours after raw or undercooked shellfish: watery diarrhea and cramps Supportive care; self-limited Traveler's diarrhea (enterotoxigenic E. coli) Watery diarrhea during or soon after travel, from water or food Fluids; an antibiotic only if moderate to severe Viral gastroenteritis (norovirus, rotavirus) Watery diarrhea, rarely blood; norovirus at any age and in outbreaks; rotavirus in unvaccinated infants Give oral rehydration; no stool testing Giardia (giardiasis) Weeks of foul, fatty diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, no blood: unpurified stream water or antibody deficiency Stool antigen test; tinidazole or metronidazole Amebiasis (E. histolytica) Poor sanitation or travel; bloody diarrhea from a parasite; liver abscess Stool antigen or molecular test; metronidazole or tinidazole, then a luminal agent Cryptosporidium Pools or day care; self-limited watery diarrhea, but chronic and severe with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection Acid-fast stain of stool for oocysts; routine ova and parasites misses it

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Bloody diarrhea with fever, a weak immune system, illness that is severe or lasts, or a cluster of cases → Stool culture Organism identified Names the organism; treat by organism → Shiga toxin test, when the stool is bloody Positive Shiga toxin E. coli: no antibiotics; CBC and creatinine in a week Targeted tests TestResultMeans Fever for more than 3 days after travel to an endemic area → Blood cultures S. Typhi Typhoid; blood cultures are usually positive in the first 2 weeks, stool cultures later Salmonella with infancy, immunocompromise or sickle cell disease → Typically blood culture; cerebrospinal fluid in infants Positive Bacteremia: antibiotics New diarrhea within 2 months of antibiotics or 72 hours into a hospital stay → C. difficile toxin or nucleic acid test Positive C. difficile infection Weeks of foul, watery diarrhea after unpurified water, or antibody deficiency → Giardia stool antigen Positive Giardiasis Bloody diarrhea after travel, culture negative → E. histolytica stool antigen or molecular test Positive Amebiasis Chronic watery diarrhea with HIV infection → Stool acid-fast stain Positive Cryptosporidiosis Diagnostic test TestResultMeans Shiga toxin E. coli found or suspected → CBC, blood smear and creatinine about a week after onset Low platelets, fragmented red cells, rising creatinine HUS: supportive care, often dialysis SkipStool tests for short-lived watery diarrhea with no fever and no blood: probably viral, and it passes; rehydrate.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Fever and bloody stools after a shared meal, on a recent antibiotic An invasive bacterium from the food; C. difficile starts watery Stool culture. A pet turtle or other reptile at home Nontyphoidal Salmonella Stool culture; supportive care unless high risk. Right lower quadrant pain with fever and bloody diarrhea Campylobacter, which can mimic appendicitis Stool culture; see Right Lower Quadrant Pain.

Pause point Bloody diarrhea days after an undercooked hamburger, little fever Offered as oral azithromycin or loperamide Shiga toxin E. coli: both make HUS more likely or worse → Fluids, then CBC and creatinine in a week A healthy child, nontyphoidal Salmonella on culture, already improving Offered as azithromycin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole Antibiotics do not shorten it and may prolong shedding → Supportive care only

Who gets an antibiotic Organism Treat when Nontyphoidal Salmonella Age under 1 year or over 50 (in practice)In practice: a major reference names infants and neonates without an age cutoff, and adds older nursing home residents; young infants also get cerebrospinal fluid testing.; immunocompromise; sickle cell disease; cardiovascular disease; more than 10 stools a day; bacteremia Campylobacter Severe: over 7 days, bloody stools or high fever; also pregnancy or immunocompromise Shigella Moderate to severe illness, a high-risk host with bloody diarrhea, or immunocompromise Traveler's diarrhea 3 or more loose stools in 8 hours, more so with fever, cramps, vomiting or blood C. difficile Every confirmed infection; fulminant disease adds IV metronidazole Shiga toxin E. coli Not given: antibiotics raise the HUS risk

1 EveryoneAny acute diarrhea Rehydrate: an oral rehydration solution for children, in small frequent sips even with vomiting. 2 Organism namedCulture, toxin or antigen result Treat by the table below; proven bacterial diarrhea does not always need an antibiotic. 3 Antimotility drugAdult with watery stool and no blood Loperamide is allowed; not in children, with fever or blood, or with suspected C. difficile or Shiga toxin E. coli.

Treatment by organism Organism Treatment Nontyphoidal Salmonella, high risk A fluoroquinolone; a third-generation cephalosporin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or azithromycin are alternatives Typhoid Ceftriaxone for 14 days; azithromycin for fluoroquinolone-resistant strains Shigella, when treated Azithromycin, ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone; may shorten illness and contagiousness Campylobacter, severe Azithromycin, the drug of choice C. difficile Stop the inciting antibiotic. First line: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, either one (recurrence)Fidaxomicin lowers the risk of recurrence more than vancomycin does.. Second line: oral metronidazole, only if neither is available. Fulminant: oral vancomycin with IV metronidazole. Giardiasis Tinidazole in a single dose or metronidazole for 5 to 7 days; nitazoxanide comes as a liquid for children Amebiasis Metronidazole or tinidazole, then a luminal agent such as paromomycin to clear the cysts Traveler's diarrhea, when treated Azithromycin for children; a fluoroquinolone for adults Shiga toxin E. coli, toxins, Vibrio, viruses No antibiotic

After the diagnosis When Do Shiga toxin E. coli CBC and creatinine about a week after symptoms began, to catch HUS early. C. difficile or Shiga toxin E. coli in hospital Contact precautions; the precaution type for each organism is in Isolation Precautions. Typhoid after treatment Watch for relapse about 2 weeks after the fever ends. Salmonella carrier who handles food or works in health care Eradication may be tried; repeat stool cultures confirm clearance. After giardiasis clears Lactose intolerance can persist for a while. Weeks after Campylobacter Guillain-Barré syndrome can follow, in about 1 per 1000 infections.

Next step1 of 7 6-week-old boy has 1 day of fever to 38.4 C and loose stools with streaks of blood; both parents had fever and diarrhea after a family picnic with undercooked chicken; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella; he feeds well and is well hydrated · Blood culture and antibiotic therapyInfants with nontyphoidal Salmonella are at high risk of bacteremia and meningitis, so they get a blood culture and an antibiotic. · Oral rehydration and supportive care onlySupportive care alone fits a healthy older child, not a young infant. · Admission for intravenous fluids aloneHe is well hydrated; the danger is bacteremia, which fluids do not treat. 6-week-old boy has 1 day of fever to 38.4 C and loose stools with streaks of blood; both parents had fever and diarrhea after a family picnic with undercooked chicken; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella; he feeds well and is well hydrated Blood culture and antibiotic therapyyoung infants with Salmonella are at risk of bacteremia and meningitis, so they are treated

Mechanism2 of 7 14-year-old girl with CVID on immunoglobulin replacement has 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and today fever and bloody stools; she just returned from a week-long summer camp; she took amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis a month ago; T 38.2 C, HR 102, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs; stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella · Inadequate cooking and refrigeration of chicken and eggsUndercooked poultry or eggs, food left warm, fever and bloody stools within 3 days: nontyphoidal Salmonella. · Lack of response to typhoid vaccinationThe typhoid vaccine covers only typhoidal strains; none exists for nontyphoidal Salmonella. · Gut microbial disruption due to antibiotic useRecent antibiotics predispose to C. difficile, which starts watery; this culture grew Salmonella. 14-year-old girl with CVID on immunoglobulin replacement has 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and today fever and bloody stools; she just returned from a week-long summer camp; she took amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis a month ago; T 38.2 C, HR 102, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs; stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella Inadequate cooking and refrigeration of chicken and eggsnontyphoidal Salmonella from undercooked poultry or eggs starts within 3 days, and warmth lets it multiply; bloody stools are common in children

Diagnosis3 of 7 10-year-old boy and his sister begin vomiting repeatedly 2 hours after a lunch of fried rice left out overnight from a takeout meal and reheated; mild cramps, no fever, no diarrhea yet; normal vital signs apart from mild tachycardia · Nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritisNontyphoidal Salmonella brings fever and diarrhea within about 3 days, not vomiting at 2 hours. · Staphylococcus aureus food poisoningS. aureus toxin comes from meats, mayonnaise or custard; rice points to B. cereus. · Bacillus cereus food poisoningVomiting within hours, no fever, reheated rice: the emetic Bacillus cereus toxin. 10-year-old boy and his sister begin vomiting repeatedly 2 hours after a lunch of fried rice left out overnight from a takeout meal and reheated; mild cramps, no fever, no diarrhea yet; normal vital signs apart from mild tachycardia Bacillus cereus food poisoningvomiting within hours from a toxin already in the food; reheated rice is the classic source; supportive care

Diagnosis4 of 7 16-year-old boy develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps 18 hours after eating raw oysters at a coastal cookout; temperature 37.9 C; no blood in the stool; he ate no poultry or eggs · Vibrio parahaemolyticus infectionRaw shellfish, watery diarrhea within a day: Vibrio parahaemolyticus. · Campylobacter jejuni enteritisCampylobacter comes from poultry or unpasteurized milk and can bleed. · Nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritisNontyphoidal Salmonella comes from poultry or eggs, which he did not eat. 16-year-old boy develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps 18 hours after eating raw oysters at a coastal cookout; temperature 37.9 C; no blood in the stool; he ate no poultry or eggs Vibrio parahaemolyticus infectionraw or undercooked shellfish; self-limited, supportive care

Avoid5 of 7 6-year-old girl has 2 days of crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a barbecue; temperature 37.4 C; mildly dry mucous membranes; stool testing for Shiga toxin is pending · Oral azithromycinAntibiotics raise the risk of HUS in Shiga toxin E. coli, so azithromycin is the order to avoid. · Oral rehydration solutionRehydration is the treatment, so it is appropriate. · Serial CBC and serum creatinineCBC and creatinine detect HUS early, so they are appropriate. 6-year-old girl has 2 days of crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a barbecue; temperature 37.4 C; mildly dry mucous membranes; stool testing for Shiga toxin is pending Oral azithromycinantibiotics and antimotility drugs raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome in Shiga toxin E. coli infection; rehydrate and watch hemoglobin, platelets and creatinine

Next step6 of 7 17-year-old girl returned 12 days ago from visiting family in rural South Asia; for 6 days she has had fever rising to 39.8 C, headache, abdominal pain and constipation; heart rate 82 at that temperature; faint pink macules on the upper abdomen; she is alert and hemodynamically stable · Outpatient oral ciprofloxacinTreatment follows blood cultures, and ceftriaxone is the first-line drug. · Stool cultureStool cultures are usually positive later, in weeks 3 to 5. · Blood culturesFever-first illness after travel: typhoid; blood cultures are usually positive in the first 2 weeks. 17-year-old girl returned 12 days ago from visiting family in rural South Asia; for 6 days she has had fever rising to 39.8 C, headache, abdominal pain and constipation; heart rate 82 at that temperature; faint pink macules on the upper abdomen; she is alert and hemodynamically stable Blood culturestyphoid presents as fever and bacteremia; the blood culture confirms it before empiric ceftriaxone

Next step7 of 7 11-year-old girl has 3 days of fever, cramps and loose stools with some blood after a summer barbecue where chicken was undercooked; she is otherwise healthy; today she is afebrile, drinking well, and her stools are fewer; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella · Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazoleNo antibiotic is needed without a high-risk host; it would prolong carriage. · Oral azithromycinAntibiotics do not shorten it and prolong shedding. · Oral rehydration and supportive careA healthy child with uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella gets supportive care only. 11-year-old girl has 3 days of fever, cramps and loose stools with some blood after a summer barbecue where chicken was undercooked; she is otherwise healthy; today she is afebrile, drinking well, and her stools are fewer; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella Oral rehydration and supportive careantibiotics do not shorten uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella in a healthy child and prolong carriage

Antibody Deficienciescovers CVID (common variable immunodeficiency): are immunoglobulin G and at least one other isotype low, with poor vaccine responses? Right Lower Quadrant Paincovers Campylobacter and Yersinia pseudoappendicitis and which of them get antibiotics: is the pain from the appendix or the ileocecum? Anemia with Thrombocytopeniacovers HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome), which follows Shiga toxin E. coli infection: is a second cell line down a week after bloody diarrhea? Sickle Cell Disease and Traitcovers Salmonella osteomyelitis: is it trait or disease?
