Right Lower Quadrant Pain covers Campylobacter and Yersinia pseudoappendicitis and which of them get antibiotics: is the pain from the appendix or the ileocecum? Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome), which follows Shiga toxin E. coli infection: is a second cell line down a week after bloody diarrhea? Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers Salmonella osteomyelitis: is it trait or disease?
In infectious diarrhea, name the organism from the exposure and the timing. That organism then determines the culture and whether to treat. A risk factor for a different organism is not the exposure.

Salient decoyAntibiotic disruption of gut flora: the recent amoxicillin-clavulanate is real, but it predisposes to C. difficile, which starts watery; the culture grew Salmonella. Class-vs-memberTyphoid vaccine failure: the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains, and there is no vaccine for nontyphoidal Salmonella; CVID blunting the response does not matter here. True-fact-wrong-slotRaw or unrefrigerated seafood: a real foodborne source, but of Vibrio parahaemolyticus, not Salmonella. Salient decoyContaminated immunoglobulin infusions: rare, and they cause bacteremia with high fever and chills found on blood culture, not gastroenteritis with a positive stool culture.

briefs.title: Hearing Loss and Chronic Ear Disease
briefs.sub: start with the Weber and Rinne tests, then read the drum: otosclerosis, cholesteatoma and the sensorineural causesWhere does the Weber go, is the drum intact, and is there a mass on it?
blocks: Hearing Loss and Chronic Ear Disease
start with the Weber and Rinne tests, then read the drum: otosclerosis, cholesteatoma and the sensorineural causesWhere does the Weber go, is the drum intact, and is there a mass on it?

The tuning forks sort every hearing loss into conductive or sensorineural; they screen, and audiometry confirms. Then the drum names the conductive cause. Conductive loss: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, and Rinne shows bone conduction greater than air conduction in that ear. Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL): Weber lateralizes away from the affected ear, and air conduction stays greater than bone conduction in both ears. Otosclerosis: a conductive loss with a normal otoscopic exam in a young adult. Cholesteatoma: painless otorrhea that fails antibiotics and a conductive loss, from a pearly white mass in a retraction pocket behind an intact drum; treated by surgical excision. Chronic suppurative otitis media: persistent otorrhea over 2 to 6 weeks through a perforated drum; discharge with an intact drum is not otitis media, and a perforation does not exclude a cholesteatoma. Sensorineural mimics: presbycusis, Ménière disease, vestibular schwannoma, aminoglycosides; all have normal otoscopy.

Lesion abnormal bone remodeling of the otic capsule, often starting at the fissula ante fenestram; an otospongiotic (hypervascular, resorptive) phase, then a sclerotic phase that fixes the stapes footplate Who autosomal dominant with about 40% penetrance, so family history is often absent; twice as common in women, suggesting a role for sex hormones; hearing loss often begins in the 20s or 30s; pregnancy appears to exacerbate it Paracusis of Willis hears conversation better in noisy surroundings Schwartze sign a reddish blush through the drum from hypervascularity in the active phase Carhart notch a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz, an artifact of ossicular fixation Measles virus its RNA (ribonucleic acid) has been found in otosclerotic foci van der Hoeve syndrome osteogenesis imperfecta, a type I collagen disorder, with otosclerosis and blue sclerae

Lesion a benign growth of keratinizing squamous epithelium with keratin debris in the middle ear: skin in the wrong place, not a tumor and not an infection; most cases are acquired and unilateral Acquired chronic middle-ear disease pulls a retraction pocket into the attic; it traps epithelium, keratin accumulates, and the mass erodes toward the ossicles; it arises from pars flaccida or posterosuperior retraction Secondary acquired follows drum injury, usually infection or trauma, so a perforation does not exclude it Congenital a white mass behind an intact drum in a child with no history of ear disease, classically anterosuperior, though surgical series find it variable Risk factors recurrent acute otitis media, chronic effusion and tympanostomy tubes; cleft palate multiplies all three through eustachian tube dysfunction Tested on chronic otorrhea when the debris becomes infected, and conductive loss once it reaches the ossicles

Hearing loss and ear drainage: the differential Diagnosis Illness script The tell Cholesteatoma Retraction pocket traps keratin, expanding toward the ossicles Pearly white mass behind an intact drum, painless refractory otorrhea Acute otitis media with perforation Infection under pressure ruptures the drum and drains Bulging, red or perforated drum; pain and fever precede the discharge Chronic suppurative otitis media Otorrhea over 2 to 6 weeks through a perforation Perforated drum; topical quinolones first; refer if refractory or a mass appears Otitis externa Canal maceration and inflammation, classically in swimmers Tragal tenderness, swollen tender canal; responds to drops Necrotizing otitis externa, can't miss Pseudomonas osteomyelitis of the temporal bone and skull base, mainly in older, immunocompromised or diabetic patients Granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction, severe pain, cranial neuropathies Foreign body in the canal Often asymptomatic; may cause pain, discharge, decreased hearing Object visible in the canal, abrasions from removal attempts Presbycusis Gradual, bilateral, high-frequency, in older adults Poor understanding of speech Ménière disease Episodic attacks Vertigo, fluctuating loss and tinnitus Vestibular schwannoma Cerebellopontine angle tumor on the cochlear nerve; neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) in the young Unilateral SNHL with tinnitus; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) Aminoglycoside ototoxicity Hair cell damage Sensorineural, never conductive

Diagnostic workup 1Is the loss conductive or sensorineural, and what does the drum show? First Otoscopy with pneumatic insufflation Normal drumWith a conductive loss, suggests otosclerosis Intact, immobile drum; pearly white mass in a retraction pocketCholesteatoma Bulging or perforated drumOtitis media: the abnormal drum names the middle-ear cause Weber and Rinne tuning forks Weber toward the affected ear, bone over airConductive: ossicles or middle ear Weber away, air over bone in both earsSensorineural: cochlea or nerve Confirms Pure-tone audiometry Air-bone gap, often a Carhart notch at 2000 HzConductive loss and its degree; otosclerosis when the drum is normal By branch MRI with gadolinium, internal auditory canals Enhancing mass in the canalVestibular schwannoma; for unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus Temporal bone computed tomography (CT) Bone erosion of the ossicles or attic wallCholesteatoma extent before surgery MRI of the brain and temporal bone Intracranial extension or abscessFor facial palsy, vertigo on canal pressure or neurologic signs: urgent surgery Confirms Excision with histology Keratinizing squamous epitheliumCholesteatoma; excision is also the treatment Skip Head CT for unilateral sensorineural loss: it can miss a small schwannoma, and MRI with gadolinium is the study. Culture of cholesteatoma drainage: it grows only the superinfecting organisms; antibiotics quiet the drainage but leave the lesion.

Diagnosis1 of 19 35-year-old woman has 2 years of worsening hearing in her left ear Hears conversation better in noisy places Weber lateralizes to the left ear Rinne: bone over air conduction on the left tympanic membranes normal Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · Sensorineural hearing loss · Cholesteatoma · Otosclerosis 35-year-old woman has 2 years of worsening hearing in her left ear Hears conversation better in noisy places Weber lateralizes to the left ear Rinne: bone over air conduction on the left tympanic membranes normal Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg Otosclerosisa conductive loss (Weber to the affected ear, bone over air there) with a normal drum in a young adult is otosclerosis: the stapes footplate is fixed. Hearing better in noisy places is paracusis of Willis. A sensorineural loss sends the Weber away, and a cholesteatoma shows a mass or retraction pocket on the drum

Diagnosis2 of 19 35-year-old woman has 3 months of reduced hearing in her right ear No ear pain, drainage or vertigo Weber lateralizes to the left ear Rinne: air over bone conduction in both ears tympanic membranes normal Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · Conductive hearing loss · Otosclerosis · Sensorineural hearing loss 35-year-old woman has 3 months of reduced hearing in her right ear No ear pain, drainage or vertigo Weber lateralizes to the left ear Rinne: air over bone conduction in both ears tympanic membranes normal Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg Sensorineural hearing lossthe Weber goes away from the affected ear and air stays louder than bone on both sides, so the loss is sensorineural. A conductive loss, otosclerosis included, sends the Weber to the affected ear with bone over air there, though otosclerosis may add a sensorineural loss when it involves the cochlea. The forks screen; audiometry confirms

Diagnosis3 of 19 5-year-old boy has a month of purulent right ear drainage Unimproved by topical, then oral antibiotics; painless Cleft palate; prior effusions and ear tubes intact, immobile tympanic membrane superior retraction pocket with a pearly white mass conductive hearing loss Afebrile · Acute otitis media with perforation · Otitis externa · Cholesteatoma 5-year-old boy has a month of purulent right ear drainage Unimproved by topical, then oral antibiotics; painless Cleft palate; prior effusions and ear tubes intact, immobile tympanic membrane superior retraction pocket with a pearly white mass conductive hearing loss Afebrile Cholesteatomapainless drainage that fails antibiotics, through an intact drum, from a pearly white mass in a retraction pocket, with a conductive loss: trapped squamous epithelium and keratin debris. Otitis media with discharge needs a perforation, and otitis externa is a tender canal that responds to drops. Cleft palate, effusions and tubes are its risk factors

Diagnosis4 of 19 50-year-old man has had right-sided hearing loss for 2 days It developed over a few hours; ear feels full canals clear; tympanic membranes normal Weber lateralizes to the left; air over bone conduction bilaterally Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg · Cerumen impaction · Sudden sensorineural hearing loss · Otosclerosis 50-year-old man has had right-sided hearing loss for 2 days It developed over a few hours; ear feels full canals clear; tympanic membranes normal Weber lateralizes to the left; air over bone conduction bilaterally Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg Sudden sensorineural hearing lossa sensorineural loss over hours is sudden sensorineural hearing loss: audiometry as soon as possible, within 14 days of symptom onset, confirms it, MRI or auditory brainstem response looks for retrocochlear disease, and corticosteroids may be offered within 2 weeks of onset; no routine head CT or labs. Cerumen would show in the canal, and otosclerosis is a slow conductive loss

Next step5 of 19 5-year-old boy was diagnosed with a right middle-ear cholesteatoma last week Drainage quieted on drops; definitive management now planned white keratin mass in an attic retraction pocket conductive hearing loss on the right Afebrile · CT: attic wall erosion · Tympanostomy tube placement · Surgical excision · Prolonged oral antibiotic therapy 5-year-old boy was diagnosed with a right middle-ear cholesteatoma last week Drainage quieted on drops; definitive management now planned white keratin mass in an attic retraction pocket conductive hearing loss on the right Afebrile · CT: attic wall erosion Surgical excisionsurgical excision is the treatment; antibiotics control the infected debris but do not remove the epithelium or stop the destruction. Tympanostomy tubes treat effusions, not a keratin mass

Surgical excision, through an otolaryngology referral, is the treatment

Distinguish sensorineural from conductive loss at the first visit, and look for bilateral loss, recurrent episodes and focal neurologic findings. Obtain audiometry as soon as possible (within 14 days of symptom onset) to confirm it, and MRI or auditory brainstem response (ABR) for retrocochlear disease; no routine head CT and no routine labs. Corticosteroids may be offered as initial therapy within 2 weeks of onset; intratympanic steroids should be offered for incomplete recovery 2 to 6 weeks after onset; hyperbaric oxygen combined with steroids may be offered within 2 weeks of onset, or within 1 month as salvage. Antivirals, thrombolytics, vasodilators and vasoactive substances are not routine. Repeat audiometry at the end of treatment and within 6 months of completion.

Treated primarily by surgical excision. Topical and oral antibiotics may quiet the superinfected debris and slow growth, but they do not stop the destructive process, so another course will not resolve it. Erosion into neighboring structures, facial nerve palsy, a labyrinthine fistula with vertigo on canal pressure, or, rarely, intracranial complications, converts an elective operation into an urgent one; the absence of vertigo argues against a fistula.

Otosclerosis: hearing aids, or stapedectomy or stapedotomy with a prosthesis. Presbycusis: hearing aids are the mainstay. Chronic suppurative otitis media: topical quinolones, equally or more effective than aminoglycosides and without their ototoxicity risk. Otitis externa: topical drops; oral antibiotics only for cellulitis beyond the canal, immunocompromise, diabetes, or when drops cannot be used. Necrotizing otitis externa: computed tomography with intravenous antipseudomonal therapy.

Canal: water exposure, trauma from swabs or ear candling, foreign material such as hearing aids and headphones, and skin conditions such as eczema. Water strips antibacterial cerumen, raises the canal pH, macerates the skin and introduces organisms; Pseudomonas aeruginosa grows in water. Middle ear, not canal: sick contacts, incomplete immunization, tobacco smoke, prior tympanostomy tubes and recurrent acute otitis media. The drum separates the two, so a middle-ear risk factor transfers no risk to the canal.

Middle-ear infection drains only through a perforation, so otorrhea with an intact drum comes from the drum itself or the canal. Purulent drainage over a month is the cholesteatoma's debris becoming superinfected, which is why antibiotics give only partial, temporary responses. A conductive loss that appears after normal audiometry is new: something in the ear has changed. A conductive loss localizes to the ossicles, so a cholesteatoma causing hearing loss is already eroding them. Immobility on insufflation means the drum is tethered by the pocket.

Acute otitis media with an inflamed drum for painless drainage: it needs a bulging or inflamed drum, and drainage implies a perforation. Foreign body: the mass is in the drum, not the canal, with no removal attempts. Otitis externa: topical therapy failed, and a discrete mass on the drum is not a canal finding. Schwannoma: sensorineural loss with tinnitus in adulthood, NF2 stigmata in a child. Head CT for unilateral sensorineural loss: MRI with gadolinium. Aminoglycosides for a conductive loss: they cause sensorineural loss. Drainage culture: it grows only the superinfecting organisms. Chronic suppurative otitis media for drainage through a perforation: a secondary acquired cholesteatoma can follow drum injury, so look for the mass.

Part II Sinusitis and Its Complications applies the same logic to the neighboring air-filled space, where a chronic infection of a bony cavity is dangerous because of what it erodes into. Congenital Infections (TORCH) covers congenital cytomegalovirus, the commonest nonhereditary cause of childhood sensorineural loss.

Sort the loss with the forks, then read the drum: is it intact, and is the mass on it or in the canal? When the options describe processes rather than diseases, translate the diagnosis into its mechanism first; discharge that fails adequate antibiotics is a symptom of something structural.

briefs.sub: migraine, cluster, tension · the autonomic tell · attack length · glaucoma and dissection · oxygen, then verapamilHow long do the attacks last, and are there autonomic signs on the same side?

Pt 27 yo M, nightly 90-minute attacks of stabbing left periorbital pain with tearing, ptosis and rhinorrhea Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned cluster headache, trigeminal neuralgia and acute angle-closure glaucoma

Acute unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs (ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection) is a cluster headache. Attacks wake the patient from sleep, peak fast, last ~90 minutes, and recur several times daily for weeks before remitting. Acute treatment is 100% oxygen; sumatriptan aborts attacks but is second-line (slower onset, side effects). Vision stays intact in cluster headache; vision change or a fixed mid-dilated pupil moves the diagnosis to angle-closure glaucoma.

Cluster attack excruciating periorbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signs, often nocturnal onset Pattern several attacks daily for 6–8 weeks, then remission lasting months to years Abortive 100% oxygen first-line; sumatriptan second Prophylaxis verapamil

Classify headache by duration and associated features: seconds = neuralgia; minutes-to-hours with autonomic signs = cluster; hours-to-days with nausea/photophobia = migraine. Establish the duration before the character of the pain.

briefs.title: Brain Tumors in a Child
briefs.sub: sellar and suprasellar masses that announce themselves on the growth chart, and posterior fossa masses that announce themselves on the neurologic examinationIs the abnormal finding endocrine or neurologic; for the sella, does the axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and for the posterior fossa, which side and which structure?
blocks: sellar and suprasellar masses that announce themselves on the growth chart, and posterior fossa masses that announce themselves on the neurologic examinationIs the abnormal finding endocrine or neurologic; for the sella, does the axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and for the posterior fossa, which side and which structure?

Ask where the abnormal finding sits. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty with a normal neurologic examination points to the sella; ataxia or crossed findings point to the posterior fossa, where you localize side first and structure second. Image with MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); with papilledema, never tap first. Suprasellar mass: classically a normal neurologic examination (no dysmetria, gait abnormality, focal weakness or skin findings); height crosses downward through percentiles while weight holds, with Tanner 1 past the pubertal gate and papilledema. Growth failure with preserved weight is a hormonal deceleration, not a nutritional one; arrested puberty with it means more than one anterior pituitary axis has failed, and multiple axes point to the stalk, not the gland. Headache and disc edema from obstructive hydrocephalus make the mass midline and suprasellar. Craniopharyngioma: from Rathke pouch remnants; cystic and calcified suprasellar mass: the cyst shows on MRI, the calcification mainly on computed tomography (CT); subtle for years before diagnosis. Posterior fossa mass: 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumors but only 15 to 20% of adult ones, so in a child, ataxia with raised pressure is infratentorial until imaged. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral. Hemisphere or vermis: limb dysmetria is hemispheric; a midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared. Both together mean a hemispheric mass large enough to disturb midline structures; ipsilateral facial numbness fits (the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally), and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression. Crossed findings: a cranial nerve palsy on one side and long-tract weakness on the other mean brainstem.

Cerebellar signs ipsilateral; the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion; face also ipsilateral; body long tracts contralateral Hemisphere limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor Vermis or midline truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation Central nystagmus direction-changing, gaze-evoked and unsuppressed; peripheral (vertigo) nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation Raised-pressure headache daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema Growth failure downward crossing of height percentiles after a stable channel, weight preserved; endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism keep a normal or increased weight, and in poor nutrition weight loss comes before height loss Pubertal delay no breast development by age 13 in girls Stalk pattern multiple anterior axes down, with or without posterior failure (diabetes insipidus); stalk compression causes panhypopituitarism, most commonly growth failure from TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) or growth hormone deficiency; morning cortisol, free T4 (thyroxine), TSH and IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) come back low in more than one axis Gland pattern a single hypersecreting axis with the others intact

Diagnosis1 of 20 14-year-old girl, a year of headaches, now worse height fell from 40th to 3rd percentile over 2 years weight steady at 70th percentile; Tanner 1 Skin, neurologic examination normal; no focal deficit Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · optic disc edema · Subependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles · Tumor in the cerebellar vermis · Cystic, calcified suprasellar mass 14-year-old girl, a year of headaches, now worse height fell from 40th to 3rd percentile over 2 years weight steady at 70th percentile; Tanner 1 Skin, neurologic examination normal; no focal deficit Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · optic disc edema Cystic, calcified suprasellar massheight falling while weight holds is endocrine, and Tanner 1 at 14, with the mass signs, suggests a second failed axis, so the stalk is involved; with headache and disc edema the mass is midline and suprasellar, cystic and calcified: craniopharyngioma. A vermian tumor brings truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared, and this examination is clean; subependymal nodules point to tuberous sclerosis, a skin-first diagnosis that does not arrest linear growth

Diagnosis2 of 20 9-year-old boy, 3 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia gait lists to the left left facial numbness No weakness or sensory loss in the limbs BP 118/72 mm Hg · bilateral papilledema · A mass in the right middle cerebellar peduncle · A mass in the left frontal lobe · A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphere 9-year-old boy, 3 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia gait lists to the left left facial numbness No weakness or sensory loss in the limbs BP 118/72 mm Hg · bilateral papilledema A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphereevery cerebellar sign is on the left, and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the output decussates twice; limb dysmetria is hemispheric, the face is served ipsilaterally, and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression. The right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side, and a frontal lobe mass gives contralateral weakness

Next step3 of 20 9-year-old girl, 2 months of bumping into door frames height fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile weight steady at the 55th percentile Misses fingers in the outer field of each eye Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg · Noncontrast CT of the head · Radiograph of the left hand for bone age · MRI of the brain with contrast 9-year-old girl, 2 months of bumping into door frames height fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile weight steady at the 55th percentile Misses fingers in the outer field of each eye Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg MRI of the brain with contrasta height percentile crossing with weight held and loss of the outer field in each eye is a suprasellar mass until imaged: MRI of the brain with contrast, sellar views. A bone age is nonspecific and delays the MRI, and a noncontrast CT shows the mass and its relation to the chiasm less well than MRI

Diagnosis4 of 20 6-year-old boy, 4 weeks of morning vomiting and unsteadiness truncal and gait ataxia; wide-based stance minimal limb dysmetria MRI: midline cerebellar mass filling the fourth ventricle, restricted diffusion, no extension through the fourth-ventricular foramina Afebrile · papilledema · Ependymoma of the fourth ventricle · Pilocytic astrocytoma of the cerebellar hemisphere · Medulloblastoma of the vermis 6-year-old boy, 4 weeks of morning vomiting and unsteadiness truncal and gait ataxia; wide-based stance minimal limb dysmetria MRI: midline cerebellar mass filling the fourth ventricle, restricted diffusion, no extension through the fourth-ventricular foramina Afebrile · papilledema Medulloblastoma of the vermistruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and relatively spared limbs localizes to the vermis; a midline fourth-ventricular mass with restricted diffusion in a child fits medulloblastoma, which seeds drop metastases through the CSF. A cerebellar hemisphere pilocytic astrocytoma gives ipsilateral limb signs and is classically a cyst with a mural nodule; ependymoma tends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle, with calcification and cysts common

Next step5 of 20 9-year-old boy is seen before planned surgery Imaging shows a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass Resection is planned for next week Height has slowed over 2 years; no medications BP 100/64 mm Hg · HR 88/min · Begin growth hormone replacement now · Repeat MRI in 6 months · Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery 9-year-old boy is seen before planned surgery Imaging shows a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass Resection is planned for next week Height has slowed over 2 years; no medications BP 100/64 mm Hg · HR 88/min Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgerystalk compression can leave several axes deficient, so measure morning cortisol, free T4 and TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery; secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism are treated before the operation, glucocorticoid first. Growth hormone does not come before the axes that threaten the operation, and a planned resection is not a reason to wait 6 months for another MRI

Diagnosis6 of 20 5-year-old girl, 4 weeks of worsening double vision progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies right hemiparesis with brisk reflexes MRI: diffuse expansion of the pons Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg · Medulloblastoma · Cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma · Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma 5-year-old girl, 4 weeks of worsening double vision progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies right hemiparesis with brisk reflexes MRI: diffuse expansion of the pons Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg Diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaa cranial nerve palsy on one side with long-tract weakness on the other is a crossed finding, which localizes to the brainstem; diffuse expansion of the pons in a child is a diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, and diplopia from an abducens palsy is often its first sign. Medulloblastoma and a cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma give ataxia rather than crossed findings

Diagnosis7 of 20 14-year-old boy, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg non-calcified suprasellar mass CSF beta-hCG mildly elevated; serum AFP normal Growth and puberty normal so far; no rash or bone pain T 36.9 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg · Suprasellar germinoma · Langerhans cell histiocytosis · Craniopharyngioma 14-year-old boy, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg non-calcified suprasellar mass CSF beta-hCG mildly elevated; serum AFP normal Growth and puberty normal so far; no rash or bone pain T 36.9 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg Suprasellar germinomadiabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes, with a mildly raised CSF beta-hCG and a normal AFP is a suprasellar germinoma (pure germinomas usually have negative markers, but low levels of beta-hCG can be detected), which is highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy, alone or after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Craniopharyngioma is cystic and calcified, and growth hormone and gonadotropin deficits are often its first endocrine failures; Langerhans cell histiocytosis thickens the stalk and brings lytic skull lesions and a seborrheic scalp rash

Workup8 of 20 9-year-old boy, 2 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting wide-based gait; right-hand dysmetria bilateral papilledema A lumbar puncture is proposed to measure the pressure T 37.0 °C · BP 116/70 mm Hg · Non-contrast CT followed by lumbar puncture · Lumbar puncture with an opening pressure · Obtain MRI of the brain instead 9-year-old boy, 2 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting wide-based gait; right-hand dysmetria bilateral papilledema A lumbar puncture is proposed to measure the pressure T 37.0 °C · BP 116/70 mm Hg Obtain MRI of the brain insteadpapilledema with cerebellar signs means a posterior fossa mass until imaged, and lumbar puncture risks herniation, so image first: MRI of the brain instead. Measuring an opening pressure does not remove that risk, and a noncontrast CT followed by a tap still ends in the tap that papilledema with a posterior fossa mass forbids

Next step9 of 20 10-year-old girl, 1 day after resection of a suprasellar tumor urine output 350 mL/h serum Na 152 mEq/L urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg Alert and thirsty BP 104/62 mm Hg · HR 112/min · Desmopressin · Hypertonic saline infusion · Free water restriction 10-year-old girl, 1 day after resection of a suprasellar tumor urine output 350 mL/h serum Na 152 mEq/L urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg Alert and thirsty BP 104/62 mm Hg · HR 112/min Desmopressindilute polyuria with a rising sodium after the stalk has been handled is central diabetes insipidus: desmopressin. Fluid restriction worsens the hypernatremia, and hypertonic saline adds sodium to a patient whose sodium is already high

Next step10 of 20 12-year-old boy, 2 months of headaches and trouble looking up upgaze palsy convergence-retraction nystagmus light-near dissociation of the pupils No head trauma; visual acuity normal Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · HR 76/min · CT of the head without contrast · Ophthalmology referral for strabismus · MRI of the brain, then serum and CSF tumor markers 12-year-old boy, 2 months of headaches and trouble looking up upgaze palsy convergence-retraction nystagmus light-near dissociation of the pupils No head trauma; visual acuity normal Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · HR 76/min MRI of the brain, then serum and CSF tumor markersupgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation are Parinaud syndrome, a pineal-region mass; in an adolescent boy that is classically a germinoma, so obtain MRI of the brain first, then serum and CSF tumor markers, the CSF once imaging shows a tap is safe. This is not strabismus, and a noncontrast CT does not characterize the mass or the markers

Avoid11 of 20 8-year-old boy with a newly found suprasellar mass Vomiting and lethargic since this morning Free thyroxine low; cortisol result pending BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · Na 128 mEq/L · glucose 52 mg/dL · IV hydrocortisone · Isotonic saline bolus · Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement 8-year-old boy with a newly found suprasellar mass Vomiting and lethargic since this morning Free thyroxine low; cortisol result pending BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · Na 128 mEq/L · glucose 52 mg/dL Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacementhypotension, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia with a new suprasellar mass is adrenal crisis; give IV hydrocortisone and isotonic saline, and avoid levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement, because thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis

Mechanism12 of 20 7-year-old boy with a right cerebellar hemisphere mass on MRI right-hand intention tremor and dysmetria falls toward the right Strength and sensation normal His parents ask why the signs are on the same side as the tumor · Cerebellar fibers do not decussate at all · Cerebellar output decussates twice · The cerebellum controls contralateral limbs directly 7-year-old boy with a right cerebellar hemisphere mass on MRI right-hand intention tremor and dysmetria falls toward the right Strength and sensation normal His parents ask why the signs are on the same side as the tumor Cerebellar output decussates twicecerebellar output decussates twice, so the two crossings cancel and the signs stay on the same side as the lesion. Cerebellar fibers do cross, and the cerebellum does not control the opposite limbs directly

Diagnosis13 of 20 15-year-old girl with amenorrhea and galactorrhea Normal growth; Tanner 4 MRI: 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification No headache; visual fields full BP 110/68 mm Hg · prolactin 180 ng/mL · TSH normal · urine pregnancy test negative · Rathke cleft cyst · Prolactinoma · Craniopharyngioma 15-year-old girl with amenorrhea and galactorrhea Normal growth; Tanner 4 MRI: 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification No headache; visual fields full BP 110/68 mm Hg · prolactin 180 ng/mL · TSH normal · urine pregnancy test negative Prolactinomagalactorrhea and amenorrhea with a raised prolactin, a normal TSH and pregnancy test, and a small, non-calcified intrasellar lesion with one axis hypersecreting is a prolactinoma; cabergoline is the preferred dopamine agonist. Craniopharyngioma is a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass, and a Rathke cleft cyst is a non-enhancing, non-calcified cyst that is usually asymptomatic

Next step14 of 20 9-year-old boy admitted with headache and vomiting MRI: posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus Over the last hour he has become drowsy Pupils equal; no seizure BP 128/70 mm Hg · HR 64/min · Acetazolamide and outpatient follow-up · Observation with serial neurologic examinations · Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation 9-year-old boy admitted with headache and vomiting MRI: posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus Over the last hour he has become drowsy Pupils equal; no seizure BP 128/70 mm Hg · HR 64/min Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultationa posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and a falling level of consciousness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection. Acetazolamide with outpatient follow-up, or observation, leaves the obstruction untreated

Next step15 of 20 6-year-old boy with declining vision and nystagmus several café-au-lait macules; axillary freckling thin despite a good appetite Normal stools; no bone pain or fractures Afebrile · HR 96/min · weight below the 5th percentile · MRI of the brain and orbits · Celiac disease serology for poor weight gain · Skeletal survey 6-year-old boy with declining vision and nystagmus several café-au-lait macules; axillary freckling thin despite a good appetite Normal stools; no bone pain or fractures Afebrile · HR 96/min · weight below the 5th percentile MRI of the brain and orbitscafé-au-lait macules and axillary freckling point to neurofibromatosis type 1, and declining vision with emaciation despite a good appetite is an optic pathway glioma with diencephalic syndrome: MRI of the brain and orbits. Celiac disease is malabsorption and brings no visual loss, and a skeletal survey looks for bone lesions he does not have

Workup16 of 20 7-year-old girl with newly confirmed medulloblastoma The tumor was resected 2 weeks ago Recovering well; no back pain Leg strength and bladder function normal Neurologic examination unchanged since discharge Afebrile · no papilledema · Whole-body PET-CT · Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy · MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology 7-year-old girl with newly confirmed medulloblastoma The tumor was resected 2 weeks ago Recovering well; no back pain Leg strength and bladder function normal Neurologic examination unchanged since discharge Afebrile · no papilledema MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytologymedulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging is MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology, the lumbar puncture done at least 10 to 14 days after surgery. Bone marrow and whole-body imaging do not look where it spreads

Next step17 of 20 11-year-old girl with a known suprasellar mass Vomiting since last night now a depressed level of consciousness CT: dilated lateral and third ventricles BP 132/60 mm Hg · HR 58/min · pupils equal · Neurosurgical CSF diversion · Lumbar puncture to measure opening pressure · Acetazolamide 11-year-old girl with a known suprasellar mass Vomiting since last night now a depressed level of consciousness CT: dilated lateral and third ventricles BP 132/60 mm Hg · HR 58/min · pupils equal Neurosurgical CSF diversiona suprasellar mass that blocks CSF flow at the third ventricle causes obstructive hydrocephalus; a falling level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion. Lumbar puncture risks herniation, and acetazolamide does not relieve an obstruction

Next step18 of 20 4-year-old boy, 3 weeks of headache headache waking him from sleep morning vomiting Normal neurologic examination; no medications Growth chart normal; no recent head injury Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 92/min · Reassurance and a headache diary · Start migraine prophylaxis · MRI of the brain 4-year-old boy, 3 weeks of headache headache waking him from sleep morning vomiting Normal neurologic examination; no medications Growth chart normal; no recent head injury Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 92/min MRI of the brainheadache that wakes him from sleep, with morning vomiting, in a child under six is a red-flag headache: MRI of the brain, because a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor. A diary or migraine prophylaxis delays the diagnosis

Mechanism19 of 20 13-year-old girl with a suprasellar mass on MRI loss of both temporal visual fields A year of headaches; height has slowed Visual acuity normal; pupils equal Her parents ask why the outer halves of her vision are missing · Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm · Interruption of Meyer loop · Compression of the optic tract 13-year-old girl with a suprasellar mass on MRI loss of both temporal visual fields A year of headaches; height has slowed Visual acuity normal; pupils equal Her parents ask why the outer halves of her vision are missing Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasma suprasellar mass presses up on the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibers, which carry the temporal fields, decussate: bitemporal hemianopsia. A lesion behind the chiasm, in the optic tract, gives a homonymous defect (the same hemifield lost in both eyes), and a Meyer loop lesion in the temporal lobe gives contralateral superior quadrantanopia

Screening20 of 20 10-year-old boy treated 1 year ago with resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma Currently asymptomatic Takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine His parents ask what follow-up he needs BP 102/64 mm Hg · height 25th percentile · Annual serum AFP and beta-hCG · Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields · Annual audiometry 10-year-old boy treated 1 year ago with resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma Currently asymptomatic Takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine His parents ask what follow-up he needs BP 102/64 mm Hg · height 25th percentile Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fieldsafter a craniopharyngioma, surveillance is lifelong and endocrine and visual: serial growth velocity with an annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields. Audiometry does not watch the axes or the visual fields this tumor threatens, and AFP and beta-hCG are germ cell tumor markers

Diagnostic workup 2Growth chart and neurologic examination first, then MRI First Growth chart: height and weight percentiles Height falling while weight holdsEndocrine growth failure, not nutritional Neurologic examination and fundoscopy Ipsilateral limb ataxia with papilledemaCerebellar hemisphere mass with raised pressure Next MRI of the brain with contrast, sellar views Cystic suprasellar mass (calcification shows mainly on CT)Craniopharyngioma; intrasellar and non-calcified suggests an adenoma Posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalusCyst with a mural nodule: pilocytic astrocytoma; midline: medulloblastoma Next, sellar mass Morning cortisol, free T4 and TSH, IGF-1 Low in more than one axisStalk compression; replace cortisol before thyroxine, before surgery By branch Serum sodium and urine osmolality Dilute urine with a high sodiumCentral diabetes insipidus; if it came first, think germinoma or histiocytosis Serum and CSF beta-hCG and AFP Raised, with diabetes insipidus or Parinaud syndromeGerm cell tumor; a pure germinoma usually has negative markers, but low levels of beta-hCG can be detected Confirms Resection with histology Adamantinomatous epithelium with calcificationCraniopharyngioma Names the tumor typePilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma or ependymoma Staging MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology Drop metastases or tumor cells in the CSFMedulloblastoma staging; the lumbar puncture at least 10 to 14 days after surgery Skip Lumbar puncture with papilledema: risk of herniation; image first. Hand radiograph for bone age: delayed bone age is nonspecific and delays the MRI when papilledema is present.

Is the neurologic examination focal? If not, the lesion is not hemispheric or in the posterior fossa. Plot the growth chart: height falling with weight holding is endocrine. Count failed axes: growth and puberty together are panhypopituitarism, which localizes to the stalk. Is there posterior pituitary failure? Polyuria makes germinoma or histiocytosis more likely. Is there raised pressure or a field cut? Papilledema or bitemporal hemianopsia makes the mass midline and suprasellar, and the imaging descriptor is cystic and calcified (calcification mainly on CT). If the examination is focal, find the side, then the structure.

Before surgery treat secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism before the operation, glucocorticoid before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis in an unrecognized cortisol deficiency. Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone in any new panhypopituitarism. After surgery diabetes insipidus can develop in 70% after craniopharyngioma surgery; expect the sodium to rise, not fall, when the stalk has been handled, and treat hypotonic polyuria with desmopressin, not fluid restriction Obstructive hydrocephalus a posterior fossa mass with drowsiness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection; a suprasellar mass with a depressed level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion, not lumbar puncture Germinoma highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy alone, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by response-based radiation therapy, which has been explored to reduce radiation doses and neurodevelopmental harm Prolactinoma cabergoline, the preferred dopamine agonist After craniopharyngioma lifelong endocrine and visual surveillance, with surveillance MRI
With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first.

Height crossing down through percentiles with weight steady is endocrine growth failure; it excludes undernutrition, which costs weight first. Tanner 1 past age 13 in a girl is delayed puberty; with growth failure and signs of a mass (headache, disc edema), it suggests a second failed axis, which can indicate hypopituitarism rather than short stature alone. Optic disc edema without fever or neck stiffness is raised intracranial pressure without meningitis, from obstructive hydrocephalus at the third ventricle. A normal neurologic examination, including finger-nose-finger testing and gait, excludes the cerebellar compartment and with it medulloblastoma. Normal skin excludes tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas) and neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling), the two phakomatoses whose intracranial lesions are on option lists. No focal deficit and no fever exclude brain abscess, which comes with focal findings and usually fever. A year of headaches before worsening is a slow-growing lesion, not a reassurance; the normal blood pressure and temperature exclude infection and crisis but say nothing about the pituitary; a morning cortisol would.

Height falling away from a stable weight with Tanner arrest and headache is a suprasellar mass until MRI says otherwise. Plot the growth chart before you order the headache imaging: a height percentile crossing is a localizing sign, and it remains detectable when the neurologic examination is normal. The exception to preserved weight is the diencephalic syndrome of a hypothalamic glioma: emaciation with a normal appetite. Diabetes insipidus first and anterior axes later makes germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis more likely than craniopharyngioma; send serum beta-hCG and AFP, and CSF levels once imaging shows a tap is safe, before assuming craniopharyngioma. Boundary: untreated acquired primary hypothyroidism reproduces this growth pattern exactly (height arrest, preserved or rising weight, delayed puberty) but does not produce papilledema; check TSH and free T4, and disc edema separates the two. Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six. Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology.

Subependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles: tuberous sclerosis is a skin-first diagnosis and does not arrest linear growth. Tumor in the cerebellar vermis: truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared; it does not touch the pituitary. Parietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim: abscess is acute, febrile and focal; a year of headaches with growth arrest is not an infection. Enhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal: acoustic neuroma is an adult disease of hearing loss and tinnitus, with no endocrine consequence. Right middle cerebellar peduncle for left-sided signs: the right region on the wrong side. Pineal mass: common in children, but it produces Parinaud syndrome. Germinoma when the anterior axes failed first and there is no polyuria; adenoma when two axes are down, there is no galactorrhea, and CSF flow is blocked; optic glioma with normal skin, normal pupils and weight preserved; Rathke cleft cyst for progressive panhypopituitarism with raised pressure, too much disease for a simple cyst; histiocytosis with normal skin, no polyuria and no bone pain.

Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatmentthe same complaint, a 13-year-old girl with worsening headaches, with the red-flag gate answered in the opposite direction. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern Headache in a School-Age Childthe workup before localization; is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infantposterior fossa tumor as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization Hyperprolactinemiathe intrasellar adenoma in the adult Polyuriathe step before this one; is the polyuria water or solute, and is the deprivation test still needed? Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern. Headache in a School-Age Child: the workup before localization; is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: posterior fossa tumor as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization. Hyperprolactinemia: the intrasellar adenoma in the adult. Polyuria: the step before this one; is the polyuria water or solute, and is the deprivation test still needed?

When a mass sits on a midline structure, the localizing finding may be endocrine rather than neurologic: a growth chart and a Tanner stage are examination findings, and in the sellar region they appear years before the field cut and the papilledema. When the finding is neurologic, localize side first and structure second; the cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion.

Pt 13 yo F, 2 years of similar headaches: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worse with activity, with nausea; now monthly instead of every other month, same characteristics; menarche at 12, periods now regular; this one began after a sleepover, she vomited twice and could not finish her homework; intermittent acetaminophen only Exam temperature 37 °C, alert and oriented, pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal, no papilledema described Q the most appropriate next step; options spanned no additional testing, computed tomography (CT) of the head, a urine toxicology screen, serum electrolytes and lumbar puncture

This headache is already diagnosable: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worsened by activity, with nausea and vomiting, in an adolescent girl with a two-year history of the same thing. Image only if a feature meets an imaging indication. None of the following three features meets one. Vomiting is a diagnostic criterion of migraine, not a pressure sign. The disability ("could not finish her homework") measures severity, and no guideline images for severity. The increase in frequency is a change in rate, not in character. The headaches "have the same characteristics" and remain monthly. The change tracks the arrival of regular menses since menarche. The examination is normal, including the pupils, and no papilledema is described. No additional testing is needed. Imaging is reserved for an abnormal neurologic examination, signs of raised intracranial pressure, or a dramatic change in headache characteristics. When papilledema is present, imaging is indicated. Then find why the pressure is high; the medication list often answers it. An adolescent on isotretinoin with a month of morning headache and vomiting, brief blurring of vision, bilateral disc edema and full visual fields has drug-induced intracranial hypertension. A mass at the optic chiasm would cut the fields. Optic neuritis is painful, acute and usually affects one eye.

Indications for neuroimaging in pediatric headache (1) abnormal neurologic examination findings, such as weakness or ataxia; (2) signs of raised intracranial pressure, such as papilledema; (3) a dramatic change in headache characteristics. None is present here Not an indication a modest rise in frequency when the headaches keep the same character, remain relatively infrequent, and have a physiologic explanation for the change Migraine, diagnostic features pulsatile, unilateral (may be bilateral in children), hours to days; photophobia and phonophobia; nausea or vomiting; ± aura; normal neurologic examination. Formal criteria add ≥5 prior attacks lasting 2–72 hours in patients under 18 (4–72 in adults); beyond 72 hours is status migrainosus (ICHD-3, International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition)

Two years of similar headaches recurrent and stereotyped; excludes "first and worst," which is the thunderclap gate Vomited twice a migraine criterion; it becomes a pressure sign only when it is morning vomiting, projectile, or paired with papilledema Pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal closes indication (1) and, in the absence of described disc edema, indication (2) Menarche at 12, now regular cycles the physiologic explanation for the change in rate, so the change is explained Afebrile, alert and oriented excludes meningitis, so lumbar puncture is not indicated Began after a sleepover sleep deprivation is a named migraine trigger, not evidence of ingestion

Classify first: headache in a child Axis The stem sentence that settles it Consequence for management Examination and fundus normal? "Pupils equal and reactive... remainder of neurologic examination normal"; no papilledema Closes both of the first two imaging indications, and the IIH (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) branch with them (in-context: papilledema would be expected) Character or only rate? "Similar headaches over the past 2 years"; "every other month… now monthly," same features Recurrent, not first-and-worst; a rate change only, which does not meet "dramatic change in characteristics" Explanation for the change? "Menarche at age 12; menstrual periods now regular" A physiologic cause is identified, so the change is accounted for Systemic signs? "Temperature 37 C," alert, normal vitals No infection, no toxidrome

done: nothing but intermittent acetaminophen failed: 2 years of attacks with inadequate abortive dosing and timing, the actual unmet need bothered: missed schoolwork, which justifies better treatment, not more testing.

Management ladder: headache in a child Tier Intervention Escalate when 1 Clinical diagnosis; trigger diary (sleep, meals, menses, screens); sleep-hygiene and hydration counseling; no laboratory or imaging Any red-flag gate is breached, or attacks recur despite trigger control 2 Abortive therapy at first symptom, at full weight-based dose: ibuprofen or acetaminophen, rest in a dark quiet room, antiemetic if vomiting blocks oral dosing An early, adequately dosed NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) fails 3 Triptan for refractory attacks, then consider daily prevention (propranolol, amitriptyline with cognitive behavioral therapy, topiramate) if attacks are frequent or disabling Reassess prevention after a trial of at least 2 months Exit / de-escalation Medication-overuse headache: withdraw the offending analgesic Simple analgesics on ≥15 days/month, or triptans, or any combination of triptans, analgesics or opioids, on ≥10 days/month, for more than 3 months

Diagnostic: up to 3 days per attack; ≥5 prior attacks of 2–72 hours. Escalation: frequent or disabling attacks (consider prevention), and the overuse thresholds above. The exam answer versus clinical practice: the exam keys the preventive rung, though a pediatric trial found amitriptyline and topiramate no better than placebo. That trial result does not change the keyed rung. Papilledema → magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with MR (magnetic resonance) venography, then LP (lumbar puncture) with an opening pressure; a normal MRI with a high opening pressure means intracranial hypertension, idiopathic or drug-induced. Fever with meningismus → lumbar puncture. A thunderclap headache → noncontrast CT, then LP if negative. Wakes from sleep, worse on waking or with Valsalva → MRI, however migrainous the rest sounds. Focal deficit or ataxia → Brain Tumors in a Child. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty → MRI with sellar views; see Brain Tumors in a Child. Household all symptomatic → carboxyhemoglobin. Image any child who is immunocompromised, shunted, or anticoagulated.

Who women of childbearing age, obesity or recent weight gain, and drugs: retinoids and vitamin A (isotretinoin for acne), tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline) and growth hormone Symptoms daily headache worse lying flat and in the morning, better standing, with nausea and vomiting; transient visual obscurations; pulsatile tinnitus; diplopia from a cranial nerve VI palsy Signs bilateral papilledema with enlarged blind spots and full visual fields, otherwise a normal neurologic exam; a lesion at the chiasm would cut the fields (bitemporal hemianopia) Workup MRI with MR venography first, to exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis; then LP (lumbar puncture): opening pressure over 250 mm H2O with normal CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) Treatment stop the offending drug, which usually resolves it; weight loss; acetazolamide

Recurrent → no urgent pathway Did the character change, or only the rate? Rate only → not a dramatic change Is there a physiologic explanation for the change? Menarche and regular cycles → yes Any systemic signal: fever, altered sensorium, abnormal vitals, growth failure? None → make a diagnosis and a treatment plan, not a test

Awakening from sleep would indicate imaging, and it is absent here. The homework detail measures disability, which sets the treatment tier and never the imaging threshold. The near-doubling of frequency is real but explained.

A change in frequency needs an explanation; a change in character, an examination finding or a pressure sign needs a scan. Reassurance is defensible only when you can name the criteria you cleared. Change in rate ≠ change in character. Ask what changed. If the only change is "more often," look for the physiologic cause (menarche, a new schedule, a new medication) before you look at the brain. MRI for chronic and progressive; CT for acute and hemorrhagic. The right decision to image still needs the right modality. Boundary: nocturnal awakening, morning vomiting, and headache worsened by Valsalva are pressure signs even when the rest is textbook migraine. They take precedence over the migraine features. Migraine onset and changes in frequency cluster around menarche. Through the same estrogen link, menstrual migraine is the commonest cause of headaches that got worse this year in an adolescent.

Brain Tumors in a Childcovers the same complaint, on the opposite side of the imaging gate. There, the headache came with papilledema, a height percentile crossing, and Tanner 1. Here it comes with a normal examination and an explained change in frequency. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? Primary Headache in an Adultcovers the headache-type differential once imaging has been excluded Low Back Pain in an Adultuses the same gating logic in a different region. The pain's severity never opens the gate, and a specific finding always does. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficienciescovers vitamin A excess as a cause of pseudotumor cerebri. Ask: is the patient taking a retinoid or a vitamin A supplement? Part I Headache in a School-Age Childcovers the whole workup once the gate opens, through the posterior fossa tumor it most often finds. Ask: does the exam show ataxia as well as papilledema? Findings, not suffering, cross an imaging threshold. The examination, the fundus, the tempo of change in character, and the systemic signs decide imaging. Frequency, duration, and disability decide only the treatment tier. When a pattern changes and you can name why, the change is explained and is not a red flag.

briefs.title: Seizure with Fever in a Child
briefs.sub: benign only inside the age window · intracranial signs · fontanelle and tone, not the neck · when to tapIs the child inside the febrile-seizure age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?
blocks: Seizure with Fever in a Child

benign only inside the age window · intracranial signs · fontanelle and tone, not the neck · when to tapIs the child inside the febrile-seizure age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?

Pt 10 wk F, fever and vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsy an hour later, open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck, decreased tone Q the most appropriate next step; options spanned lumbar puncture, neuroimaging and reassurance with discharge

At 10 weeks old, febrile seizure is excluded by age. Simple febrile seizures are defined between 6 months and 5 years. A child outside that window with fever and a seizure needs a meningitis workup by definition, before any other finding is weighed. Three other findings independently indicate the same step. A full anterior fontanelle and vomiting are signs of raised intracranial pressure. The drowsiness persisting an hour is a postictal period far beyond the ten minutes a simple febrile seizure allows. A supple neck is not reassuring, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants; read the fontanelle and the tone instead. Perform a lumbar puncture.

Simple febrile seizure age 6 months to 5 years, generalized, lasting under 15 minutes, with a brief postictal period under 10 minutes and rapid return to baseline, in a child with no signs of intracranial infection; the diagnosis is clinical and needs no laboratory studies or imaging Findings that mandate urgent lumbar puncture age outside 6 months to 5 years, signs of intracranial infection such as headache, vomiting, a bulging or full fontanelle or nuchal rigidity, prolonged altered mental status meaning a postictal period beyond 10 minutes, and a petechial rash concerning for meningococcal disease Additional considerations for tapping current antibiotic therapy, which masks meningitis, and an incomplete immunization history The open-fontanelle exemption signs of raised intracranial pressure usually require imaging before lumbar puncture, but an open fontanelle acts as a pop-off valve, limiting herniation risk and generally negating the need for a head computed tomography (CT) first

Age 10 weeks outside the febrile-seizure window entirely; this alone rules out discharge Full anterior fontanelle a sign of intracranial infection and raised pressure, and an indication to tap rather than a reason to image Fontanelle open acts as a pop-off valve, so CT is not needed first Drowsy one hour after a 4-minute seizure a postictal period beyond 10 minutes. This is prolonged altered mental status and an indication on its own Weak suck and decreased tone altered mental status in an infant, whose neurologic examination is feeding and tone rather than orientation Neck supple excludes nothing, because meningeal signs can be subtle or absent under 12 months Seizure generalized, single, 4 minutes, now stopped no benzodiazepine, since she is not seizing and it was under 5 minutes. No EEG (electroencephalography), since it was not focal, prolonged or recurrent Skin normal no petechiae, so meningococcemia is not the presentation; four other findings already indicate the tap Vaccinations up to date the incomplete-immunization consideration no longer applies, but the indication for the tap remains

Seizure with fever in a child: the differential Diagnosis Illness script The National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tell Excluded here by Bacterial meningitis Can't miss Any age, and infants localize poorly, so systemic and pressure signs substitute for neck signs Seizure with fever plus a full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia or prolonged altered mental status, with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture deciding None (the answer to pursue) Simple febrile seizure Viral fever triggers a generalized seizure in a neurologically normal child Age 6 months to 5 years, under 15 minutes, back to baseline within 10 minutes, otherwise normal examination Age 10 weeks, postictal drowsiness at 1 hour, full fontanelle Complex febrile seizure The same trigger, but focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 hours Focal features, longer than 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours; EEG may be considered, and imaging only with abnormal or focal examination findings The seizure was single, generalized and 4 minutes Herpes simplex encephalitis Can't miss Neonatal or later, and parenchymal rather than meningeal Prolonged altered mental status with focal or temporal findings and CSF lymphocytes; red cells may be present Not excluded; the same tap tests for it, and acyclovir is given until it is excluded Meningococcemia Can't miss N. meningitidis sepsis with rapid decompensation Petechial or purpuric rash with fever and shock, where antibiotics precede the tap Skin examination normal, normotensive Abusive head trauma Can't miss Infant with subdural collections Seizure with a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages, with increased irritability Not excluded by the stated findings

How old? Ten weeks → outside the window, so this is not a febrile seizure and discharge is ruled out Is she seizing now? No, it stopped in 4 minutes → no benzodiazepine Was it focal, prolonged or recurrent? No → no EEG (electroencephalography) Any sign of intracranial infection? Full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia, still drowsy → yes Does she need a CT first? The fontanelle is open → no, so perform the lumbar puncture

Temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 150/min. Now alert and playful; examination normal. He has received no pneumococcal or Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) vaccine doses Lumbar punctureincomplete immunization at 6 to 12 months lowers the bar to tap; maintenance antiseizure drugs are usually not indicated; EEG is not recommended after an initial simple febrile seizure with a normal neurologic examination

A supple neck excludes nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants. The criteria list substitutes the fontanelle, the tone and the feeding. The rest of the examination is normal: tympanic membranes, oropharynx, lungs, abdomen and skin. With no source found, this strengthens the case for tapping rather than weakening it. When every peripheral source is excluded in a febrile infant with neurologic signs, the meninges are what is left. Up-to-date vaccinations remove one of the modifiers on the list but leave the four indications already present.

Recurrence about 30% have another febrile seizure Epilepsy risk slightly raised, about 1 to 2% Antipyretics treat discomfort, do not prevent the next seizure Course resolves by school age, with no effect on development Risk factors fever of 39.5 °C or higher, a viral illness such as roseola or influenza, recent immunization, a family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy Timing usually the first day of the illness, sometimes before the viral symptoms appear Brain imaging focal neurologic signs EEG recurrent unprovoked seizures, not a simple febrile seizure Admission not back to neurologic baseline Electrolytes and glucose vomiting or diarrhea, since hypoglycemia and hyponatremia can provoke a seizure Lumbar puncture also at 6 to 12 months with incomplete pneumococcal or Hib immunization, or when already on antibiotics

Fever with seizure under 6 months, or with a full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness, needs a lumbar puncture. An open fontanelle needs no CT. The febrile-seizure diagnosis has an age gate on both ends, 6 months and 5 years. It is the fastest disqualifier, so check it before anything else. An open fontanelle is a pop-off valve, so infants tolerate rising intracranial pressure that would herniate an older child. The CT-before-tap rule therefore generally does not apply to them. The same finding can be both the indication and the apparent contraindication. Then ask what the rule is protecting against, and whether that risk exists in this patient. Infants may lack neck signs; read the fontanelle, the tone, the suck and the cry instead. A supple neck excludes nothing under 12 months. A postictal period beyond 10 minutes is altered mental status, not a long febrile seizure, and it indicates a tap on its own. With petechiae and hypotension, reverse the order: antibiotics first, tap after. A sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable price.

Part II Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn covers the workup when there is no seizure, up to the decision to tap. This brief covers what a seizure adds to that decision. Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the cerebrospinal fluid grid that interprets the fluid once it is obtained. Ask: is this child inside the age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?

For a benign diagnosis defined by an age range, check the age before weighing the findings, because age disqualifies it first. When a rule and a finding point in opposite directions, ask what the rule was built to prevent. If the anatomy has already prevented it, the rule does not apply.

True-fact-wrong-slotNeuroimaging: The rule exists to prevent herniation, and an open fontanelle decompresses the pressure, so the risk it guards against is not present and CT is generally unnecessary Mirror twinReassurance and discharge: Requires age 6 months to 5 years; at 10 weeks this was never a febrile seizure, and the postictal drowsiness and full fontanelle each independently disqualify it Salient decoyElectroencephalography: EEG may be considered for seizures that are prolonged, recurrent or focal, and this was single, generalized and four minutes True-fact-wrong-slotIntravenous lorazepam: Given for generalized convulsions lasting over 5 minutes, and she stopped at four and is no longer seizing

Pt 7 mo, born at 31 weeks, left-sided spasticity Imaging MRI shows white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle Q the most likely cause; options spanned ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity, transplacental Toxoplasma infection and inherited thrombophilia with perinatal stroke

White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia. It is ischemia and necrosis in the poorly perfused zone beside the ventricles, and the signature injury of prematurity. The examination independently confirms a unilateral injury. Increased tone, 3+ reflexes and ankle clonus on the left only, with a right-sided lesion, is spastic hemiplegia. A congenital infection produces global deficits, not one-sided spasticity.

Cerebral palsy nonprogressive motor dysfunction caused by a neurologic injury; the etiology is often multifactorial and may never be identified Periventricular leukomalacia ischemia and necrosis of the poorly perfused white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, seen as white matter injury on MRI; premature infants are at greatest risk, and their friable germinal matrix vessels also predispose to intraventricular hemorrhage Early signs that should raise suspicion motor delay (not rolling by 4 months corrected), early hand preference before age 1, persistent neonatal reflexes (tonic neck beyond 6 months), abnormal tone The tone evolution infants may be hypotonic initially, with spasticity developing over time, accompanied by hyperreflexia and often clonus

White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle periventricular leukomalacia, which points to prematurity; each other cause has a different imaging signature Born at 31 weeks prematurity is a significant risk factor for cerebral palsy Left-sided findings with a right-sided lesion spastic hemiplegia matching a unilateral injury; intrauterine infection produces global, not one-sided, deficits Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, sustained clonus upper motor neuron; excludes spinal dysraphism, where lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased Early hand preference at 7 months abnormal before age 1, and one of the earliest signs Not rolling over motor delay, judged against corrected age in a 31-weeker Head circumference at the 50th percentile no microcephaly, which argues further against congenital infection Babinski present bilaterally normal up to 24 months only in an otherwise normal examination; the abnormal sign is the asymmetry of tone and reflexes Veterinary office, inconsistent prenatal care suggest toxoplasmosis, but the MRI pattern refutes it

Cerebral palsy: the MRI pattern names the cause Etiology Illness script The National Board of Medical Examiners (NBME) tell: imaging Excluded here by Prematurity / low birth weight Ischemia in the watershed white matter beside the ventricles; friable germinal matrix vessels Periventricular leukomalacia; intraventricular hemorrhage (the answer) Hypoxic-ischemic injury Perinatal asphyxia in a term infant; low Apgars, encephalopathy, seizures Watershed injury; basal ganglia and thalamic lesions Born preterm; no depressed Apgars or neonatal encephalopathy described Perinatal stroke (± inherited thrombophilia) Arterial infarct around the time of birth; hemiplegia emerging in infancy Infarct in a vascular distribution, most often the middle cerebral artery The lesion is periventricular white matter, not a territory Intrauterine infection Cytomegalovirus (CMV), toxoplasmosis; transplacental transmission Intracranial calcifications; microcephaly; global deficits Periventricular white matter injury, normocephaly, unilateral findings Neural tube defect (folate deficiency) Spinal dysraphism A spinal lesion, and the examination is lower motor neuron: decreased lower-extremity tone and reflexes Hypertonia with hyperreflexia and clonus Magnesium sulfate exposure Given to the mother for preterm labor Transient neonatal hypotonia only Findings at 7 months, and they are hypertonic

Cerebral palsy is managed supportively and lifelong. Care includes early intervention and physical therapy, tone management, and surveillance of hips, feeding and growth, and seizures, with vision and hearing evaluation. No treatment reverses the static injury itself.

Upper or lower motor neuron? Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, clonus → upper Unilateral or global? Left side only → a single-sided lesion, so global insults are excluded What does the MRI actually say? Periventricular white matter → leukomalacia What produces that pattern? Prematurity; she was born at 31 weeks Does any exposure in the history produce it? No: infection calcifies, thrombophilia infarcts a territory, magnesium is transient, folate affects the spine

The veterinary office evokes cat litter, and the inconsistent prenatal care reinforces it, but the MRI refutes it. Of the three maternal drugs named, the antenatal corticosteroids actually lowered this infant's risk rather than raising it. The asymmetry of tone and reflexes is the abnormal sign.

White matter injury beside the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia, and prematurity is what causes it. The imaging pattern maps to the insult: periventricular white matter → prematurity · watershed or basal ganglia → hypoxic-ischemic injury · a vascular territory → perinatal stroke · calcifications → congenital infection. Distribution defines the subtype: both legs is spastic diplegia, the commonest; one side is spastic hemiplegia, which should match a unilateral lesion. Hand preference before age 1 is abnormal, and it is often the earliest sign a parent reports. Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive; losing an acquired milestone is not consistent with cerebral palsy and reopens the workup. Infants with cerebral palsy may begin hypotonic and become spastic later, so normal early tone never excludes it. Magnesium sulfate given before anticipated early preterm birth is neuroprotective and reduces cerebral palsy risk in surviving infants.
When it is not cerebral palsy

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome a boy who is hypotonic and delayed in infancy, then by about age 3 develops new dystonia, spasticity and hyperreflexia and self-mutilation (biting fingers and hands, banging limbs); X-linked recessive HGPRT deficiency (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) with high uric acid, and gouty arthritis and obstructive nephropathy later if untreated Rett syndrome a girl with normal early development who regresses after about 6 months, losing speech and purposeful hand use, with hand wringing Autism spectrum disorder social and language deficits, sometimes self-injury, but no spasticity, dystonia or pyramidal signs Progression cerebral palsy is nonprogressive, so new movement signs or self-injury after a hypotonic infancy mean a progressive or metabolic disease

Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant covers periventricular leukomalacia and intraventricular hemorrhage as prematurity outcomes, and the corrected-age arithmetic this brief uses. Part II Congenital Infections (TORCH) covers the calcification pattern and the global-deficit picture, which is where toxoplasmosis belongs. Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the upper-versus-lower motor neuron examination that separates a brain lesion from a spinal one. Part I Tics and Tic Disorders covers Tourette syndrome, and Part I Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth covers the regression red flags. Ask: what does the imaging actually describe, and are the deficits one-sided or global? Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the floppy infant before any spasticity appears: is the problem in the brain or the motor unit? Part II Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi separates Rett syndrome from Angelman syndrome. Ask: did the child lose skills, or never gain them?
An exposure in the history suggests a cause; only a described imaging pattern decides it. When a stem gives both, read the imaging first.

Salient decoyTransplacental Toxoplasma gondii: Congenital infection produces intracranial calcifications and global deficits; this MRI describes periventricular white matter and the findings are strictly one-sided, in a normocephalic infant True-fact-wrong-slotLack of maternal folic acid: Folate deficiency causes neural tube defects, in which lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased, the opposite of this examination Unchecked attributeMaternal magnesium sulfate: It causes transient hypotonia in the immediate newborn period, not lasting spasticity at 7 months Class-vs-memberInherited thrombophilia: Stroke shows an infarct in a vascular distribution, usually the middle cerebral artery, not periventricular leukomalacia
