briefs.sub: double worsening · orbital and intracranial flags · preseptal vs orbital · image before lumbar punctureAre there orbital or intracranial flags, even with a nonfocal neurologic exam?
blocks: double worsening · orbital and intracranial flags · preseptal vs orbital · image before lumbar punctureAre there orbital or intracranial flags, even with a nonfocal neurologic exam?

Pt child with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a double-worsening pattern, now with focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness; neurologic examination nonfocal Q the most appropriate next step; options spanned oral antibiotics, lumbar puncture and urgent neuroimaging

A double worsening course indicates acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness are intracranial extension flags. Vomiting is worst in the early morning because ICP (intracranial pressure) rises in recumbency. These flags call for urgent imaging rather than oral antibiotics. "Neurologic examination is nonfocal" does not exclude a brain abscess; frontal lobe abscesses are neurologically silent until late. When raised ICP is suspected, image before LP (lumbar puncture).

Sinusitis complications – features → next step Complication Features Next step Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis Eyelid swelling; normal extraocular movement (EOM), normal vision, no proptosis; often from a skin break such as an insect bite, eczema or trauma Oral antibiotics Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis Proptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegia, ↓ acuity; usual source is ethmoid or maxillary sinusitis (cheek tenderness), less often a maxillary dental infection or orbital trauma Computed tomography (CT) orbits and sinuses + IV antibiotics; surgical drainage for an abscess Pott puffy tumor Frontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess – doughy forehead swelling CT/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) + IV antibiotics + surgery Brain abscess Emergency Focal headache, early-morning vomiting, drowsiness, ± focal deficit CT/MRI → ring-enhancing lesion; IV antibiotics + drainage Meningitis Diffuse headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia Image first if ICP signs, then LP Cavernous sinus thrombosis Cranial nerve (CN) III, IV, V1–V2, VI palsies, proptosis, spreads bilaterally MRI/magnetic resonance venography (MRV) + IV antibiotics

Sinusitis the most common source; ethmoid or maxillary, spreading contiguously into the orbit (streptococci, S aureus); cheek tenderness points to the maxillary sinus Dental infection only maxillary (upper) teeth sit near the sinus and orbit; a mandibular abscess, especially on the opposite side, does not explain it Skin break (eczema, insect bite, trauma) causes preseptal cellulitis, anterior to the orbital septum, without proptosis, vision change or painful eye movements Otitis media spreads to the mastoid or meninges, not the orbit

Early-morning headache and vomiting (recumbent CO₂ retention → cerebral vasodilation) papilledema altered mental status late, the Cushing triad. Contiguous sinus spread means Streptococcus anginosus/milleri group and anaerobes; CT with contrast shows a ring-enhancing lesion, and MRI with restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging separates abscess from tumor. Treat with vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole plus drainage. Ring-enhancing differential: abscess, glioblastoma, metastasis, toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, lymphoma.

A normal neurologic exam is a low-sensitivity test for intracranial pathology. When the symptom pattern is positional and progressive (morning headache, morning vomiting, declining alertness), symptoms of raised ICP (intracranial pressure) outweigh a reassuring exam.

briefs.title: Hydrocephalus and Shunt Complications
briefs.sub: a shunt changes the raised-pressure workup · image first, never a lumbar puncture · shunt series and tap · the big infant headDoes the child have a shunt, and is there any sign of raised intracranial pressure?
blocks: a shunt changes the raised-pressure workup · image first, never a lumbar puncture · shunt series and tap · the big infant headDoes the child have a shunt, and is there any sign of raised intracranial pressure?

A child with a VP (ventriculoperitoneal) shunt presents with vomiting, irritability, lethargy, and hypertension, four signs of increased intracranial pressure. Raised ICP (intracranial pressure) calls for neuroimaging. The specific concern is shunt malfunction causing recurrent obstructive hydrocephalus. Computed tomography (CT) of the head is the first step; it shows whether the ventricles have re-dilated. Do not choose LP (lumbar puncture). LP is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus; the pressure gradient between the ventricles and the lumbar subarachnoid space can cause transtentorial herniation. In a shunt patient, obtain CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) by tapping the shunt reservoir, never by lumbar puncture.

Signs of increased ICP in children headache, vomiting (especially morning), irritability, lethargy, hypertension with bradycardia (Cushing response), papilledema, sunset sign, bulging fontanelle Shunt malfunction any ICP sign in a patient with a VP shunt VP shunt tap CSF is obtained percutaneously from the shunt reservoir, not by lumbar puncture

Management ladder – VP shunt with raised ICPCT first, shunt tap for CSF Tier Intervention Escalate when 1 CT head: compare ventricle size to baseline Ventricles enlarged → shunt malfunction confirmed 2 Shunt series (skull, chest, abdomen x-rays): trace catheter for disconnection, migration, kinking Discontinuity or migration visible 3 Shunt tap (percutaneous reservoir aspiration): cell count, Gram stain, culture; measure opening pressure Elevated pressure → obstruction; elevated white blood cell (WBC) count or positive culture → infection 4 Surgical shunt revision or externalization Clinical deterioration despite medical management

S. epidermidis – most common shunt infection organism; a skin commensal that colonizes the hardware; S. aureus second; Gram-negatives in neonates The shunt series is three plain films (skull, chest, abdomen) that trace the catheter from ventricle to peritoneum, looking for fracture, disconnection, or migration Slit ventricle syndrome – chronic overdrainage collapses the ventricles, causing intermittent obstruction and headache with small or normal ventricles on CT Shunt infection risk is highest in the first 6 months after placement or revision The open fontanelle in infants acts as a pressure pop-off valve, so papilledema and Cushing response may be absent; instead look for bulging fontanelle and increasing head circumference

Brain Tumors in a Child – shared finding: raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus; discriminator: is a shunt present? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant covers craniosynostosis; discriminator: an abnormal head shape with a ridged suture rather than a full fontanelle and a head crossing percentiles

A VP (ventriculoperitoneal) shunt changes the entire workup for raised intracranial pressure. Imaging replaces LP (lumbar puncture) as the first step. The shunt reservoir replaces the lumbar space as the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) source. The catheter itself becomes a possible cause and must be traced on plain films.

Sequencing trapLumbar puncture: it looks like the standard workup for altered mental status, but it is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus because of herniation risk. Sequencing trapEmpiric antibiotics tempt when infection is the concern, but the patient is afebrile, and antibiotics should follow culture (shunt tap), not precede it. True-fact-wrong-slotIV acetazolamide decreases CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) production but treats idiopathic intracranial hypertension, not obstructive hydrocephalus from shunt failure. True-fact-wrong-slotLP (lumbar puncture) diagnoses meningitis, but this infant is afebrile with a subacute course, and opening pressure does not diagnose hydrocephalus. Unchecked attributeReassurance fits a large head only when it grows along its own percentile with normal development; this head is crossing percentiles in a delayed infant. Mirror twinA skull film looks for craniosynostosis, which gives an abnormal head shape and ridged sutures, not a full fontanelle with split sutures. Salient decoyA large fontanelle suggests hypothyroidism, but that fontanelle is wide and soft, not full, and the head does not grow fast.

briefs.title: Night Blindness
briefs.sub: the fundus exam identifies the cause · pale disc vs cupped disc · the front of the eye · retinitis pigmentosa vs its four mimicsIs the disc pale or cupped, and is the front of the eye normal?
blocks: the fundus exam identifies the cause · pale disc vs cupped disc · the front of the eye · retinitis pigmentosa vs its four mimicsIs the disc pale or cupped, and is the front of the eye normal?

Pt 17 yo F, 2 months of progressive difficulty seeing at night while driving, with a near-collision; strict vegan eating a variety of plant products Exam visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally; lashes, conjunctivae and cornea unremarkable; pupils equal and reactive, extraocular muscles intact, red reflex equal; midperipheral visual field defect both eyes Fundus optic disc pallor, attenuation of retinal vessels and focal areas of discoloration, bilateral Q the most likely cause; options spanned cataract, open-angle glaucoma, retinal detachment, retinitis pigmentosa and vitamin A deficiency

Night blindness has a short differential, and the fundus exam settles it. Optic disc pallor with attenuated retinal vessels and patchy pigmentary change is the triad of retinitis pigmentosa. Rods degenerate first; they are densest in the midperiphery and serve dim-light vision. So the first symptom is night blindness, and the first field defect is midperipheral. Acuity stays 20/20 until cones are lost late. A normal red reflex and 20/20 vision exclude cataract. A pale rather than cupped disc excludes glaucoma. A two-month progressive course with no tear excludes detachment. The normal cornea and conjunctivae exclude vitamin A deficiency, whose ocular disease is xerophthalmia.

Retinitis pigmentosa, funduscopic triad retinal vessel attenuation from reduced metabolic demand, waxy optic disc pallor from nerve gliosis and atrophy, and abnormal retinal pigmentation in a bone-spicule pattern, which is a late finding Symptom sequence night blindness first, then progressive midperipheral field loss, then decreased acuity late when cones are involved; onset from age 10 into adulthood Xerophthalmia the mimic's gate: dryness of the cornea and conjunctivae with night blindness, which is what vitamin A deficiency looks like in the eye Glaucomatous disc an increased cup-to-disc ratio; the retinitis pigmentosa disc is pale and not cupped

Two months, progressive a degeneration, not an event; excludes retinal detachment Visual acuity 20/20 cones intact, so early disease, and inconsistent with cataract Red reflex equal bilaterally no lens opacity, closing cataract independently Cornea and conjunctivae unremarkable no xerophthalmia, closing vitamin A deficiency on examination rather than on diet Midperipheral field defect the rod-dense zone, the signature distribution of early disease Optic disc pallor, not cupping the single most efficient discriminator Vessel attenuation with focal discoloration the pigmentary retinopathy itself Age 17 open-angle glaucoma is a disease of late adulthood

Night blindness – the differential Diagnosis Illness script The NBME tell Excluded here by Retinitis pigmentosa Inherited photoreceptor degeneration, rods first; most legally blind by 40 Disc pallor plus vessel attenuation plus bone-spicule pigment; night blindness then midperipheral field loss – (the answer) Vitamin A deficiency Malabsorption, restrictive diet or poverty Xerophthalmia – dry cornea and conjunctivae, Bitot spots, corneal ulceration Cornea and conjunctivae normal; varied plant diet Open-angle glaucoma Painless gradual peripheral field loss in late adulthood Increased cup-to-disc ratio with raised intraocular pressure Age 17, and the disc is pale rather than cupped Retinal detachment Can't miss Acute; myopia, trauma or prior surgery Floaters, flashes, a curtain; tear or elevation on fundus Two-month progressive course, no tear or elevation Cataract Age, steroids, diabetes; glare from headlights at night Decreased acuity plus diminished red reflex plus lens opacity 20/20 acuity with an equal red reflex

Refer for formal visual fields and electroretinography, with genetic counselling. Treatment slows rather than reverses the disease, and most patients are legally blind by age 40. Care therefore focuses on prognosis, low-vision support and family screening rather than cure.

Is the acuity normal? Yes, so the problem is not the lens or the macula Is the red reflex intact? Yes, so cataract is out Acute or progressive? Two months and worsening, so not a detachment Pale disc or cupped disc? Pale means retinitis pigmentosa, not glaucoma Is the front of the eye normal? Yes, so no xerophthalmia and not vitamin A Where is the field defect? Midperipheral, which is the rods

Diagnostic workup Test Order Result What it points to Visual acuity and red reflex First 20/20 with a normal red reflex Excludes cataract; cones are spared early Slit-lamp exam of cornea and conjunctivae First No xerosis or Bitot spots Excludes vitamin A deficiency Dilated fundus exam Next Disc pallor, attenuated vessels, bone-spicule pigment Retinitis pigmentosa; a cupped disc is glaucoma Formal visual fields Supports Midperipheral field loss Rod loss Electroretinography Confirms Reduced or absent rod responses Retinitis pigmentosa Genetic testing, exam of relatives Cause Pathogenic variant identified Inheritance pattern; screen first-degree relatives Serum vitamin A for a vegan diet Skip Not needed with a normal cornea and conjunctivae The fundus, not the diet, names the cause

Mechanism7 of 8 Why night blindness is the earliest symptom of retinitis pigmentosa · Cone degeneration begins at the macula · Rod photoreceptors degenerate before cones · Demyelination of the optic nerve Why night blindness is the earliest symptom of retinitis pigmentosa Rod photoreceptors degenerate before conesrods serve dim-light vision and the midperiphery

Screening8 of 8 Newly diagnosed 17 yo F with retinitis pigmentosa who has an asymptomatic 12 yo brother · Annual intraocular pressure measurement alone · Ophthalmologic examination with genetic counseling for first-degree relatives · No screening is indicated unless he becomes symptomatic Newly diagnosed 17 yo F with retinitis pigmentosa who has an asymptomatic 12 yo brother Ophthalmologic examination with genetic counseling for first-degree relativesmost cases are inherited
Strict vegan is the decoy. She also eats a variety of plant products, which counters that risk factor. When a risk factor is qualified straight away, the qualifier takes precedence.

Examination versus history – diet, occupation and travel raise hypotheses, and the examination settles them; when the two disagree, trust the fundus Pale disc is retinitis pigmentosa; cupped disc is glaucoma – one descriptive word separates a teenager's genetic degeneration from an older adult's pressure disease vitamin A deficiency and retinitis pigmentosa share night blindness and differ at the front of the eye Acuity is preserved until late because rods go first, so 20/20 vision argues for the diagnosis in a patient with field loss, not against it night driving trouble in an older adult is cataract glare; in a teenager with a normal red reflex it is retinal

Part I The Red Eye covers everything anterior to the lens, the territory of xerophthalmia. Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers what a plant-only diet actually requires supplementing; that brief's answer is B12, not vitamin A. Ask: is the front of the eye normal, and is the disc pale or cupped? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin A deficiency itself (ask: is fat being malabsorbed, and are there Bitot spots?).

A demographic or lifestyle detail is a prior, not a finding. If a diet, job or country of origin is the only thing still supporting an option, that option is the decoy. Switch only when a stated finding is incompatible with your current answer.

Salient decoyVitamin A deficiency: strict vegan plus night blindness is a taught pairing and it outpolled the key, but ocular vitamin A deficiency is xerophthalmia and the front of the eye is explicitly normal. Unchecked attributeOpen-angle glaucoma: painless peripheral field loss is genuinely its presentation, but it is a disease of late adulthood and the disc is cupped, not pale. Unchecked attributeRetinal detachment: a retinal cause of field loss, but acute with floaters, flashes and a visible tear; this is two months of steady progression. True-fact-wrong-slotCataract: difficulty driving at night from headlight glare is a real cataract complaint, but it requires reduced acuity and a diminished red reflex, both normal here.

briefs.title: Tics and Tic Disorders
briefs.sub: classify the movement first · motor and vocal tics · Tourette criteria · tic vs compulsion · habit reversal, then medicationIs the behavior involuntary, or is it neutralizing an obsession?

2 or more motor tics 1 or more vocal tics, at least 1 year, onset before 18 Tourette syndrome; echolalia counts as vocal Repeated act no obsession behind it a tic, not a compulsion No impairment explain and watch. Impairment CBIT (comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics) medication: a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter type 2) inhibitor such as tetrabenazine first, or an antipsychotic; an alpha-2 agonist for milder tics, especially with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder)

What it is Sudden, rapid, nonrhythmic movements or sounds Tourette: 2 or more motor 1 or more vocal tics for at least 1 year, onset before 18 Driver Cause unknown runs in families (in some, dominant with incomplete penetrance) Triggers Family history non-modifiable male sex (about 4 boys to 1 girl) In practiceIn practiceThe Merck Manual gives a different figure: a male to female ratio of 3 to 1. non-modifiable Worse with stress fatigue downtime Chain Urge (in some) tic; some can hold it back for seconds to minutes Onset typically at 4 to 6 peak at 10 to 12 lessens in adolescence a third persist for life Insights ADHD OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder) often impair more than the tics screen every patient Tics ADHD an alpha-2 agonist first; a stimulant if the ADHD improves little, watching for worse tics

Mechanism and coursedetail behind the chain Some feel an urge first; some can hold a tic back for seconds to minutes; fewer during focused tasks, usually none in sleep Onset before 18, usually at 4 to 6 years; tics wax and wane Most severe at about 10 to 12 years Tics lessen in many About a third resolve completely, a third improve in adolescence and adulthood, and a third have lifelong tics In practice In practiceThe Merck Manual gives a different figure: most tics disappear on their own and about 1% persist into adulthood. ADHD is the most common; OCD is common too; both often interfere more than the tics; oppositional defiant disorder and autism spectrum disorder also occur A stimulant can bring out or worsen tics in some children, yet tics do not rule one outin trials of children with tics and ADHD, methylphenidate did not worsen tics on average

Course by age BirthAge 6Age 11Age 18Adult OnsetAverage age 6, most by 11; before 18 by definition Peak severityAges 10 to 12 AdolescenceSymptoms lessen in many AdulthoodA third resolve, a third improve, a third keep tics

Tourette two or more motor tics and one or more vocal tics, not always at the same time; tics for at least 1 year Persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tics, not both, for 1 year or more Provisional motor and/or vocal tics for less than 1 year All three onset before 18; not due to a medication or drug, or another medical condition (eg, seizures, Huntington disease, postviral encephalitis)

Tic types Type Motor Vocal Simple: brief, no social meaning Blinking, grimacing, head jerking, shoulder shrugging Grunting or barking, sniffing or snorting, throat clearing Complex: longer, may look intentional Combined simple tics (head turning plus shrugging); echopraxia, imitating movements; copropraxia, obscene gestures Echolalia, repeating another person's sounds or words, or one's own; coprolaliaCoprolaliaSaying obscenities: only a minority of patients, socially inappropriate words
Clinical diagnosis: no test confirms it

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Tourette syndrome Two or more motor tics plus one or more vocal tics, not always at the same time 1 year or more; both motor and vocal tics Obsessive-compulsive disorder Intrusive thoughts drive repeated acts that relieve the distress A named obsession; a tic neutralizes none. The two often coexist Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Inattention or hyperactivity in 2 or more settings 6 months or more, some before age 12; often coexists with tics Oppositional defiant disorder Angry or irritable mood, argument and defiance, vindictiveness 6 months or more of defiance, not an involuntary movement Persistent (chronic) tic disorder Motor or vocal tics, not both 1 year or more, only one type Provisional tic disorder (transient tic disorder) Motor and/or vocal tics Under 1 year Stereotypies (stereotypic movements) Repetitive, usually bilateral, such as hand flapping; with autism or intellectual disability, or in typical young children Rhythmic, where a tic is not; distraction, such as calling the child's name, typically stops it MyoclonusAlso not a ticMyoclonus is sudden and nonrhythmic like a tic, but it cannot be held back and no urge comes first. Sydenham chorea Rapid, irregular jerks, often spreading to the feet and face; may unmask OCD Often months after a strep infection; a major criterion of rheumatic fever A drug, medication or medical cause Tic-like movements with a culprit drug (eg, methylphenidate) or a condition such as seizures, Huntington disease or postviral encephalitis The culprit drug or the other condition is found

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Repeated sudden movements or sounds → Describe the movement Sudden, rapid, nonrhythmic; no obsession behind it A tic Performed to relieve an obsession A compulsion: OCD Tics confirmed → Count the tic types and time the course Motor plus vocal, 1 year or more Tourette syndrome Motor or vocal only, 1 year or more Persistent tic disorder Under 1 year Provisional tic disorder Next step TestResultMeans Any tic disorder → Screen for ADHD and OCD Inattention or hyperactivity in 2 or more settings, 6 months or more ADHD Intrusive thoughts driving rituals OCD: a dual diagnosis is allowed SkipNo test confirms it: the diagnosis is clinical. Exclude a drug, medication or medical cause, then gauge impairment.

Why time it Why time itTelling Tourette syndrome from tics that pass may take follow-up over time. Also ask Guideline detailThe American Academy of Neurology guideline adds screening for anxiety, mood and disruptive behavior disorders, and asking about suicidal thoughts and attempts.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Repeats exactly what other children say Echolalia, a vocal tic Counts toward Tourette syndrome Shrugs, turns the head, raises a hand again and again, with no obsession Motor tics Not OCD treatment One tic fades and another appears The waxing and waning course Expected; the diagnosis stands Concerns reported from school alone Only 1 setting so far Confirm a second setting before calling it ADHD

Pause point 7-year-old referred from school for behavior; his father has OCD Offered as OCD: exposure and response prevention and an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) OCD is common alongside tics, but with no obsession his repeated acts are tics; a relative’s diagnosis does not describe this child’s movements → Tics: exposure and response prevention and an SSRI miss the target; he is bullied and isolated, so the tics impair, and treatment is warranted

Treatment by impairment Situation Choose Tics with no functional impairment Explain the natural history; watchful waiting Tics that significantly interfere with activities or self-image Treat the tics: behavioral therapy (CBIT) first ADHD or OCD that impairs Treat it too; it often impairs more than the tics

1 Explainevery patient Psychoeducation on the natural history Without functional impairment, watchful waiting is enough. School and peersGuideline detailRefer teachers and peers to psychoeducation resources. 2 1st linetics interfere with activities or self-image Behavioral therapy: habit reversal training, the core of CBITWhat it isComprehensive behavioral intervention for tics: cognitive-behavioral therapy built around habit reversal training.Habit reversal training is the first-line treatment: tic awareness training (recognize the urge before a tic), then competing response training (a competing behavior, such as a deep breath, when the urge comes). Offer it before medication when it is available. 3 Medicationtics still impair A VMAT2 inhibitor such as tetrabenazine, preferred for fewer side effects; or an antipsychoticMechanismSecond-generation drugs block D2 dopamine and 5-HT2A serotonin receptors; aripiprazole is instead a D2 partial agonist. First-generation drugs carry significant extrapyramidal effects.Watch for drug-induced movement disorders; weight gain (risperidone, aripiprazole); ↑ prolactin from D2 blockade (haloperidol, pimozide, risperidone). Aripiprazole raises prolactin less. Pimozide or ziprasidone: an ECG (electrocardiogram) for the QTc (the interval from the Q wave to the end of the T wave, corrected for heart rate) before and after starting., aripiprazole first Milder tics, especially with ADHD: an alpha-2 agonist, clonidineMechanismA central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (also imidazoline receptors): lowers sympathetic outflow from the brain.Watch for sedation, low blood pressure and a slow heart rate; stopping it suddenly can cause rebound hypertension. or guanfacine, which may help both. In practiceIn practiceThe Merck Manual calls oral antipsychotics (aripiprazole, haloperidol, pimozide) second-line medications for tics that are harder to control, and the 2019 American Academy of Neurology guideline calls VMAT2 inhibitors increasingly used off-label; drowsiness, depression and parkinsonism can occur. ADHD Alpha-2 agonist: check heart rate and blood pressure; taper to stop 4 Escalatesevere tics resist these Haloperidol or pimozide, for severe, resistant tics only Risperidone also reduces tics but is not first line. If tics stay severeBeyond the ladderDeep brain stimulation for an adult with severe tics after, or unable to take, several drug classes and CBIT; multidisciplinary review first. Botulinum toxin for a localized simple motor tic in an adolescent or adult; weakness and a soft voice, all temporary. Lowest effective dose

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Tics impair, no ADHD CBIT; then a VMAT2 inhibitor (preferred) or an antipsychoticWhy these drugsBoth are antidopaminergic drugs, the most effective medications for tics: a VMAT2 inhibitor (tetrabenazine, valbenazine) depletes dopamine and is not linked to tardive dyskinesia or metabolic syndrome; an antipsychotic blocks dopamine receptors but carries more risk of weight gain, metabolic syndrome, dystonia and tardive dyskinesia.; for milder tics, an alpha-2 agonist firstAlpha-2 agonistFor less debilitating tics, with a lower risk of significant adverse effects in children; sedation and low blood pressure; weaker evidence than for antidopaminergic drugs.; if it fails and tics still impair, step up to a VMAT2 inhibitor (depletes dopamine) or an antipsychotic (blocks dopamine receptors) VMAT2 inhibitor: drowsiness, depression, parkinsonism. Antipsychotic: lowest effective dose; movement and metabolic effects. Alpha-2 agonist: heart rate, blood pressure, taper to stop Tics impair, with ADHD CBIT; then, for milder tics, clonidine or guanfacine, which may help both Stop an alpha-2 agonist by taper: rebound hypertension ADHD The ADHD is what impairs An alpha-2 agonist (guanfacine or clonidine) first; may switch to a stimulant if the ADHD improves little On a stimulant, tics can emerge or worsen in some: watch closely; tics do not rule one out. Atomoxetine is another option Tics with OCD Cognitive-behavioral therapy (exposure and response prevention), with or without an SSRI, for the OCD; treat the tics as above Exposure and response prevention targets compulsions; a tic neutralizes no obsession. SSRIs and tricyclics treat the OCD or depression; they play no primary role in the tics

Follow-up decisions When Do Tics for under 1 year Follow over time: that is how Tourette syndrome separates from tics that pass Every visit Expect waxing and waning; many improve in adolescence On an alpha-2 agonist Check heart rate and blood pressure; taper to stop On an antipsychotic Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Lowest effective dose; watch for movement, metabolic and hormonal effects; taper over weeks to months to stop ADHD that impairs Make sure the ADHD is treated

School Difficulty in a Childis the nearest relative. It shares the same referral route, a school behavior complaint. The resolution is opposite: there the private interview reveals a learning disorder, and here the examination reveals tics. Ask: what exactly is the child doing, and is it involuntary? A family history raises the prior probability, but the phenomenology decides. When a relative's diagnosis and a child's behavior are both given, first describe the behavior in neutral terms. If the behavior is sudden, rapid and nonrhythmic, with no obsession behind it, it is a tic, whatever the family carries.

For a school-age child with motor and vocal tics who is referred from school and whose father has OCD: Exposure and response prevention: the father's OCD makes it tempting, but it treats compulsions driven by obsessions, and the child describes no obsession. Fluoxetine: an SSRI is a first-line medication for OCD, but it treats obsessions and compulsions, not tics. Parent management training: it treats oppositional defiant disorder, a pattern of defiance, and does nothing for involuntary movements. Methylphenidate or atomoxetine: ADHD often coexists with tics, but these movements are tics, and concerns reported from school alone do not meet the 2-setting criterion for ADHD.

Adult: which test Why order itIn-lab polysomnography is the gold standard; home tests are cheaper and easier to get. Uncomplicated and at increased risk of moderate to severe apnea: either test. Significant heart or lung disease, neuromuscular weakness, chronic opioids, stroke or severe insomnia: polysomnography, not a home test. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2025) treats at 75 ng/mL or less, a consensus good practice statement not tested in trials; an older review used ferritin <50 ng/mL.

Treat by problem Problem First Then or watch for Sleep terrors Reassure and educateWhat to tell parentsSleep terrors are not dangerous; they usually resolve on their own within 1 to 2 years.; keep the child safe; more total sleepWhen to add sleepOnly with signs of too little sleep (moodiness, behavior change, daytime sleepiness); the need for daytime naps usually falls as children grow. Never shorten sleep Sleepwalking Reassure and educate; lock windows and outer doors; remove breakable objects Avoid sleep loss, a common trigger Nightmares Reassure: common in young children and usually pass Nightmare disorder: imagery rehearsal therapyWhat it isRewrite the dream so it is less distressing. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends it for adults with nightmares and posttraumatic stress disorder. and/or prazosin may help; CBT for anxiety-related nightmares. In a child: ask about trauma and mood. Low mood that follows the poor sleep is more likely a consequence than the cause. Lasting 3 months or more: chronic insomnia, next row Chronic insomnia, adult CBT for insomnia PartsWhat it includesCognitive restructuring, stimulus control, sleep hygiene, relaxation, and sleep restriction, the most effective part Older adult: no benzodiazepine or other sedative-hypnotic as the first choice Narcolepsy Modafinil; an oxybate also treats cataplexy; brief naps at set times Naps under 30 minutes REM sleep behavior disorder Bedroom safety; melatonin first, clonazepam second In practiceIn practice:The Merck Manual lists clonazepam first, with melatonin as the alternative; pramipexole is also used. Ask about antidepressants Restless legs syndrome Iron if stores are ↓; then gabapentin or pregabalin Alternative: a dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole) Long use can worsen symptoms (augmentation) In practiceIn practice:The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2025) advises against standard use of dopamine agonists: harms outweigh benefits. Follow-up decisions When Do Sleep terrors persist despite reassurance and safety Scheduled awakenings before the usual episode time; if still frequent or impairing: a low-dose benzodiazepine can be consideredWhen not to use itNot for infrequent episodes with no daytime impairment: reassurance only. Chronic insomnia not better with CBT for insomnia Medication may be considered, short term RisksWatch forBenzodiazepines: dependence. Z-drugs (nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotics): car crashes, falls, fractures. Antihistamines: little evidence. Other optionsOther optionsTrazodone: a sleep aid at low doses; may cause morning drowsiness; more effective with coexisting depression. Ramelteon, a melatonin agonist: fewer adverse effects; shortens time to sleep onset in older adults. briefs.title: Spinal Dysraphism
briefs.sub: grade the reflexes first · a number outranks a story · upper vs lower motor neuron · bladder, back, pes cavusAre the reflexes brisk or diminished, and is the bladder involved?
blocks: grade the reflexes first · a number outranks a story · upper vs lower motor neuron · bladder, back, pes cavusAre the reflexes brisk or diminished, and is the bladder involved?

Pt 6 yo M, 2 months of progressive gait difficulty and back pain, new incontinence, pes cavus and hammer toes, 1+ lower extremity reflexes Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned tethered cord, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and spastic diplegia

1+ reflexes are the key finding. Hyporeflexia is a lower motor neuron sign that localizes at or below the anterior horn cell. It eliminates spastic diplegia outright, since cerebral palsy is by definition an upper motor neuron disorder. Three findings then pick the lesion. Bladder involvement counts because muscle and peripheral nerve diseases spare the bladder. Back pain points at a structural spinal lesion. Pes cavus is chronic denervation of the intrinsic foot muscles. One lesion explains all four findings: a tethered cord from closed spinal dysraphism, stretched by two months of growth.

Reflex grading 0 absent, 1+ diminished, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ clonus Lower motor neuron signs weakness with hypotonia, hyporeflexia and atrophy, localizing at or below the anterior horn cell Upper motor neuron signs weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski, localizing above the anterior horn cell Secondary incontinence continence achieved and held, then lost; always pathologic Low-lying conus the conus reaches L1 to L2 by about 3 months, so below mid-L2 is low; a filum over 2 mm is thickened

The child with progressive leg weakness - the differential Diagnosis Illness script The NBME tell Tethered cord Cord anchored caudally and stretched by growth Lower motor neuron signs with bladder dysfunction, pes cavus and back pain together Duchenne muscular dystrophy 3 to 5 yo boy, progressive degeneration Proximal weakness, Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, pes planus; no bladder involvement Spastic diplegia Static perinatal insult, often prematurity Hypertonia and hyperreflexia, scissoring gait, nonprogressive Transverse myelitis Post-infectious cord demyelination Acute over hours to days with a sensory level Charcot-Marie-Tooth Hereditary neuropathy, autosomal dominant Pes cavus with foot drop and family history; no bladder involvement Friedreich ataxia Autosomal recessive, teens Pes cavus with ataxia and areflexia with upgoing toes, cardiomyopathy Spinal cord tumor Can't miss Astrocytoma or ependymoma Night-waking back pain with progressive deficits; same magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) answers both

A normal-looking back does not exclude dysraphism. Cutaneous stigmata are common but not universal. Look for a hair tuft, lipoma, hemangioma, sacral appendage, or a dimple above the gluteal cleft; a simple dimple within the cleft with a visible base is benign. Image with ultrasound before about 3 months, while the posterior elements are cartilaginous, and MRI after.

Pes cavus is a neurologic sign, not an orthopedic one: Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Friedreich ataxia, and tethered cord Secondary enuresis is never assumed functional; consider infection, diabetes, constipation, neurologic disease, stress and sleep apnea Back pain in a child under 10 is pathologic until proven otherwise Occulta – skin intact, no herniation Meningocele – meninges herniate, cord normal Myelomeningocele – meninges and neural tissue, with Chiari II and hydrocephalus Folate prevents neural tube defects: 0.4 mg periconceptionally, 4 mg with a prior affected pregnancy

Part I Enuresis is the mirror twin: it shares the complaint of a school-age child wetting, and the classification flips from functional to neurologic. Ask: was the child ever dry, and is anything else abnormal? Part I Constipation in a Child screens for this condition on every perineal examination; a sacral dimple or hair tuft converts constipation into imaging.
Grade the reflexes before you name the disease. Hyperreflexia and hyporeflexia split the weakness differential into halves that share no members. That split holds however compelling the history.

Class-vs-memberDuchenne: the right age and sex, with proximal weakness, flat feet and no bladder involvement. Mirror twinSpastic diplegia: the upper motor neuron version of the same complaint. True-fact-wrong-slotTransverse myelitis: a real cord syndrome on the wrong timeline.

briefs.title: Encephalopathy and Cerebral Edema in a Child
briefs.sub: cause of the cerebral edema, not of the illness · Reye syndrome · only ammonia swells astrocytes · the vitals eliminateWhich option causes edema rather than only encephalopathy, and do the vitals exclude the rest?
blocks: Encephalopathy and Cerebral Edema in a Child

cause of the cerebral edema, not of the illness · Reye syndrome · only ammonia swells astrocytes · the vitals eliminateWhich option causes edema rather than only encephalopathy, and do the vitals exclude the rest?

Pt 5 yo F, viral illness treated with over-the-counter medications; improved, then vomiting and lethargy; hepatomegaly with a normal spleen; no hypertension, no peripheral edema Vitals T 36.8 °C, pulse 110, BP 98/60 Imaging cerebral edema Q the most likely cause of the imaging findings; options spanned hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, uremia, adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism

The sequence is a viral prodrome, then "over-the-counter medications" (the aspirin, never named). A biphasic course follows (better, then vomiting and lethargy). Then come hepatomegaly without splenomegaly and cerebral edema. This is Reye syndrome. The cause of the imaging finding lies one level down, at the mechanism. Hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, uremia, adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism can all cloud consciousness, but only hyperammonemia causes edema. In astrocytes, glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine. Glutamine is osmotically active and cannot leave. Water follows, and the astrocytes swell, causing cytotoxic cerebral edema. Hypoglycemia, uremia and adrenal crisis produce encephalopathy by other routes and leave the brain the same size.

Option audit – which options cause encephalopathy? Option Encephalopathy? Why it fails here Hyperammonemia Yes Correct – the only one that swells astrocytes Hypoglycemia Yes Genuinely occurs in Reye (failing hepatic gluconeogenesis) but causes no edema – a true fact in the wrong slot Uremia Yes Uremic encephalopathy without edema; expect hypertension and peripheral edema, not hepatomegaly Adrenal insufficiency Yes Dysfunction is from hypoperfusion; BP is 98/60 – normal, which kills it outright Hypothyroidism Yes Myxedema coma is hypothermic and bradycardic; this child is 36.8 °C with a pulse of 110
The vitals do most of the eli…

BP 98/60 (normal) excludes adrenal crisis, which is a hypotension diagnosis pulse 110, temp 36.8 excludes myxedema coma, which is slow and cold no hypertension, no peripheral edema excludes uremia hepatomegaly with a normal spleen points to acute hepatic steatosis, not congestion or storage disease.

Toxic-metabolic encephalopathies & precipitants Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy Precipitant Hypoxic-ischemic Near-drowning, choking episode Diabetic ketoacidosis Poorly controlled diabetes; edema often follows fluid resuscitation Hyponatremia Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; or rapid correction of hypernatremia Liver failure Viral or autoimmune hepatitis; hepatotoxic drugs such as acetaminophen Reye syndrome Aspirin given for a viral illness in a child

Hypoglycemia: the sharpest trap in the set, because it is true; Reye does cause hypoglycemia through failing hepatic gluconeogenesis. It simply is not what swells the brain. Uremia: a neurotoxin, but nothing here suggests renal failure. Adrenal insufficiency: plausible until you read the blood pressure. Hypothyroidism: the pulse and temperature contradict it.

Aspirin is contraindicated in children except for Kawasaki disease and rheumatologic disease such as JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis); Kawasaki is the reason the exception exists the mechanism is mitochondrial injury → impaired β-oxidation. This causes microvesicular steatosis, which is why the liver is big but not scarred treatment is supportive; there is no antidote hyperammonemia without hepatomegaly in a neonate is a urea cycle defect, not Reye; the neurotoxin is the same, but the disease is different.

Diabetes Complications and Annual Carealso turns on reading the outcome noun ( morbidityversus mortality). Here this stem says "cause of this patient's imaging findings,"not "cause of this patient's presentation." Ask: "which effect am I being asked to explain?" Diabetes Complications and Annual Care also turns on reading the outcome noun (morbidity versus mortality). briefs.sub: find the arteriopathy · constitutional symptoms plus unequal pulses make it inflammatory · its mimicsWhat made the artery fail: constitutional symptoms with unequal pulses, a murmur, or neck strain?

find the arteriopathy · constitutional symptoms plus unequal pulses make it inflammatory · its mimicsWhat made the artery fail: constitutional symptoms with unequal pulses, a murmur, or neck strain?

Pt 15 yo with weeks of constitutional symptoms and episodic light-headedness, now an acute focal neurologic deficit, with asymmetric upper-extremity pulses Q the most likely cause of the stroke; options spanned the pediatric stroke categories: vasculitis, bacterial endocarditis, fibromuscular dysplasia and others

A stroke in a teenager is never "just a stroke"; find what made the artery fail. Weeks of fever, weight loss and aches indicate systemic inflammation. Unequal pulses or arm pressures indicate that several large arteries are narrowed at once. Inflammation plus multiple fixed large-artery stenoses is a large-vessel vasculitis; in an adolescent, that is Takayasu arteritis. Endocarditis is the exception. It also brings fever and stroke, but emboli occlude one vessel at a time and never narrow the aorta's branches, so the pulses stay equal. Look for the murmur and the embolic skin findings instead.

When a young patient has a stroke, name what made the artery fail. Systemic inflammation with unequal pulses is vasculitis; fever with a murmur is an embolus; neck strain with Horner syndrome is a dissection; a string of beads with no inflammation is fibromuscular dysplasia.

Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: fever plus stroke looks embolic, but emboli do not narrow several arteries or unequalize the pulses. Mirror twinFibromuscular dysplasia: a young woman with arterial stenoses, but no fever, weight loss or raised ESR. briefs.title: Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi
briefs.sub: Angelman vs Prader-Willi · maternal vs paternal 15q11-q13 · uniparental disomy · Rett and Williams mimicsWhich parent's copy of chromosome 15 is missing or silent?
blocks: Angelman vs Prader-Willi · maternal vs paternal 15q11-q13 · uniparental disomy · Rett and Williams mimicsWhich parent's copy of chromosome 15 is missing or silent?

Pt 3 yo F with a seizure disorder on valproic acid and strabismus; height and weight at the 25th percentile, head circumference at the 3rd Exam happy and excitable, smiles and laughs often; flat back of the head, prominent jaw, widely spaced teeth; repeated hand flapping; stiff-legged gait, needs help on stairs; short attention span; communicates with gestures and sounds, no words Q the most likely genetic defect; options spanned chromosome 15 deletions of maternal or paternal origin, a chromosome 7 deletion, an MECP2 mutation, trisomy 15 and trisomy 21

A child with no words, seizures, microcephaly, a stiff-legged, ataxic gait and a happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter has Angelman syndrome. Hand flapping, a flat occiput, a prominent jaw, widely spaced teeth and strabismus support it. The usual cause is deletion of the maternally inherited 15q11-q13 region, which contains UBE3A (ubiquitin protein ligase E3A). In neurons, imprinting silences the paternal copy of UBE3A. Losing the maternal copy therefore leaves those neurons with no working gene. The same region deleted from the paternal chromosome causes Prader-Willi syndrome. Prader-Willi follows loss of the paternally expressed genes of the region. It presents as a floppy newborn with a poor suck, followed by hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism and short stature. A less common cause of Angelman syndrome is paternal uniparental disomy. Both chromosome 15s come from the father, so no maternal UBE3A copy is present even though nothing is deleted. Maternal uniparental disomy is the mirror cause of Prader-Willi syndrome.

Angelman syndrome no active maternal copy of UBE3A in neurons, usually from a maternal 15q11-q13 deletion Prader-Willi syndrome no active paternal copy of the 15q11-q13 genes, usually from a paternal deletion Imprinting silencing of one parent's copy of a gene by DNA methylation Uniparental disomy both copies of a chromosome inherited from one parent

Developmental delay with a genetic syndrome: the differential Diagnosis Brief illness script Key discriminator Why less likely here Angelman syndrome: maternal 15q11-q13 deletion; paternal uniparental disomy less often Severe delay with little or no speech, seizures usually before age 3, microcephaly, ataxic gait Happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter; hand flapping The answer: every finding in this child fits Prader-Willi syndrome: paternal 15q11-q13 deletion; maternal uniparental disomy in about a quarter Floppy newborn with a poor suck; hyperphagia and obesity in childhood; hypogonadism, short stature, cognitive impairment Hyperphagia and obesity after a hypotonic infancy; hypogonadism Her weight is at the 25th percentile, with no hyperphagia or hypogonadism Rett syndrome: MECP2 (methyl-CpG binding protein 2) mutation, X-linked, mostly girls Normal development for 6 to 18 months, then loss of speech and purposeful hand use; head growth slows; seizures, gait problems, scoliosis Regression after normal early development; hand wringing No loss of skills is described, and her hands flap rather than wring Williams syndrome: 7q11.23 deletion that includes the elastin gene Overfriendly, usually mild intellectual disability; broad forehead, periorbital fullness, wide mouth with full lips; hypercalcemia in infancy Overfriendliness with supravalvar aortic stenosis No murmur, typical facies or hypercalcemia is described Down syndrome: trisomy 21 Hypotonia from birth, up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease; heart defects and duodenal atresia Recognizable at birth by the face, hands and low tone None of its facial or hand features is described

Workup7 of 7 3 yo F with seizures, microcephaly, an ataxic gait, no words and a happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter · Standard chromosome karyotype · Sequencing of the MECP2 gene · DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 3 yo F with seizures, microcephaly, an ataxic gait, no words and a happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects; a normal result leads to UBE3A sequencing

Other Angelman features include a fascination with water and a reduced need for sleep DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 is the first test. It detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects A normal methylation result does not exclude Angelman syndrome. A UBE3A (ubiquitin protein ligase E3A) mutation accounts for about 1 in 10 cases and needs gene sequencing
The options named the genetic defect and parent of origin, not the syndrome; the two chromosome 15 deletions differed only by parent.

Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers Down syndrome and the newborn picture of Prader-Willi syndrome. Ask: was the child floppy from birth, or delayed with seizures and laughter later? Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the methylation workup for Prader-Willi syndrome in a floppy infant. Part I Cerebral Palsy carries Rett syndrome as a regression mimic. Ask: did the child lose skills, or never gain them?

Identify the syndrome from the phenotype before choosing the genetic defect. For chromosome 15, laughter, seizures and ataxia mean the maternal copy is missing. Hyperphagia after a floppy infancy means the paternal copy is missing.

Unchecked attributeChromosome 15 deletion, paternally inherited: deletion of the same region from the paternal chromosome causes Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonic infancy, then hyperphagia, obesity and hypogonadism. Salient decoyMutation of MECP2 (methyl-CpG binding protein 2): Rett syndrome also affects girls with microcephaly, seizures and repetitive hand movements. It follows normal early development with regression, and the hands wring rather than flap. Salient decoyChromosome 7 deletion: Williams syndrome also gives a sociable child, but with overfriendliness, elfin facies, supravalvar aortic stenosis and hypercalcemia. True-fact-wrong-slotTrisomy 15: a complete trisomy 15 is typically lethal before birth. Paternal uniparental disomy, with two paternal chromosome 15s, is the less common route to Angelman syndrome. Class-vs-memberTrisomy 21: Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. It shows at birth with hypotonia, up-slanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, none of which is described.

briefs.title: Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child
briefs.sub: hordeolum vs chalazion · lid margin vs inner corner · preseptal vs orbital · warm compresses, antibiotics if it spreadsWhere is the swelling, and does it spread beyond the lump?
blocks: Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child
hordeolum vs chalazion · lid margin vs inner corner · preseptal vs orbital · warm compresses, antibiotics if it spreadsWhere is the swelling, and does it spread beyond the lump?

Pt 10 yo M, 2 days of redness and mild pain in the left eye; afebrile Exam left conjunctiva mildly red, swollen and tender; a 3-mm nodule on the lower lid margin, toward the outer corner; right eye normal Q the most appropriate treatment; options spanned nasolacrimal massage, oral amoxicillin, topical prednisolone, topical tetrahydrozoline and warm compresses

A tender nodule on the eyelid margin, with local redness and no fever, is a hordeolum (stye). It is an acute infection of an eyelid gland, usually by Staphylococcus aureus. First-line treatment is warm compresses with gentle lid massage several times a day. Heat softens the blocked gland contents so the gland can drain. Conjunctival redness and swelling beside the nodule come from surface irritation and do not make this conjunctivitis. Add oral antibiotics only when redness and swelling spread across the lid, which is preseptal cellulitis. A lesion that has not settled after several weeks of compresses goes to ophthalmology for incision and drainage.

Lump or swelling of the eyelid in a child: the differential Diagnosis Brief illness script Key discriminator Why less likely here Hordeolum (stye) Acute staphylococcal infection of a lash follicle or eyelid gland; warm compresses and lid massage Tender, red nodule on the lid margin, sometimes with a yellow point Fits: 2 days, tender 3-mm nodule on the margin, afebrile Chalazion Sterile, chronic inflammation of a blocked meibomian gland, sometimes left behind by a hordeolum; compresses, then steroid injection or incision if it persists Painless, firm nodule in the body of the lid, away from the margin, present for weeks This nodule is tender, on the margin and 2 days old Dacryocystitis Infection of the lacrimal sac behind a blocked nasolacrimal duct; oral antibiotics, with warm compresses as support Tender swelling at the inner corner of the eye, beside the nose; pus from the punctum on pressure The nodule sits on the lid margin toward the outer corner Preseptal cellulitis Infection of the lid in front of the orbital septum, from a skin break, hordeolum or dacryocystitis; oral amoxicillin-clavulanate Diffuse red, warm, swollen lid; eye movements and vision normal, no proptosis Redness and swelling stay at the nodule, and there is no fever Orbital cellulitis Can't miss Infection behind the septum, usually spread from ethmoid sinusitis; computed tomography of the orbits with contrast and intravenous antibiotics Proptosis, pain with eye movement, limited eye movement or reduced vision None of these is described, and he is afebrile Blepharitis Chronic inflammation of both lid margins, often with seborrheic dermatitis; lid hygiene and warm compresses Both lids red and crusted along the lash line, worse on waking, with no discrete nodule One focal nodule in one eye

Hordeolum Warm compresses several times a day with gentle lid massage; do not squeeze the lesion Redness and swelling spread across the lid; or no improvement after several weeks, when ophthalmology offers incision and drainage 2. Preseptal cellulitis Oral antibiotic covering Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci, such as amoxicillin-clavulanate, with close follow-up Proptosis, pain with eye movement, limited eye movement or reduced vision; or worsening on oral antibiotics 3. Orbital cellulitis Admission, computed tomography of the orbits with contrast, intravenous antibiotics and ophthalmology consultation Abscess on imaging or falling vision: surgical drainage

Squeezing a hordeolum can spread the infection into the lid A lump at the inner corner of the eye is the lacrimal sac, not an eyelid gland Topical steroid drops treat anterior uveitis and are avoided when infection is possible

The stem opened with a red, sore eye and conjunctival swelling, and it described the lump on the lid margin without ever naming a stye. Each wrong option was the right treatment for a neighboring eye problem: a blocked tear duct, preseptal cellulitis, uveitis or simple redness.

Part I The Red Eye covers conjunctivitis and the can't-miss red eyes, including uveitis, where topical steroids belong. Ask: does the redness come from the conjunctiva, or from a lump on the lid? Part I Sinusitis and Its Complications covers preseptal versus orbital cellulitis and orbital imaging. Ask: are eye movements painful or limited, and is there proptosis?

Locate the swelling before treating it. A tender nodule on the lid margin gets warm compresses. Antibiotics start when redness spreads across the lid, and imaging when the eye protrudes or eye movement hurts.

Unchecked attributeNasolacrimal massage: it sounds like the lid massage that goes with compresses; it treats a blocked tear duct at the inner corner, and this nodule is on the lid margin toward the outer corner. Sequencing trapOral amoxicillin: the nodule is an infection; there is no fever and no redness spreading across the lid, so there is no cellulitis to treat. True-fact-wrong-slotTopical prednisolone: the eye is inflamed; steroid drops treat anterior uveitis, and a tender lump on the lid margin is not uveitis; steroids are also avoided when infection is possible. Salient decoyTopical tetrahydrozoline: it clears the redness the stem opens with; this vasoconstrictor acts at alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors and does nothing for the blocked gland.

briefs.title: Headache in a School-Age Child
briefs.sub: primary, or a mass, raised pressure, infection or bleeding · red flags · the fundi and cerebellar signs · posterior fossa tumorDoes the headache come and go or progress, and are the fundi or the gait abnormal?
blocks: primary, or a mass, raised pressure, infection or bleeding · red flags · the fundi and cerebellar signs · posterior fossa tumorDoes the headache come and go or progress, and are the fundi or the gait abnormal?

Pt 7 yo with headache, Aquifer Neurology 10 / Pediatrics 20; the case works from red flags and the fundoscopic exam through cerebellar localization to a posterior fossa brain tumor Q separate primary from secondary headache, find raised intracranial pressure at the bedside, localize the lesion by site and time course, and name the likely tumor

Ask first whether a headache is primary (migraine, tension-type headache) or secondary. Causes of a secondary headache include a mass (posterior fossa or supratentorial tumor) and pressure without a mass (idiopathic intracranial hypertension). The others are blocked CSF flow (cerebrospinal fluid flow, as in hydrocephalus), infection (meningitis, abscess) and bleeding. Primary headaches come and go; secondary headaches progress. Check the vital signs for Cushing triad and fever first. Then use the pattern over time, the fundi and the neurologic exam to sort the causes. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) finds the lesion. Tissue, CSF or the typical story confirms the diagnosis.

Red flags: act before the full history Finding What it points to High blood pressure, slow pulse, irregular breathing Cushing triad: herniation; circulation, airway, breathing now Fever, stiff neck, confusion Infection: meningitis, encephalitis, abscess Wakes from sleep; vomits on waking; worse with cough or lying flat Raised intracranial pressure Weakness, numbness, clumsiness or a new gait change Space-occupying lesion Worst pain at the moment it starts Bleeding or a vascular cause Worse week by week, or a child under 6 Secondary headache until proven otherwise

Nail dystrophy together with extensor-surface scaly plaques indicates psoriasis. An extensor distribution indicates psoriasis; a flexural distribution indicates eczema. briefs.sub: border and depth · erysipelas vs cellulitis · purulent vs nonpurulent · necrotizing fasciitis · bilateral mimicsHow sharp is the border, is there pus, and is the pain out of proportion?
blocks: border and depth · erysipelas vs cellulitis · purulent vs nonpurulent · necrotizing fasciitis · bilateral mimicsHow sharp is the border, is there pus, and is the pain out of proportion?

A flat border indicates cellulitis; a raised, sharply demarcated border indicates erysipelas. Superficial infection stops at a sharp edge because superficial infection is contained by tissue planes. Deeper infection fades into an indistinct edge because deeper infection diffuses through fat.

Skin & soft-tissue infections by depth Layer Infection The tell Organism Epidermis / superficial dermis + lymphatics Erysipelas Raised, sharply demarcated, intense erythema; rapid onset, early fever S. pyogenes Deep dermis + subcutaneous fat Cellulitis (nonpurulent) Flat, poorly demarcated; indolent over days; fever later Beta-hemolytic strep, methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus Same, with drainage Cellulitis (purulent) / abscess Purulent drainage; furuncle → carbuncle S. aureus incl. methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) Fascia Necrotizing fasciitis Emergency Pain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, necrosis, anesthesia over the lesion, hourly progression Polymicrobial (type I) or group A Streptococcus ± Clostridium (type II)

Nonpurulent infection: cover streptococci with cephalexin or dicloxacillin (penicillin for erysipelas). Purulent infection: incision and drainage, plus coverage of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) with TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), doxycycline, or clindamycin. Necrotizing infection: emergent surgical exploration, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Never wait for imaging.

Mimic The tell Stasis dermatitis Bilateral, chronic, hemosiderin staining, afebrile – the single most common misdiagnosis Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) Swelling without a sharply defined rash; recent surgery or immobility Contact dermatitis Itchy, geometric border, afebrile Erythema nodosum Bilateral tender nodules on anterior shins; sarcoid, inflammatory bowel disease, strep Erythema migrans Expanding with central clearing, minimally tender Ruptured Baker cyst Popliteal fossa and posterior calf
Cellulitis is nearly always unilateral. Bilateral lower-extremity erythema is stasis dermatitis until proven otherwise; treat with compression, not antibiotics.

briefs.title: Atopic Dermatitis
briefs.sub: vesicles on eczema · punched-out erosions vs honey crust · mucosa and failed antibiotics exclude mimics · acyclovir nowAre these vesicles on eczema, and what do the mucosa and the failed antibiotic exclude?
blocks: vesicles on eczema · punched-out erosions vs honey crust · mucosa and failed antibiotics exclude mimics · acyclovir nowAre these vesicles on eczema, and what do the mucosa and the failed antibiotic exclude?

Atopic dermatitis with vesicles is eczema herpeticum until proven otherwise. The atopic dermatitis is the precondition. A disrupted barrier plus local immune dysfunction lets HSV (herpes simplex virus) spread across the skin instead of staying a single cold sore. Treatment is immediate systemic acyclovir, because the infection can disseminate to the liver and brain.

"Conjunctiva and oropharynx are clear" excludes the drug reaction. SJS (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and TEN (toxic epidermal necrolysis) require mucosal involvement (classically ≥2 sites) plus symmetric target lesions. "Progressive worsening on TMP-SMX" (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) excludes impetigo. TMP-SMX covers staph, including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus). So failure on appropriate antibacterial therapy eliminates the bacterial hypothesis, exactly as a failed antihistamine eliminates upper airway cough syndrome.

Herpes causes monomorphic vesicles that evolve into "punched-out" erosions with hemorrhagic crust and scalloped coalescing borders. Impetigo causes honey-colored crust, not hemorrhagic crust. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed with HSV PCR of vesicle fluid (herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction). A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells but is less sensitive. Give IV acyclovir if the eruption is widespread, the patient is ill-appearing, or the patient is a young infant; ophthalmology consult if periocular.

The past medical history can contain the deciding fact. Sometimes it is a risk factor that overrides a benign reading (prior cancer → spinal mets). Sometimes it is a risk factor masquerading as an explanation (Klinefelter → gynecomastia). Sometimes it is the precondition that makes the right diagnosis possible at all. Read the past medical history as information that enables a diagnosis.

Pt 8 yo, enlarging scaly bald patch with pruritus, tender occipital and postauricular nodes Q the most likely diagnosis; options spanned tinea capitis, trichotillomania and alopecia areata

Two examination findings, not the history, identify the cause. The patch has overlying scale, which means an inflammatory or infectious process in the skin rather than hair that is simply being pulled or shed. The occipital and posterior auricular nodes are enlarged and tender, which is regional lymphadenopathy draining an infected scalp. Together these findings indicate tinea capitis. Unlike tinea of the body, this dermatophyte invades the hair follicle and shaft. As a result, the hair breaks and the patch expands centrifugally over weeks. The recent school change and the anxiety suggest trichotillomania, but neither scale nor tender nodes occurs in trichotillomania.

Tinea capitis scaly erythematous patch with hair loss and localized lymphadenopathy, with or without black dots (broken hairs at the follicle) and with or without a tender boggy kerion Why systemic therapy is required the organism invades the follicle and shaft, which topical agents penetrate poorly, so oral griseofulvin or terbinafine is needed Confirmation the diagnosis is clinical; Potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture confirms it

Scale over an enlarging bald patch an inflammatory or infectious scalp process; scale is what separates infection from every non-inflammatory alopecia Tender occipital and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy the nodes that drain the scalp; expected in tinea capitis and absent in traction alopecia and trichotillomania Frequent scratching pruritus, an inflammatory feature that argues against a purely mechanical cause Recent school change with anxiety a psychosocial cue for hair-pulling, which the scale and the nodes exclude Age 8, previously healthy the peak age; tinea capitis is predominantly a disease of children and the immunocompromised

Treatment requires oral griseofulvin or terbinafine, because topical antifungals do not reach the organism inside the hair follicle.

Is there scale on the patch? Yes → an inflammatory or infectious cause, not a pulling one Are the draining nodes enlarged? Yes → infection, which excludes trichotillomania and traction alopecia Are the remaining hairs broken? Black dots are shafts snapped at the follicle; the fungus is inside the hair Any traction history or geometric pattern? No Confirm and treat KOH of the proximal shafts; oral, never topical alone

A new school and anxiety about teachers and friends make a complete, plausible causal story. The examination refutes it. "Frequently scratches at the area" seems to support it, since scratching sounds like a behavior. However, scratching reflects pruritus, an inflammatory symptom, and it points the other way. The patch is nontender, which is easy to misread as a general absence of tenderness. The nodes are tender, and that tenderness is the key finding.

A scaly, enlarging bald patch with tender occipital nodes in a child is tinea capitis, and it needs an oral antifungal. Scale plus regional lymphadenopathy means infection rather than a simple alopecia; the two pulling alopecias, traction and trichotillomania, have neither. Tinea capitis invades the follicle and shaft, so it needs an oral antifungal, the single most tested management point on the topic. Black dots are hair shafts broken at the follicular orifice; a boggy tender mass is a kerion, which is the same infection inflamed, not a bacterial abscess to drain. Alopecia areata causes a smooth, scale-free, sharply circumscribed patch with no lymphadenopathy, sometimes with nail pitting. Fomites such as combs, hats and pillowcases carry it, so the household is examined rather than treated blindly. A scaly scalp plaque that scars, in an adult woman with facial lesions, is discoid lupus rather than tinea.

Part I Scaly Rashes covers the scaly-plaque differential of the body. It also covers the rule that a scaly annular lesion needs a KOH preparation rather than a steroid. This brief covers the scalp version, where the follicle changes the therapy. Ask: is there scale, and are the draining nodes enlarged?

In hair loss, the surface of the patch identifies the diagnosis. Scale with regional nodes means infection. A smooth patch means an autoimmune or traction cause. Broken hairs of unequal length mean the hair is being pulled. Examine the scalp before you accept a psychosocial explanation.

Class-vs-memberTraction alopecia: Traction produces geometric loss along the sites of pulling (temporal areas, along braids), with no scale and no lymphadenopathy Salient decoyTrichotillomania: Hair-pulling leaves broken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular pattern, without scale or nodes Class-vs-memberCutaneous candidiasis: Candida causes intertrigo in warm moist skinfolds; it does not scale the scalp or take hair True-fact-wrong-slotSeborrheic dermatitis: It explains only the scale and the pruritus, not the hair loss or the nodes True-fact-wrong-slotDiscoid lupus erythematosus: It occurs mostly in adult women, involves the face and neck, and scars

benign newborn rashes sorted by onset, then the diaper rash split by its folds · reassure, remove a cause, or treat what was addedHow old is the baby, is there a removable cause or a red flag, and does the diaper rash involve the creases?

Reassure when a benign, self-limited rash has no modifiable cause; remove the trigger when it has an identifiable, removable one. Sort by onset age first. A rash outside its window, erythema toxicum-like pustules on the palms or soles, vesicles or crusting, or a febrile or irritable infant is not benign until the dangerous mimics are excluded. Any vesicular rash in a neonate is herpes simplex virus (HSV) until proven otherwise: polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and IV acyclovir. Erythema toxicum neonatorum: firm yellow-white pustules on a blotchy red base, on the face, trunk and proximal limbs; palms and soles usually spared; a well infant. The diagnosis is usually clinical; a smear, rarely needed, shows eosinophils. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis: pustules without surrounding erythema that rupture into hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale; may involve the palms and soles; more common in darker skin; neutrophils. Milia: firm pearly white papules on the nose and cheeks, no erythema; retained keratin. Miliaria rubra: blocked sweat glands; fine red papules and vesicles on occluded, covered and intertriginous skin (neck, axillae, groin). Its cause is in the history (a onesie under pajamas under a fleece swaddle), so treat it by unwrapping the baby, not by waiting it out. Superficial 1- to 2-mm vesicles are miliaria crystallina, usually before 2 weeks; the HSV rule still applies until herpes is excluded. Neonatal cephalic pustulosis: red papules and pustules on the face and scalp only; no comedones, unlike true neonatal acne (closed comedones); linked to Malassezia. Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy yellow scale on the scalp (cradle cap), with redness in the folds; usually not itchy, and the infant looks content. Diaper rash: irritant contact dermatitis, the most common, sits on the convex skin the wet diaper touches and usually spares the creases; Candida involves the creases, with satellite papules. A rash that got better on a barrier and then got worse has acquired something the barrier does not treat.
