Diagnosis22 of 22 4-year-old girl has had vulvar itching for 3 days Toilet trained; finished amoxicillin for otitis media last week erythema over vulva and perineum into the inguinal creases satellite papules; thick white discharge at the introitus Afebrile · Perianal group A streptococcal disease · Irritant contact dermatitis · Candidal vulvovaginitis 4-year-old girl has had vulvar itching for 3 days Toilet trained; finished amoxicillin for otitis media last week erythema over vulva and perineum into the inguinal creases satellite papules; thick white discharge at the introitus Afebrile Candidal vulvovaginitisredness of the vulva and perineum into the creases with satellite papules and a thick white discharge after antibiotics is yeast: a topical antifungal such as nystatin. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases, and perianal streptococcal disease is a sharply demarcated perianal rash

2-day-old girl examined before discharge home Term baby; uncomplicated pregnancy; spontaneous vaginal delivery length 50 cm · weight 3515 g · T 36.8 °C · HR 128/min · respirations 38/min · BP 70/54 mm Hg rash all over: tiny yellow papules on red skin mostly on the trunk Most appropriate next step? Competing answers Lesion culture and antibiotics against Staphylococcus aureus: pustules suggest a bacterial infection; but impetigo is a superficial erosion with a honey-colored crust, and localized disease takes topical mupirocin. Herpes simplex virus culture of a lesion: any newborn rash raises herpes; but herpes gives grouped vesicles, and these are papules on a red base in a well baby. Potassium hydroxide prep of a scraping for Candida: papules on a red base could be yeast; but yeast sits in the diaper area as beefy-red plaques with satellite pustules, and this rash is on the trunk. Topical corticosteroid: the skin is inflamed; but a self-limited rash needs no steroid. Down to two: reassurance or a herpes culture. Reassurance: small yellow papules on a red base, mostly over the trunk, in a well 2-day-old are erythema toxicum, a clinical diagnosis that clears without treatment; a smear, if done, shows eosinophils. Each decoy fits another rash.

5-year-old girl with 5 days of worsening dysuria and vaginal redness Her mother saw a little yellow discharge in her underwear No fever, vomiting or diarrhea; healthy, on no medications No history of sexual abuse vital signs normal moderate erythema over the vagina and whole perineum, perianal skin included no vesicles or pustules; scant white discharge at the introitus Rest of the exam normal; culture of the discharge pending Most appropriate pharmacotherapy? Competing answers Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin: a genital rash with discharge raises a sexually transmitted infection; but gonorrhea and chlamydia give mucopurulent discharge, not white, and in a prepubertal child past the newborn period either would also prompt a sexual abuse evaluation. Oral acyclovir: genital pain and redness; but herpes simplex virus gives painful vesicles on a red base, and there are none. Oral amoxicillin: burning with urination suggests cystitis; but redness over the vulva and perineum with white discharge points to yeast. Oral metronidazole: a vaginal discharge; but its spectrum is obligate anaerobic bacteria and protozoa such as Trichomonas vaginalis (it is the antibiotic of choice for bacterial vaginosis), and this is yeast; topical agents are preferred for superficial candidiasis. Down to two: topical nystatin or oral amoxicillin. Topical nystatin: candidal vulvovaginitis in a girl past the diaper years. The stem opens on burning with urination and closes on a pending culture, while the diagnosis is in the white discharge and the perineal-to-perianal redness. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, recent antibiotics and corticosteroids; none is required.

Erythema toxicum reassurance: educate the parents about its benign course; it fades over 5 to 7 days and may recur for several weeks; no treatment is needed Transient neonatal pustular melanosis observe; no treatment is necessary Milia observe; reassurance about the benign, self-limited course; do not extract Miliaria rubra a cool environment, no overbundling, loose, thin, breathable cotton; a mild- to mid-potency topical steroid may be applied if severe Cephalic pustulosis observe (weeks to months); if the look bothers the parents, a topical antifungal such as ketoconazole can be used safely and may help Seborrheic dermatitis reassurance and watchful waiting; an emollient and gentle brushing with a soft brush can loosen the scale; topical ketoconazole is safe in infants Irritant diaper dermatitis a barrier such as zinc oxide or petrolatum, and frequent diaper changes; a short course of a low-potency steroid can be used if not improving within 2 to 3 days, or in moderate to severe cases Candidal diaper dermatitis topical nystatin with every diaper change, applied under the barrier ointment; switch to an azole (clotrimazole, miconazole or ketoconazole, twice daily for 7 to 10 days) if no improvement by 1 to 3 days; add oral nystatin for thrush; avoid a high-potency steroid under a diaper, which occludes

Red flags: palms or soles involved in an otherwise erythema toxicum picture, vesicles or crusting, or fever or irritability; any one means the rash is not benign. Pustular melanosis, present at birth and nonerythematous, is the benign rash that may reach the palms and soles. Neonatal HSV: clustered vesicles on an erythematous base, days 5 to 14; PCR and IV acyclovir. Congenital syphilis: maculopapular rash that includes the palms and soles, snuffles, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, no pustules; IV penicillin. Staphylococcal pustulosis: localized pustules, vesicles or bullae that rupture to honey-colored crusts, in the diaper area or at a wound such as a circumcision; topical mupirocin. Blueberry muffin rash: TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus). Langerhans cell histiocytosis: looks seborrheic but is petechial and does not resolve. Maternal cold sores: do not diagnose HSV in a well 2-day-old with erythematous pustules and spared palms and soles; base the diagnosis on the morphology and the infant's well appearance.

The diagnosis rests on the trajectory, not the morphology. A barrier is the correct and sufficient treatment for irritant dermatitis, so a rash that improved on it and then worsened has a superinfection, not a new diagnosis; a rash failing first-line therapy from the start would instead question the original diagnosis. Two examination findings name the cause: the rash involves the skinfolds, and it has satellite lesions, discrete red papules beyond the border of the main plaque, the most characteristic and near-specific feature of Candida. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases because the convex surfaces touch the wet diaper and the depths of the folds are protected; Candida thrives in the warm, occluded crease. Recent diarrhea is the risk factor, not a diagnosis: a higher local pH can increase fecal enzyme activity and damage the barrier, and Candida albicans from the gut then colonizes the skin. Expect it after recent diarrhea, recent antibiotics, or with oral thrush. The antifungal goes under the barrier, not instead of it, because the skin is still broken and still in contact with stool.

Run the spine: did first-line therapy work and then stop? Folds involved? Satellites? Does the rash leave the diaper area (scabies)? Is the diarrhea chronic, with perioral rash and alopecia (zinc)? Is any lesion itself a sexually transmitted infection? If none is, nothing licenses an abuse workup. Afebrile, eating and sleeping normally means not systemically ill; fussiness only during changes is local pain. Social details such as separated parents or day care raise abuse and contagion, but neither is an examination finding, and no affected classmate excludes contagion. The initial improvement on the barrier is the single most informative detail.

Congenital dermal melanocytosis: blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks, most common in darker-skinned infants, benign and self-resolving by age 3 to 5 years; document them on exam to avoid confusion with non-accidental trauma. Acrocyanosis (symmetric blue-purple hands and feet with crying or cold), cutis marmorata (symmetric lacy violaceous mottling of the limbs that changes with temperature) and harlequin color change (sharply demarcated redness of one side of the body) are clinical diagnoses that need no treatment.

Oral amoxicillin for a refractory diaper rash: bacterial superinfection is real, but perianal streptococcal disease is bright red and sharply demarcated around the anus. Topical permethrin: scabies causes refractory diaper rash in infants, but it is diffuse across the trunk, axillae, palms and soles, with an affected contact. Oral zinc after a diarrheal illness: acrodermatitis enteropathica needs chronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis and alopecia. Screening for sexual abuse: triggered by findings that are themselves sexually transmitted infections; a social detail is not a finding.

Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the non-cutaneous half of the same principle (transplacental hormone, physiologic, self-limited) and vaginal discharge in a newborn girl: is the discharge white with perineal redness, or mucoid in a well newborn?

Before choosing pure reassurance, scan the history for a modifiable exposure (bundling, a soap, a detergent, a medication, a position); when the history describes the environment, removing that exposure is the treatment. When a correct treatment works and then stops working, the diagnosis was not wrong; something was added. Ask what the first treatment does not cover, and look for the finding that identifies it.

briefs.title: Scabies
briefs.sub: a close contact with the same rash outweighs morphology · permethrin specifics · itch after treatmentDoes anyone close have the same rash, and does the drug kill the cause or only treat the itch?
blocks: a close contact with the same rash outweighs morphology · permethrin specifics · itch after treatmentDoes anyone close have the same rash, and does the drug kill the cause or only treat the itch?
Pt 63 yo M, itchy web-space papules; roommate has the identical rash Q the most appropriate treatment; options spanned permethrin, topical triamcinolone and a single dose of oral ivermectin

A roommate with the identical itchy rash means the rash is transmissible by prolonged skin contact. That fact alone excludes contact dermatitis, drug eruption and every non-communicable itch. With the distribution and the timeline added, only scabies fits. Treat with permethrin 5%.

Stem findings & their diagnostic weight Finding Why it matters Severe itch Most pruritic common dermatosis; classically worse at night Hands/wrists → other hand → waistline Textbook map: finger web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, belt line, periumbilical, genitals. Spares head and neck in adults "Spots turned into scabs" Excoriations, not vesicular crusts Roommate moved in a few weeks ago Matches the 3–6 week incubation on first infestation – a sensitization delay, not a replication delay

Oral acyclovir: zoster is dermatomal, unilateral, painful. It does not migrate from one hand to the other hand and then to the waist, and it does not infect a roommate. Oral cephalexin: there is no crusting or spreading erythema, and impetigo causes honey-colored crust. Oral prednisone / topical triamcinolone: both treat the itch, not the mite, and steroids produce scabies incognito, a masked, worsening infestation. The pruritus is a type IV hypersensitivity to mite antigen, and suppressing the response does not affect the organism.

Permethrin 5%, neck-down (whole body in infants), left on 8–14 hours, repeated in 1 week because the first application does not kill eggs treat all household and close contacts simultaneously, symptomatic or not wash bedding and clothing hot, or bag 72 hours oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg, repeat day 8) for crusted scabies, outbreaks, or adherence problems; avoid in pregnancy and under 15 kg.

Post-scabetic pruritus persists 2–4 weeks after successful treatment. It is the leading reason therapy is thought to have failed. Triamcinolone and antihistamines are correct at that stage, once the mite is dead; they do not replace killing it.

A close contact with the same condition carries more weight than morphology. It narrows the differential to transmissible causes before you interpret a single lesion. When the dominant symptom is itch, check whether a drug kills the cause or only treats the sensation.

briefs.title: Vaccines in Pregnancy
briefs.sub: choosing the vaccine or immunoglobulin due now · the Tdap window optimizes protection; it is not an eligibility gateWhich one is due now, and is this window a gate or an optimization?
blocks: choosing the vaccine or immunoglobulin due now · the Tdap window optimizes protection; it is not an eligibility gateWhich one is due now, and is this window a gate or an optimization?

The patient will eventually need several vaccines or immunoglobulins; give the one that is due now. A date, a gestational age or a serology decides which one is due, not a symptom. Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis): every pregnancy, irrespective of prior Tdap; optimal at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably the earlier part, although Tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy. The window is an optimization, not a gate: for a wound needing tetanus prophylaxis or a community pertussis outbreak, give Tdap then; a dose given earlier in pregnancy is not repeated at 27 to 36 weeks. Inactivated influenza vaccine: any trimester while flu viruses circulate; in the first or second trimester, preferably September or October; in the third trimester, July or August can be considered. The classic visit is in mid-September, so it is due. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine: one dose of RSV prefusion F (RSVpreF; Abrysvo, the only one for pregnancy) at 32 0/7 through 36 6/7 weeks, September through January in most of the United States; or infant nirsevimab. Most infants will not need both. Unlike Tdap, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) does not currently recommend repeating it in a later pregnancy; after a prior-pregnancy dose, the infant gets nirsevimab instead. Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) and varicella vaccines: live, contraindicated in pregnancy; if not immune, give after pregnancy, before discharge (varicella: a second dose 4 to 8 weeks later if never vaccinated). Hepatitis B vaccine: if not already vaccinated, vaccinate in pregnancy (not PreHevbrio, which lacks pregnancy safety data). Anti-D immunoglobulin: routinely at 28 weeks when Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen.

What is due whennot to scale Inactivated influenzaAny trimester while flu circulates Conception27 wk3236DeliveryPostpartum→ Hepatitis B vaccineIf not already vaccinated Conception27 wk3236DeliveryPostpartum→ Tdap27 to 36 weeks, earlier part; any time if indicated Conception27 wk3236DeliveryPostpartum→ RSV vaccine (Abrysvo)32 to 36 weeks, September to January Conception27 wk3236DeliveryPostpartum→ MMR, varicellaIf not immune: after pregnancy, before discharge Conception27 wk3236DeliveryPostpartum→
The classic patient: Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen, non-immune to rubella, varicella immunoglobulin G (IgG) positive after a recent exposure, seen in mid-September.

Option analysis: why each fails Choice Why it tempts What kills it Anti-D immunoglobulin She is Rh-negative with a negative screen Timing: routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks MMR She is non-immune to rubella Live, contraindicated; give after pregnancy, before discharge Tdap Indicated in every pregnancy Timing, as an optimization, not a gate: 27 to 36 weeks maximizes transplacental IgG transfer Varicella vaccine Recent exposure Live, contraindicated, and she is already immune Varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) Exposure plus pregnancy is the classic postexposure prophylaxis setting Varicella IgG positive = immune; prophylaxis is for the non-immune
Two fail on timing, two on live-vaccine status, one on serology. Each distractor fails for a different reason: eliminate each on its own terms rather than comparing them.

Vaccines in pregnancy Recommended If indicated or at risk Not in pregnancy Inactivated influenza, seasonal; Tdap every pregnancy; RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks, September to January; hepatitis B if not already vaccinated (not PreHevbrio); anti-D at 28 weeks if Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen Hepatitis A if at risk for infection or a severe outcome; meningococcal vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y if indicated; VZIG if exposed and non-immune MMR, varicella, live attenuated influenza (LAIV), BCG (bacille Calmette-Guerin), oral polio: live vaccines are generally contraindicated. Human papillomavirus (HPV): not live, but deferred until after pregnancy. Recombinant zoster: no recommendation; consider delaying

No recommendation: pneumococcal vaccines (limited safety data) and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b). Newborns of mothers given the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine by mistake in pregnancy do not seem to be at increased risk.
COVID-19: recommended in pregnancy, at any trimester (ACOG 2026 maternal schedule).

28 weeks routinely; within 72 hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive; any sensitizing event: vaginal bleeding, spontaneous or threatened abortion, ectopic or molar pregnancy, amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma. A positive anti-D screen with no recent anti-D immunoglobulin means she is already alloimmunized, so anti-D can no longer help: switch to titers and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler.

Non-immune and exposed: VZIG as soon as possible, within 10 days of exposure. Maternal varicella can cause varicella pneumonia (high mortality): intravenous acyclovir. Congenital varicella syndrome at 8 to 20 weeks (first or early second trimester; small risk, 0.4 to 2.0%): limb hypoplasia, cicatricial dermatomal scarring, chorioretinitis, cataracts. Neonatal varicella if the maternal rash occurs 5 days before to 2 days after delivery: VZIG to the newborn.

Most infants will not need both. Unlike Tdap, CDC does not currently recommend repeating it in a later pregnancy. The vaccine is recommended in pregnancy, not contraindicated

Next step9 of 19 29-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Blood type B, Rh-negative No anti-D immunoglobulin this pregnancy antibody screen positive for anti-D BP 110/68 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 148/min · Give anti-D immunoglobulin now · Antibody titers with serial MCA Dopplers · Repeat the antibody screen at 28 weeks 29-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Blood type B, Rh-negative No anti-D immunoglobulin this pregnancy antibody screen positive for anti-D BP 110/68 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 148/min Antibody titers with serial MCA Dopplerswith no anti-D immunoglobulin given, a positive anti-D screen means she is already alloimmunized, and anti-D cannot undo it; follow titers and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler. The repeat screen at 24 to 28 weeks is for unsensitized women

Next step10 of 19 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Received Tdap at 29 weeks in her first pregnancy 2 years ago asks whether she needs it again BP 116/74 mm Hg · Afebrile · Give Td instead · Give Tdap again · Skip it, since she had Tdap 2 years ago 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Received Tdap at 29 weeks in her first pregnancy 2 years ago asks whether she needs it again BP 116/74 mm Hg · Afebrile Give Tdap againTdap is given during each pregnancy, irrespective of a prior dose, because it protects this infant. Td lacks the pertussis component

Next step11 of 19 21-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation asks about her human papillomavirus vaccine She received the first dose of a 3-dose series 2 months ago first prenatal visit BP 108/66 mm Hg · Afebrile · Defer to postpartum · Give the HPV vaccine now · HPV vaccine is contraindicated for life 21-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation asks about her human papillomavirus vaccine She received the first dose of a 3-dose series 2 months ago first prenatal visit BP 108/66 mm Hg · Afebrile Defer to postpartumHPV vaccines are not recommended in pregnancy; the rest of the series is delayed until the pregnancy is complete. The vaccine is not live and is not contraindicated for life; a dose given by mistake in pregnancy needs no intervention

Screening12 of 19 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit Blood type O, Rh-negative; antibody screen negative Received Tdap at 27 weeks and influenza vaccine in October BP 116/72 mm Hg · fundal height 28 cm · Anti-D immunoglobulin · Inactivated influenza vaccine · Tdap 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit Blood type O, Rh-negative; antibody screen negative Received Tdap at 27 weeks and influenza vaccine in October BP 116/72 mm Hg · fundal height 28 cm Anti-D immunoglobulinshe is Rh-negative with a negative screen, and routine prophylaxis is due at 28 weeks. Tdap given earlier in this pregnancy is not repeated, and this season's influenza dose is done

Next step13 of 19 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation is offered the nasal influenza vaccine at a pharmacy in October No influenza vaccine this season healthy; no egg allergy Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · Give the nasal formulation · Give the intramuscular inactivated vaccine · Defer influenza vaccination entirely 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation is offered the nasal influenza vaccine at a pharmacy in October No influenza vaccine this season healthy; no egg allergy Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg Give the intramuscular inactivated vaccinethe nasal formulation is live and contraindicated in pregnancy; give the intramuscular inactivated vaccine, in any trimester during the season. Influenza vaccine is right; that influenza vaccine is wrong

Next step14 of 19 26-year-old woman received MMR vaccine 3 weeks ago, then discovered she is pregnant Last menstrual period 7 weeks ago she asks whether the pregnancy is at risk Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · Counsel and reassure; not an indication for termination · Recommend termination · Serial ultrasound for congenital rubella 26-year-old woman received MMR vaccine 3 weeks ago, then discovered she is pregnant Last menstrual period 7 weeks ago she asks whether the pregnancy is at risk Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg Counsel and reassure; not an indication for terminationMMR inadvertently given in pregnancy: counsel her about the theoretical risk to the fetus; MMR vaccination during pregnancy is not a reason to terminate. The guidance calls for counseling about the theoretical risk, not fetal surveillance

Screening15 of 19 25-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit Rh-negative; received anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks Rubella IgG negative; no Tdap yet this pregnancy BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile · Tdap · Anti-D immunoglobulin · MMR 25-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit Rh-negative; received anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks Rubella IgG negative; no Tdap yet this pregnancy BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile TdapTdap is due in every pregnancy, optimally at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably early in that window, so 30 weeks is the time. Anti-D was given at 28 weeks. MMR is live and contraindicated in pregnancy; give it after pregnancy, before discharge

Next step16 of 19 31-year-old woman delivered a healthy term girl 1 day ago A vesicular rash appeared on her face and trunk 3 days before delivery No history of chickenpox mother T 37.8 °C · newborn HR 142/min · VZIG to the neonate · Maternal VZIG alone · Varicella vaccine to the neonate 31-year-old woman delivered a healthy term girl 1 day ago A vesicular rash appeared on her face and trunk 3 days before delivery No history of chickenpox mother T 37.8 °C · newborn HR 142/min VZIG to the neonatea maternal varicella rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery puts the newborn at risk: give varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) to the newborn. The live varicella vaccine is not the newborn's prophylaxis

Screening17 of 19 34-year-old man asks about vaccines; his partner is at 32 weeks' gestation He has never received Tdap His mother, who will help care for the newborn, has not received it either Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg · Only his pregnant partner needs Tdap · Vaccinate them at least 2 weeks before contact · Vaccinate them after the birth 34-year-old man asks about vaccines; his partner is at 32 weeks' gestation He has never received Tdap His mother, who will help care for the newborn, has not received it either Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg Vaccinate them at least 2 weeks before contactpeople who are not up to date should get Tdap at least 2 weeks before meeting the infant (cocooning)

Screening18 of 19 32-year-old woman is breastfeeding on the day after a vaginal delivery Rubella IgG negative on prenatal labs Received Tdap at 28 weeks; completed the HPV vaccine series at age 12 Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg · HPV vaccine · Tdap · MMR 32-year-old woman is breastfeeding on the day after a vaginal delivery Rubella IgG negative on prenatal labs Received Tdap at 28 weeks; completed the HPV vaccine series at age 12 Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg MMRMMR after pregnancy, before discharge, for a patient without rubella immunity; it is safe while breastfeeding. Tdap is given immediately postpartum only when it was not given during pregnancy and she has never had Tdap, and her HPV series is complete

Mechanism19 of 19 26-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 6-week-old son Rubella IgG and varicella IgG negative on prenatal labs asks whether vaccines are safe for her baby while she is nursing Afebrile · BP 114/70 mm Hg · Live vaccines remain contraindicated · Inactivated and live vaccines are both permitted · Defer all vaccines until weaning 26-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 6-week-old son Rubella IgG and varicella IgG negative on prenatal labs asks whether vaccines are safe for her baby while she is nursing Afebrile · BP 114/70 mm Hg Inactivated and live vaccines are both permittedneither inactivated nor live vaccines given to a lactating woman affect breastfeeding safety, so MMR and varicella vaccine can be given now: the restrictions apply to pregnancy, not lactation. The exceptions are smallpox vaccine (contraindicated) and yellow fever vaccine (avoided unless travel cannot be postponed)

Maternal Tdap is for the infant: the childhood pertussis series does not start until 2 months, and most infant pertussis deaths occur before that protection. It takes about 2 weeks after Tdap for the mother to be protected, and the antibody then needs time to cross, so late-third-trimester dosing is suboptimal; preterm delivery is the reason to dose at 27 weeks, not 36. Postpartum Tdap gives the infant no immunity. Household contacts who are not up to date get Tdap at least 2 weeks before meeting the infant.

The vaccine restrictions apply to pregnancy, not lactation: neither inactivated nor live vaccines given to a lactating woman affect breastfeeding safety. Exceptions: smallpox vaccine is contraindicated and yellow fever vaccine is avoided unless travel cannot be postponed.

Class versus member: influenza vaccine is right, but the live attenuated nasal one is wrong in pregnancy. Sequencing: Tdap today at 10 weeks, or deferred to postpartum, instead of scheduled at 27 to 36 weeks. Skipping Tdap because she had it last pregnancy: it is for this fetus.

When a patient will eventually need several vaccines or immunoglobulins, check the number (date, gestational age or titer) before weighing the indications. When a recommendation carries a time window, ask what it protects: if it optimizes an effect (antibody transfer), move outside it when the indication changes; if it defines eligibility (age 21 for cytology), you cannot.

briefs.title: Cervical Cancer Screening
briefs.sub: age gates, coverage clocks, abnormal results and special populations · eligibility depends on age, not on individual riskIs she eligible yet, which clock is running, and what does the result call for?
blocks: age gates, coverage clocks, abnormal results and special populations · eligibility depends on age, not on individual riskIs she eligible yet, which clock is running, and what does the result call for?

Screening starts at 21 whatever the sexual history: risk factors adjust intensity within the eligible window but rarely move the floor. Each negative test then starts its own interval, the test type sets its length, and screening is due when the longest valid coverage expires. Age-21 floor: no screening under 21, regardless of sexual debut, partners, sexually transmitted infection (STI) history or human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination. Why the floor ignores risk: HPV infection in adolescents is near-universal and clears in about 90% within 2 years; progression takes more than a decade, so cancer under 21 is rare. Early screening finds transient infection and leads to excisions by loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) that raise preterm-birth risk: harm without benefit. Coverage clock: negative cytology covers 3 years from that date; a negative test that includes HPV covers 5. Primary HPV testing: an HPV test alone. Co-testing: cytology plus HPV. Self-collection: patient-collected HPV testing should be offered as an option at 30 to 65 at average risk, per the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), accepted December 2025; the American Cancer Society (ACS) repeats a negative self-collected test in 3 years. Adequate prior screening: 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative co-tests within 10 years before stopping, the most recent within 5 years.

Cervical screening schedule (average risk) Age Test Interval Under 21 None, whatever the sexual history Not applicable 21 to 29 Cytology alone Every 3 years 30 to 65 Primary HPV, preferred by HRSA; clinician- or patient-collected Every 5 years 30 to 65, alternatives Co-testing; cytology alone 5 years; 3 years Older than 65 Stop after adequate prior screening, if not otherwise at high risk and no CIN2 (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2) or worse in 25 years Not applicable

Exam answer: the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) 2018 statement, still final (the 2024 draft is not), keeps cytology alone at 21 to 29 and offers primary HPV from 30, as question banks do. Answer 30 on the exam. Clinical practice: the ACS starts screening at 25, not 21, and recommends primary HPV every 5 years through 65, with co-testing every 5 years or cytology every 3 if primary HPV testing is not available; the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) keeps the start at 21 and advises that primary HPV every 5 years can be considered for average-risk patients aged 25 to 29.

Diagnostic workup 1Is she eligible, and what does the result call for? First Age Under 21, with or without human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infectionNo screening, whatever the sexual history Speculum exam Visible lesionBiopsy: diagnostic at any age, including under 21 Screen Cytology, or a primary HPV test from 30 Abnormal cytology or HPV positiveTriage by result and age, as in the table below Next Reflex HPV on ASC-US (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance; under 25, repeat cytology in 1 year is preferred, reflex acceptable) PositiveColposcopy at 25 or older; under 25, repeat cytology in 1 year NegativeCan return at 3 years from 25; routine screening under 25 By branch HPV genotyping HPV 16 or 18Colposcopy now, even with negative cytology Positive, not 16 or 18, cytology negativeRepeat HPV-based testing in 1 year Confirms Colposcopy with directed biopsy Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grade on histologyCIN1 (grade 1) observe; CIN2 or CIN3 (grade 3) treat with excision By branch Endocervical curettage (ECC) Squamocolumnar junction (SCJ) not fully seenSamples the canal; unacceptable in pregnancy Diagnostic excision Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) on biopsyNeeds an intact specimen with interpretable margins: classically cold knife conization Skip Cytology or an HPV test before 21: HPV clears in about 90% within 2 years, so it finds transient infection and leads to excisions that raise preterm-birth risk. Colposcopy for ASC-US or a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) at 21 to 24: most lesions clear on their own; repeat cytology in 1 year.

Screening1 of 17 20-year-old woman asks whether she needs a Pap test Sexual debut at 15; five lifetime male partners Uses condoms inconsistently; no symptoms normal external genitalia T 36.7 °C · BP 114/70 mm Hg · Cytology now · No screening · Co-testing now 20-year-old woman asks whether she needs a Pap test Sexual debut at 15; five lifetime male partners Uses condoms inconsistently; no symptoms normal external genitalia T 36.7 °C · BP 114/70 mm Hg No screeningshe is below the floor: screening is not recommended under 21, and her debut, partners and condom use raise HPV exposure but none lowers the starting age. Cytology now or co-testing now would find transient infection that clears in about 90% within 2 years, and the excisions that follow raise preterm-birth risk

Screening2 of 17 18-year-old woman seen to start care 2 weeks after a positive HIV test Sexually active since 15; two lifetime partners Uses condoms inconsistently pelvic examination normal T 36.8 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg · Begin at 21 as usual · Begin at 25 · Screen now, then annually × 3 18-year-old woman seen to start care 2 weeks after a positive HIV test Sexually active since 15; two lifetime partners Uses condoms inconsistently pelvic examination normal T 36.8 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg Begin at 21 as usualHIV does not lower the start age: invasive cancer incidence with HIV under 25 is exceedingly low, so screening starts at 21, per the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). From 21, cytology yearly, then every 3 years after 3 consecutive normal results, for life. Screening now follows the older Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 2021 rule (1 year after sexual debut); 25 is the American Cancer Society start for average risk, not HIV

Next step3 of 17 20-year-old woman has had postcoital bleeding for 2 months Sexually active; not yet screened because of her age exophytic friable mass on the cervix Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative · Cytology now · Biopsy the lesion · Reassure, because she is under 21 20-year-old woman has had postcoital bleeding for 2 months Sexually active; not yet screened because of her age exophytic friable mass on the cervix Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative Biopsy the lesiona visible lesion is biopsied at any age, including under 21: that is diagnosis, not screening, so the age floor does not apply. Cytology is a screening test, not the diagnosis of a visible lesion, and reassurance ignores the lesion

Screening4 of 17 21-year-old woman comes for her first well-woman visit Has never been sexually active Asks whether she can wait until she has a partner No symptoms; no medical problems normal external genitalia T 36.6 °C · BP 108/66 mm Hg · Defer until she is sexually active · Cytology now · Begin at 25 21-year-old woman comes for her first well-woman visit Has never been sexually active Asks whether she can wait until she has a partner No symptoms; no medical problems normal external genitalia T 36.6 °C · BP 108/66 mm Hg Cytology nowthe US Preventive Services Task Force rule is age-based, not activity-based: it applies to anyone with a cervix regardless of sexual history, so cytology every 3 years starts at 21. Starting at 25 is the American Cancer Society guideline, not the exam answer

Screening5 of 17 28-year-old woman asks when her next Pap test is due Cytology 2 years ago was normal; HPV testing was not done No symptoms; no abnormal results ever Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · Return in 3 years · Co-test now · Return in 1 year 28-year-old woman asks when her next Pap test is due Cytology 2 years ago was normal; HPV testing was not done No symptoms; no abnormal results ever Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg Return in 1 yearfrom 21 to 29 the schedule is cytology alone every 3 years, counted from the last negative test, so she is due in 1 year. A 3-year wait restarts the clock from today, and co-testing is one of the 30 to 65 options

Next step6 of 17 26-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) Reflex HPV test on the same sample is negative No previous abnormal results; no symptoms Afebrile · BP 112/68 mm Hg · Resume routine screening · Colposcopy · Repeat cytology in 6 months 26-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) Reflex HPV test on the same sample is negative No previous abnormal results; no symptoms Afebrile · BP 112/68 mm Hg Resume routine screeningHPV-negative ASC-US with an unknown history can return at 3 years (ASCCP), which at 26 is her routine cytology interval. Colposcopy is for HPV-positive ASC-US, and the negative HPV test already removes the reason for an early repeat

Next step7 of 17 24-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) Previous cytology at 21 was normal No symptoms; one male partner normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · Repeat cytology in 1 year · Repeat cytology in 3 years · Immediate colposcopy 24-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) Previous cytology at 21 was normal No symptoms; one male partner normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg Repeat cytology in 1 yearunder 25, repeat cytology at 1 year is preferred for ASC-US, per the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP); reflex HPV testing is acceptable, and a negative result resumes routine screening. Colposcopy is indicated only if the first 1-year repeat shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL (ASC-H), atypical glandular cells (AGC) or AIS, or the second shows ASC-US or worse; immediate colposcopy over-treats lesions that usually clear, and a 3-year wait skips the 1-year recheck

Screening8 of 17 34-year-old woman asks when her next screening test is due Co-test 3 years ago: cytology negative, HPV negative No symptoms; no abnormal results ever normal speculum exam Afebrile · HR 72/min · BP 120/78 mm Hg · Return in 3 years · Return now · Return in 2 years 34-year-old woman asks when her next screening test is due Co-test 3 years ago: cytology negative, HPV negative No symptoms; no abnormal results ever normal speculum exam Afebrile · HR 72/min · BP 120/78 mm Hg Return in 2 yearsa negative test that includes HPV covers 5 years from that date, so the 5-year clock governs and she is due in 2 years. Returning now applies the 3-year cytology clock, and 3 more years restarts the clock from today

Next step9 of 17 34-year-old woman has routine co-testing Cytology: negative for intraepithelial lesion High-risk HPV positive; genotyping shows HPV 16 Prior screening normal; no symptoms normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 116/74 mm Hg · Colposcopy · Return in 5 years · Repeat co-test in 1 year 34-year-old woman has routine co-testing Cytology: negative for intraepithelial lesion High-risk HPV positive; genotyping shows HPV 16 Prior screening normal; no symptoms normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 116/74 mm Hg ColposcopyHPV 16 or 18 escalates even with negative cytology: colposcopy is recommended now. A 1-year repeat is for HPV positivity without 16 or 18, and 5 years is for a fully negative co-test

Next step10 of 17 33-year-old woman has routine co-testing Cytology: negative for intraepithelial lesion High-risk HPV positive; genotyping negative for HPV 16 and 18 Previous screening unknown; no symptoms normal cervix on exam Afebrile · BP 114/72 mm Hg · Return in 5 years · Repeat co-test in 1 year · Immediate colposcopy 33-year-old woman has routine co-testing Cytology: negative for intraepithelial lesion High-risk HPV positive; genotyping negative for HPV 16 and 18 Previous screening unknown; no symptoms normal cervix on exam Afebrile · BP 114/72 mm Hg Repeat co-test in 1 yearHPV positive with NILM (negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy) cytology and an unknown history: repeat HPV-based testing in 1 year (ASCCP). Colposcopy now is for HPV 16 or 18, and 5 years ignores the positive HPV test

Next step11 of 17 33-year-old woman has co-testing at a new clinic Cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy HPV positive; genotyping shows HPV 18 Last screened 6 years ago, normal T 36.7 °C · BP 110/72 mm Hg · Repeat co-test in 1 year · Colposcopy · Return in 5 years 33-year-old woman has co-testing at a new clinic Cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy HPV positive; genotyping shows HPV 18 Last screened 6 years ago, normal T 36.7 °C · BP 110/72 mm Hg Colposcopythe genotype escalates: HPV 18 with negative cytology goes to colposcopy now, as HPV 16 does (ASCCP). Repeat co-testing in 1 year is for HPV positive, not 16 or 18; 5 years is for a fully negative co-test

Screening12 of 17 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has her first prenatal visit Last cytology, 2 years ago, was negative No HPV test was done with it No symptoms; no abnormal results ever T 36.9 °C · BP 110/70 mm Hg · Return in 1 year · Co-test now · Return in 3 years 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has her first prenatal visit Last cytology, 2 years ago, was negative No HPV test was done with it No symptoms; no abnormal results ever T 36.9 °C · BP 110/70 mm Hg Return in 1 yearpregnancy does not change the schedule: pregnant patients are screened at the same intervals as those who are not. Negative cytology covers 3 years from that date, so she returns in 1 year. Waiting 3 years from today stretches the interval, and co-testing is a 30 to 65 option on the exam (the American Cancer Society allows HPV-based testing, including co-testing, from 25, but her cytology still covers her until next year)

Next step13 of 17 38-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical glandular cells (AGC) Regular menses; no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding Not pregnant; no previous abnormal results normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 122/78 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative · Reflex HPV testing alone · Colposcopy with endocervical and endometrial sampling · Repeat cytology in 1 year 38-year-old woman's routine cytology shows atypical glandular cells (AGC) Regular menses; no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding Not pregnant; no previous abnormal results normal cervix on speculum exam Afebrile · BP 122/78 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative Colposcopy with endocervical and endometrial samplingevery subcategory of AGC gets colposcopy regardless of the HPV result, with endocervical sampling; at 35 or older endometrial sampling is added. Repeat cytology and HPV testing alone both leave a glandular lesion unsampled

Screening14 of 17 67-year-old woman asks whether she still needs Pap tests Three consecutive negative cytology results, at 58, 61 and 64 No history of cervical precancer or abnormal results Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg · One final cytology at 70 · Continue co-testing every 5 years · Stop screening 67-year-old woman asks whether she still needs Pap tests Three consecutive negative cytology results, at 58, 61 and 64 No history of cervical precancer or abnormal results Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg Stop screeningolder than 65 with adequate prior screening (3 consecutive negative cytology results within 10 years, the most recent within 5) and no high-grade history, she stops. Once the exit criteria are met, the USPSTF recommends against further screening, so neither co-testing every 5 years nor a final test at 70

Next step15 of 17 34-year-old woman's routine cytology shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) Not pregnant; no previous abnormal results No symptoms normal-appearing cervix on speculum exam T 36.8 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative · Repeat cytology in 1 year · Reflex HPV testing · Colposcopy, or immediate excision 34-year-old woman's routine cytology shows a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) Not pregnant; no previous abnormal results No symptoms normal-appearing cervix on speculum exam T 36.8 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative Colposcopy, or immediate excisionnonpregnant and 25 or older, she may have colposcopy with biopsy or excision without prior biopsy (see-and-treat LEEP); excision is preferred when the immediate CIN3+ risk is 60% or more, and both are acceptable from 25% to under 60%. Repeat cytology delays a high-grade result, and reflex HPV is the triage for ASC-US

Next step16 of 17 67-year-old woman asks whether she can stop Pap tests Excision for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2, 10 years ago Every test since treatment negative No symptoms; postmenopausal Afebrile · BP 132/82 mm Hg · Stop screening at 65 regardless of history · Keep screening · Stop now that treatment was over 5 years ago 67-year-old woman asks whether she can stop Pap tests Excision for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2, 10 years ago Every test since treatment negative No symptoms; postmenopausal Afebrile · BP 132/82 mm Hg Keep screeningafter treatment for CIN2+ (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse), surveillance with HPV testing or co-testing every 3 years runs at least 25 years, even past 65; 15 years remain. The age-65 exit applies only to women not otherwise at high risk

Screening17 of 17 42-year-old woman had a total hysterectomy for fibroids 1 year ago Cervix removed; pathology benign No history of cervical precancer; screening always normal No symptoms healed vaginal cuff on exam Afebrile · BP 124/80 mm Hg · Stop screening · Continue cytology every 3 years · Vaginal cuff cytology every 3 years 42-year-old woman had a total hysterectomy for fibroids 1 year ago Cervix removed; pathology benign No history of cervical precancer; screening always normal No symptoms healed vaginal cuff on exam Afebrile · BP 124/80 mm Hg Stop screeningwith the cervix removed for benign disease and no high-grade lesion in her history, screening stops. Vaginal cuff testing continues only after CIN2, CIN3 or adenocarcinoma in situ diagnosed within the previous 20 years (CDC), or after cervical cancer; a retained cervix keeps the usual schedule

Abnormal result management by age (ASCCP 2019, risk-based) Result Age 25 or older Age 21 to 24 ASC-US Reflex HPV: positive, colposcopy; negative, can return at 3 years Repeat cytology in 1 year (preferred); reflex HPV acceptable LSIL Colposcopy if HPV positive or untested; HPV negative, repeat in 1 year Repeat cytology in 1 year ASC-H (atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL) Colposcopy regardless of HPV Colposcopy HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) Colposcopy or excision without biopsy (see-and-treat LEEP) Colposcopy only AGC (atypical glandular cells) Colposcopy + ECC; endometrial sampling at 35 or older, or younger with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), chronic anovulation or obesity Same Cytology negative, HPV 16 or 18 Colposcopy now Not applicable

SCJ not fully visualized: endocervical curettage. CIN1: observation is preferred. CIN2: treat, unless her concerns about treatment's effect on future pregnancy outweigh concerns about cancer. CIN3: treat; observation is unacceptable. Adenocarcinoma in situ: diagnostic excision with an intact specimen and interpretable margins, classically cold knife conization, since a LEEP can fragment the margins. Invasive cancer: staging, not LEEP. After treatment: surveillance for at least 25 years.

HIV: start at 21 as usual, or at diagnosis if older; cytology yearly, and after 3 normal annual results every 3 years; from 30, cytology alone or co-testing, not primary HPV alone; continue for life, never stopping at 65 (Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) guideline, updated 2024, reviewed 2026). Older rule: the CDC 2021 STI guideline still screens 1 year after sexual debut, no later than 21; current HHS guidance (start at 21) sets the answer. Other immunosuppression: solid organ transplant, end-stage renal disease, hematopoietic stem cell transplant or systemic lupus erythematosus, on immunosuppressants or not; inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis or multiple sclerosis on immunosuppressants. Follow the HIV schedule, which starts at 21, for life, stopping by shared decision-making (American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) review, 2025). In-utero diethylstilbestrol (DES): an annual examination has generally been advised; its benefit over routine screening is now unclear. Treated CIN2+: HPV testing or co-testing every 3 years for at least 25 years, including past 65. Hysterectomy, cervix removed for benign disease: stop entirely. Cervix retained (supracervical): keep screening. After CIN2+, adenocarcinoma in situ or cervical cancer: keep screening the vaginal cuff (CDC: CIN2, CIN3 or adenocarcinoma in situ within the previous 20 years; HHS: annual cuff cytology in HIV). HPV-vaccinated: same intervals. Pregnant: same intervals; colposcopy is safe, but ECC and endometrial biopsy are contraindicated, and CIN2 or CIN3 treatment waits until after delivery unless invasive cancer appears.

Her risk history (salient decoy): makes no screening feel negligent, but it does not lower the floor. Colposcopy (sequencing trap): it is for an abnormal result, and she has none. HPV vaccination counseling (true-fact-wrong-slot): at 20 she is within catch-up vaccination, which runs through 26, so it is indicated, but it does not answer the screening question. A female partner: does not lower risk; HPV transmits between women, and screening is identical. Obesity: with AGC under 35 it is a listed indication for endometrial sampling, even without abnormal bleeding.
Adolescent Vaccines. Ask “Is she eligible yet?” before “Is she at risk?” Adolescent Vaccines. Ask “Is she eligible yet?” before “Is she at risk?”
Screening guidelines are population rules with age gates. Individual risk factors adjust intensity within the eligible window; they rarely move the floor. Check eligibility before you calculate risk.

briefs.sub: transvaginal ultrasound first · discriminatory zone · serial hCG · methotrexate eligibility · unstable means surgeryWhere is the pregnancy, and is the patient stable enough to image?
blocks: transvaginal ultrasound first · discriminatory zone · serial hCG · methotrexate eligibility · unstable means surgeryWhere is the pregnancy, and is the patient stable enough to image?
The urine test has already confirmed pregnancy. The next step is to find where the pregnancy is. Only transvaginal ultrasound can localize it. A single serum β-hCG localizes nothing.
Methotrexate eligibility unruptured, hCG <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up Unstable ectopic hypotension, rebound, or shoulder pain → emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy

The biggest acquired risk factor is prior PID (pelvic inflammatory disease), through tubal scarring. Others are prior ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD (intrauterine device) in place and smoking, which impairs ciliary transport half of ectopics have no palpable adnexal mass methotrexate if unruptured, hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up Rh-negative mother with any bleeding in pregnancy → RhoGAM.
When two tests both seem reasonable, choose the one whose result changes management. A single hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) does not change management tonight; the ultrasound does.

briefs.title: Adolescent Vaccines
briefs.sub: the 11 to 12 year platform, human papillomavirus (HPV) series rules, meningococcal boosters and influenza seasonIs the age gate open, is the series already complete, and is it the season?
blocks: the 11 to 12 year platform, human papillomavirus (HPV) series rules, meningococcal boosters and influenza seasonIs the age gate open, is the series already complete, and is it the season?

When every option is a real vaccine, decide by eligibility. There are only three gates: age platform, series already complete, and season; check them in that order. A date buried in line one of the stem is data. Adolescent platform: at 11 to 12 years, Tdap (tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid and acellular pertussis), HPV vaccine and MenACWY (meningococcal conjugate vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y) come due together. Catch-up principle: every encounter is a vaccination opportunity, including a sports physical. Series complete: a child up to date at 9 has finished every infant and early-childhood series: hepatitis B, MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) and pneumococcal conjugate. Season: influenza vaccine is due every year; it is gated by timing, not eligibility (below). HPV dose count: age at the first dose sets the series. A first dose at 9 to 14 years: 2 doses, at 0 and 6 to 12 months. At 15 or older: 3 doses, at 0, 1 to 2 and 6 months. Immunocompromising conditions, including HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection: 3 doses regardless of age. Never restart: a vaccine series is not restarted, regardless of the time between doses; a delayed dose is simply given late, resuming where you left off. Minimum intervals matter; there is no maximum interval. Meningococcal: MenACWY booster at 16, when the risk period begins; MenB (serogroup B meningococcal vaccine) is separate: shared decision-making at 16 to 23 when not at increased risk.

Each option and the gate it fails: June, age 11, up to date at 9 Vaccine When it is given Why not at this visit Tdap Single dose at 11 to 12 years It is the answer Influenza Every year; September and October are generally good times It is June: not the season MMR 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years Series complete before age 9 Pneumococcal conjugate Infant series at 2, 4, 6 and 12 to 15 months Complete; no routine dose in a healthy 11-year-old Hepatitis B Birth, 1 to 2 months, 6 to 18 months Series complete in infancy

When each adolescent vaccine is due (age, years)schematic TdapOne dose at 11 to 12 91112151618232645→ MenACWY11 to 12, booster at 16 91112151618232645→ MenB16 to 23, shared decision; preferred 16 to 18 91112151618232645→ HPV, 2 dosesFirst dose at 9 to 14; routine at 11 to 12 91112151618232645→ HPV, 3 dosesFirst dose at 15 or older; catch-up through 26 91112151618232645→ HPV, shared decision27 to 45 91112151618232645→

Asplenia anatomic or functional, including sickle cell disease: MenACWY becomes a 2-dose primary series (first dose at 2 years or older), at least 8 weeks apart HIV infection, persistent complement deficiency or a complement inhibitor such as eculizumab the same 2-dose MenACWY primary series MenACWY boosters at age 7 or older, a booster every 5 years while the risk remains MenB added from age 10 for asplenia, persistent complement deficiency or a complement inhibitor (not for HIV infection)

Influenza most commonly peaks from December through February. September and October are generally good times, ideally by the end of October. July and August can be considered for a child who needs only one dose; most adults, especially those 65 years and older, and pregnant women in the first or second trimester should generally not be vaccinated that early (in July or August), because protection may decrease over time. A child 6 months to 8 years old with fewer than 2 doses (at least 4 weeks apart) before July 1 of the current season, or an unknown history, needs 2 doses separated by at least 4 weeks, the first as soon as vaccine is available.

Two independent rules the age at the first dose sets the series length; a delay never restarts the series Too-early dose a dose given 5 or more days before the minimum interval does not count and is repeated; for the 2-dose series the minimum interval is 5 months Catch-up recommended through age 26, with shared decision-making at 27 to 45 Lifestyle details sexual activity, prior HPV exposure and abnormal Pap results do not change the recommendation; vaccinate anyway, since the vaccine still protects against strains not yet acquired

A January 2026 CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) revision recommended a single HPV dose. A federal court stayed that revision in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts keeps the 2-dose series when started at 9 to 14, and the AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) also recommends two doses, starting at 9 to 12; check the CDC site for the current schedule. On retired exam items, the classic keyed answer remains two doses if started before 15 and three if at 15 or older or immunocompromised: the posted schedule and the exam answer currently agree.

Influenza vaccine is excluded by timing, not eligibility: she is due for it every year, just not in June. Measles-mumps-rubella was finished at 4 to 6 years

Three doses are for a first dose at 15 or older or an immunocompromising condition. The single dose is the January 2026 revision, which a court has stayed; the posted schedule keeps 2 doses

The pneumococcal conjugate and hepatitis B series finish in infancy, with no routine dose in a healthy 11-year-old, and the MMR and varicella series both end at 4 to 6 years

Her first dose came before 15, so the second dose completes a 2-dose series; one dose alone is complete only under the stayed January 2026 revision

Influenza most commonly peaks from December through February, so waiting until December gives up protection. Every encounter, including a sports physical, is a vaccination opportunity, and the rest of the 11 to 12 platform, HPV vaccine and MenACWY, is due at this visit too

No additional dose is recommended once a series is complete, so there is no booster at 18

HIV infection, persistent complement deficiency and complement inhibitors such as eculizumab bring the same 2-dose MenACWY primary series

Repeating one dose is not restarting the series, and two doses are needed: a single dose is complete only under the stayed January 2026 revision

Next step11 of 15 11-year-old girl is seen for her adolescent vaccines with 2 days of rhinorrhea She is eating and playing normally; no ear pain or cough T 37.8 °C · HR 92/min · lungs clear · Defer all vaccines until she is afebrile · Vaccinate today · Give Tdap only; defer HPV vaccine and MenACWY until she is well 11-year-old girl is seen for her adolescent vaccines with 2 days of rhinorrhea She is eating and playing normally; no ear pain or cough T 37.8 °C · HR 92/min · lungs clear Vaccinate todaymild illness is not a contraindication: mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotics and breastfeeding are not reasons to delay these vaccines, so Tdap, HPV vaccine and MenACWY are all given today, and none waits for her to be afebrile. A moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is the precaution

briefs.title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
briefs.sub: abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) from menarche to after menopause · adolescent anovulation and bleeding disorders, fibroids, bleeding after menopause · treat the consequence, not the findingIs she pregnant, is there a consequence, and is she still in the physiologic state that the benign explanation needs?
blocks: abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) from menarche to after menopause · adolescent anovulation and bleeding disorders, fibroids, bleeding after menopause · treat the consequence, not the findingIs she pregnant, is there a consequence, and is she still in the physiologic state that the benign explanation needs?

Classify by PALM-COEIN (structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy and hyperplasia; nonstructural: coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not otherwise classified). Every patient is tested for pregnancy and anemia first. For heavy menses the levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) is the most effective medical therapy. Reassurance requires two things: a benign cause and an acceptable consequence. Anemia is a consequence, and normal physiology does not make it acceptable. Adolescent anovulation: normal in the first 1 to 2 years after menarche, from an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis; irregular, heavy and painless, and a diagnosis of exclusion. Bleeding-disorder screen: heavy bleeding since the very first period, a family history of abnormal bleeding, frequent bruising, bleeding gums, epistaxis, postpartum hemorrhage, or bleeding with surgical and dental procedures. Bleeding disorders are found in about 20% of adolescents evaluated for heavy menses (33% of those hospitalized): most commonly von Willebrand disease, platelet function defects, thrombocytopenia and clotting factor deficiencies. Fibroids (leiomyomas): symptoms, not size, drive treatment. Impressive anatomy (markedly enlarged, multiple, intramural, pedunculated) does not demand action when every symptom domain is negative; asymptomatic fibroids get observation. Postmenopausal bleeding: no period for over a year means she is postmenopausal, and any bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Amount and duration are irrelevant; a single episode of spotting counts. Endometrial sampling: at 45 or older with abnormal bleeding; younger with a significant history of unopposed estrogen exposure, persistent bleeding or failed medical management; after menopause by the workup below. Mechanism: the immature axis makes no luteinizing hormone (LH) surge, so anovulation follows; without a corpus luteum there is no progesterone. Unopposed estrogen drives continuous proliferation with no secretory differentiation, and the lining outgrows its blood supply and sheds unpredictably. Progesterone converts proliferative to secretory endometrium and produces organized withdrawal bleeding.

Normal adolescent cycle every 21 to 45 days (adults 24 to 38), lasting 7 days or fewer, 3 to 6 products a day or fewer Painless heavy irregular bleeding the anovulatory signature; ovulatory cycles are crampy Reassurance requires a benign cause and an acceptable consequence; anemia is not an acceptable consequence

Adolescent bleeding: clue, diagnosis, confirmation Clue Diagnosis Confirms, then Irregular, heavy, painless, within 2 years of menarche Anovulation from an immature axis Clinical, after a negative pregnancy test, complete blood count and ferritin; treat if anemic, otherwise reassure Heavy since the very first period, bruising, epistaxis, family history Von Willebrand disease Low von Willebrand factor activity; often repeated because levels vary; then hematology Hirsutism, acne, obesity, acanthosis nigricans Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) Androgens and glucose; in adolescents both hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction, no ultrasound; then a combined oral contraceptive Galactorrhea Prolactinoma High prolactin with pregnancy and hypothyroidism excluded; pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows the adenoma; then cabergoline Weight loss, athlete, low body mass index Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (female athlete triad) Low LH, follicle-stimulating hormone and estradiol once pregnancy, thyroid and prolactin causes are excluded; restore energy balance, check bone density Any sexually active patient Pregnancy Pregnancy test before anything else; quantitative human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and ultrasound to locate it

Diagnostic workup 1Before menopause: is she pregnant, anemic, or bleeding from a disorder or a structure? First Urine or serum hCG PositiveQuantitative level and ultrasound to locate the pregnancy NegativePregnancy excluded as the cause of bleeding or an enlarged uterus Complete blood count and ferritin Low hemoglobin (anemia) or low ferritin (iron deficiency)Anemia: the consequence that converts a normal variant or a fibroid into something you treat; give iron By branch Von Willebrand factor antigen, activity and factor VIII (antihemophilic factor) Low activityVon Willebrand disease; often repeated, because levels vary; work with hematology Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound Well-defined hypoechoic myometrial massesLeiomyoma; location predicts the symptom Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy Submucosal fibroid distorting the cavityHeavy bleeding or pregnancy loss: hysteroscopic myomectomy Pelvic MRI Thickened junctional zoneAdenomyosis; MRI also maps fibroids before myomectomy or embolization Endometrial biopsy Hyperplasia or carcinomaIndicated at 45 or older; younger with significant unopposed estrogen exposure, persistent bleeding or failed medical management Skip Routine ultrasound solely for adolescent heavy bleeding; it can be considered when initial management fails. Prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times alone: the partial thromboplastin time is part of von Willebrand testing, but the prothrombin time is normal in most von Willebrand disease and the partial thromboplastin time is normal in mild disease.

Submucosal: heavy bleeding and infertility or pregnancy loss, the most symptomatic despite often being the smallest. Intramural: bleeding and bulk. Subserosal or pedunculated: pressure, and can torse. Cervical: obstruction. Fibroids are estrogen- and progesterone-dependent and regress after menopause, so they cannot explain postmenopausal bleeding.

The enlarged uterus: the differential Diagnosis Uterus The tell Leiomyoma Irregular, firm, lumpy, mobile Heavy menses; regresses after menopause Adenomyosis Globular, symmetric, boggy, tender Severe dysmenorrhea; MRI shows a thickened junctional zone Pregnancy Symmetric, soft Amenorrhea, then beta-hCG Endometrial cancer Normal or enlarged Postmenopausal bleeding, then biopsy Leiomyosarcoma Rapidly enlarging, especially after menopause Does not arise from a leiomyoma; avoid morcellation
Treat a fibroid only for a co…

Heavy or prolonged menses, especially with anemia. Bulk symptoms: pressure, urinary frequency, constipation, hydronephrosis. Pelvic pain or dyspareunia. Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss (submucosal). Rapid growth, or any growth after menopause: leiomyosarcoma concern.

About 90% of endometrial cancer presents with postmenopausal bleeding, and about 9 to 10% of postmenopausal bleeding is cancer. Atrophy is the most common cause, about 60%, but a diagnosis of exclusion: a pale vagina with minimal rugation does not justify reassurance.

Diagnostic workup 2After menopause: is the endometrium thin, and does the bleeding stop? First Transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial biopsy Thickness 4 mm or lessNo further workup unless bleeding recurs (negative predictive value over 99%) Over 4 mmEndometrial biopsy Thin echo not clearly seenSonohysterography, office hysteroscopy or endometrial sampling Biopsy regardless Endometrial biopsy Higher risk by risk factors or presentation (for example obesity, current tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome)Sample first; the ultrasound threshold does not reassure Persistent or recurrent bleedingHistology whatever the thickness By branch Hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage (D&C) Blind biopsy insufficient or negative and bleeding persistsWarranted; the gold standard for diagnostic sampling Skip Pap test: it does not sample the endometrium. Reassurance for atrophy: atrophy is a diagnosis of exclusion; evaluate the endometrium first.

Next step1 of 25 17-year-old girl has 3 weeks of irregular vaginal bleeding Sexually active with one partner; uses condoms inconsistently Last normal period 7 weeks ago No pelvic pain BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min · Afebrile · Pelvic ultrasound first · Pregnancy test first · CBC and ferritin first 17-year-old girl has 3 weeks of irregular vaginal bleeding Sexually active with one partner; uses condoms inconsistently Last normal period 7 weeks ago No pelvic pain BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min · Afebrile Pregnancy test firstin any sexually active patient the pregnancy test comes before anything else; every patient with abnormal bleeding is tested for pregnancy and anemia. A positive test leads to a quantitative hCG level and ultrasound to locate the pregnancy. A complete blood count and ferritin follow the pregnancy test; they do not replace it

Next step2 of 25 14-year-old girl has irregular, heavy, painless periods since menarche 18 months ago Not bothered by the bleeding No bruising, nosebleeds or family bleeding history Afebrile · HR 78/min · hemoglobin 13 g/dL · urine pregnancy test negative · Combined oral contraceptive · Endometrial biopsy · Reassurance + menstrual calendar 14-year-old girl has irregular, heavy, painless periods since menarche 18 months ago Not bothered by the bleeding No bruising, nosebleeds or family bleeding history Afebrile · HR 78/min · hemoglobin 13 g/dL · urine pregnancy test negative Reassurance + menstrual calendarpainless irregular bleeding within 2 years of menarche is anovulation from an immature axis, normal for her age. The pregnancy test is negative, nothing suggests a bleeding disorder, and she is not anemic, so there is no consequence to treat: reassure and keep a menstrual calendar. A combined oral contraceptive treats a consequence she does not have. Endometrial biopsy under 45 needs a significant history of unopposed estrogen exposure, persistent bleeding or failed medical management, and her pattern is the expected one 18 months after menarche

Workup3 of 25 15-year-old girl has had heavy periods since her first period 2 years ago Bruises easily; frequent nosebleeds Her mother bled heavily after a dental extraction HR 92/min · hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · platelets 260,000/mm³ · urine pregnancy test negative · Platelet count alone · Prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times alone · Von Willebrand factor antigen, activity and factor VIII 15-year-old girl has had heavy periods since her first period 2 years ago Bruises easily; frequent nosebleeds Her mother bled heavily after a dental extraction HR 92/min · hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · platelets 260,000/mm³ · urine pregnancy test negative Von Willebrand factor antigen, activity and factor VIIIheavy bleeding since menarche with bruising, nosebleeds and a family history is the bleeding-disorder screen; bleeding disorders are found in about 20% of adolescents evaluated for heavy menses. Order von Willebrand factor antigen, activity (ristocetin cofactor) and factor VIII, often repeated because levels vary over time, and work with hematology. The prothrombin time is normal in most patients with von Willebrand disease and the partial thromboplastin time is normal in mild disease, so alone they do not exclude it; a platelet count screens for thrombocytopenia, a different disorder

Next step4 of 25 16-year-old girl has 10 days of heavy vaginal bleeding, soaking a pad every hour Light-headed on standing Urine pregnancy test negative BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL · Afebrile · Admit for intravenous conjugated estrogen · Tranexamic acid alone · Outpatient combined OCP 16-year-old girl has 10 days of heavy vaginal bleeding, soaking a pad every hour Light-headed on standing Urine pregnancy test negative BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL · Afebrile Admit for intravenous conjugated estrogena hemodynamically unstable adolescent, or one actively bleeding heavily, is hospitalized. Without contraindications to estrogen, give intravenous conjugated estrogen every 4 to 6 hours (25 mg, for 24 hours), then taper with a high-dose combined pill; tranexamic acid may be added to stop bleeding, and transfuse for instability. Outpatient pills are for the stable patient, and tranexamic acid alone leaves out the admission and the hormone

Both distractors are hormonal, which she declines. Give iron for the anemia

Check androgens and glucose, then a combined oral contraceptive. Atypical (nonclassic) congenital adrenal hyperplasia can mimic it and is excluded with a serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone, which may need an adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test. Virilization, rapid progression, or androgen levels well above the reference range point to an ovarian or adrenal neoplasm

A high level, with pregnancy and hypothyroidism excluded, leads to pituitary MRI to show the adenoma; cabergoline treats it. Thyroid-stimulating hormone alone misses the prolactin, and a pelvic ultrasound looks at the wrong organ

Luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and estradiol are low once pregnancy, thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin are excluded; restore energy balance and check bone density. Hysterectomy ends the fertility she wants, and a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist is a short-term bridge to surgery

Postmenopausal bleeding usually is caused by atrophic changes of the vagina or endometrium, about 60%, but atrophy is a diagnosis of exclusion: the endometrium is evaluated first, and with no higher-risk feature, transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial sampling is a reasonable first approach. Attributing the bleeding to the drug, or stopping it and waiting, delays the diagnosis

Sample the endometrium; transvaginal ultrasound is a reasonable first alternative for an initial episode. Waiting to see whether it recurs or lasts a week skips the evaluation

Treatment by situation Situation Treatment Notes Acute heavy bleeding, unstable or bleeding heavily Hospitalize; without contraindications to estrogen, intravenous conjugated estrogen every 4 to 6 hours (25 mg, for 24 hours), or a monophasic combined pill (30 to 50 micrograms ethinyl estradiol) every 6 to 8 hours until bleeding stops, then a taper; tranexamic acid may be used; transfuse Maintenance: combined hormonal contraceptives, oral or injectable progestins, or a levonorgestrel IUD; iron for anemia Heavy menses, stable Levonorgestrel IUD, more effective than other medical therapies (71 to 95% less blood loss); oral tranexamic acid or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs if nonhormonal is wanted; in a bleeding disorder, aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs only on a hematologist's recommendation Hysterectomy is the most effective treatment overall Symptomatic fibroids Levonorgestrel IUD or tranexamic acid for bleeding (neither shrinks fibroids); hysteroscopic myomectomy for a submucosal fibroid; myomectomy when she wants to keep fertility (it typically preserves it, though many need later procedures); hysterectomy, the definitive option, when childbearing is complete Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist before surgery, 6 months or less alone, add-back beyond; embolization is not ideal if she wants future fertility Hyperplasia without atypia Progestin, oral or by levonorgestrel IUD Typically hormonal therapy and/or curettage Atypical hyperplasia or endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN) Hysterectomy Many have a concurrent carcinoma (about 43% in one series) Endometrial carcinoma Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO) and surgical staging with nodal assessment Hysterectomy and comprehensive staging are the standard of care

The copper IUD typically makes menses heavier and occasionally longer. The levonorgestrel IUD makes them lighter and is a legitimate treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding. Any IUD is contraindicated in bleeding of unknown origin, so evaluate first.
Risk factors are unopposed estrogen: obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, PCOS, tamoxifen, granulosa cell tumor, Lynch syndrome. Combined oral contraceptives and multiparity are protective.

Treat-the-number: impressive fibroid anatomy on a computed tomography (CT) report is not, by itself, clinical significance. Uniform-answer doubt: anovulation is normal at her age, yet anemia still gets treated. True-fact-wrong-slot: fibroids do cause bleeding, but in premenopausal women; after menopause they involute. A Pap test for postmenopausal bleeding does not sample the endometrium. A same-sex relationship does not lower cervical cancer risk, and screening is identical; it does mean low pregnancy risk, so the contraceptive benefit of a combined oral contraceptive or an IUD does not offset their risks.

Part I Hereditary Polyposis Syndromes covers the hereditary colon cancer differential. In it, Lynch syndrome, the endometrial-cancer pedigree, is the polyp-poor row. Ask: is there an endometrial cancer in the family?

Treat the consequences of a finding, not the finding itself. Physiology that is normal for her age settles the diagnosis, not the management: before reassuring, look for a consequence (anemia, growth failure or functional impairment). A benign rash such as miliaria has no consequence but a removable cause, so remove it; normal anovulation with anemia is treated; impressive fibroid anatomy with no consequence is observed. And before accepting a familiar benign explanation, check that the patient is still in the physiologic state where it applies.

briefs.sub: pregnancy test first · injection window and fertility · no-estrogen situations · emergency contraception · amenorrheaCould she be pregnant, and does anything rule out estrogen?
blocks: pregnancy test first · injection window and fertility · no-estrogen situations · emergency contraception · amenorrheaCould she be pregnant, and does anything rule out estrogen?

When two explanations produce identical symptoms, test for the one that changes management and can't be missed. DMPA (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate) causes breast soreness, weight gain, fatigue and amenorrhea, which are indistinguishable from early pregnancy. DMPA is due every 13 weeks; her last injection was 4 months ago, so she has been uncovered. Inserting an IUD (intrauterine device) into an established intrauterine pregnancy can disrupt it. As a rule, a pregnancy test precedes every contraception decision, every amenorrhea workup, and absolutely every IUD placement.
DMPA dosing window every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period Return to fertility delayed up to 10 months Before any contraceptive decision a pregnancy test

Suppresses GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone), so there is no LH (luteinizing hormone) surge and no ovulation; thickens cervical mucus every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period irregular bleeding early, then amenorrhea in ~50% at 1 year weight gain from appetite stimulation reversible loss of bone mineral density (boxed warning) the unique one: delayed return to fertility up to 10 months no estrogen, so safe in smokers ≥35, migraine with aura, VTE (venous thromboembolism) history, and immediately postpartum.

Defined as no menses >3 months with previously regular cycles (or >6 months if previously irregular). Pregnancy test first, then TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), prolactin, FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone). FSH high → primary ovarian insufficiency FSH low/normal → hypothalamic or pituitary prolactin high → prolactinoma, dopamine blockers, or hypothyroidism no withdrawal bleed even to estrogen + progesterone after a D&C (dilation and curettage) → Asherman syndrome.
