Pt newborn male, growth restricted at 2.5 kg at 38 weeks, mother 29 with no prenatal care, forceps delivery for fetal heart rate abnormalities, Apgars 6 and 8 Exam microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate, and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges Q which maternal history would be found; options spanned alcohol use, cocaine use, lisinopril use, phenytoin use and untreated syphilis

Cleft palate and distal phalangeal hypoplasia are the two findings that alcohol does not cause. Together they are fetal hydantoin syndrome, from in utero exposure to a folate-antagonizing antiepileptic, classically phenytoin. The drug crosses the placenta and produces low fetal folate with high oxidative metabolites. The wide anterior fontanelle and microcephaly complete the pattern. Fetal alcohol syndrome shares the microcephaly and the midface hypoplasia but has no association with clefting. Its signature is a smooth philtrum with a thin vermilion border and short palpebral fissures, none of which is described in this newborn.

Critical periods 0–2 weeks all-or-none (death or no effect); 3–8 weeks organogenesis, the structural-malformation window; beyond 8 weeks growth restriction, central nervous system and functional deficits rather than structural defects Fetal hydantoin syndrome microcephaly, wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip and palate, distal digit and nail hypoplasia, cardiac defects, neural tube defects Fetal alcohol syndrome smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures, midface hypoplasia, microcephaly, and no clefting Antiepileptic management switch to a lower-risk agent such as levetiracetam 6 months before conception, 4 mg folic acid from 3 months before conception, and make no changes after conception; screen with alpha-fetoprotein and anatomy ultrasonography

Teratogenic medications – drug to signaturethe malformation unique to one agent Drug Signature defect Phenytoin Distal digit and nail hypoplasia, cleft lip/palate, wide fontanelle, microcephaly, cardiac, neural tube defects Valproate Neural tube defects – the highest-risk antiepileptic Carbamazepine Neural tube defects, less than valproate Topiramate Oral clefts, growth restriction, neurodevelopmental effects Phenobarbital Cardiac, orofacial and urogenital malformations Isotretinoin Microtia and small ears, microcephaly, cleft palate, cardiac, thymic hypoplasia, hydrocephalus Methotrexate Limb and craniofacial defects, cranial ossification defects, neural tube defects, abortion Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors / ARBs Renal dysgenesis → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence, growth restriction Warfarin Nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia; fetal hemorrhage later Lithium Ebstein anomaly Methimazole Aplasia cutis, esophageal atresia, facial anomalies Tetracyclines Tooth discolouration, inhibited long-bone growth Fluoroquinolones Cartilage and bone toxicity Diethylstilbestrol Clear cell adenocarcinoma of vagina and cervix, uterine malformation Thalidomide Phocomelia

Cleft palate present in hydantoin and absent in fetal alcohol syndrome; the single most discriminating finding in this newborn Hypoplasia of the distal phalanges near-specific for antiepileptic exposure Wide anterior fontanelle part of the hydantoin pattern, and easily overlooked Symmetric growth restriction with microcephaly shared by alcohol, phenytoin, isotretinoin and cocaine, so it discriminates nothing No smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border or short palpebral fissures the fetal alcohol facial triad is absent No prenatal care explains why a maternal medication history was never taken No snuffles, hepatomegaly or maculopapular rash congenital syphilis is excluded on its own features

Is there a structural malformation? Yes → exposure fell in the 3–8 week window List the findings that only one agent causes. Cleft palate and distal digit hypoplasia Which agent causes both? Phenytoin Check the nearest mimic. Alcohol shares the microcephaly but never the cleft Is there an alternative explanation for the growth restriction? It is nonspecific and fits every option What would have prevented it? Pre-conception switch plus 4 mg folate

Diagnosis9 of 9 2-week-old boy born at 38 weeks to a 27-year-old first-time mother after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with no prenatal exposure history recorded; birth weight about 2.3 kg; length, weight and head circumference at the 5th percentile; short palpebral fissures, flat midface, small jaw and thin upper lip; soft systolic murmur with normal femoral pulses; mild hypotonia · Trisomy 13 syndrome · Fetal alcohol syndrome · Down syndrome 2-week-old boy born at 38 weeks to a 27-year-old first-time mother after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with no prenatal exposure history recorded; birth weight about 2.3 kg; length, weight and head circumference at the 5th percentile; short palpebral fissures, flat midface, small jaw and thin upper lip; soft systolic murmur with normal femoral pulses; mild hypotonia Fetal alcohol syndromethe face and growth decide without an exposure history; the palpebral fissures are short, not upslanting

Low molecular weight heparin and unfractionated heparin have no fetal effects; warfarin is teratogenic to bone and cartilage. Heparins do not cross the placenta, and warfarin does. Patients with mechanical valves therefore take low-molecular-weight heparin in the first trimester, warfarin in the second and third, and unfractionated heparin near delivery.

Cleft plus distal digit hypoplasia is phenytoin; alcohol affects the philtrum and the palpebral fissures, not the palate or the fingertips Timing predicts the kind of damage – before 2 weeks all-or-none, 3–8 weeks structure, after 8 weeks growth and brain Change antiepileptics before conception, never after; once pregnancy is recognized organogenesis is mostly done, and switching adds seizure risk plus a second teratogen Valproate is the worst antiepileptic and levetiracetam the usual substitute Oligohydramnios with Potter sequence should suggest ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors as well as renal agenesis, two different first causes of the same cascade Lithium → Ebstein anomaly is the one psychiatric-drug-to-cardiac-lesion pairing worth memorizing outright

FAS (fetal alcohol syndrome) can be diagnosed from the examination when no exposure history is given. The 2016 revised Institute of Medicine criteria require all four of these. First, 2 of 3 facial features: short palpebral fissures (at or below the 10th percentile), a thin upper lip vermilion and a smooth philtrum. Second, height or weight at or below the 10th percentile. Third, a head circumference at or below the 10th percentile, a structural brain anomaly, or recurrent nonfebrile seizures. Fourth, neurobehavioral impairment, which under age 3 means developmental delay. Confirmed alcohol exposure is not required; a confirmed absence of exposure excludes the diagnosis. Short fissures point to FAS. Upslanting fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease point to Down syndrome.

No maternal alcohol history was given; the face, with length, weight and head size at the 5th percentile, made the diagnosis in a hypotonic 2-week-old. Short palpebral fissures separated it from Down syndrome, whose fissures slant upward; trisomy 13, fragile X, Klinefelter syndrome and congenital toxoplasmosis were the other decoys.

Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the oligohydramnios cascade that this brief reaches from the drug side. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers Ebstein anomaly. Ask: which single malformation does only one drug on the roster cause?
To identify a teratogen, find the one malformation unique to one agent. Ignore the shared features that every candidate agent can produce.

Unchecked attributeAlcohol use: shares microcephaly and growth restriction, but has no association with cleft lip or palate, and none of the facial triad is described. True-fact-wrong-slotCocaine use: causes preterm delivery, abruption and growth restriction, but no congenital defects. Class-vs-memberLisinopril: a named teratogen, but it produces renal failure and Potter sequence, not clefting or digit hypoplasia. True-fact-wrong-slotUntreated syphilis: symptomatic cases show snuffles, hepatomegaly and a maculopapular rash, none present here. Unchecked attributeDown syndrome: hypotonia and a soft murmur fit, but Down syndrome gives upslanting palpebral fissures with epicanthal folds, a flat facial profile and a single palmar crease. These fissures are short. True-fact-wrong-slotTrisomy 13 syndrome: it causes cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, small eyes, scalp defects and extra digits, none of which this newborn has. Unchecked attributeFragile X syndrome: the long face, large ears, prominent jaw and large testes appear later in childhood and after puberty; this newborn has a small jaw. Unchecked attributeKlinefelter syndrome (seminiferous tubule dysgenesis): boys with 47,XXY look normal at birth; small testes, tall stature and gynecomastia appear at puberty. Salient decoyCongenital toxoplasmosis: growth restriction fits, but it brings chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, scattered intracranial calcifications and an enlarged liver and spleen, not a facial pattern.

briefs.title: Primary Amenorrhea
briefs.sub: pelvic ultrasound first · uterus present or absent, then read the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) · Turner, agenesis, androgen insensitivityIs there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low; if not, is there pubic hair?
blocks: pelvic ultrasound first · uterus present or absent, then read the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) · Turner, agenesis, androgen insensitivityIs there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low; if not, is there pubic hair?

Pt 15 yo, no menses, distressed at looking younger than peers; no headache or visual change; mother and grandmother menarche at 13; height below the 3rd percentile, weight 20th Exam no breast development, normal external genitalia, Tanner 2 pubic hair; urine beta-hCG negative Imaging pelvic ultrasonography shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries Labs FSH 60 (normal under 40), luteinizing hormone (LH) 52 (normal 5–25) Q the next step in management, then the underlying cause; options spanned hormone measurements, imaging, karyotype and reassurance

Primary amenorrhea is no menarche by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without them. The first step is pelvic ultrasonography. The obstruction can sit anywhere from the hypothalamus and pituitary to the ovary, uterus and vagina. Imaging is the only test that answers the anatomical half of that chain in one move. Every hormonal test is interpretable only once you know whether there is a uterus. Uterus present → read the FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone). High FSH with high LH (luteinizing hormone) is primary ovarian insufficiency. With short stature, that is Turner syndrome: gonadal dysgenesis from loss of an X. Turner syndrome gives streak ovaries and absent oestrogen, while intact adrenals still produce pubic hair. Uterus absent → read the pubic hair. Pubic hair present means the androgen receptor works, so the diagnosis is 46,XX Müllerian agenesis. Absent pubic hair means it does not, so the diagnosis is 46,XY complete androgen insensitivity.

Primary amenorrhea no menarche by age 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 without them First step pelvic ultrasonography, to establish whether a uterus is present before any hormone is measured Uterus present, FSH high primary ovarian insufficiency; with short stature, Turner syndrome (45,X on karyotype, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) if mosaicism is suspected) Uterus present, FSH low or inappropriately normal central: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion, or GnRH deficiency, Cushing syndrome, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea Uterus absent serum testosterone: female-range with normal pubic hair is Müllerian agenesis (46,XX); male-range with absent pubic and axillary hair is complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)

Is the definition met? No menarche by 13 without secondary characteristics → yes What is the first test? Pelvic ultrasound; anatomy before hormones Is there a uterus? Yes → read the FSH Is the FSH high or low? High → ovarian failure, not a central cause Is she short? Below the 3rd percentile → Turner What confirms it? Mechanism9 of 9 Why girls with Turner syndrome develop pubic hair but no breast development · Adrenarche is intact while ovarian estrogen production fails · Androgen receptors are nonfunctional · Peripheral aromatization is absent Why girls with Turner syndrome develop pubic hair but no breast development Adrenarche is intact while ovarian estrogen production failsthe adrenal glands are unaffected by loss of an X chromosome

A 17-hydroxyprogesterone, a testosterone, a karyotype and an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) are each the right move in some branch of this algorithm. Each is uninterpretable until the ultrasound has shown whether there is a uterus, so ordering it first is one step too early. Reassurance is right for a girl under 15 who has secondary sexual characteristics. It is wrong here because the definition is already met and her height is below the 3rd percentile.

Ultrasound first, always – every hormone in this workup is uninterpretable until you know whether there is a uterus Uterus present → FSH. Uterus absent → pubic hair. These two questions, in that order, resolve almost every case of primary amenorrhea High FSH means ovarian failure; low FSH means a central cause – the gonadotropins tell you which end of the axis to investigate Turner patients have pubic hair, because adrenarche is adrenal and the adrenals are normal; pubic hair without breast development points to ovarian failure Müllerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity both present with an absent uterus and differ in pubic hair Müllerian agenesis obliges a renal ultrasound – the ducts develop alongside the urinary tract, so anomalies travel together An athlete with amenorrhea can still have a structural cause; functional hypothalamic amenorrhea never explains missing anatomy

Part I Abnormal Uterine Bleeding covers the opposite complaint on the same axis, too much bleeding rather than none, and shares the immature-axis physiology. Part II Puberty covers the staging vocabulary this brief uses throughout. Ask: is there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low?
When a workup has an anatomical branch and a hormonal branch, image first. A hormone measured before you know the anatomy produces a number you cannot interpret.

Sequencing trap17-hydroxyprogesterone: real in the amenorrhea workup for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but indicated only once a uterus is confirmed and with suggestive features. Uniform-answer doubtReassurance and observation: the definition is already met, and height below the 3rd percentile is itself a finding. Unchecked attributeAndrogen insensitivity: requires an absent uterus; she has one. Mirror twinDevelopmental failure of the urogenital sinus: produces a vaginal dimple with a uterus present, the mirror image of Müllerian agenesis. Salient decoyAbnormal GnRH pulsatility: twice-daily training is a real risk factor, but central causes give low gonadotropins and cannot remove a uterus.

briefs.title: Genital Ulcers
briefs.sub: painless vs painful ulcers · syphilis vs herpes vs chancroid · test for syphilis, herpes and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) · penicillinDoes the ulcer hurt, and are there vesicles or suppurating nodes?
blocks: painless vs painful ulcers · syphilis vs herpes vs chancroid · test for syphilis, herpes and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) · penicillinDoes the ulcer hurt, and are there vesicles or suppurating nodes?

Pt 17 yo F, 5 days of a nontender vulvar lesion; three male partners, condoms used inconsistently; afebrile, normal vital signs Exam 2 cm ulcer with raised borders on the right labium majus Q the most likely causal organism; options were organism classes: gram-negative bacillus, gram-negative diplococcus, obligate intracellular bacterium, protozoan, spirochete and virus

A single painless genital ulcer with a firm, raised border and no systemic signs is a primary syphilis chancre. The cause is Treponema pallidum, a spirochete. Genital herpes and chancroid both cause painful ulcers. HSV (herpes simplex virus) starts as grouped vesicles that break into shallow ulcers. Chancroid causes deep ulcers, often with tender suppurative inguinal nodes. A chancre can also be multiple or painful, and the exam alone often misleads. Test every genital ulcer for syphilis and HSV, and test for HIV. Early in primary syphilis the RPR (rapid plasma reagin) can still be nonreactive. Darkfield microscopy or a molecular test of the ulcer exudate detects the spirochete directly.

Genital ulcer in a sexually active patient: the differential Diagnosis Ulcer Nodes and course The NBME tell Primary syphilis: Treponema pallidum, a spirochete Usually single, painless, clean base, firm raised border Painless, rubbery inguinal nodes; heals in weeks even untreated, and secondary syphilis can follow Painless ulcer with an indurated, raised border; no vesicles Genital herpes: herpes simplex virus type 2 or herpes simplex virus type 1, a virus Painful grouped vesicles on a red base that break into shallow ulcers, then crust Tender inguinal nodes; a first episode can bring fever and dysuria; recurs Vesicles first, painful, often multiple Chancroid: Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative bacillus One or more deep, painful ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and a purulent base Tender suppurative inguinal nodes (buboes) that can rupture; rare in the United States Painful ulcer with a suppurating node Lymphogranuloma venereum: Chlamydia trachomatis L1 to L3, an obligate intracellular bacterium Small papule or ulcer that heals on its own and often goes unnoticed Tender, usually unilateral inguinal or femoral nodes; proctocolitis after rectal exposure The nodes, not the ulcer, bring the patient in Discharge infections: N. gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococcus), C. trachomatis (obligate intracellular), Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan) No ulcer Cervicitis, urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease; trichomoniasis gives a frothy, malodorous discharge Discharge without an ulcer

Spirochete Treponema pallidum: painless chancre Virus herpes simplex virus: painful vesicles, then ulcers Gram-negative bacillus Haemophilus ducreyi: painful ulcer, suppurative nodes Obligate intracellular bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis: cervicitis, or lymphogranuloma venereum with prominent nodes Gram-negative diplococcus Neisseria gonorrhoeae: cervicitis and discharge Protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis: frothy, malodorous discharge

In the United States, most genital ulcers in young, sexually active patients are genital herpes or syphilis Treat presumptively for syphilis when the ulcer looks like a chancre, before results return The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is fever, headache and myalgia within 24 hours of treating syphilis; it is not a penicillin allergy NBME framing: every option was an organism class, so the ulcer had to be named as syphilis and then matched to spirochete.

Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers secondary syphilis. Ask: is there a rash on the palms and soles? Part I Cervicitis and Pelvic Inflammatory Disease covers gonorrhea and chlamydia. Ask: is there a discharge instead of an ulcer?

For a genital ulcer, ask first whether it hurts. A painless, indurated ulcer is primary syphilis until proven otherwise. A painful ulcer is herpes when vesicles came first and chancroid when the inguinal nodes suppurate.

Unchecked attributeGram-negative bacillus: Haemophilus ducreyi causes a genital ulcer, but the chancroid ulcer is painful and comes with tender suppurative nodes. Unchecked attributeVirus: HSV (herpes simplex virus) is the most common cause of genital ulcers, but its lesions are painful and start as grouped vesicles. True-fact-wrong-slotObligate intracellular bacterium: Chlamydia trachomatis is common in sexually active adolescents, but it causes cervicitis, and its lymphogranuloma venereum strains cause only a small transient ulcer. Salient decoyGram-negative diplococcus: multiple partners suggest gonorrhea, but gonorrhea causes cervicitis and discharge, not an ulcer. True-fact-wrong-slotProtozoan: Trichomonas vaginalis causes a frothy, malodorous discharge with itching, not an ulcer.

Pt 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia Q the intervention that most reduces mortality; options spanned smoking cessation, a statin and lisinopril

When every option is guideline-supported, rank them by magnitude of benefit. Smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality more than any drug on the list. It cuts CV (cardiovascular) risk substantially within 1–2 years and approaches never-smoker risk over ~15 years.

For macrovascular outcomes, the order of benefit is smoking cessation > BP (blood pressure) control > statin > glycemic control. If the patient smokes and smoking cessation is an option, choose it. The exception is an outcome limited to a specific organ. For risk of nephropathy progression, choose an ACE-I (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor) and BP control. For microvascular complications, choose glycemic (A1c) control. Lifestyle advice ranks low when vague ("recommend exercise") and high when specific and high-magnitude (smoking or alcohol cessation).

Petechiae with a count of 8,000 in a healthy young woman → ITP (immune thrombocytopenia). Treat with steroids or IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin), not transfusion, because transfused platelets get consumed too heparin day 5–10 with a 50% drop → HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia). Stop heparin, start argatroban and never transfuse clumps on the smear → pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid). Repeat the count in a citrate tube; this is the one time "recheck the count" is correct DDAVP (desmopressin) is for qualitative defects (von Willebrand disease, mild hemophilia A, uremic platelet dysfunction), not for a low count.

briefs.title: Elder Abuse
briefs.sub: reasonable suspicion is enough · findings that build suspicion · reporting pathways · capacity determines whether to reportIs the suspicion reasonable, and is the victim a competent adult or a cognitively impaired elder?
blocks: reasonable suspicion is enough · findings that build suspicion · reporting pathways · capacity determines whether to reportIs the suspicion reasonable, and is the victim a competent adult or a cognitively impaired elder?

Reasonable suspicion → report to Adult Protective Services. You do not need proof, and you do not investigate first. Confounders such as warfarin (easy bruising) and dementia (unreliable historian) are real but irrelevant to the decision to report. Adult Protective Services investigates; you do not adjudicate.

Bruises in multiple stages of healing (the single most tested physical finding, as in child abuse) implausible or vague mechanism caregiver who cannot explain the injuries patient who becomes uncomfortable and minimizes when asked alone risk profile: dementia, dependency, caregiver stress. Interview technique: separate the patient from the caregiver, ask direct nonjudgmental questions, and do not confront the suspected abuser.

Reporting pathways Situation Path Elder / dependent adult abuse APS – report on suspicion, mandated in most states Child abuse Child Protective Services – report on suspicion, no parental consent needed Intimate partner violence in a competent adult NOT reportable without consent in most states → safety assessment, safety plan, resources, document Gunshot / stab wounds, certain infections Reportable regardless

Capacity determines whether to report. Report abuse of children and cognitively impaired elders over anyone's objection. For a competent adult experiencing IPV (intimate partner violence), offer support and respect autonomy. Once abuse is suspected, never "document and re-ask at the next visit". Doing so sends a dependent patient back into the home you suspect.

briefs.title: Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies
briefs.sub: name the vitamin by its sign · fat-soluble: why fat is not absorbed · water-soluble: what the patient drinks, takes or does not eat · the vegan diet: what must be supplementedWhich organ pattern names the vitamin, and why is this patient short of it?
blocks: name the vitamin by its sign · fat-soluble: why fat is not absorbed · water-soluble: what the patient drinks, takes or does not eat · the vegan diet: what must be supplementedWhich organ pattern names the vitamin, and why is this patient short of it?

Name the vitamin by its sign, then ask why this patient is short of it. Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K): absorbed only with bile and pancreatic enzymes, so any fat malabsorption can deplete all four: cystic fibrosis (CF) and other pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis and biliary atresia, celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, gastric bypass or short bowel. Water-soluble (B and C): the body stores little, except B12 (cobalamin), so deficiency follows chronic alcohol use, poor intake, malabsorption (bypass, short bowel, Crohn disease) or a drug. Vitamin K deficiency: the PT (prothrombin time) lengthens first, because factor VII (proconvertin) has the shortest half-life; the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) follows only when deficiency is severe, and platelets stay normal. B12 or folate: both cause a megaloblastic anemia; neurologic signs and a high methylmalonic acid mark B12. Unfortified vegan diet: B12 always, plus vitamin D and calcium, must be supplemented; iron and zinc join the list for children and menstruating women. Order of treatment: thiamine before or with glucose; no folate alone until the B12 level is known, since folate corrects the anemia but not the nerve damage.
Recognize: name it by its sign

Each vitamin: who gets it and the sign that names it Vitamin Who gets it The sign A Fat malabsorption; poor intake in low-income regions Night blindness, dry conjunctivae and cornea (xerophthalmia), Bitot spots, dry skin D Fat malabsorption; breastfed infant without supplements; little sun, dark skin; vegan diet Children: rickets (bowed legs, widened wrists, rachitic rosary). Adults: osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal weakness E Cholestatic liver disease, CF, abetalipoproteinemia Ataxia with lost vibration and position sense, neuropathy with hyporeflexia, myopathy, hemolytic anemia; mimics Friedreich ataxia K Fat malabsorption; broad-spectrum antibiotics; newborn without prophylaxis; poor intake Bruising, mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding; a long PT that corrects with vitamin K B1 (thiamine) Alcohol use (most common), malnutrition including anorexia nervosa, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery with vomiting Wernicke: confusion, ophthalmoplegia (horizontal nystagmus, bilateral abducens palsy), gait ataxia. Dry beriberi: symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy. Wet beriberi: high-output heart failure with edema B3 (niacin) Alcohol use, anorexia, Crohn disease, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome (tryptophan diverted to serotonin) Pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis of the neck (Casal necklace), hands and face, with diarrhea and dementia B6 (pyridoxine) Isoniazid, alcohol use Peripheral neuropathy, cheilitis, stomatitis; seizures when severe; microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia B9 (folate) Alcohol use, pregnancy, hemolysis, poor intake; methotrexate, trimethoprim, triamterene, phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine Megaloblastic anemia with a normal neurologic exam; neural tube defects in pregnancy B12 Pernicious anemia, atrophic gastritis, vegan diet, metformin, proton pump inhibitors, ileal resection or Crohn disease, fish tapeworm Megaloblastic anemia with lost vibration and position sense and spastic weakness (subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts), neuropathy, dementia C No fruits or vegetables: food-selective child (autism), alcohol use, severe malnutrition Swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, poor wound healing, a limp in children from bleeding under the periosteum; platelets, PT and aPTT normal

Vitamin K deficiency PT/INR (international normalized ratio) prolonged first, aPTT normal or prolonged if severe, platelets and factor V normal Liver failure PT prolonged with a low factor V (factor V does not need vitamin K) and low albumin; the PT does not correct with vitamin K Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) sepsis, trauma or malignancy; a critically ill patient oozing from lines; platelets and fibrinogen low, PT and aPTT prolonged, D-dimer high

Must supplement B12 (no unfortified plant source), vitamin D (skin synthesis covers only about half the requirement, less in northern latitudes) and calcium (plant calcium, as in spinach, is oxalate-bound and poorly absorbed) At risk iron and zinc in children (growth) and menstruating women; non-heme iron absorbs poorly, so pair it with vitamin C Not deficient folate (greens, legumes, fruit) and protein with essential amino acids in balanced diets

Diagnostic workup 1Bleeding with normal platelets: which pathway? First PT/INR with platelet count PT prolonged, platelets normalVitamin K pathway: factor VII falls first Platelets lowDIC, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) or a big spleen Next aPTT Normal, or prolonged when severeSeverity Both prolonged, platelets and fibrinogen lowDIC By branch Factor V activity NormalVitamin K deficiency LowLiver failure Confirms PT after vitamin K: it corrects in vitamin K deficiency; little change points to the liver.

Diagnostic workup 2Megaloblastic anemia: B12 or folate? First Complete blood count with mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and smear MCV over 100, hypersegmented neutrophilsMegaloblastic: B12 or folate Next Serum B12 and folate B12 under 200 pg/mLDeficient 200 to 300Order methylmalonic acid Over 300Sufficient By branch Methylmalonic acid HighB12 deficiency Normal, homocysteine highFolate deficiency Cause Intrinsic factor antibodies PositivePernicious anemia: lifelong B12 Skip Homocysteine to separate them: it is high in both.

Measure 25-hydroxyvitamin D, made in the liver; skip 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, often normal in deficiency because parathyroid hormone (PTH) drives its production Rickets labs alkaline phosphatase and PTH rise, 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls; phosphate is low (less absorbed, more lost in urine); calcium is low or normal, because PTH defends it

Vitamin K parenteral for severe coagulopathy; add fresh frozen plasma for serious bleeding (intracranial, gastrointestinal or at several sites); in CF, restart pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins Newborn one intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth Vitamin D 50,000 international units (IU) weekly for 8 weeks, then 800 to 1,000 IU daily; recheck 25-hydroxyvitamin D in 3 to 4 months, aiming for 20 ng/mL or more; 400 IU daily for every infant in the first year Thiamine IV, before or with any glucose, in Wernicke encephalopathy or any malnourished or alcohol-using patient B12 intramuscular or high-dose oral; with neurologic signs, never folate alone Folate oral folic acid once the B12 level is known, or with B12 when the cause is unclear; alongside methotrexate; 0.4 mg daily for anyone who could become pregnant, 4 mg after a prior neural tube defect, starting before conception B6 and C pyridoxine with isoniazid; oral vitamin C, improving within days to weeks

Screening1 of 27 24-year-old woman asks which supplements she needs strict vegan diet of unprocessed, unfortified plant foods Takes no supplements; eats legumes, greens and grains daily No fatigue, numbness or bone pain BP 112/70 mm Hg · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL · Vitamin B12 · Protein supplementation · Folic acid 24-year-old woman asks which supplements she needs strict vegan diet of unprocessed, unfortified plant foods Takes no supplements; eats legumes, greens and grains daily No fatigue, numbness or bone pain BP 112/70 mm Hg · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL Vitamin B12no unfortified plant source of B12 exists, so it must always be supplemented. Legumes, greens and grains supply abundant folate and protein, and balanced vegan diets supply complete protein, so neither folic acid nor protein needs supplementing; folate matters in pregnancy, but vegan diets are folate-rich

Disseminated intravascular coagulation consumes platelets and fibrinogen in a critically ill patient. Hemophilia A lacks factor VIII (antihemophilic factor), which does not need vitamin K; it prolongs the aPTT and leaves the PT normal

Porphyria cutanea tarda is also photosensitive, but it blisters on the backs of the hands and brings no diarrhea or dementia. Thiamine deficiency strikes the brain, eyes, gait or heart, not the skin

Workup4 of 27 18-month-old boy walked late, only last month Exclusively breastfed with no supplements; dark skin; rarely outdoors bowed legs and widened wrists beading along the costochondral junctions Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high · Serum ionized calcium · Serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D · Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D 18-month-old boy walked late, only last month Exclusively breastfed with no supplements; dark skin; rarely outdoors bowed legs and widened wrists beading along the costochondral junctions Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin Dnutritional rickets: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the form measured, and it falls in deficiency; replace vitamin D. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is often normal, because PTH drives its production, and PTH holds calcium low or normal, so neither confirms the cause

The glucose is needed, but not first; oral thiamine at discharge misses the emergency, which needs IV thiamine on suspicion

Mechanism6 of 27 16-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 3 days of nosebleeds bruises easily for 2 months Off her prescribed medications; low-grade fever last week no organomegaly; neurologic exam normal Normal vital signs · platelet count normal · Increased coagulation factor consumption · Vitamin C malabsorption · Absent coagulation factor activation 16-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 3 days of nosebleeds bruises easily for 2 months Off her prescribed medications; low-grade fever last week no organomegaly; neurologic exam normal Normal vital signs · platelet count normal Absent coagulation factor activationin CF the prescribed medications are usually pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins; off them, fat is not absorbed, and without vitamin K the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate (activate) factors II, VII, IX (Christmas factor) and X, so the PT lengthens first: give vitamin K. Consumption (disseminated intravascular coagulation) needs a critically ill patient with low platelets; the recent fever is the decoy. Vitamin C is water soluble, so pancreatic insufficiency does not deplete it, and scurvy leaves the PT normal

Vitamin B12 deficiency is macrocytic, not microcytic. Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause a microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia, but it follows isoniazid or alcohol use, with neuropathy

Vitamin B12 deficiency is megaloblastic and adds spastic weakness. Vitamin E deficiency mimics Friedreich ataxia, but here the cause is in sight: cystic fibrosis off enzymes, with hemolysis, and the echocardiogram is normal

Workup9 of 27 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin has 2 months of fatigue mild numbness of the feet Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL · MCV 108 fL · hypersegmented neutrophils · serum B12 240 pg/mL · folate normal · Serum homocysteine · Intrinsic factor antibodies · Serum methylmalonic acid 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin has 2 months of fatigue mild numbness of the feet Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL · MCV 108 fL · hypersegmented neutrophils · serum B12 240 pg/mL · folate normal Serum methylmalonic acida megaloblastic anemia with a B12 of 200 to 300 pg/mL needs methylmalonic acid, and a high level confirms B12 deficiency; metformin is a cause. Homocysteine is high in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot separate them. Intrinsic factor antibodies look for the cause (pernicious anemia) once the deficiency is shown

Excess vitamin D causes hypercalcemia, not raised pressure, and a normal body mass index argues against obesity-related intracranial hypertension

It mimics acute lymphoblastic leukemia, but normal white cells, platelets and coagulation studies with gum disease point to the diet. Vitamin K deficiency lengthens the PT; scurvy leaves it normal

Diagnosis12 of 27 26-year-old man who follows a vegan diet has diffuse bone aches proximal muscle weakness Lives in a northern state; takes no supplements Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high · Vitamin D deficiency · Vitamin B12 deficiency · Primary hyperparathyroidism 26-year-old man who follows a vegan diet has diffuse bone aches proximal muscle weakness Lives in a northern state; takes no supplements Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high Vitamin D deficiencyskin synthesis covers only about half the vitamin D requirement, less in northern latitudes, and an unfortified vegan diet adds little: osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal weakness. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and dorsal-column signs, not bone pain. Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium; here calcium is low-normal, held there by PTH

Wernicke encephalopathy needs confusion, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia, and these have cleared. Hepatic encephalopathy ranges from subtle cognitive change to confusion and coma, with asterixis typically in its intermediate stages; he has no asterixis and is alert and attentive

A B12 over 300 pg/mL is sufficient and the neurologic exam is normal, so intramuscular B12 replaces nothing missing. The cause is already in sight, so a bone marrow biopsy adds nothing

A normal creatinine argues against chronic kidney disease (impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation), and a normal albumin and liver enzymes against chronic liver disease (impaired hepatic 25-hydroxylation)

Switching to rifampin is not needed, because the neuropathy comes from a missing vitamin that pyridoxine replaces, and gabapentin treats the symptom, not the deficiency

Factor V does not need vitamin K, so a normal factor V points to vitamin K deficiency and a low one to hepatic synthetic failure. Factor VII depends on vitamin K, so it falls in vitamin K deficiency and cannot clear the liver; a mixing study separates a factor deficiency from an inhibitor, which is not the question

Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis alone, with a normal neurologic exam, and iron deficiency is microcytic

Diagnosis23 of 27 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is confused and unsteady 4 weeks of vomiting, 6 kg lost; intravenous dextrose twice horizontal nystagmus, weak lateral gaze bilaterally BP 104/66 mm Hg · no headache or papilledema · sodium 134 mEq/L, stable · Osmotic demyelination syndrome · Wernicke encephalopathy · Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is confused and unsteady 4 weeks of vomiting, 6 kg lost; intravenous dextrose twice horizontal nystagmus, weak lateral gaze bilaterally BP 104/66 mm Hg · no headache or papilledema · sodium 134 mEq/L, stable Wernicke encephalopathyconfusion, eye findings and ataxia after weeks of hyperemesis gravidarum and dextrose loads is Wernicke encephalopathy: IV thiamine before further dextrose. Osmotic demyelination follows rapid correction of hyponatremia, and this sodium has not moved. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis brings headache in 80 to 90%, and papilledema may join it when pressure rises significantly; she has neither

Diagnosis24 of 27 9-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis cannot see well at dusk Skips his pancreatic enzymes and vitamin supplements dry conjunctivae and cornea; Bitot spots on both eyes dry skin Afebrile · gait and reflexes normal · Vitamin E deficiency · Vitamin A deficiency · Retinitis pigmentosa 9-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis cannot see well at dusk Skips his pancreatic enzymes and vitamin supplements dry conjunctivae and cornea; Bitot spots on both eyes dry skin Afebrile · gait and reflexes normal Vitamin A deficiencycystic fibrosis off enzymes means fat malabsorption, which depletes vitamin A: night blindness, dry conjunctivae and cornea (xerophthalmia), Bitot spots and dry skin; one fat-soluble deficiency means all four need checking or replacing. Vitamin E deficiency brings ataxia and lost vibration sense with hemolysis, and his gait and reflexes are normal. Retinitis pigmentosa also brings night blindness, but the front-of-eye signs here (dry conjunctivae and cornea, Bitot spots) are the vitamin A signs, and the cause is in sight

Workup25 of 27 22-month-old girl walked late and now waddles Still drinks mostly breast milk; never had vitamin D drops bowed legs; thickened wrists and ankles Afebrile · HR 110/min · weight at the 40th percentile · Alkaline phosphatase activity · Parathyroid hormone concentration · Phosphorus concentration 22-month-old girl walked late and now waddles Still drinks mostly breast milk; never had vitamin D drops bowed legs; thickened wrists and ankles Afebrile · HR 110/min · weight at the 40th percentile Phosphorus concentrationvitamin D deficiency rickets: phosphate falls, because less is absorbed and PTH increases its loss in the urine. PTH and alkaline phosphatase both rise; osteoblasts release the enzyme as they lay down bone matrix

Screening26 of 27 27-year-old woman is planning a pregnancy Her first pregnancy was affected by anencephaly Healthy; takes no medications; eats a varied diet BP 114/72 mm Hg · body mass index 23 kg/m2 · Folic acid 4 mg daily starting before conception · Folic acid 4 mg daily starting at the first prenatal visit · Folic acid 0.4 mg daily starting before conception 27-year-old woman is planning a pregnancy Her first pregnancy was affected by anencephaly Healthy; takes no medications; eats a varied diet BP 114/72 mm Hg · body mass index 23 kg/m2 Folic acid 4 mg daily starting before conceptionafter a prior neural tube defect pregnancy the dose is 4 mg daily, started before conception; 0.4 mg daily is for anyone who could become pregnant, and the first prenatal visit is too late to start

Next step27 of 27 74-year-old woman in a nursing home has 3 months of aching hips and thighs Rarely goes outside trouble rising from a chair; tender bones Afebrile · 25-hydroxyvitamin D 8 ng/mL · calcium normal · kidney function normal · Vitamin D 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks · Vitamin D 1,000 IU daily · Calcitriol daily 74-year-old woman in a nursing home has 3 months of aching hips and thighs Rarely goes outside trouble rising from a chair; tender bones Afebrile · 25-hydroxyvitamin D 8 ng/mL · calcium normal · kidney function normal Vitamin D 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeksosteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency: 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks, then 800 to 1,000 IU daily, rechecking the level in 3 to 4 months. A daily 1,000 IU is the maintenance dose, not the load. Calcitriol, a vitamin D analog, treats low calcium and bone disease when the kidneys or parathyroid glands are not working; her kidney function and calcium are normal

5-day-old boy with bleeding from vitamin K deficiency bleeding from the nose, mouth and gastrointestinal tract subdural hemorrhage Vitamin K therapy is being given In addition to vitamin K, which is the next step? Competing answers Cryoprecipitate: a blood product for bleeding; but it carries fibrinogen, factors VIII and XIII (fibrin-stabilizing factor) and von Willebrand factor, not II, VII, IX or X. Lactated Ringer solution: he is losing blood from several sites; but it restores volume and carries no clotting factors. Platelets: a bleeding newborn; but vitamin K deficiency leaves the platelet count normal, so they replace nothing missing. Down to two: fresh frozen plasma or factor VIII concentrate. Fresh frozen plasma replaces factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S at once, while vitamin K restores them over hours. Factor VIII concentrate treats hemophilia A, and factor VIII does not need vitamin K. The lead-in grants vitamin K, so only the blood product is tested; factor VIII concentrate is the bait.

15-month-old girl has not begun to crawl or walk Exclusively breastfed since birth Length at the 50th and weight at the 85th percentile; language and social skills normal for age widened wrists; examination otherwise normal Which serum finding is most likely to be increased? Competing answers Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity: a liver enzyme beside alkaline phosphatase; but it rises with liver cell injury; a high alkaline phosphatase with normal ALT and GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase) comes from bone. Calcium concentration: a bone mineral; but PTH holds it low or normal; a high calcium points to hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D excess. Magnesium concentration: a mineral tied to calcium balance; but vitamin D deficiency does not raise it; a low magnesium impairs PTH secretion and action. Down to two: alkaline phosphatase activity or phosphorus concentration. Alkaline phosphatase: osteoblasts make it as they lay down matrix, and it is high in active rickets, often before calcium or phosphate falls. Phosphorus falls instead, because absorption drops and PTH increases urinary loss; a high phosphate points to kidney failure or hypoparathyroidism. The key was an enzyme activity set among minerals and a liver enzyme, and the infant's rickets showed only as late crawling and walking with widened wrists.

Wernicke triad confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; often incomplete, so one or two features in a drinker is enough to treat Korsakoff anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation and no insight, older long-term memories relatively preserved; it marks progression (mammillary bodies) and is often permanent Pellagra, the 4 Ds dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death Thiamine level skip it before treating suspected Wernicke: the result is not back in time, so give IV (intravenous) thiamine on suspicion

Vitamin A from excess liver, supplements or retinoids: pseudotumor cerebri (headache, papilledema, high opening pressure), bone pain and fractures, hepatomegaly, dry skin and alopecia, and teratogenicity, the reason isotretinoin needs pregnancy testing and contraception Vitamin D hypercalcemia, from massive overdose or from granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis, where macrophages make 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D without PTH control; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is the level to order for hypercalcemia with suspected sarcoidosis or lymphoma

Poor intake (milk avoidance, lactose intolerance, unfortified vegan diet); malabsorption (Crohn disease, celiac disease, gastrectomy or bariatric surgery); little sun (high latitude, dark skin, indoor life, nursing home, night work); obesity and older age; chronic kidney and liver disease; phenytoin, carbamazepine, isoniazid and rifampin, which speed its breakdown.

Increased platelet sequestration: CF liver disease can enlarge the spleen, but sequestration lowers platelets without lengthening the PT. Reduced von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity: TTP is acute, with thrombocytopenia, hemolysis and neurologic signs. Homocysteine to separate B12 from folate: high in both; only methylmalonic acid separates them. Folic acid for a megaloblastic anemia with numb feet: the blood improves, but the neurologic signs mark B12, and folate alone lets them progress. Vitamin K for bleeding gums: scurvy leaves the PT normal. Folic acid for a vegan: it matters in pregnancy, but vegan diets are folate-rich. Dextrose first in a confused drinker: needed, but thiamine goes in before or with it.

Supplements and periodic levels are lifelong, because deficiencies overlap: B12 (macrocytic anemia, neuropathy, cognitive change); A (night blindness), D and calcium (bone loss with secondary hyperparathyroidism), K (coagulopathy); iron (anemia; the duodenum is bypassed); zinc (alopecia, rash, night blindness); copper (ataxia, weakness and neuropathy that mimic B12 deficiency, with fragile, depigmented hair; check copper when B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal); folate (macrocytic anemia); thiamine (Wernicke, especially with intractable vomiting).

One malabsorption cause usually depletes several fat-soluble vitamins, so a CF or cholestatic patient with one deficiency needs all four checked or replaced. Vitamin A supplementation is standard in severe measles and where deficiency is endemic. Broad-spectrum antibiotics cut gut bacterial production of vitamin K. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 hours), then IX (Christmas factor), X and II (about 60 hours); protein C is also short (about 8 hours), so starting warfarin lowers it first and briefly makes blood hypercoagulable, the reason for heparin bridging and the cause of warfarin skin necrosis. Without vitamin K, the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX and X. Fresh frozen plasma replaces them and proteins C and S at once; vitamin K restores them over hours. B12 neurologic signs can appear before the anemia. Rarer B vitamins: B2 (riboflavin) causes angular cheilitis, stomatitis, glossitis and a normocytic anemia; B5 (pantothenic acid), rare, distal paresthesias; B7 (biotin), rare, from raw egg whites, alopecia and dermatitis. The vegan diet also lowers glucose and cholesterol and reduces cardiovascular risk; on the exam, a well-planned vegan diet is credited as nutritionally adequate except for B12.

Checked September 2026. In force: the Institute of Medicine 2011 cutoffs, still used by the National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements and matched by the 2016 Global Consensus on nutritional rickets: under 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) deficient, 12 to under 20 inadequate, 20 or more adequate, over 50 ng/mL a risk of harm. Retired: the Endocrine Society 2011 set (under 20 deficient, 21 to 29 insufficient, 30 to 100 sufficient); its 2024 guideline endorses no cutoff or target of 30 and advises against routine testing in healthy people. In 2024 it advised empiric supplementation above the daily allowance at ages 1 to 18, over 75, in pregnancy and in high-risk prediabetes; adults 19 to 74 take the usual allowance (600 IU, 800 IU over 70). Unchanged: treat symptomatic deficiency (rickets, osteomalacia) whatever the cutoff. On the exam, older questions may use the 20 and 30 cutoffs, so read the level against the symptoms. Most deficiency is silent or causes vague aches and surfaces as low bone density, fracture or osteomalacia. The vitamin D pathway: skin makes it from 7-dehydrocholesterol with ultraviolet light and diet adds more; the kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase, driven by PTH and suppressed by high calcium, makes the active form, which raises intestinal calcium absorption (its main action) and renal calcium and phosphate reabsorption, mineralizes bone and suppresses PTH.

Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease: is growth poor with greasy stools, and is the sweat chloride high? Part I Hemophilia: is the PT or the aPTT long, and are platelets normal? Part I Night Blindness: vitamin A against retinitis pigmentosa; is the front of the eye normal? Part I Hypercalcemia: vitamin D excess and sarcoidosis; is the 25-hydroxy or the 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D high? Feeding an Infant or Toddler: vitamin D 400 IU for breastfed infants. Part II Fever and Rash in a Child: measles. Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment: the papilledema workup and the other drugs that raise intracranial pressure; is the papilledema bilateral with full visual fields? Part I Tall Stature and Marfanoid Habitus: inherited high homocysteine, treated with B6, folate and B12. Part I Teratogenic Exposures: folate-antagonist antiepileptics and neural tube defects. Part I Tuberculosis: isoniazid with B6.

Read the organ pattern first: eye, bone, dorsal columns with hemolysis, bleeding, brain and eyes, sun-exposed skin with diarrhea, megaloblastic blood, or bleeding gums with normal clotting. Then ask what the patient drinks, takes or does not eat, or why fat is not absorbed. For a diet, ask where each nutrient physically comes from: no unfortified plant source means it must be supplemented. Give thiamine before glucose, and settle B12 before folate alone.

briefs.title: Adolescent Confidentiality
briefs.sub: the exceptions · services protected without parental consent · CRAFFT and brief counseling · encouraging self-disclosureWhat would have to be true to break confidentiality, and is any of it present?
blocks: the exceptions · services protected without parental consent · CRAFFT and brief counseling · encouraging self-disclosureWhat would have to be true to break confidentiality, and is any of it present?

Pt 16 yo M, well, discloses weekend marijuana use during the confidential portion of the visit Q the most appropriate next step; options spanned confidential counseling with CRAFFT screening, informing his parents and ordering a urine drug screen

A minor discloses substance use during a confidential interview. In this case, keep it confidential and counsel him directly. Substance use is a confidential service in essentially every state, and nothing he describes meets an exception. Confidentiality is what makes honest disclosure possible at all; adolescents who don't expect it don't disclose. Set the frame before he talks by saying "what you tell me stays between us, unless someone's safety is at risk". Then screen with CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble), deliver brief counseling, and encourage him to tell his parents himself. Encouraging voluntary disclosure is not the same as disclosing.

Suicidal or homicidal intent harm to self or others; break confidentiality Physical or sexual abuse including statutory abuse by partner age; break confidentiality and report Imminent danger specific and serious; imminence is the word that decides Not an exception vagueness, a parent asking, an embarrassing diagnosis, or risky behavior that is not imminently lethal

Adolescent confidentiality – what is protected Confidential without parental consent Sexually transmitted infection diagnosis and treatment (all 50 states) Contraception Pregnancy care (abortion varies – many states require notification or consent) Substance use evaluation and treatment Mental health services (age and state vary) Emancipated / mature minors: married, military, parenting, self-supporting, court-declared → consent as adults

"Inform his parents": parental authority is the higher principle for most care, but the confidential-services carve-outs exist to override it (trump-card inversion) "Tell him you can't promise confidentiality": this sounds true but is harmful; frame confidentiality as conditional, naming the specific exceptions, not as a blanket refusal "Refer to a substance-use program": escalating before you have screened severity is a sequencing trap; occasional use gets brief counseling, not a program "Order a urine drug screen": he already told you. Testing to confirm a disclosure is redundant, and a non-consented screen is its own ethics violation.
HEEADSSS (Home, Education and employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and depression, Safety) is the adolescent psychosocial history, asked privately.

Next step1 of 11 16 yo M discloses weekend marijuana use, otherwise well · Inform his parents · Order a urine drug screen · Confidential counseling, CRAFFT, encourage self-disclosure to parents 16 yo M discloses weekend marijuana use, otherwise well Confidential counseling, CRAFFT, encourage self-disclosure to parents

Next step2 of 11 16 yo M discloses use and says he's been thinking about killing himself · Break confidentiality – safety exception · Refer to outpatient counseling only · Maintain confidentiality, follow up in a week 16 yo M discloses use and says he's been thinking about killing himself Break confidentiality – safety exception

Next step3 of 11 16 yo M who drives after drinking · Break confidentiality and inform parents · Maintain confidentiality and counsel about the driving · Report him to the DMV 16 yo M who drives after drinking Maintain confidentiality and counsel about the drivingescalate only if he describes an imminent plan to drive impaired

Next step4 of 11 15 yo F requesting contraception, doesn't want her mother told · Defer until she tells her mother · Require parental consent · Provide it confidentially 15 yo F requesting contraception, doesn't want her mother told Provide it confidentially

Next step5 of 11 15 yo F at 15 weeks, sexual partner is 24 years old · Counsel about contraception only · Maintain confidentiality · Report it 15 yo F at 15 weeks, sexual partner is 24 years old Report itthe age gap converts this to statutory abuse

Next step6 of 11 17 yo M with chlamydia · Withhold partner notification · Inform his parents before treating · Treat confidentially; partner notification is a public-health obligation and does not breach his confidentiality 17 yo M with chlamydia Treat confidentially; partner notification is a public-health obligation and does not breach his confidentiality

Next step7 of 11 17 yo F, married, needs surgery · Seek a court order · She is emancipated and consents herself · Obtain parental consent 17 yo F, married, needs surgery She is emancipated and consents herself

Next step8 of 11 16 yo M whose mother calls to ask what was discussed · Disclose the full content of the visit · Decline to disclose; redirect to encouraging the conversation at home · Disclose only the substance use 16 yo M whose mother calls to ask what was discussed Decline to disclose; redirect to encouraging the conversation at home

Next step9 of 11 14 yo M with an appendectomy needed · Accept the minor's assent alone · Parental consent required · Proceed under confidential-services law 14 yo M with an appendectomy needed Parental consent requiredsurgical care is not a confidential service

Next step10 of 11 16 yo M, opioid use with withdrawal symptoms and IV track marks · Inform parents and refer without telling him · Severity now warrants treatment referral, still discussed with him first · Continue brief counseling only 16 yo M, opioid use with withdrawal symptoms and IV track marks Severity now warrants treatment referral, still discussed with him first

Next step11 of 11 16 yo M in a state where billing goes to the parent's insurance · Address the practical confidentiality limit up front; this is the real-world failure point · Decline to provide the service · Reassure that billing is always confidential 16 yo M in a state where billing goes to the parent's insurance Address the practical confidentiality limit up front; this is the real-world failure point

Set the frame before the disclosure; confidentiality cannot be promised retroactively CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble) is the validated adolescent screen; ≥2 is positive emergency care never waits for consent Management almost always includes "encourage him to tell his parents", which preserves confidentiality and the family relationship.

Elder Abuseabove covers the same axis in the opposite direction. There, impaired capacityforces reporting over the patient's wishes. Here, a minor with a confidential serviceforces confidentiality over the parent's wishes. Both turn on who holds decisional authority for this specific decision, not on who is older Elder Abuse above covers the same axis in the opposite direction. There, impaired capacity forces reporting over the patient's wishes. Here, a minor with a confidential service forces confidentiality over the parent's wishes. Both turn on who holds decisional authority for this specific decision, not on who is older.

Maintain confidentiality unless the disclosure satisfies a named exception (harm to self, harm to others, abuse). Do not weigh how serious the behavior sounds; without a named exception, confidentiality holds no matter how alarming the disclosure.

briefs.title: Decision-Making Capacity and Informed Consent
briefs.sub: the four abilities · what consent covers · WIPE exceptions · who decidesCan this patient make this decision now?
blocks: the four abilities · what consent covers · WIPE exceptions · who decidesCan this patient make this decision now?

Capacity is judged by the treating physician for the proposed treatment: the patient communicates a choice, appreciates the consequences, reasons and demonstrates understanding (CARD); competence is a legal finding by a judge Consent is sought from every patient: an involuntary hold, a psychiatric diagnosis or mild intellectual disability does not by itself remove capacity; if drugs or sedation may be interfering and the procedure is not urgent, do not proceed: reassess when the effects wear off Without capacity: the living will, then the health care proxy (the two parts of an advance directive), then family, typically the spouse, adult children, parents, siblings, though the order varies by state; with no one, the best interest standard; a life-threatening emergency is treated without consent

Informed consent needs a patient with capacity, disclosure of the diagnosis and of the benefits, risks and alternatives (including no treatment), and a voluntary choice free from coercion; a patient with capacity may refuse

Decision-making capacity (CARD) Ability The patient shows Communicates a choice Makes the decision known Appreciates How the facts and consequences apply to their own situation Reasons Describes how the choice was reached; it need not be the choice the physician prefers Demonstrates understanding The benefits, risks and alternatives, including no treatment

Exceptions to informed consent (WIPE) Exception When it applies Waiver The patient explicitly declines the discussion, as for surgery or research; a patient may also choose not to know Incompetent Under 18, or an adult who cannot make the decision: a surrogate decides for the adult; for minors, see Adolescent Confidentiality Therapeutic privilege Withholding information that may harm the patient; only when the harm is very likely, not merely hypothetical Emergency A life-threatening condition, when waiting for a surrogate would raise the risk of death or serious harm

Who decides when the patient cannot Decision maker When it decides Living will (part of an advance directive) First, when it applies to the situation Health care proxy (durable power of attorney), the other part of an advance directive has paperwork indicating that she is her mother's healthcare proxyIn a vignetteLacks capacity: Her verbal communication is limited to one-word answers Next; decides in line with the patient's wishes and overrules all family members Family surrogate With no proxy: spouse, then adult children, parents, siblings, deciding as the patient would (substituted judgment); the order varies by state Someone who knows the patient's wishes No family available Physicians, by best interest No living will or surrogate: two-physician consent; with no known relative or proxy, a court-appointed fiduciary is an option

When capacity is in doubt Step Do Before judging Remove communication barriers first Reversible causes Look for delirium, drug or medication effects, hypoxia, infection or a metabolic derangement; if drugs are the cause, reassess when their effects wear off Delirium Interview Test the four abilities for this decision; cognitive testing helps but is not required Still uncertain Consult a psychiatrist, especially with a psychiatric history; the treating physician decides; if doubt remains after a full evaluation, do not restrict the patient's choice, since restricting autonomy needs a high burden of proof Afterward Record the evaluation in the medical record

Commonly confused Pair Decides it Capacity or competence Capacity is a medical judgment by the treating physician about a proposed treatment; competence is a legal finding by a judge Refusal or incapacity Refusing a clearly beneficial treatment may prompt an evaluation, but the patient needs only to reason through the information Involuntary hold or incapacity A hold does not remove the right to refuse treatment for a condition that is not life-threatening Sedated or incapacitated Drug effects may be temporary: for a nonurgent procedure, do not proceed; reassess later Psychiatric illness or incapacity A diagnosis does not remove capacity; poor reasoning from active psychiatric illness can Surrogate or patient Family consents only after the patient is found to lack capacity Family request or disclosure A family asking to withhold a serious diagnosis is usually met by a thoughtful talk with them and sensitive disclosure; withholding (therapeutic privilege) is rare Comfort care or invasive feeding When the proxy reports the patient wanted comfort care, avoid invasive or diagnostic procedures, including IV, nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding; offer food by mouth, the least invasive way to give nutrition

Pause point Patient whose choice you disagree with Overridden for the choice, a hold or a diagnosis Can this patient make this decision now? → Outside a life-threatening emergency, none is a reason to override Impairment that may wear off means wait and reassess.

Next step1 of 6 45-year-old man brought in after a bar fight smells of alcohol and slurs his words A 2-cm scalp cut has stopped bleeding; he refuses stitches and asks to sleep it off Vital signs are normal · Ask his wife to consent by phoneA surrogate consents only after the patient is found to lack capacity · Repair it now: intoxication removes his capacityLost capacity is not assumed; only an emergency proceeds without consent · Defer the repair and reassess when he is soberDrug effects may be temporary; a nonurgent repair can wait 45-year-old man brought in after a bar fight smells of alcohol and slurs his words A 2-cm scalp cut has stopped bleeding; he refuses stitches and asks to sleep it off Vital signs are normal Defer the repair and reassess when he is soberA nonbleeding laceration poses no imminent harm, and alcohol may only temporarily affect his ability to consent, so the repair waits and he is reassessed; a surrogate decides only if he lacks capacity

Next step2 of 6 70-year-old woman hospitalized with pneumonia wants to go home on day 2 She explains the risks of leaving, including death, and says she accepts them She is alert and oriented; her son demands that she stay · Hold her until a judge rules on competenceCompetence is a legal question; her capacity is intact · Discharge her against medical adviceA patient with capacity may refuse treatment, even against advice · Keep her: her son is her surrogateA surrogate decides only when the patient lacks capacity 70-year-old woman hospitalized with pneumonia wants to go home on day 2 She explains the risks of leaving, including death, and says she accepts them She is alert and oriented; her son demands that she stay Discharge her against medical adviceShe communicates a choice and shows understanding, appreciation and reasoning, so she has capacity and may leave against medical advice; family decides only when capacity is lacking

Next step3 of 6 78-year-old man is intubated after a stroke and cannot communicate He has no living will or health care proxy His wife and his adult daughter disagree about whether he would want a feeding tube · Follow his wife's decisionThe spouse typically comes first among family surrogates · Obtain two-physician consentUsed only when there is no living will or surrogate · Follow his daughter's decisionAdult children typically come after the spouse 78-year-old man is intubated after a stroke and cannot communicate He has no living will or health care proxy His wife and his adult daughter disagree about whether he would want a feeding tube Follow his wife's decisionWithout a living will or proxy, family members typically decide in the order spouse, adult children, parents, siblings, judging what he would want; two-physician consent is for patients with no surrogate

Next step4 of 6 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia needs a decision about surgery for a hip fracture Years ago she named her close friend as her health care proxy Her three children disagree with the friend's choice · Follow the majority of her childrenFamily decides only when there is no proxy · Petition a court to appoint a health fiduciaryAn option for a patient with no known relative or proxy, not one with a proxy · Follow the health care proxyA designated proxy overrules all other decision makers 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia needs a decision about surgery for a hip fracture Years ago she named her close friend as her health care proxy Her three children disagree with the friend's choice Follow the health care proxyA health care proxy holds durable power of attorney and overrules all family members; a court-appointed health fiduciary is an option for patients with no known relative or proxy

Next step5 of 6 30-year-old man arrives unconscious after a car crash with a ruptured spleen and falling blood pressure No family can be reached, and he carries no advance directive The surgeon is ready to operate · Operate without consentA life-threatening emergency is an exception to informed consent · Wait until family can be locatedDelay for a surrogate would raise the risk of death · Obtain a court order firstEmergency care cannot wait; a reasonable person would consent 30-year-old man arrives unconscious after a car crash with a ruptured spleen and falling blood pressure No family can be reached, and he carries no advance directive The surgeon is ready to operate Operate without consentWhen delay to find a surrogate would raise the risk of death or serious harm, emergency care proceeds without formal consent, on the assumption that a reasonable person would agree

Next step6 of 6 33-year-old woman with schizophrenia is on an involuntary psychiatric hold She declines removal of a benign-appearing skin mole, citing the scar She is calm, explains the risks and benefits, and repeats her choice · Remove it: the hold allows treatmentA hold does not authorize nonemergency treatment · Ask her mother to consentA surrogate decides only when capacity is lacking · Respect her refusalShe shows capacity; a hold does not remove the right to refuse 33-year-old woman with schizophrenia is on an involuntary psychiatric hold She declines removal of a benign-appearing skin mole, citing the scar She is calm, explains the risks and benefits, and repeats her choice Respect her refusalPatients on an involuntary hold keep the right to refuse treatment for a condition that is not life-threatening, and a psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity
Adolescent Confidentialityconsent by and for minors Deliriuma reversible cause of lost capacity Adolescent Confidentiality: consent by and for minors. Delirium: a reversible cause of lost capacity.
Ask whether this patient can make this decision now; without an emergency, a capable refusal stands, and impairment that may wear off means wait and reassess.

briefs.title: Psychosis
briefs.sub: rule out a cause, then time itHow long, and only during mood episodes?
blocks: rule out a cause, then time itHow long, and only during mood episodes?

Likely harm to self or others, or unable to meet basic needs hospitalize first Toxicology chemistry and glucose TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) then time it: brief under 1 month, schizophreniform 1 to under 6 months, schizophrenia 6 months or more Delusions only, 1 month or more, Criterion A for schizophrenia (2 or more of its symptoms) never met delusional disorder; psychosis only inside mood episodes mood disorder

What it is Delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech, named by how long they last and how they relate to mood episodes Driver Schizophrenia: genes explain about 80% of the risk in twin and family studies MechanismSchizophrenia, proposed mechanismProposed: excess mesolimbic dopamine is thought to contribute to positive symptoms; lower mesocortical dopamine may be involved in negative and cognitive symptoms Triggers Family history non-modifiable heavy cannabis useCannabis risk6 times the risk in one study A marked stressor, or onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartumPostpartumPostpartum brief psychotic disorder raises the risk of suicide and infanticide. (brief psychotic disorder) Chain Schizophrenia: prodrome active psychosis, 1 month or more (less if treated) residual; 6 months in all SchizophreniformCourseSchizophreniform may evolve into schizophrenia, bipolar or schizoaffective disorder Insights Symptoms outlast a window re-time the whole illness Criterion A with a mood episode psychosis 2 weeks or more without one mood most of the illness schizoaffective

Course and specifiersdetail behind the chain 1 day to under 1 month, then full return to baseline; specifiers: with marked stressor; with postpartum onset 6 months or more, with functional decline; onset early 20s in men, later in women Age at onsetOnset runs from the late teens to the mid-30s, so a teen can have it; childhood onset is rare and has a poorer prognosis.

Criterion A, symptoms 2 or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speechIn a vignetteDisorganized speech: nonsensical or unrelated answers. Catatonia may show mutism, purposeless movement, fixed postures or staring., disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms, such as alogia (little speech): most of his replies are “yes” or “no.”In a vignetteAvolition: began to wear the same clothes for several days in a row; poorly groomedNegative symptoms: Social withdrawal, poor eye contact, neglected hygiene, lost motivation, flat affect, little speech, no pleasure. They count toward Criterion A.Disorganized behavior: sending e-mails to his friends, though he had not been connected to the internet for 3 months Criterion A, core at least 1 is delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech Duration 6 months or more in all, with at least 1 month of active symptoms (less if treated) Decline work or relationships fall since onset Cause not a substance, medication or medical condition; schizoaffective and psychotic mood disorders excluded

Time the psychosisnot to scale Brief psychotic disorder1 day to under 1 month Day 11 month6 months→ Needs1 or more core symptoms; full return to baseline Mood episodesNot only during them Schizophreniform disorder1 to under 6 months Day 11 month6 months→ NeedsCriterion A Mood episodesNone, or a minority of the illness Schizophrenia6 months or more in all ProdromeActiveResidual Day 11 month6 months→ Active symptoms 1 month or more (less if treated); prodrome and residual count toward the 6 months NeedsCriterion A; functional decline Mood episodesNone, or a minority of the illness Delusions only: Criterion A never met Delusional disorder1 month or more Day 11 month6 months→ NeedsOne or more delusions; no second Criterion A symptom; hallucinations, if any, not prominent and tied to the delusion; otherwise functioning and behavior intact Mood episodesBrief, if any Timed to a drug or its withdrawal, not a window Substance-induced psychotic disorderDuring or soon after intoxication or withdrawal Day 11 month6 months→ NeedsDelusions or hallucinations tied to a drug Mood episodesNot a criterion Every condition in a row is required. These are windows, not stages: when symptoms outlast one, re-time the whole illness.

Check it against mood episodestime → Mood disorder with psychotic featuresPsychosis only inside manic or major depressive episodes Mood Psychosis High moodLow moodPsychosis Schizoaffective disorderCriterion A with a major mood episode (a depressive one must include depressed mood), psychosis 2 weeks or more alone, and mood most of the illness Mood Psychosis 2 wk+ alone High moodLow moodPsychosisPsychosis with no mood episode SchizophreniaMood episodes, if any, a minority of the illness Mood Psychosis Low moodPsychosisPsychosis with no mood episode High moodLow moodPsychosisPsychosis with no mood episode

DangerLikely harm to self or others, or cannot meet basic needs Involuntary criteria American Psychiatric Association positionA mental disorder; hospital care can help; the patient is unable or unwilling to consent; the least restrictive option. Commitment law varies by state. If harm is likely or basic needs go unmet, choose hospitalization first, whatever the duration; involuntarily only when the criteria and state law allow. MedicalPsychosis with disturbed attention and awareness that develops over hours to days and fluctuates Delirium If it occurs only during a delirium, choose the delirium workup, not a psychotic disorder.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Schizophrenia Criterion A with functional decline 6 months or more, at least 1 month active Delusional disorder 1 or more delusions, often non-bizarreDelusion themesThemes: persecutory (being harmed), referential (cues aimed at the self), grandiose, erotomanic (another person is in love with the patient), jealous (a partner is unfaithful; the person typically searches for evidence), somatic, nihilistic (the self or world does not exist or is ending). (eg, somatic: sure of a parasite infestation); hallucinations, if any, not prominent and tied to the delusion; apart from the delusion, functioning not markedly impaired 1 month or more; no second Criterion A symptom Brief psychotic disorder 1 or more core symptoms, often after a stressor 1 day to under 1 month; full return to baseline Schizophreniform disorder Criterion A 1 to under 6 months; functional decline not required Schizoaffective disorder Criterion A with major mood episodes at the same time Psychosis 2 weeks or more without a mood episode; mood most of the illness Bipolar type includes a manic episode; depressive type, only major depressive episodes Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features Delusions with euphoric mood and less sleep Mania 1 week or more (any length if hospitalized); psychosis only inside mood episodes Substance-induced psychotic disorder (medication-induced psychotic disorder, when a medication is the cause) Delusions or hallucinations tied to a drug During or soon after intoxication or withdrawal, or after a medication; lasting about 1 month after stopping suggests an independent disorder Adjustment disorder Distress after a stressor Within 3 months of the stressor; psychosis would be atypical PTSD (posttraumatic stress disorder) Symptoms after an event More than 1 month; trauma that threatens death or injury; intrusions and avoidance Acute stress disorder Trauma symptoms soon after the eventThe pictureIntrusive re-experiencing with hyperarousal, dissociation and avoidance, for up to 1 month.
