No cause found: time the psychosis, then check it against mood episodes.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Symptoms past 1 month No longer brief psychotic disorder Re-time it: schizophreniform if Criterion A; delusions only, delusional disorder A delusion for 1 month or more, works normally, no other Criterion A symptom Delusional disorder Not schizophrenia: Criterion A needs 2 symptoms One fixed belief about one person (eg, an unfaithful spouse) in an older adult who still runs the household and finances; only occasional word-finding lapses Delusional disorder, not paranoid personality disorder or dementia Why notLook-alikesParanoid personality disorder: a lifelong pattern of distrust of others from early adulthood, generally pervasive rather than aimed at one person, and not of delusional intensity. Alzheimer disease may bring delusions of jealousy, but typically in the middle to late course; dementia needs cognitive impairment severe enough to affect activities of daily living, such as managing finances. Occasional name and word-finding lapses are relatively age-normal. Sees or hears the deceased; organized speech Normal grief SupportNot griefDisorganized speech or bizarre behavior after the loss is brief psychotic disorder, which a death can trigger. Psychosis after a stressor, no intrusions or avoidance Not a trauma disorder Under 1 month with full recovery: brief psychotic disorder, even after a life-threatening event Drank the night it began; it outlasted the drinking Substance cause unlikely One night of drinking rarely causes psychosis: keep timing it WithdrawalAlcohol withdrawalStopping differs: after heavy, prolonged drinking ends, hallucinations can come with a clear sensorium, in the window of withdrawal seizures. Began during stimulant intoxication Substance-induced Stop the drug; reassess the timing First psychosis at 40 or older, or visual hallucinations More likely medical (delusional disorder can still start then) Find the medical cause first; MRI only with a neurologic finding Older adult with voices and persecutory delusions, a psychiatric admission decades ago, on an antipsychotic; exam and MRI normal Schizophrenia, not a new late-life psychosis Chronic, persistent symptoms make schizophrenia the leading diagnosis; alcohol-induced is unlikely after a year abstinent Psychosis with seizures, abnormal movements or autonomic instability Autoimmune encephalitis, eg anti-NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor Serum and spinal fluid antibodies; linked to ovarian teratoma Loss of interest with psychosis, but no depressed mood Not a major depressive episode for schizoaffective disorder Count only episodes with depressed mood

Pause point One fixed delusion for months Offered as schizophrenia All the options The optionsBipolar disorder: grandiose claims; but no low or high mood, and normal sleep. Brief psychotic disorder: an acute presentation after an arrest; but it lasts under 1 month, and his delusion has lasted 6 months. Schizoaffective disorder: a persecutory delusion; but no mood episode and no second Criterion A symptom. Schizophrenia: a fixed persecutory delusion; but it needs a second Criterion A symptom, and delusions are his only symptom. Down to two: delusional disorder or schizophrenia. Delusional disorder: delusions alone (grandiose and persecutory) for 6 months; no voices, mood episode or disorganization; sleep and labs normal. It needs a second Criterion A symptom → Delusional disorder In practice NBME versus criteriaIn practice: NBME says no hallucinations at all; current criteria allow minor ones tied to the delusion. A week of psychosis after a stressor, full recovery Offered as delusional disorder or PTSD All the options The optionsAdjustment disorder: a clear stressor; but psychotic symptoms would be atypical. Delusional disorder: paranoid beliefs; but it needs 1 month or more, and his lasted a week. Posttraumatic stress disorder: a distressing event; but job loss is not life-threatening, and it needs intrusions and over 1 month. Schizophreniform disorder: delusions and a voice; but it needs 1 to 6 months. Substance-induced psychotic disorder: six drinks and monthly cannabis; but psychosis rarely comes from alcohol directly, and he uses cannabis only occasionally. Down to two: brief psychotic disorder or delusional disorder. Brief psychotic disorder: after a stressor, paranoid delusions and a voice that cleared within a week, well under 1 month. A week with full recovery → Brief psychotic disorder Voices and persecutory delusions in an older adult, a year abstinent from alcohol Offered as alcohol-induced psychotic disorder Symptoms persist through a year without alcohol → Schizophrenia: chronic, persistent symptoms

What it is Maintenance care after an episode, first or later: fewer relapses and admissions, better quality of life Driver Stress in a vulnerable patient can bring symptoms back support, coping skills and the antipsychotic may buffer it Triggers Stopping the antipsychotic (most relapse within 12 months of a first episode) Critical, hostile or overinvolved family substance use, especially cannabis Job or income loss, leaving home for college, a breakup, joining the Armed Forces Chain Missed doses, conflict or drugs relapse admission may be needed if severe Function may decline over the first 5 years then plateaus Insights Worse while taking every dose what changed in his life, not the drug, comes first Family conflict more stress voices take on darker meaning, less reserve to cope

Long-term course, stage by stagedetail behind the chain Outcome tracks adherence to medication and avoiding illicit drugs Continuous antipsychotic use, with long-acting forms, can bring 1-year relapse to about 30% or loweraims: fewer recurrences and admissions, better quality of life Skill training and vocational programs help many work, shop, care for themselves and get along with others Poor diet, weight gain, smoking and substance use shorten life by about 13 to 15 years About 15% to 25% recover; about a third improve but relapse or keep some disability; up to 40% do poorly Better: female sex, good premorbid function, late or sudden onset, a clear precipitant, few negative symptoms, short untreated psychosisworse: male sex, young onset, poor premorbid function, family history of schizophrenia, many negative symptoms, long untreated psychosis

DangerDanger to himself or others, or unable to care for himself (not eating or washing); for example, a voice commanding harm plus a hidden weapon Refuses to say what command voices tell him: a concerning sign. Involuntary criteria American Psychiatric Association (APA) positionA mental disorder makes harm to self or others, or unmet basic needs, likely; hospital care can help; he is unable or unwilling to consent; it is the least restrictive option. Commitment law varies by state. If he is a danger or cannot care for himself, choose hospitalization: voluntary first, involuntary if he refuses; safety before family therapy. SuicideAbout 5% die by suicide and about 20% attempt it In practiceIn practiceOther references give a lifetime risk of death by suicide of 5% to 10%. Suicidal behavior that persists: clozapine Suicide Risk Assessment If he is a danger to himself, choose hospitalization, involuntary if necessary.

Why is he relapsing, most tempting first Driver Fingerprint Decides it Family conflict or high expressed emotion Criticism, hostility or overinvolvement; he takes his doses Conflict just before the worsening; family therapy first, as an outpatient, then a dose change Nonadherence Missed or forgotten oral doses or refills; poor insight ("I don't have an illness") or stopping the drug over side effects such as weight gain; well on the drug in hospital, then relapsing within months of each discharge Poor or uncertain adherence, not a failed drug; long-acting injectable Poor engagement with services Missed injections or visits with frequent admissions, homelessness or legal trouble History of poor engagement behind the relapses; assertive community treatment Schizoaffective disorder Mood symptoms with the psychosis Mood episodes for most of the illness Treatment resistance Voices persist on adequate doses 2 or more adequate trials fail, adherence documented Substance use Especially cannabis or hallucinogens Use before the recurrence; strongly discourage it: it predicts a poor outcome Other life stressor Lost job or income, left home, a breakup A non-family stressor just before the worsening; support and coping skills for it first, since they may buffer stress; the drug continues

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Relapse: voices or delusions return or worsen → Assess danger to himself or others, and self-care Danger to himself or others, or cannot care for himself Hospitalize, involuntarily if necessary Next step TestResultMeans Safe → Ask what changed: adherenceEngagement with servicesLife events Missed or forgotten oral doses Long-acting injectable Receiving every injection on time Not an adherence problem Missed injections or visits, frequent admissions, homelessness Assertive community treatment Family conflict just before Family therapy first Substance use Strongly discourage it; it can trigger recurrence Driver treated, still worse → Adjust the treatment SkipNo test names the driver of a relapse; the history of what changed does.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Anxious and jittery after a stressor, dose unchanged Distress, not the cause Lorazepam may ease anxiety; it treats neither the psychosis nor its cause Cannot sit still, an inner urge to move, after a start or dose increase Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Akathisia, an adverse effect of the drug Lower the dose; propranolol if the dose must stay Never a manic or depressive episode Schizophrenia, not schizoaffective No lithium: unhelpful in schizophrenia Not dangerous; a stressor drives the relapse Outpatient care No partial hospital program or clozapine at this point

Pause point Voices rose after a family argument in a patient receiving his injections Offered: a higher dose, clozapine or lithium All the options The optionsPartial hospital program: his voices are worse; but it is not necessary now: address the conflict as an outpatient first. Move to a halfway house: it would separate him from critical parents; but NBME judged it not appropriate: he has no criminal history. Add lithium carbonate: an add-on drug for a relapse; but in schizoaffective disorder it is sometimes given for mood symptoms; in schizophrenia it is unhelpful. Add lorazepam: he looks anxious and jittery; it may ease anxiety but addresses neither the psychosis nor its likely root, the family conflict. Switch haloperidol to clozapine: the voices are breaking through; but a switch is not necessary at this point; the immediate stressor comes first. Increase the haloperidol dose: it targets the voices; but it is a later step, to consider once the family conflict has been addressed. Down to two: family therapy or adding lithium. Family therapy: family conflict is a risk factor for worsening psychosis, and the argument came just before the voices increased in a patient receiving his injections. Treat that stressor first, as an outpatient; then consider a higher haloperidol dose or frequency. The conflict came just before the worsening → Family therapy first; a dose change follows

1 Alwaysevery patient, once improved Continue the antipsychotic 2 Nextworse on his doses, with a stressor just before Treat the stressor as an outpatient: family therapy for a family conflict Not dangerous: a partial hospital program is not needed now. 3 Thenstressor treated, voices still more frequent A higher dose or dosing frequency A switch to clozapine is not needed yet.

Match the added treatment to the problem Situation Choose Watch for Ongoing contact with family, or a critical family (for open conflict, the family therapy in the ladder above) Family intervention: psychoeducation, understanding, communication, coping skills Not while nonadherence keeps causing relapses: add it once symptoms are stable and the cycle of relapse and admission is broken EvidenceCochrane reviewIt may cut relapses and admissions and help him take his medication; the trials were weak, so the benefit may be overstated. Poor or uncertain adherence, or he prefers it Long-acting injectable antipsychoticWho fitsAn injection every few weeks to months. It fits unstable illness, living alone, poor support, poor insight and frequent nonadherence. Haloperidol, fluphenazine, risperidone, paliperidone, olanzapine and aripiprazole all come as long-acting injectables. Not for a patient already receiving his injections Missed injections or visits with frequent relapse, homelessness or legal trouble Assertive community treatmentWhat it isA team with many staff per patient brings all or nearly all care to his home or residence. Not for a patient who keeps his visits and injections Wants competitive paid work, even if now in a sheltered workshop Supported employment: a competitive job with an on-site coach Improved on an adequate trial, adherent, but voices or delusions persist Add CBT for psychosisWhat it isCognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis, alone or in a group, aimed at lessening delusional thoughts, hallucinations and negative symptoms. alongside the drug Not in place of the antipsychotic Little or no response after 1 adequate trial (at least 4 weeks at a therapeutic dose), adherent A different antipsychotic One failed trial is not resistance: no clozapine yet 2 or more failed adequate trials, adherence documented Clozapine Psychosis Goal of getting along better with others Social skills trainingNegative symptomsIt aims at negative symptoms such as flat affect, poor eye contact and withdrawal, which antipsychotics treat less well, by practicing skills such as starting a conversation. Not while nonadherence keeps causing relapses: add it once symptoms are stable and the cycle of relapse and admission is broken Every patient, alongside the matched choice Psychoeducation

Guideline strengthsAPA 2020American Psychiatric Association 2020: recommended for continuing the antipsychotic, psychoeducation, CBT for psychosis, supported employment, assertive community treatment; suggested, the weaker grade, for family intervention, a long-acting injectable, social skills training.

Follow-up decisions When Do Improved on an antipsychotic Continue it indefinitelyIn practice:Step 2: for recurrent episodes, lifelong at the lowest effective dose. Practice references keep it for 1 to 2 years or more after a first episode, and for many years after a longer illness; Step 2 keys continue indefinitely, even after a first episode; off it, 65% to 80% relapse within 12 months of a first episode Every visit Look for adherence barriers and early signs of relapse On any antipsychotic Monitor regularly for metabolic adverse effects Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Chronic risk of suicidal behavior or aggression, once the acute danger is handled Clozapine, per the American Psychiatric Association; its label covers lowering the risk of recurrent suicidal behavior in schizophrenia Suicide Risk Assessment

Psychosiscovers which psychotic disorder by duration and the antipsychotic ladder up to clozapine; this brief covers what to add around the drug. Here, a higher dose or frequency is considered after a treated stressor in a patient already receiving his doses (NBME); that brief switches to a different antipsychotic for little or no response after 1 adequate trial (at least 4 weeks at a therapeutic dose); here, a partial response with residual voices gets CBT for psychosis added alongside the drug. Ask: is the question which disorder, which drug, or what to add? Danger to himself or others comes before every other step. When a patient who is receiving his antipsychotic gets worse, ask what changed in his life before changing the drug, and treat that first.

briefs.title: Bipolar Disorder
briefs.sub: rule out a cause, time the episode, then treatMania or hypomania, and what to start or stop?
blocks: rule out a cause, time the episode, then treatMania or hypomania, and what to start or stop?

Mania is an emergency; danger to self or others hospitalize (often needed)InsightInsight is usually limited: most do not see themselves as ill or needing treatment. Drug screen and TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) first, then time it: mania 1 week (any length if hospitalized), hypomania 4 days Stop any antidepressant; start lithium, valproate (not in anyone who could become pregnant), quetiapine, aripiprazole or risperidone

What it is At least 1 manic episode bipolar I; depression common, not required Hypomania major depression, never mania bipolar II Driver Highly heritable: 70 to 90% Triggers Family history non-modifiable childhood maltreatment, linked to developing the disorder later in life Stressful events linked to onset: childbirthPostpartumPostpartum psychosis (hallucinations, delusions and mood symptoms within 4 weeks of childbirth) is strongly linked to bipolar I., divorce, unemployment Chain Onset in the teens to 30s recurrent manic and depressive episodes Most suicide deaths occur in the depressive phase Insights Psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization mania; not the height of the mood Grandiose delusion only inside the episode bipolar, not schizophrenia

Course and risks, stage by stagedetail behind the chain Usually in the teens, 20s or 30s; men and women equally (bipolar I); a first episode late in life calls for a search for a medical or neurologic cause Childhood maltreatment, especially emotional abuse or neglect; childbirth, divorce, unemployment, disability, early parental loss Recurrent CourseRapid cycling is 4 or more mood episodes in 12 months. A worse course comes with substance use, mixed or psychotic features, rapid cycling, earlier onset and childhood adversity.; most need maintenance for many years, possibly lifelongcontinuous rather than intermittent treatment Most suicide deaths occur in the depressive phase; suicide rate about 20 to 30 times the general population In bipolar depression, an antidepressant alone risks a switch to mania or mood instability; in mania, antidepressants are stopped

Mood elevated, expansive or irritable mood plus more energy, most of the day, nearly every day Duration 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalization is necessary Symptoms 3 or more DIGFAST symptoms, 4 if the mood is only irritable Severity marked impairment, hospitalization to prevent harm, or psychotic features Cause not a substance or medical condition; an episode that outlasts an antidepressant still counts

Distractibility attention too easily drawn to irrelevant stimuli Indiscretion painful consequences: buying sprees, sexual behaviors, foolish business investments, quitting a job abruptly, trespassing Grandiosity inflated self-esteemGrandiosityIncludes a mission only that person can carry out, and confidence in areas with no training or experience. Flight of ideas thoughts are racing Activity increased goal-directed, or psychomotor agitation Sleep decreased feels rested and energetic after 2 to 3 hours or none; not insomnia, where the person is tired but cannot sleep Talkativeness pressure to keep talking; loud, joking or laughing, disinhibited with strangers

Time the episodenot to scale Hypomanic episode4 days or more in a row Day 14 days1 week2 weeks2 years→ NeedsThe same symptom count; a clear change that others notice NeverMarked impairment, hospitalization or psychosis Manic episode1 week or more; any length if hospitalized If hospitalized Day 14 days1 week2 weeks2 years→ PlusMarked impairment, hospitalization or psychosis Major depressive episode2 weeks or more Day 14 days1 week2 weeks2 years→ Needs5 or more symptoms, one of them depressed mood or loss of interest A disorder, not an episode Cyclothymic disorder2 years or more (1 year in children) Day 14 days1 week2 weeks2 years→ NeedsUp and down symptoms at least half the time, never 2 months free NeverA manic, hypomanic or major depressive episode Each bar starts at the minimum duration. Severity, not the height of the mood, separates mania from hypomania.

DangerMania with risk of harm to self or others If harm is a risk, choose psychiatric hospitalization. AgitationSevere agitation or manic psychosis Lithium takes 4 to 10 days, so a faster drug is often given If safety is compromised, choose an antipsychotic, first or second generation (eg, haloperidol), sometimes lorazepam at first. DepressionBipolar depression Suicide Risk Assessment If the episode is depressive, choose suicide risk assessment first. MedicalEpigastric pain with vomiting on valproate, at any dose or duration curled into a ball on the examination table In a vignetteEpigastric tenderness: tenderness to palpation of the middle and upper left abdomen Why Valproate pancreatitisA rare, idiosyncratic reaction, not related to dose or duration, so years on a stable dose do not exclude it; in most cases it is self-limited and resolves once the drug is stopped. Here, drinking, under the weekly maximum of 14 drinks (drinks ten glasses of wine weekly), is an unlikely cause. Other idiosyncratic valproate reactions: hepatotoxicity, bone marrow toxicity and alopecia. Lithium and anticonvulsants If a patient on valproate has epigastric pain with vomiting, choose to stop valproate and exclude other causes of pancreatitis.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Bipolar I disorder Elevated or irritable mood with DIGFAST symptoms Marked impairment, psychosis or hospitalization; 1 week or more unless hospitalized Bipolar II disorder Hypomania plus a major depressive episode No marked impairment, psychosis or hospitalization; 4 days or more; never mania Histrionic personality disorder Seductive, theatrical, attention seeking Chronic, pervasive pattern, not an episodeBorderlineBorderline personality disorder also brings unstable relationships, mood shifts and impulsivity, but persistent and pervasive, not episodic; borderline personality disorder and bipolar disorder can both be diagnosed. Schizophrenia Grandiose delusions, odd behavior 6 months or more; psychosis outside mood episodes; negative symptoms (neglected grooming, slow answers) Delusional disorder A fixed grandiose belief Delusion without mania or other symptoms Major depressive disorder Depressive episodes only, 2 weeks or more Never mania or hypomania; mania makes it bipolar I, hypomania with depression bipolar II Schizoaffective disorder Psychosis plus mood episodes 2 weeks or more of psychosis with no mood episode; mood episodes most of the illness Stimulant or other drug Symptoms tied to useCausesCocaine or amphetamine intoxication, or corticosteroids; the episode remits once the drug is gone. Medical causes include multiple sclerosis and anti-NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor encephalitis. The timing of use explains the episode Hyperthyroidism Weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia, tremor Abnormal TSH and free thyroxine Cyclothymic disorder (cyclothymia) Up and down periods below full criteria 2 years or more; never a full episode ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) Hyperactive, impulsive Chronic, in more than one setting; mania is acuteADHD onsetPersistent, not episodic, with onset by age 12. Normal adolescence, oppositional defiant disorder or conduct disorder Defiance or rule-breaking in a teenager No abrupt change from baseline, no decreased need for sleepTeen look-alikesA distinct change from baseline, with distractibility, goal-directed activity and less need for sleep, should raise suspicion for mania, not normal adolescence. Oppositional defiant disorder: irritable or angry mood, argumentative, vindictive. Conduct disorder: purposefully violates the rights of others or social norms (stealing, destroying property, assault). Neither explains an abrupt change with decreased need for sleep. Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder: temper outbursts out of proportion, onset before age 10.

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Elevated or irritable mood with more energy → Urine drug screen Drug screen negative Lowers suspicion; standard panels miss some drugs Amphetamine or cocaine Exposure, not cause: check the timing of use → TSH and free thyroxine TSH and free thyroxine normal Makes hyperthyroidism unlikely → CBC (complete blood count) and basic metabolic panel CBC and metabolic panel normal Makes another medical cause less likely Targeted tests TestResultMeans Woman who could become pregnant → Pregnancy test Positive No valproate PregnancyValproate and carbamazepine are both avoided in pregnancy: neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental disorders.; lithium in the first trimester raises the risk of cardiac malformations, mainly Ebstein anomaly Negative Valproate is still avoided in anyone who could become pregnant
No cause found: time the episode, then name the disorder from its episodes.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization A manic, not hypomanic, episode Diagnose bipolar I Mania began on an antidepressant and outlasts it Still a manic episode Diagnose bipolar I; treat the mania Weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia, tremor Hyperthyroidism Check TSH and free thyroxine First episode late in life or abrupt, or neurologic findings A medical or neurologic cause, such as a stroke Image the brain Seductive only during the episode Mania, not histrionic personality Diagnose mania Oriented, normal vital signs Not delirium or alcohol withdrawal Keep the diagnosis of mania

Pause point Grandiose delusion Offered as schizophrenia or delusional disorder All the options The optionsBrief psychotic disorder: an acute delusion; but his psychosis is secondary to mania. Delirium, alcohol withdrawal: found wandering in the cold; but vital signs are normal and he is fully oriented. Delusional disorder: a fixed delusion; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and he has it. Malingering: an odd, dangerous act; but it is unlikely that anyone would go out in the cold and cause frostbite for gain, and he has no clear source of gain. Schizoid personality disorder: an odd man; but he is playful and talkative, not detached. Schizophrenia: the god delusion and the posture; but the delusion is part of mania (NBME cites missing negative symptoms). Down to two: manic bipolar disorder or schizophrenia. Manic bipolar disorder: the god delusion rides on playful affect, rapid incessant speech and pacing; NBME also cites no negative symptoms. It sits inside an acute episode with DIGFAST symptoms; delusional disorder occurs without mania → Mania Seductiveness Offered as histrionic personality All the options The optionsADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): hyperactive and impulsive; but ADHD is chronic and in more than one setting, and this is acute. Delusional disorder: a fixed grandiose belief; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and she has it. Histrionic personality disorder: the wink and the attempted kiss; but personality disorders are chronic and pervasive. Schizophrenia: a grandiose delusion; but it sits inside a manic episode (NBME cites missing negative symptoms). Down to two: bipolar disorder or histrionic personality disorder. Bipolar disorder: the seductiveness sits inside an acute episode of euphoric, irritable mood with rapid speech, overspending and grandiosity. Personality disorders are chronic and pervasive → Bipolar disorder, manic episode In practice NBME versus criteriaIn practice: NBME gives no duration; it reads the severity and psychosis as mania. Obsession or mania?Obsession or mania?Intrusive, unwanted thoughts are obsessive-compulsive disorder; a manic preoccupation is not felt as intrusive and drives more activity.

Episode type and specifiers Episode Recognize it It means Hypomanic 4 days or more; others notice; no marked impairment, hospitalization or psychosis Bipolar II if there is also a major depressive episode and never mania Manic 1 week or more or hospitalized; marked impairment, hospitalization or psychosis Bipolar I Psychotic features Delusions or hallucinations during an elevated or irritable episode Manic by definition (a hypomanic episode cannot be psychotic), even if the patient keeps working Mixed features Full mania or hypomania plus 3 or more depressive symptoms most days A specifier: full manic or hypomanic criteria must still be met

Name the disorder from its episodestime → Bipolar I disorder1 manic episode is enough; depression common, not required; psychosis only inside episodes Mood Psychosis High moodDepression: common, not requiredPsychosis Bipolar II disorderHypomania plus a major depressive episode; never mania Mood Psychosis Hypomania: milderLow mood Schizoaffective disorderPsychosis 2 weeks or more with no mood episode; mood episodes most of the illness Mood Psychosis 2 wk+ alone High moodPsychosisPsychosis with no mood episode High moodHypomania: milderLow moodDepression: common, not requiredPsychosisPsychosis with no mood episode

1 Alongsideany drug, from the start Assess violence and self-harm risk; stop antidepressants; help stop stimulants (including caffeine) and alcohol 2 1st lineacute mania Lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic Alone, or an antipsychotic (quetiapine, aripiprazole, risperidone) plus lithium or valproate. Antipsychotic Adverse Effects 3 Add or switchno better after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses Another first-line agent, added or switched Check adherence and substance use first. 4 Severe or resistantparticularly severe or treatment-resistant mania Second-line agents, or electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) ECT may be considered alone or added on.

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Could become pregnant Lithium or a first-line antipsychotic; not valproate; in pregnancy, lamotrigine or quetiapine for maintenance Valproate: teratogenic, impaired intellectual development; lithium: Ebstein anomaly after first-trimester exposure Bipolar I depression Quetiapine or lurasidone first; partial response: add lithium or valproate; not tolerated or not working: switch to valproate alone or olanzapine plus fluoxetine. In practiceIn practiceGuidelines also list lithium and lamotrigine among first-line choices; lamotrigine treats bipolar depression and prevents its return. No antidepressant alone: risks a switch to mania Mania that started on an antidepressant Stop the antidepressant; start a first-line agent Not "continue it and add a mood stabilizer"
Severe agitation or manic psychosis: an antipsychotic, since lithium takes 4 to 10 days.

Follow-up decisions When Do After remission Continuous maintenance for years, possibly lifelong; not intermittent Choosing maintenance Lithium (linked to lower suicide risk), quetiapine, valproate (divalproex), lamotrigine (weak against mania) or aripiprazole; with kidney disease, valproate rather than lithium On lithium Lithium Therapy Levels; creatinine, TSH and calcium before starting and during maintenance On valproate Liver tests before starting and regularly afterEpigastric pain with vomiting: stop valproate On lamotrigine, a new rash Stop it at the first sign; substitute another agent

Ever manic or hypomanic? bipolar; an antidepressant alone can switch it to mania Partial response after at least 4 to 6 weeks at a therapeutic dose optimize the dose first Remission same dose for about 6 more months

What it is 5 of 9, one being depressed mood or loss of interest 2 weeks or more impairment Never manic or hypomanic no substance or medical cause Driver Not fully defined: serotonin norepinephrine dopamine Triggers First-degree relative, about 3 times the risk non-modifiable female, 1.5 to 3 times non-modifiable Chain Proposed, not settled: chronic stress hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis overactivity hippocampal and prefrontal loss Insights Depression itself often blunts dexamethasone suppression, so test for Cushing syndrome only when physical or laboratory signs point to it Benefit can lag up to 6 weeks, so judge a drug only after an adequate trial

What MDD does, by systemsupports, never diagnoses On sleep electroencephalography (EEG): shorter REM (rapid eye movement) latency; more REM, most in the first REM period; less slow-wave sleep; early-morning awakening Often ↑ cortisol; often no suppression after dexamethasone; ↑ corticotropin-releasing hormone in the cerebrospinal fluidproposed: reduced glucocorticoid receptor function, so cortisol fails to shut its own axis off Disturbed serotonin activity; norepinephrine and dopamine also implicatedreuptake blockers and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) raise them quickly, yet benefit lags weeks Smaller hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex; ↓ serum BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor)chronic stress contributes to the hippocampal and prefrontal loss ↑ inflammatory cytokines and C-reactive protein (CRP)cytokines may divert tryptophan from serotonin synthesis to the kynurenine pathway Melancholic: early waking, marked psychomotor change, anorexia or weight loss. Atypical features: mood brightens with good news, more appetite, hypersomnia

Symptoms 5 or more of 9, most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks; at least one is depressed mood or loss of interest; in children and adolescents, mood may be irritable The 9 depressed mood plus the 8 of SIGECAPS Impairment clinically significant distress or impairment Exclusions not due to a substance, a medication or a medical condition (eg, hypothyroidism); never a manic or hypomanic episode

Sleep insomnia or hypersomnia Interest loss of interest or pleasure Guilt worthlessness or excessive guilt Energy fatigue, loss of energy Concentration poor concentration or indecisiveness Appetite appetite or weight change Psychomotor agitation or retardation Suicide thoughts of death or suicide
Add depressed mood for the 9 criteria; 5 or more, and one must be depressed mood or loss of interest.
Clinical diagnosis: laboratory studies only exclude medical causes

High riskFrequent suicidal thoughts, a specific plan and intent to act soon, or rehearsal or preparation Ask about suicide directly: asking does not cause or worsen suicidal thinking Suicide Risk Assessment If high risk, choose hospitalization, involuntary if refused. Low riskNo or infrequent suicidal thoughts, no plan or intent, many protective factors Not a no-suicide contract: it does not prevent suicide If low risk, choose a safety plan, removal of firearms and medications, treatment and follow-up.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Major depressive disorder 5 of 9 symptoms for 2 weeks, with impairment Never manic or hypomanic; no cause found Bipolar disorder must not miss Depressed now, manic or hypomanic beforeNot hypomaniaBrief stretches of feeling better are likely normal mood, not hypomania, when its other symptoms are missing: inflated self-esteem, more energy, less need for sleep, pressured speech. Any past manic or hypomanic episode A substance, medication or medical cause The same symptoms with physical or laboratory abnormalities (eg, Cushing syndrome)MimicsSymptoms that began before the substance use make a primary mood disorder more likely; people with mood disorders often self-medicate. Hypothyroidism brings its own signs (cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, recent weight gain) and an abnormal examination. Chronic fatigue syndrome (systemic exertion intolerance disease): a relatively sudden onset of overwhelming fatigue, often after an infection such as mononucleosis. Medical evaluation finds the cause Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) Depressed most days for 2 years or more (1 year, possibly irritable, in children and adolescents)Persistent depressive disorderPlus 2 or more of: appetite change, sleep change, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, hopelessness. Never symptom-free for more than 2 months. Major depressive episodes can occur within it; both are then diagnosed. Forms: pure dysthymic syndrome (never a major depressive episode), with intermittent major depressive episodes, or with persistent ones (full criteria throughout the past 2 years). Treatment: a drug together with psychotherapy beats either alone. 2 years or more Adjustment disorder Distress out of proportion, within 3 months of a stressor; gone within 6 months after it ends Meets no other disorder's criteria Normal grief Sadness after a death, usually easingGrief or MDDSadness usually centers on the deceased and lessens over time. Think MDD when it worsens instead, with persistent sadness and pervasive anhedonia. Full criteria still mean major depressive disorder; bereavement does not exclude it Prolonged grief disorder (persistent complex bereavement disorder) Intense longing for, or preoccupation with, the person who died; more disabling than typical grief and longer than cultural norms expect At least a year after the death in adults (6 months in children and adolescents); full MDD criteria still mean MDD as well Schizoaffective disorder Psychosis plus mood episodes Psychosis for 2 weeks or more with no mood episode

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Depressed mood or loss of interest, 2 weeks or more → Mood history Ever manic or hypomanic A bipolar disorder, not MDD → TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone); substances and medications Abnormal TSH or a causative drug or substance A medical or substance cause Targeted tests TestResultMeans Examination or labs abnormal → Medical evaluation first Central obesity, proximal weakness, hypertension Cushing syndrome: 24-hour urinary cortisol

Criteria met and no other cause: major depressive disorder. Why order labsWhy order itLaboratory studies help exclude medical illnesses that can present as major depressive disorder, such as hypothyroidism.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Past mania or hypomania A bipolar disorder, not MDD Bipolar pathway; no antidepressant alone Depressed most days, 2 years or more Persistent depressive disorder Diagnose persistent depressive disorder Full criteria after a death or stressor Still MDD Treat as MDD Stressor within 3 months, depression criteria not met Adjustment disorder Not MDD

Pause point Depressed patient who hears voices Offered as schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder Psychosis only inside the depressive episode Not delusional disorderDelusional disorder: mood symptoms, if present, are brief and not prominent. A fixed false belief inside a severe depressive episode is MDD with psychotic features. → MDD with psychotic features Mood-congruent delusions in a full depressive episode after a recent death Offered as prolonged grief disorder (persistent complex bereavement disorder) Prolonged grief disorder needs at least 12 months in adults and is not associated with psychotic features → MDD with psychotic features Psychosis for 2 weeks or more with no mood episode, while mood episodes fill most of the illness, is schizoaffective disorder.

PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9)Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by: Item0Not at all1Several days2More than half the days3Nearly every day 1Little interest or pleasure in doing things 2Feeling down, depressed or hopeless 3Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much 4Feeling tired or having little energy 5Poor appetite or overeating 6Feeling bad about yourself, a failure, or letting yourself or your family down 7Trouble concentrating, eg, reading or watching television 8Moving or speaking slowly enough for others to notice, or so fidgety you move around more than usual 9Thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourselfAny score above 0: suicide risk assessment Score each item 0 to 3 and add them: total 0 to 27.

≥10 likely major depression AccuracySensitivity and specificity 88%. 0 to 4minimalno treatment 5 to 9mildpsychotherapy first, or watchful waiting with a repeat PHQ-9 10 to 14moderatetreatment plan: counseling and/or medication; together they beat either alone 15 to 19moderately severeactive treatment: medication and/or psychotherapy 20 to 27severestart medication now; refer if impairment is severe or response is poor

Specifiers Specifier Recognize it Choose Psychotic features Delusions or hallucinations inside the depressive episodeMood-congruentDelusions usually fit the mood: guilt or deserved punishment, worthlessness, nihilism, or a firm belief in a serious illness that normal test results do not shake. An antidepressant plus an antipsychotic, or electroconvulsive therapy (ECT); either is first line. ECT is the clear pick when severe (not eating or drinking, or persistently suicidal) CatatoniaA syndromeA syndrome, not a single disorder: it occurs in severe mood disorders with psychotic features, psychotic disorders, autism spectrum disorder and medical illness (infectious, metabolic, neurologic, rheumatologic). Mutism, abnormal postures, staring, purposeless movementSignsNegativism: resists instructions and movement. Posturing: holds positions against gravity. Waxy flexibility: resists at first, then keeps the new posture. Echolalia, echopraxia: mimics speech and movements. It ranges from stupor to marked agitation (catatonic excitement). Lorazepam first;LorazepamLorazepam challenge, intravenous 1 to 2 mg: partial, temporary relief within 5 to 10 minutes confirms catatonia. Catatonia generally responds within a week; no response by then counts as failure. ECT if it fails or is malignantAntipsychotics can worsen it: defer them Peripartum onset (postpartum depression) Onset in pregnancy or within 4 weeks after deliveryBlues: start within 2 to 3 days, gone by 2 weeks, no impairment; not a disorder. Reassure and monitor; reassess if it lasts beyond 2 weeks or suicidal ideation appears Why not treatBluesTypically self-limiting, so psychotherapy, an antidepressant or a psychiatry referral is premature. Symptoms typically peak around day 5. A past depressive episode may be associated with the blues, and the blues raise the risk of later postpartum depression.Screen every patient, whatever her psychiatric history, with a validated tool such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale Why allWhy screen everyoneSymptoms often overlap a normal postpartum course, such as fatigue and poor sleep, and are underreported. Psychotherapy and/or sertraline or escitalopram; breastfeeding can continuePostpartum psychosis: an emergency Seasonal pattern (seasonal affective disorder) Fall and winter onset, spring and summer remission, 2 years or moreThe patternSeasonal episodes far outnumber any nonseasonal ones. Atypical features are common: more sleep, more appetite, carbohydrate craving, weight gain. Light therapyLight therapyA 10,000-lux light box, about 30 minutes daily, soon after waking. Most improve in 1 to 4 weeks; continue through fall and winter until remission in spring or summer. Light alone is a reasonable first option for mild to moderate seasonal depression. Bupropion can augment a partial response or be used alone, but augmenting or switching waits until the current antidepressant reaches its optimal dose. Also: CBT (cognitive-behavioral therapy) and behavioral measures such as outdoor walks, aerobic exercise and sleep hygiene. alone or with an antidepressant Atypical features Mood brightens with good news; more appetite, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity First-line drugs; a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) if they fail
EscalateVery severe depression needing a rapid response: persistent suicidality, or refusal to eat or drink, with or without psychotic features Failed drug trials: a TCA. If any of these, choose ECT.
Before the first doseAny past mania or hypomania? If yes, choose the bipolar pathway; no antidepressant alone.

1 1st linestart here An SSRIMechanismSelective serotonin reuptake inhibitor: blocks the serotonin transporter, so more serotonin stays in the synaptic cleft; little effect on dopamine or norepinephrine. The full effect may take up to 6 weeks.Why it fits depression is linked to disturbed central serotonin activity; norepinephrine and dopamine are also implicated., SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), bupropionMechanismBlocks dopamine and norepinephrine transporters. One of very few antidepressants that does not cause sexual dysfunction.Watch for a lower seizure threshold. or mirtazapineMechanismBlocks central presynaptic alpha-2 receptors; serotonin 2A, 2C and 3 receptors; and histamine H1 receptors.Watch for drowsiness, a bigger appetite and weight gain. The table below picks the drug.Why a tableFirst-line drugs are similarly effective. Children and young adults: watch for new suicidal thoughts Pregnancy: avoid paroxetine Under 4 to 6 weeks at a therapeutic dose: same drug, same dose 2 Raisepartly better after an adequate trial Optimize the dose first Go toward the maximum tolerated dose, then give it 4 to 6 weeks before adding a drug. 3 Switchminimal or no improvement after an adequate trial A different SSRI, or a first-line drug with another mechanism For example, an SNRI such as venlafaxine. 4 Addsevere and only partly better after 6 to 12 weeks Psychotherapy, bupropion (fatigue or weight gain), or a second-generation antipsychotic Antipsychotic side effects include akathisia, sedation and weight gain. In unipolar depression, lithium is an add-on, never monotherapy. 5 Lastseveral first-line trials have failed A TCAMechanismTricyclic antidepressant: blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, and also blocks muscarinic, histamine H1 and alpha-adrenergic receptors.Watch for in overdose, a widened QRS (slowed ventricular conduction) and a prolonged QTc (QT interval corrected for heart rate). or an MAOIMechanismMonoamine oxidase inhibitor: blocks the enzyme that breaks down monoamines, so their levels rise.Watch for hypertensive reactions; serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs., or ECT, which acts rapidlyECTA brief tonic-clonic seizure under anesthesia and a muscle relaxant. Safe in pregnancy and in older adults. Side effects: temporary headache, disorientation and partial amnesia, which usually resolves within 6 months. Poor tolerability and safety limit tricyclics and MAOIs. ECT comes first when the depression is also very severe. Before an MAOI: at least 5 weeks off fluoxetine, 2 weeks off others Serotonin syndrome MAOIs

cycle timing · prospective ratings · mood and physical symptomsDo symptoms clear after menses, or persist through the cycle?

Before menses, then a symptom-free interval: suspect premenstrual syndrome (PMS) or premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Confirm with a daily symptom diary for at least 2 cycles before selecting treatment PMDD: 5 or more symptoms, including a core mood symptom, with marked distress or impaired function; symptoms become minimal or absent after menses Confirmed mild symptoms: exercise and stress reduction. Moderate or severe symptoms: a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)

What it is Recurrent menstrual-cycle symptoms affecting mood, the body, or both; PMDD is the more severe syndrome Driver Mechanism uncertain; heightened sensitivity to normal ovarian hormone fluctuations may disturb neurotransmitter signaling Triggers Reproductive years; family mood or premenstrual disorders; personal anxiety history Chain Proposed: luteal hormone sensitivity mood and bodily symptoms impaired daily function Insights Do normal hormone levels exclude PMS or PMDD? Normal hormone levels do not rule it out WhyMechanismEstrogen and progesterone concentrations are normal; altered sensitivity, rather than excess hormone, is proposed Does depression history explain a new cyclic complaint? A history of depression does not establish the cause of a new cyclic complaint TimingDiagnostic distinctionChart the entire cycle to separate baseline mood symptoms from a distinct premenstrual syndrome
Symptoms 1 to 4 physical or emotional symptoms affecting function Timing recurring in 3 successive cycles; begin premenstrually and clear in the first days of bleeding

Count At least 5 symptoms during the final premenstrual week in most cycles over the past year; at least one core mood symptom; marked distress or impaired function Symptoms SymptomsSymptom setCore: mood lability, irritability/anger, depressed mood, or anxiety. Additional features: reduced interest or concentration, low energy, altered appetite or sleep, feeling overwhelmed, and bodily symptoms Confirm Improve soon after bleeding begins; minimal or absent in the postmenstrual week. Confirm daily ratings for at least 2 symptomatic cycles; exclude substances, medical causes and mere exacerbation of another disorder
SafetyPremenstrual symptoms can include suicidal thinking If suicidal thoughts are present, choose assess intent, risks and supports; make a safety plan. Suicide Risk Assessment

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Duration Decides it PMS Fewer physical or emotional symptoms; functioning affected 1 to 2 weeks before menses; recurrent over 3 cycles Symptoms clear shortly after bleeding begins; a mood symptom is not required PMDD Prominent mood symptoms with more severe impairment Final premenstrual week; most cycles in the preceding year At least 5 symptoms including a core affective symptom; minimal or absent in the week after menses Major Depressive Disorder Persistent depressed mood or loss of pleasure Continues across menstrual phases No postmenstrual remission of the ongoing depression Premenstrual exacerbation A known mood, anxiety or other disorder worsens before menses Baseline symptoms throughout the cycle The underlying symptoms remain after menstruation starts Physiologic premenstrual changes Cyclic physical or mood changes Before menses Daily activities remain intact Medication-induced mood symptoms New symptoms after hormonal contraception starts Begins after the exposure Improves after the exogenous hormone is stopped

briefs.title: Cluster B Personality Disorders
briefs.sub: borderline · antisocial · histrionic · narcissisticA lifelong pattern, or an episode of mood or psychosis?
blocks: borderline · antisocial · histrionic · narcissisticA lifelong pattern, or an episode of mood or psychosis?

A lifelong pattern, present by early adulthood and generally stable across settings; instability that comes in episodes with a start and an end points to a mood disorder Borderline: abandonment fear, unstable relationships and self-image, self-harm, and transient stress-related paranoia lasting minutes to hours; first-line treatment is psychotherapy, with the best evidence for dialectical behavior therapy Antisocial needs age 18 or older and conduct disorder before 15; under 18, antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed; consider conduct disorder

What it is Cluster B: the dramatic, emotional or erratic personality disorders: antisocial, borderline, histrionic and narcissistic MnemonicThe three clustersCluster A weird, cluster B wild, cluster C worried Driver Rigid, pervasive patterns of thinking, feeling and relating distress or impaired function Triggers Conduct disorder in childhood (antisocial) Childhood trauma: abuse or neglect (borderline) Mood and substance use disorders in the family non-modifiable Chain Development: childhood trauma or insecure attachment fear of abandonment Pattern: splitting, people seen as all good or all bad unstable, intense relationships Crisis: a stressor such as a breakup self-injury, suicidal threats, or paranoia and dissociation for minutes to hours Insights Psychosis here is brief and tied to stress; persistent delusions more likely mean a primary psychotic disorder Borderline mood shifts moment to moment, often with stressors, and never reaches a sustained manic or hypomanic episode

Comorbidity and coursetap to open Common: screen for and treat these disordersMood and substance use disorders often coexist with cluster B Dissociation, such as depersonalization, is common after traumaAbout 10% die by suicide; most remit with treatment More common in menSome behaviors may lessen around age 40 to 50 Diagnosed more often in women

All present by early adulthood, generally stable across settings Antisocial unlawful acts, deceit, impulsivity, aggression, no remorse; age 18 or older with conduct disorder before 15 Borderline 5 or more of the features below Histrionic shifting, exaggerated emotion; overly dramatic, impressionistic speech; attention seeking; often uses appearance to draw attention; often sees relationships as closer than they are; sexually provocative Narcissistic grandiosity, entitlement, need for admiration, exploits others, lacks empathy

Borderline: the 9 features, by area Area Feature Relationships Frantic efforts to avoid abandonment; unstable, intense relationships Self Unstable self-image; chronic emptiness Behavior Self-damaging impulsivity in 2 or more areas; recurrent suicidal behavior or self-injury Mood Marked mood reactivity; intense, inappropriate anger Under stress Transient paranoia or dissociation
SuicideSuicidal threats, gestures or attempts, and often nonsuicidal self-injury such as cutting Suicide Risk Assessment If there is suicidal talk or self-harm, choose assess suicide risk.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Bipolar disorder (manic or hypomanic episode) Impulsive, unstable, seductive or reckless Mania 1 week or more, hypomania 4 days or more: episodes with a start and an end; personality traits are lifelong and pervasive Brief psychotic disorder Paranoia or voices after a stressor 1 day to under 1 month; transient stress-related paranoia in borderline personality disorder passes within minutes to hours Major depressive disorder Low mood, suicidal thoughts 2 weeks or more of sustained symptoms; loss of mood reactivity marks melancholic depression, while borderline mood reacts to each stressor Conduct disorder Lying, truancy, theft, fighting Under 18: antisocial personality disorder needs age 18 or older and conduct disorder before 15 Cluster A personality disorder Odd or eccentric; detached or suspicious Lifelong oddness, not drama or instability

Age windows Age 4151840 to 50 Conduct disorderCan start as early as age 4; before 15 for antisocial Antisocial personality disorderAge 18 or older Any personality disorderPresent by early adulthood Antisocial behaviorsMay lessen around 40 to 50

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Suspected personality disorder → History across years and settings A pattern since early adulthood across most settings A personality disorder Discrete episodes with a start and an end A mood disorder instead, or as well Next step TestResultMeans Any cluster B disorder → Suicide risk assessmentScreen for depression and substance use Comorbid disorder found Treat it as well SkipNo laboratory test or scale confirms a personality disorder; the history decides.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Staff split into all good and all bad Borderline personality disorder Diagnose it; dialectical behavior therapy Paranoia or detachment for hours after a breakup Transient stress-related paranoia of borderline personality disorder Diagnose borderline personality disorder; dialectical behavior therapy Seductive, theatrical and attention seeking for years Histrionic personality disorder Diagnose it; screen for depression and substance use Grandiose, entitled, enraged by criticism Narcissistic personality disorder Diagnose it; psychotherapy Fraud, fights and no remorse in an adult with childhood conduct problems Antisocial personality disorder Diagnose it; screen for substance use Seductive and grandiose for days, with little sleep and rapid speech A manic episode Bipolar Disorder

Pause point Mood swings, and paranoia under stress Offered as bipolar disorder or brief psychotic disorder Lifelong, reactive instability with psychosis lasting hours → Borderline personality disorder

1 First lineBorderline Psychotherapy: dialectical behavior therapy has the best evidence; transference-focused psychotherapy also works 2 AdjunctSevere mood instability or transient paranoia A mood stabilizer, or a second-generation antipsychotic 3 Comorbid disorderDepression or anxiety An antidepressant for that disorder, not for the personality disorder

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Borderline Dialectical behavior therapy; the team sees the patient jointly Splitting of staff into good and bad Antisocial Treat comorbid substance use and mood disorders; psychotherapy has not proven effective Some behaviors may lessen around 40 to 50 Histrionic Treat comorbid somatic symptom, conversion or depressive disorders; psychotherapy helps little May improve with engagement in therapy Narcissistic Psychotherapy: psychodynamic, transference-focused or dialectical behavior therapy Aggression predicts a worse course

Follow-up decisions When Do or expect Borderline, over time Expect sustained remission with treatment in most; about 10% die by suicide Antisocial, in middle age Some behaviors may lessen; the course stays chronic

Bipolar Disorder: a manic or hypomanic episode. Suicide Risk Assessment: self-harm and suicidal threats. Disruptive Behavior in a Child: conduct disorder before 18. Cluster C Personality Disorders: avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders.
Personality disorders are lifelong and pervasive: before naming one, make sure the instability is not an episode of mania or depression, and that any psychosis lasted only minutes to hours.

briefs.title: Cluster C Personality Disorders
briefs.sub: avoidant · dependent · obsessive-compulsive personality disorderWhat drives the pattern?
blocks: avoidant · dependent · obsessive-compulsive personality disorderWhat drives the pattern?

Cluster C (anxious or fearful, a pattern present by early adulthood): avoids people but wants closeness and fears rejection avoidant personality disorder; no wish for closeness is schizoid (cluster A); fear often confined to specific situations is social anxiety disorder (social phobia) Needs others to decide and care for them; submissive, clinging dependent personality disorder; order, perfectionism and control the patient sees as right (ego-syntonic) obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD), not obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), whose obsessions are unwanted Psychotherapy: CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) may help in avoidant personality disorder; CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy for dependent and OCPD; screen for and treat comorbid disorders

What it is Three lifelong, persistently maladaptive personality patterns marked by anxiety or fear: avoidant, dependent and obsessive-compulsive Driver A fear or insecurity that shapes behavior: fear of criticism and rejection (avoidant), fear of separation and of being unable to care for oneself (dependent), insecurity met by rigid order and control (OCPD) Triggers Genetic link to anxiety disorders non-modifiable Rejection or marginalization in childhood may contribute to avoidant personality disorder Chain Fear or insecurity: of rejection, of being left alone, or about the self (OCPD) a fixed coping style: avoidance, clinging, or perfectionism and control Pattern: present by early adulthood, the same at home and work social and occupational impairment Course: chronic, though it may improve with treatment; depression and anxiety disorders common alongside comorbidity typically means a poorer outlook Insights Avoidant and schizoid patients may both work alone at night; the motive decides: the avoidant patient wants people but fears rejection, the schizoid patient does not want them OCPD is ego-syntonic: the patient sees the rigid standards as right, so there are no unwanted, intrusive obsessions to neutralize as in OCD

Comorbidity and coursetap to open Depression and anxiety disorders are common with all three: screen for and treat themAvoidant personality disorder and social anxiety disorder often occur together Often stays in abusive relationships Often avoids treatment
Pattern persistent and generally stable across settings, with impairment or distress Onset by early adulthood; symptoms that began only weeks ago do not qualify Test none; clinical criteria decide

Core social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitivity to rejection Features avoids work roles with contact for fear of criticism; will not get involved unless sure of being liked; avoids new activities that might embarrass Criteria neededCriteria count4 or more of the listed features

Core an excessive need to be cared for: submissive, clinging, fears separation Features needs advice and reassurance for everyday decisions; helpless when alone; rushes into a new caretaking relationship when one ends Criteria neededCriteria count5 or more of the listed features

Core preoccupation with order, perfectionism and control; ego-syntonic Features details, rules and lists; perfectionism that blocks finishing; work before leisure and friends; reluctant to delegate unless others do it exactly their way; rigid morals; spends little, saving for disasters Criteria neededCriteria count4 or more of the listed features

Socially withdrawn: look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Avoidant personality disorder Shy and inhibited; avoids people, work contact and new activities Wants closeness but fears rejection or embarrassment; pervasive since early adulthood Schizoid personality disorder A loner with flat affect who prefers solitary activities No wish for closeness; indifferent to praise or criticism Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) Fears embarrassment while others watch, as in meetings or presentations Often tied to specific situations, not pervasive inhibition; the two often coexist Schizotypal personality disorder Few close ties; constricted affect Odd beliefs, magical thinking and odd behavior Paranoid personality disorder Socially isolated Pervasive suspicion and mistrust Schizophrenia Withdrawn and avoids others Delusions drive the avoidance, not fear of rejection Autism spectrum disorder Limited social give and take Early childhood social communication deficits with restricted, repetitive behaviors

Perfectionism or clinging: look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it OCPD Rules, lists and details; perfectionism that delays finishing; reluctant to delegate Ego-syntonic: sees the standards as right; no obsessions OCD Intrusive thoughts relieved by rituals Ego-dystonic: unwanted obsessions that cause distress Dependent personality disorder Submissive and clinging; needs advice for everyday decisions Seeks and keeps caretakers; rushes into a new caretaking relationship when one ends Borderline personality disorder Clings, then turns hostile Swings between submission and rage Adjustment disorder Clinging or anxious after a breakup or loss Began weeks ago, within 3 months of the stressor: not a lifelong pattern

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Lifelong social withdrawal → History: why the patient keeps away from people Wants closeness, fears rejection Avoidant personality disorder No wish for closeness Schizoid personality disorder Fear mainly in specific situations where others watch Social anxiety disorder Avoids people for fear of rejection → History: a second criterion of the same disorder Avoids new activities for fear of embarrassment Confirms avoidant personality disorder Needs advice for decisions, or lives by rules and lists Another cluster C disorder Next step TestResultMeans Rigid perfectionism → History: whether the patient sees the pattern as a problem Standards seen as right; no obsessions OCPD Unwanted intrusive thoughts relieved by rituals OCD Clinging, fear of being alone → History: when the pattern began By early adulthood, generally stable across settings A personality disorder Weeks ago, after a stressor Not a personality disorder SkipNo laboratory test or rating scale confirms these disorders; clinical criteria and the history decide.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Works nights to avoid people; will not date unless sure of being liked Avoidant personality disorder Confirm with a second avoidant criterion; CBT Content alone; indifferent to praise or criticism; flat affect Schizoid personality disorder, cluster A Diagnose schizoid personality disorder, as in Hears Voices or Holds Odd Beliefs Dreads mainly speaking or performing in front of others Social anxiety disorder Treat as in Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety Misses deadlines redoing work to perfection; sees no problem OCPD Start CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy Asks others to choose clothes and meals; helpless when alone Dependent personality disorder Start CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy

Pause point Shy night guard avoids people; will not date unless sure of being liked Offered as criteria of dependent, obsessive-compulsive, schizotypal or schizoid personality disorder Confirm with a criterion of the same disorder → Avoids new activities for fear of embarrassment Student loner with flat affect who wants no close friends Offered as avoidant personality disorder or social anxiety disorder Prefers to be alone; no fear of rejection or embarrassment → Schizoid personality disorder

1 First lineAny cluster C disorder Psychotherapy Avoidant: CBT may help reframe beliefs about self-worth and ease avoidance; social skills work in groups also helps. Dependent and OCPD: CBT or psychodynamic psychotherapy. In dependent personality disorder, avoid promoting dependency in the therapeutic relationship In practiceIn practiceThe Merck Manual also lists anxiolytics or antidepressants for avoidant personality disorder, with no placebo-controlled trials, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), which limited data suggest may help OCPD; the board answer is psychotherapy 2 AdjunctComorbid depression or anxiety disorder Screen for and treat the comorbid disorder Common with all three; in avoidant personality disorder it typically means a poorer outlook

Follow-up decisions When Do or expect Avoidant, over years Symptoms may ease with age; comorbid depression or social anxiety disorder typically means a poorer outlook Dependent, over years Chronic course; may improve with treatment OCPD, over years Chronic course; insight and engagement in therapy predict a better one

In a lifelong anxious pattern, ask what drives the pattern: fear of rejection (avoidant), fear of being left to fend for oneself (dependent), or insecurity met by order and control (obsessive-compulsive); a patient who simply wants to be alone is schizoid, cluster A.

briefs.title: Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety
briefs.sub: which anxiety, and how to treatAre the attacks unexpected, and have a substance and a medical cause been excluded?
blocks: which anxiety, and how to treatAre the attacks unexpected, and have a substance and a medical cause been excluded?

Exclude a cause first: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) glucose urine toxicology; consider an ECG (electrocardiogram) for palpitations or chest pain Recurrent unexpected attacks 1 month or more of worry or behavior change panic disorder; no test makes the diagnosis CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or venlafaxine XR (extended release), or both; start the drug low, raise slowly; benzodiazepine short term only

What it is Recurrent unexpected attacks worry about more of them or avoidance of their triggers Attack: abrupt surge of fear peak within minutesThe attackTypically lasts 5 to 20 minutes; often unexpected, and some attacks wake the person from sleep. 4 or more of 13 symptoms Driver Proposed: catastrophic reading of normal body sensations Triggers Affected first-degree relative non-modifiable female sex: about twice as often as in men non-modifiable Anxious temperament stressful life events Chain Proposed: body sensation appraised as catastrophic fear peaks within minutes Worry about the next attack avoidance of attack triggersAvoidanceAvoidance includes situations that mimic an attack, such as exercise, caffeine or spicy foods. Insights Attacks occur in other anxiety disorders too: ask what the fear is about Lactate can provoke attacks in panic disorder more often than in healthy people, but with no standardized criteria it is a known finding, not a diagnostic test

Who, mechanism and coursedetail behind the chain Usually starts in late adolescence or early adulthood; uncommon before age 14; women affected about twice as often as men Raised risk in first-degree relatives Proposed: oversensitive carbon dioxide detectors in the medulla, leading to breathing changes and hypocapnia (↓ blood carbon dioxide)Sodium lactate, carbon dioxide, caffeine and yohimbine can provoke attacks more often in people with panic disorder than in healthy controls Most relapse even after a symptom-free period; only about 60% remit within 6 months

Attacks recurrent unexpected panic attacks; each an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort, peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms ( STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's ) Aftermath at least 1 month, after at least 1 attack, of persistent worry about more attacks or their consequences, or a significant maladaptive behavior change, such as avoidance, tied to the attacks Cause not attributable to a substance or another medical condition Other not better explained by another mental disorder

Pause point Suspected panic disorder Offered: a lactate challenge to confirm it All the options The optionsAbnormal eye tracking: “going crazy” suggests psychosis; but abnormal eye tracking goes with schizophrenia, and patients with panic disorder do not show it. Delayed rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on polysomnography: the stem mentions sleep; but it can be found in sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder and with some drugs and alcohol; no known association exists with panic disorder. Enlarged third and lateral ventricles on head CT (computed tomography): a structural brain cause; but that pattern comes from aqueductal stenosis, the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus, which is atypical in a healthy young adult and does not explain the attacks. Cortisol not suppressed by 1 mg of dexamethasone: a stress-axis test; but nonsuppression points to Cushing syndrome, not panic disorder. Down to two: increased sensitivity to lactate infusions or cortisol nonsuppression. Lactate: recurrent attacks that come out of the blue, with a normal workup, point to panic disorder (the NBME answer), and patients with it have attacks in response to lactate at an increased rate (NBME ties this to catastrophic appraisal of body states). Its diagnostic utility is unclear: there are no standardized criteria. The stem never states worry or avoidance, and the lead-in asks for a finding, not the diagnosis. No test confirms it; lactate challenges lack standardized criteria → Panic disorder is a clinical diagnosis: recurrent unexpected attacks with worry or avoidance But when the question asks which abnormality the patient most likely has, increased sensitivity to lactate is the answer.

Obsessions (intrusive, unwanted, ego-dystonic thoughts or images) neutralized by compulsions that take more than 1 hour a day or cause impairment: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), even when the images are violent First line: exposure and response prevention (ERP) and/or a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), often at higher doses; clomipramine second line; antipsychotics only augment; buspirone and benzodiazepines do not treat it Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is ego-syntonic perfectionism with no obsessions; a tic has no obsession behind it Cluster C Personality Disorders

DSM-5 lists OCD separately from the anxiety disorders, grouped with its related disorders: body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder

What it is Intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images (obsessions) and repeated acts or mental acts performed to neutralize them (compulsions); either or both Driver A compulsion temporarily relieves the distress an obsession causes, so the ritual repeats Associated Tic disorders and Tourette syndrome; trichotillomania; major depressive disorder, which raises suicide-attempt risk Chain Obsession anxiety or distress compulsion brief relief Insights Are violent intrusive images a sign of psychosis or danger? No: images the patient finds horrifying and tries to neutralize are ego-dystonic obsessions; treat the OCD, not with an antipsychotic alone Does absent insight make it a psychotic disorder? Not by itself: OCD can be specified with absent insight (delusional beliefs), though most patients recognize their beliefs are not realistic

Obsessions intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images the patient tries to suppress or neutralize Compulsions repeated acts or mental acts driven by an obsession or by rules applied rigidly, not realistically connected to what they aim to prevent, or clearly excessive Time over 1 hour a day, or distress or impairment Exclusion not a substance, medication or medical condition
Insight good or fair, poor, or absent (delusional beliefs) Tic-related a current or past tic disorder

Suicide riskSuicidal thoughts are common in OCD; the risk of an attempt rises with major depressive disorder If OCD is diagnosed or treated, choose screen for suicidal ideation and depression. PostpartumNew intrusive fears of contaminating or harming the baby If delusions or hallucinations are present, choose treat as postpartum psychosis: hospitalization and antipsychotics.
