Pause point Violent intrusive images Offered: an antipsychotic Images the patient finds horrifying and tries to neutralize are obsessions, not psychosis; keep antipsychotics for augmenting an SSRI → An SSRI with ERP

Measure and specify Finding Action Symptom severity Rate it with the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS); aim for under 1 hour a day and minimal interference Poor or absent insight Still OCD: record the insight specifier Current or past tics Specify tic-related Tics and Tic Disorders

1 First lineOCD diagnosed ERP and/or an SSRI such as sertraline or fluoxetine How it works How it worksGraded exposure to the triggers of the obsessions while the patient refrains from the rituals Dose and choice DosingOCD often needs a higher SSRI dose than depression; an SSRI is preferred over clomipramine for its adverse-effect profile; many experts combine ERP and medication, especially when severe Not anxiolytics AvoidBuspirone and lorazepam do not treat obsessions and compulsions SSRI Adverse Effects 2 Full trialan SSRI is started Allow 8 to 12 weeks in all before judging it, at least 4 to 6 of them at the top tolerated dose 3 Switchno response to an adequate trial A different SSRI, or combine medication with ERP 4 Second lineat least two SSRIs have failed Clomipramine, a strongly serotonergic tricyclic, or venlafaxine Why second Adverse effectsClomipramine is a second-line agent because of its adverse-effect profile 5 Augmentinadequate response to an SSRI Add an atypical antipsychotic such as risperidone or aripiprazole; not indicated as monotherapy

Follow-up decisions When Do The SSRI works Continue at least 1 to 2 years, if not indefinitely The patient wants to stop Taper over several months; resume the dose if symptoms worsen Throughout treatment Repeat the suicide and depression screen

Next step1 of 7 28-year-old man has unwanted images of pushing strangers onto train tracks Horrified, he avoids platforms and silently repeats a prayer to cancel each image No hallucinations; the rituals take two hours a day · Start an SSRIFirst-line drug for OCD, with ERP · Start lorazepamAnxiolytics do not treat obsessions and compulsions · Start risperidoneAntipsychotics only augment an SSRI; not monotherapy 28-year-old man has unwanted images of pushing strangers onto train tracks Horrified, he avoids platforms and silently repeats a prayer to cancel each image No hallucinations; the rituals take two hours a day Start an SSRIEgo-dystonic violent images cancelled by a mental ritual for over an hour a day are OCD; an SSRI with ERP is first line, antipsychotics only augment an SSRI, and anxiolytics do not treat obsessions and compulsions

Diagnosis2 of 7 41-year-old accountant keeps missing deadlines because she redoes reports until every detail is perfect She insists coworkers follow her lists and will not delegate She sees her standards as correct and has no intrusive thoughts or rituals · Generalized anxiety disorderWorry, usually about real-life problems; no rigid perfectionism · Obsessive-compulsive personality disorderEgo-syntonic perfectionism and control, with no obsessions · Obsessive-compulsive disorderNeeds intrusive thoughts relieved by rituals 41-year-old accountant keeps missing deadlines because she redoes reports until every detail is perfect She insists coworkers follow her lists and will not delegate She sees her standards as correct and has no intrusive thoughts or rituals Obsessive-compulsive personality disorderPervasive perfectionism and control that she sees as correct, with no obsessions or compulsions, is OCPD; OCD is ego-dystonic

Diagnosis3 of 7 67-year-old man cannot throw away old newspapers and mail, even items of no value Stacks fill his kitchen and hallway, so he cannot cook, and a fall hazard is noted He feels distress at the idea of discarding anything · Hoarding disorderCannot discard possessions regardless of value; clutter makes rooms unusable · Obsessive-compulsive personality disorderPreoccupation with order, perfectionism and control that slows tasks · Obsessive-compulsive disorderRituals neutralize intrusive thoughts 67-year-old man cannot throw away old newspapers and mail, even items of no value Stacks fill his kitchen and hallway, so he cannot cook, and a fall hazard is noted He feels distress at the idea of discarding anything Hoarding disorderDifficulty discarding possessions regardless of their value, with clutter that makes living areas unusable or unsafe, is hoarding disorder, treated first with CBT

Next step4 of 7 24-year-old woman with OCD started sertraline at a low dose 3 weeks ago Her checking rituals have eased slightly; she has no adverse effects She asks whether the drug is failing and wants to try something else · Increase the sertraline dose and continue the trialOCD needs higher doses and 8 to 12 weeks before a trial is judged · Add aripiprazoleAugmentation follows an inadequate response to an SSRI trial · Switch to clomipramineSecond line, after at least two SSRIs fail 24-year-old woman with OCD started sertraline at a low dose 3 weeks ago Her checking rituals have eased slightly; she has no adverse effects She asks whether the drug is failing and wants to try something else Increase the sertraline dose and continue the trialOCD often needs a higher SSRI dose than depression, and a trial should continue for 8 to 12 weeks, with at least 4 to 6 of them at the top tolerated dose

Diagnosis5 of 7 Three weeks after delivery, a 30-year-old woman has repeated images of drowning her baby in the bath She knows the images are senseless, avoids bathing the infant, and checks on her often at night No hallucinations or unusual beliefs · Postpartum psychosisMarked by delusions and hallucinations; treated with hospitalization and antipsychotics · Obsessive-compulsive disorderFears of harming the baby that she knows are irrational · Major depressive disorder with peripartum onsetRumination follows a depressed theme Three weeks after delivery, a 30-year-old woman has repeated images of drowning her baby in the bath She knows the images are senseless, avoids bathing the infant, and checks on her often at night No hallucinations or unusual beliefs Obsessive-compulsive disorderAfter delivery, OCD commonly takes the form of fears of contaminating or harming the baby; she knows the thoughts are irrational, unlike a patient with psychosis

Next step6 of 7 35-year-old man with severe contamination fears has had full trials of fluoxetine and sertraline Each reached the highest tolerated dose for 12 weeks, alongside ERP He still washes his hands for 3 hours a day · BuspironeTreats generalized anxiety, not obsessions and compulsions · Haloperidol monotherapyAntipsychotics only augment an SSRI; not monotherapy · ClomipramineSecond line after at least two SSRIs fail 35-year-old man with severe contamination fears has had full trials of fluoxetine and sertraline Each reached the highest tolerated dose for 12 weeks, alongside ERP He still washes his hands for 3 hours a day ClomipramineAfter adequate trials of at least two SSRIs, clomipramine, a strongly serotonergic tricyclic, is a second-line option; antipsychotics only augment an SSRI, and anxiolytics do not treat OCD

Diagnosis7 of 7 19-year-old man is convinced his nose is crooked, though others see nothing wrong He checks mirrors for hours, has seen three plastic surgeons, and skips class He has no other repeated rituals or intrusive thoughts · Obsessive-compulsive disorderObsessions on other themes, neutralized by rituals · Body dysmorphic disorderPreoccupation with a minor or imagined defect, mirror checking, cosmetic visits · Illness anxiety disorderConcerns restricted to health and disease 19-year-old man is convinced his nose is crooked, though others see nothing wrong He checks mirrors for hours, has seen three plastic surgeons, and skips class He has no other repeated rituals or intrusive thoughts Body dysmorphic disorderPreoccupation with an imagined defect in appearance, with mirror checking and repeated cosmetic visits, is body dysmorphic disorder; it is treated with SSRIs and/or CBT

Tics and Tic Disorderstic-related OCD and exposure and response prevention Hair Loss in a Childtrichotillomania Panic Disorder and Other Anxietygeneralized anxiety disorder SSRI Adverse Effectsadverse effects of the first-line drugs Tics and Tic Disorders: tic-related OCD and exposure and response prevention. Hair Loss in a Child: trichotillomania. Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: generalized anxiety disorder. SSRI Adverse Effects: adverse effects of the first-line drugs.
If a repeated act neutralizes an unwanted thought, it is a compulsion: treat with ERP and an SSRI. If the patient sees the rigid trait as right, think of OCPD.

briefs.title: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders
briefs.sub: somatic symptom disorder · illness anxiety · functional neurological symptom disorder · factitious disorder · malingeringIs the symptom felt, feared or made on purpose, and if made, is there an external reward?
blocks: somatic symptom disorder · illness anxiety · functional neurological symptom disorder · factitious disorder · malingeringIs the symptom felt, feared or made on purpose, and if made, is there an external reward?

Distressing symptom outsized thoughts, worry or time somatic symptom disorder; typically over 6 months; real disease can coexist Illness feared, with little or nothing felt illness anxiety (hypochondriasis), 6 months or more; motor or sensory change that fits no recognized neurologic disease, not on purpose functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder); made on purpose factitious (no obvious reward) or malingering (external reward) Scheduled brief visits limit testing CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy); an SSRI or SNRI (selective serotonin or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) may also help

What it is 1 or more symptoms that distress or disrupt daily life an outsized response to them Symptomatic state lasts, typically over 6 months, even if no single symptom is constant Driver The response, not the symptom: thoughts, anxiety or time out of proportion Symptoms may or may not have a medical explanationMedically unexplainedSome sources call these symptoms medically unexplained; a medical diagnosis still does not exclude the disorder. Chain Distressing symptom outsized worry and time more health care use, many clinicians Unneeded testing more symptom-focused care Outcome: more disability, iatrogenic harm and suicidality Insights A medical diagnosis does not exclude somatic symptom disorder: judge the response, not whether the symptom is explained Deception separates factitious disorder and malingering from somatic symptom disorder; then the reward separates those two

The related disorders, side by sidesymptom, intent and reward 1 or more distressing symptoms; excess thoughts, anxiety or timenot deceiving Preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness; symptoms absent or mildchecks the body again and again, or avoids care Altered voluntary movement or sensationfindings do not fit recognized neurologic disease Falsifies or induces illness, in self or in someone else (typically a child, a dependent adult or a pet)deception even with no obvious external reward Fakes or greatly exaggerates symptomsfor an external incentive

Symptom 1 or more that distress or disrupt daily life Response thoughts about seriousness out of proportion, persistently high health anxiety, or excess time and energy on symptoms Duration symptomatic state persistent, typically over 6 months; any one symptom may come and go Cause may or may not be medically explained; a medical diagnosis does not exclude it

Fear preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness Symptoms absent, or only mild Behavior excess health behaviors, such as body checking, or avoidance, such as of doctors and hospitals Duration 6 months or more
Symptom 1 or more changes in voluntary motor or sensory function Exam findings incompatible with recognized neurologic or medical disease, such as the Hoover sign

SuicideSomatic symptom disorder carries higher rates of suicidality and disability Suicide Risk Assessment TestingIatrogenic harm from tests and procedures that are not needed If the workup for the same concern is already negative, choose limiting further evaluation. Coexisting diseaseThe diagnosis does not rule out a concurrent medical condition Symptoms may or may not be medically explained If symptoms change significantly, or a new symptom or objective sign appears, choose examining and testing as in any patient. Another personA caregiver falsifies or induces illness in a child, dependent adult or pet Factitious disorder imposed on another; no obvious external reward If a caregiver is suspected of falsifying or inducing a child's illness, even with no injury yet, choose reporting the suspicion to child protective services (adult protective services for a dependent adult).

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Somatic symptom disorder Distressing symptom with outsized worry and time spent on it Typically over 6 months; a distressing symptom is present; not deceiving Illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis) Fear of having or getting a serious illness; body checking or avoiding care 6 months or more; symptoms absent or only mild Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) Sudden blindness, yet bilateral nystagmus when the physician moves a strip of paper with vertical stripes Change in voluntary movement or sensation, such as weakness, often after an acute stressor La belle indifferenceNot a reliable signLittle concern about the deficit (la belle indifference) is not a reliable or specific sign of the disorder. Findings incompatible with recognized neurologic disease (Hoover sign); not produced on purposeFeigningMotor inconsistency alone does not prove deception. Functional weakness can allow standing or walking; factitious disorder and malingering require intentional symptom production. Factitious disorder (Munchausen syndrome) Falsified or self-induced illness Deception about one's own illness; no obvious external rewardMotiveThe motive is internal, such as psychosocial stress (exams, workload) or a wish for validation. Malingering Faked or exaggerated symptoms An external incentive Factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen syndrome by proxy) A caregiver falsifies or induces illness in a dependent The caregiver deceives; no obvious external reward Delusional disorder, somatic type AppearanceBelief about appearanceA fixed belief that a body part looks defective or ugly is body dysmorphic disorder, whose insight can be absent (delusional beliefs) A false belief about a bodily function 1 month or more; fixed belief about a bodily function (an odor, a parasite) that clear evidence does not change Panic disorder Recurrent unexpected attacks 1 month or more of worry about more attacks or a behavior change; fear typically acute and episodic Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder Pain or difficulty with attempted vaginal penetration 6 months or more; no wider preoccupation or repeated care seeking

Duration criterianot to scale Delusional disorder, somatic type1 month or more Onset1 month6 months→ Panic disorder1 month or more of worry after an attack Onset1 month6 months→ Somatic symptom disorderTypically over 6 months Onset1 month6 months→ Illness anxiety disorder6 months or more Onset1 month6 months→ Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder6 months or more Onset1 month6 months→
First exclude a medical cause: Medication- and Illness-Induced Psychiatric Disorders

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans A distressing bodily symptom, or fear of disease → History, examination and the tests the symptom itself calls for A medical cause found Treat it; somatic symptom disorder can still coexist Thoughts, worry or time out of proportion to the symptom Somatic symptom disorder when it lasts, typically over 6 months Fear of having a disease, symptoms absent or mild Illness anxiety disorder, 6 months or more Targeted tests TestResultMeans Weakness of one leg → Hoover test Other signs InconsistencyThe sign is inconsistency: a leg weak when seated, yet standing up normally; weak ankle plantar flexion, yet walking on tiptoes. Heel of the weak leg presses down as the other leg lifts against resistance Functional weakness: functional neurological symptom disorder Seizure-like episodes, often with eyes forced shut or fluttering, side-to-side head shaking, asynchronous movements, no confusion afterward → Video EEG (electroencephalography) of an event No epileptiform activity Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, a functional neurological symptom disorder Suspicion that findings are produced or faked on purpose → Look for an external reward No obvious external gain; usually cooperative; accepts invasive procedures Factitious disorder Confirm How it is confirmedDirect observation Medical supplies found (medications, syringes) Sulfonylurea screen Stool laxative screen Record review Factitious diarrhea: stool osmolality first Exogenous thyroid hormone: low thyroglobulin and low radioiodine uptake suggest it External gain at stake; usually uncooperative Malingering SkipMore tests or procedures for the same concern once its workup is negative: each new test can feed the cycle
A real disease does not rule out somatic symptom disorder, and somatic symptom disorder does not rule out a real disease.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Distressing symptom; hours a day on it; many clinicians for the same concern Somatic symptom disorder Regular, brief scheduled visits; limit further testing; CBT WhyWhyThe response to a real, distressing symptom is out of proportion Fears a serious disease; no or mild symptoms; checks the body often Illness anxiety disorder One consistent, supportive clinician; CBT or an SSRI may help WhyWhyThe fear, not a symptom, is the problem Heel of the weak leg presses down as the other leg lifts against resistance Functional neurological symptom disorder Education first: explain it as a real disorder shown by the exam findings WhyWhyFindings incompatible with recognized neurologic disease (Hoover sign); not produced on purpose Tremor of abrupt onset that eases with distraction and has changeable, inconsistent features, such as a shifting frequency Not theseOther tremorsEssential tremor: most often older adults, suppressed at rest, worse with arms outstretched. Physiologic tremor: typically low amplitude and fast, worse with movement. Cerebellar tremor: typically grows as the hand nears a target, usually with ataxia or dysmetria. Functional tremor (functional neurological symptom disorder) Education first: explain it as a real disorder shown by the exam findings WhyWhyInconsistent with known tremor syndromes; worse with attention, better with distraction Sudden blindness after an acute stressor; pupils reactive, fundi normal; nystagmus when vertical stripes move across the field of view Functional neurological symptom disorder Education first: explain it as a real disorder shown by the exam findings WhyWhyOptokinetic nystagmus is typically absent in ophthalmologic vision loss; its presence suggests a psychogenic cause Hemiplegia and hemisensory loss after a trivial crash, with no voluntary movement of the face and decreased vision, hearing, smell and taste on that side; forehead vibration sense split at the midline Functional neurological symptom disorder After trauma it is a diagnosis of exclusion: evaluate for neurologic disease first WhyWhyMidline splitting of vibration on the forehead cannot be localized. Brainstem lesions typically pair ipsilateral cranial nerve signs with contralateral body signs, not one whole side. Episodes, often with eyes forced shut or fluttering, side-to-side head shaking, asynchronous movements and no confusion afterward Other featuresSpells seen by othersSpells are seen by others while awake and wax and wane over a long time, with out-of-sync thrashing, pelvic thrusting or quick head turns. No single feature decides; video EEG does. Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (functional neurological symptom disorder) Epilepsy too?CoexistingEpilepsy also occurs in about 10% of patients with psychogenic nonepileptic seizures. Video EEG of an event: no epileptiform activity Seizure-like spell in late pregnancy with eyes fluttering shut, asynchronous limb movements and no postictal period; normal blood pressure and urinalysis Likely psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; eclampsia less likely Continuous video EEG firstWhy firstTelling an epileptic from a nonepileptic spell is always appropriate, and more so in pregnancy, where calling it eclampsia changes care. Clarify before any antiseizure drug, whose adverse effects matter in pregnancy.; antiseizure drugs have no effect on it Medical job or knowledge; self-induced wound; accepts invasive procedures; usually cooperative; no claim or lawsuit Other cluesAlsoMay refuse release of records or tamper with test samples; recovers soon after admission, or worsens before a planned discharge. Factitious disorder Early psychiatric consultation; present the diagnosis without confronting or punishing WhyWhyDeception with no obvious external reward, so not malingering Hypoglycemia in a young patient with access to a relative's diabetes drugs; insulin and C-peptide both high Factitious disorder: most likely a sulfonylurea or other secretagogue Not insulinomaInsulinomaAn insulinoma also raises both, but it is very rare and usually after age 40. Hypoglycemic drug screen to confirm; C-peptide comes only with the patient's own insulin, so injected insulin leaves it low Not alcohol or dietingOther causes of low glucoseBinge drinking can lower glucose by depleting liver glycogen and impairing gluconeogenesis; dieting or appetite suppressants rarely cause severe hypoglycemia, since counterregulatory hormones respond. Dieting does not raise C-peptide. External gain at stake; usually uncooperative; complaints stop once the gain is obtained Malingering Look for an external reward WhyWhyDeception to obtain an external incentive Believes she is pregnant: amenorrhea, morning sickness, distension; office pregnancy tests negative, thin endometrial stripe Pseudocyesis Psychiatric evaluation and treatment WhyWhyA nondelusional belief, a form of somatization.

Pause point Same concern, workup already negative Offered: one more scan or specialist referral The workup is already negative → Further testing can feed the cycle Deception with no obvious reward Offered as malingering No external reward exists → Factitious disorder

1 Every patientonce the diagnosis is made Regular, brief scheduled visits Booked on a schedule, not prompted by each new symptom. 2 Alongsideif the workup for the concern is already negative Limit further evaluation Unneeded tests and procedures can keep care focused on the symptom. 3 Psychotherapyscheduled visits alone are not enough CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) The psychotherapy with the best evidence base. In practiceIn practiceIn practice: the Merck Manual calls psychotherapy, particularly CBT, first-line; Step 2 keys regular visits with the same clinician first. 4 Medicationscheduled visits alone are not enough, especially with a coexisting psychiatric disorder An SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) Both classes improved symptoms compared with placebo.

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Asks for another scan after negative workups A scheduled brief visit; limit further testing More testing can feed the cycle Wants to come only when symptoms worsen Visits on a regular schedule Visits driven by symptoms A medical condition is also found Keep both diagnoses One does not exclude the other

Related disorders: first step Disorder Choose Illness anxiety disorder One consistent, supportive clinician; CBT or an SSRI may help Functional neurological symptom disorder Education first: explain it as a real disorder shown by exam findingsExplaining itDo not dismiss it ("everything is normal"). Appropriate communication improves symptoms in about a third of patients with psychogenic nonepileptic seizures. Then CBT second line; physical therapy can help Comorbid conditionsAlso treatScreen for and treat depression and anxiety disorders, most often panic disorder; treating them may ease the functional symptoms. Factitious disorder Early psychiatric consultation; present the diagnosis without confronting or punishing; avoid risky tests and procedures; psychotherapy (CBT if the patient agrees), often declined Factitious disorder imposed on another Report the suspicion to child protective services (adult protective services for a dependent adult)

Follow-up decisions When Do Each visit Keep it regular and time-limited, on a schedule Same concern, workup already negative Limit further evaluation Symptoms change, or a new symptom or objective sign appears Examine and test it as in any patient Throughout care Watch for suicidal threatsFunctional disorder tooFunctional neurological symptom disorder also raises suicide risk: screen for ideation, assess risk factors and plan for safety., loss of function and harm from tests, all more common in somatic symptom disorder

Diagnosis1 of 7 38-year-old woman with 18 months of back and joint pain six specialists and normal imaging; spends hours a day researching causes has stopped working; sure something serious is missed T 36.7 °C · examination normal · blood count and inflammatory markers normal · Somatic symptom disorderDistressing symptom with outsized worry and time spent on it · Illness anxiety disorderSymptoms absent or only mild; her pain is distressing · MalingeringNeeds an external incentive; nothing is faked 38-year-old woman with 18 months of back and joint pain six specialists and normal imaging; spends hours a day researching causes has stopped working; sure something serious is missed T 36.7 °C · examination normal · blood count and inflammatory markers normal Somatic symptom disordera distressing symptom with excessive thoughts and time devoted to it, persistent, typically over 6 months; illness anxiety has no or only mild symptoms, and nothing here is feigned for a reward

Diagnosis2 of 7 29-year-old man sure he has a fatal nerve disease after a friend's diagnosis no weakness; checks his grip strength many times a day worry present for 8 months examination normal · BP 122/78 mm Hg · electromyography normal · Functional neurological symptom disorderNeeds a change in movement or sensation; no weakness · Somatic symptom disorderNeeds a distressing symptom; he has none · Illness anxiety disorderFear of a serious illness, 6 months or more; symptoms absent 29-year-old man sure he has a fatal nerve disease after a friend's diagnosis no weakness; checks his grip strength many times a day worry present for 8 months examination normal · BP 122/78 mm Hg · electromyography normal Illness anxiety disorderpreoccupation with having a serious illness for at least 6 months with no or mild symptoms and repeated body checking; somatic symptom disorder needs a distressing symptom

Diagnosis3 of 7 24-year-old woman cannot move her left leg since an argument today pushing down with the left heel when she lifts the right leg against resistance reflexes normal and symmetric · toes downgoing · brain MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) normal · T 36.8 °C · Factitious disorderFalsified or self-induced illness; no deception here · Ischemic strokeNormal reflexes and MRI argue against a stroke · Functional neurological symptom disorderFindings incompatible with neurologic disease (Hoover sign) 24-year-old woman cannot move her left leg since an argument today pushing down with the left heel when she lifts the right leg against resistance reflexes normal and symmetric · toes downgoing · brain MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) normal · T 36.8 °C Functional neurological symptom disorderweakness incompatible with neurologic disease: the left heel presses down when the right leg lifts (Hoover sign); normal reflexes and MRI argue against a stroke, and nothing suggests deliberate falsification

Diagnosis4 of 7 33-year-old woman, a pharmacy technician, with a thigh wound that keeps reopening cultures grow different stool organisms each time a syringe found in her bag; no lawsuit or disability claim T 38.2 °C · leukocytes 13,000/mm³ · Somatic symptom disorderNot deceiving; here a syringe shows self-induction · Factitious disorderSelf-induced illness, deception, no obvious external reward · MalingeringNeeds an external incentive; no lawsuit or claim 33-year-old woman, a pharmacy technician, with a thigh wound that keeps reopening cultures grow different stool organisms each time a syringe found in her bag; no lawsuit or disability claim T 38.2 °C · leukocytes 13,000/mm³ Factitious disorderdeliberate induction of disease with deception and no obvious external reward; malingering needs an external incentive, and patients with somatic symptom disorder are not trying to deceive

Diagnosis5 of 7 45-year-old man in police custody asks for oxycodone for back pain pain started at the arrest; limps only when watched court date next week straight-leg raise negative seated and supine · strength and reflexes normal · BP 130/84 mm Hg · MalingeringFaked or exaggerated symptoms for an external incentive · Factitious disorderNo obvious external reward; here opioids and court · Somatic symptom disorderSomatic symptoms are not feigned; he limps only when watched 45-year-old man in police custody asks for oxycodone for back pain pain started at the arrest; limps only when watched court date next week straight-leg raise negative seated and supine · strength and reflexes normal · BP 130/84 mm Hg Malingeringsymptoms overstated to obtain external incentives; factitious disorder deceives without an obvious external reward

Diagnosis6 of 7 4-year-old boy with a 2nd admission this year for blood in his urine bleeding seen only by his mother; no custody or benefit claim repeated urinalyses normal when nurses collect them T 36.9 °C · BP 96/60 mm Hg · creatinine normal · Malingering by the motherNeeds an external incentive; no custody or benefit claim · Somatic symptom disorder in the childNeeds a distressing symptom in the child; findings exist only in her reports · Factitious disorder imposed on another (mother)Caregiver falsifies illness in a child; no obvious external reward 4-year-old boy with a 2nd admission this year for blood in his urine bleeding seen only by his mother; no custody or benefit claim repeated urinalyses normal when nurses collect them T 36.9 °C · BP 96/60 mm Hg · creatinine normal Factitious disorder imposed on another (mother)a caregiver falsifies illness in a child without external incentives; the findings exist only in her reports and vanish under observation

Next step7 of 7 36-year-old woman with abdominal pain for 3 years 11 emergency visits this year, all workups negative; fears a missed cancer asks for another computed tomography scan examination unchanged · BP 118/76 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal · Another abdominal scanMore testing can feed the cycle · Regular scheduled brief visitsRegular, time-limited visits on a schedule · Visits only when symptoms worsenVisits driven by symptoms reinforce the cycle 36-year-old woman with abdominal pain for 3 years 11 emergency visits this year, all workups negative; fears a missed cancer asks for another computed tomography scan examination unchanged · BP 118/76 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal Regular scheduled brief visitsregular, time-limited appointments rather than symptom-driven visits; limit further evaluation, since unnecessary testing can perpetuate symptom-focused health care use; CBT and an SSRI or SNRI can help
Panic Disorder and Other Anxietyis the fear about attacks, or about having a disease? Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: is the fear about attacks, or about having a disease?
Before naming a somatic symptom or related disorder, ask: is the symptom felt, feared or made on purpose, and if made, is there an external reward?

briefs.title: Trauma, Stress and Dissociative Disorders
briefs.sub: acute stress disorder · posttraumatic stress disorder · adjustment disorder · dissociative disordersTrauma or stressor, and how long since?
blocks: acute stress disorder · posttraumatic stress disorder · adjustment disorder · dissociative disordersTrauma or stressor, and how long since?

Trauma (actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violation), then intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and arousal 3 days to 1 month after the trauma: acute stress disorder; over 1 month: posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) A non-traumatic stressor with outsized distress within 3 months of the stressor; gone within 6 months after it ends, short of another disorder (in the depressed-mood type, fewer than 5 depressive symptoms) adjustment disorder; lost personal memory with negative toxicology and no neurologic cause dissociative amnesia, with fugue if the patient travels Trauma-focused CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) first; for PTSD an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or an SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) is also first line; prazosin for nightmares that persist

What it is Disorders that follow a trauma or a stressor, and dissociative disorders: disrupted memory, identity or sense of reality, often after trauma Driver A trauma raised norepinephrine and reduced serotonin activity: a heightened sympathetic response Triggers Severe trauma, such as major injury or prolonged exposure Trauma to oneself rather than witnessed Previous trauma; abuse or neglect in childhood non-modifiable Dissociation during the trauma Limited social support A psychiatric disorder before the trauma non-modifiable Chain Event: a trauma adrenergic surge: startle, fast heart rate Reaction: intrusion, avoidance, negative mood, arousal, dissociation acute stress disorder, 3 days to 1 month after the trauma Course: symptoms over 1 month the diagnosis changes to PTSD; 40% to 80% progress Insights Dissociation inside an acute stress or PTSD picture earns no separate dissociative diagnosis; intrusion, avoidance and arousal should be there too Prazosin blocks alpha-1 receptors, so it damps the adrenergic hyperactivity behind PTSD nightmares

Comorbidity and populationtap to open Common with PTSD: screen for and treat themMajor depressive disorder, bipolar disorder and substance use disorders; when depression criteria are also met, diagnose both PTSD is more common in womenDissociative identity disorder is also more common in women PTSD can start as young as age 1Young children may have nightmares not specific to the trauma, and replay its themes in play Raises the risk of PTSD, depression and suicidality

Event actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violation Symptoms intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and arousal; acute stress disorder counts dissociation too and needs 9 or more symptoms Clock acute stress disorder 3 days to 1 month after the trauma; PTSD over 1 month, with distress or impaired function Test none; the diagnosis is clinical

Stressor identifiable and not life-threatening Response distress out of proportion to the stressor, with significant functional impairment Clock within 3 months of the stressor; gone within 6 months after it ends Exclusion another disorder's criteria not met; the depressed-mood type has fewer than 5 depressive symptoms Types with anxiety, with depressed mood, or with conduct disturbance

Dissociative amnesia cannot recall important personal information, usually about a trauma or stress; with fugue when the patient travels or wanders Depersonalization/derealization disorder persistent or recurrent detachment from self or surroundings; reality testing intact Dissociative identity disorder 2 or more distinct identities that alternate in control, with memory gaps All not from a substance or a medical condition such as seizures, and not better explained by acute stress disorder or PTSD

SuicideAcute stress disorder and PTSD raise suicide risk; most patients with dissociative identity disorder attempt suicide Suicide Risk Assessment If a patient has an acute stress, posttraumatic or dissociative disorder, choose screening for suicidal ideation and a safety plan. Returning memoryRisk rises as dissociative amnesia lifts and memories return If memory is coming back in dissociative amnesia, choose screening for suicidal ideation and self-injury.

Time from the event Event3 days1 month3 months6 months after it ends Acute stress disorder3 days to 1 month after the trauma PTSDOver 1 month; onset can be delayed months or years Adjustment disorderWithin 3 months of the stressor; gone within 6 months after it ends

After a trauma or stressor: look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Major depressive disorder Low mood, poor sleep and focus after a loss 5 or more symptoms for 2 weeks or more; fewer after a stressor is adjustment disorder; sad mood, poor sleep and poor focus in response to a trauma fit the trauma disorder; when full criteria for both are met, diagnose both Panic disorder Waking with palpitations, sweating and breathlessness Recurrent, unexpected attacks; attacks likely set off by trauma dreams are not panic disorder Generalized anxiety disorder Tension, insomnia, poor focus Worry about many everyday matters for 6 months or more, not tied to one event Dependent personality disorder Clinging fear of being left A lifelong pattern; anxiety that began weeks ago, after a stressor, is not a personality disorder Brief psychotic disorder Hallucinations or delusions, often after a stressor Resolves within a month; psychosis is not part of acute stress disorder Oppositional defiant disorder A defiant, aggressive child With trauma, nightmares and avoidance, the aggression is PTSD arousal

Dissociation: medical and substance causes first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Substance blackout or intoxication A memory gap after alcohol or drugs Toxicology or the history finds the substance; rule it out before any dissociative diagnosis Transient global amnesia Sudden loss of new memories Identity kept; the loss is anterograde, for time and place Dissociative amnesia, with fugue if the patient travels Lost identity or personal history after a stressor; may wander Autobiographical memory lost, other cognition intact; no substance or neurologic cause Depersonalization/derealization disorder Detached from self or surroundings Memory and reality testing intact Dissociative identity disorder Memory gaps; may find belongings with no memory of owning them 2 or more distinct identities take turns in control Acute stress disorder or PTSD Dissociation after a trauma Intrusion, avoidance and arousal as well: no separate dissociative diagnosis

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Lost memory or identity → Urine toxicology Positive A substance effect; not a dissociative disorder Negative Go on to the neurologic check Same patient, first test negative → Neurologic evaluation Seizure, head injury or transient global amnesia A medical cause; not a dissociative disorder Normal, identity or personal history lost Dissociative amnesia Next step TestResultMeans Symptoms after a trauma or stressor → History: what the event was and how long since Trauma; symptoms 3 days to 1 month after the trauma Acute stress disorder Trauma; symptoms over 1 month PTSD Non-traumatic stressor; distress within 3 months of the stressor Adjustment disorder, if no other disorder's criteria are met Low mood after a stressor → Count the depressive symptoms 5 or more, for 2 weeks or more Major depressive disorder Fewer than 5 Adjustment disorder with depressed mood SkipDiagnosis is based on clinical criteria; the time since the event separates acute stress disorder from PTSD.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step A trauma 2 weeks ago; nightmares, startle, feels in a daze, will not talk about it Acute stress disorder Start trauma-focused CBT Neglect years ago; nightmares, avoidance and aggression in a child PTSD, not oppositional defiant disorder Treat as PTSD A breakup or job loss weeks ago; restless or tearful, short of another disorder Adjustment disorder Start brief supportive psychotherapy Found far from home, cannot say who they are, after a death Dissociative amnesia with fugue Order toxicology and a neurologic check first Flashbacks gone on an SSRI and CBT, but bad dreams continue Persistent PTSD nightmares Add prazosin

Pause point Burned 3 weeks ago; nightmares, startle, sad and tearful Offered as PTSD or major depression Still within 1 month of the trauma → Acute stress disorder Tearful, poor appetite and focus a month after a partner's affair Offered as major depressive episode Fewer than 5 symptoms, after a stressor → Adjustment disorder with depressed mood Restless and anxious 2 weeks after a breakup Offered as acute stress disorder or generalized anxiety disorder No life-threatening event; far short of 6 months of worry → Adjustment disorder with anxiety Aggressive foster child with nightmares, hiding and school refusal Offered as oppositional defiant disorder or separation anxiety Neglect years ago; symptoms over 1 month → PTSD

1 First lineAcute stress disorder or PTSD Trauma-focused CBT Start early in acute stress disorder, which raises the risk of PTSD; pharmacotherapy is typically not indicated there. For PTSD, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing is another trauma-focused therapy 2 First line, PTSDWith or instead of therapy; may also be first line when therapy is declined or unavailable, or depression or anxiety coexists An SSRI or SNRI Preferred for tolerability and efficacy; once it works, keep it: tapering risks relapse, and switching could worsen other PTSD symptoms 3 AdjunctNightmares persist on an SSRI or SNRI Add prazosin at bedtime Titrate to avoid orthostatic hypotension; a benzodiazepine does not help the nightmares and risks dependence Therapy for nightmaresPsychotherapy optionImage rehearsal therapy rewrites the nightmare with a better ending

Other disorders: first treatment Disorder Choose Watch for Adjustment disorder Brief supportive psychotherapy; a short course of a drug for a target symptom may be added Typically self-limited Dissociative amnesia A supportive environment; memory may return on its own Suicidal ideation and self-injury as memory returns Depersonalization/derealization disorder Reassurance, then CBT for grounding skills Fear of going crazy Dissociative identity disorder Trauma-focused psychotherapy aimed at integrating the identities Most attempt suicide

Follow-up decisions When Do or expect Acute stress disorder, at 1 month Reassess: symptoms over 1 month mean PTSD; 40% to 80% progress Adjustment disorder Expect it gone within 6 months after the stressor ends PTSD, over years Often chronic: about a third recover within a year; a third still have symptoms at 10 years

Diagnosis1 of 8 35-year-old man seen 2 weeks after a highway crash that killed the other driver wakes from dreams of the crash; jumps at car horns feels unreal, as if watching himself; will not drive no drug use; examination normal · Acute stress disorderTrauma, then intrusion, arousal, avoidance and dissociation, 3 days to 1 month after the trauma · Depersonalization/derealization disorderDissociation inside an acute stress picture earns no separate diagnosis · Posttraumatic stress disorderNeeds symptoms over 1 month 35-year-old man seen 2 weeks after a highway crash that killed the other driver wakes from dreams of the crash; jumps at car horns feels unreal, as if watching himself; will not drive no drug use; examination normal Acute stress disordera trauma, then intrusion, arousal, avoidance and dissociation 2 weeks later: acute stress disorder, 3 days to 1 month after the trauma; PTSD needs symptoms over 1 month, and dissociation inside an acute stress picture is not a separate disorder

Diagnosis2 of 8 9-year-old girl brought by her grandmother, who gained custody 2 years ago as a toddler she was left alone for days without food or heat nightmares, startles easily, hits classmates, will not sleep alone growth and examination normal · Oppositional defiant disorderWith trauma, nightmares and avoidance, the aggression is PTSD arousal · Separation anxiety disorderFear of separation from an attachment figure; here the trauma symptoms explain the picture · Posttraumatic stress disorderNeglect, then intrusion, arousal and avoidance over 1 month 9-year-old girl brought by her grandmother, who gained custody 2 years ago as a toddler she was left alone for days without food or heat nightmares, startles easily, hits classmates, will not sleep alone growth and examination normal Posttraumatic stress disordersevere neglect, then nightmares, startle, aggression and avoidance far longer than 1 month: PTSD; with trauma and intrusion, aggression is more likely PTSD arousal than oppositional defiant disorder

Diagnosis3 of 8 41-year-old man laid off from his job 5 weeks ago tearful, sleeping poorly, cannot focus on job applications still enjoys time with his children; no guilt or thoughts of death energy and appetite normal; no past mood episodes · Persistent depressive disorderDepressive symptoms for at least 2 years · Major depressive disorder5 or more symptoms for 2 weeks or more · Adjustment disorder with depressed moodStressor within 3 months; fewer than 5 depressive symptoms 41-year-old man laid off from his job 5 weeks ago tearful, sleeping poorly, cannot focus on job applications still enjoys time with his children; no guilt or thoughts of death energy and appetite normal; no past mood episodes Adjustment disorder with depressed mooda non-traumatic stressor 5 weeks ago and fewer than 5 depressive symptoms: adjustment disorder with depressed mood; major depressive disorder needs 5 or more, and persistent depressive disorder needs 2 years

Diagnosis4 of 8 20-year-old college student whose parents announced their divorce 1 month ago worried and restless; cannot sit through lectures grades slipping; sleeps adequately; eats normally no past anxiety; no substance use; vital signs and examination normal · Generalized anxiety disorderWorry about many everyday matters for 6 months or more · Acute stress disorderNeeds a trauma: actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violation · Adjustment disorder with anxietyStressor within 3 months; anxiety short of another disorder 20-year-old college student whose parents announced their divorce 1 month ago worried and restless; cannot sit through lectures grades slipping; sleeps adequately; eats normally no past anxiety; no substance use; vital signs and examination normal Adjustment disorder with anxietyanxiety and impaired function within 3 months of a non-traumatic stressor, short of another disorder: adjustment disorder with anxiety; generalized anxiety needs 6 months or more, and acute stress disorder needs a life-threatening trauma

Next step5 of 8 33-year-old firefighter treated for PTSD after a fatal building collapse flashbacks and avoidance much improved after CBT and 5 months of sertraline still wakes most nights from vivid dreams of the collapse blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg; drinks rarely · Switch sertraline to paroxetineNo better for nightmares; switching risks losing the response · Add clonazepamDoes not help PTSD nightmares; risks dependence · Add prazosin at bedtimeAn alpha-1 blocker for nightmares that persist on an SSRI 33-year-old firefighter treated for PTSD after a fatal building collapse flashbacks and avoidance much improved after CBT and 5 months of sertraline still wakes most nights from vivid dreams of the collapse blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg; drinks rarely Add prazosin at bedtimePTSD better on CBT and an SSRI but nightmares persist: add prazosin, an alpha-1 blocker, titrated for blood pressure; a benzodiazepine does not help the nightmares, and switching a working SSRI could worsen other PTSD symptoms

Diagnosis6 of 8 50-year-old woman found by police at a bus station 300 miles from home cannot give her name, address or job; attention and reasoning intact her son died suddenly 2 days earlier urine toxicology negative; neurologic examination normal · Dissociative identity disorder2 or more distinct identities take turns in control · Dissociative amnesia with fugueAutobiographical memory lost after a stressor, with travel · Transient global amnesiaIdentity kept; the loss is anterograde, for time and place 50-year-old woman found by police at a bus station 300 miles from home cannot give her name, address or job; attention and reasoning intact her son died suddenly 2 days earlier urine toxicology negative; neurologic examination normal Dissociative amnesia with fuguelost identity and personal history after a stressor, with travel, intact cognition and no substance or neurologic cause: dissociative amnesia with fugue; transient global amnesia keeps identity, and dissociative identity disorder needs 2 or more identities

Diagnosis7 of 8 24-year-old graduate student with months of recurrent episodes of feeling detached says she watches herself from outside, as if in a film knows the feeling is not real; memory for events intact no drug use; neurologic examination normal · Depersonalization/derealization disorderDetached from self or surroundings; memory and reality testing intact · SchizophreniaPsychosis: reality testing is lost · Dissociative amnesiaAutobiographical memory lost 24-year-old graduate student with months of recurrent episodes of feeling detached says she watches herself from outside, as if in a film knows the feeling is not real; memory for events intact no drug use; neurologic examination normal Depersonalization/derealization disorderrecurrent detachment from herself with reality testing and memory intact, and no substance or neurologic cause: depersonalization/derealization disorder; intact reality testing argues against psychosis, and intact memory against dissociative amnesia

Next step8 of 8 28-year-old woman seen 10 days after being sexually assaulted nightmares, startles easily, avoids the street where it happened feels numb and in a fog much of the day no suicidal thoughts; no substance use; examination normal · Trauma-focused CBTFirst line for acute stress disorder; early treatment lowers the risk of PTSD · Prazosin at bedtimeAn adjunct for PTSD nightmares that persist on an SSRI or SNRI · A scheduled benzodiazepineDrugs are typically not needed in acute stress disorder 28-year-old woman seen 10 days after being sexually assaulted nightmares, startles easily, avoids the street where it happened feels numb and in a fog much of the day no suicidal thoughts; no substance use; examination normal Trauma-focused CBTacute stress disorder 10 days after a sexual assault: trauma-focused CBT first, started early to lower the risk of PTSD; drugs are typically not needed, and prazosin is an adjunct for PTSD nightmares that persist on an SSRI

Major Depressive Disordercovers a full depressive episode after a loss Psychosiscovers brief psychotic disorder, often after a stressor Cluster B Personality Disorderscovers borderline personality and childhood trauma Cluster C Personality Disorderscovers dependent personality Major Depressive Disorder covers a full depressive episode after a loss. Psychosis covers brief psychotic disorder, often after a stressor. Cluster B Personality Disorders covers borderline personality and childhood trauma. Cluster C Personality Disorders covers dependent personality.

After a trauma or stressor, ask what it was and how long since: a life-threatening trauma 3 days to 1 month after the trauma is acute stress disorder and over 1 month is PTSD; any other stressor, with symptoms short of another disorder, is adjustment disorder.

briefs.title: Eating Disorders
briefs.sub: weight · compensation · medical mimicsIs the weight low, and do binges carry compensation?
blocks: weight · compensation · medical mimicsIs the weight low, and do binges carry compensation?

Weight sorts it: anorexia nervosa has a body mass index (BMI) under 18.5 with fear of weight gain; bulimia nervosa has normal weight or overweight with binges and compensatory behavior; binge eating disorder has binges without compensation Exclude a medical cause first: in long-standing type 1 diabetes with early satiety and vomiting, order a gastric emptying study after endoscopy, before psychotherapy Anorexia: nutritional rehabilitation and psychotherapy; bulimia: cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) plus fluoxetine; refeed gradually and watch phosphate

What it is Disturbed eating driven by body shape and weight concerns (anorexia and bulimia nervosa), or loss-of-control binges without compensation (binge eating disorder) Driver Excessive concern with body shape and weight drives restriction or compensation Associated Depression commonly coexists with anorexia nervosa; binges are followed by guilt and low mood Chain Restriction loss of fat lowers leptin and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) amenorrhea and low bone density Vomiting hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis Insights Does purging rule out anorexia nervosa? No: the binge-eating/purging type of anorexia can also purge; weight separates it from bulimia VomitingCompensationSelf-induced vomiting is common in bulimia but not required: fasting, excessive exercise, laxatives, enemas, diuretics and diet pills also count Is food aversion in a diabetic patient with early satiety an eating disorder? Not until gastroparesis is excluded: food aversion can follow the symptoms
BMI under 18.5 Fear intense fear of weight gain Body image distorted view of weight and shape Types restricting or binge-eating/purging
Episodes binges with compensatory behavior Frequency at least weekly for 3 months Self-view driven by shape and weight Weight normal or overweight
Episodes recurrent loss-of-control binges Compensation none
Avoidance sensory features of food Onset typically infancy or early childhood Body image not disturbed

Severe malnutritionAnorexia nervosa with BMI under 15, weight under 70% of ideal, unstable vital signs, cardiac dysfunction or acute complications of malnutrition (syncope, seizures, electrolyte disturbances) If any of these is present, choose admit for nutritional rehabilitation. RefeedingRapid feeding of a severely malnourished patient If nutrition is restarted, choose increase calories gradually; watch phosphate, potassium and magnesium. Refeeding complications: CARBS MnemonicCARBS (congestive heart failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, bloating, seizures): the complications of refeeding PurgingFrequent vomiting If vomiting is frequent, choose check potassium and chloride: hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is expected. Mallory-Weiss tear VomitingMallory-Weiss tears are usually seen with alcohol use disorder or bulimia nervosa

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Duration Decides it Bulimia nervosa Loss-of-control binges, then vomiting, fasting, exercise or laxatives; shape and weight concerns At least weekly for 3 months Normal weight or overweight; vomiting not required Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type Binges and purging with intense fear of weight gain BMI under 18.5 Binge eating disorder Recurrent loss-of-control binges; obesity and type 2 diabetes risk No compensatory behavior Anorexia nervosa, restricting type Restriction, fear of weight gain, distorted body image; amenorrhea, lanugo, bradycardia Other findingsAssociatedHypercarotenemia, mitral valve prolapse, anemia, low bone density with stress fractures BMI under 18.5 without binges Gastroparesis (medical mimic) Long-standing type 1 diabetes; early satiety, postprandial vomiting, weight loss; worried by the weight loss CausesCausesMost often idiopathic; also diabetes (type 1 more than type 2), medications such as tricyclics and calcium channel blockers, and surgery Long-standing diabetes Delayed emptying on a gastric emptying study, after endoscopy excludes obstruction Hypothyroidism (medical mimic) Constipation, cold intolerance, bradycardia Hidden anorexiaA body complaint firstPatients with anorexia often hide it, so it may arrive as constipation or feeling cold; gastrointestinal complications are extremely common in anorexia, and slowed colonic transit often causes constipation. Typically weight gain and diastolic hypertension; anorexia brings low weight and low blood pressure Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) Avoids foods for their sensory features or the experience of eating Typically begins in infancy or early childhood No body-image disturbance Body dysmorphic disorder Preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance Not diagnosed when weight concern meets eating disorder criteria Primary adrenal insufficiency May cause vomiting, weight loss and decreased appetite, without fear of eating Decreased appetite without fear of eating; an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation test can help diagnose it

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Weight loss, restriction or purging → BMI and vital signs BMI under 18.5 Anorexia nervosa range BMI under 15, unstable vital signs or another admission criterion Hospitalize → Electrolytes Hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis Vomiting Severe restriction → ECG (electrocardiogram) Bradycardia, prolonged QT Cardiac effects of starvation Targeted tests TestResultMeans Long-standing diabetes with early satiety and postprandial vomiting → Upper endoscopy No obstruction Proceed to a gastric emptying study → Gastric emptying study Delayed emptying Gastroparesis, not an eating disorder Purging suspected but denied → Urine chloride Below 20 mEq/L Vomiting

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Dorsal hand calluses, parotid enlargement, enamel erosion at normal weight Bulimia nervosa with vomiting CBT, nutritional rehabilitation and fluoxetine Lanugo, amenorrhea, bradycardia, yellow-tinged skin Anorexia nervosa Nutritional rehabilitation and psychotherapy; hospitalize for any admission criterion Binges without compensation, obesity Binge eating disorder CBT or behavioral weight loss therapy; a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), lisdexamfetamine or topiramate Type 1 diabetes with early satiety, vomiting and worry about weight loss Gastroparesis Endoscopy, then a gastric emptying study Low urine chloride with metabolic alkalosis Covert vomiting AldosteroneVolume contractionVomiting loses hydrochloric acid and potassium: a hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Volume contraction activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and secondary hyperaldosteronism worsens the losses. Peripheral edema may occur from third spacing. Treat as bulimia or binge-eating/purging anorexia, by weight Early pregnancy with vomiting plus weight loss, skipped meals then overeating, and feeling she already looks pregnant Possible eating disorder masked by nausea and vomiting of pregnancy Evaluate for disordered eating behaviors; ordinary nausea and vomiting of pregnancy is relatively mild, with no weight loss

Pause point Diabetic patient whose stress about eating follows early satiety and vomiting Offered: CBT or an SSRI An eating disorder is less likely → Medical causes are excluded before psychiatric diagnoses

Where to treat Finding Action BMI under 15, weight under 70% of ideal, unstable vital signs, cardiac dysfunction or acute complications of malnutrition (syncope, seizures, electrolyte disturbances) Hospitalize Bulimia nervosa Outpatient: hospitalization typically not required

1 Anorexiaanorexia nervosa Nutritional rehabilitation and psychotherapy 2 Addanorexia not responding to first-line treatment Olanzapine Evidence LimitsOlanzapine is used for weight gain, with limited evidence and known adverse effects; SSRIs treat comorbid anxiety or depression, not anorexia itself 3 Bulimiabulimia nervosa CBT and nutritional rehabilitation plus fluoxetine ; not bupropion: it can cause seizures in bulimia SSRI Adverse Effects 4 Binge eatingbinge eating disorder CBT or behavioral weight loss therapy; an SSRI, lisdexamfetamine or topiramate 5 Mimicgastroparesis confirmed Small, low-fat meals; metoclopramide first line, erythromycin second line

Follow-up decisions When Do Refeeding begins Increase calories gradually; watch phosphate, potassium and magnesium Long-standing anorexia Expect low bone density and stress fractures; the bone loss is typically not reversible Depression coexists It may resolve with weight gain; an SSRI may be used for it Major Depressive Disorder

Diagnosis1 of 7 24-year-old woman eats large amounts rapidly several times a week and cannot stop Afterward she fasts for a day and runs extra miles; she hates her body shape BMI 21; pulse 98; she denies vomiting · Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging typeRequires a BMI under 18.5 · Bulimia nervosaBinges with compensation at a normal weight · Binge eating disorderNo compensatory behavior 24-year-old woman eats large amounts rapidly several times a week and cannot stop Afterward she fasts for a day and runs extra miles; she hates her body shape BMI 21; pulse 98; she denies vomiting Bulimia nervosaBinges with compensatory fasting and exercise at a normal weight are bulimia nervosa; vomiting is not required, and binge-purge anorexia needs a BMI under 18.5

Next step2 of 7 25-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since childhood has lost 6 kg in 4 months She feels full after a few bites, vomits after meals, and worries about losing weight Upper endoscopy was normal; electrolytes and thyroid function normal · Gastric emptying studyConfirms delayed emptying once endoscopy has excluded obstruction · Trial of an SSRIHer distress is most likely secondary to gastroparesis · Cognitive-behavioral therapyPsychotherapy comes only after a medical cause is investigated 25-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since childhood has lost 6 kg in 4 months She feels full after a few bites, vomits after meals, and worries about losing weight Upper endoscopy was normal; electrolytes and thyroid function normal Gastric emptying studyLong-standing type 1 diabetes with early satiety and postprandial vomiting suggests gastroparesis; with obstruction excluded, a gastric emptying study confirms it before any psychiatric diagnosis

Diagnosis3 of 7 22-year-old runner has missed her periods for 5 months She eats one small meal a day, fears gaining weight and thinks her thighs are large BMI 16.8; pulse 48; fine hair on her back; no binges · Anorexia nervosaBMI under 18.5 with fear of weight gain · Bulimia nervosaNormal weight or overweight · Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorderNo body-image disturbance 22-year-old runner has missed her periods for 5 months She eats one small meal a day, fears gaining weight and thinks her thighs are large BMI 16.8; pulse 48; fine hair on her back; no binges Anorexia nervosaRestriction with fear of weight gain, a distorted body image and a BMI under 18.5, plus amenorrhea, bradycardia and lanugo, is anorexia nervosa

Next step4 of 7 23-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa comes for a scheduled visit She has lost more weight and feels dizzy whenever she stands BMI 14.5; pulse 38/min; blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg · Outpatient cognitive-behavioral therapyNot safe while vital signs are unstable · Hospital admission for nutritional rehabilitationA BMI under 15 and unstable vital signs are each an indication for admission · Start olanzapineReserved for anorexia not responding to first-line treatment 23-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa comes for a scheduled visit She has lost more weight and feels dizzy whenever she stands BMI 14.5; pulse 38/min; blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg Hospital admission for nutritional rehabilitationA BMI under 15 with unstable vital signs is an indication for hospitalization, where nutritional rehabilitation begins

Diagnosis5 of 7 26-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted to the hospital A high-calorie feeding plan is started on the first day By day 3 she has weakness, palpitations and new leg swelling · HyperkalemiaPotassium falls with refeeding · HypophosphatemiaPhosphate falls with the insulin surge of refeeding · HypermagnesemiaMagnesium falls with refeeding 26-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted to the hospital A high-calorie feeding plan is started on the first day By day 3 she has weakness, palpitations and new leg swelling HypophosphatemiaRapid refeeding triggers an insulin surge that lowers phosphate, potassium and magnesium; heart failure and arrhythmias can follow, so calories are increased gradually

Next step6 of 7 20-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa purges several times a week She has low mood and asks for a medication that could also help her quit smoking Exam shows parotid swelling and calluses on the backs of her hands · BupropionCan cause seizures in bulimia; contraindicated · Fluoxetine with CBTFirst-line drug with psychotherapy for bulimia · OlanzapineFor anorexia not responding to first-line treatment 20-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa purges several times a week She has low mood and asks for a medication that could also help her quit smoking Exam shows parotid swelling and calluses on the backs of her hands Fluoxetine with CBTBulimia nervosa is treated with CBT, nutritional rehabilitation and fluoxetine; bupropion is avoided because it can cause seizures in these patients

Diagnosis7 of 7 38-year-old man with obesity eats large meals in secret several nights a week He feels out of control and ashamed but never vomits, fasts or overexercises BMI 34; hemoglobin A1c is elevated · Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging typeRequires a BMI under 18.5 · Bulimia nervosaRequires compensatory behavior · Binge eating disorderBinges without compensatory behavior 38-year-old man with obesity eats large meals in secret several nights a week He feels out of control and ashamed but never vomits, fasts or overexercises BMI 34; hemoglobin A1c is elevated Binge eating disorderRecurrent loss-of-control binges without compensatory behavior are binge eating disorder, which raises the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes

Major Depressive Disorderdepression that coexists with an eating disorder SSRI Adverse Effectsfluoxetine, and why not bupropion Major Depressive Disorder: depression that coexists with an eating disorder. SSRI Adverse Effects: fluoxetine, and why not bupropion.
Exclude a medical cause of early satiety and vomiting, then sort by weight and by whether binges carry compensation.

briefs.title: Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder
briefs.sub: vaginismus · exclude a body cause, then treatIs it pelvic floor tightening with fear of pain, or a cause the examination finds?
blocks: vaginismus · exclude a body cause, then treatIs it pelvic floor tightening with fear of pain, or a cause the examination finds?

Penetration difficulty, pain, fear of pain or a tightening pelvic floor about 6 months distress GPPPD (genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder), the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) term that merged vaginismus and dyspareunia Exclude a body cause first: inspect the vulva, map with a cotton swab, check the pelvic floor with one finger, test any discharge Pelvic floor physical therapy psychotherapy such as CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) psychoeducation, combined, not stepped

What it is One or more of: penetration difficulty, pain, fear of pain, pelvic floor tightening on the attempt About 6 months clinically significant distress no better explanation Driver Typically levator ani (pelvic floor) dysfunction involuntary contraction when a finger is inserted NamingIn practice:Merck Manual notes that, because symptoms typically come from levator ani dysfunction, the term levator ani syndrome is increasingly used in place of vaginismus. On the exam, the answer is vaginismus or GPPPD; levator syndrome in a rectal pain stem is a different disorder, episodic rectal pain from levator ani spasm. Triggers History of abuse non-modifiable, anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; not present in every patient Can also follow a vulvar infection such as candidiasis, a gynecologic problem such as endometriosis, or pregnancy Chain Anticipated pain fear pelvic floor tightens on the attempt more pain and failed penetration more fear, and avoidance may follow Examination typically normal apart from a tight pelvic floor Insights Normal tissue and swab a pelvic floor that contracts on one finger GPPPD when about 6 months with distress; an infection, lesion or atrophy on examination treat that cause first Anxiety only about penetration: not GAD (generalized anxiety disorder); pain without preoccupation: not somatic symptom disorder

Criteria and course, part by partdetail behind the chain Persistent or recurrent trouble with one or more of four: penetration during intercourse; marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain with intercourse or attempts; marked fear or anxiety about that pain before, during or after penetration; marked tensing of the pelvic floor on the attempt About 6 months or longer: DSM-5 says approximately 6 months, and Merck Manual gives the DSM-5-TR (fifth edition, text revision) version as at least 6 months Not better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or other major stressors; not due to a substance, a medication or another medical condition Abuse, anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; some patients have none After a vulvar infection such as candidiasis, a gynecologic problem such as endometriosis, or pregnancy

Symptoms one or more of penetration difficulty, marked pain with attempts, marked fear of that pain, or marked pelvic floor tightening on the attempt Duration about 6 monthsGuideline detailDSM-5 says approximately 6 months; Merck Manual Professional gives the DSM-5-TR version as at least 6 months with significant distress. or longer Distress clinically significant Exclusions no nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or major stressor explains it better; no substance, medication or medical cause
SafetyPartner violence: ask about it directly, in private If partner violence is disclosed or suspected, choose a check of her immediate risk and a safety plan made with her.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Vulvodynia Provoked formsExam detailNBME's explanation describes the spontaneous form: vulvar, not vaginal, pain that penetration does not typically provoke. The provoked form, localized to the vestibule (provoked vestibulodynia), does hurt on entry with a tampon or intercourse. Either way, the cotton swab finds the tender spot; in GPPPD the vestibule is not tender to light touch and the pelvic floor contracts. OverlapIn practice:The two can coexist: pelvic floor tightness is often present in provoked vestibulodynia, and pelvic floor physical therapy is first line for it too. Vulvar burning, or entry pain with a tampon or intercourse 3 months or more; no identifiable cause; the cotton swab reproduces the pain at the vestibule or vulva, which it does not in GPPPD Vaginal candidiasis Recent antibiotics, diabetes, immunosuppression Red, swollen vulva and vagina; thick white discharge; organisms on microscopy Generalized anxiety disorder Worry about a range of topics 6 months or more of excessive, hard-to-control worry with at least 3 of 6 symptoms; anxiety not limited to penetration Somatic symptom disorder Preoccupied with symptoms; repeated visits More than 6 months; disproportionate thoughts, anxiety or time and energy on symptoms that distress or disrupt daily life, beyond attempted penetration Posttraumatic stress disorder Trauma, then intrusive memories or nightmares; may avoid reminders More than 1 month of symptoms; intrusions and avoidance tied to the trauma, not only to penetration Female sexual interest/arousal disorder Little interest or arousal; no pain 6 months; at least 3 of 6 symptoms; distress Genitourinary syndrome of menopause Postmenopausal burning and dryness May show pale, dry tissue (may look normal in early menopause) Lichen sclerosus Burning, dryness, itching Visible skin changes; biopsy confirms and excludes cancer Endometriosis Deep pain; painful periods common Cul-de-sac nodularity on rectovaginal examination Major depressive disorder Low mood, lost interest 2 weeks, five symptoms; low mood or anhedonia beyond sex

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Pain, fear or difficulty with penetration: examine before labeling it → Vulvar inspection Atrophy, redness, lesions, discoloration, trauma A body cause that better explains it, not GPPPD Normal vulva, or redness only at the vestibule GPPPD or vulvodynia remain unless discharge or deep pain points elsewhere; the swab and one finger decide → Cotton swab mapping, hymen included Swab: pain at the vestibule or vulva Vulvodynia; provoked vestibulodynia if localized to the vestibule Swab: no pain Points away from vulvodynia → Single-digit vaginal examination One finger: pelvic floor contracts or is tender Pelvic floor dysfunction, as in GPPPD Targeted tests TestResultMeans Discharge, burning or odor → pH testing and microscopy of the discharge Organisms Vaginitis such as candidiasis Pain is deep → Rectovaginal examinationBimanual examination Cul-de-sac nodularity Endometriosis Retroverted uterus or a pelvic mass A structural cause of deep pain Next step TestResultMeans A pelvic mass is felt on bimanual examination → Transvaginal US A myoma or other mass A structural cause of deep pain
No body cause and a swab that does not reproduce the pain, with one or more of penetration difficulty, pain, fear of pain or pelvic floor tightening for about 6 months with distress: GPPPD.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Normal vulva; painless swab; pelvic floor contracts on one finger GPPPD Pelvic floor physical therapy with CBT Swab reproduces burning or entry pain at the vestibule; normal skin, no yeast Vulvodynia (provoked vestibulodynia if only at the vestibule) Vulvar care, pelvic floor physical therapy, topical lidocaine Began after a treated yeast infection; microscopy clear; pelvic floor contracts on one finger GPPPD; active infection excluded Treat the GPPPD, not the yeast Discharge, burning or odor Vaginitis such as candidiasis Check vaginal pH and do microscopy Deep pain with painful periods Endometriosis, not an entry problem Perform a rectovaginal examination Postmenopausal; pale, dry tissue Genitourinary syndrome of menopause Lubricants or moisturizers first; low-dose vaginal estrogen for moderate to severe symptoms (most effective)

Pause point Pain at the entrance; the pelvic floor clamps against penetration Offered as vulvodynia All the options The optionsGeneralized anxiety disorder: she is anxious; but it takes 6 months or more of excessive worry over many topics, plus three other symptoms; her anxiety is specific to penetration. Somatic symptom disorder: the complaint is pain; but outside attempted penetration she shows no excessive preoccupation or repeated health-seeking. Vaginal candidiasis: it is associated with vaginismus; but it typically shows vulvar and vaginal redness, swelling and thick white discharge, and she has no antibiotic use, diabetes or immunosuppression. Vulvodynia: both hurt at the entrance; but NBME describes vulvar, not vaginal, pain that penetration does not typically provoke; its provoked form does hurt on entry, but then the cotton swab finds a tender vestibule, and neither form explains a pelvic floor that contracts to prevent penetration. Down to two: vaginismus or vulvodynia. Vaginismus: pain, anxiety before sex and a pelvic floor that tightens to block penetration, with a speculum that is hard to advance. Vulvodynia is vulvar pain the swab maps; it does not explain a clamping pelvic floor → Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (vaginismus) In practice NBME versus criteriaIn practice: the DSM-5-TR calls it genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder; the NBME question gives no duration and uses the older term. Anxious about penetration Offered as generalized anxiety disorder Anxiety confined to penetration → Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder; generalized anxiety disorder needs worry over many topics

1 Primarycommonly all together; the parts are combined (multimodal), not stepped Pelvic floor physical therapy Teaches pelvic muscle relaxation, sometimes with biofeedback; considered an effective intervention. 2 Primaryrung 1 starts, given together with it Psychotherapy such as CBT; sex therapy Aims at fear and anxiety about pain; CBT is strongly recommended. 3 Primaryrung 1 starts, given together with it Psychoeducation A primary part of treatment. 4 Addpelvic muscles stay tight Sequential vaginal dilators Self-dilation devices; part of multidisciplinary care. Other partsGuideline detailMultidisciplinary care can also include relationship and sexual counseling, lubricants and onabotulinumtoxinA injection. 5 Adjunctsex is still painful, at any stage Topical lidocaine before sex For a short time only.

Treatment by diagnosis Diagnosis Choose Not GPPPD Pelvic floor physical therapy with CBT Antifungal when microscopy is clear Genitourinary syndrome of menopause Lubricants or moisturizers first, often enough for mild symptoms; low-dose vaginal estrogen, the most effective, for moderate to severe Stopping at lubricants when symptoms stay moderate to severe Lichen sclerosus Usually a high-potency topical steroid such as clobetasol; biopsy any thickened or ulcerated area (squamous cell carcinoma risk) Vulvodynia Gentle vulvar care, pelvic floor physical therapy, topical lidocaine; amitriptyline or gabapentin may help Vestibulectomy first: only after nonsurgical options fail, pain localized to the vestibule Endometriosis Options such as nonopioid analgesics, combined oral contraceptives or progestogens; laparoscopic excision

Follow-up decisions When Do On topical lidocaine Keep it short term Working through dilators or graded self-touch Progress gradually, one stage at a time Vestibulectomy considered for vulvodynia at the vestibule Check for GPPPD (vaginismus) and treat it first
