Somatic Symptom and Related Disordersin somatic symptom disorder, distressing body symptoms with thoughts, anxiety or time out of proportion, over 6 months; pain confined to attempted penetration, with fear of that pain and a pelvic floor that tightens, is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (GPPPD) instead Sexual Dysfunctionerectile, desire, arousal and orgasm disorders Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders: in somatic symptom disorder, distressing body symptoms with thoughts, anxiety or time out of proportion, over 6 months; pain confined to attempted penetration, with fear of that pain and a pelvic floor that tightens, is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (GPPPD) instead. Sexual Dysfunction: erectile, desire, arousal and orgasm disorders.

When penetration hurts or fails, examine first: inspection looks for a body cause, microscopy tests any discharge, the swab maps vestibular pain and one finger checks the pelvic floor. Difficulty with one or more of penetration, pain, fear of pain or a pelvic floor that tightens, for about 6 months with distress and no body cause, is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, treated with pelvic floor therapy and psychotherapy together.

briefs.title: Sexual Dysfunction
briefs.sub: erectile dysfunction · desire and arousal · orgasm · sexual painOrganic or psychogenic, and what causes it?
blocks: erectile dysfunction · desire and arousal · orgasm · sexual painOrganic or psychogenic, and what causes it?

Erections that also fail with masturbation, in sleep or on waking organic; erections kept there, failing only with a partner psychogenic, such as performance anxiety Several causes in one history: ongoing heavy drinking points to alcohol; a drug started before the onset points to the drug; one taken for years before the onset, or a stable chronic disease, is less likely; a primary disorder needs 6 months or more and no drug, substance or medical cause Remove the cause. Psychogenic: sex therapy. Organic: a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor first, never with a nitrate

What it is Trouble with sexual desire, arousal (erectile dysfunction is the arousal disorder in men), orgasm, or pain with sex Driver Organic: damage to the nerves, blood supply or hormones of erection Psychogenic: may stem from performance anxiety, stress or depression; may be tied to a partner or setting Triggers Heavy alcohol use, chronic or acute Drugs: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), antipsychotics, tricyclics, beta-blockers, spironolactone Atherosclerosis, smoking and diabetes Low testosterone or high prolactin Performance anxiety, stress or depression Chain Organic: nerve, vessel or hormone injury erections fail in every setting, sleep included; at first now and then, later persistent Psychogenic: anxiety or guilt about sex sudden failure with a partner or in one setting; nocturnal and morning erections kept Overlap: organic failure reactive anxiety that compounds it Insights Erections in sleep or with masturbation show the nerves and vessels work, so a failure confined to partnered sex is psychological A side effect would be unlikely to newly emerge after years on a drug: the suspect is the drug started just before the onset

Populationtap to open Erectile dysfunction that starts after normal function often has both organic and psychological causes Slower erection and ejaculation with age Rule out medical causes such as vaginal atrophy before a desire or arousal disorder

Groups desire (male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, female sexual interest/arousal disorder), arousal (erectile dysfunction), orgasm (premature or delayed ejaculation, female orgasmic disorder), pain (genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder: vaginismus, dyspareunia) Duration 6 months or more Exclusion not from a drug, a substance or a medical condition Premature ejaculation within 1 minute of penetration; a normal time with masturbation does not rule it out

Heart diseaseNew vascular erectile dysfunction is often the first sign of cardiovascular disease Stable Ischemic Heart Disease If a man has new erectile dysfunction from a vascular cause, choose an evaluation for undiagnosed cardiovascular disease. NitratesWith a nitrate or an alpha blocker, the first-line drug for organic erectile dysfunction can cause hypotension or syncope If a man takes a nitrate, choose no phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor.

Erectile failure: substance, drug and medical causes first, most tempting first Cause Fingerprint Decides it Alcohol Heavy daily drinking; erections fail with masturbation too Chronic heavy use that continues; can improve with abstinence or cutting down An SSRI Low libido, erectile failure, delayed ejaculation or anorgasmia Started before the onset; years on it before the onset argue against it An antipsychotic Low libido or erectile failure, with gynecomastia or galactorrhea Gynecomastia points to a raised prolactin, not an SSRI An antihypertensive Erectile failure on a beta-blocker or spironolactone Started before the onset Atherosclerosis or diabetes Smoker or diabetic; erections weaken over time Gradual, from weak erections to none; a stable disease rarely explains a recent change Aortoiliac occlusion (Leriche syndrome) Erectile failure with buttock and thigh claudication Weak femoral and leg pulses Low testosterone or prolactinoma Low libido; infertility; headache with prolactinoma Morning testosterone low or low-normal, then prolactin and luteinizing hormone A statin On the medication list Not a known cause of erectile dysfunction

Psychological and primary sexual disorders, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Performance anxiety (psychogenic erectile dysfunction) Sudden; one partner or setting; libido normal Erections kept in sleep, on waking and with masturbation Depression Low libido with low mood Sexual symptoms lift with the mood; worsening as mood lifts points to the drug Female sexual interest/arousal disorder Little sexual interest or arousal 6 months or more; no drug, substance or medical cause Male hypoactive sexual desire disorder Few or no sexual thoughts or desire 6 months or more; no drug, substance or medical cause Premature ejaculation Ejaculation within 1 minute of penetration 6 months or more; a normal time with masturbation does not rule it out Delayed ejaculation Delayed or absent ejaculation 6 months or more; on an SSRI, the drug can cause it, so rule the drug out first Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (vaginismus, dyspareunia) Pain or fear with penetration Involuntary pelvic floor contraction on examination

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Erectile failure → History of erections in sleep, on waking or with masturbation Absent there too Organic: find the cause Present; fails only with a partner Psychogenic, such as performance anxiety Organic picture → Morning testosterone Low or low-normal Measure prolactin and luteinizing hormone Normal Glucose, lipids or thyroid tests only as the history suggests Next step TestResultMeans Several possible causes in one history → Line up alcohol, drugs and diseases against the onset Heavy drinking that continues Alcohol A drug started before the onset The drug A drug taken for years, or a stable disease Less likely the cause SkipNocturnal tumescence monitoring measures the same sleep erections the history already asks about.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Fails only with a new partner; morning erections and libido intact Performance anxiety Sex therapy Fails with masturbation too in a heavy daily drinker Alcohol Counsel abstinence or cutting down Buttock claudication, weak femoral pulses, erectile failure Aortoiliac occlusion (Leriche syndrome) Order a cardiovascular evaluation Ejaculation within 1 minute of penetration for months Premature ejaculation Start an SSRI

Pause point Heavy daily drinker; erections fail with a new partner and with masturbation Offered as performance anxiety, guilt or an SSRI taken for years Fails with masturbation too; the SSRI long predates the onset → Alcohol Erectile failure and breast enlargement on sertraline and risperidone Offered as sertraline or diabetic neuropathy Gynecomastia points to prolactin → Risperidone

Treat the cause first Cause Choose Watch for Alcohol Abstinence or cutting down Erections can improve A drug started before the onset Stop or replace it An SSRI: as in SSRI Adverse Effects Diabetes, prolactinoma or low testosterone Treat the disorder Testosterone alone may have little effect on erections

1 First line, psychogenicErections kept in sleep, on waking or with masturbation Sex therapy The mainstay for psychogenic erectile dysfunction; works best started promptly 2 First line, organicErections fail in every setting; the cause removed or not reversible A phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor Slows breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate, so smooth muscle relaxes and blood fills the corpus cavernosum; contraindicated with nitrates or alpha blockers 3 Second lineA phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor fails or is poorly tolerated Vacuum device or penile injection These may be used when the inhibitor fails or is poorly tolerated

Other disorders: first treatment Disorder Choose Watch for Premature ejaculation An SSRI Puts the delayed ejaculation side effect to use Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (vaginismus) Pelvic floor physical therapy Rule out a body cause first, as in Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder

Follow-up decisions When Do or expect Alcohol cut down or stopped Expect erections to improve Organic cause left untreated Failure that comes and goes becomes persistent Organic erectile dysfunction Watch for reactive anxiety that compounds it

Ask where erections still work: kept in sleep, on waking or with masturbation means psychogenic; failing there too means organic, so line the causes up against the onset: ongoing heavy drinking, a drug started just before, then vascular or hormonal disease.

briefs.title: Defense Mechanisms
briefs.sub: where the feeling goes · mature or immatureWhere does the feeling go?
blocks: where the feeling goes · mature or immatureWhere does the feeling go?

Name the defense by where the feeling goes: to a safer target (displacement), onto someone else (projection), into its opposite (reaction formation), into an acceptable activity (sublimation) Mature defenses adapt without impairing social functioning (SASH: sublimation, altruism, suppression, humor); immature ones give short-term relief but often cost long-term interpersonal difficulties Suppression is intentional; repression is involuntary
Defense mechanisms are mostly unconscious ways of adapting that protect self-image (suppression is the intentional exception); immature ones appear in children and in adults under stress

Immature defenses Defense What happens Example Displacement Moves a feeling from its upsetting source to a safer target Yelled at by the principal, a teacher criticizes her husband at home Projection Attributes one's own unacceptable feeling to someone else A man who wants to cheat accuses his wife of infidelity Reaction formation Turns an unacceptable feeling or impulse into its opposite A patient with sexual thoughts enters a monastery Passive aggression Expresses hostility indirectly, avoiding open conflict An employee is repeatedly late to get back at a manager Acting out Expresses unacceptable feelings through impulsive actions A child throws tantrums; a child with sick parents misbehaves at school; an adolescent turns to promiscuous sex during the parents' divorce Splitting Sees people or situations as all good or all bad All the nurses are cold, all the doctors warm Regression Returns to an earlier developmental pattern of coping Denial Behaves as if a painful reality does not exist Plans a full work schedule despite being warned about chemotherapy fatigue Rationalization Justifies behavior with logical reasons to avoid a difficult truth After being fired, says the job did not matter Intellectualization Focuses on facts and logic to avoid distressing feelings A patient with cancer discusses only survival rates Isolation of affect Separates feelings from ideas and events Describes a murder in graphic detail without emotion Repression Involuntarily keeps an idea or feeling out of awareness Does not remember counseling during a childhood divorce Identification Unconsciously takes on traits, good or bad, of a more powerful person A resident carries his stethoscope like his favorite attending; a child of an abusive father becomes an abuser Undoing Tries to reverse a situation by adopting a new behavior After a fantasy of sabotaging his wife's car, he has it serviced

Mature defenses (SASH) Defense What happens Example Sublimation Channels an impulse into a socially acceptable activity A teenager's aggression toward a parent goes into sports Altruism Gains satisfaction from helping others, often at a personal cost A crime boss makes a large charitable donation Suppression Deliberately sets an unwanted feeling aside to cope Chooses not to worry about the big game until it starts Humor Uses jokes to deflect anxiety or discomfort

Commonly confused pairs Pair Decides it Displacement or projection Displacement redirects the feeling to a safer target; projection says the other person has it Suppression or repression Suppression is intentional and temporary; repression is involuntary Sublimation or reaction formation Sublimation keeps the wish in an acceptable form; reaction formation flips it to the opposite Intellectualization or rationalization Intellectualization retreats into facts; rationalization supplies reasons for an action already taken Displacement or passive aggression Displacement hits a safer target; passive aggression expresses the feeling in a roundabout way instead of directly Acting out or regression Acting out is impulsive action; regression is coping like a much younger person
Pause point Angry at his boss, he yells at his children Offered as projection He keeps the anger; only its target changes → Displacement

Diagnosis1 of 5 A nurse is criticized harshly by her supervisor and says nothing in reply That evening she snaps at her teenage son over a small mess in the kitchen She later admits her anger was really at the supervisor · ProjectionAttributes one's own feeling to another person · Passive aggressionExpresses the feeling in a roundabout way instead of directly · DisplacementMoves the feeling from its source to a safer target A nurse is criticized harshly by her supervisor and says nothing in reply That evening she snaps at her teenage son over a small mess in the kitchen She later admits her anger was really at the supervisor DisplacementAnger at a superior redirected onto a safer target is displacement; passive aggression expresses the feeling in a roundabout way instead of directly, and projection attributes the feeling to someone else

Diagnosis2 of 5 A married man privately attracted to a coworker tells no one about it He repeatedly accuses his wife of flirting with other men She has given no cause for suspicion; he denies any interest in anyone else · Reaction formationTurns the feeling into its opposite · ProjectionAttributes his own unacceptable feeling to her · DisplacementRedirects a feeling to a safer target A married man privately attracted to a coworker tells no one about it He repeatedly accuses his wife of flirting with other men She has given no cause for suspicion; he denies any interest in anyone else ProjectionAttributing his own unacceptable attraction to his wife is projection; displacement would redirect a feeling to a safer target, and reaction formation would flip it

Diagnosis3 of 5 A 16-year-old has frequent angry outbursts toward his strict father He joins the wrestling team and pours the anger into training His grades and mood improve, and he now competes at the state level · SublimationChannels the impulse into an acceptable activity · Reaction formationTurns the feeling into its opposite · Acting outExpresses the feeling through impulsive action A 16-year-old has frequent angry outbursts toward his strict father He joins the wrestling team and pours the anger into training His grades and mood improve, and he now competes at the state level SublimationChanneling aggression into an acceptable activity is sublimation, a mature defense; reaction formation would show the opposite feeling, and acting out is impulsive action

Diagnosis4 of 5 A medical student learns the night before an exam that her grandmother was hospitalized She decides to set the worry aside until the exam is over Afterward she calls her family and talks openly about her fears · RepressionInvoluntarily withholds the feeling from awareness · DenialBehaves as if the reality does not exist · SuppressionIntentionally and temporarily sets the feeling aside A medical student learns the night before an exam that her grandmother was hospitalized She decides to set the worry aside until the exam is over Afterward she calls her family and talks openly about her fears SuppressionDeliberately and temporarily setting a feeling aside is suppression, a mature defense; repression is involuntary, and denial treats the reality as absent

Diagnosis5 of 5 A 52-year-old man just diagnosed with lung cancer meets his oncologist He asks only about survival statistics and staging systems When asked how he feels about the news, he cites published response rates instead · IntellectualizationFocuses on facts to avoid the feeling · DenialBehaves as if the diagnosis does not exist · RationalizationSupplies reasons for an action already taken A 52-year-old man just diagnosed with lung cancer meets his oncologist He asks only about survival statistics and staging systems When asked how he feels about the news, he cites published response rates instead IntellectualizationRetreating into facts to avoid distressing feelings is intellectualization; rationalization justifies an action, and denial would reject the diagnosis

briefs.title: Delirium
briefs.sub: tell it from dementia and psychosis, then find the causeDid attention fail over hours to days, and which drug or illness caused it?
blocks: tell it from dementia and psychosis, then find the causeDid attention fail over hours to days, and which drug or illness caused it?

Attention and awareness fail over a short time (usually hours to a few days) fluctuate: delirium; dementia starts slowly, attention spared until severe Review every drug first (anticholinergic, opioid, benzodiazepine; meperidine and tramadol highly deliriogenic) stop the culprit treat the cause, reorient, protect sleep Antipsychotic only for severe agitation that threatens safety benzodiazepine only for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal

What it is Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness an additional cognitive disturbance Hyperactive, hypoactive (often missed) or mixed Driver A physiological cause: medical illness, medication, substance intoxication or withdrawal, toxin, or several Proposed mechanism: low acetylcholine excess dopamine Triggers Age over 70 non-modifiable dementia (a leading risk factor) or mild cognitive impairment Drugs (up to 39% of cases) surgery, hypoxia, untreated pain, infection Male sex non-modifiable functional disabilities, poor vision and hearing, frailty Chain Vulnerable patient precipitant (drug, surgery, infection) inattention over hours to days Fluctuates through the day, often worse at night Usually reversible, though deficits often take weeks or months to clear Insights Sleepy and quiet with an acute change: test attention; inattention points to hypoactive delirium, often mistaken for depression New psychosis in an older adult: usually delirium or dementia; a primary psychosis rarely starts in old age

Dementia and complications, in detaildetail behind the chain An estimated 20% to 50% of hospitalized patients with dementia may develop deliriumask someone who knows the patient for the baseline Falls and injuries, aspiration pneumonia, pressure ulcers, dehydration and electrolyte disorders

Attention attention and awareness disturbed Onset over a short time (usually hours to a few days), a change from baseline, tending to fluctuate during the day Cognition an additional disturbance: memory, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception Exclusion not better explained by a preexisting, established or evolving neurocognitive disorder, and not in severely reduced arousal such as coma Cause evidence of a medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, toxin, or several

Confusion Assessment Method Bedside screenAcute onset with a fluctuating course and inattention are both required, plus either disorganized thinking or an altered level of consciousness. Timing chart: against dementia and psychosis

Time the confusionnot to scale DeliriumSudden, hours to days; lasts days to weeks, sometimes longer; fluctuates, worse at night HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears→ AttentionGreatly impaired OrientationVaries; time most often affected PsychosisVisual hallucinations common; delusions can occur Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)Slow, uncertain start; progressive, stable day to day HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears→ AttentionSpared until severe OrientationImpaired PsychosisHallucinations rare until late, except in Lewy body dementia Primary psychosisUsually slow, with a prodrome; chronic, with exacerbations HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears→ AttentionAlmost never impaired; altered consciousness suggests a medical cause OrientationDisorientation suggests a medical cause PsychosisHallucinations mainly auditory Dementia is a leading risk factor: judge the change against the baseline from someone who knows the patient.

WithdrawalDelirium tremens: confusion, fleeting hallucinations, tremor, sweating, fever and a fast pulse, usually 48 to 96 hours after the last drink It can be fatal: treat it promptly Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal If alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal is the cause, choose an intravenous (IV) benzodiazepine; in alcohol withdrawal, no haloperidol at first. NutritionalHeavy drinking or malnutrition, with confusion, nystagmus or eye-movement palsy, and an unsteady gait Glucose given first can precipitate it If Wernicke encephalopathy (from thiamine deficiency) is possible, choose IV thiamine before any glucose. DangerAgitation that puts the patient or others at risk Restraint only to prevent harm If it threatens safety despite nonpharmacologic care and withdrawal is excluded, choose a low-dose antipsychotic, with a baseline electrocardiogram (ECG) for the QTc (the QT, or Q wave to T wave, interval corrected for heart rate), especially with haloperidol. NeurologicNew focal sign or head trauma If a subdural bleed or stroke is possible, choose noncontrast CT (computed tomography) of the head, the first-line scan. InfectionSuspected bacterial meningitis If lumbar puncture must wait for imaging, choose blood cultures, then antibiotics and a glucocorticoid before the scan.

Delirium and its look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Delirium Inattention, disorientation, visual hallucinations or delusions Hours to a few days, fluctuating through the day; evidence of a medical, drug or withdrawal cause Primary psychosis Paranoid delusions; hallucinations mainly auditory Attention and orientation intact; no medical cause; usually slow onset with a prodrome, often in adolescence or young adulthood, rarely in old age; brief psychotic disorder starts suddenly, but a medical or drug cause rules it out Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia) Memory lost, especially recent events; stable day to day Slow, uncertain start; attention spared until severe Depression Depressed mood or lost interest, 5 or more symptoms; consciousness clear; concentration may be poor, but no acute, fluctuating inattention 2 weeks or more; an acute change with inattention is hypoactive delirium instead Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia); see Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM (rapid eye movement) sleep behavior disorder Swings usually span days to weeks, within a chronic dementia Delirium on top of dementia Known dementia, new drowsiness or agitation An acute change from the baseline given by someone who knows the patient Alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) Sweating, tremor, fever, fast pulse, fleeting hallucinations Usually 48 to 96 hours after the last drink; treated with a benzodiazepine Thyrotoxicosis, including too much thyroxine Tremor, anxiety or agitation, palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance ↓ TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) with ↑ free T4 (thyroxine); thyroid storm adds fever, tachycardia and confusion

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Acute, fluctuating confusion → Attention test (days of the week backward) Attention test fails Inattention, the core deficit → Every drug, including over-the-counter and alcohol Anticholinergic, opioid, benzodiazepine A drug cause: stop it → Urine drug screen → CBC (complete blood count) → Metabolic panel with glucose → Urinalysis Laboratory tests abnormal Infection, electrolyte or glucose disorder to treat → Oxygen saturation → Chest radiograph → ECG (electrocardiogram) Oxygen, radiograph or ECG abnormal Hypoxia, pneumonia: a cardiopulmonary cause Targeted tests TestResultMeans New focal sign, head trauma, suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, no cause found, or no improvement → Noncontrast CT (computed tomography) of the head Abnormal Subdural bleed, stroke, other lesion Suspected meningitis or encephalitis; or subarachnoid hemorrhage with a negative or unavailable CT → Lumbar puncture Abnormal fluid Meningitis, encephalitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage Delayed for imaging Suspected bacterial meningitis: blood cultures, then antibiotics and a glucocorticoid before imaging; confirmation must not delay treatment Suspected seizures, including nonconvulsive → EEG (electroencephalography) Seizure activity Seizures or status epilepticus, including nonconvulsive SkipRoutine head CT: order it only for the indications above; a focal sign best predicts an abnormal scan

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Meperidine with ↑ creatinine Normeperidine accumulating Stop it; treat the pain another way A new first-generation antihistamine for sleep A highly anticholinergic drug Stop it Focal weakness after a fall on an anticoagulant Subdural hemorrhage Noncontrast head CT: head trauma is itself an indication; a focal sign best predicts an abnormal scan Confusion, tremor, sweating, fast pulse, usually 48 to 96 hours after the last drink; often in the hospital, 2 to 4 days after surgery Delirium tremens IV benzodiazepine Takes a benzodiazepine; confused, tremulous, tachycardic after stopping Benzodiazepine withdrawal: short-acting within 1 to 2 days, long-acting several days to a week IV benzodiazepine, the drug of choice for withdrawal delirium Older adult, especially with cognitive impairment, agitated, confused and aggressive typically within an hour of a benzodiazepine dose; no focal signs Paradoxical agitation from the benzodiazepine Taper and stop it; a higher dose worsens it Not firstNot firstNo head CT before lowering the dose when there are no focal neurologic findings. Quetiapine only for persistent psychosis or uncontrolled agitation.

Pause point New paranoid delusions days after surgery Offered as a primary psychosis, or a tremor alone as too much thyroxine All the options The optionsChloroquine: a daily drug she takes for lupus; but the NBME explanation clears all four non-opioid options: none is linked to delirium or on the Beers list. Hydrochlorothiazide: her antihypertensive; cleared with the others, as above. Propranolol: a beta blocker that also treats tremor, and she is tremulous; cleared with the others, as above. Thyroxine: tremor and agitation point to excess thyroid hormone; but the explanation lists it as a treatment for hypothyroidism and clears it with the others. Down to two: meperidine or thyroxine. Meperidine: new agitation, disorientation to time and paranoid delusions days after surgery is delirium, and she takes an opioid. The explanation names anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines as common causes and calls meperidine and tramadol highly deliriogenic; no psychiatric or substance history argues against a primary psychosis or withdrawal. Disorientation to time; confirm inattention and fluctuation → Delirium: read the drug list for the opioid (meperidine), anticholinergic or benzodiazepine

Delirium subtypes Subtype Recognize it It means Hyperactive Agitated, more sympathetic activity; occasionally combative Antipsychotic only if safety is threatened Hypoactive Somnolent, low arousal, sluggish Often missed or called depression; test attention Mixed Swings between the two Test attention in either phase

1 Every patientfrom the start Treat the cause; stop deliriogenic drugs; reorient; glasses and hearing aids; protect sleep; mobilize The main treatment, for every patient. 2 Severe agitationbehavior puts the patient or others at risk and withdrawal is excluded Low-dose antipsychotic: haloperidol, quetiapine or risperidone Baseline ECG for the QTc, especially with haloperidol; adjust the dose daily and stop it as soon as clinically feasible. It is not shown to shorten delirium. Antipsychotic Adverse Effects
Restraint: at any rung, only to prevent harm; trained staff apply it, release it at least every 2 hours and stop it as soon as possible

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal IV benzodiazepine, the drug of choice No haloperidol at first in alcohol withdrawal: it may lower the seizure threshold; in alcohol use, thiamine before any glucose Any other cause Treat the cause; no benzodiazepine for the delirium itself Benzodiazepines bring more confusion and sedation Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia, with severe agitation Quetiapine, pimavanserin or clozapine In Parkinson disease, risperidone, olanzapine and typical antipsychotics aggravate parkinsonism; in Lewy body dementia, typical antipsychotics can acutely worsen it even at very low doses Meperidine or another deliriogenic opioid Stop it; treat the pain another way Normeperidine builds up when the kidneys clear it poorly

Follow-up decisions When Do At-risk patient, before delirium Beers criteriaGuideline detailAvoid meperidine in older adults (its neurotoxicity, delirium included, may exceed other opioids’). With delirium or a high risk of it, also avoid anticholinergics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, corticosteroids, histamine-2 receptor antagonists, zolpidem-type hypnotics and opioids, except in situations the criteria list. Two treatments stay in use: an antipsychotic for severe agitation, though not routinely, and pain control, because untreated pain also precipitates delirium. Identify the risk; fewer disturbances, protect sleep, frequent reorientation, mobility; no antipsychotic to prevent it Talking with the family Tell them it is usually reversible, but deficits often take weeks or months to clear After discharge Counsel: decline, institutionalization and death stay more likely for up to 2 years

Psychosisexclude a medical cause first; acute onset over hours to days suggests one Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonismmotor and dementia chronology in a chronic parkinsonian illness Psychosis: exclude a medical cause first; acute onset over hours to days suggests one. In a new psychosis or confusion in a hospitalized or older patient, test attention and ask when it began: acute, fluctuating inattention points to delirium. Then read the medication list and stop the anticholinergic, opioid or benzodiazepine that started it.

briefs.title: Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal
briefs.sub: PCP (phencyclidine) and stimulants · opioids · alcohol withdrawal · benzodiazepines · cannabisWhich drug do the pupils and vital signs point to, and is it intoxication or withdrawal?
blocks: PCP (phencyclidine) and stimulants · opioids · alcohol withdrawal · benzodiazepines · cannabisWhich drug do the pupils and vital signs point to, and is it intoxication or withdrawal?

Pinpoint pupils slow breathing decreased consciousness: opioid; give naloxone, with bag-mask breaths meanwhile Agitation from PCP (phencyclidine), cocaine or amphetamine: treat with a benzodiazepine; no beta-blocker for cocaine Alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremens, usually at 48 to 96 h) and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill: a benzodiazepine, thiamine before glucose; taper a benzodiazepine, never stop it abruptly

What it is Intoxication: a toxidrome read from pupils breathing vital signs Withdrawal: timed from the last dose Driver Stimulants: sympathomimetic surge Opioids: act at opioid receptors NaloxoneMechanismNaloxone is a competitive antagonist there. Sedative withdrawal: onset and length follow half-life duration of use Triggers Stopping alcohol withdrawal, timed from the last drink Stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly withdrawal, which can be life-threatening Intravenous glucose before thiamine Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, nystagmus or eye-muscle palsy, ataxia) Chain Alcohol stopped tremor, anxiety hallucinosis or seizures delirium tremens PCP: psychomotor agitation hyperthermia Cocaine: hemodynamic surge vasoconstriction acute coronary syndrome Insights Dilated pupils with autonomic overactivity fit a stimulant and opioid withdrawal alike; yawning and goose flesh mark withdrawal Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill; a spontaneous opioid stop is distressing, not life-threatening

Substance by substancedetail behind the chain Nystagmus (horizontal, vertical or rotary) in 60% to 90%; hypertension in 60%, tachycardia in 30%Complications: rhabdomyolysis, hypoglycemia, seizures, hypertensive crisis, coma Complications: seizures, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, coronary or cerebral ischemia Tearing, runny nose, goose flesh, muscle aches, diarrhea, vomiting; peaks within 48 to 72 h after heroin

Time alcohol withdrawal from the last drinknot to scale Early withdrawalBegins within 6 to 24 hours 0 h6 h12 h24 h48 h72 h96 h→ Showstremulousness, mild anxiety, insomnia, sweating, palpitations Alcoholic hallucinosisUsually 12 to 48 hours 0 h6 h12 h24 h48 h72 h96 h→ Showsauditory, tactile or visual hallucinations; clear sensorium, autonomic signs usually absent Withdrawal seizures12 to 48 hours In practiceIn practiceSome references (eg, MSD Manual) give 6 to 48 hours. 0 h6 h12 h24 h48 h72 h96 h→ Showsgeneralized tonic-clonic seizures Delirium tremensUsually 48 to 96 hours; mortality 1% to 5% 0 h6 h12 h24 h48 h72 h96 h→ Showsdisorientation, visual hallucinations, sweating, fever, tachycardia, hypertension

BreathingPinpoint pupils, slow breathing, decreased consciousness Breathing can fail again within hours as the reversal agent wears off If the opioid overdose triad is present, choose naloxone, with bag-mask breaths until it works; intubation is rarely needed when naloxone is given quickly. AlcoholSeizures at 12 to 48 h; disorientation, hallucinations, fever, usually at 48 to 96 h Delirium tremens: mortality 1% to 5% Delirium If it is delirium tremens, choose an intravenous benzodiazepine, promptly. SedativeBenzodiazepine stopped after long-term use Potentially life-threatening, like alcohol withdrawal If an outpatient dependent on a benzodiazepine must come off it, choose a slow taper of a long-acting benzodiazepine. HeartChest pain with agitation after cocaine Evaluate as any possible ischemia; beta-blockers are contraindicated If there is cardiovascular toxicity or agitation, choose a benzodiazepine first; nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists. HeatHyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis or seizures with PCP or a stimulant If agitation is driving the heat, choose benzodiazepine sedation; with a stimulant, also external cooling (ice bath or evaporative). ReversalOversedated long-term benzodiazepine user In long-term users, reversal may precipitate withdrawal and occasionally seizures If the user is long-term, choose supportive care of airway, breathing and circulation; no flumazenil.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Opioid overdose Decreased consciousness, slow breathing Pinpoint pupils with slow breathing; reverses with naloxone Sedative overdose Slurred speech, ataxia, decreased alertness AlcoholAlcohol intoxicationAlcohol intoxication looks alike: typically depressed central nervous system function and impaired motor skills. Normal-size pupils, even when breathing is slow Inhalant intoxication Incoordination, unsteadiness, lethargy Clears quickly after use CluesInhalant cluesBoys 14 to 17 are at highest risk. Effects typically last 15 to 45 minutes and may include loss of consciousness. Liver tests may rise with repeated use. Chronic nitrous oxide: vitamin B12 deficiency with polyneuropathy. Opioid withdrawal Dilated pupils, autonomic overactivity From 4 h after heroin, slower after methadone; yawning, runny nose, goose flesh, diarrhea Cocaine or amphetamine Agitation, sweating, tachycardia; chronic methamphetamine: skin sores, decayed teeth Chronic useMethamphetamineHeavy use causes weight loss, sores from skin picking, and decayed or cracked teeth ("meth mouth") from grinding and a dry mouth. Fleeting visual or tactile hallucinations (bugs under the skin) favor a drug-induced psychosis: rule out the drug before diagnosing mania or schizophrenia. Dilated pupils, hypertension, hyperthermia; can bring coronary ischemia With alcoholCocaethyleneTaken with alcohol, cocaine forms cocaethylene, which prolongs and strengthens its sympathomimetic effects.; cocaine lasts under 1 hour, amphetamine several hours Anticholinergic toxicity Dilated pupils, fever, fast pulse, delirium Dry, warm skin; urinary retention; ileus; no sweating CulpritsCauses and cautionsTricyclics (such as doxepin), clozapine and some antihistamines, alone or combined. Get an electrocardiogram (ECG) early; a tricyclic overdose can widen the QRS complex (treatment: Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity). No haloperidol: it adds anticholinergic effect. Normal muscle tone argues against neuroleptic malignant syndrome. PCP Violence, hallucinations, delusions, hypertension Nystagmus in any direction, vertical included Other featuresPCPConfusion, dissociation, ataxia and a high pain tolerance. Alcoholic hallucinosis Auditory, tactile or visual hallucinations Usually 12 to 48 h; clear sensorium, autonomic signs usually absent Delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal delirium) he refers to the physicians as sailorsIn a vignetteHallucinations: Get them off me! Confusion, fleeting hallucinations, tremor, sweating, fever, fast pulse Usually 48 to 96 h; disorientation with autonomic instability; mortality 1% to 5% Benzodiazepine withdrawal Like alcohol withdrawal; potentially life-threatening 1 to 2 days (short-acting) or several days to a week (long-acting) after stopping Stimulant withdrawal Long sleep, hunger, low mood, unpleasant dreams after a binge A crash, not arousal; the depression can bring suicide attempts Cannabis Prescription cannabinoid: dronabinolFDA labelLegal prescription use: the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label covers adults with anorexia and weight loss in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), and chemotherapy nausea and vomiting after standard antiemetics fail. Fast pulse, red conjunctivae, hunger, dry mouth, slowed time Red conjunctivae with hunger; hyperemesis (cyclical vomiting usually eased by warm showers) is a separate picture Primary psychotic disorder Delusions or hallucinations, which PCP also causes Persists about 1 month or longer after intoxication or withdrawal ends, or began before use Manic episode Agitation and high arousal, as with a stimulant A stimulant adds dilated pupils, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Altered patient, possible drug → Pupils and eyes Pinpoint pupils Opioid; small pupils are not always present Dilated pupils Stimulant (sweating), anticholinergic drug (dry skin), or opioid withdrawal Vertical or rotary nystagmus PCP. Fine lateral-gaze nystagmus: sedatives. Cannabis can also cause nystagmus → Breathing and vital signs Slow breathing Opioid, or a high sedative dose Fast pulse, high blood pressure, fever Stimulant or PCP, or alcohol or sedative withdrawal (check time since last use) Any altered patient → Fingerstick glucose Glucose ↓ Hypoglycemia, found at once at the bedside Chest pain, a drug with heart effects (such as a tricyclic, which can widen the QRS complex), or an unknown drug → ECG (electrocardiogram) Abnormal A heart effect: cardiac monitoring as well Mixed or possibly suicidal ingestion → Acetaminophen level Co-ingestants Further testsSalicylate level Urine drug screen Level detectable Acetaminophen ingestion: often silent early; delayed toxicity can be prevented Targeted tests TestResultMeans A drug stopped → Time since last use Alcohol stopped; hallucinations, clear sensorium, usually normal vital signs Alcoholic hallucinosis Alcohol stopped; disorientation with fever, fast pulse, sweating Delirium tremens Benzodiazepine stopped days earlier Benzodiazepine withdrawal Sleepy, hungry and low after a stimulant binge Stimulant withdrawal Next step TestResultMeans Possible intoxication or withdrawal → Urine toxicology Positive Exposure only: did symptoms start during or soon after use? False positives Lab caveatThe amphetamine immunoassay often cross-reacts, giving false positives; methylphenidate does not. Diphenhydramine and doxylamine can give a false-positive PCP screen. Negative Does not rule out use; standard panels miss some drugs Missed drugs Synthetic cathinonesSynthetic cathinones (bath salts), amphetamine-like, are often missed by routine screens, and their effects can last a week.
Name the drug and whether it is intoxication or withdrawal, then treat by drug.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Vertical or rotary nystagmus with violence PCP Intravenous or intramuscular benzodiazepine Seizure 12 to 48 h after the last drink In practiceIn practiceSome references (eg, MSD Manual) give 6 to 48 hours. Alcohol withdrawal seizure Benzodiazepine; routine phenytoin unlikely to help First seizure after 2 days of missed doses of a medicine taken for anxiety or sleep; no seizure history Not bupropionSeizure on stopping versus on the drugBupropion and tricyclic antidepressants can cause dose-dependent seizures while being taken; seizures are not associated with their withdrawal. Stopping paroxetine or venlafaxine gives a discontinuation syndrome (dysphoria, fatigue, dizziness, gastrointestinal upset, flu-like symptoms) without seizures. Withdrawal from a short-acting benzodiazepine such as alprazolam; can appear as early as 24 hours Treat as benzodiazepine withdrawal; prevent it with a longer-acting drug tapered over weeks to months Drinks nightly to fall asleep, then wakes during the night; macrocytosis; AST at least twice ALT Unhealthy drinkingLimitsMore than 7 drinks a week or 3 a day for women and for men 65 or older; more than 14 a week or 4 a day for men under 65 Alcohol use disorder: awakening as the alcohol level falls Screen for alcohol use disorder rather than treating insomnia alone Vomiting, diarrhea, poor sleep and muscle aches, with normal pulse, blood pressure and temperature Opioid withdrawal; alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal typically raises the vital signs Treat the withdrawal; fever or confusion points to another cause New energy drinks through the day; anxiety, insomnia, tremor, palpitations, raised blood pressure Caffeine intoxication Substance-induced comes first: not panic or adjustment disorder; alcohol withdrawal is usually associated with heavy drinking, and light drinking is very unlikely to cause it; no elevated mood or grandiosity, so not hypomania Trauma, Stress and Dissociative Disorders Party drug, alone or with an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor); hyperthermia, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, a seizure with low sodium MDMA (methylenedioxymethamphetamine, ecstasy) intoxication with serotonin syndrome ScreenUrine screenSynthetic amphetamines and analogues, such as MDMA, may not show up as amphetamines on routine urine toxicology screens. An amphetamine plus serotonin toxicity; hyponatremia from fluid intake and antidiuretic hormone release brings the seizure Seizure in pregnancy with agitation, sweating, dilated pupils, low sodium, no proteinuria and a normal head CT Amphetamine intoxication, not eclampsia Urine drug testing confirms it; telling it from eclampsia may decide whether emergency delivery is needed

Pause point Altered patient, ingestion unknown Offered: naloxone Normal-size pupils and normal breathing → Supportive care while the toxidrome is read; naloxone is for pinpoint pupils with slow breathing Chest pain and hypertension after cocaine Offered: a beta-blocker Beta-blockers are contraindicated in cocaine toxicity → A benzodiazepine first; nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists Confused, sweating and tachycardic days after the last drink Offered as alcoholic hallucinosis Disorientation with autonomic instability; hallucinosis keeps a clear sensorium → Delirium tremens: a benzodiazepine, thiamine before glucose Agitated patient, urine screen pending Offered: waiting on the screen before treating The toxidrome is read at the bedside; routine screens often miss synthetic cathinones → Treat the toxidrome now

1 Reversethe opioid overdose triad Naloxone, with bag-mask breaths until it works The reversal agent can wear off before the opioid, so observe; it can precipitate withdrawal. Given quickly, it rarely leaves a need for intubation. 2 1st lineagitation from PCP, cocaine or amphetamine A benzodiazepine, intravenous or intramuscular Lowers central sympathetic outflow. For cocaine, nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists after this first drug. PCP dosingGuideline detailLorazepam 2 to 4 mg or diazepam 5 to 10 mg, intravenous or intramuscular 3 1st linemoderate to severe alcohol withdrawal A benzodiazepine, dosed by withdrawal scale score Withdrawal scalesGuideline detailCIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) or SAWS (Short Alcohol Withdrawal Scale) scores set the as-needed doses Long-acting chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; in the hospital, intravenous lorazepam; with cirrhosis or alcoholic hepatitis, lorazepam or oxazepam, whose glucuronidation liver disease spares. Also for seizures (not routine phenytoin) and, intravenously and promptly, delirium tremens; haloperidol not at firstWhy notAntipsychotics may lower the seizure threshold, already low in alcohol withdrawal.. With intravenous fluids, thiamine before glucose. Thiamine doseGuideline detail100 mg intravenously, before any glucose 4 1st lineopioid withdrawal Buprenorphine or methadone Distressing, not dangerous, after a spontaneous stop. Start buprenorphine only once withdrawal signs are clear: a partial agonist given while a full agonist is still on board displaces it and precipitates withdrawal. DoseGuideline detailSublingual buprenorphine 4 to 12 mg to start, an alternative to methadone 5 Adjunctautonomic signs Clonidine Can ease autonomic signs, such as blood pressure, in opioid withdrawal; in alcohol withdrawal only as an adjunct to a benzodiazepine. 6 Avoidtempting but wrong Flumazenil in a long-term user; urinary acidification for PCP; beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity Where reversal fitsGuideline detailFlumazenil is best kept for respiratory depression during a procedure.

First treatment by situation Situation Choose Watch for PCP agitation Benzodiazepine; a rapid-acting antipsychotic second line No urinary acidification: acidosis, myoglobin in the kidney Opioid withdrawal Buprenorphine or methadone Not naloxone: it treats overdose Benzodiazepine withdrawal Slow outpatient taper of a long-acting one (eg clonazepam) Can last weeks Stimulant withdrawal Assess suicide risk In some users the depression is prolonged and drives relapse Cannabinoid hyperemesis Stop cannabis Warm showers usually relieve it Anticholinergic and tricyclic toxicity Supportive care; a benzodiazepine for agitation or seizures; sodium bicarbonate for a QRS over 100 ms No haloperidol; no physostigmine with a tricyclic Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity

Follow-up decisions When Do After naloxone Observe until its effect is gone; breathing can fail again within hours Alcohol withdrawal under way Keep dosing by symptom score; watch for delirium tremens Psychosis lasts about 1 month after stopping Psychosis Consider an independent psychotic disorder Active use, intoxication or withdrawal Suicide Risk Assessment Count it as a modifiable suicide risk factor; complete the risk assessment once sober, under close observation until then

Long-term care after withdrawal Use disorder Choose Watch for Alcohol Not theseOther drugsNot relapse drugs for alcohol: bupropion and varenicline (smoking cessation), fomepizole (antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol). Naltrexone or acamprosate, both first line Naltrexone helps most who take it consistently; not with acute hepatitis, liver failure or opioid use: choose acamprosate then, unless kidney impairment is significant Alcohol, still drinking Naltrexone: it can start while drinking continues Not disulfiram: abstinent patients only Alcohol, abstinent, with cravings Acamprosate, used to maintain abstinence Each drug's own limits: the Alcohol row above Alcohol, supervised Disulfiram, best in highly motivated patients, after 48 hours of abstinence Drinking on it: flushing, throbbing headache, tachycardia MoreDisulfiram reactionHeavy drinking may add vomiting and hypotension; effects may last 3 to 7 days after the last dose. Alcohol, alongside either Alcoholics Anonymous; motivational psychotherapy Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing TherapyTherapyTherapy also teaches avoiding the situations that set off drinking. Stimulant CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) to prevent relapse; an antipsychotic for psychosis No drug has proven consistently effective Opioid Buprenorphine or methadone maintenance, the standard of care over withdrawal management alone Lowers relapse and fatal overdose Opioid, buprenorphine Can be prescribed in an office Start only once withdrawal is clear, or it precipitates withdrawal In practiceIn practice:Low-dose starts give small, rising buprenorphine doses while the full agonist continues, to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Opioid, methadone Only through a licensed opioid treatment program QTc (the heart-rate-corrected Q-to-T interval) prolongation and torsades: ECG at start and during titration Opioid, naltrexone Long-acting naltrexone, from an opioid-free state Only after at least 7 days without a full dose of another opioid agonist

Pupils and breathing first: small pupils with slow breathing is an opioid; big pupils with sweating and a fast pulse is a stimulant or opioid withdrawal, while big pupils with dry, hot skin is an anticholinergic drug; nystagmus with violence is PCP.

briefs.title: Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing
briefs.sub: precontemplation to maintenance · motivational interviewingWhich stage, and which move?
blocks: Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing
precontemplation to maintenance · motivational interviewingWhich stage, and which move?

Name the stage from what the patient says now: sees no problem or has no interest in changing: precontemplation; sees a problem but is ambivalent: contemplation; committed and asking how: preparation; changing now: action; keeping the change: maintenance; back to the old habit: relapse The move is motivational interviewing: open-ended, nonjudgmental questions that let the patient explore their own reasons to change; reflect what you hear and do not argue or impose change Match the move to the stage: before commitment, explore the reasons and the ambivalence; once committed, strategies and resources; after the change, plans for coping with temptation (relapse prevention); after a relapse, a nonjudgmental review of past attempts

The stages describe readiness to change a health behavior such as substance use, diet or exercise; motivational interviewing aims to move the patient through them over time, and relapse does not always happen Where it is usedWhere it is usedMotivational interviewing is an evidence-based treatment for alcohol use disorder; it sits beside cognitive-behavioral therapy for stimulant use disorder and is one behavioral intervention for relapse prevention

Stages of change Stage The patient says Next best step Precontemplation "My drinking is not the problem; my nerves are." Sees no problem with the habit, or has no interest in changing it Open-ended, nonjudgmental questions about the habit; do not argue Contemplation "I know it hurts me, but I am not sure I want to stop." Sees a problem, ambivalent about change Explore the ambivalence: the reasons for and against change, in the patient's own words Preparation (determination) "I have decided to quit. What can help me?" Committed, asking how Discuss strategies and resources for the change Action (willpower) "I have stopped, and it is hard." Taking steps now Affirm the effort and reflect the talk of change Maintenance "I have stayed off it and want to keep it that way." Keeping a change already made Plan how to cope with temptation to return to the habit (relapse prevention) Relapse "I was doing well, then I started again." Back to the old habit after a change Without judgment, review what helped and what did not in past attempts

Motivational interviewing: techniques and stance Move What it does Open-ended question Lets the patient tell it in their own words, without being led: "What do you like about drinking, and what worries you about it?" Reflection Restates what the patient said as a statement, such as "Part of you wants to stop"; reflect most when you hear talk of change Affirmation A genuine statement about the patient's strengths, values or efforts Summary Gathers what the patient said and marks a transition in the conversation Eliciting the patient's reasons The patient, not the physician, voices the arguments for and against change; change is supported, never imposed Nonjudgmental stance Accepts ambivalence and tolerates resistance; arguing with the patient works against change

Commonly confused Pair Decides it Precontemplation or contemplation Whether the patient is weighing change at all: no problem seen or no interest in change: precontemplation; a problem seen and unsure about change: contemplation Contemplation or preparation Unsure whether to change, or committed and ready to discuss how Action or maintenance Making the change now, or keeping a change already made

Pause point Drinks daily after five treatment programs; says his drinking will be under control once his anxiety is treated Offered as contemplation, maintenance or relapse prevention Does he see the habit itself as the problem now? → No: he blames his anxiety, so precontemplation; past treatment does not set the stage

Diagnosis1 of 7 52-year-old man has had a cough all winter He smokes a pack daily and blames the cough on allergies He quit twice in the past and sees no reason to quit now · ContemplationContemplation: sees a problem but is unsure about change · PrecontemplationHe sees no problem with smoking now · RelapsePast quit attempts do not set the stage; he sees no problem now 52-year-old man has had a cough all winter He smokes a pack daily and blames the cough on allergies He quit twice in the past and sees no reason to quit now PrecontemplationHe does not see his smoking as a problem; past quit attempts do not set his stage, which is named from his present view of the habit

Diagnosis2 of 7 34-year-old woman drinks four or five glasses of wine most nights She says drinking hurts her sleep and her marriage, but it is how she unwinds She is not sure she wants to cut back · PrecontemplationPrecontemplation: sees no problem; she names the harm · Preparation (determination)Preparation: committed and asking how; she is unsure · ContemplationShe sees the harm but is ambivalent about change 34-year-old woman drinks four or five glasses of wine most nights She says drinking hurts her sleep and her marriage, but it is how she unwinds She is not sure she wants to cut back ContemplationShe names the harm yet is unsure about change: ambivalence marks contemplation

Diagnosis3 of 7 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes returns for a routine visit He says he has decided to start walking after dinner and change his diet He asks which exercise programs his insurance covers · ContemplationContemplation: unsure about change; he has decided · Action (willpower)Action: already taking steps; he has not started · Preparation (determination)Committed and ready to discuss strategies and resources 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes returns for a routine visit He says he has decided to start walking after dinner and change his diet He asks which exercise programs his insurance covers Preparation (determination)He has committed to change and wants strategies and resources but has not yet begun: preparation

Next step4 of 7 28-year-old man is treated for a hand fracture from a fight while drunk He says he drinks no more than his friends and has no problem He agrees to talk with the physician before discharge · Tell him he must stop drinking before it ruins his healthArguing and imposing change work against change · Ask what he likes about drinking and what, if anything, concerns himOpen-ended and nonjudgmental: he explores his own reasons · Tell him he has alcohol use disorder and refer him to a treatment programA label and a plan he has not agreed to impose change; he sees no problem yet 28-year-old man is treated for a hand fracture from a fight while drunk He says he drinks no more than his friends and has no problem He agrees to talk with the physician before discharge Ask what he likes about drinking and what, if anything, concerns himHe sees no problem (precontemplation), so motivational interviewing opens with open-ended, nonjudgmental questions that let him voice his own reasons; arguing or imposing a plan works against change

Next step5 of 7 31-year-old woman who smokes has two young children She says, "I want to quit for my kids, but smoking is the only thing that calms me down." She has not made any plan to quit · "Let's set a quit date for next week."A quit date is for a patient willing to quit; she is still ambivalent · "Part of you wants to quit for your children, and part of you relies on smoking to stay calm."A reflection of both sides explores her ambivalence · "Why haven't you quit yet, with two children at home?"A why-not question does not fit the nonjudgmental stance of motivational interviewing 31-year-old woman who smokes has two young children She says, "I want to quit for my kids, but smoking is the only thing that calms me down." She has not made any plan to quit "Part of you wants to quit for your children, and part of you relies on smoking to stay calm."She is ambivalent (contemplation): reflecting both sides in her own words helps her explore the ambivalence, while a quit date fits a patient who is committed to quitting

Next step6 of 7 50-year-old man who drinks daily says he has decided to stop He asks what could help him stay off alcohol He has no symptoms of withdrawal and wants to begin soon · Advise him to return once he feels readyHe is ready now; he has committed to change · Ask what he enjoys about drinkingHe is past weighing reasons: committed, he is ready for strategies · Discuss strategies and resources for stoppingCommitted and asking how: discuss strategies and resources 50-year-old man who drinks daily says he has decided to stop He asks what could help him stay off alcohol He has no symptoms of withdrawal and wants to begin soon Discuss strategies and resources for stoppingHe has committed and asks how (preparation), so the move is to discuss strategies and resources for the change

Next step7 of 7 39-year-old woman stopped drinking after an outpatient program Several months later, after a death in the family, she began drinking again She feels ashamed and says that she wants to stop again · Point out that she broke her commitment to stay soberJudging her works against change; the stance is nonjudgmental · Reassure her that relapse is rare after a full programRelapse is common: up to 70% resume heavy drinking despite psychosocial treatment · Review, without judgment, what helped and what led back to drinkingReviewing past attempts shows what helped and what did not 39-year-old woman stopped drinking after an outpatient program Several months later, after a death in the family, she began drinking again She feels ashamed and says that she wants to stop again Review, without judgment, what helped and what led back to drinkingAfter relapse, a nonjudgmental review of what helped and what did not can inform the next attempt; relapse is common, with up to 70% resuming heavy drinking despite psychosocial treatment

briefs.title: Medication- and Illness-Induced Psychiatric Disorders
briefs.sub: medication-induced psychosis · glucocorticoids · Cushing syndrome · delirium versus psychosis · medical workup before a primary diagnosisDid a drug or a disease start this, and is attention intact?
blocks: medication-induced psychosis · glucocorticoids · Cushing syndrome · delirium versus psychosis · medical workup before a primary diagnosisDid a drug or a disease start this, and is attention intact?

Rule out a drug or a medical illness before diagnosing a primary psychiatric disorder New psychosis on high-dose glucocorticoids, alert and oriented medication-induced psychotic disorder Fluctuating attention and disorientation delirium, with any psychosis secondary

What it is Psychiatric symptoms caused directly by a drug or a disease, not a primary disorder Driver A new medication or dose a disease known to cause psychosis or mood change Triggers High-dose glucocorticoids, typically in the first week but at any time Cushing syndrome, thyroid disease, lupus, Wilson disease, stroke, autoimmune encephalitis Chain Drug or disease starts symptoms follow it in time they ease when the cause is treated Insights Timing decides: what started before the symptoms, a drug, a dose or a disease? Cushing syndrome can be mistaken for a primary depressive or anxiety disorder

Medical causes by systemdetail behind the triggers Cushing syndrome (low or labile mood, anxiety, insomnia); hypothyroidism with depression; hyperthyroidism with anxiety; hypercalcemia with depression Lupus: psychosis with arthralgia, low platelets and hematuria in a young womananti-N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor encephalitis: psychiatric change, memory loss, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability; ovarian teratoma Stroke or a tumor, seizures, Wilson disease Metabolic or electrolyte disorders, central nervous system infection

Defining features Label Feature Medication-induced Acute delusions or hallucinations temporally linked to a new medication Due to another medical condition A disease known to cause psychosis (eg, central nervous system tumor, stroke, endocrine or autoimmune disorder), beginning and ending with it Delirium Fluctuating cognition with poor attention and disorientation Favors a primary psychosis Onset before 40, a prodrome, auditory (not visual, gustatory or tactile) hallucinations, family history of psychotic illness

Drug, disease or primary disorder, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Medication-induced psychotic disorder (substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder) Acute delusions or hallucinations after a new medication; alert, oriented Begins with the new drug; steroids: typically in the first week Delirium Fluctuating attention and disorientation; psychosis secondary Hours to days, fluctuating; attention fails Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition History, examination or labs show a disease known to cause psychosis Begins and ends with the illness Primary psychosis Onset before 40, a prodrome, auditory hallucinations, family history No drug or disease explains it; then time it

What it is A pattern of disruptive behavior in a child, sorted into four disorders Driver What the child does (defiance, violated rights, impulsive rage) the mood between episodes Triggers Early onset: conduct disorder before 10 carries a poorer prognosis ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), common alongside, also brings disruptive and impulsive behavior Chain Oppositional defiant disorder often comes first conduct disorder antisocial personality disorder at 18, if conduct disorder began before 15 Insights Irritable or angry mood between outbursts belongs only to disruptive mood dysregulation disorder A preschooler who cannot make himself understood: tantrums point to a language disorder

Defining rules Disorder Rule Oppositional defiant disorder 4 or more symptoms for 6 months, with someone other than a sibling; under 5 most days, 5 or older at least weekly Conduct disorder 3 or more in 12 months, from aggression, destruction, deceit or theft, serious rule violations Intermittent explosive disorder Verbal aggression on average twice a week for 3 months, or 3 destructive outbursts in 12 months; age 6 or older Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder Outbursts 3 or more a week, irritable between, in 2 or more settings, 12 months or more without a 3-month gap Precedence When disruptive mood dysregulation disorder is met, do not also diagnose oppositional defiant or intermittent explosive disorder

Time frames Disorder How often How long Oppositional defiant disorder Most days under age 5; at least weekly from 5 6 months or more Conduct disorder 3 or more behaviors Within 12 months Intermittent explosive disorder, verbal Twice a week on average 3 months Intermittent explosive disorder, destructive 3 destructive outbursts Within 12 months Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder 3 or more outbursts a week 12 months or more, no 3-month gap

Disruptive behavior, most tempting first Disorder Fingerprint Decides it Oppositional defiant disorder Argues, defies, vindictive; deliberately annoys and blames others 6 months or more; no stealing or violation of others' rights Normal adolescent development Questions family rules, argues, ignores bedtime Not excessive or impairing; educate and reassure the parents WhyWhyForming an identity as an independent person is a key adolescent task, and a degree of rebellion against authority is normal. Family therapy is for oppositional defiant or conduct disorder. Conduct disorder Aggression, destruction, theft, truancy; lies for gain or to avoid consequences 3 or more in 12 months; violates others' basic rights or major rules Intermittent explosive disorder Impulsive outbursts out of proportion, not planned; may feel remorse after Age 6 or older; appropriate behavior between outbursts Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder Severe outbursts, 3 or more a week Onset before 10, diagnosed 6 to 18; irritable or angry between outbursts Antisocial personality disorder Pervasive disregard for others' rights 18 or older, conduct disorder before 15 ADHD Disruptive and impulsive No aggression or pattern of violating norms Reactive attachment disorder After abuse or neglect: withdrawn, does not seek or respond to comfort, limited positive affect, unexplained irritability, fear or sadness even in safe settings Signs before age 5; makes eye contact and plays with varied toys, unlike autism; overfamiliarity with strangers is disinhibited social engagement disorder instead Language disorder Tantrums in a preschooler who cannot make himself understood Other milestones on target; language behind Substance use Behavior only with use The sole diagnosis when the behavior occurs only with use

briefs.sub: name the effect, then take the next stepDid it start on the drug or after stopping it, and which phase of sexual response is affected?
blocks: name the effect, then take the next stepDid it start on the drug or after stopping it, and which phase of sexual response is affected?

Clonus hyperreflexia mydriasis within hours of adding or raising a serotonergic drug serotonin syndrome FINISH symptoms typically within 3 days of a stop or taper discontinuation; relapse typically comes 2 to 3 weeks or more after Low desire, persistent and distressing lower the dose first; then taper off, or add or switch to bupropion or mirtazapine

What it is Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI): citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline Mechanism Serotonin transporter blocked more serotonin in the cleft longer postsynaptic stimulation ReceptorsDrug detailSerotonin type 2 receptor stimulation commonly causes anxiety, insomnia and sexual dysfunction. Little effect on dopamine or norepinephrine. Used for DepressionGuideline detailAbout as effective as bupropion, mirtazapine, SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) or trazodone. Panic disorder: a first-line drug, with or without CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) Bulimia nervosa: fluoxetine cuts binges and vomiting Eating Disorders Risks Serotonin syndrome with another serotonergic drug, eg, an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor), tramadol, linezolid MAOIs Suicidal thoughts in children and young adults under 25 (boxed warning) Hyponatremia, often from SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), higher risk over 65 Citalopram: more QTTermThe QT is the electrocardiogram interval of ventricular depolarization and repolarization. prolongation than other SSRIs; generally avoided after a recent MI (myocardial infarction) Sexual dysfunction in up to halfIn practiceIn practice: the Merck Manual reports sexual dysfunction in more than half of patients. Paroxetine: avoided in pregnancy (first-trimester cardiac malformations); most discontinuation symptoms Bleeding, including GI bleeding, more with aspirin, an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or an anticoagulant Insights Reflexes split the two toxic syndromes: clonus and hyperreflexia in serotonin syndrome; slow reflexes and lead-pipe rigidity in neuroleptic malignant syndrome Shorter half-life more withdrawal: paroxetine most, fluoxetine least fluoxetine may replace a drug whose slow taper fails

Adverse effects, by time coursedetail behind the risks Serotonin syndrome after a serotonergic change, about 60% within 6 hours; discontinuation reactions reported within hours of a first missed dose Sexual dysfunction in up to half (especially trouble reaching orgasm; also low libido, erectile dysfunction); sleep disturbance; weight change Discontinuation typically within 3 days, over in 1 to 2 weeks; relapse typically 2 to 3 weeks or more after, and graduala gradual taper leaves as few as 5% with symptoms Paroxetine: more anticholinergic effects; fluoxetine: more agitation and overstimulation; neither is advisedsertraline or escitalopram are good first choices

ToxicitySerotonin syndrome: mental status change, sweating, shivering, hyperthermia, mydriasis, tremor, clonus, hyperreflexia, increased bowel sounds Very high temperature Severe cases≥41.1 °C needs sedation and intubation; antipyretics such as acetaminophen do not work. Criteria Guideline detailThe Hunter criteria are recommended as the most accurate. QT and overdose Drug detailCitalopram prolongs the QT interval more than other SSRIs. SSRIs have a wide safety margin: overdose is rarely dangerous, unlike a TCA (tricyclic antidepressant) overdose. A citalopram overdose can still cause torsade de pointes; monitor the heart for longer. If clonus and hyperreflexia appear within hours of adding or raising a serotonergic drug, choose serotonin syndrome: stop every serotonergic drug. OverdoseSSRI overdose with drowsiness, slow breathing or an abnormal exam An SSRI alone is usually well tolerated Suspected Overdose or Toxidrome If an SSRI overdose comes with altered mental status or abnormal findings, choose a search for coingestants, such as acetaminophen, salicylate and ethanol levels. SuicideNew suicidal thoughts or clinical worsening on an antidepressant Risk raised in children and young adults in short-term studies Suicide Risk Assessment If any patient is on an antidepressant, choose close monitoring for worsening and suicidal thoughts. PregnancyAn SSRI in pregnancy Paroxetine: first-trimester cardiac malformations Breastfeeding Guideline detailBreastfeeding can be encouraged on an antidepressant. If a pregnant patient needs an SSRI, choose sertraline or escitalopram, good first choices; not paroxetine.

Which effect is it, most tempting first Effect Fingerprint Decides it Discontinuation syndrome headache, anxiety, nausea, muscle aches, and diarrheaIn a vignetteThe trigger: she has discontinued the dosage of her sertraline during the past monthHyperarousal: mild tremor in both hands FINISH symptoms, electric-shock sensations after a stop, taper or missed dose Typically within 3 days; gone in 1 to 2 weeks; clonus or hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome instead Relapse of depression Low mood, insomnia and psychomotor symptoms return Typically 2 to 3 weeks or longer after stopping; builds gradually Serotonin syndrome Mental status change, autonomic hyperactivity, clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, increased bowel sounds Minutes to hours after adding or raising a serotonergic drug; about 60% within 6 hours Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (antipsychotic) On an antipsychotic: fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, ↑ CK (creatine kinase) Days to weeks after an antipsychotic change; builds over 1 to 3 days; slow reflexes, rigidity Sexual dysfunction Low libido, erectile dysfunction or anorgasmia During therapy; name the phase: desire, arousal or orgasm; persists or worsens as mood improvesTiming often points to the SSRIDepression's own sexual symptoms should lift with the mood. Bupropion does not cause sexual dysfunction. Female sexual interest/arousal disorder needs 6 months or more and no drug or medical cause. Stable diabetes, high blood pressure or obesity is less likely to explain a recent change.Gynecomastia is uncommon on an SSRI; see Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Early activation Anxiety, insomnia At the start, before any benefit; especially troubling in panic disorder

F flu-like symptoms: fatigue, lethargy, malaise, muscle aches, headaches, diarrhea I insomnia N nausea I imbalance: gait instability, dizziness or lightheadedness, vertigo S sensory disturbances: paresthesia, "electric shock" sensations, visual disturbance H hyperarousal: anxiety, agitation

Timing HoursDaysWeeksMonths Serotonin syndromeMinutes to hours; about 60% by 6 hours Discontinuation syndromeTypically within 3 days of a stop; gone in 1 to 2 weeks Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (antipsychotic)Days to weeks after an antipsychotic change Relapse of depressionTypically 2 to 3 weeks or more after a stop; gradual

Pause point New symptoms 2 days after a stop Offered as relapse, so a new antidepressant is started Relapse typically arrives weeks later and builds slowly → That timing is discontinuation Low desire on an SSRI; depression in sustained remission Offered as switching to citalopram or a weekend drug holiday All the options The optionsInitiate propranolol: an add-on that leaves the antidepressant alone; but it is unlikely to help sexual dysfunction and is not helpful for major depressive disorder. Initiate sildenafil: a treatment for sexual dysfunction; but it can help arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire, her complaint, has been shown. Recommend weekend drug holidays: they seem to spare the relationship; but they are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect. Replace fluoxetine with citalopram: a switch sounds like progress; but citalopram carries a similar risk of sexual dysfunction. Down to two: lowering the dose or switching to citalopram. Lower the dose: her low desire is persistent and distressing, and NBME says initial management commonly involves decreasing the SSRI dose, especially with sustained remission. If that fails: one episode in sustained remission, so stopping can be considered; or, if she prefers to stay on medication, adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine). Citalopram carries a similar risk; holidays interfere with the antidepressant effect → Lower the dose first

Other antidepressants

Monitoring When Check Why Before starting Bipolar disorder, mania or hypomania in the patient or a relative In bipolar disorder, an antidepressant alone can set off mania 2 to 4 weeks after starting, older adults Serum sodium SIADH, higher risk over 65; ask about past hyponatremia before starting Up to 6 weeks in Response Benefit may take that long Mood rises after starting Mania or hypomania (rare) If it appears: stop the antidepressant and start a mood stabilizer Bipolar Disorder Remission of a first episode Continue about 6 more months at the dose that brought remission, then taper gradually, typically over 6 to 8 weeks (about 2 months) Lowering or stopping sooner raises the risk of relapse MaintenanceGuideline detailRecurrent, chronic or severe depression: consider maintenance at the remission dose, usually for 1 to 3 years or longer, sometimes indefinitely.

Drugs cleared by CYP2D6, such as TCAs (tricyclic antidepressants) and metoprolol: ↑ levels, most with paroxetine and fluoxetine (citalopram inhibits weakly); lower their dose if needed. Fluvoxamine strongly inhibits CYP1A2 (cytochrome P450 1A2): never with tizanidine; lower the theophylline dose; clozapine levels may rise.
