Clock it from the start or last increase: dystonia hours to days, akathisia and parkinsonism weeks, tardive dyskinesia months to years Fever, lead-pipe rigidity and confusion building over days mean neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): stop the drug, then cool and give fluids Clozapine: check the ANC (absolute neutrophil count) before and during treatment; clozapine, olanzapineInjectionOlanzapine also comes as a long-acting injection, used less because each injection needs an observation period for delirium and sedation. and quetiapine carry the most metabolic harm; screen weight, glucose and blood pressure at least yearly

What it is Dopamine receptor blockers: antipsychotics antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine Mechanism Dopamine D2 receptors blocked antipsychotic effect Blockade in the striatum acetylcholine outweighs dopamine dystonia and parkinsonism Anticholinergic balance restored dystonia usually eases within minutes Used for Psychosis: second-generation drugs favored first line Clozapine: schizophrenia after 2 or more failed adequate trials, or with increased risk of suicide or aggression Acute mania severe agitation in delirium Huntington disease: may partly suppress chorea and agitationHuntington diseaseA VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor is typically first line for chorea; avoid it with depression. Risks NMS laryngeal dystonia clozapine: severe neutropenia, myocarditis, seizures Movement: dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia Metabolic (clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine) prolactin (first-generation, risperidone) QTc (QT interval corrected for heart rate) prolongation, most with thioridazine and ziprasidone; torsades de pointes with haloperidol Insights Every class can cause NMS, second generation included switching drugs is no safeguard Anticholinergics relieve dystonia and parkinsonism, but may worsen tardive dyskinesia, so stop them there

Adverse effects, by time coursedetail behind the risks Acute dystonia, usually within hours to days of the first dose; an emergency department antiemetic can do itlaryngeal spasm can stop breathing NMS builds over 1 to 3 days, usually after a start or dose increase (the main risk factor) but possible at any timerisk highest with high-potency or depot drugs, several antipsychotics together, or added lithium Akathisia, the most common extrapyramidal effect, typically within 4 weeks (overall range hours to months); parkinsonism within days to weeks, tremor often on both sides Tardive dyskinesia after prolonged use, more than 6 months; about 10% to 20% after a year of treatmentorofacial forms are commonest Withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia after an abrupt stop, more common in children; clears in 4 to 12 weeks Agranulocytosis in just under 1%, usually within 3 months; the risk never reaches zeroseizures dose dependent, about 1% to 6%; drooling (sialorrhea); constipation that can progress to ileus Second-generation drugs differ. Extrapyramidal riskAmong second-generation drugs, risperidone carries the highest extrapyramidal risk; quetiapine and clozapine the lowest. High-potency first-generation drugs (eg haloperidol), more so at higher doses, drive extrapyramidal effects; low-potency drugs and clozapine are the most anticholinergic and sedatingseizures too are commonest with low-potency drugs and clozapine, especially at high doses Higher-potency drugs, higher doses, prior extrapyramidal effects; young men for dystonia, older women for parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia

NMSFever, rigidity, confusion and unstable vital signs on a dopamine blocker CK (creatine kinase) can be very ↑ and typically tracks severity Other labs Guideline detailLeukocytosis, myoglobin in the urine, falling kidney function. Most often high-potency first-generation (eg haloperidol), but any class, olanzapine included If NMS is suspected, choose stopping the antipsychotic, then cooling and fluids. AirwayDystonia of the larynx or pharynx If breathing is threatened, choose airway assessment and an intravenous anticholinergic. ClozapineSevere neutropenia; also myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, seizures, profound hypotension ANC before starting and throughout treatment Agranulocytosis usually within 3 months Myocarditis mostly in the first 4 weeks, at any dose If the baseline ANC is <1500/µL, choose not starting clozapine (initiation is not recommended). DementiaOlder adults with dementia-related psychosis Boxed warning, first- and second-generation alike: higher death risk in older adults with dementia Boxed warningDeath risk about 1.6 to 1.7 times higher, with more stroke and heart attack. If it was started for agitation in a delirium that has improved, choose stopping it and watching behavior.

Which effect is it, most tempting first Effect or mimic Fingerprint Decides it Acute dystonia Sustained, painful spasmNamed formsNamed forms: oculogyric crisis (eyes forced upward), torticollis (painful neck twist). of neck, jaw, eyes or tongue; mind clear; antiemetics such as metoclopramide can cause it Within hours to days of a start or increase; half by 48 hours, 90% by day 5 Akathisia Inner restlessness, a driven urge to move; pacesAkathisiaAripiprazole is commonly linked to it. (in dementia, akathisia may contribute to agitation) Typically within 4 weeks of a start or increase (overall range hours to months); the restlessness is felt from within Drug-induced parkinsonism Tremor, rigidity, slow movement, masked face, shuffling gait Days to a few weeks; tremor often symmetric; reversible Tardive dyskinesia Lip smacking, tongue darting, cheek puffing, jaw movements Months to years of treatment, usually past 6 months Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability, ↑ CK Usually after a start or increase (the main risk factor), but possible at any time; builds over 1 to 3 days; no clonus Hypocalcemia Facial muscle spasm Paresthesia, hyperreflexia and a cause such as neck surgery Serotonin syndrome Fever, agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, vomiting or diarrhea Within hours (under 24) of a serotonergic change; clonus, not rigidity Malignant hyperthermia Fever and rigidity, as in NMS During or just after a volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine Catatonia Little movement, unresponsive, posturing Plain catatonia does not explain fever or autonomic instability; the malignant form can, but shows posturing and waxy flexibility Angioedema or anaphylaxis Tongue pushed out Swelling, not spasm

Timing, from the start or a dose increase HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears Acute dystoniaHalf within 48 hours, 90% within 5 days Neuroleptic malignant syndromeUsually days to weeks after a start or increase, but possible at any time; evolves over 1 to 3 days AkathisiaTypically within 4 weeks; overall range hours to months Drug-induced parkinsonismUsually within a few weeks Tardive dyskinesiaMonths or years after starting

Pause point Fever and rigidity on a dopamine blocker Offered as serotonin syndrome from a drug interaction, or as malignant hyperthermia Rigidity and fever building over days → NMS Sudden muscle spasm on a dopamine blocker Offered as hypocalcemia, or as agitation needing more haloperidol Within hours, in an alert patient → Dystonia: an anticholinergic treats it

Manage by effect Effect or situation Do Avoid Acute dystonia A parenteral anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine); intravenous relief in about 3 to 5 minutes; intravenous benztropine is followed by an oral dose More haloperidol: further blockade would likely worsen it Akathisia Lower the dose, or stop the antipsychotic if the lower dose helps little; or switch (clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine); propranolol if the dose must stay Raising the dose (akathisia is dose dependent); reaching first for a benzodiazepineIn dementiaIn dementia, benzodiazepines generally have no role: falls, dependence, paradoxical agitation. Memantine, a dementia drug, has no evidence for akathisia, and moving the patient to a nursing home is premature before a treatable drug cause is addressed. or benztropine (less favorable safety) Parkinsonism Lower the dose or switch to a second-generation drug; amantadine, or an anticholinergic short term Anticholinergics in older adults Tardive dyskinesia Stop anticholinergics; valbenazine or deutetrabenazine if moderate to severe; stop the antipsychotic or switch (eg clozapine) if possible Anticholinergics: they may worsen it Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Stop the antipsychotic, then cool and correct fluids and electrolytes (ladder below) Swapping in another antipsychotic: every class can cause it Metabolic harm Switch to a lower-risk drug: aripiprazole, ziprasidone or lurasidone carry the leastAlsoAlongside lifestyle measures, metformin can counter the weight gain. Clozapine, olanzapine and quetiapine carry the mostIn practiceAn American Family Physician review places quetiapine one tier lower, in a middle group with less metabolic harm than the top three. Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia; see Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism Quetiapine, pimavanserin or clozapine Risperidone, olanzapine, typical drugsGuideline detailIn Lewy body dementia, typical drugs, even at very low doses, tend to worsen extrapyramidal signs. High-risk patient (eg young man, prior dystonia) given an intramuscular first-generation drug Give diphenhydramine or benztropine with it Waiting for dystonia to appear before giving the anticholinergic

1 FirstNMS suspected Stop the antipsychotic 2 Supportivethe antipsychotic is stopped Aggressive cooling; correct volume deficits and electrolytes Admit to an intensive care unit for close monitoring; a benzodiazepine may help agitation. RefractoryCase reportsElectroconvulsive therapy (ECT) has been reported to work in refractory cases. Restarting laterRestarting after NMSThe recommended cautious rechallenge: wait at least 2 weeks after it resolves, then a lower-potency drug at a low dose with slow titration. 3 Optionsbeyond supportive care Bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist) or dantrolene (a muscle relaxant)

Monitoring When Check Why Every patient Weight, glucose and blood pressure at least yearly, with counseling against weight gain Clozapine, olanzapine and quetiapine carry the most metabolic risk Second-generation drug, from the start Fasting glucose and lipids, weight and blood pressure from baselineGuideline detailWeight at baseline, 4, 8 and 12 weeks, then quarterly; glucose and blood pressure at baseline, 12 weeks, then yearly; lipids at baseline, 12 weeks, then every 5 years (adapted from the 2004 American Diabetes Association consensus). Metabolic harm On clozapine ANC before starting, weekly to month 6, every 2 weeks to month 12, then monthly Severe neutropenia, likeliest early, never zero Starting haloperidol (eg, for delirium) Baseline ECG (electrocardiogram) for the QTc (rate-corrected QT interval) Haloperidol can cause torsades de pointes; QTc prolongation is most marked with thioridazine and ziprasidone. Second-generationQTAmong second-generation drugs, ziprasidone and quetiapine carry the greatest QT risk. Long-term use Orofacial movements About 10% to 20% develop tardive dyskinesia after a year of treatment Missed periods or nipple dischargeAripiprazoleLow-dose aripiprazole can counter the prolactin rise through partial D2 agonism. Hyperprolactinemia Whether the patient takes a drug that commonly raises prolactin (any first-generation drug, risperidone) Dopamine D2 block in the tuberoinfundibular tract raises prolactin: galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, bone loss Sexual Dysfunction

Time the movement from the start or the last dose increase before naming it: hours to days is dystonia, weeks is akathisia or parkinsonism, months to years is tardive dyskinesia.

briefs.title: Lithium Therapy
briefs.sub: which complication, and what to doIs this toxicity, diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism or an expected effect?
blocks: which complication, and what to doIs this toxicity, diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism or an expected effect?

Coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech ↑ level toxicity: stop lithium IV isotonic fluids; hemodialysis for altered mental status, seizures, a life-threatening dysrhythmia or a level past the dialysis cutoffs ↑ sodium dilute urine after years of use nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: restore volume; stop lithium if possible ↑ TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) ↓ free thyroxine add levothyroxine; keep lithium going

What it is Mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder Mechanism Handled like sodium; the kidney is its only real exit Thiazide, NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug), ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker) more lithium reabsorbed level rises Narrow therapeutic range Used for Acute mania: first line, alone or with an antipsychotic Bipolar maintenance (linked to lower suicide risk) bipolar I depression, both first line Kidney disease: valproate for maintenance instead Risks Toxicity nephrogenic diabetes insipidus hypothyroidism Ebstein anomaly in pregnancy ( LMNOP ) Insights Collecting duct: lithium blunts the signal of ADH (antidiuretic hormone) fewer aquaporins desmopressin barely changes the urine Lithium enters collecting-duct cells through the epithelial sodium channel; amiloride blocks that entry, so it can treat the diabetes insipidus when lithium must continue

Adverse effects, by systemroutine effects and complications Fine tremor is routine; coarse tremor, slurred speech, ataxia or drowsiness suggest toxicity; seizures and worsening mental status when severe Metallic taste and diarrhea are common Polyuria and thirst are common; long-term use is linked to chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy Hypothyroidism may develop in about 25% (up to 50%), usually within 1 to 2 years of starting

ToxicityToxicity: findings commonly appear >1.5 mmol/L If lithium toxicity (↑ level) brings altered mental status, seizures or a life-threatening dysrhythmia, choose hemodialysis, whatever the level. LevelLevel >5.0 mmol/L, or >4.0 or >2.5 mmol/L with a conditionHemodialysis cutoffs>4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function (creatinine >2.0 mg/dL); >2.5 mmol/L with prominent signs of toxicity, such as tremor, fasciculations or confusion. In practice: toxicology guidance recommends dialysis >4.0 mmol/L only with impaired kidneys, and only suggests it >5.0 mmol/L. If any one of these is present, choose hemodialysis. IngestionRecent large ingestion; alert, kidneys working, level ≤2.5 mmol/L Activated charcoal does not bind lithium If no dialysis criterion is met, choose IV isotonic fluids and serial levels. Water lossDrowsy and volume-depleted with diabetes insipidus Dehydration also raises the lithium level If sodium is ↑ and the urine dilute, choose volume replacement and a lithium level. PregnancyFirst-trimester exposure: Ebstein anomaly Teratogenic Exposures If exposure fell in the first trimester, choose fetal echocardiography.

Which effect is it, most tempting first Effect Fingerprint Decides it Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Thirst, polyuria; confusion with dehydration Years of use; ↑ sodium with dilute urine; little or no desmopressin response Hypothyroidism Tiredness, cold intolerance, mental fogginess; constipation, myalgias, bradycardia Statin baitNot the statinMyalgias can come from a statin; constipation, a slow pulse and tiredness typically do not. Usually within 1 to 2 years; ↑ TSH with ↓ free thyroxine, or TSH >10 μU/mL Routine side effects Fine tremor, polyuria, metallic taste, mildly ↑ TSH Sodium, mental status, level and free thyroxine all normal Chronic toxicity can no longer hold a coffee cup without spilling its contentsIn a vignetteAsked as: Addition of which of the following medications most likely contributed Long-term user; new thiazide, NSAID, ACE inhibitor or ARB, or dehydration Neurologic findings lead; ↑ level (after a thiazide it usually rises within 10 days) Acute toxicity Recent large ingestion Soon after ingestion: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea often come first; ↑ level Type 2 diabetes mellitus Obesity with polyuria suggests glucose diuresis ↑ glucose; urine not dilute (solute diuresis) Primary polydipsia Polyuria with dilute urine; especially common in psychiatric patients Sodium usually ↓, not ↑; urine concentrates >600 mOsm/kg after water deprivation Central diabetes insipidus Polyuria with dilute urine Desmopressin clearly raises urine osmolality Hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemia ↑ calcium on routine labs Years of lithium; ↑ calcium on the yearly check, then ↑ PTH (parathyroid hormone)

Timing HoursDaysWeeksMonthsYears Acute toxicitySoon after a large ingestion Chronic toxicity after a thiazideLevel usually rises within 10 days HypothyroidismUsually within 1 to 2 years Nephrogenic diabetes insipidusYears of use Hyperparathyroidism, hypercalcemiaYears of lithium; found on the yearly calcium
L lithium M movement: tremor N nephrology: kidney injury and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (thirst, heavy urination) O hypothyroidism P pregnancy: Ebstein anomaly

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans New symptoms on lithium: read all three pairs together → Serum lithium level and creatinine Level ↑, with neurologic findings Toxicity; hemodialysis when a dialysis criterion is met → Serum sodium and urine osmolality Sodium ↑, urine dilute Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus → TSH and free thyroxine ↑ TSH, ↓ free thyroxine Hypothyroidism Mildly ↑ TSH, normal free thyroxine, no symptoms The routine thyroid change Targeted tests TestResultMeans Toxicity suspected → ECG (electrocardiogram) Bradycardia, atrioventricular block, flat T waves Cardiac toxicity Diabetes insipidus suspected → Desmopressin response Urine osmolality rises little (usually <50 mOsm/kg) or not at all Nephrogenic; a clear rise means central

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Thirst and polyuria plus confusion Water loss, not the routine polyuria Sodium with urine osmolality, plus a lithium level Mildly ↑ TSH beside ↑ sodium and dilute urine A decoy: the thyroid explains neither Read the sodium against the urine; also check free thyroxine

Pause point Years of lithium: a mildly ↑ TSH, confusion, a high sodium Offered as hypothyroidism, or the confusion as acute toxicity All the options The optionsAcute lithium toxicity: confusion and trouble walking fit toxicity; but the labs here point to the kidney. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism: the TSH of 5.5 is mildly high; but no free thyroxine is given, and hypothyroidism explains neither the hypernatremia nor the dilute urine. Routine side effects of lithium: polyuria alone is routine; but with dehydration, confusion, hypernatremia and dilute urine, this can be life-threatening. Type 2 diabetes mellitus: a body mass index of 29 with polyuria suggests glucose diuresis; but hypernatremia after years of lithium fits the kidney better. Down to two: lithium-induced diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. Diabetes insipidus: 20 years of lithium, thirst and polyuria, then a sodium of 150 with urine osmolality 200; the kidney is losing water it should keep. With no lithium level and no mention of diabetes insipidus in the stem, the answer comes from reading the sodium against the urine. Four of the five options are effects of lithium; the one tempting lab, a mildly high TSH, points to the wrong effect. Hypernatremia with dilute urine after years of use → The kidney Check a level too, since water loss can raise it.

1 1st linetoxicity with nausea, diarrhea, a coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech or an unsteady gait; mental status intact, level 2.5 or under, no dialysis criterion met Stop lithium; IV isotonic fluids; serial levels 2 Escalatealtered mental status, seizures, a life-threatening dysrhythmia, or a level past the dialysis cutoffs Hemodialysis

Manage by effect Effect Do Avoid Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Stop lithium if possible, then restrict salt. If lithium must continue, amiloride may be used instead of salt restriction, since a low-sodium diet would raise the level A thiazide, or an NSAID other than aspirin or sulindac, without close levels: both raise the lithium level Hypothyroidism Add levothyroxine; continue lithium Stopping lithium: thyroid changes are not a reason

Monitoring Before startingBaselines: creatinine, BUN (blood urea nitrogen), TSH, calcium with albumin Day 7First level Every 1 to 2 weeksLevel, until stable in range Every 6 to 12 monthsLevel, electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, TSH YearlyCalcium with albumin; PTH if calcium is ↑ When Check Why Before starting Creatinine, BUN (blood urea nitrogen), TSH, calcium with albumin; weight, height, blood pressure; a pregnancy test when relevant Higher riskGuideline detailWith cardiac disease or cardiac risk factors, or in older adults, add an ECG before starting Baselines for kidney, thyroid and calcium effects; teratogenic risk After starting Level at 7 days, then every 1 to 2 weeks until stable in range Narrow range: the dose is titrated to the level Every 6 to 12 months Level, electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, TSH Kidney and thyroid effects build over time Yearly Calcium with albumin; PTH if calcium is ↑ Long-term use is linked to hyperparathyroidism ↑ TSH, normal free thyroxine Recheck in 4 to 6 months; add levothyroxine once free thyroxine falls or TSH >10 μU/mL; a trial is reasonable if symptoms appear Not a reason to stop lithium

Levels are troughs, about 12 hours after the last dose. Target 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/LIn practice:Guidelines split the target: acute mania 0.8 to 1.2 under age 65; maintenance 0.6 to 1.0, some using 0.8 as the floor (= mmol/L); toxic >1.5.

Interactions With Effect Do Thiazide diuretic Level usually rises within 10 days Level and creatinine more often NSAID Raises the level (more is reabsorbed); aspirin and sulindac are exceptions Level and creatinine more often ACE inhibitor or ARB Raises the level Level and kidney function more often Metronidazole Can raise the level Check the level Dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, low-sodium diet Raise the level Check the level; consider a lower dose with infection, heavy sweating or diarrhea

When a patient on a drug with several known complications presents, choose the complication that explains every abnormal value. On lithium, a high sodium with dilute urine points to the kidney, and a mildly high TSH beside it is not the answer.

briefs.title: Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity
briefs.sub: anticholinergic toxidrome · tricyclic cardiotoxicity · bicarbonate, benzodiazepine, physostigmineIs the QRS wide, and is a tricyclic involved?
blocks: anticholinergic toxidrome · tricyclic cardiotoxicity · bicarbonate, benzodiazepine, physostigmineIs the QRS wide, and is a tricyclic involved?

Anticholinergic signs or any tricyclic overdose: an ECG (electrocardiogram) first; a QRS over 100 ms, a ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension calls for sodium bicarbonate Agitation or seizures: a benzodiazepine. No haloperidol; no physostigmine once a tricyclic is involved QRS width, not pupil size, bowel sounds or a drug level, predicts seizures and arrhythmia

What it is Anticholinergic toxicity: muscarinic receptors blocked by one drug or several, often psychiatric medications A tricyclic overdose adds sodium-channel cardiotoxicity, seizures and coma Mechanism Muscarinic block hot, dry, flushed skin big pupils ileus, urinary retention, delirium MnemonicAnticholinergic toxidromeHot as a hare (fever), dry as a bone (no sweating), red as a beet (flushing), blind as a bat (big pupils), mad as a hatter (delirium) Cardiac fast sodium channels blocked wide QRS ventricular arrhythmia Alpha-1 block hypotension; gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) antagonism seizures Culprits Tricyclics: amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine and doxepin (tertiary, most anticholinergic); nortriptyline and desipramine (secondary, least) First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine; clozapine; phenothiazine and butyrophenone antipsychotics, haloperidol included Used for Tricyclics: depression after first-line drugs fail; obsessive-compulsive disorder (clomipramine); insomnia (doxepin); neuropathic pain and migraine (amitriptyline, nortriptyline); enuresis (imipramine) Risks Cardiotoxicity, the most common cause of death; convulsions and coma also occur ( Tri-C ); fatal at relatively low doses Insights Bicarbonate works on the sodium-channel block, not on drug removal: it raises the pH and the extracellular sodium Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, reverses anticholinergic toxicity, yet it is contraindicated in tricyclic poisoning because it can worsen cardiotoxicity

Convulsions GABA-A antagonism Coma sedation and confusion, progressing to unresponsiveness Cardiotoxicity wide QRS; QT prolongation that can bring torsades de pointes; ventricular arrhythmia; hypotension

Adverse effects at usual doses, by receptortap to open Dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation, urinary retention, fast pulse, confusionStrongest with amitriptyline; tricyclics are relatively contraindicated in older adults Orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, reflex tachycardiaFalls in older adults Sedation, weight gain Sexual dysfunction, tremor, seizures; serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs, such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) QRS widening; ventricular tachycardia or fibrillationContraindicated with conduction disease

CardiotoxicityWide QRS, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension If the QRS is over 100 ms, or arrhythmia or hypotension appears, choose IV sodium bicarbonate. SeizuresOne or more convulsions after a tricyclic overdose If a seizure occurs, choose a benzodiazepine. Looks wellA normal early appearance can still progress to collapse, because absorption varies If a tricyclic was taken, choose ECGs repeated and close monitoring. Suicide attemptOverdose taken to attempt suicide Suicide Risk Assessment If the patient is medically stable and thinking clearly, choose assess suicide risk.

Look-alikes, most tempting first Diagnosis Fingerprint Decides it Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Fever, confusion, unstable vital signs, lead-pipe rigidity Builds over 1 to 3 days after a dopamine blocker is started or raised; rigid; normal tone makes it unlikely Primary psychosis flare Hallucinations in a patient on several psychiatric drugs Anticholinergic signs (big pupils, dry hot skin, fast pulse) mean toxicity; haloperidol can worsen it Serotonin syndrome Sweating, clonus, hyperreflexia, increased bowel sounds Minutes to hours after a serotonergic drug is added or raised; clonus Seizure or postictal state Confusion after a convulsion Seconds to minutes, typically abrupt; fever, hypertension and hallucinations point to anticholinergic toxicity Stimulant (cocaine, amphetamine) Fever, big pupils, fast pulse, agitation Sweating; anticholinergic skin stays dry Delirium in an older adult New confusion, agitation or hallucinations on an anticholinergic drug An anticholinergic drug in an older adult: dry, warm skin and big pupils point to the drug as the cause

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Anticholinergic signs, or a tricyclic taken → ECG now, then serial ECGs QRS over 100 ms, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension Cardiotoxicity: sodium bicarbonate Normal at first Repeat the ECG: the patient can worsen quickly Any intentional overdose → Acetaminophen level → Salicylate level → Urine drug screen SkipSerum or urine tricyclic levels: late, and they do not track toxicity. No laboratory test confirms anticholinergic toxicity.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Big pupils and quiet bowel after a tricyclic Common anticholinergic effects with no prognostic value Follow the QRS width Normal muscle tone and reflexes Not neuroleptic malignant syndrome No bromocriptine Clonus or hyperreflexia with sweating Serotonin syndrome SSRI Adverse Effects Agitated and hallucinating, with hot, dry, flushed skin and big pupils Anticholinergic delirium A benzodiazepine; no haloperidol Diphenhydramine or another first-generation antihistamine an empty bottle of “sleep aids” Anticholinergic; some lengthen the QT interval ECG Hard, infrequent stools on nightly diphenhydramine for sleep; otherwise well A relatively common anticholinergic adverse effect Decrease or stop the diphenhydramine; constipation testing waits for that trial

Pause point Agitation and fever on anticholinergic drugs Offered: haloperidol for the agitation, or bromocriptine for the fever Big pupils, dry skin and normal tone → Anticholinergic toxicity; the ECG comes first

1 FirstEvery patient Supportive care: airway, breathing, circulation; IV fluids for hypotension 2 DecontaminateUnder 2 hours, airway protected Activated charcoal 3 CardiotoxicityQRS over 100 ms, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension IV sodium bicarbonate infusion Not physostigmine 4 Agitation or seizuresAt any point A benzodiazepine Not haloperidol or a phenothiazine: they add anticholinergic effect 5 Antidote, with careSevere central and peripheral anticholinergic signs, no tricyclic Physostigmine Contraindicated with any sign of a tricyclic or a wide QRS, as it can worsen cardiotoxicity

Prescribing a tricyclic safely When Check Why Before starting Potassium; an ECG if age 40 or older, cardiac symptoms, or a QT-prolonging drug such as methadone Low potassium and QT prolongation add arrhythmia risk Conduction or coronary artery disease Conduction disease: do not use; coronary disease: avoid QT prolongation and arrhythmia Epilepsy, angle-closure glaucoma, older age Prescribe cautiously, with close monitoring Lower seizure threshold; pupil dilation; anticholinergic effects and falls Suicide risk Dispense a small supply, such as 1 week Fatal at relatively low doses After an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor) Wait 14 days Serotonin syndrome risk Stopping Taper over weeks to months An abrupt stop brings cholinergic rebound: nausea, sweating, headache, insomnia

briefs.title: Suicide Risk Assessment
briefs.sub: screening by age · ideation, plan and intent · risk and protective factors · level of care · antidepressant warningIs the risk imminent, and what does that decide about the level of care?
blocks: screening by age · ideation, plan and intent · risk and protective factors · level of care · antidepressant warningIs the risk imminent, and what does that decide about the level of care?

Ask directly asking does not cause or worsen suicidal thinking Plan with intent to act, or uncertain whether he will act hospitalize, involuntarily if he refuses Thoughts without plan or intent safety plan, intensive outpatient treatment, follow-up

What it is A bedside assessment of ideation, plan and intent that sets the level of care Driver Ideation with a plan and intent to act risk factors outweighing protective ones Low cerebrospinal fluid 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the main serotonin metabolite, is associated with suicidal behavior Triggers Prior attempt (non-modifiable; the strongest predictor) Firearm at home, alcohol or drugs, hopelessness, a recent loss, living alone Chain Passive thoughts active thoughts plan rehearsal or preparatory acts Each step raises the risk Insights A prior attempt outranks a firearm or alcohol: both are real but lesser, and modifiable; in the acute setting, active alcohol or drug use (disinhibition) weighs more than the other static factors: age, sex and family history Intoxicated or delirious no valid assessment until cognition is intact

Risk and protective factorsdetail behind the triggers Prior attempt, age (adolescents and young adults; over 70 has the highest rates), male sex for death (females attempt more), family history of suicide or psychiatric illness Plan or intent, access to weapons or medications, intoxication or substance use (disinhibition), impulsivity, psychosis or agitation, psychiatric or medical illness, stopping treatment, hopelessness, a recent stressor, living alone A firearm at home is an independent risk factor, about 3 times the risk of death by suicide; the most common method in the US Effective mental health care, connectedness, beliefs that discourage suicide

Risk factors in one mnemonic: SAD PERSONSRisk factor mnemonicSex (male), Age (teenage or elderly), Depression, Previous attempt (the highest risk), Ethanol or drug use, Rational thinking impaired (psychosis), Sickness (medical illness), Organized plan, No spouse or other support, Stated future intent.

ImminentA specific plan with intent to act now, rehearsal or preparatory acts, few or no protective factors If he refuses admission, choose involuntary hospitalization under local law. ImpairedIntoxicated or delirious, cannot answer questions about a plan If cognition is impaired, choose one-to-one observation with suicide precautions until he is sober, then the full assessment.

Which level of risk, most tempting first Picture Fingerprint Decides it High (imminent) risk Frequent thoughts, a specific plan, intent to act now, rehearsal or preparation Intent to act now; hospitalize even if he looks calm Uncertain intent Suicidal thoughts, and no one can say whether he will act Uncertainty is not low risk; emergency hospitalization Low (nonimminent) risk Passive or infrequent thoughts, no plan or intent, protective factors No plan and no intent; outpatient care, not admission Assessment not yet valid Intoxication or delirium Cognition impaired; a steady gait does not replace the assessment

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Any disclosure, positive screen, depression or life-threatening act → Ask directly about thoughts of suicide Passive or active, how often Ideation and its severity Next step TestResultMeans Thoughts present → Plan, access to the method, lethality, chance of rescue Rehearsal or preparatory acts Higher risk Risk unclear → Risk and protective factors; collateral from family Prior attempt The most predictive risk factor Firearm at home Independent risk factor; discuss removing it SkipThe assessment is the history: ideation, intent and plan, asked directly.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Age 12 or older, routine visit Universal screening Validated screen (eg, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions); a positive screen gets a brief safety assessment Age 8 to 11 Screen when clinically indicated Under 8: not indicated, but assess if warning signs Adult with current depression or a prior attempt Targeted screening Ask directly Minor with active concerns for suicide Safety outranks privacy Telling a parent or guardian is permissible; hospitalize for safety Adolescent Confidentiality Paranoid and impulsive, with a gun at home; no threats, no suicidal or homicidal ideation Acute risk to others and to himself Restrict access to the firearm first, within an outpatient safety plan Why not warn or contractWhyThe firearm at home is the most immediate risk. Notifying others is not needed without homicidal ideation or specific threats. Safety contracts have not been shown to prevent violence. Hospitalization should be considered with several acute risk factors; with no threats and no suicidal or homicidal ideation, an outpatient safety plan is reasonable.

Pause point Calm, sober patient with a rehearsed plan Read as safe because he promises to stay safe Intent and preparation set the risk; a no-suicide contract does not prevent suicide → Admit, involuntarily if he refuses

Risk tier and level of care Tier Features Level of care Low No or infrequent thoughts; no apparent plan or intent; few risk factors, many protective ones Outpatient: safety plan, means removal, treatment, follow-up Uncertain Thoughts present; whether he will act is unclear Emergency hospitalization High (imminent) Frequent thoughts, specific plan, intent to act now, rehearsal, few protective factors Inpatient hospitalization; involuntary if he refuses

1 Lowthoughts without plan or intent Collaborative safety plan: coping, supports, emergency and crisis contacts; discuss removing means, with family help if he agrees Treat the condition and arrange follow-up; intensive outpatient treatment, not admission. Not a No-suicide contractWhy notA promise not to harm himself. It does not prevent suicide; a safety plan replaces it.. 2 Highspecific plan with imminent intent, rehearsal or preparation, or uncertain whether he will act Inpatient hospitalization with precautions: remove hazards, one-to-one sitter 3 Refuseshe refuses admission Involuntary hospitalization under local law

By situation Situation Do Minor with active suicidal ideation Hospitalize for safety; telling a parent or guardian is permissible Adolescent Confidentiality Firearm or stockpiled medication at home Discuss removing access, with family help if he agrees Depression driving the risk Treat the condition driving the risk Major Depressive Disorder

Follow-up decisions When Do Starting an antidepressant such as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), especially in a child, adolescent or young adult Monitor closely for worsening and new suicidal thoughts; short-term studies showed more suicidal thoughts and behaviors in these agesWas it the drug or a new stressor?Improvement on the drug before a new stressor makes the drug a less likely cause of the suicidal thoughts; look for the stressor and for substance use. The evidence that the drug causes suicidal thoughts is inconclusive, and expert consensus favors treating. SSRI Adverse Effects Low risk, managed as an outpatient Follow-up visits; reassess if high-risk features appear

briefs.title: Intimate Partner Violence
briefs.sub: plan for safety, report by who is at riskIs she safe at home, and who decides what happens next?
blocks: plan for safety, report by who is at riskIs she safe at home, and who decides what happens next?

Injuries that do not fit the story, or bruises on the lower abdomen, back or forearms ask her alone whether she feels safe Every patient an emergency safety plan, whether or not she discloses abuse or is ready to leave A child abused in the home report on suspicion; reporting her own abuse varies by state and is not the first step

What it is Abuse by a partner at home (domestic abuse); the danger is her home, not a psychiatric condition Driver A competent adult decides when to leave many are not yet willing or able to Triggers Recent job loss or financial instability; substance use Pregnancy (it often begins or increases, especially if unintended) and the postpartum period Chain Repeated injury frequent emergency visits In pregnancy trauma, placental abruption, miscarriage, preterm labor, low birth weight Insights Police or a protective order before she is ready to leave may escalate the violence A partner who speaks for her is a reason to see her alone

ChildSuspected abuse of a child in the home If a child in the home may be abused, choose a report to child protective services on suspicion. CapacityAn older or dependent adult who cannot decide for herself If she cannot protect herself, choose a report per state law; most states require it. Immediate harmRisk of immediate harm, assessed at every visit If she discloses abuse, choose assess her readiness to act; she decides when to leave.

Who is at risk, and who decides Situation Fingerprint Decides it Competent adult, only she at risk Alert, oriented, judgment intact; not older or disabled She decides what to do and when; safety plan with her, no report as the first step State lawReporting her own abuseMost states require reports of specified injuries and wounds, and very few require reporting domestic violence itself; know your state's law. Child abuse in the home Suspected abuse of a child she lives with Report on suspicion to child protective services Older or dependent adult Cannot decide for herself; unexplained change in health, behavior or finances Report; most states require it Weapon injury Injury from a gun, knife or other weapon Reportable in most states

Diagnostic workup First step TestResultMeans Injuries that do not fit the story; suspicious bruises → See her aloneAsk, tactfully, whether she feels safe Partner present He can intimidate her: see her alone if possible Not possible or not offered The safety plan comes first Next step TestResultMeans Every patient → Emergency safety plan She says she is abused Assess readiness to act She denies it Plan anyway; the findings raised it Woman of reproductive age, including pregnancy and after delivery → Screen with a brief questionnaire, in private Positive screen Evaluate; offer or refer for interventions with ongoing support SkipNo test raises it; the injury pattern and the history do.

Clues that change the answer Clue Points to Next best step Bruised forearms Defensive movements during an attack Ask her alone about safety Lower-abdominal bruises in pregnancy Partner violence, which often begins or increases in pregnancy Ask her alone about safety Partner answers for her Intimidation See her alone first, if possible Older patient with an unexplained change in health, behavior or finances Elder abuse Report per state law

Pause point Woman with serious injuries who is not ready to leave Offered: police, a protective order, psychiatric admission or anger management for the partner All the options The optionsContact the police: Serious injuries, but she is not ready to go; involving police now can make the violence worse An order of protection: Sounds protective, but filed too early it may raise her risk of harm Psychiatric admission: She is in danger from her home situation, not from a mental illness; a stay only removes her briefly Anger management for the partner: Not conclusively shown to lower the risk of violence A pamphlet to take home: The abuser may find written materials Adult Protective Services for a competent adult: Reporting abuse of a competent adult depends on state law Down to two: a safety plan or contacting the police. Safety plan: all patients with suspected abuse get help with one, whether or not they disclose abuse. The stem never says abuse: repeated injuries, an apologetic story that does not match the bruises, and a patient who looks at her husband before answering; four options act through the police, the courts, a psychiatric unit or the husband, and only the safety plan acts with her. Each may escalate harm, may only remove her for a while, or has not conclusively been shown to lower the risk → A safety plan she can use today

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block serotonin reuptake early nausea, headache, insomnia and anxiety; later sexual dysfunction and weight gain Class risks: suicidal thoughts under 25 (boxed warning), hyponatremia, and bleeding with an anti-inflammatory or an anticoagulant Citalopram: dose-dependent QT prolongation, avoided after a recent heart attack; paroxetine: the most interactions and a first-trimester heart-defect signal; fluoxetine: long half-life, so no taper

Drugs Citalopram Celexa: dose-dependent QT prolongation, fewest interactions Escitalopram Lexapro: few interactions Fluoxetine Prozac: long half-life, so no taper is needed; strong cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) inhibitor Fluvoxamine: strong cytochrome P450 1A2 (CYP1A2) inhibitor Paroxetine Paxil: most interactions, most discontinuation symptoms, anticholinergic Sertraline Zoloft: few interactions Mechanism Serotonin transporter blocked more serotonin in the synapse longer postsynaptic stimulation ReceptorsSerotonin receptorsType 1 receptors carry the antidepressant and anti-anxiety effect; type 2 receptors bring anxiety, insomnia and sexual dysfunction; type 3 receptors bring nausea and headache. Dopamine and norepinephrine are barely touched. Few anticholinergic or cardiac conduction effects wide safety margin; isolated overdose is usually well tolerated, except with citalopram Uses Depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic, generalized and social anxiety, premenstrual dysphoric disorder; fluoxetine for bulimia nervosa AlsoOther usesSSRIs also treat premature ejaculation and menopausal hot flashes (paroxetine, citalopram). Adverse effects Early: nausea, headache, insomnia or sleepiness, anxiety, dizziness LabelSertraline labelThe Zoloft label also lists diarrhea, tremor, indigestion, less appetite and sweating among the most common effects. Later: sexual dysfunction in up to half, weight gain In practiceIn practiceHigher in the Merck Manual: sexual dysfunction above half of patients, most often trouble reaching orgasm. Hyponatremia, often from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), higher risk over 65 MnemonicDrug causes of SIADH"Can't Concentrate Serum Na+": carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, SSRIs and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can all cause SIADH. SSRI Adverse Effects Paroxetine: anticholinergic; fluoxetine: agitation, early appetite loss Abrupt stop of a short half-life SSRI such as paroxetine: flu-like, neurologic and psychiatric symptoms within days SSRI Adverse Effects Monitoring Before starting: screen for bipolar disorder Bipolar Disorder Older adults: serum sodium SSRI Adverse Effects

QT prolongation on citalopramDose-dependent; label maximum 40 mg a day, 20 mg over age 60 or with hepatic impairment LabelCitalopram labelThe Celexa label also avoids it with congenital long QT, a slow heart rate, low potassium or magnesium, uncompensated heart failure or another QT-prolonging drug, and checks electrolytes when they may run low. If a patient with a recent heart attack needs an SSRI, choose sertraline or escitalopram, not citalopram. A citalopram overdose can still bring torsade de pointes, and it may be delayed: keep the heart monitored Suspected Overdose or Toxidrome Suicidal thoughts under 25Boxed warning: more suicidal thoughts in children and adults under 25 in short-term studies If a patient of any age starts an antidepressant, choose a close watch for worsening mood and suicidal thinking. Suicide Risk Assessment Paroxetine in pregnancyFirst-trimester exposure: under a 2-fold rise in cardiac malformations If an SSRI is needed in pregnancy, choose sertraline or escitalopram over paroxetine. NewbornNewborn riskAny SSRI late in pregnancy, paroxetine included, can cause persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. On the Zoloft label, newborns exposed to an SSRI late in the third trimester have needed prolonged hospital care, breathing support and tube feeding.

Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake blocked dose-dependent hypertension, the most common adverse effect of serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs); venlafaxine is typically avoided in hypertension Abrupt stop, most of all with short half-life venlafaxine flu-like discontinuation symptoms within days, without seizures; a slow taper prevents them First line, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), for generalized anxiety, panic, social anxiety and posttraumatic stress disorders; duloxetine also treats diabetic neuropathy and fibromyalgia With a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), linezolid or another serotonergic drug serotonin syndrome

Drugs Venlafaxine Effexor XR (extended release): short half-life, so more discontinuation symptoms Desvenlafaxine Pristiq: the active metabolite of venlafaxine Duloxetine: like venlafaxine in benefit and adverse effects; also treats pain Levomilnacipran Fetzima Milnacipran Savella: fibromyalgia Mechanism Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake blocked at the presynaptic neuron More norepinephrine blood pressure up, dose-dependent Short half-life (venlafaxine) abrupt stop discontinuation symptoms Uses Depression: an alternative to SSRIs Major Depressive Disorder Generalized anxiety, panic and social anxiety disorders: first line with SSRIs Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety Posttraumatic stress disorder: first line with SSRIs Trauma, Stress and Dissociative Disorders Obsessive-compulsive disorder: venlafaxine is second line Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders Duloxetine: diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia (milnacipran too); may help chronic low back pain still present after exercise and acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs Low Back Pain in an Adult Pain orderNeuropathic painFor neuropathic pain, tricyclics or gabapentinoids come first; duloxetine is an option. Adverse effects Hypertension, dose-dependent: the most common SNRI adverse effect; block below Nausea, mostly in the first 2 weeks; also stimulant effects or sedation Sexual dysfunction, as with SSRIs SSRI Adverse Effects Discontinuation syndrome after an abrupt stop, without seizures; block below MnemonicDiscontinuation mnemonicFlu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances, hyperarousal: the initials spell "finish" Serotonin syndrome with another serotonergic drug; block below Other Venlafaxine may give a false-positive phencyclidine (PCP) result on a standard urine drug screen Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal

Dose-dependent hypertensionBlood pressure up, more at higher doses; heart rate may rise too If hypertension is present before starting, choose an antidepressant other than venlafaxine. Discontinuation syndromeFlu-like aches, dizziness, nausea, irritability or electric shock-like sensations within days of an abrupt stop SSRI Adverse Effects Symptoms after an abrupt stop are discontinuation, not relapse or influenza; a patient willing to restart venlafaxine restarts it, then tapers slowly, as the board teaches for paroxetine, another short half-life drug; a patient who will not restart venlafaxine: SSRI Adverse Effects. If venlafaxine is to be stopped, choose a slow taper. Serotonin syndromeTypically fever, mental status changes, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia and clonus after, for example, an MAOI, linezolid, tramadol, a triptan or ondansetron joins an SNRI SSRI Adverse Effects

Interactions, by result Combined with Result Rule An MAOI, or linezolid (a weak MAOI) Serotonin syndrome Never together; washout as on the MAOIs card Tramadol, meperidine, dextromethorphan, triptans, ondansetron Serotonin syndrome Risk adds up; watch for clonus and fever

Monitoring When Check Why Before starting Blood pressure; control it first Dose-dependent rise During treatment Blood pressure and pulse, checked more often at higher doses The rise tracks the dose Stopping Taper slowly Short half-life: discontinuation symptoms

Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold avoid it with a seizure disorder, bulimia or anorexia, or an abrupt stop of alcohol, a benzodiazepine, a barbiturate or an antiepileptic Trazodone blocks alpha-1 receptors priapism and orthostatic hypotension; an erection over 4 hours is a urologic emergency Mirtazapine sedates and raises appetite and weight; it and bupropion cause no sexual dysfunction

Drugs Bupropion Wellbutrin SR (sustained release), XL (extended release): norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor Mirtazapine Remeron: alpha-2 antagonist Trazodone: serotonin 2 antagonist, used mostly for sleep Vilazodone Viibryd: serotonin 1A partial agonist LabelVilazodone labelViibryd is taken with food; diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and insomnia are its most common effects. With a strong cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibitor, its dose stays at 20 mg a day or less. Vortioxetine Trintellix: serotonin 1A agonist Mechanism Bupropion: norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake blocked mild stimulant; seizure threshold lowered Mirtazapine: alpha-2 autoreceptor blocked more serotonin and norepinephrine released; histamine H1 blocked sedation, appetite ReceptorsSerotonin receptorsMirtazapine also blocks serotonin 2 and 3 receptors, so serotonergic and noradrenergic function rise without sexual dysfunction or nausea. Trazodone: serotonin 2 blocked, weak serotonin reuptake block; alpha-1 blocked vasodilation orthostatic hypotension, priapism; H1 blocked sedation Uses Bupropion: depression with fatigue or hypersomnia, concern about weight gain, or a wish to quit smoking Major Depressive Disorder Mirtazapine: depression with insomnia or weight loss; older adults Major Depressive Disorder Trazodone: mainly insomnia (off label), at low doses; sedation limits antidepressant doses Sleep Problems Adverse effects Bupropion: insomnia, fast pulse; seizures, dose-related (below); less weight gain; no sexual dysfunction, and it may relieve it LabelBupropion labelThe Wellbutrin XL label adds dry mouth and raised blood pressure; check blood pressure before starting and during treatment. Mirtazapine: sedation, appetite and weight gain, raised cholesterol, dry mouth; no sexual dysfunction LabelMirtazapine labelThe Remeron label warns of agranulocytosis: with sore throat, fever, mouth sores or infection and a low white blood cell count, stop the drug. Trazodone: sedation, orthostatic hypotension, priapism, sexual dysfunction; QT prolongation Vortioxetine: sexual dysfunction, abnormal dreams Other Urine drug screen: bupropion can give a false positive for amphetamines LabelConfirming the screenThe Wellbutrin XL label: a confirmatory test (gas chromatography with mass spectrometry) tells bupropion from amphetamines.

Bupropion seizuresRisk climbs with the dose and with fast dose increases; electrolyte abnormalities, as in bulimia or anorexia, raise it further If there is a seizure disorder, bulimia or anorexia, or an abrupt stop of alcohol, a benzodiazepine, a barbiturate or an antiepileptic, choose another antidepressant, such as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). A seizure on bupropion: stop it and never restart it Ischemic priapismAn erection lasting over 4 hours on trazodone, usually painful, from alpha-1 block; sildenafil and sickle cell disease are other causes If an erection lasts over 4 hours on trazodone, choose corporal aspiration or intracavernosal phenylephrine. WhyHow it worksAn alpha-1 agonist constricts the helicine arterioles. A urologic emergency: untreated, it may end in permanent erectile dysfunction or penile necrosis LabelTrazodone labelThe trazodone label: with an erection past 4 hours, painful or not, stop the drug and seek emergency care at once.

The bupropion label instead bars starting it on linezolid for hypertensive reactions; the mirtazapine label bars it as well. Avoid Drugs cleared by cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6), eg, nortriptyline, paroxetine, metoprolol, flecainide Their levels rise on bupropion Consider a lower dose

Tricyclics block muscarinic, alpha-1 and histamine H1 receptors besides reuptake dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, confusion; orthostatic hypotension; sedation and weight gain Fatal at relatively low doses: cardiac fast sodium channels blocked wide QRS and ventricular arrhythmia, the usual cause of death Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity Tertiary amines (amitriptyline most) are the most anticholinergic and sedating; tricyclics are relatively contraindicated in older adults, and if one is needed, a secondary amine such as nortriptyline

Drugs Amitriptyline: tertiary; the most anticholinergic Clomipramine Anafranil: tertiary; the most serotonergic Doxepin Silenor (3 or 6 mg, for sleep): tertiary; strong H1 block Imipramine: tertiary Nortriptyline Pamelor: secondary; among the least anticholinergic Desipramine Norpramin: secondary; among the least anticholinergic Protriptyline: secondary Tertiary or secondaryThe two amine groupsTertiary amines lean toward serotonin reuptake block and are more anticholinergic and sedating. Secondary amines lean toward norepinephrine reuptake block and are less of both. Mechanism Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake blocked effects on mood and pain Muscarinic block anticholinergic effects; alpha-1 block orthostatic hypotension; H1 block sedation, weight gain Cardiac fast sodium channels blocked slower conduction QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmia Like class IAAnalogyAnalogy from the source: the sodium-channel block resembles class IA antiarrhythmics such as quinidine. Gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) antagonism seizures Uses Depression that has not answered first-line drugs Major Depressive Disorder Clomipramine: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), second line after selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders Imipramine: enuresis, second line after desmopressin and rarely used Enuresis Amitriptyline, nortriptyline at low doses: neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, migraine prophylaxis OrderPain and headacheNeuropathic pain: a tricyclic or a gabapentinoid comes first. Migraine prophylaxis: tricyclics are second line. Amitriptyline is the first-line preventive for chronic tension headache. Tricyclics also help diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia. Doxepin: insomnia, from its histamine block LabelDoxepin labelSilenor, low-dose doxepin, is labeled for insomnia with trouble staying asleep. Adverse effects Anticholinergic: dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation, urinary retention, fast pulse, confusion; worst with amitriptyline MoreOther effectsTricyclics can also cause gastroparesis; respiratory depression and hyperpyrexia are listed too. Alpha-1: orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, reflex tachycardia falls in older adults H1: sedation, more appetite, weight gain; sedation adds to delirium in older adults Reuptake: sexual dysfunction (low libido, anorgasmia), tremor GABA-A antagonism: seizures ClomipramineClomipramine labelOn the Anafranil label, seizure is the most significant risk of the drug. Cardiac: QRS widening; QT prolongation torsades de pointes Abrupt stop cholinergic rebound: nausea, vomiting, sweating, headache, muscle aches, irritability, insomnia

Tricyclic overdoseConfusion, seizures, hot dry skin, big pupils, low blood pressure and a wide QRS; can look well at first and then worsen fast Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity No physostigmine in a tricyclic overdose: it can worsen the cardiotoxicity If the QRS is over 100 ms, or a ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension appears, choose a sodium bicarbonate infusion. Serotonin syndromeTypically fever, mental status changes, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia and clonus; often with another serotonergic drug SSRI Adverse Effects If serotonin syndrome appears, choose stopping every serotonergic drug.

Interactions, by result Combined with Result Rule A monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), or one stopped inside its washout MAOIs Serotonin syndrome Never together Fluoxetine, paroxetine, other cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) blockers; quinidine, cimetidine Tricyclic level rises; a stable patient can turn toxic Consider a lower dose Other anticholinergic drugs, eg, clozapine Anticholinergic toxicity Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity Electrocardiogram (ECG) if toxicity appears Alcohol Stronger effect; more danger in an overdose Warn the patient

Monitoring and limits When Check Why Before starting Potassium; an ECG at 40 or older, with cardiac symptoms, or on a QT-prolonging drug such as methadone An abnormal result adds to the arrhythmia risk Conduction disease (bundle branch or heart block, long QT); coronary artery disease Conduction disease: do not use; coronary disease: avoid QT prolongation and arrhythmia Recovery from a recent myocardial infarction Do not use The nortriptyline and amitriptyline labels both warn about the acute recovery period Epilepsy, angle-closure glaucoma, older age Prescribe cautiously, with close monitoring Lower seizure threshold; pupil dilation; anticholinergic effects and falls Suicide risk A small supply, such as 1 week Fatal at relatively low doses Stopping Taper over weeks to months Avoids cholinergic rebound

Tyramine (aged cheese, wine) or a sympathomimetic such as pseudoephedrine on an MAOI hypertensive crisis; treat with phentolamine Any other serotonergic drug with an MAOI serotonin syndrome; wait 2 weeks between them, 5 weeks after fluoxetine Not first line; used for treatment-resistant or atypical depression; lethal in overdose

Drugs Phenelzine Nardil Tranylcypromine Parnate Isocarboxazid Marplan Selegiline patch Emsam: selective for MAO‑B at low doses Mechanism Monoamine oxidase (MAO) A and B blocked, irreversibly less breakdown of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine A and BThe two enzymesMAO‑A breaks down serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine. MAO‑B breaks down dopamine. Phenelzine, tranylcypromine and isocarboxazid block both; selegiline at low doses and rasagiline block MAO‑B selectively. Gut MAO‑A blocked dietary tyramine enters the circulation norepinephrine pushed out of nerve endings hypertensive crisis Irreversible block new enzyme must be made diet limits and washout outlast the last dose (timeline below) Selegiline: MAO‑B only at low doses gut MAO‑A spared at the low-dose patch Uses Treatment-resistant depression, atypical depression, anxiety; not first line Why reservedWhy MAOIs are reservedKept for severe, treatment-resistant depression because of the hypertensive crisis and their lethality in overdose. Tranylcypromine often works after several failed antidepressant trials. Atypical features (mood brightens with good news, more sleep and appetite, leaden paralysis): other first-line drugs first, an MAOI if they fail Major Depressive Disorder Selegiline: also Parkinson disease, as an MAO‑B inhibitor added when levodopa starts to wear off; may worsen levodopa adverse effects Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism Adverse effects Hypertensive crisis and serotonin syndrome: the two blocks below Lethal in overdose Suspected Overdose or Toxidrome Common: erectile dysfunction, insomnia and anxiety (central nervous system stimulation), dizziness, nausea, pedal edema, weight gain TimingDose timingDoses go in the morning and early afternoon to avoid overstimulation. Erectile dysfunction is least common with tranylcypromine. Withdrawal after an abrupt stop: vivid nightmares, agitation, psychosis, seizures; timing below Orthostatic (postural) hypotension

Tyramine crisisSevere hypertension, occipital headache, blurry vision and sweating within minutes of aged cheese, aged meats, wine or malted beer, or a decongestant such as pseudoephedrine If a hypertensive crisis follows tyramine on an MAOI, choose phentolamine, an alpha blocker that dilates vessels. Not theseOther antidotes offeredCyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome. Physostigmine treats severe anticholinergic toxicity, with hot, dry skin. Headache, a fast or slow pulse, or chest pain on an MAOI may mean a rise in blood pressure; intracranial bleeding has been reported Serotonin syndromeFever, mental status changes, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia and clonus after a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), tricyclic, meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, linezolid or St. John's wort SSRI Adverse Effects If serotonin syndrome appears, choose stopping every serotonergic drug.

Adverse effects Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention (worst with an enlarged prostate), big pupils, fast pulse Less sweating heat intolerance and hyperthermia Confusion and delirium, most in older adults; can worsen psychosis LabelBenztropine labelThe benztropine label lists toxic psychosis with confusion, disorientation, memory loss and visual hallucinations, and worsening of earlier psychotic symptoms. Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine inhibit vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) less dopamine stored for release the drugs for tardive dyskinesia Tetrabenazine and reserpine also deplete dopamine, for Huntington chorea; tetrabenazine also treats Tourette tics In Huntington disease they can deepen depression and suicidality, a boxed warning on all three labels

Drugs Valbenazine Ingrezza: tardive dyskinesia and Huntington chorea Deutetrabenazine Austedo: tardive dyskinesia and Huntington chorea; appears better tolerated than tetrabenazine SwitchingLabel dosingLabel: stop tetrabenazine and start deutetrabenazine the next day. Tetrabenazine Xenazine: Huntington chorea on its label; the board example for tics BoardTetrabenazine and tardive dyskinesiaOn a board card, reserpine and tetrabenazine may also treat tardive dyskinesia; the labeled drugs are valbenazine and deutetrabenazine. Mechanism VMAT2 carries monoamines from the cytoplasm into synaptic vesicles for storage and release Reversible VMAT2 block dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine stores deplete less dopamine on supersensitive dopamine receptors fewer dyskinetic movements Mechanism in tardive dyskinesiaMechanismThe labels call the mechanism in tardive dyskinesia unclear; VMAT2 inhibition is the accepted account. Depleting, not blocking no tardive dyskinesia or metabolic syndrome from these drugs Reserpine irreversible VMAT2 block lasting days Uses Tardive dyskinesia, moderate to severe: valbenazine or deutetrabenazine Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Huntington chorea: a VMAT2 inhibitor is typically first line Tourette tics that still impair: tetrabenazine as the dopamine-depleting option Tics and Tic Disorders Adverse effects Somnolence and sedation, the most common with valbenazine; no driving until the effect is known Depression and suicidality in Huntington disease (boxed warning) Parkinsonism and akathisia: lower the dose or stop if clinically significant QT prolongation (all three labels): avoid with congenital long QT syndrome or QT-related arrhythmias Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stop the drug Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

Depression and suicidalityHuntington disease already carries high rates of depression and suicide; monoamine depletion can worsen both; this is the boxed warning on all three drugs Tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine labels rule them out with active suicidality or untreated depression If Huntington chorea comes with untreated depression or suicidal thoughts, choose an antipsychotic for the chorea, not a VMAT2 inhibitor.

Lithium: a narrow window (0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L), cleared by the kidneys; for its levels, toxicity and interactions, see Lithium Therapy Any rash on lamotrigine: stop it; valproate raises its level and rash risk; after a sudden stop, restart at the starting dose Valproate: check ammonia when confused and lipase with epigastric pain (pancreatitis: stop it); liver tests at the start and throughout; neural tube defects in pregnancy Carbamazepine: in Asian ancestry, screen for human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B*1502 before starting; follow the CBC and sodium; it induces liver enzymes, so a contraceptive pill can fail

Drugs Lithium Lithobid (lithium carbonate) Valproate (valproic acid; divalproex Depakote) Carbamazepine Tegretol Equetro Oxcarbazepine Trileptal Lamotrigine Lamictal Topiramate Topamax The anticonvulsants that stabilize mood: valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine ("Valentine Cards are Lame") Mechanism Lithium: how it calms mania is unknown; the kidneys clear nearly all of it avoided in kidney disease Valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine: block voltage-gated sodium channels neurons fire less Valproate: inhibits gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) transaminase more GABA Carbamazepine: liver enzymes induced (cytochrome P450 3A4), its own metabolism included levels typically stabilize at 2 to 4 weeks Topiramate: more GABA action sedation and fatigue Uses Lithium: acute treatment and maintenance in bipolar disorder Valproate: mania, acute and maintenance; also seizures and migraine prevention Carbamazepine: acute mania; seizures; trigeminal neuralgia (first line, with oxcarbazepine) Lamotrigine: maintenance and bipolar depression, not acute mania MnemonicLamotrigine"Relapsigine": lamotrigine prevents relapse. Oxcarbazepine: matches carbamazepine for mood with fewer adverse effects, including less rash and less liver toxicity Topiramate: prevents migraine and treats binge eating disorder; it has shown no benefit in bipolar disorder Eating Disorders Adverse effects Lithium: tremor, nystagmus, polyuria and thirst, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, or arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic) Why the urine is diluteNephrogenic diabetes insipidusLithium builds up in collecting duct cells and blocks the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), so free water is lost. Lithium Therapy Valproate: GI upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), weight gain, sedation, tremor, ataxia, hair loss MoreValproateHair loss in 5% to 10%. Hyperandrogenism in women; it may raise the risk of polycystic ovary syndrome. Valproate, rare but serious: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonemic encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia Urea cycleHyperammonemiaA valproate metabolite, propionic acid, stops the urea cycle clearing ammonia; liver failure or a urea cycle disorder is a reason not to use it. Carbamazepine: sleepiness, nausea, diarrhea, rash; double vision (diplopia), ataxia Vitamin DCarbamazepineVitamin D deficiency may occur: the induced enzyme breaks vitamin D down. Carbamazepine, serious: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, low sodium, liver toxicity Oxcarbazepine: fatigue, dizziness, somnolence, double vision; hyponatremia Cross-reactionOxcarbazepineAbout 25% to 30% of patients with a carbamazepine hypersensitivity reaction react to oxcarbazepine too (label). Lamotrigine: the most common effects are nausea, dizziness, fatigue, insomnia; up to 10% get a benign rash; SJS or TEN in about 0.1% LabelLamotrigine labelThe label also warns of aseptic meningitis. Topiramate: weight loss, kidney stones, sedation, cognitive slowing, speech dysfunction; myopia with acute angle-closure glaucoma; metabolic acidosis MoreTopiramate labelThe acidosis is hyperchloremic, with a normal anion gap. Decreased sweating (oligohidrosis) is reported. Other Pregnancy, valproate: neural tube defects and other major malformations MoreValproate in pregnancyAlso oral clefts, heart and urogenital malformations; in childhood, cognitive deficits, autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Pregnancy, carbamazepine: neural tube, heart and craniofacial defects Pregnancy, lithium: Ebstein anomaly and other heart defects Pregnancy, topiramate: cleft lip or palate; lamotrigine: relatively safe LamotriginePregnancyUse in the first trimester may raise the risk of oral clefts slightly. Topiramate can also leave the baby small for gestational age.

Rash on lamotrigineA benign rash and early SJS or TEN cannot be told apart Risk is higher in children, with valproate, or with a fast titration If a rash of any kind appears on lamotrigine, choose stopping lamotrigine and switching to another agent. DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)A polymorphic rash, typically with liver or other organ involvement, 2 to 8 weeks into carbamazepine or lamotrigine Eosinophilia is often present (lamotrigine label) Most seriousLamotrigine skinSJS is the most serious skin reaction on lamotrigine. If DRESS appears, choose stopping the drug. Valproate pancreatitisEpigastric pain and vomiting with a raised lipase; idiosyncratic, so dose and years on the drug do not rule it out In most cases it resolves after the cause is removed If acute pancreatitis appears on valproate, choose stopping valproate. Confusion on valproateDrowsiness or confusion on valproate: a metabolite blocks the urea cycle Once the diagnosis is confirmed: stop valproate and look for an underlying urea cycle disorder If confusion develops on valproate, choose checking plasma ammonia. Valproate toxicity with GI symptomsVomiting, diarrhea and confusion on valproate If GI symptoms and altered mental status appear on valproate and the question asks which result is abnormal, choose liver function tests, which are likely abnormal with a high ammonia. Carbamazepine blood dyscrasiaAgranulocytosis or aplastic anemia, typically in the first 3 to 4 months Antipsychotic Adverse Effects Clozapine also causes agranulocytosis If a blood dyscrasia appears on carbamazepine, choose stopping carbamazepine; some of these recover after the stop. Carbamazepine in Asian ancestryAn allele typical of Asian ancestry carries the SJS and TEN risk on carbamazepine If carbamazepine is planned in a patient of Asian ancestry, choose HLA-B*1502 testing first, and avoiding the drug if the allele is present. Low sodium on carbamazepine or oxcarbazepineConfusion with a low sodium: syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), dose-dependent, on carbamazepine; hyponatremia on oxcarbazepine If the hyponatremia is symptomatic, choose considering a stop of carbamazepine; with oxcarbazepine, some patients need a lower dose, a stop or fluid limits. Carbamazepine overdoseSodium channel block can widen the QRS Other signsCarbamazepine overdoseAnticholinergic effects (hyperthermia, flushed skin, dilated pupils), tachycardia and hypotension. Care is mainly supportive. Levels are repeated until they fall: the peak can take days If the QRS is wide or the rhythm is abnormal, choose sodium bicarbonate; continuous cardiac monitoring may be needed. Valproate overdoseLethargy; anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypernatremia, hypocalcemia, high ammonia Also checkValproate overdoseGlucose, acetaminophen and salicylate levels, and an electrocardiogram; in severe cases sodium, bicarbonate, calcium, ammonia, platelets and liver tests. Hemodialysis may remove much of the drug in overdose If a valproate overdose is suspected, choose valproate levels every 2 to 3 hours, since a delayed-release tablet can peak late.

briefs.title: Cognitive agents
briefs.sub: cholinesterase inhibitors · donepezil · rivastigmine · galantamine · memantine
blocks: cholinesterase inhibitors · donepezil · rivastigmine · galantamine · memantine

Donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine block acetylcholinesterase more acetylcholine modest gain in cognition, no change in the course Memantine blocks N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors less glutamate excitotoxicity; for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, often added to a cholinesterase inhibitor Extra acetylcholine brings nausea, diarrhea and weight loss and slows the heart bradycardia, heart block, syncope; anticholinergic drugs work against these drugs

Drugs Donepezil Aricept: once a day, in the evening; every stage of Alzheimer disease Rivastigmine Exelon: by mouth or a daily skin patch; Alzheimer disease and mild-to-moderate Parkinson disease dementia PatchLabelOne patch at a time, replaced every 24 hours; most medication errors reported on the label were an old patch left on or several worn at once, and some needed a hospital stay. Galantamine: also modulates nicotinic receptors, which adds to acetylcholine release Memantine: uncompetitive, open-channel NMDA receptor antagonist; moderate to severe disease Mechanism Alzheimer disease: the nucleus basalis of Meynert loses choline acetyltransferase low acetylcholine Acetylcholinesterase blocked, reversibly less acetylcholine broken down more at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors The same surplus outside the brain gut and bladder smooth muscle contract, vagal tone slows the heart Glutamate keeps NMDA receptors open calcium entry excitotoxicity; memantine plugs the open channel Uses Alzheimer disease: a cholinesterase inhibitor, the three about equally effective; memantine for moderate to severe disease, alone or added Cognitive Decline and Dementia in an Adult Dementia with Lewy bodies (Lewy body dementia): cholinesterase inhibitors first, for cognition, attention and visual hallucinations Cognitive Decline and Dementia in an Adult Parkinson disease dementia: cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism No data to support use in mild cognitive impairment, and no help in delirium caused by a drug Delirium Adverse effects Cholinesterase inhibitors: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, anorexia and weight loss; insomnia, dizziness, muscle cramps, urinary incontinence LabelLabelOften transient; a slow dose climb reduces them. On the patch they can force a pause, and long vomiting or diarrhea can dehydrate. Vagal slowing at the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes may bring bradycardia, heart block or syncope, with or without known conduction disease More gastric acid ulcer and GI bleeding risk; caution in asthma or obstructive lung disease LabelLabelCholinomimetics may also cause bladder outflow obstruction and may carry some potential for generalized seizures. Memantine: dizziness, headache, confusion, constipation; hallucinations

Interactions, by result Combined with Result Rule Anticholinergic drugs, such as oxybutynin or tolterodine Each works against the other; anticholinergic toxicity brings delirium, sedation and hallucinations Delirium Avoid unless clinically necessary Beta-blockers, especially atenolol (rivastigmine label) Additive slowing of the heart, which can bring fainting Not recommended once signs appear Succinylcholine during anesthesia Muscle relaxation is altered Expect it exaggerated: a deeper block Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs May add gastric acid Watch for active or hidden bleeding Metoclopramide (rivastigmine label) Additive extrapyramidal reactions Not recommended Memantine with sodium bicarbonate or a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor LabelMemantine labelMemantine with other NMDA antagonists (amantadine, ketamine, dextromethorphan) is unstudied; the label advises caution. Alkaline urine cuts memantine clearance by about 80%: it may accumulate Watch for more adverse effects

Titration and restart limits, from the last dose changeweeks Donepezil: 5 mg, then 10 mgAfter 4 to 6 weeks on 5 mg 01 wk2 wk3 wk4 wk5 wk6 wk→ Whygradual increases reduce the cholinergic effects Rivastigmine patch: each step upAt least 4 weeks, if the dose was tolerated 01 wk2 wk3 wk4 wk5 wk6 wk→ Whynausea, vomiting and weight loss can force a pause Rivastigmine patch: doses missedMore than 3 days 01 wk2 wk3 wk4 wk5 wk6 wk→ Whyrestart on the lowest patch and titrate again Memantine: each step upAt least 1 week 01 wk2 wk3 wk4 wk5 wk6 wk→ Whythe dose rises in 5 mg steps to 20 mg a day

Monitoring When Check Why During treatment, most of all with sick sinus syndrome or other conduction disease Pulse; ask about fainting Vagal slowing of the heart If that check is abnormal Electrocardiogram ⚠︎ pharm document line; no board source found yet Bradycardia or heart block During treatment Appetite and weight Its gastrointestinal adverse effects After several months Daily function, with the caregiver report Decides whether to continue or stop Memantine with severe kidney disease Creatinine clearance Severe impairment: target 5 mg twice daily
