briefs.title: Benzodiazepines
briefs.sub: benzodiazepines · alprazolam · lorazepam · clonazepam · diazepam · chlordiazepoxide · oxazepam · temazepam · midazolam · triazolam
blocks: benzodiazepines · alprazolam · lorazepam · clonazepam · diazepam · chlordiazepoxide · oxazepam · temazepam · midazolam · triazolam

A benzodiazepine with an opioid or alcohol respiratory depression and hypotension; alone, breathing is usually only mildly slowed Short half-life (alprazolam) rebound anxiety between doses and harsher withdrawal; a long-acting agent such as clonazepam lowers both After daily use, avoid stopping abruptly: withdrawal seizures; flumazenil in a long-term user can set them off too Liver disease or old age: lorazepam, oxazepam or temazepam, cleared by glucuronidation alone

Drugs Alprazolam Xanax: short-acting on the NBME LabelAlprazolam labelThe Xanax label contraindicates strong CYP3A (cytochrome P450 3A) inhibitors such as ketoconazole and itraconazole, ritonavir excepted. Lorazepam Ativan: glucuronidation only; intravenous or intramuscular LabelLorazepam labelThe Ativan label lists acute narrow-angle glaucoma as a contraindication. Clonazepam Klonopin: the long-acting alternative to alprazolam Diazepam Valium, chlordiazepoxide, flurazepam: long-acting Oxazepam, temazepam Restoril: glucuronidation only Midazolam, triazolam: short-acting Half-life classesHalf-life classesShort, under 6 hours: triazolam, midazolam. Intermediate, 6 to 50 hours: alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam, clonazepam. Long, over 50 hours: diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, flurazepam. Tables differ: the NBME treats alprazolam as short-acting and clonazepam as the long-acting switch. Clorazepate ⚠︎ pharm document line; no board source found yet Mechanism Binds its own site on the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) type A receptor chloride channel opens more often sedation, anxiolysis, seizure control FrequencyVersus barbituratesBenzodiazepines raise how often the channel opens ("frenzodiazepines"). Barbiturates bind a different site, carry more risk of respiratory depression and coma, and are not reversed by flumazenil. Long use GABA-A receptors downregulate tolerance withdrawal after an abrupt stop Agents cleared by glucuronidation alone skip the oxidative liver step safer in liver disease and old age LOTMnemonicLOT may help recall them: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam, safe in liver disease. Uses Anxiety, panic: a short-term bridge until a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) works Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety Insomnia: not first line (dependence) Sleep agents Alcohol withdrawal: long-acting agents, or lorazepam with liver disease Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal Catatonia (first line) Major Depressive Disorder Status epilepticus, procedural sedation, acute agitation Adverse effects Sedation, ataxia, anterograde amnesia; older adults: falls, confusion Rebound anxiety between doses of a short-acting agent LabelInterdose symptomsThe Xanax label reports early-morning anxiety and anxiety between doses in panic disorder on maintenance doses. Physiologic dependence on prescribed use is not a use disorder Addiction: higher with short-acting agents ATOMMnemonicATOM may help recall the more addictive group: alprazolam, triazolam, oxazepam, midazolam (alprazolam and oxazepam are intermediate in some tables). Withdrawal after an abrupt stop; timing below Disinhibition in an adolescent raises acute suicide risk Suicide Risk Assessment

Respiratory depressionStupor, slow breathing, low blood pressure with an opioid or alcohol; alone, near-normal vital signs and pupils Suspected Overdose or Toxidrome Flumazenil needs caution: in a long-term user it can set off withdrawal and seizures If breathing slows or blood pressure falls, choose airway, breathing and circulation support; naloxone if an opioid may be involved. Withdrawal seizuresTremor, anxiety, then a seizure within 1 to 2 days of stopping a short-acting agent such as alprazolam Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal If a daily user must come off a benzodiazepine, choose a slow taper, ideally of a longer-acting agent. Paradoxical agitationAn older adult or child turns confused and aggressive, typically within an hour of a dose Delirium If agitation follows a benzodiazepine dose, choose tapering and stopping it; a higher dose only worsens it.

briefs.title: Other anxiety agents
briefs.sub: buspirone · hydroxyzine · gabapentin · pregabalin
blocks: Buspirone, a serotonin 1A partial agonist: no sedation, no tolerance or addiction and no alcohol interaction; second line for generalized anxiety disorder, alone or added when a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) falls short Hydroxyzine, a sedating first-generation antihistamine: a short-term add-on while the SSRI or SNRI is titrated; in an older adult, its anticholinergic action can lead to delirium Buspirone does not treat obsessive-compulsive disorder and gives no cover for benzodiazepine withdrawal

Drugs Buspirone: not related to benzodiazepines or barbiturates Benzodiazepines ClearanceBuspirone clearanceCleared by cytochrome P450 3A4; the label advises against large amounts of grapefruit juice. Hydroxyzine: a first-generation antihistamine, as are meclizine and promethazine MnemonicAntihistamine mnemonicThe "-zine" ending marks these first-generation antihistamines. Gabapentin Neurontin: a gabapentinoid that resembles gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) but does not act like it Pregabalin Lyrica: the same mechanism as gabapentin Mechanism Serotonin 1A receptors partially stimulated (buspirone) anxiety eased without the sedation of typical anxiolytics MnemonicBuspirone mnemonicAnxious when the bus does not arrive at one: buspirone acts at serotonin 1A. Histamine 1 receptors blocked (hydroxyzine) drowsiness; anticholinergic action dry mouth Alpha-2-delta subunit bound (gabapentinoids) voltage-gated calcium channels blocked Uses Buspirone: generalized anxiety disorder, second line, alone or as an add-on Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety In practice:Buspirone dosingAnxiety symptoms typically ease only once the dose reaches the upper range; buspirone is taken on a schedule, not as a rescue dose ⚠︎ pharm document line; no board source found yet Buspirone does not treat obsessive-compulsive disorder or somatic symptom disorder Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders Hydroxyzine: a short-term add-on for severe anxiety, agitation or insomnia during SSRI or SNRI titration Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety LabelHydroxyzine usesThe label also lists itching from allergic conditions such as chronic urticaria. Pregabalin: generalized anxiety disorder, second line; gabapentin: often used as an add-on for anxiety, sleep and neuropathic pain Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety ⚠︎ pharm document line; no board source found yet gabapentin for anxiety is off-label Adverse effects Buspirone: dizziness, nausea, headache, nervousness; no sedation, no dependence Hydroxyzine: drowsiness, dry mouth; in older adults, possible confusion, delirium (see Anticholinergic delirium below) and falls ⚠︎ pharm document line; no board source found yet QTHydroxyzine and QTLabel: contraindicated with a prolonged QT interval; QT prolongation and torsades de pointes have been reported; use caution with other QT-prolonging drugs. Disruptive Behavior in a Child Atomoxetine when a stimulant is ruled out, as with a high risk of misuse or diversion; alpha-2 agonists when stimulants fail, in children and teens Which alpha-2Alpha-2 agonists in ADHDGuanfacine works better than clonidine for childhood ADHD. Both are less effective than stimulants and have limited data in adults. Lisdexamfetamine: also binge eating disorder Eating Disorders Narcolepsy: methylphenidate or an amphetamine, second line after modafinil Sleep Problems Methylphenidate: also used in severe depression when life expectancy is short Clonidine, guanfacine: also tics Tics and Tic Disorders Adverse effects Stimulants: appetite suppression (the dose can be taken after a meal), insomnia, higher HR and BP MoreOther effectsHeadache and stomachache are also common. On average, a stimulant raises the heart rate by 5-10 beats/min and systolic BP by 4-6 mm Hg. Growth in height slows over 2 years of use; adult height may be lower Tics can emerge on a stimulant; they do not rule one out New psychotic or manic symptoms are a label warning; in diagnosed bipolar disorder, a small risk of switching to mania Label warningsStimulant labelsSudden death is reported with structural heart disease. Peripheral vasculopathy, including Raynaud phenomenon: watch the fingers and toes. Misuse and diversion: high abuse potential; family members prescribed stimulants are one route to misuse Not a use disorderPrescribed useOn a prescribed, supervised stimulant, tolerance and withdrawal alone do not make a stimulant use disorder. Atomoxetine: nausea, sedation, irritability; rare liver injury; suicidal ideation in children and teens (boxed warning) Avoid withAtomoxetine contraindicationsContraindicated with narrow-angle glaucoma, a present or past pheochromocytoma, or severe heart or vessel disease that a rise in BP or HR would worsen. Alpha-2 agonists: sleepiness, low BP, slow pulse, fainting on standing (orthostatic syncope); rebound hypertension after an abrupt stop With sedativesAdded sedationOther central nervous system depressants add to the sleepiness.

Mania on a stimulantAn episodic course fits bipolar disorder better than chronic ADHD Bipolar Disorder Dilated pupils (mydriasis) and a fast pulse point to stimulant intoxication instead If a manic episode begins on a stimulant, choose tapering or stopping the stimulant and treating the mania first. Atomoxetine liver injuryItching, dark urine, jaundice or right upper quadrant tenderness on atomoxetine, with raised liver enzymes If jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury appears, choose stopping atomoxetine and never restarting it. Alpha-2 reboundHeadache, agitation, tremor, then a sharp rise in BP and pulse after guanfacine or clonidine is stopped suddenly or doses are missed Worst caseReboundHypertensive encephalopathy has followed an abrupt stop. Doses often missed favor another drug If guanfacine or clonidine is to be stopped, choose a slow taper, with BP and HR checked at each step.

briefs.sub: nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics (Z-drugs) · zolpidem · zaleplon · eszopiclone · ramelteon

Zolpidem, zaleplon and eszopiclone (the Z-drugs) act on gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) type A receptors at the benzodiazepine site faster sleep onset, with less tolerance and dependence than benzodiazepines; flumazenil reverses them Zaleplon helps sleep onset only; zolpidem and eszopiclone (longest half-life) help onset and maintenance Ramelteon, a melatonin agonist: sleep onset, few adverse effects, no dependence, safe in older adults Never with alcohol or another central nervous system (CNS) depressant; in older adults, ataxia and falls

Drugs Zolpidem Ambien: sleep onset and maintenance Zaleplon: sleep onset only MnemonicZaleplon mnemonicZaleplON(SET): onset Eszopiclone Lunesta: onset and maintenance; the longest half-life of the three MnemonicEszopiclone mnemonicLongest name, longest half-life Ramelteon Rozerem: sleep onset only; not a controlled substance MnemonicRamelteon mnemonicRamelteON: onset Mechanism Z-drug the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A, more selective for benzodiazepine type 1 (BZ1) than benzodiazepines are shorter sleep latency; less likely to change the sleep cycle Rapid liver metabolism short duration of action Ramelteon melatonin receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus sleep onset Uses Insomnia that stays severe after cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I): lowest dose, shortest time Sleep Problems Orexin antagonists Zolpidem, brief use: situational insomnia, including the insomnia of adjustment disorder Ramelteon: trouble falling asleep Sleep Problems Melatonin, acting at melatonin receptors, first; clonazepam if symptoms persist: rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder Sleep Problems Adverse effects Older adults are more sensitive: cognitive impairment, headache, delirium; central ataxia falls; see the danger rows below Delirium Long-term use: tolerance to the hypnotic effect, somnolence, dependence, cognitive impairment, though less tolerance and dependence than benzodiazepines On the board: no significant day-after psychomotor depression or amnesia In practiceNext-day impairmentIn practice: the zolpidem and eszopiclone labels warn of next-day impairment, driving included, when a dose leaves too little of the night for sleep (the zolpidem label gives 7 to 8 hours), and the zolpidem label gives 5 mg as the starting dose for women and as the dose for older adults. Label warningComplex sleep behaviorsBoxed warning on the zolpidem and eszopiclone labels: complex sleep behaviors (sleep-walking, sleep-driving, other acts while not fully awake) may occur; the drug is stopped at once if one occurs. No board question on it found yet. Ramelteon: few, nonspecific (dizziness, nausea, fatigue, headache) LabelRamelteon and fluvoxamineThe ramelteon label bars fluvoxamine with it. No board question on it found yet.

Additive CNS depressionDeeper sedation and slowed breathing when alcohol, an opioid, a benzodiazepine, a barbiturate or a first-generation antihistamine joins a Z-drug If an opioid or nightly alcohol is on the history, choose no Z-drug; a benzodiazepine carries the same risk. Ataxia and falls in older adultsUnsteady gait, confusion or delirium after a bedtime dose; night falls Delirium Diphenhydramine is no better choice: heavy sedation for questionable benefit If an older adult needs a drug for trouble falling asleep, choose ramelteon. OversedationHeavy sedation after a Z-drug overdose Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal In a long-term benzodiazepine user, the antidote can set off withdrawal and seizures If Z-drug sedation must be reversed, choose flumazenil.

briefs.title: Orexin antagonists
briefs.sub: orexin receptor antagonists · suvorexant · lemborexant · daridorexant
blocks: orexin receptor antagonists · suvorexant · lemborexant · daridorexant

Suvorexant, lemborexant and daridorexant block orexin (hypocretin) receptors less wake drive sleep, for insomnia In narcolepsy orexin can already be low blocking its receptors worsens the loss: contraindicated Avoid in liver disease and with a strong cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibitor; the board answer for physical dependence is none or low In practiceIn practiceIn practice: the label bars only severe hepatic impairment and needs no change for mild or moderate disease.

Drugs Suvorexant Belsomra: the agent the board asks about MnemonicMnemonicSuv-orex-ant: the orexin antagonist is in the name DosingLabel dosingOnce a night at most, within 30 minutes of bed, with at least 7 hours left before waking. Lemborexant Dayvigo: same class, same narcolepsy contraindication Daridorexant Quviviq: same class, same narcolepsy contraindication Mechanism Orexin A and B from the lateral hypothalamus both orexin receptor types wakefulness Both receptors blocked wake drive thought to be suppressed sleep comes and lasts Narcolepsy: orexin output can already be low the blockade deepens the deficit Uses Insomnia, trouble falling or staying asleep, after cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia Sleep Problems Adverse effects Somnolence, the most common with suvorexant, and next-day impairment, driving included, that grows with dose Headache, dizziness, abnormal dreams, upper respiratory tract infection Sleep paralysis, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations and cataplexy-like symptoms, more at higher doses Complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-walking or sleep-driving: stop the drug Suicidal ideation, dose-related (suvorexant label) Dependence: none or low on the board In practiceIn practiceIn practice: suvorexant is Schedule IV; in abuse studies it produced effects similar to zolpidem on subjective ratings, and trials found no physical dependence.

Narcolepsy made worseOrexin can already be deficient; blocking its receptors worsens the deficiency, and the drug itself can bring sleep paralysis and cataplexy-like symptoms Sleep Problems If narcolepsy is on the problem list and a sleep aid is requested, choose any option other than an orexin antagonist.

Interactions, by result Combined with Result Rule Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor: ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir In practiceIn practiceIn practice: the label says not recommended rather than contraindicated, and caps the dose at 5 mg with a moderate inhibitor such as diltiazem. Higher suvorexant exposure: next-day sleepiness Do not combine Alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, tricyclics Additive central nervous system depression No dose after evening alcohol; doses of both may need adjusting

briefs.title: Substance use and cessation
briefs.sub: naltrexone · acamprosate · disulfiram · buprenorphine · methadone · varenicline · nicotine replacement
blocks: 06 Substance use and other · class card
naltrexone · acamprosate · disulfiram · buprenorphine · methadone · varenicline · nicotine replacement

Buprenorphine: binds tighter than a full agonist, activates less if dosed before withdrawal signs, it displaces the full agonist precipitated withdrawal Naltrexone: for alcohol it can start while still drinking; for opioids only after withdrawal is complete; avoid with liver disease, never with acute hepatitis or liver failure Methadone: long-acting full agonist accumulates; QT prolongation; CYP3A4 (cytochrome P450 3A4) inhibitors raise the level opioid toxicity Varenicline is the most effective single smoking drug, then combination nicotine replacement, then bupropion

Drugs Naltrexone Vivitrol (monthly injection): mu-opioid antagonist Acamprosate: glutamate modulator Disulfiram: a deterrent Buprenorphine, with naloxone as Suboxone: partial mu agonist Methadone Methadose: long-acting full agonist Varenicline Chantix: nicotinic partial agonist Nicotine replacement: NicoDerm CQ (patch), gum or lozenge Nicorette for cravings; the patch keeps a steady level In practiceNicotine replacementIn practice: combined nicotine forms work about as well as varenicline. Mechanism Naltrexone: mu receptor blocked opioid euphoria blocked; less craving and fewer heavy drinking days MnemonicNaloxone or naltrexoneNaloxone treats toxicity; naltrexone prevents relapse. Acamprosate: glutamate modulated less craving once abstinent Disulfiram: acetaldehyde dehydrogenase blocked acetaldehyde builds after a drink HangoverDisulfiram reactionThink of the reaction as a really bad hangover: acetaldehyde causes hangover symptoms. Buprenorphine: high affinity, low efficacy a ceiling on respiratory depression Naloxone in the combination: inactive under the tongue; injected, it precipitates withdrawal deters misuse Methadone: long half-life steady receptor activation no withdrawal, less craving Build-upMethadone accumulationIt can build up faster than it is cleared. Varenicline: nicotinic partial agonist less withdrawal and craving ReceptorVarenicline receptorThe alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptor (label). It also partly blocks the effects of nicotine. Nicotine withdrawal brings irritability, anxiety, restlessness and poor concentration. Uses Alcohol use disorder: naltrexone or acamprosate first line, acamprosate preferred with liver disease or opioid use; disulfiram second line; alongside psychosocial treatment Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal Opioid use disorder: buprenorphine or methadone maintenance first line, often long term; long-acting naltrexone after withdrawal, for mild disorder TaperOpioid maintenanceWhen maintenance is going well, continue it; in a highly motivated patient a slow taper may be tried, with close watch for relapse. Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal Opioid use disorder in pregnancy: methadone or buprenorphine WhyPregnancyBetter maternal and newborn outcomes than abstinence. Quitting smoking: varenicline, nicotine replacement and bupropion are all first line Other antidepressants Adverse effects Naltrexone: hepatotoxicity; precipitated withdrawal with opioids on board Acamprosate: diarrhea; kidney-cleared, so avoid with significant impairment In practiceAcamprosate labelIn practice: the label contraindicates it at a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min or less. Disulfiram: reaction with any alcohol (see the disulfiram reaction row below); not in pregnancy or cardiac decompensation LabelDisulfiram labelHepatitis, sometimes fatal, may develop even after months; optic and peripheral neuritis may occur; contraindicated with psychosis or severe myocardial disease. Never given to an intoxicated patient or without the patient knowing. Methadone: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes; accumulation and overdose Varenicline: nausea, headaches, insomnia, abnormal dreams, depressed mood LabelVarenicline labelNausea and sleep complaints lead. New or worsening seizures were seen in people taking it; severe kidney impairment starts a lower dose. Nicotine replacement: angina is not a contraindication; caution with serious angina or within 2 weeks of a myocardial infarction AnginaNicotine replacement and anginaUse cautiously with certain cardiovascular risks; most data suggest it is safe.

Precipitated withdrawalRapid, severe withdrawal after a first buprenorphine or naltrexone dose with a full agonist on board Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal If opioid withdrawal signs are not yet present, choose waiting, then buprenorphine once withdrawal signs appear. If drinking has not stopped, choose naltrexone; disulfiram needs abstinence. wake-promoting and weight-loss agents · modafinil · armodafinil · phentermine · phentermine-topiramate

Modafinil and its R-enantiomer armodafinil are non-amphetamine wake-promoting drugs the first-line choice for narcolepsy sleepiness Phentermine is a sympathomimetic that releases norepinephrine weight loss; contraindicated in cardiovascular disease, hypertension and heart failure In practiceIn practiceIn practice: the label lists uncontrolled hypertension, with coronary artery disease, stroke, arrhythmias and congestive heart failure. Modafinil induces cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) hormonal contraceptive levels may fall a second method is needed

Drugs Modafinil Provigil: wake-promoting drug, first line for narcolepsy sleepiness Armodafinil Nuvigil: the R-enantiomer of modafinil, same uses and warnings Phentermine: sympathomimetic appetite suppressant for obesity Phentermine-topiramate Qsymia: the combination, for long-term weight reduction; topiramate's own effects are on its card Lithium and anticonvulsants Mechanism Modafinil: exact action unclear; thought to raise orexin and monoamine signaling wakefulness Wakes like amphetamine or methylphenidate, though its drug profile differs Phentermine: norepinephrine release appetite suppression weight loss; an amphetamine-like amine Uses Narcolepsy daytime sleepiness: modafinil is first line Sleep Problems Hypersomnolence disorder (first line); sleepiness at work in shift work disorder Sleep Problems Obstructive sleep apnea: modafinil treats the sleepiness only, not the underlying obstruction Obesity: phentermine for weight loss, and most patients regain the weight after stopping; phentermine-topiramate to reduce weight and keep it off long term In practiceIn practiceIn practice: phentermine alone is labeled as a short-term adjunct of a few weeks, alongside diet, exercise and behavior change; tolerance to the appetite effect usually comes within a few weeks, and the drug is then stopped. The topiramate combination is labeled for long-term use. Adverse effects Modafinil: headache, nausea, nervousness, anxiety, insomnia Serious rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome included: stop modafinil at the first sign of rash, unless clearly not drug-related LabelModafinil labelToxic epidermal necrolysis and drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms are also reported; suspected angioedema or anaphylaxis also means stopping. Psychiatric symptoms: use caution after psychosis, depression or mania Phentermine: palpitations, tachycardia, raised blood pressure, ischemic events; rarely primary pulmonary hypertension or valvular heart disease Abuse potential: modafinil and phentermine are Schedule IV

Weight-loss drug in heart diseaseNorepinephrine release raises heart rate and blood pressure; ischemic events are reported If a patient with coronary disease, heart failure or hypertension asks for a weight-loss drug, choose an option that is not a norepinephrine-releasing sympathomimetic (phentermine, diethylpropion or benzphetamine).
